Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Jātaka

Catuttho bhāgo

The fourth part.

10. Dasakanipāto

10. The Book of the Tens

[439] 1. Catudvārajātakavaṇṇanā

[439] 1. The Commentary on the Catudvāra Jātaka

Catudvāramidaṃ [V 4.0001][P 4.0001][M 4.0001] nagaranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu navakanipātassa paṭhamajātake vitthāritameva. Idha pana satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbaco”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “pubbepi tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbacatāya paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā khuracakkaṃ āpādesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This city has four gates...” This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain difficult-to-admonish monk. The present story has been detailed in the first Jātaka of the Navaka Nipāta. Here, however, the Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to admonish?” When he replied, “It is true, Bhante,” the Teacher said, “In the past too, monk, because you were difficult to admonish, you did not follow the words of the wise and encountered the razor-wheel.” Having said this, he related the past story.

Atīte [V 4.0002] kassapadasabalassa kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ asītikoṭivibhavassa seṭṭhino eko putto mittavindako nāma ahosi. Tassa mātāpitaro sotāpannā ahesuṃ, so pana dussīlo assaddho. Atha naṃ aparabhāge pitari kālakate mātā kuṭumbaṃ vicārentī āha – “tāta, tayā dullabhaṃ manussattaṃ laddhaṃ, dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, uposathakammaṃ karohi, dhammaṃ suṇāhī”ti. Amma, na mayhaṃ dānādīhi attho, mā maṃ kiñci avacuttha, ahaṃ yathākammaṃ gamissāmīti. Evaṃ vadantampi naṃ ekadivasaṃ [M 4.0002] puṇṇamuposathadivase mātā āha – “tāta, ajja abhilakkhito mahāuposathadivaso, ajja uposathaṃ samādiyitvā vihāraṃ gantvā sabbarattiṃ dhammaṃ sutvā ehi, ahaṃ te sahassaṃ dassāmī”ti. So “sādhū”ti dhanalobhena uposathaṃ samādiyitvā bhuttapātarāso vihāraṃ gantvā divasaṃ vītināmetvā rattiṃ yathā ekampi dhammapadaṃ kaṇṇaṃ na paharati, tathā ekasmiṃ [P 4.0002] padese nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkamitvā punadivase pātova mukhaṃ dhovitvā gehaṃ gantvā nisīdi.

In the past, during the time of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One, in Bārāṇasī, there was a son named Mittavindaka of a merchant who possessed eighty crores of wealth. His parents were stream-enterers, but he was immoral and faithless. Later, when his father had passed away, his mother, managing the household, said to him, “Dear son, human birth is hard to obtain; give alms, observe the precepts, perform the Uposatha duties, and listen to the Dhamma.” He said, “Mother, I have no need for almsgiving and such; do not say anything to me, I will go according to my own deeds.” Even as he said this, one day on the full-moon Uposatha day, his mother said to him, “Dear son, today is a designated great Uposatha day; today, having undertaken the Uposatha, go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma all night, and I will give you a thousand coins.” He, greedy for the money, undertook the Uposatha, and after eating his morning meal, went to the monastery and spent the day there. At night, in such a way that not even a single verse of the Dhamma would strike his ear, he lay down in a certain place and fell asleep. The next day, having washed his face early in the morning, he went home and sat down.

Mātā panassa “ajja me putto dhammaṃ sutvā pātova dhammakathikattheraṃ ādāya āgamissatī”ti yāguṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā tassāgamanaṃ paṭimānentī taṃ ekakaṃ āgataṃ disvā “tāta, dhammakathiko kena na ānīto”ti vatvā “na mayhaṃ dhammakathikena attho”ti vutte “tena hi yāguṃ pivā”ti āha. So “tumhehi mayhaṃ sahassaṃ paṭissutaṃ, taṃ tāva me detha, pacchā pivissāmī”ti āha. “Piva, tāta, pacchā dassāmī”ti. “Gahetvāva pivissāmī”ti. Athassa mātā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ purato ṭhapesi. So yāguṃ pivitvā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ gahetvā vohāraṃ karonto na cirasseva vīsasatasahassaṃ uppādesi. Athassa etadahosi – “nāvaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā vohāraṃ karissāmī”ti. So nāvaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā “amma, ahaṃ nāvāya vohāraṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mātā “tvaṃ tāta, ekaputtako, imasmiṃ ghare dhanampi bahu, samuddo anekādīnavo, mā gamī”ti nivāresi. So “ahaṃ gamissāmeva, na sakkā maṃ nivāretu”nti vatvā “ahaṃ taṃ, tāta, vāressāmī”ti mātarā hatthe gahito hatthaṃ vissajjāpetvā mātaraṃ paharitvā pātetvā antaraṃ katvā gantvā nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhandi.

His mother, thinking, “Today my son will return early having heard the Dhamma and bringing a Dhamma-preaching elder,” prepared rice porridge and various foods, arranged a seat, and awaited his arrival. Seeing him return alone, she said, “Dear son, why did you not bring a Dhamma-preacher?” When he said, “I have no need for a Dhamma-preacher,” she said, “In that case, drink some rice porridge.” He said, “You promised me a thousand coins; give them to me first, then I will drink.” “Drink, dear son, and I will give them later.” “I will drink only after receiving them.” Then his mother placed a bag of a thousand coins before him. He drank the porridge, took the bag of a thousand coins, and while trading, he soon gained one hundred and twenty thousand. Then he thought, “I will prepare a ship and trade.” He prepared a ship and said, “Mother, I will go trading by ship.” Then his mother restrained him, saying, “Dear son, you are my only son; there is much wealth in this house, and the ocean has many dangers; do not go.” He said, “I will certainly go; you cannot stop me.” When his mother held him by the hand, saying, “I will stop you, dear son,” he forced her to let go, struck her and knocked her down, and having treated her with such disregard, he went and boarded the ship and set out to sea.

Nāvā sattame divase mittavindakaṃ nissāya samuddapiṭṭhe niccalā aṭṭhāsi. Kāḷakaṇṇisalākā kariyamānā mittavindakasseva hatthe tikkhattuṃ pati. Athassa uḷumpaṃ datvā “imaṃ ekaṃ nissāya bahū mā nassantū”ti taṃ samuddapiṭṭhe khipiṃsu. Tāvadeva nāvā javena mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandi. Sopi uḷumpe nipajjitvā ekaṃ dīpakaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha phalikavimāne catasso [V 4.0003] vemānikapetiyo addasa. Tā sattāhaṃ dukkhaṃ [P 4.0003] anubhavanti, sattāhaṃ sukhaṃ[M 4.0003]. So tāhi saddhiṃ sattāhaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavi. Atha naṃ tā dukkhānubhavanatthāya gacchamānā “sāmi, mayaṃ sattame divase āgamissāma, yāva mayaṃ āgacchāma, tāva anukkaṇṭhamāno idheva vasā”ti vatvā agamaṃsu. So taṇhāvasiko hutvā tasmiṃyeva phalake nipajjitvā puna samuddapiṭṭhena gacchanto aparaṃ dīpakaṃ patvā tattha rajatavimāne aṭṭha vemānikapetiyo disvā eteneva upāyena aparasmiṃ dīpake maṇivimāne soḷasa, aparasmiṃ dīpake kanakavimāne dvattiṃsa vemānikapetiyo disvā tāhi saddhiṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tāsampi dukkhaṃ anubhavituṃ gatakāle puna samuddapiṭṭhena gacchanto ekaṃ pākāraparikkhittaṃ catudvāraṃ nagaraṃ addasa. Ussadanirayo kiresa, bahūnaṃ nerayikasattānaṃ kammakaraṇānubhavanaṭṭhānaṃ mittavindakassa alaṅkatapaṭiyattanagaraṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāsi.

On the seventh day, because of Mittavindaka, the ship stood motionless on the surface of the ocean. When the lots for the ill-fated one were cast, the lot fell into Mittavindaka’s hand three times. Then, giving him a raft, they said, “Let not many perish because of this one,” and they threw him onto the surface of the ocean. Immediately, the ship sped swiftly across the great ocean. He, lying on the raft, reached a small island. There, in a crystal mansion, he saw four mansion-pretis (vemānikapetiyo). They experienced suffering for seven days and happiness for seven days. He enjoyed divine bliss with them for seven days. Then, when they were departing to undergo their suffering, they said, “Master, we will return on the seventh day; until we return, stay here without becoming restless,” and they left. Being overcome by craving, he lay on that same raft and, traveling again across the ocean's surface, reached another island. There, in a silver mansion, he saw eight mansion-pretis. In the same manner, on another island, he saw sixteen in a gem mansion, and on yet another island, thirty-two in a golden mansion. Having enjoyed divine bliss with them, when they also left to undergo their suffering, he again traveled across the ocean's surface and saw a city surrounded by a wall with four gates. That, indeed, was the Ussada Hell, the place where many hell-beings undergo their punishment; but to Mittavindaka, it appeared like a decorated and prepared city.

So “imaṃ nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājā bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā khuracakkaṃ ukkhipitvā sīse paccamānaṃ nerayikasattaṃ addasa. Athassa taṃ tassa sīse khuracakkaṃ padumaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāsi. Ure pañcaṅgikabandhanaṃ uracchadapasādhanaṃ hutvā sīsato galantaṃ lohitaṃ lohitacandanavilepanaṃ viya hutvā paridevanasaddo madhurasaro gītasaddo viya hutvā upaṭṭhāsi. So tassa santikaṃ gantvā “bho purisa, ciraṃ tayā padumaṃ dhāritaṃ, dehi me eta”nti āha. “Samma, nayidaṃ padumaṃ, khuracakkaṃ eta”nti. “Tvaṃ mayhaṃ adātukāmatāya evaṃ vadasī”ti. Nerayikasatto cintesi “mayhaṃ kammaṃ khīṇaṃ bhavissati, imināpi mayā viya mātaraṃ paharitvā āgatena bhavitabbaṃ, dassāmissa khuracakka”nti. Atha naṃ “ehi bho, gaṇha ima”nti vatvā khuracakkaṃ tassa sīse khipi, taṃ tassa matthakaṃ pisamānaṃ bhassi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mittavindako [P 4.0004] tassa khuracakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tava khuracakkaṃ gaṇha, tava khuracakkaṃ gaṇhā”ti vedanāppatto paridevi, itaro antaradhāyi. Tadā bodhisatto rukkhadevatā hutvā mahantena parivārena ussadacārikaṃ caramāno taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Mittavindako taṃ oloketvā “sāmi devarāja, idaṃ maṃ cakkaṃ saṇhakaraṇiyaṃ viya tilāni pisamānaṃ otarati, kiṃ nu kho mayā pāpaṃ pakata”nti pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thinking, 'Having entered this city, I will become king,' he saw a hell-being with a razor-wheel on his head, suffering. Then to him, that razor-wheel on his head appeared like a lotus. The five-point restraint on his chest appeared like a breast-ornament; the blood flowing from his head appeared like red sandalwood ointment; and the sound of lamentation appeared like the sweet sound of a song. Approaching him, he said, 'O man, you have worn this lotus for a long time; give it to me.' 'Friend, this is not a lotus; it is a razor-wheel.' 'You say this only because you do not wish to give it to me.' The hell-being thought, 'My karma must be exhausted. This man must also have come here after striking his mother, just as I did. I will give him the razor-wheel.' Then he said to him, 'Come, friend, take this,' and threw the razor-wheel onto Mittavindaka's head. It fell, crushing his head. At that moment, Mittavindaka, realizing it was a razor-wheel, cried out in pain, 'Take your razor-wheel, take your razor-wheel!' The other vanished. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a tree-deity, arrived at that place with a great retinue while wandering through the Ussada hells. Mittavindaka, seeing him, asked, 'Lord, king of gods, this wheel descends upon me, crushing me like sesame seeds; what evil have I done?' and spoke these two verses:

1.

1.

“Catudvāramidaṃ [M 4.0004] nagaraṃ, āyasaṃ daḷhapākāraṃ;

Oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi, kiṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā.

This city has four gates, with an iron wall firmly built; I am confined and hemmed in. What evil have I done?

2.

2.

“Sabbe [V 4.0004] apihitā dvārā, oruddhosmi yathā dijo;

Kimādhikaraṇaṃ yakkha, cakkābhinihato aha”nti.

All the gates are shut; I am confined like a bird in a cage. For what reason, O Yakkha, am I struck down by this wheel?

Tattha daḷhapākāranti thirapākāraṃ. “Daḷhatoraṇa”ntipi pāṭho, thiradvāranti attho. Oruddhapaṭiruddhosmīti anto katvā samantā pākārena ruddho, palāyanaṭṭhānaṃ na paññāyati. Kiṃ pāpaṃ pakatanti kiṃ nu kho mayā pāpakammaṃ kataṃ. Apihitāti thakitā. Yathā dijoti pañjare pakkhitto sakuṇo viya. Kimādhikaraṇanti kiṃ kāraṇaṃ. Cakkābhinihatoti cakkena abhinihato.

Therein, 'daḷhapākāra' means a firm wall. There is also a reading 'daḷhatoraṇa,' meaning a firm gate. 'Oruddhapaṭiruddhosmi' means confined within and blocked on all sides by a wall, such that no way of escape is seen. 'Kiṃ pāpaṃ pakata' means what evil deed have I done. 'Apihitā' means closed. 'Yathā dijo' means like a bird thrown into a cage. 'Kimādhikaraṇa' means for what reason. 'Cakkābhinihato' means struck down by the wheel.

Athassa devarājā kāraṇaṃ kathetuṃ cha gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king of gods, to tell him the reason, spoke these six verses:

3.

3.

“Laddhā satasahassāni, atirekāni vīsati;

Anukampakānaṃ ñātīnaṃ, vacanaṃ samma nākari.

Having gained a hundred thousand, and twenty thousand more, you did not follow the advice of your compassionate kinsfolk, friend.

4.

4.

“Laṅghiṃ samuddaṃ pakkhandi, sāgaraṃ appasiddhikaṃ;

Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhāhipi ca soḷasa.

You crossed the ocean, you plunged into the sea that brings little success. From four you went to eight, and from eight to sixteen.

5.

5.

“Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, aticchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake.

From sixteen you went to thirty-two; through excessive greed you came to the wheel. Upon the man overcome by desire, the wheel whirls on his head.

6.

6.

“Uparivisālā duppūrā, icchā visaṭagāminī;

Ye ca taṃ anugijjhanti, te honti cakkadhārino.

Ever-expanding and hard to fill, desire spreads far and wide. Those who are greedy for it become the wearers of the wheel.

7.

7.

“Bahubhaṇḍaṃ avahāya, maggaṃ appaṭivekkhiya;

Yesañcetaṃ asaṅkhātaṃ, te honti cakkadhārino.

Leaving behind great wealth, not examining the path, those for whom this is not considered become the wearers of the wheel.

8.

8.

“Kammaṃ [P 4.0005] samekkhe vipulañca bhogaṃ, icchaṃ na seveyya anatthasaṃhitaṃ;

Kareyya vākyaṃ anukampakānaṃ, taṃ tādisaṃ nātivatteyya cakka”nti.

One should reflect on one's actions and the abundance of wealth; one should not indulge in desire connected with harm. One should follow the words of those who are compassionate; the wheel would not overcome such a person.

Tattha laddhā satasahassāni, atirekāni vīsatīti tvaṃ uposathaṃ katvā mātu santikā sahassaṃ [V 4.0005] gahetvā vohāraṃ karonto satasahassāni [M 4.0005] ca atirekāni vīsatisahassāni labhitvā. Nākarīti tena dhanena asantuṭṭho nāvāya samuddaṃ pavisanto samudde ādīnavañca kathetvā mātuyā vāriyamānopi anukampakānaṃ ñātīnaṃ vacanaṃ na karosi, sotāpannaṃ mātaraṃ paharitvā antaraṃ katvā nikkhantoyevāsīti dīpeti.

Therein, 'laddhā satasahassāni, atirekāni vīsatī' means: you, having observed the Uposatha and taken a thousand from your mother, engaged in trade and gained a hundred thousand and twenty thousand extra. 'Nākarī' shows: being dissatisfied with that wealth, entering the ocean in a ship, you did not follow the words of your compassionate kinsfolk, even though your mother forbade you, pointing out the dangers of the sea; and having struck your mother, who was a Stream-enterer, and pushed her aside, you departed.

Laṅghinti nāvaṃ ullaṅghanasamatthaṃ. Pakkhandīti pakkhandosi. Appasiddhikanti mandasiddhiṃ vināsabahulaṃ. Catubbhi aṭṭhāti atha naṃ nissāya ṭhitāya nāvāya phalakaṃ datvā samudde khittopi tvaṃ mātaraṃ nissāya ekadivasaṃ katassa uposathakammassa nissandena phalikavimāne catasso itthiyo labhitvā tato rajatavimāne aṭṭha, maṇivimāne soḷasa, kanakavimāne dvattiṃsa adhigatosīti. Aticchaṃ cakkamāsadoti atha tvaṃ yathāladdhena asantuṭṭho “atra uttaritaraṃ labhissāmī”ti evaṃ laddhaṃ laddhaṃ atikkamanalobhasaṅkhātāya aticchāya samannāgatattā aticcho pāpapuggalo tassa uposathakammassa khīṇattā dvattiṃsa itthiyo atikkamitvā imaṃ petanagaraṃ āgantvā tassa mātupahāradānaakusalassa nissandena idaṃ khuracakkaṃ sampattosi. “Atriccha”ntipi pāṭho, atra atra icchamānoti attho. “Atricchā”tipi pāṭho, atricchāyāti attho. Bhamatīti tassa te icchāhatassa posassa idaṃ cakkaṃ matthakaṃ pisamānaṃ idāni kumbhakāracakkaṃ viya matthake bhamatīti attho.

'Laṅghiṃ' refers to one capable of leaping with a boat. 'Pakkhandī' means you plunged in. 'Appasiddhikaṃ' means of little success, full of destruction. 'Catubbhi aṭṭha' means that although you were thrown into the sea, having given up the plank of the ship on which you relied, due to the result of the Uposatha you observed for one day on account of your mother, you first obtained four women in a crystal palace, then eight in a silver palace, sixteen in a gem palace, and thirty-two in a golden palace. 'Aticchaṃ cakkamāsado' means that being dissatisfied with what you had obtained, thinking 'I will get something better further on,' you are an excessively greedy, evil person, possessed of 'aticchā' (excessive desire), which is the greed of bypassing what is already gained; and because the merit of that Uposatha is exhausted, you bypassed the thirty-two women, came to this city of Petas, and reached this razor-wheel as a result of the unwholesome deed of striking your mother. There is also a reading 'atricchaṃ,' meaning desiring 'here and there.' Another reading is 'atricchā,' meaning by excessive desire. 'Bhamati' means for you, a man overcome by desire, this wheel now whirls on your head, crushing it, like a potter's wheel.

Ye ca taṃ anugijjhantīti taṇhā nāmesā gacchantī uparūpari visālā hoti, samuddo viya ca duppūrā, rūpādīsu tassa tassa icchanaicchāya visaṭagāminī, taṃ evarūpaṃ taṇhaṃ ye ca anugijjhanti giddhā gadhitā hutvā punappunaṃ allīyanti. Te honti cakkadhārinoti te evaṃ paccantā khuracakkaṃ dhārenti. Bahubhaṇḍanti mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ bahudhanaṃ ohāya. Magganti gantabbaṃ appasiddhikaṃ samuddamaggaṃ apaccavekkhitvā yathā tvaṃ paṭipanno, evameva aññesampi yesañcetaṃ asaṅkhātaṃ avīmaṃsitaṃ, te yathā tvaṃ tatheva taṇhāvasikā hutvā dhanaṃ pahāya gamanamaggaṃ anapekkhitvā paṭipannā cakkadhārino honti. Kammaṃ samekkheti tasmā paṇḍito puriso attanā kattabbakammaṃ “sadosaṃ nu kho, niddosa”nti samekkheyya [M 4.0006] paccavekkheyya. Vipulañca [P 4.0006] bhoganti attano dhammaladdhaṃ dhanarāsimpi samekkheyya. Nātivatteyyāti taṃ tādisaṃ puggalaṃ idaṃ cakkaṃ na ativatteyya nāvatthareyya. “Nātivattetī”tipi pāṭho, nāvattharatīti attho.

'Those who lust after that' refers to craving (taṇhā); as it proceeds, it becomes wider and wider at the top, and like the ocean, it is difficult to fill. It goes spreading towards various objects like sights and so on according to one's desires. Those who lust after such craving, being greedy and attached, cling to it again and again. 'They are wheel-bearers' means they carry the razor-wheel while being thus tormented. 'Much wealth' refers to abandoning the great wealth belonging to one's parents. 'The path' refers to the path across the sea which is to be traveled; having set out without considering it as you have done, so too for others, for whomsoever this is unconsidered and unexamined, they, like you, being under the power of craving, having abandoned their wealth and having set out without considering the path of travel, become wheel-bearers. 'Should examine the action'—therefore, a wise person should examine and reflect on the action to be done by himself, whether it is faulty or faultless. 'And vast wealth' means he should also examine his own accumulation of wealth obtained righteously. 'Should not overcome' means this wheel would not overcome or overwhelm such a person. There is also a reading 'nātivatteti', meaning it does not overwhelm.

Taṃ [V 4.0006] sutvā mittavindako “iminā devaputtena mayā katakammaṃ tathato ñātaṃ, ayaṃ mayhaṃ paccanapamāṇampi jānissati, pucchāmi na”nti cintetvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Mittavindaka thought, 'This deity knows exactly what I have done. He will also know the measure of my suffering; I will ask him,' and he spoke the ninth verse:

9.

9.

“Kīvaciraṃ nu me yakkha, cakkaṃ sirasi ṭhassati;

Kati vassasahassāni, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

'How long, O Yakkha, will the wheel stay on my head? For how many thousands of years? Tell me that when you are asked.'

Athassa kathento mahāsatto dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, speaking to him, the Great Being spoke the tenth verse:

10.

10.

“Atisaro paccasaro, mittavinda suṇohi me;

Cakkaṃ te sirasi māviddhaṃ, na taṃ jīvaṃ pamokkhasī”ti.

'One who overreaches and persists, O Mittavinda, listen to me; the wheel is spinning on your head, you shall not be released from it while alive.'

Tattha atisaroti atisarītipi atisaro, atisarissatītipi atisaro. Paccasaroti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma mittavindaka, suṇohi me vacanaṃ, tvañhi atidāruṇassa kammassa katattā atisaro, tassa pana na sakkā vassagaṇanāya vipāko paññāpetunti aparimāṇaṃ atimahantaṃ vipākadukkhaṃ sarissasi paṭipajjissasīti atisaro. Tena te “ettakāni vassasahassānī”ti vattuṃ na sakkomi. Sirasimāviddhanti yaṃ pana te idaṃ cakkaṃ sirasmiṃ āviddhaṃ kumbhakāracakkamiva bhamati. Na taṃ jīvaṃ pamokkhasīti taṃ tvaṃ yāva te kammavipāko na khīyati, tāva jīvamāno na pamokkhasi, kammavipāke pana khīṇe idaṃ cakkaṃ pahāya yathākammaṃ gamissasīti.

id

Idaṃ vatvā devaputto attano devaṭṭhānameva gato, itaropi mahādukkhaṃ paṭipajji.

Having said this, the deity went to his own divine abode, while the other person underwent great suffering.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mittavindako ayaṃ dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, devarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jataka: 'At that time, Mittavindaka was this difficult-to-admonish monk, but the King of Devas was I myself.'

Catudvārajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The commentary on the Catudvāra Jātaka is the first.

[440] 2. Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā

[440] 2. Commentary on the Kaṇha Jātaka

Kaṇho [V 4.0007][M 4.0007] vatāyaṃ purisoti idaṃ satthā kapilavatthuṃ upanissāya nigrodhārāme viharanto sitapātukammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira satthā sāyanhasamaye [P 4.0007] nigrodhārāme bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto jaṅghavihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno aññatarasmiṃ padese sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Ānandatthero “ko nu kho hetu, ko paccayo bhagavato sitassa pātukammāya, na ahetu tathāgatā sitaṃ pātukaronti, pucchissāmi tāvā”ti añjaliṃ paggayha sitakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Athassa satthā “bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, kaṇho nāma isi ahosi, so imasmiṃ bhūmippadese vihāsi jhāyī jhānarato, tassa sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampī”ti sitakāraṇaṃ vatvā tassa vatthuno apākaṭattā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while residing in the Nigrodha Grove near Kapilavatthu, spoke this discourse beginning with the words, 'This man is dark indeed,' concerning the manifestation of a smile. At that time, it is said, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was walking up and down in the evening at the Nigrodha Grove when he manifested a smile at a certain spot. The Venerable Ānanda thought, 'What indeed is the reason, what is the cause for the manifestation of the Blessed One's smile? Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a cause. I shall ask him.' Raising his joined hands in salutation, he asked the reason for the smile. Then the Teacher said to him, 'Ānanda, formerly there was an ascetic named Kaṇha who lived in this very spot of ground, a meditator delighting in meditation. Through the power of his virtue, the abode of Sakka shook.' Having explained the reason for the smile, and because that matter was unclear, when requested by the Elder, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiyaṃ ekena asītikoṭivibhavena aputtakena brāhmaṇena sīlaṃ samādiyitvā putte patthite bodhisatto tassa brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Kāḷavaṇṇattā panassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “kaṇhakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So soḷasavassakāle maṇipaṭimā viya sobhaggappatto hutvā pitarā sippuggahaṇatthāya pesito takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggahetvā paccāgacchi. Atha naṃ pitā anurūpena dārena saṃyojesi. So aparabhāge mātāpitūnaṃ accayena sabbissariyaṃ paṭipajji. Athekadivasaṃ ratanakoṭṭhāgārāni viloketvā varapallaṅkamajjhagato suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ āharāpetvā “ettakaṃ dhanaṃ asukena uppāditaṃ, ettakaṃ asukenā”ti pubbañātīhi suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhitāni akkharāni disvā cintesi “yehi imaṃ dhanaṃ uppāditaṃ, te na paññāyanti, dhanameva paññāyati, ekopi idaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā gato nāma natthi, na kho pana sakkā dhanabhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā paralokaṃ gantuṃ. Pañcannaṃ verānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvena hi asārassa dhanassa dānaṃ sāro, bahurogasādhāraṇabhāvena asārassa sarīrassa sīlavantesu abhivādanādikammaṃ sāro, aniccābhibhūtabhāvena asārassa [M 4.0008] jīvitassa aniccādivasena vipassanāyogo sāro, tasmā asārehi bhogehi sāraggahaṇatthaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a childless Brahmin with eighty crores of wealth undertook the precepts and wished for a son. The Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of that Brahmin’s wife. Due to his dark complexion, on the naming-ceremony day they named him 'Kaṇhakumāra.' At sixteen years of age, having attained a radiant beauty like a jeweled statue, he was sent by his father to Takkasilā to learn all the arts. After mastering all the arts, he returned. Then his father united him with a suitable wife. Later, after the passing of his parents, he took charge of the entire estate. One day, while inspecting the treasure houses and seated on a splendid couch, he had a golden tablet brought to him. Seeing the inscriptions written on the golden tablet by his ancestors—'So much wealth was produced by this one, so much by that one'—he reflected: 'Those by whom this wealth was produced are not to be seen; only the wealth is seen. Not a single one has taken this wealth and departed. Indeed, it is not possible to bind up a bundle of wealth and go to the next world. Since wealth, being essenceless, is common to the five enemies, its essence is giving. Since the body, being essenceless, is common to many diseases, its essence is the act of paying respect to the virtuous. And since life, being essenceless, is overcome by impermanence, its essence is the practice of insight meditation on impermanence and so forth. Therefore, to grasp the essence from these essenceless possessions, I shall give alms.'

So āsanā vuṭṭhāya rañño santikaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ āpucchitvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Yāva sattamā divasā dhanaṃ aparikkhīyamānaṃ [P 4.0008] disvā “kiṃ me dhanena, yāva maṃ jarā nābhibhavati, tāvadeva pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā gehe sabbadvārāni vivarāpetvā “dinnaṃ me, harantū”ti asuciṃ viya jigucchanto [V 4.0008] vatthukāme pahāya mahājanassa rodantassa paridevantassa nagarā nikkhamitvā himavantapadesaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā attano vasanatthāya ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ olokento imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā “idha vasissāmī”ti ekaṃ indavāruṇīrukkhaṃ gocaragāmaṃ adhiṭṭhāya tasseva rukkhassa mūle vihāsi. Gāmantasenāsanaṃ pahāya āraññiko ahosi, paṇṇasālaṃ akatvā rukkhamūliko ahosi, abbhokāsiko nesajjiko. Sace nipajjitukāmo, bhūmiyaṃyeva nipajjati, dantamūsaliko hutvā anaggipakkameva khādati, thusaparikkhittaṃ kiñci na khādati, ekadivasaṃ ekavārameva khādati, ekāsaniko ahosi. Khamāya pathavīāpatejavāyusamo hutvā ete ettake dhutaṅgaguṇe samādāya vattati, imasmiṃ kira jātake bodhisatto paramappiccho ahosi. So na cirasseva abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto tattheva vasati, phalāphalatthampi aññattha na gacchati, rukkhassa phalitakāle phalaṃ khādati, pupphitakāle pupphaṃ khādati, sapattakāle pattāni khādati, nippattakāle papaṭikaṃ khādati. Evaṃ paramasantuṭṭho hutvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ciraṃ vasati.

Rising from his seat, he went to the king, took his leave, and initiated a great giving of alms. Seeing that the wealth was not exhausted even by the seventh day, he thought, 'What is this wealth to me? Before old age overcomes me, I shall go forth, produce the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and be destined for the Brahma-world.' Having all the doors of his house opened, he declared, 'It is given by me, let them take it!' Disgusted with sensual pleasures as if with filth, he abandoned them. As the great crowd of people wept and lamented, he departed from the city, entered the Himalayan region, and went forth into the ascetic life of a sage. Searching for a pleasant place to dwell, he arrived at this spot and thought, 'I will live here.' Resolving upon a single indavāruṇī tree as his alms-resort, he dwelt at the root of that very tree. Abandoning lodgings near a village, he became a forest-dweller. Not making a leaf-hut, he became a tree-root-dweller, an open-air-dweller, and one who maintains the sitting posture. If he wished to lie down, he lay upon the ground itself. He used his teeth as a pestle, eating only what was uncooked by fire; he ate nothing covered with husks. He ate only once a day, in a single session. In patience, he was like the earth, water, fire, and air. He undertook and observed these many ascetic qualities; for in this birth, it is said, the Bodhisatta was supremely desireless. Before long, he produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments and dwelt there, delighting in the play of absorption. He did not go elsewhere even for fruits and roots. When the tree bore fruit, he ate the fruit; when it flowered, he ate the flowers; when it had leaves, he ate the leaves; and when it was without leaves, he ate the bark. Thus, being supremely content, he dwelt in that place for a long time.

So ekadivasaṃ pubbaṇhasamaye tassa rukkhassa pakkāni phalāni gaṇhi, gaṇhanto pana loluppacārena uṭṭhāya aññasmiṃ padese na gaṇhāti, yathānisinnova hatthaṃ pasāretvā hatthappasāraṇaṭṭhāne ṭhitāni phalāni saṃharati, tesupi manāpāmanāpaṃ avicinitvā sampattasampattameva gaṇhāti. Evaṃ paramasantuṭṭhassa tassa sīlatejena sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Taṃ kira sakkassa āyukkhayena vā uṇhaṃ hoti puññakkhayena [M 4.0009] vā, aññasmiṃ [P 4.0009] vā mahānubhāvasatte taṃ ṭhānaṃ patthente, dhammikānaṃ vā mahiddhikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlatejena uṇhaṃ hoti. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti āvajjetvā imasmiṃ padese vasantaṃ kaṇhaṃ isiṃ rukkhaphalāni uccinantaṃ disvā cintesi “ayaṃ isi ghoratapo paramajitindriyo, imaṃ dhammakathāya sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā sukāraṇaṃ sutvā varena santappetvā imamassa rukkhaṃ dhuvaphalaṃ katvā āgamissāmī”ti. So mahantenānubhāvena sīghaṃ otaritvā tasmiṃ rukkhamūle tassa piṭṭhipasse ṭhatvā “attano avaṇṇe kathite kujjhissati nu kho, no”ti vīmaṃsanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, in the early morning, he gathered the ripe fruits from that tree. While gathering them, however, he did not, out of greed, get up and gather them from another spot; but remaining seated as he was, he stretched out his hand and collected the fruits that were within his reach. Among those, he did not discriminate between the pleasant and the unpleasant, but took whatever he happened to get. Due to the supreme contentment of one such as this, the power of his virtue caused Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone seat to show signs of heat. It is said that this seat becomes hot either when Sakka’s lifespan is ending, or when his merit is exhausted, or when another being of great power aspires to that position, or through the power of the virtue of righteous ascetics and brahmins of great spiritual power. Sakka, thinking, 'Who now wishes to dislodge me from my position?' reflected and saw the sage Kaṇha dwelling in that place, gathering fruits from the tree. He thought, 'This sage is of severe austerity and has perfectly subdued his senses. I shall make him roar a lion's roar with a Dhamma talk, and having heard the reason for happiness, I will satisfy him with a boon, make this tree of his perpetually fruitful, and then return.' With his great power, he descended swiftly and stood at the foot of that tree behind the sage. To test him, wondering, 'Will he become angry if his faults are spoken of, or not?' he spoke the first verse:

11.

11.

“Kaṇho vatāyaṃ puriso, kaṇhaṃ bhuñjati bhojanaṃ;

Kaṇhe bhūmipadesasmiṃ, na mayhaṃ manaso piyo”ti.

Dark indeed is this man, dark is the food he eats; in a dark spot of ground he stays, he is not pleasing to my mind.

Tattha kaṇhoti kāḷavaṇṇo. Bhojananti rukkhaphalabhojanaṃ.

Therein, 'dark' means of a dark complexion. 'Food' means the eating of the fruit of the tree.

Kaṇho [V 4.0009] isi sakkassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ko nu kho mayā saddhiṃ kathetī”ti dibbacakkhunā upadhārento “sakko”ti ñatvā anivattitvā anoloketvāva dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The sage Kaṇha, hearing Sakka's words, thought, 'Who is it that speaks with me?' Investigating with the divine eye, he knew it was Sakka. Without turning back or even looking around, he spoke the second verse:

12.

12.

“Na kaṇho tacasā hoti, antosāro hi brāhmaṇo;

Yasmiṃ pāpāni kammāni, sa ve kaṇho sujampatī”ti.

One is not dark by skin; a brahmin has his essence within. He in whom evil deeds are found, he is truly dark, O Sujampati.

Tattha tacasāti tacena kaṇho nāma na hotīti attho. Antosāroti abbhantare sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasārehi samannāgato. Evarūpo hi bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo nāma hoti. Sa veti yasmiṃ pana pāpāni kammāni atthi, so yattha katthaci kule jātopi yena kenaci sarīravaṇṇena samannāgatopi kāḷakova.

Therein, 'by skin' means that one is not called dark because of one's skin. 'Having his essence within' means being endowed with the inner essences of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. For one of such a nature, having cast out evil, is called a brahmin. But as for 'he is truly dark': whoever has evil deeds, no matter in what family he is born or with what bodily complexion he is endowed, he is a dark one indeed.

Evañca pana vatvā imesaṃ sattānaṃ kaṇhabhāvakarāni pāpakammāni ekavidhādibhedehi vitthāretvā sabbānipi tāni garahitvā sīlādayo guṇe pasaṃsitvā ākāse candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya [P 4.0010] sakkassa dhammaṃ desesi. Sakko tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pamudito somanassajāto mahāsattaṃ varena nimantento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he explained in detail the evil deeds that make beings dark, through classifications such as the singlefold and so on. Censuring all of those and praising virtues such as morality, he preached the Dhamma to Sakka as if making the moon rise in the sky. Having heard his Dhamma talk, Sakka was delighted and joyful. Inviting the Great Being with a boon, he spoke the third verse:

13.

13.

“Etasmiṃ [M 4.0010] te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ brāhmaṇa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti.

Since you have spoken so well, in words that are suitable and well-said, I grant you a boon, O Brahmin—whatever you desire in your heart.

Tattha etasminti yaṃ idaṃ tayā sabbaññubuddhena viya sulapitaṃ, tasmiṃ sulapite tumhākameva anucchavikattā patirūpe subhāsite yaṃ kiñci manasā icchasi, sabbaṃ te yaṃ varaṃ icchitaṃ patthitaṃ, taṃ dammīti attho.

Therein, 'since you have spoken so well' (etasmiṃ sulapite) refers to this which was well-spoken by you as if by an Omniscient Buddha. 'In words that are suitable and well-said' (patirūpe subhāsite) means words fitting for you. 'Whatever you desire in your heart' means I grant you all of that, whatever boon is desired or wished for; this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto cintesi “ayaṃ kiṃ nu kho attano avaṇṇe kathite kujjhissati, noti maṃ vīmaṃsanto mayhaṃ chavivaṇṇañca bhojanañca vasanaṭṭhānañca garahitvā idāni mayhaṃ akuddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā pasannacitto varaṃ deti, maṃ kho panesa ‘sakkissariyabrahmissariyānaṃ atthāya brahmacariyaṃ caratī’tipi maññeyya, tatrassa nikkaṅkhabhāvatthaṃ mayhaṃ paresu kodho vā doso vā mā uppajjatu, parasampattiyaṃ lobho vā paresu sineho vā mā uppajjatu, majjhattova bhaveyyanti ime mayā cattāro vare gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tassa nikkaṅkhabhāvatthāya cattāro vare gaṇhanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Great Being thought: 'Will Sakka get angry when I mention his lack of virtue? Testing me, he disparaged my appearance, my food, and my dwelling; now, knowing my lack of anger and being pleased at heart, he offers me a boon. But he might also think, "He practices the holy life for the sake of attaining the status of Sakka or the status of Brahma." To remove any doubt in him, I should accept these four boons: "May no anger or malice arise in me toward others; may no greed for others' prosperity or affection for others arise in me; may I remain equanimous."’ To clear Sakka's doubt, choosing the four boons, he spoke the fourth verse:

14.

14.

“Varañce [V 4.0010] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Sunikkodhaṃ suniddosaṃ, nillobhaṃ vuttimattano;

Nisnehamabhikaṅkhāmi, ete me caturo vare”ti.

14. 'If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings, I desire a life of total freedom from anger, total freedom from malice, and freedom from greed. I long for a life free from attachment; these are the four boons I seek.'

Tattha varañce me ado sakkāti sace tvaṃ mayhaṃ varaṃ adāsi. Sunikkodhanti akujjhanavasena suṭṭhu nikkodhaṃ. Suniddosanti adussanavasena suṭṭhu niddosaṃ. Nillobhanti parasampattīsu nillobhaṃ. Vuttimattanoti evarūpaṃ attano vuttiṃ. Nisnehanti puttadhītādīsu vā saviññāṇakesu dhanadhaññādīsu vā aviññāṇakesu attano santakesupi nisnehaṃ apagatalobhaṃ. Abhikaṅkhāmīti evarūpaṃ imehi catūhaṅgehi samannāgataṃ attano vuttiṃ abhikaṅkhāmi. Ete me caturo vareti ete nikkodhādike caturo mayhaṃ vare dehīti.

Therein, 'If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka' (varañce me ado sakka) means if you were to give me a boon. 'Total freedom from anger' (sunikkodhaṃ) means being well-freed from anger through non-irascibility. 'Total freedom from malice' (suniddosaṃ) means being well-freed from malice through non-offensiveness. 'Freedom from greed' (nillobhaṃ) means being free from greed for the prosperity of others. 'A life for oneself' (vuttimattano) means such a way of living for oneself. 'Free from attachment' (nisnehaṃ) means being free from affection and devoid of greed regarding one’s own possessions, whether they be sentient beings like sons and daughters, or inanimate objects like wealth and grain. 'I desire' (abhikaṅkhāmi) means I long for such a life for myself, endowed with these four factors. 'These are the four boons I seek' (ete me caturo vare) means give me these four boons, such as freedom from anger and so on.

Kiṃ panesa na jānāti “yathā na sakkā sakkassa santike varaṃ gahetvā varena kodhādayo hanitu”nti. No na jānāti, sakke kho pana varaṃ [P 4.0011] dente na gaṇhāmīti vacanaṃ na yuttanti tassa ca nikkaṅkhabhāvatthāya gaṇhi[M 4.0011]. Tato sakko cintesi “kaṇhapaṇḍito varaṃ gaṇhanto ativiya anavajje vare gaṇhi, etesu varesu guṇadosaṃ etameva pucchissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ pucchanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Now, did he not know that 'it is not possible to eradicate anger and so forth by receiving a boon from Sakka'? It is not that he did not know; he did indeed know. However, when Sakka offers a boon, it is not proper to say 'I will not accept it.' Therefore, he accepted the boons in that manner to clear Sakka's doubt. Then Sakka thought: 'The wise Kaṇha, in choosing boons, chose boons that are extremely blameless. I will ask this very wise Kaṇha about the merits and faults of these boons.' Then, questioning him, he spoke the fifth verse:

15.

15.

“Kiṃnu kodhe vā dose vā, lobhe snehe ca brāhmaṇa;

Ādīnavaṃ tvaṃ passasi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

15. 'What danger do you see, O Brahmin, in anger or malice, in greed or in attachment? Being asked, please tell me that.'

Tassattho – brāhmaṇa kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ kodhe dose lobhe snehe ca ādīnavaṃ passasi, taṃ tāva me pucchito akkhāhi, na hi mayaṃ ettha ādīnavaṃ jānāmāti.

Its meaning is: O Brahmin, what danger indeed do you see in anger, malice, greed, and attachment? Please tell me that since you have been asked; for we do not know the danger in these things.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto “tena hi suṇāhī”ti vatvā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Great Being said to him, 'In that case, listen,' and spoke four verses:

16.

16.

“Appo hutvā bahu hoti, vaḍḍhate so akhantijo;

Āsaṅgī bahupāyāso, tasmā kodhaṃ na rocaye.

16. 'Starting small, it becomes great; that which is born of impatience grows. It causes attachment and much distress; therefore, one should not delight in anger.'

17.

17.

“Duṭṭhassa [V 4.0011] pharusā vācā, parāmāso anantarā;

Tato pāṇi tato daṇḍo, satthassa paramā gati;

Doso kodhasamuṭṭhāno, tasmā dosaṃ na rocaye.

17. 'For one who is corrupted, there are harsh words, followed by physical assault; then the hand, then the stick, and finally the weapon is the ultimate resort. Malice originates from anger; therefore, one should not delight in malice.'

18.

18.

“Ālopasāhasākārā, nikatī vañcanāni ca;

Dissanti lobhadhammesu, tasmā lobhaṃ na rocaye.

18. 'Plunder, acts of violence, fraud, and deception are seen in states of greed; therefore, one should not delight in greed.'

19.

19.

“Snehasaṅgathitā ganthā, senti manomayā puthū;

Te bhusaṃ upatāpenti, tasmā snehaṃ na rocaye”ti.

19. 'The bonds tied by attachment are many and mind-made; they cause intense torment. Therefore, one should not delight in attachment.'

Tattha akhantijoti so anadhivāsakajātikassa akhantito jāto kodho paṭhamaṃ paritto hutvā pacchā bahu hoti aparāparaṃ vaḍḍhati. Tassa vaḍḍhanabhāvo khantivādījātakena (jā. 1.4.49 ādayo) ceva cūḷadhammapālajātakena (jā. 1.5.44 ādayo) ca vaṇṇetabbo. Apica tissāmaccassapettha bhariyaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ saparijanaṃ māretvā pacchā attano māritavatthu kathetabbaṃ. Āsaṅgīti āsaṅgakaraṇo. Yassa uppajjati, taṃ āsattaṃ laggitaṃ karoti, taṃ vatthuṃ vissajjetvā [M 4.0012] gantuṃ na deti, nivattitvā akkosanādīni kāreti. Bahupāyāsoti bahunā kāyikacetasikadukkhasaṅkhātena upāyāsena kilamathena samannāgato. Kodhaṃ nissāya hi kodhavasena ariyādīsu katavītikkamā diṭṭhadhamme ceva samparāye ca vadhabandhavippaṭisārādīni [P 4.0012] ceva pañcavidhabandhanakammakaraṇādīni ca bahūni dukkhāni anubhavantīti kodho bahupāyāso nāma. Tasmāti yasmā esa evaṃ anekādīnavo, tasmā kodhaṃ na rocemi.

Therein, 'born of impatience' (akhantijo) means that anger, born of the impatience of a person with an intolerant nature, is small at first but later becomes great and grows more and more. Its growth should be described by the Khantivāda Jātaka and the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka. Furthermore, the story of the minister Tissa should be told here, starting from the killing of his wife, then all his attendants, and finally the matter of his own execution. 'Causes attachment' (āsaṅgī) means it creates entanglement. In whomever it arises, it makes them entangled and stuck; it does not allow them to let go of that object and leave, but makes them turn back and commit verbal abuse and so on. 'Much distress' (bahupāyāso) means endowed with great distress and exhaustion, consisting of physical and mental suffering. For, depending on anger, due to the power of anger, those who commit transgressions against Noble Ones and others experience many sufferings such as execution, imprisonment, and remorse, as well as the fivefold punishment in both the present life and the future state; thus anger is called 'having much distress.' 'Therefore' (tasmā) means because it has such manifold dangers, for that reason I do not delight in anger.

Duṭṭhassāti kujjhanalakkhaṇena kodhena kujjhitvā aparabhāge dussanalakkhaṇena dosena duṭṭhassa paṭhamaṃ tāva “are, dāsa, pessā”ti pharusavācā niccharati, vācāya anantarā ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanavasena hatthaparāmāso, tato anantarā upakkamanavasena pāṇi pavattati, tato daṇḍo, daṇḍappahāre atikkamitvā pana ekatodhāraubhatodhārassa satthassa paramā gati, sabbapariyantā satthanipphatti hoti. Yadā hi satthena paraṃ jīvitā voropetvā pacchā teneva satthena attānaṃ jīvitā voropeti, tadā doso matthakappatto hoti. Doso kodhasamuṭṭhānoti yathā anambilaṃ takkaṃ vā kañjikaṃ vā pariṇāmavasena parivattitvā ambilaṃ hoti, taṃ ekajātikampi samānaṃ ambilaṃ anambilanti nānā vuccati, tathā pubbakāle kodho pariṇamitvā [V 4.0012] aparabhāge doso hoti. So akusalamūlattena ekajātikopi samāno kodho dosoti nānā vuccati. Yathā anambilato ambilaṃ, evaṃ sopi kodhato samuṭṭhātīti kodhasamuṭṭhāno. Tasmāti yasmā evaṃ anekādīnavo doso, tasmā dosampi na rocemi.

'To one who is corrupt' (duṭṭhassa): Having become angry through anger characterized by irritation (kujjhanalakkhaṇena), one later becomes corrupt through ill-will characterized by malice (dussanalakkhaṇena). First, harsh speech such as 'Hey, you slave, you servant!' is uttered. Immediately after the speech, there is physical contact by way of pulling and dragging. After that, the hand is used to attack; then a stick. Transgressing the use of a stick, the ultimate resort is a weapon, either single-edged or double-edged, which is the finality of weapons. For when one kills another with a weapon and later kills oneself with that same weapon, then ill-will has reached its peak. 'Ill-will is born of anger' (doso kodhasamuṭṭhāno): Just as non-sour buttermilk or sour gruel turns sour through the process of fermentation—though it is of the same nature, it is called differently as 'sour' and 'non-sour'—similarly, anger in the earlier stage transforms into ill-will in the later stage. Although they are of the same class due to being unwholesome roots, anger is called 'ill-will'. Just as the sour comes from the non-sour, so also this [ill-will] arises from anger; hence it is called 'born of anger'. 'Therefore': Since ill-will has such manifold dangers, I do not approve of ill-will either.

Ālopasāhasākārāti divā divasseva gāmaṃ paharitvā vilumpanāni ca āvudhaṃ sarīre ṭhapetvā “idaṃ nāma me dehī”ti sāhasākārā ca. Nikatī vañcanāni cāti patirūpakaṃ dassetvā parassa haraṇaṃ nikati nāma, sā asuvaṇṇameva “suvaṇṇa”nti kūṭakahāpaṇaṃ “kahāpaṇo”ti datvā parasantakaggahaṇe daṭṭhabbā. Paṭibhānavasena pana upāyakusalatāya parasantakaggahaṇaṃ vañcanaṃ nāma. Tassevaṃ pavatti daṭṭhabbā – eko kira ujujātiko gāmikapuriso araññato sasakaṃ ānetvā nadītīre ṭhapetvā nhāyituṃ otari. Atheko dhutto taṃ sasakaṃ sīse katvā nhāyituṃ otiṇṇo. Itaro uttaritvā sasakaṃ apassanto ito cito ca vilokesi. Tamenaṃ dhutto “kiṃ bho vilokesī”ti vatvā “imasmiṃ me ṭhāne sasako ṭhapito, taṃ na passāmī”ti vutte “andhabāla, tvaṃ na jānāsi, sasakā nāma nadītīre ṭhapitā palāyanti, passa ahaṃ attano sasakaṃ [M 4.0013] sīse ṭhapetvāva nhāyāmī”ti āha. So appaṭibhānatāya “evaṃ bhavissatī”ti pakkāmi. Ekakahāpaṇena migapotakaṃ gahetvā puna taṃ datvā dvikahāpaṇagghanakassa migassa gahitavatthupettha kathetabbaṃ. Dissanti lobhadhammesūti sakka, ime ālopādayo pāpadhammā lobhasabhāvesu lobhābhibhūtesu sattesu dissanti. Na hi aluddhā evarūpāni kammāni karonti. Evaṃ lobho anekādīnavo, tasmā lobhampi na rocemi.

'Plunder and acts of violence' (ālopasāhasākārā): This refers to plundering a village in broad daylight, as well as acts of violence such as placing a weapon against someone's body and saying, 'Give me such-and-such.' 'Fraud and deception' (nikatī vañcanāni): Displaying a counterfeit to take another's property is called fraud; this should be understood as taking another's belongings by giving non-gold as 'gold' or a counterfeit coin as a 'kahāpaṇa'. Taking another's property through cleverness and skillful means is called deception. Its occurrence should be understood thus: It is said that an honest villager brought a hare from the forest, placed it by the riverbank, and went down to bathe. A rogue placed that hare on his head and went down to bathe. The other, having come up and not seeing the hare, looked here and there. The rogue said to him, 'What are you looking for, friend?' When he said, 'I placed a hare in this spot and do not see it,' the rogue replied, 'You blind fool, don't you know? Hares placed on a riverbank run away. Look, I am bathing while keeping my hare on my head!' Due to his lack of wit, the villager thought, 'It must be so,' and went away. The story of taking a young deer for one kahāpaṇa, then giving it back and taking a deer worth two kahāpaṇas should also be told here. 'Are seen among those with greedy natures' (dissanti lobhadhammesu): O Sakka, these evil states such as plundering are seen among beings whose nature is greed and who are overwhelmed by greed. For those without greed do not perform such actions. Thus, greed has manifold dangers; therefore, I do not approve of greed either.

Snehasaṅgathitā ganthāti ārammaṇesu allīyanalakkhaṇena snehena saṅgathitā punappunaṃ uppādavasena ghaṭitā suttena pupphāni [P 4.0013] viya baddhā nānappakāresu ārammaṇesu pavattamānā abhijjhākāyaganthā. Senti manomayā puthūti te puthūsu ārammaṇesu uppannā suvaṇṇādīhi nibbattāni suvaṇṇādimayāni ābharaṇādīni viya manena nibbattattā manomayā abhijjhākāyaganthā tesu ārammaṇesu senti anusenti. Te bhusaṃ upatāpentīti te evaṃ anusayitā balavatāpaṃ janentā bhusaṃ upatāpenti atikilamenti. Tesaṃ pana bhusaṃ upatāpane “sallaviddhova ruppatī”ti (su. ni. 773) gāthāya vatthu, “piyajātikā hi gahapati, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā piyappabhutikā” (ma. ni. 2.353), “piyato jāyatī soko”tiādīni (dha. pa. 212) suttāni ca āharitabbāni. Apica maṅgalabodhisattassa dārake datvā balavasokena hadayaṃ phali, vessantarabodhisattassa mahantaṃ domanassaṃ udapādi. Evaṃ pūritapāramīnaṃ [V 4.0013] mahāsattānaṃ pemaṃ upatāpaṃ karotiyeva. Ayaṃ snehe ādīnavo, tasmā snehampi na rocemīti.

'Bonds tied by affection' (snehasaṅgathitā ganthā): These are the bodily bonds of covetousness occurring in various objects, tied by affection characterized by clinging to objects, linked by repeated arising like flowers strung together by a thread. 'Manifold, mind-made, they lie' (senti manomayā puthū): These bodily bonds of covetousness, having arisen in manifold objects, are called 'mind-made' because they are produced by the mind, just as ornaments made of gold and so forth are produced from gold. They lie and lie latent in those objects. 'They torment severely' (te bhusaṃ upatāpenti): Being thus latent, they generate intense heat and torment severely, causing great distress. Regarding this severe torment, the story for the verse 'One suffers like one pierced by a dart' (Sn 773) and the suttas such as 'Sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, O householder, are born of the beloved' (MN 87) and 'From the beloved arises sorrow' (Dhp 212) should be cited. Furthermore, after the Bodhisatta Maṅgala gave away his children, his heart broke with intense grief; and for the Bodhisatta Vessantara, great distress arose. Thus, even for Great Beings who have fulfilled the perfections, affection indeed causes torment. This is the danger in affection; therefore, I do not approve of affection either.

Sakko pañhavissajjanaṃ sutvā “kaṇhapaṇḍita tayā ime pañhā buddhalīḷāya sādhukaṃ kathitā, ativiya tuṭṭhosmi te, aparampi varaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka, having heard the solution to the questions, said, "Wise Kaṇha, these questions have been well answered by you with the grace of a Buddha. I am exceedingly pleased with you. Take another boon," and spoke the tenth verse:

20.

20.

“Etasmiṃ [M 4.0014] te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ brāhmaṇa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti.

"For this well-spoken, fitting, and well-expressed statement of yours, O Brahmin, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish in your mind."

Tato bodhisatto anantaragāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the following verse:

21.

21.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Araññe me viharato, niccaṃ ekavihārino;

Ābādhā mā uppajjeyyuṃ, antarāyakarā bhusā”ti.

"If, O Sakka, lord of all beings, you should grant me a boon, while I dwell in the forest, ever living alone, may no severe, obstructive illnesses arise for me."

Tattha antarāyakarā bhusāti imassa me tapokammassa antarāyakarā.

Therein, 'severe, obstructive' (antarāyakarā bhusa) means obstructive to this ascetic practice of mine.

Taṃ sutvā sakko “kaṇhapaṇḍito varaṃ gaṇhanto na āmisasannissitaṃ gaṇhāti, tapokammanissitameva gaṇhātī”ti cintetvā bhiyyosomattāya pasanno aparampi varaṃ dadamāno itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka, thinking, "The wise Kaṇha, in choosing a boon, does not take one connected with material things; he takes only what is connected with his ascetic practice," became even more pleased and, offering another boon, spoke the other verse:

22.

22.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ brāhmaṇa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti.

"For this well-spoken, fitting, and well-expressed statement of yours, O Brahmin, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish in your mind."

Bodhisattopi varaggahaṇāpadesena tassa dhammaṃ desento osānagāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, under the pretext of choosing a boon, teaching him the Dhamma, spoke the concluding verse:

23.

23.

“Varañce [P 4.0014] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Na mano vā sarīraṃ vā, maṃ-kate sakka kassaci;

Kadāci upahaññetha, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare”ti.

"If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings, may no one's mind or body ever be harmed on my account at any time, O Sakka; this is the boon I choose."

Tattha [V 4.0014] mano vāti manodvāraṃ vā. Sarīraṃ vāti kāyadvāraṃ vā, vacīdvārampi etesaṃ gahaṇena gahitamevāti veditabbaṃ. Maṃ-kateti mama kāraṇā. Upahaññethāti upaghātaṃ āpajjeyya aparisuddhaṃ assa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sakka devarāja, mama kāraṇā maṃ nissāya mama anatthakāmatāya kassaci sattassa kismiñci kāle idaṃ tividhampi kammadvāraṃ na upahaññetha, pāṇātipātādīhi dasahi akusalakammapathehi vimuttaṃ parisuddhameva bhaveyyāti.

In this context, 'mind' refers to the mind-door. 'Body' refers to the body-door; it should be understood that the speech-door is also included by the mention of these. 'On my account' means because of me. 'May it be harmed' means may it come to harm or become impure. This is what is meant: 'O Sakka, king of the gods, on my account, because of me, or due to a desire to harm me, may the threefold door of action of any being never be harmed at any time; rather, may it be released and completely pure from the ten unwholesome paths of action, beginning with the taking of life.'"

Iti [M 4.0015] mahāsatto chasupi ṭhānesu varaṃ gaṇhanto nekkhammanissitameva gaṇhi, jānāti cesa “sarīraṃ nāma byādhidhammaṃ, na taṃ sakkā sakkena abyādhidhammaṃ kātu”nti. Sattānañhi tīsu dvāresu parisuddhabhāvo asakkāyattova, evaṃ santepi tassa dhammadesanatthaṃ ime vare gaṇhi. Sakkopi taṃ rukkhaṃ dhuvaphalaṃ katvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā sirasi añjaliṃ patiṭṭhapetvā “arogā idheva vasathā”ti vatvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisattopi aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, in choosing boons in all six instances, the Great Being chose only those based on renunciation. He knew, 'The body is by nature subject to disease; even Sakka cannot make it free from disease.' For the purity of beings in the three doors of action is indeed not dependent on others but on oneself; nevertheless, he chose these boons for the sake of preaching the Dhamma to Sakka. Sakka, having made that tree bear fruit perpetually, paid homage to the Great Being, placed his joined hands on his head in reverence, and said, 'May you dwell right here in health and free from disease,' and then returned to his own abode. The Bodhisatta, with his meditative absorption (jhāna) undiminished, was later reborn in the Brahma world."

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “ānanda, pubbe mayā nivutthabhūmippadeso ceso”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi, kaṇhapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, 'Ānanda, this is the very place where I resided in the past,' and then identified the rebirths of the Jātaka: 'At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, but the wise Kaṇha was I myself.'"

Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇha Jātaka is the second.

[441] 3. Catuposathikajātakavaṇṇanā

[441] 3. The Commentary on the Catuposathika Jātaka

24-38. Yo kopaneyyoti idaṃ catuposathikajātakaṃ puṇṇakajātake āvi bhavissati.

24-38. "One who is provoking"—this Catuposathika Jātaka will be fully explained in the Puṇṇaka Jātaka.

Catuposathikajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Catuposathika Jātaka is the third.

[442] 4. Saṅkhajātakavaṇṇanā

[442] 4. The Commentary on the Saṅkha Jātaka

Bahussutoti [P 4.0015] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko upāsako tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacitto svātanāya nimantetvā attano gharadvāre maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā alaṅkaritvā punadivase tathāgatassa kālaṃ ārocāpesi. Satthā [V 4.0015] pañcasatabhikkhuparivāro tattha gantvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Upāsako saputtadāro saparijano buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā puna svātanāyāti evaṃ sattāhaṃ nimantetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāraṃ adāsi. Taṃ pana dadamāno upāhanadānaṃ ussannaṃ katvā adāsi. Dasabalassa dinno upāhanasaṅghāṭo sahassagghanako [M 4.0016] ahosi, dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ pañcasatagghanako, sesānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ satagghanako. Iti so sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ datvā attano parisāya saddhiṃ bhagavato santike nisīdi. Athassa satthā madhurena sarena anumodanaṃ karonto “upāsaka, uḷāraṃ te sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ, attamano hohi, pubbe anuppanne buddhe paccekabuddhassa ekaṃ upāhanasaṅghāṭaṃ datvā nāvāya bhinnāya appatiṭṭhe mahāsamuddepi upāhanadānanissandena patiṭṭhaṃ labhiṃsu, tvaṃ pana buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ adāsi, tassa te upāhanadānassa phalaṃ kasmā na patiṭṭhā bhavissatī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"He who is learned"—the Teacher told this story while staying at Jetavana, concerning the gift of all the requisites. It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain lay devotee, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Tathāgata and being filled with devotion, invited the Buddha for the following day. He had a pavilion erected and decorated at his house door, and the next day he announced the time to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, accompanied by five hundred monks, went there and sat on the prepared seat. The lay devotee, with his wife, children, and retinue, offered a great gift to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. He continued this for seven days, and on the seventh day, he offered all the requisites. In making this gift, he provided an abundance of sandals. The pair of sandals given to the Ten-Powered One was worth a thousand pieces; those for the two chief disciples were worth five hundred; and for the remaining five hundred monks, they were worth one hundred each. Having given all the requisites, he sat with his followers near the Blessed One. Then the Teacher, in a sweet voice, gave the words of appreciation: 'Lay devotee, your gift of all the requisites is magnificent. Be joyful! In the past, before a Buddha had arisen, people who gave a single pair of sandals to a Paccekabuddha found firm support through the result of that gift even in the trackless great ocean when their ship was wrecked. You have given all the requisites to the Sangha headed by the Buddha; why then should the fruit of your gift of sandals not be a firm support for you?' Being requested by the devotee, he related a story of the past."

Atīte ayaṃ bārāṇasī moḷinī nāma ahosi. Moḷininagare brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente saṅkho nāma brāhmaṇo aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo pahūtavittupakaraṇo pahūtadhanadhaññasuvaṇṇarajato catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāre cāti chasu ṭhānesu cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassāni vissajjento kapaṇaddhikānaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattesi. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi “ahaṃ gehe dhane khīṇe dātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, aparikkhīṇeyeva dhane nāvāya suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gantvā dhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti. So nāvaṃ bandhāpetvā bhaṇḍassa pūrāpetvā puttadāraṃ āmantetvā “yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi[P 4.0016], tāva me dānaṃ anupacchinditvā pavatteyyāthā”ti vatvā dāsakammakaraparivuto chattaṃ ādāya upāhanaṃ āruyha majjhanhikasamaye paṭṭanagāmābhimukho pāyāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe gandhamādane eko paccekabuddho āvajjetvā taṃ dhanāharaṇatthāya gacchantaṃ disvā “mahāpuriso dhanaṃ āharituṃ gacchati, bhavissati nu kho assa samudde antarāyo, no”ti āvajjetvā “bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “esa maṃ disvā chattañca upāhanañca mayhaṃ datvā upāhanadānanissandena samudde bhinnāya nāvāya patiṭṭhaṃ labhissati, karissāmissa anuggaha”nti ākāsenāgantvā tassāvidūre otaritvā caṇḍavātātape aṅgārasantharasadisaṃ uṇhavālukaṃ maddanto tassa abhimukho āgacchi.

In the past, this Bārāṇasī was named Moḷinī. While King Brahmadatta was ruling in Moḷinī, there was a brahmin named Saṅkha, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and property, with abundant gold, silver, and grain. He had six alms-halls built—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at the entrance of his residence—and daily distributed six hundred thousand pieces of money, maintaining a great charity for the poor and travelers. One day, he thought, 'When the wealth in my house is exhausted, I will be unable to give. While the wealth is still undiminished, I will go by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi and bring back more wealth.' He had a ship built, loaded it with goods, and told his wife and children, 'Until I return, keep my charity going without interruption.' Then, surrounded by servants, taking a parasol and putting on his sandals, he set out at midday toward the port town. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana, reflecting and seeing him going to fetch wealth, thought, 'This great man is going to acquire wealth. Will he face danger at sea or not?' Knowing there would be danger, he thought, 'When he sees me, he will give me his parasol and sandals. By the result of this gift, when his ship is wrecked at sea, he will find a firm support. I shall favor him.' Coming through the sky, he descended nearby and, treading on the hot sand which was like a bed of embers in the fierce heat, he approached the Brahmin."

So taṃ disvāva “puññakkhettaṃ me āgataṃ, ajja mayā ettha dānabījaṃ ropetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tuṭṭhacitto vegena taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “bhante, mayhaṃ anuggahatthāya thokaṃ maggā okkamma imaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upasaṅkamathā”ti vatvā [M 4.0017] tasmiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upasaṅkamante rukkhamūle [V 4.0016] vālukaṃ ussāpetvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ paññapetvā paccekabuddhaṃ nisīdāpetvā vanditvā vāsitaparissāvitena udakena pāde dhovitvā gandhatelena makkhetvā attano upāhanā omuñcitvā papphoṭetvā gandhatelena makkhetvā tassa pādesu paṭimuñcitvā “bhante, imā upāhanā āruyha chattaṃ matthake katvā gacchathā”ti chattupāhanaṃ adāsi. So assa anuggahatthāya taṃ gahetvā pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthaṃ passantassevassa uppatitvā gandhamādanameva agamāsi. Bodhisattopi taṃ disvā ativiya pasannacitto paṭṭanaṃ gantvā nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Athassa mahāsamuddaṃ paṭipannassa sattame divase nāvā vivaraṃ adāsi, udakaṃ ussiñcituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Mahājano maraṇabhayabhīto attano attano devatā namassitvā mahāviravaṃ viravi. Mahāsatto ekaṃ upaṭṭhākaṃ [P 4.0017] gahetvā sakalasarīraṃ telena makkhetvā sappinā saddhiṃ sakkharacuṇṇaṃ yāvadatthaṃ khāditvā tampi khādāpetvā tena saddhiṃ kūpakayaṭṭhimatthakaṃ āruyha “imāya disāya amhākaṃ nagara”nti disaṃ vavatthapetvā macchakacchapaparipanthato attānaṃ mocento tena saddhiṃ usabhamattaṃ atikkamitvā pati. Mahājano vināsaṃ pāpuṇi. Mahāsatto pana upaṭṭhākena saddhiṃ samuddaṃ tarituṃ ārabhi. Tassa tarantasseva sattamo divaso jāto. So tasmimpi kāle loṇodakena mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathiko ahosiyeva.

Seeing him, he thought with a joyful heart: 'A field of merit has come to me. Today, it is fitting for me to plant a seed of merit here.' Quickly approaching, he paid homage and said: 'Venerable sir, for my benefit, please step aside from the path a little and come to the foot of this tree.' When the Paccekabuddha reached the foot of the tree, he heaped up the sand there, spread out his upper robe, and seated the Paccekabuddha. Having paid homage, he washed the Paccekabuddha’s feet with perfumed and filtered water, anointed them with fragrant oil, removed his own sandals, dusted them off, anointed them with fragrant oil, and put them on the Paccekabuddha’s feet, saying: 'Venerable sir, please put on these sandals, place the parasol over your head, and go on your way.' Thus he gave him the parasol and sandals. The Paccekabuddha, for his benefit, accepted them. To increase his faith, while the Bodhisatta was watching, he rose into the air and went right to Gandhamādana. The Bodhisatta, seeing this, was exceedingly gladdened in heart and went to the port to board the ship. Then, on the seventh day after he had set out upon the great ocean, the ship broke apart and began to take on water. They were unable to bail out the water. The great crowd of people, terrified by the fear of death, paid homage to their respective deities and cried out with a great cry. The Great Being took one attendant, anointed his entire body with oil, ate his fill of ghee mixed with powdered sugar, and had the attendant eat as well. Then, together with him, he climbed to the top of the mast. Determining the direction, thinking 'Our city is in this direction,' and freeing himself from the danger of fish and turtles, he jumped with the attendant, landing beyond the distance of an usabha. The rest of the crew perished. But the Great Being, together with his attendant, began to swim across the ocean. As he was swimming, the seventh day arrived. Even at that time, he rinsed his mouth with saltwater and remained one observing the Uposatha.

Tadā pana catūhi lokapālehi maṇimekhalā nāma devadhītā “sace samudde nāvāya bhinnāya tisaraṇagatā vā sīlasampannā vā mātāpitupaṭṭhākā vā manussā dukkhappattā honti, te rakkheyyāsī”ti samudde ārakkhaṇatthāya ṭhapitā hoti. Sā attano issariyena sattāhamanubhavitvā pamajjitvā sattame divase samuddaṃ olokentī sīlācārasaṃyuttaṃ saṅkhabrāhmaṇaṃ disvā “imassa sattamo divaso samudde patitassa, sace so marissati ativiya gārayhā me bhavissatī”ti saṃviggamānahadayā hutvā ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ nānaggarasabhojanassa pūretvā vātavegena tattha gantvā tassa purato ākāse ṭhatvā “brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ sattāhaṃ nirāhāro, idaṃ dibbabhojanaṃ bhuñjā”ti āha. So taṃ oloketvā “apanehi tava bhattaṃ, ahaṃ uposathiko”ti āha. Athassa [M 4.0018] upaṭṭhāko pacchato āgato devataṃ adisvā saddameva sutvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo pakatisukhumālo sattāhaṃ nirāhāratāya dukkhito maraṇabhayena vilapati maññe, assāsessāmi na”nti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, a celestial maiden named Maṇimekhalā had been appointed by the four world-guarding kings to guard the ocean with the instruction: 'If, when a ship is wrecked at sea, humans who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, or are endowed with virtue, or are attendants to their parents, fall into distress, you should protect and rescue them.' Having enjoyed her own celestial dominion for seven days, she became negligent. On the seventh day, looking over the ocean, she saw the brahmin Saṅkha, who was endowed with virtue and good conduct, and thought: 'This is the seventh day since he fell into the ocean. If he dies, it will be highly blameworthy for me.' With an agitated heart, she filled a golden bowl with food of various excellent flavors, went there with the speed of the wind, stood in the air before the Bodhisatta, and said: 'Brahmin, you have been without food for seven days. Eat this divine food.' He looked at her and said: 'Take away your food. I am observing the Uposatha.' Then his attendant, coming from behind, did not see the deity but only heard her voice. He thought: 'This brahmin is naturally delicate. Suffering from being without food for seven days, he is surely babbling out of fear of death. I shall comfort him.' Thinking thus, he spoke the first verse:

39.

39.

“Bahussuto sutadhammosi saṅkha, diṭṭhā tayā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca;

Athakkhaṇe [P 4.0018] dassayase vilāpaṃ, añño nu ko te paṭimantako mayā”ti.

“You are learned, O Saṅkha, you have heard the Dhamma from the Paccekabuddhas, and you have seen ascetics and brahmins. Yet at this inopportune moment you display lamentation; who other than I is here to be your interlocutor?”

Tattha [V 4.0017] sutadhammosīti dhammopi tayā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ santike suto asi. Diṭṭhā tayāti tesaṃ paccaye dentena veyyāvaccaṃ karontena dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā ca tayā diṭṭhā. Evaṃ akaronto hi passantopi te na passatiyeva. Athakkhaṇeti atha akkhaṇe sallapantassa kassaci abhāvena vacanassa anokāse. Dassayaseti “ahaṃ uposathiko”ti vadanto vilāpaṃ dassesi. Paṭimantakoti mayā añño ko tava paṭimantako paṭivacanadāyako, kiṃkāraṇā evaṃ vippalapasīti?

In those verses, 'sutadhammosi' means that the Dhamma has also been heard by you from the presence of righteous ascetics and brahmins. 'Diṭṭhā tayā' means that righteous ascetics and brahmins have also been seen by you as you gave them requisites and performed services for them. For one who does not act thus, even while seeing them, he does not truly see them. 'Athakkhaṇe' means at an inopportune time, when there is no occasion for speech due to the absence of anyone else to converse with. 'Dassayase' means that by saying 'I am observing the Uposatha,' you are displaying lamentation. 'Paṭimantako' means: 'Who other than me is your interlocutor, your giver of a reply? For what reason are you thus babbling?'

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “imassa devatā na paññāyati maññe”ti cintetvā “samma, nāhaṃ maraṇassa bhāyāmi, atthi pana me añño paṭimantako”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, the brahmin thought, 'I suppose this attendant does not perceive the deity,' and then said, 'Friend, I do not fear death, but I have another interlocutor besides you.' Then he spoke the second verse:

40.

40.

“Subbhū subhā suppaṭimukkakambu, paggayha sovaṇṇamayāya pātiyā;

‘Bhuñjassu bhattaṃ’ iti maṃ vadeti, saddhāvittā, tamahaṃ noti brūmī”ti.

“Of beautiful countenance, radiant, with a well-adorned neck, holding out a golden bowl, she says to me, ‘Eat this food.’ But because I am observing the Uposatha, I say to her, ‘No.’”

Tattha subbhūti subhamukhā. Subhāti pāsādikā uttamarūpadharā. Suppaṭimukkakambūti paṭimukkasuvaṇṇālaṅkārā. Paggayhāti suvaṇṇapātiyā bhattaṃ gahetvā ukkhipitvā. Saddhāvittāti saddhā ceva tuṭṭhacittā ca. “Saddhaṃ citta”ntipi pāṭho, tassattho saddhanti saddahantaṃ, cittanti tuṭṭhacittaṃ. Tamahaṃ [M 4.0019] notīti tamahaṃ devataṃ uposathikattā paṭikkhipanto noti brūmi, na vippalapāmi sammāti.

Here, 'subbhū' means one with a beautiful face. 'Subhā' means delightful, bearing an excellent form. 'Suppaṭimukkakambū' means adorned with golden ornaments. 'Paggayha' means having taken the food in the golden bowl and lifted it up. 'Saddhāvittā' means one who has a mind of faith and joy. There is also a reading 'saddhaṃ cittaṃ'; its meaning is 'saddhaṃ' as believing and 'cittaṃ' as a joyful heart. 'Tamahaṃ noti' means 'I say "No" to that deity,' rejecting her because of being one observing the Uposatha; 'I am not babbling, friend.'

Athassa so tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the attendant spoke this third verse to the brahmin Saṅkha:

41.

41.

“Etādisaṃ brāhmaṇa disvāna yakkhaṃ, puccheyya poso sukhamāsisāno;

Uṭṭhehi naṃ pañjalikābhipuccha, devī nusi tvaṃ uda mānusī nū”ti.

“Seeing such a deity, O brahmin, a person desiring happiness should ask her; rise and with hands clasped in reverence, inquire: ‘Are you a goddess or a human being?’”

Tattha sukhamāsisānoti etādisaṃ yakkhaṃ disvā attano sukhaṃ āsīsanto paṇḍito puriso “amhākaṃ sukhaṃ bhavissati, na bhavissatī”ti puccheyya. Uṭṭhehīti udakato uṭṭhānākāraṃ dassento uṭṭhaha. Pañjalikābhipucchāti añjaliko [P 4.0019] hutvā abhipuccha. Uda mānusīti udāhu mahiddhikā mānusī tvanti.

Here, ‘desiring happiness’ means that a wise person, seeing such a deity (yakkha) and wishing for his own happiness, would ask, ‘Will there be happiness for us or not?’ ‘Rise!’ means indicating the manner of rising from the water, [saying] ‘Rise!’ ‘Inquire with hands joined in reverence’ means inquiring while having one’s hands joined in reverence. ‘Or a human being?’ means ‘Or are you a human being of great power?’

Bodhisatto “yuttaṃ kathesī”ti taṃ pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, thinking, ‘He speaks appropriately,’ and wishing to ask her, spoke the fourth verse:

42.

42.

“Yaṃ [V 4.0018] tvaṃ sukhenābhisamekkhase maṃ, bhuñjassu bhattaṃ iti maṃ vadesi;

Pucchāmi taṃ nāri mahānubhāve, devī nusi tvaṃ uda mānusī nū”ti.

“Since you look upon me with a kindly eye and say to me, ‘Partake of the food,’ I ask you, O lady of great power: Are you a goddess or are you a human being?”

Tattha yaṃ tvanti yasmā tvaṃ sukhena maṃ abhisamekkhase, piyacakkhūhi olokesi. Pucchāmi tanti tena kāraṇena taṃ pucchāmi.

In that verse, ‘Since you’ means ‘because you look upon me with a kindly eye; you look with loving eyes.’ ‘I ask you’ means ‘for that reason I ask you.’

Tato devadhītā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the daughter of the gods spoke two verses:

43.

43.

“Devī ahaṃ saṅkha mahānubhāvā, idhāgatā sāgaravārimajjhe;

Anukampikā no ca paduṭṭhacittā, taveva atthāya idhāgatāsmi.

“I am a goddess, O Saṅkha, of great power, come here to the midst of the ocean waters. I am compassionate and not of a wicked mind; I have come here for your sake only.”

44.

44.

“Idhannapānaṃ sayanāsanañca, yānāni nānāvividhāni saṅkha;

Sabbassa tyāhaṃ paṭipādayāmi, yaṃ kiñci tuyhaṃ manasābhipatthita”nti.

“Here is food and drink, beds and seats, and various kinds of vehicles, O Saṅkha. All of this I bestow upon you, whatever is desired by your mind.”

Tattha [M 4.0020] idhāti imasmiṃ mahāsamudde. Nānāvividhānīti bahūni ca anekappakārāni ca hatthiyānaassayānādīni atthi. Sabbassa tyāhanti tassa annapānādino sabbassa sāmikaṃ katvā taṃ te annapānādiṃ paṭipādayāmi dadāmi. Yaṃ kiñcīti aññampi yaṃ kiñci manasā icchitaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ te dammīti.

In that verse, ‘here’ means in this great ocean. ‘Various kinds’ means there are many and various types, such as elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and so on. ‘All of this I bestow upon you’ means I bestow that food, drink, and so on upon you, making you the master of all that food and drink; I give it. ‘Whatever’ means whatever else is desired by the mind, all that I give to you.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ devadhītā samuddapiṭṭhe mayhaṃ ‘idañcidañca dammī’ti vadati, kiṃ nu kho esā mayā katena puññakammena dātukāmā, udāhu attano balena, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā pucchanto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being thought: ‘This daughter of the gods, on the surface of the ocean, says to me, “I will give you this and that.” Is she wishing to give this because of some meritorious deed done by me, or by her own power? I will ask her.’ Thinking thus, he asked her with the seventh verse:

45.

45.

“Yaṃ kiñci yiṭṭhañca hutañca mayhaṃ, sabbassa no issarā tvaṃ sugatte;

Sussoṇi subbhamu suvilaggamajjhe, kissa me kammassa ayaṃ vipāko”ti.

“Whatever sacrifice or offering of mine there be, you are the master of it all, O beautiful-limbed one. O lady of beautiful thighs, beautiful eyebrows, and slender waist, of which deed of mine is this the result?”

Tattha [P 4.0020] yiṭṭhanti dānavasena yajitaṃ. Hutanti āhunapāhunavasena dinnaṃ. Sabbassa no issarā tvanti tassa amhākaṃ puññakammassa tvaṃ issarā, “imassa ayaṃ vipāko, imassa aya”nti byākarituṃ samatthāti attho. Sussoṇīti sundaraūrulakkhaṇe. Subbhamūti sundarabhamuke[V 4.0019]. Suvilaggamajjheti suṭṭhuvilaggitatanumajjhe. Kissa meti mayā katakammesu katarakammassa ayaṃ vipāko, yenāhaṃ appatiṭṭhe samudde patiṭṭhaṃ labhāmīti.

In that verse, ‘sacrifice’ (yiṭṭhaṃ) means what was sacrificed in the form of a gift. ‘Offering’ (hutaṃ) means what was given as an offering to guests. ‘You are the master of it all’ means you are the master of that meritorious deed of ours; the meaning is that you are capable of explaining, ‘This is the result of this [deed], this is the result of that [deed].’ ‘O lady of beautiful thighs’ refers to the mark of beautiful thighs. ‘Beautiful eyebrows’ means having beautiful eyebrows. ‘Slender waist’ means a very slender and thin waist. ‘Of which deed of mine’ means, of the deeds done by me, of which deed is this the result, by which I gain a footing in the ocean where there is no footing?

Taṃ sutvā devadhītā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo ‘yaṃ tena kusalaṃ kataṃ, taṃ kammaṃ na jānātī’ti aññāya pucchati maññe, kathayissāmi dānissā”ti taṃ kathentī aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the daughter of the gods, thinking, ‘This brahmin, it seems, asks because he does not know the meritorious deed he has done. I will now explain it to him,’ spoke the eighth verse to tell him:

46.

46.

“Ghamme pathe brāhmaṇa ekabhikkhuṃ, ugghaṭṭapādaṃ tasitaṃ kilantaṃ;

Paṭipādayī saṅkha upāhanāni, sā dakkhiṇā kāmaduhā tavajjā”ti.

“On a parched road, O brahmin, to a lone monk whose feet were chafed, who was thirsty and weary, you provided sandals, O Saṅkha; that gift of yours today yields all your desires.”

Tattha ekabhikkhunti ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ sandhāyāha. Ugghaṭṭapādanti uṇhavālukāya ghaṭṭitapādaṃ. Tasitanti pipāsitaṃ. Paṭipādayīti paṭipādesi, yojesīti attho. Kāmaduhāti sabbakāmadāyikā.

In that verse, ‘a lone monk’ refers to a certain Paccekabuddha. ‘With feet chafed’ means feet rubbed by hot sand. ‘Thirsty’ means parched with thirst. ‘You provided’ means you bestowed or supplied; this is the meaning. ‘Yielding all desires’ means granting all desires.

Taṃ [M 4.0021] sutvā mahāsatto “evarūpepi nāma appatiṭṭhe mahāsamudde mayā dinnaupāhanadānaṃ mama sabbakāmadadaṃ jātaṃ, aho sudinnaṃ me paccekabuddhassa dāna”nti tuṭṭhacitto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being, with a delighted mind, thinking, ‘Even in such a supportless great ocean, my gift of sandals has become one that grants all my desires! Oh, well given indeed was my gift to the Paccekabuddha!’ spoke the ninth verse:

47.

47.

“Sā hotu nāvā phalakūpapannā, anavassutā erakavātayuttā;

Aññassa yānassa na hettha bhūmi, ajjeva maṃ moḷiniṃ pāpayassū”ti.

“Let there be a ship, well-planked, not leaking, and equipped with sails and wind; for there is no place for any other vehicle here. This very day, convey me to Moḷinī.”

Tassattho – devate, evaṃ sante mayhaṃ ekaṃ nāvaṃ māpehi, khuddakaṃ pana ekadoṇikanāvaṃ māpehi, yaṃ nāvaṃ māpessasi, sā hotu nāvā bahūhi susibbitehi phalakehi upapannā, udakapavesanassābhāvena anavassutā, erakena sammā [P 4.0021] gahetvā gacchantena vātena yuttā, ṭhapetvā dibbanāvaṃ aññassa yānassa ettha bhūmi natthi, tāya pana dibbanāvāya ajjeva maṃ moḷininagaraṃ pāpayassūti.

The meaning is: ‘O deity, such being the case, create a ship for me—not a small, single-log boat—but whatever ship you create, let it be a ship provided with many well-joined planks, not leaking because no water can enter, and equipped with a sail properly catching the wind. Except for a celestial ship, there is no place here for any other vehicle. By that celestial ship, convey me to the city of Moḷinī this very day.’

Devadhītā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhacittā sattaratanamayaṃ nāvaṃ māpesi. Sā dīghato aṭṭhausabhā ahosi vitthārato catuusabhā, gambhīrato vīsatiyaṭṭhikā. Tassā indanīlamayā tayo kūpakā, sovaṇṇamayāni yottāni rajatamayāni pattāni sovaṇṇamayāni ca phiyārittāni ahesuṃ. Devatā taṃ nāvaṃ sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ pūretvā brāhmaṇaṃ āliṅgitvā alaṅkatanāvāya [V 4.0020] āropesi, upaṭṭhākaṃ panassa na olokesi. Brāhmaṇo attanā katakalyāṇato tassa pattiṃ adāsi, so anumodi. Tadā devatā tampi āliṅgitvā nāvāya patiṭṭhāpesi. Atha naṃ nāvaṃ moḷininagaraṃ netvā brāhmaṇassa ghare dhanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Satthā abhisambuddho hutvā –

The daughter of the gods, hearing his words, with a delighted heart, created a ship made of the seven jewels. It was eight usabhas in length, four usabhas in width, and twenty yaṭṭhis in depth. It had three masts made of sapphire, golden riggings, silver sails, and oars and rudders of pure gold. The deity filled the ship with the seven jewels, embraced the brahmin, and placed him upon the adorned ship, but she did not even look at his attendant. The brahmin shared the merit of his own good deed with the attendant, and he rejoiced. Then the deity embraced him also and placed him in the ship. Then, having brought the ship to the city of Moḷinī and deposited the wealth in the brahmin’s house, she went back to her own abode. The Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke:

48.

48.

“Sā tattha vittā sumanā patītā, nāvaṃ sucittaṃ abhinimminitvā;

Ādāya saṅkhaṃ purisena saddhiṃ, upānayī nagaraṃ sādhuramma”nti. –

“She, being joyful, glad-minded, and pleased, having created a splendid ship, took Saṅkha together with the man and brought them to the delightful city.”

Imaṃ osānagāthaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this concluding verse.
