Tattha [M 4.0022] sāti bhikkhave, sā devatā tattha samuddamajjhe tassa vacanaṃ sutvā vittisaṅkhātāya pītiyā samannāgatattā vittā. Sumanāti sundaramanā pāmojjena patītacittā hutvā vicitranāvaṃ nimminitvā brāhmaṇaṃ paricārakena saddhiṃ ādāya sādhurammaṃ atiramaṇīyaṃ nagaraṃ upānayīti.

Therein, monks, 'she' refers to that deity. 'There' means in the midst of the ocean. Having heard his words, she was 'delighted' (vittā), being endowed with the joy known as delight. 'Glad-minded' (sumanā) means having a beautiful mind. 'Pleased' (patītā) means her heart was pleased with gladness. Having created a marvelous boat and taking the brahmin along with his attendant, she brought them to the 'very delightful' (sādhurammaṃ), that is, the exceedingly delightful city.

Brāhmaṇopi yāvajīvaṃ aparimitadhanaṃ gehaṃ ajjhāvasanto dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā jīvitapariyosāne sapariso devanagaraṃ paripūresi.

The brahmin also, dwelling in a house of immeasurable wealth for his entire life, giving alms and observing the precepts, at the end of his life, together with his retinue, filled the heavenly city.

Satthā [P 4.0022] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, upaṭṭhākapuriso ānando, saṅkhabrāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, the attendant was Ānanda, and the brahmin Saṅkha was none other than myself.

Saṅkhajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The fourth commentary on the Saṅkha Jātaka.

[443] 5. Cūḷabodhijātakavaṇṇanā

[443] 5. The Commentary on the Cūḷabodhi Jātaka

Yo te imaṃ visālakkhinti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kodhanaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhikkhu niyyānike buddhasāsane pabbajitvāpi kodhaṃ niggahetuṃ nāsakkhi, kodhano ahosi upāyāsabahulo, appampi vutto samāno abhisajji kuppi byāpajji [V 4.0021] patiṭṭhayi. Satthā tassa kodhanabhāvaṃ sutvā pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ kodhano”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu kodho nāma vāretabbo, evarūpo hi idhaloke ca paraloke ca anatthakārako, tvaṃ nikkodhassa buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā kasmā kujjhasi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā bāhirasāsane pabbajitvāpi kodhaṃ na kariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Yo te imaṃ visālakkhiṃ”—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain angry monk. It is said that this monk, though he had gone forth in the Buddha’s dispensation which leads to liberation, could not restrain his anger. He was prone to anger, full of resentment, and would become irritated, upset, hostile, and stubborn even when spoken to slightly. Hearing of his angry nature, the Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true that you are angry?” When he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Monk, anger should be restrained, for such a thing brings harm both in this world and the next. Having gone forth in the dispensation of the Buddha, who is free from anger, why do you get angry? Even the wise of old, though they went forth in external teachings, did not give way to anger.” Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente aññatarasmiṃ kāsinigame eko brāhmaṇo aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo aputtako ahosi, tassa brāhmaṇī puttaṃ patthesi. Tadā bodhisatto brahmalokā cavitvā tassā kucchiyaṃ nibbatti, tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “bodhikumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa vayappattakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā [M 4.0023] sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgatassa anicchantasseva mātāpitaro samānajātikā kulā kumārikaṃ ānesuṃ. Sāpi brahmalokā cutāva uttamarūpadharā devaccharapaṭibhāgā. Tesaṃ anicchamānānaññeva aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ kariṃsu. Ubhinnaṃ panetesaṃ kilesasamudācāro nāma na bhūtapubbo, saṃrāgavasena aññamaññassa olokanaṃ nāma nāhosi, supinepi methunadhammo nāma na diṭṭhapubbo, evaṃ parisuddhasīlā ahesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, in a certain village in Kāsi there lived a brahmin who was rich, very wealthy, and possessed great riches, yet was without a son. His brahmin wife desired a son. Then the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Brahma world, was conceived in her womb. On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name 'Bodhikumāra.' When he came of age, having gone to Takkasilā, he mastered all the arts and returned home. Although he was unwilling, his parents brought a maiden from a family of equal status. She too, having passed away from the Brahma world, possessed a supreme form like a celestial nymph. Though both were unwilling, their marriage was arranged. But for them, the arising of defilements had never occurred. There was not even a mutual glance with passion. They had never seen sexual intercourse even in a dream. Thus, they were of perfectly pure virtue.

Athāparabhāge mahāsatto mātāpitūsu kālakatesu tesaṃ sarīrakiccaṃ katvā taṃ pakkositvā “bhadde, tvaṃ imaṃ [P 4.0023] asītikoṭidhanaṃ gahetvā sukhena jīvāhī”ti āha. “Kiṃ karissatha tumhe pana, ayyaputtā”ti? “Mayhaṃ dhanena kiccaṃ natthi, himavantapadesaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana ayyaputta pabbajjā nāma purisānaññeva vaṭṭatī”ti? “Itthīnampi vaṭṭati, bhadde”ti. “Tena hi ahaṃ tumhehi chaṭṭitakheḷaṃ na gaṇhissāmi, mayhampi dhanena kiccaṃ natthi, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhadde”ti. Te ubhopi mahādānaṃ datvā nikkhamitvā ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge assamaṃ katvā pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya phalāphalehi yāpentā tattha dasamattāni saṃvaccharāni vasiṃsu, jhānaṃ pana nesaṃ na tāva uppajjati. Te tattha pabbajjāsukheneva dasa saṃvacchare vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ carantā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasiṃsu.

Then, at a later time, when his parents had passed away, the Great Being performed their funeral rites. He called his wife and said, “Dear one, take this wealth of eighty crores and live happily.” “But what will you do, noble lord?” she asked. “I have no need for wealth. I will enter the Himalayan region, go forth as an ascetic, and establish myself.” “But noble lord, is renunciation fitting only for men?” she asked. “It is fitting for women too, dear one,” he replied. “In that case, I will not take what you have discarded like spittle. I too have no need for wealth—I will also go forth.” “Very well, dear one,” he said. Both of them gave great alms, departed, and in a delightful region built a hermitage. Having gone forth, they sustained themselves by gleaning and on fruits, and lived there for ten years. However, meditative absorption did not yet arise for them. After living in the joy of renunciation for ten years, they set out on a journey through the countryside to obtain salt and sour seasoning. Gradually, they reached Benares and took up residence in the royal garden.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānapālaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya āgataṃ disvā “uyyānakīḷikaṃ kīḷissāma, uyyānaṃ sodhehī”ti vatvā tena sodhitaṃ sajjitaṃ uyyānaṃ mahantena parivārena agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe te ubhopi janā uyyānassa ekapasse pabbajjāsukhena vītināmetvā nisinnā [V 4.0022] honti. Atha rājā uyyāne vicaranto te ubhopi nisinnake disvā paramapāsādikaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ paribbājikaṃ olokento paṭibaddhacitto ahosi. So kilesavasena kampanto “pucchissāmi tāva, ayaṃ paribbājikā imassa kiṃ hotī”ti bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “pabbajita ayaṃ te paribbājikā kiṃ hotī”ti pucchi. Mahārāja, kiñci na hoti, kevalaṃ ekapabbajjāya pabbajitā, apica kho pana me gihikāle pādaparicārikā ahosīti. Taṃ sutvā rājā “ayaṃ kiretassa kiñci na hoti, apica kho pana gihikāle pādaparicārikā kirassa ahosi[M 4.0024], sace panāhaṃ issariyabalena gahetvā gaccheyyaṃ, kiṃ nu kho esa karissati, pariggaṇhissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, the king saw the park keeper coming with a tribute and said, “We will enjoy the park; clean the park.” After it was cleaned and prepared, he went to the park with a large retinue. At that moment, the two of them were sitting on one side of the park, passing the time in the bliss of renunciation. Then, as the king wandered through the park, he saw the two of them sitting there. Gazing at the female ascetic, who was extremely pleasing and possessed of the highest beauty, his heart became attached. Trembling with the power of defilement, he thought, “I shall first ask what this female ascetic is to him.” Approaching the Bodhisatta, he asked, “Ascetic, what is this female ascetic to you?” “Great king, she is nothing to me, but has simply gone forth in the same renunciation. However, in my lay life, she was my attendant.” Hearing this, the king thought, “He says she is nothing to him, though in lay life she was his attendant. If I were to take her by the force of my power, what would he do? I shall first test him.” Having reflected thus, he approached and spoke the first verse:

49.

49.

“Yo [P 4.0024] te imaṃ visālakkhiṃ, piyaṃ saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ;

Ādāya balā gaccheyya, kiṃ nu kayirāsi brāhmaṇā”ti.

"If someone were to forcibly take away this broad-eyed one, dear and speaking with a gentle smile, what would you do, O Brahmin?"

Tattha saṃmhitabhāsininti mandahasitabhāsiniṃ. Balā gaccheyyāti balakkārena ādāya gaccheyya. Kiṃ nu kayirāsīti tassa tvaṃ brāhmaṇa kiṃ kareyyāsīti?

Therein, 'saṃmhitabhāsiniṃ' means speaking with a gentle smile. 'Balā gaccheyya' means one would take away by force. 'Kiṃ nu kayirāsi' means, 'What would you, O Brahmin, do to him?'

Athassa kathaṃ sutvā mahāsatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having heard his words, the Great Being spoke the second verse:

50.

50.

“Uppajje me na mucceyya, na me mucceyya jīvato;

Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhi, khippameva nivāraye”ti.

"Should it arise in me, may it not be released; may it not be released from me while I live. As a great rain lays the dust, so would I swiftly restrain it."

Tassattho – mahārāja, sace imaṃ gahetvā gacchante kismiñci mama abbhantare kopo uppajjeyya, so me anto uppajjitvā na mucceyya, yāvāhaṃ jīvāmi, tāva me na mucceyya. Nāssa anto ghanasannivāsena patiṭṭhātuṃ dassāmi, atha kho yathā uppannaṃ rajaṃ vipulā meghavuṭṭhi khippaṃ nivāreti, tathā khippameva naṃ mettābhāvanāya niggahetvā vāressāmīti.

The meaning is: O great king, if anger should arise within me while she is being led away, once arisen within, it would not be released. As long as I live, it would not be released from me. I would not allow it to gain a firm foothold within, but just as a great rain quickly dispels arisen dust, so too would I swiftly restrain and ward it off through the cultivation of loving-kindness.

Evaṃ mahāsatto sīhanādaṃ nadi. Rājā panassa kathaṃ sutvāpi andhabālatāya paṭibaddhaṃ attano cittaṃ nivāretuṃ asakkonto aññataraṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi “imaṃ paribbājikaṃ rājanivesanaṃ nehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā “adhammo loke vattati, ayutta”ntiādīni [V 4.0023] vatvā paridevamānaṃyeva naṃ ādāya pāyāsi. Bodhisatto tassā paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā ekavāraṃ oloketvā puna na olokesi. Taṃ rodantiṃ paridevantiṃ rājanivesanameva nayiṃsu. Sopi bārāṇasirājā uyyāne papañcaṃ akatvāva sīghataraṃ gantvā taṃ paribbājikaṃ pakkosāpetvā mahantena yasena nimantesi. Sā yasassa aguṇaṃ pabbajāya eva guṇaṃ kathesi. Rājā kenaci pariyāyena tassā manaṃ alabhanto taṃ ekasmiṃ gabbhe kāretvā cintesi “ayaṃ paribbājikā evarūpaṃ yasaṃ na icchati, sopi tāpaso evarūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ gahetvā gacchante kujjhitvā olokitamattampi [M 4.0025] na akāsi, pabbajitā kho pana bahumāyā honti, kiñci payojetvā anatthampi me kareyya, gacchāmi [P 4.0025] tāva jānāmi kiṃ karonto nisinno”ti saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonto uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisattopi cīvaraṃ sibbanto nisīdi. Rājā mandaparivārova padasaddaṃ akaronto saṇikaṃ upasaṅkami. Bodhisatto rājānaṃ anoloketvā cīvarameva sibbi. Rājā “ayaṃ kujjhitvā mayā saddhiṃ na sallapatī”ti maññamāno “ayaṃ kūṭatāpaso ‘kodhassa uppajjituṃ na dassāmi, uppannampi naṃ khippameva niggaṇhissāmī’ti paṭhamameva gajjitvā idāni kodhena thaddho hutvā mayā saddhiṃ na sallapatī”ti saññāya tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, the Great Being roared a lion's roar. The king, however, even after hearing his words, was unable to restrain his own mind, which was bound by blind foolishness, and commanded a certain minister, 'Take this female ascetic to the royal palace.' He, agreeing with 'Very well,' took her away even as she was lamenting and saying, 'Unrighteousness prevails in the world; this is improper,' and so on. The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of her lamentation, glanced once but did not look again. They led her, weeping and wailing, straight to the royal palace. That king of Benares, without dallying in the park, went very quickly and, having summoned that female ascetic, offered her great royal splendor. She spoke of the lack of benefit in splendor and the benefit only in renunciation. The king, unable to win her over by any means, had her placed in a chamber and thought, 'This female ascetic does not desire such splendor, and that ascetic, while such a woman was being taken away, did not even give a mere look in anger. Renunciants, however, are full of guile; they might cause me harm by employing some means. I will go and find out what he is doing as he sits there.' Unable to remain still, he went to the park. The Bodhisatta sat sewing his robe. The king, with a small retinue, approached quietly, making no sound with his feet. The Bodhisatta, without looking at the king, continued to sew his robe. The king, thinking, 'He is angry and does not speak with me,' and perceiving, 'This rogue ascetic, having first boasted, "I will not allow anger to arise, and if it does arise, I will quickly suppress it," is now stiff with anger and does not speak with me,' spoke the third stanza:

51.

51.

“Yaṃ nu pubbe vikatthittho, balamhiva apassito;

Svajja tuṇhikato dāni, saṅghāṭiṃ sibbamacchasī”ti.

That which you boasted of before, as if relying on strength; now today you are silent, sitting and sewing your robe.

Tattha balamhiva apassitoti balanissito viya hutvā. Tuṇhikatoti kiñci avadanto. Sibbamacchasīti sibbanto acchasi.

Therein, 'as if relying on strength' means having become as if dependent on strength. 'Silent' means not saying anything. 'Sitting and sewing' means you sit while sewing.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “ayaṃ rājā kodhavasena maṃ nālapatīti maññati, kathessāmi dānissa uppannassa kodhassa vasaṃ agatabhāva”nti cintetvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being thought, 'This king thinks I do not speak to him under the influence of anger. I will now explain to him that I have not fallen under the sway of the anger that arose.' Thinking thus, he spoke the fourth stanza:

52.

52.

“Uppajji me na muccittha, na me muccittha jīvato;

Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhi, khippameva nivārayi”nti.

It arose in me, but was not released; it was not released from me while I live. As a great rain quickly dispels dust, I quickly warded it off.

Tassattho – mahārāja, uppajji me, na na uppajji, na pana me muccittha, nāssa pavisitvā hadaye ṭhātuṃ adāsiṃ, iti so mama jīvato na muccittheva, rajaṃ vipulā vuṭṭhi viya khippameva naṃ nivāresinti.

The meaning is: O great king, it arose in me—it is not that it did not arise—but it was not released from me, for I did not allow it to enter and remain in my heart. Thus, while I live, it was indeed not released; I quickly warded it off, just as a great rain wards off dust.

Taṃ [V 4.0024] sutvā rājā “kiṃ nu kho esa kopameva sandhāya vadati, udāhu aññaṃ kiñci sippaṃ sandhāya kathesi, pucchissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā pucchanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king thought, 'I wonder, is he speaking with reference to anger itself, or did he speak with reference to some other skill? I will ask him.' Thinking thus, he asked the fifth stanza:

53.

53.

“Kiṃ te uppajji no mucci, kiṃ te na mucci jīvato;

Rajaṃva vipulā vuṭṭhi, katamaṃ taṃ nivārayī”ti.

What arose for you that was not released? What was not released from you while you live? As a great rain dispels dust, what was it that you restrained?

Tattha [P 4.0026] kiṃ te uppajji no muccīti kiṃ tava uppajji ceva na mucci ca.

Therein, 'What arose for you that was not released?' means 'What both arose for you and was not released?'

Taṃ [M 4.0026] sutvā bodhisatto “mahārāja, evaṃ kodho bahuādīnavo mahāvināsadāyako, eso mama uppajji, uppannañca naṃ mettābhāvanāya nivāresi”nti kodhe ādīnavaṃ pakāsento –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta, declaring the dangers in anger, said: 'O great king, anger has many dangers and brings great destruction. This arose in me, and having arisen, I warded it off by cultivating loving-kindness.'

54.

54.

“Yamhi jāte na passati, ajāte sādhu passati;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

When it has arisen, one does not see; when it has not arisen, one sees well. That arose in me, but was not released: anger, the domain of the foolish.

55.

55.

“Yena jātena nandanti, amittā dukkhamesino;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

By whose arising enemies rejoice, those who seek one's suffering; that arose in me, but was not released: anger, the domain of the foolish.

56.

56.

“Yasmiñca jāyamānamhi, sadatthaṃ nāvabujjhati;

So me uppajji no mucci, kodho dummedhagocaro.

And when it is arising, one does not comprehend one's own good. That arose in me, but was not released: anger, the domain of the foolish.

57.

57.

“Yenābhibhūto kusalaṃ jahāti, parakkare vipulañcāpi atthaṃ;

Sa bhīmaseno balavā pamaddī, kodho mahārāja na me amuccatha.

Overcome by which, one abandons what is wholesome, and rejects even great benefit. That fierce, powerful, crushing anger, O great king, was not released from me.

58.

58.

“Kaṭṭhasmiṃ matthamānasmiṃ, pāvako nāma jāyati;

Tameva kaṭṭhaṃ ḍahati, yasmā so jāyate gini.

When wood is being rubbed, fire is born; it burns that very wood from which that fire is born.

59.

59.

“Evaṃ mandassa posassa, bālassa avijānato;

Sārambhā jāyate kodho, sopi teneva ḍayhati.

Thus, for the dull person, the fool who does not understand, anger arises from contention, and he too is burned by it.

60.

60.

“Aggīva [V 4.0025] tiṇakaṭṭhasmiṃ, kodho yassa pavaḍḍhati;

Nihīyati tassa yaso, kāḷapakkheva candimā.

For whom anger grows, like a fire in grass and wood, his glory wanes, like the moon in the dark fortnight.

61.

61.

“Anedho dhūmaketūva, kodho yassūpasammati;

Āpūrati tassa yaso, sukkapakkheva candimā”ti. – imā gāthā āha;

For whom anger subsides, like a fire without fuel, his glory increases, like the moon in the bright fortnight." Thus he spoke these verses.

Tattha na passatīti attatthampi na passati, pageva paratthaṃ. Sādhu passatīti attatthaṃ paratthaṃ ubhayatthampi sādhu passati. Dummedhagocaroti nippaññānaṃ ādhārabhūto gocaro. Dukkhamesinoti dukkhaṃ icchantā. Sadatthanti attano [M 4.0027] atthabhūtaṃ atthato ceva dhammato ca vuddhiṃ. Parakkareti vipulampi atthaṃ uppannaṃ parato kāreti, apanetha, na me iminā atthoti vadati. Sa bhīmasenoti so kodho bhīmāya bhayajananiyā mahatiyā kilesasenāya [P 4.0027] samannāgato. Pamaddīti attano balavabhāvena uḷārepi satte gahetvā attano vase karaṇena maddanasamattho. Na me amuccathāti mama santikā mokkhaṃ na labhati, hadaye vā pana me khīraṃ viya muhuttaṃ dadhibhāvena na patiṭṭhahitthātipi attho.

Therein, 'one does not see' means one does not see even one's own benefit, let alone the benefit of others. 'One sees well' means one sees well one's own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. 'The domain of the foolish' means the foundation and domain of the unwise. 'Those who seek suffering' means those who desire suffering. 'One's own good' means one's own welfare, which is growth in both worldly benefit and in the Dhamma. 'Rejects' means even when great benefit arises, one has another take it away, saying, 'Take it away, this is of no use to me.' 'That fierce one' means that anger is endowed with a great and fearsome army of defilements that generates terror. 'The crusher' means that through its own power, it is capable of crushing even great beings by seizing them and bringing them under its control. 'Was not released from me' means it did not gain release from me; or it means that it did not establish itself in my heart for even a moment, like milk turning into curds.

Kaṭṭhasmiṃ matthamānasminti araṇīsahitena matthiyamāne, “maddamānasmi”ntipi pāṭho. Yasmāti yato kaṭṭhā jāyati, tameva ḍahati. Ginīti aggi. Bālassa avijānatoti bālassa avijānantassa. Sārambhā jāyateti ahaṃ tvanti ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanaṃ karontassa karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇā sārambhā araṇīmatthanā viya pāvako kodho jāyati. Sopi tenevāti sopi bālo teneva kodhena kaṭṭhaṃ viya agginā ḍayhati. Anedho dhūmaketūvāti anindhano aggi viya. Tassāti tassa adhivāsanakhantiyā samannāgatassa puggalassa sukkapakkhe cando viya laddho yaso aparāparaṃ āpūratīti.

Therein, 'when wood is being rubbed' means when it is being rubbed together with a fire-drill; 'maddamānasmiṃ' is also a reading. 'From which' means from whatever wood it is born, it burns that very wood. 'Ginī' means fire. 'Of the fool who does not understand' means of the fool who is not understanding. 'Anger arises from contention' means for one who engages in pulling and pushing, saying 'I' and 'you', from the contention characterized by aggressive behavior, the fire of anger is born, like fire from the rubbing of fire-drills. 'He too is burned by it' means that fool too is burned by that very anger, like wood by fire. 'Like a fire without fuel' means like a fire without kindling. 'His' means for that person endowed with the patience of forbearance, his attained glory continually increases, like the moon in the bright fortnight.

Rājā mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā tuṭṭho ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpetvā paribbājikaṃ āharāpetvā “bhante nikkodhatāpasa, ubhopi tumhe pabbajjāsukhena vītināmentā idheva uyyāne vasatha, ahaṃ vo dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā khamāpetvā vanditvā pakkāmi. Te ubhopi tattheva vasiṃsu. Aparabhāge paribbājikā kālamakāsi. Bodhisatto tassā kālakatāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having heard the Great Being's discourse on the Dhamma, the king was pleased and, ordering a minister to bring the female wanderer, said, 'Venerable ascetic free from anger, may both of you spend your time in the bliss of renunciation and dwell right here in this park. I will provide righteous protection, shelter, and security for you.' Having asked for forgiveness and paid homage, he departed. Both of them stayed there. Later, the female wanderer passed away. After her death, the Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas, developed supernormal powers and meditative attainments, cultivated the four divine abidings, and became destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [V 4.0026] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kodhano bhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the irritable monk was established in the fruit of Non-Returning.

Tadā paribbājikā rāhulamātā ahosi, rājā ānando, paribbājako pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the female wanderer was Rāhula’s mother; the king was Ānanda; and the male wanderer was I myself.

Cūḷabodhijātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth story, the Cūḷabodhi Jātaka, is concluded.

[444] 6. Kaṇhadīpāyanajātakavaṇṇanā

[444] 6. 6. Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka

Sattāhamevāhanti [M 4.0028] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu kusajātake (jā. 2.20.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ bhante”ti [P 4.0028] vutte “bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppanne buddhe bāhirakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā atirekapaññāsavassāni anabhiratā brahmacariyaṃ carantā hirottappabhedabhayena attano ukkaṇṭhitabhāvaṃ na kassaci kathesuṃ, tvaṃ kasmā evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā mādisassa garuno buddhassa sammukhe ṭhatvā catuparisamajjhe ukkaṇṭhitabhāvaṃ āvi karosi, kimatthaṃ attano hirottappaṃ na rakkhasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'I have been for only seven days'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was discontented. The story will appear in the Kusa Jātaka. The Teacher asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true, Venerable Sir,' the Teacher said, 'Monk, wise men of old, before a Buddha had arisen, went forth into an ascetic life outside the dispensation and lived the holy life for more than fifty years without finding delight. Yet, fearing to break their sense of shame and dread of blame, they did not speak of their discontent to anyone. Why then, having gone forth in a dispensation that leads to deliverance, and standing in the presence of a teacher like me, the Buddha, in the midst of the fourfold assembly, do you reveal your discontent? Why do you not protect your sense of shame and dread of blame?' Having said this, he told a story of the past.

Atīte vaṃsaraṭṭhe kosambiyaṃ nāma nagare kosambako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā aññatarasmiṃ nigame dve brāhmaṇā asītikoṭidhanavibhavā aññamaññaṃ piyasahāyakā kāmesu dosaṃ disvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā ubhopi kāme pahāya mahājanassa rodantassa paridevantassa nikkhamitvā himavantapadese assamapadaṃ katvā pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāphalena yāpentā paṇṇāsa vassāni vasiṃsu, jhānaṃ uppādetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Te paṇṇāsavassaccayena loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadaṃ carantā kāsiraṭṭhaṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Tatra aññatarasmiṃ nigamagāme dīpāyanatāpasassa gihisahāyo maṇḍabyo nāma atthi, te ubhopi tassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. So te disvāva attamano paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā ubhopi te catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahi. Te tattha tīṇi cattāri vassāni vasitvā taṃ āpucchitvā cārikaṃ carantā bārāṇasiṃ patvā atimuttakasusāne vasiṃsu. Tattha dīpāyano yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā puna tasseva sahāyassa santikaṃ gato. Maṇḍabyatāpaso tattheva vasi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Vaṃsa, in the city of Kosambī, a king named Kosambaka reigned. At that time, in a certain market town, there were two brahmins who possessed eighty crores of wealth and were dear friends. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, they gave a great gift and, both abandoning sensual pleasures, departed while the populace wept and lamented. They made a hermitage in the Himalayan region and, having become ascetics, lived for fifty years, sustaining themselves by gleaning and with the roots and fruits of the forest. They were unable to generate jhāna. After fifty years had passed, while wandering in the countryside in search of salt and vinegar, they arrived in the Kāsi kingdom. There, in a certain market town, lived a householder named Maṇḍabya, who had been a friend of the ascetic Dīpāyana during his lay life. Both went to him. Seeing them, he was delighted and had a leaf-hut built, attending to both with the four requisites. They stayed there for three or four years, and after taking leave of him, they traveled on and reached Bārāṇasī, where they lived in the Atimuttaka charnel ground. There, Dīpāyana stayed as long as he pleased and then returned to that same friend's place. The ascetic Maṇḍabya remained there.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 4.0027] eko coro antonagare corikaṃ katvā dhanasāraṃ ādāya nikkhanto “coro”ti ñatvā paṭibuddhehi gharassāmikehi ceva ārakkhamanussehi ca anubaddho niddhamanena nikkhamitvā vegena susānaṃ pavisitvā tāpasassa paṇṇasāladvāre bhaṇḍikaṃ chaṭṭetvā palāyi[M 4.0029]. Manussā bhaṇḍikaṃ disvā “are duṭṭhajaṭila, tvaṃ rattiṃ corikaṃ katvā [P 4.0029] divā tāpasarūpena carasī”ti tajjetvā pothetvā taṃ ādāya netvā rañño dassayiṃsu. Rājā anupaparikkhitvāva “gacchatha, naṃ sūle uttāsethā”ti āha. Te taṃ susānaṃ netvā khadirasūlaṃ āropayiṃsu, tāpasassa sarīre sūlaṃ na pavisati. Tato nimbasūlaṃ āhariṃsu, tampi na pavisati. Ayasūlaṃ āhariṃsu, tampi na pavisati. Tāpaso “kiṃ nu kho me pubbakamma”nti olokesi, athassa jātissarañāṇaṃ uppajji, tena pubbakammaṃ oloketvā addasa. Kiṃ panassa pubbakammanti? Koviḷārasūle makkhikāvedhanaṃ. So kira purimabhave vaḍḍhakiputto hutvā pitu rukkhatacchanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ekaṃ makkhikaṃ gahetvā koviḷārasalākāya sūle viya vijjhi. Tamenaṃ pāpakammaṃ imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā gaṇhi. So “na sakkā ito pāpā mayā muccitu”nti ñatvā rājapurise āha “sace maṃ sūle uttāsetukāmattha, koviḷārasūlaṃ āharathā”ti. Te tathā katvā taṃ sūle uttāsetvā ārakkhaṃ datvā pakkamiṃsu.

Then one day, a thief, having committed a robbery inside the city and taken valuable goods, was leaving. Realizing he was a thief, the awakened householders and guards pursued him. Exiting through a drainage pipe, he quickly entered the cemetery and, throwing the bundle of goods at the door of the ascetic’s leaf hut, he fled. The people, seeing the bundle, threatened and beat the ascetic, saying, "You wicked, matted-hair ascetic! You commit theft by night and wander in the guise of an ascetic by day!" They took him and presented him to the king. Without investigation, the king said, "Go, impale him on a stake." They took him to the cemetery and tried to impale him on a khadira stake, but the stake did not pierce the ascetic’s body. Then they brought a neem stake, but that too did not pierce him. They brought an iron stake, and that also did not pierce him. The ascetic reflected, "What past kamma of mine could this be?" Then the knowledge of his past lives arose, and through it, he looked back and saw his past kamma. And what was his past kamma? It was the piercing of a fly on a koviḷāra splinter. It seems that in a past life, he had been the son of a carpenter. Going to his father’s woodworking area, he had caught a fly and pierced it on a koviḷāra splinter as if on a stake. That evil kamma, having reached this state, now took hold of him. Realizing, "It is not possible for me to be freed from this evil kamma," he told the king’s men, "If you wish to impale me, bring a koviḷāra stake." They did so, impaled him on the stake, set a guard, and departed.

Ārakkhakā paṭicchannā hutvā tassa santikaṃ āgacchante olokenti. Tadā dīpāyano “ciradiṭṭho me sahāyo”ti maṇḍabyassa santikaṃ āgacchanto “sūle uttāsito”ti taṃ divasaññeva antarāmagge sutvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “kiṃ samma kārakosī”ti pucchitvā “akārakomhī”ti vutte “attano manopadosaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkhi, nāsakkhī”ti pucchi. “Samma, yehi ahaṃ gahito, neva tesaṃ, na rañño upari mayhaṃ manopadoso atthī”ti. “Evaṃ sante tādisassa sīlavato chāyā mayhaṃ sukhā”ti vatvā dīpāyano sūlaṃ nissāya nisīdi. Athassa sarīre maṇḍabyassa sarīrato lohitabindūni patiṃsu. Tāni suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīre patitapatitāni sussitvā kāḷakāni uppajjiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāyeva so kaṇhadīpāyano nāma ahosi. So sabbarattiṃ tattheva nisīdi.

The guards, remaining hidden, watched those who approached him. At that time, the ascetic Dīpāyana, thinking, "I have not seen my friend Maṇḍabya for a long time," was approaching Maṇḍabya. Having heard on the road that very day that he had been impaled, he went to the place where he was impaled and, standing to one side, asked, "Friend Maṇḍabya, are you at fault?" When he replied, "I am not at fault," Dīpāyana asked, "Are you able to prevent ill-will in your heart, or are you not?" "Friend, I have no ill-will toward those who seized me, nor toward the king," he replied. "Since you are without anger, the shadow of a virtuous one like you is a cause of happiness for me," said Dīpāyana, and sat down leaning against the stake. Then drops of blood fell from Maṇḍabya’s body onto Dīpāyana’s body. Wherever they fell on his golden-hued body, the drops of blood dried and turned into black spots. From the time those black spots appeared on his body, he became known as Kaṇhadīpāyana (Black Dīpāyana). He sat there at that stake throughout all three watches of the night.

Punadivase ārakkhapurisā āgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “anisāmetvāva me kata”nti vegena tattha gantvā [P 4.0030] “pabbajita, kasmā sūlaṃ nissāya nisinnosī”ti dīpāyanaṃ pucchi. Mahārāja, imaṃ tāpasaṃ rakkhanto nisinnomhi. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ mahārāja, imassa kārakabhāvaṃ vā akārakabhāvaṃ vā ñatvā evaṃ kāresīti? So kammassa asodhitabhāvaṃ ācikkhi. Athassa [M 4.0030] so “mahārāja, raññā nāma nisammakārinā bhavitabbaṃ[V 4.0028], alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhū”tiādīni vatvā dhammaṃ desesi. Rājā maṇḍabyassa niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sūlaṃ harathā”ti āṇāpesi. Sūlaṃ harantā harituṃ na sakkhiṃsu. Maṇḍabyo āha – “mahārāja, ahaṃ pubbe katakammadosena evarūpaṃ bhayaṃ sampatto, mama sarīrato sūlaṃ harituṃ na sakkā, sace mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dātukāmo, kakacaṃ āharāpetvā imaṃ sūlaṃ cammasamaṃ chindāpehī”ti. Rājā tathā kāresi. Antosarīre sūlo antoyeva ahosi. Tadā kira so sukhumaṃ koviḷārasalākaṃ gahetvā makkhikāya vaccamaggaṃ pavesesi, taṃ tassa antosarīreyeva ahosi. So tena kāraṇena amaritvā attano āyukkhayeneva mari, tasmā ayampi na mato. Rājā tāpase vanditvā khamāpetvā ubhopi uyyāne vasāpento paṭijaggi, tato paṭṭhāya maṇḍabyo āṇimaṇḍabyo nāma jāto. So rājānaṃ upanissāya tattheva vasi, dīpāyano pana tassa vaṇaṃ phāsukaṃ katvā attano gihisahāyamaṇḍabyassa santikameva gato.

At dawn, the guards came and reported the matter to the king. The king, thinking, "I have acted without investigation," quickly went there and asked Dīpāyana, "Ascetic, why are you sitting leaning on the stake?" "Great king, I am guarding this ascetic," he replied. "Do you guard him because you know whether he is guilty or innocent?" the king asked. Dīpāyana, having investigated the matter and heard of his innocence, then spoke to the king, "Great king, a ruler of the land should act only after careful consideration; a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures is not good if he is lazy," and so forth, teaching him the Tenfold Virtue of Kings. The king, realizing Maṇḍabya was innocent, ordered, "Remove the stake." When they tried to remove it, Maṇḍabya said, "They will not be able to remove it. Great king, I have encountered such danger because of the fault of past kamma. The stake cannot be pulled from my body. If you wish to grant me life, have a saw brought and saw the stake off level with the skin." The king did as the ascetic requested. The stake remained inside his body. (It is said that when he was the carpenter's son, he took a fine koviḷāra splinter and inserted it into a fly's anus. That splinter remained inside the fly’s body. Because of that, the fly did not die, but died only when its lifespan was exhausted. Therefore, this ascetic also did not die; this was his past evil kamma.) The King of Benares paid homage to the ascetics, asked for forgiveness, and provided for them while they stayed in the royal park. From the time the stake was cut level with the flesh, Maṇḍabya became known as Āṇimaṇḍabya (Maṇḍabya with the Pin). He lived in that park supported by the King of Benares. As for the ascetic Kaṇhadīpāyana, after he had eased the pain from Āṇimaṇḍabya's wound, he went to the house of his friend Maṇḍabya the householder, whom he had known in his lay life.

Taṃ paṇṇasālaṃ pavisantaṃ disvā eko puriso sahāyassa ārocesi. So sutvāva tuṭṭhacitto saputtadāro bahū gandhamālatelaphāṇitādīni ādāya taṃ paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā dīpāyanaṃ vanditvā pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā pānakaṃ pāyetvā āṇimaṇḍabyassa pavattiṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Athassa putto yaññadattakumāro nāma caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ geṇḍukena kīḷi, tatra cekasmiṃ vammike āsīviso vasati. Kumārassa bhūmiyaṃ pahaṭageṇḍuko gantvā vammikabile āsīvisassa matthake pati. So ajānanto bile hatthaṃ pavesesi. Atha naṃ kuddho āsīviso hatthe ḍaṃsi. So visavegena mucchito tattheva pati. Athassa mātāpitaro [P 4.0031] sappena ḍaṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā kumārakaṃ ukkhipitvā tāpasassa santikaṃ ānetvā pādamūle nipajjāpetvā “bhante, pabbajitā nāma osadhaṃ vā parittaṃ vā jānanti, puttakaṃ no ārogaṃ karothā”ti āhaṃsu. Ahaṃ osadhaṃ na jānāmi, nāhaṃ vejjakammaṃ karissāmīti. “Tena hi bhante, imasmiṃ kumārake mettaṃ katvā saccakiriyaṃ karothā”ti [M 4.0031] vutte tāpaso “sādhu, saccakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā yaññadattassa sīse hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing him enter the leaf hut, a man informed his friend, the householder Maṇḍabya. Hearing this, the delighted man, along with his wife and son, took many perfumes, garlands, oils, molasses, and other items, went to the leaf hut, paid respects to Dīpāyana, washed his feet, anointed them with oil, offered him a drink, and sat down to listen to the news of Āṇimaṇḍabya. Meanwhile, his son, a youth named Yaññadatta, was playing with a ball at the end of the walking path. There, in an anthill, lived a venomous snake. The youth's ball, having been struck on the ground, went and fell on the head of the venomous snake in the anthill's hole. Not knowing, he put his hand into the hole. Then the enraged venomous snake bit his hand. Overcome by the force of the venom, he fell right there. Then his mother and father, knowing he had been bitten by a snake, lifted the youth, brought him to the ascetic, and laid him at his feet, saying, “Venerable sir, renunciants are known to know medicine or protective chants. Please make our son well.” “I do not know medicine, nor will I perform medical treatment,” said the ascetic. “Then, venerable sir, having compassion for this youth, please perform an act of truth,” they said. The ascetic, saying, “Good, I will perform an act of truth,” placed his hand on Yaññadatta’s head and spoke the first verse:

62.

62.

“Sattāhamevāhaṃ pasannacitto, puññatthiko ācariṃ brahmacariyaṃ;

Athāparaṃ yaṃ caritaṃ mamedaṃ, vassāni paññāsa samādhikāni;

Akāmakovāpi ahaṃ carāmi, etena saccena suvatthi hotu;

Hataṃ visaṃ jīvatu yaññadatto”ti.

“For only seven days, with a serene mind, seeking merit, I practiced the holy life. Thereafter, this practice of mine has been for fifty years and more; though unwillingly I practice. By this truth, may there be well-being! May the poison be overcome! May Yaññadatta live!”

Tattha [V 4.0029] athāparaṃ yaṃ caritanti tasmā sattāhā uttari yaṃ mama brahmacariyaṃ. Akāmakovāpīti pabbajjaṃ anicchantoyeva. Etena saccena suvatthi hotūti sace atirekapaṇṇāsavassāni anabhirativāsaṃ vasantena mayā kassaci anārocitabhāvo saccaṃ, etena saccena yaññadattakumārassa sotthibhāvo hotu, jīvitaṃ paṭilabhatūti.

Therein, ‘athāparaṃ yaṃ caritaṃ’ means ‘that holy life of mine which is beyond those seven days.’ ‘Akāmakovāpi’ means ‘not desiring the going forth at all.’ ‘Etena saccena suvatthi hotu’ means: ‘If it is true that for more than fifty years, while dwelling without delight, I have not told this to anyone, by this truth may there be well-being for the youth Yaññadatta, may he regain his life.’”

Athassa saha saccakiriyāya yaññadattassa thanappadesato uddhaṃ visaṃ bhassitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Kumāro akkhīni ummīletvā mātāpitaro oloketvā “ammatātā”ti vatvā parivattitvā nipajji. Athassa pitaraṃ kaṇhadīpāyano āha – “mayā tāva mama balaṃ kataṃ, tvampi attano balaṃ karohī”ti. So “ahampi saccakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti puttassa ure hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, together with this act of truth, the poison in Yaññadatta above the region of his breast fell and entered the earth. The youth opened his eyes, looked at his mother and father, said, “Mother, father,” and turned over and lay down. Then Kaṇhadīpāyana said to his father, “For my part, I have done what I can. You too do what you can.” He said, “I too will perform an act of truth,” and placing his hand on his son’s chest, he spoke the second verse:

63.

63.

“Yasmā dānaṃ nābhinandiṃ kadāci, disvānahaṃ atithiṃ vāsakāle;

Na [P 4.0032] cāpi me appiyataṃ aveduṃ, bahussutā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca;

Akāmakovāpi ahaṃ dadāmi, etena saccena suvatthi hotu;

Hataṃ visaṃ jīvatu yaññadatto”ti.

“Because I never once rejoiced in giving, having seen a guest at my dwelling time; and yet the learned ascetics and brahmins never knew my displeasure; though unwillingly I give. By this truth, may there be well-being! May the poison be overcome! May Yaññadatta live!”

Tattha vāsakāleti vasanatthāya gehaṃ āgatakāle. Na cāpi me appiyataṃ avedunti bahussutāpi samaṇabrāhmaṇā “ayaṃ neva dānaṃ abhinandati [M 4.0032] na amhe”ti imaṃ mama appiyabhāvaṃ neva jāniṃsu. Ahañhi te piyacakkhūhiyeva olokemīti dīpeti. Etena saccenāti sace ahaṃ dānaṃ dadamāno vipākaṃ asaddahitvā attano anicchāya dammi, anicchanabhāvaṃ mama pare na jānanti, etena saccena suvatthi hotūti attho.

Here, ‘vāsakāle’ means ‘at the time of coming to the house for lodging.’ ‘Na cāpi me appiyataṃ aveduṃ’ means that even the learned ascetics and brahmins did not know this displeasure of mine, thinking, ‘This person neither rejoices in giving nor in us.’ It is explained: ‘For I look upon them only with affectionate eyes.’ ‘Etena saccena’ means: ‘If I, when giving a gift, do so with my own unwillingness, not having faith in the result, and others do not know of my unwillingness, by this truth may there be well-being’—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ tassa saccakiriyāya saha kaṭito uddhaṃ visaṃ bhassitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Kumāro uṭṭhāya nisīdi, ṭhātuṃ pana na sakkoti. Athassa pitā mātaraṃ āha “bhadde, mayā attano balaṃ kataṃ, tvaṃ idāni saccakiriyaṃ katvā puttassa uṭṭhāya gamanabhāvaṃ karohī”ti. “Sāmi, atthi mayhaṃ ekaṃ saccaṃ, tava pana santike kathetuṃ na sakkomī”ti. “Bhadde, yathā tathā me puttaṃ arogaṃ karohī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā saccaṃ karontī tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, together with his act of truth, the poison above his waist fell and entered the earth. The youth got up and sat, but he could not stand. Then his father said to his mother, “My dear, I have done what I can. Now you perform an act of truth and make it so our son can get up and walk.” “Husband, I have one truth, but I cannot speak of it in your presence,” she said. “My dear, whatever it takes, make our son well.” She, having agreed, saying “Good,” performed her act of truth and spoke the third verse:

64.

64.

“Āsīviso [V 4.0030] tāta pahūtatejo, yo taṃ aḍaṃsī bilarā udicca;

Tasmiñca me appiyatāya ajja, pitarañca te natthi koci viseso;

Etena saccena suvatthi hotu, hataṃ visaṃ jīvatu yaññadatto”ti.

“My son, that venomous snake of great power, which bit you emerging from its hole—for me, in my dislike, there is no difference today between it and your father. By this truth, may there be well-being! May the poison be overcome! May Yaññadatta live!”

Tattha tātāti puttaṃ ālapati. Pahūtatejoti balavaviso. Bilarāti vivarā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Udiccāti uṭṭhahitvā, vammikabilato uṭṭhāyāti attho. Pitarañca teti pitari ca te. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ayameva pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “tāta, yaññadatta tasmiñca āsīvise tava pitari [P 4.0033] ca appiyabhāvena mayhaṃ koci viseso natthi. Tañca pana appiyabhāvaṃ ṭhapetvā ajja mayā koci jānāpitapubbo nāma natthi, sace etaṃ saccaṃ, etena saccena tava sotthi hotū”ti.

Here, ‘tāta’ is an address to the son. ‘Pahūtatejo’ means ‘of potent venom.’ ‘Bilarā’ means ‘from the hole’; or this is the reading itself. ‘Udicca’ means ‘having arisen’; the meaning is ‘having arisen from the anthill hole.’ ‘Pitarañca te’ means ‘and in your father.’ In the commentary, however, this is the reading. This is what was said: “My son, Yaññadatta, for me, in my dislike, there is no difference between that venomous snake and your father. And moreover, I have never before made this dislike known to anyone. If this is true, by this truth may you be well.”

Saha ca saccakiriyāya sabbaṃ visaṃ bhassitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Yaññadatto nibbisena sarīrena uṭṭhāya kīḷituṃ āraddho. Evaṃ putte uṭṭhite maṇḍabyo dīpāyanassa ajjhāsayaṃ pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

As soon as she made the act of truth, all the poison fell down and entered the earth. Yaññadatta rose with a body free of poison and began to play. When his son had thus risen, Maṇḍabya, inquiring about Dīpāyana’s intention, spoke the fourth verse:

65.

65.

“Santā [M 4.0033] dantāyeva paribbajanti, aññatra kaṇhā natthākāmarūpā;

Dīpāyana kissa jigucchamāno, akāmako carasi brahmacariya”nti.

“Peaceful and tamed, they go forth; apart from Kaṇha, there are none who are of an unwilling nature. Dīpāyana, disgusted with what, do you live the holy life unwillingly?”

Tassattho – ye keci khattiyādayo kāme pahāya idha loke pabbajanti, te aññatra kaṇhā bhavantaṃ kaṇhaṃ ṭhapetvā aññe akāmarūpā nāma natthi, sabbe jhānabhāvanāya kilesānaṃ samitattā santā, cakkhādīni dvārāni yathā nibbisevanāni honti, tathā tesaṃ damitattā dantā hutvā abhiratāva brahmacariyaṃ caranti, tvaṃ pana bhante dīpāyana, kiṃkāraṇā tapaṃ jigucchamāno akāmako hutvā brahmacariyaṃ carasi, kasmā puna na agārameva ajjhāvasasīti.

The meaning is this: All those who, having given up sensual pleasures, go forth in this world—whether khattiyas or others—with the exception of Kaṇha, setting aside the venerable Kaṇha, there are no others who are discontented. All are peaceful because they have calmed the defilements through the development of meditation. Their sense faculties, such as the eye, are not indulged, and thus, because they are restrained, they become tamed and live the holy life with delight. But you, venerable Dīpāyana, for what reason do you loathe the state of an ascetic and live the holy life unwillingly? Why do you not just dwell at home?

Athassa so kāraṇaṃ kathento pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining the reason to him, he spoke the fifth verse:

66.

66.

“Saddhāya nikkhamma punaṃ nivatto, so eḷamūgova bālo vatāyaṃ;

Etassa vādassa jigucchamāno, akāmako carāmi brahmacariyaṃ;

Viññuppasatthañca satañca ṭhānaṃ, evampahaṃ puññakaro bhavāmī”ti.

“Having gone forth out of faith, he returns again—that fool is like a mute sheep. Disgusted with this saying, I live the holy life unwillingly. This is praised by the wise, a state of the good; thus I will be a doer of merit.”

Tassattho [V 4.0031] – kaṇho kammañca phalañca saddahitvā tāva mahantaṃ vibhavaṃ pahāya agārā nikkhamitvā yaṃ jahi, puna tadatthameva nivatto. So ayaṃ eḷamūgo gāmadārako viya bālo vatāti imaṃ vādaṃ jigucchamāno ahaṃ attano hirottappabhedabhayena anicchamānopi brahmacariyaṃ carāmi. Kiñca bhiyyo pabbajjāpuññañca nāmetaṃ viññūhi buddhādīhi pasatthaṃ, tesaṃyeva ca sataṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ imināpi kāraṇena ahaṃ puññakaro bhavāmi, assumukhopi rudamāno brahmacariyaṃ carāmiyevāti.

The meaning is this: Kaṇha, having had faith in action and its result, abandoned such great wealth and went forth from home, yet he has returned again to that very thing he abandoned. ‘This fool is like a mute village boy!’ Loathing this saying, I live the holy life unwillingly, out of fear for my own sense of shame and moral dread. Moreover, this merit of going forth is praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas, and is the dwelling place of those very good ones. Thus, for this reason too, I become a doer of merit—even weeping with a tearful face, I still live the holy life.

Evaṃ [P 4.0034] so attano ajjhāsayaṃ kathetvā puna maṇḍabyaṃ pucchanto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus declared his intention, he then questioned Maṇḍabya again, speaking the sixth verse:

67.

67.

“Samaṇe [M 4.0034] tuvaṃ brāhmaṇe addhike ca, santappayāsi annapānena bhikkhaṃ;

Opānabhūtaṃva gharaṃ tava yidaṃ, annena pānena upetarūpaṃ;

Atha kissa vādassa jigucchamāno, akāmako dānamimaṃ dadāsī”ti.

“You gratify ascetics, brahmins, and travelers with alms of food and drink. Your house is like a public well, well-provided with food and drink. Then, disgusted with what saying, do you give this gift unwillingly?”

Tattha bhikkhanti bhikkhāya carantānaṃ bhikkhañca sampādetvā dadāsi. Opānabhūtaṃvāti catumahāpathe khatasādhāraṇapokkharaṇī viya.

Here, ‘bhikkhaṃ’ means you provide and give alms to those who wander for alms. ‘Opānabhūtaṃva’ means like a common pond dug at a great crossroads.

Tato maṇḍabyo attano ajjhāsayaṃ kathento sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Maṇḍabya, explaining his disposition, spoke the seventh verse:

68.

68.

“Pitaro ca me āsuṃ pitāmahā ca, saddhā ahuṃ dānapatī vadaññū;

Taṃ kullavattaṃ anuvattamāno, māhaṃ kule antimagandhano ahuṃ;

Etassa vādassa jigucchamāno, akāmako dānamimaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“My fathers and grandfathers were faithful, generous givers, munificent. Following that family custom, may I not become the final disgrace of the family. Disgusted with this saying, I give this gift unwillingly.”

Tattha “āsu”nti padassa “saddhā”ti iminā sambandho, saddhā ahesunti attho. Ahunti saddhā hutvā tato uttari dānajeṭṭhakā ceva “detha karothā”ti vuttavacanassa atthajānanakā ca ahesuṃ. Taṃ kullavattanti taṃ kulavattaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ayameva pāṭho. Māhaṃ kule antimagandhano ahunti “ahaṃ attano kule sabbapacchimako ceva kulapalāpo ca mā ahu”nti sallakkhetvā etaṃ “kulaantimo kulapalāpo”ti vādaṃ jigucchamāno dānaṃ anicchantopi idaṃ dānaṃ dadāmīti dīpeti.

Here, the word ‘āsuṃ’ is connected with ‘saddhā,’ meaning ‘they were faithful.’ Having become faithful, they were, moreover, foremost in generosity and understood the meaning of the words, “Give, do.” ‘Taṃ kullavattaṃ’ means ‘that family custom’; however, in the commentary, this is the reading. ‘Māhaṃ kule antimagandhano ahuṃ’ means, reflecting, “May I not be the very last in my family, nor the family's ruin.” And detesting the saying, “the last of the family, the family’s ruin,” even though unwilling to give, he declares, “I give this gift.”

Evañca pana vatvā maṇḍabyo attano bhariyaṃ pucchamāno aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, Maṇḍabya, questioning his wife, spoke the eighth verse:

69.

69.

“Dahariṃ [V 4.0032][P 4.0035][M 4.0035] kumāriṃ asamatthapaññaṃ, yaṃ tānayiṃ ñātikulā sugatte;

Na cāpi me appiyataṃ avedi, aññatra kāmā paricārayantā;

Atha kena vaṇṇena mayā te bhoti, saṃvāsadhammo ahu evarūpo”ti.

“A young maiden, of incapable intelligence, whom I brought from her family, O you of beautiful form—you never showed me any dislike, even while attending on me without desire. Then for what reason, O lady, has our life together become like this?”

Tattha asamatthapaññanti kuṭumbaṃ vicāretuṃ appaṭibalapaññaṃ atitaruṇiññeva samānaṃ. Yaṃ tānayinti yaṃ taṃ ānayiṃ, ahaṃ daharimeva samānaṃ taṃ ñātikulato ānesinti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññatra kāmā paricārayantāti ettakaṃ kālaṃ vinā kāmena anicchāya maṃ paricārayantāpi attano appiyataṃ maṃ na jānāpesi, sampiyāyamānarūpāva paricari. Kena vaṇṇenāti kena kāraṇena. Bhotīti taṃ ālapati. Evarūpoti āsīvisasamānapaṭikūlabhāvena mayā saddhiṃ tava saṃvāsadhammo evarūpo piyasaṃvāso viya kathaṃ jātoti.

Here, ‘asamatthapaññaṃ’ means having intelligence incapable of managing the household, being very young. ‘Yaṃ tānayiṃ’ means ‘whom I brought’; it is said that I brought her while she was very young from her relatives’ family. ‘Aññatra kāmā paricārayantā’ means for so long, even while serving me without desire, unwillingly, she did not reveal her dislike to me, but served as if showing affection. ‘Kena vaṇṇena’ means for what reason. ‘Bhoti’ is addressing her. ‘Evarūpo’ means how did your life together with me, which is repulsive like a viper, become like this, as if a pleasant life together?

Athassa sā kathentī navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then she, speaking to him, uttered this ninth verse:

70.

70.

“Ārā dūre nayidha kadāci atthi, paramparā nāma kule imasmiṃ;

Taṃ kullavattaṃ anuvattamānā, māhaṃ kule antimagandhinī ahuṃ;

Etassa vādassa jigucchamānā, akāmikā paddhacarāmhi tuyha”nti.

“Far from this, there has never been in our family a succession of husbands. Following that family custom, may I not be the last one of ill repute in the family. Disgusted with that very saying, unwilling, I attend upon you.”

Tattha ārā dūreti aññamaññavevacanaṃ. Atidūreti vā dassentī evamāha. Idhāti nipātamattaṃ, na kadācīti attho. Paramparāti purisaparamparā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sāmi, imasmiṃ amhākaṃ ñātikule dūrato paṭṭhāya yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā purisaparamparā nāma na kadāci atthi, ekitthiyāpi sāmikaṃ chaḍḍetvā añño puriso gahitapubbo nāma natthīti. Taṃ kullavattanti ahampi taṃ kulavattaṃ kulapaveṇiṃ anuvattamānā attano kule pacchimikā palālabhūtā mā ahunti sallakkhetvā etaṃ kulaantimā [M 4.0036] kulagandhinīti vādaṃ jigucchamānā akāmikāpi tuyhaṃ paddhacarāmhi veyyāvaccakārikā pādaparicārikā jātāmhīti.

Here, ‘ārā dūre’ are synonyms. Or, she said this to indicate extreme distance. ‘Idha’ is merely a particle, meaning ‘never at any time.’ ‘Paramparā’ means a succession of men. This is what is meant: ‘Master, in this our family lineage, from distant times up to the seventh generation, there has never been a succession of men—nor has any woman ever taken another man after abandoning her husband.’ Then, reflecting, ‘I too, following this family custom and tradition, should not become the last in my family, a mere husk,’ and despising the saying, ‘the last of the family, the family's disgrace,’ even unwillingly, I have become your attendant, a performer of services, a foot-servant.

Evañca [P 4.0036] pana vatvā “mayā sāmikassa santike abhāsitapubbaṃ guyhaṃ bhāsitaṃ, kujjheyyapi me ayaṃ, amhākaṃ kulūpakatāpasassa sammukheyeva khamāpessāmī”ti cintetvā khamāpentī dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, she thought: “I have spoken a secret to my husband that I had never spoken before. He might be angry with me. I will ask for his forgiveness right in front of the ascetic who has served our family.” Then, seeking forgiveness, she spoke the tenth verse:

71.

71.

“Maṇḍabya [V 4.0033] bhāsiṃ yamabhāsaneyyaṃ, taṃ khamyataṃ puttakahetu majja;

Puttapemā na idha paratthi kiñci, so no ayaṃ jīvati yaññadatto”ti.

“Maṇḍabya, I spoke what should not have been spoken; forgive that today for the sake of the child. There is nothing else here but love for a son, and this our Yaññadatta lives.”

Tattha taṃ khamyatanti taṃ khamayatu. Puttakahetu majjāti taṃ mama bhāsitaṃ ajja imassa puttassa hetu khamayatu. So no ayanti yassa puttassa kāraṇā mayā etaṃ bhāsitaṃ, so no putto jīvati, imassa jīvitalābhabhāvena me khama sāmi, ajjato paṭṭhāya tava vasavattinī bhavissāmīti.

Here, ‘taṃ khamyataṃ’ means ‘let that be forgiven.’ ‘Puttakahetu majja’ means ‘forgive today what I said for the sake of this child.’ ‘So no ayaṃ’ means ‘the child for whose sake I spoke this, our son lives. Because of his recovery of life, forgive me, lord; from today onwards, I shall be under your power.’

Atha naṃ maṇḍabyo “uṭṭhehi bhadde, khamāmi te, ito pana paṭṭhāya mā pharusacittā ahosi, ahampi te appiyaṃ na karissāmī”ti āha. Bodhisatto maṇḍabyaṃ āha – “āvuso, tayā dussaṅgharaṃ dhanaṃ saṅgharitvā kammañca phalañca asaddahitvā dānaṃ dadantena ayuttaṃ kataṃ, ito paṭṭhāya dānaṃ saddahitvā dehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā bodhisattaṃ āha – “bhante, tayā amhākaṃ dakkhiṇeyyabhāve ṭhatvā anabhiratena brahmacariyaṃ carantena ayuttaṃ kataṃ, ito paṭṭhāya idāni yathā tayi katakārā mahapphalā honti, evaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā suddhacitto abhirato hutvā brahmacariyaṃ carāhī”ti. Te mahāsattaṃ vanditvā uṭṭhāya agamaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya bhariyā sāmike sasnehā ahosi, maṇḍabyo pasannacitto saddhāya dānaṃ adāsi. Bodhisatto anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā jhānābhiññaṃ uppādetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Then Maṇḍabya said to her, 'Arise, dear lady, I forgive you. From now on, do not have a harsh mind, and I too will not do anything unpleasant to you.' The Bodhisatta said to Maṇḍabya, 'Friend, having accumulated wealth improperly, and giving gifts without believing in kamma and its fruit, you have acted wrongly. From now on, give gifts with faith.' He replied, 'Very well,' and accepting this, said to the Bodhisatta, 'Venerable sir, by remaining in a state worthy of offerings for us while living the holy life without delight, you have acted wrongly. From now on, so that deeds done towards you may be of great fruit, live the holy life with a gladdened and pure mind, finding delight in it.' They paid homage to the Great Being, rose, and departed. From then on, the wife was affectionate toward her husband, and Maṇḍabya, with a serene mind, gave gifts with faith. The Bodhisatta, having dispelled his discontent and developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, became destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhito bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi[M 4.0037]. Tadā maṇḍabyo ānando ahosi, bhariyā [P 4.0037] visākhā, putto rāhulo, āṇimaṇḍabyo sāriputto, kaṇhadīpāyano pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Maṇḍabya was Ānanda, the wife was Visākhā, the son was Rāhula, Āṇimaṇḍabya was Sāriputta, and Kaṇhadīpāyana was none other than myself.

Kaṇhadīpāyanajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇhadīpāyana Jātaka is the sixth.

[445] 7. Nigrodhajātakavaṇṇanā

[445] 7. The Commentary on the Nigrodha Jātaka

Na vāhametaṃ jānāmīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi bhikkhū tena “āvuso devadatta, satthā tava bahūpakāro, tvañhi satthāraṃ nissāya pabbajjaṃ labhi upasampadaṃ labhi, tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhi, jhānaṃ uppādesi, lābhasakkāropi [V 4.0034] te dasabalasseva santako”ti bhikkhūhi vutte tiṇasalākaṃ ukkhipitvā “ettakampi samaṇena gotamena mayhaṃ kataṃ guṇaṃ na passāmī”ti vutte dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto akataññū mittadubbhī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'I do not know this,'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta. For one day, when the monks said to him, 'Friend Devadatta, the Teacher has done you great favors. It is because of the Teacher that you obtained the going forth, obtained the higher ordination, learned the Three Baskets of the Buddha's word, and aroused meditative states; and the gain and honor you receive is that which belongs to the Ten-Powered One,' Devadatta, lifting a blade of grass, replied, 'I do not see even this much good done to me by the ascetic Gotama.' At this, the monks stirred up talk in the Dhamma hall. The Teacher, arriving, asked, 'What is the subject you are discussing now, monks?' When told, 'This,' he said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Devadatta was ungrateful and a betrayer of friends,' and at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte rājagahe magadhamahārājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā rājagahaseṭṭhi attano puttassa janapadaseṭṭhino dhītaraṃ ānesi, sā vañjhā ahosi. Athassā aparabhāge sakkāro parihāyi. “Amhākaṃ puttassa gehe vañjhitthiyā vasantiyā kathaṃ kulavaṃso vaḍḍhissatī”ti yathā sā suṇāti, evampi kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti. Sā taṃ sutvā “hotu gabbhiniālayaṃ katvā ete vañcessāmī”ti cintetvā attano atthacārikaṃ dhātiṃ āha “amma, gabbhiniyo nāma kiñca kiñca karontī”ti gabbhiniparihāraṃ pucchitvā utunikāle paṭicchādetvā ambilādirucikā hutvā hatthapādānaṃ uddhumāyanakāle hatthapādapiṭṭhiyo koṭṭāpetvā bahalaṃ kāresi, divase divasepi pilotikāveṭhanena ca udaravaḍḍhanaṃ vaḍḍhesi, thanamukhāni kāḷāni kāresi, sarīrakiccaṃ karontīpi aññatra tassā dhātiyā aññesaṃ sammukhaṭṭhāne na karoti. Sāmikopissā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Evaṃ nava māse vasitvā “idāni janapade pitu gharaṃ gantvā vijāyissāmī”ti sasure āpucchitvā rathamāruhitvā mahantena parivārena [P 4.0038] rājagahā nikkhamitvā [M 4.0038] maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tassā pana purato eko sattho gacchati. Satthena vasitvā gataṭṭhānaṃ esā pātarāsakāle pāpuṇāti.

In the past, a great king of Magadha ruled in Rājagaha. At that time, the merchant of Rājagaha brought a daughter of a provincial merchant for his son, but she was barren. Later, her honor declined. 'How will our family lineage grow if a barren woman lives in our son's house?' they would say, spreading such talk in a way that she could hear it. Hearing this, she thought, 'Very well, I will deceive them by making a pretense of pregnancy.' She then asked her personal maid, 'Mother, what do pregnant women do?' After inquiring about the care of a pregnant woman, she concealed her menstrual periods, craved sour and other tastes, and when her hands and feet would swell, she had the backs of her hands and feet pounded to make them appear plump. Day by day, she also increased the size of her belly by wrapping it with cloths. She darkened her nipples and performed her bodily functions only in the presence of that maid, not in front of others. Her husband also provided her with pregnancy care. Having lived thus for nine months, she said, 'Now I will go to my father’s house in the province to give birth.' Taking leave of her in-laws, she mounted a chariot and left Rājagaha with a large retinue, proceeding along the road. Ahead of her, a caravan was traveling. She would reach the place where the caravan had stayed and departed at breakfast time.

Athekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ satthe ekā duggatitthī rattiyā ekasmiṃ nigrodhamūle puttaṃ vijāyitvā pātova satthe gacchante “ahaṃ vinā satthena gantuṃ na sakkhissāmi, sakkā kho pana jīvantiyā puttaṃ labhitu”nti nigrodhamūlajāle jalābuñceva gabbhamalañca attharitvā puttaṃ chaṭṭetvā agamāsi. Dārakassapi devatā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. So hi na yo vā so vā, bodhisattoyeva. So pana tadā tādisaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Itarā pātarāsakāle taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā “sarīrakiccaṃ karissāmī”ti tāya dhātiyā saddhiṃ nigrodhamūlaṃ gatā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ dārakaṃ disvā “amma, nipphannaṃ no kicca”nti pilotikāyo apanetvā ucchaṅgapadesaṃ lohitena ca gabbhamalena ca makkhetvā attano gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ārocesi. Tāvadeva naṃ sāṇiyā parikkhipitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho saparijano rājagahaṃ paṇṇaṃ pesesi. Athassā sassusasurā vijātakālato paṭṭhāya “pitu kule kiṃ karissati, idheva āgacchatū”ti pesayiṃsu. Sā paṭinivattitvā [V 4.0035] rājagahameva pāvisi. Tattha taṃ sampaṭicchitvā dārakassa nāmaṃ karontā nigrodhamūle jātattā “nigrodhakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ divasaññeva anuseṭṭhisuṇisāpi vijāyanatthāya kulagharaṃ gacchantī antarāmagge ekissā rukkhasākhāya heṭṭhā puttaṃ vijāyi, tassa “sākhakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ divasaññeva seṭṭhiṃ nissāya vasantassa tunnakārassa bhariyāpi pilotikantare puttaṃ vijāyi, tassa “pottiko”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu.

Then one day in that caravan, a certain poor woman gave birth to a son at night at the root of a banyan tree. Early in the morning, as the caravan was leaving, she thought, 'I will not be able to go without the caravan. But if I survive, it is possible to have a child.' So she spread out the placenta and the impurities of the womb in the root-network of the banyan tree, abandoned the son, and departed with the caravan. Deities protected the boy. Indeed, he was no ordinary child, but the Bodhisatta himself. Even so, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of such a poor woman in that life. The other woman, reaching that place at breakfast time, went to the root of the banyan tree with her nurse to attend to a bodily need. Seeing the golden-hued boy, she said, 'Mother, our task is accomplished!' Removing her soiled clothes, she smeared her lap area with blood and the impurities of the womb and announced her own delivery. Immediately, having screened her with a curtain, she, overjoyed and together with her attendants, sent word to Rājagaha. Then her mother-in-law and father-in-law sent word, saying, 'Since the child is born, what will she do at her parents' house? Let her come right here to Rājagaha.' She returned and entered Rājagaha. There, welcoming the child, they named him; because he was born at the root of a banyan tree, they called him 'Nigrodhakumāra.' On that same day, the daughter-in-law of a junior treasurer, while going to her parents' house to give birth, delivered a son under a tree branch along the way. They named him 'Sākhakumāra.' Also on that same day, the wife of a tailor who lived in dependence on the treasurer gave birth to a son among some soiled cloths. They named him 'Pottika.'

Mahāseṭṭhi ubhopi te dārake “nigrodhakumārassa jātadivasaññeva jātā”ti āṇāpetvā teneva saddhiṃ saṃvaḍḍhesi. Te ekato vaḍḍhitvā vayappattā takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhiṃsu. Ubhopi seṭṭhiputtā ācariyassa dve sahassāni adaṃsu. Nigrodhakumāro [P 4.0039] pottikassa attano santike sippaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Te nipphannasippā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā nikkhantā “janapadacārikaṃ carissāmā”ti anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle nipajjiṃsu. Tadā bārāṇasirañño kālakatassa sattamo divaso, “sve phussarathaṃ yojessāmā”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Tesupi sahāyesu rukkhamūle nipajjitvā niddāyantesu pottiko [M 4.0039] paccūsakāle uṭṭhāya nigrodhakumārassa pāde parimajjanto nisīdi. Tasmiṃ rukkhe vutthakukkuṭesu uparikukkuṭo heṭṭhākukkuṭassa sarīre vaccaṃ pātesi. Atha naṃ so “kenetaṃ pātita”nti āha. “Samma, mā kujjhi, mayā ajānantena pātita”nti āha. “Are, tvaṃ mama sarīraṃ attano vaccaṭṭhānaṃ maññasi, kiṃ mama pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī”ti. Atha naṃ itaro “are tvaṃ ‘ajānantena me kata’nti vuttepi kujjhasiyeva, kiṃ pana te pamāṇa”nti āha. “Yo maṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ khādati, so pātova sahassaṃ labhati, tasmā ahaṃ mānaṃ karomī”ti. Atha naṃ itaro “are ettakamattena tvaṃ mānaṃ karosi, maṃ pana māretvā yo thūlamaṃsaṃ khādati, so pātova rājā hoti, yo majjhimamaṃsaṃ khādati, so senāpati, yo aṭṭhinissitaṃ khādati, so bhaṇḍāgāriko hotī”ti āha.

The High Treasurer, having ordered that both those boys were born on the very day of Nigrodhakumāra’s birth, raised them together with him. Growing up together, when they came of age, they went to Takkasilā and learned the arts. Both sons of the merchants gave two thousand pieces to the teacher. Nigrodhakumāra had Pottika learn the art in his presence. Having mastered their arts, they took leave of the teacher and set out, saying, 'We will wander through the countryside.' Gradually reaching Bārāṇasī, they lay down under a tree. At that time, it was the seventh day since the King of Bārāṇasī had died, and they had a drum beaten in the city, announcing, 'Tomorrow we will send out the Pusya-chariot.' While those companions lay asleep under the tree, Pottika rose at dawn and sat massaging Nigrodhakumāra’s feet. Among the roosters living in that tree, the one above dropped its excrement on the body of the one below. Then the other said, 'Who dropped this?' The upper one said, 'Friend, do not be angry; I dropped it unknowingly.' The lower one said, 'Hey, do you think my body is a place for your excrement? Do you not know my worth?' Then the other said, 'Hey, even when I say "it was done by me unknowingly," you still get angry; what then is your worth?' The lower rooster said, 'Whoever kills me and eats my flesh will gain a thousand pieces in the morning; therefore, I am proud.' Then the other said, 'Hey, you are proud of such a small thing? But whoever kills me and eats my fat flesh will become a king in the morning; whoever eats my middle flesh will become the commander-in-chief; and whoever eats the flesh clinging to my bones will become the treasurer.'

Pottiko tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “kiṃ no sahassena, rajjameva vara”nti saṇikaṃ rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā uparisayitakukkuṭaṃ gahetvā māretvā aṅgāre pacitvā thūlamaṃsaṃ nigrodhassa adāsi, majjhimamaṃsaṃ sākhassa adāsi, aṭṭhimaṃsaṃ attanā khādi. Khāditvā pana “samma nigrodha, tvaṃ ajja rājā bhavissasi, samma sākha, tvaṃ senāpati bhavissasi, ahaṃ pana bhaṇḍāgāriko bhavissāmī”ti vatvā “kathaṃ jānāsī”ti puṭṭho taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Te tayopi janā pātarāsavelāya bārāṇasiṃ pavisitvā ekassa brāhmaṇassa gehe sappisakkarayuttaṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjitvā nagarā nikkhamitvā uyyānaṃ [P 4.0040] pavisiṃsu. Nigrodhakumāro silāpaṭṭe nipajji[V 4.0036], itare dve bahi nipajjiṃsu. Tasmiṃ samaye pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni anto ṭhapetvā phussarathaṃ vissajjesuṃ. Tattha vitthārakathā mahājanakajātake (jā. 2.22.123 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Phussaratho uyyānaṃ gantvā nivattitvā ārohanasajjo hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Purohito “uyyāne puññavatā sattena bhavitabba”nti uyyānaṃ pavisitvā kumāraṃ disvā pādantato sāṭakaṃ apanetvā pādesu lakkhaṇāni upadhāretvā “tiṭṭhatu bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ, sakalajambudīpassa adhipatirājā bhavituṃ yutto”ti sabbatālāvacare paggaṇhāpesi. Nigrodhakumāro pabujjhitvā mukhato sāṭakaṃ apanetvā mahājanaṃ oloketvā parivattitvā nipanno thokaṃ vītināmetvā silāpaṭṭe pallaṅkena nisīdi. Atha [M 4.0040] naṃ purohito jaṇṇunā patiṭṭhāya “rajjaṃ te deva pāpuṇātī”ti vatvā “‘sādhū”ti vutte tattheva ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisiñci. So rajjaṃ patvā sākhassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ datvā mahantena sakkārena nagaraṃ pāvisi, pottikopi tehi saddhiññeva agamāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya mahāsatto bārāṇasiyaṃ dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi.

Hearing the conversation of those two roosters, Pottika thought, 'What use to us is a thousand pieces of money? Only kingship is best.' Gently climbing the tree, he caught the rooster sleeping above, killed it, and cooked it on the coals. He gave the fatty meat to Nigrodha, the meat of the middle part to Sākha, and ate the meat adhering to the bones himself. After eating, he said, 'Friend Nigrodha, today you will become king; friend Sākha, you will become the commander-in-chief; and I will become the treasurer.' When asked how he knew, he related the matter. At the time of the morning meal, the three of them entered Bārāṇasī, ate rice porridge mixed with ghee and sugar in a brahmin’s house, left the city, and entered the royal park. The young Nigrodha lay down on a stone slab, while the other two lay down outside. At that time, the five royal insignia were placed in the chariot and the Phussa chariot was sent out. The detailed account of the Phussa chariot being sent out will become clear in the Mahājanaka Jātaka. The Phussa chariot went to the park, turned back, and stood ready to be mounted according to the ceremony. The purohita, thinking, 'There must be a meritorious being in the park,' entered the park and saw the young man. Removing the cloth from the end of his feet and examining the marks on his feet, he declared, 'Let alone the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, he is fit to be the sovereign king of all Jambudīpa.' He then had all kinds of music played. The young Nigrodha awoke, removed the cloth from his face, looked at the crowd, turned over, and after a short while, sat cross-legged on the stone slab. Then the purohita, kneeling down, announced, 'The kingdom comes to you, Your Majesty.' When he replied, 'Good,' they placed him on a heap of jewels right there on the stone slab and consecrated him. Having attained the kingdom, he gave the position of commander-in-chief to Sākha and entered the city of Bārāṇasī with great honor. Pottika also went with them. From then on, the Great Being ruled in Bārāṇasī according to the ten royal virtues.

So ekadivasaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ saritvā sākhaṃ āha – “samma, na sakkā mātāpitūhi vinā vattituṃ, mahantena parivārena gantvā mātāpitaro no ānehī”ti. Sākho “na me tattha gamanakammaṃ atthī”ti paṭikkhipi. Tato pottikaṃ āṇāpesi. So “sādhū”ti tattha gantvā nigrodhassa mātāpitaro “putto vo rajje patiṭṭhito, etha gacchāmā”ti āha. Te “atthi no tāva vibhavamattaṃ, alaṃ tattha gamanenā”ti paṭikkhipiṃsu. Sākhassapi mātāpitaro avoca, tepi na icchiṃsu. Attano mātāpitaro avoca, “mayaṃ tāta tunnakārakammena jīvissāma ala”nti paṭikkhipiṃsu. So tesaṃ manaṃ alabhitvā bārāṇasimeva paccāgantvā “senāpatissa ghare maggakilamathaṃ vinodetvā pacchā nigrodhasahāyaṃ passissāmī”ti cintetvā tassa nivesanadvāraṃ gantvā “sahāyo kira [P 4.0041] te pottiko nāma āgatoti senāpatissa ārocehī”ti dovārikaṃ āha, so tathā akāsi. Sākho pana “ayaṃ mayhaṃ rajjaṃ adatvā sahāyanigrodhassa adāsī”ti tasmiṃ veraṃ bandhi. So taṃ kathaṃ sutvāva kuddho āgantvā “ko imassa sahāyo ummattako dāsiputto, gaṇhatha na”nti vatvā hatthapādajaṇṇukapparehi koṭṭāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpesi.

One day, remembering his parents, the Great Being said to the commander-in-chief, 'Friend, I am unable to live without my parents. Go with a large retinue and bring our parents here.' Sākha refused, saying, 'It is not my duty to go to the place where the parents of the king reside.' Then he commanded Pottika. He said, 'Very well,' went to the parents, and said to Nigrodha's parents, 'Your son has become the king in Bārāṇasī. Come, let us go.' They refused, saying, 'Dear son, we have sufficient wealth; it is not proper to go to our son.' He also spoke to Sākha's parents, but they too did not wish to go. He spoke to his own parents, who refused, saying, 'Dear son, we will live by our tailor's craft; it is not proper to go to our son.' Unable to gain their consent, Pottika returned to Bārāṇasī. Thinking, 'I will relieve my travel fatigue at the commander-in-chief's house and afterwards see my friend Nigrodha,' he went to Sākha's gate and told the gatekeeper, 'Inform the commander-in-chief that your friend named Pottika has arrived.' The gatekeeper did so. But Sākha had conceived a grudge against him, thinking, 'He did not give the kingdom to me, but gave it to my friend Nigrodha.' Upon hearing that Pottika had arrived, Sākha came out in a rage and said, 'Who is this friend of his? He is a madman, the son of a slave! Seize him!' Then he had him beaten with hands, feet, knees, and elbows, and had him seized by the neck and driven out.

So cintesi “sākho mama santikā senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ labhitvā akataññū mittadubbhī, maṃ koṭṭāpetvā nīharāpesi, nigrodho pana paṇḍito kataññū sappuriso, tasseva santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti. So rājadvāraṃ gantvā “deva, pottiko kira nāma te sahāyo dvāre ṭhito”ti [V 4.0037] rañño ārocāpesi. Rājā pakkosāpetvā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā āsanā vuṭṭhāya paccuggantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā massukammādīni kārāpetvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitena paribhuttanānaggarasabhojanena tena saddhiṃ sukhanisinno mātāpitūnaṃ pavattiṃ pucchitvā anāgamanabhāvaṃ suṇi. Sākhopi “pottiko maṃ rañño santike paribhindeyya[M 4.0041], mayi pana gate kiñci vattuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti tattheva agamāsi. Pottiko tassa santikeyeva rājānaṃ āmantetvā “deva, ahaṃ maggakilanto ‘sākhassa gehaṃ gantvā vissamitvā idhāgamissāmī’ti agamiṃ. Atha maṃ sākho ‘nāhaṃ taṃ jānāmī’ti vatvā koṭṭāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpesīti saddaheyyāsi tvaṃ eta”nti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Pottika thought, 'Sākha, having received the position of commander-in-chief from me, is ungrateful and a betrayer of friends; he had a benefactor like me beaten and driven out. But Nigrodha is wise, grateful, and a virtuous man—I will go to him.' He went to the king's gate and had it announced to the king, 'Your Majesty, your friend named Pottika is standing at the gate.' The king had him summoned, and seeing him approaching, rose from his seat, went to meet him, and made a friendly greeting. He had his beard and hair attended to, had him adorned with all ornaments, and after Pottika had eaten a meal of various excellent flavors, the king sat comfortably with him and asked about his parents, and heard that they had not come. Sākha also went to the palace, thinking, 'Pottika might speak to the king to break our friendship, but if I am there, he will not be able to say anything.' In Sākha's very presence, Pottika addressed the king, 'Your Majesty, weary from my journey, I went to Sākha’s house to rest before coming to you. But Sākha said, "I do not know him," had me beaten, and had me seized by the neck and driven out. Your Majesty, please believe this.' Having said this, he spoke these three verses:

72.

72.

“Na vāhametaṃ jānāmi, ko vāyaṃ kassa vāti vā;

Yathā sākho vadi eva, nigrodha kinti maññasi.

'I do not know this man, or who he is, or to whom he belongs'—thus Sākha spoke. O Nigrodha, what do you think of this?

73.

73.

“Tato galavinītena, purisā nīhariṃsu maṃ;

Datvā mukhapahārāni, sākhassa vacanaṃkarā.

Then, led by the neck, men dragged me out, having struck me on the face, doing the bidding of Sākha.

74.

74.

“Etādisaṃ dummatinā, akataññuna dubbhinā;

Kataṃ anariyaṃ sākhena, sakhinā te janādhipā”ti.

Such an ignoble deed was done by your friend Sākha, who is ill-minded, ungrateful, and a betrayer of friends, O lord of men.

Tattha [P 4.0042] kinti maññasīti yathā maṃ sākho acari, kiṃ tvampi evameva maññasi, udāhu aññathā maññasi, maṃ sākho evaṃ vadeyyāti saddahasi, taṃ na saddahasīti adhippāyo. Galavinītenāti galaggāhena. Dubbhināti mittadubbhinā.

In those verses, 'what do you think?' means: 'Just as Sākha treated me, do you also think the same, or do you think otherwise? Do you believe that Sākha would speak to me thus, or do you not believe it?'—this is the intention. 'Led by the neck' (galavinītena) means by seizing the neck. 'Treacherous' (dubbhinā) means a betrayer of friends.

Taṃ sutvā nigrodho catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, King Nigrodha spoke these four verses:

75.

75.

“Na vāhametaṃ jānāmi, napi me koci saṃsati;

Yaṃ me tvaṃ samma akkhāsi, sākhena kāraṇaṃ kataṃ.

"I do not know about this, nor did anyone tell me; that which you have told me, friend, is the harm done by Sākha."

76.

76.

“Sakhīnaṃ sājīvakaro, mama sākhassa cūbhayaṃ;

Tvaṃ nosissariyaṃ dātā, manussesu mahantataṃ;

Tayāmā labbhitā iddhī, ettha me natthi saṃsayo.

"You are the provider of livelihood for friends, for both me and Sākha. You are the giver to us of sovereignty and greatness among humans. By you, this prosperity has been obtained by us; of this I have no doubt."

77.

77.

“Yathāpi [V 4.0038] bījamaggimhi, ḍayhati na virūhati;

Evaṃ kataṃ asappurise, nassati na virūhati.

"Just as a seed in a fire is burnt and does not sprout, so too, a service done for an unworthy person perishes and does not flourish."

78.

78.

“Kataññumhi ca posamhi, sīlavante ariyavuttine;

Sukhette viya bījāni, kataṃ tamhi na nassatī”ti.

"But for a person who is grateful, virtuous, and of noble conduct, a service done for him does not perish, like seeds sown in a fertile field."

Tattha [M 4.0042] saṃsatīti ācikkhati. Kāraṇaṃ katanti ākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanapothanakoṭṭanasaṅkhātaṃ kāraṇaṃ katanti attho. Sakhīnaṃ sājīvakaroti samma, pottika tvaṃ sahāyakānaṃ suājīvakaro jīvikāya uppādetā. Mama sākhassa cūbhayanti mayhañca sākhassa ca ubhinnampi sakhīnanti attho. Tvaṃ nosissariyanti tvaṃ no asi issariyaṃ dātā, tava santikā imā sampattī amhehi laddhā. Mahantatanti mahantabhāvaṃ.

In this context, 'saṃsati' means 'tells'. 'Kāraṇaṃ kataṃ' means 'the harm done', referring to the treatment consisting of dragging, pulling about, beating, and pounding. 'Sakhīnaṃ sājīvakaro' means: friend Pottika, you are the provider of a good livelihood for your companions, the one who secures a living for them. 'Mama sākhassa cūbhayaṃ' means for both myself and Sākha, referring to both friends. 'Tvaṃ nosissariyaṃ' means you are the giver of sovereignty to us; from you, these fortunes were obtained by us. 'Mahantataṃ' means greatness.

Evañca pana vatvā ettakaṃ kathente nigrodhe sākho tattheva aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ rājā “sākha imaṃ pottikaṃ sañjānāsī”ti pucchi. So tuṇhī ahosi. Athassa rājā daṇḍaṃ āṇāpento aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, while Nigrodha was saying this much, Sākha was standing right there. Then the king asked him, "Sākha, do you recognize this Pottika?" He remained silent. Then the king, intending to punish him, spoke the eighth verse:

79.

79.

“Imaṃ jammaṃ nekatikaṃ, asappurisacintakaṃ;

Hanantu sākhaṃ sattīhi, nāssa icchāmi jīvita”nti.

"This wretched and deceitful person, who thinks like an unworthy man—let them strike Sākha with spears; I do not wish for him to live."

Tattha jammanti lāmakaṃ. Nekatikanti vañcakaṃ.

In this context, 'jamma' means base or wretched. 'Nekatika' means deceitful or fraudulent.

Taṃ sutvā pottiko “mā esa bālo maṃ nissāya nassatū”ti cintetvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Pottika thought, "Let not this fool be ruined on account of me," and spoke the ninth verse:

80.

80.

“Khamatassa [P 4.0043] mahārāja, pāṇā na paṭiānayā;

Khama deva asappurisassa, nāssa icchāmahaṃ vadha”nti.

"Forgive him, O great king; life cannot be brought back. Forgive this unworthy man, O Lord; I do not desire his death."

Tattha khamatassāti khamataṃ assa, etassa asappurisassa khamathāti attho. Na paṭiānayāti matassa nāma pāṇā paṭiānetuṃ na sakkā.

In this context, 'khamatassa' means forgive him; the meaning is 'forgive this unworthy man'. 'Na paṭiānayā' means it is not possible to bring back the life of one who is dead.
