Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sākhassa khami, senāpatiṭṭhānampi pottikasseva dātukāmo ahosi[V 4.0039], so pana na icchi. Athassa sabbasenānīnaṃ vicāraṇārahaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikaṭṭhānaṃ nāma adāsi. Pubbe kiretaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ nāhosi, tato paṭṭhāya jātaṃ. Aparabhāge pottiko bhaṇḍāgāriko puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamāno attano puttadhītānaṃ ovādavasena osānagāthamāha –

The king, hearing his words, forgave Sākha. He even wished to give the position of commander-in-chief to Pottika himself, but Pottika did not desire it. Then the king gave him the position of treasurer, which involved the administration of all the army forces. It is said that previously this specific rank did not exist; it was established from that time onward. Later, Pottika the treasurer, flourishing with sons and daughters, spoke the final verse as advice to them:

81.

81.

“Nigrodhameva seveyya, na sākhamupasaṃvase;

Nigrodhasmiṃ mataṃ seyyo, yañce sākhasmi jīvita”nti.

"One should serve only a Nigrodha, and not live with a Sākha. Death with a Nigrodha is better than life with a Sākha."

Satthā [M 4.0043] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, devadatto pubbepi akataññūyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sākho devadatto ahosi, pottiko ānando, nigrodho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, "Thus, bhikkhus, Devadatta was ungrateful even in the past." Then he identified the birth-story: "At that time, Sākha was Devadatta, Pottika was Ānanda, and King Nigrodha was I myself."

Nigrodhajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Nigrodha Jātaka, the seventh.

[446] 8. Takkalajātakavaṇṇanā

[446] 8. The Commentary on the Takkala Jātaka

Na takkalā santi na āluvānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ pituposakaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira daliddakule paccājāto mātari kālakatāya pātova uṭṭhāya dantakaṭṭhamukhodakadānādīni karonto bhatiṃ vā kasiṃ vā katvā laddhavibhavānurūpena yāgubhattādīni sampādetvā pitaraṃ posesi. Atha naṃ pitā āha – “tāta, tvaṃ ekakova anto ca bahi ca kattabbaṃ karosi, ekaṃ te kuladārikaṃ ānessāmi, sā te gehe kattabbaṃ karissatī”ti. “Tāta, itthiyo nāma gharaṃ āgatā neva mayhaṃ, na tumhākaṃ cittasukhaṃ karissanti, mā evarūpaṃ cintayittha, ahaṃ yāvajīvaṃ tumhe posetvā tumhākaṃ [P 4.0044] accayena jānissāmī”ti. Athassa pitā anicchamānasseva ekaṃ kumārikaṃ ānesi. Sā sasurassa ca sāmikassa ca upakārikā ahosi nīcavutti. Sāmikopissā “mama pitu upakārikā”ti tussitvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ manāpaṃ āharitvā deti, sāpi taṃ sasurasseva upanāmesi. Sā aparabhāge cintesi “mayhaṃ sāmiko laddhaṃ laddhaṃ pitu adatvā mayhameva deti, addhā pitari nisneho jāto, imaṃ mahallakaṃ ekenupāyena mama sāmikassa paṭikkūlaṃ katvā gehā nikkaḍḍhāpessāmī”ti.

"There are no tubers, no yams"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower who supported his father. He was born into a poor family, and after his mother passed away, he would rise early in the morning to provide items such as a tooth-stick and water for the mouth. By working for wages or by farming, he would prepare gruel, rice, and so on, according to his means, and thus supported his father. Then his father said to him, "Son, you alone perform all the duties both inside and outside the house. I will bring you a girl from a suitable family; she will do the household work for you." "Father," he replied, "women, having come into the house, will bring no peace of mind either to me or to you. Do not think of such a thing. I will support you as long as you live, and I will see to things after you pass away." But his father, even though the son was unwilling, brought a young girl. She was helpful to both her father-in-law and her husband, and was of humble conduct. Her husband, too, being pleased that "she is helpful to my father," would bring and give her whatever pleasing things he obtained, and she, in turn, would offer them to her father-in-law. Later, she thought: "My husband gives whatever he obtains to me, not to his father. Surely, he has become devoid of affection for his father. By some stratagem, I will make this old man repulsive to my husband and have him driven out of the house."

Sā tato paṭṭhāya udakaṃ atisītaṃ vā accuṇhaṃ vā, āhāraṃ atiloṇaṃ vā aloṇaṃ vā[V 4.0040], bhattaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ vā atikilinnaṃ vāti evamādīni tassa kodhuppattikāraṇāni katvā tasmiṃ kujjhante “ko imaṃ mahallakaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ sakkhissatī”ti pharusāni vatvā kalahaṃ vaḍḍhesi. Tattha tattha kheḷapiṇḍādīni chaḍḍetvāpi sāmikaṃ ujjhāpesi “passa pitu kammaṃ, ‘idañcidañca mā karī’ti vutte kujjhati, imasmiṃ gehe pitaraṃ vā vasāpehi maṃ vā”ti. Atha naṃ so “bhadde, tvaṃ daharā yattha katthaci jīvituṃ sakkhissasi, mayhaṃ [M 4.0044] pitā mahallako, tvaṃ tassa asahantī imamhā gehā nikkhamā”ti āha. Sā bhītā “ito paṭṭhāya evaṃ na karissāmī”ti sasurassa pādesu patitvā khamāpetvā pakatiniyāmeneva paṭijaggituṃ ārabhi. Atha so upāsako purimadivasesu tāya ubbāḷho satthu santikaṃ dhammassavanāya agantvā tassā pakatiyā patiṭṭhitakāle agamāsi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ, upāsaka, sattaṭṭha divasāni dhammassavanāya nāgatosī”ti pucchi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathesi. Satthā “idāni tāva tassā kathaṃ aggahetvā pitaraṃ na nīharāpesi, pubbe pana etissā kathaṃ gahetvā pitaraṃ āmakasusānaṃ netvā āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā tattha naṃ pakkhipitvā māraṇakāle ahaṃ sattavassiko hutvā mātāpitūnaṃ guṇaṃ kathetvā pitughātakakammā nivāresiṃ, tadā tvaṃ mama kathaṃ sutvā tava pitaraṃ yāvajīvaṃ paṭijaggitvā saggaparāyaṇo jāto, svāyaṃ mayā dinno ovādo bhavantaragatampi na vijahati, iminā kāraṇena tassā kathaṃ aggahetvā idāni tayā pitā na nīhaṭo”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

From that time onwards, she prepared water that was either too cold or too hot, food that was either too salty or saltless, and rice that was either undercooked or overcooked. By doing these and other things to provoke his anger, when he became angry, she would say harsh words such as, 'Who can attend to this old man?' and thus escalate the quarrel. By throwing lumps of phlegm and such like here and there, she also made her husband dissatisfied, saying, 'See your father's conduct! When told, "Do not do this or that," he gets angry. In this house, either let your father stay or let me.' Then he said to her, 'Good lady, you are young and can make a living anywhere; my father is old. Since you cannot endure him, leave this house of mine.' Frightened, she said, 'From now on I will not do such things,' and falling at her father-in-law's feet, she begged for forgiveness and began to care for him as before. Then that lay follower, who had been troubled by her in previous days and had not gone to the Teacher's presence to hear the Dhamma, went at the time when she was re-established in her normal conduct. Then the Teacher asked him, 'Lay follower, why have you not come to hear the Dhamma for seven or eight days?' He told him the reason. The Teacher said, 'Now, at least, you did not take her word and drive out your father. But in the past, listening to her words, you took your father to a charnel ground, dug a pit, and after throwing him into it, at the time of killing him, I, being only seven years old, understood the virtues of parents and prevented you from the crime of patricide. Then, listening to my words, you cared for your father with respect for the rest of his life and became one destined for heaven. This advice given by me does not leave you even in another existence. Because of this advice given in a past life, you did not take her word and drive your father out now.' Having said this, being requested by him, he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente aññatarasmiṃ kāsigāme ekassa kulassa ghare ekaputtako ahosi nāmena saviṭṭhako nāma. So mātāpitaro paṭijagganto [P 4.0045] aparabhāge mātari kālakatāya pitaraṃ posesīti sabbaṃ vatthu paccuppannavatthuniyāmeneva kathetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha viseso. Tadā sā itthī “passa pitu kammaṃ, ‘idañcidañca mā karī’ti vutte kujjhatī”ti vatvā “sāmi, pitā te caṇḍo pharuso niccaṃ kalahaṃ karoti, jarājiṇṇo byādhipīḷito na cirasseva marissati, ahañca etena saddhiṃ ekagehe vasituṃ na sakkomi, sayampesa katipāhena marissatiyeva, tvaṃ etaṃ āmakasusānaṃ netvā āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā tattha naṃ pakkhipitvā kuddālena sīsaṃ chinditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā upari paṃsunā chādetvā āgacchāhī”ti āha. So tāya punappunaṃ vuccamāno “bhadde, purisamāraṇaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ māressāmī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ te upāyaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti. “Ācikkha tāvā”ti. “Sāmi, tvaṃ paccūsakāle pitu nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yathā sabbe suṇanti, evaṃ mahāsaddaṃ katvā ‘tāta, asukagāme tumhākaṃ uddhāraṇako [M 4.0045] atthi, mayi gate na deti, tumhākaṃ accayena na dassateva, sve yānake nisīditvā pātova gacchissāmā’ti vatvā tena vuttavelāyameva [V 4.0041] uṭṭhāya yānakaṃ yojetvā tattha nisīdāpetvā āmakasusānaṃ netvā āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā corehi acchinnasaddaṃ katvā māretvā āvāṭe pakkhipitvā sīsaṃ chinditvā nhāyitvā āgacchā”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Varanasi, there was an only son named Saviṭṭhaka in the house of a certain family in a village of Kāsi. This Saviṭṭhaka looked after his parents and, after his mother passed away later on, he supported his father. (The entire story should be told exactly like the present event, but this is the difference in this past story:) At that time, the woman said, 'See your father's conduct! When told, "Do not do this or that," he gets angry again.' She said, 'Lord, your father is fierce and harsh, always creating conflict. He is very old and oppressed by disease; he will die before long. I cannot live in the same house as your father, and he will surely die in a few days anyway. You should take him to the charnel ground, dig a pit, throw him in, strike his head with a spade to break it and end his life, cover him with earth, and return.' Being urged repeatedly by her, he said, 'Good lady, killing a person is a very grave matter. How can I kill my father?' When she said, 'I will tell you a way,' he replied, 'Tell me then.' She said, 'Lord, in the early morning, go to the place where your father sits and, in such a way that everyone can hear, make a loud noise and say, "Father, in such-and-such a village there is a debt belonging to your parents. When I went to ask for it, they did not give it; if you pass away, it will surely be lost. Let us go early tomorrow morning in a small cart." When your father says he will follow, rise, harness the cart, seat him in it, take him to the charnel ground, and after digging a pit, make a sound as if being plundered by robbers. Then kill him, throw him into the pit, break his head, bathe, and only then return.'

Saviṭṭhako “atthesa upāyo”ti tassā vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā yānakaṃ gamanasajjaṃ akāsi. Tassa paneko sattavassiko putto atthi paṇḍito byatto. So mātu vacanaṃ sutvā “mayhaṃ mātā pāpadhammā pitaraṃ me pitughātakammaṃ kāreti, ahaṃ imassa pitughātakammaṃ kātuṃ na dassāmī”ti saṇikaṃ gantvā ayyakena saddhiṃ nipajji. Saviṭṭhakopi itarāya vuttavelāya yānakaṃ yojetvā “ehi, tāta, uddhāraṃ sodhessāmā”ti pitaraṃ yānake nisīdāpesi. Kumāropi paṭhamataraṃ yānakaṃ abhiruhi. Saviṭṭhako taṃ [P 4.0046] nivāretuṃ asakkonto teneva saddhiṃ āmakasusānaṃ gantvā pitarañca kumārakena saddhiṃ ekamante ṭhapetvā sayaṃ otaritvā kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya ekasmiṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne caturassāvāṭaṃ khaṇituṃ ārabhi. Kumārako otaritvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā ajānanto viya kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Saviṭṭhaka, thinking, 'This is a way,' accepted her words and made preparations to go to the charnel ground. Now, he had a seven-year-old son who was wise and discerning. The boy, hearing his mother's words, thought, 'My mother is of evil conduct; she is making my father commit the crime of patricide. I will not allow him to perform this act of killing his father.' He went quietly and lay down with his grandfather. Saviṭṭhaka, at the time told by the other, harnessed the cart and said, 'Come, father, let us settle the debt,' and seated his father in the cart. The young boy also climbed into the cart first. Saviṭṭhaka, being unable to prevent the boy, went to the charnel ground together with him. Placing his father and the boy together in one place, he himself descended from the cart, took a spade and a basket, and in a concealed spot began to dig a four-cornered pit. The boy descended, went to his father Saviṭṭhaka, and as if not knowing, initiated a conversation and spoke the first verse:

82.

82.

“Na takkalā santi na āluvāni, na biḷāliyo na kaḷambāni tāta;

Eko araññamhi susānamajjhe, kimatthiko tāta khaṇāsi kāsu”nti.

'There are no takkalā tubers, no ālu, no biḷāli, and no kaḷamba here, father. Alone in the forest in the middle of the charnel ground, for what purpose, father, are you digging a pit?'

Tattha na takkalā santīti piṇḍālukandā na santi. Āluvānīti āluvakandā. Biḷāliyoti biḷārivallikandā. Kaḷambānīti tālakandā.

Therein, 'na takkalā santi' means there are no piṇḍālu tubers. 'Āluvāni' means ālu tubers. 'Biḷāliyoti' means biḷāri creeper tubers. 'Kaḷambāni' means tāla tubers.

Athassa pitā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his father spoke the second verse:

83.

83.

“Pitāmaho tāta sudubbalo te, anekabyādhīhi dukhena phuṭṭho;

Tamajjahaṃ nikhaṇissāmi sobbhe, na hissa taṃ jīvitaṃ rocayāmī”ti.

'Your grandfather, son, is very weak, afflicted with many diseases and suffering. Today I will bury him in a pit, for I do not approve of that life of his.'

Tattha [M 4.0046] anekabyādhīhīti anekehi byādhīhi uppannena dukkhena phuṭṭho. Na hissa tanti ahañhi tassa tava pitāmahassa taṃ dujjīvitaṃ na icchāmi, “evarūpā jīvitā maraṇamevassa vara”nti maññamāno taṃ sobbhe nikhaṇissāmīti.

Therein, ‘anekabyādhĦhi’ means ‘touched by suffering arising from many illnesses’. ‘Na hissa taᅃ’ means: ‘I indeed do not wish for that miserable life for your grandfather, thinking, ‘Death would indeed be better for him than such a life,’ and so I will bury him in that pit.’

Taṃ sutvā kumāro upaḍḍhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the boy spoke half a verse:

84.

84.

“Saṅkappametaṃ [V 4.0042] paṭiladdha pāpakaṃ, accāhitaṃ kamma karosi ludda”nti.

‘Having conceived this evil resolve, you do a very harmful deed, O cruel one.’

Tassattho – tāta, tvaṃ “pītaraṃ dukkhā pamocessāmī”ti maraṇadukkhena yojento etaṃ pāpakaṃ saṅkappaṃ paṭiladdhā tassa ca saṅkappavasena hitaṃ atikkamma ṭhitattā accāhitaṃ kammaṃ karosi luddanti.

Its meaning is this: ‘Father, thinking, ‘I will free my father from suffering,’ you are linking him to the suffering of death. Having acquired this evil resolve, and because you have transgressed what is beneficial due to the force of that resolve, you are doing a very harmful deed, O cruel one.’

Evañca pana vatvā kumāro pitu hatthato kuddālaṃ gahetvā avidūre aññataraṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ pitā upasaṅkamitvā [P 4.0047] “kasmā, tāta, āvāṭaṃ khaṇasī”ti pucchi. So tassa kathento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the boy took the spade from his father’s hand and began to dig another pit not far away. Then his father approached him and asked, ‘Why, son, are you digging a pit?’ Explaining to him, he spoke the third verse:

“Mayāpi tāta paṭilacchase tuvaṃ, etādisaṃ kamma jarūpanīto;

Taṃ kullavattaṃ anuvattamāno, ahampi taṃ nikhaṇissāmi sobbhe”ti.

‘You too, father, will receive such a deed from me when brought on by old age. Following that family custom, I too will bury you in a pit.’

Tassattho – tāta, ahampi etasmiṃ sobbhe taṃ mahallakakāle nikhaṇissāmi, iti kho tāta, mayāpi kate imasmiṃ sobbhe tuvaṃ jarūpanīto etādisaṃ kammaṃ paṭilacchase, yaṃ etaṃ tayā pavattitaṃ kulavattaṃ, taṃ anuvattamāno vayappatto bhariyāya saddhiṃ vasanto ahampi taṃ nikhaṇissāmi sobbheti.

Its meaning is this: Father, I too will bury you in this pit when you are old. Thus, father, when you are brought on by old age, you will receive such a deed from me in this pit that I have made. Following this family custom that you have started, when I am grown up and living with my wife, I too will bury you in a pit.

Athassa pitā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his father spoke the fourth verse:

85.

85.

“Pharusāhi vācāhi pakubbamāno, āsajja maṃ tvaṃ vadase kumāra;

Putto mamaṃ orasako samāno, ahītānukampī mama tvaṃsi puttā”ti.

‘Overpowering me with harsh words, assailing me, you speak, O boy; though you are my own son, born of my breast, you show no compassion for my well-being, my son.’

Tattha pakubbamānoti abhibhavanto. Āsajjāti ghaṭṭetvā.

Therein, ‘pakubbamāno’ means ‘overpowering’. ‘Āsajja’ means ‘having assailed’.

Evaṃ [M 4.0047] vutte paṇḍitakumārako ekaṃ paṭivacanagāthaṃ, dve udānagāthāti tisso gāthā abhāsi –

When this was said, the wise boy spoke three verses—one verse of reply and two verses of inspired utterance:

86.

86.

“Na tāhaṃ tāta ahitānukampī, hitānukampī te ahampi tāta;

Pāpañca taṃ kamma pakubbamānaṃ, arahāmi no vārayituṃ tato.

‘I am not uncompassionate for your well-being, father; I am indeed compassionate for your well-being, father. And as you are performing that evil deed, I am right to restrain you from it, even as you should restrain us.’

87.

87.

“Yo [V 4.0043] mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ saviṭṭha, adūsake hiṃsati pāpadhammo;

Kāyassa bhedā abhisamparāyaṃ, asaṃsayaṃ so nirayaṃ upeti.

‘Whoever harms mother or father, O Savittha, who are blameless, that wicked one, after the breakup of the body, in the next life, without doubt, goes to hell.’

88.

88.

“Yo mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ saviṭṭha, annena pānena upaṭṭhahāti;

Kāyassa [P 4.0048] bhedā abhisamparāyaṃ, asaṃsayaṃ so sugatiṃ upetī”ti. –

‘Whoever attends to mother or father, O Savittha, with food and drink, after the breakup of the body, in the next life, without doubt, goes to a good destination.’

Imaṃ pana puttassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pitā aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma from his son, the father spoke the eighth verse:

89.

89.

“Na me tvaṃ putta ahitānukampī, hitānukampī me tvaṃsi putta;

Ahañca taṃ mātarā vuccamāno, etādisaṃ kamma karomi ludda”nti.

‘My son, you are not uncompassionate for my well-being; you are compassionate for my well-being. It is I who, being urged by your mother, am doing this cruel deed.’

Tattha ahañca taṃ mātarāti ahañca te mātarā, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Therein, ‘ahañca taṃ mātarā’ means ‘ahañca te mātarā’ (and I, by your mother); or this is the reading.

Taṃ sutvā kumāro “tāta, itthiyo nāma uppanne dose aniggayhamānā punappunaṃ pāpaṃ karonti, mama mātā yathā puna evarūpaṃ na karoti, tathā naṃ paṇāmetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the boy said, ‘Father, women, when faults arise, if they are not checked, repeatedly do evil. It is fitting to banish my mother so that she does not do such a thing again.’ Then he spoke the ninth verse:

90.

90.

“Yā te sā bhariyā anariyarūpā, mātā mamesā sakiyā janetti;

Niddhāpaye tañca sakā agārā, aññampi te sā dukhamāvaheyyā”ti.

‘That woman who is your wife, of ignoble nature, she is my mother, my own birth-giver; drive her out from your house, lest she bring you other suffering.’

Saviṭṭhako [M 4.0048] paṇḍitaputtassa kathaṃ sutvā somanassajāto hutvā “gacchāma, tātā”ti saddhiṃ puttena ca pitarā ca yānake nisīditvā pāyāsi. Sāpi kho anācārā “nikkhantā no gehā kāḷakaṇṇī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā allagomayena gehaṃ upalimpetvā pāyāsaṃ pacitvā āgamanamaggaṃ olokentī te āgacchante disvā “nikkhantaṃ kāḷakaṇṇiṃ puna gahetvā āgato”ti kujjhitvā “are nikatika, nikkhantaṃ kāḷakaṇṇiṃ puna ādāya āgatosī”ti paribhāsi. Saviṭṭhako kiñci avatvā yānakaṃ mocetvā “anācāre kiṃ vadesī”ti taṃ sukoṭṭitaṃ koṭṭetvā “ito paṭṭhāya mā imaṃ gehaṃ pāvisī”ti pāde gahetvā nikkaḍḍhi. Tato pitarañca puttañca nhāpetvā sayampi nhāyitvā tayopi [P 4.0049] pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjiṃsu. Sāpi pāpadhammā katipāhaṃ aññasmiṃ gehe vasi. Tasmiṃ kāle putto pitaraṃ āha – “tāta, mama mātā ettakena na bujjhati, tumhe mama mātu maṅkubhāvakaraṇatthaṃ ‘asukagāmake mama mātuladhītā atthi[V 4.0044], sā mayhaṃ pitarañca puttañca mañca paṭijaggissati, taṃ ānessāmī’ti vatvā mālāgandhādīni ādāya yānakena nikkhamitvā khettaṃ anuvicaritvā sāyaṃ āgacchathā”ti. So tathā akāsi.

Having heard the wise son's words, Saviᅩᅩhaka was filled with joy and said, 'Let us go, my dears!' He then set out in a carriage with his son and his father. That ill-behaved woman, thinking, 'The unlucky one has left our house,' was overjoyed. She smeared the house with fresh cow dung, cooked rice porridge, and kept looking down the road for their return. When she saw them coming, she became angry, thinking, 'He has brought back the unlucky one who had departed,' and reviled him, saying, 'Hey, you trickster, you have brought back the unlucky one!' Without saying a word, Saviᅩᅩhaka unyoked the carriage and asked, 'Ill-behaved woman, what are you saying?' Then he gave her a thorough beating, and seizing her by the feet, he dragged her out, saying, 'From now on, do not enter this house!' After that, he bathed his father and son, bathed himself, and the three of them ate the rice porridge. That wicked woman stayed in another house for a few days. At that time, the son said to his father, 'Father, my mother does not understand even after all this. To make her feel abashed, you should say, "In such-and-such a village, I have a maternal uncle's daughter; she will take care of my father, my son, and me. I will bring her here." Then, taking garlands, perfumes, and so on, leave by carriage, wander about the fields, and return in the evening.' He did so.

Paṭivissakakule itthiyo “sāmiko kira te aññaṃ bhariyaṃ ānetuṃ asukagāmaṃ nāma gato”ti tassā ācikkhiṃsu. Sā “dānimhi naṭṭhā, natthi me puna okāso”ti bhītā tasitā hutvā “puttameva yācissāmī”ti paṇḍitaputtassa santikaṃ gantvā tassa pādesu patitvā “tāta, taṃ ṭhapetvā añño mama paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, ito paṭṭhāya tava pitarañca pitāmahañca alaṅkatacetiyaṃ viya paṭijaggissāmi, puna mayhaṃ imasmiṃ ghare pavesanaṃ karohī”ti āha. So “sādhu, amma, sace puna evarūpaṃ na karissatha, karissāmi, appamattā hothā”ti vatvā pitu āgatakāle dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

In a neighboring household, the women told her, 'Your husband, it seems, has gone to such-and-such a village to bring another wife.' She, frightened and distressed, thought, 'Now I am ruined; there is no opportunity for me again,' and went to her wise son. Falling at his feet, she said, 'Dear son, besides you, I have no other refuge. From now on, I will look after your father and grandfather as if they were adorned shrines. Please allow me entrance into this house again.' He replied, 'Very well, mother. If you will not do such a thing again, I will arrange it. Be heedful.' Then, when his father arrived, he spoke the tenth verse:

91.

91.

“Yā te sā bhariyā anariyarūpā, mātā mamesā sakiyā janetti;

Dantā kareṇūva vasūpanītā, sā pāpadhammā punarāvajātū”ti.

‘She who was your wife, of ignoble nature, this mother of mine, my own birth-giver; like a tamed female elephant brought under control, may that woman of wicked nature return.’

Tattha [M 4.0049] kareṇūvāti tāta, idāni sā āneñjakāraṇaṃ kārikā hatthinī viya dantā vasaṃ upanītā nibbisevanā jātā. Punarāgajātūti puna imaṃ gehaṃ āgacchatūti.

Herein, 'like a female elephant' means, 'Dear father, she has now, by being the cause of her own steadiness, become like a female elephant that is tamed, brought under control, and free from bad conduct.' 'Punarāgajātū' means 'may she come to this house again.'

Evaṃ so pitu dhammaṃ kathetvā gantvā mātaraṃ ānesi. Sā sāmikañca sasurañca khamāpetvā tato paṭṭhāya dantā dhammena samannāgatā hutvā sāmikañca sasurañca puttañca paṭijaggi. Ubhopi ca puttassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni karitvā saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Having thus spoken the Dhamma to his father, he went and brought his mother. She, having asked for forgiveness from her husband and father-in-law, from then on, being tamed and endowed with Dhamma, attended to her husband, father-in-law, and son. Both of them, abiding by their son's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and were destined for heaven.

Satthā [P 4.0050] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne pituposako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā pitā ca putto ca suṇisā ca teyeva ahesuṃ, paṇḍitakumāro pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher revealed the truths and connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the truths, the father-supporter was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the father, the son, and the daughter-in-law were those very same individuals, but the wise youth was none other than myself.

Takkalajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Takkala Jātaka, the eighth.

[447] 9. Mahādhammapālajātakavaṇṇanā

[447] 9. The Commentary on the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka.

Kiṃ [V 4.0045] te vatanti idaṃ satthā paṭhamagamanena kapilapuraṃ gantvā nigrodhārāme viharanto pitu nivesane rañño asaddahanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi suddhodanamahārājā vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivārassa bhagavato attano nivesane yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā antarābhatte sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathento “bhante, tumhākaṃ padhānakāle devatā āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā ‘putto te siddhatthakumāro appāhāratāya mato’ti mayhaṃ ārocesu”nti āha. Satthārā ca “saddahi, mahārājā”ti vutte “na saddahiṃ, bhante, ākāse ṭhatvā kathentiyopi devatā, ‘mama puttassa bodhitale buddhattaṃ appatvā parinibbānaṃ nāma natthī’ti paṭikkhipi”nti āha. “Mahārāja, pubbepi tvaṃ mahādhammapālakālepi ‘putto te mato imānissa aṭṭhīnī’ti dassetvā vadantassapi disāpāmokkhācariyassa ‘amhākaṃ kule taruṇakāle kālakiriyā nāma natthī’ti na saddahi, idāni pana kasmā saddahissasī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'What is your vow?' The Teacher, on his first journey after reaching Kapilavatthu and dwelling in the Nigrodha Grove, related this in his father's residence concerning the king's disbelief. At that time, King Suddhodana, having given rice-gruel and solid food to the Blessed One surrounded by twenty thousand monks in his own residence, while engaging in pleasant conversation during the meal, said: 'Venerable sir, during the time of your Great Striving, deities came and stood in the sky, announcing to me, "Your son, Prince Siddhattha, has died from lack of food."' When the Teacher said, 'Great king, did you believe them?' he replied, 'I did not believe them, venerable sir; even though the deities were speaking while standing in the sky, I rejected it, thinking, "For my son, there is no such thing as passing away without achieving Buddhahood at the foot of the Bodhi tree."' The Teacher said, 'Great king, in the past, during the time of Mahādhammapāla, even when the world-renowned teacher showed you bones and said, "Your son has died, these are his bones," you did not believe, saying, "In our family, there is no such thing as dying at a young age." Why then would you believe now?' Having said this, and being requested by the king, the Teacher related the past.

Atīte [M 4.0050] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kāsiraṭṭhe dhammapālagāmo nāma ahosi. So dhammapālakulassa vasanatāya etaṃ nāmaṃ labhi. Tattha dasannaṃ kusalakammapathānaṃ pālanato “dhammapālo”tveva paññāto brāhmaṇo paṭivasati, tassa kule antamaso dāsakammakarāpi dānaṃ denti, sīlaṃ rakkhanti, uposathakammaṃ karonti. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ kule nibbatti, “dhammapālakumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Atha naṃ vayappattaṃ pitā sahassaṃ datvā sippuggahaṇatthāya takkasilaṃ pesesi. So tattha gantvā disāpāmokkhācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhi, pañcannaṃ māṇavakasatānaṃ jeṭṭhantevāsiko ahosi. Tadā ācariyassa jeṭṭhaputto kālamakāsi. Ācariyo māṇavakaparivuto [P 4.0051] ñātigaṇena saddhiṃ rodanto kandanto susāne tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāreti. Tattha ācariyo ca ñātivaggo cassa antevāsikā ca rodanti paridevanti, dhammapāloyeveko na rodati na paridevati. Apica kho pana tesu pañcasatesu māṇavesu susānā āgamma ācariyassa santike nisīditvā “aho evarūpo nāma ācārasampanno taruṇamāṇavo taruṇakāleyeva mātāpitūhi vippayutto maraṇappatto”ti vadantesu “sammā, tumhe ‘taruṇo’ti bhaṇatha, atha kasmā taruṇakāleyeva marati, nanu ayuttaṃ taruṇakāle maritu”nti āha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a village named Dhammapāla in the kingdom of Kāsi. It received this name because the Dhammapāla family resided there. There lived a brahmin known as Dhammapāla, so-called for his upholding of the ten wholesome courses of action. In his household, even the servants and laborers gave alms, observed the moral precepts, and performed the Uposatha duties. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into that family, and they named him Dhammapālakumāra. When he came of age, his father gave him a thousand coins and sent him to Takkasilā for the purpose of learning the arts. Going there, he studied under the world-renowned teacher and became the senior pupil among five hundred students. Then, the teacher’s eldest son passed away. The teacher, surrounded by his students and relatives, weeping and lamenting, had the funeral rites performed at the charnel ground. There, the teacher, his relatives, and his pupils all wept and mourned—only Dhammapāla did not weep or lament. Moreover, when those five hundred students returned from the charnel ground and sat near the teacher, saying, 'Alas, such a well-behaved young man, separated from his parents at a young age, has met his death,' Dhammapāla said, 'Friends, you say "young," but why does he die while still young? Is it not improper to die at a young age?'

Atha naṃ te āhaṃsu “kiṃ pana samma, tvaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ maraṇabhāvaṃ na jānāsī”ti? Jānāmi, taruṇakāle pana na maranti, mahallakakāleyeva marantīti. Nanu aniccā sabbe saṅkhārā [V 4.0046] hutvā abhāvinoti? “Saccaṃ aniccā, daharakāle pana sattā na maranti, mahallakakāle maranti, aniccataṃ pāpuṇantī”ti. “Kiṃ samma, dhammapāla, tumhākaṃ gehe na keci marantī”ti? “Daharakāle pana na maranti, mahallakakāleyeva marantī”ti. “Kiṃ panesā tumhākaṃ kulapaveṇī”ti? “Āma kulapaveṇī”ti. Māṇavā taṃ tassa kathaṃ ācariyassa ārocesuṃ. Atha naṃ so pakkosāpetvā pucchi “saccaṃ kira tāta dhammapāla, tumhākaṃ kule daharakāle na mīyantī”ti? “Saccaṃ ācariyā”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi “ayaṃ ativiya acchariyaṃ vadati, imassa pitu santikaṃ gantvā pucchitvā sace etaṃ saccaṃ, ahampi tameva [M 4.0051] dhammaṃ pūressāmī”ti. So puttassa kattabbakiccaṃ katvā sattaṭṭhadivasaccayena dhammapālaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, ahaṃ khippaṃ āgamissāmi, yāva mamāgamanā ime māṇave sippaṃ vācehī”ti vatvā ekassa eḷakassa [P 4.0052] aṭṭhīni gahetvā dhovitvā pasibbake katvā ekaṃ cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ ādāya takkasilato nikkhamitvā anupubbena taṃ gāmaṃ patvā “kataraṃ mahādhammapālassa geha”nti pucchitvā gantvā dvāre aṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇassa dāsamanussesu yo yo paṭhamaṃ addasa, so so ācariyassa hatthato chattaṃ gaṇhi, upāhanaṃ gaṇhi, upaṭṭhākassapi hatthato pasibbakaṃ gaṇhi. “Puttassa vo dhammapālakumārassa ācariyo dvāre ṭhitoti kumārassa pitu ārocethā”ti ca vuttā “sādhū”ti gantvā ārocayiṃsu. So vegena dvāramūlaṃ gantvā “ito ethā”ti taṃ gharaṃ abhinetvā pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā sabbaṃ pādadhovanādikiccaṃ akāsi.

Then they said to him, "But friend, do you not know that these beings are subject to death?" "I know, but in our family they do not die in their youth; they die only in old age." "But are not all conditioned things impermanent, having come into being, do they not cease to exist?" "It is true they are impermanent, but beings do not die in youth; they die in old age, when they reach the state of impermanence." "But friend Dhammapāla, does no one die in your household?" "They do not die in youth; they die only in old age." "Is this a family tradition of yours?" "Yes, it is a family tradition." The young men reported this conversation to their teacher. Then the teacher summoned him and asked, "Is it true, dear Dhammapāla, that in your family they do not die young?" "It is true, teacher." Hearing his words, the teacher thought, "This is most extraordinary. I will go to his father and ask. If this is true, I too will fulfill that very practice." After performing the funeral rites for his deceased son, and after seven or eight days had passed, he summoned Dhammapāla and said, "Dear Dhammapāla, I will return soon. Until my return, teach these young men their craft." Then, taking the bones of a goat, he washed them, put them in a bag, took a young attendant, and left Takkasilā. In due course, he reached that village and asked, "Which is the house of Mahādhammapāla?" Going there, he stood at the door. Among the brahmin’s servants, whoever saw him first took the umbrella from the teacher’s hand, another took his sandals, and another took the bag from the attendant’s hand. They were told, "Inform the youth's father that your son Dhammapālakumāra's teacher is standing at the door." Saying, "Very well," they went and announced it. He quickly went to the doorway, said, "Come this way," led him into the house, seated him on a couch, and performed all the duties such as washing his feet.

Ācariyo bhuttabhojano sukhakathāya nisinnakāle “brāhmaṇa, putto te dhammapālakumāro paññavā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ aṭṭhārasannañca sippānaṃ nipphattiṃ patto, apica kho panekena aphāsukena jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, mā socitthā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo pāṇiṃ paharitvā mahāhasitaṃ hasi. “Kiṃ nu brāhmaṇa, hasasī”ti ca vutte “mayhaṃ putto na marati, añño koci mato bhavissatī”ti āha. “Brāhmaṇa, puttoyeva te mato, puttasseva te aṭṭhīni disvā saddahā”ti aṭṭhīni nīharitvā “imāni te puttassa aṭṭhīnī”ti āha. Etāni eḷakassa vā sunakhassa vā bhavissanti, mayhaṃ pana putto na marati, amhākāñhi kule yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā taruṇakāle matapubbā nāma natthi, tvaṃ musā bhaṇasīti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sabbepi pāṇiṃ paharitvā mahāhasitaṃ hasiṃsu. Ācariyo taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā somanassappatto hutvā “brāhmaṇa, tumhākaṃ kulapaveṇiyaṃ daharānaṃ amaraṇena na sakkā ahetukena bhavituṃ, kena vo kāraṇena daharā na mīyantī”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The teacher, having finished his meal, was seated for pleasant conversation when he said, "Brahmin, your son Dhammapālakumāra was wise, accomplished in the three Vedas and the eighteen arts. Yet, due to some ailment, he has died. All conditioned things are impermanent; do not grieve." The brahmin clapped his hands and laughed loudly. When asked, "Why do you laugh, brahmin?" he replied, "My son is not dead. Someone else must have died." "Brahmin, it is indeed your son who has died. Seeing his bones, you will believe," said the teacher, and bringing out the bones, he said, "These are your son’s bones." "These might be the bones of a goat or a dog, but my son is not dead. In our lineage, for seven generations, no one has ever died young. You speak falsely!" At that moment, all those present clapped their hands and laughed loudly. The teacher, seeing this marvel, was filled with joy and said, "Brahmin, this lack of death among the young in your family tradition cannot be without a cause. For what reason do your young ones not die?" Asking this, he spoke the first verse:

92.

92.

“Kiṃ [V 4.0047] te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ, kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Akkhāhi me brāhmaṇa etamatthaṃ, kasmā nu tumhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti.

"What is your vow, and what is your holy life? Of what good practice is this the fruit? Explain this matter to me, brahmin: why is it that your young ones do not die?"

Tattha [P 4.0053][M 4.0052] vatanti vatasamādānaṃ. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Kissa suciṇṇassāti tumhākaṃ kule daharānaṃ amaraṇaṃ nāma katarasucaritassa vipākoti.

In that verse, 'vow' (vatan) means the undertaking of a vow. 'Holy life' (brahmacariyan) means the excellent conduct. 'Of what good practice' (kissa suciṇṇassa) means: 'Of what good conduct is this the result, namely, the deathlessness of the young in your family?'

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo yesaṃ guṇānaṃ ānubhāvena tasmiṃ kule daharā na mīyanti, te vaṇṇayanto –

Having heard that, the brahmin, describing the virtues by the power of which the young do not die in that family, said:

93.

93.

“Dhammaṃ carāma na musā bhaṇāma, pāpāni kammāni parivajjayāma;

Anariyaṃ parivajjemu sabbaṃ, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"We practice the Dhamma, we do not speak falsehood; we avoid evil actions. We shun all that is ignoble; therefore our young ones do not die."

94.

94.

“Suṇoma dhammaṃ asataṃ satañca, na cāpi dhammaṃ asataṃ rocayāma;

Hitvā asante na jahāma sante, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"We hear the Dhamma of both the unvirtuous and the virtuous, yet we do not delight in the Dhamma of the unvirtuous. Having abandoned the unvirtuous, we do not forsake the virtuous; therefore our young ones do not die."

95.

95.

“Pubbeva dānā sumanā bhavāma, dadampi ve attamanā bhavāma;

Datvāpi ve nānutappāma pacchā, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"Before giving, we are glad-minded; while giving, our minds are uplifted. Having given, we do not repent afterwards; therefore our young ones do not die."

96.

96.

“Samaṇe mayaṃ brāhmaṇe addhike ca, vanibbake yācanake dalidde;

Annena pānena abhitappayāma, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"We satisfy ascetics, brahmins, travelers, mendicants, and the destitute with food and drink; therefore our young ones do not die."

97.

97.

“Mayañca bhariyaṃ nātikkamāma, amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us. Apart from them, we lead a life of purity; therefore our young ones do not die."

98.

98.

“Pāṇātipātā [M 4.0053] viramāma sabbe, loke adinnaṃ parivajjayāma;

Amajjapā nopi musā bhaṇāma, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"We all abstain from killing living beings; we avoid taking what is not given in the world. We are not drinkers of intoxicants, nor do we speak falsehood; therefore our young ones do not die."

99.

99.

“Etāsu ve jāyare suttamāsu, medhāvino honti pahūtapaññā;

Bahussutā vedaguno ca honti, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"From these excellent women are born the wise; they become intelligent, possessing abundant wisdom. They are very learned and attain mastery of the Veda; therefore our young ones do not die."

100.

100.

“Mātā [V 4.0048] pitā ca bhaginī bhātaro ca, puttā ca dārā ca mayañca sabbe;

Dhammaṃ carāma paralokahetu, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare.

"Mother and father, sister and brothers, children and wives, and all of us—we practice the Dhamma for the sake of the next world; therefore our young ones do not die."

101.

101.

“Dāsā ca dāsyo anujīvino ca, paricārakā kammakarā ca sabbe;

Dhammaṃ [P 4.0054] caranti paralokahetu, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti. –

"Male and female slaves, dependents, attendants, and all the workers practice the Dhamma for the sake of the next world; therefore our young ones do not die."

Imā gāthā āha.

He spoke these nine verses.

Tattha dhammaṃ carāmāti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ carāma, attano jīvitahetu antamaso kunthakipillikampi jīvitā na voropema, parabhaṇḍaṃ lobhacittena na olokemāti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Musāvādo cettha musāvādissa akaraṇapāpaṃ nāma natthīti ussannavasena puna vutto. Te kira hasādhippāyenapi musā na bhaṇanti. Pāpānīti sabbāni nirayagāmikammāni. Anariyanti ariyagarahitaṃ sabbaṃ asundaraṃ aparisuddhaṃ kammaṃ parivajjayāma. Tasmā hi amhanti ettha hi-kāro nipātamatto, tena kāraṇena amhākaṃ daharā na mīyanti, antarā akālamaraṇaṃ nāma no natthīti attho. “Tasmā amha”ntipi pāṭho. Suṇomāti mayaṃ kiriyavādānaṃ sappurisānaṃ kusaladīpanampi asappurisānaṃ akusaladīpanampi dhammaṃ suṇoma[M 4.0054], so pana no sutamattakova hoti, taṃ na rocayāma. Tehi pana no saddhiṃ viggaho vā vivādo vā mā hotūti dhammaṃ suṇāma, sutvāpi hitvā asante sante vattāma, ekampi khaṇaṃ na jahāma sante, pāpamitte pahāya kalyāṇamittasevinova homāti.

Here, 'We practice the Dhamma' means we practice the Dhamma of the tenfold path of wholesome actions; for the sake of our own lives, we do not deprive even a small insect or an ant of life, nor do we look with a greedy mind at others' belongings—all this should be elaborated. Here, false speech is mentioned again emphatically because, for one who speaks falsely, there is no evil they would not do. It is said that they do not speak falsely even for amusement. 'Evil deeds' refers to all actions that lead to hell. 'Ignoble' means we avoid all actions censured by the noble ones, all that is unlovely and impure. In the phrase 'Therefore our young ones,' the particle 'hi' is merely an indeclinable; the meaning is that for this reason our young ones do not die, that there is no untimely death among us. There is also the reading 'tasmā amha.' 'We hear' means we hear the teaching that explains the wholesome from virtuous people who teach the efficacy of action, and the teaching that explains the unwholesome from unvirtuous people, but for us it is merely heard; we do not approve of it. We hear their teaching so that there may be no quarrel or dispute with them; but having heard, we abandon the unvirtuous and conduct ourselves according to the virtuous, not forsaking the virtuous even for a moment; having abandoned evil friends, we associate only with good friends.

Samaṇe mayaṃ brāhmaṇeti mayaṃ samitapāpe bāhitapāpe paccekabuddhasamaṇabrāhmaṇepi avasesadhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇepi addhikayācake sesajanepi annapānena abhitappemāti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana ayaṃ gāthā “pubbeva dānā”ti gāthāya pacchato āgatā. Nātikkamāmāti attano bhariyaṃ atikkamitvā bahi aññaṃ micchācāraṃ na karoma. Aññatra tāhīti tā attano bhariyā ṭhapetvā sesaitthīsu brahmacariyaṃ carāma, amhākaṃ bhariyāpi sesapurisesu evameva vattanti. Jāyareti jāyanti. Suttamāsūti susīlāsu uttamitthīsu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye etāsu sampannasīlāsu uttamitthīsu amhākaṃ puttā jāyanti, te medhāvinoti evaṃpakārā honti, kuto tesaṃ antarā maraṇaṃ, tasmāpi amhākaṃ kule daharā na marantīti. Dhammaṃ carāmāti paralokatthāya tividhasucaritadhammaṃ carāma. Dāsyoti dāsiyo.

In 'We gratify ascetics and brahmins,' it means we gratify with food and drink those who have pacified evil and banished evil—such as Paccekabuddhas, ascetics, and brahmins, as well as other righteous ascetics and brahmins, travelers, beggars, and other people; this is the meaning. In the Pāli text, however, this verse comes after the verse beginning 'Pubbeva dānā.' 'We do not transgress' means we do not transgress against our own wives to engage in misconduct with other women. 'Apart from them' means that, setting aside our own wives, we practice celibacy towards other women, and our wives conduct themselves in the same way towards other men. 'They are born' means they are born. 'In the best' means in virtuous, excellent women. This is what is said: 'Those children who are born to us from these women endowed with virtue, the best of women, become wise and of such a kind. How could death come to them prematurely? Therefore, in our family, the young do not die.' 'We practice the Dhamma' means we practice the Dhamma of threefold good conduct for the sake of the next world. 'Dāsyoti' means female slaves.

Avasāne [V 4.0049] –

In conclusion:

102.

102.

“Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahati;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe, na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī.

“Indeed, the Dhamma protects the Dhamma-farer; the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness. This is the benefit in the Dhamma well-practiced: the Dhamma-farer does not go to a bad destination.”

103.

103.

“Dhammo [P 4.0055] have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, chattaṃ mahantaṃ viya vassakāle;

Dhammena gutto mama dhammapālo, aññassa aṭṭhīni sukhī kumāro”ti. –

“Indeed, the Dhamma protects the Dhamma-farer, like a great parasol in the rainy season. Protected by the Dhamma is my Dhammapāla; the prince is happy, and these are the bones of another.”

Imāhi dvīhi gāthāhi dhammacārīnaṃ guṇaṃ kathesi.

With these two verses, he spoke of the virtues of Dhamma-farers.

Tattha rakkhatīti dhammo nāmeso rakkhito attano rakkhitaṃ paṭirakkhati. Sukhamāvahatīti devamanussasukhañceva nibbānasukhañca āvahati. Na [M 4.0055] duggatinti nirayādibhedaṃ duggatiṃ na gacchati. Evaṃ brāhmaṇa, mayaṃ dhammaṃ rakkhāma, dhammopi amhe rakkhatīti dasseti. Dhammena guttoti mahāchattasadisena attanā gopitadhammena gutto. Aññassa aṭṭhīnīti tayā ānītāni aṭṭhīni aññassa eḷakassa vā sunakhassa vā aṭṭhīni bhavissanti, chaḍḍethetāni, mama putto sukhī kumāroti.

Here, 'protects' means this Dhamma, being protected, protects its protector in return. 'Brings happiness' means it brings the happiness of both devas and humans, and the happiness of Nibbāna. 'Not to a bad destination' means one does not go to a bad destination such as hell. Thus, brahmin, it shows: 'We protect the Dhamma, and the Dhamma protects us.' 'Guarded by the Dhamma' means guarded by the Dhamma that one has protected, which is like a great parasol. 'Bones of another' means: 'These bones you have brought are the bones of another, either a goat or a dog. Discard them! My son, the prince, is happy.'

Taṃ sutvā ācariyo “mayhaṃ āgamanaṃ suāgamanaṃ, saphalaṃ, no nipphala”nti sañjātasomanasso dhammapālassa pitaraṃ khamāpetvā “mayā āgacchantena tumhākaṃ vīmaṃsanatthāya imāni eḷakaaṭṭhīni ābhatāni, putto te arogoyeva, tumhākaṃ rakkhitadhammaṃ mayhampi dethā”ti paṇṇe likhitvā katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā takkasilaṃ gantvā dhammapālaṃ sabbasippāni sikkhāpetvā mahantena parivārena pesesi.

Hearing this, the teacher, filled with joy, said, “My coming has been a good coming, successful and not fruitless.” After asking for forgiveness from Dhammapāla’s father, he said, “I brought these goat bones merely to test you. Your son is indeed healthy. Give me also the Dhamma you have protected.” After writing it on a leaf and staying there for a few days, he went to Takkasilā, taught Dhammapāla all the arts, and sent him back with a great retinue.

Satthā suddhodanamahārājassa imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne rājā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, ācariyo sāriputto, parisā buddhaparisā, dhammapālakumāro pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse to King Suddhodana and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the king was established in the fruition of non-returning. At that time, the parents were of the great royal family, the teacher was Sāriputta, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Prince Dhammapāla was I myself.

Mahādhammapālajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, the Ninth.

[448] 10. Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[448] 10. The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka

Nāsmase [V 4.0050] katapāpamhīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhū devadattassa aguṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto dhanuggahādipayojanena dasabalassa vadhatthameva upāyaṃ karotī”ti. Satthā [P 4.0056] āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi esa mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“One should not trust one who has done evil…”: This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta's scheming to kill him. In the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion about Devadatta’s faults: “Friends, Devadatta is making an effort to kill the Ten-Powered One, employing archers and other means.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you assembled here now?” When told, he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he schemed to kill me,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte kosambiyaṃ kosambako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto ekasmiṃ veḷuvane kukkuṭayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā anekasatakukkuṭaparivāro araññe vasati, tassāvidūre eko seno vasati[M 4.0056]. So upāyena ekekaṃ kukkuṭaṃ gahetvā khādanto ṭhapetvā bodhisattaṃ sese khādi, bodhisatto ekakova ahosi. So appamatto velāya gocaraṃ gahetvā veḷuvanaṃ pavisitvā vasati. So seno taṃ gaṇhituṃ asakkonto “ekena naṃ upāyena upalāpetvā gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā tassāvidūre sākhāya nilīyitvā “samma kukkuṭarāja, tvaṃ mayhaṃ kasmā bhāyasi, ahaṃ tayā saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ kattukāmo, asukasmiṃ nāma padese sampannagocaro, tattha ubhopi gocaraṃ gahetvā aññamaññaṃ piyasaṃvāsaṃ vasissāmā”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha “samma, mayhaṃ tayā saddhiṃ vissāso nāma natthi, gaccha tva”nti. “Samma, tvaṃ mayā pubbe katapāpatāya na saddahasi, ito paṭṭhāya evarūpaṃ na karissāmī”ti. “Na mayhaṃ tādisena sahāyenattho, gaccha tva”nti. Iti naṃ yāvatatiyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “etehi aṅgehi samannāgatena puggalena saddhiṃ vissāso nāma kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vanaghaṭaṃ unnādento devatāsu sādhukāraṃ dadamānāsu dhammakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpento –

In the past, in Kosambi, a king named Kosambaka reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a hen in a bamboo grove, living in the forest with a retinue of many hundreds of cocks. Not far from him lived a hawk. The hawk, by a trick, caught and ate the cocks one by one until, apart from the Bodhisatta, he had eaten all the rest; the Bodhisatta was the only one left. Being vigilant, he would go out for food at the proper time and return to the bamboo grove to live. The hawk, unable to catch him, thought, “I will deceive him with a trick and catch him.” Perching on a branch nearby, he said, “Friend, King Cock, why do you fear me? I wish to make friends with you. In a certain place there is abundant food; let us both go there for food and live together in pleasant companionship.” Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Friend, I have no trust in you. Go away.” The hawk said, “Friend, you do not believe me because of the evil I have done in the past, but from now on I will not do such things.” The Bodhisatta replied, “I have no need for such a companion. Go away.” Having thus rejected him three times, making the forest thicket resound as the deities gave their approval, he raised a Dhamma talk, declaring, “It is not proper to place trust in a person endowed with these qualities”:

104.

104.

“Nāsmase katapāpamhi, nāsmase alikavādine;

Nāsmase attatthapaññamhi, atisantepi nāsmase.

“One should not trust one who has done evil, nor should one trust a liar; one should not trust one who is wise only for his own gain, nor one who appears excessively serene.”

105.

105.

“Bhavanti heke purisā, gopipāsikajātikā;

Ghasanti maññe mittāni, vācāya na ca kammunā.

“For there are some men of the nature of thirsty cows; they seem to devour friends with words, but not with deeds.”

106.

106.

“Sukkhañjalipaggahitā[V 4.0051], vācāya paliguṇṭhitā;

Manussapheggū nāsīde, yasmiṃ natthi kataññutā.

“With empty cupped hands raised, veiled by words—one should not approach the chaff of humanity, in whom there is no gratitude.”

107.

107.

“Na [P 4.0057] hi aññaññacittānaṃ, itthīnaṃ purisāna vā;

Nānāvikatvā saṃsaggaṃ, tādisampi ca nāsmase.

“For one should not trust women or men of fickle minds, nor such a one who forms associations in various ways.”

108.

108.

“Anariyakammamokkantaṃ, athetaṃ sabbaghātinaṃ;

Nisitaṃva paṭicchannaṃ, tādisampi ca nāsmase.

“One who has resorted to ignoble deeds, who is unreliable, a destroyer of all, like a sharpened blade concealed—one should not trust such a one.”

109.

109.

“Mittarūpenidhekacce, sākhalyena acetasā;

Vividhehi upāyanti, tādisampi ca nāsmase.

“Some here, in the guise of friends, with affability but without sincerity, approach with various schemes—one should not trust such a one.”

110.

110.

“Āmisaṃ [M 4.0057] vā dhanaṃ vāpi, yattha passati tādiso;

Dubbhiṃ karoti dummedho, tañca hantvāna gacchatī”ti. – imā gāthā āha;

“Wherever such a one sees material gain or wealth, the fool commits treachery, and having struck that person, he departs.” — He spoke these verses.

Tattha nāsmaseti nāssase. Ayameva vā pāṭho, na vissaseti vuttaṃ hoti. Katapāpamhīti paṭhamaṃ katapāpe puggale. Alikavādineti musāvādimhipi na vissase. Tassa hi akattabbaṃ nāma pāpaṃ natthi. Nāsmase attatthapaññamhīti attano atthāya eva yassa paññā snehavasena na bhajati, dhanatthikova bhajati, tasmiṃ attatthapaññepi na vissase. Atisanteti anto upasame avijjamāneyeva ca bahi upasamadassanena atisante viya paṭicchannakammantepi bilapaṭicchannaāsīvisasadise kuhakapuggale. Gopipāsikajātikāti gunnaṃ pipāsakajātikā viya, pipāsitagosadisāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathā pipāsitagāvo titthaṃ otaritvā mukhapūraṃ udakaṃ pivanti, na pana udakassa kattabbayuttakaṃ karonti, evameva ekacce “idañcidañca karissāmā”ti madhuravacanena mittāni ghasanti, piyavacanānucchavikaṃ pana na karonti, tādisesu vissāso mahato anatthāya hotīti dīpeti.

Here, 'nāsmase' means 'one should not trust.' Or, this is the reading: 'one should not trust' is said. 'Katapāpamhi' refers, first, to a person who has committed evil. 'Alikavādine' means one should not trust even a liar. For there is no evil deed that such a one would not do. 'Nāsmase attatthapaññamhi' means one should not trust even one wise for his own gain, whose wisdom is not based on affection but only serves the purpose of wealth. 'Atisante' refers to a deceptive person, like a snake hidden in a hole, whose actions are concealed, appearing outwardly peaceful as if very serene, even though inner peace is absent. 'Gopipāsikajātikā' means 'of the nature of thirsty cows,' or it is said, 'like a thirsty cow.' Just as thirsty cows, having descended to a watering place, drink a mouthful of water but do not perform what is proper for the water, so too some, saying, 'We will do this and that,' devour friends with sweet words but do not act in accordance with their pleasant words. Trust in such people leads to great harm—this is explained.

Sukkhañjalipaggahitāti paggahitatucchaañjalino. Vācāya paliguṇṭhitāti “idaṃ dassāma, idaṃ karissāmā”ti vacanena paṭicchādikā. Manussapheggūti evarūpā asārakā manussā manussapheggū nāma. Nāsīdeti na āsīde evarūpe na upagaccheyya. Yasmiṃ natthīti yasmiñca puggale kataññutā natthi, tampi nāsīdeti attho. Aññaññacittānanti aññenaññena cittena samannāgatānaṃ[V 4.0052], lahucittānanti attho. Evarūpānaṃ itthīnaṃ vā purisānaṃ vā na vissaseti dīpeti. Nānāvikatvā saṃsagganti yopi na sakkā anupagantvā etassa antarāyaṃ kātunti antarāyakaraṇatthaṃ nānākāraṇehi saṃsaggamāvikatvā daḷhaṃ karitvā pacchā antarāyaṃ karoti, tādisampi puggalaṃ nāsmase na vissaseyyāti dīpeti.

'Sukkhañjalipaggahitā' means 'with cupped hands holding nothing.' 'Vācāya paliguṇṭhitā' means 'concealed by words,' by saying, 'We will give this, we will do that.' 'Manussapheggū' refers to such insubstantial people, who are called the chaff of humanity. 'Nāsīde' means 'one should not approach,' one should not go near such a one. 'Yasmiṃ natthi' means, 'in whom there is no gratitude,' that is, one should not approach a person in whom gratitude is lacking. 'Aññaññacittānaṃ' means 'endowed with minds that are different at different times,' that is, 'light-minded.' It indicates that one should not trust such women or men. 'Nānāvikatvā saṃsaggaṃ' refers to one who, for the purpose of causing harm, creates a firm association by various means, thinking, 'It is not possible to cause harm to this one without approaching him,' and then later causes harm. It indicates that one should not trust such a person.

Anariyakammamokkantati anariyānaṃ dussīlānaṃ kammaṃ otaritvā ṭhitaṃ. Athetanti athiraṃ appatiṭṭhitavacanaṃ. Sabbaghātinanti okāsaṃ labhitvā sabbesaṃ [M 4.0058] upaghātakaraṃ. Nisitaṃva [P 4.0058] paṭicchannanti kosiyā vā pilotikāya vā paṭicchannaṃ nisitakhaggamiva. Tādisampīti evarūpampi amittaṃ mittapatirūpakaṃ na vissaseyya. Sākhalyenāti maṭṭhavacanena. Acetasāti acittakena. Vacanameva hi nesaṃ maṭṭhaṃ, cittaṃ pana thaddhaṃ pharusaṃ. Vividhehīti vividhehi upāyehi otārāpekkhā upagacchanti. Tādisampīti yo etehi amittehi mittapatirūpakehi sadiso hoti, tampi na vissaseti attho. Āmisanti khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ. Dhananti mañcapaṭipādakaṃ ādiṃ katvā avasesaṃ. Yattha passatīti sahāyakagehe yasmiṃ ṭhāne passati. Dubbhiṃ karotīti dubbhicittaṃ uppādeti, taṃ dhanaṃ harati. Tañca hantvānāti tañca sahāyakampi chetvā gacchati. Iti imā satta gāthā kukkuṭarājā kathesi.

'Anariyakammamokkantā' means 'one who has descended to the deeds of the ignoble, the immoral.' 'Atheta' means 'unstable, unestablished speech.' 'Sabbaghātina' means 'one who, having found an opportunity, harms all.' 'Nisitaṃva paṭicchanna' means 'like a sharp sword concealed by a sheath or a cloth.' 'Tādisampi' means 'even such a one,' that is, an enemy disguised as a friend, should not be trusted. 'Sākhalyena' means 'with smooth words.' 'Acetasā' means 'without a mind.' For their speech is smooth, but their mind is obstinate and harsh. 'Vividhehi' means 'with various methods,' they approach seeking an opportunity. 'Tādisampi' means that one who resembles such enemies disguised as friends should also not be trusted—that is the meaning. 'Āmisa' means 'edible food.' 'Dhana' means 'wealth,' including beds, footstools, and the rest. 'Yattha passati' means 'in a companion's house, in whatever place he sees it.' 'Dubbhiṃ karoti' means 'he generates a malicious thought and steals that wealth.' 'Tañca hantvāna' means 'and having cut off that companion, he departs.' Thus, the king of cocks spoke these seven verses.

111.

111.

“Mittarūpena bahavo, channā sevanti sattavo;

Jahe kāpurise hete, kukkuṭo viya senakaṃ.

“Many foes, concealed in the guise of friends, attend on one; one should abandon these base persons, as a cock abandons a hawk.”

112.

112.

“Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

Amittavasamanveti, pacchā ca manutappati.

“And he who does not quickly discern a matter that has arisen, falls under the sway of enemies, and afterward regrets.”

113.

113.

“Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate sattusambādhā, kukkuṭo viya senakā.

“And he who quickly discerns a matter that has arisen, is freed from the oppression of enemies, like a cock from a hawk.”

114.

114.

“Taṃ tādisaṃ kūṭamivoḍḍitaṃ vane, adhammikaṃ niccavidhaṃsakārinaṃ;

Ārā vivajjeyya naro vicakkhaṇo, senaṃ yathā kukkuṭo vaṃsakānane”ti. –

“Such a one, like a trap set up in the forest, unrighteous, always causing destruction—a discerning person should avoid him from afar, as a cock avoids a hawk in a bamboo grove.”

Imā catasso dhammarājena bhāsitā abhisambuddhagāthā.

These four verses were spoken by the King of the Dhamma; they are verses of full enlightenment.

Tattha [V 4.0053] jahe kāpurise heteti bhikkhave, ete kāpurise paṇḍito jaheyya. Ha-kāro panettha nipātamattaṃ. Pacchā ca manutappatīti pacchā ca anutappati. Kūṭamivoḍḍitanti vane migānaṃ bandhanatthāya kūṭapāsaṃ viya oḍḍitaṃ. Niccavidhaṃsakārinanti niccaṃ viddhaṃsanakaraṃ. Vaṃsakānaneti yathā vaṃsavane kukkuṭo senaṃ vivajjeti, evaṃ vicakkhaṇo pāpamitte vivajjeyya.

Here, 'jahe kāpurise hete' means, 'Bhikkhus, the wise person should abandon these base persons.' The syllable 'ha' here is merely a particle. 'Pacchā ca manutappati' means 'and afterward he regrets.' 'Kūṭamivoḍḍita' means 'like a snare set up in the forest to trap animals.' 'Niccavidhaṃsakārin' means 'always causing destruction.' 'Vaṃsakānane' means 'in a bamboo grove,' that is, just as a cock avoids a hawk in a bamboo grove, so should the discerning one avoid evil friends.

Sopi [M 4.0059] tā gāthā vatvā senaṃ āmantetvā “sace imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasissasi, jānissāmi te kattabba”nti tajjesi. Seno tato palāyitvā aññatra gato.

Having spoken those verses, he addressed the hawk and threatened him, saying, 'If you stay in this place, I will know what should be done to you.' The hawk then fled from there and went elsewhere.

Satthā [P 4.0059] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhave devadatto pubbepi mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā seno devadatto ahosi, kukkuṭo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Master, having delivered this discourse, said: 'Thus, bhikkhus, Devadatta formerly also tried to kill me.' Then he connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the hawk was Devadatta, but the cock was indeed I myself.'

Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Cock Jātaka (Tenth).

[449] 11. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalījātakavaṇṇanā

[449] 11. The Commentary on the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Jātaka

Alaṅkato maṭṭhakuṇḍalīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mataputtaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekassa buddhupaṭṭhākassa kuṭumbikassa piyaputto kālamakāsi. So puttasokasamappito na nhāyati na bhuñjati na kammante vicāreti, na buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, kevalaṃ “piyaputtaka, maṃ ohāya paṭhamataraṃ gatosī”tiādīni vatvā vippalapati. Satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento tassa sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ disvā punadivase bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco bhikkhū uyyojetvā ānandattherena pacchāsamaṇena tassa gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. Satthu āgatabhāvaṃ kuṭumbikassa ārocesuṃ. Athassa gehajano āsanaṃ paññapetvā satthāraṃ nisīdāpetvā kuṭumbikaṃ pariggahetvā satthu santikaṃ ānesi. Taṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ satthā karuṇāsītalena vacanena āmantetvā “kiṃ, upāsaka, puttakaṃ anusocasī”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “upāsaka, porāṇakapaṇḍitā putte kālakate sokasamappitā vicarantāpi paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā ‘alabbhanīyaṭṭhāna’nti tathato ñatvā appamattakampi sokaṃ na kariṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Adorned, with polished earrings”—this the Master spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a householder whose son had died. It is said that in Sāvatthī, the beloved son of a householder, a lay follower of the Buddha, passed away. Overcome by grief for his son, he neither bathed nor ate, nor attended to his business, nor went to attend upon the Buddha. He merely lamented, saying, “My dear son, you have gone first, leaving me behind!” and so on, rambling incoherently. At dawn, the Master, surveying the world, saw that he had the potential for attaining the fruit of stream-entry. The next day, surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having finished his meal, he dismissed the bhikkhus and, with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant, went to the householder’s door. The householder’s people announced the Master’s arrival. Then the household prepared a seat and had the Master sit down. They took hold of the grieving householder and brought him into the Master’s presence. After paying homage, he sat down to one side. The Master, with words cool with compassion, addressed him: “Why, lay follower, do you grieve for your son?” When he replied, “Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Master said, “Lay follower, the wise of old, though stricken with grief for their departed sons, even while wandering about, upon hearing the words of the wise and realizing ‘this is an unobtainable matter,’ did not grieve even a little.” Having been entreated by him, he then related a story from the past.

Atīte [V 4.0054][M 4.0060] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente ekassa mahāvibhavassa brāhmaṇassa putto pañcadasasoḷasavassakāle ekena byādhinā phuṭṭho kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatti. Brāhmaṇo tassa kālakiriyato paṭṭhāya susānaṃ gantvā chārikapuñjaṃ āvijjhanto paridevati, sabbakammante pariccajitvā sokasamappito vicarati. Tadā devaputto anuvicaranto taṃ disvā “ekaṃ upamaṃ katvā sokaṃ harissāmī”ti tassa susānaṃ gantvā paridevanakāle tasseva puttavaṇṇī hutvā sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍito ekasmiṃ padese ṭhatvā ubho hatthe sīse ṭhapetvā [P 4.0060] mahāsaddena paridevi. Brāhmaṇo saddaṃ sutvā taṃ oloketvā puttapemaṃ paṭilabhitvā tassa santike ṭhatvā “tāta māṇava, imasmiṃ susānamajjhe kasmā paridevasī”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the son of a very wealthy brahmin, at the age of fifteen or sixteen, was afflicted by an illness and died, being reborn in the heavenly realm. From the time of his death, the brahmin would go to the charnel ground, sifting through piles of ashes and lamenting. Abandoning all his duties, he wandered about, consumed by grief. At that time, a devaputta, while wandering, saw him and thought, “I will dispel his sorrow by giving him a simile.” He went to the charnel ground, and at the moment the brahmin was lamenting, took on the appearance of his son, adorned with all ornaments. Standing in one spot, he raised both hands to his head and wailed loudly. Hearing the sound, the brahmin looked over and, his love for his son reawakening, stood near him and asked, “Dear boy, why do you wail in the middle of this charnel ground?” Then he spoke the first verse:

115.

115.

“Alaṅkato maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, māladhārī haricandanussado;

Bāhā paggayha kandasi, vanamajjhe kiṃ dukkhito tuva”nti.

“Adorned, with polished earrings, wearing garlands, anointed with yellow sandalwood, you raise your arms and cry in the middle of the forest. For what are you sorrowful?”

Tattha alaṅkatoti nānābharaṇavibhūsito. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīti karaṇapariniṭṭhitehi maṭṭhehi kuṇḍalehi samannāgato. Māladhārīti vicitrakusumamāladharo. Haricandanussadoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇena candanena anulitto. Vanamajjheti susānamajjhe. Kiṃ dukkhito tuvanti kiṃkāraṇā dukkhito tvaṃ, ācikkha, ahaṃ te yaṃ icchasi, taṃ dassāmīti āha.

Here, “adorned” means decorated with various ornaments. “Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī” means possessed of polished earrings, beautifully crafted. “Wearing garlands” means wearing a garland of colorful flowers. “Anointed with yellow sandalwood” means anointed with golden-hued sandalwood. “In the middle of the forest” means in the middle of the cemetery. “Why are you sorrowful?” means, “For what reason are you sorrowful? Tell me, and I will give you whatever you desire.”

Athassa kathento māṇavo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the young man, wishing to speak to the brahmin, spoke the second verse:

116.

116.

“Sovaṇṇamayo pabhassaro, uppanno rathapañjaro mama;

Tassa cakkayugaṃ na vindāmi, tena dukkhena jahāmi jīvita”nti.

“A golden, radiant chariot frame has arisen for me; but I cannot find a pair of wheels for it. Because of that sorrow, I am abandoning my life.”

Brāhmaṇo sampaṭicchanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin, wishing to grant the request, spoke the third verse:

117.

117.

“Sovaṇṇamayaṃ maṇīmayaṃ, lohamayaṃ atha rūpiyāmayaṃ;

Pāvada rathaṃ karissāmi te, cakkayugaṃ paṭipādayāmi ta”nti.

“Made of gold, of gems, of copper, or of silver—tell me; I will have a chariot made for you, I will provide you with a pair of wheels.”

Tattha [M 4.0061] pāvadāti yādisena te attho yādisaṃ rocesi, tādisaṃ vada, ahaṃ te ratha karissāmi. Paṭipādayāmi tanti taṃ pañjarānurūpaṃ cakkayugaṃ adhigacchāpemi.

In this context, “tell me” means, “Whatever kind you need or desire, say it, and I will have a chariot made for you.” “I will provide you with a pair of wheels” means, “I will cause you to obtain a pair of wheels suitable for that frame.”

Taṃ [V 4.0055] sutvā māṇavena kathitāya gāthāya paṭhamapādaṃ satthā abhisambuddho hutvā kathesi, sesaṃ māṇavo.

Hearing this, the Master, having become fully enlightened, spoke the first line of the verse that was said by the young man; the rest was spoken by the young man.

118.

118.

“So māṇavo tassa pāvadi, candasūriyā [P 4.0061] ubhayettha bhātaro;

Sovaṇṇamayo ratho mama, tena cakkayugena sobhatī”ti.

That young man said to him, “The sun and moon, both of them here, are brothers; my golden chariot would be glorious with that pair of wheels.”

Brāhmaṇo tadanantaraṃ āha –

Immediately after that, the brahmin said:

119.

119.

“Bālo kho tvaṃsi māṇava, yo tvaṃ patthayasi apatthiyaṃ;

Maññāmi tuvaṃ marissasi, na hi tvaṃ lacchasi candasūriye”ti. –

“You are foolish indeed, young man, for you desire what should not be desired. I think you will die, for you will not obtain the sun and moon.”

Brāhmaṇena vuttagāthāya apatthiyanti apatthetabbaṃ.

In the verse spoken by the brahmin, “what is not to be desired” means what ought not to be desired.

Tato māṇavo āha –

Then the young man said:

120.

120.

“Gamanāgamanampi dissati, vaṇṇadhātu ubhayettha vīthiyo;

Peto pana neva dissati, ko nu kho kandataṃ bālyataro”ti.

“The coming and going of the sun and moon is seen, as are their paths; but the departed one is not seen at all. Who then, of those who lament, is the more foolish?”

Māṇavena vuttagāthāya gamanāgamananti uggamanañca atthagamanañca. Vaṇṇoyeva vaṇṇadhātu. Ubhayettha vīthiyoti ettha ākāse “ayaṃ candassa vīthi, ayaṃ sūriyassa vīthī”ti evaṃ ubhayagamanāgamanabhūmiyopi paññāyanti. Peto panāti paralokaṃ gatasatto pana na dissateva. Ko nu khoti evaṃ sante amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ kandantānaṃ ko nu kho bālyataroti.

In the verse spoken by the young man, “coming and going” means rising and setting. “The sun and moon” refers to the entities of light. “The paths of both” means that here in the sky, “this is the moon’s path, this is the sun’s path”—thus the grounds for the coming and going of both are perceived. “But the departed one” means a being gone to the next world is simply not seen. “Who then is more foolish?” means, “This being so, between the two of us lamenting, who then is more foolish?”

Evaṃ [M 4.0062] māṇave kathente brāhmaṇo sallakkhetvā gāthamāha –

As the young man was speaking thus, the brahmin, taking it to heart, spoke a verse:

121.

121.

“Saccaṃ kho vadesi māṇava, ahameva kandataṃ bālyataro;

Candaṃ viya dārako rudaṃ, petaṃ kālakatābhipatthaye”ti.

“You speak the truth, young man, I am indeed the more foolish of us who lament; like a child weeping for the moon, I long for the one who is dead and gone.”

Tattha candaṃ viya dārakoti yathā daharo gāmadārako “candaṃ dethā”ti candassatthāya rodeyya, evaṃ ahampi petaṃ kālakataṃ abhipatthemīti.

In that verse, “like a child for the moon” means: just as a young village boy might cry for the moon, saying, “Give me the moon!”, so too do I long for the one who has passed away.

Iti [V 4.0056] brāhmaṇo māṇavassa kathāya nissoko hutvā tassa thutiṃ karonto sesagāthā abhāsi –

Thus the brahmin, freed from sorrow by the young man’s words, praising him, spoke the remaining verses:

122.

122.

“Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

“I was indeed burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee; you have extinguished all my distress, as though drenching it with water.”

123.

123.

“Abbahī [P 4.0062] vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

“Indeed, you have drawn out the dart that was lodged in my heart; you have dispelled the sorrow for my son from me, who was overcome by grief.”

124.

124.

“Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna māṇavā”ti.

“With the dart drawn out, I am without sorrow, untroubled. I neither grieve nor weep, having heard you, young man.”

Atha naṃ māṇavo “brāhmaṇa, yassatthāya tvaṃ rodasi, ahaṃ te putto, ahaṃ devaloke nibbatto, ito paṭṭhāya mā maṃ anusoci, dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, uposathaṃ karohī”ti ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Brāhmaṇopi tassovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā kālakato devaloke nibbatti.

Then the young man said to him, “Brahmin, I am your son for whom you weep; I have been reborn in the heavenly world. From now on, do not grieve for me. Give alms, observe the precepts, and keep the Uposatha.” After advising him, he returned to his own place. The brahmin, abiding by his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and after death was reborn in the heavenly world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānehi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.Tadā dhammadesakadevaputto ahameva ahosinti.

The Master, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. To connect the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the devaputta who taught the Dhamma.”

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalījātakavaṇṇanā ekādasamā.

The Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī Jātaka is finished.

[450] 12. Bilārakosiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[450] 12. 12. Bilārakosiya Jātaka

Apacantāpīti [M 4.0063] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dānavittaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sāsane pabbajitvā pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya dānavitto ahosi dānajjhāsayo, pattapariyāpannampi piṇḍapātaṃ aññassa adatvā na bhuñji, antamaso pānīyampi labhitvā aññassa adatvā na pivi, evaṃ dānābhirato ahosi. Athassa dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū guṇakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ [V 4.0057] bhikkhu dānavitto dānajjhāsayo”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhave ayaṃ pubbe assaddho ahosi appasanno, tiṇaggena telabindumpi uddharitvā kassaci na adāsi, atha naṃ ahaṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā dānaphalaṃ ñāpesiṃ, tameva dānaninnaṃ cittaṃ bhavantarepi na pajahatī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Apacantāpīti.” The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this in reference to a certain monk who was a generous giver. It is said that after hearing the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching, he went forth into the Dispensation. From the time of his going forth, he was a generous giver, inclined to generosity. He would not eat even the almsfood in his bowl without giving some to another; he would not even drink water he had obtained without giving some to someone else. Thus, he was devoted to giving. Then, in the Dhamma hall, the monks discussed his virtues. The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they told him, he had that monk summoned and questioned him, “Is it true, monk, that you are a generous giver and inclined to generosity?” When he replied, “It is true, Blessed One,” the Teacher said, “Monks, in the past, this man was faithless and without confidence. He would not give even a drop of oil taken up on the tip of a blade of grass to anyone. But I tamed him, made him have no other refuge [but me], and taught him the fruit of giving. That same mind, inclined to generosity, does not forsake him even in another existence.” Requested by the monks, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ patvā ekadivasaṃ dhanavilokanaṃ katvā “dhanaṃ paññāyati, etassa [P 4.0063] uppādakā na paññāyanti, imaṃ dhanaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dānasālaṃ kāretvā yāvajīvaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā āyupariyosāne “idaṃ dānavattaṃ mā upacchindī”ti puttassa ovādaṃ datvā tāvatiṃsabhavane sakko hutvā nibbatti. Puttopissa tatheva dānaṃ datvā puttaṃ ovaditvā āyupariyosāne cando devaputto hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto sūriyo hutvā nibbatti, tassapi putto mātalisaṅgāhako hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto pañcasikho gandhabbadevaputto hutvā nibbatti. Chaṭṭho pana assaddho ahosi thaddhacitto nisneho maccharī, dānasālaṃ viddhaṃsetvā jhāpetvā yācake pothetvā nīharāpesi, kassaci tiṇaggena uddharitvā telabindumpi na deti. Tadā sakko devarājā attano pubbakammaṃ oloketvā “pavattati nu kho me dānavaṃso, udāhu no”ti upadhārento “putto me dānaṃ pavattetvā [M 4.0064] cando hutvā nibbatti, tassa putto sūriyo, tassa putto mātali, tassa putto pañcasikho gandhabbadevaputto hutvā nibbatti, chaṭṭho pana taṃ vaṃsaṃ upacchindī”ti passi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Varanasi, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a treasurer's family. Having come of age, he established his household and, upon his father's death, attained the position of treasurer. One day, while inspecting his wealth, he thought, 'Wealth is evident, but those who produced it are not. It is fitting for me to distribute this wealth and give great alms.' He had an alms-hall built and provided great alms throughout his life. At the end of his life, he gave an instruction to his son, 'Do not discontinue this practice of giving,' and was reborn as Sakka in the Tavatimsa heaven. His son likewise gave alms and, after instructing his own son at the end of his life, was reborn as the deity Canda. His son was reborn as the deity Suriya, his son as Matali the Charioteer, and his son as the Gandhabba deity Pancasikha. However, the sixth descendant was faithless, hard-hearted, devoid of affection, and miserly. He destroyed the alms-hall, burned it down, and had the beggars beaten and driven away. He would not give even a drop of oil lifted on the tip of a blade of grass. At that time, Sakka, the king of the gods, reflecting on his own past deeds, wondered, 'Does my lineage of giving continue, or not?' Observing, he saw, 'My son maintained the giving and was reborn as Canda. His son became Suriya, his son Matali, and his son the Gandhabba deity Pancasikha. But the sixth has cut off that lineage.'

Athassa etadahosi “imaṃ pāpadhammaṃ dametvā dānaphalaṃ jānāpetvā āgamissāmī”ti. So candasūriyamātalipañcasikhe pakkosāpetvā “sammā, amhākaṃ vaṃse chaṭṭho kulavaṃsaṃ samucchinditvā dānasālaṃ jhāpetvā yācake nīharāpesi, na kassaci kiñci deti, etha naṃ damessāmā”ti tehi saddhiṃ bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe seṭṭhi rājupaṭṭhānaṃ katvā āgantvā sattame dvārakoṭṭhake antaravīthiṃ olokento caṅkamati. Sakko “tumhe mama paviṭṭhakāle pacchato paṭipāṭiyā āgacchathā”ti vatvā gantvā seṭṭhissa santike ṭhatvā “bho mahāseṭṭhi, bhojanaṃ me dehī”ti āha. “Brāhmaṇa natthi tava idha bhattaṃ, aññattha gacchā”ti. “Bho mahāseṭṭhi, brāhmaṇehi bhatte yācite [P 4.0064] na dātuṃ na labbhatī”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, mama gehe pakkampi pacitabbampi bhattaṃ natthi, aññattha gacchā”ti. “Mahāseṭṭhi, ekaṃ te silokaṃ kathessāmi, taṃ suṇāhī”ti. “Natthi mayhaṃ tava silokenattho, mā idha tiṭṭhā”ti. Sakko tassa kathaṃ asuṇanto viya dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then it occurred to him: 'I shall tame this evil person, make him understand the fruit of giving, and then return.' He summoned Canda, Suriya, Matali, and Pancasikha and said, 'Friends, the sixth in our lineage has cut off the family tradition, burned down the alms-hall, and driven away the beggars; he gives nothing to anyone. Come, let us tame him.' Together with them, he went to Varanasi. At that moment, the treasurer, having attended upon the king, returned and was walking to and fro at the seventh gateway, looking down the street. Sakka said, 'When I have entered, you follow in succession.' Then he went and stood near the treasurer, saying, 'O great treasurer, give me food.' 'Brahmin, there is no food for you here. Go elsewhere.' 'O great treasurer, when brahmins ask for food, it is not that it is impossible to give; it is indeed available.' 'Brahmin, in my house, there is neither cooked food nor food yet to be cooked. Go elsewhere.' 'Great treasurer, I will recite a verse for you. Listen to it.' 'I have no need of your verse. Do not stand here.' As if not hearing his words, Sakka spoke two verses—

125.

125.

“Apacantāpi [V 4.0058] dicchanti, santo laddhāna bhojanaṃ;

Kimeva tvaṃ pacamāno, yaṃ na dajjā na taṃ samaṃ.

The virtuous, even when not cooking, wish to give from the food they have obtained. What then of you who cook? That you do not give is not proper.

126.

126.

“Maccherā ca pamādā ca, evaṃ dānaṃ na dīyati;

Puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānena, deyyaṃ hoti vijānatā”ti.

Through miserliness and heedlessness, a gift is not given; by one who is wise, desiring merit, a gift should indeed be given.

Tāsaṃ attho – mahāseṭṭhi apacantāpi santo sappurisā bhikkhācariyāya laddhampi bhojanaṃ dātuṃ icchanti, na ekakā paribhuñjanti. Kimeva tvaṃ pacamāno yaṃ na dadeyyāsi, na taṃ samaṃ, taṃ tava anurūpaṃ anucchavikaṃ na hoti. Dānañhi maccherena ca pamādena cāti dvīhi dosehi na dīyati, puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānena vijānatā paṇḍitamanussena dātabbameva hotīti.

This is the meaning: Great treasurer, even the virtuous, good people, though they do not cook, wish to give the food obtained by wandering for alms; they do not eat alone. How then could you, who are cooking, not give? That is not proper; it is not fitting or suitable for you. For a gift is not given because of two faults: miserliness and heedlessness. By a wise person who understands, desiring merit, a gift should indeed be given.

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “tena hi gehaṃ pavisitvā nisīda, thokaṃ lacchasī”ti āha. Sakko pavisitvā te siloke sajjhāyanto nisīdi.
