Atha naṃ cando āgantvā bhattaṃ yāci. “Natthi te bhattaṃ, gacchā”ti ca [M 4.0065] vutto “mahāseṭṭhi anto eko brāhmaṇo nisinno, brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ maññe bhavissati, ahampi bhavissāmī”ti vatvā “natthi brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ, nikkhamā”ti vuccamānopi “mahāseṭṭhi iṅgha tāva silokaṃ suṇāhī”ti dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, the treasurer said, 'Well then, enter the house and sit down; you will get a little.' Sakka entered and sat down, reciting those verses. Then Canda came and asked for food. When told, 'There is no food for you, go away,' he said, 'Great treasurer, there is a brahmin sitting inside. I suppose there will be a feeding of brahmins; I too shall be there.' Though he was told, 'There is no feeding of brahmins, get out,' he said, 'Great treasurer, come now, listen to a verse,' and he spoke two verses—

127.

127.

“Yasseva bhīto na dadāti maccharī, tadevādadato bhayaṃ;

Jighacchā ca pipāsā ca, yassa bhāyati maccharī;

Tameva bālaṃ phusati, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

That which the miser fears and so does not give—that very thing is the danger for him who does not give. Hunger and thirst, of which the miser is afraid, afflict that fool both in this world and the next.

128.

128.

“Tasmā vineyya maccheraṃ, dajjā dānaṃ malābhibhū;

Puññāni paralokasmiṃ, patiṭṭhā honti pāṇina”nti.

Therefore, having removed miserliness, one should give a gift, overcoming the stain. Meritorious deeds are the support for living beings in the world beyond.

Tattha yassa bhāyatīti “ahaṃ aññesaṃ datvā sayaṃ jighacchito ca pipāsito ca bhavissāmī”ti yassā jighacchāya pipāsāya bhāyati. Tamevāti [P 4.0065] taññeva jighacchāpipāsāsaṅkhātaṃ bhayaṃ etaṃ bālaṃ nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne idhaloke paraloke ca phusati pīḷeti, accantadāliddiyaṃ pāpuṇāti. Malābhibhūti macchariyamalaṃ abhibhavanto.

Therein, 'which he fears' means the hunger and thirst he fears, thinking, 'If I give to others, I myself will become hungry and thirsty.' 'That very thing' means that this danger, characterized as hunger and thirst, afflicts and torments this fool in every place he is reborn, in this world and the next; he attains extreme poverty. 'Overcoming the stain' (malābhibhū) means overcoming the stain of miserliness.

Tassapi vacanaṃ sutvā “tena hi pavisa, thokaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. Sopi pavisitvā [V 4.0059] sakkassa santike nisīdi. Tato thokaṃ vītināmetvā sūriyo āgantvā bhattaṃ yācanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard his words as well, the treasurer said, 'Then enter, you will receive a little.' He also entered and sat near Sakka. After a short time had passed, Suriya arrived, and while asking for food, spoke two verses—

129.

129.

“Duddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ, dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ;

Asanto nānukubbanti, sataṃ dhammo durannayo.

Giving is hard for those who give; a difficult deed is performed by those who act. The unvirtuous do not emulate the virtuous, whose practice is hard to follow.

130.

130.

“Tasmā satañca asataṃ, nānā hoti ito gati;

Asanto nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyaṇā”ti.

Therefore, the destination of the virtuous and the unvirtuous, departing from here, is different. The unvirtuous go to hell, while the virtuous have heaven as their destination.

Tattha duddadanti dānaṃ nāma duddadaṃ maccheraṃ abhibhavitvā dātabbato, taṃ dadamānānaṃ. Dukkaranti tadeva dānakammaṃ dukkaraṃ yuddhasadisaṃ, taṃ kubbataṃ. Nānukubbantīti asappurisā dānaphalaṃ ajānantā tesaṃ gatamaggaṃ nānugacchanti. Sataṃ dhammoti sappurisānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ dhammo aññehi duranugamo. Asantoti macchariyavasena dānaṃ adatvā asappurisā nirayaṃ yanti.

Herein, 'duddadaṃ' means that a gift is difficult to give, because it must be given by overcoming miserliness; this applies to those who give. 'Dukkaraṃ' means that this same act of giving is a difficult deed, like a battle; this applies to those who perform it. 'Nānukubbanti' means that unworthy people, not knowing the fruit of giving, do not follow the path taken by the virtuous. 'Sataṃ dhammo' means the way of the virtuous, of Bodhisattas, is difficult for others to follow. 'Asanto' means that unworthy people, who do not give on account of miserliness, go to hell.

Seṭṭhi [M 4.0066] gahetabbagahaṇaṃ apassanto “tena hi pavisitvā brāhmaṇānaṃ santike nisīda, thokaṃ lacchasī”ti āha. Tato thokaṃ vītināmetvā mātali āgantvā bhattaṃ yācitvā “natthī”ti vacanamattakālameva sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

The treasurer, seeing no way to refuse, said, 'Then enter and sit near the brahmins; you will get a little.' After a short time had passed, Mātali arrived, begged for food, and at the very moment he heard the words 'There is none,' he spoke the seventh verse—

131.

131.

“Appasmeke pavecchanti, bahuneke na dicchare;

Appasmā dakkhiṇā dinnā, sahassena samaṃ mitā”ti.

Some give from the little they have, while some with much do not wish to give. A gift given from little is considered equal to a thousand.

Tattha appasmeke pavecchantīti mahāseṭṭhi ekacce paṇḍitapurisā appasmimpi deyyadhamme pavecchanti, dadantiyevāti attho. Bahunāpi deyyadhammena samannāgatā eke sattā na dicchare na dadanti. Dakkhiṇāti kammañca phalañca saddahitvā dinnadānaṃ. Sahassena samaṃ mitāti evaṃ dinnā kaṭacchubhattamattāpi dakkhiṇā sahassadānena saddhiṃ mitā, mahāphalattā sahassadānasadisāva hotīti attho.

Herein, 'appasmeke pavecchantīti' means that certain wise people bestow even from a small amount of what should be given; that is, they simply give. Some beings, though endowed with much to give, do not desire to give, nor do they give. 'Dakkhiṇā' means a gift given with faith in the action and its result. 'Sahassena samaṃ mitā' means that even a gift as small as a ladleful of food, when given in this way, is measured as equal to a thousand gifts; that is, because of its great fruit, it is just like a thousand gifts.

Tampi [P 4.0066] so “tena hi pavisitvā nisīdā”ti āha. Tato thokaṃ vītināmetvā pañcasikho āgantvā bhattaṃ yācitvā “natthi gacchā”ti vutte “ahaṃ na gatapubbo, imasmiṃ gehe brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ bhavissati maññe”ti tassa dhammakathaṃ ārabhanto aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after a short while, Pañcasikha came and asked for food. When told, 'There is none, go away,' he replied, 'I have never gone away before. There must be a feeding of brahmins in this house, I suppose.' Beginning a discourse on the Dhamma for him, he spoke the eighth verse:

132.

132.

“Dhammaṃ [V 4.0060] care yopi samuñchakaṃ care, dārañca posaṃ dadamappakasmiṃ;

Sataṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāginaṃ, kalampi nāgghanti tathāvidhassa te”ti.

Should one practice the Dhamma, even living by gleaning, supporting his wife and giving from what little he has; a hundred thousand of those who perform a thousand sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of such a one.

Tattha dhammanti tividhasucaritadhammaṃ. Samuñchakanti gāme vā āmakapakkabhikkhācariyaṃ araññe vā phalāphalaharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ uñchaṃ yo careyya, sopi dhammameva care. Dārañca posanti attano ca puttadāraṃ posentoyeva. Dadamappakasminti paritte vā deyyadhamme dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ dadamāno dhammaṃ careti attho. Sataṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāginanti paraṃ pothetvā viheṭhetvā sahassena yāgaṃ yajantānaṃ sahassayāgīnaṃ issarānaṃ satasahassampi. Kalampi nāgghanti tathāvidhassa teti tesaṃ satasahassasaṅkhātānaṃ sahassayāgīnaṃ yāgā tathāvidhassa dhammena samena [M 4.0067] deyyadhammaṃ uppādetvā dentassa duggatamanussassa soḷasiṃ kalaṃ na agghantīti.

Herein, 'Dhamma' refers to the threefold good conduct. 'Samuñchakaṃ' means that whoever should live by gleaning—whether by the practice of seeking alms of raw or cooked food in a village, or by what is known as collecting fruits in the forest—that one also practices the Dhamma. 'Dārañca posaṃ' means supporting one’s own wife and children. 'Dadamappakasmiṃ' means that, while giving to righteous ascetics and brahmins from the little that is to be given, one practices the Dhamma. 'Sataṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāginaṃ' refers to even a hundred thousand of those powerful ones who perform a thousand sacrifices, having crushed and harmed others. 'Kalampi nāgghanti tathāvidhassa te' means that the sacrifices of those hundred thousand who perform a thousand sacrifices are not worth the sixteenth part of such a poor person who gives after having produced the gift righteously and justly.

Seṭṭhi pañcasikhassa kathaṃ sutvā sallakkhesi. Atha naṃ anagghakāraṇaṃ pucchanto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

The merchant, having heard Pañcasikha’s discourse, considered it. Then, asking him the reason for its lack of value, he spoke the ninth verse:

133.

133.

“Kenesa yañño vipulo mahagghato, samena dinnassa na agghameti;

Kathaṃ sataṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāginaṃ, kalampi nāgghanti tathāvidhassa te”ti.

For what reason does this vast and costly sacrifice not attain the value of that which is given justly? How is it that a hundred thousand of those who perform a thousand sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of such a one?

Tattha yaññoti dānayāgo satasahassapariccāgavasena vipulo, vipulattāva mahagghato. Samena dinnassāti dhammena dinnassa kena kāraṇena agghaṃ na upeti. Kathaṃ sataṃ sahassānanti brāhmaṇa, kathaṃ [P 4.0067] sahassayāgīnaṃ purisānaṃ bahūnaṃ sahassānaṃ satasahassasaṅkhātā issarā tathāvidhassa dhammena uppādetvā dāyakassa ekassa duggatamanussassa kalaṃ nāgghantīti.

Herein, 'yañña' means a sacrifice of giving, vast by way of an expenditure of a hundred thousand; and because of its vastness, it is of great price. 'Samena dinnassa na agghameti' means: for what reason does it not attain the value of that which is given righteously? 'Kathaṃ sataṃ sahassānaṃ...' means: How, O brahmin, are the powerful ones, numbered at a hundred thousand among many thousands of men who perform a thousand sacrifices, not worth a fraction of a single poor person, a giver who gives after having produced the gift righteously?

Athassa kathento pañcasikho osānagāthamāha –

Then, explaining to him, Pañcasikha spoke the concluding verse:

134.

134.

“Dadanti heke visame niviṭṭhā, chetvā vadhitvā atha socayitvā;

Sā dakkhiṇā assumukhā sadaṇḍā, samena dinnassa na agghameti;

Evaṃ sataṃ sahassānaṃ sahassayāginaṃ, kalampi nāgghanti tathāvidhassa te”ti.

Some give while established in injustice, having maimed, killed, and then caused sorrow. That gift, given with tearful faces and violence, does not attain the value of that which is given justly. Thus, a hundred thousand of those who perform a thousand sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of such a one.

Tattha visameti visame kāyakammādimhi niviṭṭhā. Chetvāti kilametvā. Vadhitvāti māretvā. Socayitvāti sasoke katvā.

Herein, 'visame' means established in unjust bodily action and the like. 'Chetvā' means having tormented. 'Vadhitvā' means having killed. 'Socayitvā' means having made sorrowful.

So [V 4.0061] pañcasikhassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā “tena hi gaccha, gehaṃ pavisitvā nisīda, thokaṃ lacchasī”ti āha. Sopi gantvā tesaṃ santike nisīdi. Tato bilārakosiyo seṭṭhi ekaṃ dāsiṃ āmantetvā “etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ palāpavīhīnaṃ nāḷiṃ nāḷiṃ dehī”ti āha. Sā vīhī gahetvā brāhmaṇe [M 4.0068] upasaṅkamitvā “ime ādāya yattha katthaci pacāpetvā bhuñjathā”ti āha. “Na amhākaṃ vīhinā attho, na mayaṃ vīhiṃ āmasāmā”ti. “Ayya, vīhiṃ kirete nāmasantī”ti? “Tena hi tesaṃ taṇḍule dehī”ti. Sā taṇḍule ādāya gantvā “brāhmaṇā taṇḍule gaṇhathā”ti āha. “Mayaṃ āmakaṃ na paṭiggaṇhāmā”ti. “Ayya, āmakaṃ kira na gaṇhantī”ti. “Tena hi tesaṃ karoṭiyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā gobhattaṃ dehī”ti. Sā tesaṃ karoṭiyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā mahāgoṇānaṃ pakkabhattaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Pañcapi janā kabaḷe vaḍḍhetvā mukhe pakkhipitvā gale laggāpetvā akkhīni parivattetvā vissaṭṭhasaññā matā viya nipajjiṃsu. Dāsī te disvā “matā bhavissantī”ti bhītā gantvā seṭṭhino ārocesi “ayya, te brāhmaṇā gobhattaṃ gilituṃ asakkontā [P 4.0068] matā”ti.

Having heard Pañcasikha’s discourse on the Dhamma, he said: "In that case, go, enter the house and sit down; you will receive a little." So he went and sat near them. Then the merchant Bilārakosiya summoned a servant girl and said: "Give each of these brahmins a measure of paddy with chaff." She took the paddy, approached the brahmins, and said: "Take these and, having them cooked anywhere, eat." They replied: "We have no use for paddy; we do not touch paddy." She asked the merchant: "Sir, it is said that they do not touch paddy?" He said: "In that case, give them husked rice." She took the rice, went and said: "Brahmins, take the rice." They replied: "We do not accept raw food." She asked: "Sir, it is said they do not accept raw food?" He said: "In that case, serve them cow-food in a bowl." She served the cooked food intended for the great oxen into a bowl for them, brought it, and gave it to them. The five men, having made large mouthfuls and putting them in their mouths, letting them get stuck in their throats and rolling their eyes, they lost consciousness and lay down as if dead. The servant girl, seeing them and fearing they were dead, went and reported to the merchant: "Sir, those brahmins, unable to swallow the cow-food, are dead."

So cintesi “idāni ayaṃ pāpadhammo sukhumālabrāhmaṇānaṃ gobhattaṃ dāpesi, te taṃ gilituṃ asakkontā matāti maṃ garahissantī”ti. Tato dāsiṃ āha – “khippaṃ gantvā etesaṃ karoṭikesu bhattaṃ haritvā nānaggarasaṃ sālibhattaṃ vaḍḍhehī”ti. Sā tathā akāsi. Seṭṭhi antarapīthiṃ paṭipannamanusse pakkosāpetvā “ahaṃ mama bhuñjananiyāmena etesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhattaṃ dāpesiṃ, ete lobhena mahante piṇḍe katvā bhuñjamānā gale laggāpetvā matā, mama niddosabhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti vatvā parisaṃ sannipātesi. Mahājane sannipatite brāhmaṇā uṭṭhāya mahājanaṃ oloketvā “passathimassa seṭṭhissa musāvāditaṃ, ‘amhākaṃ attano bhuñjanabhattaṃ dāpesi’nti vadati, paṭhamaṃ gobhattaṃ amhākaṃ datvā amhesu matesu viya nipannesu imaṃ bhattaṃ vaḍḍhāpesī”ti vatvā attano mukhehi gahitabhattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā dassesuṃ. Mahājano seṭṭhiṃ garahi “andhabāla, attano kulavaṃsaṃ nāsesi, dānasālaṃ jhāpesi, yācake gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīharāpesi, idāni imesaṃ sukhumālabrāhmaṇānaṃ bhattaṃ dento gobhattaṃ dāpesi, paralokaṃ gacchanto tava ghare vibhavaṃ gīvāyaṃ bandhitvā gamissasi maññe”ti.

He thought: "Now [people] will reproach me, saying: 'This wicked man had cow-food given to delicate brahmins, and they, unable to swallow it, died.'" Then he said to the servant girl: "Go quickly, remove the food from their bowls and serve them fine rice of various excellent flavors." She did so. The merchant summoned the people who had entered the street and said: "I had food given to these brahmins according to my own manner of eating. These men, out of greed, made large mouthfuls and while eating, got them stuck in their throats and died. Know that I am blameless." Having said this, he gathered the crowd. When the great crowd had gathered, the brahmins stood up, looked at the crowd and said: "Behold this merchant's falsehood! He says, 'I had my own eating-food given to them,' but first he gave us cow-food, and only when we were lying as if dead did he have this food served." Having said this, they spat out the food taken in their mouths onto the ground and showed it. The great crowd reproached the merchant: "Blind fool! You have destroyed your family lineage, you had the alms-hall burned, you had beggars seized by the neck and thrown out, and now, when giving food to these delicate brahmins, you have cow-food given to them! When you go to the next world, I suppose you will go with the wealth in your house tied around your neck!"

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko mahājanaṃ pucchi “jānātha, tumhe imasmiṃ gehe dhanaṃ kassa santaka”nti? “Na jānāmā”ti. “Imasmiṃ nagare asukakāle bārāṇasiyaṃ [M 4.0069] mahāseṭṭhi nāma dānasālaṃ kāretvā mahādānaṃ pavattayī”ti sutapubbaṃ tumhehīti. “Āma suṇāmā”ti. “Ahaṃ so seṭṭhi, dānaṃ datvā sakko devarājā hutvā puttopi me taṃ vaṃsaṃ avināsetvā dānaṃ datvā cando [V 4.0062] devaputto hutvā nibbatto, tassa putto sūriyo, tassa putto mātali, tassa putto pañcasikho gandhabbadevaputto hutvā nibbatto. Tesu ayaṃ cando, ayaṃ sūriyo, ayaṃ mātalisaṅgāhako, ayaṃ imassa [P 4.0069] pāpadhammassa pitā pañcasikho gandhabbadevaputto, evaṃ bahuguṇaṃ etaṃ dānaṃ nāma, kattabbameva kusalaṃ paṇḍitehī”ti kathentā mahājanassa kaṅkhacchedanatthaṃ ākāse uppatitvā mahantenānubhāvena mahantena parivārena jalamānasarīrā aṭṭhaṃsu, sakalanagaraṃ pajjalantaṃ viya ahosi. Sakko mahājanaṃ āmantetvā “mayaṃ attano dibbasampattiṃ pahāya āgacchantā imaṃ kulavaṃsanāsakaraṃ pāpadhammabilārakosiyaṃ nissāya āgatā, ayaṃ pāpadhammo attano kulavaṃsaṃ nāsetvā dānasālaṃ jhāpetvā yācake gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīharāpetvā amhākaṃ vaṃsaṃ samucchindi, ‘ayaṃ adānasīlo hutvā niraye nibbatteyyā’ti imassa anukampāya āgatāmhā”ti vatvā dānaguṇaṃ pakāsento mahājanassa dhammaṃ desesi. Bilārakosiyo sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ patiṭṭhapetvā “deva, ahaṃ ito paṭṭhāya porāṇakulavaṃsaṃ anāsāpetvā dānaṃ pavattessāmi, ajja ādiṃ katvā antamaso udakadantaponaṃ upādāya attano laddhāhāraṃ parassa adatvā na khādissāmī”ti sakkassa paṭiññaṃ adāsi. Sakko taṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhapetvā cattāro devaputte ādāya sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Sopi seṭṭhi yāvajīvaṃ dānaṃ datvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti.

At that moment, Sakka asked the great crowd: "Do you know to whom the wealth in this house belongs?" "We do not know," they replied. "In this city, at such a time in Bārāṇasī, have you heard before that a merchant named Mahāseṭṭhi had an alms-hall built and maintained a great gift?" "Yes, we have heard." "I am that merchant. Having given the gift, I became Sakka, king of the gods. My son also, without destroying that lineage, gave the gift and was born as the divine son Canda. His son was Sūriya, his son was Mātali, and his son was born as the celestial musician divine son Pañcasikha. Among them, this is Canda, this is Sūriya, this is Mātali the charioteer, and this is the father of this wicked man, Pañcasikha, the celestial musician divine son. Thus, giving has many benefits; indeed, merit should be performed by the wise." While saying this, to dispel the doubts of the great crowd, they rose into the air and by their great power, stood with glowing bodies; the whole city was as if ablaze. Sakka addressed the great crowd: "We, having left our divine splendor, have come here on account of this wicked Bilārakosiya who destroys the family lineage. This wicked man, having destroyed his own family lineage, burned the alms-hall, and having the beggars seized by the neck and driven out, cut off our lineage. Thinking, 'Let this man not be reborn in hell by being ungenerous,' we have come out of compassion for him." Having said this, proclaiming the virtue of giving, he taught the Dhamma to the great crowd. Bilārakosiya, placing his joined hands on his head, gave a promise to Sakka: "Lord, from now on, I will maintain the gift without destroying the ancient family lineage. From today onwards, even including a tooth-stick and water, I will not eat my obtained food without first giving to others." Sakka, having tamed him and made him free from the poison of greed, established him in the five precepts and, taking the four divine sons, went to his own place. That merchant also, having given gifts as long as he lived, was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-Three.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, ayaṃ bhikkhu pubbe assaddho ahosi kassaci kiñci adātā, ahaṃ pana naṃ dametvā dānaphalaṃ jānāpesiṃ, tameva cittaṃ bhavantaragatampi na jahātī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā seṭṭhi ayaṃ dānapatiko bhikkhu ahosi, cando sāriputto, sūriyo moggallāno, mātali kassapo, pañcasikho ānando, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said: 'Thus, monks, this monk was formerly faithless and gave nothing to anyone. But I, having tamed him, made him know the fruit of giving. That same mind of giving does not abandon him even when gone to another existence.' Having said this, he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the merchant was this monk who is a donor; Canda was Sāriputta; Sūriya was Moggallāna; Mātali was Kassapa; Pañcasikha was Ānanda; and Sakka was indeed myself.'

Bilārakosiyajātakavaṇṇanā dvādasamā.

The Commentary on the Bilārakosiya Jātaka, the twelfth.

[451] 13. Cakkavākajātakavaṇṇanā

[451] 13. The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka

Vaṇṇavā [P 4.0070][M 4.0070] abhirūposīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira cīvarādīhi atitto “kahaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ, kahaṃ nimantana”nti pariyesanto vicarati, āmisakathāyameva abhiramati. Athaññe pesalā bhikkhū tassānuggahena satthu ārocesuṃ. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu lolo”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti [V 4.0063] vutte “bhikkhu kasmā evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā lolo ahosi, lolabhāvo ca nāma pāpako, pubbepi tvaṃ lolabhāvaṃ nissāya bārāṇasiyaṃ hatthikuṇapādīhi atitto mahāaraññaṃ paviṭṭho”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'You are of fine complexion and handsome'—this the Teacher said while dwelling in Jetavana, with reference to a certain fickle monk. It is said that he was unsatisfied with robes and other requisites, and went about searching, 'Where is a meal for the Saṅgha? Where is an invitation?' He delighted only in talk concerning material gains. Then other virtuous monks, out of compassion for him, informed the Teacher. The Teacher had him summoned and asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are fickle?' When he replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' the Teacher said, 'Monk, why, after going forth in such a dispensation leading to liberation, have you become fickle? Fickleness is indeed evil. In the past, on account of your fickleness, being unsatisfied with elephant carcasses and such in Bārāṇasī, you entered the great forest.' Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko lolakāko bārāṇasiyaṃ hatthikuṇapādīhi atitto “araññaṃ nu kho kīdisa”nti araññaṃ gantvā tatthapi phalāphalehi asantuṭṭho gaṅgāya tīraṃ gantvā vicaranto jayampatike cakkavāke disvā “ime sakuṇā ativiya sobhanti, ime imasmiṃ gaṅgātīre bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khādanti maññe, ime paṭipucchitvā mayāpi imesaṃ bhojanaṃ gocaraṃ khāditvā vaṇṇavantena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tesaṃ avidūre nisīditvā cakkavākaṃ pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a greedy crow, unsatisfied with elephant carcasses and such in Bārāṇasī, thinking, 'What is the forest like?' went to the forest. There too, being discontented with various fruits, he went to the bank of the Ganges and, while wandering about, saw a pair of ruddy geese. 'These birds are exceedingly beautiful,' he thought. 'I suppose they eat much fish and meat on this bank of the Ganges. Having questioned them, it is proper for me to eat their food and range, and become of fine complexion.' Sitting not far from them and wishing to question the ruddy goose, he spoke these two verses:

135.

135.

“Vaṇṇavā abhirūposi, ghano sañjātarohito;

Cakkavāka surūposi, vippasannamukhindriyo.

'You are of fine complexion and handsome, with a firm body and a ruddy hue; O ruddy goose, you are beautiful, with a serene face and clear senses.'

136.

136.

“Pāṭhīnaṃ pāvusaṃ macchaṃ, balajaṃ muñjarohitaṃ;

Gaṅgāya tīre nisinno, evaṃ bhuñjasi bhojana”nti.

'Eating the Pāṭhīna and Pāvusa fish, the Balaja, the Muñja, and the Rohita; sitting on the bank of the Ganges, do you eat such food?'

Tattha ghanoti ghanasarīro. Sañjātarohitoti uttattasuvaṇṇaṃ viya suṭṭhujātarohitavaṇṇo. Pāṭhīnanti pāṭhīnanāmakaṃ pāsāṇamacchaṃ. Pāvusanti mahāmukhamacchaṃ, “pāhusa”ntipi pāṭho. Balajanti balajamacchaṃ. Muñjarohitanti muñjamacchañca rohitamacchañca. Evaṃ bhuñjasīti evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ maññe bhuñjasīti pucchati.

In this context, 'ghana' means having a firm body. 'Sañjātarohita' means having a well-produced ruddy color like refined gold. 'Pāṭhīna' refers to the stone-fish named Pāṭhīna. 'Pāvusa' means a large-mouthed fish; 'pāhusa' is also a reading. 'Balaja' is the Balaja fish. 'Muñjarohita' refers to the Muñja fish and the Rohita fish. 'Evaṃ bhuñjasi' means he asks, 'I suppose you eat such food?'

Cakkavāko [M 4.0071] tassa vacanaṃ paṭikkhipanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The ruddy goose, rejecting his words, spoke the third verse:

137.

137.

“Na [P 4.0071] vāhametaṃ bhuñjāmi, jaṅgalānodakāni vā;

Aññatra sevālapaṇakā, etaṃ me samma bhojana”nti.

'I do not eat this, nor meat from the land or the water; except for moss and duckweed, this, friend, is my food.'

Tassattho – ahaṃ samma, aññatra sevālā ca paṇakā ca sesāni jaṅgalāni vā odakāni vā maṃsāni ādāya etaṃ bhojanaṃ na bhuñjāmi, yaṃ panetaṃ sevālapaṇakaṃ, etaṃ me samma, bhojananti.

The meaning is: 'Friend, apart from moss and duckweed, I do not take and eat other meats from the land or the water as food. But as for this moss and duckweed, this, friend, is my food.'

Tato [V 4.0064] kāko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the crow spoke two verses:

138.

138.

“Na vāhametaṃ saddahāmi, cakkavākassa bhojanaṃ;

Ahampi samma bhuñjāmi, gāme loṇiyateliyaṃ.

'I do not believe this is the food of the ruddy goose. I too, friend, eat in the village food that is salty and oily.'

139.

139.

“Manussesu kataṃ bhattaṃ, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Na ca me tādiso vaṇṇo, cakkavāka yathā tuva”nti.

'Food prepared among humans, pure and seasoned with meat; yet I do not have such a complexion, O ruddy goose, as you do.'

Tattha yathā tuvanti yathā tuvaṃ sobhaggappatto sarīravaṇṇo, tādiso mayhaṃ vaṇṇo natthi, etena kāraṇena ahaṃ tava “sevālapaṇakaṃ mama bhojana”nti vadantassa vacanaṃ na saddahāmīti.

In this context, 'as you do' means: 'I do not have such a complexion as your body's complexion, which has attained such beauty.' For this reason, I do not believe your words when you say, 'Moss and duckweed are my food.'

Athassa cakkavāko dubbaṇṇakāraṇaṃ kathetvā dhammaṃ desento sesagāthā abhāsi –

Then the ruddy goose, explaining the cause of his bad complexion and teaching the Dhamma, spoke the remaining verses:

140.

140.

“Sampassaṃ attani veraṃ, hiṃsayaṃ mānusiṃ pajaṃ;

Utrasto ghasasī bhīto, tena vaṇṇo tavediso.

'Perceiving enmity towards yourself while harming the human populace, you eat terrified and in fear; that is why your complexion is such.'

141.

141.

“Sabbalokaviruddhosi, dhaṅka pāpena kammunā;

Laddho piṇḍo na pīṇeti, tena vaṇṇo tavediso.

'You are at odds with the whole world, O crow, because of your evil deeds; the morsel you obtain does not satisfy you; that is why your complexion is such.'

142.

142.

“Ahampi samma bhuñjāmi, ahiṃsaṃ sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Appossukko nirāsaṅkī, asoko akutobhayo.

'I too, friend, eat, while harming no living being; I am carefree, without apprehension, sorrowless, and fearless from any quarter.'

143.

143.

“So karassu ānubhāvaṃ, vītivattassu sīliyaṃ;

Ahiṃsāya cara loke, piyo hohisi maṃmiva.

'Therefore, exert yourself and transcend your bad habits; wander in the world with harmlessness, and you will be dear to others, just like me.'

144.

144.

“Yo [M 4.0072] na hanti na ghāteti, na jināti na jāpaye;

Mettaṃso sabbabhūtesu, veraṃ tassa na kenacī”ti.

'He who neither kills nor causes to kill, who neither robs nor causes to rob; who has a share of loving-kindness for all beings, has enmity with none.'

Tattha sampassanti samma kāka tvaṃ paresu uppannaṃ attani veracittaṃ sampassamāno mānusiṃ pajaṃ hiṃsanto viheṭhento. Utrastoti bhīto. Ghasasīti bhuñjasi. Tena te ediso bībhacchavaṇṇo [V 4.0065] jāto. Dhaṅkāti kākaṃ ālapati. Piṇḍoti bhojanaṃ. Ahiṃsaṃ sabbapāṇinanti ahaṃ pana sabbasatte ahiṃsanto [P 4.0072] bhuñjāmīti vadati. So karassu ānubhāvanti so tvampi vīriyaṃ karohi, attano sīliyasaṅkhātaṃ dussīlabhāvaṃ vītivattassu. Ahiṃsāyāti ahiṃsāya samannāgato hutvā loke cara. Piyo hohisi maṃmivāti evaṃ sante mayā sadisova lokassa piyo hohisi. Na jinātīti dhanajāniṃ na karoti. Na jāpayeti aññepi na kāreti. Mettaṃsoti mettakoṭṭhāso mettacitto. Na kenacīti kenaci ekasattenapi saddhiṃ tassa veraṃ nāma natthīti.

In this context, 'sampassaṃ' means: 'O friend crow, seeing clearly the hostile intention arisen in others towards yourself while harming and harassing the human populace.' 'Utrasto' means 'frightened.' 'Ghasasī' means 'you eat.' Because of that, such a repulsive color has arisen in you. 'Dhaṅka' is an address for a crow. 'Piṇḍo' means 'food.' 'Ahiṃsaṃ sabbapāṇinaṃ' means: 'But I eat without harming any beings,' he says. 'So karassu ānubhāvaṃ' means: 'You too should make an effort; transcend your immoral nature called "sīliya".' 'Ahiṃsāya' means: 'Wander in the world being endowed with harmlessness.' 'Piyo hohisi maṃmiva' means: 'If this is so, you will be dear to the world just like me.' 'Na jināti' means he does not cause loss of wealth. 'Na jāpaye' means he does not cause others to do so. 'Mettaṃso' means one with a share of loving-kindness or a mind of loving-kindness. 'Na kenaci' means there is no enmity with even a single being.

Tasmā sace lokassa piyo bhavituṃ icchasi, sabbaverehi viramāhīti evaṃ cakkavāko kākassa dhammaṃ desesi. Kāko “tumhe attano gocaraṃ mayhaṃ na kathetha, kā kā”ti vassanto uppatitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ ukkārabhūmiyaññeva otari.

'Therefore, if you wish to be dear to the world, refrain from all enmities.' Thus the ruddy shelduck taught the Dhamma to the crow. The crow, crying, 'You do not tell me your own feeding ground, caw caw!' flew up and landed right on the refuse heap in Bārāṇasī.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, cakkavākī rāhulamātā, cakkavāko pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of non-returning. At that time, the crow was the greedy monk, the female ruddy shelduck was Rāhula’s mother, and the male ruddy shelduck was indeed myself.

Cakkavākajātakavaṇṇanā terasamā.

The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka is the thirteenth.

[452] 14. Bhūripaññajātakavaṇṇanā

[452] 14. The Commentary on the Bhūripañña Jātaka

145-154. Saccaṃ kirāti idaṃ bhūripaññajātakaṃ mahāumaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

145-154. "It is true, indeed..." This Bhūripañña Jātaka will become manifest in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka (Jā 546).

Bhūripaññajātakavaṇṇanā cuddasamā.

The Commentary on the Bhūripañña Jātaka is the fourteenth.

[453] 15. Mahāmaṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā

[453] 15. The Commentary on the Mahāmaṅgala Jātaka

Kiṃsu [M 4.0073] naroti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahāmaṅgalasuttaṃ (khu. pā. 5.1 ādayo) ārabbha kathesi. Rājagahanagarasmiñhi kenacideva karaṇīyena santhāgāre sannipatitassa mahājanassa majjhe eko puriso “ajja me maṅgalakiriyā atthī”ti uṭṭhāya agamāsi. Aparo tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ ‘maṅgala’nti vatvāva gato, kiṃ etaṃ maṅgalaṃ nāmā”ti āha[V 4.0066]. Tamañño “abhimaṅgalarūpadassanaṃ maṅgalaṃ nāma. Ekacco hi kālasseva uṭṭhāya sabbasetaṃ usabhaṃ vā passati, gabbhinitthiṃ vā rohitamacchaṃ vā puṇṇaghaṭaṃ vā navanītaṃ vā gosappiṃ vā ahatavatthaṃ vā pāyāsaṃ vā passati, ito uttari maṅgalaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. Tena kathitaṃ ekacce “sukathita”nti abhinandiṃsu. Aparo “netaṃ [P 4.0073] maṅgalaṃ, sutaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ. Ekacco hi ‘puṇṇā’ti vadantānaṃ suṇāti, tathā ‘vaḍḍhā’ti ‘vaḍḍhamānā’ti suṇāti, ‘bhuñjā’ti ‘khādā’ti vadantānaṃ suṇāti, ito uttari maṅgalaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. Tena kathitampi ekacce “sukathita”nti abhinandiṃsu. Aparo “na etaṃ maṅgalaṃ, mutaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ. Ekacco hi kālasseva uṭṭhāya pathaviṃ āmasati, haritatiṇaṃ allagomayaṃ parisuddhasāṭakaṃ rohitamacchaṃ suvaṇṇarajatabhājanaṃ āmasati, ito uttari maṅgalaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. Tena kathitampi ekacce “sukathita”nti abhinandiṃsu. Evaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikā sutamaṅgalikā mutamaṅgalikāti tissopi parisā hutvā aññamaññaṃ saññāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, bhummadevatā ādiṃ katvā yāva brahmalokā “idaṃ maṅgala”nti tathato na jāniṃsu.

"What is auspicious for man?" This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Mahāmaṅgala Sutta. For in the city of Rājagaha, among the great multitude gathered in the assembly hall for some business, one man rose and said, "Today I have an auspicious act to perform," and left. Another, hearing his words, said, "This man said 'auspicious' and left. What is this thing called 'auspicious'?" Another replied, "Seeing an auspicious form is called 'auspicious.' For some, rising early in the morning, see a completely white bull, or a pregnant woman, or a red fish, or a full pot, or fresh butter, or cow’s ghee, or new cloth, or milk-rice—beyond this, there is nothing called 'auspicious.'" Some, hearing this, approved, saying, "Well spoken." Another said, "That is not 'auspicious.' What is heard is called 'auspicious.' For some hear others saying 'full,' or 'increase,' or 'growing,' or 'eat,' or 'consume'—beyond this, there is nothing called 'auspicious.'" Some, hearing this, also approved, saying, "Well spoken." Another said, "That is not 'auspicious.' What is sensed by touch is called 'auspicious.' For some, rising early in the morning, touch the earth, green grass, fresh cow dung, a very clean cloth, a red fish, or gold and silver vessels—beyond this, there is nothing called 'auspicious.'" Some, hearing this, also approved, saying, "Well spoken." Thus, the assembly, having become three groups—those who held to auspicious signs seen, auspicious signs heard, and auspicious signs sensed by touch—could not convince one another. From the earth deities up to the Brahmā world, none knew for certain, "This is auspicious."

Sakko cintesi “imaṃ maṅgalapañhaṃ sadevake loke aññatra bhagavatā añño kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā imaṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti. So rattibhāge satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha “bahū devā manussā cā”ti pañhaṃ pucchi. Athassa satthā dvādasahi gāthāhi aṭṭhatiṃsa mahāmaṅgalāni kathesi. Maṅgalasutte vinivaṭṭanteyeva koṭisatasahassamattā devatā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, sotāpannādīnaṃ gaṇanapatho natthi. Sakko maṅgalaṃ sutvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Satthārā maṅgale kathite sadevako loko “sukathita”nti abhinandi. Tadā [M 4.0074] dhammasabhāyaṃ tathāgatassa guṇakathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthā aññesaṃ avisayaṃ maṅgalapañhaṃ sadevakassa lokassa cittaṃ gahetvā kukkuccaṃ chinditvā gaganatale candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya kathesi, evaṃ mahāpañño, āvuso, tathāgato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, idāneva sambodhippattassa mama maṅgalapañhakathanaṃ, svāhaṃ bodhisattacariyaṃ carantopi devamanussānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chinditvā maṅgalapañhaṃ kathesi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Sakka thought: "In this world with its gods, there is no one other than the Blessed One capable of explaining this question on auspicious signs. I will approach the Blessed One and ask him this question." So, in the night, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and with hands reverently joined, asked the question, "Many gods and humans..." Then the Teacher explained the thirty-eight great auspicious signs in twelve verses. At the very moment the Discourse on Auspicious Signs was concluded, a hundred thousand koṭis of deities attained Arahantship, while the number of those who became stream-enterers and so on was beyond reckoning. Having heard the auspicious signs, Sakka returned to his own abode. When the Teacher had spoken on the auspicious signs, the world with its gods rejoiced, saying, "Well spoken!" At that time, in the Dhamma assembly, they began extolling the virtues of the Tathāgata: "Friends, the Teacher, grasping the minds of the world with its gods and resolving their doubts on the question of auspicious signs—a topic beyond others' reach—spoke as if raising the moon in the sky. Truly, friends, the Tathāgata is of great wisdom." When the Teacher arrived, he asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you seated together now?" Being told, "About this matter," he said, "It is not astonishing, monks, that I, having just now attained full enlightenment, should explain the question on auspicious signs. Even while practicing the Bodhisatta path, I dispelled the doubts of gods and humans and spoke on the question of auspicious signs." Having said this, he related a past event.

Atīte [P 4.0074] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāme vibhavasampannassa brāhmaṇassa kule nibbatti, “rakkhitakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo katadārapariggaho mātāpitūnaṃ accayena ratanavilokanaṃ katvā saṃviggamānaso mahādānaṃ pavattetvā kāme pahāya himavantapadese pabbajitvā jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā [V 4.0067] vanamūlaphalāhāro ekasmiṃ padese vāsaṃ kappesi. Anupubbenassa parivāro mahā ahosi, pañca antevāsikasatāni ahesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ te tāpasā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “ācariya, vassārattasamaye himavantato otaritvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadacārikaṃ gacchāma, evaṃ no sarīrañca thiraṃ bhavissati, jaṅghavihāro ca kato bhavissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Te “tena hi tumhe gacchatha, ahaṃ idheva vasissāmī”ti vutte taṃ vanditvā himavantā otaritvā cārikaṃ caramānā bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasiṃsu. Tesaṃ mahāsakkārasammāno ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ santhāgāre sannipatite mahājanakāye maṅgalapañho samuṭṭhāti. Sabbaṃ paccuppannavatthunayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a wealthy brahmin in a certain village. They named him 'Rakkhitakumāra.' When he came of age, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā, married, and after his parents passed away, he inspected his storehouse of wealth. Stirred in heart, he gave a great donation, renounced sensual pleasures, and went forth as an ascetic into the Himalayan region. There, he developed meditative attainments and psychic powers, living on wild roots and fruits in a certain place. Gradually, his following grew large, with five hundred disciples. One day, those ascetics approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and said, 'Teacher, during the rainy season, we wish to descend from the Himalayas and wander through the countryside to obtain salt and sour condiments. In this way, our bodies will become strong and firm, and we will have the benefit of a journey on foot.' When he said, 'Very well, you may go; I will remain here,' they paid homage to him, descended from the Himalayas, and while wandering, arrived in Bārāṇasī, where they stayed in the royal park. They received great honor and respect there. One day, a great crowd gathered in the assembly hall of Bārāṇasī, and a question about auspicious signs arose. The entire matter should be understood in the same way as the present story.

Tadā pana manussānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chinditvā maṅgalapañhaṃ kathetuṃ samatthaṃ apassanto mahājano uyyānaṃ gantvā isigaṇaṃ maṅgalapañhaṃ pucchi. Isayo rājānaṃ āmantetvā “mahārāja, mayaṃ etaṃ kathetuṃ na sakkhissāma, apica kho amhākaṃ ācariyo rakkhitatāpaso nāma mahāpañño himavante vasati, so sadevakassa lokassa cittaṃ gahetvā etaṃ maṅgalapañhaṃ kathessatī”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā “bhante, himavanto [M 4.0075] nāma dūre duggamova, na sakkhissāma mayaṃ tattha gantuṃ, sādhu vata tumheyeva ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā pucchitvā uggaṇhitvā punāgantvā amhākaṃ kathethā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā katapaṭisanthārā ācariyena rañño dhammikabhāve janapadacāritte ca pucchite taṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalādīnaṃ uppattiṃ ādito paṭṭhāya kathetvā [P 4.0075] rañño yācanāya ca attano pañhasavanatthaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā “sādhu no bhante, maṅgalapañhaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā kathethā”ti yāciṃsu. Tato jeṭṭhantevāsiko ācariyaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, unable to find anyone capable of resolving their doubts and explaining the question of auspicious signs, the great multitude went to the park and asked the group of ascetics. The ascetics addressed the king, saying, 'Great king, we are unable to explain this. However, our teacher named Rakkhita is a man of great wisdom who dwells in the Himalayas. He will satisfy the minds of the entire world with its gods and explain this question of auspicious signs.' The king replied, 'Venerable sirs, the Himalayas are far and difficult to reach. We cannot go there. It would be good if you yourselves went to your teacher, asked him, learned the answer, and then returned to explain it to us.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and went to their teacher. After paying respects and exchanging friendly greetings, they were asked by the teacher about the king’s righteousness and the conduct of the country. They then explained the origin of the debate over seen auspicious signs and other matters from the beginning. Revealing that they had come at the king’s request to hear the question answered, they pleaded, 'Venerable sir, please make the question of auspicious signs clear and explain it to us.' Thereupon, the senior disciple, wishing to question the teacher, spoke the first verse:

155.

155.

“Kiṃsu naro jappamadhicca kāle, kaṃ vā vijjaṃ katamaṃ vā sutānaṃ;

So macco asmiñca paramhi loke, kathaṃ karo sotthānena gutto”ti.

What recitation having studied at the proper time, or what knowledge, or which of the sacred traditions, how should a mortal act so as to be protected by well-being in this world and in the next?

Tattha kāleti maṅgalapatthanakāle. Vijjanti vedaṃ. Sutānanti sikkhitabbayuttakapariyattīnaṃ. Asmiñcāti ettha cāti nipātamattaṃ. Sotthānenāti sotthibhāvāvahena maṅgalena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ācariya, puriso maṅgalaṃ icchanto maṅgalakāle kiṃsu nāma jappanto tīsu vedesu kataraṃ vā vedaṃ kataraṃ vā sutānaṃ antare sutapariyattiṃ adhīyitvā so macco imasmiñca loke paramhi ca kathaṃ karo etesu jappādīsu kiṃ kena niyāmena karonto sotthānena niraparādhamaṅgalena gutto rakkhito hoti, taṃ ubhayalokahitaṃ gahetvā ṭhitamaṅgalaṃ amhākaṃ kathehī”ti.

Herein, 'at the time' means at the time of aspiring for an auspicious sign. 'Knowledge' means the Veda. 'Of the sacred traditions' means the scriptural texts suitable to be learned. 'And in this'—the word 'ca' here is a mere particle. 'By well-being' means by the auspicious sign that brings about a state of safety and purity. This is what was said: 'Teacher, a person desiring an auspicious sign, what recitation should he mutter at the proper time? Which of the three Vedas, or which scriptural text among the sacred traditions should he study? How should that mortal act, and by what principle among these recitations and so forth, so as to be guarded and protected by well-being, by a faultless auspicious sign? Please tell us that auspicious sign which brings benefit to both worlds.'

Evaṃ [V 4.0068] jeṭṭhantevāsikena maṅgalapañhaṃ puṭṭho mahāsatto devamanussānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindanto “idañcidañca maṅgala”nti buddhalīḷāya maṅgalaṃ kathento āha –

Thus questioned about the question of auspicious signs by the senior disciple, the Great Being, dispelling the doubts of gods and humans, and explaining the auspicious sign with the grace of a Buddha, saying, 'This and this is an auspicious sign,' spoke thus:

156.

156.

“Yassa [M 4.0076] devā pitaro ca sabbe, sarīsapā sabbabhūtāni cāpi;

Mettāya niccaṃ apacitāni honti, bhūtesu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhū”ti.

For whom the devas and all the ancestors, creeping things and all beings too, are constantly honored with loving-kindness—that, they say, is well-being among beings.

Tattha yassāti yassa puggalassa. Devāti bhummadeve ādiṃ katvā sabbepi kāmāvacaradevā. Pitaro cāti tatuttari rūpāvacarabrahmāno. Sarīsapāti dīghajātikā. Sabbabhūtāni cāpīti vuttāvasesāni ca sabbānipi bhūtāni. Mettāya niccaṃ apacitāni hontīti ete sabbe sattā dasadisāpharaṇavasena pavattāya appanāppattāya mettābhāvanāya apacitā honti. Bhūtesu veti taṃ tassa puggalassa sabbasattesu sotthānaṃ nirantaraṃ pavattaṃ niraparādhamaṅgalaṃ [P 4.0076] āhu. Mettāvihārī hi puggalo sabbesaṃ piyo hoti parūpakkamena avikopiyo. Iti so iminā maṅgalena rakkhito gopito hotīti.

Herein, 'for whom' means for which person. 'Devas' means all the sense-sphere devas, beginning with the earth-devas. 'And ancestors' means the form-sphere Brahmas beyond them. 'Creeping things' means long-bodied creatures. 'And all beings too' means all remaining beings. 'Are constantly honored with loving-kindness' means all these beings are honored through the development of loving-kindness that has reached absorption and proceeds by pervading the ten directions. 'Among beings' means they say that for that person, it is a faultless auspicious sign that proceeds uninterruptedly among all beings. For a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to all and cannot be harmed by the aggression of others. Thus, by this auspicious sign, one is guarded and protected.

Iti mahāsatto paṭhamaṃ maṅgalaṃ kathetvā dutiyādīni kathento –

Thus, having explained the first auspicious sign, the Great Being, explaining the second and the others, said:

157.

157.

“Yo sabbalokassa nivātavutti, itthīpumānaṃ sahadārakānaṃ;

Khantā duruttānamappaṭikūlavādī, adhivāsanaṃ sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

One who is of humble conduct toward all the world, toward women and men together with their children; who is patient with harsh words and does not speak contentiously—that forbearance, they say, is well-being.

158.

158.

“Yo nāvajānāti sahāyamatte, sippena kulyāhi dhanena jaccā;

Rucipañño atthakāle matīmā, sahāyesu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

One who does not despise companions on account of skill, family, wealth, or birth; who is of bright wisdom and discerning in time of need—that, they say, is well-being among companions.

159.

159.

“Mittāni ve yassa bhavanti santo, saṃvissatthā avisaṃvādakassa;

Na mittadubbhī saṃvibhāgī dhanena, mittesu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

For one who is not deceitful, whose friends are the virtuous and trusting; who is not a betrayer of friends and is a sharer of wealth—that, they say, is well-being among friends.

160.

160.

“Yassa [M 4.0077] bhariyā tulyavayā samaggā, anubbatā dhammakāmā pajātā;

Koliniyā sīlavatī patibbatā, dāresu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

One whose wife is of similar age, harmonious, compliant, devoted to the Dhamma, a mother of children, of good family, virtuous, and faithful to her husband—that, they say, is well-being in a wife.

161.

161.

“Yassa rājā bhūtapati yasassī, jānāti soceyyaṃ parakkamañca;

Advejjhatā suhadayaṃ mamanti, rājūsu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

When a glorious king, a lord of beings, knows one's purity and effort, and knowing 'his sincerity and good heart are toward me'—that, indeed, is what they call well-being among kings.

162.

162.

“Annañca [V 4.0069] pānañca dadāti saddho, mālañca gandhañca vilepanañca;

Pasannacitto anumodamāno, saggesu ve sotthānaṃ tadāhu.

When a faithful person, with a confident mind and rejoicing, gives food and drink, garlands, perfumes, and ointments—that, indeed, is what they call well-being leading to the heavens.

163.

163.

“Yamariyadhammena punanti vuddhā, ārādhitā samacariyāya santo;

Bahussutā [P 4.0077] isayo sīlavanto, arahantamajjhe sotthānaṃ tadāhū”ti. –

Whom the elders—the peaceful, learned, and virtuous sages—having been pleased by his right conduct, purify with the noble Dhamma—that, indeed, they say, is well-being in the midst of Arahants.

Imā gāthā abhāsi.

He spoke these verses.

Tattha nivātavuttīti muducittatāya sabbalokassa nīcavutti hoti. Khantā duruttānanti parehi vuttānaṃ duṭṭhavacanānaṃ adhivāsako hoti. Appaṭikūlavādīti “akkocchi maṃ, avadhi ma”nti yugaggāhaṃ akaronto anukūlameva vadati. Adhivāsananti idaṃ adhivāsanaṃ tassa sotthānaṃ niraparādhamaṅgalaṃ paṇḍitā vadanti.

Herein, 'humble conduct' means that due to gentleness of heart, one has a lowly demeanor toward the whole world. 'Patient with harsh words' means one is a forbearer of wicked words spoken by others. 'Not speaking contentiously' means not taking up the challenge of 'He abused me, he struck me,' but speaking only what is agreeable. 'Forbearance' means this forbearance is what the wise call his well-being, a faultless blessing.

Sahāyamatteti sahāye ca sahāyamatte ca. Tattha sahapaṃsukīḷitā sahāyā nāma, dasa dvādasa vassāni ekato vutthā sahāyamattā nāma, te sabbepi “ahaṃ sippavā, ime nisippā”ti evaṃ sippena vā “ahaṃ kulīno, ime na kulīnā”ti evaṃ kulasampattisaṅkhātāhi kulyāhi vā, “ahaṃ aḍḍho, ime duggatā”ti evaṃ dhanena vā, “ahaṃ jātisampanno, ime dujjātā”ti evaṃ jaccā vā nāvajānāti. Rucipaññoti sādhupañño sundarapañño[M 4.0078]. Atthakāleti kassacideva atthassa kāraṇassa uppannakāle. Matīmāti taṃ taṃ atthaṃ paricchinditvā vicāraṇasamatthatāya matimā hutvā te sahāye nāvajānāti. Sahāyesūti taṃ tassa anavajānanaṃ sahāyesu sotthānaṃ nāmāti porāṇakapaṇḍitā āhu. Tena hi so niraparādhamaṅgalena idhaloke ca paraloke ca gutto hoti. Tattha paṇḍite sahāye nissāya sotthibhāvo kusanāḷijātakena (jā. 1.1.121 ādayo) kathetabbo.

Herein, 'companions and associates' refers to both close friends and mere acquaintances. Among them, those who played in the dust together are called 'companions'; those who have lived together for ten or twelve years are called 'associates.' One does not despise any of them on account of skill, thinking, 'I am skilled, these are unskilled'; or on account of family accomplishment, thinking, 'I am of high family, these are not'; or on account of wealth, thinking, 'I am rich, these are poor'; or on account of birth, thinking, 'I am well-born, these are of low birth.' 'Of bright wisdom' means of good and excellent wisdom. 'In time of need' means at a time when some purpose or cause has arisen. 'Discerning' means being discerning through the ability to investigate and determine various matters, one does not despise those companions. 'Among companions' means the ancient wise say this non-despising is well-being among companions. Therefore, guarded by this faultless blessing, one is protected in this world and the next. Here, the state of well-being from relying on wise companions should be discussed with the Kusanāḷi Jātaka.

Santoti paṇḍitā sappurisā yassa mittāni bhavanti. Saṃvissatthāti gharaṃ pavisitvā icchiticchitasseva gahaṇavasena vissāsamāpannā. Avisaṃvādakassāti avisaṃvādanasīlassa. Na mittadubbhīti yo ca mittadubbhī na hoti. Saṃvibhāgī dhanenāti attano dhanena mittānaṃ saṃvibhāgaṃ karoti. Mittesūti mitte nissāya laddhabbaṃ tassa taṃ mittesu sotthānaṃ nāma hoti. So hi evarūpehi mittehi rakkhito sotthiṃ pāpuṇāti. Tattha mitte nissāya sotthibhāvo mahāukkusajātakādīhi (jā. 1.14.44 ādayo) kathetabbo.

Herein, 'the virtuous' means wise and good people who become one's friends. 'Trusting' means they have reached a state of confidence such that, having entered his house, they take whatever they desire. 'Of one who is not deceitful' means of one whose nature is not to deceive. 'Not a betrayer of friends' means one who does not betray a friend's trust. 'A sharer of wealth' means one who shares his own wealth with friends. 'Among friends' means that which is to be gained by relying on friends; for him, that is called well-being among friends. For, protected by such friends, he attains safety. Here, the state of well-being from relying on friends should be discussed with the Mahāukkusa Jātaka and others.

Tulyavayāti [V 4.0070] samānavayā. Samaggāti samaggavāsā. Anubbatāti anuvattitā. Dhammakāmāti tividhasucaritadhammaṃ roceti. Pajātāti vijāyinī, na vañjhā. Dāresūti etehi sīlaguṇehi samannāgate mātugāme gehe vasante sāmikassa sotthi hotīti paṇḍitā kathenti. Tattha sīlavantaṃ mātugāmaṃ nissāya sotthibhāvo maṇicorajātaka- (jā. 1.2.87 ādayo) sambūlajātaka- (jā. 1.16.297 ādayo) khaṇḍahālajātakehi (jā. 2.22.982 ādayo) kathetabbo.

Here, 'of equal age' means of the same age. 'Harmonious' means living together in harmony. 'Compliant' means following the husband's will. 'Fond of Dhamma' means one delights in the Dhamma of threefold good conduct. 'Prolific' means one who has given birth and is not barren. 'Among wives' means the wise say that when women endowed with these qualities of virtue dwell in the home, the husband attains well-being. Here, the state of well-being through reliance on a virtuous woman should be explained with the Maṇicora Jātaka, the Sambūla Jātaka, and the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka.

Soceyyanti sucibhāvaṃ. Advejjhatāti advejjhatāya na esa mayā saddhiṃ bhijjitvā dvidhā bhavissatīti evaṃ advejjhabhāvena yaṃ jānāti. Suhadayaṃ mamanti suhado ayaṃ mamanti ca yaṃ jānāti. Rājūsu veti evaṃ rājūsu sevakānaṃ sotthānaṃ nāmāti paṇḍitā kathenti. Dadāti [P 4.0078] saddhoti kammañca phalañca saddahitvā dadāti. Saggesu veti evaṃ sagge devaloke sotthānaṃ niraparādhamaṅgalanti paṇḍitā kathenti, taṃ petavatthuvimānavatthūhi vitthāretvā kathetabbaṃ.

Here, 'purity' means the state of being clean. 'Non-duplicity' means knowing, by the state of non-duplicity, 'He will not break with me and become of two minds.' 'My good-hearted one' means knowing, 'This person is my well-wisher.' 'Among kings' means the wise say this is called well-being for a servant among kings. 'One gives with faith' means one gives having faith in action and its result. 'Among heavens' means the wise say this is called well-being in the heavenly realm, a faultless blessing; this should be discussed in detail using the Petavatthu and Vimānavatthu.

Punanti [M 4.0079] vuddhāti yaṃ puggalaṃ ñāṇavuddhā ariyadhammena punanti parisodhenti. Samacariyāyāti sammāpaṭipattiyā. Bahussutāti paṭivedhabahussutā. Isayoti esitaguṇā. Sīlavantoti ariyasīlena samannāgatā. Arahantamajjheti arahantānaṃ majjhe paṭilabhitabbaṃ taṃ sotthānanti paṇḍitā kathenti. Arahanto hi attanā paṭividdhamaggaṃ ācikkhitvā paṭipādentā ārādhakaṃ puggalaṃ ariyamaggena punanti, sopi arahāva hoti.

Here, 'the wise purify' means those mature in knowledge purify and cleanse a person with the noble Dhamma. 'Through right conduct' means through right practice. 'Learned' means having the great learning of penetration. 'Sages' means those who have sought after virtues. 'Virtuous' means endowed with noble virtue. 'Among Arahants' means the wise say that what is to be obtained in the midst of Arahants is well-being. For Arahants, having themselves penetrated the path, by teaching it and guiding others in practice, purify the person who achieves success with the noble path, and he too becomes an Arahant.

Evaṃ mahāsatto arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto aṭṭhahi gāthāhi aṭṭha mahāmaṅgalāni kathetvā tesaññeva maṅgalānaṃ thutiṃ karonto osānagāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being, bringing the teaching to its peak with Arahantship, having explained the eight great blessings in eight verses, spoke the final verse, praising those very blessings:

164.

164.

“Etāni kho sotthānāni loke, viññuppasatthāni sukhudrayāni;

Tānīdha sevetha naro sapañño, na hi maṅgale kiñcanamatthi sacca”nti.

“These, indeed, are well-beings in the world, praised by the wise, bringing about happiness. A wise person should cultivate these here, for in auspicious signs there is no truth at all.”

Tattha na hi maṅgaleti tasmiṃ pana diṭṭhasutamutappabhede maṅgale kiñcanaṃ ekamaṅgalampi saccaṃ nāma natthi, nibbānameva panekaṃ paramatthasaccanti.

Here, 'for in auspicious signs there is no truth' means that regarding those auspicious signs classified as what is seen, heard, or sensed, there is no truth in any single one of them at all. Nibbāna alone is the single ultimate truth.

Isayo tāni maṅgalāni sutvā sattaṭṭhadivasaccayena ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā tattheva agamaṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā pucchi. Te tassa ācariyena kathitaniyāmena maṅgalapañhaṃ [V 4.0071] kathetvā himavantameva āgamaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya loke maṅgalaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Maṅgalesu vattitvā matamatā saggapathaṃ pūresuṃ. Bodhisatto cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā isigaṇaṃ ādāya brahmaloke nibbatti.

The seers, having heard those blessings, after seven or eight days, took leave of their teacher and went to that same city. The king went to them and asked. They explained the question of blessings in the manner taught by their teacher and then returned to the Himalayas. From that time onward, the blessings became well-known in the world. Those who lived rightly according to the blessings, upon dying, filled the heavenly realms. The Bodhisatta, having developed the four divine abodes, was reborn in the Brahma world together with the company of seers.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ maṅgalapañhaṃ kathesi”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā isigaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi[P 4.0079], maṅgalapañhapucchako jeṭṭhantevāsiko sāriputto, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, I explained the question of blessings.” Then he connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the company of seers was the Buddha's assembly, the senior disciple who asked the question about blessings was Sāriputta, and the teacher was none other than myself.”

Mahāmaṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā pannarasamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāmaṅgala Jātaka, the fifteenth.

[454] 16. Ghaṭapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā

[454] 16. The Commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka

Uṭṭhehi [M 4.0080] kaṇhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mataputtaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu maṭṭhakuṇḍalisadisameva. Idha pana satthā taṃ upāsakaṃ “kiṃ, upāsaka, socasī”ti vatvā “āma, bhante”nti vutte “upāsaka, porāṇakapaṇḍitā paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā mataputtaṃ nānusociṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Arise, Kaṇhā”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a householder whose son had died. The story is just like that of Maṭṭhakuṇḍali. Here, however, the Teacher said to that lay follower, “Why do you grieve, lay follower?” When he replied, “Yes, Bhante,” the Teacher said, “Lay follower, wise men of old, having heard the words of the wise, did not grieve for a dead son.” Being requested by him, he then related the past.

Atīte uttarapathe kaṃsabhoge asitañjananagare mahākaṃso nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa kaṃso ca, upakaṃso cāti dve puttā ahesuṃ, devagabbhā nāma ekā dhītā. Tassā jātadivase nemittakā brāhmaṇā “etissā kucchiyaṃ nibbattaputtā kaṃsagottaṃ kaṃsavaṃsaṃ nāsessantī”ti byākariṃsu. Rājā balavasinehena dhītaraṃ vināsetuṃ nāsakkhi, “bhātaro jānissantī”ti yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā kālamakāsi. Tasmiṃ kālakate kaṃso rājā ahosi, upakaṃso uparājā. Te cintayiṃsu “sace mayaṃ bhaginiṃ nāsessāma, gārayhā bhavissāma, etaṃ kassaci adatvā nissāmikaṃ katvā paṭijaggissāmā”ti. Te ekathūṇakaṃ pāsādaṃ kāretvā taṃ tattha vasāpesuṃ. Nandigopā nāma tassā paricārikā ahosi. Andhakaveṇḍo nāma dāso tassā sāmiko ārakkhamakāsi.

In the past, in the northern country, in the territory of the Kaṃsas, in the city of Asitañjana, there reigned a king named Mahākaṃsa. He had two sons, Kaṃsa and Upakaṃsa, and one daughter named Devagabbhā. On the day of her birth, soothsaying Brahmins predicted, “The sons born from her womb will destroy the Kaṃsa clan and the Kaṃsa lineage.” The king, due to strong affection, could not bring himself to destroy his daughter. Thinking, “The brothers will know what to do,” he lived out his life and passed away. After his death, Kaṃsa became king, and Upakaṃsa became the viceroy. They thought, “If we destroy our sister, we will be blamed. Let us not give her to anyone; let us keep her without a husband and take care of her.” They had a single-pillared palace built and made her reside there. A servant named Nandigopā was her attendant, and her husband, a slave named Andhakaveṇḍa, acted as guard.

Tadā uttaramadhurāya mahāsāgaro nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa sāgaro, upasāgaro cāti dve puttā ahesuṃ. Tesu pitu accayena sāgaro rājā ahosi, upasāgaro uparājā. So upakaṃsassa sahāyako ekācariyakule ekato uggahitasippo. So sāgarassa bhātu antepure [V 4.0072] dubbhitvā bhāyamāno palāyitvā kaṃsabhoge upakaṃsassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Upakaṃso taṃ rañño dassesi, rājā tassa [P 4.0080] mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. So rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto devagabbhāya nivāsaṃ ekathambhaṃ pāsādaṃ disvā “kasseso nivāso”ti pucchitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā devagabbhāya paṭibaddhacitto ahosi. Devagabbhāpi ekadivasaṃ taṃ upakaṃsena saddhiṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “ko eso”ti pucchitvā “mahāsāgarassa putto upasāgaro nāmā”ti nandigopāya [M 4.0081] santikā sutvā tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā ahosi. Upasāgaro nandigopāya lañjaṃ datvā “bhagini, sakkhissasi me devagabbhaṃ dassetu”nti āha. Sā “na etaṃ sāmi, garuka”nti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ devagabbhāya ārocesi. Sā pakatiyāva tasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā nandigopā upasāgarassa saññaṃ datvā rattibhāge taṃ pāsādaṃ āropesi. So devagabbhāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Atha nesaṃ punappunaṃ saṃvāsena devagabbhā gabbhaṃ paṭilabhi.

At that time, a king named Mahāsāgara ruled in Uttarā Madhurā. He had two sons: Sāgara and Upasāgara. After their father’s death, Sāgara became king, and Upasāgara became the viceroy. He was a companion of Upakaṃsa, and they had learned their arts together under the same teacher. Having offended in his brother Sāgara's inner apartments, Upasāgara, being afraid, fled to the territory of the Kaṃsas, to Upakaṃsa. Upakaṃsa presented him to the king, who granted him great honor. While going to attend upon the king, he saw the single-pillared palace, the dwelling of Devagabbhā. He asked, “Whose dwelling is this?” and upon hearing the reason, his heart became attached to Devagabbhā. One day, Devagabbhā also saw him coming to attend upon the king with Upakaṃsa and asked, “Who is this?” When she heard from Nandigopā that he was Upasāgara, the son of Mahāsāgara, her heart became drawn to him. Upasāgara gave a bribe to Nandigopā, saying, “Sister, will you be able to show me Devagabbhā?” She said, “This is not difficult, lord,” and informed Devagabbhā of the matter. Since Devagabbhā was already naturally inclined toward him, upon hearing this, she gladly accepted. Nandigopā then gave a signal to Upasāgara and led him up into the palace at night. He cohabited with Devagabbhā. Then, through their repeated cohabitation, Devagabbhā conceived.

Aparabhāge tassā gabbhapatiṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Bhātaro nandigopaṃ pucchiṃsu, sā abhayaṃ yācitvā taṃ antaraṃ kathesi. Te sutvā “bhaginiṃ nāsetuṃ na sakkā, sace dhītaraṃ vijāyissati, tampi na nāsessāma, sace pana putto bhavissati, nāsessāmā”ti cintetvā devagabbhaṃ upasāgarasseva adaṃsu. Sā paripuṇṇagabbhā dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Bhātaro sutvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā tassā “añjanadevī”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tesaṃ bhogavaḍḍhamānaṃ nāma bhogagāmaṃ adaṃsu. Upasāgaro devagabbhaṃ gahetvā bhogavaḍḍhamānagāme vasi. Devagabbhāya punapi gabbho patiṭṭhāsi, nandigopāpi taṃ divasameva gabbhaṃ paṭilabhi. Tāsu paripuṇṇagabbhāsu ekadivasameva devagabbhā puttaṃ vijāyi, nandigopā dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Devagabbhā puttassa vināsanabhayena puttaṃ nandigopāya rahassena pesetvā tassā dhītaraṃ āharāpesi. Tassā vijātabhāvaṃ bhātikānaṃ ārocesuṃ. Te “puttaṃ vijātā, dhītara”nti pucchitvā “dhītara”nti [P 4.0081] vutte “tena hi posethā”ti āhaṃsu. Etenupāyena devagabbhā dasa putte vijāyi, dasa dhītaro nandigopā vijāyi. Dasa puttā nandigopāya santike vaḍḍhanti, dhītaro devagabbhāya. Taṃ antaraṃ koci na jānāti. Devagabbhāya jeṭṭhaputto vāsudevo nāma ahosi, dutiyo baladevo, tatiyo candadevo, catuttho sūriyadevo, pañcamo aggidevo, chaṭṭho varuṇadevo, sattamo ajjuno, aṭṭhamo pajjuno, navamo ghaṭapaṇḍito, dasamo aṅkuro nāma ahosi. Te andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā dasa bhātikā ceṭakāti pākaṭā ahesuṃ.

Later, her pregnancy became evident. Her brothers questioned Nandigopā, and she, having requested immunity, revealed the secret. Hearing this, they thought, 'We cannot destroy our sister; if she gives birth to a daughter, we will not destroy her either, but if it is a son, we will destroy him.' So they gave Devagabbhā to Upasāgara alone. When her pregnancy was complete, she gave birth to a daughter. The brothers, overjoyed upon hearing this, named the niece Añjanadevī. They granted the couple a village for their maintenance called Bhogavaḍḍhamāna. Upasāgara took Devagabbhā and lived in the village of Bhogavaḍḍhamāna. Devagabbhā conceived again, and Nandigopā also conceived on that very day. When their pregnancies were complete, on the very same day Devagabbhā gave birth to a son and Nandigopā gave birth to a daughter. Fearing the destruction of her son, Devagabbhā secretly sent her son to Nandigopā and had Nandigopā’s daughter brought to her. They informed her brothers of the birth. When they asked, 'Did she give birth to a son or a daughter?' and were told, 'A daughter,' they said, 'In that case, raise her.' By this stratagem, Devagabbhā gave birth to ten sons, and Nandigopā gave birth to ten daughters. The ten sons grew up with Nandigopā, and the daughters with Devagabbhā. No one knew the secret. Devagabbhā’s eldest son was named Vāsudeva, the second Baladeva, the third Candadeva, the fourth Sūriyadeva, the fifth Aggideva, the sixth Varuṇadeva, the seventh Ajjuna, the eighth Pajjuno, the ninth Ghaṭapaṇḍita, and the tenth Aṅkura. These ten brothers, the sons of the slave Andhakaveṇḍa, became widely known as the Ceṭakas.

Te aparabhāge vuddhimanvāya thāmabalasampannā kakkhaḷā pharusā hutvā vilopaṃ karontā vicaranti[V 4.0073], rañño gacchante paṇṇākārepi vilumpanteva. Manussā [M 4.0082] sannipatitvā “andhakaveṇḍadāsaputtā dasa bhātikā raṭṭhaṃ vilumpantī”ti rājaṅgaṇe upakkosiṃsu. Rājā andhakaveṇḍaṃ pakkosāpetvā “kasmā puttehi vilopaṃ kārāpesī”ti tajjesi. Evaṃ dutiyampi tatiyampi manussehi upakkose kate rājā taṃ santajjesi. So maraṇabhayabhīto rājānaṃ abhayaṃ yācitvā “deva, ete na mayhaṃ puttā, upasāgarassa puttā”ti taṃ antaraṃ ārocesi. Rājā bhīto “kena te upāyena gaṇhāmā”ti amacce pucchitvā “ete, deva, mallayuddhavittakā, nagare yuddhaṃ kāretvā tattha ne yuddhamaṇḍalaṃ āgate gāhāpetvā māressāmā”ti vutte cārurañca, muṭṭhikañcāti dve malle posetvā “ito sattame divase yuddhaṃ bhavissatī”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe yuddhamaṇḍalaṃ sajjāpetvā akkhavāṭaṃ kāretvā yuddhamaṇḍalaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā dhajapaṭākaṃ bandhāpesi. Sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. Cakkāticakkaṃ mañcātimañcaṃ bandhitvā cāruramuṭṭhikā yuddhamaṇḍalaṃ āgantvā vaggantā gajjantā apphoṭentā vicariṃsu. Dasa bhātikāpi āgantvā rajakavīthiṃ vilumpitvā vaṇṇasāṭake nivāsetvā gandhāpaṇesu gandhaṃ[P 4.0082], mālākārāpaṇesu mālaṃ vilumpitvā vilittagattā māladhārino katakaṇṇapūrā vaggantā gajjantā apphoṭentā yuddhamaṇḍalaṃ pavisiṃsu.

In later times, having grown up and become strong and powerful, they became rough and cruel, roaming about plundering, even looting the king’s tribute as it was being brought. People gathered and complained in the royal court, saying, 'The ten brothers, the sons of the slave Andhakaveṇḍa, are plundering the kingdom.' The king summoned Andhakaveṇḍa and threatened him, saying, 'Why do you have your sons commit robbery?' When the people complained a second and a third time, the king threatened him again. Fearing for his life, Andhakaveṇḍa begged the king for immunity and revealed the secret: 'Your Majesty, these are not my sons—they are the sons of Upasāgara.' Terrified, the king asked his ministers, 'By what means can we capture them?' They replied, 'These men are fond of wrestling, O king. Let us arrange a wrestling match in the city, and when they enter the wrestling arena, we will have them seized and killed.' The king then retained two wrestlers, Cārura and Muṭṭhika, and had a drum beaten throughout the city to announce, 'On the seventh day from now, there will be a wrestling match.' He had the royal wrestling arena prepared, had an enclosure built, and had the wrestling arena adorned with banners and flags. The whole city was in an uproar. Tiered platforms were built, and Cārura and Muṭṭhika entered the wrestling arena, leaping, roaring, and clapping their hands. The ten brothers also arrived, having plundered the washermen's street and dressed in crimson robes. They stole perfumes from the perfume shops and garlands from the florists, and with their bodies anointed and adorned with garlands and ear ornaments, they entered the wrestling arena, leaping, roaring, and clapping their hands.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe cāruro apphoṭento vicarati. Baladevo taṃ disvā “na naṃ hatthena chupissāmī”ti hatthisālato mahantaṃ hatthiyottaṃ āharitvā vaggitvā gajjitvā yottaṃ khipitvā cāruraṃ udare veṭhetvā dve yottakoṭiyo ekato katvā vattetvā ukkhipitvā sīsamatthake bhametvā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā bahi akkhavāṭe khipi. Cārure mate rājā muṭṭhikamallaṃ āṇāpesi. So uṭṭhāya vaggitvā gajjitvā apphoṭesi. Baladevo taṃ pothetvā aṭṭhīni sañcuṇṇetvā “amallomhi, amallomhī”ti vadantameva “nāhaṃ tava mallabhāvaṃ vā amallabhāvaṃ vā jānāmī”ti hatthe gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā bahi akkhavāṭe khipi. Muṭṭhiko maranto “yakkho hutvā taṃ khādituṃ labhissāmī”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. So kālamattikaaṭaviyaṃ nāma yakkho hutvā nibbatti. Rājā “gaṇhatha dasa bhātike ceṭake”ti uṭṭhahi[M 4.0083]. Tasmiṃ khaṇe vāsudevo cakkaṃ khipi. Taṃ dvinnampi bhātikānaṃ sīsāni pātesi. Mahājano bhītatasito “avassayā no hothā”ti tesaṃ pādesu patitvā nipajji. Te dvepi mātule māretvā asitañjananagare rajjaṃ gahetvā mātāpitaro tattha katvā “sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti nikkhamitvā anupubbena kālayonakarañño nivāsaṃ ayujjhanagaraṃ gantvā taṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ parikhārukkhagahanaṃ viddhaṃsetvā pākāraṃ bhinditvā rājānaṃ [V 4.0074] gahetvā taṃ rajjaṃ attano hatthagataṃ katvā dvāravatiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tassa pana nagarassa ekato samuddo ekato pabbato, amanussapariggahitaṃ kira taṃ ahosi.

At that moment, Cārura was walking about, clapping his hands. Seeing him, Baladeva thought, 'I will not touch him with my hand.' So he brought a large elephant-rope from the elephant stable, and leaping and roaring, he threw the rope, wrapped it around Cārura’s belly, brought the two ends of the rope together and twisted them, lifted him up, whirled him over his head, slammed him to the ground, and threw him outside the enclosure. When Cārura was dead, the king ordered the wrestler Muṭṭhika forward. He got up, leaping, roaring, and clapping his hands. Baladeva struck him and crushed his bones. As Muṭṭhika was saying, 'I am not a wrestler! I am not a wrestler!' Baladeva, saying, 'I do not know whether you are a wrestler or not,' grabbed him by the hand, slammed him to the ground, ended his life, and threw him outside the enclosure. As Muṭṭhika was dying, he made a wish: 'May I become a yakkha and be able to devour him!' He was reborn as a yakkha in the Kālamattika forest. The king rose and said, 'Seize the ten Ceṭaka brothers!' At that moment, Vāsudeva threw his discus. It cut off the heads of both royal brothers. The terrified populace fell at their feet and lay prostrate, pleading, 'Be our refuge!' Having killed their two maternal uncles, they took the kingdom in the city of Asitañjana and established their parents there. Declaring, 'We will conquer all of Jambudīpa!' they set out and proceeded in due course to the city of Ayujjha, the residence of King Kālayonaka. They surrounded it, cleared the thicket of trees around the moat, broke through the wall, captured the king, took his kingdom into their own hands, and finally reached Dvāravatī. That city had the ocean on one side and a mountain on the other, and it was said to be guarded by non-human beings.

Tassa ārakkhaṃ gahetvā ṭhitayakkho paccāmitte disvā gadrabhavesena gadrabharavaṃ ravati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe yakkhānubhāvena [P 4.0083] sakalanagaraṃ uppatitvā mahāsamudde ekasmiṃ dīpake tiṭṭhati. Paccāmittesu gatesu punāgantvā sakaṭṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhāti. Tadāpi so gadrabho tesaṃ dasannaṃ bhātikānaṃ āgamanaṃ ñatvā gadrabharavaṃ ravi. Nagaraṃ uppatitvā dīpake patiṭṭhāya tesu nagaraṃ adisvā nivattantesu punāgantvā sakaṭṭhāne patiṭṭhāsi. Te puna nivattiṃsu, punapi gadrabho tatheva akāsi. Te dvāravatinagare rajjaṃ gaṇhituṃ asakkontā kaṇhadīpāyanassa isino santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, mayaṃ dvāravatiyaṃ rajjaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoma, ekaṃ no upāyaṃ karothā”ti pucchitvā “parikhāpiṭṭhe asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne eko gadrabho carati. So hi amitte disvā viravati, tasmiṃ khaṇe nagaraṃ uppatitvā gacchati, tumhe tassa pāde gaṇhatha, ayaṃ vo nipphajjanūpāyo”ti vutte tāpasaṃ vanditvā gantvā gadrabhassa pādesu gahetvā nipatitvā “sāmi, ṭhapetvā tumhe añño amhākaṃ avassayo natthi, amhākaṃ nagaraṃ gaṇhanakāle mā ravitthā”ti yāciṃsu. Gadrabho “na sakkā na viravituṃ, tumhe pana paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā cattāro janā mahantāni ayanaṅgalāni gahetvā catūsu nagaradvāresu mahante ayakhāṇuke bhūmiyaṃ ākoṭetvā nagarassa uppatanakāle naṅgalāni gahetvā naṅgalabaddhaṃ ayasaṅkhalikaṃ ayakhāṇuke bandheyyātha, nagaraṃ uppatituṃ na sakkhissatī”ti āha.

The yakkha who stood guard over it, seeing the enemies, took the form of a donkey and brayed like a donkey. At that moment, by the power of the yakkha, the entire city rose up and stood on a small island in the great ocean. When the enemies had gone, it returned and settled back in its original place. Then again, that donkey, knowing of the arrival of those ten brothers, brayed like a donkey. The city rose up and stood on the small island. When they, not seeing the city, turned back, it returned and settled in its original place. They turned back again, and again the donkey acted in the same way. Unable to seize the kingdom in Dvāravatī, they went to the ascetic Kaṇhadīpāyana, paid homage, and asked, 'Venerable sir, we are unable to take the kingdom of Dvāravatī. Please devise a means for us.' He replied, 'On the bank of the moat, in a certain place, a donkey roams. When it sees enemies, it brays. At that moment, the city rises up and departs. You must seize its feet—this will be your means of success.' Having paid homage to the ascetic, they went and, seizing the donkey’s feet, fell down before it. They pleaded, 'Master, other than you, we have no other refuge. When we are about to take the city, do not bray.' The donkey said, 'It is not possible not to bray. But you, arriving first, four men should take large iron plows and drive large iron stakes into the ground at the four city gates. When the city is about to rise, take the plows and bind the iron chain attached to the plows to the iron stakes. The city will not be able to rise.'

Te [M 4.0084] “sādhū”ti vatvā tasmiṃ aviravanteyeva naṅgalāni ādāya catūsu nagaradvāresu khāṇuke bhūmiyaṃ ākoṭetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe gadrabho viravi, nagaraṃ uppatitumārabhi. Catūsu dvāresu ṭhitā catūhi ayanaṅgalehi gahetvā naṅgalabaddhā ayasaṅkhalikā khāṇukesu bandhiṃsu, nagaraṃ uppatituṃ nāsakkhi. Dasa bhātikā tato nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājānaṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Evaṃ te sakalajambudīpe tesaṭṭhiyā [P 4.0084] nagarasahassesu sabbarājāno cakkena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā dvāravatiyaṃ vasamānā rajjaṃ dasa koṭṭhāse katvā vibhajiṃsu, bhaginiṃ pana añjanadeviṃ na sariṃsu. Tato puna “ekādasa koṭṭhāse karomā”ti vutte aṅkuro “mama koṭṭhāsaṃ tassā detha, ahaṃ vohāraṃ katvā jīvissāmi, kevalaṃ tumhe attano janapade mayhaṃ suṅkaṃ vissajjethā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tassa koṭṭhāsaṃ bhaginiyā datvā saddhiṃ tāya nava rājāno dvāravatiyaṃ vasiṃsu. Aṅkuro pana vaṇijjamakāsi. Evaṃ tesu aparāparaṃ puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamānesu addhāne gate mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu.

Saying, 'Good,' they took the plows while it was not braying, drove stakes into the ground at the four city gates, and stood ready. At that moment, the donkey brayed, and the city began to rise. Those stationed at the four gates took the four iron plows and bound the iron chains attached to the plows to the stakes; the city was unable to rise. The ten brothers then entered the city, killed the king, and seized the kingdom. Thus, having brought all the kings in the sixty-three thousand cities throughout Jambudīpa to the end of their lives with their wheel-weapon, they resided in Dvāravatī and divided the kingdom into ten shares, but they did not remember their sister, Añjanadevī. Then, when it was said, 'Let us make eleven shares,' Aṅkura said, 'Give my share to her; I will make a living through trade. You must only remit the taxes for me in your own territories.' They agreed, saying, 'Good,' and gave his share to their sister. The nine kings then lived with her in Dvāravatī, while Aṅkura engaged in trade. Thus, as time passed and they prospered with sons and daughters, their parents died.

Tadā [V 4.0075] kira manussānaṃ vīsativassasahassāyukakālo ahosi. Tadā vāsudevamahārājassa eko putto kālamakāsi. Rājā sokapareto sabbakiccāni pahāya mañcassa aṭaniṃ pariggahetvā vilapanto nipajji. Tasmiṃ kāle ghaṭapaṇḍito cintesi “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño koci mama bhātu sokaṃ harituṃ samattho nāma natthi, upāyenassa sokaṃ harissāmī”ti. So ummattakavesaṃ gahetvā “sasaṃ me detha, sasaṃ me dethā”ti ākāsaṃ ullokento sakalanagaraṃ vicari. “Ghaṭapaṇḍito ummattako jāto”ti sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. Tasmiṃ kāle rohiṇeyyo nāma amacco vāsudevarañño santikaṃ gantvā tena saddhiṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, it is said, the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years. Then, a son of the great king Vāsudeva died. The king, overcome with grief, abandoned all his duties, and grasping the frame of his bed, lay down lamenting. At that time, Ghaṭapaṇ胆ita thought, 'Except for me, there is no one else capable of removing my brother's sorrow. I will remove his grief by some stratagem.' He took on the guise of a madman and, looking up at the sky, wandered through the entire city, crying, 'Give me a hare! Give me a hare!' The whole city was in an uproar, saying, 'Ghaṭapaṇḍita has gone mad!' At that time, a minister named Rohiṇeyya went to King Vāsudeva and, initiating a conversation with him, spoke the first verse:

165.

165.

“Uṭṭhehi kaṇha kiṃ sesi, ko attho supanena te;

Yopi tuyhaṃ sako bhātā, hadayaṃ cakkhu ca dakkhiṇaṃ;

Tassa vātā balīyanti, ghaṭo jappati kesavā”ti.

"Arise, Kaṇha, why do you lie down? What is the use of sleep to you? He who is your own brother, your very heart and right eye—for him the winds grow strong; Ghaṭa babbles, O Kesava."

Tattha [M 4.0085] kaṇhāti gottenālapati, kaṇhāyanagotto kiresa. Ko atthoti katarā nāma vaḍḍhi. Hadayaṃ cakkhu ca dakkhiṇanti hadayena ceva dakkhiṇacakkhunā ca samānoti attho. Tassa vātā balīyantīti tassa hadayaṃ apasmāravātā avattharantīti attho. Jappatīti “sasaṃ me dethā”ti vippalapati. Kesavāti so kira kesasobhanatāya “kesavā”ti paññāyittha, tena taṃ nāmenālapati.

Herein, 'Kaṇha': he addresses him by his clan name; it is said he is of the Kaṇhāyana clan. 'Ko attho' means 'what benefit?'. 'Hadayaṃ cakkhu ca dakkhiṇaṃ' means he is like the heart and the right eye. 'Tassa vātā balīyanti' means winds of epilepsy overwhelm his heart. 'Jappati' means he raves, 'Give me a hare!' 'Kesava': it is said he was known as 'Kesava' because of the beauty of his hair; thus he addresses him by that name.

Evaṃ [P 4.0085] amaccena vutte tassa ummattakabhāvaṃ ñatvā satthā abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

When the minister had spoken thus, the Teacher, knowing his state of madness, having become fully enlightened, spoke the second verse:

166.

166.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, rohiṇeyyassa kesavo;

Taramānarūpo vuṭṭhāsi, bhātusokena aṭṭito”ti.

"Having heard that speech of Rohiṇeyya, Kesava, afflicted by sorrow for his brother, rose up in haste."

Rājā uṭṭhāya sīghaṃ pāsādā otaritvā ghaṭapaṇḍitassa santikaṃ gantvā ubhosu hatthesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king rose quickly, descended from the palace, approached Ghaṭapaṇḍita, firmly grasped both his hands, and while conversing with him, spoke the third verse:

167.

167.

“Kiṃ nu ummattarūpova, kevalaṃ dvārakaṃ imaṃ;

Saso sasoti lapasi, ko nu te sasamāharī”ti.

"Why, like one who is mad, do you wander through this entire Dvārakā, muttering, 'A hare, a hare'? Who, then, has taken your hare?"

Tattha [V 4.0076] kevalaṃ dvārakaṃ imanti kasmā ummattako viya hutvā sakalaṃ imaṃ dvāravatinagaraṃ vicaranto “saso saso”ti lapasi. Ko tava sasaṃ hari, kena te saso gahitoti pucchati.

Herein, 'this entire Dvārakā' means: 'Why, like a madman, do you wander throughout this entire city of Dvāravatī, muttering, "A hare, a hare"?' He asks: 'Who took your hare? By whom was your hare seized?'

So raññā evaṃ vuttepi punappunaṃ tadeva vacanaṃ vadati. Rājā puna dve gāthā abhāsi –

Even though the king spoke thus, he repeated the same words again and again. The king spoke two further verses:

168.

168.

“Sovaṇṇamayaṃ maṇīmayaṃ, lohamayaṃ atha rūpiyāmayaṃ;

Saṅkhasilāpavāḷamayaṃ, kārayissāmi te sasaṃ.
