"Be it made of gold or jewels, of bronze or of silver, or made of conch, crystal, or coral, I will have a hare made for you."

169.

169.

“Santi aññepi sasakā, araññe vanagocarā;

Tepi te ānayissāmi, kīdisaṃ sasamicchasī”ti.

"There are other hares, too, that roam the forest wilderness; those also I will bring for you. What kind of hare do you desire?"

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – tesu suvaṇṇamayādīsu yaṃ icchasi, taṃ vada, ahaṃ te kāretvā dassāmi, athāpi te na rocesi, aññepi araññe [M 4.0086] vanagocarā sasakā atthi, tepi te ānayissāmi, vada bhadramukha, kīdisaṃ sasamicchasīti.

Herein, this is the meaning in brief: Among those made of gold and so on, whichever you desire, say so; I will have it made and given to you. Or if these do not please you, there are other hares that roam the forest wilderness; those also I will bring for you. Speak, good sir, what kind of hare do you desire?

Rañño kathaṃ sutvā ghaṭapaṇḍito chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard the king's words, Ghaṭapaṇḍita spoke the sixth verse:

170.

170.

“Na cāhamete icchāmi, ye sasā pathavissitā;

Candato sasamicchāmi, taṃ me ohara kesavā”ti.

"I do not desire these hares that are on the earth; I desire the hare from the moon; bring that down for me, O Kesava."

Tattha oharāti otārehi.

Herein, 'ohara' means 'bring down'.

Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “nissaṃsayaṃ me bhātā ummattakova jāto”ti domanassappatto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, the king became distressed, thinking, 'Without a doubt, my brother has become like a madman,' and spoke the seventh verse:

171.

171.

“So [P 4.0086] nūna madhuraṃ ñāti, jīvitaṃ vijahissasi;

Apatthiyaṃ yo patthayasi, candato sasamicchasī”ti.

"Surely, kinsman, you will give up your sweet life, for you desire what should not be desired: you desire the hare from the moon."

Tattha [V 4.0077] ñātīti kaniṭṭhaṃ ālapanto āha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “tāta, mayhaṃ piyañāti so tvaṃ nūna atimadhuraṃ attano jīvitaṃ vijahissasi, yo apatthetabbaṃ patthayasī”ti.

Herein, 'kinsman' means he spoke addressing his younger brother. This is what was said: 'Dear one, you who are my beloved kinsman will surely give up your own very sweet life, since you desire that which is not to be desired.'

Ghaṭapaṇḍito rañño vacanaṃ sutvā niccalo ṭhatvā “bhātika, tvaṃ candato sasakaṃ patthentassa taṃ alabhitvā jīvitakkhayabhāvaṃ jānanto kiṃ kāraṇā mataputtaṃ anusocasī”ti vatvā aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Ghaṭapaṇḍita, having heard the king's words, stood motionless and said, "Brother, knowing that one who desires a hare from the moon, and not obtaining it, thereby meets with the destruction of life, for what reason do you grieve for your dead son?" Then he spoke the eighth verse:

172.

172.

“Evaṃ ce kaṇha jānāsi, yadaññamanusāsasi;

Kasmā pure mataṃ puttaṃ, ajjāpi manusocasī”ti.

"If you know this, Kaṇha, as you instruct others, why do you still grieve today for a son who died in the past?"

Tattha evanti idaṃ alabbhaneyyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na patthetabbanti yadi evaṃ jānāsi. Yadaññamanusāsasīti evaṃ jānantova yadi aññaṃ anusāsasīti attho. Pureti atha kasmā ito catumāsamatthake mataputtaṃ ajjāpi anusocasīti vadati.

Here, 'evaṃ' means: 'this is a state impossible to obtain, not to be desired'—if you know it thus. 'Yadaññamanusāsasi' means: 'if you instruct another, knowing thus.' Regarding 'pure', he says: 'then why do you still grieve today for a son who died four months ago?'

Evaṃ so antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitakova “bhātika, ahaṃ tāva paññāyamānaṃ patthemi, tvaṃ pana apaññāyamānassa socasī”ti vatvā tassa dhammaṃ desento puna dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, standing in the middle of the street, he said, "Brother, I am seeking one who is discernible, but you grieve for one who is indiscernible." Then, teaching him the Dhamma, he spoke two further verses:

173.

173.

“Yaṃ [M 4.0087] na labbhā manussena, amanussena vā puna;

Jāto me mā marī putto, kuto labbhā alabbhiyaṃ.

"That which cannot be obtained by a human being, nor again by a non-human being—'May my son who is born not die'—how can the unobtainable be obtained?"

174.

174.

“Na mantā mūlabhesajjā, osadhehi dhanena vā;

Sakkā ānayituṃ kaṇha, yaṃ petamanusocasī”ti.

"Not by spells, nor by root medicines, nor by herbs, nor by wealth is it possible, Kaṇha, to bring back the deceased for whom you grieve."

Tattha yanti bhātika yaṃ evaṃ jāto me putto mā marīti manussena vā devena vā puna na labbhā na sakkā laddhuṃ, taṃ tvaṃ patthesi, tadetaṃ kuto labbhā kena kāraṇena sakkā laddhuṃ, na sakkāti dīpeti. Kasmā? Yasmā alabbhiyaṃ, alabbhaneyyaṭṭhānañhi nāmetanti attho. Mantāti mantapayogena. Mūlabhesajjāti mūlabhesajjena. Osadhehīti nānāvidhosadhehi. Dhanena vāti koṭisatasaṅkhyenapi dhanena vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yaṃ tvaṃ petamanusocasi, taṃ etehi mantapayogādīhi ānetuṃ na sakkā”ti.

Here, 'yaṃ' means: brother, that which is expressed as 'may my son who is born not die' cannot be obtained or achieved again by a human being or by a deva, yet that you desire. From where can this be obtained? By what cause can it be achieved? 'It cannot be'—this is made clear. Why? Because it is unobtainable; for it is, indeed, called an unobtainable state—this is the meaning. 'Mantā' means by the application of incantations. 'Mūlabhesajjā' means by root-based medicines. 'Osadhehi' means by various kinds of medicines. 'Dhanena vā' means even by wealth amounting to hundreds of millions. This is what was said: "The deceased for whom you grieve cannot be brought back by these means, such as the application of incantations."

Rājā [V 4.0078] taṃ sutvā “yuttaṃ, tāta, sallakkhitaṃ me, mama sokaharaṇatthāya tayā idaṃ kata”nti ghaṭapaṇḍitaṃ vaṇṇento catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the king said, "It is right, dear one, I have rightly discerned; you have done this to dispel my sorrow," and praising Ghaṭapaṇḍita, he spoke four verses:

175.

175.

“Yassa [P 4.0087] etādisā assu, amaccā purisapaṇḍitā;

Yathā nijjhāpaye ajja, ghaṭo purisapaṇḍito.

"Would that one had such ministers, wise sages, as Ghaṭa, the wise man, has enlightened me today."

176.

176.

“Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

"Alas, I who am burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee—he, drenching me as if with water, has extinguished all my distress."

177.

177.

“Abbahī vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

"Indeed, he has drawn out my dart, which was lodged in my heart; he who, for me, overwhelmed by sorrow, has removed the grief for my son."

178.

178.

“Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna māṇavā”ti.

"I am one whose dart has been drawn out, free from sorrow, untroubled. I neither grieve nor weep, having heard you, young man."

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya saṅkhepattho – yathā yena kāraṇena ajja maṃ puttasokaparetaṃ ghaṭo purisapaṇḍito sokaharaṇatthāya nijjhāpaye nijjhāpesi bodhesi. Yassa aññassapi etādisā purisapaṇḍitā amaccā assu, tassa kuto sokoti. Sesagāthā vuttatthāyeva.

Here, the concise meaning of the first verse is: Just as today Ghaṭa, the wise man, for the purpose of removing sorrow, enlightened, made understand, and awakened me, who was overwhelmed by grief for my son. If another person also had such wise men as ministers, whence could sorrow arise for them? The remaining verses have the meaning already stated.

Avasāne [M 4.0088] –

At the end:

179.

179.

“Evaṃ karonti sappaññā, ye honti anukampakā;

Nivattayanti sokamhā, ghaṭo jeṭṭhaṃva bhātara”nti. –

"Thus act the wise, who are compassionate; they turn one back from sorrow, as Ghaṭa did his elder brother."

Ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā uttānatthāyeva.

This verse of the Fully Enlightened One has a clear meaning.

Evaṃ ghaṭakumārena vītasoke kate vāsudeve rajjaṃ anusāsante dīghassa addhuno accayena dasabhātikaputtā kumārā cintayiṃsu “kaṇhadīpāyanaṃ ‘dibbacakkhuko’ti vadanti, vīmaṃsissāma tāva na”nti. Te ekaṃ daharakumāraṃ alaṅkaritvā gabbhiniākārena dassetvā udare masūrakaṃ bandhitvā tassa santikaṃ netvā “bhante, ayaṃ kumārikā kiṃ vijāyissatī”ti pucchiṃsu. Tāpaso “dasabhātikarājūnaṃ vināsakālo patto, mayhaṃ nu kho āyusaṅkhāro kīdiso [V 4.0079] hotī”ti olokento “ajjeva maraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “kumārā iminā tumhākaṃ ko attho”ti vatvā “kathetheva no, bhante”ti nibaddho “ayaṃ ito sattame divase khadiraghaṭikaṃ vijāyissati, tāya vāsudevakulaṃ nassissati, apica kho pana tumhe taṃ khadiraghaṭikaṃ gahetvā jhāpetvā chārikaṃ nadiyaṃ pakkhipeyyāthā”ti āha. Atha naṃ te “kūṭajaṭila, puriso vijāyanako nāma natthī”ti vatvā tantarajjukaṃ nāma kammakaraṇaṃ katvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpayiṃsu. Rājāno kumāre pakkosāpetvā “kiṃ kāraṇā tāpasaṃ mārayitthā”ti [P 4.0088] pucchitvā sabbaṃ sutvā bhītā tassa ārakkhaṃ datvā sattame divase tassa kucchito nikkhantaṃ khadiraghaṭikaṃ jhāpetvā chārikaṃ nadiyaṃ khipiṃsu. Sā nadiyā vuyhamānā mukhadvāre ekapasse laggi, tato erakaṃ nibbatti.

Thus, when Vāsudeva had been made free from sorrow by Prince Ghaṭa and was ruling the kingdom, after a long time had passed, the princes, the sons of the ten brothers, thought: "They say Kaṇhadīpāyana has the divine eye. Let us test him." They adorned a young boy, made him appear as a pregnant woman, tied a cushion to his belly, and brought him before the ascetic. They asked, "Venerable sir, what will this girl give birth to?" The ascetic, observing, "The time for the destruction of the ten brother-kings has come. What, then, is the measure of my own lifespan?" and realizing, "Death will come today," said, "Princes, what is your purpose in this?" Pressed by them, "Just tell us, venerable sir," he replied, "On the seventh day from now, this one will give birth to a khadira-wood club, and by it the lineage of Vāsudeva will perish. However, you should take that khadira-wood club, burn it, and throw the ashes into the river." Then they said, "Deceitful ascetic! There is no such thing as a man giving birth," and having performed a punishment called tantarajjuka, they ended his life right there. The kings summoned the princes and asked, "For what reason did you kill the ascetic?" Hearing everything, they became frightened and, placing the boy under guard, on the seventh day, when the khadira-wood club emerged from his belly, they burned it and threw the ashes into the river. Carried by the river, the ashes lodged on one side of the river mouth, and from there, eraka grass sprouted.

Athekadivasaṃ te rājāno “samuddakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti mukhadvāraṃ gantvā mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā alaṅkatamaṇḍape khādantā pivantā kīḷāvaseneva pavattahatthapādaparāmāsā dvidhā bhijjitvā mahākalahaṃ kariṃsu. Atheko aññaṃ muggaraṃ alabhanto erakavanato ekaṃ erakapattaṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ gahitamattameva khadiramusalaṃ ahosi. So tena mahājanaṃ pothesi[M 4.0089]. Athaññehi sabbehi gahitagahitaṃ khadiramusalameva ahosi. Te aññamaññaṃ paharitvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tesu mahāvināsaṃ vinassantesu vāsudevo ca baladevo ca bhaginī añjanadevī ca purohito cāti cattāro janā rathaṃ abhiruhitvā palāyiṃsu, sesā sabbepi vinaṭṭhā. Tepi cattāro rathena palāyantā kāḷamattikaaṭaviṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. So hi muṭṭhikamallo patthanaṃ katvā yakkho hutvā tattha nibbatto baladevassa āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā tattha gāmaṃ māpetvā mallavesaṃ gahetvā “ko yujjhitukāmo”ti vagganto gajjanto apphoṭento vicari. Baladevo taṃ disvāva “bhātika, ahaṃ iminā saddhiṃ yujjhissāmī”ti vatvā vāsudeve vārenteyeva rathā oruyha tassa santikaṃ gantvā vagganto gajjanto apphoṭesi. Atha naṃ so pasāritahattheyeva gahetvā mūlakandaṃ viya khādi. Vāsudevo tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhaginiñca purohitañca ādāya sabbarattiṃ gantvā sūriyodaye ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ patvā “āhāraṃ pacitvā āharathā”ti bhaginiñca purohitañca gāmaṃ pahiṇitvā sayaṃ ekasmiṃ gacchantare paṭicchanno nipajji.

Then one day, those kings thought, "Let us play a water game," and went to the river mouth. Having had a great pavilion built, they were eating and drinking in the decorated pavilion when, in the course of their play, they began to strike one another with hands and feet, split into two factions, and started a great brawl. One of them, not finding a club, grabbed a blade of eraka grass from a thicket. As soon as he took it, it became a khadira-wood club. With it, he struck the crowd. Then, whatever anyone else grabbed also became a khadira-wood club. They struck one another and met with great destruction. As they were being destroyed, four people—Vāsudeva, Baladeva, their sister Añjanadevī, and the chaplain—boarded a chariot and fled. All the rest perished. Those four, fleeing by chariot, reached the Black Clay Wilderness. A wrestler named Muṭṭhika, having made an aspiration and being reborn there as a yakkha, knew of Baladeva’s arrival. He created a village there, took on the guise of a wrestler, and was roaming about, challenging, roaring, and clapping his arms, saying, "Who wants to fight?" As soon as Baladeva saw him, he said, "Brother, I will fight with him," and though Vāsudeva tried to stop him, he descended from the chariot, went to him, and began to challenge, roar, and clap his arms. Then the yakkha seized him with outstretched hands and devoured him like a root bulb. Vāsudeva, realizing he was dead, took his sister and the chaplain and traveled all night. At sunrise, they reached a border village. Sending his sister and the chaplain into the village, saying, "Cook some food and bring it," he himself lay down, hidden in a thicket.

Atha naṃ jarā nāma eko luddako gacchaṃ calantaṃ disvā “sūkaro ettha bhavissatī”ti saññāya sattiṃ khipitvā pāde vijjhitvā “ko maṃ vijjhī”ti vutte manussassa viddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhīto palāyituṃ ārabhi[P 4.0089]. Rājā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā uṭṭhāya “mātula, mā bhāyi, ehī”ti pakkositvā āgataṃ “kosi nāma tva”nti pucchitvā “ahaṃ sāmi, jarā nāmā”ti [V 4.0080] vutte “jarāya viddho marissatīti kira maṃ porāṇā byākariṃsu, nissaṃsayaṃ ajja mayā maritabba”nti ñatvā “mātula, mā bhāyi, ehi pahāraṃ me bandhā”ti tena pahāramukhaṃ bandhāpetvā taṃ uyyojesi. Balavavedanā pavattiṃsu, itarehi ābhataṃ āhāraṃ paribhuñjituṃ nāsakkhi. Atha te āmantetvā “ajja ahaṃ marissāmi, tumhe pana sukhumālā aññaṃ kammaṃ katvā jīvituṃ na sakkhissatha, imaṃ vijjaṃ sikkhathā”ti ekaṃ vijjaṃ sikkhāpetvā te uyyojetvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Evaṃ añjanadeviṃ ṭhapetvā sabbeva vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

Then a hunter named Jarā, seeing a thicket moving and thinking, "There must be a boar here," threw a spear and pierced his foot. When the king cried out, "Who has pierced me?", the hunter, realizing that he had pierced a human, became frightened and began to flee. The king, re-establishing his mindfulness, rose and called out, "Uncle, do not be afraid, come here!" When he came, the king asked, "What is your name?" When he replied, "Master, I am named Jarā," the king, knowing, "The wise predicted that I would die pierced by Jarā; undoubtedly I must die today," said, "Uncle, do not be afraid; come and bind my wound." Having had him bind the opening of the wound, he dismissed him. Intense pain arose, and he was unable to eat the food brought by the others. Then he addressed them, saying, "Today I shall die. You, however, are delicate and will not be able to make a living by doing any other work; learn this art." After teaching them a certain art and dismissing them, he met the end of his life right there. Thus, with the exception of Añjanādevī, all of them perished.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “upāsaka, evaṃ porāṇakapaṇḍitā paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā attano puttasokaṃ hariṃsu, mā cintayī”ti vatvā [M 4.0090] saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rohiṇeyyo ānando ahosi, vāsudevo sāriputto, avasesā buddhaparisā, ghaṭapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, said, "Layman, thus did the wise men of old, having heard the words of the wise, dispel their sorrow for their son. Do not grieve." Having said this, he revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the layman was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, Rohiṇeyya was Ānanda, Vāsudeva was Sāriputta, the rest were the Buddha's assembly, and Ghaṭapaṇḍita was I myself.

Ghaṭapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā soḷasamā.

The Commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka, the Sixteenth.

Iti soḷasajātakapaṭimaṇḍitassa

Thus, of that which is adorned with sixteen Jātakas.

Dasakanipātajātakassa atthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Jātakas of the Book of Ten is concluded.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Recapitulation of the Jātakas:

Catudvāro kaṇhuposo, saṅkha bodhi dīpāyano;

Nigrodha takkala dhamma-pālo kukkuṭa kuṇḍalī;

Bilāra cakka bhūri ca, maṅgala ghaṭa soḷasa.

Catudvāra, Kaṇha, Saṅkha, Bodhi, Dīpāyana; Nigrodha, Takkala, Dhammapāla, Kukkuṭa, Kuṇḍalī; Bilāra, Cakka, Bhūri, Maṅgala, and Ghaṭa make sixteen.

Dasakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Ten is concluded.

11. Ekādasakanipāto

11. The Book of Eleven

[455] 1. Mātuposakajātakavaṇṇanā

[455] 1. The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Jātaka

Tassa [V 4.0081][P 4.0090][M 4.0091] nāgassa vippavāsenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu sāmajātakavatthusadisameva. Satthā pana bhikkhū āmantetvā “mā bhikkhave, etaṃ bhikkhuṃ ujjhāyittha, porāṇakapaṇḍitā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattāpi mātarā viyuttā sattāhaṃ nirāhāratāya sussamānā rājārahaṃ bhojanaṃ labhitvāpi ‘mātarā vinā na bhuñjissāmā’ti mātaraṃ disvāva gocaraṃ gaṇhiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītamāhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Jātaka concerning a monk who supported his mother, beginning with: 'Tassa nāgassa vippavāsena.' The story of the present is just like that of the Sāma Jātaka. But here, the Teacher addressed the monks, saying: 'Monks, do not find fault with this monk. Wise men of old, even when reborn in the animal realm, when separated from their mothers, languished for seven days without food. Even when they obtained food worthy of a king, they thought, "Without our mother, we will not eat," and they only took their food after seeing their mother.' Having said this, at their request, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā sabbaseto ahosi abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko lakkhaṇasampanno asītihatthisahassaparivāro. So jarājiṇṇaṃ mātaraṃ posesi, mātā panassa andhā. So madhuramadhurāni phalāphalāni hatthīnaṃ datvā mātu santikaṃ pesesi. Hatthī tassā adatvā attanāva khādanti. So pariggaṇhanto taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “yūthaṃ chaḍḍetvā mātarameva posessāmī”ti rattibhāge aññesaṃ hatthīnaṃ ajānantānaṃ mātaraṃ gahetvā caṇḍoraṇapabbatapādaṃ gantvā ekaṃ naḷiniṃ upanissāya ṭhitāya pabbataguhāyaṃ mātaraṃ ṭhapetvā posesi. Atheko bārāṇasivāsī vanacarako maggamūḷho disaṃ vavatthapetuṃ asakkonto mahantena [P 4.0091] saddena paridevi. Bodhisatto tassa saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ puriso anātho, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ esa mayi ṭhite idha vinasseyyā”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ bhayena palāyantaṃ disvā “ambho purisa, natthi te maṃ nissāya bhayaṃ, mā palāyi, kasmā tvaṃ paridevanto vicarasī”ti pucchitvā “sāmi, ahaṃ maggamūḷho, ajja me sattamo divaso”ti vutte “bho purisa, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ taṃ manussapathe ṭhapessāmī”ti taṃ attano piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā araññā nīharitvā nivatti. Sopi pāpo “nagaraṃ gantvā rañño ārocessāmī”ti rukkhasaññaṃ pabbatasaññaṃ karontova nikkhamitvā bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himalayan region as an elephant. He was completely white, beautiful, pleasing to behold, charming, endowed with auspicious marks, and had a retinue of eighty thousand elephants. He supported his aged and frail mother, who was blind. He would select sweet and delicious fruits and send them to his mother via other elephants. However, those elephants would eat the fruits themselves without giving them to her. Investigating this, he came to know what was happening and thought, 'I will abandon the herd and care for my mother alone.' In the middle of the night, without the other elephants knowing, he took his mother and went to the foot of Mount Caṇḍoraṇa. There, he placed his mother in a mountain cave situated near a lotus pond and cared for her. Then a certain forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī lost his way. Unable to determine his direction, he lamented with a great cry. The Bodhisatta heard his cry and thought, 'This man is helpless. It is not right that he should perish here while I am present.' He went to him, and seeing him fleeing in fear, said, 'Good man, there is no danger to you from me. Do not flee. Why do you wander about lamenting?' When the man said, 'Lord, I have lost my way; today is my seventh day,' the Bodhisatta said, 'Good man, do not be afraid. I will set you on the path to human habitation.' He had the man sit on his back, carried him out of the forest, and then turned back. But that wicked man, making note of the trees and mountains as he departed, went to Bārāṇasī, thinking, 'When I get to the city, I will inform the king.'

Tasmiṃ [V 4.0082][M 4.0092] kāle rañño maṅgalahatthī kālamakāsi. Rājā “sace kenaci katthaci opavayhaṃ kātuṃ yuttarūpo hatthī diṭṭho atthi, so ācikkhatū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. So puriso rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mayā, deva, tumhākaṃ opavayho bhavituṃ yuttarūpo sabbaseto sīlavā hatthirājā diṭṭho, ahaṃ maggaṃ dassessāmi, mayā saddhiṃ hatthācariye pesetvā taṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti “imaṃ maggadesakaṃ katvā araññaṃ gantvā iminā vuttaṃ hatthināgaṃ ānethā”ti tena saddhiṃ mahantena parivārena hatthācariyaṃ pesesi. So tena saddhiṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ naḷiniṃ pavisitvā gocaraṃ gaṇhantaṃ passi. Bodhisattopi hatthācariyaṃ disvā “idaṃ bhayaṃ na aññato uppannaṃ, tassa purisassa santikā uppannaṃ bhavissati, ahaṃ kho pana mahābalo hatthisahassampi viddhaṃsetuṃ samattho homi, kujjhitvā saraṭṭhakaṃ senāvāhanaṃ nāsetuṃ, sace pana kujjhissāmi, sīlaṃ me bhijjissati, tasmā ajja sattīhi koṭṭiyamānopi na kujjhissāmī”ti adhiṭṭhāya sīsaṃ nāmetvā niccalova aṭṭhāsi. Hatthācariyo padumasaraṃ otaritvā tassa lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “ehi puttā”ti rajatadāmasadisāya soṇḍāya gahetvā sattame divase bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi. Bodhisattamātā pana putte anāgacchante “putto me rājarājamahāmattādīhi nīto [P 4.0092] bhavissati, idāni tassa vippavāsena ayaṃ vanasaṇḍo vaḍḍhissatī”ti paridevamānā dve gāthā abhāsi –

At that time, the king’s state elephant died. The king had a drum beaten, proclaiming, 'If anyone anywhere has seen an elephant fit to be a royal mount, let him report it.' That man approached the king and said, 'Your Majesty, I have seen an all-white, virtuous elephant king, fit to be your royal mount. I will show the way. Send elephant trainers with me and have him captured.' The king said, 'Good,' and sent the chief elephant trainer with a great retinue along with him, saying, 'Taking this man as a guide, go to the forest and bring back the noble elephant he described.' The trainer went with him and saw the Bodhisatta entering a lotus pond to feed. The Bodhisatta, seeing the elephant trainer, thought, 'This danger has not arisen from anywhere else; it must have come from that man. I am so powerful that I am capable of destroying a thousand elephants, or of destroying a kingdom along with its army if I were to become angry. But if I become angry, my virtue will be broken. Therefore, today, even if I am pierced with spears, I will not become angry.' Having made this resolution, he lowered his head and stood perfectly still. The elephant trainer descended into the lotus lake, observed the perfection of his marks, and said, 'Come, my son.' Taking him by his trunk, which was like a silver chain, he led him away and reached Bārāṇasī on the seventh day. Meanwhile, as her son did not return, the Bodhisatta’s mother lamented, 'My son must have been taken by the king or royal ministers. Now, in his absence, this forest thicket will overgrow.' Lamenting, she spoke these two verses:

1.

1.

“Tassa nāgassa vippavāsena, virūḷho sallakī ca kuṭajā ca;

Kuruvindakaravīrā bhisasāmā ca, nivāte pupphitā ca kaṇikārā.

“Due to the absence of that noble elephant, the sallakī and kuṭaja trees have overgrown; the kuruvinda, karavīra, bhisa, and sāmā have grown, and the kaṇikāra trees have blossomed in a sheltered place.”

2.

2.

“Kocideva suvaṇṇakāyurā, nāgarājaṃ bharanti piṇḍena;

Yattha rājā rājakumāro vā, kavacamabhihessati achambhito”ti.

“Surely now some men with golden armlets feed the elephant king with morsels of food; in whose service the king or a prince, fearless, will strike through armor.”

Tattha [M 4.0093] virūḷhāti vaḍḍhitā nāma, natthettha saṃsayoti asaṃsayavasenevamāha. Sallakī ca kuṭajā cāti indasālarukkhā ca kuṭajarukkhā ca. Kuruvindakaravīrā bhisasāmā cāti kuruvindarukkhā ca karavīranāmakāni mahātiṇāni ca bhisāni ca sāmākāni cāti attho. Ete ca sabbe idāni vaḍḍhissantīti paridevati. Nivāteti pabbatapāde. Pupphitāti mama puttena sākhaṃ bhañjitvā akhādiyamānā kaṇikārāpi pupphitā bhavissantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kocidevāti katthacideva gāme vā nagare vā. Suvaṇṇakāyurāti suvaṇṇābharaṇā rājarājamahāmattā. Bharanti piṇḍenāti ajja mātuposakaṃ nāgarājaṃ rājārahassa bhojanassa suvaḍḍhitena piṇḍena posenti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ nāgarāje rājā nisīditvā. Kavacamabhihessatīti [V 4.0083] saṅgāmaṃ pavisitvā paccāmittānaṃ kavacaṃ abhihanissati bhindissati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yattha mama putte nisinno rājā vā rājakumāro vā achambhito hutvā sapattānaṃ kavacaṃ hanissati, taṃ me puttaṃ nāgarājānaṃ suvaṇṇābharaṇā ajja piṇḍena bharantī”ti.

There, ‘virūḷhā’ means grown, that is, increased; ‘there is no doubt here’—he says this with certainty. ‘Sallakī’ and ‘kuṭajā’ refer to indasāla trees and kuṭaja trees. ‘Kuruvindakaravīrā bhisasāmā’ means the kuruvinda trees, the great grasses called karavīra, lotus roots, and sāmāka grain—this is the meaning. He laments that all these will now grow. ‘Nivāte’ means at the foot of the mountain where the wind is still. ‘Pupphitā’ means that the kaṇikāra trees, no longer having their branches broken and eaten by my son, will now be in bloom—this is what is said. ‘Kocideva’ means in some place, in a village or a city. ‘Suvaṇṇakāyurā’ refers to the king's ministers adorned with golden ornaments. ‘Bharanti piṇḍena’ means: today they sustain the mother-supporting elephant king with a portion of food fit for a king. ‘Yattha’ means upon which elephant king the king sits. ‘Kavacamabhihessati’ means: having entered the battle, he will strike and shatter the armor of his enemies. This is what is said: ‘Mounted upon my son, the elephant king, the king or prince, being fearless, will strike the armor of his foes; today, those adorned with golden ornaments sustain him with a portion of food.’

Hatthācariyopi antarāmaggeva rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpesi. Hatthācariyo bodhisattaṃ katagandhaparibhaṇḍaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ hatthisālaṃ netvā vicitrasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā rañño ārocāpesi. Rājā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ ādāya gantvā bodhisattassa dāpesi. So “mātaraṃ vinā gocaraṃ na gaṇhissāmī”ti piṇḍaṃ na gaṇhi. Atha naṃ yācanto rājā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The elephant trainer sent a message to the king while still on the way. Hearing this, the king had the city adorned. The elephant trainer brought the Bodhisatta, fragrant with perfumes and fully decorated, to the elephant stable, had it surrounded with a colorful curtain, and then informed the king. The king, taking various choice foods, went and had them offered to the Bodhisatta. But thinking, “Without my mother, I will not take food,” he did not accept the morsel. Then the king, imploring him, spoke the third verse:

3.

3.

“Gaṇhāhi [P 4.0093] nāga kabaḷaṃ, mā nāga kisako bhava;

Bahūni rājakiccāni, tāni nāga karissasī”ti.

“Take the morsel, O elephant, do not become emaciated, O elephant; many are the king’s tasks, and those you, O elephant, will perform.”

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse:

4.

4.

“Sā nūnasā kapaṇikā, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti.

“Surely she is a wretched one, blind and without a guide; she strikes a stump with her foot, heading towards Mount Caṇḍoraṇa.”

Tattha sā nūnasāti mahārāja, nūna sā esā. Kapaṇikāti puttaviyogena kapaṇā. Khāṇunti tattha tattha patitaṃ rukkhakaliṅgaraṃ. Ghaṭṭetīti paridevamānā tattha tattha pādena pothentī nūna pādena hanati[M 4.0094]. Giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patīti caṇḍoraṇapabbatābhimukhī, pabbatapāde paripphandamānāti attho.

There, ‘sā nūnasā’ means, “Great King, surely that is she.” ‘Kapaṇikā’ means wretched due to separation from her son. ‘Khāṇu’ refers to fallen tree stumps scattered here and there. ‘Ghaṭṭeti’ means, “wailing, she must be striking them here and there with her foot; surely she strikes them with her foot.” ‘Giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī’ means heading towards Mount Caṇḍoraṇa, floundering about at the foot of the mountain—that is the meaning.

Atha naṃ pucchanto rājā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king, questioning him, spoke the fifth verse:

5.

5.

“Kā nu te sā mahānāga, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti.

“Who is she to you, O great elephant, blind and without a guide? She strikes a stump with her foot, heading towards Mount Caṇḍoraṇa.”

Bodhisatto [V 4.0084] chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta spoke the sixth verse:

6.

6.

“Mātā me sā mahārāja, andhā apariṇāyikā;

Khāṇuṃ pādena ghaṭṭeti, giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti.

“She is my mother, Great King, blind and without a guide; she strikes a stump with her foot, heading towards Mount Caṇḍoraṇa.”

Rājā chaṭṭhagāthāya tamatthaṃ sutvā muñcāpento sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having heard the meaning of that sixth verse and wishing to release him, spoke the seventh verse:

7.

7.

“Muñcathetaṃ mahānāgaṃ, yoyaṃ bharati mātaraṃ;

Sametu mātarā nāgo, saha sabbehi ñātibhī”ti.

“Release this great elephant, who supports his mother; let the elephant be reunited with his mother, together with all his relatives.”

Tattha yoyaṃ bharatīti ayaṃ nāgo “ahaṃ, mahārāja, andhaṃ mātaraṃ posemi, mayā vinā mayhaṃ mātā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissati, tāya vinā mayhaṃ issariyena attho natthi, ajja me mātu gocaraṃ alabhantiyā sattamo divaso”ti vadati, tasmā yo ayaṃ mātaraṃ bharati, etaṃ mahānāgaṃ khippaṃ muñcatha. Sabbehi ñātibhīti saddhiṃ esa mātarā sametu samāgacchatūti.

There, ‘yoyaṃ bharati’ means, “This elephant says, ‘Great King, I support my blind mother. Without me, my mother will meet her end. Without her, sovereignty is of no use to me. Today is the seventh day since my mother has obtained no food.’” Therefore, quickly release this great elephant who supports his mother. ‘Sabbehi ñātibhī’ means, “Let him be reunited and come together with his mother, together with all his relatives.”

Aṭṭhamanavamā abhisambuddhagāthā honti –

The eighth and ninth verses were spoken by the Teacher after his Enlightenment:

8.

8.

“Mutto ca bandhanā nāgo, muttamādāya kuñjaro;

Muhuttaṃ assāsayitvā, agamā yena pabbato.

“Freed from his bonds, the elephant, taking his freedom, the noble beast; after resting for a moment, he went to where the mountain was.”

9.

9.

“Tato [P 4.0094] so naḷiniṃ gantvā, sītaṃ kuñjarasevitaṃ;

Soṇḍāyūdakamāhatvā, mātaraṃ abhisiñcathā”ti.

“Then he went to the lotus pond, cool and frequented by elephants; drawing up water with his trunk, he sprinkled his mother.”

So kira nāgo bandhanā mutto thokaṃ vissamitvā rañño dasarājadhammagāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti ovādaṃ [M 4.0095] datvā mahājanena gandhamālādīhi pūjiyamāno nagarā nikkhamitvā tadaheva taṃ padumasaraṃ patvā “mama mātaraṃ gocaraṃ gāhāpetvāva sayaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti bahuṃ bhisamuḷālaṃ ādāya soṇḍapūraṃ udakaṃ gahetvā guhāleṇato nikkhamitvā guhādvāre nisinnāya mātuyā santikaṃ gantvā sattāhaṃ nirāhāratāya mātu sarīrassa phassapaṭilābhatthaṃ [V 4.0085] upari udakaṃ siñci, tamatthaṃ āvikaronto satthā dve gāthā abhāsi. Bodhisattassa mātāpi “devo vassatī”ti saññāya taṃ akkosantī dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

It is said that the elephant, once freed from bondage, rested briefly, taught the king the Dhamma with a verse on the Ten Royal Virtues, and advised him, saying, “Be diligent, great king.” Honored by the people with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he left the city and reached that very lotus pond that same day. Thinking, “I will only eat after I have made my mother take her food,” he gathered many lotus roots and stalks, filled his trunk with water, and emerged from the mountain cave. Approaching his mother, who was sitting at the cave entrance, he sprinkled water upon her to restore the sensation of touch to her body, which had been without nourishment for seven days. To make this meaning clear, the Teacher spoke these two verses. The Bodhisatta’s mother, thinking it was rain, scolded the sky and spoke the tenth verse:

10.

10.

“Koyaṃ anariyo devo, akālenapi vassati;

Gato me atrajo putto, yo mayhaṃ paricārako”ti.

“Who is this ignoble deva, raining out of season? Gone is my son, born of my breast, who was my attendant.”

Tattha atrajoti attato jāto.

There, ‘atrajo’ means born of one’s own body.

Atha naṃ samassāsento bodhisatto ekādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, comforting her, spoke the eleventh verse:

11.

11.

“Uṭṭhehi amma kiṃ sesi, āgato tyāhamatrajo;

Muttomhi kāsirājena, vedehena yasassinā”ti.

“Arise, mother, why do you lie there? I, your son, have come. I have been freed by the glorious King of Kāsi, the wise one.”

Tattha āgato tyāhanti āgato te ahaṃ. Vedehenāti ñāṇasampannena. Yasassināti mahāparivārena tena raññā maṅgalahatthibhāvāya gahitopi ahaṃ mutto, idāni tava santikaṃ āgato uṭṭhehi gocaraṃ gaṇhāhīti.

There, ‘āgato tyāhaṃ’ means I have come to you. ‘Vedehena’ means by one endowed with wisdom. ‘Yasassinā’ means by him with a great retinue. “Even though I was taken by that king to be the state elephant, I was released. Now I have come to you. Arise and take your food.”

Sā tuṭṭhamānasā rañño anumodanaṃ karontī osānagāthamāha –

With a joyful heart, expressing her appreciation for the king, she spoke the final verse:

12.

12.

“Ciraṃ jīvatu so rājā, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Yo me puttaṃ pamocesi, sadā vuddhāpacāyika”nti.

“Long live that king, the increaser of the Kāsi realm, who released my son, who is ever respectful to his elders.”

Tadā rājā bodhisattassa guṇe pasīditvā naḷiniyā avidūre gāmaṃ māpetvā bodhisattassa ca mātu cassa nibaddhaṃ vattaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Aparabhāge bodhisatto mātari kālakatāya tassā sarīraparihāraṃ katvā [P 4.0095] kāraṇḍakaassamapadaṃ nāma gato. Tasmiṃ pana ṭhāne himavantato otaritvā pañcasatā isayo vasiṃsu, taṃ vattaṃ tesaṃ adāsi. Rājā bodhisattassa samānarūpaṃ silāpaṭimaṃ kāretvā mahāsakkāraṃ pavattesi[M 4.0096]. Sakalajambudīpavāsino anusaṃvaccharaṃ sannipatitvā hatthimahaṃ nāma kariṃsu.

Then the king, pleased with the virtues of the Bodhisatta, had a village built not far from the lotus pond and established a regular provision for the Bodhisatta and his mother. Later, when his mother died, the Bodhisatta performed her funeral rites and went to the Kāraṇḍaka hermitage. At that place, five hundred sages who had come down from the Himalayas lived; he gave that provision to them. The king had a stone statue made in the likeness of the Bodhisatta and instituted great honor. The inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa, gathering every year, held a festival called the Elephant Festival.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne [V 4.0086] mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, pāpapuriso devadatto, hatthācariyo sāriputto, mātā hatthinī mahāmāyā, mātuposakanāgo pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and declared the Truths, identified the Birth Story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king was Ānanda, the evil man was Devadatta, the elephant trainer was Sāriputta, the mother elephant was Mahāmāyā, and the elephant king who supported his mother was I myself.

Mātuposakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first, the Commentary on the Mātuposaka Jātaka.

[456] 2. Juṇhajātakavaṇṇanā

[456] 2. The Commentary on the Juṇha Jātaka

Suṇohi mayhaṃ vacanaṃ janindāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ānandattherena laddhavare ārabbha kathesi. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi vīsati vassāni bhagavato anibaddhupaṭṭhākā ahesuṃ. Ekadā thero nāgasamālo, ekadā nāgito, ekadā upavāṇo, ekadā sunakkhatto, ekadā cundo, ekadā nando, ekadā sāgato, ekadā meghiyo bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Athekadivasaṃ bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi “bhikkhave, idānimhi mahallako, ekacce bhikkhū ‘iminā maggena gacchāmā’ti vutte aññena gacchanti, ekacce mayhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipanti, nibaddhupaṭṭhākaṃ me ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ jānāthā”ti. “Bhante, ahaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmi, ahaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti sirasi añjaliṃ katvā uṭṭhite sāriputtattherādayo “tumhākaṃ patthanā matthakaṃ pattā, ala”nti paṭikkhipi. Tato bhikkhū ānandattheraṃ “tvaṃ āvuso, upaṭṭhākaṭṭhānaṃ yācāhī”ti āhaṃsu. Thero “sace me bhante, bhagavā attanā laddhacīvaraṃ na dassati, piṇḍapātaṃ na dassati, ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasituṃ na dassati, maṃ gahetvā nimantanaṃ na gamissati, sace pana bhagavā mayā gahitaṃ nimantanaṃ gamissati, sace ahaṃ tiroraṭṭhā tirojanapadā bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgataṃ parisaṃ āgatakkhaṇeyeva dassetuṃ labhissāmi[P 4.0096], yadā me kaṅkhā uppajjati, tasmiṃ khaṇeyeva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ labhissāmi, sace yaṃ bhagavā mama parammukhā dhammaṃ katheti, taṃ āgantvā mayhaṃ kathessati, evāhaṃ [M 4.0097] bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti ime cattāro paṭikkhepe catasso ca āyācanāti aṭṭha vare yāci, bhagavāpissa adāsi.

‘Listen to my words, O lord of men’—this the Teacher told while staying at Jetavana, concerning the boons obtained by the Elder Ānanda. For the first twenty years after the Enlightenment, the Blessed One had no permanent attendant. At one time the Elder Nāgasamāla, at another Nāgita, at another Upavāṇa, at another Sunakkhatta, at another Cunda, at another Nanda, at another Sāgata, and at another Meghiya attended the Blessed One. Then one day, the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks, I am now old. Some monks, when told "Let us go by this path," go by another. Some drop my bowl and robe on the ground. Find me one monk to be a permanent attendant.’ ‘Venerable sir, I will attend you! I will attend you!’—so saying, the Elder Sāriputta and others rose, with hands clasped in reverence on their heads. But he declined them, saying, ‘Your aspirations have reached their goal; enough.’ Then the monks said to the Elder Ānanda: ‘Friend, you should request the position of attendant.’ The Elder replied: ‘Venerable sir, if the Blessed One will not give me a robe that he himself has received, nor give me almsfood, nor allow me to dwell in the same fragrant hut, nor take me along when he is invited; but if the Blessed One will go to an invitation accepted by me; if I may present to him any company of people who come from other kingdoms and districts to see the Blessed One at the very moment they arrive; if I may approach the Blessed One at the very moment a doubt arises in me; and if the Blessed One will repeat to me whatever Dhamma he teaches in my absence—then I will attend upon the Blessed One.’ He thus requested these eight boons—four rejections and four requests—and the Blessed One granted them to him.

So tato paṭṭhāya pañcavīsati vassāni nibaddhupaṭṭhāko ahosi. So pañcasu ṭhānesu etadagge ṭhapanaṃ patvā āgamasampadā, adhigamasampadā, pubbahetusampadā, attatthaparipucchāsampadā, titthavāsasampadā, yonisomanasikārasampadā, buddhūpanissayasampadāti imāhi sattahi sampadāhi samannāgato buddhassa santike aṭṭhavaradāyajjaṃ labhitvā buddhasāsane paññāto gaganamajjhe cando viya pākaṭo ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, tathāgato ānandattheraṃ [V 4.0087] varadānena santappesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ ānandaṃ varena santappesiṃ, pubbepāhaṃ yaṃ yaṃ esa yāci, taṃ taṃ adāsiṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

From then on, he served as a permanent attendant for twenty-five years. Having attained the foremost position in five respects and being endowed with these seven accomplishments: accomplishment in scripture, accomplishment in attainment, accomplishment through past causes, accomplishment in inquiring for his own benefit, accomplishment in dwelling in the Presence, accomplishment in wise attention, and accomplishment in having the Buddha as his support—having received the inheritance of the eight boons in the presence of the Buddha, he became renowned in the Buddha's Dispensation, as prominent as the moon in the midst of the sky. Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: ‘Friends, the Tathāgata pleased the Elder Ānanda by granting him boons.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?’ When they told him, he replied, ‘Not only now, monks, but in the past also, I pleased Ānanda with a boon. In the past also, whatever he asked for, I granted it.’ Then he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa putto juṇhakumāro nāma hutvā takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggahetvā ācariyassa anuyogaṃ datvā rattibhāge andhakāre ācariyassa gharā nikkhamitvā attano nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ vegena gacchanto aññataraṃ brāhmaṇaṃ bhikkhaṃ caritvā attano nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantaṃ apassanto bāhunā paharitvā tassa bhattapātiṃ bhindiṃ, brāhmaṇo patitvā viravi. Kumāro kāruññena nivattitvā taṃ hatthe gahetvā uṭṭhāpesi. Brāhmaṇo “tayā, tāta, mama bhikkhābhājanaṃ bhinnaṃ, bhattamūlaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Kumāro “brāhmaṇa, na dānāhaṃ tava bhattamūlaṃ dātuṃ sakkomi, ahaṃ kho pana kāsikarañño putto juṇhakumāro nāma, mayi rajje patiṭṭhite āgantvā maṃ dhanaṃ yāceyyāsī”ti vatvā niṭṭhitasippo ācariyaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā pitu sippaṃ dassesi. Pitā “jīvantena me putto diṭṭho, rājabhūtampi naṃ passissāmī”ti rajje abhisiñci. So [P 4.0097] juṇharājā nāma hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “idāni mama bhattamūlaṃ āharissāmī”ti bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājānaṃ alaṅkatanagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karontameva disvā ekasmiṃ unnatappadese ṭhito hatthaṃ pasāretvā jayāpesi. Atha naṃ rājā anoloketvāva atikkami. Brāhmaṇo tena adiṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his son, named Prince Juṇha. Having learned the arts in Takkasilā and having completed his revision with his teacher, he left the teacher’s house at night in the darkness. Hurrying back to his own dwelling, he did not see a certain brahmin who was returning to his own dwelling after going about for alms. Striking him with his arm, he broke the brahmin’s food bowl. The brahmin fell down and cried out. Moved by compassion, the prince turned back, took him by the hand, and helped him up. The brahmin said, “Dear boy, you have broken my alms bowl; give me the price of my meal.” The prince replied, “Brahmin, I cannot give you the price of your meal now. But I am Prince Juṇha, the son of the king of Kāsi. When I am established on the throne, come to me and ask for wealth.” Having said this, and having completed his training, he paid respects to his teacher and went to Benares, where he showed his skills to his father. His father thought, “I have seen my son alive; I shall also see him as king,” and had him consecrated on the throne. He became known as King Juṇha and ruled righteously. The brahmin, hearing of this, thought, “Now I shall get the price of my meal,” and went to Benares. Seeing the king making a ceremonial procession around the adorned city, he stood on an elevated spot, stretched out his hand, and hailed him with cries of victory. But the king passed by without even looking at him. Realizing he had not been noticed, the brahmin, wishing to initiate a conversation, spoke the first verse:

13.

13.

“Suṇohi [M 4.0098] mayhaṃ vacanaṃ janinda, atthena juṇhamhi idhānupatto;

Na brāhmaṇe addhike tiṭṭhamāne, gantabbamāhu dvipadinda seṭṭhā”ti.

“Listen to my words, O lord of men; I have come here to you, Juṇha, for a purpose. O best of men, lord of bipeds, the wise say one should not depart without looking when a brahmin traveler is standing by.”

Tattha juṇhamhīti mahārāja, tayi juṇhamhi ahaṃ ekena atthena idhānuppatto, na nikkāraṇā idhāgatomhīti dīpeti. Addhiketi addhānaṃ āgate. Gantabbanti taṃ addhikaṃ addhānamāgataṃ yācamānaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ anoloketvāva gantabbanti paṇḍitā na āhu na kathentīti.

Herein, ‘to you, Juṇha’ means, O great king, ‘I have come here to you, Juṇha, for a certain purpose, I have not come here without cause,’ so it is shown. ‘Traveler’ means one who has come on a long journey. ‘Should not depart’ means that the wise do not say or declare that one should depart without even looking at that traveler, the brahmin who has come on a journey and is making a request.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā hatthiṃ vajiraṅkusena niggahetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Upon hearing the brahmin's words, the king restrained his elephant with a goad and spoke the second verse:

14.

14.

“Suṇomi [V 4.0088] tiṭṭhāmi vadehi brahme, yenāsi atthena idhānupatto;

Kaṃ vā tvamatthaṃ mayi patthayāno, idhāgamo brahme tadiṅgha brūhī”ti.

“I listen, I stand—speak, O brahmin, for what purpose you have come here. What favor do you desire from me, having come here, O brahmin? Pray, tell me that.”

Tattha iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto.

Herein, ‘iṅgha’ is a particle in the sense of urging.

Tato paraṃ brāhmaṇassa ca rañño ca vacanapaṭivacanavasena sesagāthā kathitā –

Thereafter, the remaining verses were spoken by way of the exchange of words between the brahmin and the king:

15.

15.

“Dadāhi me gāmavarāni pañca, dāsīsataṃ satta gavaṃsatāni;

Parosahassañca suvaṇṇanikkhe, bhariyā ca me sādisī dve dadāhi.

“Give me five excellent villages, a hundred female slaves, seven hundred head of cattle, and more than a thousand gold coins; and give me two wives of similar birth to myself.”

16.

16.

“Tapo [P 4.0098] nu te brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpo, mantā nu te brāhmaṇa cittarūpā;

Yakkhā nu te assavā santi keci, atthaṃ vā me abhijānāsi kattaṃ.

“Is your asceticism, O brahmin, of a fearsome kind? Or are your mantras, O brahmin, of a wondrous kind? Do you have any obedient yakkhas? Or do you recognize some service done for me in the past?”

17.

17.

“Na [M 4.0099] me tapo atthi na cāpi mantā, yakkhāpi me assavā natthi keci;

Atthampi te nābhijānāmi kattaṃ, pubbe ca kho saṅgatimattamāsi.

“I have no asceticism, nor any mantras. Nor are there any obedient yakkhas for me. Nor do I recognize any service done for you. But indeed, there was just a meeting in the past.”

18.

18.

“Paṭhamaṃ idaṃ dassanaṃ jānato me, na tābhijānāmi ito puratthā;

Akkhāhi me pucchito etamatthaṃ, kadā kuhiṃ vā ahu saṅgamo no.

“To me, who recognizes you not, this is the first sight of you; I do not recognize you from before this. Being asked, explain this matter to me: when or where was our meeting?”

19.

19.

“Gandhārarājassa puramhi ramme, avasimhase takkasīlāyaṃ deva;

Tatthandhakāramhi timīsikāyaṃ, aṃsena aṃsaṃ samaghaṭṭayimha.

“In the lovely city of the Gandhāra king, in Takkasilā, we dwelt, O king. There, in the thick darkness of the night, we struck shoulder against shoulder.”

20.

20.

“Te tattha ṭhatvāna ubho janinda, sārāṇiyaṃ vītisārayimha tattha;

Sāyeva no saṅgatimattamāsi, tato na pacchā na pure ahosi.

“We both stood there, O lord of men, and exchanged friendly greetings. That alone was our meeting; there was none after that, nor before.”

21.

21.

“Yadā kadāci manujesu brahme, samāgamo sappurisena hoti;

Na paṇḍitā saṅgatisanthavāni, pubbe kataṃ vāpi vināsayanti.

“Whenever, O brahmin, among humans, a meeting with a good person occurs, the wise do not destroy the benefits of that meeting and intimacy, nor what was done before.”

22.

22.

“Bālāva kho saṅgatisanthavāni, pubbe kataṃ vāpi vināsayanti;

Bahumpi bālesu kataṃ vinassati, tathā hi bālā akataññurūpā.

“Fools indeed destroy the benefits of meeting and intimacy, and also what was done before. Even much done for fools is wasted, for fools are indeed ungrateful by nature.”

23.

23.

“Dhīrā [V 4.0089] ca kho saṅgatisanthavāni, pubbe kataṃ vāpi na nāsayanti;

Appampi [P 4.0099] dhīresu kataṃ na nassati, tathā hi dhīrā sukataññurūpā.

“But the wise indeed do not destroy the benefits of meeting and intimacy, nor what was done before. Even a little done for the wise is not lost, for the wise are indeed grateful by nature.”

24.

24.

“Dadāmi [M 4.0100] te gāmavarāni pañca, dāsīsataṃ satta gavaṃsatāni;

Parosahassañca suvaṇṇanikkhe, bhariyā ca te sādisī dve dadāmi.

“I give you five excellent villages, a hundred female slaves, seven hundred head of cattle, and more than a thousand gold coins; and I give you two wives similar to yourself.”

25.

25.

“Evaṃ sataṃ hoti samecca rāja, nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ;

Āpūratī kāsipatī tathāhaṃ, tayāpi me saṅgamo ajja laddho”ti.

“Thus it is for the good when they meet, O king, like the moon among the stars which becomes full; so am I, O lord of the Kasis; for today a meeting with you has been gained by me.”

Tattha sādisīti rūpavaṇṇajātikulapadesena mayā sādisī ekasadisā dve mahāyasā bhariyā ca me dehīti attho. Bhiṃsarūpoti kiṃ nu te brāhmaṇa balavarūpasīlācāraguṇasaṅkhātaṃ tapokammaṃ atthīti pucchati. Mantā nu teti udāhu vicitrarūpā sabbatthasādhakā mantā te atthi. Assavāti vacanakārakā icchiticchitadāyakā yakkhā vā te keci santi. Kattanti kataṃ, udāhu tayā kataṃ kiñci mama atthaṃ abhijānāsīti pucchati. Saṅgatimattanti samāgamamattaṃ tayā saddhiṃ pubbe mama āsīti vadati. Jānato meti jānantassa mama idaṃ paṭhamaṃ tava dassanaṃ. Na tābhijānāmīti na taṃ abhijānāmi. Timīsikāyanti bahalatimirāyaṃ rattiyaṃ. Te tattha ṭhatvānāti te mayaṃ tasmiṃ aṃsena aṃsaṃ ghaṭṭitaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā vītisārayimha tatthāti tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne saritabbayuttakaṃ kathaṃ vītisārayimha, ahaṃ “bhikkhābhājanaṃ me tayā bhinnaṃ, bhattamūlaṃ me dehī”ti avacaṃ, tvaṃ “idānāhaṃ tava bhattamūlaṃ dātuṃ na sakkomi, ahaṃ kho pana kāsikarañño putto juṇhakumāro nāma, mayi rajje patiṭṭhite āgantvā maṃ dhanaṃ yāceyyāsī”ti avacāti imaṃ sāraṇīyakathaṃ karimhāti āha. Sāyeva no saṅgatimattamāsīti deva, amhākaṃ sāyeva aññamaññaṃ saṅgatimattamāsi, ekamuhuttikamahosīti dīpeti. Tatoti tato pana taṃmuhuttikamittadhammato pacchā vā pure vā kadāci amhākaṃ saṅgati nāma na bhūtapubbā.

Here, ‘sādisī’ means ‘similar to me’ in terms of beauty, complexion, birth, and lineage, meaning ‘give me two great wives similar to me, of the same kind.’ ‘Bhiṃsarūpo’ asks, ‘O brahmin, do you possess any ascetic practice characterized by power, beauty, virtue, conduct, and good qualities?’ ‘Mantā nu te’ inquires, ‘Or do you possess mantras that are varied and effective in all situations?’ ‘Assavā’ questions, ‘Are there any yakkhas for you who are obedient, who grant whatever is desired?’ ‘Kattaṃ’ means ‘done’, or he asks, ‘Do you recognize any benefit for me that you have done?’ ‘Saṅgatimattaṃ’ states, ‘There was merely a meeting with you in the past.’ ‘Jānato me’ means, ‘For me who knows, this is my first sight of you.’ ‘Na tābhijānāmi’ declares, ‘I do not recognize you.’ ‘Timīsikāyaṃ’ refers to ‘a night of thick darkness.’ ‘Te tattha ṭhatvāna’ explains, ‘We stood there in that place where we brushed shoulder to shoulder.’ ‘Vītisārayimha tattha’ indicates, ‘In that very spot, we exchanged conversation worthy of being remembered.’ For example, I said, ‘You broke my alms bowl, give me the price of the meal.’ You replied, ‘I cannot give you the price of the meal now. I am Prince Juṇhakumāra, son of the king of Kāsi. Once I am established on the throne, come to me and ask for wealth.’ Thus, he says, ‘we had this memorable conversation.’ ‘Sāyeva no saṅgatimattamāsi’ clarifies, ‘O king, that was merely our brief encounter with each other, lasting only a moment,’ so it indicates. ‘Tato’ concludes, ‘After that momentary friendship, never before or after have we ever met.’

Na paṇḍitāti brāhmaṇa paṇḍitā nāma taṃmuhuttikaṃ saṅgatiṃ vā cirakālasanthavāni vā yaṃ kiñci pubbe kataguṇaṃ vā na nāsenti. Bahumpīti bahukampi[M 4.0101]. Akataññurūpāti yasmā bālā akataññusabhāvā, tasmā tesu bahumpi kataṃ nassatīti attho. Sukataññurūpāti suṭṭhu kataññusabhāvā. Etthāpi tatthāpi tathā hīti hi-kāro kāraṇattho. Dadāmi teti brāhmaṇena yācitayācitaṃ dadanto evamāha. Evaṃ satanti brāhmaṇo rañño [P 4.0100] anumodanaṃ karonto vadati, sataṃ [V 4.0090] sappurisānaṃ ekavārampi samecca saṅgati nāma evaṃ hoti. Nakkhattarājārivāti ettha ra-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Tārakānanti tārakagaṇamajjhe. Kāsipatīti rājānamālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “deva, kāsiraṭṭhādhipati yathā cando tārakānaṃ majjhe ṭhito tārakagaṇaparivuto pāṭipadato paṭṭhāya yāva puṇṇamā āpūrati, tathā ahampi ajja tayā dinnehi gāmavarādīhi āpūrāmī”ti. Tayāpi meti mayā pubbe tayā saddhiṃ laddhopi saṅgamo aladdhova, ajja pana mama manorathassa nipphannattā mayā tayā saha saṅgamo laddho nāmāti nipphannaṃ me tayā saddhiṃ mittaphalanti vadati. Bodhisatto tassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

By ‘Na paṇḍitā’ it means, O brahmin, that the wise do not destroy even a momentary meeting or long-standing friendships, nor any good deed done in the past. ‘Bahumpi’ means ‘even much.’ ‘Akataññurūpā’ means that since fools are ungrateful by nature, therefore much done for them is lost. ‘Sukataññurūpā’ means ‘of a truly grateful nature.’ In both cases, the particle ‘hi’ in ‘tathā hi’ indicates the cause. ‘Dadāmi te’ means that giving what was repeatedly asked for by the brahmin, he spoke thus. ‘Evaṃ sataṃ’ means the brahmin, expressing his appreciation to the king, says: ‘Even a single meeting with good people is truly like this.’ In ‘Nakkhattarājāriva’, the letter ‘ra’ is merely a euphonic particle. ‘Tārakānaṃ’ means ‘amidst the host of stars.’ ‘Kāsipatī’ is an address to the king. This is what is meant: ‘O king, just as the moon, the king of stars, standing amidst the stars and surrounded by the host of stars, waxes from the first day until the full moon, so too today, I am fulfilled by the choice villages and other gifts you have given me.’ ‘Tayāpi me’ means that although I had previously met you, it was as if I had not; but today, because my heart’s desire has been fulfilled, I have truly gained the benefit of a meeting with you—thus he says that the fruit of friendship with you has been achieved for me. The Bodhisatta granted him great renown.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ ānandaṃ varena santappesiṃ yevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, ‘Not only now, monks, but in former times also I gratified Ānanda with a boon.’ Then he connected the Jātaka: ‘At that time Ānanda was the brahmin, and I myself was the king.’

Juṇhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Juṇha Jātaka, the Second.

[457] 3. Dhammadevaputtajātakavaṇṇanā

[457] 3. Commentary on the Dhammadevaputta Jātaka

Yasokaro puññakarohamasmīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa pathavipavesanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto tathāgatena saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhitvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na idānevesa, bhikkhave, mama jinacakke pahāraṃ datvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho, pubbepi dhammacakke [M 4.0102] pahāraṃ datvā pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīciparāyaṇo jātoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with ‘I am a maker of renown, a maker of merit,’ regarding Devadatta’s entering the earth. At that time, the monks in the Dhamma hall raised a discussion: ‘Friends, Devadatta, having opposed the Tathāgata, has entered the earth.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?’ When they said, ‘For this one,’ he said, ‘Not only now, monks, has he struck against my Wheel of the Conqueror and entered the earth; even in the past, having struck against the Wheel of Dhamma, he entered the earth and was destined for Avīci.’ Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāmāvacaradevaloke dhammo nāma devaputto hutvā nibbatti, devadatto adhammo nāma. Tesu dhammo dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito dibbarathavaramabhiruyha accharāgaṇaparivuto manussesu sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā attano attano gharadvāre sukhakathāya nisinnesu puṇṇamuposathadivase gāmanigamajanapadarājadhānīsu ākāse ṭhatvā “pāṇātipātādīhi dasahi akusalakammapathehi viramitvā mātupaṭṭhānadhammaṃ pitupaṭṭhānadhammaṃ tividhasucaritadhammañca pūretha[P 4.0101], evaṃ saggaparāyaṇā hutvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavissathā”ti manusse dasa kusalakammapathe samādapento jambudīpaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. Adhammo pana devaputto “pāṇaṃ hanathā”tiādinā nayena dasa akusalakammapathe samādapento jambudīpaṃ vāmaṃ karoti. Atha tesaṃ [V 4.0091] ākāse rathā sammukhā ahesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ parisā “tumhe kassa, tumhe kassā”ti pucchitvā “mayaṃ dhammassa, mayaṃ adhammassā”ti vatvā maggā okkamitvā dvidhā jātā. Dhammopi adhammaṃ āmantetvā “samma, tvaṃ adhammo, ahaṃ dhammo, maggo mayhaṃ anucchaviko, tava rathaṃ okkāmetvā mayhaṃ maggaṃ dehī”ti paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Kāmāvacara deva-world as a deva-son named Dhamma, while Devadatta was reborn as one named Adhamma. Among them, Dhamma, adorned with divine ornaments and riding a splendid celestial chariot, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, would appear in the sky on the full-moon Uposatha day when people, having eaten their evening meal, were seated at their doorsteps engaged in pleasant conversation. Standing in the sky above villages, towns, districts, and royal capitals, he would exhort them: “Refrain from the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as the destruction of life. Fulfill the duties of attending to your mother and father, and the threefold good conduct. Thus, being destined for heaven, you will experience great glory.” In this way, he would circumambulate Jambudīpa to the right, encouraging people to undertake the ten wholesome courses of action. The deva-son Adhamma, however, would circumambulate Jambudīpa to the left, urging people to adopt the ten unwholesome courses of action, saying, “Destroy living beings,” and so forth. Then their chariots met face to face in the sky. Their retinues asked one another, “To whom do you belong?” and replying, “We belong to Dhamma,” or “We belong to Adhamma,” they moved off the path and divided into two groups. Dhamma then addressed Adhamma, saying, “Friend, you are Adhamma, and I am Dhamma. The path is proper for me. Move your chariot aside and give the way to me.” First, he spoke this verse:

26.

26.

“Yasokaro puññakarohamasmi, sadātthuto samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ;

Maggāraho devamanussapūjito, dhammo ahaṃ dehi adhamma magga”nti.

“I am a maker of renown, a maker of merit, always praised by recluses and brahmins. Worthy of the way, honored by devas and humans, I am Dhamma; give way, Adhamma.”

Tattha yasokaroti ahaṃ devamanussānaṃ yasadāyako. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Sadātthutoti sadā thuto niccapasattho. Tato parā –

Here, ‘maker of renown’ means I am the giver of renown to devas and humans. The same applies to the second phrase. ‘Always praised’ means always lauded, constantly extolled. Then, the next verse:

27.

27.

“Adhammayānaṃ daḷhamāruhitvā, asantasanto balavāhamasmi;

Sa kissa hetumhi tavajja dajjaṃ, maggaṃ ahaṃ dhamma adinnapubbaṃ.

“Having firmly mounted the chariot of unrighteousness, I am strong and fearless. For what reason should I give you the way today, Dhamma, a way I have never given before?”

28.

28.

“Dhammo [M 4.0103] have pāturahosi pubbe, pacchā adhammo udapādi loke;

Jeṭṭho ca seṭṭho ca sanantano ca, uyyāhi jeṭṭhassa kaniṭṭha maggā.

“Dhamma, indeed, arose first; later Adhamma arose in the world. I am the eldest, the best, and the most ancient. Therefore, younger one, give way from the path to the eldest!”

29.

29.

“Na yācanāya napi pātirūpā, na arahatā tehaṃ dadeyyaṃ maggaṃ;

Yuddhañca [P 4.0102] no hotu ubhinnamajja, yuddhamhi yo jessati tassa maggo.

“Neither by begging, nor by fitting words, nor by my worthiness would I give you the way. Let there be a battle between us two today. To him who conquers in battle belongs the way.”

30.

30.

“Sabbā disā anuvisaṭohamasmi, mahabbalo amitayaso atulyo;

Guṇehi sabbehi upetarūpo, dhammo adhamma tvaṃ kathaṃ vijessasi.

“I have spread throughout all directions; I am of great power, boundless renown, and incomparable. Endowed with all virtues, how will you, Adhamma, conquer Dhamma?”

31.

31.

“Lohena ve haññati jātarūpaṃ, na jātarūpena hananti lohaṃ;

Sace adhammo hañchati dhammamajja, ayo suvaṇṇaṃ viya dassaneyyaṃ.

“Gold is indeed struck by iron, but iron is not struck by gold. If Adhamma were to strike Dhamma today, it would be as if one saw iron [destroying] gold.”

32.

32.

“Sace tuvaṃ yuddhabalo adhamma, na tuyha vuḍḍhā ca garū ca atthi;

Maggañca te dammi piyāppiyena, vācāduruttānipi te khamāmī”ti. –

“If you, Adhamma, are strong in battle, and you have no elders or revered ones, I will give you the way, whether out of love or not, and I will endure your harsh words.”

Imā cha gāthā tesaññeva vacanapaṭivacanavasena kathitā.

These six verses were spoken by them by way of an exchange of words.

Tattha [V 4.0092] sa kissa hetumhi tavajja dajjanti somhi ahaṃ adhammo adhammayānaṃ rathaṃ āruḷho abhīto balavā. Kiṃkāraṇā ajja bho dhamma, kassaci adinnapubbaṃ maggaṃ tuyhaṃ dammīti. Pubbeti paṭhamakappikakāle imasmiṃ loke dasakusalakammapathadhammo ca pubbe pāturahosi, pacchā adhammo. Jeṭṭho cāti pure nibbattabhāvena ahaṃ jeṭṭho ca seṭṭho ca porāṇako ca, tvaṃ pana kaniṭṭho, tasmā maggā uyyāhīti vadati. Napi [M 4.0104] pātirūpāti ahañhi te neva yācanāya na patirūpavacanena maggārahatāya maggaṃ dadeyyaṃ. Anuvisaṭoti ahaṃ catasso disā catasso anudisāti sabbā disā attano guṇena patthaṭo paññāto pākaṭo. Lohenāti ayamuṭṭhikena. Hañchatīti hanissati. Tuvaṃ yuddhabalo adhammāti sace tvaṃ yuddhabalosi adhamma. Vuḍḍhā ca garū cāti yadi tuyhaṃ “ime vuḍḍhā, ime garū paṇḍitā”ti evaṃ natthi. Piyāppiyenāti piyenāpi appiyenāpi dadanto piyena viya te maggaṃ dadāmīti attho.

Therein, 'For what reason should I give you the way today?': I am Adhamma, riding the chariot of unrighteousness, fearless and powerful. For what reason today, O Dhamma, should I give you a way never given before? 'Formerly' (pubbe): In the first aeon, the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action appeared first in this world, and Adhamma came later. 'Eldest' (jeṭṭho ca): Because I arose first, I am the eldest, the best, and the ancient one. You, however, are the younger. Therefore, he says, 'Step aside from the way!' 'Nor by fitting words' (napi pātirūpā): I would not give you the way, neither by begging, nor by fitting words, nor by the fact that I am worthy of the way. 'Spread throughout' (anuvisaṭo): I am spread, known, and manifest throughout all directions—the four cardinal and four intermediate directions—by my own virtues. 'By iron' (lohena): By an iron hammer. 'Will strike' (hañchati) means will strike (hanissati). 'You, Adhamma, strong in battle' (tuvaṃ yuddhabalo adhamma) means if you are strong in battle, Adhamma. 'And elders and revered ones' (vuḍḍhā ca garū ca): If for you there is no such thought as 'These are elders, these are revered and wise.' 'Whether out of love or not' (piyāppiyena): Whether giving with what is pleasant or unpleasant, the meaning is 'I give you the way as if it were out of love for you.'

Bodhisattena [P 4.0103] pana imāya gāthāya kathitakkhaṇeyeva adhammo rathe ṭhātuṃ asakkonto avaṃsiro pathaviyaṃ patitvā pathaviyā vivare dinne gantvā avīcimhiyeva nibbatti. Etamatthaṃ viditvā bhagavā abhisambuddho hutvā sesagāthā abhāsi –

But at the very moment the Bodhisatta spoke this verse, Adhamma, unable to remain in the chariot, fell headfirst to the ground. The earth opened up and he was reborn in the Avīci hell. Knowing this matter, the Blessed One, having become fully enlightened, spoke the remaining verses:

33.

33.

“Idañca sutvā vacanaṃ adhammo, avaṃsiro patito uddhapādo;

Yuddhatthiko ce na labhāmi yuddhaṃ, ettāvatā hoti hato adhammo.

“Having heard these words, Adhamma fell headfirst, with feet upwards. If I, seeking battle, do not obtain battle, by that much alone is Adhamma defeated.”

34.

34.

“Khantībalo yuddhabalaṃ vijetvā, hantvā adhammaṃ nihanitva bhūmyā;

Pāyāsi vitto abhiruyha sandanaṃ, maggeneva atibalo saccanikkamo.

“He whose strength is patience, having conquered the strength of battle, having struck down Adhamma and laid him low on the earth, delighted, mounted his chariot and went along the path, exceedingly powerful and of true endeavor.”

35.

35.

“Mātā pitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca, asammānitā yassa sake agāre;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā nirayaṃ vajanti te;

Yathā adhammo patito avaṃsiro.

“Those in whose own home mother, father, recluses, and brahmins are not honored—they, having laid aside the body here, go to hell at the breakup of the body, just as Adhamma fell headfirst.”

36.

36.

“Mātā pitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca, susammānitā yassa sake agāre;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ vajanti te;

Yathāpi dhammo abhiruyha sandana”nti.

“Those in whose own home mother, father, recluses, and brahmins are well honored—they, having laid aside the body here, go to a happy destination at the breakup of the body, just as Dhamma mounted his chariot.”

Tattha [M 4.0105] yuddhatthiko ceti ayaṃ tassa vilāpo, so kirevaṃ vilapantoyeva patitvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho[V 4.0093]. Ettāvatāti bhikkhave, yāvatā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho, tāvatā adhammo hato nāma hoti. Khantībaloti bhikkhave, evaṃ adhammo pathaviṃ paviṭṭho adhivāsanakhantībalo taṃ yuddhabalaṃ vijetvā vadhitvā bhūmiyaṃ nihanitvā pātetvā vittajātatāya vitto attano rathaṃ āruyha maggeneva saccanikkamo tathaparakkamo dhammadevaputto pāyāsi. Asammānitāti asakkatā. Sarīradehanti imasmiṃyeva loke sarīrasaṅkhātaṃ dehaṃ nikkhipitvā. Nirayaṃ vajantīti yassa pāpapuggalassa ete sakkārārahā gehe asakkatā, tathārūpā yathā adhammo patito avaṃsiro, evaṃ avaṃsirā [P 4.0104] nirayaṃ vajantīti attho. Sugatiṃ vajantīti yassa panete sakkatā, tādisā paṇḍitā yathāpi dhammo sandanaṃ abhiruyha devalokaṃ gato, evaṃ sugatiṃ vajantīti.

Herein, 'Desiring battle' (yuddhatthiko): this is his lament. It is said that while he was lamenting in this way, he fell and entered the earth. 'To this extent' (ettāvatā): monks, in as far as he entered the earth, to that extent Adhamma is said to be slain. 'He whose strength is patience' (khantībalo): monks, when Adhamma had thus entered the earth, the Dhamma-devaputta, whose strength was enduring patience, having conquered that battle-force, having slain him, struck him down into the earth and felled him, being joyful because of the joy that had arisen, mounted his own chariot and went forth along the way, steadfast in truth and with such exertion. 'Not honored' (asammānitā): not respected. 'The bodily frame' (sarīradehaṃ): having laid aside the body-aggregate in this very world. 'They go to hell' (nirayaṃ vajanti): this means that for whatever wicked person these who are worthy of honor are not respected in his home, just as Adhamma fell headfirst, so do they go to hell headfirst. 'They go to a good destination' (sugatiṃ vajanti): this means that for those by whom these are respected, such wise ones go to a good destination, just as Dhamma, having mounted his chariot, went to the celestial world.

Satthā evaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhitvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā adhammo devaputto devadatto ahosi, parisāpissa devadattaparisā, dhammo pana ahameva, parisā buddhaparisāyevā”ti.

The Teacher, having thus taught this Dhamma, said: 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta opposed me and entered the earth.' Then he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the deva-son Adhamma was Devadatta, and his retinue was Devadatta’s retinue. But Dhamma was I myself, and his retinue was the Buddha’s retinue.'

Dhammadevaputtajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Dhammadevaputta Jātaka, the third.

[458] 4. Udayajātakavaṇṇanā

[458] 4. The Commentary on the Udaya Jātaka.

Ekā nisinnāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu kusajātake (jā. 2.20.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu kasmā kilesavasena evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā ukkaṇṭhitosi? Porāṇakapaṇḍitā samiddhe dvādasayojanike surundhananagare rajjaṃ kārentā devaccharapaṭibhāgāya itthiyā saddhiṃ satta vassasatāni ekagabbhe vasantāpi indriyāni bhinditvā lobhavasena na olokesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Alone she sits': this the Teacher told while staying in Jetavana, concerning a certain disaffected monk. The story will become clear in the Kusa Jātaka. But the Teacher, having asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that you are disaffected?' and when he replied, 'It is true, Bhante,' said: 'Monk, why, having gone forth in such a liberating Dispensation, are you disaffected under the influence of defilements? Wise men of old, while ruling in the prosperous city of Surundhana, twelve leagues in extent, even though they lived for seven hundred years in a single chamber with a woman who was like a celestial nymph, they did not look at her through the power of greed, breaking their sense-restraint.' Having said this, he brought up the past story.

Atīte [M 4.0106] kāsiraṭṭhe surundhananagare kāsirājā rajjaṃ kāresi, tassa neva putto, na dhītā ahosi. So attano deviyo “putte patthethā”ti āha. Aggamahesīpi rañño vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tathā akāsi. Tadā bodhisatto brahmalokā cavitvā tasseva rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Athassa mahājanassa hadayaṃ vaḍḍhetvā jātabhāvena “udayabhaddo”ti [V 4.0094] nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Kumārassa padasā caraṇakāle aññopi satto brahmalokā cavitvā tasseva rañño aññatarāya deviyā kucchimhi kumārikā hutvā nibbatti, tassāpi “udayabhaddā”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Kumāro vayappatto sabbasippanipphattiṃ pāpuṇi[P 4.0105], jātabrahmacārī pana ahosi, supinantenapi methunadhammaṃ na jānāti, na tassa kilesesu cittaṃ allīyi. Rājā puttaṃ rajje abhisiñcitukāmo “kumārassa idāni rajjasukhasevanakālo, nāṭakāpissa paccupaṭṭhāpessāmī”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. Bodhisatto “na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, kilesesu me cittaṃ na allīyatī”ti paṭikkhipitvā punappunaṃ vuccamāno rattajambunadamayaṃ itthirūpaṃ kāretvā “evarūpaṃ itthiṃ labhamāno rajjaṃ sampaṭicchissāmī”ti mātāpitūnaṃ pesesi. Te taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ parihārāpetvā tathārūpaṃ itthiṃ alabhantā udayabhaddaṃ alaṅkāretvā tassa santike ṭhapesuṃ. Sā taṃ suvaṇṇarūpakaṃ abhibhavitvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha nesaṃ anicchamānānaññeva vemātikaṃ bhaginiṃ udayabhaddakumāriṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā bodhisattaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Te pana dvepi brahmacariyavāsameva vasiṃsu.

In the past, when the king of Kāsi was reigning in the city of Surundhana in the kingdom of Kāsi, he had neither a son nor a daughter. He said to his queens, 'Pray for a son.' The chief queen, accepting the king's word, did so. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Brahma world, was reborn in the womb of that very king's chief queen. Then, because he was born increasing the joy of the people's hearts, they gave him the name 'Udayabhadda'. At the time when the prince was able to walk on foot, another being passed away from the Brahma world and was reborn in the womb of another of that same king's queens, becoming a princess. They gave her the name 'Udayabhaddā' as well. When the prince came of age, he attained proficiency in all the arts, but he was celibate from birth. Even in a dream, he did not know of sexual intercourse, and his mind did not cling to defilements. The king, wishing to consecrate his son in the kingship, sent a message: 'Now is the time for the prince to enjoy the pleasures of royalty; I shall provide him with performers.' The Bodhisatta refused, saying, 'I have no need for kingship; my mind does not cling to defilements.' Being urged again and again, he had a female figure made of red gold and sent it to his parents, saying: 'If I obtain a woman of this kind, I will accept the kingship.' They had that golden image carried throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, but not finding such a woman, they adorned Udayabhaddā and placed her near it. She stood there, surpassing the golden image. Then, though they were unwilling, they made his half-sister, the princess Udayabhaddā, the chief queen and consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingship. However, the two of them lived only a life of celibacy.

Aparabhāge mātāpitūnaṃ accayena bodhisatto rajjaṃ kāresi. Ubho ekagabbhe vasamānāpi lobhavasena indriyāni bhinditvā aññamaññaṃ na olokesuṃ, apica kho pana “yo amhesu paṭhamataraṃ kālaṃ karoti, so nibbattaṭṭhānato āgantvā ‘asukaṭṭhāne nibbattosmī’ti ārocetū”ti saṅgaramakaṃsu. Atha kho bodhisatto abhisekato sattavassasataccayena kālamakāsi. Añño rājā nāhosi, udayabhaddāyayeva āṇā pavatti. Amaccā rajjaṃ anusāsiṃsu. Bodhisattopi cutikkhaṇe tāvatiṃsabhavane sakkattaṃ patvā yasamahantatāya sattāhaṃ anussarituṃ nāsakkhi. Iti so manussagaṇanāya sattavassasataccayena āvajjetvā “udayabhaddaṃ rājadhītaraṃ dhanena vīmaṃsitvā sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā dhammaṃ desetvā saṅgaraṃ mocetvā āgamissāmī”ti cintesi. Tadā [M 4.0107] kira manussānaṃ dasavassasahassāyukakālo hoti. Rājadhītāpi taṃ divasaṃ rattibhāge pihitesu dvāresu ṭhapitaārakkhe sattabhūmikapāsādavaratale alaṅkatasirigabbhe ekikāva niccalā attano [P 4.0106] sīlaṃ āvajjamānā nisīdi. Atha sakko suvaṇṇamāsakapūraṃ ekaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ ādāya āgantvā sayanagabbheyeva pātubhavitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Later, after the passing of his parents, the Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom. Though they lived in the same chamber, they did not allow their sense-faculties to be broken through the power of desire and look at one another. Instead, they made a pact: "Whoever among us dies first, let them return from their place of rebirth and announce, 'I have been reborn in such-and-such a place.'" Then, the Bodhisatta passed away seven hundred years after his coronation. There was no other king; only Princess Udayabhaddā's command was followed. The ministers governed the kingdom. At the moment of his passing, the Bodhisatta attained the state of Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Due to his immense glory, he was unable to recollect for seven days. Thus, after seven hundred years in human reckoning, he reflected: "I will test the princess Udayabhaddā with wealth, cause her to utter a lion's roar, teach her the Dhamma, release her from the pact, and then return." At that time, it is said, the lifespan of humans was ten thousand years. That very day, during the night, with the doors bolted and guards posted, the princess sat alone and motionless in the adorned, splendid chamber on the excellent floor of the seven-storied palace, reflecting on her own virtue. Then Sakka, taking a golden bowl filled with golden māsaka coins, appeared right there in her bedchamber. Standing to one side, he conversed with her and spoke the first verse:

37.

37.

“Ekā nisinnā suci saññatūrū, pāsādamāruyha aninditaṅgī;

Yācāmi taṃ kinnaranettacakkhu, imekarattiṃ ubhayo vasemā”ti.

"Alone you sit, pure, with well-composed thighs, having ascended the palace, flawless of limb; I beg of you, O one with eyes like a kinnara's, let us both dwell together for this one night."

Tattha [V 4.0095] sucīti sucivatthanivatthā. Saññatūrūti suṭṭhu ṭhapitaūrū, iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapetvā sucivatthā ekikāva nisinnāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Aninditaṅgīti pādantato yāva kesaggā aninditasarīrā paramasobhaggappattasarīrā. Kinnaranettacakkhūti tīhi maṇḍalehi pañcahi ca pasādehi upasobhitattā kinnarānaṃ nettasadisehi cakkhūhi samannāgate. Imekarattinti imaṃ ekarattaṃ ajja imasmiṃ alaṅkatasayanagabbhe ekato vaseyyāmāti yācati.

There, 'sucī' means clothed in clean garments. 'Saññatūrū' means with well-placed thighs; it is said that having composed her posture, she sat alone in clean garments. 'Aninditaṅgī' means from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair, her body is flawless, a body that has attained supreme beauty. 'Kinnaranettacakkhu' means 'O one endowed with eyes like those of a kinnara,' because they are adorned with three circles and five kinds of clarity. 'Imekarattinti' means he begs, 'May we dwell together this one night—today, in this adorned bedchamber.'

Tato rājadhītā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the princess spoke two verses:

38.

38.

“Okiṇṇantaraparikhaṃ, daḷhamaṭṭālakoṭṭhakaṃ;

Rakkhitaṃ khaggahatthehi, duppavesamidaṃ puraṃ.

"Filled with inner moats, with strong towers and gatehouses; guarded by swordsmen, this city is difficult to enter."

39.

39.

“Daharassa yuvino cāpi, āgamo ca na vijjati;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, saṅgamaṃ icchase mayā”ti.

"For a youth, even one in his prime, there is no access; for what reason, then, do you desire union with me?"

Tattha okiṇṇantaraparikhanti idaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ surundhanapuraṃ antarantarā udakaparikhānaṃ kaddamaparikhānaṃ sukkhaparikhānaṃ okiṇṇattā okiṇṇantaraparikhaṃ. Daḷhamaṭṭālakoṭṭhakanti thiratarehi aṭṭālakehi dvārakoṭṭhakehi ca samannāgataṃ. Khaggahatthehīti āvudhahatthehi dasahi yodhasahassehi rakkhitaṃ. Duppavesamidaṃ puranti idaṃ sakalapurampi tassa anto māpitaṃ mayhaṃ nivāsapurampi ubhayaṃ kassaci pavisituṃ na sakkā. Āgamo cāti idha imāya [M 4.0108] velāya taruṇassa vā yobbanappattassa vā thāmasampannayodhassa vā aññassa vā mahantampi paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgacchantassa āgamo nāma natthi. Saṅgamanti atha tvaṃ kena kāraṇena imāya velāya mayā saha samāgamaṃ icchasīti.

There, 'okiṇṇantaraparikhaṃ' means this city of Surundhana, twelve yojanas in extent, is 'filled with inner moats' because it is filled with alternating water moats, mud moats, and dry moats. 'Daḷhamaṭṭālakoṭṭhakaṃ' means endowed with very firm towers and gatehouses. 'Khaggahatthehi' means guarded by weapons in their hands, by ten thousand soldiers. 'Duppavesamidaṃ puraṃ' means both this entire city and my own residence built within it are impossible for anyone to enter. 'Āgamo cāti' means that at this time, there is no such thing as arrival for anyone coming, whether a youth, a man in his prime, a strong warrior, or any other, even bearing a large tribute. 'Saṅgamanti' means 'for what reason, then, do you wish for union with me at this time?'

Atha sakko catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka spoke the fourth verse:

40.

40.

“Yakkhohamasmi [P 4.0107] kalyāṇi, āgatosmi tavantike;

Tvaṃ maṃ nandaya bhaddante, puṇṇakaṃsaṃ dadāmi te”ti.

"I am a yakkha, O fair one, and I have come to your presence; delight me, O blessed one, and I will give you a bowl full [of gold coins]."

Tassattho – kalyāṇi, sundaradassane ahameko devaputto devatānubhāvena idhāgato, tvaṃ ajja maṃ nandaya tosehi, ahaṃ te imaṃ suvaṇṇamāsakapuṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ dadāmīti.

The meaning is: O fair one, lovely to behold, I am a devaputta who has come here through divine power. Today, delight me, please me, and I will give you this golden bowl filled with golden māsaka coins.

Taṃ [V 4.0096] sutvā rājadhītā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the princess spoke the fifth verse:

41.

41.

“Devaṃva yakkhaṃ atha vā manussaṃ, na patthaye udayamaticca aññaṃ;

Gaccheva tvaṃ yakkha mahānubhāva, mā cassu gantvā punarāvajitthā”ti.

"Whether a god, a yakkha, or a human, I desire no other, transgressing Udaya; go, O mighty yakkha, and having gone, do not return here again."

Tassattho – ahaṃ devarāja, devaṃ vā yakkhaṃ vā udayaṃ atikkamitvā aññaṃ na patthemi, so tvaṃ gaccheva, mā idha aṭṭhāsi, na me tayā ābhatena paṇṇākārena attho, gantvā ca mā imaṃ ṭhānaṃ punarāvajitthāti.
