The meaning is: O king of gods, I do not desire another, whether god or yakkha, transgressing Udaya. Therefore, you must go, do not stay here. I have no need of the gift you have brought. And having gone, do not return to this place again.

So tassā sīhanādaṃ sutvā aṭṭhatvā gatasadiso hutvā tattheva antarahito aṭṭhāsi. So punadivase tāya velāyameva suvaṇṇamāsakapūraṃ rajatapātiṃ ādāya tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing her lion's roar, he became as one who has departed, and vanishing on the spot, he remained there. The next day, at that very time, he took a silver bowl filled with golden māsaka coins and, conversing with her, spoke the sixth verse:

42.

42.

“Yā sā rati uttamā kāmabhoginaṃ, yaṃhetu sattā visamaṃ caranti;

Mā taṃ ratiṃ jīyi tuvaṃ sucimhite, dadāmi te rūpiyaṃ kaṃsapūra”nti.

"That which is the highest delight for those who enjoy sensual pleasures, for which reason beings act wrongly—do not be deprived of that delight, O you of the beautiful smile. I will give you a silver bowl, full [of gold coins]."

Tassattho [M 4.0109] – bhadde, rājadhīte yā esā kāmabhogisattānaṃ ratīsu methunakāmarati nāma uttamā rati, yassā ratiyā kāraṇā sattā kāyaduccaritādivisamaṃ caranti, taṃ ratiṃ tvaṃ bhadde, sucimhite manāpahasite mā jīyi, ahampi āgacchanto na tucchahattho āgato, hiyyo suvaṇṇamāsakapūraṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ āhariṃ, ajja rūpiyapātiṃ, imaṃ te ahaṃ rūpiyapātiṃ suvaṇṇapūraṃ dadāmīti.

The meaning is this: 'O good lady, princess, that highest delight among beings who enjoy sensual pleasures, which is called sexual pleasure, on account of which beings engage in misconduct such as bodily misdeeds—do not, O good lady with your beautiful smile and charming laughter, lose that delight. I too have not come empty-handed. Yesterday I brought a golden bowl filled with golden māsaka coins; today, a silver bowl. This silver bowl, filled with gold, I give to you.'

Rājadhītā cintesi “ayaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ labhanto punappunaṃ āgamissati, na dāni tena saddhiṃ kathessāmī”ti. Sā kiñci na [P 4.0108] kathesi.

The princess thought, 'If he obtains an opportunity to converse, he will come again and again. I will not speak with him from now on.' She said nothing.

Sakko tassā akathitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tattheva antarahito hutvā punadivase tāyameva velāya lohapātiṃ kahāpaṇapūraṃ ādāya “bhadde, tvaṃ maṃ kāmaratiyā santappehi, imaṃ te kahāpaṇapūraṃ lohapātiṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Taṃ disvā rājadhītā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka, knowing her silence, vanished on the spot. The next day, at the same time, he brought a copper bowl filled with kahāpaṇas and said, "Good lady, gratify me with sensual pleasure, and I will give you this copper bowl filled with kahāpaṇas." Seeing this, the princess spoke the seventh verse:

43.

43.

“Nāriṃ [V 4.0097] naro nijjhapayaṃ dhanena, ukkaṃsatī yattha karoti chandaṃ;

Vipaccanīko tava devadhammo, paccakkhato thokatarena esī”ti.

"A man, when persuading a woman with wealth, exalts her for whom he feels desire. Your divine nature is contrary, for you come before my very eyes with an ever smaller offering."

Tassattho – bho purisa, tvaṃ jaḷo. Naro hi nāma nāriṃ kilesaratikāraṇā dhanena nijjhāpento saññāpento yattha nāriyā chandaṃ karoti, taṃ ukkaṃsati vaṇṇetvā thometvā bahutarena dhanena palobheti, tuyhaṃ paneso devasabhāvo vipaccanīko, tvañhi mayā paccakkhato thokatarena esi, paṭhamadivase suvaṇṇapūraṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ āharitvā, dutiyadivase suvaṇṇapūraṃ rūpiyapātiṃ, tatiyadivase kahāpaṇapūraṃ lohapātiṃ āharasīti.

The meaning is: 'O man, you are very foolish. Indeed, a man, for the sake of sensual pleasure, when persuading and convincing a woman with wealth, exalts the one for whom he feels desire; he entices her with more and more wealth, praising and extolling her. But this divine nature of yours is contrary, for you come before my very eyes with less and less: on the first day bringing a golden bowl filled with gold, on the second day a silver bowl filled with gold, and on the third day a copper bowl filled with kahāpaṇas.'

Taṃ sutvā sakko “bhadde rājakumāri, ahaṃ chekavāṇijo na niratthakena atthaṃ nāsemi, sace tvaṃ āyunā vā vaṇṇena vā vaḍḍheyyāsi, ahaṃ te paṇṇākāraṃ vaḍḍhetvā āhareyyaṃ, tvaṃ pana parihāyaseva, tenāhampi dhanaṃ parihāpemī”ti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, Sakka said, "Good princess, I am a skilled merchant. I do not waste my profit for nothing. If you were to increase in lifespan or beauty, I would increase the gift I bring you. But you are only declining, so I too diminish the wealth." Then he spoke three verses:

44.

44.

“Āyu [M 4.0110] ca vaṇṇo ca manussaloke, nihīyati manujānaṃ sugatte;

Teneva vaṇṇena dhanampi tuyhaṃ, nihīyati jiṇṇatarāsi ajja.

"Lifespan and beauty in the human world decline for mortals, O lady of fair limbs. For that very reason, your wealth too declines; you are older today."

45.

45.

“Evaṃ me pekkhamānassa, rājaputti yasassini;

Hāyateva tava vaṇṇo, ahorattānamaccaye.

"Thus, as I watch, O glorious princess, your beauty indeed fades with the passing of days and nights."

46.

46.

“Imināva tvaṃ vayasā, rājaputti sumedhase;

Brahmacariyaṃ careyyāsi, bhiyyo vaṇṇavatī siyā”ti.

"With this very age, O wise princess, you should practice the holy life; you would become even more beautiful."

Tattha nihīyatīti parissāvane āsittaudakaṃ viya parihāyati. Manussalokasmiñhi sattā jīvitena vaṇṇena cakkhupasādādīhi ca dine dine parihāyanteva. Jiṇṇatarāsīti [P 4.0109] mama paṭhamaṃ āgatadivase pavattañhi te āyu hiyyo divasaṃ na pāpuṇi, kuṭhāriyā chinnaṃ viya tattheva nirujjhi, hiyyo pavattampi ajjadivasaṃ na pāpuṇi, hiyyova kuṭhāriyā chinnaṃ viya nirujjhi, tasmā ajja jiṇṇatarāsi jātā. Evaṃ meti tiṭṭhatu hiyyo ca parahiyyo ca, ajjeva pana mayhaṃ evaṃ pekkhamānasseva hāyateva tava vaṇṇo. Ahorattānamaccayeti ito paṭṭhāya rattindivesu vītivattesu ahorattānaṃ accayena apaṇṇattikabhāvameva gamissasīti dasseti. Imināvāti tasmā bhadde, sace tvaṃ iminā vayeneva imasmiṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇe sarīre rajāya [V 4.0098] avilutteyeva seṭṭhacariyaṃ careyyāsi, pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ kareyyāsi. Bhiyyo vaṇṇavatī siyāti atirekataravaṇṇā bhaveyyāsīti.

Therein, 'it declines' means it dwindles away just like water poured into a strainer. Indeed, beings in the human world decline day by day in life, beauty, and the clarity of the eye and other faculties. 'You are older' means that the lifespan that was present on the day I first arrived did not reach yesterday; like something cut by an axe, it ceased right there. And the lifespan that was present yesterday did not reach today; it ceased just yesterday, like something cut by an axe. Therefore, today you have become older. 'Thus, as I watch' means, let yesterday and the day before be; but even today, as I observe, your beauty indeed fades away. 'With the passing of days and nights' indicates that from this point on, as nights and days pass by, with the passing of days and nights, you will only move toward a state of non-existence. 'With this very age' means, therefore, good lady, if you, with this very age, while still in this golden-hued body, not yet defiled by dust, were to live the supreme life, if you were to go forth and practice the ascetic's way, 'you would become even more beautiful' means you would possess an even more excellent beauty.

Tato rājadhītā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the princess spoke another verse:

47.

47.

“Devā na jīranti yathā manussā, gattesu tesaṃ valiyo na honti;

Pucchāmi taṃ yakkha mahānubhāva, kathaṃ nu devāna sarīradeho”ti.

"Devas do not age as humans do; wrinkles do not appear on their bodies. I ask you, O yakkha of great power, how indeed is the physical body of the devas?"

Tattha [M 4.0111] sarīradehoti sarīrasaṅkhāto deho, devānaṃ sarīraṃ kathaṃ na jīrati, idaṃ ahaṃ taṃ pucchāmīti vadati.

Therein, 'physical body' (sarīradeho) means the body designated as the physical frame. She says, 'How does the body of the devas not age? This I ask you.'

Athassā kathento sakko itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka, explaining to her, spoke another verse:

48.

48.

“Devā na jīranti yathā manussā, gattesu tesaṃ valiyo na honti;

Suve suve bhiyyatarova tesaṃ, dibbo ca vaṇṇo vipulā ca bhogā”ti.

"Devas do not age as humans do; wrinkles do not appear on their bodies. Day by day their divine beauty and vast enjoyments become ever greater."

Tattha yathā manussāti yathā manussā jīrantā rūpena vaṇṇena bhogena cakkhupasādādīhi ca jīranti, na evaṃ devā. Tesañhi gattesu valiyopi na santi, maṭṭhakañcanapaṭṭamiva sarīraṃ hoti. Suve suveti divase divase. Bhiyyatarovāti atirekatarova tesaṃ dibbo ca vaṇṇo vipulā ca bhogā honti, manussesu hi rūpaparihāni cirajātabhāvassa sakkhi, devesu atirekarūpasampatti ca atirekaparivārasampatti ca. Evaṃ aparihānadhammo nāmesa devaloko[P 4.0110]. Tasmā tvaṃ jaraṃ appatvāva nikkhamitvā pabbaja, evaṃ parihāniyasabhāvā manussalokā cavitvā aparihāniyasabhāvaṃ evarūpaṃ devalokaṃ gamissasīti.

Herein, 'as humans' means that just as humans, in aging, decline in form, beauty, enjoyments, and the clarity of the eye and other faculties, so it is not with the devas. For on their bodies there are no wrinkles; their bodies are like a polished gold plate. 'Day by day' means daily. 'Ever greater' means their divine beauty and vast enjoyments become even more excellent. Among humans, the decline in appearance is evidence of having been born long ago; among the devas, there is an abundance of beauty and an abundance of retinue. Thus, the deva-world is of a nature without decline. Therefore, before reaching old age, you should go forth and renounce. In this way, having passed away from the human world, which is subject to decline, you will reach such a deva-world, which has a nature free from decline.

Sā devalokassa vaṇṇaṃ sutvā tassa gamanamaggaṃ pucchantī itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard the praise of the deva-world, she, asking about the path to go there, spoke another verse:

49.

49.

“Kiṃsūdha bhītā janatā anekā, maggo ca nekāyatanaṃ pavutto;

Pucchāmi taṃ yakkha mahānubhāva, katthaṭṭhito paralokaṃ na bhāye”ti.

"Why indeed are the many people here afraid, and a path of many foundations proclaimed? I ask you, O yakkha of great power, standing where would one not fear the next world?"

Tattha kiṃsūdha bhītāti devarāja, ayaṃ khattiyādibhedā anekā janatā kiṃbhītā kassa bhayena [V 4.0099] parihāniyasabhāvā manussalokā devalokaṃ na gacchatīti pucchati. Maggoti devalokagāmimaggo. Idha pana “ki”nti āharitvā “ko”ti pucchā kātabbā. Ayañhettha attho “anekatitthāyatanavasena paṇḍitehi pavutto devalokamaggo ko kataro”ti vutto. Katthaṭṭhitoti paralokaṃ gacchanto katarasmiṃ magge ṭhito na bhāyatīti.

Herein, 'Why indeed are the many people here afraid?' means she asks, 'O king of devas, this diverse multitude of people, such as nobles and others—afraid of what, or through what fear, do they not go from the human world, which is of a declining nature, to the deva-world?' 'Path' means the path leading to the deva-world. Here, however, instead of 'what' (kiṃ), the question 'which' (ko) should be understood. This is the meaning here: 'Which is the path to the deva-world proclaimed by the wise according to various sectarian foundations?' 'Standing where?' means, while journeying to the next world, standing on which path would one not be afraid?

Athassā [M 4.0112] kathento sakko itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka, explaining to her, spoke another verse:

50.

50.

“Vācaṃ manañca paṇidhāya sammā, kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno;

Bahunnapānaṃ gharamāvasanto, saddho mudū saṃvibhāgī vadaññū;

Saṅgāhako sakhilo saṇhavāco, etthaṭṭhito paralokaṃ na bhāye”ti.

"Having rightly directed speech and mind, not doing evil deeds with the body; dwelling in a house with abundant food and drink, faithful, gentle, sharing one's portions, knowing the needs of others; helpful, friendly, and of smooth speech—standing in these qualities, one would not fear the next world."

Tassattho – bhadde, udaye vācaṃ manañca sammā ṭhapetvā kāyena pāpāni akaronto ime dasa kusalakammapathe samādāya vattanto bahuannapāne pahūtadeyyadhamme ghare vasanto “dānassa vipāko atthī”ti saddhāya samannāgato muducitto dānasaṃvibhāgatāya saṃvibhāgī pabbajitā bhikkhāya caramānā vadanti nāma, tesaṃ paccayadānena tassa vādassa jānanato vadaññū catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgahatāya saṅgāhako piyavāditāya sakhilo maṭṭhavacanatāya saṇhavāco ettha ettake guṇarāsimhi ṭhito paralokaṃ gacchanto na bhāyatīti.

The meaning is: Good lady, O Udayā, having rightly established speech and mind, not doing evil deeds with the body, thus undertaking and observing these ten wholesome courses of action; dwelling in a house with abundant food and drink and plentiful things fit to be given; endowed with faith that 'there is a result of giving'; gentle-hearted; 'one who shares' (saṃvibhāgī) because of a disposition to share gifts; 'liberal' (vadaññū) because one knows the request of the renunciants who wander for alms and speak, by means of giving them requisites; 'one who is inclusive' (saṅgāhako) because of inclusiveness through the four bases of sympathy; 'friendly' (sakhilo) because of pleasant speech; 'of gentle speech' (saṇhavāco) because of polished words—one who stands here amidst such a mass of virtues does not fear when going to the next world.

Tato [P 4.0111] rājadhītā taṃ tassa vacanaṃ sutvā thutiṃ karontī itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the princess, having heard his speech and wishing to praise him, spoke another verse:

51.

51.

“Anusāsasi maṃ yakkha, yathā mātā yathā pitā;

Uḷāravaṇṇa pucchāmi, ko nu tvamasi subrahā”ti.

51. You advise me, O spirit, as a mother, as a father. O one of sublime appearance, I ask you, who are you, O radiant one?

Tassattho – yathā mātāpitaro puttake anusāsanti, tathā maṃ anusāsasi. Uḷāravaṇṇa sobhaggappattarūpadāraka ko nu asi tvaṃ evaṃ accuggatasarīroti.

The meaning of that verse is: Just as parents instruct their children, so you instruct me. O spirit of sublime appearance and beautiful form, who are you, with such an exceedingly radiant body?

Tato bodhisatto itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke another verse:

52.

52.

“Udayohamasmi kalyāṇi, saṅgarattā idhāgato;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāmi, muttosmi tava saṅgarā”ti.

52. I am Udaya, O fair one, come here on account of a promise. Now I take my leave of you; I am freed from your promise.

Tassattho [V 4.0100][M 4.0113] – kalyāṇadassane ahaṃ purimabhave tava sāmiko udayo nāma tāvatiṃsabhavane sakko hutvā nibbatto, idhāgacchanto na kilesavasenāgato, taṃ vīmaṃsitvā pana saṅgaraṃ mocessāmīti saṅgarattā pubbe saṅgarassa katattā āgatosmi, idāni taṃ āmantetvā gacchāmi, muttosmi tava saṅgarāti.

The meaning of that verse is: O one of beautiful appearance, in a former existence I was your husband named Udaya, reborn as Sakka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In coming here, I have not come under the power of defilements; but thinking, 'Having investigated you, I will fulfill the promise,' I have come on account of that promise, because a promise was made previously. Now, taking leave of you, I go; I am released from your promise.

Rājadhītā assasitvā “sāmi, tvaṃ udayabhaddarājā”ti assudhārā pavattayamānā “ahaṃ tumhehi vinā vasituṃ na sakkomi, yathā tumhākaṃ santike vasāmi, tathā maṃ anusāsathā”ti vatvā itaraṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The princess was pleased and, saying, "Lord, you are King Udayabhadda," while shedding streams of tears, she said, "I cannot live separated from you. Instruct me so that I may live in your presence," and spoke another verse:

53.

53.

“Sace kho tvaṃ udayosi, saṅgarattā idhāgato;

Anusāsa maṃ rājaputta, yathāssa puna saṅgamo”ti.

53. If you are indeed Udaya, come here on account of a promise, advise me, O prince, so that there may be another union.

Atha naṃ anusāsanto mahāsatto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, wishing to instruct the princess, spoke these four verses:

54.

54.

“Atipatati vayo khaṇo tatheva, ṭhānaṃ natthi dhuvaṃ cavanti sattā;

Parijīyati addhuvaṃ sarīraṃ, udaye mā pamāda carassu dhammaṃ.

54. Life-stage passes swiftly, and the moment likewise; there is no permanent state, for beings surely pass away. The impermanent body decays. O Udayā, be not heedless; practice the Dhamma.

55.

55.

“Kasiṇā pathavī dhanassa pūrā, ekasseva siyā anaññadheyyā;

Taṃ cāpi jahati avītarāgo, udaye mā pamāda carassu dhammaṃ.

55. Though the entire earth were full of wealth, belonging to one alone and not shared with another, even that one abandons it, not being free from passion. O Udayā, be not heedless; practice the Dhamma.

56.

56.

“Mātā [P 4.0112] ca pitā ca bhātaro ca, bhariyā yāpi dhanena hoti kītā;

Te cāpi jahanti aññamaññaṃ, udaye mā pamāda carassu dhammaṃ.

56. Mother and father and brothers, and even a wife who has been bought with wealth; they too abandon one another. O Udayā, be not heedless; practice the Dhamma.

57.

57.

“Kāyo [M 4.0114] parabhojananti ñatvā, saṃsāre sugatiñca duggatiñca;

Ittaravāsoti jāniyāna, udaye mā pamāda carassu dhamma”nti.

57. Knowing the body is food for others, and knowing that both happy and unhappy destinies in saṃsāra are but a temporary dwelling, O Udayā, be not heedless; practice the Dhamma.

Tattha atipatatīti ativiya patati, sīghaṃ atikkamati. Vayoti paṭhamavayāditividhopi vayo. Khaṇo tathevāti uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇopi tatheva atipatati. Ubhayenapi bhinno imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyusaṅkhāro nāma sīghasotā nadī viya anivattanto sīghaṃ atikkamatīti dasseti. Ṭhānaṃ natthīti “uppannā saṅkhārā abhijjitvā tiṭṭhantū”ti patthanāyapi [V 4.0101] tesaṃ ṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, dhuvaṃ ekaṃseneva buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbepi sattā cavanti, “dhuvaṃ maraṇaṃ, addhuvaṃ jīvita”nti evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāvehīti dīpeti. Parijīyatīti idaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇampi sarīraṃ jīrateva, evaṃ jānāhi. Mā pamādanti tasmā tvaṃ udayabhadde mā pamādaṃ āpajji, appamattā hutvā dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ carāhīti.

54. Therein, 'atipatatī' means it passes exceedingly, it passes swiftly. 'Vayo' refers to the three stages of life, such as youth. 'Khaṇo tatheva' means the moment of arising, persistence, and cessation also passes swiftly in the same way. By both of these, he shows that the life-span of these beings, like a swift-flowing river that does not turn back, passes on quickly. 'Ṭhānaṃ natthi' means that even with the wish, 'May arisen formations remain without breaking,' there is no such state for them. Certainly, without a doubt, all beings, beginning with the Buddha, the Blessed One, pass away. Thus it shows one should develop mindfulness of death: 'Death is certain, life is uncertain.' 'Parijīyati' means: know that this body, even if of golden hue, indeed decays. 'Mā pamāda' means: therefore, you, O Udayabhaddā, do not fall into heedlessness; being heedful, practice the Dhamma of the ten wholesome paths of action.

Kasiṇāti sakalā. Ekassevāti yadi ekasseva rañño, tasmiṃ ekasmiṃyeva anaññādhīnā assa. Taṃ cāpi jahati avītarāgoti taṇhāvasiko puggalo ettakenapi yasena atitto maraṇakāle avītarāgova taṃ vijahati. Evaṃ taṇhāya apūraṇīyabhāvaṃ jānāhīti dīpeti. Te cāpīti mātā puttaṃ, putto mātaraṃ, pitā puttaṃ, putto pitaraṃ, bhātā bhaginiṃ, bhaginī bhātaraṃ, bhariyā sāmikaṃ, sāmiko bhariyanti ete aññamaññaṃ jahanti, nānā honti. Evaṃ sattānaṃ nānābhāvavinābhāvaṃ jānāhīti dīpeti.

55-56. 'Kasiṇā' means entire. 'Ekasseva' means: if it belonged to one king alone, it would be his alone, not subject to another. 'Taṃ cāpi jahati avītarāgo' means: a person under the sway of craving, unsatisfied even with so much glory, abandons it at the time of death, still not free from passion. Thus it shows the insatiable nature of craving. 'Te cāpi' means: mother and son, son and mother, father and son, son and father, brother and sister, sister and brother, wife and husband, husband and wife—these abandon one another and become separate. Thus it shows the state of being separate and parted from one another among beings.

Parabhojananti vividhānaṃ kākādīnaṃ parasattānaṃ bhojanaṃ. Ittaravāsoti yā esā imasmiṃ saṃsāre manussabhūtā suggati ca tiracchānabhūtā duggati ca, etaṃ ubhayampi “ittaravāso”ti jānitvā mā pamādaṃ, carassu dhammaṃ. Imesaṃ sattānaṃ nānāṭhānato āgantvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samāgamo paritto, ime sattā appakasmiṃyeva kāle ekato vasanti, tasmā appamattā hohīti.

57. 'Parabhojanaṃ' means food for other beings, such as various crows and so on. 'Ittaravāso' means: knowing that both this happy destiny as a human and the unhappy destiny as an animal in this saṃsāra are but a 'temporary dwelling,' do not be heedless; practice the Dhamma. The coming together in one place of these beings who have come from various places is brief; these beings dwell together for only a short time. Therefore, be heedful.

Evaṃ [M 4.0115] mahāsatto tassā ovādamadāsi. Sāpi tassa dhammakathāya pasīditvā thutiṃ karontī osānagāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being gave her this advice. And she, pleased by the Great Being's Dhamma talk and wishing to praise him, spoke the concluding verse:

58.

58.

“Sādhu [P 4.0113] bhāsatiyaṃ yakkho, appaṃ maccāna jīvitaṃ;

Kasirañca parittañca, tañca dukkhena saṃyutaṃ;

Sāhaṃ ekā pabbajissāmi, hitvā kāsiṃ surundhana”nti.

58. Well does the spirit speak: short is the life of mortals. It is difficult and brief, and it is conjoined with suffering. I shall go forth alone, having left Kāsi and the city of Surundhana.

Tattha sādhūti “appaṃ maccāna jīvita”nti bhāsamāno ayaṃ devarājā sādhu bhāsati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Idañhi kasirañca dukkhaṃ assādarahitaṃ, parittañca na bahukaṃ ittarakālaṃ. Sace hi kasirampi samānaṃ dīghakālaṃ pavatteyya, parittakampi samānaṃ sukhaṃ bhaveyya, idaṃ pana kasirañceva parittañca sakalena vaṭṭadukkhena saṃyutaṃ sannihitaṃ. Sāhanti sā ahaṃ. Surundhananti surundhananagarañca kāsiraṭṭhañca chaḍḍetvā ekikāva pabbajissāmīti āha.

Herein, 'sādhu' means: in saying, 'short is the life of mortals,' this king of gods speaks well. For what reason? For this life is difficult, suffering, and devoid of delight; it is brief, not long, and of short duration. If, being difficult, it were to last a long time, or, being brief, it were pleasant—but this life is both difficult and brief, conjoined with the entire suffering of the round of existence and ever-present. 'Sāhaṃ' means 'I, that one.' 'Surundhana' means she said: 'Having abandoned the city of Surundhana and the kingdom of Kāsi, I will go forth alone.'

Bodhisatto [V 4.0102] tassā ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Sāpi punadivase amacce rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā antonagareyeva ramaṇīye uyyāne isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā dhammaṃ caritvā āyupariyosāne tāvatiṃsabhavane bodhisattassa pādaparicārikā hutvā nibbatti.

The Bodhisatta, having given her this advice, went to his own abode. On the next day, she had the ministers accept the kingdom and, in a delightful park within the city itself, she went forth into the life of an ascetic. Having practiced the Dhamma, at the end of her life she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the consort of the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājadhītā rāhulamātā ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, proclaimed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of Stream-Entry. At that time, the king’s daughter was Rāhula’s mother, and Sakka was I myself.

Udayajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Udaya Jātaka, the Fourth.

[459] 5. Pānīyajātakavaṇṇanā

[459] 5. The Commentary on the Pānīya Jātaka

Mitto mittassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye sāvatthivāsino pañcasatā gihisahāyakā tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā upasampannā antokoṭisanthāre vasantā aḍḍharattasamaye kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkesuṃ. Sabbaṃ [M 4.0116] heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Bhagavato āṇattiyā panāyasmatā ānandena bhikkhusaṅghe sannipātite satthā paññattāsane nisīditvā anodissakaṃ katvā “kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkayitthā”ti avatvā sabbasaṅgāhikavaseneva “bhikkhave, kileso khuddako nāma natthi, bhikkhunā nāma uppannuppannā kilesā niggahetabbā, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppannepi buddhe kilese niggahetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ pattā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning with 'Mitto mittassā,' concerning the suppression of defilements. At one time, five hundred lay companions from Sāvatthī, having heard the Tathāgata's teaching, went forth, received the higher ordination, and while dwelling in the inner quarters, at midnight they entertained thoughts of sensual desire. All this should be understood in the way stated previously. Then, by the Blessed One's command, when the community of monks had been assembled by the Venerable Ānanda, the Teacher, seated on the prepared seat, without specifying anyone and without saying, 'You entertained thoughts of sensual desire,' but in a comprehensive manner, said: 'Monks, there is no such thing as a small defilement. A monk must restrain defilements as they arise. The wise ones of old, even when no Buddha had arisen, restrained their defilements and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 4.0114] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ gāmake dve sahāyakā pānīyatumbāni ādāya khettaṃ gantvā ekamantaṃ ṭhapetvā khettaṃ koṭṭetvā pipāsitakāle āgantvā pānīyaṃ pivanti. Tesu eko pānīyatthāya āgantvā attano pānīyaṃ rakkhanto itarassa tumbato pivitvā sāyaṃ araññā nikkhamitvā nhāyitvā ṭhito “atthi nu kho me kāyadvārādīhi ajja kiñci pāpaṃ kata”nti upadhārento thenetvā pānīyassa pivitabhāvaṃ disvā saṃvegappatto hutvā “ayaṃ taṇhā vaḍḍhamānā maṃ apāyesu khipissati, imaṃ kilesaṃ niggaṇhissāmī”ti pānīyassa thenetvā pivitabhāvaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ āvajjento aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ itaro nhāyitvā uṭṭhito “ehi, samma, gharaṃ gacchāmā”ti āha. “Gaccha tvaṃ, mama gharena kiccaṃ natthi, paccekabuddhā [V 4.0103] nāma maya”nti. “Paccekabuddhā nāma tumhādisā na hontī”ti. “Atha kīdisā paccekabuddhā hontī”ti? “Dvaṅgulakesā kāsāyavatthavasanā uttarahimavante nandamūlakapabbhāre vasantī”ti. So sīsaṃ parāmasi, taṃ khaṇaññevassa gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivatthameva, vijjulatāsadisaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ baddhameva, alattakapāṭalavaṇṇaṃ uttarāsaṅgacīvaraṃ ekaṃsaṃ katameva, meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭe ṭhapitameva, bhamaravaṇṇo mattikāpatto vāmaaṃsakūṭe laggitova ahosi. So ākāse ṭhatvā dhammaṃ desetvā uppatitvā nandamūlakapabbhāreyeva otari.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, in the Kāsi country, in a certain village, two friends, taking water gourds, went to a field. They set them aside, tilled the field, and when thirsty, returned to drink the water. One of them, coming for water, while guarding his own water, drank from the other’s gourd. In the evening, having left the wilds, he bathed and stood reflecting, 'Have I done any evil today through the doors of the body and so forth?' Realizing he had stolen and drunk the water, he was struck with spiritual urgency. 'This craving, as it grows, will cast me into the lower realms. I will subdue this defilement.' Taking the theft of the water as his object, he developed insight, gave rise to the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and stood reflecting on the qualities he had attained. Then the other, having bathed and risen, said, 'Come, friend, let us go home.' 'You go. I have no business with a home. I am a Paccekabuddha.' 'Paccekabuddhas are not like you.' 'Then what are Paccekabuddhas like?' 'They have hair two fingers’ breadth long, wear saffron robes, and dwell in the northern Himalayas, in the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.' He touched his head, and in that instant his lay appearance vanished. A bright red double-layered undergarment was already worn, a waistband like a streak of lightning was already fastened, an upper robe the color of red lac was already draped over one shoulder, a rag-robe the color of a dark cloud was already placed on his shoulder-point, and a bee-colored clay bowl was already hanging from his left shoulder. Standing in the air, he taught the Dhamma, then soared up and descended at the Nandamūlaka cave.

Aparopi kāsigāmeyeva kuṭumbiko āpaṇe nisinno ekaṃ purisaṃ attano bhariyaṃ ādāya gacchantaṃ disvā taṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ itthiṃ indriyāni bhinditvā oloketvā puna cintesi “ayaṃ lobho vaḍḍhamāno maṃ [M 4.0117] apāyesu khipissatī”ti saṃviggamānaso vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā ākāse ṭhito dhammaṃ desetvā nandamūlakapabbhārameva [P 4.0115] gato.

Another householder, also from a Kāsi village, was sitting in a shop when he saw a man going by with his own wife. Seeing that woman who possessed excellent beauty, he looked at her, breaking the restraint of his senses, and then he thought, 'This greed, as it grows, will cast me into the lower realms.' With a mind stirred by spiritual urgency, he developed insight, brought forth the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, stood in the sky, taught the Dhamma, and went to the Nandamūlaka cave.

Aparepi kāsigāmavāsinoyeva dve pitāputtā ekato maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Aṭavīmukhe pana corā uṭṭhitā honti. Te pitāputte labhitvā puttaṃ gahetvā “dhanaṃ āharitvā tava puttaṃ gaṇhā”ti pitaraṃ vissajjenti, dve bhātaro labhitvā kaniṭṭhaṃ gahetvā jeṭṭhaṃ vissajjenti, ācariyantevāsike labhitvā ācariyaṃ gahetvā antevāsikaṃ vissajjenti, antevāsiko sippalobhena dhanaṃ āharitvā ācariyaṃ gaṇhitvā gacchati. Atha te pitāputtāpi tattha corānaṃ uṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tvaṃ maṃ ‘pitā’ti mā vada, ahampi taṃ ‘putto’ti na vakkhāmī”ti katikaṃ katvā corehi gahitakāle “tumhe aññamaññaṃ kiṃ hothā”ti puṭṭhā “na kiñci homā”ti sampajānamusāvādaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu aṭavito nikkhamitvā sāyaṃ nhāyitvā ṭhitesu putto attano sīlaṃ sodhento taṃ musāvādaṃ disvā “idaṃ pāpaṃ vaḍḍhamānaṃ maṃ apāyesu khipissati, imaṃ kilesaṃ niggaṇhissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā ākāse ṭhito pitu dhammaṃ desetvā nandamūlakapabbhārameva gato.

Furthermore, two—a father and a son—who were inhabitants of a Kāsi village, were traveling together along a road. Now, robbers had emerged at the entrance to the forest. When those robbers seize a father and a son, they hold the son and release the father, saying, 'Bring wealth and take your son.' When they seize two brothers, they hold the younger and release the elder. When they seize a teacher and a student, they hold the teacher and release the student; the student, out of desire for the craft, brings wealth, takes his teacher, and goes. Now, that father and son also, knowing that robbers had emerged there, made an agreement: 'You must not call me "father," and I also will not call you "son."' When they were seized by the robbers and asked, 'What are you to each other?' they, knowing the truth, spoke a deliberate falsehood, saying, 'We are nothing to each other.' After they had emerged from the forest and were standing there having bathed in the evening, the son, while purifying his own virtue, saw that falsehood and thought, 'This evil, if it increases, will cast me into the planes of misery; I shall subdue this defilement.' Developing insight, he attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha and, standing in the sky, taught the Dhamma to his father and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.

Aparopi kāsigāmeyeva pana eko gāmabhojako māghātaṃ kārāpesi. Atha naṃ balikammakāle mahājano sannipatitvā āha “sāmi, mayaṃ migasūkarādayo māretvā yakkhānaṃ balikammaṃ karissāma, balikammakālo eso”ti. Tumhākaṃ pubbe karaṇaniyāmeneva karothāti manussā bahuṃ pāṇātipātamakaṃsu. So bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ disvā “ime manussā ettake pāṇe mārentā mamevekassa vacanena mārayiṃsū”ti kukkuccaṃ katvā vātapānaṃ nissāya ṭhitakova vipassanaṃ [V 4.0104] vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā ākāse ṭhito mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā nandamūlakapabbhārameva gato.

Furthermore, another village headman in a Kāsi village had a ban on slaughter proclaimed. Then, at the time of the sacrificial offering, a great crowd gathered and said, 'Master, we shall kill deer, boars, and so on and perform a sacrificial offering to the spirits; this is the time for the sacrifice.' When he said, 'Do just as you have done according to your former custom,' the people committed much destruction of life. Seeing so much fish and meat, he became remorseful, thinking, 'While these people are killing so many living beings, they killed them only because of my word.' While standing leaning against a window, he developed insight, attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha and, standing in the sky, taught the Dhamma to the great crowd and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.

Aparopi kāsiraṭṭheyeva gāmabhojako majjavikkayaṃ vāretvā “sāmi, pubbe imasmiṃ kāle surāchaṇo nāma hoti, kiṃ karomā”ti mahājanena vutto “tumhākaṃ porāṇakaniyāmeneva karothā”ti [P 4.0116][M 4.0118] āha. Manussā chaṇaṃ katvā suraṃ pivitvā kalahaṃ karontā hatthapāde bhañjitvā sīsaṃ bhinditvā kaṇṇe chinditvā bahudaṇḍena bajjhiṃsu. Gāmabhojako te disvā cintesi “mayi ananujānante ime imaṃ dukkhaṃ na vindeyyu”nti. So ettakena kukkuccaṃ katvā vātapānaṃ nissāya ṭhitakova vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā “appamattā hothā”ti ākāse ṭhatvā dhammaṃ desetvā nandamūlakapabbhārameva gato.

Another village headman, also in the Kāsi country, prohibited the sale of liquor. When he was told by the great crowd, 'Master, formerly at this time there was a liquor festival; what shall we do?' he said, 'Do just as you have done according to your ancient custom.' The people held the festival, drank liquor, and while quarreling, broke their hands and feet, split their heads, tore their ears, and were bound with many punishments. Seeing them, the village headman thought, 'If I had not given permission, these people would not have experienced this suffering.' Becoming remorseful over this, while standing leaning against a window, he developed insight, attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and standing in the sky, taught the Dhamma, saying, 'Be heedful!' and went to the Nandamūlaka mountain cave.

Aparabhāge te pañca paccekabuddhā bhikkhācāratthāya bārāṇasidvāre otaritvā sunivatthā supārutā pāsādikehi abhikkamādīhi piṇḍāya carantā rājadvāraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Rājā te disvā pasannacitto rājanivesanaṃ pavesetvā pāde dhovitvā gandhatelena makkhetvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisitvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ paṭhamavaye pabbajjā sobhati, imasmiṃ vaye pabbajantā kathaṃ kāmesu ādīnavaṃ passittha, kiṃ vo ārammaṇaṃ ahosī”ti pucchi. Te tassa kathentā –

At a later time, those five Paccekabuddhas, descending at the gate of Bārāṇasī for the purpose of the alms-round, well-clothed and well-robed, wandering for alms with pleasing deportment in their movements and so forth, arrived at the palace gate. The king, seeing them, with a mind inspired by confidence, had them enter the royal residence, washed their feet, anointed them with fragrant oil, served them with excellent hard and soft food, and sitting down to one side, asked, 'Venerable sirs, renunciation in the prime of life is beautiful for you. While renouncing at this age, how did you see the danger in sensual pleasures? What was the basis for your awakening?' They, in telling him, replied:

59.

59.

“Mitto mittassa pānīyaṃ, adinnaṃ paribhuñjisaṃ;

Tena pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, tasmā pabbajito ahaṃ.

'Being a friend, I consumed a friend's water that was not given. Because of that, I was afterwards disgusted; that evil was done by me. May I not do evil again; therefore, I have gone forth.'

60.

60.

“Paradārañca disvāna, chando me udapajjatha;

Tena pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, tasmā pabbajito ahaṃ.

'And having seen another's wife, desire arose in me. Because of that, I was afterwards disgusted; that evil was done by me. May I not do evil again; therefore, I have gone forth.'

61.

61.

“Pitaraṃ me mahārāja, corā agaṇhu kānane;

Tesāhaṃ pucchito jānaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākariṃ.

'O great king, robbers seized my father in the forest. When questioned by them, although I knew the truth, I explained it to them otherwise.'

62.

62.

“Tena [V 4.0105] pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, tasmā pabbajito ahaṃ.

'Because of that, I was afterwards disgusted; that evil was done by me. May I not do evil again; therefore, I have gone forth.'

63.

63.

“Pāṇātipātamakaruṃ, somayāge upaṭṭhite;

Tesāhaṃ samanuññāsiṃ.

'They committed the destruction of life when the Soma sacrifice was prepared. I gave my consent to them.'

64.

64.

“Tena [M 4.0119] pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, tasmā pabbajito ahaṃ.

'Because of that, I was afterwards disgusted; that evil was done by me. May I not do evil again; therefore, I have gone forth.'

65.

65.

“Surāmerayamādhukā, ye janā paṭhamāsu no;

Bahūnaṃ te anatthāya, majjapānamakappayuṃ;

Tesāhaṃ [P 4.0117] samanuññāsiṃ.

'Those people who were first among us perceived liquor and wine as sweet; for the harm of many, they devised the drinking of intoxicants. I gave my consent to them.'

66.

66.

“Tena pacchā vijigucchiṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, tasmā pabbajito aha”nti. –

'Because of that, I was afterwards disgusted; that evil was done by me. May I not do evil again; therefore, I have gone forth.'

Imā paṭipāṭiyā pañca gāthā abhāsiṃsu. Rājāpi ekamekassa byākaraṇaṃ sutvā “bhante, ayaṃ pabbajjā tumhākaṃ yevānucchavikā”ti thutimakāsi.

They spoke these five verses in succession. The king also, hearing each one's explanation, praised them, saying, 'Venerable sirs, this renunciation is indeed suitable for you.'

Tattha mitto mittassāti mahārāja, ahaṃ ekassa mitto hutvā tassa mittassa santakaṃ pānīyaṃ iminā niyāmeneva paribhuñjiṃ. Tasmāti yasmā puthujjanā nāma pāpakammaṃ karonti, tasmā ahaṃ mā puna akaraṃ pāpaṃ, taṃ pāpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pabbajitomhi. Chandoti mahārāja, imināva niyāmena mama paradāraṃ disvā kāme chando uppajji. Agaṇhūti agaṇhiṃsu. Jānanti tesaṃ corānaṃ “ayaṃ kiṃ te hotī”ti pucchito jānantoyeva “na kiñci hotī”ti aññathā byākāsiṃ. Somayāgeti navacande uṭṭhite somayāgaṃ nāma yakkhabaliṃ kariṃsu, tasmiṃ upaṭṭhite. Samanuññāsinti samanuñño āsiṃ. Surāmerayamādhukāti piṭṭhasurādisurañca pupphāsavādimerayañca pakkamadhu viya madhuraṃ maññamānā. Ye janā paṭhamāsu noti ye no gāme janā paṭhamaṃ evarūpā āsuṃ ahesuṃ. Bahūnaṃ teti te ekadivasaṃ ekasmiṃ chaṇe patte bahūnaṃ anatthāya majjapānaṃ akappayiṃsu.

Therein, 'a friend's': O great king, I, being a friend to one, consumed that friend's water in this very manner. 'Therefore': Because ordinary people indeed commit evil deeds, therefore I, lest I do evil again, having made that evil my object, have gone forth. 'Desire': O great king, in this very manner, upon seeing another's wife, desire for sensual pleasures arose in me. 'Agaṇhu' (they seized): They seized. 'Knowing': When asked by those robbers, 'What is this to you?' I, knowing full well, falsely declared, 'It is nothing to me.' 'Soma sacrifice': When the new moon had risen, they performed a sacrifice called the Soma offering, a yakkha offering, when that was undertaken. 'Samanuññāsiṃ' (I approved): I was agreeable. 'Liquor, wine, and honey-liquor': Considering flour-based liquor and other liquors, and flower-juice and other wines, to be sweet like ripe honey. 'Those people who were first in our village': Those people in our village who were formerly of such a kind. 'For many': They, one day, when a certain festival arrived, prepared intoxicating drink to the harm of many.

Rājā [V 4.0106] tesaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā pasannacitto cīvarasāṭake ca bhesajjāni ca datvā paccekabuddhe uyyojesi. Tepi tassa anumodanaṃ katvā tattheva agamaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya rājā vatthukāmesu viratto anapekkho hutvā [M 4.0120] nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā itthiyo anālapitvā anoloketvā virattacitto uṭṭhāya sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā nisinno setabhittiyaṃ kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ nibbattesi. So jhānappatto kāme garahanto –

The king, hearing their Dhamma, with a mind inspired by confidence, gave them robe-cloths and medicines and sent the Paccekabuddhas on their way. They also, having expressed their appreciation to him, went to that very same place. From then on, the king became detached and without longing for material sensual pleasures, and after eating food of various excellent flavors, he did not talk to or look at women. With a detached mind, he rose and entered his auspicious chamber, and while sitting, he performed the kasiṇa-preliminary on a white wall and generated jhāna. Having attained jhāna, censuring sensual pleasures, he spoke this verse:

67.

67.

“Dhiratthu subahū kāme, duggandhe bahukaṇṭake;

Ye ahaṃ paṭisevanto, nālabhiṃ tādisaṃ sukha”nti. – gāthamāha;

'Woe to these many sensual pleasures, foul-smelling and full of many thorns! While I was indulging in them, I did not obtain such happiness.' Thus he spoke the verse.

Tattha bahukaṇṭaketi bahū paccāmitte. Ye ahanti yo ahaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tādisanti etādisaṃ kilesarahitaṃ jhānasukhaṃ.

Herein, 'full of many thorns' means 'many enemies.' 'Ye ahaṃ' (which I): Or 'yo ahaṃ' (who I) is also a reading. 'Such' refers to such jhāna happiness, free from defilements.

Athassa [P 4.0118] aggamahesī “ayaṃ rājā paccekabuddhānaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā ukkaṇṭhitarūpo ahosi, amhehi saddhiṃ akathetvāva sirigabbhaṃ paviṭṭho, pariggaṇhissāmi tāva na”nti cintetvā sirigabbhadvāre ṭhitā rañño kāmesu garahantassa udānaṃ sutvā “mahārāja, tvaṃ kāme garahasi, kāmasukhasadisaṃ nāma sukhaṃ natthī”ti kāme vaṇṇentī itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then his chief queen, thinking, 'This king, having heard the Dhamma talk of the Paccekabuddhas, has become discontented. Without speaking to us, he has entered the splendid chamber. I will investigate him first,' stood at the door of the splendid chamber. Hearing the king's inspired utterance disparaging sensual pleasures, she praised sensual pleasures, speaking the following verse: 'Great king, you disparage sensual pleasures, but there is no happiness like the happiness of sensual pleasure.'

68.

68.

“Mahassādā sukhā kāmā, natthi kāmā paraṃ sukhaṃ;

Ye kāme paṭisevanti, saggaṃ te upapajjare”ti.

"Sensual pleasures are greatly delightful and pleasant; there is no happiness beyond sensual pleasures. Those who indulge in sensual pleasures are reborn in heaven."

Tattha mahassādāti mahārāja, ete kāmā nāma mahāassādā, ito uttariṃ aññaṃ sukhaṃ natthi. Kāmasevino hi apāye anupagamma sagge nibbattantīti attho.

Herein, 'greatly delightful': O great king, these sensual pleasures are indeed greatly delightful; there is no other happiness superior to this. The meaning is that those who indulge in sensual pleasures, without going to the lower realms, are reborn in heaven.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto tassā “nassa vasali, kiṃ kathesi, kāmesu sukhaṃ nāma kuto atthi, vipariṇāmadukkhā ete”ti garahanto sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta, rebuking her, said: "Perish, you wretched woman! What are you saying? Where can there be happiness in sensual pleasures? These are suffering through change." Then he spoke the remaining verses:

69.

69.

“Appassādā dukhā kāmā, natthi kāmā paraṃ dukhaṃ;

Ye kāme paṭisevanti, nirayaṃ te upapajjare.

"Sensual pleasures are of little gratification and are painful; there is no suffering greater than sensual pleasures. Those who indulge in sensual pleasures are reborn in hell."

70.

70.

“Asī [V 4.0107] yathā sunisito, nettiṃsova supāyiko;

Sattīva urasi khittā, kāmā dukkhatarā tato.

"Like a well-sharpened sword, like a blade that drinks blood; like a spear thrust into the chest, sensual pleasures are more painful than that."

71.

71.

“Aṅgārānaṃva [M 4.0121] jalitaṃ, kāsuṃ sādhikaporisaṃ;

Phālaṃva divasaṃtattaṃ, kāmā dukkhatarā tato.

"Like a pit of burning coals, more than a man's height; like a ploughshare heated all day, sensual pleasures are more painful than that."

72.

72.

“Visaṃ yathā halāhalaṃ, telaṃ pakkuthitaṃ yathā;

Tambalohavilīnaṃva, kāmā dukkhatarā tato”ti.

"Like the deadly poison halāhala, like boiling oil, or like molten copper; sensual pleasures are more painful than these."

Tattha nettiṃsoti nikkaruṇo, idampi ekassa khaggassa nāmaṃ. Dukkhatarāti evaṃ jalitaṅgārakāsuṃ vā divasaṃ tattaṃ phālaṃ vā paṭicca yaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tatopi kāmāyeva dukkhatarāti attho. Anantaragāthāya yathā etāni visādīni dukkhāvahanato dukkhāni, evaṃ kāmāpi dukkhā, taṃ pana kāmadukkhaṃ itarehi dukkhehi dukkhataranti attho.

Herein, 'nettiṃsa' means merciless; it is also the name of a certain sword. The meaning of 'more painful' is that the suffering arising from a pit of burning coals or a ploughshare heated all day is less than that of sensual pleasures. In the immediately preceding verse, just as these, such as poisons, are painful because they bring suffering, so too are sensual pleasures painful; but the suffering of sensual pleasures is more painful than those other sufferings—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ [P 4.0119] mahāsatto deviyā dhammaṃ desetvā amacce sannipātetvā “bhonto amaccā, tumhe rajjaṃ paṭipajjatha, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti vatvā mahājanassa rodantassa paridevantassa uṭṭhāya ākāse ṭhatvā ovādaṃ datvā anilapatheneva uttarahimavantaṃ gantvā ramaṇīye padese assamaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the queen, the Great Being assembled his ministers and said: "Honorable ministers, you take charge of the kingdom; I will go forth." With these words, as the people wept and lamented, he rose into the sky, gave them advice, and by the path of the wind, went to the Northern Himalayas. There, in a delightful place, he had a hermitage built, embraced the ascetic life, and at the end of his life, was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “bhikkhave, kileso khuddako nāma natthi, appamattakopi paṇḍitehi niggahitabboyevā”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne pañcasatā bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tadā paccekabuddhā parinibbāyiṃsu, devī rāhulamātā ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said: "Monks, there is no defilement that is small; even the slightest should be subdued by the wise." Having revealed the Truths, he connected the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, five hundred monks were established in Arahantship. At that time, the Paccekabuddhas attained final Nibbāna, the queen was Rāhula's mother, and the king was none other than myself.

Pānīyajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Pānīya Jātaka, the Fifth.

[460] 6. Yudhañcayajātakavaṇṇanā

[460] 6. The Commentary on the Yudhañcaya Jātaka

Mittāmaccaparibyūḷhanti [V 4.0108] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “āvuso, sace dasabalo agāraṃ ajjhāvasissa, sakalacakkavāḷagabbhe cakkavattirājā abhavissa sattaratanasamannāgato caturiddhīhi samiddho parosahassaputtaparivāro[M 4.0122], so evarūpaṃ sirivibhavaṃ pahāya kāmesu dosaṃ disvā aḍḍharattasamaye channasahāyova kaṇṭakamāruyha nikkhamitvā anomanadītīre pabbajitvā chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ katvā sammāsambodhiṃ patto”ti satthu guṇakathaṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, pubbepi dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare rajjaṃ pahāya nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Surrounded by friends and ministers," the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the great renunciation. One day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and discussed: "Friends, if the Ten-Powered One had remained a householder, he would have become a wheel-turning monarch in the entire world-sphere, endowed with the seven treasures, flourishing with the four psychic powers, surrounded by over a thousand sons. Yet, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced such glory, mounted his horse Kaṇṭhaka at midnight with Channa as his companion, departed, and after going forth on the banks of the Anomā River, practiced arduous austerities for six years before attaining perfect enlightenment." Thus, they spoke in praise of the Teacher's virtues. When the Teacher arrived and asked: "Monks, with what discussion are you now assembled?" and they replied: "With this very one," he said: "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has undertaken the great renunciation. Even in the past, he renounced kingship in the twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī." Then he related a past event.

Atīte rammanagare sabbadatto nāma rājā ahosi. Ayañhi bārāṇasī udayajātake (jā. 1.11.37 ādayo) surundhananagaraṃ nāma jātā, cūḷasutasomajātake (jā. 2.17.195 ādayo) sudassanaṃ nāma, soṇanandajātake (jā. 2.20.92 ādayo) brahmavaḍḍhanaṃ nāma, khaṇḍahālajātake (jā. 2.22.982 ādayo) pupphavatī [P 4.0120] nāma, saṅkhabrāhmaṇajātake (jā. 1.10.39 ādayo) moḷinī nāma, imasmiṃ pana yudhañcayajātake rammanagaraṃ nāma ahosi. Evamassā kadāci nāmaṃ parivattati. Tattha sabbadattarañño puttasahassaṃ ahosi. Yudhañcayassa nāma jeṭṭhaputtassa uparajjaṃ adāsi. So divase divase mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Evaṃ gacchante kāle bodhisatto ekadivasaṃ pātova rathavaramāruyha mahantena sirivibhavena uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchanto rukkhaggatiṇaggasākhaggamakkaṭakasuttajālādīsu muttājālākārena laggitaussavabindūni disvā “samma sārathi, kiṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā “ete deva, himasamaye patanakaussavabindūni nāmā”ti sutvā divasabhāgaṃ uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhakāle paccāgacchanto te adisvāva “samma sārathi, kahaṃ nu kho ete ussavabindū, na te idāni passāmī”ti pucchi. “Deva, te sūriye uggacchante sabbeva bhijjitvā pathaviyaṃ patantī”ti sutvā saṃvegappatto hutvā “imesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitasaṅkhārāpi tiṇagge ussavabindusadisāva, mayā byādhijarāmaraṇehi apīḷiteyeva mātāpitaro āpucchitvā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ussavabindumeva ārammaṇaṃ katvā āditte viya tayo bhave passanto attano gehaṃ agantvā alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya vinicchayasālāya nisinnassa pitu santikaṃyeva gantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito pabbajjaṃ yācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in the city of Rammanagara, there was a king named Sabbadatta. Indeed, this city of Bārāṇasī was called Surundhana in the Udaya Jātaka (Jā. 1.11.37, etc.); Sudassana in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka (Jā. 2.17.195, etc.); Brahmavaḍḍhana in the Soṇananda Jātaka (Jā. 2.20.92, etc.); Pupphavatī in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.982, etc.); Moḷinī in the Saṅkha Brāhmaṇa Jātaka (Jā. 1.10.39, etc.); but in this Yudhañcaya Jātaka, it was called Rammanagara. Thus, its name changes from time to time. There, King Sabbadatta had a thousand sons. He gave the viceroyalty to his eldest son, named Yudhañcaya. Day by day, he held great almsgivings. As time passed, one morning the Bodhisatta mounted his excellent chariot and, with great royal splendor, went to the park for amusement. Seeing dewdrops clinging to the tips of trees, grass, branches, spider webs, and the like, resembling strings of pearls, he asked: "Good charioteer, what are these?" Hearing: "Your Majesty, these are dewdrops that fall in the cold season," he spent part of the day playing in the park. Returning in the evening, he no longer saw them and asked: "Good charioteer, where have those dewdrops gone? I do not see them now." Hearing: "Your Majesty, when the sun rises, they all break and fall to the ground," he was struck with a sense of urgency and thought: "The life-constituents of these beings are just like dewdrops on grass tips. Though I am not yet afflicted by sickness, old age, and death, I should take leave of my parents and go forth." Taking the dewdrops as his object of reflection, seeing the three realms of existence as if on fire, he did not go to his own house, but went to his father, who was seated in the decorated judgment hall. He paid homage to his father and stood to one side. Requesting permission to go forth, he first spoke this verse:

73.

73.

“Mittāmaccaparibyūḷhaṃ[V 4.0109][M 4.0123], ahaṃ vande rathesabhaṃ;

Pabbajissāmahaṃ rāja, taṃ devo anumaññatū”ti.

"Surrounded by friends and ministers, I pay homage to you, O noblest of charioteers. I shall go forth, O king; may Your Majesty grant me permission."

Tattha paribyūḷhanti parivāritaṃ. Taṃ devoti taṃ mama pabbajjaṃ devo anujānātūti attho.

Here, 'paribyūḷhaṃ' means surrounded or encircled. The meaning of 'taṃ devo' is: May Your Majesty approve of my going forth.

Atha naṃ rājā nivārento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king, seeking to restrain him, spoke a second verse:

74.

74.

“Sace te ūnaṃ kāmehi, ahaṃ paripūrayāmi te;

Yo taṃ hiṃ sati vāremi, mā pabbaja yudhañcayā”ti.

"If you are deficient in sensual pleasures, I will fulfill them for you; and I will restrain whoever harms you. Do not go forth, Yudhañcaya."

Taṃ [P 4.0121] sutvā kumāro tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince spoke a third verse:

75.

75.

“Na matthi ūnaṃ kāmehi, hiṃsitā me na vijjati;

Dīpañca kātumicchāmi, yaṃ jarā nābhikīratī”ti.

"There is no deficiency in sensual pleasures for me, nor is there anyone who harms me; I wish to make a refuge that old age cannot overwhelm."

Tattha dīpañcāti tāta neva mayhaṃ kāmehi ūnaṃ atthi, na maṃ hiṃsanto koci vijjati, ahaṃ pana paralokagamanāya attano patiṭṭhaṃ kātumicchāmi. Kīdisaṃ? Yaṃ jarā nābhikīrati na viddhaṃseti, tamahaṃ kātumicchāmi, amatamahānibbānaṃ gavesissāmi, na me kāmehi attho, anujānātha maṃ, mahārājāti vadati.

Here, 'dīpañca' means: 'Father, I have no lack of sensual pleasures, nor does anyone harm me. Yet, I wish to establish a refuge for myself for the journey to the next world. What kind of refuge? That which old age does not overwhelm or destroy—that I wish to create. I will seek the great deathless Nibbāna. I have no need for sensual pleasures. Grant me permission, O great king,' he says.

Iti punappunaṃ kumāro pabbajjaṃ yāci, rājā “mā pabbajā”ti vāreti. Tamatthamāvikaronto satthā upaḍḍhaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus again and again the prince requested to go forth, but the king prevented him, saying: "Do not go forth." To reveal that matter, the Teacher spoke half a verse:

76.

76.

“Putto vā pitaraṃ yāce, pitā vā puttamorasa”nti.

"A son may beg from his father, or a father from his own son."

Tattha vā-kāro sampiṇḍanattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “evaṃ, bhikkhave, putto ca pitaraṃ yācati, pitā ca orasaṃ puttaṃ yācatī”ti.

Here, the particle 'vā' has the meaning of aggregation. This is what is said: "Thus, monks, a son asks his father, and a father asks his own son."

Sesaṃ upaḍḍhagāthaṃ rājā āha –

The king spoke the remaining half-verse:

“Negamo [V 4.0110] taṃ yāce tāta, mā pabbaja yudhañcayā”ti.

"The townspeople beg you, my dear: do not go forth, Yudhañcaya."

Tassattho – ayaṃ te tāta nigamavāsimahājano yācati, nagarajanopi mā tvaṃ pabbajāti.

Its meaning is: "Dear son, this great multitude of townspeople, as well as the city people, entreat you that you should not go forth."

Kumāro punapi pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince then spoke a fifth verse:

77.

77.

“Mā [M 4.0124] maṃ deva nivārehi, pabbajantaṃ rathesabha;

Māhaṃ kāmehi sammatto, jarāya vasamanvagū”ti.

"O king, do not hinder me as I go forth, O noblest of charioteers; let me not, infatuated with sensual pleasures, come under the power of old age."

Tattha vasamanvagūti mā ahaṃ kāmehi sammatto pamatto jarāya vasagāmī nāma homi, vaṭṭadukkhaṃ pana khepetvā yathā ca sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivijjhanako homi,. Tathā maṃ olokehīti adhippāyo.

Here, 'vasamanvagū' means: 'May I not be intoxicated or heedless regarding sensual pleasures, nor subject to aging. Rather, having exhausted the suffering of the round of existence, may I become one who penetrates the knowledge of omniscience. Look upon me in such a way.' This is the intention.

Evaṃ vutte rājā appaṭibhāṇo ahosi. Mātā panassa “putto te, devi, pitaraṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetī”ti sutvā “kiṃ tumhe kathethā”ti nirassāsena mukhena suvaṇṇasivikāya nisīditvā sīghaṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yācamānā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

When this was said, the king was speechless. But his mother, hearing, "Your son, O queen, is asking his father for permission to go forth," said, "What are you saying?" and with a breathless face, sitting in a golden palanquin, she quickly went to the judgment hall and, pleading, spoke the sixth verse:

78.

78.

“Ahaṃ taṃ tāta yācāmi, ahaṃ putta nivāraye;

Ciraṃ taṃ daṭṭhumicchāmi, mā pabbaja yudhañcayā”ti.

"My dear, I beg you; son, I restrain you. I wish to see you for a long time; do not go forth, Yudhañcaya."

Taṃ [P 4.0122] sutvā kumāro sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince spoke the seventh verse:

79.

79.

“Ussāvova tiṇaggamhi, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Evamāyu manussānaṃ, mā maṃ amma nivārayā”ti.

"Like a dewdrop on a blade of grass at sunrise, so is the life of humans. O mother, do not hinder me."

Tassattho – amma, yathā tiṇagge ussavabindu sūriyassa uggamanaṃ patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, pathaviyaṃ patati, evaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ parittaṃ tāvakālikaṃ aciraṭṭhitikaṃ, evarūpe lokasannivāse kathaṃ tvaṃ ciraṃ maṃ passasi, mā maṃ nivārehīti.

Its meaning is: "Mother, just as a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass cannot remain when the sun rises but falls to the ground, so too is the life of these beings—limited, temporary, and short-lived. In such a world as this, why do you wish to see me for a long time? Do not hinder me."

Evaṃ [V 4.0111] vuttepi sā punappunaṃ yāciyeva. Tato mahāsatto pitaraṃ āmantetvā aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Even when this was said, she kept begging again and again. Then the Great Being, addressing his father, spoke the eighth verse:

80.

80.

“Taramāno imaṃ yānaṃ, āropetu rathesabha;

Mā me mātā tarantassa, antarāyakarā ahū”ti.

"Hurry and place her upon this vehicle, O noblest of charioteers; lest my mother create an obstacle for me while I am hurrying."

Tassattho – tāta rathesabha, imaṃ mama mātaraṃ taramāno puriso suvaṇṇasivikāyānaṃ āropetu, mā me jātijarābyādhimaraṇakantāraṃ tarantassa atikkamantassa mātā antarāyakarā ahūti.

Its meaning is: “Dear father, noblest of charioteers, let a hurrying man place this mother of mine in the golden palanquin, lest my mother become an obstacle to me as I cross and overcome the wilderness of birth, aging, sickness, and death.”

Rājā [M 4.0125] puttassa vacanaṃ sutvā “gaccha, bhadde, tava sivikāya nisīditvā rativaḍḍhanapāsādaṃ abhiruhā”ti āha. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā ṭhātuṃ asakkontī nārīgaṇaparivutā gantvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā “kā nu kho puttassa pavattī”ti vinicchayaṭṭhānaṃ olokentī aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto mātu gatakāle puna pitaraṃ yāci. Rājā paṭibāhituṃ asakkonto “tena hi tāta, tava manaṃ matthakaṃ pāpehi, pabbajāhī”ti anujāni. Rañño anuññātakāle bodhisattassa kaniṭṭho yudhiṭṭhilakumāro nāma pitaraṃ vanditvā “tāta, mayhaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāthā”ti anujānāpesi. Ubhopi bhātaro pitaraṃ vanditvā kāme pahāya mahājanaparivutā vinicchayato nikkhamiṃsu. Devīpi mahāsattaṃ oloketvā “mama putte pabbajite rammanagaraṃ tucchaṃ bhavissatī”ti paridevamānā gāthādvayamāha –

The king, hearing his son's words, said, “Go, dear lady, sit in your palanquin and ascend the Rativaḍḍhana Palace.” Hearing his words, she, unable to remain still, surrounded by a group of women, went and ascended the palace, and stood there, looking at the judgment hall, thinking, “What now is the news of my son?” When his mother had gone, the Bodhisatta once again entreated his father. The king, unable to refuse, granted permission, saying, “Then, dear son, fulfill your heart's desire and go forth.” At the time the king gave his consent, the Bodhisatta's younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, having paid homage to his father, requested and received permission to go forth, saying, “Father, grant me permission to go forth as well.” Both brothers, having paid homage to their father, renounced sensual pleasures and left the judgment hall surrounded by a great crowd. The queen, looking at the Great Being, lamented, “With my sons gone forth, the city of Rammaka will become empty,” and spoke these two verses:

81.

81.

“Abhidhāvatha bhaddante, suññaṃ hessati rammakaṃ;

Yudhañcayo anuññāto, sabbadattena rājinā.

“Run forth! [Say,] ‘Prosperity to you!’ Rammaka will be empty; for Yudhañcaya has been granted permission by King Sabbadatta.”

82.

82.

“Yohu [P 4.0123] seṭṭho sahassassa, yuvā kañcanasannibho;

Soyaṃ kumāro pabbajito, kāsāyavasano balī”ti.

“He who was the best of a thousand, a youth like burnished gold—this very prince has gone forth, clad in saffron robes, a powerful one.”

Tattha abhidhāvathāti parivāretvā ṭhitā nāriyo sabbā vegena dhāvathāti āṇāpeti. Bhaddanteti evaṃ gantvā “bhaddaṃ tava hotū”ti vadatha. Rammakanti rammanagaraṃ sandhāyāha. Yohu seṭṭhoti yo rañño putto sahassassa seṭṭho ahosi, so pabbajitoti pabbajjāya gacchantaṃ sandhāyevamāha.

Here, “Run forth!” means she commanded all the women standing around to run quickly. As for “Bhaddante,” it means, “Go and say, ‘May good fortune be yours.’” “Rammaka” refers to the city of Ramma. “He who was the foremost” means the king’s son, who was the best of a thousand, has gone forth—thus she spoke referring to him departing for the going-forth.

Bodhisattopi [V 4.0112] na tāva pabbajati. So hi mātāpitaro vanditvā kaniṭṭhaṃ yudhiṭṭhilakumāraṃ gahetvā nagarā nikkhamma mahājanaṃ nivattetvā ubhopi bhātaro himavantaṃ pavisitvā manorame ṭhāne assamapadaṃ karitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā vanamūlaphalādīhi yāvajīvaṃ yāpetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ osāne abhisambuddhagāthāya dīpeti –

The Bodhisatta, however, did not go forth immediately. He paid respects to his parents, took his younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, and left the city. After turning back the great crowd, both brothers entered the Himalayas. There, in a delightful spot, they established a hermitage, undertook the ascetic life, developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and sustained themselves with forest roots and fruits for the rest of their lives, destined for the Brahma-world. He reveals this meaning at the end with the Buddha’s verse of perfect enlightenment:

83.

83.

“Ubho kumārā pabbajitā, yudhañcayo yudhiṭṭhilo;

Pahāya mātāpitaro, saṅgaṃ chetvāna maccuno”ti.

“Both princes have gone forth, Yudhañcaya and Yudhiṭṭhila; having abandoned mother and father, having cut the attachment of Death.”

Tattha [M 4.0126] maccunoti mārassa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhikkhave, yudhañcayo ca yudhiṭṭhilo ca te ubhopi kumārā mātāpitaro pahāya mārassa santakaṃ rāgadosamohasaṅgaṃ chinditvā pabbajitāti.

Therein, ‘of Death’ means of Māra. This is what is said: “Monks, both princes, Yudhañcaya and Yudhiṭṭhila, having abandoned their parents and cut off the attachment of greed, hatred, and delusion belonging to Māra, went forth.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā “na bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajitoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, yudhiṭṭhilakumāro ānando, yudhañcayo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, the Teacher said: “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, the Tathāgata abandoned a kingdom and went forth.” Then he made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the parents were the members of the great royal family, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila was Ānanda, and Yudhañcaya was indeed myself.”

Yudhañcayajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Yudhañcaya Jātaka is concluded.

[461] 7. Dasarathajātakavaṇṇanā

[461] 7. 7. Dasaratha Jātaka

Etha lakkhaṇa sītā cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ matapitikaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi pitari kālakate sokābhibhūto sabbakiccāni pahāya sokānuvattakova ahosi. Satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento tassa sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ disvā punadivase sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco bhikkhū uyyojetvā ekaṃ pacchāsamaṇaṃ [P 4.0124] gahetvā tassa gehaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ madhuravacanena ālapanto “kiṃ socasi upāsakā”ti vatvā “āma, bhante, pitusoko maṃ bādhatī”ti vutte “upāsaka, porāṇakapaṇḍitā aṭṭhavidhe lokadhamme tathato jānantā pitari kālakate appamattakampi sokaṃ na kariṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Come, Lakkhana and Sītā”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain householder whose father had died. When his father passed away, he was overwhelmed by grief and, abandoning all his duties, became one who was given over only to his sorrow. The Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw his potential for attaining the fruit of stream-entry. The next day, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī and finishing his meal, he dismissed the monks, took a single attendant monk, and went to that man’s house. Having been greeted and seated, he addressed him with kind words, asking, “Why are you grieving, lay follower?” When the man replied, “Venerable sir, grief for my father torments me,” the Teacher said, “Lay follower, the wise of old, knowing the eight worldly conditions as they truly are, did not grieve even slightly when their father passed away.” Being entreated by him, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ dasarathamahārājā nāma agatigamanaṃ pahāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa [V 4.0113] soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhikā aggamahesī dve putte ekañca dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Jeṭṭhaputto rāmapaṇḍito nāma ahosi, dutiyo lakkhaṇakumāro nāma, dhītā sītā devī nāma. Aparabhāge mahesī kālamakāsi. Rājā tassā kālakatāya cirataraṃ sokavasaṃ gantvā amaccehi saññāpito tassā kattabbaparihāraṃ [M 4.0127] katvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā rañño piyā ahosi manāpā. Sāpi aparabhāge gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā laddhagabbhaparihārā puttaṃ vijāyi, “bharatakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Rājā puttasinehena “bhadde, varaṃ te dammi, gaṇhāhī”ti āha. Sā gahitakaṃ katvā ṭhapetvā kumārassa sattaṭṭhavassakāle rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, tumhehi mayhaṃ puttassa varo dinno, idānissa varaṃ dethā”ti āha. Gaṇha, bhaddeti. “Deva, puttassa me rajjaṃ dethā”ti vutte rājā accharaṃ paharitvā “nassa, vasali, mayhaṃ dve puttā aggikkhandhā viya jalanti, te mārāpetvā tava puttassa rajjaṃ yācasī”ti tajjesi. Sā bhītā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā aññesupi divasesu rājānaṃ punappunaṃ rajjameva yāci.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a great king named Dasaratha ruled righteously, having abandoned the four wrong courses of action. Of his sixteen thousand women, the eldest, his chief queen, gave birth to two sons and one daughter. The eldest son was named Rāma the Wise, the second was named Prince Lakkhaṇa, and the daughter was named Princess Sītā. In time, the chief queen passed away. The king, overcome by prolonged grief at her death, was consoled by his ministers. After performing the necessary funeral rites for her, he appointed another to the position of chief queen. She was dear and pleasing to the king. In time, she too conceived, and after receiving the care due to a pregnant woman, she gave birth to a son; they gave him the name Prince Bharata. Out of affection for his son, the king said to her, 'My lady, I grant you a boon; take it.' She accepted the boon but set it aside. When the prince was seven or eight years old, she approached the king and said, 'Your Majesty, a boon was given by you for my son; now, grant him that boon.' 'Take it, my lady,' he said. When she said, 'Your Majesty, give my son the kingdom,' the king snapped his fingers and rebuked her, 'Be gone, you wretch! My two sons blaze like masses of fire. Do you ask for the kingdom for your son, having had them killed?' Terrified, she retreated to her royal chamber. Yet, on other days, she repeatedly begged the king for the kingdom.

Rājā tassā taṃ varaṃ adatvāva cintesi “mātugāmo nāma akataññū mittadubbhī, ayaṃ me kūṭapaṇṇaṃ vā kūṭalañjaṃ vā katvā putte ghātāpeyyā”ti. So putte pakkosāpetvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “tātā, tumhākaṃ idha vasantānaṃ antarāyopi bhaveyya, tumhe sāmantarajjaṃ vā araññaṃ vā gantvā mama maraṇakāle āgantvā kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇheyyāthā”ti vatvā puna nemittake brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā attano āyuparicchedaṃ pucchitvā “aññāni dvādasa vassāni [P 4.0125] pavattissatī”ti sutvā “tātā, ito dvādasavassaccayena āgantvā chattaṃ ussāpeyyāthā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti vatvā pitaraṃ vanditvā rodantā pāsādā otariṃsu. Sītā devī “ahampi bhātikehi saddhiṃ gamissāmī”ti pitaraṃ vanditvā rodantī nikkhami. Tayopi janā mahāparivārā nikkhamitvā mahājanaṃ nivattetvā anupubbena himavantaṃ pavisitvā sampannodake sulabhaphalāphale padese assamaṃ māpetvā phalāphalena yāpentā vasiṃsu.

The king, without granting her that boon, thought, 'Women are indeed ungrateful and treacherous to friends. This queen might create a forged letter or a deceitful gift and have my sons killed.' He summoned his sons, explained the matter to them, and said, 'My dears, if you remain living here, danger may befall you. You should go to a neighboring kingdom or to the forest, and at the time of my death, return and take the kingdom that belongs to our family.' Then he summoned the soothsaying brahmins and asked about the limit of his own lifespan. Hearing that 'it will continue for another twelve years,' he said, 'My dears, come back after the passing of twelve years from now and raise the royal parasol.' They replied, 'Very well,' paid respects to their father, and descended from the palace weeping. Princess Sītā said, 'I too will go with my brothers,' paid respects to her father, and left weeping. Those three, with a great retinue, departed, and after turning back the great crowd, they gradually entered the Himalayas. There, in a region with abundant water and readily available fruits, they had a hermitage built and lived there, sustaining themselves on various fruits.

Lakkhaṇapaṇḍito ca sītā ca rāmapaṇḍitaṃ yācitvā “tumhe amhākaṃ pituṭṭhāne ṭhitā, tasmā assameyeva hotha, mayaṃ phalāphalaṃ āharitvā tumhe posessāmā”ti paṭiññaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya rāmapaṇḍito tattheva hoti. Itare dve phalāphalaṃ āharitvā taṃ paṭijaggiṃsu. Evaṃ tesaṃ phalāphalena yāpetvā vasantānaṃ dasarathamahārājā puttasokena navame saṃvacchare kālamakāsi. Tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā [M 4.0128] devī “attano puttassa bharatakumārassa chattaṃ ussāpethā”ti āha. Amaccā pana “chattassāmikā araññe vasantī”ti na adaṃsu. Bharatakumāro [V 4.0114] “mama bhātaraṃ rāmapaṇḍitaṃ araññato ānetvā chattaṃ ussāpessāmī”ti pañcarājakakudhabhaṇḍāni gahetvā caturaṅginiyā senāya tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā avidūre khandhāvāraṃ katvā tattha nivāsetvā katipayehi amaccehi saddhiṃ lakkhaṇapaṇḍitassa ca sītāya ca araññaṃ gatakāle assamapadaṃ pavisitvā assamapadadvāre ṭhapitakañcanarūpakaṃ viya rāmapaṇḍitaṃ nirāsaṅkaṃ sukhanisinnaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito rañño pavattiṃ ārocetvā saddhiṃ amaccehi pādesu patitvā rodati. Rāmapaṇḍito pana neva soci, na paridevi, indriyavikāramattampissa nāhosi. Bharatassa pana roditvā nisinnakāle sāyanhasamaye itare dve phalāphalaṃ ādāya āgamiṃsu. Rāmapaṇḍito cintesi “ime daharā mayhaṃ viya pariggaṇhanapaññā etesaṃ natthi, sahasā [P 4.0126] ‘pitā vo mato’ti vutte sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontānaṃ hadayampi tesaṃ phaleyya, upāyena te udakaṃ otāretvā etaṃ pavattiṃ ārocessāmī”ti. Atha nesaṃ purato ekaṃ udakaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā “tumhe aticirena āgatā, idaṃ vo daṇḍakammaṃ hotu, imaṃ udakaṃ otaritvā tiṭṭhathā”ti upaḍḍhagāthaṃ tāva āha –

Lakkhaṇa the Wise and Sītā, having requested Rāma the Wise, received his promise, saying, 'You stand in our father's place; therefore, remain in the hermitage. We will gather various fruits and sustain you.' From then on, Rāma the Wise stayed there. The other two would bring various fruits and attend to him. While they were thus living, sustaining themselves on various fruits, in the ninth year, King Dasaratha passed away from grief for his children. After having his funeral rites performed, the queen said, 'Raise the parasol for my son, Prince Bharata.' But the ministers, saying, 'The lords of the parasol dwell in the forest,' did not grant it. Prince Bharata thought, 'I will bring my brother, Rāma the Wise, from the forest and raise the parasol.' Taking the five royal insignia, he went with a fourfold army to the place where Rāma resided. Having set up camp not far away and settled there, he entered the hermitage with a few ministers at a time when Lakkhaṇa the Wise and Sītā had gone into the forest. He approached Rāma the Wise, who was seated without apprehension and serene like a golden statue placed at the hermitage door, paid homage to him, and, standing to one side, informed him of the king's passing. Then, together with the ministers, he fell at his feet and wept. But Rāma the Wise neither grieved nor lamented; there was not even the slightest change in his faculties. While Bharata, having wept, was sitting down, the other two returned in the evening, bringing various fruits. Rāma the Wise thought, 'These young ones do not have the same reflective wisdom as I do. If they were told abruptly, "Your father is dead," they would be unable to bear the sorrow, and their hearts might even break. By a stratagem, I will have them enter the water and then announce this news.' Then, pointing to a place with water before them, he said, 'You have returned very late. Let this be your punishment: enter this water and stand there.' First, he spoke this half-verse:

84.

84.

“Etha lakkhaṇa sītā ca, ubho otarathodaka”nti.

Tassattho – etha lakkhaṇa sītā ca āgacchatha, ubhopi otaratha udakanti;

'Come, Lakkhaṇa and Sītā, both of you, descend into the water.' The meaning of this is: Come, Lakkhaṇa and Sītā; both of you, descend into the water.

Te ekavacaneneva otaritvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ pitu pavattiṃ ārocento sesaṃ upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

At his single word, they descended and stood there. Then, informing them of the news about their father, he spoke the remaining half-verse:

“Evāyaṃ bharato āha, rājā dasaratho mato”ti.

'Thus this Bharata says: King Dasaratha is dead.'

Te pitu matasāsanaṃ sutvāva visaññā ahesuṃ. Punapi nesaṃ kathesi, punapi te visaññā ahesunti evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ visaññitaṃ patte te amaccā ukkhipitvā udakā nīharitvā thale nisīdāpetvā laddhassāsesu tesu [M 4.0129] sabbe aññamaññaṃ roditvā paridevitvā nisīdiṃsu. Tadā bharatakumāro cintesi – “mayhaṃ bhātā lakkhaṇakumāro ca bhaginī ca sītā devī pitu matasāsanaṃ sutvāva sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkonti, rāmapaṇḍito pana neva socati, na paridevati, kiṃ nu kho tassa asocanakāraṇaṃ, pucchissāmi na”nti. So taṃ pucchanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Upon hearing the news of their father's death, they both fainted. He spoke to them again, and again they fainted. When they had thus fainted for a third time, the ministers lifted them up, brought them out of the water, and seated them on dry land. Once they had regained their composure, they all sat weeping and lamenting with one another. Then Prince Bharata thought: 'My brother Prince Lakkhaṇa and my sister Princess Sītā, upon hearing the news of our father's death, are unable to restrain their grief. But Rāma the Wise neither grieves nor laments. What, I wonder, is the reason for his lack of sorrow? I shall ask him.' So, questioning him, he spoke the second verse:

85.

85.

“Kena [V 4.0115] rāmappabhāvena, socitabbaṃ na socasi;

Pitaraṃ kālakataṃ sutvā, na taṃ pasahate dukha”nti.

'By what power, O Rāma, do you not grieve for that which should be grieved? Having heard that your father has passed away, sorrow does not overwhelm you.'

Tattha pabhāvenāti ānubhāvena. Na taṃ pasahate dukhanti evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ kena kāraṇena taṃ na pīḷeti, kiṃ te asocanakāraṇaṃ, kathehi tāva nanti.

In this context, 'by power' (pabhāvena) means by majesty or spiritual power. 'Sorrow does not overwhelm you' means: for what reason does such suffering not afflict you? What is your reason for not grieving? Pray, tell me.

Athassa rāmapaṇḍito attano asocanakāraṇaṃ kathento –

Then Rāma the Wise, explaining his reason for not grieving, said:

86.

86.

“Yaṃ na sakkā nipāletuṃ, posena lapataṃ bahuṃ;

Sa kissa viññū medhāvī, attānamupatāpaye.

'If a person, though lamenting much, cannot protect that which is destined to perish, why then should a discerning and intelligent person torment himself over it?'

87.

87.

“Daharā [P 4.0127] ca hi vuddhā ca, ye bālā ye ca paṇḍitā;

Aḍḍhā ceva daliddā ca, sabbe maccuparāyaṇā.

'Both the young and the old, the foolish and the wise, the rich and the poor—all have death as their final destination.'

88.

88.

“Phalānamiva pakkānaṃ, niccaṃ patanato bhayaṃ;

Evaṃ jātāna maccānaṃ, niccaṃ maraṇato bhayaṃ.

'Just as for ripe fruits there is the constant fear of falling, so for mortals, once born, there is the constant fear of death.'

89.

89.

“Sāyameke na dissanti, pāto diṭṭhā bahujjanā;

Pāto eke na dissanti, sāyaṃ diṭṭhā bahujjanā.

'Of the many people seen in the morning, some are not seen by evening; of the many people seen in the evening, some are not seen by morning.'

90.

90.

“Paridevayamāno ce, kiñcidatthaṃ udabbahe;

Sammūḷho hiṃsamattānaṃ, kayirā taṃ vicakkhaṇo.

'If by lamenting and thus harming himself, a deluded person could achieve any benefit, then a discerning person would also do so.'

91.

91.

“Kiso vivaṇṇo bhavati, hiṃsamattānamattano;

Na tena petā pālenti, niratthā paridevanā.

'One becomes lean and pale, only harming oneself; the departed are not sustained by that—lamentation is therefore useless.'

92.

92.

“Yathā saraṇamādittaṃ, vārinā parinibbaye;

Evampi dhīro sutavā, medhāvī paṇḍito naro;

Khippamuppatitaṃ sokaṃ, vāto tūlaṃva dhaṃsaye.

'Just as one would extinguish a burning house with water, so too a steadfast, learned, intelligent, and wise person would quickly dispel arisen sorrow, just as the wind scatters a tuft of cotton.'

93.

93.

“Macco [V 4.0116][M 4.0130] ekova acceti, ekova jāyate kule;

Saṃyogaparamātveva, sambhogā sabbapāṇinaṃ.

'A mortal passes away alone, and alone one is born into a family. The shared lives of all beings are ultimately nothing more than a temporary association.'

94.

94.

“Tasmā hi dhīrassa bahussutassa, sampassato lokamimaṃ parañca;

Aññāya dhammaṃ hadayaṃ manañca, sokā mahantāpi na tāpayanti.

'Therefore, for the steadfast and very learned one, who clearly sees this world and the next, having understood the Dhamma, even great sorrows do not torment the heart and mind.'

95.

95.

“Sohaṃ dassañca bhokkhañca, bharissāmi ca ñātake;

Sesañca pālayissāmi, kiccametaṃ vijānato”ti. –

'I shall give and I shall enjoy; I shall support my relatives and protect the rest. This is the duty of one who understands the truth of things.'

Imāhi dasahi gāthāhi aniccataṃ pakāseti.

With these ten verses, he elucidated the nature of impermanence.

Tattha nipāletunti rakkhituṃ. Lapatanti lapantānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “tāta bharata, yaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ bahumpi vilapantānaṃ purisānaṃ ekenāpi mā ucchijjīti na sakkā rakkhituṃ, so dāni mādiso aṭṭha lokadhamme tathato jānanto viññū medhāvī paṇḍito maraṇapariyosānajīvitesu sattesu kissa attānamupatāpaye, kiṃkāraṇā anupakārena sokadukkhena attānaṃ santāpeyyā”ti.

In this context, 'nipāletuṃ' means to protect or preserve. 'Lapatant' refers to those who are lamenting. This is what is meant: 'Dear Bharata, if the life of beings—which even many men lamenting greatly cannot protect by wishing "May it not be cut off!"—then why should one like me, a discerning and wise person who knows the eight worldly conditions as they truly are, torment himself over beings whose lives end in death? For what reason should I afflict myself with futile grief and sorrow?'

Daharā cāti gāthā “maccu nāmesa tāta bharata, neva [P 4.0128] suvaṇṇarūpakasadisānaṃ daharānaṃ khattiyakumārakādīnaṃ, na vuddhippattānaṃ mahāyodhānaṃ, na bālānaṃ puthujjanasattānaṃ, na buddhādīnaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ, na cakkavattiādīnaṃ issarānaṃ, na niddhanānaṃ daliddādīnaṃ lajjati, sabbepime sattā maccuparāyaṇā maraṇamukhe saṃbhaggavibhaggā bhavantiyevā”ti dassanatthaṃ vuttā.
