The verse beginning 'Daharā ca' was spoken to show this: 'Death, dear Bharata, feels no shame before the young, such as warrior princes who resemble golden statues, nor before great warriors who have reached old age, nor before foolish ordinary people, nor before the wise such as Buddhas, nor before the powerful such as universal monarchs, nor before the destitute and poor. All these beings have death as their final destination; they are indeed broken and shattered in the mouth of death.'

Niccaṃ patanatoti idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā hi tāta bharata, pakkānaṃ phalānaṃ pakkakālato paṭṭhāya “idāni vaṇṭā chijjitvā patissanti, idāni patissantī”ti patanato bhayaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ ekaṃsikameva bhavati, evaṃ āsaṅkanīyato evaṃ jātānaṃ maccānampi ekaṃsikaṃyeva maraṇato bhayaṃ, natthi so khaṇo vā layo vā yattha tesaṃ maraṇaṃ na āsaṅkitabbaṃ bhaveyyāti.

By 'constant fear of falling,' this is what is meant: Just as, dear Bharata, for ripe fruits, from the moment they are ripe, the fear of falling—'Now the stems will break and they will fall; now they will fall!'—is constant, certain, and inevitable; so too for mortals thus born, the fear of death is absolutely certain. There is no moment or instant when their death is not to be expected.

Sāyanti [M 4.0131] vikāle. Iminā rattibhāge ca diṭṭhānaṃ divasabhāge adassanaṃ, divasabhāge ca diṭṭhānaṃ rattibhāge adassanaṃ dīpeti. Kiñcidatthanti “pitā me, putto me”tiādīhi paridevamānova poso sammūḷho attānaṃ hiṃsanto kilamento appamattakampi atthaṃ āhareyya. Kayirā [V 4.0117] taṃ vicakkhaṇoti atha paṇḍito puriso evaṃ paridevaṃ kareyya, yasmā pana paridevanto mataṃ vā ānetuṃ aññaṃ vā tassa vaḍḍhiṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā niratthakattā paridevitassa paṇḍitā na paridevanti.

“Evening” refers to the late hour. This clarifies that those seen in the night may not be seen in the day, and those seen in the day may not be seen in the night. “Some benefit” means that if a person, bewildered and lamenting with thoughts like ‘my father, my son,’ harming and exhausting himself, could bring about even a minimal benefit, then a wise person would likewise lament. However, since one who laments cannot bring back the dead or increase their welfare, and because lamentation is pointless, the wise do not lament.

Attānamattanoti attano attabhāvaṃ sokaparidevadukkhena hiṃsanto. Na tenāti tena paridevena paralokaṃ gatā sattā na pālenti na yāpenti. Niratthāti tasmā tesaṃ matasattānaṃ ayaṃ paridevanā niratthakā. Saraṇanti nivāsagehaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā paṇḍito puriso attano vasanāgāre āditte muhuttampi vosānaṃ anāpajjitvā ghaṭasatena ghaṭasahassena vārinā nibbāpayateva, evaṃ dhīro uppatitaṃ sokaṃ khippameva nibbāpaye. Tūlaṃ viya ca vāto yathā saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ dhaṃsaye viddhaṃseyyāti attho.

“Harming oneself by oneself” means afflicting one's own being with the suffering of sorrow and lamentation. “Not by that” means that by such lamentation, beings who have passed to the other world are neither protected nor sustained. “Useless” means that for those who have died, this lamentation is without benefit. “Refuge” (saraṇaṃ) refers to a dwelling house. This is what is meant: Just as a wise man, when his own home is on fire, does not give in to despair for even a moment but extinguishes it with a hundred or a thousand pots of water, so too should the wise quickly extinguish arisen sorrow. And just as the wind does not allow a tuft of cotton to remain still, so should one destroy and scatter sorrow—this is the meaning.

Macco ekova accetīti ettha tāta bharata, ime sattā kammassakā nāma, tathā hi ito paralokaṃ gacchanto satto ekova acceti atikkamati, khattiyādikule jāyamānopi ekova gantvā jāyati. Tattha tattha pana ñātimittasaṃyogena “ayaṃ me pitā, ayaṃ me mātā, ayaṃ me mitto”ti saṃyogaparamātveva sambhogā sabbapāṇīnaṃ, paramatthena pana tīsupi bhavesu kammassakāvete sattāti attho.

"A mortal passes away alone"—here, dear Bharata, these beings are indeed owners of their kamma. For when a being goes from this world to the next, they pass away alone, they transcend. Even if born in a khattiya or other family, they go alone and are born. There, however, through association with relatives and friends, with the thought, "This is my father, this is my mother, this is my friend," enjoyment for all beings is based on nothing more than this connection. But in the ultimate sense, in all three realms of existence, these beings are owners of their kamma—this is the meaning.

Tasmāti yasmā etesaṃ sattānaṃ ñātimittasaṃyogaṃ ñātimittaparibhogamattaṃ ṭhapetvā ito paraṃ aññaṃ natthi, tasmā. Sampassatoti imañca parañca lokaṃ nānābhāvavinābhāvameva sammā passato. Aññāya dhammanti aṭṭhavidhalokadhammaṃ jānitvā. Hadayaṃ manañcāti [P 4.0129] idaṃ ubhayampi cittasseva nāmaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti –

"Therefore"—because for these beings, apart from the mere association and enjoyment of relatives and friends, there is nothing else, therefore. "One who sees rightly"—one who rightly sees this world and the next as being of different natures and subject to separation. "Knowing the Dhamma"—having understood the eight worldly conditions. "Heart and mind"—both of these are names for the mind. This is said:

“Lābho [M 4.0132] alābho yaso ayaso ca, nindā pasaṃsā ca sukhañca dukkhaṃ;

Ete aniccā manujesu dhammā, mā soca kiṃ socasi poṭṭhapādā”ti. (jā. 1.4.114) –

“Gain and loss, fame and infamy, censure and praise, pleasure and pain—these conditions are impermanent among humans. Do not grieve; why do you grieve, O Poṭṭhapāda?”

Imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ lokadhammānaṃ yena kenaci cittaṃ pariyādīyati, tassa ca aniccataṃ ñatvā ṭhitassa dhīrassa pituputtamaraṇādivatthukā mahantāpi sokā hadayaṃ na tāpayantīti. Etaṃ vā aṭṭhavidhaṃ lokadhammaṃ ñatvā ṭhitassa hadayavatthuñca manañca mahantāpi sokā na tāpayantīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Of these eight worldly conditions, by any of which the mind is overwhelmed, for the wise person who stands firm having known their impermanence, even great sorrows arising from such things as the death of a father or son do not torment the heart. Or, for one who stands firm having known this eightfold worldly condition, great sorrows do not torment the heart and the mind—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

Sohaṃ [V 4.0118] dassañca bhokkhañcāti gāthāya – tāta bharata, andhabālānaṃ sattānaṃ viya mama rodanaparidevanaṃ nāma na anucchavikaṃ, ahaṃ pana pitu accayena tassa ṭhāne ṭhatvā kapaṇādīnaṃ dānārahānaṃ dānaṃ, ṭhānantarārahānaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ, yasārahānaṃ yasaṃ dassāmi, pitarā me paribhuttanayena issariyaṃ paribhuñjissāmi, ñātake ca posessāmi, avasesañca antoparijanādikaṃ janaṃ pālessāmi, dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ karissāmīti evañhi jānato paṇḍitapurisassa anurūpaṃ kiccanti attho.

By the verse, "I shall give and I shall enjoy"— "Dear Bharata, weeping and lamentation are indeed unfitting for me, as they are for blind and foolish beings. But I, having taken my father's place after his passing, will give gifts to the poor and others worthy of them, appoint the deserving to their rightful positions, and bestow honor upon those worthy of honor. I will enjoy sovereignty in the manner my father enjoyed it, support my relatives, and protect the remaining people, including the household. I shall provide righteous protection, shelter, and security to righteous ascetics and brahmins." Thus, for a wise man who understands, such deeds are fitting—this is the meaning.

Parisā imaṃ rāmapaṇḍitassa aniccatāpakāsanaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nissokā ahesuṃ. Tato bharatakumāro rāmapaṇḍitaṃ vanditvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ sampaṭicchathā”ti āha. Tāta lakkhaṇañca, sītādeviñca gahetvā gantvā rajjaṃ anusāsathāti. Tumhe pana, devāti. Tāta, mama pitā “dvādasavassaccayena āgantvā rajjaṃ kāreyyāsī”ti maṃ avoca, ahaṃ idāneva gacchanto tassa vacanakaro nāma na homi, aññānipi tīṇi vassāni atikkamitvā āgamissāmīti. “Ettakaṃ kālaṃ ko rajjaṃ kāressatī”ti? “Tumhe kārethā”ti. “Na mayaṃ kāressāmā”ti. “Tena hi yāva mamāgamanā imā pādukā kāressantī”ti attano tiṇapādukā omuñcitvā adāsi. Te tayopi janā pādukā gahetvā rāmapaṇḍitaṃ vanditvā mahājanaparivutā bārāṇasiṃ agamaṃsu. Tīṇi saṃvaccharāni pādukā rajjaṃ kāresuṃ. Amaccā tiṇapādukā rājapallaṅke ṭhapetvā [M 4.0133] aḍḍaṃ vinicchinanti. Sace dubbinicchito hoti, pādukā aññamaññaṃ [P 4.0130] paṭihaññanti. Tāya saññāya puna vinicchinanti. Sammā vinicchitakāle pādukā nissaddā sannisīdanti. Rāmapaṇḍito tiṇṇaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena araññā nikkhamitvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ patvā uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Tassa āgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā kumārā amaccagaṇaparivutā uyyānaṃ gantvā sītaṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā ubhinnampi abhisekaṃ akaṃsu. Evaṃ abhisekappatto mahāsatto alaṅkatarathe ṭhatvā mahantena parivārena nagaraṃ pavisitvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā candakapāsādavarassa mahātalaṃ abhiruhi. Tato paṭṭhāya soḷasa vassasahassāni dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā āyupariyosāne saggapuraṃ pūresi.

The assembly, having heard this Dhamma teaching by the wise Rāma revealing impermanence, became free from sorrow. Then Prince Bharata, having paid homage to the wise Rāma, said, "Accept the kingdom of Bārāṇasī." "Take Lakkhaṇa and Queen Sītā with you and go, rule the kingdom." "And you, my lord?" "Dear one, my father told me, 'After twelve years have passed, return and rule the kingdom.' If I go now, I would not be acting according to his word. I will return after another three years have passed." "Who will rule the kingdom for that long?" "You shall rule." "We will not rule." "Then, until my return, let these sandals rule." So saying, he took off his grass sandals and gave them to them. Those three took the sandals, paid homage to the wise Rāma, and, surrounded by a great crowd, went to Bārāṇasī. For three years, the sandals ruled the kingdom. The ministers would place the grass sandals on the royal throne and decide cases. If a case was decided wrongly, the sandals would strike against each other. By that sign, they would decide it again. When a case was decided rightly, the sandals would settle down in silence. At the end of three years, Rāma the wise left the forest, reached the city of Bārāṇasī, and entered the park. Having learned of his arrival, the princes, surrounded by a retinue of ministers, went to the park, made Sītā the chief queen, and performed the consecration for both of them. Thus, having received the consecration, the great being, standing in a decorated chariot, entered the city with a large entourage, circumambulated it, and ascended to the great terrace of the excellent Candaka Palace. From then on, he ruled the kingdom righteously for sixteen thousand years, and at the end of his life, he filled the city of the gods.

96.

96.

“Dasa vassasahassāni, saṭṭhi vassasatāni ca;

Kambugīvo mahābāhu, rāmo rajjamakārayī”ti. –

"For ten thousand years, and sixty hundred years besides, Kambugīva, the mighty-armed Rāma, ruled the kingdom."

Ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā tamatthaṃ dīpeti.

This verse spoken by the Fully Enlightened One illuminates that meaning.

Tattha [V 4.0119] kambugīvoti suvaṇṇāḷiṅgasadisagīvo. Suvaṇṇañhi kambūti vuccati.

Here, 'kambugīvo' means one with a neck like a golden drum. For 'kambu' is indeed said to be gold.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā dasarathamahārājā suddhodanamahārājā ahosi, mātā mahāmāyādevī, sītā rāhulamātā, bharato ānando, lakkhaṇo sāriputto, parisā buddhaparisā, rāmapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, made the connection for the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, King Dasaratha was King Suddhodana, the mother was Mahāmāyādevī, Sītā was Rāhula's mother, Bharata was Ānanda, Lakkhaṇa was Sāriputta, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Rāma the wise was I myself.

Dasarathajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The seventh exposition, on the Dasaratha Jātaka.

[462] 8. Saṃvarajātakavaṇṇanā

[462] 8. The Exposition of the Saṃvara Jātaka

Jānanto no mahārājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ pūrento ubhayāni pātimokkhāni paguṇāni katvā paripuṇṇapañcavasso [M 4.0134] kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā “araññe vasissāmī”ti ācariyupajjhāye āpucchitvā kosalaraṭṭhe ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ gantvā tattha iriyāpathe pasannamanussehi [P 4.0131] paṇṇasālaṃ katvā upaṭṭhiyamāno vassaṃ upagantvā yuñjanto ghaṭento vāyamanto accāraddhena vīriyena temāsaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā obhāsamattampi uppādetuṃ asakkonto cintesi “addhā ahaṃ satthārā desitesu catūsu puggalesu padaparamo, kiṃ me araññavāsena, jetavanaṃ gantvā tathāgatassa rūpasiriṃ passanto madhuradhammadesanaṃ suṇanto vītināmessāmī”ti. So vīriyaṃ ossajitvā tato nikkhanto anupubbena jetavanaṃ gantvā ācariyupajjhāyehi ceva sandiṭṭhasambhattehi ca āgamanakāraṇaṃ puṭṭho tamatthaṃ kathetvā tehi “kasmā evamakāsī”ti garahitvā satthu santikaṃ netvā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, anicchamānaṃ bhikkhuṃ ānayitthā”ti vutte “ayaṃ, bhante, vīriyaṃ ossajitvā āgato”ti ārocite satthā “saccaṃ kirā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kasmā bhikkhu vīriyaṃ ossaji, imasmiñhi sāsane nibbīriyassa kusītapuggalassa aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ nāma natthi, āraddhavīriyā imaṃ dhammaṃ ārādhenti, tvaṃ kho pana pubbe vīriyavā ovādakkhamo, teneva kāraṇena bārāṇasirañño puttasatassa sabbakaniṭṭho hutvāpi paṇḍitānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā setacchattaṃ pattosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Knowing, O great king"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had slackened his effort. It seems that a clansman from Sāvatthī, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, went forth and received full ordination. Fulfilling his duties toward his teachers and preceptor, mastering both Pātimokkhas, and completing five years, he took up a meditation subject. Thinking, "I will dwell in the forest," he took leave of his teachers and preceptor and went to a border village in the Kosala country. There, people who were pleased with his conduct built him a leaf hut and supported him. Entering the rains retreat, striving, exerting, and endeavoring with excessive effort for three months, he was unable to produce even a glimmer of light. He thought, "Surely, among the four types of persons taught by the Teacher, I am merely one for whom the word is the maximum. What use is forest dwelling for me? Going to Jetavana, seeing the Tathāgata’s glorious form and listening to his sweet Dhamma teachings, I will pass my time." So, abandoning his effort, he left and gradually went to Jetavana. When questioned by his teachers, preceptor, and acquaintances about his reason for coming, he explained the matter. They rebuked him, saying, "Why did you act thus?" and took him to the Teacher. When asked, "Monks, why have you brought this monk against his will?" they replied, "Venerable sir, this monk has abandoned his effort and come." The Teacher asked, "Is it true?" and being told, "It is true, venerable sir," he said, "Why, monk, have you abandoned effort? For in this dispensation, there is no supreme fruit of arahantship for the lazy and indolent. Those who exert effort attain this Dhamma. But you, in a former life, were energetic and amenable to advice. Because of that, though you were the youngest among the hundred sons of the king of Bārāṇasī, you stood by the advice of the wise and obtained the white parasol." Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte [V 4.0120] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente saṃvarakumāro nāma puttasatassa sabbakaniṭṭho ahosi. Rājā ekekaṃ puttaṃ “sikkhitabbayuttakaṃ sikkhāpethā”ti ekekassa amaccassa adāsi. Saṃvarakumārassa ācariyo amacco bodhisatto ahosi paṇḍito byatto rājaputtassa pituṭṭhāne ṭhito. Amaccā sikkhitasippe rājaputte rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā tesaṃ janapadaṃ datvā uyyojesi. Saṃvarakumāro sabbasippassa nipphattiṃ patvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi “tāta, sace maṃ pitā janapadaṃ peseti, kiṃ karomī”ti? “Tāta, tvaṃ janapade dīyamāne taṃ aggahetvā ‘deva ahaṃ sabbakaniṭṭho, mayipi gate tumhākaṃ pādamūlaṃ tucchaṃ bhavissati, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pādamūleyeva vasissāmī’ti vadeyyāsī”ti. Athekadivasaṃ rājā saṃvarakumāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ [M 4.0135] nisinnaṃ pucchi “kiṃ tāta, sippaṃ te niṭṭhita”nti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Tuyhampi janapadaṃ demī”ti. “Deva tumhākaṃ pādamūlaṃ [P 4.0132] tucchaṃ bhavissati, pādamūleyeva vasissāmī”ti. Rājā tussitvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. So tato paṭṭhāya rañño pādamūleyeva hutvā punapi bodhisattaṃ pucchi “tāta aññaṃ kiṃ karomī”ti? “Tāta rājānaṃ ekaṃ purāṇuyyānaṃ yācāhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti uyyānaṃ yācitvā tattha jātakehi pupphaphalehi nagare issarajanaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā puna “kiṃ karomī”ti pucchi. “Tāta, rājānaṃ āpucchitvā antonagare bhattavetanaṃ tvameva dehī”ti. So tathā katvā antonagare kassaci kiñci ahāpetvā bhattavetanaṃ datvā puna bodhisattaṃ pucchitvā rājānaṃ viññāpetvā antonivesane dāsaporisānampi hatthīnampi assānampi balakāyassapi vattaṃ aparihāpetvā adāsi, tirojanapadehi āgatānaṃ dūtādīnaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānādīni vāṇijānaṃ suṅkanti sabbakaraṇīyāni attanāva akāsi. Evaṃ so mahāsattassa ovāde ṭhatvā sabbaṃ antojanañca bahijanañca nāgare ca raṭṭhavāsino ca āgantuke ca āyavattane ca tena tena saṅgahavatthunā ābandhitvā saṅgaṇhi, sabbesaṃ piyo ahosi manāpo.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, Prince Saṃvara was the youngest of a hundred sons. The king entrusted each son to a minister, saying, "Teach them the skills they ought to learn." The minister who was the teacher of Prince Saṃvara was the Bodhisatta—wise, skilled, and standing in the place of a father to the prince. When the ministers had trained the princes in their crafts, they presented them to the king. The king granted them provinces and sent them away. Having mastered all the skills, Prince Saṃvara asked the Bodhisatta, "Father, if my father sends me to a province, what should I do?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Dear one, if a province is offered to you, decline it and say, 'Your Majesty, I am the very youngest; if I too should go, the place at your feet will be empty. I will stay right here at your feet.'" One day, the king, seeing Prince Saṃvara seated to one side after paying his respects, asked, "Dear son, have you completed your training?" "Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "I shall grant you a province as well," said the king. "Your Majesty, the place at your feet would be empty; I will stay right here at your feet," the prince answered. Pleased, the king accepted his words, saying, "Very well." From then on, the prince remained at the king’s feet. Later, he asked the Bodhisatta again, "Father, what else should I do?" "Dear one, ask the king for an old park," advised the Bodhisatta. Agreeing, the prince requested the park and, having won over the city’s influential people with the flowers and fruits that grew there, he then asked again, "What should I do now?" "Dear one, ask the king’s permission to personally distribute food and wages within the city," instructed the Bodhisatta. Following this advice, the prince ensured no one within the city was deprived of anything, providing food and wages himself. Later, after consulting the Bodhisatta again and informing the king, he took charge of distributing provisions to the servants and slaves in the royal residence, as well as to the elephants, horses, and the army, without any deficiency. He also personally attended to all duties, such as providing lodging for messengers arriving from foreign lands and collecting tolls from merchants. Thus, abiding by the Great Being’s guidance, he won over and bound to himself with various bases of sympathy all people—those within the palace and without, city dwellers, country folk, visitors, and those involved in revenue—and became beloved and dear to all.

Aparabhāge rājānaṃ maraṇamañce nipannaṃ amaccā pucchiṃsu “deva, tumhākaṃ accayena setacchattaṃ kassa demā”ti? “Tāta, mama puttā sabbepi setacchattassa sāminova. Yo pana tumhākaṃ manaṃ gaṇhāti, tasseva setacchatthaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti. Te tasmiṃ kālakate tassa sarīraparihāraṃ katvā sattame divase sannipatitvā “raññā ‘yo tumhākaṃ manaṃ gaṇhāti, tassa setacchattaṃ ussāpeyyāthā’ti vuttaṃ, amhākañca ayaṃ saṃvarakumāro manaṃ gaṇhātī”ti ñātakehi parivāritā tassa kañcanamālaṃ setacchattaṃ ussāpayiṃsu. Saṃvaramahārājā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Itare ekūnasatakumārā “pitā kira no kālakato, saṃvarakumārassa kira setacchattaṃ [P 4.0133] ussāpesuṃ, so sabbakaniṭṭho, tassa chattaṃ na pāpuṇāti, sabbajeṭṭhakassa [V 4.0121] chattaṃ ussāpessāmā”ti ekato āgantvā “chattaṃ vā no detu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti saṃvaramahārājassa paṇṇaṃ pesetvā nagaraṃ uparundhiṃsu. Rājā bodhisattassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “idāni kiṃ karomā”ti pucchi. Mahārāja, tava bhātikehi [M 4.0136] saddhiṃ yujjhanakiccaṃ natthi, tvaṃ pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ satakoṭṭhāse kāretvā ekūnasataṃ bhātikānaṃ pesetvā “imaṃ tumhākaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ pitu santakaṃ gaṇhatha, nāhaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ yujjhāmī”ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇāhīti. So tathā akāsi. Athassa sabbajeṭṭhabhātiko uposathakumāro nāma sese āmantetvā “tātā, rājānaṃ nāma abhibhavituṃ samatthā nāma natthi, ayañca no kaniṭṭhabhātiko paṭisattupi hutvā na tiṭṭhati, amhākaṃ pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ pesetvā ‘nāhaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ yujjhāmī’ti pesesi, na kho pana mayaṃ sabbepi ekakkhaṇe chattaṃ ussāpessāma, ekasseva chattaṃ ussāpessāma, ayameva rājā hotu, etha taṃ passitvā rājakuṭumbaṃ paṭicchādetvā amhākaṃ janapadameva gacchāmā”ti āha. Atha te sabbepi kumārā nagaradvāraṃ vivarāpetvā paṭisattuno ahutvā nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu.

Later, when the king was lying on his deathbed, the ministers asked him, "Your Majesty, after your passing, to whom shall we give the white parasol?" "My dears," he replied, "all my sons are worthy of the white parasol. However, you should give the white parasol to the one who wins your hearts." After the king passed away, they performed his funeral rites. On the seventh day, they gathered and said, "Our lord the king instructed us to give the white parasol to the one who wins our hearts. And this Prince Sa၃vara has won our hearts." Thus, they raised the golden garland and the white parasol for Prince Sa၃vara. King Sa၃vara, established in the advice of the Bodhisatta, ruled righteously. The other ninety-nine princes thought, "Our father has passed away, and they have raised the white parasol for Prince Sa၃vara. He is the youngest of all, yet the parasol has gone to him. We shall give it to the eldest, Uposatha, instead." Having conspired together, they all came and sent a message to King Sa၃vara: "Either give us the throne or give us battle." Then they besieged the city. The king informed the Bodhisatta of this and asked, "What should I do now?" "Great king," the Bodhisatta said, "there is no need for you to fight with your brothers. Divide your father’s wealth into a hundred portions, send ninety-nine to your brothers, and send this message: 'Please take this, your portion of our father’s inheritance. I do not wish to fight with you.'" The king did exactly as the Bodhisatta suggested. Then his eldest brother, Prince Uposatha, called the other brothers and said, "My brothers, no one is able to overcome a king. Our youngest brother Sa၃vara does not resist us as an enemy; he has sent us our father’s wealth with the message that he does not wish to fight. We cannot all wear the white parasol at the same time. Let our youngest brother alone wear it; let him be the king. Come, let us see our youngest brother Sa၃vara, entrust the royal estate to him, and return to our own provinces." Then all the princes had the city gates opened and, no longer acting as enemies, entered the city.

Rājāpi tesaṃ amaccehi paṇṇākāraṃ gāhāpetvā paṭimaggaṃ peseti. Kumārā nātimahantena parivārena pattikāva āgantvā rājanivesanaṃ abhiruhitvā saṃvaramahārājassa nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā nīcāsane nisīdiṃsu. Saṃvaramahārājā setacchattassa heṭṭhā sīhāsane nisīdi, mahanto yaso mahantaṃ sirisobhaggaṃ ahosi, olokitolokitaṭṭhānaṃ kampi. Uposathakumāro saṃvaramahārājassa sirivibhavaṃ oloketvā “amhākaṃ pitā attano accayena saṃvarakumārassa rājabhāvaṃ ñatvā maññe amhākaṃ janapade datvā imassa na adāsī”ti cintetvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The king then had his ministers take gifts to meet and welcome his brothers. The princes, with a modest retinue, came on foot and ascended to the palace. Having shown their respect to King Sa၃vara, they sat on low seats. King Sa၃vara sat on the magnificent lion throne beneath the white parasol in great glory and splendor; wherever he looked, things seemed to tremble. Prince Uposatha, observing King Sa၃vara’s glorious majesty, thought, ‘Our father, knowing that Sa၃vara would become king after his passing, must have given us provinces but gave none to him.’ Thinking thus, while conversing with his brothers, he spoke these three verses:

97.

97.

“Jānanto [P 4.0134] no mahārāja, tava sīlaṃ janādhipo;

Ime kumāre pūjento, na taṃ kenaci maññatha.

‘O great king, did the lord of men, our father, know your virtue? When he honored these ninety-nine princes with provinces, did he not consider you for even a single town?’

98.

98.

“Tiṭṭhante no mahārāje, adu deve divaṅgate;

Ñātī taṃ samanuññiṃsu, sampassaṃ atthamattano.

‘Was it while our great father was still living, or was it after the king had passed to heaven, that your kinsmen, seeing your own advantage, gave you their consent?’

99.

99.

“Kena saṃvara vattena, sañjāte abhitiṭṭhasi;

Kena taṃ nātivattanti, ñātisaṅghā samāgatā”ti.

‘By what conduct, O Sa၃vara, do you excel your ninety-nine brothers of equal birth? For what reason do your assembled kinsmen not overcome you?’

Tattha [V 4.0122][M 4.0137] jānanto noti jānanto nu. Janādhipoti amhākaṃ pitā narindo. Imeti ime ekūnasate kumāre. Pāḷipotthakesu pana “aññe kumāre”ti likhitaṃ. Pūjentoti tena tena janapadena mānento. Na taṃ kenacīti khuddakenāpi kenaci janapadena taṃ pūjetabbaṃ na maññittha, “ayaṃ mama accayena rājā bhavissatī”ti ñatvā maññe attano pādamūleyeva vāsesīti. Tiṭṭhante noti tiṭṭhante nu, dharamāneyeva nūti pucchati, adu deveti udāhu amhākaṃ pitari divaṅgate attano atthaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ passantā saddhiṃ rājakārakehi negamajānapadehi ñātayo taṃ “rājā hohī”ti samanuññiṃsu. Vattenāti sīlācārena. Sañjāte abhitiṭṭhasīti samānajātike ekūnasatabhātaro abhibhavitvā tiṭṭhasi. Nātivattantīti na abhibhavanti.

Herein, jānanto no means jānanto nu (knowing, indeed?). Janādhipo means our father, the king. Ime means these ninety-nine princes. In the Pāli books, however, it is written as ‘other princes’. Pūjento means honoring with this and that province. Na taṃ kenaci means he did not think you should be honored with any province, even a small one, knowing, ‘This one will be king after my passing,’ I suppose, and so he kept you at his own feet. Tiṭṭhante no means tiṭṭhante nu (while he was still living, indeed?); he asks if it was while he was still living. Adu deve means or, when our father, the deva, had passed away, did the kinsmen, along with the king-makers, the townspeople, and the country-folk, seeing their own benefit and prosperity, consent, saying, ‘Be king’? Vattena means by virtuous conduct. Sañjāte abhitiṭṭhasi means you stand, having overcome your ninety-nine brothers of equal birth. Nātivattanti means they do not overcome.

Taṃ sutvā saṃvaramahārājā attano guṇaṃ kathento cha gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, King Sa၃vara, wishing to declare his own virtues, spoke these six verses:

100.

100.

“Na rājaputta usūyāmi, samaṇānaṃ mahesinaṃ;

Sakkaccaṃ te namassāmi, pāde vandāmi tādinaṃ.

‘O prince Uposatha, I am not envious. I pay homage to the feet of the ascetics, the great seers. I honor them with reverence and bow to such stable ones.’

101.

101.

“Te maṃ dhammaguṇe yuttaṃ, sussūsamanusūyakaṃ;

Samaṇā manusāsanti, isī dhammaguṇe ratā.

‘Those ascetics and sages, delighting in the qualities of the Dhamma, instruct me, who am devoted to the Dhamma, eager to listen, and free from envy.’

102.

102.

“Tesāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, samaṇānaṃ mahesinaṃ;

Na kiñci atimaññāmi, dhamme me nirato mano.

‘Having heard the words of those ascetics, the great seers, I do not disparage anyone; my mind is always devoted to the Dhamma.’

103.

103.

“Hatthārohā anīkaṭṭhā, rathikā pattikārakā;

Tesaṃ nappaṭibandhāmi, niviṭṭhaṃ bhattavetanaṃ.

‘Elephant riders, horsemen who stand near the elephants, charioteers, and foot soldiers—I do not withhold from them their established food and wages.’

104.

104.

“Mahāmattā ca me atthi, mantino paricārakā;

Bārāṇasiṃ voharanti, bahumaṃsasurodanaṃ.

‘I have great ministers and attendants, all of whom are wise in counsel.’

105.

105.

“Athopi [P 4.0135] vāṇijā phītā, nānāraṭṭhehi āgatā;

Tesu me vihitā rakkhā, evaṃ jānāhuposathā”ti.

‘Moreover, prosperous merchants come from various countries and trade in Benares, which is rich in meat, liquor, and rice. For them, I have provided protection. Know this, Uposatha.’

Tattha [M 4.0138] na rājaputtāti ahaṃ rājaputta, kañci sattaṃ “ayaṃ sampatti imassa mā [V 4.0123] hotū”ti na usūyāmi. Tādinanti tādilakkhaṇayuttānaṃ samitapāpatāya samaṇānaṃ mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ esitatāya mahesīnaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena pāde vandāmi, dānaṃ dadanto dhammikañca nesaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ paccupaṭṭhapento sakkaccaṃ te namassāmi, manena sampiyāyanto ca pūjemīti attho. Te manti te samaṇā maṃ “ayaṃ dhammakoṭṭhāse yuttapayutto sussūsaṃ anusūyako”ti tathato ñatvā maṃ dhammaguṇe yuttaṃ sussūsaṃ anusūyakaṃ anusāsanti, “idaṃ kara, idaṃ mā karī”ti ovadantīti attho. Tesāhanti tesaṃ ahaṃ. Hatthārohāti hatthiṃ āruyha yujjhanakā yodhā. Anīkaṭṭhāti hatthānīkādīsu ṭhitā. Rathikāti rathayodhā. Pattikārakāti pattinova. Niviṭṭhanti yaṃ tehi sajjitaṃ bhattañca vetanañca, ahaṃ taṃ nappaṭibandhāmi, aparihāpetvā dadāmīti attho.

Herein, Na rājaputta usūyāmi means: I, a prince, do not envy any being, thinking, ‘May this prosperity not be theirs.’ Tādinaṃ refers to those endowed with the quality of being ‘such a one’: I bow at the feet of righteous ascetics and brahmins—who are ascetics because they have quelled evil, and great seers because they seek great virtues such as the aggregate of morality—with the five-point prostration. The meaning is: while giving gifts and establishing for them righteous protection, guarding, and security, I honor them respectfully and cherish them in my heart. Te maṃ means: those ascetics, truly knowing me as one who is diligently engaged in the portion of Dhamma, eager to listen, and not envious, instruct me; the meaning is that they advise me, saying, ‘Do this, do not do that.’ Tesāhaṃ means tesaṃ ahaṃ (of them, I). Hatthārohā means warriors who fight mounted on elephants. Anīkaṭṭhā means those stationed in the divisions, such as the elephant corps. Rathikā means chariot warriors. Pattikārakā means foot soldiers. Niviṭṭhaṃ means the food and wages that have been arranged for them; I do not withhold them, meaning I give them without reduction.

Mahāmattāti bhātika, mayhaṃ mahāpaññā mantesu kusalā mahāamaccā ceva avasesamantino ca paricārakā atthi. Iminā imaṃ dasseti “tumhe mantasampanne paṇḍite ācariye na labhittha, amhākaṃ pana ācariyā paṇḍitā upāyakusalā, te no setacchattena yojesu”nti. Bārāṇasinti bhātika, mama chattaṃ ussāpitakālato paṭṭhāya “amhākaṃ rājā dhammiko anvaddhamāsaṃ devo vassati, tena sassāni sampajjanti, bārāṇasiyaṃ bahuṃ khāditabbayuttakaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ pāyitabbayuttakaṃ surodakañca jāta”nti evaṃ raṭṭhavāsino bahumaṃsasurodakaṃ katvā bārāṇasiṃ voharanti. Phītāti hatthiratanaassaratanamuttaratanādīni āharitvā nirupaddavā vohāraṃ karontā phītā samiddhā. Evaṃ jānāhīti bhātika uposatha ahaṃ imehi ettakehi kāraṇehi sabbakaniṭṭhopi hutvā mama bhātike abhibhavitvā setacchattaṃ patto, evaṃ jānāhīti.

Mahāmattā means: Brother, I have great ministers, as well as other counselors and attendants, who are of great wisdom and skilled in counsel. By this he shows: ‘You did not find wise teachers accomplished in counsel, but our teachers are wise and skilled in means; they are the ones who provided us with the white parasol.’ Bārāṇasiṃ means: Brother, from the time my parasol was raised, the country-dwellers say, ‘Our king is righteous, the heavens rain every fortnight, and because of that the crops are abundant. In Benares, much edible fish and meat, and drinkable liquor and water have appeared.’ Thus the inhabitants of the land, with this abundance of meat, liquor, and water, conduct their affairs in Benares. Phītā means: bringing treasures such as elephant-jewels, horse-jewels, pearl-jewels, and so on, they trade without misfortune, thus they are prosperous and successful. Evaṃ jānāhi means: Brother Uposatha, know that it is for these many reasons that I, though the very youngest, have overcome my brothers and attained the white parasol. Thus you should know.

Athassa guṇaṃ sutvā uposathakumāro dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then, having heard of his virtues, Prince Uposatha spoke these two verses to praise his younger brother Sa၃vara:

106.

106.

“Dhammena kira ñātīnaṃ, rajjaṃ kārehi saṃvara;

Medhāvī paṇḍito cāsi, athopi ñātinaṃ hito.

‘Truly, O Sa၃vara, you have excelled your ninety-nine elder brothers by righteousness! Rule the kingdom; you are wise, learned, and a benefactor to your kinsmen.’

107.

107.

“Taṃ [M 4.0139] taṃ ñātiparibyūḷhaṃ, nānāratanamocitaṃ;

Amittā nappasahanti, indaṃva asurādhipo”ti.

‘Enemies cannot overcome you, surrounded as you are by your ninety-nine kinsmen and endowed with various virtues, just as the lord of the Asuras cannot overcome Indra.’

Tattha [P 4.0136] dhammena kira ñātīnanti tāta saṃvara mahārāja, dhammena kira tvaṃ ekūnasatānaṃ ñātīnaṃ [V 4.0124] attano jeṭṭhabhātikānaṃ ānubhāvaṃ abhibhavasi, ito paṭṭhāya tvameva rajjaṃ kārehi, tvameva medhāvī ceva paṇḍito ca ñātīnañca hitoti attho. Taṃ tanti evaṃ vividhaguṇasampannaṃ taṃ. Ñātiparibyūḷhanti amhehi ekūnasatehi ñātakehi parivāritaṃ. Nānāratanamocitanti nānāratanehi ocitaṃ sañcitaṃ bahuratanasañcayaṃ. Asurādhipoti yathā tāvatiṃsehi parivāritaṃ indaṃ asurarājā nappasahati, evaṃ amhehi ārakkhaṃ karontehi parivāritaṃ taṃ tiyojanasatike kāsiraṭṭhe dvādasayojanikāya bārāṇasiyā rajjaṃ kārentaṃ amittā nappasahantīti dīpeti.

Herein, "Dhammena kira %%%tĩna၃" means: Dear King Sa၃vara, it is truly by righteousness that you excel the power of your ninety-nine elder brothers. From now on, you alone should rule; you are wise, learned, and seek the welfare of your kin. "Ta၃ ta၃" means you, who are endowed with such various virtues. "%%%tiparibyũ့ha၃" means surrounded by us, the ninety-nine kinsmen. "Nānāratanamocita၃" means filled and accumulated with various jewels and treasures. "Asurādhipo" shows that just as the king of the asuras cannot overcome Indra when he is surrounded by the Tāvati၃sa devas, so too enemies cannot overcome you while you are protected by us, ruling the kingdom of Kāsi, which is three hundred yojanas in extent, from Bārā၃asĩ, a city twelve yojanas in size.

Saṃvaramahārājā sabbesampi bhātikānaṃ mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. Te tassa santike māsaḍḍhamāsaṃ vasitvā “mahārāja janapadesu coresu uṭṭhahantesu mayaṃ jānissāma, tvaṃ rajjasukhaṃ anubhavā”ti vatvā attano attano janapadaṃ gatā. Rājāpi bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā āyupariyosāne devanagaraṃ pūrento agamāsi.

King Saṃvara bestowed great glory and retinue upon all his brothers. They stayed with him for a month and a half and then, saying, "Great king, should thieves arise in the provinces, we shall know of it. You may enjoy the bliss of kingship," they each returned to their own province. The king, too, having abided by the Bodhisatta’s advice, at the end of his life, went on to fill the city of the devas.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “bhikkhu evaṃ tvaṃ pubbe ovādakkhamo, idāni kasmā vīriyaṃ na akāsī”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said: "Monk, formerly you were amenable to advice; why do you not exert effort now?" Having spoken thus, he revealed the Truths and made the connection of the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā saṃvaramahārājā ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, uposathakumāro sāriputto, sesabhātikā therānutherā, parisā buddhaparisā, ovādadāyako amacco pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, King Saṃvara was this monk, Prince Uposatha was Sāriputta, the remaining brothers were the senior and junior elders, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the minister who gave the advice was I myself.

Saṃvarajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The commentary on the Saṃvara Jātaka, the eighth.

[463] 9. Suppārakajātakavaṇṇanā

[463] 9. The Commentary on the Suppāraka Jātaka.

Ummujjanti nimujjantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi sāyanhasamaye tathāgatassa dhammaṃ desetuṃ nikkhamanaṃ āgamayamānā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā “āvuso, aho [M 4.0140] satthā mahāpañño puthupañño hāsapañño javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño tatra tatra upāyapaññāya samannāgato vipulāya pathavīsamāya, mahāsamuddo viya gambhīrāya, ākāso viya vitthiṇṇāya, sakalajambudīpasmiñhi uṭṭhitapañho dasabalaṃ atikkamitvā gantuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Yathā mahāsamudde uṭṭhitaūmiyo velaṃ nātikkamanti, velaṃ patvāva bhijjanti, evaṃ [P 4.0137] na koci pañho dasabalaṃ atikkamati, satthu pādamūlaṃ [V 4.0125] patvā bhijjatevā”ti dasabalassa mahāpaññāpāramiṃ vaṇṇesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva paññavā, pubbepi aparipakke ñāṇe paññavāva, andho hutvāpi mahāsamudde udakasaññāya ‘imasmiṃ imasmiṃ samudde idaṃ nāma idaṃ nāma ratana’nti aññāsī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"They rise up and sink down"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the perfection of wisdom. One evening, as the monks were awaiting the Tathāgata's departure to teach the Dhamma, they sat in the Dhamma hall and said, "Friends, truly the Teacher is of great wisdom, wide wisdom, bright wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, endowed here and there with wisdom in skillful means, with wisdom as expansive as the earth, as deep as the great ocean, and as vast as the sky. Indeed, in all of Jambudīpa, there is no question that arises which is capable of surpassing the Ten-Powered One. Just as waves that arise in the great ocean do not cross the shore, but break upon reaching the shore, so too no question surpasses the Ten-Powered One; having reached the Teacher's feet, it simply shatters." Thus they were praising the great perfection of wisdom of the Ten-Powered One. The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you now gathered here?" When they said, "With this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is wise; even in the past, when his knowledge was not yet fully ripened, he was wise. Though blind, by the perception of water, he knew, 'In this and that ocean are jewels named such and such.'" Then he brought forth a past story.

Atīte kururaṭṭhe kururājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi, kurukacchaṃ nāma paṭṭanagāmo ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto kurukacche niyāmakajeṭṭhakassa putto hutvā nibbatti pāsādiko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, “suppārakakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So mahantena parivārena vaḍḍhanto soḷasavassakāleyeva niyāmakasippe nipphattiṃ patvā aparabhāge pitu accayena niyāmakajeṭṭhako hutvā niyāmakakammaṃ akāsi, paṇḍito ñāṇasampanno ahosi. Tena āruḷhanāvāya byāpatti nāma natthi. Tassa aparabhāge loṇajalapahaṭāni dvepi cakkhūni nassiṃsu. So tato paṭṭhāya niyāmakajeṭṭhako hutvāpi niyāmakakammaṃ akatvā “rājānaṃ nissāya jīvissāmī”ti rājānaṃ upasaṅkami. Atha naṃ rājā agghāpaniyakamme ṭhapesi. So tato paṭṭhāya rañño hatthiratanaassaratanamuttasāramaṇisārādīni agghāpesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kuru, a king named Kururāja reigned, and there was a port village called Kurukaccha. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in Kurukaccha as the son of the chief navigator, handsome and golden-skinned. They named him "Suppārakakumāra." Growing up with a large retinue, by the age of sixteen, he had mastered the navigator's craft. Later, after his father's death, he became the chief navigator and carried out the navigator's work. He was wise and full of knowledge. No ship piloted by him ever met with disaster. Later, both his eyes were destroyed by salty water. From then on, though he was still the chief navigator, he no longer engaged in the navigator's work, thinking, "I will live depending on the king." So he approached the king. Then the king appointed him to the office of valuer. From that time onward, he evaluated the king’s elephant-gem, horse-gem, the finest pearls, the finest gems, and other precious items.

Athekadivasaṃ “rañño maṅgalahatthī bhavissatī”ti kāḷapāsāṇakūṭavaṇṇaṃ ekaṃ vāraṇaṃ ānesuṃ. Taṃ disvā rājā “paṇḍitassa dassethā”ti āha. Atha naṃ tassa santikaṃ nayiṃsu. So hatthena tassa sarīraṃ parimajjitvā “nāyaṃ maṅgalahatthī bhavituṃ anucchaviko, pādehi vāmanadhātuko esa, etañhi mātā vijāyamānā aṅkena sampaṭicchituṃ nāsakkhi, tasmā bhūmiyaṃ patitvā pacchimapādehi vāmanadhātuko hotī”ti [M 4.0141] āha. Hatthiṃ gahetvā āgate pucchiṃsu. Te “saccaṃ paṇḍito kathetī”ti vadiṃsu. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ [P 4.0138] rājā sutvā tuṭṭho tassa aṭṭha kahāpaṇe dāpesi.

One day, they brought a certain elephant resembling a peak of black stone, saying, "This will be the king's auspicious elephant." Seeing it, the king said, "Show it to the wise man." Then they led it to him. He stroked its body with his hand and said, "This is not suitable to be an auspicious elephant; it is stunted in its legs. Indeed, when its mother was giving birth, she was unable to receive it in her lap, so it fell to the ground and thus became stunted in its hind legs." Those who had brought the elephant were questioned, and they said, "The wise man speaks the truth." Hearing this, the king was pleased and had eight kahāpaṇas given to him.

Punekadivasaṃ “rañño maṅgalaasso bhavissatī”ti ekaṃ assaṃ ānayiṃsu. Tampi rājā paṇḍitassa santikaṃ pesesi. So tampi hatthena parāmasitvā “ayaṃ maṅgalaasso bhavituṃ na yutto, etassa hi jātadivaseyeva mātā mari, tasmā mātu khīraṃ alabhanto na sammā vaḍḍhito”ti āha. Sāpissa kathā saccāva ahosi. Tampi sutvā rājā tussitvā aṭṭha kahāpaṇe dāpesi. Athekadivasaṃ “rañño maṅgalaratho bhavissatī”ti rathaṃ āhariṃsu. Tampi rājā tassa santikaṃ pesesi. So tampi hatthena parāmasitvā “ayaṃ ratho susirarukkhena kato, tasmā rañño nānucchaviko”ti āha. Sāpissa kathā saccāva ahosi. Rājā tampi sutvā aṭṭheva [V 4.0126] kahāpaṇe dāpesi. Athassa mahagghaṃ kambalaratanaṃ āhariṃsu. Tampi tasseva pesesi. So tampi hatthena parāmasitvā “imassa mūsikacchinnaṃ ekaṭṭhānaṃ atthī”ti āha. Sodhentā taṃ disvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā sutvā tussitvā aṭṭheva kahāpaṇe dāpesi.

Again one day, they brought a horse, saying, "This will be the king's auspicious horse." The king sent it to the wise man as well. He also touched it with his hand and said, "This horse is not fit to be an auspicious one, for its mother died on the very day it was born. Therefore, not having received its mother's milk, it was not properly nourished." His words also proved to be true. Hearing this too, the king was pleased and gave him eight kahāpaṇas. Then one day, they brought a chariot, saying, "This will be the king's auspicious chariot." The king sent it to him as well. He also touched it with his hand and said, "This chariot is made from hollow wood, so it is not suitable for the king." His words also proved to be true. The king, hearing this too, gave him eight kahāpaṇas. Then they brought him a precious woolen blanket. The king sent that to him as well. He also touched it with his hand and said, "This has a place where it was gnawed by a mouse." Upon cleaning it, they saw it and reported to the king. Hearing this, the king was pleased and gave him eight kahāpaṇas.

So cintesi “ayaṃ rājā evarūpānipi acchariyāni disvā aṭṭheva kahāpaṇe dāpesi, imassa dāyo nhāpitadāyo, nhāpitajātiko bhavissati, kiṃ me evarūpena rājupaṭṭhānena, attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gamissāmī”ti. So kurukacchapaṭṭanameva paccāgami. Tasmiṃ tattha vasante vāṇijā nāvaṃ sajjetvā “kaṃ niyāmakaṃ karissāmā”ti mantesuṃ. “Suppārakapaṇḍitena āruḷhanāvā na byāpajjati, esa paṇḍito upāyakusalo, andho samānopi suppārakapaṇḍitova uttamo”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “niyāmako no hohī”ti vatvā “tātā, ahaṃ andho, kathaṃ niyāmakakammaṃ karissāmī”ti vutte “sāmi, andhāpi tumheyeva amhākaṃ uttamā”ti punappunaṃ yāciyamāno “sādhu tātā, tumhehi ārocitasaññāya niyāmako bhavissāmī”ti tesaṃ [P 4.0139] nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Te nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Nāvā satta divasāni nirupaddavā agamāsi, tato akālavātaṃ uppātitaṃ uppajji, nāvā cattāro māse pakatisamuddapiṭṭhe vicaritvā khuramālīsamuddaṃ nāma pattā. Tattha [M 4.0142] macchā manussasamānasarīrā khuranāsā udake ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti. Vāṇijā te disvā mahāsattaṃ tassa samuddassa nāmaṃ pucchantā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

He thought, "This king, having seen such wonders, gave only eight kahāpaṇas. This gift is a barber's gift; he must be a barber by birth. What use is such royal service to me? I will return to my own dwelling place." So he returned to the port of Kurukaccha. While he was living there, merchants prepared a ship and consulted, "Whom shall we appoint as navigator?" They said, "A ship boarded by Suppāraka the Wise does not come to harm. He is wise and skilled in means. Even though blind, Suppāraka the Wise is the best." Approaching him, they said, "Be our navigator." He replied, "Friends, I am blind. How can I perform the duties of a navigator?" When they insisted, "Sir, even though blind, you are still the best for us," and repeatedly entreated him, he agreed, "Very well, friends. I will be your navigator, relying on the signs you report." He boarded their ship. They set sail into the great ocean. For seven days, the ship sailed without mishap. Then, a sudden, untimely storm arose. The ship drifted for four months on the surface of the ordinary ocean and reached a sea called Khuramālī. There, fish with human-like bodies and razor-sharp noses were diving and surfacing in the water. Seeing them, the merchants, wishing to ask the Great Being the name of that sea, spoke the first verse:

108.

108.

“Ummujjanti nimujjanti, manussā khuranāsikā;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti.

"They rise and sink, these human-like beings with razor noses! We ask you, Suppāraka, what ocean is this?"

Evaṃ tehi puṭṭho mahāsatto attano niyāmakasuttena saṃsanditvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus questioned by them, the Great Being, checking it against his navigator's lore, spoke the second verse:

109.

109.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, khuramālīti vuccatī”ti.

"For the wealth-seeking merchants who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, when their ship has gone astray, this sea is called Khuramālī."

Tattha payātānanti kurukacchapaṭṭanā nikkhamitvā gacchantānaṃ. Dhanesinanti tumhākaṃ vāṇijānaṃ dhanaṃ pariyesantānaṃ. Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāyāti tāta tumhākaṃ imāya videsaṃ pakkhandanāvāya kammakārakaṃ pakatisamuddaṃ atikkamitvā sampatto ayaṃ samuddo “khuramālī”ti vuccati, evametaṃ paṇḍitā kathentīti.

Here, 'of those who have set out' means of those departing from the city of Kurukaccha and going forth. 'Of those seeking wealth' means of you merchants seeking wealth. And 'for the destruction of the ship' means, Fathers, this ocean, which has been reached by your ship journeying to a foreign land, having crossed the ordinary sea, is called 'Khuramālī'; thus do the wise say.

Tasmiṃ [V 4.0127] pana samudde vajiraṃ ussannaṃ hoti. Mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ ‘ayaṃ vajirasamuddo’ti evaṃ etesaṃ kathessāmi, lobhena bahuṃ vajiraṃ gaṇhitvā nāvaṃ osīdāpessantī”ti tesaṃ anācikkhitvāva nāvaṃ laggāpetvā upāyenekaṃ yottaṃ gahetvā macchagahaṇaniyāmena jālaṃ khipāpetvā vajirasāraṃ uddharitvā nāvāyaṃ pakkhipitvā aññaṃ appagghabhaṇḍaṃ chaḍḍāpesi. Nāvā taṃ samuddaṃ atikkamitvā purato aggimāliṃ nāma gatā. So pajjalitaaggikkhandho viya majjhanhikasūriyo viya ca obhāsaṃ muñcanto aṭṭhāsi. Vāṇijā –

In that ocean, diamonds were abundant. The Great Being thought, "If I tell them, 'This is a diamond ocean,' they will greedily take many diamonds and sink the ship." Without informing them, he had the ship anchored. Then, using a stratagem, he took a rope, and in the manner of catching fish, he had a net cast. He drew out the essence of diamonds, placed them in the ship, and had other goods of little value discarded. The ship crossed that ocean and reached a sea called Aggimālī ahead. It stood there, emitting light like a blazing mass of fire or like the midday sun. The merchants, wishing to ask the Great Being about this sea, spoke the third verse:

110.

110.

“Yathā aggīva sūriyova, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti. – gāthāya taṃ pucchiṃsu;

“Like fire or the sun, the ocean appears; We ask you, Suppāraka, which ocean is this?”

Mahāsattopi [M 4.0143] tesaṃ anantaragāthāya kathesi –

The Great Being also spoke to them in the following verse:

111.

111.

“Kurukacchā [P 4.0140] payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, aggimālīti vuccatī”ti.

“For the wealth-seeking merchants who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, when their ship has gone astray, this sea is called Aggimālī.”

Tasmiṃ pana samudde suvaṇṇaṃ ussannaṃ ahosi. Mahāsatto purimanayeneva tatopi suvaṇṇaṃ gāhāpetvā nāvāyaṃ pakkhipāpesi. Nāvā tampi samuddaṃ atikkamitvā khīraṃ viya dadhiṃ viya ca obhāsantaṃ dadhimāliṃ nāma samuddaṃ pāpuṇi. Vāṇijā –

In that ocean, gold was abundant. The Great Being, in the same way as before, had gold collected and loaded onto the ship. The ship, having crossed that ocean also, reached a sea called Dadhimālī, shining like milk or curds. The merchants wished to ask the Great Being about that ocean:

112.

112.

“Yathā dadhīva khīraṃva, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti. –

“Like curd or milk, the ocean appears; We ask you, Suppāraka, which ocean is this?”

Gāthāya tassapi nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu.

With a verse they asked its name also.

Mahāsatto anantaragāthāya ācikkhi –

The Great Being informed them in the following verse:

113.

113.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, dadhimālīti vuccatī”ti.

“For the wealth-seeking merchants who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, when their ship has gone astray, this sea is called Dadhimālī.”

Tasmiṃ pana samudde rajataṃ ussannaṃ ahosi. So tampi upāyena gāhāpetvā nāvāyaṃ pakkhipāpesi[V 4.0128]. Nāvā tampi samuddaṃ atikkamitvā nīlakusatiṇaṃ viya sampannasassaṃ viya ca obhāsamānaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ kusamāliṃ nāma samuddaṃ pāpuṇi. Vāṇijā –

In that ocean, silver was abundant. He had that also collected by a stratagem and loaded onto the ship. The ship, having crossed that ocean also, reached a sea called Kusamālī, which had a dark blue color and shone like blue kusa grass or a flourishing crop. The merchants wished to ask the Great Being about it:

114.

114.

“Yathā kusova sassova, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti. –

“Like kusa grass or a crop, the ocean appears; We ask you, Suppāraka, which ocean is this?”

Gāthāya tassapi nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu.

With a verse they asked its name also.

So anantaragāthāya ācikkhi –

He informed them in the following verse:

115.

115.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, kusamālīti vuccatī”ti.

“For the wealth-seeking merchants who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, when their ship has gone astray, this sea is called Kusamālī.”

Tasmiṃ pana samudde nīlamaṇiratanaṃ ussannaṃ ahosi. So tampi upāyeneva gāhāpetvā nāvāyaṃ pakkhipāpesi. Nāvā tampi samuddaṃ atikkamitvā [M 4.0144] naḷavanaṃ viya veḷuvanaṃ viya ca khāyamānaṃ naḷamāliṃ nāma samuddaṃ pāpuṇi. Vāṇijā –

In that ocean, dark sapphire gems were abundant. He had those also obtained by a stratagem and loaded onto the ship. The ship, having crossed that ocean also, reached a sea called Naḷamālī, appearing like a reed forest or a bamboo grove. The merchants wished to ask the Great Being the name of that sea:

116.

116.

“Yathā [P 4.0141] naḷova veḷūva, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti. –

“Like a reed or bamboo, the ocean appears; We ask you, Suppāraka, which ocean is this?”

Gāthāya tassapi nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu.

With a verse they asked its name also.

Mahāsatto anantaragāthāya kathesi –

Wishing to inform the sailors of the name of that sea, the Great Being spoke:

117.

117.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, naḷamālīti vuccatī”ti.

“For the wealth-seeking merchants who set out from the port of Kurukaccha, when their ship has gone astray, this sea is called Naḷamālī.”

Tasmiṃ pana samudde masāragallaṃ veḷuriyaṃ ussannaṃ ahosi. So tampi upāyena gāhāpetvā nāvāyaṃ pakkhipāpesi. Aparo nayo – naḷoti vicchikanaḷopi kakkaṭakanaḷopi, so [V 4.0129] rattavaṇṇo hoti. Veḷūti pana pavāḷassetaṃ nāmaṃ, so ca samuddo pavāḷussanno rattobhāso ahosi, tasmā “yathā naḷova veḷuvā”ti pucchiṃsu. Mahāsatto tato pavāḷaṃ gāhāpesīti.

In that ocean, masāragalla gems and beryl were abundant. He had those also gathered by a stratagem and loaded onto the ship. According to another explanation: 'Reed' (naḷa) refers to both scorpion-reeds and crab-reeds, which are red in color. 'Bamboo' (veḷu) is a name for coral; that sea was abundant in coral and had a red lustre. Hence, they asked, 'Like a reed or bamboo?' The Great Being then had the coral collected.

Vāṇijā naḷamāliṃ atikkantā balavāmukhasamuddaṃ nāma passiṃsu. Tattha udakaṃ kaḍḍhitvā kaḍḍhitvā sabbato bhāgena uggacchati. Tasmiṃ sabbato bhāgena uggate udakaṃ sabbato bhāgena chinnapapātamahāsobbho viya paññāyati, ūmiyā uggatāya ekato papātasadisaṃ hoti, bhayajanano saddo uppajjati sotāni bhindanto viya hadayaṃ phālento viya ca. Taṃ disvā vāṇijā bhītatasitā –

The merchants, having passed Naḷamālī, saw a sea named Balavāmukha. There, water was drawn up again and again and surged up on all sides. When the water surged up from all directions, it appeared like a great chasm with a sheer drop on all sides. As a wave rose, one side became like a precipice, and a fear-inspiring sound arose, as if shattering the ears and splitting the heart. Seeing this, the merchants, frightened and terrified—

118.

118.

“Mahabbhayo bhiṃsanako, saddo suyyatimānuso;

Yathā sobbho papātova, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo aya”nti. –

“A sound of great terror, terrifying, an inhuman sound is heard; like a chasm or a precipice, the ocean appears; we ask you, Suppāraka, which ocean is this?”

Gāthāya tassapi nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu.

With a verse they asked its name also.

Tattha [M 4.0145] suyyatimānusoti suyyati amānuso saddo.

Here, 'suyyatimānuso' means 'an inhuman sound is heard'.

119.

119.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, balavāmukhīti vuccatī”ti. –

“For the merchants who set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth, it is called Balavāmukhī when the ship has gone astray.”

Bodhisatto anantaragāthāya tassa nāmaṃ ācikkhitvā “tātā, imaṃ balavāmukhasamuddaṃ [P 4.0142] patvā nivattituṃ samatthā nāvā nāma natthi, ayaṃ sampattanāvaṃ nimujjāpetvā vināsaṃ pāpetī”ti āha. Tañca nāvaṃ satta manussasatāni abhiruhiṃsu. Te sabbe maraṇabhayabhītā ekappahāreneva avīcimhi paccamānasattā viya atikāruññaṃ ravaṃ muñciṃsu. Mahāsatto “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño etesaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ kātuṃ samattho nāma natthi, saccakiriyāya tesaṃ sotthiṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā te āmantetvā āha – “tātā, khippaṃ maṃ gandhodakena nhāpetvā ahatavatthāni nivāsāpetvā puṇṇapātiṃ sajjetvā nāvāya dhure ṭhapethā”ti. Te vegena tathā kariṃsu. Mahāsatto ubhohi hatthehi puṇṇapātiṃ gahetvā nāvāya dhure ṭhito saccakiriyaṃ karonto osānagāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, having declared its name in the immediately following verse, said, “Fathers, there is no ship whatsoever capable of turning back once it reaches this Balavāmukha sea; it causes any ship that arrives to sink and brings it to destruction.” And seven hundred people had boarded that ship. Terrified by the fear of death, they all at once let out a most piteous cry, like beings being cooked in Avīci hell. The Great Being thought, “Except for me, no one else is capable of bringing them to safety. I will ensure their safety through an act of truth.” He then addressed them, saying, “Fathers, quickly bathe me with fragrant water, clothe me in new garments, prepare a full bowl, and place me at the bow of the ship.” They swiftly did so. The Great Being, holding the full bowl with both hands, stood at the bow of the ship and, making an act of truth, spoke the concluding verse:

120.

120.

“Yato [V 4.0130] sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ;

Nābhijānāmi sañcicca, ekapāṇampi hiṃsitaṃ;

Etena saccavajjena, sotthiṃ nāvā nivattatū”ti.

“From the time I remember myself, from the time I attained understanding, I do not recall intentionally harming even a single living being. By this statement of truth, may the ship return in safety.”

Tattha yatoti yato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ attānaṃ sarāmi, yato paṭṭhāya camhi viññutaṃ pattoti attho. Ekapāṇampi hiṃsitanti etthantare sañcicca ekaṃ kunthakipillikapāṇampi hiṃsitaṃ nābhijānāmi. Desanāmattamevetaṃ, bodhisatto pana tiṇasalākampi upādāya mayā parasantakaṃ na gahitapubbaṃ, lobhavasena paradāraṃ na olokitapubbaṃ, musā na bhāsitapubbā, tiṇaggenāpi majjaṃ na pivitapubbanti evaṃ pañcasīlavasena pana saccakiriyaṃ akāsi, katvā ca pana puṇṇapātiyā udakaṃ nāvāya dhure abhisiñci.

Here, 'from when' means: from when onwards I remember myself, and from when onwards I attained understanding. 'Harming even a single living being' means: in this interval, I do not recall intentionally harming even a single tiny insect or ant. This is merely a summary statement, for the Bodhisatta had never before taken another's possessions, even so much as a blade of grass; had never before looked at another's wife out of greed; had never before spoken falsely; had never before drunk intoxicants, even with the tip of a grass-blade. Thus he performed the act of truth based on the five precepts. And having done so, he sprinkled water from the full bowl onto the bow of the ship.

Cattāro māse videsaṃ pakkhandanāvā nivattitvā iddhimā viya saccānubhāvena ekadivaseneva kurukacchapaṭṭanaṃ agamāsi. Gantvā ca pana thalepi aṭṭhusabhamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ pakkhanditvā nāvikassa gharadvāreyeva aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto tesaṃ vāṇijānaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇipavāḷamuttavajirāni bhājetvā [M 4.0146] adāsi. “Ettakehi [P 4.0143] vo ratanehi alaṃ, mā puna samuddaṃ pavisathā”ti tesaṃ ovādaṃ datvā yāvajīvaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā devapuraṃ pūresi.

The ship, which had been sailing towards a foreign land for four months, turned back as if by psychic power. By the power of truth, it reached the port of Kurukaccha in just one day. Upon arriving, it leaped onto land for a distance of eight usabhas and stopped right at the navigator's door. The Great Being distributed gold, silver, gems, coral, pearls, and diamonds to those merchants and gave them advice: “With these jewels, you have enough. Do not venture into the ocean again.” After giving them this counsel, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving for the rest of his life and filled the heavenly city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi tathāgato mahāpaññoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā parisā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, suppārakapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said: “Thus, monks, even in the past, the Tathāgata was indeed of great wisdom.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time, the assembly was the assembly of the Buddha, but Suppāraka the wise was none other than myself.”

Suppārakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the Commentary on the Suppāraka Jātaka.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Mātuposaka juṇho ca, dhamma udaya pānīyo;

Yudhañcayo dasaratho, saṃvaro ca suppārako;

Ekādasanipātamhi, saṅgītā nava jātakā.

Mātuposaka, and Juṇha, Dhamma, Udaya, Pānīya; Yudhañcaya, Dasaratha, Saṃvara, and Suppāraka; In the Eleventh Nipāta, nine Jātakas are recited.

Ekādasakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of the Elevens is completed.

12. Dvādasakanipāto

12. The Book of Twelves

[464] 1. Cūḷakuṇālajātakavaṇṇanā

[464] 1. 1. The Commentary on the Cūḷakuṇāla Jātaka

1-12.

1-12.

Luddhānaṃ [V 4.0131][P 4.0144][M 4.0147] lahucittānanti idaṃ jātakaṃ kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati;

“Of the greedy and the fickle-minded...” — this Jātaka will become clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka (Jā. 536).

Cūḷakuṇālajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first, the Commentary on the Cūḷakuṇāla Jātaka.

[465] 2. Bhaddasālajātakavaṇṇanā

[465] 2. 2. The Commentary on the Bhaddasāla Jātaka

Kā tvaṃ suddhehi vatthehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ñātatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi anāthapiṇḍikassa nivesane pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ nibaddhabhojanaṃ pavattati, tathā visākhāya ca kosalarañño ca. Tattha pana kiñcāpi nānaggarasabhojanaṃ dīyati, bhikkhūnaṃ panettha koci vissāsiko natthi, tasmā bhikkhū rājanivesane na bhuñjanti, bhattaṃ gahetvā anāthapiṇḍikassa vā visākhāya vā aññesaṃ vā vissāsikānaṃ gharaṃ gantvā bhuñjanti. Rājā ekadivasaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ āhaṭaṃ “bhikkhūnaṃ dethā”ti bhattaggaṃ pesetvā “bhattagge bhikkhū natthī”ti vutte “kahaṃ gatā”ti pucchitvā “attano vissāsikagehesu nisīditvā bhuñjantī”ti sutvā bhuttapātarāso satthu santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, bhojanaṃ nāma kiṃ parama”nti pucchi. Vissāsaparamaṃ mahārāja, kañjikamattakampi vissāsikena dinnaṃ madhuraṃ hotīti. Bhante, kena pana saddhiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vissāso hotīti? “Ñātīhi vā sekkhakulehi vā, mahārājā”ti. Tato rājā cintesi “ekaṃ sakyadhītaraṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṃ karissāmi, evaṃ mayā saddhiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ñātake viya [P 4.0145] vissāso bhavissatī”ti. So uṭṭhāyāsanā attano nivesanaṃ gantvā kapilavatthuṃ dūtaṃ pesesi “dhītaraṃ me detha, ahaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ ñātibhāvaṃ icchāmī”ti.

“Who are you, in pure garments?” — this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning conduct for the benefit of relatives. In Sāvatthī, at the residence of Anāthapiṇḍika, a regular meal was provided for five hundred monks, as well as at the residences of Visākhā and the King of Kosala. Though various delicious foods were offered there, the monks had no trusted person there. Therefore, the monks did not eat at the king’s residence but, taking their meal, went to the houses of trusted persons like Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, or others, and ate there. One day, the king sent a gift that had been brought to him, saying, “Give this to the monks,” and sent it to the dining hall. When told, “There are no monks in the dining hall,” he asked, “Where have they gone?” Hearing that they were sitting and eating in the houses of their trusted persons, the king, after finishing his morning meal, went to the Teacher and asked, “Venerable sir, what is the most excellent food?” “Trust is most excellent, great king. Even a little gruel given by a trusted person is delicious.” “Venerable sir, with whom do the monks have trust?” “With relatives or with families of noble disciples, great king.” Then the king thought, “I will bring a Sakyan daughter and make her my chief queen. Thus, I will have a relationship with the monks as if through relatives.” Rising from his seat, he returned to his palace and sent a messenger to Kapilavatthu, saying, “Give me a daughter. I wish to establish kinship with you.”

Sākiyā [V 4.0132][M 4.0148] dūtavacanaṃ sutvā sannipatitvā mantayiṃsu “mayaṃ kosalarañño āṇāpavattiṭṭhāne vasāma, sace dārikaṃ na dassāma, mahantaṃ veraṃ bhavissati, sace dassāma, kulavaṃso no bhijjissati, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti. Atha ne mahānāmo āha – “mā cintayittha, mama dhītā vāsabhakhattiyā nāma nāgamuṇḍāya nāma dāsiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Sā soḷasavassuddesikā uttamarūpadharā sobhaggappattā pitu vaṃsena khattiyajātikā, tamassa ‘khattiyakaññā’ti pesessāmā”ti. Sākiyā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā dūte pakkosāpetvā “sādhu, dārikaṃ dassāma, idāneva naṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti āhaṃsu. Dūtā cintesuṃ “ime sākiyā nāma jātiṃ nissāya atimānino, ‘sadisī no’ti vatvā asadisimpi dadeyyuṃ, etehi saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjamānameva gaṇhissāmā”ti. Te evamāhaṃsu “mayaṃ gahetvā gacchantā yā tumhehi saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjati, taṃ gahetvā gamissāmā”ti. Sākiyā tesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ dāpetvā “kiṃ karissāmā”ti cintayiṃsu. Mahānāmo āha – “tumhe mā cintayittha, ahaṃ upāyaṃ karissāmi, tumhe mama bhojanakāle vāsabhakhattiyaṃ alaṅkaritvā ānetvā mayā ekasmiṃ kabaḷe gahitamatte ‘deva, asukarājā paṇṇaṃ pahiṇi, imaṃ tāva sāsanaṃ suṇāthā’ti paṇṇaṃ dasseyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tasmiṃ bhuñjamāne kumārikaṃ alaṅkariṃsu.

Having heard the messenger's words, the Sākiyans assembled and deliberated: 'We live in a place where the command of King Kosala prevails. If we do not give the maiden, there will be great enmity. If we do give her, our family lineage will be broken. What should be done?' Then Mahānāma said to them, 'Do not worry. My daughter is named Vāsabhakhattiyā; she was born from the womb of a slave-woman named Nāgamuṇḍā. She is about sixteen years of age, possesses supreme beauty, has reached the height of loveliness, and by her father’s lineage is of the Khattiya caste. We shall send her as a "Khattiya maiden."' The Sākiyans agreed, saying, 'Very well.' They summoned the messengers and said, 'Very well, we will give a maiden. Take her and go now.' The messengers thought, 'These Sākiyans are very proud of their birth. Claiming she is equal to us, they might give one who is not equal. We will take only the one who eats together with them.' They said this: 'When we depart, we will take only her who eats together with you.' The Sākiyans provided them with a place to stay and thought, 'What shall we do?' Mahānāma said, 'Do not worry; I will employ a stratagem. At my mealtime, bring Vāsabhakhattiyā after adorning her. Just as I have taken a single morsel, you should show a letter, saying: "Your Majesty, such-and-such a king has sent a letter. Please hear this message first."' They agreed, and while he was eating, they adorned the maiden.

Mahānāmo “dhītaraṃ me ānetha, mayā saddhiṃ bhuñjatū”ti āha. Atha naṃ alaṅkaritvā tāvadeva thokaṃ papañcaṃ katvā ānayiṃsu. Sā “pitarā saddhiṃ bhuñjissāmī”ti ekapātiyaṃ hatthaṃ otāresi. Mahānāmopi tāya saddhiṃ ekapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā mukhe ṭhapesi. Dutiyapiṇḍāya hatthe pasārite “deva, asukaraññā paṇṇaṃ pahitaṃ, imaṃ tāva sāsanaṃ suṇāthā”ti paṇṇaṃ upanāmesuṃ. Mahānāmo “amma, tvaṃ bhuñjāhī”ti dakkhiṇahatthaṃ [P 4.0146] pātiyāyeva katvā vāmahatthena gahetvā paṇṇaṃ olokesi. Tassa taṃ sāsanaṃ upadhārentasseva itarā bhuñji. So tassā bhuttakāle hatthaṃ dhovitvā mukhaṃ vikkhālesi. Taṃ disvā dūtā “nicchayenesā etassa dhītā”ti niṭṭhamakaṃsu, na taṃ antaraṃ jānituṃ sakkhiṃsu. Mahānāmo mahantena parivārena [M 4.0149] dhītaraṃ pesesi. Dūtāpi naṃ sāvatthiṃ netvā “ayaṃ kumārikā jātisampannā mahānāmassa dhītā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā tussitvā sakalanagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā taṃ ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne abhisiñcāpesi. Sā rañño piyā ahosi manāpā.

Mahānāma said, 'Bring my daughter; let her eat with me.' Then they adorned her and, having made a slight delay, brought her. She, thinking, 'I will eat with my father,' placed her hand in the same plate. Mahānāma also took a single morsel together with her and put it in his mouth. When his hand was extended for a second morsel, they presented the letter, saying, 'Your Majesty, a letter has been sent by such-and-such a king; please hear this message first.' Mahānāma said, 'Dear, you eat,' and keeping his right hand in the plate itself, he took the letter with his left hand and examined it. While he was considering the message, the other ate. When she had finished eating, he washed his hand and rinsed his mouth. Seeing that they ate from the same plate, the messengers made a firm conclusion, 'She is certainly his daughter.' They were unable to know the secret. Mahānāma sent his daughter with a large retinue. The messengers also took her to Sāvatthi and reported, 'This maiden is of noble birth, the daughter of Mahānāma.' The king, being delighted, had the entire city decorated, placed her on a heap of jewels, and had her consecrated in the position of chief queen. She became dear and pleasing to the king.

Athassā na cirasseva gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Rājā gabbhaparihāramadāsi. Sā dasamāsaccayena suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase rājā attano ayyakassa santikaṃ pesesi “sakyarājadhītā vāsabhakhattiyā puttaṃ vijāyi, kimassa nāmaṃ karomā”ti. Taṃ pana sāsanaṃ [V 4.0133] gahetvā gato amacco thokaṃ badhiradhātuko, so gantvā rañño ayyakassārocesi. So taṃ sutvā “vāsabhakhattiyā puttaṃ avijāyitvāpi sabbaṃ janaṃ abhibhavati, idāni pana ativiya rañño vallabhā bhavissatī”ti āha. So badhiraamacco “vallabhā”ti vacanaṃ dussutaṃ sutvā “viṭaṭūbho”ti sallakkhetvā rājānaṃ upagantvā “deva, kumārassa kira ‘viṭaṭūbho’ti nāmaṃ karothā”ti āha. Rājā “porāṇakaṃ no kuladattikaṃ nāmaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “viṭaṭūbho”ti nāmaṃ akāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya kumāro kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhanto sattavassikakāle aññesaṃ kumārānaṃ mātāmahakulato hatthirūpakaassarūpakādīni āhariyamānāni disvā mātaraṃ pucchi “amma, aññesaṃ mātāmahakulato paṇṇākāro āhariyati, mayhaṃ koci kiñci na pesesi, kiṃ tvaṃ nimmātā nippitāsī”ti? Atha naṃ sā “tāta, sakyarājāno mātāmahā dūre pana vasanti, tena te kiñci na pesentī”ti vatvā vañcesi.

Not long after, her pregnancy was established. The king provided protection for the fetus. After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son with a golden complexion. Then, on the day of his naming, the king sent word to the prince's grandfather, saying, 'The Sākyan princess Vāsabhakhattiyā has given birth to a son; what name shall we give him?' The minister who went taking that message was somewhat hard of hearing. He went and informed the king's grandfather. Upon hearing that, the grandfather said, 'Even without having born a son, Vāsabhakhattiyā overcomes all the people. Now she will be exceedingly beloved (vallabhā) by the king.' That deaf minister, having misheard the word 'vallabhā,' perceived it as 'Viṭaṭūbha' and, approaching the king, said, 'Your Majesty, it is said you should name the prince Viṭaṭūbha.' The king, thinking, 'It must be an ancient family name of ours,' gave him the name 'Viṭaṭūbha.' From then on, the prince grew up with the care befitting a prince. When he was seven years old, seeing toy elephants, toy horses, and so on being brought for other princes from the houses of their maternal grandfathers, he asked his mother, 'Mother, gifts are brought for other princes from their maternal grandfathers’ houses, but no one sends anything to me. Why is that? Are you without a mother or a father?' Then she deceived him, saying, 'Dear son, the Sākyan kings are your maternal grandfathers, but they live far away; that is why they send nothing.'

Puna soḷasavassikakāle “amma, mātāmahakulaṃ passitukāmomhī”ti vatvā “alaṃ tāta, kiṃ tattha gantvā karissasī”ti vāriyamānopi punappunaṃ yāci. Athassa mātā “tena hi [P 4.0147] gacchāhī”ti sampaṭicchi. So pitu ārocetvā mahantena parivārena nikkhami. Vāsabhakhattiyā puretaraṃ paṇṇaṃ pesesi “ahaṃ idha sukhaṃ vasāmi, sāmino kiñci antaraṃ mā dassayiṃsū”ti. Sākiyā viṭaṭūbhassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā “vandituṃ na sakkā”ti tassa daharadahare kumārake janapadaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Kumāre kapilavatthuṃ sampatte sākiyā santhāgāre sannipatiṃsu. Kumāro santhāgāraṃ [M 4.0150] gantvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ “ayaṃ te, tāta, mātāmaho, ayaṃ mātulo”ti vadiṃsu so sabbe vandamāno vicari. So yāvapiṭṭhiyā rujanappamāṇā vanditvā ekampi attānaṃ vandamānaṃ adisvā “kiṃ nu kho maṃ vandantā natthī”ti pucchi. Sākiyā “tāta, tava kaniṭṭhakumārā janapadaṃ gatā”ti vatvā tassa mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. So katipāhaṃ vasitvā mahantena parivārena nikkhami. Athekā dāsī santhāgāre tena nisinnaphalakaṃ “idaṃ vāsabhakhattiyāya dāsiyā puttassa nisinnaphalaka”nti akkositvā paribhāsitvā khīrodakena dhovi. Eko puriso attano āvudhaṃ pamussitvā nivatto taṃ gaṇhanto viṭaṭūbhakumārassa akkosanasaddaṃ sutvā taṃ antaraṃ pucchitvā “vāsabhakhattiyā dāsiyā kucchismiṃ mahānāmasakkassa jātā”ti ñatvā gantvā balakāyassa kathesi. “Vāsabhakhattiyā kira dāsiyā dhītā”ti mahākolāhalaṃ ahosi.

Again, at the age of sixteen, he said, 'Mother, I wish to see my maternal grandfather's family.' Although she tried to dissuade him, saying, 'Enough, dear son, what will you do by going there?' he repeatedly requested it. Finally, his mother consented, saying, 'In that case, you may go.' Having informed his father, he set out with a large retinue. Vāsabhakhattiyā sent a letter ahead, saying, 'I am living happily here; do not let my lords show any distinction.' The Sākyas, knowing of Viṭaṭūbha’s arrival and thinking, 'It is not possible to pay homage to him,' sent their youngest princes away to the countryside. When the prince arrived in Kapilavatthu, the Sākyas gathered in the assembly hall. The prince entered the assembly hall and stood there. Then they said to him, 'This, dear son, is your grandfather; this is your uncle.' He went about paying homage to all the Sākyas. Although he bowed until his back ached, he did not see a single person paying homage to him and asked, 'Why is it that no one is paying respects to me?' The Sākyas replied, 'Dear son, the princes younger than you have gone to the countryside,' and they showed him great honor. After staying for a few days, he departed with his large retinue. Then a slave woman in the assembly hall reviled the plank on which he had sat, saying, 'This is the sitting plank of the son of the slave woman Vāsabhakhattiyā!' and washed it with milk-water. A man who had forgotten his weapon returned to retrieve it and overheard the insults against Prince Viṭaṭūbha. He inquired about the matter and, learning that 'Vāsabhakhattiyā was born from the womb of a slave woman of Mahānāma the Sākya,' went and told the army. A great uproar arose: 'Vāsabhakhattiyā, it is said, is the daughter of a slave woman!'

Kumāro taṃ sutvā “ete tāva mama nisinnaphalakaṃ khīrodakena dhovantu, ahaṃ pana rajje patiṭṭhitakāle [V 4.0134] etesaṃ galalohitaṃ gahetvā mama nisinnaphalakaṃ dhovissāmī”ti cittaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ sāvatthiṃ gate amaccā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “sabbe mayhaṃ dāsidhītaraṃ adaṃsū”ti sākiyānaṃ kujjhitvā vāsabhakhattiyāya ca puttassa ca dinnaparihāraṃ acchinditvā dāsadāsīhi laddhabbaparihāramattameva dāpesi. Tato katipāhaccayena satthā rājanivesanaṃ āgantvā nisīdi. Rājā satthāraṃ vanditvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ kira ñātakehi dāsidhītā mayhaṃ dinnā, tenassā ahaṃ saputtāya parihāraṃ acchinditvā dāsadāsīhi laddhabbaparihāramattameva dāpesi”nti āha. Satthā “ayuttaṃ, mahārāja, sākiyehi [P 4.0148] kataṃ, dadantehi nāma samānajātikā dātabbā assa. Taṃ pana mahārāja, vadāmi vāsabhakhattiyā khattiyarājadhītā khattiyassa rañño gehe abhisekaṃ labhi, viṭaṭūbhopi khattiyarājānameva paṭicca jāto, mātugottaṃ nāma kiṃ karissati, pitugottameva pamāṇanti porāṇakapaṇḍitā dalidditthiyā kaṭṭhahārikāyapi aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ adaṃsu, tassā ca kucchimhi jātakumāro dvādasayojanikāya bārāṇasiyā rajjaṃ katvā kaṭṭhavāhanarājā nāma jāto”ti kaṭṭhavāhanajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.7) kathesi[M 4.0151]. Rājā satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā “pitugottameva kira pamāṇa”nti sutvā tussitvā mātāputtānaṃ pakatiparihārameva dāpesi.

Hearing this, the prince resolved in his mind, 'For now, let them wash my sitting plank with milk-water. But when I am established in the kingdom, I will wash my sitting plank with the blood from their throats.' When he arrived in Sāvatthī, the ministers reported the whole matter to the king. The king, becoming angry with the Sākyas, thinking, 'They all gave me a slave’s daughter!' rescinded the privileges granted to Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son, and gave them only as much as male and female slaves receive. A few days later, the Teacher came to the king's palace and sat down. The king paid homage to the Teacher and said, 'Venerable sir, it seems your kinsmen gave me a slave’s daughter. Therefore, I have rescinded the privileges granted to her and her son and have allowed them only what male and female slaves receive.' The Teacher said, 'Great king, what the Sākyas did was improper. When giving in marriage, they should give one of equal birth. However, great king, I say to you: Vāsabhakhattiyā is the daughter of a Khattiya king and received her consecration in the house of a Khattiya king, and Viṭaṭūbha too was born depending on a Khattiya king. What does the mother’s lineage matter? Only the father’s lineage is the standard. The wise men of old gave the position of chief queen even to a poor woman gathering firewood, and the prince born in her womb ruled the twelve-league kingdom of Bārāṇasī and became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana.' Then he told the Kaṭṭhavāhana Jātaka. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse and understanding that 'Indeed, the father’s lineage is the standard,' the king was pleased and restored the mother and son to their former privileges.

Rañño pana bandhulo nāma senāpati mallikaṃ nāma attano bhariyaṃ vañjhaṃ “tava kulagharameva gacchāhī”ti kusinārameva pesesi. Sā “satthāraṃ disvāva gamissāmī”ti jetavanaṃ pavisitvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā “kahaṃ gacchasī”ti ca puṭṭhā “sāmiko me, bhante, kulagharaṃ pesesī”ti vatvā “kasmā”ti vuttā “vañjhā aputtikā, bhante”ti vatvā satthārā “yadi evaṃ gamanakiccaṃ natthi, nivattāhī”ti vuttā tuṭṭhā satthāraṃ vanditvā nivesanameva puna agamāsi. “Kasmā nivattasī”ti puṭṭhā “dasabalena nivattitāmhī”ti āha. Senāpati “diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati tathāgatena kāraṇa”nti āha. Sā na cirasseva gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā uppannadohaḷā “dohaḷo me uppanno”ti ārocesi. “Kiṃ dohaḷo”ti? “Vesāliyā nagare licchavirājānaṃ abhisekamaṅgalapokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā nhatvā pānīyaṃ pivitukāmāmhi, sāmī”ti. Senāpati “sādhū”ti vatvā sahassathāmadhanuṃ gahetvā taṃ rathaṃ āropetvā sāvatthito nikkhamitvā rathaṃ pājento vesāliṃ pāvisi.

Now, the king’s general, Bandhula by name, sent his wife, Mallikā, who was barren, to her family home in Kusinārā, saying, 'Go to your family home.' She thought, 'I will go only after seeing the Teacher,' and entering Jetavana, she paid homage to the Tathāgata and stood to one side. When asked, 'Where are you going?' she replied, 'My husband, venerable sir, is sending me to my family home.' When asked, 'Why?' she said, 'Because I am barren and childless, venerable sir.' The Teacher then said, 'If that is so, there is no need to go; turn back.' Delighted, she paid homage to the Teacher and returned home. When asked, 'Why have you turned back?' she replied, 'I was turned back by the One of Ten Powers.' The general thought, 'The Tathāgata must have seen a reason.' Not long after, she conceived, and when a pregnancy craving arose, she announced, 'A craving has arisen in me.' 'What is the craving?' 'My lord, I wish to descend into the auspicious ceremonial consecration pond of the Licchavi kings in the city of Vesālī, to bathe and drink the water.' The general said, 'Very well,' and taking his bow with the strength of a thousand men, he placed her in the chariot. Setting out from Sāvatthī, he drove the chariot and entered Vesālī.

Tasmiñca kāle kosalarañño bandhulasenāpatinā saddhiṃ ekācariyakule uggahitasippo mahāli nāma licchavī andho licchavīnaṃ atthañca dhammañca anusāsanto dvārasamīpe vasati. So rathassa ummāre paṭighaṭṭanasaddaṃ sutvā “bandhulamallassa rathapatanasaddo [P 4.0149] eso, ajja licchavīnaṃ [V 4.0135] bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti āha. Pokkharaṇiyā anto ca bahi ca ārakkhā balavā, upari lohajālaṃ patthaṭaṃ, sakuṇānampi okāso natthi. Senāpati pana rathā otaritvā ārakkhake khaggena paharanto palāpetvā lohajālaṃ chinditvā antopokkharaṇiyaṃ bhariyaṃ otāretvā nhāpetvā pāyetvā sayampi nhatvā mallikaṃ rathaṃ āropetvā nagarā nikkhamitvā āgatamaggeneva pāyāsi. Ārakkhakā gantvā licchavīnaṃ ārocesuṃ. Licchavirājāno kujjhitvā pañca rathasatāni āruyha “bandhulamallaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti nikkhamiṃsu. Taṃ pavattiṃ mahālissa ārocesuṃ. Mahāli “mā gamittha, so hi vo sabbe ghātayissatī”ti āha. Tepi “mayaṃ gamissāmayevā”ti vadiṃsu.
