Tena hi cakkassa yāva nābhito pathaviṃ paviṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ [M 4.0152] disvā nivatteyyātha, tato anivattantā purato asanisaddaṃ viya suṇissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha, tato anivattantā tumhākaṃ rathadhuresu chiddaṃ passissatha, tamhā ṭhānā nivatteyyātha, purato māgamitthāti. Te tassa vacanena anivattitvā taṃ anubandhiṃsuyeva.

At that time, a Licchavi named Mahāli, who was blind and had learned his craft in the same teacher’s house as Bandhula, the Kosalan king’s general, lived near the gate, advising the Licchavis on their welfare and the Dhamma. Hearing the sound of the chariot striking against the threshold, he said, "That is the sound of Bandhula the Malla’s chariot; today, danger will arise for the Licchavis." Now, the security around the lotus pond was strong both inside and outside, with an iron net spread above it so that not even birds could find an opening. But the general, descending from his chariot and driving away the guards by striking them with his sword, cut through the iron net and let his wife Mallikā descend into the pond. After she had bathed and drunk, and he himself had bathed, he placed Mallikā back on the chariot and left the city, traveling back by the same way he had come. The guards went and reported this to the Licchavi kings. Enraged, the Licchavis mounted five hundred chariots and set out, saying, "We will capture Bandhula the Malla!" They reported this to Mahāli. Mahāli said, "Do not go, for he will kill you all." But they insisted, "We will surely go." "In that case," he said, "when you see the place where the chariot wheels have sunk into the earth up to the hubs, turn back. If you do not turn back from there, you will hear a sound like a thunderbolt ahead—turn back from there. If you still do not turn back from there, you will see holes in your chariot poles—turn back from there. Do not proceed further!" But they did not turn back at his words and pursued him anyway.

Mallikā disvā “rathā, sāmi, paññāyantī”ti āha. Tena hi ekassa rathassa viya paññāyanakāle mama āroceyyāsīti. Sā yadā sabbe eko viya hutvā paññāyiṃsu, tadā “ekameva sāmi rathasīsaṃ paññāyatī”ti āha. Bandhulo “tena hi imā rasmiyo gaṇhāhī”ti tassā rasmiyo datvā rathe ṭhitova dhanuṃ āropeti, rathacakkaṃ yāva nābhito pathaviṃ pāvisi, licchavino taṃ ṭhānaṃ disvāpi na nivattiṃsu. Itaro thokaṃ gantvā jiyaṃ pothesi, asanisaddo viya ahosi. Te tatopi na nivattiṃsu, anubandhantā gacchanteva. Bandhulo rathe ṭhitakova ekaṃ saraṃ khipi. So pañcannaṃ rathasatānaṃ rathasīsaṃ chiddaṃ katvā pañca rājasatāni parikarabandhanaṭṭhāne vijjhitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Te attano viddhabhāvaṃ ajānitvā “tiṭṭha re, tiṭṭha re”ti vadantā anubandhiṃsuyeva. Bandhulo rathaṃ ṭhapetvā “tumhe matakā, matakehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ yuddhaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. Te “matakā nāma amhādisā neva hontī”ti vadiṃsu. “Tena hi sabbapacchimassa parikaraṃ mocethā”ti. Te [P 4.0150] mocayiṃsu. So muttamatteyeva maritvā patito. Atha ne “sabbepi tumhe evarūpā, attano gharāni gantvā saṃvidhātabbaṃ saṃvidahitvā puttadāre anusāsitvā sannāhaṃ mocethā”ti āha. Te tathā katvā sabbe jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā.

Mallikā, seeing them, said, "Lord, the chariots are visible." He replied, "In that case, tell me when they all appear as a single chariot." When all five hundred chariots appeared as one, she said, "Lord, only a single chariot-front is visible." Bandhula said, "Then take these reins," and giving her the reins, he stood in the chariot and strung his bow. The chariot wheels sank into the earth up to the hubs, but the Licchavis, even seeing that spot, did not turn back. He went a little further and twanged the bowstring; the sound was like a thunderbolt. Still, they did not turn back but continued the pursuit. Standing in the chariot, Bandhula shot a single arrow. It pierced the front of the five hundred chariots, struck the five hundred kings at the place where their girdles were fastened, and then entered the earth. Unaware that they had been shot, they shouted, "Stop, you rogue! Stop!" and continued to pursue. Bandhula halted his chariot and said, "You are dead men; I do not fight with the dead." They replied, "Dead men are not like us." "In that case," he said, "loosen the girdle of the very last man." They loosened it. As soon as it was loosened, he fell dead. Then he told them, "All of you are just like this. Go to your own homes, make whatever arrangements need to be made, instruct your wives and children, and then remove your armor." They did as he said, and all five hundred Licchavis met their end.

Bandhulopi mallikaṃ sāvatthiṃ ānesi. Sā soḷasakkhattuṃ yamake putte vijāyi, sabbepi sūrā thāmasampannā ahesuṃ, sabbasippe nipphattiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Ekekassapi purisasahassaparivāro ahosi[V 4.0136]. Pitarā saddhiṃ rājanivesanaṃ gacchantehi teheva rājaṅgaṇaṃ paripūri. Athekadivasaṃ vinicchaye kūṭaḍḍaparājitā manussā bandhulaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā mahāravaṃ viravantā vinicchayaamaccānaṃ kūṭaḍḍakāraṇaṃ tassa ārocesuṃ. Sopi vinicchayaṃ gantvā taṃ aḍḍaṃ tīretvā sāmikameva sāmikaṃ, assāmikameva assāmikaṃ [M 4.0153] akāsi. Mahājano mahāsaddena sādhukāraṃ pavattesi. Rājā “kimida”nti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā tussitvā sabbepi te amacce hāretvā bandhulasseva vinicchayaṃ niyyādesi. So tato paṭṭhāya sammā vinicchini. Tato porāṇakavinicchayikā lañjaṃ alabhantā appalābhā hutvā “bandhulo rajjaṃ patthetī”ti rājakule paribhindiṃsu. Rājā taṃ kathaṃ gahetvā cittaṃ niggahetuṃ nāsakkhi, “imasmiṃ idheva ghātiyamāne garahā me uppajjissatī”ti puna cintetvā “payuttapurisehi paccantaṃ paharāpetvā te palāpetvā nivattakāle antarāmagge puttehi saddhiṃ māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti bandhulaṃ pakkosāpetvā “paccanto kira kupito, tava puttehi saddhiṃ gantvā core gaṇhāhī”ti pahiṇitvā “etthevassa dvattiṃsāya puttehi saddhiṃ sīsaṃ chinditvā āharathā”ti tehi saddhiṃ aññepi samatthe mahāyodhe pesesi. Tasmiṃ paccantaṃ gacchanteyeva “senāpati kira āgacchatī”ti sutvāva payuttakacorā palāyiṃsu. So taṃ padesaṃ āvāsāpetvā janapadaṃ saṇṭhapetvā nivatti.

Bandhula then brought Mallikā to Sāvatthī. She gave birth to sixteen pairs of twin sons, all of whom were brave, strong, and masters of every craft. Each of them had an entourage of a thousand men. When they went to the royal palace with their father, the royal courtyard was filled with them alone. One day, people who had been defeated in the court due to fraudulent lawsuits saw Bandhula coming and, crying out loudly, informed the general of the judges’ deceitful rulings. Bandhula went to the court, settled the cases, and made the rightful owner the owner and the non-owner the non-owner. The crowd raised a great shout of approval. The king, asking "What is this?" and hearing the matter, was highly pleased; he dismissed all those judges and entrusted the office of judge to Bandhula alone. From then on, Bandhula judged cases justly. Consequently, the former judges, unable to get bribes and having little gain, slandered him in the royal court, saying, "Bandhula desires the kingdom." The king, believing their words, could not restrain his mind. Thinking, "If he is killed right here, I will face blame," he then thought, "It is better to have the border region attacked by my agents, have them flee, and then have him killed with his sons on the way back." So he summoned Bandhula and said, "The border is in revolt; go with your sons and capture the thieves." He sent them off, but also sent other capable warriors with them, instructing them, "Cut off his head along with his thirty-two sons right there and bring them back." While he was on his way to the border, the agents acting as thieves fled as soon as they heard "The general is coming." He had that region settled, restored order to the countryside, and then turned back.

Athassa nagarato avidūre ṭhāne te yodhā puttehi saddhiṃ sīsaṃ chindiṃsu. Taṃ divasaṃ mallikāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ dve aggasāvakā nimantitā honti. Athassā pubbaṇhasamaye “sāmikassa te saddhiṃ puttehi sīsaṃ chindiṃsū”ti paṇṇaṃ āharitvā adaṃsu. Sā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā [P 4.0151] kassaci kiñci avatvā paṇṇaṃ ucchaṅge katvā bhikkhusaṅghameva parivisi. Athassā paricārikā bhikkhūnaṃ bhattaṃ datvā sappicāṭiṃ āharantiyo therānaṃ purato cāṭiṃ bhindiṃsu. Dhammasenāpati “upāsike, bhedanadhammaṃ bhinnaṃ, na cintetabba”nti āha. Sā ucchaṅgato paṇṇaṃ nīharitvā “dvattiṃsaputtehi saddhiṃ pitu sīsaṃ chinnanti me imaṃ paṇṇaṃ āhariṃsu, ahaṃ idaṃ sutvāpi na cintemi, sappicāṭiyā bhinnāya kiṃ cintemi, bhante”ti āha. Dhammasenāpati “animittamanaññāta”ntiādīni (su. ni. 579) vatvā dhammaṃ desetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāpi dvattiṃsa suṇisāyo pakkosāpetvā “tumhākaṃ sāmikā attano purimakammaphalaṃ labhiṃsu, tumhe mā socittha mā paridevittha, rañño upari manopadosaṃ mā karitthā”ti ovadi.

Not far from the city, at that place, those warriors beheaded Bandhula along with his sons. On that day, Mallikā had invited the two chief disciples together with five hundred monks. Then, in the morning, they brought and gave her a letter, saying, 'Your husband has been beheaded along with his sons.' Upon learning this news, she said nothing to anyone, but placed the letter in her lap and continued to serve the community of monks. Then, as her female attendants were serving food to the monks and bringing jars of ghee, a jar broke in front of the elders. The Marshal of the Dhamma said, 'Laywoman, what is subject to breaking has broken; do not worry.' She took the letter out from her lap and said, 'They brought me this letter saying that my husband’s head has been cut off along with his thirty-two sons. Even upon hearing this, I do not worry; why should I worry about a broken jar of ghee, Venerable Sir?' The Marshal of the Dhamma, having spoken the verses beginning with "Unindicated and unknown" (Sutta Nipāta 579) and having taught the Dhamma, rose from his seat and went to the monastery. She too summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law and advised them, 'Your husbands have reaped the fruit of their own past deeds. Do not grieve, do not lament, and do not harbor ill will toward the king.'

Rañño carapurisā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tesaṃ niddosabhāvaṃ rañño kathayiṃsu. Rājā saṃvegappatto tassā nivesanaṃ gantvā mallikañca suṇisāyo [M 4.0154] cassā khamāpetvā mallikāya varaṃ adāsi. Sā [V 4.0137] “gahito me hotū”ti vatvā tasmiṃ gate matakabhattaṃ datvā nhatvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “deva, tumhehi me varo dinno, mayhañca aññena attho natthi, dvattiṃsāya me suṇisānaṃ mama ca kulagharagamanaṃ anujānāthā”ti āha. Rājā sampaṭicchi. Sā dvattiṃsāya suṇisānaṃ sakakulaṃ pesetvā sayaṃ kusināranagare attano kulagharaṃ agamāsi. Rājā bandhulasenāpatino bhāgineyyassa dīghakārāyanassa nāma senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So pana “mātulo me iminā mārito”ti rañño otāraṃ gavesanto vicarati. Rājāpi nipparādhassa bandhulassa māritakālato paṭṭhāya vippaṭisārī cittassādaṃ na labhati, rajjasukhaṃ nānubhoti.

The king’s spies, having heard that talk, reported their lack of malice to the king. The king, struck with a sense of urgency, went to her house, and having asked for forgiveness from Mallikā and her daughters-in-law, granted Mallikā a boon. She said, 'Let it be accepted by me.' After he had gone, she offered a funeral meal, bathed, and approached the king. Having paid homage, she said, 'Your Majesty, you have granted me a boon, and I have no other need. Please permit me and my thirty-two daughters-in-law to return to our parental homes.' The king consented. She sent the thirty-two daughters-in-law to their own families and went herself to her parental home in the city of Kusinārā. The king gave the position of general to Dīghakārāyana, the nephew of General Bandhula. But he, thinking, 'My uncle was killed by this king,' wandered about seeking an opportunity against the king. The king, too, from the time the innocent Bandhula was killed, felt remorse, found no mental pleasure, and did not enjoy the bliss of kingship.

Tadā satthā sākiyānaṃ veḷuṃ nāma nigamaṃ upanissāya viharati. Rājā tattha gantvā ārāmato avidūre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsetvā “mahantena parivārena satthāraṃ vandissāmā”ti vihāraṃ gantvā pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni dīghakārāyanassa datvā ekakova gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Sabbaṃ dhammacetiyasuttaniyāmeneva (ma. ni. 2.364 ādayo) veditabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe dīghakārāyano tāni pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni gahetvā viṭaṭūbhaṃ [P 4.0152] rājānaṃ katvā rañño ekaṃ assaṃ ekañca upaṭṭhānakārikaṃ mātugāmaṃ nivattetvā sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Rājā satthārā saddhiṃ piyakathaṃ kathetvā nikkhanto senaṃ adisvā taṃ mātugāmaṃ pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “ahaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ ajātasattuṃ ādāya āgantvā viṭaṭūbhaṃ gahessāmī”ti rājagahanagaraṃ gacchanto vikāle dvāresu pihitesu nagaraṃ pavisitumasakkonto ekissāya sālāya nipajjitvā vātātapena kilanto rattibhāge tattheva kālamakāsi. Vibhātāya rattiyā “deva kosalanarinda, idāni anāthosi jāto”ti vilapantiyā tassā itthiyā saddaṃ sutvā rañño ārocesuṃ. So mātulassa mahantena sakkārena sarīrakiccaṃ kāresi.

At that time, the Teacher was dwelling near the Sakyan market town named Veḷu. The king went there and, having established his camp not far from the monastery, went to the monastery, thinking, 'I will pay homage to the Teacher with a large retinue.' He gave the five articles of royal regalia to Dīghakārāyana and entered the Perfumed Chamber alone. The whole account should be understood according to the manner of the Dhammacetiya Sutta. When he had entered the Perfumed Chamber, Dīghakārāyana took those five articles of royal regalia, made Viṭaṭūbha king, and having sent back the king’s horse and one female attendant, went to Sāvatthī. The king, after having a pleasant conversation with the Teacher, came out. Not seeing his army, he questioned the woman and, hearing what had happened, thought, 'I will take my nephew Ajātasattu and go seize Viṭaṭūbha.' As he was going to the city of Rājagaha, he arrived late when the gates were closed and could not enter the city. He lay down in a certain rest-house and, exhausted by wind and heat, died right there during the night. At daybreak, hearing the sound of that woman wailing, 'Your Majesty, King of Kosala, now you have become helpless!' they reported it to King Ajātasattu. He performed the funeral rites for his uncle with great honor.

Viṭaṭūbhopi rajjaṃ labhitvā taṃ veraṃ saritvā “sabbepi sākiye māressāmī”ti mahatiyā senāya nikkhami. Taṃ divasaṃ satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento ñātisaṅghassa vināsaṃ disvā “ñātisaṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā pubbaṇhasamaye piṇḍāya caritvā [M 4.0155] piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiyaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā sāyanhasamaye ākāsena gantvā kapilavatthusāmante ekasmiṃ kabaracchāye rukkhamūle nisīdi. Tato avidūre viṭaṭūbhassa rajjasīmāya anto sandacchāyo nigrodharukkho atthi, viṭaṭūbho satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “bhante, kiṃkāraṇā evarūpāya uṇhavelāya imasmiṃ kabaracchāye rukkhamūle nisīdatha, etasmiṃ sandacchāye nigrodharukkhamūle nisīdatha, bhante”ti vatvā “hotu, mahārāja, ñātakānaṃ chāyā [V 4.0138] nāma sītalā”ti vutte “ñātakānaṃ rakkhaṇatthāya satthā āgato bhavissatī”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā sāvatthimeva paccāgami. Satthāpi uppatitvā jetavanameva gato.

Viṭaṭūbha, having obtained the kingship and remembering that enmity, thought, 'I will kill all the Sakyans,' and set out with a large army. That day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the destruction of his kinsmen and thought, 'It is fitting to render assistance to my kinsmen.' In the morning, after walking for alms and returning from his alms round, he took the lion’s posture in the Perfumed Chamber. In the evening, he traveled through the air and sat at the foot of a tree with sparse shade near Kapilavatthu. Not far from there, within the borders of Viṭaṭūbha’s kingdom, there was a banyan tree with dense shade. Viṭaṭūbha saw the Teacher, approached, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, for what reason do you sit at the foot of this tree with sparse shade in such hot weather? Please, venerable sir, sit at the foot of this banyan tree with dense shade.' When the Teacher replied, 'Let it be, Great King; the shade of kinsmen is indeed cool,' Viṭaṭūbha thought, 'The Teacher must have come to protect his kinsmen.' Having paid homage to the Teacher, he returned to Sāvatthī itself. The Teacher also flew up and went back to Jetavana.

Rājā sākiyānaṃ dosaṃ saritvā dutiyaṃ nikkhamitvā tatheva satthāraṃ passitvā puna nivattitvā tatiyavāre nikkhamitvā tattheva satthāraṃ passitvā nivatti. Catutthavāre pana tasmiṃ nikkhante satthā sākiyānaṃ pubbakammaṃ oloketvā tesaṃ nadiyaṃ visapakkhipanapāpakammassa appaṭibāhirabhāvaṃ ñatvā catutthavāre na agamāsi. Viṭaṭūbharājā khīrapāyake dārake ādiṃ katvā sabbe sākiye ghātetvā galalohitena nisinnaphalakaṃ dhovitvā paccāgami. Satthari tatiyavāre gamanato paccāgantvā punadivase piṇḍāya caritvā [P 4.0153] niṭṭhāpitabhattakicce gandhakuṭiyaṃ pavisante disāhi sannipatitā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā “āvuso, satthā attānaṃ dassetvā rājānaṃ nivattāpetvā ñātake maraṇabhayā mocesi, evaṃ ñātakānaṃ atthacaro satthā”ti bhagavato guṇakathaṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva tathāgato ñātakānaṃ atthaṃ carati, pubbepi cariyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The king, remembering his grievance against the Sākiyans, set out a second time. Seeing the Teacher just as before, he turned back. Setting out a third time, he saw the Teacher in the same place and turned back. But when he set out for the fourth time, the Teacher, having considered the Sākiyans' past kamma and knowing the unavoidable nature of their evil deed of poisoning the river, did not go the fourth time. King Viṭaṭūbha, starting with the infants at the breast, had all the Sākiyans slain, washed the board on which he sat with the blood from their throats, and returned. On the day after the Teacher had returned from his third journey, when he had finished his alms round and meal and was entering the perfumed chamber, monks who had gathered from all directions were seated in the hall of Dhamma, saying, "Friends, the Teacher, by showing himself, made the king turn back and freed his kinsmen from the fear of death. Thus does the Teacher act for the welfare of his kinsmen." They were discussing the virtues of the Blessed One. The Teacher arrived and asked, "For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered together?" When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of his kinsmen; he did so in the past as well," and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto nāma rājā dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento ekadivasaṃ cintesi “jambudīpatale rājāno bahuthambhesu pāsādesu vasanti, tasmā bahūhi thambhehi pāsādakaraṇaṃ nāma anacchariyaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ekathambhakaṃ pāsādaṃ kāreyyaṃ, evaṃ sabbarājūnaṃ aggarājā bhavissāmī”ti. So vaḍḍhakī pakkosāpetvā “mayhaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ ekathambhakaṃ pāsādaṃ karothā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti [M 4.0156] sampaṭicchitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā ujū mahante ekathambhakapāsādārahe bahū rukkhe disvā “ime rukkhā santi, maggo pana visamo, na sakkā otāretuṃ, rañño ācikkhissāmā”ti cintetvā tathā akaṃsu. Rājā “kenaci upāyena saṇikaṃ otārethā”ti vatvā “deva, yena kenaci upāyena na sakkā”ti vutte “tena hi mama uyyāne ekaṃ rukkhaṃ upadhārethā”ti āha. Vaḍḍhakī uyyānaṃ gantvā ekaṃ sujātaṃ ujukaṃ gāmanigamapūjitaṃ rājakulatopi laddhabalikammaṃ maṅgalasālarukkhaṃ disvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā “uyyāne rukkho nāma mama paṭibaddho, gacchatha bho taṃ chindathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā gandhamālādihatthā uyyānaṃ gantvā rukkhe gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ datvā suttena parikkhipitvā pupphakaṇṇikaṃ bandhitvā dīpaṃ jāletvā balikammaṃ katvā “ito [P 4.0154] sattame divase āgantvā rukkhaṃ chindissāma, rājā chindāpeti, imasmiṃ rukkhe nibbattadevatā aññattha gacchatu, amhākaṃ doso natthī”ti sāvesuṃ.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta was ruling righteously, without violating the ten royal virtues. One day, he thought: "Kings on the continent of Jambudīpa live in palaces with many pillars; therefore, building a palace with many pillars is nothing extraordinary. What if I were to have a palace with a single pillar built? In that way, I would become the foremost of all kings." He had carpenters summoned and said, "Build me a magnificent single-pillared palace." They agreed, saying, "Very well," and entered the forest. There they saw many straight, great trees suitable for a single-pillared palace, but thinking, "These trees are available, but the path is rough and it is not possible to transport them; we shall inform the king," they did so. The king said, "Transport them slowly, by some means." When they replied, "Your Majesty, it is not possible by any means whatsoever," he said, "In that case, find a suitable tree in my own park." The carpenters went to the park and saw a well-formed, straight, auspicious sāl tree, which was worshipped by the villages and towns and had even received offerings from the royal family. They went to the king and reported the matter. The king said, "A tree in the park is my own property. Go, sirs, and cut it down." They agreed, saying, "Very well," and went to the park with perfumes, garlands, and other things in hand. They made a five-fingered mark with fragrant paste on the tree, encircled it with a thread, tied a floral ornament to it, lit a lamp, made an offering, and announced: "Seven days from now, we will come and cut down this tree. The king has ordered it to be cut. Let the deity dwelling in this tree go elsewhere. There is no fault on our part."

Atha [V 4.0139] tasmiṃ nibbatto devaputto taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “nissaṃsayaṃ ime vaḍḍhakī imaṃ rukkhaṃ chindissanti, vimānaṃ me nassissati, vimānapariyantikameva kho pana mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ, imañca rakkhaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitesu taruṇasālarukkhesu nibbattānaṃ mama ñātidevatānampi bahūni vimānāni nassissanti. Vimānapariyantikameva mama ñātīnaṃ devatānampi jīvitaṃ, na kho pana maṃ tathā attano vināso bādhati, yathā ñātīnaṃ, tasmā nesaṃ mayā jīvitaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā aḍḍharattasamaye dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito rañño sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sakalagabbhaṃ ekobhāsaṃ katvā ussisakapasse rodamāno aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā bhītatasito tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, the deity who was born in that sāl tree, hearing those words, thought: "Without a doubt, these carpenters will cut down this tree; my celestial mansion will perish, and indeed, my life is co-terminous with this mansion. Moreover, many celestial mansions belonging to my divine relatives born among the young sāl trees surrounding this tree will also perish. The lives of my divine relatives are also co-terminous with their mansions. My own destruction does not afflict me as much as that of my relatives; therefore, it is fitting for me to give life to them." Having reflected thus, at midnight, adorned with divine ornaments, he entered the king's bedchamber, illuminating the entire chamber with a single radiance, and stood weeping at the head of the bed. The king, seeing him, frightened and terrified, conversed with him and first uttered this verse:

13.

13.

“Kā tvaṃ suddhehi vatthehi, aghe vehāyasaṃ ṭhitā;

Kena tyāssūni vattanti, kuto taṃ bhayamāgata”nti.

"Who are you, with pure garments, standing in the unobstructed sky? For what reason do your tears fall? From where has this fear come to you?"

Tattha kā tvanti nāgayakkhasupaṇṇasakkādīsu kā nāma tvanti pucchati. Vatthehīti vacanamattamevetaṃ, sabbepi pana dibbālaṅkāre sandhāyevamāha. Agheti appaṭighe ākāse. Vehāyasanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Kena tyāssūni vattantīti kena kāraṇena tava assūni vattanti. Kutoti ñātiviyogadhanavināsādīnaṃ kiṃ nissāya taṃ bhayamāgatanti pucchati.

Herein, 'Who are you?' means he asks, "Among nāgas, yakkhas, supaṇṇas, Sakka, and others, who are you?" 'With garments' is merely a manner of speaking; he says this referring to all divine ornaments. 'In the unobstructed' means in the air where there is no resistance. 'In the sky' is a synonym for the same. 'For what reason do your tears fall?' means for what cause do your tears fall. 'From where?' means he asks, "Based on what—such as separation from relatives or loss of wealth—has this fear come to you?"

Tato [M 4.0157] devarājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the divine king spoke two verses:

14.

14.

“Taveva deva vijite, bhaddasāloti maṃ vidū;

Saṭṭhi vassasahassāni, tiṭṭhato pūjitassa me.

"O king, in your own realm, they know me as Bhaddasāla. For sixty thousand years I have stood here, being honored.

15.

15.

“Kārayantā nagarāni, agāre ca disampati;

Vividhe cāpi pāsāde, na maṃ te accamaññisuṃ;

"While building cities, houses, and various palaces, O lord of the land, they did not disrespect me;

Yatheva maṃ te pūjesuṃ, tatheva tvampi pūjayā”ti.

Just as they honored me, so too should you honor me."

Tattha [P 4.0155] tiṭṭhatoti sakalabārāṇasinagarehi ceva gāmanigamehi ca tayā ca pūjitassa niccaṃ balikammañca sakkārañca labhantassa mayhaṃ imasmiṃ uyyāne tiṭṭhantassa ettako kālo gatoti dasseti. Nagarānīti nagarapaṭisaṅkharaṇakammāni. Agārecāti bhūmigehāni. Disampatīti disānaṃ [V 4.0140] pati, mahārāja. Na maṃ teti te nagarapaṭisaṅkharaṇādīni karontā imasmiṃ nagare porāṇakarājāno maṃ nātimaññisuṃ nātikkamiṃsu na viheṭhayiṃsu, mama nivāsarukkhaṃ chinditvā attano kammaṃ na kariṃsu, mayhaṃ pana sakkārameva kariṃsūti avaca. Yathevāti tasmā yatheva te porāṇakarājāno maṃ pūjayiṃsu, ekopi imaṃ rukkhaṃ na chindāpesi, tvañcāpi maṃ tatheva pūjaya, mā me rukkhaṃ chedayīti.

Herein, 'standing' shows that so much time has passed for me standing in this park, honored by the entire city of Bārāṇasī, its villages and towns, and by you, constantly receiving offerings and respect. 'Cities' refers to the work of renovating cities. 'Houses' means ground-level dwellings. 'Lord of the land' means lord of the directions, O great king. 'They did not disrespect me' means that those ancient kings in this city, while undertaking city renovations and the like, did not disrespect me, did not transgress against me, did not harm me; they did not do their work by cutting down my dwelling-tree, but rather paid me respect. 'Just as' means: therefore, just as those ancient kings honored me, and not a single one had this tree cut down, so too should you honor me; do not have my tree cut down.

Tato rājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke two verses:

16.

16.

“Taṃ ivāhaṃ na passāmi, thūlaṃ kāyena te dumaṃ;

Ārohapariṇāhena, abhirūposi jātiyā.

"I do not see another tree as massive in body as you; in height and girth, you are beautiful by nature.

17.

17.

“Pāsādaṃ kārayissāmi, ekatthambhaṃ manoramaṃ;

Tattha taṃ upanessāmi, ciraṃ te yakkha jīvita”nti.

"I will have a delightful, single-pillared palace built; there I will install you. Long may you live, O yakkha!"

Tattha kāyenāti pamāṇena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tava pamāṇena taṃ viya thūlaṃ mahantaṃ aññaṃ dumaṃ na passāmi, tvaññeva pana ārohapariṇāhena sujātasaṅkhātāya samasaṇṭhānaujubhāvappakārāya jātiyā ca abhirūpo sobhaggappatto ekathambhapāsādārahoti. Pāsādanti tasmā taṃ chedāpetvā ahaṃ pāsādaṃ kārāpessāmeva. Tattha tanti taṃ [M 4.0158] panāhaṃ samma devarāja, tattha pāsāde upanessāmi, so tvaṃ mayā saddhiṃ ekato vasanto aggagandhamālādīni labhanto sakkārappatto sukhaṃ jīvissasi, nivāsaṭṭhānābhāvena me vināso bhavissatīti mā cintayi, ciraṃ te yakkha jīvitaṃ bhavissatīti.

Herein, 'in body' means in size. This is what is said: 'I do not see another tree as large and massive as you in size. You, by your height and girth, and by your nature—described as well-born, a kind possessing a symmetrical form and straightness—are handsome, endowed with beauty, and worthy of a single-pillared palace.' 'Palace' means: therefore, having had you cut down, I will indeed have a palace built. 'There I will install you' means: but, my dear divine king, I will install you in that palace. Living together with me, you will receive the finest perfumes, garlands, and so on, and being honored, you will live happily. Do not think, 'My destruction will occur due to the lack of a dwelling place.' Long will be your life, O yakkha.

Taṃ sutvā devarājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the divine king spoke two verses:

18.

18.

“Evaṃ cittaṃ udapādi, sarīrena vinābhāvo;

Puthuso maṃ vikantitvā, khaṇḍaso avakantatha.

"Since this thought has arisen for you—separation from my body—then cut me up in many ways; cut me into pieces.

19.

19.

“Agge [P 4.0156] ca chetvā majjhe ca, pacchā mūlamhi chindatha;

Evaṃ me chijjamānassa, na dukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ siyā”ti.

"Having cut the top and the middle, afterwards cut at the root. For me, being cut in this way, death would not be painful."

Tattha [V 4.0141] evaṃ cittaṃ udapādīti yadi evaṃ cittaṃ tava uppannaṃ. Sarīrena vinābhāvoti yadi te mama sarīrena bhaddasālarukkhena saddhiṃ mama vinābhāvo patthito. Puthusoti bahudhā. Vikantitvāti chinditvā. Khaṇḍasoti khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ katvā avakantatha. Agge cāti avakantantā pana paṭhamaṃ agge, tato majjhe chetvā sabbapacchā mūle chindatha. Evañhi me chijjamānassa na dukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ siyā, sukhaṃ nu khaṇḍaso bhaveyyāti yācati.

Herein, 'Thus a thought arose' means 'if such a thought has arisen in you.' 'Separation from the body' means 'if you desire my separation from my body, the Bhaddasāla tree.' 'In many ways' means in various ways. 'Having cut up' means having cut. 'Cut into pieces' means having made it into fragments. 'And at the top' means: while cutting, first cut at the top, then in the middle, and last of all at the root. He begs, saying, "For in this way, while I am being cut, my death would not be painful; may it be pleasant, piece by piece."

Tato rājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke two verses:

20.

20.

“Hatthapādaṃ yathā chinde, kaṇṇanāsañca jīvato;

Tato pacchā siro chinde, taṃ dukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ siyā.

"Just as one might cut off the hands and feet, and the ears and nose, of a living person, and then afterwards cut off the head—that would be a painful death.

21.

21.

“Sukhaṃ nu khaṇḍaso chinnaṃ, bhaddasāla vanappati;

Kiṃhetu kiṃ upādāya, khaṇḍaso chinnamicchasī”ti.

"Is it pleasant to be cut piece by piece, O Bhaddasāla, lord of the forest? For what reason, on what account, do you wish to be cut piece by piece?"

Tattha hatthapādanti hatthe ca pāde ca. Taṃ dukkhanti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā chijjantassa corassa taṃ maraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ siyā. Sukhaṃ nūti samma bhaddasāla, vajjhappattā corā sukhena maritukāmā sīsacchedaṃ yācanti, na khaṇḍaso chedanaṃ, tvaṃ pana evaṃ yācasi, tena taṃ pucchāmi “sukhaṃ nu khaṇḍaso chinna”nti. Kiṃhetūti khaṇḍaso chinnaṃ nāma na sukhaṃ, kāraṇena panettha bhavitabbanti taṃ pucchanto evamāha.

Herein, 'hands and feet' means hands and feet. 'That painful' means that for a thief being cut in sequence in this way, that death would be painful. 'Is it pleasant, then?' means: 'Friend Bhaddasāla, condemned thieves, wishing to die pleasantly, request beheading, not being cut into pieces. Yet you request it thus. Therefore I ask you, 'Is it pleasant to be cut piece by piece?'' 'For what reason?' means: being cut piece by piece is certainly not pleasant; there must be a reason for this. Thus questioning, he says this.

Athassa [M 4.0159] ācikkhanto bhaddasālo dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then Bhaddasāla, explaining to him, spoke two verses:

22.

22.

“Yañca hetumupādāya, hetuṃ dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ;

Khaṇḍaso chinnamicchāmi, mahārāja suṇohi me.

"The reason, a reason connected with the Dhamma, on account of which I wish to be cut to pieces—listen to it from me, O great king.

23.

23.

“Ñātī me sukhasaṃvaddhā, mama passe nivātajā;

Tepihaṃ upahiṃseyya, paresaṃ asukhocita”nti.

"My relatives, happily raised, born in a sheltered place beside me—I would injure even them, thereby accumulating unhappiness for others."

Tattha [P 4.0157] hetuṃ dhammūpasaṃhitanti mahārāja, yaṃ hetusabhāvayuttameva, na hetupatirūpakaṃ, hetuṃ upādāya ārabbha sandhāyāhaṃ khaṇḍaso chinnamicchāmi, taṃ ohitasoto suṇohīti attho. Ñātī [V 4.0142] meti mama bhaddasālarukkhassa chāyāya sukhasaṃvaddhā mama passe taruṇasālarukkhesu nibbattā mayā katavātaparittāṇattā nivātajā mama ñātakā devasaṅghā atthi, te ahaṃ visālasākhaviṭapo mūle chinditvā patanto upahiṃseyyaṃ, saṃbhaggavimāne karonto vināseyyanti attho. Paresaṃ asukhocitanti evaṃ sante mayā tesaṃ paresaṃ ñātidevasaṅghānaṃ asukhaṃ dukkhaṃ ocitaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, na cāhaṃ tesaṃ dukkhakāmo, tasmā bhaddasālaṃ khaṇḍaso khaṇḍaso chindāpemīti ayametthādhippāyo.

Herein, 'a reason connected with the Dhamma' means: O great king, the reason on account of which I wish to be cut to pieces is one truly connected with the nature of a cause, not a mere semblance of one; listen to that reason with an attentive ear—this is the meaning. 'My relatives' means: there are hosts of deities, my kinsfolk, who have grown up happily in the shade of my Bhaddasāla tree, born among the young sāl trees beside me, and born in a sheltered place because I protect them from the wind. I, with my great branches and boughs, would harm them by falling when cut at the root, destroying them by shattering their celestial mansions—this is the meaning. 'Accumulating unhappiness for others' means that, in such a case, unhappiness and suffering would be accumulated and increased by me for those other hosts of deities, my relatives. And I do not wish them to suffer. Therefore, I wish to have the Bhaddasāla tree cut piece by piece—this is the intent here.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “dhammiko vatāyaṃ, devaputto, attano vimānavināsatopi ñātīnaṃ vimānavināsaṃ na icchati, ñātīnaṃ atthacariyaṃ carati, abhayamassa dassāmī”ti tussitvā osānagāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king thought: "Truly, this son of a deva is righteous! Even at the cost of his own celestial mansion's destruction, he does not wish for the destruction of his relatives’ mansions; he practices conduct beneficial to his relatives. I will grant him safety." Pleased, he spoke this concluding verse:

24.

24.

“Ceteyyarūpaṃ cetesi, bhaddasāla vanappati;

Hitakāmosi ñātīnaṃ, abhayaṃ samma dammi te”ti.

"You have conceived a thought worthy of conception, Bhaddasāla, lord of the forest; you are one who desires the good of your relatives. Friend, I grant you safety."

Tattha ceteyyarūpaṃ cetesīti ñātīsu muducittatāya cintento cintetabbayuttakameva cintesi. Chedeyyarūpaṃ chedesītipi pāṭho. Tassattho – khaṇḍaso chinnamicchanto chedetabbayuttakameva chedesīti. Abhayanti etasmiṃ te samma, guṇe pasīditvā abhayaṃ dadāmi, na me pāsādenattho, nāhaṃ taṃ chedāpessāmi, gaccha ñātisaṅghaparivuto sakkatagarukato sukhaṃ jīvāti āha.

Here, 'you have conceived a thought worthy of conception' (ceteyyarūpaṃ cetesi) means that, with a mind tender toward his relatives, he conceived only what was fitting to conceive. There is also the reading, 'you wished to cut what was fitting to be cut' (chedeyyarūpaṃ chedesi), meaning, wishing it to be cut into pieces, he wished to cut only what was fitting to be cut. 'Safety' (abhayaṃ) refers to this; the King said, 'Friend, pleased with this quality in you, I grant you safety. I have no need for the palace. I will not have you cut down. Go, surrounded by your assembly of relatives, honored and respected, and live happily.'

Devarājā [M 4.0160] rañño dhammaṃ desetvā agamāsi. Rājā tassovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Having taught the Dhamma to the king, the king of devas departed. The king, abiding by his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and thus filled the heavenly city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi tathāgato ñātatthacariyaṃ acariyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, taruṇasālesu nibbattadevatā buddhaparisā, bhaddasāladevarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, "Thus, monks, even in the past the Tathāgata practiced conduct for the benefit of his relatives." Then he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, the deities born among the young Sāla trees were the Buddha’s assembly, and the king of the Bhaddasāla devas was myself."

Bhaddasālajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Bhaddasāla Jātaka, the second.

[466] 3. Samuddavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā

[466] 3. The Commentary on the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka

Kasanti [V 4.0143][P 4.0158] vapanti te janāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa pañca kulasatāni gahetvā niraye patitabhāvaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi aggasāvakesu parisaṃ gahetvā pakkantesu sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto uṇhalohite mukhato nikkhante balavavedanāpīḷito tathāgatassa guṇaṃ anussaritvā “ahameva nava māse tathāgatassa anatthaṃ cintesiṃ, satthu pana mayi pāpacittaṃ nāma natthi, asītimahātherānampi mayi āghāto nāma natthi, mayā katakammena ahameva idāni anātho jāto, satthārāpimhi vissaṭṭho mahātherehipi ñātiseṭṭhena rāhulattherenapi sakyarājakulehipi, gantvā satthāraṃ khamāpessāmī”ti parisāya saññaṃ datvā attānaṃ pañcakena gāhāpetvā rattiṃ rattiṃ gacchanto kosalaraṭṭhaṃ sampāpuṇi. Ānandatthero satthu ārocesi “devadatto kira, bhante, tumhākaṃ khamāpetuṃ āgacchatī”ti. “Ānanda, devadatto mama dassanaṃ na labhissatī”ti.

"Those people plow and sow": this the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning Devadatta's fall into hell after taking five hundred families with him. Indeed, when the chief disciples had departed with the assembly, Devadatta, unable to bear his sorrow, with hot blood gushing from his mouth and overwhelmed by intense pain, reflected on the virtues of the Tathāgata and thought: "For nine months, I alone schemed harm against the Tathāgata, yet the Teacher harbored no ill will toward me. Even the eighty great elders held no grudge against me. By my own deeds, I have now become helpless. I have been abandoned by the Teacher, by the great elders, by the elder Rāhula, the best of my kinsmen, and by the Sakyan royal families. I will go and ask forgiveness from the Teacher." Having given the assembly a signal, he had himself carried on a litter and, traveling night after night, he reached the Kosala country. The elder Ānanda informed the Teacher: "Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta is coming to ask for your forgiveness." The Teacher replied, "Ānanda, Devadatta will not get to see me."

Atha tasmiṃ sāvatthinagaradvāraṃ sampatte puna thero ārocesi, bhagavāpi tatheva avaca. Tassa jetavane pokkharaṇiyā samīpaṃ āgatassa pāpaṃ matthakaṃ pāpuṇi, sarīre ḍāho uppajji, nhatvā pānīyaṃ pivitukāmo hutvā “mañcakato maṃ āvuso otāretha, pānīyaṃ pivissāmī”ti āha. Tassa otāretvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitamattassa cittassāde aladdheyeva mahāpathavī vivaramadāsi. Tāvadeva taṃ avīcito [M 4.0161] aggijālā uṭṭhāya parikkhipitvā gaṇhi. So “pāpakammaṃ me matthakaṃ patta”nti tathāgatassa guṇe anussaritvā –

Then, when he reached the gate of Sāvatthī city, the elder announced it again, and the Blessed One spoke in the same way. As he approached the lotus pond in Jetavana, his evil deed came to a head. A burning sensation arose in his body, and desiring to drink water after bathing, he said, "Friends, lower me from the litter; I wish to drink water." As soon as they lowered him and placed him on the ground, before he could even obtain any mental relief, the great earth split open. Immediately, flames from Avīci hell rose up, surrounded him, and seized him. He, realizing, "My evil deed has come to a head," recollected the virtues of the Tathāgata—

“Imehi aṭṭhīhi tamaggapuggalaṃ, devātidevaṃ naradammasārathiṃ;

Samantacakkhuṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ, pāṇehi buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ upemī”ti. (mi. pa. 4.1.3) –

"With these bones, I go for refuge to that foremost individual, the God beyond gods, the charioteer of mortals to be tamed, the All-Seeing One, marked with a hundred signs of merit; with my very life, I go for refuge to the Buddha."

Imāya gāthāya saraṇe patiṭṭhahanto avīciparāyaṇo ahosi. Tassa pana pañca upaṭṭhākakulasatāni ahesuṃ. Tānipi tappakkhikāni hutvā dasabalaṃ akkositvā avīcimhiyeva nibbattiṃsu. Evaṃ so tāni pañca kulasatāni gaṇhitvā avīcimhi patiṭṭhito.

By this verse, while establishing himself in the refuge, he became destined for Avīci hell. He had five hundred families as his supporters. They too, siding with him, reviled the Ten-Powered One and were reborn in Avīci hell itself. Thus, taking those five hundred families with him, he was established in Avīci hell.

Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto pāpo lābhasakkāragiddhatāya [V 4.0144][P 4.0159] sammāsambuddhe aṭṭhāne kopaṃ bandhitvā anāgatabhayamanoloketvā pañcahi kulasatehi saddhiṃ avīciparāyaṇo jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto lābhasakkāragiddho hutvā anāgatabhayaṃ na olokesi, pubbepi anāgatabhayaṃ anoloketvā paccuppannasukhagiddhena saddhiṃ parisāya mahāvināsaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, the wicked Devadatta, due to his greed for gain and honor, harbored anger toward the Fully Enlightened One without reason, failed to foresee future danger, and has become destined for Avīci, along with five hundred families." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta, greedy for gain and honor, has failed to foresee future danger. In the past too, failing to foresee future danger and siding with one greedy for present pleasure, he brought great ruin upon an assembly." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasito avidūre kulasahassanivāso mahāvaḍḍhakīgāmo ahosi. Tattha vaḍḍhakī “tumhākaṃ mañcaṃ karissāma, pīṭhaṃ karissāma, gehaṃ karissāmā”ti vatvā manussānaṃ hatthato bahuṃ iṇaṃ gahetvā kiñci kātuṃ na sakkhiṃsu. Manussā diṭṭhadiṭṭhe vaḍḍhakī codenti palibuddhanti. Te iṇāyikehi upaddutā sukhaṃ vasituṃ asakkontā “videsaṃ gantvā yattha katthaci vasissāmā”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā rukkhe chinditvā mahatiṃ nāvaṃ bandhitvā nadiṃ otāretvā āharitvā gāmato gāvutaḍḍhayojanamatte ṭhāne ṭhapetvā aḍḍharattasamaye gāmaṃ āgantvā puttadāramādāya nāvaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā nāvaṃ [M 4.0162] āruyha anukkamena mahāsamuddaṃ pavisitvā vātavegena vicarantā samuddamajjhe ekaṃ dīpakaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pana dīpake sayaṃjātasāliucchukadaliambajambupanasatālanāḷikerādīni vividhaphalāni atthi, aññataro pabhinnanāvo puriso paṭhamataraṃ taṃ dīpakaṃ patvā sālibhattaṃ bhuñjamāno ucchuādīni khādamāno thūlasarīro naggo parūḷhakesamassu tasmiṃ dīpake paṭivasati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, not far from Benares there was a large village of carpenters, home to a thousand families. There, the carpenters would say to people, "We will make you a bed, we will make you a stool, we will make you a house," and having taken large advances from people, they were unable to do anything. People would accuse and harass the carpenters whenever they saw them. Harassed by their creditors and unable to live in peace, they thought, "Let us go abroad and settle somewhere." Entering the forest, they cut down trees, built a large boat, launched it into the river, and placed it at a distance of a league or two from the village. At midnight, they came to the village, took their wives and children, went to where the boat was, boarded it, and gradually entered the great ocean. Driven by the wind, they wandered until they reached a small island in the middle of the ocean. On that island, there were various self-grown fruits such as rice, sugarcane, plantains, mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruits, palmyra palms, and coconuts. A certain man whose boat had been wrecked had reached that island earlier. Eating cooked rice and chewing sugarcane and other things, he lived there naked, with a stout body and overgrown hair and beard.

Vaḍḍhakī cintayiṃsu “sace ayaṃ dīpako rakkhasapariggahito bhavissati, sabbepi amhe vināsaṃ pāpuṇissāma, pariggaṇhissāma tāva na”nti. Atha sattaṭṭha purisā sūrā balavanto [P 4.0160] sannaddhapañcāvudhā hutvā otaritvā dīpakaṃ pariggaṇhiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so puriso bhuttapātarāso ucchurasaṃ pivitvā sukhappatto ramaṇīye padese rajatapaṭṭasadise vālukatale sītacchāyāya uttānako nipajjitvā “jambudīpavāsino kasantā vapantā evarūpaṃ sukhaṃ na labhanti, jambudīpato mayhaṃ ayameva dīpako vara”nti gāyamāno udānaṃ udānesi. Atha satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā “so bhikkhave puriso imaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti dassento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The carpenters thought, "If this island is possessed by ogres, we will all be destroyed. Let us first investigate it." Then seven or eight brave, strong men, armed with the five kinds of weapons, disembarked and explored the island. At that moment, that man, having eaten his morning meal and drunk sugarcane juice, feeling happy, lay down on his back in a delightful spot on a sandy ground resembling a silver sheet, in the cool shade. Singing, he uttered an inspired utterance: "The people of Jambudīpa, plowing and sowing, do not obtain such happiness. For me, this island is better than Jambudīpa." Then the Teacher, addressing the monks, said, "Monks, that man uttered this inspired utterance," and he recited the first verse:

25.

25.

“Kasanti vapanti te janā, manujā kammaphalūpajīvino;

Nayimassa dīpakassa bhāgino, jambudīpā idameva no vara”nti.

"Those people plow and sow, humans living on the fruits of their labor; they do not share in the benefits of this island. This indeed is better for us than Jambudīpa."

Tattha [V 4.0145] te janāti te jambudīpavāsino janā. Kammaphalūpajīvinoti nānākammānaṃ phalūpajīvino sattā.

There, 'those people' means the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. 'Living on the fruits of their actions' means beings who live dependent on the results of various deeds.

Atha te dīpakaṃ pariggaṇhantā purisā tassa gītasaddaṃ sutvā “manussasaddo viya suyyati, jānissāma na”nti saddānusārena gantvā taṃ purisaṃ disvā “yakkho bhavissatī”ti bhītatasitā sare sannahiṃsu. Sopi te disvā attano vadhabhayena “nāhaṃ, sāmi, yakkho, purisomhi, jīvitaṃ me dethā”ti yācanto “purisā nāma tumhādisā naggā na hontī”ti vutte punappunaṃ yācitvā manussabhāvaṃ viññāpesi. Te taṃ purisaṃ upasaṅkamitvā sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sutvā tassa tattha āgataniyāmaṃ pucchiṃsu. Sopi sabbaṃ tesaṃ kathetvā “tumhe attano puññasampattiyā idhāgatā[M 4.0163], ayaṃ uttamadīpo, na ettha sahatthena kammaṃ katvā jīvanti, sayaṃjātasālīnañceva ucchuādīnañcettha anto natthīti anukkaṇṭhantā vasathā”ti āha. Idha pana vasantānaṃ amhākaṃ añño paripantho [P 4.0161] natthi, aññaṃ bhayaṃ ettha natthi, ayaṃ pana amanussapariggahito, amanussā tumhākaṃ uccārapassāvaṃ disvā kujjheyyuṃ, tasmā taṃ karontā vālukaṃ viyūhitvā vālukāya paṭicchādeyyātha, ettakaṃ idha bhayaṃ, aññaṃ natthi, niccaṃ appamattā bhaveyyāthāti. Te tattha vāsaṃ upagacchiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pana kulasahasse pañcannaṃ pañcannaṃ kulasatānaṃ jeṭṭhakā dve vaḍḍhakī ahesuṃ. Tesu eko bālo ahosi rasagiddho, eko paṇḍito rasesu anallīno.

Then those men, while exploring the island, heard the sound of his singing and thought, "It sounds like a human voice; let us find out." Following the sound, they saw the man. Frightened and terrified, they prepared their arrows, thinking, "He must be a yakkha!" Seeing them, he feared for his life and pleaded, "Sirs, I am not a yakkha, I am a man. Please grant me my life!" When they said, "Humans are not usually naked like you," he repeatedly begged and convinced them of his human nature. Approaching him, they exchanged pleasantries and asked how he had come there. He told them everything and said, "You have come here due to your own meritorious attainments. This is an excellent island. Here, no one works with their own hands to survive. There is no end to the self-grown rice, sugarcane, and so on. Live here without discontent." "However, for us living here, there is no other obstacle, there is no other danger here. But this place is possessed by non-humans. The non-humans may become angry if they see your urine and excrement. Therefore, when you do so, you should push aside the sand and cover it with sand. That is the only danger here; there is no other. You should always be heedful." They took up residence there. Among those thousand families, there were two carpenters who were the chiefs of five hundred families each. One of them was a fool, greedy for flavors; one was wise, unattached to flavors.

Aparabhāge sabbepi te tattha sukhaṃ vasantā thūlasarīrā hutvā cintayiṃsu “ciraṃ pītā no surā, ucchurasena merayaṃ katvā pivissāmā”ti. Te merayaṃ kāretvā pivitvā madavasena gāyantā naccantā kīḷantā pamattā tattha tattha uccārapassāvaṃ katvā appaṭicchādetvā dīpakaṃ jegucchaṃ paṭikūlaṃ kariṃsu. Devatā “ime amhākaṃ kīḷāmaṇḍalaṃ paṭikūlaṃ karontī”ti kujjhitvā “mahāsamuddaṃ uttarāpetvā dīpakadhovanaṃ karissāmā”ti mantetvā “ayaṃ kāḷapakkho, ajja amhākaṃ samāgamo ca bhinno, ito dāni pannarasame divase puṇṇamīuposathadivase candassuggamanavelāya samuddaṃ ubbattetvā sabbepime ghātessāmā”ti divasaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ antare eko dhammiko devaputto “mā ime mama passantassa nassiṃsū”ti anukampāya tesu sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā gharadvāre sukhakathāya nisinnesu sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito sakaladīpaṃ ekobhāsaṃ katvā uttarāya disāya ākāse ṭhatvā “ambho vaḍḍhakī, devatā tumhākaṃ kuddhā. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne mā vasittha, ito aḍḍhamāsaccayena hi devatā samuddaṃ ubbattetvā [P 4.0162] sabbeva tumhe ghātessanti, ito nikkhamitvā palāyathā”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Later, all of them, living happily there, became stout-bodied and thought, 'We have not drunk spirits for a long time; let us make liquor with sugarcane juice and drink it.' Having had the liquor made and having drunk it, intoxicated, they sang, danced, played, and became heedless. They urinated and defecated here and there without covering it, making the island disgusting and repulsive. The deities, thinking, 'These people are making our playground repulsive,' became angry. They conferred, 'We will make the great ocean swell up and wash the island.' They set the day, saying, 'This is the dark fortnight, and today our assembly is broken. Fifteen days from now, on the full moon observance day, at the time of the moon's rising, we will make the ocean swell up and kill all of them.' Then, among them, a righteous deity, out of compassion, thought, 'May these people not perish before my eyes.' In the evening, after they had eaten their meal and were sitting at their house doors in pleasant conversation, he, adorned with all his ornaments, making the entire island a single radiance, stood in the sky in the northern direction and said, 'Ho, carpenters, the deities are angry with you. Do not live in this place. In half a month, the deities will make the ocean swell up and will kill all of you. Leave this place and flee!' Then he spoke a second verse:

26.

26.

“Tipañcarattūpagatamhi [V 4.0146] cande, vego mahā hehiti sāgarassa;

Uplavissaṃ dīpamimaṃ uḷāraṃ, mā vo vadhī gacchatha leṇamañña”nti.

"When the moon has reached fifteen nights, a great surge of the ocean will occur; it will inundate this splendid island. May it not kill you; go to another refuge."

Tattha [M 4.0164] uplavissanti imaṃ dīpakaṃ uplavanto ajjhottharanto abhibhavissati. Mā vo vadhīti so sāgaravego tumhe mā vadhi.

Here, 'it will inundate' means it will flood this island; flooding, overwhelming, it will overcome it. 'May it not kill you' means may that ocean surge not kill you.

Iti so tesaṃ ovādaṃ datvā attano ṭhānameva gato. Tasmiṃ gate aparo sāhasiko kakkhaḷo devaputto “ime imassa vacanaṃ gahetvā palāyeyyuṃ, ahaṃ nesaṃ gamanaṃ nivāretvā sabbepime mahāvināsaṃ pāpessāmī”ti cintetvā dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito sakaladīpaṃ ekobhāsaṃ karonto āgantvā dakkhiṇāya disāya ākāse ṭhatvā “eko devaputto idhāgato, no”ti pucchitvā “āgato”ti vutte “so vo kiṃ kathesī”ti vatvā “imaṃ nāma, sāmī”ti vutte “so tumhākaṃ idha nivāsaṃ na icchati, dosena katheti, tumhe aññattha agantvā idheva vasathā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, having given them this advice, he went to his own abode. When he had gone, another reckless and harsh deity thought, 'These people might take his word and flee. I will prevent their departure and lead them all to great destruction.' Adorned with divine ornaments, making the entire island a single radiance, he came and stood in the sky in the southern direction. He asked, 'Did a deity come here, or not?' When they said, 'He came,' he asked, 'What did he tell you?' When they replied, 'Such and such, sir,' he said, 'He does not want you to live here; he speaks out of malice. Do not go elsewhere, but live right here.' Then he spoke two verses:

27.

27.

“Na jātuyaṃ sāgaravārivego, uplavissaṃ dīpamimaṃ uḷāraṃ;

Taṃ me nimittehi bahūhi diṭṭhaṃ, mā bhetha kiṃ socatha modathavho.

"Never will the ocean's watery surge inundate this splendid island; this I have seen by many signs. Do not be afraid! Why do you grieve? Rejoice!"

28.

28.

“Pahūtabhakkhaṃ bahuannapānaṃ, pattattha āvāsamimaṃ uḷāraṃ;

Na vo bhayaṃ paṭipassāmi kiñci, āputtaputtehi pamodathavho”ti.

You have obtained this noble dwelling with abundant food and much to eat and drink. I foresee no danger for you at all; rejoice with your children and your grandchildren!

Tattha [P 4.0163] na jātuyanti na jātu ayaṃ. Mā bhethāti mā bhāyittha. Modathavhoti pamoditā pītisomanassajātā hotha. Āputtaputtehīti yāva puttānampi puttehi pamodatha, natthi vo imasmiṃ ṭhāne bhayanti.

Here, 'na jātuyanti' means 'this will indeed not be'. 'Mā bhetha' means 'do not be afraid'. 'Modathavho' means 'be joyful, be filled with joy and happiness'. 'Āputtaputtehi' means 'rejoice even with your children's children; there is no danger for you in this place'.

Evaṃ so imāhi dvīhi gāthāhi te assāsetvā pakkāmi. Tassa pakkantakāle dhammikadevaputtassa vacanaṃ anādiyanto bālavaḍḍhakī “suṇantu me, bhonto, vacana”nti sesavaḍḍhakī āmantetvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, having reassured them with these two verses, he departed. After his departure, the foolish carpenter, not heeding the words of the righteous divine son, addressed the remaining carpenters, saying, 'Sirs, listen to my words,' and spoke the fifth verse:

29.

29.

“Yo [M 4.0165] devoyaṃ dakkhiṇāyaṃ disāyaṃ, khemanti pakkosati tassa saccaṃ;

Na uttaro vedi bhayābhayassa, mā bhetha kiṃ socatha modathavho”ti.

This deva who is in the southern direction, who proclaims 'safety'—his word is true. The northern one does not know of danger and safety. Do not be afraid! Why do you grieve? Rejoice!

Tattha [V 4.0147] dakkhiṇāyanti dakkhiṇāya, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Here, 'dakkhiṇāyanti' means 'in the south,' or this is simply the reading.

Taṃ sutvā rasagiddhā pañcasatā vaḍḍhakī tassa bālassa vacanaṃ ādiyiṃsu. Itaro pana paṇḍitavaḍḍhakī tassa vacanaṃ anādiyanto te vaḍḍhakī āmantetvā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the five hundred carpenters who were greedy for tastes accepted the words of that fool. But the other, the wise carpenter, not heeding his words, addressed those carpenters and spoke four verses:

30.

30.

“Yathā ime vippavadanti yakkhā, eko bhayaṃ saṃsati khemameko;

Tadiṅgha mayhaṃ vacanaṃ suṇātha, khippaṃ lahuṃ mā vinassimha sabbe.

Since these yakkhas contradict each other—one declares danger, another safety—come now, listen to my words, quickly and swiftly, lest we all perish.

31.

31.

“Sabbe samāgamma karoma nāvaṃ, doṇiṃ daḷhaṃ sabbayantūpapannaṃ;

Sace ayaṃ dakkhiṇo saccamāha, moghaṃ paṭikkosati uttaroyaṃ;

Sā ceva no hehiti āpadatthā, imañca dīpaṃ na pariccajema.

Let us all come together and build a boat, a sturdy vessel fully equipped with all gear. If this southerner speaks the truth and the northern one objects in vain, it will be for our benefit in case of calamity, and we will not have to abandon this island.

32.

32.

“Sace ca kho uttaro saccamāha, moghaṃ paṭikkosati dakkhiṇoyaṃ;

Tameva [P 4.0164] nāvaṃ abhiruyha sabbe, evaṃ mayaṃ sotthi taremu pāraṃ.

But if the northern one speaks the truth and this southern one objects in vain, then, having all boarded that very boat, we will thus safely cross to the far shore.

33.

33.

“Na ve sugaṇhaṃ paṭhamena seṭṭhaṃ, kaniṭṭhamāpāthagataṃ gahetvā;

Yo cīdha tacchaṃ paviceyya gaṇhati, sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

One should not easily take the first as best, nor the later statement that has come into range. But whoever here investigates and grasps what is true, that person indeed attains the highest state.

Tattha [M 4.0166] vippavadantīti aññamaññaṃ viruddhaṃ vadanti. Lahunti purimassa atthadīpanaṃ. Doṇinti gambhīraṃ mahānāvaṃ. Sabbayantūpapannanti sabbehi phiyārittādīhi yantehi upapannaṃ. Sā ceva no hehiti āpadatthāti sā ca no nāvā pacchāpi uppannāya āpadāya atthā bhavissati, imañca dīpaṃ na pariccajissāma. Taremūti tarissāma. Na ve sugaṇhanti na ve sukhena gaṇhitabbaṃ. Seṭṭhanti uttamaṃ tathaṃ saccaṃ. Kaniṭṭhanti paṭhamavacanaṃ upādāya pacchimavacanaṃ kaniṭṭhaṃ nāma. Idhāpi “na ve sugaṇha”nti anuvattateva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ambho vaḍḍhakī, yena kenaci paṭhamena vuttavacanaṃ “idameva seṭṭhaṃ tathaṃ sacca”nti sukhaṃ na gaṇhitabbameva, yathā ca taṃ, evaṃ kaniṭṭhaṃ gacchā vuttavacanampi “idameva tathaṃ sacca”nti na gaṇhitabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana sotavisayaṃ āpāthagataṃ hoti, taṃ āpāthagataṃ gahetvā yo idha paṇḍitapuriso purimavacanañca pacchimavacanañca paviceyya vicinitvā tīretvā upaparikkhitvā tacchaṃ gaṇhāti, yaṃ tathaṃ saccaṃ sabhāvabhūtaṃ, tadeva paccakkhaṃ katvā gaṇhāti. Sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhānanti so uttamaṃ ṭhānaṃ upeti adhigacchati vindati labhatīti.

Herein, 'they dispute' (vippavadanti) means they speak in opposition to each other. 'Lahunti' is an elucidation of the meaning of the preceding word. 'A boat' (doṇi) means a large, deep boat. 'Fully equipped with all gear' (sabbayantūpapanna) means equipped with all equipment such as oars and rudders. 'And that will be for our benefit in a calamity' (sā ceva no hehiti āpadatthā) means that this boat of ours will be for our benefit in a calamity that may arise later, and we will not abandon this island. 'We shall cross' (taremū) means we will cross over. 'It is not easily grasped' (na ve sugaṇha) means it is not indeed to be easily accepted. 'The best' (seṭṭha) means the supreme, the factual, the true. 'The lesser' (kaniṭṭha) means the latter statement, taking the first statement as the basis; it is called 'lesser'. Here too, 'it is not easily grasped' continues to apply. This is what is said: 'O carpenters, a statement spoken first by anyone should not be easily accepted as “this alone is the best, the factual, the true”; and just as that, so too a statement spoken later should not be accepted as “this alone is the factual, the true.” But whatever comes within the range of hearing, having grasped what has come within range, the wise person here investigates, discerns, evaluates, and scrutinizes both the former statement and the latter statement and grasps what is factual, what is true, real, and natural, grasping it after having made it directly evident. 'That person indeed attains the highest state' (sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhāna) means that person attains, reaches, finds, and obtains the supreme state.

So [V 4.0148] evañca pana vatvā āha – “ambho, mayaṃ dvinnampi devatānaṃ vacanaṃ karissāma, nāvaṃ tāva sajjeyyāma. Sace paṭhamassa vacanaṃ saccaṃ bhavissati, taṃ nāvaṃ abhiruhitvā palāyissāma, atha itarassa vacanaṃ saccaṃ bhavissati, nāvaṃ ekamante ṭhapetvā idheva vasissāmā”ti. Evaṃ vutte bālavaḍḍhakī “ambho, tvaṃ udakapātiyaṃ [P 4.0165] susumāraṃ passasi, atīva dīghaṃ passasi, paṭhamadevaputto amhesu dosavasena kathesi, pacchimo sineheneva, imaṃ evarūpaṃ varadīpaṃ pahāya kuhiṃ gamissāma, sace pana tvaṃ gantukāmo, tava parisaṃ gaṇhitvā nāvaṃ karohi, amhākaṃ nāvāya kiccaṃ natthī”ti āha. Paṇḍito attano parisaṃ gahetvā nāvaṃ sajjetvā nāvāya sabbūpakaraṇāni āropetvā sapariso nāvāya aṭṭhāsi.

Having spoken thus, he said: 'Sirs, we shall follow the words of both deities; let us first prepare a boat. If the words of the first one prove true, we will board that boat and flee. But if the words of the other prove true, we will set the boat aside and remain right here.' When this was said, the foolish carpenter said, 'Sir, you see a crocodile in a water pot, you see it as extremely long. The first divine son spoke to us out of ill will, but the latter out of affection. Abandoning such an excellent island, where would we go? If you wish to go, take your company and make a boat; we have no need for a boat.' The wise man, taking his company, prepared the boat, loaded all the equipment onto the boat, and stayed on the boat with his followers.

Tato puṇṇamadivase candassa uggamanavelāya samuddato ūmi uttaritvā jāṇukapamāṇā hutvā dīpakaṃ dhovitvā gatā. Paṇḍito samuddassa uttaraṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā nāvaṃ vissajjesi. Bālavaḍḍhakipakkhikāni pañca kulasatāni “samuddato ūmi dīpadhovanatthāya āgatā, ettakameva eta”nti kathentā [M 4.0167] nisīdiṃsu. Tato paṭipāṭiyā kaṭippamāṇā purisappamāṇā tālappamāṇā sattatālappamāṇā sāgaraūmi dīpakampi vuyhamānā āgañchi. Paṇḍito upāyakusalatāya rase alaggo sotthinā gato, bālavaḍḍhakī rasagiddhena anāgatabhayaṃ anolokento pañcahi kulasatehi saddhiṃ vināsaṃ patto.

Then, on the full moon day, at the time of the moon's rising, a wave rose from the ocean, became knee-high, washed over the small island, and receded. The wise man, knowing the ocean was rising, launched the boat. The five hundred families on the foolish carpenter's side, saying, 'A wave has come from the ocean to wash the island, that is all it is,' remained there. Then, in succession, ocean waves came, waist-high, man-high, palm-tree-high, and seven palm-trees-high, sweeping away even the small island. The wise man, through his skill in means, being unattached to tastes, went safely. The foolish carpenter, greedy for tastes and not looking at the future danger, met with destruction along with the five hundred families.

Ito parā sānusāsanī tamatthaṃ dīpayamānā tisso abhisambuddhagāthā honti –

Hereafter, there are three verses of the Fully Enlightened One, being an instruction which illuminates that matter:

34.

34.

“Yathāpi te sāgaravārimajjhe, sakammunā sotthi vahiṃsu vāṇijā;

Anāgatatthaṃ paṭivijjhiyāna, appampi nācceti sa bhūripañño.

Just as those merchants in the midst of the ocean's waters were carried to safety by their own action; having penetrated the meaning of the future, that one of great wisdom does not neglect even a little.

35.

35.

“Bālā ca mohena rasānugiddhā, anāgataṃ appaṭivijjhiyatthaṃ;

Paccuppanne sīdanti atthajāte, samuddamajjhe yathā te manussā.

“But fools, deluded and greedy for tastes, not realizing the future benefit, sink when a present matter arises, like those men in the middle of the ocean.”

36.

36.

“Anāgataṃ [P 4.0166] paṭikayirātha kiccaṃ, ‘mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi’;

Taṃ tādisaṃ paṭikatakiccakāriṃ, na taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhetī”ti.

“One should perform a future task beforehand, thinking, ‘May the task not afflict me at the time for the task.’ For such a one who performs the task beforehand, that task does not afflict them at the time for the task.”

Tattha sakammunāti anāgatabhayaṃ disvā puretaraṃ katena attano kammena. Sotthi vahiṃsūti khemena gamiṃsu. Vāṇijāti samudde vicaraṇabhāvena vaḍḍhakī vuttā. Paṭivijjhiyānāti evaṃ, bhikkhave[V 4.0149], paṭhamataraṃ kattabbaṃ anāgataṃ atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā idhaloke bhūripañño kulaputto appamattakampi attano atthaṃ na acceti nātivattati, na hāpetīti attho. Appaṭivijjhiyatthanti appaṭivijjhitvā atthaṃ, paṭhamameva kattabbaṃ akatvāti attho. Paccuppanneti yadā taṃ anāgataṃ atthajātaṃ uppajjati, tadā tasmiṃ paccuppanne sīdanti, atthe jāte attano patiṭṭhaṃ na labhanti, samudde te bālavaḍḍhakī manussā viya vināsaṃ pāpuṇanti.

Therein, ‘by their own action’ (sakammunā) means by their own deed done beforehand, having seen the future danger. ‘Carried safely’ (sotthi vahiṃsu) means they went in safety. ‘Merchants’ (vāṇijā) refers to the carpenters, because of their traveling on the ocean. ‘Having penetrated’ (paṭivijjhiyāna) means: ‘Monks, having first penetrated a future benefit that should be acted upon, a clansman of broad wisdom in this world does not neglect, overstep, or lose even a small benefit of his own’—this is the meaning. ‘Not penetrating the benefit’ (appaṭivijjhiyatthaṃ) means not having penetrated the benefit, not having done first what ought to be done—this is the meaning. ‘In the present’ (paccuppanne) means when that future matter arises, then they sink in that present situation; when the matter has arisen, they do not find a footing for themselves, and like those foolish carpenters in the ocean, they come to ruin.

Anāgatanti [M 4.0168] bhikkhave, paṇḍitapuriso anāgataṃ paṭhamataraṃ kattabbakiccaṃ samparāyikaṃ vā diṭṭhadhammikaṃ vā paṭikayirātha, puretarameva kareyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi, pure kattabbañhi pure akayiramānaṃ pacchā paccuppannabhāvappattaṃ attano kiccakāle kāyacittābādhena byadheti, taṃ maṃ mā byadhesīti paṭhamameva naṃ paṇḍito kareyya. Taṃ tādisanti yathā paṇḍitaṃ purisaṃ. Paṭikatakiccakārinti paṭikacceva kattabbakiccakārinaṃ. Taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāleti anāgataṃ kiccaṃ kayiramānaṃ pacchā paccuppannabhāvappattaṃ attano kiccakāle kāyacittābādhakāle tādisaṃ purimaṃ na byadheti na bādhati. Kasmā? Pureyeva katattāti.

‘Future’ (anāgataṃ) means, monks, a wise person should perform a future task that should be done first, whether it relates to the next life or to the present life; he should do it beforehand. For what reason? ‘May the task not afflict me at the time for the task.’ For a task that should be done beforehand, if not done beforehand, it later reaches a present state and afflicts one with bodily and mental suffering at the time for the task. Thinking, ‘May that not afflict me,’ a wise person should do it first. ‘Such a one’ (taṃ tādisaṃ) means a person like that wise man. ‘One who performs the task beforehand’ (paṭikatakiccakāriṃ) means one who does the task that ought to be done beforehand. ‘That task at the time for the task’ (taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle) means a future task, which, having been performed, when it later reaches a present state at the time for the task—a time of bodily and mental affliction—does not afflict or harm such a person as before. Why? Because it was done beforehand.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto paccuppannasukhe laggo anāgatabhayaṃ anoloketvā sapariso vināsaṃ patto”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bālavaḍḍhakī devadatto ahosi, dakkhiṇadisāya ṭhito adhammikadevaputto kokāliko, uttaradisāya ṭhito dhammikadevaputto sāriputto, paṇḍitavaḍḍhakī pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Devadatta, attached to present pleasure and not looking to the future danger, met with destruction along with his company.” Then he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the foolish carpenter was Devadatta, the unrighteous son of a deva standing in the southern direction was Kokālika, the righteous son of a deva standing in the northern direction was Sāriputta, and I myself was the wise carpenter.”

Samuddavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Explanation of the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka, the Third.

[467] 4. Kāmajātakavaṇṇanā

[467] 4. The Explanation of the Kāma Jātaka.

Kāmaṃ [P 4.0167] kāmayamānassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī brāhmaṇo aciravatītīre khettakaraṇatthāya araññaṃ koṭesi. Satthā tassa upanissayaṃ disvā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisanto maggā okkamma tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ karosi brāhmaṇā”ti vatvā “khettaṭṭhānaṃ koṭāpemi bho, gotamā”ti vutte “sādhu, brāhmaṇa, kammaṃ karohī”ti vatvā agamāsi. Eteneva upāyena chinnarukkhe hāretvā khettassa sodhanakāle kasanakāle kedārabandhanakāle vapanakāleti punappunaṃ gantvā tena saddhiṃ [V 4.0150] paṭisanthāramakāsi. Vapanadivase pana so brāhmaṇo “ajja, bho gotama, mayhaṃ vappamaṅgalaṃ, ahaṃ imasmiṃ sasse nipphanne buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa [M 4.0169] mahādānaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Satthā tuṇhībhāvena adhivāsetvā pakkāmi. Punekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇo sassaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi. Satthāpi tattha gantvā “kiṃ karosi brāhmaṇā”ti pucchitvā “sassaṃ olokemi bho gotamā”ti vutte “sādhu brāhmaṇā”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tadā brāhmaṇo cintesi “samaṇo gotamo abhiṇhaṃ āgacchati, nissaṃsayaṃ bhattena atthiko, dassāmahaṃ tassa bhatta”nti. Tassevaṃ cintetvā gehaṃ gatadivase satthāpi tattha agamāsi. Atha brāhmaṇassa ativiya vissāso ahosi. Aparabhāge pariṇate sasse “sve khettaṃ lāyissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā nipanne brāhmaṇe aciravatiyā upari sabbarattiṃ karakavassaṃ vassi. Mahogho āgantvā ekanāḷimattampi anavasesaṃ katvā sabbaṃ sassaṃ samuddaṃ pavesesi. Brāhmaṇo oghamhi patite sassavināsaṃ oloketvā sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ nāhosi, balavasokābhibhūto hatthena uraṃ paharitvā paridevamāno rodanto nipajji.

This story, beginning with ‘For one desiring desires,’ the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, in reference to a certain brahmin. It is said that a certain brahmin living in Sāvatthī was clearing a forest on the bank of the Aciravatī River for the purpose of making a field. The Teacher, seeing his spiritual potential, while entering Sāvatthī for alms, turned aside from the path, exchanged pleasantries with him, and asked, ‘What are you doing, brahmin?’ When he replied, ‘Venerable Gotama, I am clearing a place for a field,’ the Teacher said, ‘Good, brahmin, do your work,’ and departed. In this same way, after the trees were removed, at the time of clearing the field, plowing, making the bunds, and sowing, he went again and again and exchanged pleasantries with him. On the day of sowing, the brahmin said, ‘Today, Venerable Gotama, is my sowing festival. When this crop is produced, I will give a great donation to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha.’ The Teacher consented by silence and departed. On another day, the brahmin stood inspecting his crop. The Teacher also went there and asked, ‘What are you doing, brahmin?’ When he said, ‘Venerable Gotama, I am inspecting the crop,’ the Teacher said, ‘Good, brahmin,’ and departed. Then the brahmin thought, ‘The ascetic Gotama comes frequently; undoubtedly he is in need of food. I will give him food.’ On the day he went home after thinking thus, the Teacher also went there. Then the brahmin’s trust became very strong. Later, when the crop was ripe, the brahmin decided, ‘Tomorrow I will harvest the field,’ and went to sleep. That night, a hailstorm rained over the upper Aciravatī throughout the night. A great flood came and, leaving not even a single nāḷi-measure, swept the entire crop into the sea. The brahmin, seeing the destruction of his crop by the flood, could not maintain his composure; overcome by intense grief, he struck his chest with his hands, and lay down lamenting and weeping.

Satthā paccūsasamaye sokābhibhūtaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā “brāhmaṇassāvassayo bhavissāmī”ti punadivase sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhū vihāraṃ pesetvā pacchāsamaṇena saddhiṃ tassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Brāhmaṇo satthu āgatabhāvaṃ [P 4.0168] sutvā “paṭisanthāratthāya me sahāyo āgato bhavissatī”ti paṭiladdhassāso āsanaṃ paññapesi. Satthā pavisitvā paññattāsane nisīditvā “brāhmaṇa, kasmā tvaṃ dummanosi, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Bho gotama, aciravatītīre mayā rukkhacchedanato paṭṭhāya kataṃ kammaṃ tumhe jānātha, ahaṃ “imasmiṃ sasse nipphanne tumhākaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī”ti vicarāmi, idāni me sabbaṃ taṃ sassaṃ mahogho samuddameva pavesesi, kiñci avasiṭṭhaṃ natthi, sakaṭasatamattaṃ dhaññaṃ vinaṭṭhaṃ, tena me mahāsoko uppannoti. “Kiṃ pana, brāhmaṇa, socantassa naṭṭhaṃ punāgacchatī”ti. “No hetaṃ bho gotamā”ti. “Evaṃ sante kasmā socasi, imesaṃ sattānaṃ dhanadhaññaṃ nāma uppajjanakāle uppajjati, nassanakāle nassati, kiñci saṅkhāragataṃ anassanadhammaṃ nāma natthi, mā cintayī”ti. Iti naṃ satthā samassāsetvā tassa sappāyadhammaṃ desento kāmasuttaṃ (su. ni. 772 ādayo) kathesi. Suttapariyosāne [M 4.0170] socanto brāhmaṇo sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthā taṃ nissokaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ agamāsi. “Satthā asukaṃ nāma brāhmaṇaṃ sokasallasamappitaṃ nissokaṃ katvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesī”ti sakalanagaraṃ aññāsi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, dasabalo brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ mittaṃ katvā vissāsiko hutvā upāyeneva tassa sokasallasamappitassa dhammaṃ desetvā taṃ [V 4.0151] nissokaṃ katvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ etaṃ nissokamakāsi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

At dawn, the Teacher, seeing the brahmin overwhelmed by sorrow, thought, 'I will be the brahmin's refuge.' The following day, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his alms round, he sent the monks back to the monastery and went to the brahmin's door with an attendant monk. The brahmin, hearing of the Teacher's arrival, regained his composure, thinking, 'My friend must have come to greet me,' and prepared a seat. The Teacher entered, sat on the prepared seat, and asked, 'Brahmin, why are you distressed? What is your discomfort?' 'Venerable Gotama, you know the work I have done since I started cutting trees on the banks of the Aciravatī. I have been going about thinking, "When this crop is produced, I will give a gift to you." But now, a great flood has swept all that crop into the sea. Nothing remains; about a hundred cartloads of grain have been destroyed. Because of that, great sorrow has arisen in me.' 'But, brahmin, does what is lost return to one who grieves?' 'No, Venerable Gotama.' 'If that is so, why do you grieve? For these beings, wealth and grain arise when it is time to arise and perish when it is time to perish. There is no conditioned thing that is of a nature not to perish. Do not worry.' Thus consoling him, the Teacher, preaching the Dhamma suitable for him, taught the Kāma Sutta. At the end of the discourse, the grieving brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, having freed him from sorrow, rose from his seat and returned to the monastery. The entire city came to know: 'The Teacher has freed a certain brahmin, who was pierced by the dart of sorrow, from sorrow and established him in the fruit of stream-entry.' In the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: 'Friends, the Ten-Powered One befriended the brahmin, and having gained his trust, by skillful means he taught the Dhamma to him who was pierced by the dart of sorrow, freeing him from sorrow and establishing him in the fruit of stream-entry.' When the Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' and they told him, 'For this one,' he said, 'Not only now, monks; in the past too, I freed him from sorrow,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadattassa rañño dve puttā ahesuṃ. So jeṭṭhakassa uparajjaṃ adāsi, kaniṭṭhassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ. Aparabhāge brahmadatte kālakate amaccā jeṭṭhakassa abhisekaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. So “na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, kaniṭṭhassa me dethā”ti vatvā punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi paṭikkhipitvā kaniṭṭhassa abhiseke kate “na me issariyenattho”ti uparajjādīnipi na icchi. “Tena hi sādūni bhojanāni bhuñjanto idheva vasāhī”ti vuttepi “na me imasmiṃ nagare kiccaṃ atthī”ti bārāṇasito [P 4.0169] nikkhamitvā paccantaṃ gantvā ekaṃ seṭṭhikulaṃ nissāya sahatthena kammaṃ karonto vasi. Te aparabhāge tassa rājakumārabhāvaṃ ñatvā kammaṃ kātuṃ nādaṃsu, kumāraparihāreneva taṃ parihariṃsu. Aparabhāge rājakammikā khettappamāṇaggahaṇatthāya taṃ gāmaṃ agamaṃsu. Seṭṭhi rājakumāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “sāmi, mayaṃ tumhe posema, kaniṭṭhabhātikassa paṇṇaṃ pesetvā amhākaṃ baliṃ hārethā”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “ahaṃ asukaseṭṭhikulaṃ nāma upanissāya vasāmi, maṃ nissāya etesaṃ baliṃ vissajjehī”ti paṇṇaṃ pesesi. Rājā “sādhū”ti vatvā tathā kāresi.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta had two sons. He gave the eldest the viceregency and the youngest the position of commander of the army. Later, when King Brahmadatta passed away, the ministers began the preparations for the eldest son's consecration. But he said, 'I have no need for the kingdom; give the kingship to my younger brother.' Though he was repeatedly urged, he refused. When the younger brother had been consecrated, he said, 'I have no need for power,' and did not even desire the viceregency or other such positions. When they said, 'Then at least stay here and enjoy delicious food,' he replied, 'I have no business in this city,' and left Bārāṇasī for a border region. There, he took up residence with a merchant's family and lived by working with his own hands. Later, when they learned of his status as a prince, they no longer allowed him to work, but attended to him with the care due to a prince. Sometime later, royal officials came to that village to take measurements of the fields. The merchant approached the prince and said, 'Lord, we support you. Please send a letter to your younger brother and have our tax remitted.' The prince agreed and sent a letter saying, 'I am staying in dependence on a certain merchant's family; on my account, remit their tax.' The king said, 'Very well,' and did so.

Atha naṃ sakalagāmavāsinopi janapadavāsinopi upasaṅkamitvā “mayaṃ tumhākaññeva baliṃ dassāma, amhākampi suṅkaṃ vissajjāpehī”ti āhaṃsu. So tesampi atthāya paṇṇaṃ pesetvā vissajjāpesi. Tato [M 4.0171] paṭṭhāya te tasseva baliṃ adaṃsu. Athassa mahālābhasakkāro ahosi, tena saddhiññevassa taṇhāpi mahatī jātā. So aparabhāgepi sabbaṃ janapadaṃ yāci, upaḍḍharajjaṃ yāci, kaniṭṭhopi tassa adāsiyeva. So taṇhāya vaḍḍhamānāya upaḍḍharajjenapi asantuṭṭho “rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti janapadaparivuto taṃ nagaraṃ gantvā bahinagare ṭhatvā “rajjaṃ vā me detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti kaniṭṭhassa paṇṇaṃ pahiṇi. Kaniṭṭho cintesi “ayaṃ bālo pubbe rajjampi uparajjādīnipi paṭikkhipitvā idāni ‘yuddhena gaṇhāmī’ti vadati, sace kho panāhaṃ imaṃ yuddhena māressāmi, garahā me bhavissati, kiṃ me rajjenā”ti. Athassa “alaṃ yuddhena, rajjaṃ gaṇhatū”ti pesesi. So rajjaṃ gaṇhitvā kaniṭṭhassa uparajjaṃ datvā tato paṭṭhāya rajjaṃ kārento taṇhāvasiko hutvā ekena rajjena asantuṭṭho dve tīṇi rajjāni patthetvā [P 4.0170] taṇhāya koṭiṃ nāddasa.

Then all the villagers and the country folk approached him and said, 'We will give tribute to you alone; please have our taxes remitted as well.' For their sake, he sent a letter and had them remitted. From then on, they gave tribute to him alone. Then great gain and honor came to him, and along with it, great craving arose in him. Later, he asked for the entire country, then he asked for half the kingdom, and his younger brother gave it to him. But as his craving grew, he was not satisfied even with half the kingdom and thought, 'I will seize the kingdom.' Surrounded by the country folk, he went to that city and, staying outside the city, sent a letter to his younger brother: 'Either give me the kingdom or give me battle.' The younger brother reflected, 'This fool previously refused the kingdom and the viceregency, and now he says, "I will take it by battle." If I were to kill him in battle, I would be censured. What use is the kingdom to me?' Then he sent a message, saying, 'Enough of battle; let him take the kingdom.' Having taken the kingdom, he gave the viceregency to his younger brother. From then on, while ruling the kingdom, he was a slave to craving. Unsatisfied with one kingdom, he desired two or three kingdoms, and he never saw an end to his craving.

Tadā [V 4.0152] sakko devarājā “ke nu kho loke mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti, ke dānādīni puññāni karonti, ke taṇhāvasikā”ti olokento tassa taṇhāvasikabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ bālo bārāṇasirajjenapi na tussati, ahaṃ sikkhāpessāmi na”nti māṇavakavesena rājadvāre ṭhatvā “eko upāyakusalo māṇavo dvāre ṭhito”ti ārocāpetvā “pavisatū”ti vutte pavisitvā rājānaṃ jayāpetvā “kiṃkāraṇā āgatosī”ti vutte “mahārāja tumhākaṃ kiñci vattabbaṃ atthi, raho paccāsīsāmī”ti āha. Sakkānubhāvena tāvadeva manussā paṭikkamiṃsu. Atha naṃ māṇavo “ahaṃ, mahārāja, phītāni ākiṇṇamanussāni sampannabalavāhanāni tīṇi nagarāni passāmi, ahaṃ te attano ānubhāvena tesu rajjaṃ gahetvā dassāmi, papañcaṃ akatvā sīghaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha.
