So taṇhāvasiko rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sakkānubhāvena “ko vā tvaṃ, kuto vā āgato, kiṃ vā te laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti na pucchi. Sopi ettakaṃ vatvā tāvatiṃsabhavanameva agamāsi.

At that time Sakka, king of the gods, looking about to see, “Who in the world attends to their parents? Who performs meritorious deeds such as giving? Who are slaves to craving?” and perceiving that this king was a slave to craving, he thought: “This fool is not satisfied even with the kingdom of Bārāᅇasī; I shall teach him a lesson.” Assuming the guise of a young man, he stood at the palace gate and had it announced: ‐A young man skilled in expedients is standing at the gate.” When told to enter, he went in, wished the king victory, and when asked, “For what reason have you come?” he replied, “Great king, I have something to tell you; I wish for a private audience.” By Sakka’s power, the people immediately withdrew. Then the young man said to him, “Great king, I see three prosperous cities, teeming with people and endowed with powerful armies and vehicles. By my own power, I will seize the kingdoms in them and give them to you. Without delay, it is best to go quickly.” The king, being a slave to craving, agreed, saying “Very well,” and by Sakka’s power, he did not ask, “Who are you, where have you come from, or what should you receive in return?” Having said this much, Sakka went to the Tāvatiᅇsa heaven.

Rājā amacce pakkosāpetvā “eko māṇavo ‘amhākaṃ tīṇi rajjāni gahetvā dassāmī’ti āha, taṃ pakkosatha, nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā [M 4.0172] balakāyaṃ sannipātāpetha, papañcaṃ akatvā tīṇi rajjāni gaṇhissāmī”ti vatvā “kiṃ pana te, mahārāja, tassa māṇavassa sakkāro vā kato, nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ vā pucchita”nti vutte “neva sakkāraṃ akāsiṃ, na nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ pucchiṃ, gacchatha naṃ upadhārethā”ti āha. Upadhārentā naṃ adisvā “mahārāja, sakalanagare māṇavaṃ na passāmā”ti ārocesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā rājā domanassajāto “tīsu nagaresu rajjaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, mahantenamhi yasena parihīno, ‘neva me paribbayaṃ adāsi, na ca pucchi nivāsaṭṭhāna’nti mayhaṃ kujjhitvā māṇavo [P 4.0171] anāgato bhavissatī”ti punappunaṃ cintesi. Athassa taṇhāvasikassa sarīre ḍāho uppajji, sarīre pariḍayhante udaraṃ khobhetvā lohitapakkhandikā udapādi. Ekaṃ bhājanaṃ pavisati, ekaṃ nikkhamati, vejjā tikicchituṃ na sakkonti, rājā kilamati. Athassa byādhitabhāvo sakalanagare pākaṭo ahosi.

The king summoned his ministers and said, ‐A young man has said, ‘I will seize three kingdoms and give them to us.’ Summon him, have the drum beaten throughout the city, and assemble the army. Without delay, I will seize the three kingdoms.” When they asked, “But, great king, was any honor shown to that young man, or was his dwelling place asked?” he replied, ‐I showed him no honor, nor did I ask his dwelling place. Go and find him.” Searching for him but not finding him, they reported, “Great king, we do not see the young man anywhere in the entire city.” Hearing this, the king became distressed, thinking repeatedly, “The rule over three cities is lost; I am deprived of great glory. Thinking, ‘He gave me no reward, nor did he ask my dwelling place,’ the young man has become angry with me and will not return.” Then, for him who was a slave to craving, a burning fever arose in his body. As his body burned, his stomach was agitated, and a bloody flux arose. One vessel was brought in as another was taken out. The physicians could not cure him, and the king grew weary. Then his illness became known throughout the entire city.

Tadā bodhisatto takkasilato sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasinagare mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ āgato taṃ rañño pavattiṃ sutvā “ahaṃ tikicchissāmī”ti rājadvāraṃ gantvā “eko kira taruṇamāṇavo tumhe tikicchituṃ āgato”ti ārocāpesi. Rājā “mahantamahantā disāpāmokkhavejjāpi maṃ tikicchituṃ na sakkonti, kiṃ taruṇamāṇavo sakkhissati, paribbayaṃ datvā vissajjetha na”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā māṇavo “mayhaṃ vejjakammena vetanaṃ natthi, ahaṃ tikicchāmi, kevalaṃ bhesajjamūlamattaṃ detū”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā [V 4.0153] rājā “sādhū”ti pakkosāpesi. Māṇavo rājānaṃ vanditvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ahaṃ te tikicchāmi, apica kho pana me rogassa samuṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhāhī”ti āha. Rājā harāyamāno “kiṃ te samuṭṭhānena, bhesajjaṃ eva karohī”ti āha. Mahārāja, vejjā nāma “ayaṃ byādhi imaṃ nissāya samuṭṭhito”ti ñatvā anucchavikaṃ bhesajjaṃ karontīti. Rājā “sādhu tātā”ti samuṭṭhānaṃ kathento “ekena māṇavena āgantvā tīsu nagaresu rajjaṃ gahetvā dassāmī”tiādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ kathetvā “iti me tāta, taṇhaṃ nissāya byādhi uppanno, sace tikicchituṃ sakkosi, tikicchāhī”ti āha. Kiṃ pana mahārāja, socanāya tāni nagarāni sakkā laddhunti? “Na sakkā tātā”ti. “Evaṃ sante kasmā socasi, mahārāja, sabbameva hi saviññāṇakāviññāṇakavatthuṃ [M 4.0173] attano kāyaṃ ādiṃ katvā pahāya gamanīyaṃ[P 4.0172], catūsu nagaresu rajjaṃ gahetvāpi tvaṃ ekappahāreneva na catasso bhattapātiyo bhuñjissasi, na catūsu sayanesu sayissasi, na cattāri vatthayugāni acchādessasi, taṇhāvasikena nāma bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, ayañhi taṇhā nāma vaḍḍhamānā catūhi apāyehi muccituṃ na detīti.

At that time the Bodhisatta, having learned all the arts at Takkasilā, had come to his parents in the city of Bārāᅇasī. Hearing of the king’s condition, he thought, ‐I will treat him,” and went to the king’s gate, having it announced, ‐A certain young man has come to treat you.” The king said, ‐Even the greatest world-renowned physicians cannot cure me. What can a young man do? Give him a payment and send him away.” Hearing this, the young man said, ‐There is no fee for my medical service. I will provide the treatment; let the king provide only the cost of the medicine.” Hearing this, the king said, ‐Very well,” and had him summoned. The young man paid homage to the king and said, ‐Do not fear, great king, I will treat you. However, you must tell me the origin of the illness.” The king, being ashamed, said, ‐What concern is the origin to you? Just prepare the medicine.” ‐Great king, physicians, knowing ‘this illness has arisen from this cause,’ prepare a suitable remedy.” The king said, ‐Very well, my dear,” and relating the origin, he told him everything, beginning with, ‐A young man came and said, ‘I will seize the kingdoms in three cities and give them to you.’” He concluded, ‐Thus, my dear, my illness has arisen from craving. If you are able to cure it, then do so.” ‐But, great king, can those cities be obtained by sorrowing?” ‐They cannot, my dear.” ‐That being so, why do you sorrow, great king? For every single thing, both animate and inanimate, beginning with one’s own body, must be left behind. Even if you were to seize the kingdoms in four cities, you would not eat from four bowls of rice at a single time, nor sleep on four beds, nor wear four pairs of garments. It is not right to be a slave to craving, for this craving, as it grows, does not allow one to be freed from the four states of misery.”

Iti naṃ mahāsatto ovaditvā athassa dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Thus the Great Being, having advised him and wishing to teach him the Dhamma, uttered these verses:

37.

37.

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa ce taṃ samijjhati;

Addhā pītimano hoti, laddhā macco yadicchati.

For one who desires sensual pleasures, should that be fulfilled for him, he surely becomes joyful in mind, a mortal having obtained what he wished.

38.

38.

“Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa ce taṃ samijjhati;

Tato naṃ aparaṃ kāme, ghamme taṇhaṃva vindati.

For one who desires sensual pleasures, should that be fulfilled for him, then another desire finds him, like thirst in the heat.

39.

39.

“Gavaṃva siṅgino siṅgaṃ, vaḍḍhamānassa vaḍḍhati;

Evaṃ mandassa posassa, bālassa avijānato;

Bhiyyo taṇhā pipāsā ca, vaḍḍhamānassa vaḍḍhati.

Just as the horn of a horned bull grows as the bull grows, so for a dull, foolish person without understanding, craving and thirst grow ever more as he grows.

40.

40.

“Pathabyā sāliyavakaṃ, gavāssaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Datvā ca nālamekassa, iti vidvā samaṃ care.

The earth with its rice and barley, cattle and horses, servants and followers—giving all this is not enough for one person. Knowing this, the wise one should live with equanimity.

41.

41.

“Rājā pasayha pathaviṃ vijitvā, sasāgarantaṃ mahimāvasanto;

Oraṃ samuddassa atittarūpo, pāraṃ samuddassapi patthayetha.

A king, having forcibly conquered the earth and ruling over it to the ocean’s shore, unsatisfied with this side of the sea, would still long for the other side of the sea.

42.

42.

“Yāva [V 4.0154] anussaraṃ kāme, manasā titti nājjhagā;

Tato nivattā paṭikkamma disvā, te ve sutittā ye paññāya tittā.

While one is recollecting sensual pleasures, one does not find satisfaction of mind. Having turned away and withdrawn from them, having seen [the danger], they are indeed well-satisfied who are satisfied by wisdom.

43.

43.

“Paññāya tittinaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, na so kāmehi tappati;

Paññāya tittaṃ purisaṃ, taṇhā na kurute vasaṃ.

Of all satisfactions, that of wisdom is supreme; such a one is not tormented by sensual pleasures. Craving does not bring under its power a person satisfied by wisdom.

44.

44.

“Apacinetheva [M 4.0174] kāmānaṃ, appicchassa alolupo;

Samuddamatto puriso, na so kāmehi tappati.

One should indeed discard sensual pleasures, being of few wants and not greedy. A person vast as the ocean is not tormented by sensual pleasures.

45.

45.

“Rathakārova cammassa, parikantaṃ upāhanaṃ;

Yaṃ [P 4.0173] yaṃ cajati kāmānaṃ, taṃ taṃ sampajjate sukhaṃ;

Sabbañce sukhamiccheyya, sabbe kāme pariccaje”ti.

Just like a leather worker cutting leather for a shoe; whatever portion of sensual pleasures one gives up, to that extent one attains happiness. If one should desire complete happiness, one should renounce all sensual pleasures.

Tattha kāmanti vatthukāmampi kilesakāmampi. Kāmayamānassāti patthayamānassa. Tassa ce taṃ samijjhatīti tassa puggalassa taṃ kāmitavatthu samijjhati ce, nipphajjati ceti attho. Tato naṃ aparaṃ kāmeti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ. Aparanti parabhāgadīpanaṃ. Kāmeti upayogabahuvacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa taṃ kāmitavatthu samijjhati, tasmiṃ samiddhe tato paraṃ so puggalo kāmayamāno yathā nāma ghamme gimhakāle vātātapena kilanto taṇhaṃ vindati, pānīyapipāsaṃ paṭilabhati, evaṃ bhiyyo kāmataṇhāsaṅkhāte kāme vindati paṭilabhati, rūpataṇhādikā taṇhā cassa vaḍḍhatiyevāti. Gavaṃvāti gorūpassa viya. Siṅginoti matthakaṃ padāletvā uṭṭhitasiṅgassa. Mandassāti mandapaññassa. Bālassāti bāladhamme yuttassa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā vacchakassa vaḍḍhantassa sarīreneva saddhiṃ siṅgaṃ vaḍḍhati, evaṃ andhabālassapi appattakāmataṇhā ca pattakāmapipāsā ca aparāparaṃ vaḍḍhatīti.

Here, 'sensual pleasures' (kāmaṃ) refers to both objective sensual pleasures and defilement-based sensual pleasures. 'Desiring them' means longing for them. 'If that succeeds for him' means if that desired object is attained or accomplished by that person. In the phrase 'then he [desires] more' (tato naṃ aparaṃ kāme), 'naṃ' is a mere particle; 'aparaṃ' indicates the subsequent part; 'kāme' is the accusative plural. This is what is said: If a person desiring sensual pleasures attains that desired object, then, having obtained it, that person still desiring—just as one exhausted by the heat and wind in the hot summer finds thirst and obtains a craving for water—so even more does he find and obtain the sensual pleasures known as craving for sensual pleasures, and his craving for forms and so on only increases. 'Like an ox' refers to a bovine. 'Growing horns' refers to one whose horns have emerged, having split through the head. 'Of a fool' means of one with weak wisdom. 'Of a deluded one' means of one engaged in foolish things. This is what is said: Just as for a growing calf, the horns increase along with its body, so too for the blind fool, both the craving for unobtained sensual pleasures and the thirst for obtained sensual pleasures grow again and again.

Sāliyavakanti sālikhettayavakhettaṃ. Etena sāliyavādikaṃ sabbaṃ dhaññaṃ dasseti, dutiyapadena sabbaṃ dvipadacatuppadaṃ dasseti. Paṭhamapadena vā sabbaṃ aviññāṇakaṃ, itarena saviññāṇakaṃ. Datvā cāti datvāpi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tiṭṭhantu tīṇi rajjāni, sace so māṇavo aññaṃ vā sakalampi pathaviṃ saviññāṇakāviññāṇakaratanapūraṃ kassaci datvā gaccheyya, idampi ettakaṃ vatthu ekasseva apariyantaṃ, evaṃ duppūrā esā taṇhā nāma. Iti vidvā samaṃ careti evaṃ jānanto puriso taṇhāvasiko ahutvā kāyasamācārādīni pūrento careyya.

'Rice and barley' means the rice field and the barley field. By this, all grains are indicated; by the second phrase, all bipeds and quadrupeds are shown. Alternatively, by the first phrase, all non-sentient things are indicated; by the other, all sentient things. 'And having given' means even after giving. This is what is said: Let alone the three kingdoms, if that young man were to give away even the entire earth filled with sentient and non-sentient treasures to someone and then depart, even this much substance would be insufficient for one person alone; thus this craving is indeed hard to fill. 'Knowing thus, one should live equanimously' means knowing this, a person, not being under the power of craving, should live fulfilling right bodily conduct and so forth.

Oranti [V 4.0155][M 4.0175] orimakoṭṭhāsaṃ patvā tena atittarūpo puna samuddapārampi patthayetha. Evaṃ taṇhāvasikasattā nāma duppūrāti dasseti. Yāvāti aniyāmitaparicchedo. Anussaranti anussaranto. Nājjhagāti na vindati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, puriso apariyantepi kāme [P 4.0174] manasā anussaranto tittiṃ na vindati, pattukāmova hoti, evaṃ kāmesu sattānaṃ taṇhā vaḍḍhateva. Tato nivattāti tato pana vatthukāmakilesakāmato cittena nivattitvā kāyena paṭikkamma ñāṇena ādīnavaṃ disvā ye paññāya tittā paripuṇṇā, te tittā nāma.

'The shore' means having reached the near shore, and being unsatisfied with that, one would again long for the far shore of the ocean. This shows that beings under the power of craving are insatiable. 'Yāva' indicates an indefinite limit. 'Recollecting' (anussaraṃ) means while recollecting. 'Did not find' (nājjhagā) means he does not find. This is what is said: O Great King, even while recollecting limitless sensual pleasures with the mind, a person does not find satisfaction; he remains one who simply desires to obtain more. Thus, for beings attached to sensual pleasures, craving only increases. 'Turned away from that' means: having turned away with the mind from objective and defilement-based sensual pleasures, having withdrawn with the body, and having seen the danger with knowledge—those who are satisfied and fulfilled by wisdom, they are called 'truly satisfied'.

Paññāya tittinaṃ seṭṭhanti paññāya tittīnaṃ ayaṃ paripuṇṇaseṭṭho, ayameva vā pāṭho. Na so kāmehi tappatīti “na hī”tipi pāṭho. Yasmā paññāya titto puriso kāmehi na pariḍayhatīti attho. Na kurute vasanti tādisañhi purisaṃ taṇhā vase vattetuṃ na sakkoti, sveva pana taṇhāya ādīnavaṃ disvā sarabhaṅgamāṇavo viya ca aḍḍhamāsakarājā viya ca taṇhāvase na pavattatīti attho. Apacinethevāti viddhaṃsetheva. Samuddamattoti mahatiyā paññāya samannāgatattā samuddappamāṇo. So mahantena aggināpi samuddo viya kilesakāmehi na tappati na ḍayhati.

'Of satisfactions, that of wisdom is supreme' means: this is the supreme fulfillment among satisfactions of wisdom; this is also a reading. 'He is not tormented by sensual pleasures'—there is also a reading 'na hī' (for 'not'). The meaning is that a person satisfied by wisdom is not burned by sensual pleasures. 'Does not bring under its power' means: craving is not able to bring such a person under its power; rather, having seen the danger in craving, he does not proceed under its power, like the youth Sarabhaṅga or King Aḍḍhamāsaka. 'One should indeed diminish' means: one should indeed destroy them. 'Measured by the ocean' means: one who, being endowed with great wisdom, is like the ocean in extent. Just as the ocean is not tormented or burned even by a great fire, so too, such a person is not tormented or burned by defilement-based sensual pleasures.

Rathakāroti cammakāro. Parikantanti parikantanto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā cammakāro upāhanaṃ parikantanto yaṃ yaṃ cammassa agayhūpagaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ cajitvā upāhanaṃ katvā upāhanamūlaṃ labhitvā sukhito hoti, evameva paṇḍito cammakārasatthasadisāya paññāya kantanto yaṃ yaṃ odhiṃ kāmānaṃ cajati, tena tenassa kāmodhinā rahitaṃ taṃ taṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammañca sukhaṃ sampajjati vigatadarathaṃ, sace pana sabbampi kāyakammādisukhaṃ vigatapariḷāhameva iccheyya, kasiṇaṃ bhāvetvā jhānaṃ nibbattetvā sabbe kāme pariccajeti.

'Rathakāro' means a leather worker. 'Parikantaṃ' means while cutting around. This is what is said: Just as a leather worker, while cutting a shoe, discards whatever parts of the leather are unsuitable, and having made the shoe, obtains the price for it and is happy; in the same way, the wise person, cutting with wisdom like the leather-worker's knife, gives up whatever limit of sensual pleasures he can. By that, those bodily, verbal, and mental actions of his, which are free from that limit of sensual pleasures, become happy and free from distress. But if one should desire all happiness, including bodily happiness, to be entirely free from feverish burning, one should develop a kasiṇa, produce a jhāna, and renounce all sensual pleasures.

Bodhisattassa pana imaṃ gāthaṃ kathentassa rañño setacchattaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā odātakasiṇajjhānaṃ udapādi, rājāpi arogo ahosi. So tuṭṭho sayanā vuṭṭhahitvā “ettakā vejjā maṃ tikicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, [M 4.0176] paṇḍitamāṇavo pana attano ñāṇosadhena maṃ nirogaṃ akāsī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

While the Bodhisatta was speaking these verses, the white-kasiṇa jhāna arose in him using the king's white parasol as the object, and the king also became free from illness. Delighted, the king rose from his bed and said, 'So many great physicians were unable to heal me, but this wise youth, through the medicine of his wisdom, has made me healthy.' Desiring to converse with him, he spoke the tenth verse:

46.

46.

“Aṭṭha [P 4.0175] te bhāsitā gāthā, sabbā honti sahassiyā;

Paṭigaṇha mahābrahme, sādhetaṃ tava bhāsita”nti.

Eight verses have been spoken by you, each worth a thousand; accept [the eight thousand], O Great Brahmin, for this which you have spoken is excellent.

Tattha [V 4.0156] aṭṭhāti dutiyagāthaṃ ādiṃ katvā kāmādīnavasaṃyuttā aṭṭha. Sahassiyāti sahassārahā. Paṭigaṇhāti aṭṭha sahassāni gaṇha. Sādhetaṃ tava bhāsitanti sādhu etaṃ tava vacanaṃ.

Therein, 'eight' means the eight verses connected with the danger of sensual pleasures, beginning with the second verse. 'Worthy of a thousand' means deserving a thousand. 'Accept' means take eight thousand. 'Excellent is this utterance of yours' means: good is this word of yours.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto ekādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being spoke the eleventh verse:

47.

47.

“Na me attho sahassehi, satehi nahutehi vā;

Pacchimaṃ bhāsato gāthaṃ, kāme me na rato mano”ti.

I have no need for thousands, nor for hundreds, nor for myriads; while speaking this last verse, my mind finds no delight in sensual pleasures.

Tattha pacchimanti “rathakārova cammassā”ti gāthaṃ. Kāme me na rato manoti imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsamānasseva mama vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepi mano nābhiramāmi. Ahañhi imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsamāno attanova dhammadesanāya jhānaṃ nibbattesiṃ, mahārājāti.

Therein, 'the last' refers to the verse, 'Like a chariot-maker with leather...' 'My mind finds no delight in sensual pleasures' means: even while speaking this verse, my mind does not delight in objective sensual pleasures or in defilement-sensual pleasures. For while speaking this verse, I myself produced jhāna through my own teaching of the Dhamma, O great king.

Rājā bhiyyosomattāya tussitvā mahāsattaṃ vaṇṇento osānagāthamāha –

The king, exceedingly pleased, praising the Great Being, spoke the concluding verse:

48.

48.

“Bhadrako vatāyaṃ māṇavako, sabbalokavidū muni;

Yo imaṃ taṇhaṃ dukkhajananiṃ, parijānāti paṇḍito”ti.

Excellent indeed is this young man, the sage, knower of the whole world; this wise one fully understands this craving, the generator of suffering.

Tattha dukkhajananinti sakalavaṭṭadukkhajananiṃ. Parijānātīti parijāni paricchindi, luñcitvā nīharīti bodhisattaṃ vaṇṇento evamāha.

Therein, 'generator of suffering' means the generator of all the suffering of the round of existence. 'Fully understands' means: he fully understood, discerned, plucked out, and removed—praising the Bodhisatta, he spoke thus.

Bodhisattopi “mahārāja, appamatto hutvā dhammaṃ carā”ti rājānaṃ ovaditvā ākāsena himavantaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā aparihīnajjhāno hutvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, having advised the king, 'Great king, be diligent and practice the Dhamma,' then went through the air to the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life, lived there as long as his life lasted, developed the divine abidings, and without falling away from jhāna, arose in the Brahma-world.

Satthā [M 4.0177] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepāhaṃ etaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ nissokamakāsi”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā esa brāhmaṇo ahosi, paṇḍitamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, "Thus, monks, in the past I freed this brahmin from sorrow." Then he identified the birth: "At that time, the king was that brahmin, but the wise youth was none other than myself."

Kāmajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Kāma Jātaka, the Fourth.

[468] 5. Janasandhajātakavaṇṇanā

[468] 5. The Exposition of the Janasandha Jātaka

Dasa [V 4.0157][P 4.0176] khalūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño ovādatthāya kathesi. Ekasmiñhi kāle rājā issariyamadamatto kilesasukhanissito vinicchayampi na paṭṭhapesi, buddhupaṭṭhānampi pamajji. So ekadivase dasabalaṃ anussaritvā “satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti bhuttapātarāso rathavaramāruyha vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ mahārāja ciraṃ na paññāyasī”ti vatvā “bahukiccatāya no bhante buddhupaṭṭhānassa okāso na jāto”ti vutte “mahārāja, mādise nāma ovādadāyake sabbaññubuddhe dhuravihāre viharante ayuttaṃ tava pamajjituṃ, raññā nāma rājakiccesu appamattena bhavitabbaṃ, raṭṭhavāsīnaṃ mātāpitusamena agatigamanaṃ pahāya dasa rājadhamme akopentena rajjaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭati, rañño hi dhammikabhāve sati parisāpissa dhammikā honti, anacchariyaṃ kho panetaṃ, yaṃ mayi anusāsante tvaṃ dhammena rajjaṃ kāreyyāsi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anusāsakaācariye avijjamānepi attano matiyāva tividhasucaritadhamme patiṭṭhāya mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā saggapathaṃ pūrayamānā agamaṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

This discourse beginning 'Indeed, ten things...' the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, for the instruction of the king of Kosala. At one time, the king, intoxicated with power and indulging in sensual pleasures, neglected even judicial matters and grew heedless of attending upon the Buddha. One day, recalling the Ten-Powered One, he thought, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher." After his morning meal, he mounted his splendid chariot and went to the monastery. Having paid respects to the Teacher, he sat down. Then the Teacher said to him, "Great king, why have you not been seen for so long?" The king replied, "Venerable sir, due to many duties, I have had no opportunity to attend upon the Buddha." The Teacher then said, "Great king, it is unfitting for you to be heedless when omniscient Buddhas, who bear the burden of teaching, are dwelling here to give advice. A king should be diligent in his royal duties. Having abandoned partiality, he should rule without wavering in the ten royal virtues, treating his subjects as a mother and father would. When a king is righteous, his court becomes righteous too. It is no surprise that, under my guidance, you should rule righteously. Even in the past, when there were no teachers or instructors present, ancient sages, relying solely on their own wisdom, established themselves in the threefold good conduct, taught the Dhamma to the people, and went on their way, filling the path to heaven." Having spoken thus, at the king's request, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, “janasandhakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Athassa vayappattassa takkasilato sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā āgatakāle rājā sabbāni bandhanāgārāni sodhāpetvā uparajjaṃ adāsi. So aparabhāge pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya catūsu nagaradvāresu [M 4.0178] nagaramajjhe rājadvāre cāti cha dānasālāyo kārāpetvā divase divase cha satasahassāni pariccajitvā sakalajambudīpaṃ saṅkhobhetvā mahādānaṃ pavattento bandhanāgārāni niccaṃ vivaṭāni kārāpetvā dhammabhaṇḍikaṃ sodhāpetvā catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi lokaṃ saṅgaṇhanto pañca sīlāni [P 4.0177] rakkhanto uposathavāsaṃ vasanto dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Antarantarā ca raṭṭhavāsino sannipātāpetvā “dānaṃ detha, sīlaṃ samādiyatha, bhāvanaṃ bhāvetha, dhammena kammante ca vohāre ca payojetha, daharakāleyeva sippāni uggaṇhatha, dhanaṃ uppādetha, gāmakūṭakammaṃ vā pisuṇavācākammaṃ vā mā karittha, caṇḍā pharusā mā ahuvattha, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ pitupaṭṭhānaṃ pūretha, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino bhavathā”ti dhammaṃ desetvā mahājane sucaritadhamme patiṭṭhāpesi. So ekadivasaṃ pannarasīuposathe samādinnuposatho “mahājanassa bhiyyo hitasukhatthāya appamādavihāratthāya dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti cintetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā attano orodhe ādiṃ katvā sabbanagarajanaṃ sannipātāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe alaṅkaritvā alaṅkataratanamaṇḍapamajjhe supaññattavarapallaṅke nisīditvā “ambho, nagaravāsino tumhākaṃ [V 4.0158] tapanīye ca atapanīye ca dhamme desessāmi, appamattā hutvā ohitasotā sakkaccaṃ suṇāthā”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, and they named him Prince Janasandha. When he had learned all the arts from Takkasilā and returned, the king had all the prisons cleared and gave him the viceroyalty. Later, upon his father’s passing, he ascended the throne and established six alms halls: at the four city gates, in the city center, and at the palace gate. Daily, he gave away six hundred thousand, shaking all of Jambudīpa with his great generosity. He kept the prison gates always open, had the administration of justice purified, and ruled righteously, winning over the populace with the four bases of sympathy, observing the five precepts, and keeping the Uposatha. From time to time, he gathered the citizens of the kingdom and taught them: "Give alms, observe the precepts, cultivate meditation, conduct your work and business righteously, learn skills while young, accumulate wealth, avoid fraudulent practices or malicious speech, do not be violent or harsh, fulfill your duties to your mother and father, and honor the elders in your families." Thus, he established the people in good conduct. One day, on the fifteenth Uposatha, having undertaken the Uposatha observance, he thought, "For the greater welfare and happiness of the people, for the sake of living heedfully, I shall teach them the Dhamma." He had drums beaten throughout the city, assembled all the townsfolk, beginning with those in his own inner court, adorned the royal courtyard, and sat upon a splendid throne in a magnificently decorated jeweled pavilion. He said, "Listen carefully, citizens of the city, I shall teach you the Dhamma concerning what causes regret and what does not. Be heedful and attentive." Then he taught the Dhamma.

Satthā saccaparibhāvitaṃ mukharatanaṃ vivaritvā taṃ dhammadesanaṃ madhurena sarena kosalarañño āvi karonto –

The Teacher, opening his jewel-like mouth, imbued with truth, made that Dhamma teaching clear to the Kosalan king with a sweet voice:

49.

49.

“Dasa khalu imāni ṭhānāni, yāni pubbe akaritvā;

Sa pacchā manutappati, iccevāha janasandho.

"Indeed, these are the ten things which, if not done before, one later regrets; thus spoke Janasandha.

50.

50.

“Aladdhā vittaṃ tappati, pubbe asamudānitaṃ;

Na pubbe dhanamesissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

"Not having gained wealth, he suffers, wealth not amassed before; 'I did not seek wealth before!' thus one later regrets.

51.

51.

“Sakyarūpaṃ pure santaṃ, mayā sippaṃ na sikkhitaṃ;

Kicchā vutti asippassa, iti pacchānutappati.

"While it was possible before, I did not learn a craft; hard is the livelihood of the unskilled, thus one later regrets.

52.

52.

“Kūṭavedī pure āsiṃ, pisuṇo piṭṭhimaṃsiko;

Caṇḍo ca pharuso cāpi, iti pacchānutappati.

"I was deceitful before, a slanderer, a backbiter; and fierce and harsh too, thus one later regrets.

53.

53.

“Pāṇātipātī [P 4.0178][M 4.0179] pure āsiṃ, luddo cāpi anāriyo;

Bhūtānaṃ nāpacāyissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

I was a taker of life before, and also cruel and ignoble; I did not show respect to living beings; thus one regrets later.

54.

54.

“Bahūsu vata santīsu, anāpādāsu itthisu;

Paradāraṃ asevissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

Indeed, while there were many women not possessed by others, I consorted with another's wife; thus one regrets later.

55.

55.

“Bahumhi vata santamhi, annapāne upaṭṭhite;

Na pubbe adadaṃ dānaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

Indeed, while much food and drink was provided, I did not give gifts before; thus one regrets later.

56.

56.

“Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ cāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Pahu santo na posissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

Mother and father, aged and past their youth; though I was capable, I did not support them; thus one regrets later.

57.

57.

“Ācariyamanusatthāraṃ[V 4.0159], sabbakāmarasāharaṃ;

Pitaraṃ atimaññissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

My father, my teacher and instructor, the provider of all desired pleasures; I looked down on him; thus one regrets later.

58.

58.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe cāpi, sīlavante bahussute;

Na pubbe payirupāsissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

Ascetics and brahmins, virtuous and learned; I did not attend upon them before; thus one regrets later.

59.

59.

“Sādhu hoti tapo ciṇṇo, santo ca payirupāsito;

Na ca pubbe tapo ciṇṇo, iti pacchānutappati.

Good is austerity practiced, and good is the peaceful one attended upon; but I did not practice austerity before; thus one regrets later.

60.

60.

“Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni, yoniso paṭipajjati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, sa pacchā nānutappatī”ti. – imā gāthā āha;

"And whoever wisely undertakes these ten points, performing the duties of a man, he does not regret later." — He spoke these verses.

Tattha ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni. Pubbeti paṭhamameva akaritvā. Sa pacchā manutappatīti so paṭhamaṃ kattabbānaṃ akārako puggalo pacchā idhalokepi paralokepi tappati kilamati. “Pacchā vā anutappatī”tipi pāṭho. Iccevāhāti iti evaṃ āhāti padacchedo, iti evaṃ rājā janasandho avoca. Iccassuhātipi pāṭho. Tattha assu-kāro nipātamattaṃ iti assu āhāti padacchedo. Idāni tāni dasa tapanīyakāraṇāni pakāsetuṃ bodhisattassa dhammakathā hoti. Tattha pubbeti paṭhamameva taruṇakāle parakkamaṃ katvā asamudānitaṃ asambhataṃ dhanaṃ [M 4.0180] mahallakakāle alabhitvā tappati socati, pare ca sukhite disvā sayaṃ dukkhaṃ jīvanto “pubbe dhanaṃ na pariyesissa”nti evaṃ pacchā anutappati, tasmā mahallakakāle sukhaṃ jīvitukāmā daharakāleyeva dhammikāni kasikammādīni katvā dhanaṃ pariyesathāti dasseti.

Here, 'points' (ṭhānāni) means causes. 'Before' (pubbe) means without having done it first. 'He later regrets' (sa pacchā manutappati) means that person, not being a doer of what should be done first, later suffers and is weary in both this world and the next. There is also the reading 'pacchā vā anutappati'. 'Iccevāha' means 'iti evaṃ āha'; thus King Janasandha spoke. There is also the reading 'Iccassuhā'. There 'assu' is a mere particle, so it is 'iti assu āha'. Now, the Bodhisatta's discourse is for revealing those ten causes of regret. There, 'before' (pubbe) means in youth, if one does not strive and fails to accumulate wealth, one suffers and grieves in old age when not obtaining it. Seeing others happy while living in misery oneself, one regrets, thinking, 'I did not seek wealth before.' Therefore, he shows that those who wish to live happily in old age should seek wealth by righteous farming and such in their youth.

Pure santanti pure daharakāle ācariye payirupāsitvā mayā kātuṃ sakyarūpaṃ samānaṃ hatthisippādikaṃ kiñci sippaṃ na [P 4.0179] sikkhitaṃ. Kicchāti mahallakakāle asippassa dukkhā jīvitavutti, neva sakkā tadā sippaṃ sikkhituṃ, tasmā mahallakakāle sukhaṃ jīvitukāmā taruṇakāleyeva sippaṃ sikkhathāti dasseti. Kuṭavedīti kūṭajānanako gāmakūṭako vā lokassa anatthakārako vā tulākūṭādikārako vā kūṭaṭṭakārako vāti attho. Āsinti evarūpo ahaṃ pubbe ahosiṃ. Pisuṇoti pesuññakāraṇo. Piṭṭhimaṃsikoti lañjaṃ gahetvā asāmike sāmike karonto paresaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsakhādako. Iti pacchāti evaṃ maraṇamañce nipanno anutappati[V 4.0160], tasmā sace niraye na vasitukāmāttha, mā evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ karitthāti ovadati.

'While before' (pure santaṃ) means in youth, having attended upon a teacher, I did not learn any craft such as the craft of elephants that I was capable of doing. 'Hard' (kicchā) means that for the unskilled in old age, the livelihood is difficult; it is not possible to learn a craft then. Therefore, he shows that those who wish to live happily in old age should learn a craft while young. 'Deceitful' (kūṭavedī) means a village cheat, one who harms the world, or a user of false weights, or a false litigant. 'I was' (āsiṃ) means I was such a one before. 'Slanderer' (pisuṇo) means one who slanders. 'Backbiter' (piṭṭhimaṃsiko) means one who takes bribes and makes owners of non-owners, devouring the back-flesh of others. 'Thus later' (iti pacchā) means lying on one's deathbed, one regrets. Therefore, he advises: 'If you do not wish to dwell in hell, do not commit such evil deeds.'

Luddoti dāruṇo. Anāriyoti na ariyo nīcasamācāro. Nāpacāyissanti khantimettānuddayavasena nīcavuttiko nāhosiṃ. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Anāpādāsūti āpādānaṃ āpādo, pariggahoti attho. Natthi āpādo yāsaṃ tā anāpādā, aññehi akatapariggahāsūti attho. Upaṭṭhiteti paccupaṭṭhite. Na pubbeti ito pubbe dānaṃ na adadaṃ. Pahu santoti dhanabalenāpi kāyabalenāpi posituṃ samattho paṭibalo samāno. Ācariyanti ācāre sikkhāpanato idha pitā “ācariyo”ti adhippeto. Anusatthāranti anusāsakaṃ. Sabbakāmarasāharanti sabbe vatthukāmarase āharitvā positāraṃ. Atimaññissanti tassa ovādaṃ agaṇhanto atikkamitvā maññissaṃ.

'Cruel' (luddo) means harsh. 'Ignoble' (anāriyo) means not noble, of low conduct. 'I did not show respect' (nāpacāyissaṃ) means I was not humble through patience, love, and compassion. The rest should be construed in the same way as before. 'Unclaimed' (anāpādāsu) means taking up or possession; 'anāpādā' means those for whom there is no possession, meaning not possessed by others. 'At hand' (upaṭṭhite) means present. 'Not before' (na pubbe) means I did not give gifts before this. 'Being capable' (pahu santo) means being able and strong enough to support by wealth and physical strength. 'Teacher' (ācariyaṃ) means the father is intended here as 'teacher' because he teaches conduct. 'Instructor' (anusatthāraṃ) means one who advises. 'Bringer of all sensual pleasures' (sabbakāmarasāharaṃ) means one who supports by bringing all objects of sensual pleasure. 'I looked down on' (atimaññissaṃ) means I looked down on him, not accepting his advice.

Na pubbeti ito pubbe dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇepi gilānāgilānepi cīvarādīni datvā appaṭijagganena na payirupāsissaṃ. Tapoti sucaritatapo. Santoti tīhi dvārehi upasanto sīlavā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tividhasucaritasaṅkhāto [M 4.0181] tapo ciṇṇo evarūpo ca upasanto payirupāsito nāma sādhu sundaro. Na pubbeti mayā daharakāle evarūpo tapo na ciṇṇo, iti pacchā jarājiṇṇo maraṇabhayatajjito anutappati socati. Sace tumhe evaṃ na socitukāmā, tapokammaṃ karothāti vadati. Yo ca etānīti yo pana etāni dasa kāraṇāni paṭhamameva upāyena paṭipajjati samādāya vattati, purisehi kattabbāni dhammikakiccāni karonto so appamādavihārī puriso pacchā nānutappati, somanassappattova hotīti.

'Not before' (na pubbe) means before this, I did not attend upon righteous ascetics and brahmins, whether sick or healthy, by giving robes and so forth and looking after them. 'Austerity' (tapo) means the austerity of good conduct. 'Peaceful' (santo) means one who is peaceful through the three doors, a virtuous person. This is what is said: the austerity known as the three types of good conduct when practiced, and such a peaceful one attended upon, are good and excellent. 'Not before' (na pubbe) means such austerity was not practiced by me in my youth; thus, later, worn out by old age and terrified by the fear of death, one regrets and grieves. He says, 'If you do not wish to grieve so, perform acts of austerity.' 'And whoever these' (yo ca etāni) means whoever undertakes and practices these ten points from the very beginning by skillful means, doing the righteous duties to be done by men, that person who dwells in heedfulness does not regret later, but is indeed happy.

Iti [P 4.0180] mahāsatto anvaddhamāsaṃ iminā niyāmena mahājanassa dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājanopissa ovāde ṭhatvā tāni dasa ṭhānāni pūretvā saggaparāyaṇova ahosi.

Thus the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the public every fortnight in this manner. The people, abiding by his advice and fulfilling those ten points, were destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, mahārāja, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anācariyakāpi attano matiyāva dhammaṃ desetvā mahājanaṃ saggapathe patiṭṭhāpesu”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā parisā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, janasandharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, said: "Thus, O Great King, ancient wise ones, even without a teacher, taught the Dhamma by their own wisdom and established the public on the path to heaven." Then he connected the Jātaka: "At that time the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and King Janasandha was I myself."

Janasandhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Janasandha Jātaka is the fifth.

[469] 6. Mahākaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā

[469] 6. The Commentary on the Mahākaṇha Jātaka

Kaṇho [V 4.0161] kaṇho cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lokatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā “yāvañcidaṃ, āvuso, satthā bahujanahitāya paṭipanno attano phāsuvihāraṃ pahāya lokasseva atthaṃ carati, paramābhisambodhiṃ patvā sayaṃ pattacīvaramādāya aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ gantvā pañcavaggiyattherānaṃ dhammacakkaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 13 ādayo; paṭi. ma. 2.30) pavattetvā pañcamiyā pakkhassa anattalakkhaṇasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.59; mahāva. 20 ādayo) kathetvā sabbesaṃ arahattaṃ adāsi. Uruvelaṃ gantvā tebhātikajaṭilānaṃ aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni dassetvā pabbājetvā gayāsīse ādittapariyāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.235; mahāva. 54) kathetvā jaṭilasahassānaṃ arahattaṃ adāsi, mahākassapassa tīṇi gāvutāni [M 4.0182] paccuggamanaṃ gantvā tīhi ovādehi upasampadaṃ adāsi. Eko pacchābhattaṃ pañcacattālīsayojanamaggaṃ gantvā pukkusātikulaputtaṃ anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpesi, mahākappinassa vīsayojanasataṃ paccuggamanaṃ katvā arahattaṃ adāsi, eko pacchābhattaṃ tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ gantvā tāva kakkhaḷaṃ pharusaṃ aṅgulimālaṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāpesi, tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ gantvā āḷavakaṃ yakkhaṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā kumārassa sotthiṃ akāsi. Tāvatiṃsabhavane temāsaṃ vasanto asītiyā devatākoṭīnaṃ dhammābhisamayaṃ sampādesi, brahmalokaṃ gantvā bakabrahmuno diṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā dasannaṃ brahmasahassānaṃ arahattaṃ adāsi, anusaṃvaccharaṃ tīsu maṇḍalesu cārikaṃ caramāno upanissayasampannānaṃ manussānaṃ saraṇāni ceva sīlānica maggaphalāni ca deti, nāgasupaṇṇādīnampi [P 4.0181] nānappakāraṃ atthaṃ caratī”ti dasabalassa lokatthacariyaguṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, sohaṃ idāni abhisambodhiṃ patvā lokassa atthaṃ careyyaṃ, pubbe sarāgakālepi lokassa atthaṃ acari”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Kaṇho kaṇho ca"—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his conduct for the world's welfare. One day, the monks, seated in the Dhamma hall, discussed: "Indeed, friends, the Teacher, for the welfare of many, abandoning his own comfort, works for the good of the world. Having attained supreme enlightenment, he himself took bowl and robe, traveled eighteen yojanas, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma for the group of five elders, and taught the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta on the fifth day of the fortnight, granting them all arahantship. Going to Uruvelā, he displayed three thousand five hundred miraculous feats to the three matted-hair ascetic brothers, ordained them, and on Gayāsīsa, delivered the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, granting arahantship to a thousand matted-hair ascetics. He went three gāvutas to meet Mahākassapa and gave him higher ordination with three exhortations. Alone, after the meal, he traveled forty-five yojanas and established Pukkusāti the clansman in the fruit of non-return. For Mahākappina, he went one hundred and twenty yojanas to meet him and granted him arahantship. Alone, after the meal, he traveled thirty yojanas and established the harsh and cruel Aṅgulimāla in arahantship. Traveling thirty yojanas, he established the yakkha Āḷavaka in the fruit of stream-entry and ensured the prince’s safety. Dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa realm for three months, he brought about the realization of Dhamma for eight hundred million devas. Going to the Brahma world, he shattered the view of Baka Brahmā and granted arahantship to ten thousand Brahmas. Year after year, he wandered in the three regions, giving refuge and precepts, as well as the path and fruits, to humans endowed with supporting conditions. He also worked various benefits for nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others." Thus, they spoke of the Ten-Powered One’s virtue of working for the world’s welfare. The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?" When told, "This one," he said, "It is no surprise, monks, that now, having attained enlightenment, I work for the world’s welfare. Even in the past, during times of passion, I worked for the world’s welfare," and he recounted a past event.

Atīte kassapasammāsambuddhakāle bārāṇasiyaṃ usīnako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Kassapasammāsambuddhe catusaccadesanāya mahājanaṃ kilesabandhanā mocetvā nibbānanagaraṃ pūretvā parinibbute dīghassa addhuno accayena sāsanaṃ osakki. Bhikkhū ekavīsatiyā anesanāhi jīvikaṃ kappenti, bhikkhū gihisaṃsaggaṃ karonti, puttadhītādīhi vaḍḍhanti. Bhikkhuniyopi gihisaṃsaggaṃ karonti, puttadhītādīhi vaḍḍhanti. Bhikkhū bhikkhudhammaṃ, bhikkhuniyo bhikkhunidhammaṃ, uposakā upāsakadhammaṃ, upāsikā upāsikadhammaṃ, brāhmaṇā brāhmaṇadhammaṃ vissajjesuṃ. Yebhuyyena manussā [V 4.0162] dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattiṃsu, matamatā apāyesu paripūresuṃ. Tadā sakko devarājā nave nave deve apassanto manussalokaṃ oloketvā manussānaṃ apāyesu nibbattitabhāvaṃ ñatvā satthu sāsanaṃ osakkitaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu karissāmī”ti cintetvā “attheko upāyo, mahājanaṃ tāsetvā bhītabhāvaṃ ñatvā pacchā assāsetvā dhammaṃ desetvā osakkitaṃ sāsanaṃ paggayha aparampi vassasahassaṃ pavattanakāraṇaṃ karissāmī”ti [M 4.0183] sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā mātalidevaputtaṃ mocappamāṇadāṭhaṃ catūhi dāṭhāhi viniggatarasmiyā bhayānakaṃ katvā gabbhinīnaṃ dassaneneva gabbhapātanasamatthaṃ ghorarūpaṃ ājāneyyappamāṇaṃ kāḷavaṇṇaṃ mahākaṇhasunakhaṃ māpetvā pañcabandhanena bandhitvā rattamālaṃ [P 4.0182] kaṇṭhe piḷandhitvā rajjukoṭikaṃ ādāya sayaṃ dve kāsāyāni nivāsetvā pacchāmukhe pañcadhā kese bandhitvā rattamālaṃ piḷandhitvā āropitapavāḷavaṇṇajiyaṃ mahādhanuṃ gahetvā vajiragganārācaṃ nakhena parivaṭṭento vanacarakavesaṃ gahetvā nagarato yojanamatte ṭhāne otaritvā “nassati loko, nassati loko”ti tikkhattuṃ saddaṃ anusāvetvā manusse uttāsetvā nagarūpacāraṃ patvā puna saddamakāsi.

In the past, during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, a king named Usīnaka reigned in Bārāṇasī. When Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, having liberated the great multitude from the bonds of defilements through the teaching of the Four Noble Truths and filled the city of Nibbāna, attained final Nibbāna, after a long time had passed, the Dispensation declined. Monks sustained their livelihood through twenty-one improper means; monks associated with householders and increased with sons and daughters. Nuns also associated with householders and increased with sons and daughters. Monks abandoned the duties of monks, nuns the duties of nuns, male lay followers the duties of male lay followers, female lay followers the duties of female lay followers, and brahmins the duties of brahmins. For the most part, people engaged in the ten unwholesome courses of action, and whenever they died, they filled the realms of misery. Then Sakka, the king of the gods, not seeing any new gods, looked upon the human world. Knowing that humans were being reborn in the realms of misery and seeing that the Teacher’s Dispensation had declined, he thought, “What now shall I do?” He resolved, “There is one way: I will frighten the great multitude, and having made them aware of their fear, I will then console them, teach them the Dhamma, uplift the declined Dispensation, and make it last for another thousand years.” Having made this resolution, he transformed the devaputta Mātali into a great black dog, the size of a noble steed, with a terrifying form capable of causing miscarriages in pregnant women at the mere sight of it. It had fangs the size of plantain buds, with rays emanating from its four fangs. He bound it with five restraints, placed a red garland around its neck, and took the end of the rope in his hand. He himself donned two ochre robes, tied his hair in five knots at the back, and put on a red garland. Taking up a great bow with a strung, coral-colored bowstring, and twirling a diamond-tipped arrow with his nail, he assumed the guise of a forest dweller. Descending to a place a yojana from the city, he proclaimed three times, “The world is perishing! The world is perishing!” Having terrified the people, he approached the city’s vicinity and made the sound again.

Manussā sunakhaṃ disvā utrastā nagaraṃ pavisitvā taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā sīghaṃ nagaradvārāni pidahāpesi. Sakkopi aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ pākāraṃ ullaṅghitvā sunakhena saddhiṃ antonagare patiṭṭhahi. Manussā bhītatasitā palāyitvā gehāni pavisitvā nilīyiṃsu. Mahākaṇhopi diṭṭhadiṭṭhe manusse upadhāvitvā santāsento rājanivesanaṃ agamāsi. Rājaṅgaṇe manussā bhayena palāyitvā rājanivesanaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidahiṃsu. Usīnakarājāpi orodhe gahetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Mahākaṇho sunakho purimapāde ukkhipitvā vātapāne ṭhatvā mahābhussitaṃ bhussi. Tassa saddo heṭṭhā avīciṃ, upari bhavaggaṃ patvā sakalacakkavāḷaṃ ekaninnādaṃ ahosi. Vidhurajātake (jā. 2.22.1346 ādayo) hi puṇṇakayakkharañño, kusajātake (jā. 2.20.1 ādayo) kusarañño, bhūridattajātake (jā. 2.22.784 ādayo) sudassananāgarañño, imasmiṃ mahākaṇhajātake ayaṃ saddoti ime cattāro saddā jambudipe mahāsaddā nāma ahesuṃ.

Seeing the dog, the people were terrified and, entering the city, reported the matter to the king. The king quickly had the city gates closed. Sakka, too, leaped over the eighteen-cubit wall and stood inside the city with the dog. Frightened and trembling, the people fled, entered their houses, and hid. The great black dog, Mahākaṇha, ran towards and terrified whomever it saw, and went to the royal palace. In the royal courtyard, people fled in fear, entered the royal residence, and closed the doors. King Usīnaka also took the women of his harem and ascended to the upper palace. The dog Mahākaṇha lifted its front paws, stood at a window, and let out a mighty bark. Its sound reached Avīci below and the summit of existence above, and the entire world-system resounded with one roar. Indeed, in the Vidhura Jātaka, it was the roar of the yakkha Puṇṇaka; in the Kusa Jātaka, the roar of King Kusa; in the Bhūridatta Jātaka, the roar of the nāga king Sudassana; and in this Mahākaṇha Jātaka, this sound—these four sounds were known as the great sounds in Jambudīpa.

Nagaravāsino bhītatasitā hutvā ekapurisopi sakkena saddhiṃ kathetuṃ nāsakkhi, rājāyeva satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā vātapānaṃ nissāya sakkaṃ āmantetvā “ambho luddaka, kasmā te [P 4.0183] sunakho bhussatī”ti āha. “Chātabhāvena, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi tassa bhattaṃ dāpessāmī”ti antojanassa ca attano ca pakkabhattaṃ sabbaṃ dāpesi. Taṃ sabbaṃ sunakho ekakabaḷaṃ viya katvā puna saddamakāsi. Puna rājā pucchitvā “idānipi me sunakho [M 4.0184] chātoyevā”ti [V 4.0163] sutvā hatthiassādīnaṃ pakkabhattaṃ sabbaṃ āharāpetvā dāpesi. Tasmiṃ ekappahāreneva niṭṭhāpite sakalanagarassa pakkabhattaṃ dāpesi. Tampi so tatheva bhuñjitvā puna saddamakāsi. Rājā “na esa sunakho, nissaṃsayaṃ esa yakkho bhavissati, āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchissāmī”ti bhītatasito hutvā pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The city dwellers were so terrified and trembling that not a single person dared to speak with Sakka. Only the king, establishing mindfulness, leaned against a window and addressed Sakka, saying, ‘Ho, hunter, why does your dog bark?’ ‘Because of hunger, great king.’ ‘In that case, I shall have food given to it.’ He had all the cooked food for his retinue and for himself given to it. The dog, making it as if a single mouthful, devoured it all and barked again. The king asked again, and hearing, ‘Even now my dog is hungry,’ he had all the cooked food for the elephants, horses, and other animals brought and given. When that was finished in a single gulp, he had all the cooked food in the entire city given. The dog ate that in the same way and barked again. The king, terrified and trembling, thought, ‘This is no dog; without a doubt, this must be a yakkha. I shall ask the reason for its coming.’ So thinking, he asked, speaking the first verse:

61.

61.

“Kaṇho kaṇho ca ghoro ca, sukkadāṭho pabhāsavā;

Baddho pañcahi rajjūhi, kiṃ ravi sunakho tavā”ti.

‘Black, black and terrible, with white fangs and radiant; bound by five ropes—why does your dog bark?’

Tattha kaṇho kaṇhoti bhayavasena daḷhīvasena vā āmeḍitaṃ. Ghoroti passantānaṃ bhayajanako. Pabhāsavāti dāṭhā nikkhantaraṃsipabhāsena pabhāsavā. Kiṃ ravīti kiṃ viravi. Tavesa evarūpo kakkhaḷo sunakho kiṃ karoti, kiṃ mige gaṇhāti, udāhu te amitte, kiṃ te iminā, vissajjehi nanti adhippāyenevamāha.

Herein, ‘black, black’ is a repetition due to fear or for emphasis. ‘Terrible’ means it generates fear in those who see it. ‘Radiant’ means it is radiant with the splendor of the rays issuing from its fangs. ‘Why does it bark?’ means ‘why did it bark?’ He spoke thus with the intention: ‘What does this fierce dog of yours do? Does it catch deer, or your enemies? What use is it to you? Release it!’

Taṃ sutvā sakko dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka spoke the second verse:

62.

62.

“Nāyaṃ migānamatthāya, usīnaka bhavissati;

Manussānaṃ anayo hutvā, tadā kaṇho pamokkhatī”ti.

‘This one will not be for the benefit of deer, O Usĩnaka; having become a calamity for humankind, then Kaᅅha will be set free.’

Tassattho – ayañhi “migamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti idha nāgato, tasmā migānaṃ attho na bhavissati, manussamaṃsaṃ pana khādituṃ āgato, tasmā tesaṃ anayo mahāvināsakārako hutvā yadā anena manussā vināsaṃ pāpitā bhavissanti, tadā ayaṃ kaṇho pamokkhati, mama hatthato muccissatīti.

Its meaning is: This one has not come here thinking, ‘I will eat the flesh of deer,’ therefore it will not be for the benefit of deer. Rather, it has come to eat the flesh of humans. Therefore, having become a calamity for them and a cause of great destruction, when humans have been brought to ruin by it, then this Kaᅅha will be set free; it will be released from my hand.

Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ pana te bho luddaka-sunakho sabbesaṃyeva manussānaṃ maṃsaṃ khādissati, udāhu tava amittānaññevā”ti [P 4.0184] pucchitvā “amittānaññeva me, mahārājā”ti vutte “ke pana idha te amittā”ti pucchitvā “adhammābhiratā visamacārino, mahārājā”ti vutte “kathehi tāva ne amhāka”nti pucchi. Athassa kathento devarājā dasa gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king asked him, ‘But, good hunter, will your dog eat the flesh of all humans, or only of your enemies?’ When he was told, ‘Only of my enemies, great king,’ he asked, ‘And who are your enemies here?’ When he was told, ‘Those who delight in unrighteousness and live crookedly, great king,’ he asked, ‘Then tell us of them.’ Then the king of the gods, explaining to him, spoke ten verses:

63.

63.

“Pattahatthā [M 4.0185] samaṇakā, muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā;

Naṅgalehi kasissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When vile ascetics with bowls in hand, shaven-headed and wearing the outer robe, plow with plows, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

64.

64.

“Tapassiniyo [V 4.0164] pabbajitā, muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā;

Yadā loke gamissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When female ascetics who have gone forth, shaven-headed and wearing the outer robe, go about in the world pursuing sensual pleasures, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

65.

65.

“Dīghottaroṭṭhā jaṭilā, paṅkadantā rajassirā;

Iṇaṃ codāya gacchanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When matted-haired ascetics with long upper lips, muddy teeth, and dust on their heads, go about demanding the repayment of debts, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

66.

66.

“Adhicca vede sāvittiṃ, yaññatantañca brāhmaṇā;

Bhatikāya yajissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When brahmins who have studied the Vedas, the Sāvitrĩ, and the sacrificial texts, perform sacrifices for a fee, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

67.

67.

“Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ cāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Pahū santo na bharanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When those who are able do not support their mother and father, aged and past their youth, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

68.

68.

“Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ cāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Bālā tumheti vakkhanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When they say to their mother and father, aged and past their youth, ‘You are fools,’ then Kaᅅha will be set free.

69.

69.

“Ācariyabhariyaṃ sakhiṃ, mātulāniṃ pitucchakiṃ;

Yadā loke gamissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When people in the world consort with their teacher’s wife, their friend’s wife, their maternal aunt, or their paternal aunt, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

70.

70.

“Asicammaṃ gahetvāna, khaggaṃ paggayha brāhmaṇā;

Panthaghātaṃ karissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When brahmins, taking up shield and sword, brandishing their swords, commit highway robbery, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

71.

71.

“Sukkacchavī vedhaverā, thūlabāhū apātubhā;

Mittabhedaṃ karissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

‘When fair-skinned men, desiring widows, with thick arms but no wealth, cause division among friends, then Kaᅅha will be set free.

72.

72.

“Māyāvino nekatikā, asappurisacintakā;

Yadā loke bhavissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhatī”ti.

‘When deceivers, tricksters, and those who think like the wicked are in the world, then Kaᅅha will be set free.’

Tattha [P 4.0185] samaṇakāti “mayaṃ samaṇāmhā”ti paṭiññāmattakena hīḷitavohārenevamāha. Kasissantīti te tadāpi kasantiyeva. Ayaṃ pana [M 4.0186] ajānanto viya evamāha. Ayañhissa adhippāyo – ete evarūpā dussīlā mama amittā, yadā mama sunakhena ete māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditaṃ [V 4.0165] bhavissati, tadā esa kaṇho ito pañcarajjubandhanā pamokkhatīti. Iminā upāyena sabbagāthāsu adhippāyayojanā veditabbā.

Herein, 'ascetics' refers to those who merely claim, 'We are ascetics,' with contemptuous language. 'They will plow' means they are indeed plowing even then. But this one speaks thus as if not knowing. His intention is this: 'These immoral ones, my enemies, when my dog has killed them and eaten their flesh, then this dark one will be freed from his fivefold bondage.' By this means, the intended meaning in all the verses should be understood.

Pabbajitāti buddhasāsane pabbajitā. Gamissantīti agāramajjhe pañca kāmaguṇe paribhuñjantiyo vicarissanti. Dīghottaroṭṭhāti dāṭhikānaṃ vaḍḍhitattā dīghuttaroṭṭhā. Paṅkadantāti paṅkena malena samannāgatadantā. Iṇaṃ codāyāti bhikkhācariyāya dhanaṃ saṃharitvā vaḍḍhiyā iṇaṃ payojetvā taṃ codetvā tato laddhena jīvikaṃ kappentā yadā gacchantīti attho.

"'Gone forth' means those who have gone forth in the Buddha’s dispensation. 'They will go' means they will roam indulging in the five sensual pleasures amidst households. 'Long-upper-lipped' means their upper lips are long due to the growth of their tusks. 'Filthy-toothed' means their teeth are covered with dirt. 'They will demand debts' means they will collect wealth by alms-seeking, lend it out for interest, demand repayment, and live off what they gain—that is the meaning.

Sāvittinti sāvittiñca adhiyitvā. Yaññatantañcāti yaññavidhāyakatantaṃ, yaññaṃ adhiyitvāti attho. Bhatikāyāti te te rājarājamahāmatte upasaṅkamitvā “tumhākaṃ yaññaṃ yajissāma, dhanaṃ dethā”ti evaṃ bhatiatthāya yadā yaññaṃ yajissanti. Pahū santoti bharituṃ posetuṃ samatthā samānā. Bālā tumheti tumhe bālā na kiñci jānāthāti yadā vakkhanti. Gamissantīti lokadhammasevanavasena gamissanti. Panthaghātanti panthe ṭhatvā manusse māretvā tesaṃ bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ.

"'Having studied the Sāvitti' means having learned the Sāvitti. 'And the sacrificial rites' refers to the treatise that regulates sacrifices; having studied the sacrifice, that is the meaning. 'For wages' means when they approach various kings and high ministers, saying, "We will perform sacrifices for you, give us wealth," and thus perform sacrifices for the sake of wages. 'Capable' means being capable of supporting and nourishing. 'Fools, you' means when they will say, "You are fools, knowing nothing." 'They will go' means they will go in dependence on indulgence in worldly ways. 'Highway robbery' means standing on the road, killing people, and taking their goods.

Sukkacchavīti kasāvacuṇṇādighaṃsanena samuṭṭhāpitasukkacchavivaṇṇā. Vedhaverāti vidhavā apatikā, tāhi vidhavāhi veraṃ carantīti vedhaverā. Thūlabāhūti pādaparimaddanādīhi samuṭṭhāpitamaṃsatāya mahābāhū. Apātubhāti apātubhāvā, dhanuppādarahitāti attho. Mittabhedanti mithubhedaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadā evarūpā itthidhuttā “imā amhe na jahissantī”ti sahiraññā vidhavā upagantvā saṃvāsaṃ kappetvā tāsaṃ santakaṃ khāditvā tāhi saddhiṃ mittabhedaṃ [P 4.0186] karissanti[M 4.0187], vissāsaṃ bhinditvā aññaṃ sahiraññaṃ gamissanti, tadā esa te core sabbeva khāditvā muccissati. Asappurisacintakāti asappurisacittehi paradukkhacintanasīlā. Tadāti tadā sabbepime ghātetvā khāditamaṃso kaṇho pamokkhatīti.

"'Pale-skinned' means their skin is pale-colored, made so by rubbing with astringent powder and such. 'Hostile to widows' means: a widow is without a husband; because they behave with hostility towards such widows, they are called 'hostile to widows.' 'Thick-armed' means having large arms because of flesh developed from massaging feet and such. 'Inconspicuous' means being unmanifest, that is, devoid of producing wealth. 'Breaking friendships' means causing discord, or this is the reading. This is what is said: when such female swindlers, thinking, "These will not abandon us," approach wealthy widows, establish relationships, devour their possessions, and then break their friendships with them, betraying their trust to go to another wealthy one, then this one, having devoured all those thieves, will be freed. 'Of base thoughts' means habitually thinking of others' suffering with the minds of base people. 'Then' means: then, having killed all these and eaten their flesh, the dark one will be released.

Evañca pana vatvā “ime mayhaṃ, mahārāja, amittā”ti te te adhammakārake pakkhanditvā khāditukāmataṃ viya katvā dasseti. So tato mahājanassa utrastakāle sunakhaṃ rajjuyā ākaḍḍhitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya katvā luddakavesaṃ vijahitvā attano ānubhāvena ākāse jalamāno ṭhatvā “mahārāja, ahaṃ sakko devarājā, ‘ayaṃ loko vinassatī’ti āgato, pamattā hi mahājanā, adhammaṃ vattitvā matamatā sampati apāye pūrenti, devaloko tuccho viya [V 4.0166] vito, ito paṭṭhāya adhammikesu kattabbaṃ ahaṃ jānissāmi, tvaṃ appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti catūhi satārahagāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā manussānaṃ dānasīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā osakkitasāsanaṃ aññaṃ vassasahassaṃ pavattanasamatthaṃ katvā mātaliṃ ādāya sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Mahājanā dānasīlādīni puññāni katvā devaloke nibbattiṃsu.

And having spoken thus, saying, 'O great king, these wrongdoers are my enemies,' he made it appear as though he desired to pounce upon and devour those various workers of unrighteousness. Then, at the moment when the people were terrified, he acted as though he had pulled back the dog with a rope and restrained it. Casting off his hunter’s disguise, he stood blazing in the sky by his own power and declared, 'O great king, I am Sakka, king of the gods. I have come because this world is perishing. For the people, being heedless, act unrighteously, and dying one after another, they now fill the lower realms. The heavenly world is becoming empty, as it were. From now on, I will know what must be done to the unrighteous. Be vigilant, O great king!' Then, teaching the Dhamma with four verses worth a hundred pieces each, he established the people in generosity and virtue. Having made the declining Dispensation capable of lasting for another thousand years, he took Mātali and returned to his own abode. The people, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and virtue, were reborn in the heavenly world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhave pubbepāhaṃ lokassa atthameva carāmī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātali ānando ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, 'Thus, monks, even in the past I acted for the welfare of the world.' Then he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, Mātali was Ānanda, and Sakka was indeed I myself.'

Mahākaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Mahākaṇha Jātaka, the Sixth.

[470] 7. Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[470] 7. The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka

73-93. Kosiyajātakaṃ sudhābhojanajātake (jā. 2.21.192 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

73-93. The Kosiya Jātaka will become clear in the Sudhābhojana Jātaka (Jā. 535).

Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka, the Seventh.

[471] 8. Meṇḍakapañhajātakavaṇṇanā

[471] 8. The Commentary on the Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka

94-105. Meṇḍakapañhajātakaṃ [M 4.0188] umaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

94-105. The Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka will become clear in the Maha-umaṅga Jātaka (Jā. 546).

Meṇḍakapañhajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Meṇḍakapañha Jātaka, the Eighth.

[472] 9. Mahāpadumajātakavaṇṇanā

[472] 9. The Commentary on the Mahāpaduma Jātaka

Nādaṭṭhā [P 4.0187] parato dosanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ciñcamāṇavikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi dasabalassa puthubhūtesu sāvakesu aparimāṇesu devamanussesu ariyabhūmiṃ okkantesu patthaṭesu guṇasamudayesu mahālābhasakkāro udapādi. Titthiyā sūriyuggamane khajjopanakasadisā ahesuṃ hatalābhasakkārā. Te antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā “kiṃ samaṇo gotamova buddho, mayampi buddhā, kiṃ tasseva dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, amhākampi dinnaṃ mahapphalameva, amhākampi [V 4.0167] detha karothā”ti evaṃ manusse viññāpentāpi lābhasakkāraṃ alabhantā raho sannipatitvā “kena nu kho upāyena samaṇassa gotamassa manussānaṃ antare avaṇṇaṃ uppādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nāseyyāmā”ti mantayiṃsu. Tadā sāvatthiyaṃ ciñcamāṇavikā nāmekā paribbājikā uttamarūpadharā sobhaggappattā devaccharā viya. Tassā sarīrato rasmiyo niccharanti. Atheko kharamantī evamāha – “ciñcamāṇavikaṃ paṭicca samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ uppādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nāsessāmā”ti. Te “attheso upāyo”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. Atha sā titthiyārāmaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi, titthiyā tāya saddhiṃ na kathesuṃ. Sā “ko nu kho me doso”ti yāvatatiyaṃ “vandāmi ayyā”ti vatvā “ayyā, ko nu kho me doso, kiṃ mayā saddhiṃ na kathethā”ti āha. “Bhagini, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ amhe viheṭhentaṃ hatalābhasakkāre katvā vicarantaṃ na jānāsī”ti. “Nāhaṃ jānāmi ayyā, mayā kiṃ panettha kattabbanti. Sace tvaṃ bhagini, amhākaṃ sukhamicchasi, attānaṃ paṭicca samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ uppādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nāsehī”ti.

'Not having seen the fault in another'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Ciñcamāṇavikā. For during the period of the First Enlightenment, when the Ten-Powered One's disciples had become numerous, countless devas and humans had entered the noble stage, and his virtues had spread far and wide, great gain and honor arose. The sectarians became like fireflies at sunrise, deprived of their gain and honor. Standing in the streets, they proclaimed, 'Is only the ascetic Gotama a Buddha? We too are Buddhas! Why is only a gift to him of great fruit? A gift to us is also of great fruit! Give to us, support us!' Yet despite such persuasions, they failed to obtain gain and honor. Gathering in secret, they deliberated, 'By what means can we stir up disrepute against the ascetic Gotama among people and destroy his gain and honor?' At that time, in Sāvatthī, there was a female wanderer named Ciñcamāṇavikā, endowed with supreme beauty, radiant like a celestial nymph. Rays of light emanated from her body. Then a certain sectarian of harsh counsel said, 'By means of Ciñcamāṇavikā, we can stir up disrepute against the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gain and honor.' They agreed, 'This is the way.' Then she went to the sectarians' monastery, paid homage, and stood there, but the sectarians did not speak with her. She said, 'What is my fault?' and up to the third time, she said, 'I pay homage to you, venerable sirs,' and asked, 'Venerable sirs, what is my fault? Why do you not speak with me?' They replied, 'Sister, do you not know that the ascetic Gotama is harassing us, depriving us of our gain and honor?' 'I do not know, venerable sirs. But what can I do about it?' 'If you, sister, wish for our happiness, then by your own means, stir up disrepute against the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gain and honor.'

Sā [M 4.0189] “sādhu ayyā, mayhameveso bhāro, mā cintayitthā”ti vatvā pakkamitvā itthimāyāsu kusalatāya tato paṭṭhāya sāvatthivāsīnaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā jetavanā nikkhamanasamaye indagopakavaṇṇaṃ paṭaṃ pārupitvā gandhamālādihatthā jetavanābhimukhī [P 4.0188] gacchantī “imāya velāya kuhiṃ gacchasī”ti vutte “kiṃ tumhākaṃ mama gamanaṭṭhānenā”ti vatvā jetavanasamīpe titthiyārāme vasitvā pātova “aggavandanaṃ vandissāmā”ti nagarā nikkhamante upāsakajane jetavane vutthā viya hutvā nagaraṃ pavisati. “Kuhiṃ vutthāsī”ti vutte “kiṃ tumhākaṃ mama vutthaṭṭhānenā”ti vatvā māsaḍḍhamāsaccayena pucchiyamānā “jetavane samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyā vutthāmhī”ti āha. Puthujjanānaṃ “saccaṃ nu kho etaṃ, no”ti kaṅkhaṃ uppādetvā temāsacatumāsaccayena pilotikāhi udaraṃ veṭhetvā gabbhinivaṇṇaṃ dassetvā upari rattapaṭaṃ pārupitvā “samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṭicca gabbho me laddho”ti andhabāle gāhāpetvā aṭṭhanavamāsaccayena udare dārumaṇḍalikaṃ bandhitvā upari rattapaṭaṃ pārupitvā hatthapādapiṭṭhiyo gohanukena koṭṭāpetvā ussade dassetvā kilantindriyā hutvā sāyanhasamaye tathāgate alaṅkatadhammāsane nisīditvā dhammaṃ desente dhammasabhaṃ gantvā tathāgatassa purato ṭhatvā “mahāsamaṇa, mahājanassa tāva dhammaṃ desesi, madhuro te saddo, suphusitaṃ dantāvaraṇaṃ, ahaṃ pana taṃ paṭicca gabbhaṃ labhitvā paripuṇṇagabbhā jātā, neva me sūtigharaṃ jānāsi, na sappitelādīni, sayaṃ akaronto upaṭṭhākānampi aññataraṃ kosalarājānaṃ vā anāthapiṇḍikaṃ vā visākhaṃ upāsikaṃ vā “imissā ciñcamāṇavikāya kattabbayuttaṃ karohī’ti na vadasi, abhiramituṃyeva [V 4.0168] jānāsi, gabbhaparihāraṃ na jānāsī”ti gūthapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā candamaṇḍalaṃ dūsetuṃ vāyamantī viya parisamajjhe tathāgataṃ akkosi. Tathāgato dhammakathaṃ ṭhapetvā sīho viya abhinadanto “bhagini, tayā kathitassa tathabhāvaṃ vā atathabhāvaṃ vā ahañceva tvañca jānāmā”ti āha. Āma, samaṇa, tayā ca mayā ca ñātabhāvenetaṃ jātanti.

She said, 'Very well, sirs, this burden is mine alone; do not worry.' Having spoken thus, she departed. Being skilled in women's wiles, from then on, at the time when the residents of Sāvatthī were leaving Jetavana after hearing a Dhamma talk, she would wrap herself in a cloak the color of an indagopaka beetle, carry perfumes and garlands, and walk towards Jetavana. When asked, 'Where are you going at this time?' she would reply, 'What is it to you where I go?' and would stay in a monastery of the heretics near Jetavana. Early in the morning, as the lay devotees were leaving the city, saying, 'We will go to pay homage,' she would enter the city as if she had stayed in Jetavana. When asked, 'Where did you stay?' she would reply, 'What is it to you where I stayed?' After a month or a half-month, when questioned, she said, 'I stayed in the same Fragrant Chamber with the ascetic Gotama.' She created doubt among the common people as to whether this was true or not. After three or four months, wrapping her belly with rags to show the appearance of pregnancy and covering herself with a red upper cloth, she made the fools believe her, saying, 'I have conceived on account of the ascetic Gotama.' After eight or nine months, she tied a wooden disc to her belly, covered it with a red cloth, and had the backs of her hands and feet struck with a cow's jawbone to show swelling. With weary faculties, in the evening, when the Tathāgata was seated on the adorned Dhamma-seat teaching the Dhamma, she went to the Dhamma assembly. Standing before the Tathāgata, she reviled him in the midst of the assembly, like one trying to defile the orb of the moon with a lump of dung: 'Great ascetic, you teach the Dhamma to the people; your voice is sweet, and your lips are well-formed. But I, having conceived on account of you, am now far along in pregnancy. You neither arrange for a lying-in room, nor for ghee, oil, and so on. Not doing it yourself, you do not even tell one of your attendants—King Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, or the lay devotee Visākhā—"Do what is necessary for this Ciñcamāṇavikā." You only know how to enjoy yourself; you do not know how to provide for a pregnancy.' The Tathāgata stopped his Dhamma talk and, roaring like a lion, said: 'Sister, whether what you have said is true or untrue, only I and you know.' 'Yes, ascetic,' she said, 'this has come about as a matter known by you and me.'

Tasmiṃ [M 4.0190] khaṇe sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjamāno “ciñcamāṇavikā tathāgataṃ abhūtena akkosatī”ti ñatvā “imaṃ vatthuṃ sodhessāmī”ti catūhi devaputtehi saddhiṃ āgami. Devaputtā mūsikapotakā hutvā dārumaṇḍalikassa [P 4.0189] bandhanarajjuke ekappahāreneva chindiṃsu, pārutapaṭaṃ vāto ukkhipi, dārumaṇḍalikaṃ patamānaṃ tassā pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ pati, ubho aggapādā chijjiṃsu. Manussā uṭṭhāya “kāḷakaṇṇi, sammāsambuddhaṃ akkosasī”ti sīse kheḷaṃ pātetvā leḍḍudaṇḍādihatthā jetavanā nīhariṃsu. Athassā tathāgatassa cakkhupathaṃ atikkantakāle mahāpathavī bhijjitvā vivaramadāsi, avīcito aggijālā uṭṭhahi. Sā kuladattiyaṃ kambalaṃ pārupamānā viya gantvā avīcimhi nibbatti. Aññatitthiyānaṃ lābhasakkāro parihāyi, dasabalassa bhiyyosomattāya vaḍḍhi. Punadivase dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, ciñcamāṇavikā evaṃ uḷāraguṇaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ abhūtena akkositvā mahāvināsaṃ pattā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi esā maṃ abhūtena akkositvā mahāvināsaṃ pattā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

At that moment, Sakka’s throne showed signs of heat. Reflecting, he realized: 'Ciñcamāṇavikā is falsely reviling the Tathāgata.' Thinking, 'I shall clear up this matter,' he came with four devas. The devas, becoming young mice, severed the ropes binding the wooden disc with a single bite. The wind blew up her cloak, and as the wooden disc fell, it struck the tops of her feet, and the toes of both feet were cut off. The people rose up, crying: 'You wretch! You revile the Perfectly Enlightened One!' They spat on her head and, with clods and sticks in hand, drove her out of Jetavana. Then, as soon as she passed out of the Tathāgata’s sight, the great earth split open and gave way; flames arose from the Avīci hell. As if wrapping herself in a red blanket given by her family, she went and was reborn in Avīci. The gain and honor of the other sectarians declined, while that of the Ten-Powered One increased even more. The next day, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, Ciñcamāṇavikā, having falsely reviled the Perfectly Enlightened One—one of such noble quality and the supreme recipient of offerings—has met with great ruin.' The Teacher arrived and asked: 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' When they told him, he said: 'Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, she falsely reviled me and met with great ruin.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, phullapadumasassirikamukhattā panassa “padumakumāro”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā āgami. Athassa mātā kālamakāsi. Rājā aññaṃ aggamahesiṃ katvā puttassa uparajjaṃ adāsi. Aparabhāge rājā paccantaṃ kupitaṃ vūpasametuṃ aggamahesiṃ āha “bhadde, idheva vasa, ahaṃ paccantaṃ kupitaṃ vūpasametuṃ gacchāmī”ti vatvā “nāhaṃ idheva vasissāmi, ahampi gamissāmī”ti vutte yuddhabhūmiyā ādīnavaṃ dassetvā “yāva mamāgamanā anukkaṇṭhamānā vasa, ahaṃ padumakumāraṃ yathā tava kattabbakiccesu appamatto hoti, evaṃ āṇāpetvā gamissāmī”ti vatvā tathā katvā gantvā paccāmitte palāpetvā janapadaṃ santappetvā paccāgantvā bahinagare khandhāvāraṃ nivāsesi[V 4.0169]. Bodhisatto pitu āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā [M 4.0191] nagaraṃ [P 4.0190] alaṅkārāpetvā rājagehaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā ekakova tassā santikaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of his chief queen. Because his face was as radiant as a full-blown lotus, they named him Prince Paduma. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and returned. Then his mother passed away. The king appointed another chief queen and gave his son the position of viceroy. Later, when the king was about to go to pacify a rebellion on the border, he said to the chief queen: 'Dear lady, stay here; I am going to pacify the border rebellion.' When she said, 'I will not stay here; I too will go,' he pointed out the dangers of the battlefield and said: 'Stay here without anxiety until my return. I will instruct Prince Paduma to be diligent in his duties toward you, and then I will go.' Having done so, he departed. After putting the enemies to flight and pacifying the country, he returned and set up camp outside the city. The Bodhisatta, knowing of his father’s arrival, had the city decorated and the royal palace cleaned, and then went alone into her presence.

Sā tassa rūpasampattiṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā ahosi. Bodhisatto taṃ vanditvā “amma, kiṃ amhākaṃ kattabba”nti pucchi. Atha naṃ “ammāti maṃ vadasī”ti uṭṭhāya hatthe gahetvā “sayanaṃ abhiruhā”ti āha. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Yāva rājā na āgacchati, tāva ubhopi kilesaratiyā ramissāmā”ti. “Amma, tvaṃ mama mātā ca sasāmikā ca, mayā sapariggaho mātugāmo nāma kilesavasena indriyāni bhinditvā na olokitapubbo, kathaṃ tayā saddhiṃ evarūpaṃ kiliṭṭhakammaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā dve tayo vāre kathetvā tasmiṃ anicchamāne “mama vacanaṃ na karosī”ti āha. “Āma, na karomī”ti. “Tena hi rañño kathetvā sīsaṃ te chindāpessāmī”ti. Mahāsatto “tava ruciṃ karohī”ti vatvā taṃ lajjāpetvā pakkāmi.

She, seeing the perfection of his form, became infatuated with him. The Bodhisatta paid homage to her and asked: 'Mother, what is to be done by us?' Then, exclaiming, 'You call me "mother"?' she rose, took his hand, and said: 'Ascend the bed.' 'For what reason?' he asked. 'Until the king arrives, we shall both delight in the pleasure of defilement.' 'Mother, you are my mother and a married woman. I have never before, driven by defilement, broken my senses and looked upon a woman who belongs to another. How could I commit such a defiled act with you?' She repeated her request two or three times, but when he still refused, she said: 'Will you not do my bidding?' 'Indeed, I will not,' he replied. 'In that case, I shall tell the king and have your head cut off.' The Great Being said: 'Do as you please,' and having shamed her, he departed.

Sā bhītatasitā cintesi “sace ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ pitu ārocessati, jīvitaṃ me natthi, ahameva puretaraṃ kathessāmī”ti bhattaṃ abhuñjitvā kiliṭṭhalomavatthaṃ nivāsetvā sarīre nakharājiyo dassetvā “kuhiṃ devīti rañño pucchanakāle “gilānā’ti katheyyāthā”ti paricārikānaṃ saññaṃ datvā gilānālayaṃ katvā nipajji. Rājāpi nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nivesanaṃ āruyha taṃ apassanto “kuhiṃ devī”ti pucchitvā “gilānā”ti sutvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā “kiṃ te devi, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Sā tassa vacanaṃ asuṇantī viya hutvā dve tayo vāre pucchitā “mahārāja, kasmā kathesi, tuṇhī hohi, sasāmikaitthiyo nāma mādisā na hontī”ti vatvā “kena tvaṃ viheṭhitāsi, sīghaṃ me kathehi[P 4.0191], sīsamassa chindissāmī”ti vutte “kaṃsi tvaṃ, mahārāja, nagare ṭhapetvā gato”ti vatvā “padumakumāra”nti vutte “so mayhaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā ‘tāta, mā evaṃ karohi, ahaṃ tava mātā’ti vuccamānopi ‘ṭhapetvā maṃ añño rājā natthi, ahaṃ taṃ gehe karitvā kilesaratiyā ramissāmī’ti maṃ kesesu [M 4.0192] gahetvā aparāparaṃ luñcitvā attano vacanaṃ akarontiṃ maṃ pātetvā koṭṭetvā gato”ti āha.

She, frightened and terrified, thought: 'If he reports this to his father first, my life is forfeit. I myself must speak first.' Without eating her meal, she put on a soiled garment, showed scratch marks on her body, and gave instructions to her attendants, saying: 'When the king asks where the queen is, tell him she is ill.' Then, feigning illness, she lay down. The king, having circumambulated the city and ascended to his residence, did not see her and asked: 'Where is the queen?' Hearing she was ill, he entered the royal chamber and asked: 'What ails you, queen?' As if not hearing his words, she remained silent. When he had asked two or three times, she said: 'Great king, why do you speak? Be silent. Married women like me are not treated thus.' When he said: 'Who has harmed you? Tell me quickly, I will cut off his head,' she replied: 'Whom did you leave in charge of the city when you went away?' When he said: 'Prince Paduma,' she said: 'He came to my dwelling place and, though I said, "Dear son, do not do this, I am your mother," he said, "Apart from me, there is no other king. I will make you mine and delight in the pleasure of defilement." Then he seized me by the hair, dragged me to and fro, and when I would not do his bidding, he threw me down, beat me, and left.'

Rājā anupaparikkhitvāva āsīviso viya kuddho purise āṇāpesi “gacchatha, bhaṇe, padumakumāraṃ bandhitvā ānethā”ti. Te nagaraṃ avattharantā viya tassa gehaṃ gantvā taṃ bandhitvā paharitvā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā rattakaṇaveramālaṃ gīvāyaṃ paṭimuñcitvā vajjhaṃ katvā ānayiṃsu[V 4.0170]. So “deviyā idaṃ kamma”nti ñatvā “bho purisā, nāhaṃ rañño dosakārako, nipparādhohamasmī”ti vilapanto āgacchati. Sakalanagaraṃ saṃkhubbhitvā “rājā kira mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvā mahāpadumakumāraṃ ghātāpesī”ti sannipatitvā rājakumārassa pādamūle nipatitvā “idaṃ te sāmi, ananucchavika”nti mahāsaddena paridevi. Atha naṃ netvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā disvāva cittaṃ niggaṇhituṃ asakkonto “ayaṃ arājāva rājalīḷaṃ karoti, mama putto hutvā aggamahesiyā aparajjhati, gacchatha naṃ corapapāte pātetvā vināsaṃ pāpethā”ti āha. Mahāsatto “na mayhaṃ, tāta, evarūpo aparādho atthi, mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvā mā maṃ nāsehī”ti pitaraṃ yāci. So tassa kathaṃ na gaṇhi.

The king, without any investigation, became enraged like a venomous snake and ordered his men: 'Go, sirs, bind Prince Paduma and bring him here.' As if overrunning the city, they went to his house, bound him, struck him, tied his hands tightly behind his back, placed a garland of red oleanders around his neck, and, having marked him for execution, brought him forth. Knowing that 'this is the queen’s doing,' he lamented as he was brought, crying: 'Sirs, I have not wronged the king! I am innocent!' The entire city was in turmoil. The people gathered and, falling at the prince’s feet, wailed with a great cry: 'The king, they say, taking the word of a woman, is having the great Prince Paduma executed! This, lord, is unfitting for you!' Then they brought him and showed him to the king.
