The moment the king saw him, unable to control his anger, he declared: 'This one acts with royal airs as if he were king; though my own son, he offends the chief queen! Go, cast him from the robbers’ precipice and bring him to ruin!' The Great Being pleaded with his father: 'Father, I have committed no such offense. Do not destroy me on the word of a woman!' But he did not heed his words.

Tato soḷasasahassā antepurikā “tāta mahāpadumakumāra, attano ananucchavikaṃ idaṃ laddha”nti mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Sabbe [P 4.0192] khattiyamahāsālādayopi amaccaparijanāpi “deva, kumāro sīlācāraguṇasampanno vaṃsānurakkhito rajjadāyādo, mā naṃ mātugāmassa vacanaṃ gahetvā anupaparikkhitvāva vināsehi, raññā nāma nisammakārinā bhavitabba”nti vatvā satta gāthā abhāsiṃsu –

Then sixteen thousand palace women cried out with a great cry: 'Dear Prince Mahāpaduma, you have met with this unfitting fate!' All the noble khattiyas, ministers, and attendants also said: 'Your Majesty, the prince is endowed with morality, good conduct, and virtue, a protector of the lineage, and the heir to the kingdom. Do not, taking the word of a woman and without investigation, destroy him. A king should be one who acts with careful consideration.' Having said this, they spoke these seven verses:

106.

106.

“Nādaṭṭhā parato dosaṃ, aṇuṃ thūlāni sabbaso;

Issaro paṇaye daṇḍaṃ, sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiya.

Not having seen for himself the fault in another, whether subtle or gross in every way, a ruler should not impose punishment without personal investigation.

107.

107.

“Yo ca appaṭivekkhitvā, daṇḍaṃ kubbati khattiyo;

Sakaṇṭakaṃ so gilati, jaccandhova samakkhikaṃ.

The ruler who, without investigation, imposes punishment, swallows that which has thorns, like one born blind swallowing food with flies.

108.

108.

“Adaṇḍiyaṃ [M 4.0193] daṇḍayati, daṇḍiyañca adaṇḍiyaṃ;

Andhova visamaṃ maggaṃ, na jānāti samāsamaṃ.

He punishes one who is not to be punished, and leaves unpunished one who is to be punished; like a blind man on an uneven path, he knows not the level from the unlevel.

109.

109.

“Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni, aṇuṃ thūlāni sabbaso;

Sudiṭṭhamanusāseyya, sa ve voharitu marahati.

But he who, having well examined these matters, subtle and gross in every way, would rule justly, he is truly worthy to administer the law.

110.

110.

“Nekantamudunā sakkā, ekantatikhiṇena vā;

Attaṃ mahante ṭhapetuṃ, tasmā ubhayamācare.

Not by extreme gentleness alone, nor by extreme harshness, can one establish oneself in greatness. Therefore, one should practice both.

111.

111.

“Paribhūto [V 4.0171] mudu hoti, atitikkho ca veravā;

Etañca ubhayaṃ ñatvā, anumajjhaṃ samācare.

The gentle one is despised, while the overly harsh one creates enemies; having understood both these, one should follow a middle course.

112.

112.

“Bahumpi ratto bhāseyya, duṭṭhopi bahu bhāsati;

Na itthikāraṇā rāja, puttaṃ ghātetumarahasī”ti.

One who is infatuated may speak much, and a wicked one also speaks much; for a woman’s sake, O king, you should not have your son killed.

Tattha nādaṭṭhāti na adisvā. Paratoti parassa. Sabbasoti sabbāni. Aṇuṃthūlānīti khuddakamahantāni vajjāni. Sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiyāti parassa vacanaṃ gahetvā attano paccakkhaṃ akatvā pathavissaro rājā daṇḍaṃ na paṇaye na paṭṭhapeyya. Mahāsammatarājakālasmiñhi satato uttari daṇḍo nāma natthi, tāḷanagarahaṇapabbājanato uddhaṃ hatthapādacchedanaghātanaṃ nāma natthi, pacchā kakkhaḷarājūnaṃyeva kāle etaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ sandhāya te amaccā “ekanteneva parassa dosaṃ sāmaṃ adisvā kātuṃ na yutta”nti kathentā evamāhaṃsu.

Herein, 'nādaṭṭhā' means not having seen. 'Parato' means of another. 'Sabbaso' means in every way. 'Aṇuṃthūlāni' means small and great faults. 'Sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiyā' means that a king, a lord of the earth, should not impose or establish punishment by taking another’s word without personally investigating and making it clear to himself. For in the time of King Mahāsammata, there was no punishment beyond beating, censure, and banishment; there was no cutting off of hands and feet or execution. It was only later, in the time of harsh kings, that such things arose. With reference to this, those ministers, saying, 'It is not at all proper to act without seeing another’s fault for oneself,' spoke thus.

Yo ca appaṭivekkhitvāti mahārāja, evaṃ appaṭivekkhitvā dosānucchavike daṇḍe paṇetabbe yo rājā agatigamane ṭhito taṃ dosaṃ appaṭivekkhitvā hatthacchedādidaṇḍaṃ karoti, so [P 4.0193] attano dukkhakāraṇaṃ karonto sakaṇṭakaṃ bhojanaṃ gilati nāma, jaccandho viya ca samakkhikaṃ bhuñjati nāma. Adaṇḍiyanti yo adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍapaṇetabbañca daṇḍetvā daṇḍiyañca daṇḍapaṇetabbaṃ adaṇḍetvā attano rucimeva karoti, so andho viya visamaṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno, na jānāti samāsamaṃ, tato pāsāṇādīsu pakkhalanto andho viya catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti [M 4.0194] attho. Etāni ṭhānānīti etāni daṇḍiyādaṇḍiyakāraṇāni ceva daṇḍiyakāraṇesupi aṇuṃthūlāni ca sabbāni sudiṭṭhaṃ disvā anusāseyya, sa ve voharituṃ rajjamanusāsituṃ arahatīti attho.

'And who, without investigation': O great king, thus, when a king who is biased and acts partially imposes a punishment like cutting off hands without investigating whether the punishment is appropriate for the offense, he, creating the cause of his own suffering, is said to swallow food with thorns, or like one blind from birth, he is said to eat food full of flies. 'One who is not to be punished': he who punishes one who should not be punished and leaves unpunished one who should be punished, acting only according to his own preference, is like a blind man who has entered an uneven path; he does not know the level from the unlevel. Then, just as a blind man stumbling over stones and the like, he attains great suffering in the four woeful states—this is the meaning. 'These matters': these are the grounds for punishing and not punishing, and even within the grounds for punishment, all aspects, small and great. Having seen these well, one should govern. Such a one is truly worthy to judge and to rule the kingdom—this is the meaning.

Attaṃ mahante ṭhapetunti evarūpo anuppanne bhoge uppādetvā uppanne thāvare katvā attānaṃ mahante uḷāre issariye ṭhapetuṃ na sakkotīti attho. Mudūti mudurājā raṭṭhavāsīnaṃ paribhūto hoti avaññāto, so rajjaṃ niccoraṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Veravāti atitikkhassa pana sabbepi raṭṭhavāsino verino hontīti so veravā nāma hoti. Anumajjhanti anubhūtaṃ mudutikhiṇabhāvānaṃ majjhaṃ samācare, amudu atikkho hutvā rajjaṃ kāreyyāti attho. Na itthikāraṇāti pāpaṃ lāmakaṃ mātugāmaṃ nissāya vaṃsānurakkhakaṃ chattadāyādaṃ puttaṃ ghātetuṃ nārahasi, mahārājāti.

'To establish oneself in greatness': The meaning is that such a person who is either too soft or too harsh is not able to generate wealth that has not yet arisen, make stable the wealth that has arisen, or establish himself in great and lofty sovereignty. 'Gentle': A gentle king is despised and looked down upon by the citizens; he cannot keep the kingdom free from thieves. 'Creates enemies': As for one who is too harsh, all the citizens become his enemies; thus he is called one who has enemies. 'A middle course': One should practice the middle way between gentleness and harshness. The meaning is that one should rule being neither too soft nor too harsh. 'Not for a woman’s sake': O great king, you should not kill your son, who is the protector of the lineage and heir to the throne, by relying on a wicked and base woman.

Evaṃ [V 4.0172] nānākāraṇehi kathentāpi amaccā attano kathaṃ gāhāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Bodhisattopi yācanto attano kathaṃ gāhāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. Andhabālo pana rājā “gacchatha naṃ corapapāte khipathā”ti āṇāpento aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, even though they spoke with various reasons, the ministers could not make the king accept their words. Even the Bodhisatta, though pleading, could not make him accept his words. But the blind and foolish king, ordering, 'Go, throw him from the robbers' precipice,' spoke the eighth verse:

113.

113.

“Sabbova loko ekato, itthī ca ayamekikā;

Tenāhaṃ paṭipajjissaṃ, gacchatha pakkhipatheva ta”nti.

“The whole world is on one side, and this woman is alone; therefore, I will act [on her word]. Go, just cast him down the precipice.”

Tattha tenāhanti yena kāraṇena sabbo loko ekato kumārasseva pakkho hutvā ṭhito, ayañca itthī ekikāva, tena kāraṇena ahaṃ imissā vacanaṃ paṭipajjissaṃ, gacchatha taṃ pabbataṃ āropetvā papāte khipathevāti.

Therein, 'therefore, I will act' means: because the whole world stood united on the prince’s side, and this woman was all alone, for that reason I will comply with her words. Go, take him up the mountain and throw him into the precipice.

Evaṃ vutte soḷasasahassāsu rājaitthīsu ekāpi sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, sakalanagaravāsino bāhā paggayha kanditvā kese vikirayamānā vilapiṃsu. Rājā “ime imassa papāte khipanaṃ [P 4.0194] paṭibāheyyu”nti saparivāro gantvā mahājanassa paridevantasseva naṃ uddhaṃpādaṃ avaṃsiraṃ katvā gāhāpetvā papāte khipāpesi. Athassa mettānubhāvena pabbate adhivatthā devatā “mā bhāyi mahāpadumā”ti taṃ samassāsetvā [M 4.0195] ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā hadaye ṭhapetvā dibbasamphassaṃ pharāpetvā otaritvā pabbatapāde patiṭṭhitanāgarājassa phaṇagabbhe ṭhapesi. Nāgarājā bodhisattaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ netvā attano yasaṃ majjhe bhinditvā adāsi. So tattha ekasaṃvaccharaṃ vasitvā “manussapathaṃ gamissāmī”ti vatvā “kataraṃ ṭhāna”nti vutte “himavantaṃ gantvā pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Nāgarājā “sādhū”ti taṃ gahetvā manussapathe patiṭṭhāpetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Sopi himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro tattha paṭivasati.

When this was said, not one of the sixteen thousand royal women could maintain her composure. All the city-dwellers raised their arms, wept, and wailed, scattering their hair. The king, thinking, 'They might prevent him from being thrown into the precipice,' went with his retinue and, while the crowd was lamenting, had him seized, turned upside down with his feet up and head down, and thrown into the precipice. Then, by the power of the Bodhisatta’s loving-kindness, a deity dwelling on the mountain comforted him, saying, 'Fear not, Mahāpaduma,' and taking him with both hands, placed him on her breast, suffused him with divine touch to comfort him, descended, and set him down on the hollow of the hood of the Nāga king established at the foot of the mountain. The Nāga king took the Bodhisatta to the Nāga realm and, dividing his own majesty and wealth in half, gave it to him. The Bodhisatta lived there for one year and then said, 'O noble Nāga king, I will return to the human world.' When asked, 'To which place will you go?' he replied, 'I will go to the Himalayas and become a renunciate.' The Nāga king said, 'Very well,' took him and set him on the path to the human world, gave him the requisites for a renunciate, and returned to his own abode. The Bodhisatta then entered the Himalayas, was ordained as an ascetic, developed meditative attainments and higher knowledge, and lived there subsisting on roots and fruits.

Atheko bārāṇasivāsī vanacarako taṃ ṭhānaṃ patto mahāsattaṃ sañjānitvā “nanu tvaṃ deva, mahāpadumakumāro”ti vatvā “āma, sammā”ti vutte taṃ vanditvā katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rañño ārocesi “deva, putto te himavantapadese isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasati, ahaṃ tassa santike vasitvā āgato”ti. “Paccakkhato te diṭṭho”ti? “Āma devā”ti. Rājā mahābalakāyaparivuto tattha gantvā vanapariyante khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā amaccagaṇaparivuto paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā kañcanarūpasadisaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre nisinnaṃ mahāsattaṃ disvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Amaccāpi vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā [V 4.0173] nisīdiṃsu. Bodhisattopi rājānaṃ paṭipucchitvā paṭisanthāramakāsi. Atha naṃ rājā “tāta, mayā tvaṃ gambhīre [P 4.0195] papāte khipāpito, kathaṃ sajīvitosī”ti pucchanto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then a forest-dweller from Bārāṇasī arrived at that place, recognized the Great Being, and said, “Are you not, sire, Prince Mahāpaduma?” When he replied, “Yes, friend,” he paid homage to him, stayed there for a few days, then went to Bārāṇasī and informed the king: “Sire, your son has renounced the world as an ascetic in the Himalayan region and dwells in a leaf-hut. I stayed near him and have returned.” “Did you see him with your own eyes?” “Yes, sire.” The king, surrounded by a great army, went there, set up camp at the edge of the forest, and with his retinue of ministers approached the leaf-hut. Seeing the Great Being seated at the door of the leaf-hut, looking like a golden statue, he paid homage and sat to one side. The ministers also paid homage, offered greetings, and sat down. The Bodhisatta also inquired after the king and offered greetings in return. Then the king, wishing to ask him, “Dear son, when I had you thrown into a deep precipice, how did you survive?” spoke the ninth verse:

114.

114.

“Anekatāle narake, gambhīre ca suduttare;

Pātito giriduggasmiṃ, kena tvaṃ tattha nāmarī”ti.

“Into a chasm many palms deep, profound and very hard to climb out of; cast into a mountain abyss, by what means did you not die there?”

Tattha anekatāleti anekatālappamāṇe. Nāmarīti na amari.

Therein, ‘anekatāle’ means of the measure of many palm trees. ‘Nāmarī’ means ‘na amari’, he did not die.

Tatoparaṃ –

Thereafter, the Great Being, wishing to inform his father how he survived, said:

115.

115.

“Nāgo jātaphaṇo tattha, thāmavā girisānujo;

Paccaggahi maṃ bhogehi, tenāhaṃ tattha nāmariṃ.

“A Nāga with hood displayed, mighty, born of the mountain slopes, received me with his coils; therefore I did not die there.”

116.

116.

“Ehi [M 4.0196] taṃ paṭinessāmi, rājaputta sakaṃ gharaṃ;

Rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasi.

“Come, prince, I will lead you back to your own home. Rule the kingdom, blessed one; what will you do in the forest?”

117.

117.

“Yathā gilitvā baḷisaṃ, uddhareyya salohitaṃ;

Uddharitvā sukhī assa, evaṃ passāmi attanaṃ.

“Just as one who has swallowed a fishhook would vomit it out along with blood; having vomited it out, one would be at ease; so do I see myself.”

118.

118.

“Kiṃ nu tvaṃ baḷisaṃ brūsi, kiṃ tvaṃ brūsi salohitaṃ;

Kiṃ nu tvaṃ ubbhataṃ brūsi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

“What do you call the fishhook? What do you call the ‘with blood’? What do you call the ‘vomited out’? Tell me this, as I ask.”

119.

119.

“Kāmāhaṃ baḷisaṃ brūmi, hatthiassaṃ salohitaṃ;

Cattāhaṃ ubbhataṃ brūmi, evaṃ jānāhi khattiyā”ti. –

“Sensual pleasures I call the fishhook; elephants and horses, the ‘with blood’. Renunciation I call the ‘vomited out’; know this, O King.”

Imāsu pañcasu ekantarikā tisso gāthā bodhisattassa, dve rañño.

Among these five alternating verses, three are the Bodhisatta’s and two are the king’s.

Tattha [V 4.0174] paccaggahi manti pabbatapatanakāle devatāya pariggahetvā dibbasamphassena samassāsetvā upanītaṃ maṃ paṭiggaṇhi, gahetvā ca pana nāgabhavanaṃ ānetvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā “manussapathaṃ maṃ nehī”ti vutto maṃ manussapathaṃ ānesi. Ahaṃ idhāgantvā pabbajito, iti tena devatāya ca nāgarājassa ca ānubhāvena ahaṃ tattha nāmarinti sabbaṃ ārocesi.

Therein, paccaggahi maṃ means: at the time of falling from the mountain, having been taken hold of by a deity, comforted with a divine touch, and brought near, the Nāga king received me. And having taken me to the Nāga realm and given me great glory, when I said, “Take me to the human world,” he brought me to the human path. Having come here, I became a renunciate. Thus, by the power of that deity and the Nāga king, I did not die there—he recounted everything.

Ehīti rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā somanassappatto hutvā “tāta, ahaṃ bālabhāvena itthiyā vacanaṃ gahetvā evaṃ sīlācārasampanne tayi aparajjhiṃ, khamāhi me dosa”nti pādesu nipatitvā “uṭṭhehi, mahārāja, khamāma te dosaṃ, ito paraṃ puna mā evaṃ anisammakārī bhaveyyāsī”ti vutte “tāta, tvaṃ attano kulasantakaṃ setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjaṃ anusāsanto mayhaṃ khamasi nāmā”ti evamāha.

Hearing his words, the king was filled with joy and said, “Son, in my foolishness, having taken a woman’s words, I wronged you, who are so accomplished in virtue and conduct. Forgive me my fault,” and fell at his feet. When the Bodhisatta said, “Rise, great king, I forgive you your fault. From now on, do not be so unreflecting in your actions,” the king said, “Son, you truly forgive me if you will raise aloft the white umbrella, the possession of your lineage, and rule the kingdom.”

Uddharitvāti [P 4.0196] hadayavakkādīni asampattameva taṃ uddharitvā sukhī assa. Evaṃ passāmi attananti attānaṃ mahārāja, evaṃ ahampi puna sotthibhāvappattaṃ gilitabaḷisaṃ purisamiva attānaṃ passāmīti. “Kiṃ nu tva”nti idaṃ rājā tamatthaṃ vitthārato sotuṃ pucchati. Kāmāhanti pañca kāmaguṇe ahaṃ. Hatthiassaṃ salohitanti evaṃ hatthiassarathavāhanaṃ sattaratanādivibhavaṃ “salohita”nti brūmi. Cattāhanti cattaṃ ahaṃ, yadā taṃ sabbampi cattaṃ hoti pariccattaṃ, taṃ dānāhaṃ “ubbhata”nti brūmi.

Uddharitvā means that even if it has not reached the heart, kidneys, and so on, having drawn it out, one would be happy. Evaṃ passāmi attanaṃ means: O great king, I see myself thus; I see myself as having again attained a state of well-being, like a man who has swallowed a fishhook. Kiṃ nu tvaṃ—this the king asks to hear the matter in detail. Kāmāhaṃ refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. Hatthiassaṃ salohitaṃ means: thus I call elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, the seven treasures, and other wealth ‘the bloody thing’. Cattāhaṃ means ‘I who have relinquished’; when all that is given up, relinquished, then I call that ‘drawn out’.

“Iti [M 4.0197] kho, mahārāja, mayhaṃ rajjena kiccaṃ natthi, tvaṃ pana dasa rājadhamme akopetvā agatigamanaṃ pahāya dhammena rajjaṃ kārehī”ti mahāsatto pitu ovādaṃ adāsi. So rājā roditvā paridevitvā nagaraṃ gacchanto antarāmagge amacce pucchi. “Ahaṃ kaṃ nissāya evarūpena ācāraguṇasampannena puttena viyogaṃ patto”ti? “Aggamahesiṃ, devā”ti. Rājā taṃ uddhaṃpādaṃ gāhāpetvā corapapāte khipāpetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi.

“Great king, I have no need for the kingdom. But you, without violating the ten royal virtues, abandoning the four wrong paths, should rule the kingdom righteously,” the Great Being thus gave advice to his father. The king, weeping and lamenting, as he went back to the city, asked his ministers along the way, “On whose account have I been separated from a son possessed of such conduct and virtue?” “On account of the chief queen, sire,” they replied. The king then had her seized by the feet and thrown into the robbers’ precipice. Having entered the city, he ruled righteously.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepesā maṃ akkositvā mahāvināsaṃ pattā”ti vatvā –

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, “Monks, in the past also, Ciñca Māṇavikā, having slandered me, met with great ruin,” and then spoke:

120.

120.

“Ciñcamāṇavikā [V 4.0175] mātā, devadatto ca me pitā;

Ānando paṇḍito nāgo, sāriputto ca devatā;

Rājaputto ahaṃ āsiṃ, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti. –

“Ciñca Māṇavikā was the mother, Devadatta was my father; Ānanda the wise nāga, Sāriputta the deity; I was the royal son—remember this birth-story thus.”

Osānagāthāya jātakaṃ samodhānesi.

With this concluding verse, he identified the Jātaka.

Mahāpadumajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāpaduma Jātaka, the ninth.

[473] 10. Mittāmittajātakavaṇṇanā

[473] 10. Commentary on the Mittāmitta Jātaka

Kāni kammānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño atthacarakaṃ amaccaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira rañño bahūpakāro ahosi. Athassa rājā atirekasammānaṃ kāresi. Avasesā naṃ asahamānā “deva, asuko nāma amacco tumhākaṃ anatthakārako”ti paribhindiṃsu. Rājā taṃ pariggaṇhanto kiñci dosaṃ adisvā “ahaṃ imassa kiñci dosaṃ na passāmi, kathaṃ nu kho sakkā mayā imassa mittabhāvaṃ vā amittabhāvaṃ vā jānitu”nti cintetvā “imaṃ pañhaṃ ṭhapetvā tathāgataṃ [P 4.0197] añño jānituṃ na sakkhissati, gantvā pucchissāmī”ti bhuttapātarāso satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, kathaṃ nu kho sakkā purisena attano mittabhāvaṃ vā amittabhāvaṃ vā jānitu”nti pucchi. Atha naṃ satthā “pubbepi mahārāja, paṇḍitā imaṃ pañhaṃ cintetvā paṇḍite pucchitvā tehi kathitavasena [M 4.0198] ñatvā amitte vajjetvā mitte seviṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Regarding ‘What actions…’, the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a minister of the King of Kosala who served his interests. This minister had been of great benefit to the king, who in return showed him excessive honor. The other ministers, unable to bear this, slandered him, saying, ‘Sire, this named minister is working for your ruin.’ The king, investigating him and finding no fault, thought, ‘I see no fault in him—how can I know whether he is a friend or a foe?’ Pondering further, ‘No one but the Tathāgata can answer this question,’ he went to the Teacher after his morning meal and asked, ‘Venerable sir, how can a person know whether someone is their friend or foe?’ The Teacher replied, ‘Great king, even in the past, the wise pondered this question, and upon asking the wise and knowing through their answers, they avoided foes and cultivated friends.’ At the king's request, he then recounted the past tale.”

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. Tadā bārāṇasirañño ekaṃ atthacarakaṃ amaccaṃ sesā paribhindiṃsu. Rājā tassa dosaṃ apassanto “kathaṃ nu kho sakkā mittaṃ vā amittaṃ vā ñātu”nti mahāsattaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his advisor in matters of welfare and Dhamma. At that time, the other ministers slandered a minister who acted for the king’s welfare. The king, seeing no fault in him, and wondering, “How indeed can one know a friend from a foe?” questioned the Great Being, speaking the first verse:

121.

121.

“Kāni kammāni kubbānaṃ, kathaṃ viññū parakkame;

Amittaṃ jāneyya medhāvī, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito”ti.

“By what actions being performed, and how should a discerning person strive, so that a wise and intelligent person may recognize an enemy after seeing and hearing?”

Tassattho – kāni kammāni karontaṃ medhāvī paṇḍito puriso cakkhunā disvā vā sotena [V 4.0176] sutvā vā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ amitto”ti jāneyya, tassa jānanatthāya kathaṃ viññū parakkameyyāti.

The meaning is: By seeing a person performing what actions with the eye or hearing with the ear should a wise and intelligent person recognize, ‘This is my enemy’? And for the sake of knowing that, how should a discerning person strive?

Athassa amittalakkhaṇaṃ kathento āha –

Then, describing the characteristics of an enemy to him, he said:

122.

122.

“Na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandati;

Cakkhūni cassa na dadāti, paṭilomañca vattati.

“Seeing him, he does not smile, nor does he welcome him; he does not look him in the eye, and he behaves in a contrary manner.

123.

123.

“Amitte tassa bhajati, mitte tassa na sevati;

Vaṇṇakāme nivāreti, akkosante pasaṃsati.

“He associates with that person’s enemies and does not associate with his friends; he discourages those who wish to praise him and praises those who revile him.

124.

124.

“Guyhañca tassa nakkhāti, tassa guyhaṃ na gūhati;

Kammaṃ tassa na vaṇṇeti, paññassa nappasaṃsati.

“He does not reveal his own secrets to him, nor does he keep the other’s secrets; he does not praise his deeds, nor does he commend his wisdom.

125.

125.

“Abhave nandati tassa, bhave tassa na nandati;

Accheraṃ bhojanaṃ laddhā, tassa nuppajjate sati;

Tato naṃ nānukampati, aho sopi labheyyito.

“He rejoices in his decline and does not rejoice in his prosperity; upon obtaining excellent food, the thought of him does not arise, nor does he feel compassion, thinking, ‘Oh, may he also obtain this!’

126.

126.

“Iccete soḷasākārā, amittasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā;

Yehi amittaṃ jāneyya, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito”ti.

“These sixteen characteristics are established in an enemy; by these, a wise person, having seen and heard, should recognize an enemy.”

Mahāsatto [M 4.0199] imā pañca gāthā vatvāna puna –

Having spoken these five verses, the Great Being then further said:

127.

127.

“Kāni [P 4.0198] kammāni kubbānaṃ, kathaṃ viññū parakkame;

Mittaṃ jāneyya medhāvī, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito”ti. –

“By performing what actions, and in what way should a discerning person strive, so that a wise and intelligent person, having seen and heard, may recognize a friend?”

Imāya gāthāya mittalakkhaṇaṃ puṭṭho sesagāthā abhāsi –

Asked by this verse about the characteristics of a friend, he spoke the remaining verses:

128.

128.

“Pavutthaṃ [V 4.0177] tassa sarati, āgataṃ abhinandati;

Tato kelāyito hoti, vācāya paṭinandati.

“He remembers him when he is away and rejoices when he arrives; thus, he is affectionate toward him and welcomes him with kind words.

129.

129.

“Mitte tasseva bhajati, amitte tassa na sevati;

Akkosante nivāreti, vaṇṇakāme pasaṃsati.

“He associates only with that person’s friends and does not associate with his enemies; he restrains those who revile him and praises those who speak his praise.

130.

130.

“Guyhañca tassa akkhāti, tassa guyhañca gūhati;

Kammañca tassa vaṇṇeti, paññaṃ tassa pasaṃsati.

“He reveals his own secrets to him and keeps the other’s secrets; he praises his deeds and commends his wisdom.

131.

131.

“Bhave ca nandati tassa, abhave tassa na nandati;

Accheraṃ bhojanaṃ laddhā, tassa uppajjate sati;

Tato naṃ anukampati, aho sopi labheyyito.

“He rejoices in his prosperity and does not rejoice in his decline; having obtained excellent food, the thought of him arises and he feels compassion, thinking, ‘Oh, may he also obtain this!’

132.

132.

“Iccete soḷasākārā, mittasmiṃ suppatiṭṭhitā;

Yehi mittañca jāneyya, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito”ti.

“These sixteen characteristics are well-established in a friend; by these, a wise person, having seen and heard, should recognize a friend.”

Tattha na naṃ umhayate disvāti taṃ mittaṃ mittapatirūpako disvā sitaṃ na karoti, pahaṭṭhākāraṃ na dasseti. Na ca naṃ paṭinandatīti tassa kathaṃ paggaṇhanto na paṭinandati na tussati. Cakkhūni cassa na dadātīti olokentaṃ na oloketi. Paṭilomañcāti tassa kathaṃ paṭippharati paṭisattu hoti. Vaṇṇakāmeti tassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇante. Nakkhātīti attano guyhaṃ tassa na ācikkhati. Kammaṃ tassāti tena katakammaṃ na vaṇṇayati. Paññassāti assa paññaṃ nappasaṃsati, ñāṇasampadaṃ na pasaṃsati. Abhaveti avaḍḍhiyaṃ. Tassa nuppajjate satīti tassa mittapatirūpakassa “mama mittassapi ito dassāmī”ti sati na uppajjati. Nānukampatīti muducittena na cinteti. Labheyyitoti labheyya ito. Ākārāti kāraṇāni. Pavutthanti videsagataṃ[M 4.0200]. Kelāyitoti kelāyati mamāyati pattheti piheti icchatīti attho. Vācāyāti madhuravacanena taṃ samudācaranto paṭinandati tussati. Sesaṃ vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbaṃ. Rājā [P 4.0199] mahāsattassa kathāya attamano hutvā tassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

Therein, regarding ‘Seeing him, he does not smile’: seeing that person, a friend in name only does not smile, nor show a delighted expression. Regarding ‘nor does he welcome him’: he does not welcome or take pleasure in his speech. Regarding ‘he does not look him in the eye’: when looked at, he does not look back. Regarding ‘and behaves in a contrary manner’: he contradicts his words and acts as an adversary. Regarding ‘those who wish to praise him’: those who speak in his praise. Regarding ‘does not reveal’: he does not tell his own secrets to him. Regarding ‘his deeds’: he does not praise the work done by him. Regarding ‘his wisdom’: he does not praise his wisdom or his attainment of knowledge. Regarding ‘in decline’: in the loss of wealth. Regarding ‘the thought of him does not arise’: the thought, ‘I should give some of this to my friend,’ does not occur to that friend in name only. Regarding ‘nor does he feel compassion’: he does not think of him with a gentle heart. Regarding ‘may he obtain’: he might obtain from this. Regarding ‘characteristics’: reasons. Regarding ‘away’: gone to another country. Regarding ‘he is affectionate’: the meaning is he cherishes, considers him as his own, longs for, and desires him. Regarding ‘with kind words’: he welcomes and is pleased by him, addressing him with sweet speech. The rest is to be understood as the opposite of what was said for the enemy. The king, delighted by the Great Being’s words, bestowed great honor upon him.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, mahārāja, pubbepesa pañho samuṭṭhahi, paṇḍitāva naṃ [V 4.0178] kathayiṃsu, imehi dvattiṃsāya ākārehi mittāmitto jānitabbo”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said: “Thus, O great king, this question arose in the past, and the wise answered it; by these thirty-two characteristics, a friend and an enemy are to be known.” Having said this, he identified the birth story: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself.”

Mittāmittajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Mittāmitta Jātaka is finished.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kuṇālaṃ bhaddasālañca, samuddavāṇija paṇḍitaṃ;

Janasandhaṃ mahākaṇhaṃ, kosiyaṃ sirimantakaṃ.

Kuṇāla, Bhaddasāla, the wise Samuddavāṇija, Janasandha, Mahākaṇha, Kosiya, Sirimantaka,

Padumaṃ mittāmittañca, iccete dasa jātake;

Saṅgāyiṃsu mahātherā, dvādasamhi nipātake.

Paduma and Mittāmitta—these ten Jātakas the Great Elders recited in the twelfth section.

Dvādasakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Twelfth Nipāta is concluded.

13. Terasakanipāto

13. The Nipāta of Thirteen

[474] 1. Ambajātakavaṇṇanā

[474] 1. 1. Commentary on the Amba Jātaka

Ahāsi [V 4.0179][P 4.0200][M 4.0201] me ambaphalāni pubbeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatto hi “ahaṃ buddho bhavissāmi, mayhaṃ samaṇo gotamo neva ācariyo na upajjhāyo”ti ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya jhānaparihīno saṅghaṃ bhinditvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ āgacchanto bahijetavane pathaviyā vivare dinne avīciṃ pāvisi. Tadā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya mahāvināsaṃ patto, avīcimahāniraye nibbatto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya mahāvināsaṃ pattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“He took my mango fruits in the past.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning Devadatta. For Devadatta, having declared, “I will become a Buddha; the ascetic Gotama is neither my teacher nor my preceptor,” renounced his teacher, fell away from his meditative attainments, split the Saṅgha, and, gradually coming to Sāvatthī, entered Avīci when a fissure opened in the earth outside Jetavana. Then the monks raised a discussion in the hall of Dhamma: “Friends, Devadatta, having renounced his teacher, has met with great ruin and has been reborn in the great Avīci hell.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what discussion are you now gathered, monks?” When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Devadatta renounced his teacher and met with great ruin,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa purohitakulaṃ ahivātarogena vinassi. Ekova putto bhittiṃ bhinditvā palāto. So takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhassācariyassa santike tayo vede ca avasesasippāni ca uggahetvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā nikkhanto “desacārittaṃ jānissāmī”ti caranto ekaṃ paccantanagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ nissāya mahācaṇḍālagāmako ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ gāme paṭivasati, paṇḍito byatto akāle phalaṃ gaṇhāpanamantaṃ jānāti. So pātova vuṭṭhāya kājaṃ ādāya tato gāmā nikkhimitvā araññe ekaṃ ambarukkhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā sattapadamatthake ṭhito taṃ mantaṃ parivattetvā ambarukkhaṃ ekena [P 4.0201] udakapasatena paharati. Rukkhato taṅkhaṇaññeva purāṇapaṇṇāni patanti, navāni uṭṭhahanti, pupphāni pupphitvā patanti, ambaphalāni uṭṭhāya muhutteneva paccitvā madhurāni ojavantāni dibbarasasadisāni hutvā rukkhato patanti. Mahāsatto tāni uccinitvā yāvadatthaṃ khāditvā kājaṃ pūrāpetvā gehaṃ gantvā tāni vikkiṇitvā puttadāraṃ posesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the family of his royal chaplain was destroyed by the snake-wind disease. Only one son broke through the wall and fled. He went to Takkasilā and, under a world-renowned teacher, mastered the three Vedas and the remaining arts. Having paid respects to his teacher, he departed, thinking, 'I will learn the customs of the regions.' While wandering, he reached a border town. Near it was a large outcaste village. At that time, the Bodhisatta was living in that village; he was wise, skilled, and knew a mantra for producing fruit out of season. Rising early in the morning, he took his carrying pole, left the village, and approached a mango tree in the forest. Standing at a distance of seven paces, he recited the mantra and struck the mango tree with a handful of water. Instantly, the old leaves fell from the tree, new ones sprouted, flowers bloomed and fell, and mango fruits appeared, ripened in a moment, and fell from the tree, being sweet, flavorful, and like divine nectar. The Great Being gathered them, ate his fill, filled his baskets, returned home, sold them, and supported his wife and children.

So [V 4.0180][M 4.0202] brāhmaṇakumāro mahāsattaṃ akāle ambapakkāni āharitvā vikkiṇantaṃ disvā “nissaṃsayena tehi mantabalena uppannehi bhavitabbaṃ, imaṃ purisaṃ nissāya idaṃ anagghamantaṃ labhissāmī”ti cintetvā mahāsattassa ambāni āharaṇaniyāmaṃ pariggaṇhanto tathato ñatvā tasmiṃ araññato anāgateyeva tassa gehaṃ gantvā ajānanto viya hutvā tassa bhariyaṃ “kuhiṃ ayyo, ācariyo”ti pucchitvā “araññaṃ gato”ti vutte taṃ āgataṃ āgamayamānova ṭhatvā āgacchantaṃ disvā hatthato pacchiṃ gahetvā āharitvā gehe ṭhapesi. Mahāsatto taṃ oloketvā bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, ayaṃ māṇavo mantatthāya āgato, tassa hatthe manto nassati, asappuriso eso”ti. Māṇavopi “ahaṃ imaṃ mantaṃ ācariyassa upakārako hutvā labhissāmī”ti cintetvā tato paṭṭhāya tassa gehe sabbakiccāni karoti. Dārūni āharati, vīhiṃ koṭṭeti, bhattaṃ pacati, dantakaṭṭhamukhadhovanādīni deti, pādaṃ dhovati.

That young brahmin, seeing the Great Being bringing and selling ripe mangoes out of season, thought, 'Without a doubt, these must have been produced by the power of a mantra. By depending on this man, I shall obtain this priceless mantra.' Having carefully observed and learned the Great Being's manner of fetching the mangoes, he went to his house before the Great Being had returned from the forest and, pretending not to know, asked his wife, 'Where is the master, the teacher?' When she replied, 'He has gone to the forest,' he stood waiting for his arrival. Seeing him coming, he took the basket from his hand, carried it, and placed it in the house. The Great Being, observing him, said to his wife, 'My dear, this young man has come for the sake of the mantra. The mantra will not stay in his hands; he is an unworthy person.' The young man, for his part, thought, 'I will obtain this mantra by being of service to the teacher.' From then on, he performed all the duties in the house: he fetched firewood, pounded the paddy, cooked the rice, provided tooth-sticks and water for washing the face, and washed his feet.

Ekadivasaṃ mahāsattena “tāta māṇava, mañcapādānaṃ me upadhānaṃ dehī”ti vutte aññaṃ apassitvā sabbarattiṃ ūrumhi ṭhapetvā nisīdi. Aparabhāge mahāsattassa bhariyā puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassā pasūtikāle parikammaṃ sabbamakāsi. Sā ekadivasaṃ mahāsattaṃ āha “sāmi, ayaṃ māṇavo jātisampanno hutvā mantatthāya amhākaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karoti, etassa hatthe manto tiṭṭhatu vā mā vā, detha tassa manta”nti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā [P 4.0202] tassa mantaṃ datvā evamāha – “tāta, anagghoyaṃ manto, tava imaṃ nissāya mahālābhasakkāro bhavissati, raññā vā rājamahāmattena vā ‘ko te ācariyo’ti puṭṭhakāle mā maṃ nigūhittho, sace hi ‘caṇḍālassa me santikā manto gahito’ti lajjanto ‘brāhmaṇamahāsālo me ācariyo’ti kathessasi, imassa mantassa phalaṃ na labhissasī”ti. So “kiṃ kāraṇā taṃ nigūhissāmi, kenaci puṭṭhakāle tumheyeva kathessāmī”ti vatvā taṃ vanditvā caṇḍālagāmato nikkhamitvā mantaṃ vīmaṃsitvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā ambāni vikkiṇitvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhi.

One day, when the Great Being said, 'My dear boy, give me a support for the legs of the bed,' he, seeing no other support, sat all night with them placed upon his thighs. Later, the Great Being's wife gave birth to a son. He performed all the services for her during her confinement. One day, she said to the Great Being, 'My lord, this young man, though of high birth, performs services for us for the sake of the mantra. Whether the mantra remains with him or not, give him the mantra.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and after giving him the mantra, he said this: 'My dear, this mantra is priceless. By depending on it, you will gain great wealth and honor. When asked by the king or a royal minister, "Who is your teacher?" do not conceal me. If, being ashamed to say, "I received the mantra from an outcaste," you say, "A great and wealthy brahmin is my teacher," you will not receive the fruit of this mantra.' He replied, 'For what reason would I conceal you? If asked by anyone, I will speak only of you.' Then, having paid his respects, he departed from the outcaste village, tested the mantra, and in due course reached Benares. There, he sold mangoes and gained much wealth.

Athekadivasaṃ uyyānapālo tassa hatthato ambaṃ kiṇitvā rañño adāsi. Rājā taṃ paribhuñjitvā “kuto samma, tayā evarūpaṃ ambaṃ [M 4.0203] laddha”nti pucchi. Deva, eko māṇavo akālaambaphalāni ānetvā vikkiṇāti, tato me gahitanti. Tena hi “ito paṭṭhāya idheva ambāni āharatū”ti naṃ vadehīti. So tathā akāsi. Māṇavopi tato paṭṭhāya ambāni rājakulaṃ harati. Atha raññā “upaṭṭhaha ma”nti vutte rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahanto bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhitvā anukkamena vissāsiko jāto. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ rājā pucchi “māṇava, kuto akāle evaṃ [V 4.0181] vaṇṇagandharasasampannāni ambāni labhasi, kiṃ te nāgo vā supaṇṇo vā devo vā koci deti, udāhu mantabalaṃ eta”nti? “Na me mahārāja, koci deti, anaggho pana me manto atthi, tasseva bala”nti. “Tena hi mayampi te ekadivasaṃ mantabalaṃ daṭṭhukāmā”ti. “Sādhu, deva, dassessāmī”ti. Rājā punadivase tena saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā “dassehī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti ambarukkhaṃ upagantvā sattapadamatthake ṭhito mantaṃ parivattetvā rukkhaṃ udakena pahari. Taṅkhaṇaññeva ambarukkho heṭṭhā vuttaniyāmeneva phalaṃ gahetvā [P 4.0203] mahāmegho viya ambavassaṃ vassi. Mahājano sādhukāraṃ adāsi, celukkhepā pavattiṃsu.

One day, the park keeper bought a mango from him and gave it to the king. The king, after eating it, asked, 'Friend, where did you get such a mango?' 'Your Majesty, a young man brings unseasonal mangoes and sells them; I got it from him.' 'In that case, tell him to bring the mangoes here from now on.' He did so. From then on, the young man brought mangoes to the royal palace. Then, when the king said, 'Attend upon me,' he served the king, gained much wealth, and gradually became a trusted confidant. One day, the king asked him, 'Young man, how do you obtain such mangoes out of season, so rich in color, fragrance, and taste? Does a nāga, a supaṇṇa, a deva, or someone give them to you, or is it the power of a mantra?' 'Great king, no one gives them to me, but I possess a priceless mantra; it is by its power.' 'Then we too wish to see the power of your mantra one day.' 'Very well, Your Majesty, I will show you.' The next day, the king went to the park with him and said, 'Show me.' He replied, 'Very well,' approached a mango tree, stood at a distance of seven paces, recited the mantra, and struck the tree with water. Instantly, the mango tree bore fruit as described before, and mangoes rained down like a great cloud. The people shouted their approval, and the waving of cloths began.

Rājā ambaphalāni khāditvā tassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā “māṇavaka, evarūpo te acchariyamanto kassa santike gahito”ti pucchi. Māṇavo “sacāhaṃ ‘caṇḍālassa santike’ti vakkhāmi, lajjitabbakaṃ bhavissati, mañca garahissanti, manto kho pana me paguṇo, idāni na nassissati, disāpāmokkhaṃ ācariyaṃ apadisāmī”ti cintetvā musāvādaṃ katvā “takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhācariyassa santike gahito me”ti vadanto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāsi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva manto antaradhāyi. Rājā somanassajāto taṃ ādāya nagaraṃ pavisitvā punadivase “ambāni khādissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīditvā māṇava, ambāni āharāti āha. So “sādhū”ti ambaṃ upagantvā sattapadamatthake ṭhito “mantaṃ parivattessāmī”ti mante anupaṭṭhahante antarahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā lajjito aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “ayaṃ pubbe parisamajjheyeva ambāni āharitvā amhākaṃ deti, ghanameghavassaṃ viya ambavassaṃ vassāpeti, idāni thaddho viya ṭhito, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintetvā taṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having eaten the mangoes and given him much wealth, asked, 'Young man, from whom did you obtain such a marvelous mantra?' The young man thought, 'If I say, "From an outcaste," it will be shameful, and they will reproach me. But the mantra is mastered; it will not be lost now. I shall name the world-renowned teacher.' Having resolved to lie, he said, 'I obtained it from the world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā,' thus disowning his teacher. At that very moment, the mantra vanished. The king, filled with joy, took him and entered the city. The next day, wishing to eat mangoes, he went to the park and sat on the ceremonial stone slab. He said to the young man, 'Bring the mangoes.' He replied, 'Very well,' and approached the mango tree. Standing at a height of seven feet in the air, he thought, 'I shall recite the mantra,' but when the mantra did not occur to him, he stood there ashamed, knowing it had disappeared. The king thought, 'Before, he would bring mangoes and give them to us even in the midst of an assembly, causing a rain of mangoes like a downpour from a thick cloud. Now he stands as if rigid—what could be the reason?' Pondering thus, he questioned him and spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Ahāsi [M 4.0204] me ambaphalāni pubbe, aṇūni thūlāni ca brahmacāri;

Teheva mantehi na dāni tuyhaṃ, dumapphalā pātubhavanti brahme”ti.

“You brought me mango fruits before, both small and large, O holy man; now, with those very same mantras, the fruits of the tree do not appear for you, O brahmin.”

Tattha ahāsīti āhari. Dumapphalāti rukkhaphalāni.

In this context, 'ahāsi' means 'you brought.' 'Dumapphalā' means 'fruits of the tree.'

Taṃ sutvā māṇavo “sace ‘ajja ambaphalaṃ na gaṇhāmī’ti vakkhāmi, rājā me kujjhissati, musāvādena naṃ vañcessāmī”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the young man thought, 'If I say, “I cannot get mango fruits today,” the king will be angry with me; I shall deceive him with a lie.' Then he spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Nakkhattayogaṃ [V 4.0182] paṭimānayāmi, khaṇaṃ muhuttañca mante na passaṃ;

Nakkhattayogañca [P 4.0204] khaṇañca laddhā, addhā harissambaphalaṃ pahūta”nti.

“I await the conjunction of stars, not seeing the moment or instant in the mantra; having obtained the conjunction of stars and the moment, surely I shall bring abundant mango fruit.”

Tattha addhāharissambaphalanti addhā ambaphalaṃ āharissāmi.

Therein, 'addhā harissambaphalaṃ' means 'surely I shall bring mango fruit.'

Rājā “ayaṃ aññadā nakkhattayogaṃ na vadati, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The king, asking, 'This man did not speak of the conjunction of stars before. What, then, is this?' spoke two verses:

3.

3.

“Nakkhattayogaṃ na pure abhāṇi, khaṇaṃ muhuttaṃ na pure asaṃsi;

Sayaṃ harī ambaphalaṃ pahūtaṃ, vaṇṇena gandhena rasenupetaṃ.

“You did not speak of the conjunction of stars before, nor did you mention the moment or the instant; you yourself brought abundant mango fruit, endowed with color, fragrance, and taste.”

4.

4.

“Mantābhijappena pure hi tuyhaṃ, dumapphalā pātubhavanti brahme;

Svājja na pāresi jappampi mantaṃ, ayaṃ so ko nāma tavajja dhammo”ti.

“Indeed, in the past, O brahmin, through your chanting of mantras, the fruits of the tree appeared. Yet today you are unable even to chant the mantra; what, then, is this state of yours today?”

Tattha na pāresīti na sakkosi. Jappampīti jappantopi parivattentopi. Ayaṃ soti ayameva so tava sabhāvo ajja ko nāma jātoti.

Therein, 'na pāresi' means 'you are not able.' 'Jappampi' means 'even while muttering or reciting.' The phrase beginning 'ayaṃ so' means: 'this very nature of yours, what has it become today?'

Taṃ sutvā māṇavo “na sakkā rājānaṃ musāvādena vañcetuṃ, sacepi me sabhāve kathite āṇaṃ kareyya, karotu, sabhāvameva kathessāmī”ti cintetvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the young man thought, 'It is not possible to deceive the king with a lie. Even if he were to exercise his authority against me when my true situation is revealed, let him do so; I will speak only the truth.' Reflecting thus, he uttered two verses:

5.

5.

“Caṇḍālaputto [M 4.0205] mama sampadāsi, dhammena mante pakatiñca saṃsi;

Mā cassu me pucchito nāmagottaṃ, guyhittho atthaṃ vijaheyya manto.

“A son of an outcaste bestowed them upon me; he taught the mantras and their nature rightly, and said: ‘Do not, when questioned about my name and lineage, conceal it. Should it be hidden, the mantra would lose its power.’

6.

6.

“Sohaṃ janindena janamhi puṭṭho, makkhābhibhūto alikaṃ abhāṇiṃ;

‘Mantā ime brāhmaṇassā’ti micchā, pahīnamanto kapaṇo rudāmī”ti.

“Thus I, being questioned by the lord of the people in the midst of the folk, overwhelmed by ingratitude, spoke a lie: ‘These mantras belong to a brahmin’—this was false. Now, with the mantra lost, miserable, I weep.”

Tattha dhammenāti samena kāraṇena appaṭicchādetvāva adāsi. Pakatiñca saṃsīti “mā me pucchito nāmagottaṃ guyhittho, sace gūhasi[P 4.0205], mantā te nassissantī”ti tesaṃ nassanapakatiñca mayhaṃ saṃsi. Brāhmaṇassāti micchāti “brāhmaṇassa santike mayā ime mantā gahitā”ti [V 4.0183] micchāya abhaṇiṃ, tena me te mantā naṭṭhā, svāhaṃ pahīnamanto idāni kapaṇo rudāmīti.

Therein, 'dhammena' means he gave it with a fair reason, without concealing anything. And 'pakatiñca saṃsi' means he told me their nature of being lost, saying, 'Do not, when asked by me, conceal your name and lineage; if you conceal it, your mantras will be lost.' And the words 'brāhmaṇassa' and 'micchā' mean: 'I falsely said, “These mantras were received by me from a brahmin,” and because of that, those mantras were lost to me. Now, deprived of the mantras, I weep wretchedly.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā “ayaṃ pāpadhammo evarūpaṃ ratanamantaṃ na olokesi, evarūpasmiñhi uttamaratanamante laddhe jāti kiṃ karissatī”ti kujjhitvā tassa garahanto –

Hearing this, the king grew angry, thinking, 'This wicked man did not respect such a precious mantra. When such a supreme, precious mantra has been obtained, what does birth matter?' Rebuking him, he spoke these three verses:

7.

7.

“Eraṇḍā pucimandā vā, atha vā pālibhaddakā;

Madhuṃ madhutthiko vinde, so hi tassa dumuttamo.

“Whether from a castor-oil plant or a neem tree, or even from a coral tree, if a honey-seeker finds honey, then for him, that is the best of trees.”

8.

8.

“Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Yamhā dhammaṃ vijāneyya, so hi tassa naruttamo.

“Be they Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, or pukkusas—from whomever one might learn the Dhamma, that person is for him the supreme man.”

9.

9.

“Imassa daṇḍañca vadhañca datvā, gale gahetvā khalayātha jammaṃ;

Yo uttamatthaṃ kasirena laddhaṃ, mānātimānena vināsayitthā”ti. –

“Having imposed punishment and thrashing on this one, seize this wretch by the neck and cast him out—he who, through conceit and arrogance, has destroyed the supreme goal gained with difficulty.”

Imā gāthā āha.

He spoke these verses.

Tattha [M 4.0206] madhutthikoti madhuatthiko puriso araññe madhuṃ olokento etesaṃ rukkhānaṃ yato madhuṃ labhati, sova dumo tassa dumuttamo nāma. Tatheva khattiyādīsu yamhā purisā dhammaṃ kāraṇaṃ yuttaṃ atthaṃ vijāneyya, sova tassa uttamo naro nāma. Imassa daṇḍañcāti imassa pāpadhammassa sabbassaharaṇadaṇḍañca veḷupesikādīhi piṭṭhicammaṃ uppāṭetvā vadhañca datvā imaṃ jammaṃ gale gahetvā khalayātha, khalikārattaṃ pāpetvā niddhamatha nikkaḍḍhatha, kiṃ iminā idha vasantenāti.

Therein, 'madhutthiko' means a man desiring honey, who, while looking for honey in the forest, finds it from one of those trees; that very tree is indeed 'the best of trees' for him. Likewise, among Khattiyas and the rest, from whichever person one might learn the Dhamma—the cause and the proper meaning—that very person is the supreme man for him. 'Imassa daṇḍañca' means: 'having imposed upon this wicked man the punishment of confiscation of property and a beating by tearing the skin from his back with bamboo slivers and the like, seize this wretch by the neck and cast him out, drive him away; what use is his staying here?'

Rājapurisā tathā katvā “tavācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ ārādhetvāva sace puna mante labhissasi, idha āgaccheyyāsi, no ce, imaṃ disaṃ mā olokeyyāsī”ti taṃ nibbisayamakaṃsu. So anātho hutvā “ṭhapetvā ācariyaṃ na me aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ atthi, tasseva santikaṃ gantvā taṃ ārādhetvā puna mantaṃ yācissāmī”ti rodanto taṃ gāmaṃ agamāsi. Atha [P 4.0206] naṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā mahāsatto bhariyaṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, passa taṃ pāpadhammaṃ parihīnamantaṃ puna āgacchanta”nti āha. So mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ [V 4.0184] nisinno “kiṃkāraṇā āgatosī”ti puṭṭho “ācariya, musāvādaṃ katvā ācariyaṃ paccakkhitvā mahāvināsaṃ pattomhī”ti vatvā accayaṃ dassetvā puna mante yācanto –

The king's men, having done so, said to him, 'Go to your teacher, appease him, and only if you obtain the mantras again may you return here. If not, do not even look in this direction again.' Thus, they expelled him from the territory. Left without support, he thought, 'Apart from the teacher, I have no other refuge. I will go to him, appease him, and beg for the mantra once more.' Weeping, he went to that village. Seeing him approaching, the Great Being addressed his wife, 'My dear, look at that wicked man, his mantra lost, returning again.' The man approached the Great Being, paid homage, and sat to one side. When asked, 'For what reason have you come?' he replied, 'Teacher, by speaking falsely and denying my teacher, I have met with great ruin.' Confessing his transgression, he begged again for the mantras, saying:

10.

10.

“Yathā samaṃ maññamāno pateyya, sobbhaṃ guhaṃ narakaṃ pūtipādaṃ;

Rajjūti vā akkame kaṇhasappaṃ, andho yathā jotimadhiṭṭhaheyya;

Evampi maṃ taṃ khalitaṃ sapañña, pahīnamantassa punappadāhī”ti. – gāthamāha;

“Just as one, thinking it level, might fall into a chasm, a cave, a precipice, or a pit with rotting roots; or might tread upon a black snake, thinking it a rope; or as a blind man might step on fire; even so, O wise one, forgive that stumble of mine and give the mantra again to me, who have lost it.”

Tattha yathā samanti yathā puriso idaṃ samaṃ ṭhānanti maññamāno sobbhaṃ vā guhaṃ vā bhūmiyā phalitaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ narakaṃ vā pūtipādaṃ vā pateyya. Pūtipādoti himavantapadese mahārukkhe sussitvā mate tassa [M 4.0207] mūlesu pūtikesu jātesu tasmiṃ ṭhāne mahāāvāṭo hoti, tassa nāmaṃ. Jotimadhiṭṭhaheyyāti aggiṃ akkameyya. Evampīti evaṃ ahampi paññācakkhuno abhāvā andho tumhākaṃ visesaṃ ajānanto tumhesu khalito, taṃ maṃ khalitaṃ viditvā sapañña ñāṇasampanna pahīnamantassa mama punapi dethāti.

Therein, 'yathā samaṃ' means: just as a person, thinking 'this ground is level,' might fall into a chasm, a cave, a precipice—meaning a place where the earth has split open—or a Pūtipāda pit. 'Pūtipāda' refers to a place in the Himalayan region where, when a great tree has withered and died and its roots have rotted, a great pit forms; that is its name. 'Jotimadhiṭṭhaheyya' means he might step on fire. 'Evampi' means: 'In this way, I too, being blind because of the absence of the eye of wisdom and unaware of your special quality, have stumbled in regard to you. Recognizing that stumble of mine, O wise one endowed with knowledge, give the mantra again to me, who have lost it.'

Atha naṃ ācariyo “tāta, kiṃ kathesi, andho hi saññāya dinnāya sobbhādīni pariharati, mayā paṭhamameva tava kathitaṃ, idāni kimatthaṃ mama santikaṃ āgatosī”ti vatvā –

Then the teacher said to him, 'My dear man, what are you saying? Indeed, a blind man avoids chasms and the like when a sign is given to him. I told you this at the very beginning. Now for what reason have you come back to me?' Rebuking him and wishing to dismiss him, he spoke these verses:

11.

11.

“Dhammena mantaṃ tava sampadāsiṃ, tuvampi dhammena paṭiggahesi;

Pakatimpi te attamano asaṃsiṃ, dhamme ṭhitaṃ taṃ na jaheyya manto.

“Righteously I gave you the mantra, and you too accepted it righteously; being pleased, I even told you its natural benefit. The mantra would not abandon one who is established in righteousness.

12.

12.

“Yo [P 4.0207] bāla-mantaṃ kasirena laddhaṃ, yaṃ dullabhaṃ ajja manussaloke;

Kiñcāpi laddhā jīvituṃ appapañño, vināsayī alikaṃ bhāsamāno.

“That fool who, with difficulty, obtained the powerful mantra, which is rare today in the human world—that witless one, though having obtained it for his livelihood, destroys the mantra by speaking falsely.

13.

13.

“Bālassa mūḷhassa akataññuno ca, musā bhaṇantassa asaññatassa;

Mante mayaṃ tādisake na dema, kuto mantā gaccha na mayhaṃ ruccasī”ti. –

“To the fool, the deluded, the ungrateful, the liar, and the unrestrained, we do not give such mantras. How could you have the mantras? Go! You do not please me.”

Imā gāthā āha.

He spoke these three verses.

Tattha dhammenāti ahampi tava ācariyabhāgaṃ hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā aggahetvā dhammeneva mantaṃ sampadāsiṃ, tvampi kiñci adatvā dhammena sameneva paṭiggahesi. Dhamme ṭhitanti ācariyapūjakadhamme [V 4.0185] ṭhitaṃ. Tādisaketi tathārūpe akālaphalagaṇhāpake mante na dema, gaccha na me ruccasīti.

Therein, 'dhammena' means: I, without taking a teacher's fee of silver or gold, gave the mantra according to the Dhamma; and you, without giving anything, received it according to the Dhamma. 'Dhamme ṭhitaṃ' means 'established in the duty of honoring one’s teacher.' 'Tādisake' means such mantras that cause mangoes to be obtained at any time. 'Gaccha na me ruccasī' means 'Go, you do not please me.'

So evaṃ ācariyena uyyojito “kiṃ mayhaṃ jīvitenā”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā anāthamaraṇaṃ mari.

Thus dismissed by his teacher, thinking, 'Of what use is life to me?' he entered the forest and died a helpless death.

Satthā [M 4.0208] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto ācariyaṃ paccakkhāya mahāvināsaṃ patto”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā akataññū māṇavo devadatto ahosi, rājā ānando, caṇḍālaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, 'Not only now, monks, but also in the past, Devadatta, having rejected his teacher, met with great ruin.' Having said this, he connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the ungrateful youth was Devadatta, King Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, and the Caṇḍāla's son was none other than myself.'

Ambajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Amba Jātaka is finished.

[475] 2. Phandanajātakavaṇṇanā

[475] 2. 2. The Phandana Jātaka

Kuṭhārihattho purisoti idaṃ satthā rohiṇīnadītīre viharanto ñātakānaṃ kalahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā ñātake āmantetvā – mahārājā, atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bahinagare vaḍḍhakigāmo ahosi. Tatreko brāhmaṇavaḍḍhakī araññato dārūni āharitvā rathaṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tadā himavantapadese mahāphandanarukkho ahosi[P 4.0208]. Eko kāḷasīho gocaraṃ pariyesitvā āgantvā tassa mūle nipajji. Athassa ekadivasaṃ vāte paharante eko sukkhadaṇḍako patitvā khandhe avatthāsi. So thokaṃ khandhena rujantena bhītatasito uṭṭhāya pakkhanditvā puna nivatto āgatamaggaṃ olokento kiñci adisvā “añño maṃ sīho vā byaggho vā anubandhanto natthi, imasmiṃ pana rukkhe nibbattadevatā maṃ ettha nipajjantaṃ na sahati maññe, hotu jānissāmī”ti aṭṭhāne kopaṃ bandhitvā rukkhaṃ paharitvā “neva tava rukkhassa pattaṃ khādāmi, na sākhaṃ bhañjāmi, idha aññe mige vasante sahasi, maṃ na sahasi, ko mayhaṃ doso atthi, katipāhaṃ āgamehi, samūlaṃ te rukkhaṃ uppāṭetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chedāpessāmī”ti rukkhadevataṃ tajjetvā ekaṃ purisaṃ upadhārento vicari. Tadā so brāhmaṇavaḍḍhakī dve tayo manusse ādāya rathadārūnaṃ atthāya yānakena taṃ padesaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne yānakaṃ ṭhapetvā vāsipharasuhattho rukkhe upadhārento phandanasamīpaṃ agamāsi. Kāḷasīho taṃ disvā “ajja, mayā paccāmittassa piṭṭhiṃ daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti gantvā rukkhamūle aṭṭhāsi[V 4.0186]. Vaḍḍhakī ca ito cito oloketvā [M 4.0209] phandanasamīpena pāyāsi. So “yāva eso nātikkamati, tāvadevassa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

“A man with an axe in hand”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Jetavana monastery, concerning a quarrel among his kinsmen. The story, however, will be made clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. On this occasion, the Teacher addressed his kinsmen: “Great Kings, in the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a village of carpenters. There, a Brahmin carpenter, having brought timber from the forest, made carts and earned his living. At that time, in the region of the Himalayas, there was a great phandana tree. A bear, having sought food, came and lay down at its foot. Then one day, as the wind was blowing against the tree, a dry branch fell and landed on its back. Feeling a slight pain in its back, frightened and terrified, it sprang up and fled, then turned back. Seeing nothing upon looking back at the path, it thought, ‘No lion or tiger is pursuing me. I think the deity dwelling in this tree does not tolerate my lying here. Very well, I shall find out.’ Harboring anger where there was no cause, it struck the tree and threatened the tree-deity, ‘I neither eat the leaves of your tree, nor do I break its branches. You tolerate other beasts dwelling here, but not me. What fault is there in me? Wait a few days, and I will have your tree uprooted by the roots and chopped into pieces!’ Having thus intimidated the tree-deity, it wandered about, looking for a man. At that time, that Brahmin carpenter, taking two or three men, went by vehicle to that region for timber for carts. Leaving the vehicle in one place, with adze and axe in hand, he approached the phandana tree while searching for timber. The bear, seeing him, thought, ‘Today, it is fitting for me to see the ruin of my enemy,’ and went and stood at the foot of the tree. The carpenter, looking here and there, proceeded towards the phandana tree. The bear, thinking, ‘Before he passes by, I will speak to him,’ uttered this first verse—"

14.

14.

“Kuṭhārihattho puriso, vanamogayha tiṭṭhasi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ dāruṃ chetumicchasī”ti.

“O man with an axe in hand, you stand having entered the forest. Asked by me, friend, tell me: what wood do you wish to cut?”

Tattha purisoti tvaṃ kuṭhārihattho eko puriso imaṃ vanaṃ ogayha tiṭṭhasīti.

Therein, “man” means: ‘You, a single man with an axe in hand, stand having entered this forest.’

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “acchariyaṃ vata bho, na vata me ito pubbe migo manussavācaṃ bhāsanto diṭṭhapubbo, esa rathānucchavikaṃ [P 4.0209] dāruṃ jānissati, pucchissāmi na”nti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing its words, he thought: ‘How wonderful, indeed! Never before have I seen a bear speaking with a human voice. This bear will surely know the wood suitable for making a chariot. I shall ask it.’ Then he spoke the second verse:

15.

15.

“Isso vanāni carasi, samāni visamāni ca;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷha”nti.

“O bear, you roam the forests, both level and uneven. Asked by me, friend, tell me: what wood is strong for a wheel’s rim?”

Tattha issoti tvampi eko kāḷasīho vanāni carasi, tvaṃ rathānucchavikaṃ dāruṃ jānissasīti.

Herein, “lord” means: ‘You too, a solitary black lion, roam the forests; you will know the wood suitable for a chariot.’

Taṃ sutvā kāḷasīho “idāni me manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti cintetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the bear thought, ‘Now my wish will reach its consummation,’ and spoke a third verse:

16.

16.

“Neva sālo na khadiro, nāssakaṇṇo kuto dhavo;

Rukkho ca phandano nāma, taṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷha”nti.

“Neither sāla nor khadira, nor assakaṇṇa, much less dhava; but the tree named phandana—that wood is strong for a wheel’s rim.”

So taṃ sutvā somanassajāto “sudivasena vatamhi ajja araññaṃ paviṭṭho, tiracchānagato me rathānucchavikaṃ dāruṃ ācikkhati, aho sādhū”ti pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, he was filled with joy and thought, ‘Auspiciously have I entered the forest today! A beast tells me of wood fit for a chariot. How excellent!’ And asking further, he spoke the fourth verse:

17.

17.

“Kīdisānissa pattāni, khandho vā pana kīdiso;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, yathā jānemu phandana”nti.

“What are its leaves like, and what is its trunk like? Asked by me, good sir, tell me, so that we may recognize the phandana.”

Athassa [V 4.0187] so ācikkhanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then, explaining to him, the bear uttered two verses:

18.

18.

“Yassa sākhā palambanti, namanti na ca bhañjare;

So rukkho phandano nāma, yassa mūle ahaṃ ṭhito.

“The tree whose branches hang down, bending but not breaking—that is the tree named phandana, at whose root I stand.

19.

19.

“Arānaṃ [M 4.0210] cakkanābhīnaṃ, īsānemirathassa ca;

Sabbassa te kammaniyo, ayaṃ hessati phandano”ti.

“For spokes, wheel-hubs, and for the pole and rim of the chariot; for all of this, this phandana will be suitable for you.”

Tattha “arāna”nti idaṃ so “kadācesa imaṃ rukkhaṃ na gaṇheyya, guṇampissa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā evamāha. Tattha īsānemirathassa cāti īsāya ca nemiyā ca sesassa ca rathassa sabbassa te esa kammaniyo kammakkhamo bhavissatīti.

Herein, he spoke the word “for spokes” thinking, ‘Lest he should not take this tree, I will also describe its virtues.’ Herein, “and for the pole and rim of the chariot” means: ‘for the pole, the rim, and for all the rest of the chariot, this will be suitable for you, fit for the work.’

So evaṃ ācikkhitvā tuṭṭhamānaso ekamante vicari, vaḍḍhakīpi rukkhaṃ chindituṃ ārabhi. Rukkhadevatā cintesi “mayā etassa upari na kiñci pātitaṃ, ayaṃ aṭṭhāne āghātaṃ bandhitvā mama vimānaṃ nāseti, ahañca vinassissāmi, ekenupāyena [P 4.0210] imañca issaṃ vināsessāmī”ti. Sā vanakammikapuriso viya hutvā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā pucchi “bho purisa manāpo te rukkho laddho, imaṃ chinditvā kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Rathanemiṃ karissāmī”ti. “Iminā rukkhena ratho bhavissatī”ti kena te akkhātanti. “Ekena kāḷasīhenā”ti. “Sādhu suṭṭhu tena akkhātaṃ, iminā rukkhena ratho sundaro bhavissati, kāḷasīhassa galacammaṃ uppāṭetvā caturaṅgulamatte ṭhāne ayapaṭṭena viya nemimaṇḍale parikkhitte nemi ca thirā bhavissati, bahuñca dhanaṃ labhissasī”ti. “Kāḷasīhacammaṃ kuto lacchāmī”ti? “Tvaṃ bālakosi, ayaṃ tava rukkho vane ṭhito na palāyati, tvaṃ yena te rukkho akkhāto, tassa santikaṃ gantvā ‘sāmi tayā dassitarukkhaṃ kataraṭṭhāne chindāmī’ti vañcetvā ānehi, atha naṃ nirāsaṅkaṃ ‘idha ca ettha ca chindā’ti mukhatuṇḍaṃ pasāretvā ācikkhantaṃ tikhiṇena mahāpharasunā koṭṭetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā cammaṃ ādāya varamaṃsaṃ khāditvā rukkhaṃ chindā”ti veraṃ appesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imā gāthā āha –

Having thus explained, the bear, with a pleased mind, went aside, and the carpenter began to cut the tree. The tree-deity thought, ‘I have dropped nothing upon him, yet he, harboring anger without cause, is destroying my abode, and I too shall perish. By some means, I will destroy this bear.’ Assuming the form of a forest worker, she approached him and asked, ‘Good man, you have found a pleasing tree. What will you do after cutting it?’ ‘I will make a chariot rim,’ he replied. ‘Who told you that a chariot can be made from this tree?’ ‘A certain bear,’ he said. ‘He has told you well. From this tree, a beautiful chariot can be made. If you strip the skin from the bear’s neck and wrap the rim with it in a four-finger-wide strip, like an iron band, the rim will be strong, and you will gain much wealth.’ ‘But where can I get a bear’s skin?’ ‘You are a fool. This tree of yours stands in the forest and does not flee. Go to the one who pointed out the tree to you and deceive him, saying, “Master, at what place should I cut the tree you showed me?” and bring him here. Then, when he unsuspectingly stretches out his snout to point, saying, “Cut here and here,” strike him with a sharp, great axe, bring his life to an end, take his skin, eat the choice meat, and then cut the tree.’ Thus, she instigated enmity. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:

20.

20.

“Iti phandanarukkhopi, tāvade ajjhabhāsatha;

Mayhampi vacanaṃ atthi, bhāradvāja suṇohi me.

“Thus the phandana tree also spoke at that very moment: ‘I too have something to say, Bhāradvāja, listen to me.

21.

21.

“Issassa [V 4.0188] upakkhandhamhā, ukkacca caturaṅgulaṃ;

Tena nemiṃ pasāresi, evaṃ daḷhataraṃ siyā.

“‘From the bear’s shoulder, having cut off a four-finger-breadth strip, with it you should bind the rim; thus it would be all the more firm.’

22.

22.

“Iti phandanarukkhopi, veraṃ appesi tāvade;

Jātānañca ajātānaṃ, issānaṃ dukkhamāvahī”ti.

“Thus the phandana tree also instigated enmity at that very moment; it brought suffering to bears, both born and unborn.”

Tattha [M 4.0211] bhāradvājāti taṃ gottena ālapati. Upakkhandhamhāti khandhato. Ukkaccāti ukkantitvā.

Herein, by “Bhāradvāja” she addresses him by his clan name. “From the shoulder” means from the shoulder. “Having cut off” means having cut off.

Vaḍḍhakī rukkhadevatāya vacanaṃ sutvā “aho ajja mayhaṃ maṅgaladivaso”ti kāḷasīhaṃ ghātetvā rukkhaṃ chetvā pakkāmi. Tamatthaṃ [P 4.0211] pakāsento satthā āha –

The carpenter, hearing the words of the tree-deity, and thinking, ‘Oh, today is an auspicious day for me,’ killed the bear, cut down the tree, and departed. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

23.

23.

“Iccevaṃ phandano issaṃ, isso ca pana phandanaṃ;

Aññamaññaṃ vivādena, aññamaññamaghātayuṃ.

“Thus the phandana tree destroyed the bear, and the bear the phandana tree; through mutual dispute, they caused each other to be killed.

24.

24.

“Evameva manussānaṃ, vivādo yattha jāyati;

Mayūranaccaṃ naccanti, yathā te issaphandanā.

“Just so among humans, wherever quarrels arise, they dance the peacock dance, like that bear and phandana tree.

25.

25.

“Taṃ vo vadāmi bhaddaṃ vo, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Sammodatha mā vivadatha, mā hotha issaphandanā.

“Therefore I tell you, may it be well with you, as many as are gathered here: rejoice together, do not quarrel, do not be like the bear and the phandana tree.

26.

26.

“Sāmaggimeva sikkhetha, buddhehetaṃ pasaṃsitaṃ;

Sāmaggirato dhammaṭṭho, yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatī”ti.

“Learn only concord, for this is praised by the Buddhas. Delighting in concord, established in the Dhamma, one does not fall away from security from bondage.”

Tattha aghātayunti ghātāpesuṃ. Mayūranaccaṃ naccantīti mahārājā yattha hi manussānaṃ vivādo hoti, tattha yathā nāma mayūrā naccantā paṭicchādetabbaṃ rahassaṅgaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonti, evaṃ manussā aññamaññassa randhaṃ pakāsentā mayūranaccaṃ naccanti nāma. Yathā te issaphandanā aññamaññassa randhaṃ pakāsentā nacciṃsu nāma. Taṃ voti tena kāraṇena tumhe vadāmi. Bhaddaṃ voti bhaddaṃ tumhākaṃ hotu. Yāvantetthāti yāvanto ettha issaphandanasadisā mā ahuvattha. Sāmaggimeva sikkhethāti samaggabhāvameva tumhe sikkhatha, idaṃ paññāvuddhehi paṇḍitehi pasaṃsitaṃ[V 4.0189]. Dhammaṭṭhoti sucaritadhamme ṭhito. Yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatīti yogehi khemā nibbānā na parihāyatīti nibbānena desanākūṭaṃ gaṇhi. Sakyarājāno dhammakathaṃ sutvā samaggā jātā.

Here, ‘aghātayuṃ’ means they caused to be killed. Here, ‘they dance the peacock dance’ means, great king, that wherever there is strife among people, just as peacocks dancing reveal their private parts that should be concealed, so too do people, exposing each other’s faults, dance the peacock dance, as it were. Just as that bear and phandana tree, exposing each other’s faults, danced, as it were. ‘Taṃ vo’ means: ‘For that reason, I tell you.’ ‘Bhaddaṃ vo’ means: ‘May it be well with you.’ ‘Yāvantettha’ means: ‘As many as are here, do not be like the bear and the phandana tree.’ ‘Sāmaggimeva sikkhetha’ means: ‘You should learn only concord; this is praised by the wise, those mature in wisdom.’ ‘Dhammaṭṭho’ means: ‘established in the Dhamma of good conduct.’ ‘Yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatī’ means: ‘one who is secure from the bonds does not fall away from Nibbāna’—thus he brought the teaching to its climax with Nibbāna. The Sakyan kings, having heard the Dhamma talk, became harmonious.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā taṃ kāraṇaṃ viditvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nivutthadevatā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: ‘At that time, I myself was the deity who dwelt in that forest grove, having understood that matter.’

Phandanajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Phandana Jātaka, the second.

[476] 3. Javanahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[476] 3. The Commentary on the Javanahaṃsa Jātaka

Idheva [M 4.0212] haṃsa nipatāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto daḷhadhammadhanuggahasuttantadesanaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.228) ārabbha kathesi. Bhagavatā hi –

“Here, O swan, alight”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana with reference to the discourse on the Strong-bowed Archers (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.228). For the Blessed One said—

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, cattāro daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā susikkhitā katahatthā katūpāsanā catuddisā ṭhitā assu, atha puriso āgaccheyya ‘ahaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ daḷhadhammānaṃ dhanuggahānaṃ susikkhitānaṃ katahatthānaṃ katūpāsanānaṃ [P 4.0212] catuddisā kaṇḍe khitte apatiṭṭhite pathaviyaṃ gahetvā āharissāmī’ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, ‘javano puriso paramena javena samannāgato’ti alaṃ vacanāyā”ti? “Evaṃ bhante”ti. Yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṃ javo, tato sīghataro. Yathā ca, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa javo, yathā ca candimasūriyānaṃ javo, yathā ca yā devatā candimasūriyānaṃ purato dhāvanti, tāsaṃ devatānaṃ javo, tato sīghataraṃ āyusaṅkhārā khīyanti, tasmātiha, bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘appamattā viharissāmā’ti. Evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba”nti –

“Just as, bhikkhus, there might be four strong-bowed archers—well-trained, skillful-handed, and practiced—standing in the four directions, and a man were to come, thinking: ‘I will catch and bring back the arrows shot in the four directions by these four strong-bowed archers—well-trained, skillful-handed, and practiced—before they land on the ground.’ What do you think, bhikkhus? Would it be right to say that this man is endowed with supreme speed?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, as swift as that man’s speed is, the speed of the moon and the sun is swifter than that. As swift as that man’s speed and the speed of the moon and the sun are, the speed of the deities who run ahead of the moon and the sun is swifter than that. Even swifter than the speed of that man, the moon and the sun, and those deities, life-formations waste away. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell heedfully.’ This is how you should train yourselves.”

Imassa suttassa kathitadivasato dutiyadivase bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthā attano buddhavisaye ṭhatvā imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyusaṅkhāre ittare dubbale katvā paridīpento puthujjanabhikkhū ativiya santāsaṃ pāpesi, aho buddhabalaṃ nāmā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, svāhaṃ idāni sabbaññutaṃ patto āyusaṅkhārānaṃ ittarabhāvaṃ dassetvā bhikkhū saṃvejetvā dhammaṃ desemi, mayā hi pubbe ahetukahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattenapi āyusaṅkhārānaṃ ittarabhāvaṃ [V 4.0190] dassetvā bārāṇasirājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sakalarājaparisaṃ saṃvejetvā dhammo desito”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

On the second day after this discourse was given, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, the Teacher, standing within his own Buddha-domain, by showing the life-formations of these beings to be so transient and weak, has caused the worldling monks to feel great terror. Ah, how wonderful is the power of a Buddha!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered together?” When they told him, he said: “It is no wonder, bhikkhus, that I, who have now attained omniscience, teach the Dhamma, stirring the monks with a sense of urgency by showing the transient nature of life-formations. For even in the past, when I was born in the womb of an irrational goose, I taught the Dhamma, stirring the king of Benares and his entire royal retinue with a sense of urgency by showing the transient nature of life-formations.” And then he related a past incident.

Atīte [M 4.0213] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto javanahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā navutihaṃsasahassaparivuto cittakūṭe paṭivasati. So ekadivasaṃ jambudīpatale ekasmiṃ sare saparivāro sayaṃjātasāliṃ khāditvā ākāse suvaṇṇakilañjaṃ pattharanto viya mahantena parivārena bārāṇasinagarassa matthakena mandamandāya vilāsagatiyā cittakūṭaṃ gacchati. Atha naṃ bārāṇasirājā disvā “imināpi mādisena raññā bhavitabba”nti amaccānaṃ vatvā tasmiṃ sinehaṃ uppādetvā mālāgandhavilepanaṃ gahetvā mahāsattaṃ oloketvā sabbatūriyāni paggaṇhāpesi. Mahāsatto attano sakkāraṃ karontaṃ disvā haṃse pucchi “rājā[P 4.0213], mama evarūpaṃ sakkāraṃ karonto kiṃ paccāsīsatī”ti? “Tumhehi saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ devā”ti. “Tena hi rañño amhehi saddhiṃ mittabhāvo hotū”ti raññā saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Athekadivasaṃ rañño uyyānaṃ gatakāle anotattadahaṃ gantvā ekena pakkhena udakaṃ, ekena candanacuṇṇaṃ ādāya āgantvā rājānaṃ tena udakena nhāpetvā candanacuṇṇena okiritvā mahājanassa passantasseva saparivāro cittakūṭaṃ agamāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya rājā mahāsattaṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā “sahāyo me ajja āgamissati, sahāyo me ajja āgamissatī”ti āgamanamaggaṃ olokento acchati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a swift goose and lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety thousand geese. One day, after feeding on self-grown rice in a lake in Jambudīpa with his flock, he flew through the sky as if spreading a golden mat, moving very slowly and gracefully with his great retinue over the city of Benares toward Cittakūṭa. Then the king of Benares, seeing him, said to his ministers, “This one too must be a king like me.” Feeling affection for him, he took flowers, perfumes, and unguents, and as he watched the Great Being, he had all musical instruments played. The Great Being, seeing the king honoring him, asked the geese, “What does the king hope for in showing me such honor?” “He desires friendship with you, lord.” “In that case, let there be friendship between us and the king.” Having established friendship with the king, he departed. Then one day, when the king had gone to his park, the goose went to Lake Anotatta, and taking water with one wing and sandalwood powder with the other, he returned and bathed the king with that water and sprinkled him with the sandalwood powder. Then, in full view of the people, he departed for Cittakūṭa with his retinue. From that time on, the king, desiring to see the Great Being, would wait, watching the path of his arrival, thinking, “My friend will come today, my friend will come today.”

Tadā mahāsattassa kaniṭṭhā dve haṃsapotakā “sūriyena saddhiṃ javissāmā”ti mantetvā mahāsattassa ārocesuṃ “mayaṃ sūriyena saddhiṃ javissāmā”ti. “Tātā, sūriyajavo nāma sīgho, sūriyena saddhiṃ javituṃ na sakkhissatha, antarāva vinassissatha, mā gamitthā”ti. Te dutiyampi tatiyampi yāciṃsu, bodhisattopi te yāvatatiyaṃ vāresiyeva. Te mānathaddhā attano balaṃ ajānantā mahāsattassa anācikkhitvāva “sūriyena saddhiṃ javissāmā”ti sūriye anuggateyeva gantvā yugandharamatthake nisīdiṃsu. Mahāsatto te adisvā “kahaṃ nu kho gatā”ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā cintesi “te sūriyena saddhiṃ javituṃ na sakkhissanti, antarāva vinassissanti, jīvitaṃ tesaṃ dassāmī”ti. Sopi gantvā yugandharamatthakeyeva nisīdi. Atha uggate sūriyamaṇḍale haṃsapotakā uppatitvā sūriyena saddhiṃ pakkhandiṃsu, mahāsattopi tehi saddhiṃ pakkhandi. Kaniṭṭhabhātiko [M 4.0214] yāva pubbaṇhasamayā javitvā kilami, pakkhasandhīsu aggiuṭṭhānakālo viya ahosi. So bodhisattassa saññaṃ adāsi “bhātika, na sakkomī”ti. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “mā bhāyi, jīvitaṃ te dassāmī”ti pakkhapañjarena parikkhipitvā [V 4.0191] assāsetvā cittakūṭapabbataṃ netvā haṃsānaṃ majjhe ṭhapetvā puna pakkhanditvā sūriyaṃ patvā itarena saddhiṃ pāyāsi. Sopi yāva upakaṭṭhamajjhanhikā sūriyena [P 4.0214] saddhiṃ javitvā kilami, pakkhasandhīsu aggiuṭṭhānakālo viya ahosi. Tadā bodhisattassa saññaṃ adāsi “bhātika, na sakkomī”ti. Tampi mahāsatto tatheva samassāsetvā pakkhapañjarenādāya cittakūṭameva agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sūriyo nabhamajjhaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then the Great Being’s two younger brother swans, having discussed, 'We will race with the sun,' informed the Great Being, 'We will race with the sun.' 'Dear ones, the speed of the sun is fast; you will not be able to race with the sun. You will perish along the way—do not go.' They asked a second and a third time, but the Bodhisatta still restrained them up to the third time. They, stiff with pride and not knowing their own strength, without informing the Great Being, resolved, 'We will race with the sun,' and went before the sun had risen, sitting on the summit of Mount Yugandhara. Not seeing them, the Great Being asked, 'Where can they have gone?' and hearing what had happened, he thought, 'They will not be able to race with the sun; they will perish along the way. I will save their lives.' He too went and sat on the summit of Mount Yugandhara. Then, when the sun’s orb rose, the young swans flew up and raced with the sun, and the Great Being also raced with them. The younger brother, having raced until the forenoon, grew weary; it was as if fire were arising in his wing-joints. He gave a signal to the Bodhisatta, 'Brother, I cannot go on.' Then the Great Being said, 'Do not fear, I will save your life,' and enclosing him within the cage of his wings, he comforted him, took him to Mount Cittakūṭa, and placed him among the swans. Then he flew again and, reaching the sun, went on with the other. That one too, having raced with the sun until close to midday, grew weary; it was as if fire were arising in his wing-joints. Then he gave a signal to the Bodhisatta, 'Brother, I cannot go on.' The Great Being likewise comforted him and, taking him within the cage of his wings, went to Mount Cittakūṭa. At that moment, the sun reached the middle of the sky.

Atha mahāsatto “mama ajja sarīrabalaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti cintetvā ekavegena pakkhanditvā yugandharamatthake nisīditvā tato uppatitvā ekavegena sūriyaṃ pāpuṇitvā kālena purato, kālena pacchato javitvā cintesi “mayhaṃ sūriyena saddhiṃ javanaṃ nāma niratthakaṃ ayonisomanasikārasambhūtaṃ, kiṃ me iminā, bārāṇasiṃ gantvā mama sahāyakassa rañño atthayuttaṃ dhammayuttaṃ kathaṃ kathessāmī”ti. So nivattitvā sūriye nabhamajjhaṃ anatikkanteyeva sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ antantena anusaṃyāyitvā vegaṃ parihāpento sakalajambudīpaṃ antantena anusaṃyāyitvā bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇi. Dvādasayojanikaṃ sakalanagaraṃ haṃsacchannaṃ viya ahosi, chiddaṃ nāma na paññāyi, anukkamena vege parihāyante ākāse chiddāni paññāyiṃsu. Mahāsatto vegaṃ parihāpetvā ākāsato otaritvā sīhapañjarassa abhimukhaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “āgato me sahāyo”ti somanassappatto tassa nisīdanatthāya kañcanapīṭhaṃ paññapetvā “samma, pavisa, idha nisīdā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being thought, 'Today I will test my bodily strength.' With a single burst of speed, he rushed forth and sat on the summit of Mount Yugandhara. Then, rising from there, he reached the sun in a single burst of speed, at times racing ahead and at times behind, and he thought: 'This racing with the sun is useless, born of improper attention.
