What is the use of this to me? I will go to Benares and speak a discourse connected with benefit and the Dhamma to my friend, the king.' Turning back, while the sun had not yet passed the zenith, he traversed the interior of the entire world-sphere along its inner circumference, and reducing his speed, he traversed the whole of Jambudīpa along its inner circumference and reached Benares. The entire twelve-yojana city was as if covered by a swan; no gap was seen. As his speed gradually decreased, gaps appeared in the sky. The Great Being, having reduced his speed, descended from the sky and stood in a place facing the lion-window. The king, filled with joy, thinking, 'My friend has come,' had a golden seat prepared for him to sit on and said, 'Friend, enter, sit here,' and spoke the first verse:

27.

27.

“Idheva haṃsa nipata, piyaṃ me tava dassanaṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yamidhatthi pavedayā”ti.

“Alight here, O swan, pleasing to me is the sight of you; you have arrived as master, declare whatever you desire here.”

Tattha “idhā”ti kañcanapīṭhaṃ sandhāyāha. Nipatāti nisīda. Issarosīti tvaṃ imassa ṭhānassa issaro sāmi hutvā āgatosīti vadati. Yamidhatthi pavedayāti [M 4.0215] yaṃ imasmiṃ nivesane atthi, taṃ aparisaṅkanto amhākaṃ kathehīti.

Herein, 'here' refers to the golden seat. 'Alight' (nipata) means sit down. 'You have arrived as master' (issarosi) means he says, 'You have come as the lord and master of this place.' 'Declare whatever you desire here' (yamidhatthi pavedaya) means, 'Whatever there is in this dwelling, tell it to us without hesitation.'

Mahāsatto kañcanapīṭhe nisīdi. Rājā satapākasahassapākehi telehi tassa pakkhantarāni makkhetvā kañcanataṭṭake madhulāje ca madhurodakañca sakkharodakañca dāpetvā madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā [P 4.0215] “samma, tvaṃ ekakova āgatosi, kuhiṃ agamitthā”ti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ vitthārena kathesi. Atha naṃ rājā āha “samma, mamapi sūriyena saddhiṃ javitavegaṃ dassehī”ti. Mahārāja, na sakkā so vego dassetunti. Tena hi me sarikkhakamattaṃ [V 4.0192] dassehīti. Sādhu, mahārāja, sarikkhakamattaṃ dassessāmi, akkhaṇavedhī dhanuggahe sannipātehīti. Rājā sannipātesi. Mahāsatto cattāro dhanuggahe gahetvā nivesanā oruyha rājaṅgaṇe silāthambhaṃ nikhaṇāpetvā attano gīvāyaṃ ghaṇṭaṃ bandhāpetvā silāthambhamatthake nisīditvā cattāro dhanuggahe thambhaṃ nissāya catuddisābhimukhe ṭhapetvā “mahārāja, ime cattāro janā ekappahāreneva catuddisābhimukhā cattāri kaṇḍāni khipantu, tāni ahaṃ pathaviṃ appattāneva āharitvā etesaṃ pādamūle pātessāmi. Mama kaṇḍagahaṇatthāya gatabhāvaṃ ghaṇṭasaddasaññāya jāneyyāsi, maṃ pana na passissasī”ti vatvā tehi ekappahāreneva khittakaṇḍāni āharitvā tesaṃ pādamūle pātetvā silāthambhamatthake nisinnameva attānaṃ dassetvā “diṭṭho te, mahārāja, mayhaṃ vego”ti vatvā “mahārāja, ayaṃ vego mayhaṃ neva uttamo, majjhimo, paritto lāmakavego esa, evaṃ sīgho, mahārāja, amhākaṃ vego”ti āha.

The Great Being sat on the golden seat. The king had the joints of his wings anointed with oils cooked a hundred and a thousand times, and after giving him honey-puffed rice, honeyed water, and sugar-water in golden bowls, and showing him sweet hospitality, he asked, 'Friend, you have come alone; where did you go?' He told the story in detail. Then the king said to him, 'Friend, show me too the speed of racing with the sun.' 'Great king, that speed cannot be shown.' 'Then show me just a comparable amount.' 'Very well, great king, I will show you a comparable amount. Assemble archers who hit the mark in a flash.' The king assembled them. The Great Being, taking four archers, descended from the palace and had a stone pillar planted in the royal courtyard. Having a bell fastened around his own neck, he sat on the top of the stone pillar. He positioned the four archers leaning against the pillar, facing the four directions, and said, 'Great king, let these four people shoot four arrows simultaneously in the four directions. I will retrieve those arrows before they even reach the ground and drop them at their feet. You will know that I have gone to catch the arrows by the signal of the bell’s sound, but you will not see me.' Having said this, he retrieved the arrows shot by them simultaneously and dropped them at their feet. Then, showing himself still seated on the top of the stone pillar, he said, 'Great king, have you seen my speed?' He continued, 'Great king, this speed is neither my supreme nor my middling speed; this is a slight, inferior speed. Such, great king, is our swiftness.'

Atha naṃ rājā pucchi “samma, atthi pana tumhākaṃ vegato añño sīghataro vego”ti? “Āma, mahārāja, amhākaṃ uttamavegatopi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena imesaṃ sattānaṃ āyusaṅkhārā sīghataraṃ khīyanti bhijjanti, khayaṃ gacchantī”ti khaṇikanirodhavasena rūpadhammānaṃ nirodhaṃ dasseti, tato nāmadhammānaṃ. Rājā mahāsattassa kathaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayabhīto satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto bhūmiyaṃ pati, mahājano utrāsaṃ patto ahosi. Rañño mukhaṃ udakena siñcitvā [M 4.0216] satiṃ labhāpesi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “mahārāja, mā bhāyi, maraṇassatiṃ [P 4.0216] bhāvehi, dhammaṃ carāhi, dānādīni puññāni karohi, appamatto hohi, devā”ti ovadi. Atha rājā “sāmi, mayaṃ tumhādisena ñāṇabalasampannena ācariyena vinā vasituṃ na sakkhissāma, cittakūṭaṃ agantvā mayhaṃ dhammaṃ desento mayhaṃ ovādācariyo hutvā idheva vasāhī”ti yācanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king asked him, "Friend, is there any speed faster than your speed?" "Yes, great king. A hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times faster than even our supreme speed, the life-formations of these beings waste away, break up, and reach destruction." Thus he showed the cessation of material phenomena by way of momentary cessation, and then of mental phenomena. Hearing the Great Being's words, the king, terrified by the fear of death and unable to establish mindfulness, fell to the ground. The great crowd was struck with terror. They sprinkled water on the king's face and caused him to regain consciousness. Then the Great Being advised him, "Great king, do not fear. Develop mindfulness of death. Practice the Dhamma. Perform meritorious deeds such as giving, and be heedful, O King." Then the king, pleading, "Master, we cannot live without a teacher like you, endowed with the power of knowledge. Do not go to Cittakūṭa; please stay right here, teaching me the Dhamma and being my advising teacher," spoke two verses:

28.

28.

“Savanena ekassa piyā bhavanti, disvā panekassa viyeti chando;

Disvā ca sutvā ca piyā bhavanti, kaccinnu me pīyasi dassanena.

“For one, some become dear through hearing, but upon seeing, for another, desire vanishes; some become dear through both seeing and hearing. I wonder, are you fond of me upon seeing me?”

29.

29.

“Savanena piyo mesi, bhiyyo cāgamma dassanaṃ;

Evaṃ piyadassano me, vasa haṃsa mamantike”ti.

“By hearing, you are dear to me, and even more so by coming into my sight. Thus, being one whose sight is dear to me, O swan, dwell near me.”

Tāsaṃ attho – samma haṃsarāja savanena ekassa ekacce piyā honti, “evaṃ guṇo nāmā”ti sutvā savanena piyāyati, ekassa pana ekacce disvāva chando vigacchati, pemaṃ antaradhāyati[V 4.0193], khādituṃ āgatā yakkhā viya upaṭṭhahanti, ekassa ekacce disvā ca sutvā cāti ubhayathāpi piyā honti, tena taṃ pucchāmi. Kaccinnu me pīyasi dassanenāti kacci nu tvaṃ maṃ piyāyasi, mayhaṃ pana tvaṃ savanena piyova, dassanaṃ panāgamma atipiyova. Evaṃ mama piyadassano samāno cittakūṭaṃ agantvā idha mama santike vasāti.

The meaning of this is: Friend swan king, for some, certain ones become dear by hearing; having heard, 'Such is his virtue,' one holds them dear. For another, however, upon seeing certain ones, desire vanishes, affection disappears; they appear like yakkhas come to devour. For yet another, certain ones are dear both by seeing and by hearing, in both ways. Therefore, I ask you. 'Are you fond of me by sight?' means 'Do you hold me dear?' For me, however, you are dear by hearing, and having come into my sight, you are exceedingly dear. Thus, being one whose sight is dear to me, do not go to Cittakūṭa, but dwell here near me.

Bodhisatto āha –

The Bodhisatta said:

30.

30.

“Vaseyyāma tavāgāre, niccaṃ sakkatapūjitā;

Matto ca ekadā vajje, haṃsarājaṃ pacantu me”ti.

“We would dwell in your house, always honored and revered. But if, intoxicated, you should one day say, ‘Let them cook the king of geese for me!’”

Tattha matto ca ekadāti mahārāja, mayaṃ tava ghare niccaṃ pūjitā vaseyyāma, tvaṃ pana kadāci surāmadamatto maṃsakhādanatthaṃ “haṃsarājaṃ pacantu me”ti vadeyyāsi, atha evaṃ tava anujīvino maṃ māretvā paceyyuṃ, tadāhaṃ kiṃ karissāmīti.

There, 'intoxicated, one day,' O great king, means this: we would always dwell honored in your house, but you, sometimes intoxicated with liquor, might say for the sake of eating meat, 'Let them cook the king of geese for me!' Then your servants might kill me and cook me. What would I do then?

Athassa [P 4.0217][M 4.0217] rājā “tena hi majjameva na pivissāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ dātuṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king, in order to give a promise, saying, “In that case, I shall not drink liquor at all,” spoke this verse:

31.

31.

“Dhiratthu taṃ majjapānaṃ, yaṃ me piyataraṃ tayā;

Na cāpi majjaṃ pissāmi, yāva me vacchasī ghare”ti.

“Fie on that drinking of intoxicants, for you are dearer to me than it. And I will not drink intoxicants as long as you dwell in my house.”

Tato paraṃ bodhisatto cha gāthā āha –

Thereupon, the Bodhisatta spoke six stanzas:

32.

32.

“Suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato.

“The howling of jackals is easily known, and the calls of birds; the speech of humans, O king, is more difficult to know than that.

33.

33.

“Api ce maññatī poso, ñāti mitto sakhāti vā;

Yo pubbe sumano hutvā, pacchā sampajjate diso.

“Even if a person thinks, ‘This is a relative, a friend, or a companion,’ one who was previously well-disposed later becomes an enemy.

34.

34.

“Yasmiṃ mano nivisati, avidūre sahāpi so;

Santikepi hi so dūre, yasmiṃ nāvisate mano.

“He in whom the mind settles is near, even if far away; but he in whom the mind does not settle is far away, even if near.

35.

35.

“Antopi [V 4.0194] so hoti pasannacitto, pāraṃ samuddassa pasannacitto;

Antopi so hoti paduṭṭhacitto, pāraṃ samuddassa paduṭṭhacitto.

“He is nearby who has a pure heart, though on the far shore of the ocean; he is as if on the far shore of the ocean who has a corrupt heart, though nearby.

36.

36.

“Saṃvasantā vivasanti, ye disā te rathesabha;

Ārā santo saṃvasanti, manasā raṭṭhavaḍḍhana.

“Those who are hostile, O lord of chariots, live apart though living together; the virtuous, O enhancer of the kingdom, live together in mind though far away.

37.

37.

“Aticiraṃ nivāsena, piyo bhavati appiyo;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma, purā te homa appiyā”ti.

“By dwelling too long, one who is dear becomes disliked. We take our leave of you and shall go, before we become disliked by you.”

Tattha vassitanti mahārāja, tiracchānagatā ujuhadayā, tena tesaṃ vassitaṃ suvijānaṃ, manussā pana kakkhaḷā, tasmā tesaṃ vacanaṃ dubbijānataranti attho. Yo pubbeti yo puggalo paṭhamameva attamano hutvā “tvaṃ mayhaṃ ñātako mitto pāṇasamo sakhā”ti api evaṃ maññati, sveva pacchā diso verī sampajjati, evaṃ dubbijānaṃ nāma manussahadayanti. Nivisatīti mahārāja, yasmiṃ puggale pemavasena mano nivisati, so dūre [M 4.0218] vasantopi avidūre sahāpi vasatiyeva nāma. Yasmiṃ pana puggale mano na nivisati apeti, so santike vasantopi dūreyeva.

There, 'utterance' (vassitaṃ), O great king, means that animals are straightforward in heart; therefore, their utterances are easily known. Humans, however, are harsh; therefore, their speech is more difficult to know—this is the meaning. 'He who previously' means a person who, being initially pleased, thinks, 'You are my relative, friend, dear as life, companion,' yet that very one later becomes an enemy, a foe. Thus, the human heart is indeed difficult to know. 'Settles' (Nivisati), O great king, means that the person in whom the mind settles through affection, even if living far away, is indeed considered to be living nearby. But the person in whom the mind does not settle and departs, even if living nearby, is indeed far away.

Antopi so hotīti mahārāja, yo sahāyo pasannacitto, so cittena allīnattā pāraṃ samuddassa vasantopi antoyeva [P 4.0218] hoti. Yo pana paduṭṭhacitto, so cittena anallīnattā anto vasantopi pāraṃ samuddassa nāma. Ye disā teti ye verino paccatthikā, te ekato vasantāpi dūre vasantiyeva nāma. Santo pana paṇḍitā ārā ṭhitāpi mettābhāvitena manasā āvajjentā saṃvasantiyeva. Purā te homāti yāva tava appiyā na homa, tāvadeva taṃ āmantetvā gacchāmāti vadati.

“He is indeed nearby,” O great king, means this: a companion with a serene mind, even dwelling beyond the ocean, is nearby because his mind is attached. But one with a corrupt mind, even dwelling nearby, is as if beyond the ocean because his mind is not attached. “Those who are enemies” means foes and adversaries; though living together, they are indeed living far apart. But the virtuous and wise, even when at a distance, dwell together, turning their minds developed with loving-kindness. “Before we become disliked by you” means he is saying, “We shall take our leave and go before we become disliked by you.”

Atha naṃ rājā āha –

Then the king said to him:

38.

38.

“Evaṃ ce yācamānānaṃ, añjaliṃ nāvabujjhasi;

Paricārakānaṃ sataṃ, vacanaṃ na karosi no;

Evaṃ taṃ abhiyācāma, puna kayirāsi pariyāya”nti.

“If, when we beg you thus, you do not acknowledge our joined palms; if you do not heed the words of us, your good attendants; thus we implore you, may you make an occasion to return again.”

Tattha [V 4.0195] evaṃ ceti sace haṃsarāja, evaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha yācamānānaṃ amhākaṃ imaṃ añjaliṃ nāvabujjhasi, tava paricārakānaṃ samānānaṃ vacanaṃ na karosi, atha naṃ evaṃ yācāma. Puna kayirāsi pariyāyanti kālena kālaṃ idha āgamanāya vāraṃ kareyyāsīti attho.

There, 'If thus' means: 'If, O swan king, you do not acknowledge this gesture of respect from us who beg with palms joined in reverence, and do not heed the words of those who are your attendants, then we beg you thus.' 'May you again make an occasion' means 'may you make a turn to come here from time to time'—this is the meaning.

Tato bodhisatto āha –

Then the Bodhisatta said:

39.

39.

“Evaṃ ce no viharataṃ, antarāyo na hessati;

Tuyhaṃ cāpi mahārāja, mayhañca raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Appeva nāma passemu, ahorattānamaccaye”ti.

“If, as we live thus, no obstacle should arise for us, nor for you, O great king, enhancer of the kingdom, then perhaps we may see each other again with the passing of days and nights.”

Tattha evaṃ ce noti mahārāja, mā cintayittha, sace amhākampi evaṃ viharantānaṃ jīvitantarāyo na bhavissati, appeva nāma ubho aññamaññaṃ passissāma, apica tvaṃ mayā dinnaṃ ovādameva mama ṭhāne ṭhapetvā evaṃ ittarajīvite lokasannivāse appamatto hutvā dānādīni puññāni karonto dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārehi, evañhi [M 4.0219] me ovādaṃ karonto maṃ passissatiyevāti. Evaṃ mahāsatto rājānaṃ ovaditvā cittakūṭapabbatameva gato.

There, 'If thus for us' means: O great king, do not worry. If, for us too, living thus, there will be no danger to life, perhaps indeed we both shall see each other. Moreover, you should establish the advice given by me in my place, and being diligent in this short-lived existence in the world, perform meritorious deeds such as giving, and rule the kingdom righteously without violating the ten royal virtues. For indeed, by acting according to my advice, you will surely see me. Having thus advised the king, the Great Being went to Mount Cittakūṭa.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattenapi mayā āyusaṅkhārānaṃ dubbalabhāvaṃ dassetvā dhammo desito”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, kaniṭṭho moggallāno, majjhimo sāriputto, sesahaṃsagaṇā buddhaparisā, javanahaṃso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “Thus, monks, in the past, even when reborn in an animal existence, I taught the Dhamma, showing the frailty of the life-formations.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, the youngest goose was Moggallāna, the middle one was Sāriputta, the remaining flock of geese were the Buddha's assembly, but the swift goose was I myself.”

Javanahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Explanation of the Javanahaṃsa Jātaka, the Third.

[477] 4. Cūḷanāradajātakavaṇṇanā

[477] 4. The Explanation of the Cūḷanārada Jātaka.

Na [P 4.0219] te kaṭṭhāni bhinnānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthivāsino kirekassa kulassa pannarasasoḷasavassuddesikā dhītā ahosi sobhaggappattā, na ca naṃ koci vāresi. Athassā mātā cintesi “mama dhītā vayappattā, na ca naṃ koci vāreti, āmisena macchaṃ viya etāya ekaṃ sākiyabhikkhuṃ palobhetvā uppabbājetvā [V 4.0196] taṃ nissāya jīvissāmī”ti. Tadā ca sāvatthivāsī eko kulaputto sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā upasampannakālato paṭṭhāya sikkhākāmataṃ pahāya ālasiyo sarīramaṇḍanamanuyutto vihāsi. Mahāupāsikā gehe yāgukhādanīyabhojanīyāni sampādetvā dvāre ṭhatvā antaravīthiyā gacchantesu bhikkhūsu ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ rasataṇhāya bandhitvā gahetuṃ sakkuṇeyyarūpaṃ upadhārentī tepiṭakaābhidhammikavinayadharānaṃ mahantena parivārena gacchantānaṃ antare kañci gayhupagaṃ adisvā tesaṃ pacchato gacchantānaṃ madhuradhammakathikānaṃ acchinnavalāhakasadisānaṃ piṇḍapātikānampi antare kañci adisvāva ekaṃ yāva bahi apaṅgā akkhīni añjetvā kese osaṇhetvā dukūlantaravāsakaṃ nivāsetvā ghaṭitamaṭṭhaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā maṇivaṇṇapattaṃ ādāya manoramaṃ chattaṃ dhārayamānaṃ vissaṭṭhindriyaṃ kāyadaḷhibahulaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “imaṃ sakkā gaṇhitu”nti gantvā vanditvā pattaṃ gahetvā “etha[M 4.0220], bhante”ti gharaṃ ānetvā nisīdāpetvā yāguādīhi parivisitvā katabhattakiccaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ “bhante, ito paṭṭhāya idhevāgaccheyyāthā”ti āha. Sopi tato paṭṭhāya tattheva gantvā aparabhāge vissāsiko ahosi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning the seduction of a plump young woman, beginning with the words 'Na te kaṭṭhāni bhinnāni' (Your logs are not split). It is said that in Sāvatthi, there was a daughter of a certain family, about fifteen or sixteen years old, who had attained beauty, yet no one courted her. Then her mother thought, 'My daughter has come of age, yet no one asks for her hand. Like a fish lured by bait, I will tempt a monk of the Sakyan lineage with her, make him disrobe, and then depend on him for our livelihood.' At that time, a young man from Sāvatthi had gone forth into the monastic life, having given his heart to the Dispensation. But from the time of his higher ordination, he abandoned the desire for training, indulging in laziness and adorning his body. The great laywoman, having prepared rice porridge, edibles, and food in her house, stood at the door, observing among the monks passing through the street for one who seemed capable of being ensnared and caught by craving for flavors. She saw none suitable among the great retinues of monks learned in the Tipiṭaka, the Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya. Nor did she see any among the sweet Dhamma speakers resembling unbroken rain clouds who walked behind them, who were alms-goers. Then she saw a monk approaching who had applied collyrium to his eyes extending to the outer corners, with his hair dressed, wearing a fine inner garment, and having put on a carefully arranged robe, carrying a jewel-colored bowl and holding an attractive parasol, with unrestrained senses and a sturdy body. Thinking, 'This one can be caught,' she approached, paid respects, took his bowl, and saying, 'Come, venerable sir,' led him to her house, seated him, served him porridge and other food, and after the meal, told that monk, 'Venerable sir, from now on, please come only here.' From then on, he went there regularly and later became intimate.

Athekadivasaṃ mahāupāsikā tassa savanapathe ṭhatvā “imasmiṃ gehe upabhogaparibhogamattā atthi, tathārūpo pana me putto vā jāmātā vā gehaṃ vicārituṃ samattho natthī”ti āha. So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “kimatthaṃ nu kho kathetī”ti thokaṃ hadaye viddho viya ahosi. Sā dhītaraṃ āha “imaṃ palobhetvā tava vase vattāpehī”ti. Sā tato paṭṭhāya maṇḍitapasādhitā itthikuttavilāsehi taṃ palobhesi. Thullakumārikāti [P 4.0220] na ca thūlasarīrā daṭṭhabbā, thūlā vā hotu kisā vā, pañcakāmaguṇikarāgena pana thūlatāya “thullakumārikā”ti vuccati. So daharo kilesavasiko hutvā “na dānāhaṃ buddhasāsane patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti cintetvā “vihāraṃ gantvā pattacīvaraṃ niyyādetvā asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma gamissāmi, tatra me vatthāni pesethā”ti vatvā vihāraṃ gantvā pattacīvaraṃ niyyādetvā “ukkaṇṭhitosmī”ti ācariyupajjhāye āha. Te taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ netvā “ayaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhito”ti ārocesuṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti vatvā “thullakumārikāya, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu pubbepesā tava araññe vasantassa brahmacariyantarāyaṃ katvā mahantaṃ anatthamakāsi, puna tvaṃ etameva nissāya kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, the great laywoman, standing within his earshot, said, 'In this house, there are only things for use and enjoyment, but there is no son or son-in-law of mine capable of managing the household.' Hearing her words, he thought, 'Why indeed is she saying this?' and felt as if slightly struck in his heart. She then told her daughter, 'Entice him and make him subject to your control.' From that time onward, adorned and embellished, she enticed him with feminine wiles and flirtations. 'Thullakumārikā' (plump young woman) should not be understood only as having a large body; whether she was stout or thin, she was called 'Thullakumārikā' because of the coarseness of her passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Being young and under the sway of defilements, he thought, 'I will no longer be able to abide in the Buddha’s dispensation.' Deciding, 'I will go to the monastery, return my bowl and robes, and then go to such-and-such a place; send my lay clothes there,' he went to the monastery, returned his bowl and robes, and said to his teachers and preceptors, 'I am discontented.' They took him to the Teacher and reported, 'This monk is discontented.' The Teacher asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true, venerable sir,' the Teacher asked, 'What has made you discontented?' He answered, 'The Thullakumārikā, venerable sir.' The Teacher then said, 'Monk, in the past also, while you were dwelling in the forest, she created an obstruction to your holy life and caused you great harm. Now, relying on her again, why are you discontented?' Having said this, at the request of the monks, he related the past.

Atīte [V 4.0197] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe mahābhoge brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā uggahitasippo kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapesi, athassa bhariyā ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyitvā kālamakāsi. So “yatheva me piyabhariyāya, evaṃ mayipi maraṇaṃ āgamissati, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā kāme pahāya puttaṃ ādāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā tena saddhiṃ isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro araññe vihāsi. Tadā paccantavāsino corā janapadaṃ pavisitvā [M 4.0221] gāmaṃ paharitvā karamare gahetvā bhaṇḍikaṃ ukkhipāpetvā puna paccantaṃ pāpayiṃsu. Tesaṃ antare ekā abhirūpā kumārikā kerāṭikapaññāya samannāgatā cintesi “ime amhe gahetvā dāsibhogena paribhuñjissanti, ekena upāyena palāyituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā “sāmi, sarīrakiccaṃ kātukāmāmhi, thokaṃ paṭikkamitvā tiṭṭhathā”ti vatvā core vañcetvā palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisantī bodhisattassa puttaṃ assame ṭhapetvā phalāphalatthāya gatakāle pubbaṇhasamaye taṃ assamaṃ pāpuṇitvā taṃ tāpasakumāraṃ [P 4.0221] kāmaratiyā palobhetvā sīlamassa bhinditvā attano vase vattetvā “kiṃ te araññavāsena, ehi gāmaṃ gantvā vasissāma, tatra hi rūpādayo kāmaguṇā sulabhā”ti āha. Sopi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “pitā tāva me araññato phalāphalaṃ āharituṃ gato, taṃ disvā ubhopi ekatova gamissāmā”ti āha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy brahmin family in the Kasi country. Having mastered his craft, he established a household. Later, his wife gave birth to a son and then died. He thought, "Just as death has come to my beloved wife, so too will death come to me. What is the use of living in a house? I shall go forth." Reflecting thus, he abandoned sensual pleasures and, taking his young son, entered the Himalayas. There, together with his son, he embraced the life of an ascetic, developed jhānas and higher knowledges, and lived in the forest, subsisting on forest roots and fruits. At that time, border-dwelling bandits entered the countryside, raided a village, took captives, made them carry the goods, and then returned to the borderlands. Among them was a beautiful young girl, endowed with sharp wisdom, who thought, "These bandits will take us and use us as slaves in their homes. I must find a way to escape." She said to the bandits, "Sirs, I wish to relieve myself. Please step aside a little and wait." Deceiving them, she fled and entered the forest. While the Bodhisatta had gone to gather fruits and roots, leaving the young ascetic at the hermitage, she reached the hermitage in the early morning. She seduced the young ascetic with sensual allure, broke his virtue, and brought him under her sway. She said, "What is the use of living in the forest? Come, let us go to the village and settle there. In the village, sensual pleasures such as forms are easily found." He agreed, saying, "Very well. But my father has gone into the forest to gather fruits and roots; when we see him, we shall both go together."

Sā cintesi – “ayaṃ taruṇadārako na kiñci jānāti, pitarā panassa mahallakakāle pabbajitena bhavitabbaṃ, so āgantvā ‘idha kiṃ karosī’ti maṃ pothetvā pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhetvā araññe khipissati, tasmiṃ anāgateyeva palāyissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ “ahaṃ purato gacchāmi, tvaṃ pacchā āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā maggasaññaṃ ācikkhitvā pakkāmi. So tassā gatakālato paṭṭhāya uppannadomanasso yathā pure kiñci vattaṃ akatvā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā antopaṇṇasālāya pajjhāyanto nipajji. Mahāsatto phalāphalaṃ ādāya āgantvā tassā padavalañjaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mātugāmassa padavalañjo, “puttassa mama sīlaṃ bhinnaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintento paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā phalāphalaṃ otāretvā puttaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

She thought, "This young ascetic is just a youth; he knows nothing. His father, however, must have gone forth when he was old. When that father returns, he will say, 'What are you doing in the hermitage?' and will beat me, grab me by the feet, drag me, and throw me into the forest. Therefore, I must flee before the elder ascetic returns." Having thought thus, she said to the young ascetic, "My dear, I will go ahead; you follow behind," and after indicating the route, she departed. From the time she left, the young ascetic became distressed. Without performing any of his duties as before, he covered his head and lay down inside the leaf hut, brooding. When the Great Being returned with fruits and roots, he saw the woman's footprints and thought, "These are a woman's footprints. My son's virtue must have been broken." Entering the leaf hut, he set down the fruits and roots and, wishing to question his son, spoke the first verse:

40.

40.

“Na te kaṭṭhāni bhinnāni, na te udakamābhataṃ;

Aggīpi te na hāpito, kiṃ nu mandova jhāyasī”ti.

"Your firewood is not split, your water is not fetched; your fire is not kindled, why do you brood like a dullard?"

Tattha [V 4.0198] aggīpi te na hāpitoti aggipi te na jālito. Mandovāti nippañño andhabālo viya.

In this context, 'aggīpi te na hāpito' means 'your fire is not kindled'. 'Mandova' means 'like one with little wisdom, like a blind fool'.

So pitu kathaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāya pitaraṃ vanditvā gāraveneva araññavāse anussāhaṃ pavedento gāthādvayamāha –

Having heard his father's words, the young ascetic rose, paid respects to his father, and with reverence, wishing to ask permission to leave the forest for the life of a householder, spoke these two verses:

41.

41.

“Na [M 4.0222] ussahe vane vatthuṃ, kassapāmantayāmi taṃ;

Dukkho vāso araññamhi, raṭṭhaṃ icchāmi gantave.

"I cannot bear to dwell in the forest, Kassapa, I address you; dwelling in the wilderness is difficult, I wish to go to the country.

42.

42.

“Yathā ahaṃ ito gantvā, yasmiṃ janapade vasaṃ;

Ācāraṃ brahme sikkheyyaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ anusāsa ma”nti.

“O noble one, teach me that principle by which, having gone from here, I might dwell in whatever country and learn its conduct.”

Tattha [P 4.0222] kassapāmantayāmi tanti kassapa āmantayāmi taṃ. Gantaveti gantuṃ. Ācāranti yasmiṃ janapade vasāmi, tattha vasanto yathā ācāraṃ janapadacārittaṃ sikkheyyaṃ jāneyyaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ anusāsa ovadāhīti vadati.

In this context, 'kassapāmantayāmi taṃ' means 'Kassapa, I address you.' 'Gantave' means 'to go.' 'Ācāraṃ' refers to the noble conduct: 'In whichever country I dwell, dwelling there, I should learn and know the customary practices of that country.' He says, 'Instruct and advise me in that principle.'

Mahāsatto “sādhu, tāta, desacārittaṃ te kathessāmī”ti vatvā gāthādvayamāha –

The Great Being said, "Very well, my son, I will tell you about the conduct of the region," and spoke these two verses:

43.

43.

“Sace araññaṃ hitvāna, vanamūlaphalāni ca;

Raṭṭhe rocayase vāsaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ nisāmehi me.

“If, having left the forest and forest roots and fruits, you find delight in dwelling in the realm, then listen to this teaching from me.

44.

44.

“Visaṃ mā paṭisevittho, papātaṃ parivajjaya;

Paṅke ca mā visīdittho, yatto cāsīvise care”ti.

“Do not partake of poison, avoid a precipice; do not sink into the mud, and conduct yourself with care near a viper.”

Tattha dhammanti sace raṭṭhavāsaṃ rocesi, tena hi tvaṃ janapadacārittaṃ dhammaṃ nisāmehi. Yatto cāsīviseti āsīvisassa santike yatto paṭiyatto careyyāsi, sakkonto āsīvisaṃ parivajjeyyāsīti attho.

In this context, 'dhammaṃ' means: 'If you delight in dwelling in the country, then listen to the teaching of the country's customs.' 'Yatto cāsīvise' means: 'You should conduct yourself with diligence and care near a viper, meaning you should avoid the viper altogether.'

Tāpasakumāro saṃkhittena bhāsitassa atthaṃ ajānanto pucchi –

The young ascetic, not understanding the meaning of what was briefly spoken, asked:

45.

45.

“Kiṃ [V 4.0199] nu visaṃ papāto vā, paṅko vā brahmacārinaṃ;

Kaṃ tvaṃ āsīvisaṃ brūsi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“What is poison, or a precipice, or a mire for those leading the holy life? Whom do you call a viper? Tell me, as I ask you.”

Itaropissa byākāsi –

The other explained to him in detail:

46.

46.

“Āsavo tāta lokasmiṃ, surā nāma pavuccati;

Manuñño surabhī vaggu, sādu khuddarasūpamo;

Visaṃ tadāhu ariyā se, brahmacariyassa nārada.

“Dear one, in this world, an intoxicant called liquor is spoken of; delightful, fragrant, lovely, sweet like the essence of honey. The noble ones call that poison, O Nārada, for the holy life.

47.

47.

“Itthiyo [M 4.0223] tāta lokasmiṃ, pamattaṃ pamathenti tā;

Haranti yuvino cittaṃ, tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva māluto;

Papāto eso akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

“Women in the world, dear one, overwhelm the heedless; they steal the hearts of young men, like the wind scatters cotton fallen from a tree. This is declared a precipice, O Nārada, for the holy life.

48.

48.

“Lābho siloko sakkāro, pūjā parakulesu ca;

Paṅko eso ca akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

“Gain, renown, honor, and veneration in other families—this, O Nārada, is declared the mire for the holy life.

49.

49.

“Sasatthā tāta rājāno, āvasanti mahiṃ imaṃ;

Te tādise manussinde, mahante tāta nārada.

“Kings, dear one, with their weapons, inhabit this earth. Such lords of men, great ones, dear Nārada,

50.

50.

“Issarānaṃ [P 4.0223] adhipatīnaṃ, na tesaṃ pādato care;

Āsīvisoti akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

“One should not walk at the feet of those rulers and overlords; this is declared a viper, O Nārada, for the holy life.

51.

51.

“Bhattattho bhattakāle ca, yaṃ gehamupasaṅkame;

Yadettha kusalaṃ jaññā, tattha ghāsesanaṃ care.

“One who seeks food should approach a house at mealtime. Knowing what is wholesome there, one should conduct oneself in seeking alms.

52.

52.

“Pavisitvā parakulaṃ, pānatthaṃ bhojanāya vā;

Mitaṃ khāde mitaṃ bhuñje, na ca rūpe manaṃ kare.

“Entering another’s home for drink or food, eat and partake in moderation, and do not fix your mind on forms.”

53.

53.

“Goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāṭañca, sabhā nikiraṇāni ca;

Ārakā parivajjehi, yānīva visamaṃ patha”nti.

“Avoid cattle pens, taverns, gamblers' haunts, assembly halls, and places for amassing wealth, just as a vehicle would avoid a rough path.”

Tattha [V 4.0200] āsavoti pupphāsavādi. Visaṃ tadāhūti taṃ āsavasaṅkhātaṃ suraṃ ariyā “brahmacariyassa visa”nti vadanti. Pamattanti muṭṭhassatiṃ. Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃvāti rukkhā bhassitvā patitatūlaṃ viya. Akkhātoti buddhādīhi kathito. Silokoti kittivaṇṇo. Sakkāroti añjalikammādi. Pūjāti gandhamālādīhi pūjā. Paṅkoti esa osīdāpanaṭṭhena “paṅko”ti akkhāto. Mahanteti mahantabhāvappatte. Na tesaṃ pādato careti tesaṃ santike na care, rājakulūpako na bhaveyyāsīti attho. Rājāno hi āsīvisā viya muhutteneva kujjhitvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti. Apica antepurappavesane vuttādīnavavasenapettha attho veditabbo.

In those verses, ‘āsavo’ refers to fermented liquor made from flowers and the like. ‘Visaṃ tadāhu’ means the noble ones call that liquor, known as ‘āsava,’ ‘the poison for the holy life.’ ‘Pamatta’ means one with muddled mindfulness. ‘Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva’ means like cotton that has fallen from a tree. ‘Akkhāto’ means declared by the Buddhas and others. ‘Siloka’ means fame and renown. ‘Sakkāro’ means acts of respect such as folding the hands in homage. ‘Pūjā’ means veneration with perfumes, garlands, and so forth. ‘Paṅka’ is declared to be ‘mire’ because it causes one to sink down. ‘Mahante’ means those who have attained a great state. ‘Na tesaṃ pādato care’ means one should not walk near them; the meaning is that one should not become a courtier. For kings, like vipers, can become angry in an instant and cause ruin and destruction. Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood in terms of the dangers mentioned regarding entering the inner palace.

Bhattatthoti [M 4.0224] bhattena atthiko hutvā. Yadettha kusalanti yaṃ tesu upasaṅkamitabbesu gehesu kusalaṃ anavajjaṃ pañcaagocararahitaṃ jāneyyāsi, tattha ghāsesanaṃ careyyāsīti attho. Na ca rūpe manaṃ kareti parakule mattaññū hutvā bhojanaṃ bhuñjantopi tattha itthirūpe manaṃ mā kareyyāsi, mā cakkhuṃ ummīletvā itthirūpe nimittaṃ gaṇheyyāsīti vadati. Goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāṭanti ayaṃ potthakesu pāṭho, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāsañcā”ti vatvā “goṭṭhanti gunnaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Majjanti pānāgāraṃ. Kirāsanti dhuttakerāṭikajana”nti vuttaṃ. Sabhā nikiraṇāni cāti sabhāyo ca hiraññasuvaṇṇānaṃ nikiraṇaṭṭhānāni ca. Ārakāti etāni sabbāni dūrato parivajjeyyāsi. Yānīvāti sappitelayānena gacchanto visamaṃ maggaṃ viya.

‘Bhattattho’ means being in need of food. ‘Yadettha kusalaṃ’ means whatever house among those to be approached you should know as wholesome, blameless, and free from the five wrong resorts; there you should conduct your search for food. This is the meaning. ‘Na ca rūpe manaṃ kare’ means even while eating food in moderation in another's family, you should not fix your mind on the forms of women there; he is saying, ‘do not open your eyes and take a sign from the forms of women.’ ‘Goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāṭañca’ is the reading in the books, but in the commentary it says ‘goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāsañca,’ explaining ‘goṭṭha’ as the standing place of cattle, ‘majja’ as a drinking house, and ‘kirāsa’ as rogues and swindlers. ‘Sabhā nikiraṇāni ca’ means assembly halls and places where gold and silver are stored. ‘Ārakā’ means you should avoid all these from afar. ‘Yānīva’ means like a vehicle avoids a rough path.

Māṇavo pitu kathentasseva satiṃ paṭilabhitvā “tāta, alaṃ me manussapathenā”ti āha. Athassa pitā [P 4.0224] mettādibhāvanaṃ ācikkhi. So tassovāde ṭhatvā na cirasseva jhānābhiññā nibbattesi. Ubhopi pitāputtā aparihīnajjhānā kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbattiṃsu.

As his father was speaking, the young ascetic regained mindfulness and said, “Father, I have no more need for the ways of the world.” Then his father explained to him the development of loving-kindness and the other brahmavihāras. Standing firm in his father's advice, he soon produced the jhānas and higher knowledges. Both father and son, with their jhānas undiminished, passed away and were reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sā kumārikā ayaṃ kumārikā ahosi, tāpasakumāro ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, pitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, that maiden was this maiden; the ascetic youth was the discontented monk; and the father was I myself.”

Cūḷanāradajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The fourth, the Commentary on the Cūḷanārada Jātaka, is finished.

[478] 5. Dūtajātakavaṇṇanā

[478] 5. 5. Dūta Jātaka

(Relating one’s distress only to those who can help.)

Dūte te brahme pāhesinti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto attano paññāpasaṃsanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “passatha, āvuso, dasabalassa upāyakosallaṃ, nandassa [V 4.0201] sakyaputtassa accharāgaṇaṃ dassetvā arahattaṃ adāsi, cūḷapanthakassa pilotikaṃ datvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ adāsi, kammāraputtassa padumaṃ dassetvā arahattaṃ adāsi, evaṃ nānāupāyehi satte vinetī”ti[M 4.0225]. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva ‘iminā idaṃ hotī’ti upāyakusalo, pubbepi upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“I sent them as messengers to you, O Brahmin”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the praise of his own wisdom. In the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, see the skill in means of the One of Ten Powers! By showing a host of celestial nymphs to Nanda the Sakyan, he gave him the fruit of arahantship. By giving a piece of cloth to Cūḷapanthaka, he granted him arahantship along with the four analytical knowledges. By showing a lotus to the goldsmith’s son, he bestowed arahantship. Thus, he trains beings through various means.” The Teacher, arriving, asked, “Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?” When they replied, “With this discussion,” he said, “Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata skilled in means, knowing, ‘By this cause, this effect happens.’ Even in the past, he was skilled in means,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente janapado ahirañño ahosi. So hi janapadaṃ pīḷetvā dhanameva saṃkaḍḍhi. Tadā bodhisatto kāsigāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā “pacchā dhammena bhikkhaṃ caritvā ācariyadhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti vatvā sippaṃ paṭṭhapetvā niṭṭhitasippo anuyogaṃ datvā “ācariya, tumhākaṃ dhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti āpucchitvā nikkhamma janapade caranto dhammena samena pariyesitvā satta nikkhe labhitvā “ācariyassa dassāmī”ti gacchanto antarāmagge gaṅgaṃ otarituṃ nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Tassa tattha nāvāya viparivattamānāya taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ udake pati. So cintesi “dullabhaṃ hiraññaṃ, janapade puna ācariyadhane pariyesiyamāne [P 4.0225] papañco bhavissati, yaṃnūnāhaṃ gaṅgātīreyeva nirāhāro nisīdeyyaṃ, tassa me nisinnabhāvaṃ anupubbena rājā jānissati, tato amacce pesessati, ahaṃ tehi saddhiṃ na mantessāmi, tato rājā sayaṃ āgamissati, iminā upāyena tassa santike ācariyadhanaṃ labhissāmī”ti. So gaṅgātīre uttarisāṭakaṃ pārupitvā yaññasuttaṃ bahi ṭhapetvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇe vālukatale suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya nisīdi. Taṃ nirāhāraṃ nisinnaṃ disvā mahājano “kasmā nisinnosī”ti pucchi, kassaci na kathesi. Punadivase dvāragāmavāsino tassa tattha nisinnabhāvaṃ sutvā āgantvā pucchiṃsu, tesampi na kathesi. Te tassa kilamathaṃ disvā paridevantā pakkamiṃsu. Tatiyadivase nagaravāsino āgamiṃsu, catutthadivase nagarato issarajanā, pañcamadivase rājapurisā. Chaṭṭhadivase rājā amacce pesesi, tehipi saddhiṃ na kathesi. Sattamadivase rājā bhayaṭṭito hutvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the country was without gold and silver. For the king oppressed the country and collected only wealth. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kasi country. When he came of age, he went to Takkasila and said, “Teacher, I will later wander for alms righteously and bring back the teacher’s fee.” Having begun his studies and completed his craft, he took his leave, saying, “Teacher, I will bring your fee,” then departed from Takkasila. Wandering through the country, he searched righteously and obtained seven nikkhas of gold. Thinking, “I will give these to the teacher,” he set out. On the way, he boarded a boat to cross the Ganges. While the boat was tossing about, that gold fell into the water. He thought, “Gold is very hard to obtain. If I search again in the country for the teacher’s fee, it will take a long time. What if I were to sit here on the bank of the Ganges without food? The king will eventually learn of my state. Then he will send his ministers. I will not speak with them. Then the king will come himself. By this means, I will obtain the teacher’s fee from him.” Having so planned, on the bank of the Ganges, he wrapped his upper robe around him, placed his sacrificial thread outside, and sat on the sand which was the color of a silver plate, like a golden statue. Seeing him sitting there without food, the people asked, “Why are you sitting here?” He spoke to no one. The next day, the people living at the village gate heard of him sitting there, came, and asked him, but he did not speak to them either. Seeing his exhaustion, they lamented and left. On the third day, the city dwellers came; on the fourth day, the authorities from the city; on the fifth day, the king’s men. On the sixth day, the king sent his ministers, but he did not speak with them either. On the seventh day, the king, overcome by fear, went to the Bodhisatta and, wishing to question him, spoke the first verse:

54.

54.

“Dūte te brahme pāhesiṃ, gaṅgātīrasmi jhāyato;

Tesaṃ puṭṭho na byākāsi, dukkhaṃ guyhamataṃ nu te”ti.

“Brahmin, I sent messengers to you as you were brooding on the bank of the Ganges; questioned by them, you did not answer. Is your suffering a matter to be kept secret by you?”

Tattha [M 4.0226] dukkhaṃ guyhamataṃ nu teti kiṃ nu kho, brāhmaṇa, yaṃ tava dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ te guyhameva mataṃ, na aññassa ācikkhitabbanti.

Here, “Is your suffering a matter to be kept secret?” means, “Brahmin, is the suffering that has arisen for you considered something to be kept secret, not to be told to another?”

Taṃ [V 4.0202] sutvā mahāsatto “mahārāja, dukkhaṃ nāma harituṃ samatthasseva ācikkhitabbaṃ, na aññassā”ti vatvā satta gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Great Being said, “Great king, suffering should be told only to one capable of removing it, not to another,” and intending to inform the king, he spoke these seven verses:

55.

55.

“Sace te dukkhamuppajje, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Mā kho naṃ tassa akkhāhi, yo taṃ dukkhā na mocaye.

“If suffering should arise for you, O increaser of the Kasi realm, do not tell it to one who cannot free you from that suffering.

56.

56.

“Yo tassa dukkhajātassa, ekaṅgamapi bhāgaso;

Vippamoceyya dhammena, kāmaṃ tassa pavedaya.

“To one who, by righteous means, could relieve even a single part of the suffering that has arisen, you should surely declare it.

57.

57.

“Suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato.

“The howling of jackals is easily known, as is the crying of birds; but the speech of humans, O king, is more difficult to understand than that.

58.

58.

“Api [P 4.0226] ce maññatī poso, ñāti mitto sakhāti vā;

Yo pubbe sumano hutvā, pacchā sampajjate diso.

“A person may think another is a relative, a friend, or a companion; yet one who was formerly well-disposed may later become an enemy.

59.

59.

“Yo attano dukkhamanānupuṭṭho, pavedaye jantu akālarūpe;

Ānandino tassa bhavanti mittā, hitesino tassa dukhī bhavanti.

“The person who, when asked repeatedly and at an inopportune time, reveals their own suffering—their enemies rejoice, while their well-wishers are saddened.

60.

60.

“Kālañca ñatvāna tathāvidhassa, medhāvinaṃ ekamanaṃ viditvā;

Akkheyya tibbāni parassa dhīro, saṇhaṃ giraṃ atthavatiṃ pamuñce.

“Knowing the right time, and having recognized a wise person of such a kind to be of one mind, a steadfast person should speak of intense sufferings to another, uttering gentle and meaningful speech.

61.

61.

“Sace ca jaññā avisayhamattano, na te hi mayhaṃ sukhāgamāya;

Ekova tibbāni saheyya dhīro, saccaṃ hirottappamapekkhamāno”ti.

“And if one should know one's suffering to be unbearable and that these conditions do not bring about one's happiness, then the steadfast person, having regard for truth, moral shame, and moral dread, should endure intense sufferings alone.”

Tattha [M 4.0227] uppajjeti sace tava uppajjeyya. Mā akkhāhīti mā kathehi. Dubbijānataraṃ tatoti tato tiracchānagatavassitatopi dubbijānataraṃ, tasmā tathato ajānitvā harituṃ asamatthassa attano dukkhaṃ na kathetabbamevāti. Api ceti gāthā vuttatthāva. Anānupuṭṭhoti punappunaṃ puṭṭho. Pavedayeti katheti. Akālarūpeti akāle. Kālanti attano guyhassa kathanakālaṃ. Tathāvidhassāti paṇḍitapurisaṃ attanā saddhiṃ ekamanaṃ viditvā tathāvidhassa ācikkheyya. Tibbānīti dukkhāni.

In those verses, ‘uppajje’ means ‘should it arise for you.’ ‘Mā akkhāhi’ means ‘do not speak of it.’ ‘Dubbijānataraṃ tato’ means harder to understand than even the cries of animals; therefore, without knowing for certain, one should not speak of one’s suffering to one who is unable to remove it. The verse beginning ‘Api ce’ has the meaning already stated. ‘Anānupuṭṭho’ means asked repeatedly. ‘Pavedaye’ means speaks of it. ‘Akālarūpe’ means at an improper time. ‘Kālaṃ’ means the time to speak of one’s own secret. ‘Tathāvidhassa’ means having recognized a wise person as being of one mind with oneself, one should disclose it to such a person. ‘Tibbāni’ means intense sufferings.

Saceti [V 4.0203] yadi attano dukkhaṃ avisayhaṃ attano vā paresaṃ vā purisakārena atekicchaṃ jāneyya. Te hīti te eva lokapaveṇikā, aṭṭhalokadhammāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – atha ayaṃ lokapaveṇī na mayhaṃ eva sukhāgamāya uppannā, aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi parimutto nāma natthi, evaṃ sante sukhameva patthentena parassa dukkhāropanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ, netaṃ hirottappasampannena kattabbaṃ, atthi ca me hirī ottappanti saccaṃ saṃvijjamānaṃ attani hirottappaṃ apekkhamānova aññassa anārocetvā ekova tibbāni saheyya dhīroti.

‘Sace’ means if one should know one’s own suffering to be unbearable and incurable by human effort, whether by oneself or by others. ‘Te hi’ refers to these worldly traditions, that is, the eight worldly conditions. This is what is meant: ‘This worldly tradition has not arisen for my happiness alone; there is no one exempt from the eight worldly conditions.’ This being so, it is not fitting for one who seeks only happiness to impose suffering on another. This should not be done by one endowed with moral shame and moral dread. Considering the truth and the moral shame and moral dread that truly exist in oneself, and not revealing it to another, the steadfast person should endure intense sufferings alone.

Evaṃ [P 4.0227] mahāsatto sattahi gāthāhi rañño dhammaṃ desetvā attano ācariyadhanassa pariyesitabhāvaṃ dassento catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to the king with seven verses, and wishing to show that he was seeking wealth for his teacher, spoke these four verses:

62.

62.

“Ahaṃ raṭṭhe vicaranto, nigame rājadhāniyo;

Bhikkhamāno mahārāja, ācariyassa dhanatthiko.

“Wandering through the country, in market towns and royal cities, I was requesting alms, O great king, being in need of wealth for my teacher.

63.

63.

“Gahapatī rājapurise, mahāsāle ca brāhmaṇe;

Alatthaṃ satta nikkhāni, suvaṇṇassa janādhipa;

Te me naṭṭhā mahārāja, tasmā socāmahaṃ bhusaṃ.

“From householders, royal officials, and wealthy brahmins, I obtained seven nikkhas of gold, O lord of men. They were lost to me, great king; therefore, I grieve deeply.

64.

64.

“Purisā te mahārāja, manasānuvicintitā;

Nālaṃ dukkhā pamocetuṃ, tasmā tesaṃ na byāhariṃ.

“Your men, great king, I have considered in my mind; they are not able to free me from suffering, therefore I did not speak to them.

65.

65.

“Tvañca [M 4.0228] kho me mahārāja, manasānuvicintito;

Alaṃ dukkhā pamocetuṃ, tasmā tuyhaṃ pavedayi”nti.

“But you, great king, have been considered by me in my mind; you are capable of freeing me from suffering; therefore, I have revealed it to you.”

Tattha bhikkhamānoti ete gahapatiādayo yācamāno. Te meti te satta nikkhā mama gaṅgaṃ tarantassa naṭṭhā, gaṅgāyaṃ patitā. Purisā teti mahārāja, tava dūtapurisā. Anuvicintitāti “nālaṃ ime maṃ dukkhā mocetu”nti mayā ñātā. Tasmāti tena kāraṇena tesaṃ attano dukkhaṃ nācikkhiṃ. Pavedayinti kathesiṃ.

In those verses, ‘bhikkhamāno’ means asking those householders and others. ‘Te me’ means those seven nikkhas were lost while I was crossing the Ganges, having fallen into the river. ‘Purisā te’ means your messengers, great king. ‘Anuvicintitā’ means it was understood by me that ‘they are not able to free me from suffering.’ ‘Tasmā’ means for that reason I did not declare my suffering to them. ‘Pavedayiṃ’ means I spoke.

Rājā tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā “mā cintayi, brāhmaṇa, ahaṃ te ācariyadhanaṃ dassāmī”ti dviguṇadhanamadāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā osānagāthamāha –

Hearing his Dhamma talk, the king said, “Brahmin, do not worry; I will give you the wealth for your teacher,” and gave him double the amount. Explaining this matter, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:

66.

66.

“Tassādāsi [V 4.0204] pasannatto, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Jātarūpamaye nikkhe, suvaṇṇassa catuddasā”ti.

“With a pleased mind, the increaser of the Kasi realm gave him fourteen nikkhas made of gold.”

Tattha jātarūpamayeti te suvaṇṇassa catuddasa nikkhe jātarūpamayeyeva adāsi, na yassa vā tassa vā suvaṇṇassāti attho.

In that verse, ‘jātarūpamaye’ means he gave fourteen nikkhas of gold that was indeed pure gold, not just any gold.

Mahāsatto rañño ovādaṃ datvā ācariyassa dhanaṃ datvā dānādīni puññāni katvā rājāpi tassovāde ṭhito dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā ubhopi yathākammaṃ gatā.

The Great Being gave counsel to the king and delivered the wealth to his teacher, and then performed meritorious deeds such as generosity. The king, remaining established in that counsel, ruled righteously, and both passed away according to their deeds.

Satthā [P 4.0228] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, ācariyo sāriputto, brāhmaṇamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to a close, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, the Tathāgata was skilled in means,” and he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, the teacher was Sāriputta, and the brahmin youth was none other than myself.”

Dūtajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Dūta Jātaka is finished.

[479] 6. Kāliṅgabodhijātakavaṇṇanā

[479] 6. 6. Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka

The account of the worship of the Great Bodhi Tree worthy of being a shrine of use.

Rājā kāliṅgo cakkavattīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ānandattherena kataṃ mahābodhipūjaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Veneyyasaṅgahatthāya hi tathāgate janapadacārikaṃ pakkante sāvatthivāsino gandhamālādihatthā jetavanaṃ gantvā aññaṃ pūjanīyaṭṭhānaṃ alabhitvā gandhakuṭidvāre pātetvā [M 4.0229] gacchanti, te uḷārapāmojjā na honti. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā anāthapiṇḍiko tathāgatassa jetavanaṃ āgatakāle ānandattherassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, ayaṃ vihāro tathāgate cārikaṃ pakkante nipaccayo hoti, manussānaṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjanīyaṭṭhānaṃ na hoti, sādhu, bhante, tathāgatassa imamatthaṃ ārocetvā ekassa pūjanīyaṭṭhānassa sakkuṇeyyabhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathāgataṃ pucchi “kati nu kho, bhante, cetiyānī”ti? “Tīṇi ānandā”ti. “Katamāni, bhante, tīṇī”ti? “Sārīrikaṃ pāribhogikaṃ uddissaka”nti. “Sakkā pana, bhante, tumhesu dharantesuyeva cetiyaṃ kātu”nti. “Ānanda, sārīrikaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ. Tañhi buddhānaṃ parinibbānakāle hoti, uddissakaṃ avatthukaṃ mamāyanamattameva hoti, buddhehi paribhutto mahābodhirukkho buddhesu dharantesupi cetiyamevā”ti. “Bhante, tumhesu pakkantesu jetavanavihāro appaṭisaraṇo hoti, mahājano pūjanīyaṭṭhānaṃ [V 4.0205] na labhati, mahābodhito bījaṃ āharitvā jetavanadvāre ropessāmi, bhante”ti. “Sādhu, ānanda, ropehi, evaṃ sante jetavane mama nibaddhavāso viya bhavissatī”ti.

“The king of Kāliṅga, a universal monarch…” This the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the great worship of the Bodhi tree performed by the Elder Ānanda. For the sake of favoring those who can be trained, when the Tathāgata went on a journey through the countryside, the residents of Sāvatthī, carrying perfumes and garlands, would go to Jetavana. Not finding any other place of worship, they would drop them at the door of the perfumed chamber and depart, not feeling great joy. Knowing this reason, Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Elder Ānanda when the Tathāgata had returned to Jetavana and said, "Venerable sir, this monastery becomes devoid of support when the Tathāgata goes on a journey. People have no place to worship with perfumes and garlands. It would be good, venerable sir, if you would inform the Tathāgata of this matter and find out the possibility of a place of worship." He agreed, saying, "Good," and asked the Tathāgata, "How many kinds of shrines are there, Lord?" "Three, Ānanda." "What are the three, Lord?" "Relic shrines, shrines of use, and commemorative shrines." "But is it possible, Lord, to create a shrine while you are still living?" "Ānanda, a relic shrine cannot be made. That arises only at the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas. A commemorative shrine is without a physical basis—it is merely for the sake of devotion. The great Bodhi tree, used by the Buddhas, is a shrine even while the Buddhas are living." "Lord, when you are away, the Jetavana monastery is without a refuge. The multitude finds no place of worship. I will bring a seed from the great Bodhi tree and plant it at the gate of Jetavana, Lord." "Good, Ānanda, plant it. Thus, it will be as if I have a continuous dwelling at Jetavana."

Thero kosalanarindassa anāthapiṇḍikassa visākhādīnañca ārocetvā jetavanadvāre bodhiropanaṭṭhāne āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpetvā mahāmoggallānattheraṃ āha – “bhante, ahaṃ jetavanadvāre bodhiṃ ropessāmi, mahābodhito me bodhipakkaṃ āharathā”ti. Thero “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ākāsena bodhimaṇḍaṃ gantvā vaṇṭā parigalantaṃ [P 4.0229] pakkaṃ bhūmiṃ asampattameva cīvarena sampaṭicchitvā gahetvā ānandattherassa adāsi. Ānandatthero “ajja bodhiṃ ropessāmī”ti kosalarājādīnaṃ ārocesi. Rājā sāyanhasamaye mahantena parivārena sabbūpakaraṇāni gāhāpetvā āgami, tathā anāthapiṇḍiko visākhā ca añño ca saddho jano. Thero mahābodhiropanaṭṭhāne mahantaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ ṭhapetvā heṭṭhā chiddaṃ kāretvā gandhakalalassa pūretvā “idaṃ bodhipakkaṃ ropehi, mahārājā”ti rañño adāsi. So cintesi “rajjaṃ nāma na sabbakālaṃ amhākaṃ hatthe tiṭṭhati, idaṃ mayā anāthapiṇḍikena ropāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti[M 4.0230]. So taṃ bodhipakkaṃ mahāseṭṭhissa hatthe ṭhapesi. Anāthapiṇḍiko gandhakalalaṃ viyūhitvā tattha pātesi. Tasmiṃ tassa hatthato muttamatteyeva sabbesaṃ passantānaññeva naṅgalasīsappamāṇo bodhikhandho paṇṇāsahatthubbedho uṭṭhahi, catūsu disāsu uddhañcāti pañca mahāsākhā paṇṇāsahatthāva nikkhamiṃsu. Iti so taṅkhaṇaññeva vanappatijeṭṭhako hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā aṭṭhārasamatte suvaṇṇarajataghaṭe gandhodakena pūretvā nīluppalahatthakādipaṭimaṇḍite mahābodhiṃ parikkhipitvā puṇṇaghaṭe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapesi, sattaratanamayaṃ vedikaṃ kāresi, suvaṇṇamissakaṃ vālukaṃ okiri, pākāraparikkhepaṃ kāresi, sattaratanamayaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ kāresi, sakkāro mahā ahosi.

The elder informed the King of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and others, and had a pit dug at the spot for planting the Bodhi tree near the gate of Jetavana. Then he addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: "Venerable sir, I will plant the Bodhi tree at the gate of Jetavana. Please bring me a ripe fruit from the Great Bodhi tree." The elder consented, saying, "Very well," and traveled through the air to the Bodhi terrace. There, he caught in his robe a ripe fruit that was falling from its stalk just before it reached the ground, and gave it to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda announced to the King of Kosala and others, "Today I will plant the Bodhi tree." In the evening, the king arrived with a large retinue, having them bring all the necessary items. Likewise, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā, and other faithful people came. The elder placed a large golden bowl at the site for planting the Great Bodhi tree, had a hole made at the bottom, filled it with fragrant mud, and said to the king, "Great king, plant this ripe Bodhi fruit." The king thought, "Kingship does not remain in our hands forever; it is fitting that I have Anāthapiṇḍika plant this." So he placed the Bodhi fruit in the hands of the great merchant. Anāthapiṇḍika parted the fragrant mud and dropped it there. The moment it left his hand, before the eyes of all present, a Bodhi trunk the size of a plow-shaft instantly sprang up to a height of fifty cubits. Five great branches, each fifty cubits long, spread out in the four directions and upwards. Thus, in that very instant, it stood as the foremost of forest trees. The king had eighteen golden and silver pots filled with fragrant water, adorned with handfuls of blue lotuses and other flowers, and arranged them in rows around the Great Bodhi tree. He had a railing made of the seven precious gems constructed, scattered sand mixed with gold, built a surrounding wall, and constructed a gatehouse of the seven precious gems. The honor shown was immense.

Thero tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, tumhehi mahābodhimūle samāpannasamāpattiṃ mayā ropitabodhimūle nisīditvā mahājanassa hitatthāya samāpajjathā”ti āha. “Ānanda, kiṃ kathesi, mayi mahābodhimūle samāpannasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisinne añño padeso dhāretuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Bhante, mahājanassa hitatthāya imassa bhūmippadesassa dhuvaniyāmena samāpattisukhena taṃ bodhimūlaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti. Satthā ekarattiṃ samāpattisukhena paribhuñji. Thero kosalarājādīnaṃ kathetvā bodhimahaṃ nāma kāresi. Sopi kho bodhirukkho ānandattherena ropitattā ānandabodhiyevāti paññāyittha. Tadā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso āyasmā ānando dharanteyeva tathāgate bodhiṃ ropetvā mahāpūjaṃ kāresi[P 4.0230], aho mahāguṇo thero”ti[V 4.0206]. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānando saparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu manusse gahetvā bahugandhamālādīni āharitvā mahābodhimaṇḍe bodhimahaṃ kāresiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The elder approached the Tathāgata and said, "Venerable sir, may you, who attained absorption at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, now sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree I planted and enter that same absorption for the welfare of the multitude." "Ānanda, what are you saying? When I am seated, having entered the absorption I attained at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, no other place is able to bear it." "Venerable sir, for the welfare of the multitude, by the fixed nature of this spot of earth, may you enjoy the base of that Bodhi tree with the bliss of absorption." The Teacher enjoyed it with the bliss of absorption for one night. The elder spoke to the King of Kosala and others and had a great Bodhi festival conducted. That very Bodhi tree, having been planted by the Elder Ānanda, became known as the Ānanda Bodhi. Then the monks in the Dhamma hall started a discussion: "Friends, the venerable Ānanda, while the Tathāgata was still living, planted a Bodhi tree and had a great offering made—ah, how great are the elder’s virtues!" The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Ānanda, taking people from the four great continents along with their retinues, bringing many perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, had a great Bodhi festival conducted at the great Bodhi terrace." Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte kaliṅgaraṭṭhe dantapuranagare kāliṅgo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa mahākāliṅgo, cūḷakāliṅgoti dve puttā ahesuṃ. Nemittakā “jeṭṭhaputto pitu accayena rajjaṃ kāressati, kaniṭṭho pana isipabbajjaṃ [M 4.0231] pabbajitvā bhikkhāya carissati, putto panassa cakkavattī bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Aparabhāge jeṭṭhaputto pitu accayena rājā ahosi, kaniṭṭho pana uparājā. So “putto kira me cakkavattī bhavissatī”ti puttaṃ nissāya mānaṃ akāsi. Rājā asahanto “cūḷakāliṅgaṃ gaṇhā”ti ekaṃ atthacarakaṃ āṇāpesi. So gantvā “kumāra, rājā taṃ gaṇhāpetukāmo, tava jīvitaṃ rakkhāhī”ti āha. So attano lañjanamuddikañca sukhumakambalañca khaggañcāti imāni tīṇi atthacarakāmaccassa dassetvā “imāya saññāya mama puttassa rajjaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti vatvā araññaṃ pavisitvā ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge assamaṃ katvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā nadītīre vāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, in the city of Dantapura, a king named Kāliṅga ruled. He had two sons: Mahākāliṅga and Cūḷakāliṅga. Fortune-tellers predicted, 'The eldest son, Mahākāliṅga, will rule the kingdom after his father's passing; the younger son, Cūḷakāliṅga, will go forth into the life of an ascetic and live by alms, but his son will become a Universal Monarch.' Later, the eldest son became king after his father's passing, and he appointed his younger brother, Cūḷakāliṅga, as viceroy. The viceroy, thinking, 'It is said my son will be a Universal Monarch,' became arrogant on account of his son. King Mahākāliṅga, unable to bear this, ordered a trusted agent, 'Go and seize Prince Cūḷakāliṅga!' The agent went and said, 'Prince, your elder brother the king wishes to have you seized. Protect your life!' The prince then showed a trusted minister his signet ring, a fine woolen blanket, and a sword—these three items—and instructed, 'By this token, give the kingdom to my son.' Having said this, he entered the forest, built a hermitage in a pleasant spot, went forth into the life of an ascetic, and lived on the riverbank.

Maddaraṭṭhepi sāgalanagare maddarañño aggamahesī dhītaraṃ vijāyi. Taṃ nemittakā “ayaṃ bhikkhaṃ caritvā jīvikaṃ kappessati, putto panassā cakkavattī bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Sakalajambudīpe rājāno taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā ekappahāreneva āgantvā sāgalanagaraṃ rundhiṃsu. Maddarājā cintesi “sacāhaṃ imaṃ ekassa dassāmi, sesarājāno kujjhissanti, mama dhītaraṃ rakkhissāmī”ti dhītarañca bhariyañca gahetvā aññātakavesena palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā cūḷakāliṅgakumārassa assamapadato uparibhāge assamaṃ [P 4.0231] katvā pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya jīvikaṃ kappento tattha paṭivasati. Mātāpitaro “dhītaraṃ rakkhissāmā”ti taṃ assamapade katvā phalāphalatthāya gacchanti. Sā tesaṃ gatakāle nānāpupphāni gahetvā pupphacumbaṭakaṃ katvā gaṅgātīre ṭhapitasopānapanti viya jāto eko supupphito ambarukkho atthi, taṃ abhiruhitvā kīḷitvā pupphacumbaṭakaṃ udake khipi. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ gaṅgāyaṃ nhāyantassa cūḷakāliṅgakumārassa sīse laggi. So taṃ oloketvā “idaṃ ekāya itthiyā kataṃ, no ca kho mahallikāya, taruṇakumārikāya katakammaṃ, vīmaṃsissāmi tāva na”nti kilesavasena uparigaṅgaṃ gantvā tassā ambarukkhe nisīditvā madhurena sarena gāyantiyā saddaṃ sutvā rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā taṃ disvā “bhadde, kā nāma tva”nti āha. “Manussitthīhamasmi sāmī”ti[V 4.0207]. “Tena hi otarāhī”ti. “Na sakkā sāmi, ahaṃ khattiyā”ti. “Bhadde, ahampi khattiyoyeva, otarāhī”ti. Sāmi, na vacanamatteneva khattiyo hoti, yadisi khattiyo, khattiyamāyaṃ [M 4.0232] kathehī”ti. Te ubhopi aññamaññaṃ khattiyamāyaṃ kathayiṃsu. Rājadhītā otari.

In the kingdom of Madda, in the city of Sāgala, the chief queen of the King of Madda gave birth to a daughter. Fortune-tellers predicted, 'This princess will sustain her life by wandering for alms, but her son will be a Universal Monarch.' When the kings of all Jambudīpa heard this news, they arrived all at once and besieged the city of Sāgala. The King of Madda thought, 'If I give her to one king, the others will be angry. I will protect my daughter.' Taking his daughter and wife, he fled in disguise, entered the forest, and built a hermitage in a place further upstream from Prince Cūḷakāliṅga’s hermitage. Having gone forth as an ascetic, he lived there, sustaining his life by gleaning. The parents, thinking, 'We will protect our daughter,' would leave her at the hermitage and go out for various fruits. In their absence, she would take various flowers, weave them into a wreath, and climb a well-blossomed mango tree that stood on the bank of the Ganges like a flight of stairs. After playing there, she would toss the floral wreath into the water. One day, the wreath floated down and got caught in the hair of Prince Cūḷakāliṅga as he was bathing in the Ganges. Looking at it, he thought, 'This was woven by a young maiden, not an old woman. I will investigate.' Driven by passion, he went upstream and heard the sweet voice of the princess singing while sitting in the mango tree. Going to the foot of the tree and seeing her, he asked, 'Good lady, who are you?' She replied, 'I am a human woman, sir.' 'In that case, come down,' he said. 'I cannot, sir, I am a princess,' she replied. 'Good lady, I too am a prince. Come down.' 'Sir, one is not a prince by words alone. If you are a prince, speak the lore of the Khattiyas.' They both then spoke the Khattiya-lore to each other. The princess then descended from the mango tree.

Te aññamaññaṃ ajjhācāraṃ cariṃsu. Sā mātāpitūsu āgatesu tassa kāliṅgarājaputtabhāvañceva araññaṃ paviṭṭhakāraṇañca vitthārena tesaṃ kathesi. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ tassa adaṃsu. Tesaṃ piyasaṃvāsena vasantānaṃ rājadhītā gabbhaṃ labhitvā dasamāsaccayena dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi, “kāliṅgo”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto pitu ceva ayyakassa ca santike sabbasippānaṃ nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa pitā nakkhattayogavasena bhātu matabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tāta, mā tvaṃ araññe vasa, petteyyo te mahākāliṅgo kālakato, tvaṃ dantapuranagaraṃ gantvā kulasantakaṃ sakalarajjaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā attanā [P 4.0232] ānītaṃ muddikañca kambalañca khaggañca datvā “tāta, dantapuranagare asukavīthiyaṃ amhākaṃ atthacarako amacco atthi, tassa gehe sayanamajjhe otaritvā imāni tīṇi ratanāni tassa dassetvā mama puttabhāvaṃ ācikkha, so taṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpessatī”ti uyyojesi. So mātāpitaro ca ayyakāyyike ca vanditvā puññamahiddhiyā ākāsena gantvā amaccassa sayanapiṭṭheyeva otaritvā “kosi tva”nti puṭṭho “cūḷakāliṅgassa puttomhī”ti ācikkhitvā tāni ratanāni dassesi. Amacco rājaparisāya ārocesi. Amaccā nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā tassa setacchattaṃ ussāpayiṃsu.

After she descended, they committed an act of transgression with each other. When her parents returned from the forest, she told them in detail that he was the son of the King of Kāliṅga and explained the reason for his coming to the forest. They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and gave their daughter to the Kāliṅga prince. While they were living together in a loving union, the princess conceived, and after ten months, she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of merit and fortune. They named him 'Kāliṅga.' When the prince came of age, he mastered all the arts in the presence of his father and grandfather. Then his father, Cūḷakāliṅga, knowing by the conjunction of the stars that his elder brother had died, said, 'Son, do not live in the forest. Your paternal uncle, Mahākāliṅga, has passed away. Go to the city of Dantapura and take the entire kingdom which is your family's inheritance.' Giving him the signet ring, the blanket, and the sword he had brought, he instructed him, 'Son, in the city of Dantapura, on such-and-such a street, there is a minister who serves our interests. Enter his house, descend onto the middle of his bed, show him these three treasures, and announce that you are my son. He will establish you in the kingdom.' Having sent him off, the prince paid homage to his parents and grandparents and, by the great power of his merit, traveled through the air and descended right onto the minister's bed. When asked, 'Who are you?' he replied, 'I am the son of Cūḷakāliṅga,' and showed the treasures. The minister informed the royal assembly. The ministers then had the city decorated and raised the white parasol over the prince.

Athassa kāliṅgabhāradvājo nāma purohito tassa dasa cakkavattivattāni ācikkhi. So taṃ vattaṃ pūresi. Athassa pannarasauposathadivase cakkadahato cakkaratanaṃ, uposathakulato hatthiratanaṃ, valāhakakulato assaratanaṃ, vepullapabbatato maṇiratanaṃ āgami, itthiratanagahapatiratanapariṇāyakaratanāni pātubhavanti. So sakalacakkavāḷagabbhe rajjaṃ gaṇhitvā ekadivasañca chattiṃsayojanāya parisāya parivuto sabbasetaṃ kelāsakūṭapaṭibhāgaṃ hatthiṃ āruyha mahantena sirivilāsena mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ pāyāsi. Athassa sabbabuddhānaṃ jayapallaṅkassa pathavīnābhibhūtassa mahābodhimaṇḍassa uparibhāge nāgo gantuṃ nāsakkhi. Rājā punappunaṃ codesi, so nāsakkhiyeva. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, his chaplain, named Kāliṅgabhāradvāja, instructed him in the ten duties of a wheel-turning monarch. He fulfilled those duties. Then, on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, the wheel-treasure came from the Wheel Lake, the elephant-treasure from the Uposatha clan, the horse-treasure from the Valāhaka clan, and the jewel-treasure from Mount Vepulla; the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the crown prince treasure also manifested. Having taken sovereignty over the entire world-system, one day, surrounded by a retinue extending thirty-six yojanas, he mounted a completely white royal elephant that resembled a peak of Mount Kelāsa and set out with great royal splendor to his parents' presence. But as he was proceeding, above the Great Bodhimaṇḍa—the navel of the earth and the throne of victory for all Buddhas—the royal elephant was unable to go. The king urged it again and again, but it simply could not proceed. To make this matter clear, the Teacher spoke the first verse:

67.

67.

“Rājā [V 4.0208][M 4.0233] kāliṅgo cakkavatti, dhammena pathavimanusāsaṃ;

Agamā bodhisamīpaṃ, nāgena mahānubhāvenā”ti.

King Kāliṅga, the wheel-turning monarch, ruling the earth with righteousness, approached the vicinity of the Bodhi tree upon his greatly powerful elephant.

Atha rañño purohito raññā saddhiṃ gacchanto “ākāse āvaraṇaṃ nāma natthi, kiṃ nu kho rājā hatthiṃ pesetuṃ na sakkoti[P 4.0233], vīmaṃsissāmī”ti ākāsato oruyha sabbabuddhānaṃyeva jayapallaṅkaṃ pathavīnābhimaṇḍalabhūtaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ passi. Tadā kira tattha aṭṭharājakarīsamatte ṭhāne kesamassumattampi tiṇaṃ nāma natthi, rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇavālukā vippakiṇṇā honti, samantā tiṇalatāvanappatiyo bodhimaṇḍaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā āvaṭṭetvā bodhimaṇḍābhimukhāva aṭṭhaṃsu. Brāhmaṇo taṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ oloketvā “idañhi sabbabuddhānaṃ sabbakilesaviddhaṃsanaṭṭhānaṃ, imassa uparibhāge sakkādīhipi na sakkā gantu”nti cintetvā kāliṅgarañño santikaṃ gantvā bodhimaṇḍassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā rājānaṃ “otarā”ti āha. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imā gāthā āha –

Then the king's chaplain, traveling with the king, thought, 'There is no obstruction in the sky. Why is the king unable to make the royal elephant go forward? I will investigate.' Descending from the sky, he saw that stretch of ground which is the throne of victory for all Buddhas, the navel-circle of the earth. At that time, it is said, in that place measuring about eight royal karīsas, there was not even a blade of grass the size of a hair. It was strewn with sand the color of a silver sheet, and all around, the grasses, creepers, and forest trees, having circumambulated the Bodhimaṇḍa to the right, stood turned towards it, facing the Bodhimaṇḍa. The brahmin, observing that stretch of ground, thought, 'This is indeed the place where all Buddhas shatter all defilements. Even Sakka and others are unable to travel above it.' He went to King Kāliṅga, described the qualities of the Bodhimaṇḍa, and said to the king, 'Descend from the royal elephant.' To make this matter clear, the Teacher spoke these verses:

68.

68.

“Kāliṅgo bhāradvājo ca, rājānaṃ kāliṅgaṃ samaṇakolaññaṃ;

Cakkaṃ vattayato pariggahetvā, pañjalī idamavoca.

Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja, with hands joined in reverence, addressed King Kāliṅga, the wheel-turner and descendant of a line of recluses, and spoke this:

69.

69.

“Paccoroha mahārāja, bhūmibhāgo yathā samaṇuggato;

Idha anadhivarā buddhā, abhisambuddhā virocanti.

Descend, O Great King, for this stretch of ground is praised by the Sages. Here the unexcelled Buddhas, having attained full enlightenment, shine forth.

70.

70.

“Padakkhiṇato āvaṭṭā, tiṇalatā asmiṃ bhūmibhāgasmiṃ;

Pathaviyā nābhiyaṃ maṇḍo, iti no sutaṃ mante mahārāja.

The grasses and creepers on this stretch of ground turn to the right. This is the essence at the navel of the earth; thus have we heard in our sacred texts, O Great King.

71.

71.

“Sāgarapariyantāya, mediniyā sabbabhūtadharaṇiyā;

Pathaviyā ayaṃ maṇḍo, orohitvā namo karohi.

Of the earth that is bounded by the ocean, the supporter of all beings, this is the sacred center; descend and pay homage.

72.

72.

“Ye te bhavanti nāgā ca, abhijātā ca kuñjarā;

Ettāvatā padesaṃ te, nāgā neva mupayanti.

Those elephants that are of noble breed, the great tuskers, even they cannot approach this region.

73.

73.

“Abhijāto nāgo kāmaṃ, pesehi kuñjaraṃ dantiṃ;

Ettāvatā padeso, sakkā nāgena mupagantuṃ.

Your elephant is indeed of noble breed; if you wish, urge on the tusker. This region can only be approached so far by a royal elephant.

74.

74.

“Taṃ [V 4.0209][M 4.0234] sutvā rājā kāliṅgo, veyyañjanikavaco nisāmetvā;

Sampesesi nāgaṃ ñassāma, mayaṃ yathimassidaṃ vacanaṃ.

Hearing that, King Kāliṅga, having heeded the words of the interpreter of signs, urged the elephant forward, thinking, 'We shall know if this word of his is true.'

75.

75.

“Sampesito ca raññā, nāgo koñcova abhinaditvāna;

Paṭisakkitvā nisīdi, garuṃva bhāraṃ asahamāno”ti.

And being urged on by the king, the elephant, trumpeting like a crane, retreated and sat down, as if unable to bear a heavy burden.

Tattha [P 4.0234] samaṇakolaññanti tāpasānaṃ puttaṃ. Cakkaṃ vattayatoti cakkaṃ vattayamānaṃ, cakkavattinti attho. Pariggahetvāti bhūmibhāgaṃ vīmaṃsitvā. Samaṇuggatoti sabbabuddhehi vaṇṇito. Anadhivarāti atulyā appameyyā. Virocantīti vihatasabbakilesandhakārā taruṇasūriyā viya idha nisinnā virocanti. Tiṇalatāti tiṇāni ca latāyo ca. Maṇḍoti catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalāya pathaviyā maṇḍo sāro nābhibhūto acalaṭṭhānaṃ, kappe saṇṭhahante paṭhamaṃ saṇṭhahati, vinassante pacchā vinassati. Iti no sutanti evaṃ amhehi lakkhaṇamantavasena sutaṃ. Orohitvāti ākāsato otaritvā imassa sabbabuddhānaṃ kilesaviddhaṃsanaṭṭhānassa namo karohi, pūjāsakkāraṃ karohi.

Therein, 'samaṇakolañña' means the son of recluses. 'Cakkaṃ vattayato' means turning the wheel; the sense is 'wheel-turner' (cakkavattī). 'Pariggahetvā' means having examined the region. 'Samaṇuggato' means praised by all Buddhas. 'Anadhivarā' means incomparable and immeasurable. 'Virocanti' means, having dispelled all the darkness of defilements, they shine, seated here like the morning sun. 'Tiṇalatā' means grasses and creepers. 'Maṇḍo' refers to the essence of the earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, the navel and unmoving place; when the aeon forms, it is the first to form, and when it perishes, it is the last to perish. 'Iti no sutaṃ' means thus have we heard through the lore of marks in the Vedas. 'Orohitvā' means descending from the sky, pay homage to this place where all Buddhas have destroyed the defilements; make offerings and show honor.

Ye teti ye cakkavattirañño hatthiratanasaṅkhātā uposathakule nibbattanāgā. Ettāvatāti sabbepi te ettakaṃ padesaṃ neva upayanti, koṭṭiyamānāpi na upagacchantiyeva. Abhijātoti gocariyādīni aṭṭha hatthikulāni abhibhavitvā atikkamitvā uposathakule jāto. Kuñjaranti uttamaṃ. Ettāvatāti ettako padeso sakkā etena nāgena upagantuṃ, ito uttari na sakkā, abhikaṅkhanto vajiraṅkusena saññaṃ datvā pesehīti. Veyyañjanikavaco nisāmetvāti bhikkhave, so rājā tassa lakkhaṇapāṭhakassa veyyañjanikassa kāliṅgabhāradvājassa vaco nisāmetvā upadhāretvā “ñassāma mayaṃ yathā imassa vacanaṃ yadi vā saccaṃ yadi vā alika”nti vīmaṃsanto nāgaṃ pesesīti attho. Koñcova abhinaditvānāti bhikkhave, so nāgo tena raññā vajiraṅkusena codetvā pesito koñcasakuṇo viya naditvā paṭisakkitvā soṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā gīvaṃ unnāmetvā garuṃ bhāraṃ vahituṃ asakkonto viya ākāseyeva nisīdi.

'Ye te' refers to those elephants born in the Uposatha family, known as the elephant-jewels of a wheel-turning king. 'Ettāvatā' means all of them cannot reach even this area; even when prodded, they do not proceed further. 'Abhijāto' means born in the Uposatha family, having surpassed the eight elephant families, such as Gocariya and others. 'Kuñjara' means excellent. 'Ettāvatā' means this much area can be traversed by this elephant; beyond this, it is not possible; if you desire, give the signal with the diamond goad and send it forth. 'Veyyañjanikavaco nisāmetvā' means, monks, the king, having heeded and reflected on the words of that reader of marks, the soothsayer Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja, thinking, 'We shall know whether his words are true or false,' sent the elephant forth. 'Koñcova abhinaditvāna' means, monks, that elephant, urged on by the king with the diamond goad, trumpeted like a crane, retreated, and as if unable to bear the heavy burden, sat down right there in the air.

So [M 4.0235] tena punappunaṃ vijjhiyamāno vedanaṃ sahituṃ asakkonto kālamakāsi. Rājā panassa matabhāvaṃ ajānanto piṭṭhe nisinnova ahosi. Kāliṅgabhāradvājo “mahārāja, tava nāgo niruddho, aññaṃ hatthiṃ saṅkamā”ti āha. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Being prodded again and again by the goad, and unable to endure the pain, the noble elephant died. The king, however, unaware of its death, remained seated on its back. Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja said, "Great King, your noble elephant's life-force has ceased; please mount another elephant." To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke the tenth verse:

76.

76.

“Kāliṅgabhāradvājo[V 4.0210], nāgaṃ khīṇāyukaṃ viditvāna;

Rājānaṃ kāliṅgaṃ, taramāno ajjhabhāsittha;

Aññaṃ saṅkama nāgaṃ, nāgo khīṇāyuko mahārājā”ti.

"Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja, knowing the elephant's life was exhausted, urgently addressed King Kāliṅga: 'Mount another elephant; the elephant's life is exhausted, Great King.'"

Tattha [P 4.0235] nāgo khīṇāyukoti nāgo te jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, yaṃ kiñci karontena na sakkā piṭṭhe nisinnena bodhimaṇḍamatthakena gantuṃ. Aññaṃ nāgaṃ saṅkamāti rañño puññiddhibalena añño nāgo uposathakulato āgantvā piṭṭhiṃ upanāmesi.

Therein, 'nāgo khīṇāyuko' means the elephant has reached the end of its life; it is not possible for one seated on its back to go to the summit of the Bodhi-maṇḍa, whatever one might do. 'Aññaṃ nāgaṃ saṅkama' means that by the power of the king's merit, another elephant from the Uposatha clan arrived and offered its back.

Rājā tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe matahatthī bhūmiyaṃ pati. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

The king sat upon its back. At that moment, the dead elephant fell to the ground. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke the next verse:

77.

77.

“Taṃ sutvā kāliṅgo, taramāno saṅkamī nāgaṃ;

Saṅkanteva raññe nāgo, tattheva pati bhumyā;

Veyyañjanikavaco, yathā tathā ahu nāgo”ti.
