"Having heard that, Kāliṅga, hurrying, mounted the other elephant. As soon as the king had mounted, the first elephant fell to the ground right there. Just as the soothsayer had spoken, so it happened to the elephant."

Atha rājā ākāsato oruyha bodhimaṇḍaṃ oloketvā pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā bhāradvājassa thutiṃ karonto āha –

Then the king, descending from the sky and gazing upon the Bodhi-maṇḍa, saw the miracle and, in praise of Bhāradvāja, said:

78.

78.

“Kāliṅgo rājā kāliṅgaṃ, brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca;

Tvameva asi sambuddho, sabbaññū sabbadassāvī”ti.

"King Kāliṅga said this to the brahmin Kāliṅga: 'You yourself are the Perfectly Awakened One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing.'"

Brāhmaṇo taṃ anadhivāsento attānaṃ nīcaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā buddheyeva ukkhipitvā vaṇṇesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The brahmin, not accepting that praise and placing himself in a humble position, extolled only the Buddhas. To explain this matter, the Teacher uttered these verses:

79.

79.

“Taṃ anadhivāsento kāliṅga, brāhmaṇo idamavoca;

Veyyañjanikā hi mayaṃ, buddhā sabbaññuno mahārāja.

"Not accepting that, the brahmin said this to Kāliṅga: 'We are merely soothsayers, Great King; it is the Buddhas who are omniscient.

80.

80.

“Sabbaññū [M 4.0236] sabbavidū ca, buddhā na lakkhaṇena jānanti;

Āgamabalasā hi mayaṃ, buddhā sabbaṃ pajānantī”ti.

The Buddhas, the All-Knowing and All-Wise, do not know by means of signs. We know by the power of tradition, but the Buddhas know everything fully.'"

Tattha [V 4.0211] veyyañjanikāti mahārāja, mayaṃ byañjanaṃ disvā byākaraṇasamatthā sutabuddhā nāma, buddhā pana sabbaññū sabbavidū. Buddhā hi atītādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ jānanti ceva passanti ca, sabbaññutaññāṇena te sabbaṃ jānanti, na lakkhaṇena. Mayaṃ pana āgamabalasā attano sippabaleneva jānāma, tañca ekadesameva, buddhā pana sabbaṃ pajānantīti.

Therein, 'veyyañjanikā' means: Great King, we are those who, upon seeing a sign, are capable of making a prediction; we are called 'Buddhas by hearsay'. The Buddhas, however, are omniscient and all-wise. Indeed, the Buddhas both know and see everything, divided into past, present, and future; they know everything through the knowledge of omniscience, not by signs. We, however, know by the power of tradition and by the power of our own skill, and that only in part; but the Buddhas know everything fully.

Rājā buddhaguṇe sutvā somanassappatto hutvā sakalacakkavāḷavāsikehi bahugandhamālaṃ āharāpetvā mahābodhimaṇḍe sattāhaṃ vasitvā mahābodhipūjaṃ kāresi. Tamatthaṃ [P 4.0236] pakāsento satthā imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

The king, having heard the virtues of the Buddha, became filled with joy and had many perfumes and flowers brought by the inhabitants of the entire world-system. Residing at the great Bodhi-maṇḍa for seven days, he had a great offering made to the Great Bodhi. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:

81.

81.

“Mahayitvā sambodhiṃ, nānāturiyehi vajjamānehi;

Mālāvilepanaṃ abhiharitvā, atha rājā manupāyāsi.

"Having honored the Bodhi with various musical instruments being played, and having offered garlands and perfumes, the king then departed."

82.

82.

“Saṭṭhi vāhasahassāni, pupphānaṃ sannipātayi;

Pūjesi rājā kāliṅgo, bodhimaṇḍamanuttara”nti.

"Sixty thousand cartloads of flowers he gathered; King Kāliṅga honored the unsurpassed Bodhi-maṇḍa."

Tattha manupāyāsīti mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. So mahābodhimaṇḍe aṭṭhārasahatthaṃ suvaṇṇatthambhaṃ ussāpesi. Tassa sattaratanamayā vedikā kāresi, ratanamissakaṃ vālukaṃ okirāpetvā pākāraparikkhittaṃ kāresi, sattaratanamayaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakaṃ kāresi, devasikaṃ pupphānaṃ saṭṭhivāhasahassāni sannipātayi, evaṃ bodhimaṇḍaṃ pūjesi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “saṭṭhi vāhasahassāni pupphāna”nti ettakameva āgataṃ.

Therein, 'manupāyāsi' means he went to his parents. At the great Bodhi-maṇḍa, he had a golden pillar eighteen cubits high erected. He had a railing made of the seven precious materials constructed for it, had sand mixed with jewels scattered, and had it surrounded by a wall. He had a gatehouse made of the seven precious materials constructed. He gathered sixty thousand cartloads of flowers daily, and thus he honored the Bodhi-maṇḍa. In the canonical text, however, only 'sixty thousand cartloads of flowers' is mentioned.

Evaṃ mahābodhipūjaṃ katvā mātāpitaro ayyakāyyike ca ādāya dantapurameva ānetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti.

Having thus performed the great Bodhi-pūjā, he took his parents and grandparents and brought them to Dantapura. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

Satthā [M 4.0237] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānando bodhipūjaṃ kāresiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā māṇavakakāliṅgo ānando ahosi, kāliṅgabhāradvājo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Ānanda had Bodhi-pūjā performed." Then he made the connection to the Jātaka: "At that time, the young prince Kāliṅga was Ānanda, and Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja was I myself."

Kāliṅgabodhijātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Kāliṅga Bodhi Jātaka is finished.

[480] 7. Akittijātakavaṇṇanā

[480] 7. 7. Akitti Jātaka

Akittiṃ [V 4.0212] disvā sammantanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sāvatthivāsiṃ dānapatiṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira satthāraṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā pariyosānadivase ariyasaṅghassa sabbaparikkhāre adāsi. Athassa satthā parisamajjheyeva anumodanaṃ karonto “upāsaka, mahā te pariccāgo, aho dukkaraṃ tayā kataṃ, ayañhi dānavaṃso nāma porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, dānaṃ nāma gihināpi pabbajitenāpi dātabbameva. Porāṇakapaṇḍitā pana pabbajitvā araññe vasantāpi aloṇakaṃ vidhūpanaṃ udakamattasittaṃ kārapaṇṇaṃ [P 4.0237] khādamānāpi sampattayācakānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ datvā sayaṃ pītisukhena yāpayiṃsū”ti vatvā “bhante, idaṃ tāva sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ mahājanassa pākaṭaṃ, tumhehi vuttaṃ apākaṭaṃ, taṃ no kathethā”ti tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"Seeing Akitti, they deliberated": this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a lay devotee in Sāvatthī who was a generous donor. He, it is said, invited the Teacher and for seven days gave a great offering to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. On the final day, he gave all the requisites to the Noble Sangha. Then the Teacher, performing the anumodanā in the midst of the assembly, said, "Lay devotee, great is your sacrifice. Ah, what you have done is difficult! This is the lineage of giving, the lineage of the ancient wise. Giving is to be done by both householders and renunciants. The ancient wise, though they renounced and lived in the forest, even when eating kāra leaves steamed in water without salt, gave to those who asked as much as they desired and sustained themselves with the bliss of joy." When asked, "Venerable sir, this giving of all requisites is evident to the people, but what you spoke of is not evident—please tell us that," he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa kule nibbatti, “akittī”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa padasā gamanakāle bhaginīpi jāyi, “yasavatī”tissā nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Mahāsatto soḷasavassakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgami. Athassa mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. So tesaṃ petakiccāni kāretvā dhanavilokanaṃ karonto “asuko nāma ettakaṃ dhanaṃ saṇṭhapetvā atīto, asuko ettaka”nti vacanaṃ sutvā saṃviggamānaso hutvā “idaṃ dhanameva paññāyati, na dhanassa saṃhārakā, sabbe imaṃ dhanaṃ pahāyeva gatā, ahaṃ pana taṃ ādāya gamissāmī”ti bhaginiṃ pakkosāpetvā “tvaṃ imaṃ dhanaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha[M 4.0238]. “Tumhākaṃ pana ko ajjhāsayo”ti? “Pabbajitukāmomhī”ti. “Bhātika, ahaṃ tumhehi chaḍḍitaṃ kheḷaṃ na sirasā sampaṭicchāmi, na me iminā attho, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti. So rājānaṃ āpucchitvā bheriṃ carāpesi “dhanena atthikā akittipaṇḍitassa gehaṃ āgacchantū”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a brahmin of great wealth, eighty crores in value. They named him 'Akitti.' When he was able to walk, his sister was also born, and they named her 'Yasavatī.' When the Great Being was sixteen years old, he went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and returned. Then his parents passed away. After performing their funeral rites, he examined their wealth and, hearing people say, 'So-and-so passed away, having amassed this much wealth; so-and-so, that much,' he became agitated in mind, thinking, 'Only this wealth is seen, but not those who amassed it. All have departed, leaving this wealth behind. But I shall take it and depart.' He summoned his sister and said, 'You take possession of this wealth.' 'But what is your intention?' she asked. 'I wish to renounce the world.' 'Brother, I would not accept on my head even the spittle you discard. I have no use for this. I too shall renounce.' He took leave of the king and had a drum beaten: 'Let those in need of wealth come to the house of Akitti the wise.'

So sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā dhane akhīyamāne cintesi “ime saṅkhārā khīyanti, kiṃ me dhanakīḷāya, atthikā taṃ gaṇhissantī”ti nivesanadvāraṃ vivaritvā “dinnaññeva harantū”ti sahiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ gehaṃ pahāya ñātimaṇḍalassa paridevantassa bhaginiṃ gahetvā bārāṇasito nikkhami. Yena dvārena nikkhami, taṃ akittidvāraṃ nāma jātaṃ, yena titthena nadiṃ otiṇṇo, tampi akittititthaṃ nāma jātaṃ. So dve tīṇi yojanāni gantvā ramaṇīye ṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ katvā bhaginiyā saddhiṃ pabbaji. Tassa pabbajitakālato [P 4.0238] paṭṭhāya bahugāmanigamarājadhānivāsino [V 4.0213] pabbajiṃsu. Mahāparivāro ahosi, mahālābhasakkāro nibbatti, buddhuppādakālo viya pavatti. Atha mahāsatto “ayaṃ lābhasakkāro mahā, parivāropi mahanto, mayā ekakeneva viharituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā avelāya antamaso bhaginimpi ajānāpetvā ekakova nikkhamitvā anupubbena damiḷaraṭṭhaṃ patvā kāvīrapaṭṭanasamīpe uyyāne viharanto jhānābhiññāyo nibbattesi. Tatrāpissa mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. So taṃ jigucchitvā chaḍḍetvā ākāsena gantvā nāgadīpasamīpe kāradīpe otari. Tadā kāradīpo ahidīpo nāma ahosi. So tattha mahantaṃ kārarukkhaṃ upanissāya paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tattha tassa vasanabhāvaṃ na koci jānāti. Athassa bhaginī bhātaraṃ gavesamānā anupubbena damiḷaraṭṭhaṃ patvā taṃ adisvā tena vasitaṭṭhāneyeva vasi, jhānaṃ pana nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi.

For seven days he held a great almsgiving, and when the wealth was not diminishing, he thought, 'These conditioned things perish; what is the use of my delighting in wealth? Those who need it will take it.' Then he opened the doors of his house and declared, 'Let them take what is given.' Abandoning his home with its gold and silver, he left Bārāṇasī with his sister, while his circle of relatives lamented. The gate by which he departed became known as 'Akitti Gate,' and the ford where he crossed the river was called 'Akitti Ford.' After traveling two or three yojanas, he built a leaf-hut in a pleasant place and went forth into homelessness with his sister. From the time of his going forth, many inhabitants of villages, towns, and royal cities also went forth. He had a great following, and great gains and honor arose—it was as if the time of a Buddha’s appearance had arrived. Then the Great Being thought, 'These gains and honor are great, and the retinue is large. It is fitting for me to dwell alone.' Without informing even his sister, even at an unseasonable time, he left alone and gradually reached the Damila country. Dwelling in a grove near Kāvīrapaṭṭana, he developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges. There too, great gains and honor arose for him. Disgusted by them, he abandoned that place and, traveling through the air, descended on Kāra Island near Nāga Island. At that time, Kāra Island was called Ahidīpa. There, relying on a large kāra tree, he built a leaf-hut and took up residence. No one knew of his dwelling there. Meanwhile, his sister, searching for her brother, gradually reached the Damila country. Not finding him, she settled in the very place where he had lived, but she was unable to develop meditative absorption.

Mahāsatto appicchatāya katthaci agantvā tassa rukkhassa phalakāle phalāni khādati, pattakāle pattāni udakasittāni khādati. Tassa sīlatejena sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti āvajjento akittipaṇḍitaṃ disvā “kimatthaṃ esa tāpaso sīlāni rakkhati, sakkattaṃ nu kho pattheti, udāhu aññaṃ, vīmiṃsissāmi naṃ. Ayañhi dukkhena jīvikaṃ kappesi, udakasittāni kārapaṇṇāni [M 4.0239] khādati, sace sakkattaṃ pattheti, attano sittapattāni mayhaṃ dassati, no ce, na dassatī”ti brāhmaṇavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisatto kārapaṇṇāni sedetvā otāretvā “sītalabhūtāni khādissāmī”ti paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Athassa purato sakko bhikkhāya aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto taṃ disvā somanassappatto hutvā “lābhā vata me, yohaṃ yācakaṃ passāmi, ajja me manorathaṃ matthakaṃ [P 4.0239] pāpetvā dānaṃ dassāmī”ti pakkabhājaneneva ādāya gantvā “idaṃ me dānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇassa paccayo hotū”ti attano asesetvāva tassa bhājane pakkhipi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ gahetvā thokaṃ gantvā antaradhāyi. Mahāsattopi tassa datvā puna apacitvā pītisukheneva vītināmetvā punadivase pacitvā tattheva paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi.

The Great Being, due to his fewness of wishes, did not go anywhere. When it was the fruit season of that tree, he ate the fruits; when it was the leaf season, he ate the leaves sprinkled with water. Through the power of his virtue, Sakka’s Pandukambala stone seat showed a sign of heat. Sakka, wondering, 'Who is trying to dislodge me from my place?' and reflecting, saw Akitti the wise. He thought, 'For what purpose does this ascetic maintain his virtues? Does he aspire to the state of Sakka, or something else? I will test him. He lives a life of hardship, eating water-sprinkled kāra leaves. If he aspires to the state of Sakka, he will give me his own sprinkled leaves; if not, he will not give them.' Assuming the form of a brahmin, he approached him. The Bodhisatta, having steamed the kāra leaves and taken them down, thought, 'I will eat them when they are cool,' and sat at the door of his leaf-hut. Then Sakka stood before him for alms. The Great Being, seeing him, was filled with joy and thought, 'What a gain for me, that I see a mendicant! Today I will bring my wish to fulfillment by giving alms.' Taking the vessel of cooked food itself, he went and, thinking, 'May this gift be a condition for the attainment of omniscience,' he placed all of it into the brahmin’s bowl without keeping any for himself. The brahmin took it, went a short distance, and disappeared. The Great Being, having given it to him, did not cook again, but spent the time in the bliss of rapture. On the next day, after cooking, he sat again at the door of his leaf-hut.

Sakko puna brāhmaṇavesena agamāsi. Punapissa datvā mahāsatto tatheva vītināmesi. Tatiyadivasepi tatheva datvā “aho me lābhā vata, kārapaṇṇāni nissāya mahantaṃ puññaṃ pasuta”nti somanassappatto tayo divase anāhāratāya dubbalopi samāno majjhanhikasamaye paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā dānaṃ āvajjento paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Sakkopi cintesi “ayaṃ [V 4.0214] brāhmaṇo tayo divase nirāhāro hutvā evaṃ dubbalopi dānaṃ dento tuṭṭhacittova deti, cittassa aññathattampi natthi, ahaṃ imaṃ ‘idaṃ nāma patthetvā detī’ti na jānāmi, pucchitvā ajjhāsayamassa sutvā dānakāraṇaṃ jānissāmī”ti. So majjhanhike vītivatte mahantena sirisobhaggena gaganatale taruṇasūriyo viya jalamāno āgantvā mahāsattassa puratova ṭhatvā “ambho tāpasa, evaṃ uṇhavāte paharante evarūpe loṇajalaparikkhitte araññe kimatthaṃ tapokammaṃ karosī”ti pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka again approached in the guise of a brahmin. Once more, the Great Being gave to him and spent the day in the same manner. On the third day as well, after giving in the same way, he was filled with joy, thinking, "Ah, what good fortune is mine! Relying on these kāra leaves, I have generated great merit!" Though weakened by three days without food, at midday he left his leaf-hut and sat at its door, reflecting on his gift. Sakka thought, "This brahmin, though so weak from three days without food, gives with a delighted mind. There is no change in his mind. I do not know for what he gives, aspiring for something in return. I will ask him, learn his intention, and understand the reason for his generosity." When midday had passed, Sakka, shining with great splendor like a young sun ablaze in the sky, approached and stood right before the Great Being. He asked, "O ascetic, in this scorching wind, in such a wilderness surrounded by salty water and without shelter, for what purpose do you undertake this ascetic practice?" To explain this matter, the Teacher first spoke this verse:

83.

83.

“Akittiṃ disvā sammantaṃ, sakko bhūtapatī bravi;

Kiṃ patthayaṃ mahābrahme, eko sammasi ghammanī”ti.

Seeing Akitti dwelling in peace, Sakka, lord of beings, said: 'Aspiring for what, O great brahmin, do you dwell alone in the heat?'

Tattha kiṃ patthayanti kiṃ manussasampattiṃ patthento, udāhu sakkasampattiādīnaṃ aññataranti.

Herein, what is he aspiring for? Is he aspiring for human attainment, or for one of the divine attainments, such as that of Sakka?

Mahāsatto [M 4.0240] taṃ sutvā sakkabhāvañcassa ñatvā “nāhaṃ etā sampattiyo patthemi, sabbaññutaṃ pana patthento tapokammaṃ karomī”ti pakāsetuṃ dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, hearing those words and recognizing his status as Sakka, spoke the second verse to declare: 'I do not aspire for these attainments, but fulfilling the perfections for omniscience, I practice asceticism.'

84.

84.

“Dukkho [P 4.0240] punabbhavo sakka, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ;

Sammohamaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā sammāmi vāsavā”ti.

'Painful is rebirth, O Sakka, and the dissolution of the body; death with delusion is painful; therefore, O Vāsava, I dwell in peace.'

Tattha tasmāti yasmā punappunaṃ jāti khandhānaṃ bhedanaṃ sammohamaraṇañca dukkhaṃ, tasmā yatthetāni natthi, taṃ nibbānaṃ patthento idha sammāmīti evaṃ attano nibbānajjhāsayataṃ dīpeti.

Herein, 'therefore' means: because repeated birth, the breaking up of the aggregates, and death with delusion are suffering; therefore, aspiring for Nibbāna where these do not exist, I dwell in peace here. Thus he reveals his inclination toward Nibbāna.

Taṃ sutvā sakko tuṭṭhamānaso “sabbabhavesu kirāyaṃ ukkaṇṭhito nibbānatthāya araññe viharati, varamassa dassāmī”ti varena nimantento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka, with a pleased mind, thought, "Indeed, this ascetic is weary of all states of existence and dwells in the forest for the sake of Nibbāna. I shall grant him a boon." Then, inviting him to choose a boon, he spoke the third verse:

85.

85.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

Tattha yaṃ kiñci manasicchasīti yaṃ manasā icchasi, taṃ dammi, varaṃ gaṇhāhīti.

Herein, 'whatever you wish for in your mind' means: 'whatever you desire in your mind, I give it to you; take the boon.'

Mahāsatto [V 4.0215] varaṃ gaṇhanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, wishing to accept the boon, spoke the fourth verse:

86.

86.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Yena putte ca dāre ca, dhanadhaññaṃ piyāni ca;

Laddhā narā na tappanti, so lobho na mayī vase”ti.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may that greed not dwell in me, by which men, having obtained sons, wives, wealth, grain, and beloved things, are never satisfied.'

Tattha varañce me adoti sace varaṃ mayhaṃ desi. Piyāni cāti aññāni ca yāni piyabhaṇḍāni. Na tappantīti punappunaṃ puttādayo patthentiyeva, na tittiṃ upagacchanti. Na mayī vaseti mayi mā vasatu mā uppajjatu.

Herein, 'If you grant me a boon' means 'if you give a boon to me.' 'And beloved things' means other cherished possessions. 'Are not satisfied' means they desire sons and so forth again and again; they do not reach fulfillment. 'May it not dwell in me' means may it not arise within me.

Athassa sakko tussitvā uttarimpi varaṃ dento mahāsatto ca varaṃ gaṇhanto imā gāthā abhāsiṃsu –

Then Sakka, being pleased with the Great Being and offering further boons, and the Great Being, accepting those boons, spoke these verses:

87.

87.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

88.

88.

“Varañce [M 4.0241] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Khettaṃ vatthuṃ hiraññañca, gavāssaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Yena jātena jīyanti, so doso na mayī vase.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may that hatred not dwell in me, by which, when it arises, fields, property, gold, cattle and horses, slaves and servants are lost.'

89.

89.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

90.

90.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Bālaṃ na passe na suṇe, na ca bālena saṃvase;

Bālenallāpasallāpaṃ, na kare na ca rocaye.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I not see a fool, nor hear a fool, nor associate with a fool; may I not engage in conversation with a fool, nor find pleasure in a fool.'

91.

91.

“Kiṃ [P 4.0241] nu te akaraṃ bālo, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa bālassa, dassanaṃ nābhikaṅkhasi.

'What wrong did the fool do to you? Speak, Kassapa, the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you not desire to even see a fool?'

92.

92.

“Anayaṃ [V 4.0216] nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati;

Dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati;

Vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassanaṃ.

'The fool leads to ruin; he engages in what is unbeneficial. He is difficult to lead toward the better; when rightly spoken to, he gets angry. He does not know discipline—it is good not to see him.'

93.

93.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

94.

94.

“Varañce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Dhīraṃ passe suṇe dhīraṃ, dhīrena saha saṃvase;

Dhīrenallāpasallāpaṃ, taṃ kare tañca rocaye.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I see the wise, may I hear the wise, may I associate with the wise; may I engage in conversation with the wise, and find pleasure in them.'

95.

95.

“Kiṃ nu te akaraṃ dhīro, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa dhīrassa, dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

'What then has the wise one done for you? Speak, Kassapa, the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you long for the sight of the wise?'

96.

96.

“Nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati;

Sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati;

Vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo.

'The wise one leads to what is beneficial; he does not engage in what is unbeneficial. He is easy to lead toward the better; when rightly spoken to, he does not get angry. He understands discipline; association with him is good.'

97.

97.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

98.

98.

“Varañce [M 4.0242] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Dibbā bhakkhā pātubhaveyyuṃ, sīlavanto ca yācakā.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: then at the end of the night, at the rising of the sun, may divine food appear, and may virtuous mendicants come.'

99.

99.

“Dadato me na khīyetha, datvā nānutapeyyahaṃ;

Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyyaṃ, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

'May my store not be exhausted while I am giving; having given, may I not regret it; while giving, may I gladden my mind—this, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.'

100.

100.

“Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

'For this well-spoken, fitting, and eloquent speech of yours, Kassapa, I grant you a boon, whatever you wish for in your mind.'

101.

101.

“Varañce [V 4.0217] me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Na maṃ puna upeyyāsi, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

'If you grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may you not come near me again. This, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.'

102.

102.

“Bahūhi vatacariyāhi, narā ca atha nāriyo;

Dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhanti, kiṃ nu me dassane bhayaṃ.

'Many men and women, through various religious observances, long for a sight of me. What fear could there be in seeing me?'

103.

103.

“Taṃ tādisaṃ devavaṇṇaṃ, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Disvā tapo pamajjeyyaṃ, etaṃ te dassane bhaya”nti.

'Seeing you of such a divine form, endowed with all sensual fulfillments, I might become negligent in my ascetic practice; this is the danger in seeing you.'

Tattha yena jātenāti yena cittena jātena kuddhā sattā pāṇavadhādīnaṃ katattā rājadaṇḍavasena visakhādanādīhi vā attano maraṇavasena [P 4.0242] etāni khettādīni jīyanti, so doso mayi na vaseyyāti yācati. Na suṇeti asukaṭṭhāne nāma vasatītipi imehi kāraṇehi na suṇeyyaṃ. Kiṃ nu te akaranti kiṃ nu tava bālena mātā māritā, udāhu tava pitā, aññaṃ vā pana te kiṃ nāma anatthaṃ bālo akaraṃ.

Herein, 'by which having arisen' means: by which mind having arisen, angry beings, because they have committed acts such as killing living beings, lose these fields and so forth by way of the king's punishment, or by consuming poison and so on, or by way of their own death. He requests: 'May that fault not dwell in me.' 'May I not hear' means: 'May I not even hear that he lives in such-and-such a place.' 'What has he done to you?' means: 'What, was your mother killed by the fool, or your father? Or what other harm indeed has the fool done to you?'

Anayaṃ nayatīti akāraṇaṃ “kāraṇa”nti gaṇhāti, pāṇātipātādīni katvā jīvikaṃ kappessāmīti evarūpāni anatthakammāni cinteti. Adhurāyanti saddhādhurasīladhurapaññādhuresu ayojetvā ayoge niyuñjati. Dunnayo seyyaso hotīti dunnayova tassa seyyo hoti. Pañca dussīlakammāni samādāya vattanameva seyyoti gaṇhāti, hitapaṭipattiyā vā dunnayo hoti netuṃ asakkuṇeyyo. Sammā vuttoti hetunā [M 4.0243] kāraṇena vutto kuppati. Vinayanti “evaṃ abhikkamitabba”ntiādikaṃ ācāravinayaṃ na jānāti, ovādañca na sampaṭicchati. Sādhu tassāti etehi kāraṇehi tassa adassanameva sādhu.

'He leads to ruin' means he takes what is not a cause as a cause; he thinks, 'I will make a living by killing living beings and the like,' contemplating such unprofitable actions. 'He applies himself to what is unsuitable' means not applying himself to the burdens of faith, virtue, and wisdom, he applies himself to what is not suitable. 'Misconduct is preferable to him' means misconduct itself is preferable to him; he embraces the five kinds of immoral conduct and considers that way of life itself as better, or he is too difficult to lead to beneficial practice. 'When rightly spoken to' means when spoken to with reason and cause, he gets angry. 'He does not know discipline' means he does not know the discipline of conduct, such as 'one should proceed thus,' and he does not accept advice. 'Not seeing him is good' means for these reasons, it is indeed good not to see him.

Sūriyuggamanaṃ patīti sūriyuggamanavelāya. Dibbā bhakkhāti dibbabhojanaṃ yācakāti tassa dibbabhojanassa paṭiggāhakā. Vatacariyāhīti dānasīlauposathakammehi. Dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhantīti dassanaṃ mama abhikaṅkhanti. Taṃ tādisanti evarūpaṃ dibbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ. Pamajjeyyanti pamādaṃ āpajjeyyaṃ. Tava sirisampattiṃ pattheyyaṃ, evaṃ nibbānatthāya pavattite tapokamme sakkaṭṭhānaṃ patthento pamatto nāma bhaveyyaṃ, etaṃ tava dassane mayhaṃ bhayanti.

'Towards the rising of the sun' means at the time of sunrise. 'Divine food' means divine food. 'Beggars' means the recipients of that divine food. 'By virtuous practice' means by deeds of generosity, virtue, and the observance days. 'Desiring to see' means they desire my sight. 'Such a one' means adorned with such divine ornaments. 'I might become negligent' means 'I might fall into negligence.' 'I would aspire to your glorious prosperity; thus, in ascetic practice undertaken for the sake of Nibbāna, if I were to aspire to Sakka's place, I would indeed be negligent. This is my fear at the sight of you.'

Sakko “sādhu, bhante, ito paṭṭhāya na te santikaṃ āgamissāmā”ti taṃ vanditvā khamāpetvā [V 4.0218] pakkāmi. Mahāsatto yāvajīvaṃ tattheva vasanto brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmaloke nibbatti.

Sakka said, 'Good, venerable sir, from now on I will not come into your presence,' and having paid homage and asked for forgiveness, he departed. The Great Being, dwelling there for the rest of his life, cultivated the divine abidings and was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi, akittipaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth story: 'At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, but Akitti the Wise was indeed myself.'

Akittijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh: The Commentary on the Akitti Jātaka.

[481] 8. Takkāriyajātakavaṇṇanā

[481] 8. 8. The Commentary on the Takkāriya Jātaka

Ahameva dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsi bāloti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi antovasse dve aggasāvakā gaṇaṃ pahāya vivittāvāsaṃ vasitukāmā satthāraṃ āpucchitvā kokālikaraṭṭhe kokālikassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ evamāhaṃsu “āvuso kokālika, taṃ [P 4.0243] nissāya amhākaṃ, amhe ca nissāya tava phāsuvihāro bhavissati, imaṃ temāsaṃ idha vaseyyāmā”ti. “Ko panāvuso, maṃ nissāya tumhākaṃ phāsuvihāro”ti. Sace tvaṃ āvuso “dve aggasāvakā idha viharantī”ti kassaci nāroceyyāsi, mayaṃ sukhaṃ vihareyyāma, ayaṃ taṃ nissāya amhākaṃ phāsuvihāroti. “Atha [M 4.0244] tumhe nissāya mayhaṃ ko phāsuvihāro”ti? “Mayaṃ tuyhaṃ antotemāsaṃ dhammaṃ vācessāma, dhammakathaṃ kathessāma, esa tuyhaṃ amhe nissāya phāsuvihāro”ti. “Vasathāvuso, yathājjhāsayenā”ti. So tesaṃ patirūpaṃ senāsanaṃ adāsi. Te phalasamāpattisukhena sukhaṃ vasiṃsu. Koci nesaṃ tattha vasanabhāvaṃ na jānāti.

'It was I myself, the fool, who spoke ill-spoken words.' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning Kokālika. During one rainy season, the two chief disciples, wishing to leave the community and dwell in seclusion, took leave of the Teacher and went to Kokālika’s dwelling place in the Kokālika country. They said to him: 'Friend Kokālika, depending on you, we will have a comfortable stay, and depending on us, you will also have a comfortable stay. Let us stay here for these three months.' 'But, friends, how will your comfortable stay depend on me?' 'If you, friend, do not tell anyone that the two chief disciples are staying here, we will dwell happily. This is how our comfortable stay depends on you.' 'Then how will my comfortable stay depend on you?' 'We will teach you the Dhamma and give Dhamma talks during these three months. This is how your comfortable stay will depend on us.' 'Stay, friends, as you wish.' He provided them with suitable lodging. They dwelled happily in the bliss of fruition attainment. No one knew of their staying there.

Te vutthavassā pavāretvā “āvuso, taṃ nissāya sukhaṃ vutthāmha, satthāraṃ vandituṃ gacchāmā”ti taṃ āpucchiṃsu. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā te ādāya dhuragāme piṇḍāya cari. Therā katabhattakiccā gāmato nikkhamiṃsu. Kokāliko te uyyojetvā nivattitvā manussānaṃ ārocesi “upāsakā, tumhe tiracchānasadisā, dve aggasāvake temāsaṃ dhuravihāre vasante na jānittha, idāni te gatā”ti. Manussā “kasmā pana, bhante, amhākaṃ nārocitthā”ti vatvā bahuṃ sappitelādibhesajjañceva vatthacchādanañca gahetvā there upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “khamatha no, bhante, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ aggasāvakabhāvaṃ na jānāma, ajja no kokālikabhadantassa vacanena ñātā, amhākaṃ anukampāya imāni bhesajjavatthacchādanāni gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu.

Having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they took leave of him, saying, 'Friend, we have stayed happily depending on you; now we are going to pay homage to the Teacher.' He consented, saying, 'Good.' Taking them along, he went for alms in the neighboring village. The elders, having finished their meal, left the village. Kokālika, having sent them off and turning back, informed the people, saying, 'Lay devotees, you are like animals. You did not know that the two chief disciples were staying in the nearby monastery for three months. Now they have left.' The people replied, 'But why, venerable sir, did you not inform us?' Then, taking much medicine like ghee and oil, as well as cloth for robes, they approached the elders, paid homage, and said, 'Forgive us, venerable sirs; we did not know of your being the chief disciples. Today we learned of it through the words of the Venerable Kokālika. Out of compassion for us, please accept these medicines and robes.'

Kokāliko [V 4.0219] “therā appicchā santuṭṭhā, imāni vatthāni attanā aggahetvā mayhaṃ dassantī”ti cintetvā upāsakehi saddhiṃyeva therānaṃ santikaṃ gato. Therā bhikkhuparipācitattā tato kiñci neva attanā gaṇhiṃsu, na kokālikassa dāpesuṃ. Upāsakā “bhante, idāni agaṇhantā puna amhākaṃ anukampāya idha āgaccheyyāthā”ti yāciṃsu. Therā anadhivāsetvā satthu santikaṃ agamiṃsu. Kokāliko “ime therā attanā agaṇhantā mayhaṃ na dāpesu”nti āghātaṃ bandhi. Therāpi satthu santike thokaṃ vasitvā attano parivāre pañcabhikkhusate ca ādāya bhikkhusahassena saddhiṃ cārikaṃ caramānā kokālikaraṭṭhaṃ pattā. Te upāsakā paccuggamanaṃ katvā there ādāya tameva vihāraṃ netvā devasikaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Pahutaṃ bhesajjavatthacchādanaṃ [P 4.0244] uppajji, therehi saddhiṃ āgatabhikkhū cīvarāni vicārentā saddhiṃ āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaññeva denti[M 4.0245], kokālikassa na denti, therāpi tassa na dāpenti. Kokāliko cīvaraṃ alabhitvā “pāpicchā sāriputtamoggallānā, pubbe dīyamānaṃ lābhaṃ aggahetvā idāni gaṇhanti, pūretuṃ na sakkā, aññe na olokentī”ti there akkosati paribhāsati. Therā “ayaṃ amhe nissāya akusalaṃ pasavatī”ti saparivārā nikkhamitvā “aññaṃ, bhante, katipāhaṃ vasathā”ti manussehi yāciyamānāpi nivattituṃ na icchiṃsu.

Kokālika thought, "The elders are of few wishes and content; not taking these items for themselves, they will give them to me." With this thought, he went to the elders along with the lay devotees. The elders, because the items had been solicited by the monk Kokālika, neither took anything for themselves nor had anything given to Kokālika. The lay devotees requested, "Venerable sirs, since you are not taking them now, please come here again out of compassion for us." The elders, without consenting, went to the Teacher's presence. Kokālika became resentful, thinking, "These elders, not taking them for themselves, did not have them given to me." After staying near the Teacher for a short while, the elders, taking their retinue of five hundred monks each, set out on a journey with a thousand monks and arrived in the Kokālika territory. The lay devotees welcomed them, led them to that same monastery, and showed them great honor daily. Abundant medicines, robes, and materials were offered. The monks who had come with the elders, while distributing the robes, gave only to the monks who had come with them; they did not give any to Kokālika, nor did the elders have any given to him. Unable to obtain a robe, Kokālika reviled and insulted the elders, saying, "Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires. Previously, they did not accept offered gains, but now they take them. They can never be satisfied; they have no regard for others." The elders thought, "This man is generating unwholesome karma because of us," and left with their retinue. Even when the people pleaded, "Venerable sirs, stay for a few more days," they did not wish to turn back.

Atheko daharo bhikkhu āha – “upāsakā, kathaṃ therā vasissanti, tumhākaṃ kulūpako thero idha imesaṃ vāsaṃ na sahatī”ti. Te tassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, tumhe kira therānaṃ idha vāsaṃ na sahatha, gacchatha ne khamāpetvā nivattetha, sace na nivattetha, palāyitvā aññattha vasathā”ti āhaṃsu. So upāsakānaṃ bhayena gantvā there yāci. Therā “gacchāvuso, na mayaṃ nivattāmā”ti pakkamiṃsu. So there nivattetuṃ asakkonto vihārameva paccāgato. Atha naṃ upāsakā pucchiṃsu “nivattitā te, bhante, therā”ti. “Nivattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃ āvuso”ti. Atha naṃ “imasmiṃ pāpadhamme vasante idha pesalā bhikkhū na vasissanti, nikkaḍḍhāma na”nti cintetvā “bhante, mā tvaṃ idha vasi, amhe nissāya tuyhaṃ kiñci natthī”ti āhaṃsu. So tehi nikkaḍḍhito pattacīvaramādāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “pāpicchā, bhante, sāriputtamoggallānā, pāpikānaṃ icchānaṃ vasaṃ gatā”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “mā hevaṃ kokālika, avaca, mā hevaṃ kokālika avaca, pasādehi kokālika, sāriputtamoggallānesu cittaṃ, te pesalā bhikkhū”ti vāreti. Vāritopi kokāliko “tumhe, bhante, tumhākaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ saddahatha, ahaṃ paccakkhato addasaṃ, pāpicchā ete paṭicchannakammantā dussīlā”ti vatvā yāvatatiyaṃ satthārā vāritopi tatheva vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Tassa pakkantamattasseva sakalasarīre sāsapamattā piḷakā uṭṭhahitvā anupubbena vaḍḍhitvā [V 4.0220] beḷuvapakkamattā hutvā bhijjitvā pubbalohitāni pagghariṃsu. So nitthunanto vedanāppatto jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake nipajji. “Kokālikena dve aggasāvakā akkuṭṭhā”ti yāva brahmalokā ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi.

Then a young monk said, "Lay followers, how will the elders stay here? Your family-supporter elder cannot endure their stay in this place." They went to him and said, "Venerable sir, it is said that you cannot endure the elders staying here. Go, apologize to them and bring them back. If you do not bring them back, flee and live elsewhere." Out of fear of the lay followers, he went and begged the elders. The elders said, "Go, friend, we will not return," and departed. Unable to make them return, he went back to the monastery. Then the lay followers asked him, "Venerable sir, did the elders return?" "I could not make them return, friends." Then, thinking, "As long as this wicked one stays here, virtuous monks will not dwell here; let us drive him out," they said, "Venerable sir, do not stay here. Depending on us, there is nothing for you." Driven out by them, he took his bowl and robes, went to Jetavana, and approaching the Teacher, said, "Venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil wishes." Then the Teacher restrained him, saying, "Do not say so, Kokālika; do not say so, Kokālika. Settle your heart with faith in Sāriputta and Moggallāna; they are virtuous monks." Although restrained, Kokālika said, "Venerable sir, you trust your chief disciples, but I have seen it for myself—they have evil desires, their actions are hidden, and they are immoral." Though the Teacher restrained him up to three times, he said the same thing, rose from his seat, and left. Just as he had left, boils the size of mustard seeds broke out over his whole body; they grew progressively until they were the size of ripe bael fruits, then burst, oozing pus and blood. Groaning and in great pain, he lay down in the gatehouse of Jetavana. An uproar arose all the way to the Brahma world, saying, "Kokālika has reviled the two chief disciples!"

Athassa [M 4.0246] upajjhāyo turū nāma brahmā [P 4.0245] taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “there khamāpessāmī”ti āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā “kokālika, pharusaṃ te kammaṃ kataṃ, aggasāvake pasādehī”ti āha. “Ko pana tvaṃ āvuso”ti? “Turū brahmā nāmāha”nti. “Nanu tvaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā anāgāmīti byākato, anāgāmī ca anāvattidhammo asmā lokāti vuttaṃ, tvaṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne yakkho bhavissasī”ti mahābrahmaṃ apasādesi. So taṃ attano vacanaṃ gāhāpetuṃ asakkonto “tava vācāya tvaññeva paññāyissasī”ti vatvā suddhāvāsameva gato. Kokālikopi kālaṃ katvā padumaniraye uppajji. Tassa tattha nibbattabhāvaṃ ñatvā sahampatibrahmā tathāgatassa ārocesi, satthā bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhū tassa aguṇaṃ kathentā dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, kokāliko kira sāriputtamoggallāne akkositvā attano mukhaṃ nissāya padumaniraye uppanno”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva kokāliko vacanena hato attano mukhaṃ nissāya dukkhaṃ anubhoti, pubbepi esa attano mukhaṃ nissāya dukkhaṃ anubhosiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then his preceptor, a Brahma named Turu, knowing the matter and thinking, "I will have him ask the elders for forgiveness," came and, standing in the air, said, "Kokālika, you have committed a harsh deed. Settle your heart with faith in the chief disciples." "But who are you, friend?" "I am the Brahma named Turu." "Friend, were you not declared a non-returner by the Blessed One? And has it not been said that a non-returner is one who does not return from that world? You will become a yakkha at a rubbish heap!" Thus he rebuked the Great Brahma. Unable to make him accept his words, the Brahma said, "By your own words, you yourself will be known," and went back to the Suddhāvāsa heaven. Kokālika also passed away and was reborn in the Paduma hell. Knowing of his rebirth there, the Brahma Sahampati informed the Tathāgata, and the Teacher informed the monks. The monks, discussing his faults, raised a conversation in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, it is said that Kokālika, having reviled Sāriputta and Moggallāna, was reborn in the Paduma hell on account of his own mouth." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now has Kokālika been destroyed by his speech and suffered on account of his own mouth; in the past, too, he suffered on account of his own mouth." Having said this, he brought up the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa purohito piṅgalo nikkhantadāṭho ahosi. Tassa brāhmaṇī aññena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ aticari, sopi tādisova. Purohito brāhmaṇiṃ punappunaṃ vārentopi vāretuṃ asakkonto cintesi “imaṃ mama veriṃ sahatthā māretuṃ na sakkā, upāyena naṃ māressāmī”ti. So rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha “mahārāja, tava nagaraṃ sakalajambudīpe agganagaraṃ, tvaṃ aggarājā, evaṃ aggarañño nāma tava dakkhiṇadvāraṃ duyuttaṃ avamaṅgala”nti. “Ācariya, idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Maṅgalaṃ katvā yojetabba”nti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Purāṇadvāraṃ hāretvā maṅgalayuttāni dārūni gahetvā nagarapariggāhakānaṃ bhūtānaṃ baliṃ datvā maṅgalanakkhattena patiṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Tena hi evaṃ karothā”ti. Tadā bodhisatto takkāriyo nāma māṇavo [M 4.0247] hutvā [P 4.0246] tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhāti. Purohito purāṇadvāraṃ hāretvā navaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā rājānaṃ āha – “niṭṭhitaṃ, deva, dvāraṃ, sve bhaddakaṃ nakkhattaṃ, taṃ anatikkamitvā baliṃ katvā dvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Ācariya, balikammatthāya kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Deva, mahesakkhaṃ dvāraṃ mahesakkhāhi devatāhi [V 4.0221] pariggahitaṃ, ekaṃ piṅgalaṃ nikkhantadāṭhaṃ ubhatovisuddhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ māretvā tassa maṃsalohitena baliṃ katvā sarīraṃ heṭṭhā khipitvā dvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpetabbaṃ, evaṃ tumhākañca nagarassa ca vuḍḍhi bhavissatī”ti. “Sādhu ācariya, evarūpaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ māretvā dvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, his chaplain was Piṅgala, whose teeth protruded. His brahmin wife committed adultery with another brahmin, who was just like him. Although the chaplain repeatedly restrained the brahmin woman, he was unable to do so and thought, "I cannot kill this enemy of mine with my own hands; I will kill him by a stratagem." He approached the king and said, "Great king, your city is the foremost city in all Jambudīpa, and you are the foremost king. Yet for such a foremost king, your southern gate is poorly constructed and inauspicious." "Teacher, what should be done now?" "It should be reconstructed with a blessing ceremony." "What is it necessary to obtain?" "The old gate should be removed, auspicious timbers taken, and after giving an offering to the spirits who protect the city, it should be established under an auspicious constellation." "Then do so." At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young student named Takkāriya and was learning the arts under him. The chaplain had the old gate removed, and after finishing the new one, he said to the king, "Sire, the gate is finished. Tomorrow is an auspicious constellation; without missing it, the gate should be established after making an offering." "Teacher, what is required for the offering?" "Sire, the gate is of great power and is guarded by deities of great power. One yellow-eyed, tooth-protruding brahmin, pure on both sides, should be killed; after making an offering with his flesh and blood and throwing the body beneath, the gate should be established. Thus there will be prosperity for you and the city." "Good, teacher. Kill such a brahmin and establish the gate."Requested JSON array

So tuṭṭhamānaso “sve paccāmittassa piṭṭhiṃ passissāmī”ti ussāhajāto attano gehaṃ gantvā mukhaṃ rakkhituṃ asakkonto turitaturito bhariyaṃ āha – “pāpe caṇḍāli ito paṭṭhāya kena saddhiṃ abhiramissasi, sve te jāraṃ māretvā balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Niraparādhaṃ kiṃkāraṇā māressasī”ti? Rājā “kaḷārapiṅgalassa brāhmaṇassa maṃsalohitena balikammaṃ katvā nagaradvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpehī”ti āha, “jāro ca te kaḷārapiṅgalo, taṃ māretvā balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā jārassa santikaṃ sāsanaṃ pāhesi “rājā kira kaḷārapiṅgalaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ māretvā baliṃ kātukāmo, sace jīvitukāmo, aññepi tayā sadise brāhmaṇe gahetvā kālasseva palāyassū”ti. So tathā akāsi. Taṃ nagare pākaṭaṃ ahosi, sakalanagarato sabbe kaḷārapiṅgalā palāyiṃsu.

Pleased at heart, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall see the defeat of my enemy," and full of effort, he went home. Unable to guard his mouth, he hastily said to his wife, "You wicked woman! From this day forth, with whom will you take your pleasure? Tomorrow, after killing your lover, I will perform a sacrificial offering." "Why would you kill an innocent man?" she asked. He replied, "The king has said, 'Establish the city gate by making a sacrificial offering with the flesh and blood of a tawny-eyed brahmin with protruding teeth.' Your lover is such a brahmin; I shall kill him and perform the sacrifice." She sent word to her lover: "The king, it is said, wishes to perform a sacrifice by killing a tawny-eyed brahmin with protruding teeth. If you wish to live, take other brahmins like yourself and flee while there is still time." He did as she said. This became known in the city, and all the tawny-eyed brahmins with protruding teeth fled the entire city.

Purohito paccāmittassa palātabhāvaṃ ajānitvā pātova rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, asukaṭṭhāne kaḷārapiṅgalo brāhmaṇo atthi, taṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti āha. Rājā amacce pesesi. Te taṃ apassantā āgantvā “palāto kirā”ti ārocesuṃ. “Aññattha upadhārethā”ti [P 4.0247] sakalanagaraṃ upadhārentāpi na passiṃsu. Tato “aññaṃ upadhārethā”ti vutte “deva, ṭhapetvā purohitaṃ añño evarūpo natthī”ti vadiṃsu. Purohitaṃ na sakkā māretunti. “Deva, kiṃ kathetha, purohitassa kāraṇā ajja dvāre appatiṭṭhāpite nagaraṃ aguttaṃ bhavissati, ācariyo kathento “ajja nakkhattaṃ atikkamitvā ito saṃvaccharaccayena nakkhattaṃ labhissatī”ti kathesi, saṃvaccharaṃ nagare advārake paccatthikānaṃ okāso bhavissati, imaṃ māretvā aññena byattena [M 4.0248] brāhmaṇena balikammaṃ kāretvā dvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpessāmā”ti. “Atthi pana añño ācariyasadiso paṇḍito brāhmaṇo”ti? “Atthi deva, tassa antevāsī takkāriyamāṇavo nāma, tassa purohitaṭṭhānaṃ datvā maṅgalaṃ karothā”ti.

The chaplain, unaware of his enemy's flight, approached the king early in the morning and said, "Your Majesty, in such-and-such a place there is a tawny-eyed brahmin with protruding teeth; have him seized." The king sent his ministers. They, not seeing him, returned and reported, "He has fled, it seems." "Search elsewhere," said the king. Though they searched the whole city, they did not see him. Then, when told to search for another, they said, "Your Majesty, except for the chaplain, there is no other brahmin of this description." When it was said that it was impossible to kill the chaplain, they replied, "Your Majesty, what are you saying? If the gate is not established today because of the chaplain, the city will be insecure. The teacher said, 'If today's constellation is passed, a favorable constellation will be found only after a year has passed.' If the city gate remains unfinished for a whole year, enemies will find an opportunity. Therefore, let us kill this chaplain, have another clever brahmin perform the sacrifice, and establish the gate." "Is there another wise brahmin equal to the teacher?" "Your Majesty, there is a young man named Takkāriya, a pupil of that chaplain. Give the position of chaplain to the young Takkāriya and perform the auspicious ceremony."

Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā sammānaṃ kāretvā purohitaṭṭhānaṃ datvā tathā kātuṃ āṇāpesi. So mahantena parivārena nagaradvāraṃ agamāsi. Purohitaṃ rājānubhāvena bandhitvā ānayiṃsu. Mahāsatto dvāraṭṭhapanaṭṭhāne āvāṭaṃ khaṇāpetvā sāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā ācariyena saddhiṃ antosāṇiyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ācariyo āvāṭaṃ oloketvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ alabhanto “attho tāva [V 4.0222] me nipphādito ahosi, bālattā pana mukhaṃ rakkhituṃ asakkonto vegena pāpitthiyā kathesiṃ, attanāva attano vadho ābhato”ti mahāsattaṃ ālapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king summoned the young Takkāriya, showed him great honor, gave him the chaplain's position, and ordered him to do as the ministers had said. The young Takkāriya went to the city gate with a large retinue. They bound the chaplain by the king's authority and brought him there. The Bodhisatta had a pit dug where the gate-pillar was to be placed, had a screen set up around it, and stood inside the screen with his teacher. The teacher, looking into the pit and finding no way to save himself, thought, "My purpose was achieved, yet because of my foolishness and inability to guard my mouth, I spoke to that wicked woman. I myself have brought about my own death." Addressing the Bodhisatta, and wishing to declare his own fault, he spoke this first verse:

104.

104.

“Ahameva dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsi bālo, bhekovaraññe ahimavhāyamāno;

Takkāriye sobbhamimaṃ patāmi, na kireva sādhu ativelabhāṇī”ti.

"It is I myself, foolish as I am, who spoke ill-chosen words, like a frog in the forest calling out to a snake. Takkāriya, I fall into this pit; indeed, they say it is not good to be one who speaks out of season."

Tattha [P 4.0248] dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsīti dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsiṃ. Bhekovāti yathā araññe maṇḍūko vassanto attano khādakaṃ ahiṃ avhāyamāno dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsati nāma, evaṃ ahameva dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsiṃ. Takkāriyeti tassa nāmaṃ, takkāriyāti itthiliṅgaṃ nāmaṃ, teneva taṃ ālapanto evamāha.

In this verse, 'spoke ill-chosen words' (dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsi) means I spoke speech without restraint. 'Like a frog' (bhekovā): just as a frog in the forest, by croaking, calls out to the snake that will devour it and thus speaks what is ill-chosen, so I too spoke ill-chosen words. 'Takkāriye' is his name; 'Takkāriyā' is a feminine-form name, and addressing him thus, he spoke.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

105.

105.

“Pappoti macco ativelabhāṇī, bandhaṃ vadhaṃ sokapariddavañca;

Attānameva garahāsi ettha, ācera yaṃ taṃ nikhaṇanti sobbhe”ti.

"A mortal who speaks out of season meets with bondage, death, sorrow, and lamentation. In this matter, teacher, blame only yourself, for it is because of your own actions that they bury you in the pit."

Tattha [M 4.0249] ativelabhāṇīti velātikkantaṃ pamāṇātikkantaṃ katvā kathanaṃ nāma na sādhu, ativelabhāṇī puriso na sādhūti attho. Sokapariddavañcāti ācariya, evameva ativelabhāṇī puriso vadhaṃ bandhañca sokañca mahantena saddena paridevañca pappoti. Garahāsīti paraṃ agarahitvā attānaṃyeva garaheyyāsi. Etthāti etasmiṃ kāraṇe. Ācera yaṃ tanti ācariya, yena kāraṇena taṃ nikhaṇanti sobbhe, taṃ tayāva kataṃ, tasmā attānameva garaheyyāsīti vadati.

In this verse, 'one who speaks out of season' (ativelabhāṇī) means speaking beyond the proper time or limit is not good; the meaning is that a person who speaks out of season is not good. 'Sorrow and lamentation' (sokapariddavañca): Teacher, in this very way, a person who speaks out of season undergoes death, bondage, sorrow, and loud wailing. 'Blame yourself' (garahāsī): instead of blaming others, you should blame only yourself. 'In this matter' (etthā): in this cause. 'Teacher, for which...' (ācera yaṃ taṃ): Teacher, the reason they bury you in a pit was done by you alone; therefore, he says, 'you should blame only yourself.'

Evañca pana vatvā “ācariya, vācaṃ arakkhitvā na kevalaṃ tvameva dukkhappatto, aññopi dukkhappattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āharitvā dassesi.

Having spoken these words, he said, "Teacher, it is not only you who have come to ruin by not guarding your tongue; others also have come to ruin before," and he brought forward a story of the past.

Pubbe kira bārāṇasiyaṃ kāḷī nāma gaṇikā ahosi, tassā tuṇḍilo nāma bhātā. Kāḷī ekadivasaṃ sahassaṃ gaṇhāti. Tuṇḍilo pana itthidhutto surādhutto akkhadhutto ahosi. Sā tassa dhanaṃ deti, so laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vināseti. Sā taṃ vārentīpi vāretuṃ nāsakkhi. So ekadivasaṃ jūtaparājito nivatthavatthāni datvā kaṭasārakakhaṇḍaṃ nivāsetvā tassā gehaṃ āgami[V 4.0223]. Tāya ca dāsiyo āṇattā honti “tuṇḍilassa āgatakāle [P 4.0249] kiñci adatvā gīvāyaṃ naṃ gahetvā nīhareyyāthā”ti. Tā tathā kariṃsu. So dvāramūle rodanto aṭṭhāsi.

Teacher, it is heard that formerly in the city of Bārāṇasī there was a courtesan named Kāḷī. Her brother was named Tuṇḍila. Kāḷī would receive a thousand pieces of money in a single day. Her brother Tuṇḍila, however, was a womanizer, a drunkard, and a gambler. Kāḷī would give money to her brother Tuṇḍila, and he would squander whatever he received. Kāḷī was unable to restrain her brother Tuṇḍila. One day, Tuṇḍila lost at dice and, having even lost his clothes, he came to his sister Kāḷī's house wearing only pieces of a tattered mat. Kāḷī had instructed her slave-girls, "When Tuṇḍila comes, do not give him anything, but seize him by the neck and cast him out." The slave-girls did as Kāḷī had said. Tuṇḍila stood weeping at the doorway.

Atheko seṭṭhiputto niccakālaṃ kāḷiyā sahassaṃ āharāpento disvā “kasmā tuṇḍila rodasī”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, jūtaparājito mama bhaginiyā santikaṃ āgatomhi, taṃ maṃ dāsiyo gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīhariṃsū”ti. “Tena hi tiṭṭha, bhaginiyā te kathessāmī”ti so gantvā “bhātā te kaṭasārakakhaṇḍaṃ nivāsetvā dvāramūle ṭhito, vatthānissa kimatthaṃ na desī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ tāva na demi, sace pana te sineho atthi, tvaṃ dehī”ti. Tasmiṃ pana gaṇikāya ghare idaṃcārittaṃ – ābhatasahassato pañcasatāni gaṇikāya honti, pañcasatāni vatthagandhamālamūlāni honti. Āgatapurisā tasmiṃ ghare laddhavatthāni nivāsetvā rattiṃ vasitvā punadivase gacchantā ābhatavatthāneva nivāsetvā gacchanti. Tasmā so seṭṭhiputto tāya dinnavatthāni nivāsetvā attano sāṭake tuṇḍilassa dāpesi. So nivāsetvā nadanto [M 4.0250] gajjanto gantvā surāgehaṃ pāvisi. Kāḷīpi dāsiyo āṇāpesi “sve etassa gamanakāle vatthāni acchindeyyāthā”ti. Tā tassa nikkhamanakāle ito cito ca upadhāvitvā vilumpamānā sāṭake gahetvā “idāni yāhi kumārā”ti naggaṃ katvā vissajjesuṃ. So naggova nikkhami. Jano parihāsaṃ karoti. So lajjitvā “mayāvetaṃ kataṃ, ahameva attano mukhaṃ rakkhituṃ nāsakkhi”nti paridevi. Idaṃ tāva dassetuṃ tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then a merchant's son, who always had a thousand coins brought to Kāḷī, saw him and asked, 'Why are you crying, Tuṇḍila?' 'Master, I was defeated in gambling and came to my sister's place, but her maids grabbed me by the neck and threw me out.' 'Then stay here, I will speak to your sister for you,' he said and went. 'Your brother is standing at the door wearing a piece of an old mat—why don't you give him clothes?' he asked. 'I won't give them, but if you have affection for him, you give them.' Now, in that courtesan's house, this was the custom: out of a thousand coins brought, five hundred belonged to the courtesan, and five hundred were for the price of clothes, perfumes, and garlands. The men who came to that house, having put on the clothes received in that house and stayed the night, would put on the clothes they had brought with them when leaving the next day. So the merchant's son, having put on the clothes given by her, had his own garments given to Tuṇḍila. He put them on and went, shouting and roaring, into a tavern. Kāḷī also ordered her maids, 'Tomorrow when he leaves, you should snatch his clothes.' As he was leaving, they ran here and there, plundering him, took his garments, and said, 'Now go, young man,' making him naked and sending him away. He left naked. The people mocked him. Ashamed, he lamented, 'I did this to myself; I was unable to guard my own mouth.' To show this, he spoke the third verse:

106.

106.

“Kimevahaṃ tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ, kareyya saṃ bhātaraṃ kāḷikāyaṃ;

Naggovahaṃ vatthayugañca jīno, ayampi attho bahutādisovā”ti.

'Why indeed did I ask about Tuṇḍila? Why did I show courtesy to Kāḷī's brother? I am naked and deprived of my pair of clothes. This matter, too, is very much like that.'

Tattha [P 4.0250] bahutādisovāti seṭṭhiputto hi attanā katena dukkhaṃ patto, tvampi tasmā ayampi tuyhaṃ dukkhappatti attho. Bahūhi kāraṇehi tādisova.

Herein, 'is very much like that' means: the merchant's son reached suffering by his own action, and so have you; therefore, this matter of your reaching suffering is similar. For many reasons, it is just like that.

Aparopi bārāṇasiyaṃ ajapālānaṃ pamādena gocarabhūmiyaṃ dvīsu meṇḍesu yujjhantesu eko kuliṅgasakuṇo “ime dāni bhinnehi sīsehi marissanti, vāressāmi teti mātulā mā yujjhathā”ti vāretvā tesaṃ kathaṃ aggahetvā yujjhantānaññeva piṭṭhiyampi sīsepi nisīditvā yācitvā vāretuṃ asakkonto “tena hi maṃ māretvā yujjhathā”ti ubhinnampi sīsantaraṃ pāvisi. Te aññamaññaṃ yujjhiṃsuyeva. So saṇhakaraṇiyaṃ pisito viya attanā kateneva vināsaṃ patto. Idampi aparaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Another story: in Bārāṇasī, while two rams were fighting in the grazing ground due to the negligence of the goatherds, a kuliṅga bird thought, 'Now these will die with their heads split; I will stop them,' and said, 'Uncles, do not fight!' Having forbidden them, they did not heed his words; and while they were fighting, he perched on their backs and heads, pleading but unable to stop them. Then he said, 'Well then, kill me and fight!' and entered between the heads of both. They just continued fighting. He was crushed as if in a grinder and met destruction by his own action. To show this other reason, he spoke the fourth verse:

107.

107.

“Yo [V 4.0224] yujjhamānānamayujjhamāno, meṇḍantaraṃ accupatī kuliṅgo;

So piṃsito meṇḍasirehi tattha, ayampi attho bahutādisovā”ti.

'The kuliṅga bird that, not fighting itself, flew between the fighting rams, was crushed there by the rams' heads. This matter, too, is very much like that.'

Tattha meṇḍantaranti meṇḍānaṃ antaraṃ. Accupatīti atigantvā uppati, ākāse sīsānaṃ vemajjhe aṭṭhāsīti attho. Piṃsitoti pīḷito.

Herein, 'between the rams' means the space between the rams. 'Flew between' means having gone beyond, it flew up; the meaning is that it stood in the air in the middle of their heads. 'Crushed' means pressed.

Aparepi [M 4.0251] bārāṇasivāsino gopālakā phalitaṃ tālarukkhaṃ disvā ekaṃ tālaphalatthāya rukkhaṃ āropesuṃ. Tasmiṃ phalāni pātente eko kaṇhasappo vammikā nikkhamitvā tālarukkhaṃ āruhi. Heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitā daṇḍehi paharantā nivāretuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Te “sappo tālaṃ abhiruhatī”ti itarassa ācikkhiṃsu. So bhīto mahāviravaṃ viravi. Heṭṭhā ṭhitā ekaṃ thirasāṭakaṃ catūsu kaṇṇesu gahetvā “imasmiṃ sāṭake patā”ti āhaṃsu. So patanto catunnampi antare sāṭakamajjhe pati. Tassa pana pātanavegena te sandhāretuṃ asakkontā aññamaññaṃ [P 4.0251] sīsehi paharitvā bhinnehi sīsehi jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā. Idampi kāraṇaṃ dassento pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Another story: some cowherds living in Bārāṇasī, seeing a palm tree laden with fruit, made one of them climb the tree for the sake of the palm fruit. While he was making the fruits fall, a black snake came out of an anthill and climbed the palm tree. Those standing below were unable to prevent it by striking with sticks. They told the other, 'A snake is climbing the palm tree!' Terrified, he uttered a great cry. Those standing below took a sturdy cloth by its four corners and said, 'Fall into this cloth!' As he fell, he landed in the middle of the cloth among the four of them. Being unable to withstand the force of his fall, they struck one another with their heads and, with their heads split, they met their end. To show this reason also, he spoke the fifth verse:

108.

108.

“Caturo janā potthakamaggahesuṃ, ekañca posaṃ anurakkhamānā;

Sabbeva te bhinnasirā sayiṃsu, ayampi attho bahutādisovā”ti.

'Four men held a cloth, protecting one person; all of them lay with their heads split. This matter, too, is very much like that.'

Tattha potthakanti sāṇasāṭakaṃ. Sabbeva teti tepi cattāro janā attanā kateneva bhinnasīsā sayiṃsu.

Herein, 'cloth' means a hempen cloth. 'All of them indeed' means those four men also lay with their heads split by their own doing.

Aparepi bārāṇasivāsino eḷakacorā rattiṃ ekaṃ ajaṃ thenetvā “divā araññe khādissāmā”ti tassā avassanatthāya mukhaṃ bandhitvā veḷugumbe ṭhapesuṃ. Punadivase taṃ khādituṃ gacchantā āvudhaṃ pamussitvā agamaṃsu. Te “ajaṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādissāma, āharathāvudha”nti ekassapi hatthe āvudhaṃ adisvā “vinā āvudhena etaṃ māretvāpi maṃsaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, vissajjetha naṃ, puññamassa atthī”ti vissajjesuṃ. Tadā eko naḷakāro veḷuṃ gahetvā “punapi āgantvā gahessāmī”ti naḷakārasatthaṃ veḷugumbantare ṭhapetvā pakkāmi. Ajā “muttāmhī”ti tussitvā veḷumūle kīḷamānā pacchimapādehi paharitvā taṃ satthaṃ pātesi. Corā satthasaddaṃ sutvā upadhārentā taṃ disvā tuṭṭhamānasā ajaṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu. Iti “sāpi ajā attanā kateneva matā”ti dassetuṃ chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Another story: some goat-thieves living in Bārāṇasī stole a goat at night. Thinking, 'We will eat it in the forest by day,' they tied its mouth so it would not bleat and placed it in a bamboo grove. The next day, when they went to eat it, they forgot their weapon. When they said, 'Let's kill the goat, cook the meat and eat it; bring the weapon!', not seeing a weapon in anyone's hand, they said, 'Without a weapon, even if we kill it, we cannot take the meat. Let it go; it has merit,' and they released it. Then a reed-worker, having taken bamboo, thought, 'I will come back and take more later,' and having placed his reed-worker's knife in the middle of the bamboo grove, he departed. The goat, rejoicing that 'I am free!', while playing at the base of the bamboo, kicked with its hind legs and knocked down that knife. The thieves, hearing the sound of the knife, investigated and, seeing it, with delighted minds, killed the goat and ate the meat. Thus, to show that 'that goat also died by its own doing,' he spoke the sixth verse:

109.

109.

“Ajā [V 4.0225][M 4.0252] yathā veḷugumbasmiṃ baddhā, avakkhipantī asimajjhagacchi;

Teneva tassā galakāvakantaṃ, ayampi attho bahutādisovā”ti.

'Just as a goat bound in a bamboo grove, while kicking about, came upon a sword; by that very thing her throat was cut. This matter, too, is very much like that.'

Tattha avakkhipantīti kīḷamānā pacchimapāde khipantī.

Herein, 'kicking about' means playing, kicking with the hind legs.

Evañca [P 4.0252] pana vatvā “attano vacanaṃ rakkhitvā mitabhāṇino nāma maraṇadukkhā muccantī”ti dassetvā kinnaravatthuṃ āhari.

Having said this, and showing that 'by guarding their speech and speaking measuredly, people are freed from the suffering of death,' he introduced the Kinnara story.

Bārāṇasivāsī kireko luddako himavantaṃ gantvā ekenupāyena jayampatike dve kinnare gahetvā ānetvā rañño adāsi. Rājā adiṭṭhapubbe kinnare disvā tussitvā “ludda, imesaṃ ko guṇo”ti pucchi. “Deva, ete madhurena saddena gāyanti, manuññaṃ naccanti, manussā evaṃ gāyituñca naccituñca na jānantī”ti. Rājā luddassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā kinnare “gāyatha naccathā”ti āha. Kinnarā “sace mayaṃ gāyantā byañjanaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissāma, duggītaṃ hoti, amhe garahissanti vadhissanti, bahuṃ kathentānañca pana musāvādopi hotī”ti musāvādabhayena raññā punappunaṃ vuttāpi na gāyiṃsu na nacciṃsu. Rājā kujjhitvā “ime māretvā maṃsaṃ pacitvā āharathā”ti āṇāpento sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

A hunter from Bārāṇasī, it is said, went to the Himālaya and by a certain stratagem captured a couple of kinnaras, husband and wife, brought them back, and presented them to the king. The king, having never seen kinnaras before, was delighted and asked, 'Hunter, what is their special quality?' 'Your Majesty, they sing with sweet voices and dance charmingly; humans do not know how to sing and dance like that,' he replied. The king gave the hunter much wealth and said to the kinnaras, 'Sing and dance!' But the kinnaras, fearing to speak falsely—thinking, 'If we sing but cannot make the syllables perfect, it will be a poor song, and they will censure and kill us; moreover, for those who speak much, there can also be false speech'—did not sing or dance, despite the king's repeated requests. Enraged, the king, while ordering, 'Kill them, cook their flesh, and bring it to me!', spoke the seventh verse:

110.

110.

“Ime na devā na gandhabbaputtā, migā ime atthavasaṃ gatā me;

Ekañca naṃ sāyamāse pacantu, ekaṃ punappātarāse pacantū”ti.

These are not devas, nor sons of gandhabbas; these are beasts that have come under my control. Let one be cooked for the evening meal, and another be cooked for the morning meal.

Tattha migā imeti ime sace devā gandhabbā vā bhaveyyuṃ, nacceyyuñceva gāyeyyuñca, ime pana migā tiracchānagatā. Atthavasaṃ gatā meti atthaṃ paccāsīsantena luddena ānītattā atthavasena mama hatthaṃ gatā. Etesu ekaṃ sāyamāse, ekaṃ pātarāse pacantūti.

Herein, 'these are beasts' means: if they were devas or gandhabbas, they would dance and sing. But these are beasts, born in the animal realm. 'Have come under my control' means: having been brought by the hunter desiring gain, they have come into my hands by way of that gain. Let one of these be cooked for the evening meal and one for the morning meal.

Kinnarī cintesi “rājā kuddho nissaṃsayaṃ māressati, idāni kathetuṃ kālo”ti aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The kinnarī thought, 'The king is angry; he will kill us without a doubt. Now is the time to speak,' and she spoke the eighth verse:

111.

111.

“Sataṃ [M 4.0253] sahassāni dubhāsitāni, kalampi nāgghanti subhāsitassa;

Dubbhāsitaṃ saṅkamāno kileso, tasmā tuṇhī kimpurisā na bālyā”ti.

A hundred thousand ill-spoken words are not worth even a sixteenth part of one well-spoken word. Being anxious over ill-spoken speech is a defilement; therefore, kimpurisas are silent not from foolishness.

Tattha [V 4.0226][P 4.0253] saṅkamāno kilesoti kadāci ahaṃ bhāsamāno dubbhāsitaṃ bhāseyyaṃ, evaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ saṅkamāno kilissati kilamati. Tasmāti tena kāraṇena tumhākaṃ na gāyiṃ, na bālabhāvenāti.

Herein, 'saṅkamāno kileso' means: 'Sometimes, while speaking, I might utter ill-spoken speech. Thus, being anxious about ill-spoken speech, one becomes defiled and wearied.' 'Therefore' means: 'For that reason, I did not sing for you, not out of foolishness.'

Rājā kinnariyā tussitvā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

The king, pleased with the kinnarī, then spoke the following verse:

112.

112.

“Yā mesā byāhāsi pamuñcathetaṃ, giriñca naṃ himavantaṃ nayantu;

Imañca kho dentu mahānasāya, pātova naṃ pātarāse pacantū”ti.

This one who has spoken, release her, and let them lead her to the Himālaya mountain. But this one, indeed, let them give to the great kitchen; in the morning, let them cook him for the morning meal.

Tattha yā mesāti yā me esā. Dentūti mahānasatthāya dentu.

Herein, 'yā mesā' means 'she who is this of mine'. 'Dentū' means 'let them give for the purpose of the great kitchen'.

Kinnaro rañño vacanaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ maṃ akathentaṃ avassaṃ māressati, idāni kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the king's words, the kinnara, thinking, 'He will surely kill me if I do not speak; now it is fitting to speak,' uttered the other verse:

113.

113.

“Pajjunnanāthā pasavo, pasunāthā ayaṃ pajā;

Tvaṃ nāthosi mahārāja, nāthohaṃ bhariyāya me;

Dvinnamaññataraṃ ñatvā, mutto gaccheyya pabbata”nti.

Cattle have the rain-god as their protector; this populace has cattle as its protector; you are my protector, great king, and I am the protector of my wife. When one of us knows the other is dead, the survivor, freed, may go to the mountain.

Tattha pajjunnanāthā pasavoti tiṇabhakkhā pasavo meghanāthā nāma. Pasunāthā ayaṃ pajāti ayaṃ pana manussapajā pañcagorasena upajīvantī pasunāthā pasupatiṭṭhā. Tvaṃ nāthosīti tvaṃ mama patiṭṭhā asi. Nāthohanti mama bhariyāya ahaṃ nātho, ahamassā patiṭṭhā. Dvinnamaññataraṃ ñatvā, mutto gaccheyya pabbatanti amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ antare eko ekaṃ mataṃ ñatvā sayaṃ maraṇato mutto himavantaṃ gaccheyya, jīvamānā pana mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ na jahāma, tasmā sacepi imaṃ himavantaṃ pesetukāmo, maṃ paṭhamaṃ māretvā pacchā pesehīti.

Herein, 'cattle have the rain-god as protector' means: grass-eating cattle are said to be protected by the clouds. 'This populace has cattle as protector' means: this human populace, living by means of the five products of the cow, has cattle as its protector, is supported by cattle. 'You are my protector' means: you are my support. 'I am the protector' means: I am the protector of my wife, I am her support. 'When one of us knows the other is dead, the survivor, freed, may go to the mountain' means: between the two of us, one, having known the other to be dead, being freed from death oneself, would go to the Himālaya. But while living, we do not abandon each other. Therefore, if you wish to send this one to the Himālaya, kill me first, then send her.

Evañca [M 4.0254] pana vatvā “mahārāja, na mayaṃ tava vacanaṃ akātukāmatāya tuṇhī ahumha, mayaṃ kathāya pana dosaṃ disvā na kathayimhā”ti dīpento imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

And having said this, explaining, 'Great king, we were not silent from an unwillingness to follow your word; rather, seeing the fault in speech, we did not speak,' he then spoke this pair of verses:

114.

114.

“Na ve nindā suparivajjayetha, nānā janā sevitabbā janinda;

Yeneva [P 4.0254] eko labhate pasaṃsaṃ, teneva añño labhate ninditāraṃ.

Indeed, blame is not easily avoided, and diverse people must be associated with, O lord of men. For by the very thing for which one gains praise, by that same thing another finds a critic.

115.

115.

“Sabbo [V 4.0227] loko paricitto aticitto, sabbo loko cittavā samhi citte;

Paccekacittā puthu sabbasattā, kassīdha cittassa vasena vatte”ti.

The whole world is varied by mind, exceedingly varied by mind; the whole world is endowed with mind, each in its own mind. With individual minds, all beings are diverse. Under the power of whose mind here should one live?

Tattha suparivajjayethāti mahārāja, nindā nāma sukhena parivajjetuṃ na sakkā. Nānā janāti nānāchandā janā. Yenevāti yena sīlādiguṇena eko pasaṃsaṃ labhati, teneva añño ninditāraṃ labhati. Amhākañhi kinnarānaṃ antare kathanena pasaṃsaṃ labhati, manussānaṃ antare nindaṃ, iti nindā nāma dupparivajjiyā, svāhaṃ kathaṃ tava santikā pasaṃsaṃ labhissāmīti.

Herein, regarding 'su-parivajjayetha' (avoided well): O great king, blame cannot be easily avoided. 'Diverse people' means people with diverse desires. 'For the very reason' means by the very same virtue, such as morality, by which one gains praise, another finds a critic. Indeed, among us kinnaras, speaking brings praise, but among humans it brings blame. Thus, blame is hard to avoid. How then shall I gain praise from you?

Sabbo loko paricittoti mahārāja, asappuriso nāma pāṇātipātādicittena, sappuriso pāṇātipātā veramaṇi ādicittena aticittoti, evaṃ sabbo loko paricitto aticittoti attho. Cittavā samhi citteti sabbo pana loko attano hīnena vā paṇītena vā cittena cittavā nāma. Paccekacittāti pāṭiyekkacittā puthuppabhedā sabbe sattā. Tesu kassekassa tava vā aññassa vā cittena kinnarī vā mādiso vā añño vā vatteyya, tasmā “ayaṃ mama cittavasena na vattatī”ti, mā mayhaṃ kujjhi. Sabbasattā [M 4.0255] hi attano cittavasena gacchanti, devāti. Kimpuriso rañño dhammaṃ desesi.

Herein, 'the whole world is varied by mind' means: O great king, an unworthy person has a mind inclined to killing living beings and so forth, while a worthy person has a mind inclined to abstaining from killing living beings and so forth; thus, 'the whole world is varied by mind, exceedingly varied by mind'—this is the meaning. Regarding 'is endowed with mind, in its own mind': indeed, the whole world is called 'endowed with mind' because of its own inferior or superior mind. 'Each with a distinct mind' means: all beings have individual, diverse minds. Among them, by whose mind—whether yours or another's—might a kinnarī or one like me or another act? Therefore, thinking, 'This one does not act according to my mind,' do not be angry with me. Indeed, all beings proceed according to the power of their own minds, O king. The kimpurisa taught the Dhamma to the king.

Rājā “sabhāvameva katheti paṇḍito kinnaro”ti somanassappatto hutvā osānagāthamāha –

The king, thinking, "The wise kinnara speaks the very truth," became filled with joy and recited the concluding verse:

116.

116.

“Tuṇhī ahū kimpuriso sabhariyo, yo dāni byāhāsi bhayassa bhīto;

So dāni mutto sukhito arogo, vācākirevatthavatī narāna”nti.

“Silent was the kimpurisa with his wife, who, now afraid of what was to be feared, has spoken out. Now he is freed, happy, and free from disease; indeed, speech is fruitful for humankind.”

Tattha vācākirevatthavatī narānanti vācāgirā eva imesaṃ sattānaṃ atthavatī hitāvahā hotīti attho.

Herein, 'indeed, speech is fruitful for humankind' means: speech itself is meaningful and brings welfare to these beings.

Rājā kinnare suvaṇṇapañjare nisīdāpetvā tameva luddaṃ pakkosāpetvā “gaccha bhaṇe, gahitaṭṭhāneyeva vissajjehī”ti vissajjāpesi. Mahāsattopi [P 4.0255] “ācariya, evaṃ kinnarā vācaṃ rakkhitvā pattakāle kathitena subhāsiteneva muttā, tvaṃ pana dukkathitena mahādukkhaṃ patto”ti idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ dassetvā “ācariya, mā bhāyi, jīvitaṃ te ahaṃ dassāmī”ti assāsesi, “apica kho pana tumhe maṃ rakkheyyāthā”tivutte “na tāva nakkhattayogo labbhatī”ti [V 4.0228] divasaṃ vītināmetvā majjhimayāmasamanantare mataṃ eḷakaṃ āharāpetvā “brāhmaṇa, yattha katthaci gantvā jīvāhī”ti kañci ajānāpetvā uyyojetvā eḷakamaṃsena baliṃ katvā dvāraṃ patiṭṭhāpesi.

The king, having had the kinnara seated in a golden cage, summoned that very hunter and had the kinnara released, saying to the hunter, 'Go, fellow, release him in the very place you captured him.' The Great Being also said, 'Teacher, thus the kinnaras, having guarded their speech, were freed by a well-spoken word uttered at the proper time; but you, having spoken wrongly, have met with great suffering.' Giving this example, he reassured him, 'Teacher, do not fear, I will grant you your life.' When the teacher said, 'But you must protect me,' he replied, 'The auspicious conjunction is not yet obtained.' After passing the day, just after the middle watch of the night, he had a dead ram brought and, without letting anyone know, sent the brahmin away, saying, 'Brahmin, go and live wherever you wish.' Then, making an offering with the ram's flesh, he set up the door.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi kokāliko vācāya hatoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kaḷārapiṅgalo kokāliko ahosi, takkāriyapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, said: "Not only now, monks, but also in the past was Kokālika ruined by his speech." Then he made the connection to the Jātaka: "At that time, Kaḷārapiṅgala was Kokālika, and I myself was the wise Takkāriya."

Takkāriyajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The eighth, the commentary on the Takkāriya Jātaka.

[482] 9. Rurumigarājajātakavaṇṇanā

[482] 9. The Commentary on the Ruru-deer King Jātaka

Tassa [M 4.0256] gāmavaraṃ dammīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhikkhūhi “bahūpakāro te āvuso, devadattasatthā, tvaṃ tathāgataṃ nissāya pabbajjaṃ labhi, tīṇi piṭakāni uggaṇhi, lābhasakkāraṃ pāpuṇī”ti vutto “āvuso, satthārā mama tiṇaggamattopi upakāro na kato, ahaṃ sayameva pabbajiṃ, sayaṃ tīṇi piṭakāni uggaṇhiṃ, sayaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ pāpuṇi”nti kathesi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “akataññū āvuso, devadatto akatavedī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva akataññū, pubbepi akataññūyeva, pubbepesa mayā jīvite dinnepi mama guṇamattaṃ na jānātī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, spoke this concerning Devadatta, beginning with the words: 'I will give him a choice village.' It is said that when the monks told him, "Friend Devadatta, the Teacher has been of great help to you. Dependent on the Tathāgata, you gained the going forth, learned the three Piṭakas, and attained gain and honor," he replied, "Friends, the Teacher has not helped me even as much as the tip of a blade of grass. I went forth on my own, learned the three Piṭakas on my own, and attained gain and honor on my own." The monks raised this matter in the Dhamma assembly, saying, "Friends, Devadatta is ungrateful and does not acknowledge kindness." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?" When they told him what it was, he said, "Monks, Devadatta is not only ungrateful now; he was ungrateful in the past as well. In the past, even when I gave him his life, he did not recognize even a particle of my virtue." Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko asītikoṭivibhavo seṭṭhi puttaṃ labhitvā “mahādhanako”tissa, nāmaṃ katvā “sippaṃ uggaṇhanto mama putto kilamissatī”ti na kiñci sippaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. So gītanaccavāditakhādanabhojanato uddhaṃ na kiñci aññāsi. Taṃ vayappattaṃ patirūpena dārena saṃyojetvā mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. So tesaṃ accayena itthidhuttasurādhuttādīhi parivuto nānābyasanamukhehi [P 4.0256] iṇaṃ ādāya taṃ dātuṃ asakkonto iṇāyikehi codiyamāno cintesi “kiṃ mayhaṃ jīvitena, ekenamhi attabhāvena añño viya jāto, mataṃ me seyyo”ti. So iṇāyike āha – “tumhākaṃ iṇapaṇṇāni gahetvā āgacchatha, gaṅgātīre me nidahitaṃ kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ atthi, taṃ vo dassāmī”ti. Te tena [V 4.0229] saddhiṃ agamaṃsu. So “idha dhana”nti nidhiṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhanto viya “gaṅgāyaṃ patitvā marissāmī”ti palāyitvā gaṅgāyaṃ pati. So caṇḍasotena vuyhanto kāruññaravaṃ viravi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a wealthy merchant with a fortune of eighty crores had a son. Naming him 'Mahādhanaka,' he thought, 'My son will become weary if he learns a skill,' so he did not have him learn any skill whatsoever. He knew nothing beyond singing, dancing, playing instruments, eating, and feasting. When he came of age, his parents joined him in marriage with a suitable wife, and then they passed away. After their passing, surrounded by libertines, drunkards, and the like, he took out loans through various ruinous means, and being unable to repay them, he was pressed by his creditors. He thought, 'What is this life to me? In this very existence, I have become like another person. Death would be better for me.' He told his creditors, 'Take your loan documents and come. I have ancestral wealth buried on the banks of the Ganges; I will give it to you.' They went with him. As if pointing out the location of the treasure, saying, 'The wealth is here,' he fled and fell into the Ganges. Swept away by the strong current, he cried out piteously.

Tadā mahāsatto rurumigayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā parivāraṃ chaḍḍetvā ekakova gaṅgānivattane ramaṇīye sālamissake supupphitaambavane vasati uposathaṃ upavutthāya.
