Tassa sarīracchavi sumajjitakañcanapaṭṭavaṇṇā ahosi, hatthapādā [M 4.0257] lākhārasaparikammakatā viya, naṅguṭṭhaṃ cāmarīnaṅguṭṭhaṃ viya, siṅgāni rajatadāmasadisāni, akkhīni sumajjitamaṇiguḷikā viya, mukhaṃ odahitvā ṭhapitarattakambalageṇḍukaṃ viya. Evarūpaṃ tassa rūpaṃ ahosi. So aḍḍharattasamaye tassa kāruññasaddaṃ sutvā “manussasaddo sūyati, mā mayi dharante maratu, jīvitamassa dassāmī”ti cintetvā sayanagumbā uṭṭhāya nadītīraṃ gantvā “ambho purisa, mā bhāyi, jīvitaṃ te dassāmī”ti assāsetvā sotaṃ chindanto gantvā taṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā tīraṃ pāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā phalāphalāni datvā dvīhatīhaccayena “bho purisa, ahaṃ taṃ ito araññato nīharitvā bārāṇasimagge ṭhapessāmi, tvaṃ sotthinā gamissasi, apica kho pana tvaṃ ‘asukaṭṭhāne nāma kañcanamigo vasatī’ti dhanakāraṇā maṃ rañño ceva rājamahāmattassa ca mā ācikkhāhī”ti āha. So “sādhu sāmī”ti sampaṭicchi.

At that time, the Great Being was reborn as a ruru deer and, leaving his herd, lived alone in a delightful grove of sal trees mixed with mango trees in full bloom near a bend in the Ganges, observing the Uposatha. The complexion of his body was the color of a polished golden plate; his hooves were as if lacquered with red lac; his tail was like a yak’s tail; his antlers were like silver chains; his eyes were like polished jewel-orbs; and his mouth was like a ball of red wool. Such was his beautiful form. At midnight, hearing the man’s piteous cry, he thought, 'A human voice is heard. Let him not die while I am living; I will give him his life!' Rising from his resting place in the thicket, he went to the riverbank and reassured the man, saying, 'Fear not, good man, I will give you your life!' Cutting through the current, he went and, placing the man on his back, brought him to the shore. He led him to his own dwelling place and gave him various fruits. After two or three days had passed, he said, 'Good man, I will take you out of this wilderness and set you on the road to Benares. You will go in safety. However, do not, for the sake of wealth, reveal to the king or the king's great ministers, saying, "A golden deer lives in such-and-such a place."' The man replied, 'Very well, lord,' and agreed.

Mahāsatto tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā taṃ attano piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā bārāṇasimagge otāretvā nivatti. Tassa bārāṇasipavisanadivaseyeva khemā nāma rañño aggamahesī paccūsakāle supinante suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ migaṃ attano dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā [P 4.0257] cintesi “sace evarūpo migo na bhaveyya, nāhaṃ supine passeyyaṃ, addhā bhavissati, rañño ārocessāmī”ti. Sā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, ahaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ migaṃ passituṃ icchāmi, suvaṇṇavaṇṇamigassa dhammaṃ sotukāmāmhi, labhissāmi ce, jīveyyaṃ, no ce, natthi me jīvita”nti āha. Rājā taṃ assāsetvā “sace manussaloke atthi, labhissasī”ti vatvā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇā migā nāma hontī”ti pucchitvā “āma, deva, hontī”ti sutvā alaṅkatahatthikkhandhe suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭake sahassathavikaṃ ṭhapetvā yo suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ migaṃ ācikkhissati, tassa saddhiṃ sahassathavikasuvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakena tañca hatthiṃ tato ca uttari dātukāmo hutvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe gāthaṃ likhāpetvā ekaṃ amaccaṃ pakkosāpetvā “ehi tāta, mama vacanena imaṃ gāthaṃ nagaravāsīnaṃ kathehī”ti imasmiṃ jātake paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, having accepted his promise, placed him on his back and, setting him down on the road to Benares, returned. On the very day he entered Benares, Queen Khemā, the chief queen of the king, saw in her dream at dawn a golden-colored deer teaching her the Dhamma. She thought, 'If such a deer did not exist, I would not have seen it in my dream. Surely, it must exist. I shall inform the king.' She approached the king and said, 'Great king, I wish to see a golden-colored deer. I long to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored deer. If I obtain it, I shall live; if not, my life is at an end.' The king consoled her, saying, 'If it exists in the human world, you shall obtain it.' Then he summoned the brahmins and asked, 'Do golden-colored deer exist?' Hearing their reply, 'Yes, lord, they do,' he placed a purse of a thousand coins in a golden casket on the back of a decorated elephant and had a golden plate inscribed with a verse. He declared that whoever pointed out the golden-colored deer would receive the purse of a thousand coins along with the golden casket and the elephant, and even more beyond that. Calling a minister, he said, 'Come, dear one, by my command, recite this verse to the city dwellers.' In this Jātaka, he spoke the first verse:

117.

117.

“Tassa [V 4.0230][M 4.0258] gāmavaraṃ dammi, nāriyo ca alaṅkatā;

Yo me taṃ migamakkhāti, migānaṃ migamuttama”nti.

“I will give a choice village and women adorned to whoever points out to me that deer, the best of deer.”

Amacco suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ gahetvā sakalanagare vācāpesi. Atha so seṭṭhiputto bārāṇasiṃ pavisantova taṃ kathaṃ sutvā amaccassa santikaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ rañño evarūpaṃ migaṃ ācikkhissāmi, maṃ rañño dassehī”ti āha. Amacco hatthikkhandhato otaritvā taṃ rañño santikaṃ netvā “ayaṃ kira, deva, taṃ migaṃ ācikkhissatī”ti dassesi. Rājā “saccaṃ ambho purisā”ti pucchi. So “saccaṃ mahārāja, tvaṃ etaṃ yasaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti vadanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The minister, taking the golden plate, had it read throughout the whole city. Then, the merchant's son, just as he was entering Benares, heard that news and went to the minister, saying, 'I will point out such a deer to the king; present me to the king.' The minister descended from the elephant's back and brought him to the king, saying, 'This man, O king, will reportedly point out that deer.' The king asked, 'Is it true, good man?' He replied, 'It is true, great king. Therefore, grant me that wealth and fortune,' and while asking for it, he spoke the second verse:

118.

118.

“Mayhaṃ gāmavaraṃ dehi, nāriyo ca alaṅkatā;

Ahaṃ te migamakkhissaṃ, migānaṃ migamuttama”nti.

“Give me a choice village and women adorned; I will point out to you the deer, the best of deer.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā tassa mittadubbhissa tussitvā “abbho kuhiṃ so migo vasatī”ti pucchitvā “asukaṭṭhāne nāma devā”ti vutte tameva maggadesakaṃ katvā mahantena parivārena taṃ ṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ so mittadubbhī “senaṃ, deva, sannisīdāpehī”ti [P 4.0258] vatvā sannisinnāya senāya eso, deva, suvaṇṇamigo etasmiṃ vane vasatī”ti hatthaṃ pasāretvā ācikkhanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, pleased with that treacherous friend, asked, 'Good man, where does that deer live?' When told, 'In such and such a place, lord,' he made him his guide and went to that place with a large retinue. Then that treacherous friend said, 'Lord, have the army halt,' and when the army had halted, he pointed with outstretched hand and, wishing to show it, said, 'Lord, that golden-colored deer lives in this forest,' and spoke the third verse:

119.

119.

“Etasmiṃ vanasaṇḍasmiṃ, ambā sālā ca pupphitā;

Indagopakasañchannā, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti.

“In this forest grove, mango and sal trees are in bloom; and the ground is covered with ladybirds; here stands that deer.”

Tattha indagopakasañchannāti etassa vanasaṇḍassa bhūmi indagopakavaṇṇāya rattāya sukhasamphassāya tiṇajātiyā sañchannā, sasakucchi viya mudukā, ettha etasmiṃ ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe eso tiṭṭhatīti dasseti.

In that passage, 'covered with ladybirds' means the ground of that forest grove is covered with a species of red grass the color of ladybirds, which is pleasant to the touch and soft like a hare's belly; it shows that in this delightful forest grove, he stands.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā amacce āṇāpesi “tassa migassa palāyituṃ adatvā khippaṃ āvudhahatthehi purisehi saddhiṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ parivārethā”ti. Te tathā katvā unnadiṃsu. Rājā katipayehi janehi saddhiṃ ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi, sopissa avidūre aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā cintesi “mahanto balakāyasaddo, tamhā me purisā [M 4.0259] bhayena uppannena bhavitabba”nti[V 4.0231]. So uṭṭhāya sakalaparisaṃ oloketvā rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ disvā “rañño ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva me sotthi bhavissati, ettheva mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā rājābhimukho pāyāsi. Rājā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “nāgabalo migo avattharanto viya āgaccheyya, saraṃ sannayhitvā imaṃ migaṃ santāsetvā sace palāyati, vijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā gaṇhissāmī”ti dhanuṃ āropetvā bodhisattābhimukho ahosi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imaṃ gāthādvayamāha –

The king, hearing his words, commanded his ministers, 'Without giving that deer a chance to escape, quickly surround the forest grove with men armed with weapons.' They did as they were told and made the forest echo. The king stood to one side with a few men, and that wicked man also stood not far away. The Great Being, hearing that sound, thought, 'The sound of the army is great; danger must have arisen for me from that man.' Rising, he looked around at the entire assembly and, seeing where the king stood, thought, 'My safety will be only in the place where the king stands; therefore, I should go to where the king is.' So he set out towards the king. The king, seeing him approach, thought, 'This deer comes with the strength of a noble elephant, as if to overwhelm. If this deer should flee out of fear, I will shoot him, weaken him, and capture him.' So he strung his bow and faced the Bodhisatta. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke these two verses:

120.

120.

“Dhanuṃ advejjhaṃ katvāna, usuṃ sannayhupāgami;

Migo ca disvā rājānaṃ, dūrato ajjhabhāsatha.

Having strung the bow and fitted an arrow, the king approached; and the deer, seeing the king from afar, addressed him.

121.

121.

“Āgamehi mahārāja, mā maṃ vijjhi rathesabha;

Ko nu te idamakkhāsi, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti.

“Wait, O great king, do not shoot me, O best of charioteers; who indeed told you, 'Here this deer stands'?”

Tattha [P 4.0259] advejjhaṃ katvānāti jiyāya ca sarena ca saddhiṃ ekameva katvā. Sannayhāti sannayhitvā. Āgamehīti “tiṭṭha, mahārāja, mā maṃ vijjhi, jīvaggāhameva gaṇhāhī”ti madhurāya manussavācāya abhāsi.

Here, “unwaveringly” means making it one with the bowstring and the arrow. “Fitted” means having fitted it. “Hold” means, “Stay, great king, do not shoot me; seize me alive,” he spoke with sweet human speech.

Rājā tassa madhurakathāya bandhitvā dhanuṃ otāretvā gāravena aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsattopi rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Mahājanopi sabbāvudhāni chaḍḍetvā āgantvā rājānaṃ parivāresi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikaṃ cālento viya madhurena sarena rājānaṃ pucchi “ko nu te idamakkhāsi, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe pāpapuriso thokaṃ paṭikkamitvā sotapatheva aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “iminā me dassito”ti kathento chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, captivated by his sweet speech, lowered his bow and stood respectfully. The Great Being also approached the king, greeting him warmly, and stood in a suitable place. The great crowd, having laid down all their weapons, came and surrounded the king. At that moment, the Great Being, with a voice as sweet as the sound of a shaken golden bell, asked the king, 'Who indeed told you, "The deer stands here"?' At that moment, the wicked man stepped back a little and stood right there. The king, saying, 'This man showed me,' spoke the sixth verse:

122.

122.

“Esa pāpacaro poso, samma tiṭṭhati ārakā;

Soyaṃ me idamakkhāsi, ettheso tiṭṭhate migo”ti.

“This man of evil conduct, my friend, stands at a distance; it was he who told me, 'Here this deer stands.'”

Tattha pāpacaroti vissaṭṭhācāro.

In that passage, 'of evil conduct' means one of corrupt conduct.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto taṃ mittadubbhiṃ garahitvā raññā saddhiṃ sallapanto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being rebuked that treacherous friend and, conversing with the king, spoke the seventh verse:

123.

123.

“Saccaṃ [V 4.0232][M 4.0260] kireva māhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;

Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyo, na tvevekacciyo naro”ti.

“Truly, it seems, some men here have spoken rightly: ‘A log rescued from the water is better, but never a certain kind of man.’”

Tattha niplavitanti uttāritaṃ. Ekacciyoti ekacco pana mittadubbhī pāpapuggalo udake patantopi uttārito na tveva seyyo. Kaṭṭhañhi nānappakārena upakārāya saṃvattati, mittadubbhī pana pāpapuggalo vināsāya, tasmā tato kaṭṭhameva varataranti porāṇakapaṇḍitā kathayiṃsu, mayā pana tesaṃ vacanaṃ na katanti.

Here, “rescued from the water” means lifted up. “A certain kind of man” refers to a treacherous and wicked person—even if he were falling into water, lifting him up would not be better. For a piece of wood can be useful in various ways, but a treacherous and wicked person only leads to ruin. Therefore, the ancient sages declared that a piece of wood is even preferable to him. But I did not act according to their words.

Taṃ sutvā rājā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king spoke another verse:

124.

124.

“Kiṃ nu ruru garahasi migānaṃ, kiṃ pakkhīnaṃ kiṃ pana mānusānaṃ;

Bhayaṃ [P 4.0260] hi maṃ vindatinapparūpaṃ, sutvāna taṃ mānusiṃ bhāsamāna”nti.

“Whom do you reproach, Ruru? Is it one of the deer, one of the birds, or one of humankind? For a great fear finds me, hearing you speak with a human voice.”

Tattha migānanti migānamaññataraṃ garahasi, udāhu pakkhīnaṃ, mānusānanti pucchi. Bhayañhi maṃ vindatīti bhayaṃ maṃ paṭilabhati, ahaṃ attani anissaro bhayasantako viya homi. Anapparūpanti mahantaṃ.

Here, “of the deer” means: “Do you blame a certain one of the deer, or of the birds, or of men?” he asked. “For fear finds me” means fear overtakes me; I am not my own master, as if possessed by fear. “Not small” means great.

Tato mahāsatto “mahārāja, na migaṃ, na pakkhiṃ garahāmi, manussaṃ pana garahāmī”ti dassento navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, indicating, “Great king, I do not blame the deer or the birds, but I do blame humans,” spoke the ninth verse:

125.

125.

“Yamuddhariṃ vāhane vuyhamānaṃ, mahodake salile sīghasote;

Tatonidānaṃ bhayamāgataṃ mama, dukkho have rāja asabbhi saṅgamo”ti.

“One whom I rescued, being carried away in the current, in the great water, in a swiftly flowing stream—from that cause, danger has come to me. Truly, O king, association with the ignoble is suffering.”

Tattha vāhaneti patitapatite vahituṃ samatthe gaṅgāvahe. Mahodake salileti mahāudake mahāsalileti attho. Ubhayenāpi gaṅgāvahasseva bahuudakataṃ dasseti. Tatonidānanti mahārāja, yo mayhaṃ tayā dassito puriso, eso mayā gaṅgāya vuyhamāno aḍḍharattasamaye kāruññaravaṃ viravanto uddharito, tatonidānaṃ me idamajja bhayaṃ āgataṃ, asappurisehi samāgamo nāma dukkho, mahārājāti.

There, 'vāhane' means in the current of the Ganges, capable of carrying away whatever has fallen. 'Mahodake salile' means in great water, in vast water. Both phrases indicate the great volume of water in the Ganges current. 'Tatonidānaṃ' means, O great king, that man whom you showed me—he was being carried away by the Ganges, crying out piteously at midnight, and I rescued him. From that cause, this fear has come upon me today. Association with the wicked is indeed suffering, O great king.

Taṃ [V 4.0233][M 4.0261] sutvā rājā tassa kujjhitvā “evaṃ bahūpakārassa nāma guṇaṃ na jānāti, vijjhitvā naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, angered at him, said, “So, he does not recognize the virtue of such a great benefactor? I shall pierce him and bring about his death!” Then he spoke the tenth verse:

126.

126.

“Sohaṃ catuppattamimaṃ vihaṅgamaṃ, tanucchidaṃ hadaye ossajāmi;

Hanāmi taṃ mittadubbhiṃ akiccakāriṃ, yo tādisaṃ kammakataṃ na jāne”ti.

“This four-feathered, sky-going, body-piercing arrow of mine, I shall plunge into his heart. I shall kill that betrayer of friends, that doer of what should not be done, who does not recognize such a deed done.”

Tattha catuppattanti catūhi vājapattehi samannāgataṃ. Vihaṅgamanti ākāsagāmiṃ. Tanucchidanti sarīrachindanaṃ. Ossajāmīti etassa hadaye vissajjemi.

Here, 'catuppattaṃ' means endowed with four feathers. 'Vihaṅgamaṃ' means sky-going. 'Tanucchidaṃ' means body-piercing. 'Ossajāmi' means I cast it into his heart.

Tato mahāsatto “mā esa maṃ nissāya nassatū”ti cintetvā ekādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, thinking, “Let this one not perish on account of me,” spoke the eleventh verse:

127.

127.

“Dhīrassa [P 4.0261] bālassa have janinda, santo vadhaṃ nappasaṃsanti jātu;

Kāmaṃ gharaṃ gacchatu pāpadhammo, yañcassa bhaṭṭhaṃ tadetassa dehi;

Ahañca te kāmakaro bhavāmī”ti.

“O lord of men, the good never praise the killing, whether of the wise or of a fool. Let the one of evil conduct go home as he pleases, and give him whatever was promised to him. And I shall do your bidding.”

Tattha kāmanti kāmena yathāruciyā attano gharaṃ gacchatu. Yañcassa bhaṭṭhaṃ tadetassa dehīti yañca tassa “idaṃ nāma te dassāmī”ti tayā kathitaṃ, taṃ tassa dehi. Kāmakaroti icchākaro, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ karohi, maṃsaṃ vā me khāda, kīḷāmigaṃ vā karohi, sabbattha te anukūlavattī bhavissāmīti attho.

Here, 'kāmaṃ' means let him go to his own home according to his wish, as he pleases. 'Yañcassa bhaṭṭhaṃ tadetassa dehi' means whatever you promised him, saying, “I will give this to you,” give that to him. 'Kāmakaro' means a doer of your wish—whatever you wish, do that; eat my flesh or make me a play-deer; in all things, I shall act in accordance with your will.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tuṭṭhamānaso mahāsattassa thutiṃ karonto anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, with a pleased mind, praising the Great Being, spoke the next verse:

128.

128.

“Addhā rurū aññataro sataṃ so, yo dubbhato mānusassa na dubbhi;

Kāmaṃ gharaṃ gacchatu pāpadhammo, yañcassa bhaṭṭhaṃ tadetassa dammi;

Ahañca te kāmacāraṃ dadāmī”ti.

“Truly, Ruru, you are one of the good, who does not betray a man even when betrayed. Let the one of evil conduct go home as he pleases, and whatever was promised to him, that I give to him. And I grant you freedom to go as you wish.”

Tattha [M 4.0262] sataṃ soti addhā tvaṃ sataṃ paṇḍitānaṃ aññataro. Kāmacāranti ahaṃ tava dhammakathāya pasīditvā tuyhaṃ kāmacāraṃ abhayaṃ dadāmi, ito paṭṭhāya tumhe nibbhayā yathāruciyā viharathāti mahāsattassa varaṃ adāsi.

Here, 'sataṃ so' means truly you are one of the wise. 'Kāmacāraṃ' means, pleased by your discourse on the Dhamma, I grant you freedom of movement and safety. From now on, live without fear as you wish—thus he granted the Great Being a boon.

Atha [V 4.0234] naṃ mahāsatto “mahārāja, manussā nāma aññaṃ mukhena bhāsanti, aññaṃ kāyena karontī”ti pariggaṇhanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, reflecting, “O king, humans speak one thing with their mouth, but do another with their body,” spoke two verses:

129.

129.

“Suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato.

“The howling of jackals is easily known, and the calls of birds; the speech of humans, O king, is more difficult to understand than that.”

130.

130.

“Api ce maññatī poso, ñāti mitto sakhāti vā;

Yo pubbe sumano hutvā, pacchā sampajjate diso”ti.

“Even if one considers another to be a relative, friend, or companion, that person, having formerly been well-disposed, may later become an enemy.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā “migarāja, mā maṃ evaṃ maññi, ahañhi rajjaṃ jahantopi na tuyhaṃ dinnavaraṃ jahissaṃ, saddahatha, mayha”nti [P 4.0262] varaṃ adāsi. Mahāsatto tassa santike varaṃ gaṇhanto attānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayadānaṃ varaṃ gaṇhi. Rājāpi taṃ varaṃ datvā bodhisattaṃ nagaraṃ netvā mahāsattañca nagarañca alaṅkārāpetvā deviyā dhammaṃ desāpesi. Mahāsatto deviṃ ādiṃ katvā rañño ca rājaparisāya ca madhurāya manussabhāsāya dhammaṃ desetvā rājānaṃ dasahi rājadhammehi ovaditvā mahājanaṃ anusāsitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā migagaṇaparivuto vāsaṃ kappesi. Rājā “sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ dammī”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya migapakkhīnaṃ koci hatthaṃ pasāretuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Migagaṇo manussānaṃ sassāni khādati, koci vāretuṃ na sakkoti. Mahājano rājaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā upakkosi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king said, “O king of deer, do not think of me thus. For even if I were to abandon my kingdom, I would not forsake the boon I granted you. Believe me,” and he granted the boon. The Great Being, receiving the boon from him, taking himself as the starting point, accepted the boon of granting safety to all beings. The king, having granted that boon, led the Bodhisatta to the city and, having adorned both the Great Being and the city, had the Dhamma preached to the queen. The Great Being, beginning with the queen, taught the Dhamma to the king and his court in sweet human speech. He advised the king with the ten royal virtues and instructed the people before entering the forest, where he lived surrounded by herds of deer. The king proclaimed, “I grant safety to all beings,” and had a drum beaten throughout the city. From that time onward, no one was able to raise a hand against any deer or bird. The herds of deer began to eat the crops of the people, yet no one could stop them. The people went to the royal courtyard and complained. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke this verse:

131.

131.

“Samāgatā jānapadā, negamā ca samāgatā;

Migā sassāni khādanti, taṃ devo paṭisedhatū”ti.

“The country people have gathered, and the townspeople have gathered; the deer are eating the crops—may Your Majesty restrain them.”

Tattha taṃ devoti taṃ migagaṇaṃ devo paṭisedhatūti.

In this context, 'taṃ devo' means 'may Your Majesty restrain that herd of deer.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke these two verses:

132.

132.

“Kāmaṃ janapado māsi, raṭṭhañcāpi vinassatu;

Na tvevāhaṃ ruruṃ dubbhe, datvā abhayadakkhiṇaṃ.

“Let the countryside be no more, and let the kingdom too be destroyed; but I would never betray Ruru, having given him the assurance of safety.”

133.

133.

“Mā [V 4.0235][M 4.0263] me janapado āsi, raṭṭhañcāpi vinassatu;

Na tvevāhaṃ migarājassa, varaṃ datvā musā bhaṇe”ti.

“Let my countryside be no more, and let the kingdom too be destroyed; but I would never speak falsely, having given a promise to the king of deer.”

Tattha māsīti kāmaṃ mayhaṃ janapado mā hotu. Rurunti na tveva ahaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa rurumigarājassa abhayadakkhiṇaṃ datvā dubbhissāmīti.

In this context, 'māsi' means 'let my countryside not be.' The line concerning Ruru means: 'Indeed, I will not betray Ruru, the golden-hued king of deer, after having given him the assurance of safety.'

Mahājano rañño vacanaṃ sutvā kiñci vattuṃ avisahanto paṭikkami. Sā kathā vitthārikā ahosi. Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto migagaṇaṃ sannipātāpetvā “ito paṭṭhāya manussānaṃ sassāni mā khādathā”ti ovaditvā “attano khettesu paṇṇasaññaṃ bandhantū”ti [P 4.0263] manussānaṃ ghosāpesi. Te tathā bandhiṃsu, tāya saññāya migā yāvajjatanā sassāni na khādanti.

The people, hearing the king’s words and not daring to say anything, departed. That story became widespread. Hearing it, the Great Being assembled the herds of deer and advised them, “From now on, do not eat the crops of humans.” He then had it proclaimed to the people, “Let them tie a sign made of leaves in their fields.” They did so, and because of that sign, the deer do not eat the crops to this day.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto akataññūyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā seṭṭhiputto devadatto ahosi, rājā ānando, rurumigarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta was ungrateful.” Then he made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the merchant’s son was Devadatta, the king was Ānanda, and the Ruru deer king was I myself.”

Rurumigarājajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Ninth, the Commentary on the Rurumigarāja Jātaka.

[483] 10. Sarabhamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[483] 10. The Commentary on the Sarabhamiga Jātaka

Āsīsetheva purisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto attanā saṃkhittena pucchitapañhassa dhammasenāpatino vitthārena byākaraṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kadā pana satthā theraṃ saṃkhittena pañhaṃ pucchīti? Devorohane. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepato anupubbikathā. Rājagahaseṭṭhino hi santake candanapatte āyasmatā piṇḍolabhāradvājena iddhiyā gahite satthā bhikkhūnaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ paṭikkhipi. Tadā titthiyā “paṭikkhittaṃ samaṇena gotamena iddhipāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ, idāni sayampi na karissatī”ti cintetvā maṅkubhūtehi attano sāvakehi “kiṃ, bhante, iddhiyā pattaṃ na gaṇhathā”ti vuccamānā “netaṃ āvuso, amhākaṃ dukkaraṃ, chavassa pana dārupattassatthāya attano saṇhasukhumaguṇaṃ ko gihīnaṃ pakāsessatīti na gaṇhimha, samaṇā pana sakyaputtiyā lolatāya iddhiṃ dassetvā [M 4.0264] gaṇhiṃsu. Mā ‘amhākaṃ iddhikaraṇaṃ bhāro’ti cintayittha, mayañhi tiṭṭhantu samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā, ākaṅkhamānā pana [V 4.0236] samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ iddhiṃ dassessāma, sace hi samaṇo gotamo ekaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ karissati, mayaṃ dviguṇaṃ karissāmā”ti kathayiṃsu.

‘A person should indeed maintain hope’—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this concerning the detailed explanation given by the General of the Dhamma in response to a question the Teacher himself had asked concisely. When did the Teacher ask the elder a concise question? At the time of the Descent from Heaven. Here is a summary of the narrative in order. When the sandalwood bowl belonging to the merchant of Rājagaha was taken by the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja by means of psychic power, the Teacher forbade the monks from performing psychic marvels. Then the sectarians, thinking, ‘The ascetic Gotama has forbidden the performance of psychic marvels; now he himself will not perform them,’ were addressed by their own disheartened disciples, who said, ‘Venerable sirs, why do you not take the bowl by psychic power?’ They replied, ‘Friends, this is not difficult for us. But for the sake of a worthless wooden bowl, who would reveal their own refined and subtle qualities to householders? That is why we did not take it. However, the Sakyan ascetics, due to their frivolity, displayed psychic power and took it. Do not think that performing psychic power is a burden for us. Let the disciples of the ascetic Gotama be; if we wish, we will display psychic power along with the ascetic Gotama. If the ascetic Gotama performs one miracle, we will perform twice as many.’ Thus they spoke.

Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ “bhante, titthiyā kira pāṭihāriyaṃ karissantī”ti. Satthā “bhikkhave, karontu, ahampi karissāmī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā bimbisāro āgantvā bhagavantaṃ pucchi “bhante, pāṭihāriyaṃ kira karissathā”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Nanu, bhante, sikkhāpadaṃ paññatta”nti. “Mahārāja, taṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ paññattaṃ, buddhānaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ nāma [P 4.0264] natthi. “Yathā hi, mahārāja, tava uyyāne pupphaphalaṃ aññesaṃ vāritaṃ, na tava, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti. “Kattha pana, bhante, pāṭihāriyaṃ karissathā”ti? “Sāvatthinagaradvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle”ti. “Amhehi tattha kiṃ kattabba”nti? “Natthi kiñci mahārājā”ti. Punadivase satthā katabhattakicco cārikaṃ pakkāmi. Manussā “kuhiṃ, bhante, satthā gacchatī”ti pucchanti. “Sāvatthinagaradvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle titthiyamaddanaṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ kātu”nti tesaṃ bhikkhū kathayanti. Mahājano “acchariyarūpaṃ kira pāṭihāriyaṃ bhavissati, passissāma na”nti gharadvārāni chaḍḍetvā satthārā saddhiṃyeva agamāsi.

Hearing that, the monks informed the Blessed One, ‘Venerable sir, it is said that the sectarians will perform a miracle.’ The Teacher said, ‘Monks, let them do so; I too will perform one.’ Hearing this, King Bimbisāra came and asked the Blessed One, ‘Venerable sir, will you indeed perform a miracle?’ ‘Yes, great king.’ ‘But, venerable sir, has not a training rule been laid down?’ ‘Great king, that rule was laid down by me for my disciples; but for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a training rule. Just as, great king, in your park, others are forbidden from taking flowers and fruits, but not you, so should this be understood.’ ‘Where then, venerable sir, will you perform the miracle?’ ‘At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī.’ ‘What should we do there?’ ‘There is nothing for you to do, great king.’ The next day, the Teacher, having finished his meal, set out on his journey. People asked, ‘Where is the Teacher going?’ The monks told them, ‘To the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, to perform the twin miracle to subdue the sectarians.’ A great crowd, thinking, ‘A wonderful miracle will surely take place; let us see it!’ left their homes and went along with the Teacher.

Aññatitthiyā “mayampi samaṇassa gotamassa pāṭihāriyakaraṇaṭṭhāne pāṭihāriyaṃ karissāmā”ti upaṭṭhākehi saddhiṃ satthārameva anubandhiṃsu. Satthā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā raññā “pāṭihāriyaṃ kira, bhante, karissathā”ti pucchito “karissāmī”ti vatvā “kadā, bhante”ti vutte “ito sattame divase āsāḷhipuṇṇamāsiya”nti āha. “Maṇḍapaṃ karomi bhante”ti? “Alaṃ mahārāja, mama pāṭihāriyakaraṇaṭṭhāne sakko devarājā dvādasayojanikaṃ ratanamaṇḍapaṃ karissatī”ti. “Etaṃ kāraṇaṃ nagare ugghosāpemi, bhante”ti? “Ugghosāpehi mahārājā”ti. Rājā dhammaghosakaṃ alaṅkatahatthipiṭṭhiṃ āropetvā “bhagavā kira sāvatthinagaradvāre kaṇḍambarukkhamūle titthiyamaddanaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ karissati ito sattame divase”ti yāva chaṭṭhadivasā devasikaṃ ghosanaṃ kāresi. Titthiyā “kaṇḍambarukkhamūle kira karissatī”ti sāmikānaṃ dhanaṃ [M 4.0265] datvā sāvatthisāmante ambarukkhe chindāpayiṃsu. Dhammaghosako puṇṇamīdivase pātova “ajja, bhagavato pāṭihāriyaṃ bhavissatī”ti ugghosesi. Devatānubhāvena sakalajambudīpe dvāre ṭhatvā ugghositaṃ viya ahosi. Ye ye gantuṃ cittaṃ uppādenti, te te sāvatthiṃ pattameva attānaṃ passiṃsu, dvādasayojanikā parisā ahosi.

The other sectarians, thinking, ‘We too will perform a miracle in the place where the ascetic Gotama performs his miracle,’ followed the Teacher along with their supporters. The Teacher, gradually arriving at Sāvatthī, was asked by the king, ‘Venerable sir, will you indeed perform a miracle?’ He replied, ‘I will.’ When asked, ‘When, venerable sir?’ he said, ‘On the seventh day from today, on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī.’ The king asked, ‘Venerable sir, shall I prepare a pavilion?’ The Teacher replied, ‘There is no need, great king. In the place where I perform the miracle, Sakka, the king of the gods, will prepare a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas in size.’ The king asked, ‘Venerable sir, shall I announce this matter in the city?’ The Teacher said, ‘Announce it, great king.’ The king had a public announcer mounted on an adorned elephant and, until the sixth day, had this daily proclamation made: ‘The Blessed One will perform a miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree by the gate of Sāvatthī, subduing the sectarians, on the seventh day from today.’ The sectarians, hearing it would be at the foot of a Kaṇḍamba tree, paid money to the owners and had the mango trees in the vicinity of Sāvatthī cut down. On the full moon day, the public announcer proclaimed early in the morning, ‘Today, the Blessed One’s miracle will take place.’ By the power of the deities, it was as if this proclamation was made while standing at every door throughout all of Jambudīpa. All those who formed the intention to go found themselves already arrived in Sāvatthī, and an assembly twelve yojanas in size gathered.

Satthā [V 4.0237] pātova sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisituṃ nikkhami. Kaṇḍo nāma uyyānapālo piṇḍipakkameva kumbhapamāṇaṃ mahantaṃ ambapakkaṃ rañño haranto satthāraṃ nagaradvāre disvā “idaṃ tathāgatasseva anucchavika”nti adāsi. Satthā paṭiggahetvā tattheva ekamantaṃ nisinno paribhuñjitvā “ānanda, imaṃ ambaṭṭhiṃ uyyānapālakassa imasmiṃ ṭhāne ropanatthāya dehi, esa kaṇḍambo [P 4.0265] nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Thero tathā akāsi. Uyyānapālo paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā ropesi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva aṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā mūlāni otariṃsu, naṅgalasīsapamāṇo rattaṅkuro uṭṭhahi, mahājanassa olokentasseva paṇṇāsahatthakkhandho paṇṇāsahatthasākho ubbedhato ca hatthasatiko ambarukkho sampajji, tāvadevassa pupphāni ca phalāni ca uṭṭhahiṃsu. So madhukaraparivuto suvaṇṇavaṇṇaphalabharito nabhaṃ pūretvā aṭṭhāsi, vātappaharaṇakāle madhurapakkāni patiṃsu. Pacchā āgacchantā bhikkhū paribhuñjitvāva āgamiṃsu.

Early in the morning, the Teacher set out to enter Sāvatthī for alms. A park keeper named Kaṇḍa, while bringing a large ripe mango the size of a water pot to the king, saw the Teacher at the city gate and, thinking, ‘This is fitting for the Tathāgata,’ offered it to him. The Teacher accepted it, sat down to one side, and after eating, said, ‘Ānanda, give this mango stone to the park keeper to plant in this very spot; it will be known as the Kaṇḍamba mango tree.’ The elder did so. The park keeper cleared the ground and planted it. At that very moment, the stone split, roots descended, and a red shoot the size of a plowshare sprouted. As the great crowd watched, a mango tree one hundred cubits in height came into being, with a trunk of fifty cubits and main branches of fifty cubits. Instantly, flowers and fruits appeared on it. Surrounded by bees and laden with golden-colored fruit, it stood filling the sky. When the wind blew, sweet, ripe fruits fell. The monks who came afterwards ate them before proceeding.

Sāyanhasamaye sakko devarājā āvajjento “satthu ratanamaṇḍapakaraṇaṃ amhākaṃ bhāro”ti ñatvā vissakammadevaputtaṃ pesetvā dvādasayojanikaṃ nīluppalasañchannaṃ sattaratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāresi. Evaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatiṃsu. Satthā titthiyamaddanaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehi yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā bahujanassa pasannabhāvaṃ ñatvā oruyha buddhāsane nisinno dhammaṃ desesi. Vīsati pāṇakoṭiyo amatapānaṃ piviṃsu. Tato “purimabuddhā pana pāṭihāriyaṃ katvā kattha gacchantī”ti āvajjento “tāvatiṃsabhavana”nti ñatvā buddhāsanā uṭṭhāya dakkhiṇapādaṃ yugandharamuddhani ṭhapetvā vāmapādena sinerumatthakaṃ akkamitvā pāricchattakamūle paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ vassaṃ upagantvā antotemāsaṃ devānaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ kathesi. Parisā satthu gataṭṭhānaṃ ajānantī [M 4.0266] “disvāva gamissāmā”ti tattheva temāsaṃ vasi. Upakaṭṭhāya pavāraṇāya mahāmoggallānatthero gantvā bhagavato ārocesi. Atha naṃ satthā pucchi “kahaṃ pana etarahi sāriputto”ti? “Eso, bhante, pāṭihāriye pasīditvā pabbajitehi pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ saṅkassanagaradvāre vasī”ti. “Moggallāna, ahaṃ ito sattame divase saṅkassanagaradvāre otarissāmi, tathāgataṃ daṭṭhukāmā saṅkassanagare ekato sannipatantū”ti. Thero “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā āgantvā parisāya ārocetvā sakalaparisaṃ sāvatthito tiṃsayojanaṃ saṅkassanagaraṃ ekamuhutteneva pāpesi.

In the evening, Sakka, king of the devas, reflecting, realized, 'The construction of the jeweled pavilion for the Teacher is our responsibility.' Knowing this, he sent the devaputta Vissakamma and had a seven-jeweled pavilion, twelve yojanas in size and covered with blue lotuses, constructed. Thus, the deities of the ten thousand world-systems gathered. The Teacher, having performed the Twin Miracle to subdue the sectarians—a miracle not shared with his disciples—and knowing the faithful disposition of the multitude, descended and sat on the Buddha’s seat to teach the Dhamma. Twenty crores of beings drank the nectar of immortality. Then, reflecting, 'Where did the previous Buddhas go after performing miracles?' and knowing it was the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he rose from the Buddha’s seat, placed his right foot on the summit of Mount Yugandhara, and with his left foot stepped onto the peak of Mount Sineru. He then went to the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, sat on the Paṇḍukambala stone, and spent the three months of the rainy season there, teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the devas. The assembly, unaware of where the Teacher had gone, thought, 'We will leave only after seeing him,' and stayed there for those three months. As the Pavāraṇā day drew near, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna went and informed the Blessed One. Then the Teacher asked him, 'Where is Sāriputta now?' 'Venerable sir, he, pleased by the miracle, is dwelling at the gate of Saṅkassa city with five hundred monks who had gone forth.' 'Moggallāna, on the seventh day from now, I will descend at the gate of Saṅkassa city. Let those who wish to see the Tathāgata gather together in Saṅkassa city.' The elder replied, 'Very well,' and having returned, informed the assembly. He then brought the entire assembly from Sāvatthī, a distance of thirty yojanas, to Saṅkassa city in a single moment.

Satthā vutthavasso pavāretvā “mahārāja, manussalokaṃ gamissāmī”ti sakkassa ārocesi. Sakko vissakammaṃ āmantetvā “dasabalassa manussalokagamanatthāya tīṇi sopānāni karohī”ti āha. So sinerumatthake sopānasīsaṃ saṅkassanagaradvāre dhurasopānaṃ katvā [V 4.0238] majjhe maṇimayaṃ, ekasmiṃ passe rajatamayaṃ, ekasmiṃ passe suvaṇṇamayanti [P 4.0266] tīṇi sopānāni māpesi, sattaratanamayā vedikāparikkhepā. Satthā lokavivaraṇaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ katvā majjhe maṇimayena sopānena otari. Sakko pattacīvaraṃ aggahesi, suyāmo vālabījaniṃ, sahampati mahābrahmā chattaṃ dhāresi, dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā dibbagandhamālādīhi pūjayiṃsu. Satthāraṃ dhurasopāne patiṭṭhitaṃ paṭhamameva sāriputtatthero vandi, pacchā sesaparisā. Tasmiṃ samāgame satthā cintesi “moggallāno “iddhimā’ti pākaṭo, upāli ‘vinayadharo’ti. Sāriputtassa pana mahāpaññaguṇo apākaṭo, ṭhapetvā maṃ añño etena sadiso samapañño nāma natthi, paññāguṇamassa pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ tāva puthujjanānaṃ visaye pañhaṃ pucchi, taṃ puthujjanāva kathayiṃsu tato sotāpannānaṃ visaye pañhaṃ pucchi, tampi sotāpannāva kathayiṃsu, puthujjanā na jāniṃsu. Evaṃ sakadāgāmivisaye anāgāmivisaye khīṇāsavavisaye mahāsāvakavisaye ca pañhaṃ pucchi, tampi heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā na jāniṃsu, uparimā uparimāva kathayiṃsu. Aggasāvakavisaye puṭṭhapañhampi aggasāvakāva kathayiṃsu, aññe na jāniṃsu. Tato sāriputtattherassa visaye pañhaṃ pucchi, taṃ therova kathesi, aññe na jāniṃsu.

The Teacher, having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, informed Sakka, 'Great king, I shall go to the human world.' Sakka summoned Vissakamma and said, 'Make three staircases for the descent of the One of Ten Powers to the human world.' He then created three staircases, with their tops at the peak of Mount Sineru and their bases at the city gate of Saṅkassa: a jeweled one in the middle, a silver one on one side, and a golden one on the other, all surrounded by railings made of the seven precious gems. The Teacher performed the miracle of opening up the worlds and descended by the central jeweled staircase. Sakka took the bowl and robe, Suyāma held the yak-tail whisk, Sahampati Mahābrahmā carried the parasol, and the deities of the ten-thousand world-systems honored him with divine perfumes and garlands. The Elder Sāriputta was the first to pay homage to the Teacher as he stood at the base of the staircase, followed by the rest of the assembly. At that gathering, the Teacher reflected: 'Moggallāna is renowned as being "possessed of psychic power," and Upāli as "an expert in the Vinaya." But Sāriputta’s great quality of wisdom is not yet renowned. Except for me, there is no one else equal to him in wisdom—I shall make his quality of wisdom renowned.' First, he posed a question within the scope of ordinary people, and the ordinary people answered it. Then he asked a question within the scope of stream-enterers, and the stream-enterers answered it, while the ordinary people did not know. In this way, he asked questions within the scope of once-returners, non-returners, those who have destroyed the taints, and the great disciples; and each time, those of lower attainment did not know, while those of higher attainment answered. When he asked a question within the scope of the chief disciples, the chief disciples answered, while others did not know. Then he posed a question within the scope of the Elder Sāriputta, and only the elder answered it—no one else knew.

Manussā [M 4.0267] “ko nāma esa thero satthārā saddhiṃ kathesī”ti pucchitvā “dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero nāmā”ti sutvā “aho mahāpañño”ti vadiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya devamanussānaṃ antare therassa mahāpaññaguṇo pākaṭo jāto. Atha naṃ satthā –

People asked, 'Who is this elder who converses with the Teacher?' and hearing, 'He is the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta,' they said, 'Ah, how great is his wisdom!' From then on, the elder’s quality of great wisdom became renowned among gods and humans. Then, wishing to pose a question to him, the Teacher said—

“Ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse, ye ca sekhā puthū idha;

Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhi mārisā”ti. (su. ni. 1044; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchā 63; netti. 14) –

'Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and the many who are still in training here—tell me, O wise one, when asked, what is their conduct, dear sir.'

Buddhavisaye pañhaṃ pucchitvā “imassa nu kho sāriputta, saṃkhittena bhāsitassa kathaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti āha. Thero pañhaṃ oloketvā “satthā maṃ sekhāsekhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āgamanapaṭipadaṃ pucchatī”ti pañhe nikkaṅkho hutvā “āgamanapaṭipadā nāma khandhādivasena bahūhi mukhehi sakkā kathetuṃ, kataṃ nu kho kathento satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti ajjhāsaye kaṅkhi. Satthā “sāriputto pañhe nikkaṅkho, ajjhāsaye pana me kaṅkhati, mayā naye adinne kathetuṃ na sakkhissati, nayamassa dassāmī”ti [P 4.0267] nayaṃ dadanto “bhūtamidaṃ sāriputta samanupassā”ti āha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “sāriputto mama ajjhāsayaṃ [V 4.0239] gahetvā kathento khandhavasena kathessatī”ti. Therassa saha nayadānena so pañho nayasatena nayasahassena upaṭṭhāsi. So satthārā dinnanaye ṭhatvā buddhavisaye pañhaṃ kathesi.

Having asked a question within the Buddha’s range, he said, 'Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?' The elder, looking at the question, thought, 'The Teacher is asking me about the path of progress for monks, both those in training and those beyond training.' Being certain about the question, he felt uncertain about the Teacher’s intention, thinking, 'The path of progress can be explained in many ways, such as by way of the aggregates; by which way of explaining will I be able to grasp the Teacher’s intention?' The Teacher thought, 'Sāriputta is certain about the question but is uncertain about my intention. He will not be able to explain it without me giving him a lead; I will give him a lead.' So, giving him the lead, he said, 'Sāriputta, contemplate this as it is.' The Teacher thought, 'Sāriputta, having grasped my intention, will explain it by way of the aggregates.' Along with the giving of the lead, the question became clear to the elder in a hundred, a thousand ways. Standing firm in the lead given by the Teacher, he explained the question within the Buddha’s range.

Satthā dvādasayojanikāya parisāya dhammaṃ desesi. Tiṃsa pāṇakoṭiyo amatapānaṃ piviṃsu. Satthā parisaṃ uyyojetvā cārikaṃ caranto anupubbena sāvatthiṃ gantvā punadivase sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhūhi vatte dassite gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Sāyanhasamaye bhikkhū therassa guṇakathaṃ kathentā dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu “mahāpañño, āvuso, sāriputto puthupañño javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño dasabalena saṃkhittena pucchitapañhaṃ vitthārena kathesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi esa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ kathesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher taught the Dhamma to an assembly twelve yojanas in extent. Thirty crores of beings drank the nectar of the deathless. Having dismissed the assembly, the Teacher wandered on tour and in due course reached Sāvatthī. The next day, he wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, and having returned from the alms-round, he entered the Perfumed Chamber after the monks had performed their duties. In the evening, the monks sat in the Dhamma hall, discussing the elder’s virtues: 'Friends, the Elder Sāriputta is of great wisdom, wide wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. He has explained in detail a question asked concisely by the One of Ten Powers.' The Teacher came and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he explained in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief.' Having said this, he brought forth the past.

Atīte [M 4.0268] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sarabhamigayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā araññe vasati. Rājā migavittako ahosi thāmasampanno, aññaṃ manussaṃ “manusso”tipi na gaṇeti. So ekadivasaṃ migavaṃ gantvā amacce āha – “yassa passena migo palāyati, tena so daṇḍo dātabbo”ti. Te cintayiṃsu “kadāci vemajjhe ṭhitamigaṃ vijjhanti, kadāci uṭṭhitaṃ, kadāci palāyantampi, ajja pana yena kenaci upāyena rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānaññeva āropessāmā”ti. Cintetvā ca pana katikaṃ katvā rañño dhuramaggaṃ adaṃsu. Te mahantaṃ gumbaṃ parikkhipitvā muggarādīhi bhūmiṃ pothayiṃsu. Paṭhamameva sarabhamigo uṭṭhāya tikkhattuṃ gubbhaṃ anuparigantvā palāyanokāsaṃ olokento sesadisāsu manusse bāhāya bāhaṃ dhanunā dhanuṃ āhacca nirantare ṭhite disvā rañño ṭhitaṭṭhāneyeva okāsaṃ addasa. So ummīlitesu akkhīsu [P 4.0268] vālukaṃ khipamāno viya rājānaṃ abhimukho agamāsi. Rājā taṃ lahusampattaṃ disvā saraṃ ukkhipitvā vijjhi. Sarabhamigā nāma saraṃ vañcetuṃ chekā honti, sare abhimukhaṃ āgacchante vegaṃ hāpetvā tiṭṭhanti, pacchato āgacchante vegena purato javanti, uparibhāgenāgacchante piṭṭhiṃ nāmenti, passenāgacchante thokaṃ apagacchanti, kucchiṃ sandhāyāgacchante parivattitvā patanti, sare atikkante vātacchinnavalāhakavegena palāyanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a sarabha deer and lived in the forest. The king was fond of hunting and was very strong; he did not even consider other people to be human beings. One day, while going hunting, he told his ministers, “Whoever lets a deer escape past him shall be punished.” They thought, “Sometimes they shoot a deer standing in the middle, sometimes when it has risen, and sometimes even when it is fleeing. But today, by some means or other, we must make it go to the king’s standing place.” Having decided this, they made an agreement and gave the king the head of the path. They surrounded a large thicket and beat the ground with clubs and such. At the very first sound, the sarabha deer rose and circled the thicket three times, looking for an escape route. Seeing men standing shoulder to shoulder and bow to bow without a gap in every other direction, he saw an opening only where the king stood. As if throwing sand into wide-open eyes, he charged straight toward the king. The king, seeing him swiftly approaching, raised his arrow and shot. Sarabha deer are skilled at dodging arrows: when an arrow comes straight at them, they slow down and stop; when it comes from behind, they speed forward; when it comes from above, they bend their backs; when it comes from the side, they move slightly aside; when it aims at their belly, they turn and fall; and when the arrow has passed, they flee with the speed of a cloud scattered by the wind.

Sopi rājā tasmiṃ parivattitvā patite “sarabhamigo me viddho”ti nādaṃ muñci. Sarabho uṭṭhāya vātavegena palāyi. Balamaṇḍalaṃ bhijjitvā ubhosu passesu ṭhitaamaccā sarabhaṃ palāyamānaṃ disvā ekato hutvā pucchiṃsu “migo kassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhī”ti? “Rañño ṭhitaṭṭhāna”nti[V 4.0240]. “Rājā ‘viddho me’ti vadati, konena viddho, nibbirajjho bho amhākaṃ rājā, bhūminena viddhā”ti te nānappakārena raññā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ kariṃsu. Rājā cintesi “ime maṃ parihasanti, na mama pamāṇaṃ jānantī”ti gāḷhaṃ nivāsetvā pattikova khaggaṃ ādāya “sarabhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti vegena pakkhandi. Atha naṃ disvā tīṇi yojanāni anubandhi. Sarabho araññaṃ pāvisi, rājāpi pāvisi. Tattha sarabhamigassa gamanamagge saṭṭhihatthamatto mahāpūtipādanarakāvāṭo [M 4.0269] atthi, so tiṃsahatthamattaṃ udakena puṇṇo tiṇehi ca paṭicchanno. Sarabho udakagandhaṃ ghāyitvāva āvāṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā thokaṃ osakkitvā gato. Rājā pana ujukameva gacchanto tasmiṃ pati.

When the deer turned and fell, the king cried out, “The sarabha deer has been shot by me!” The sarabha rose and fled with the speed of the wind. The circle of men broke, and the ministers standing on both sides, seeing the sarabha fleeing, gathered together and asked, “Whose standing place did the deer go past?” “The king’s standing place,” they replied. “The king says, ‘It has been shot by me,’ but by whom was it shot? Our king has missed, sirs; he shot the earth!” Thus, they mocked the king in various ways. The king thought, “These men mock me; they do not know my capacity.” Tightly fastening his garment and taking his sword, he set out on foot and swiftly charged forward, declaring, “I will capture the sarabha!” Then, seeing it, he pursued for three leagues. The sarabha entered the forest, and the king followed. There, on the path where the sarabha deer had gone, was a great pit of rotten roots, sixty cubits deep, filled with water to a depth of thirty cubits and covered with grass and leaves. The sarabha, smelling the scent of the water, knew it was a pit and turned slightly aside. But the king, walking straight ahead, fell into it.

Sarabho tassa padasaddaṃ asuṇanto nivattitvā taṃ apassanto “narakāvāṭe patito bhavissatī”ti ñatvā āgantvā olokento taṃ gambhīraudake apatiṭṭhaṃ kilamantaṃ disvā tena kataṃ aparādhaṃ hadaye akatvā [P 4.0269] sañjātakāruñño “mā mayi passanteva rājā nassatu, imamhā dukkhā naṃ mocessāmī”ti āvāṭatīre ṭhito “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, mahantā dukkhā taṃ mocessāmī”ti vatvā attano piyaputtaṃ uddharituṃ ussāhaṃ karonto viya tassuddharaṇatthāya silāya yoggaṃ katvāva “vijjhissāmī”ti āgataṃ rājānaṃ saṭṭhihatthā narakā uddharitvā assāsetvā piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā araññā nīharitvā senāya avidūre otāretvā ovādamassa datvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Rājā mahāsattaṃ vinā vasituṃ asakkonto āha “sāmi sarabhamigarāja, mayā saddhiṃ bārāṇasiṃ ehi, dvādasayojanikāya te bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ dammi, taṃ kārehī”ti. “Mahārāja, mayaṃ tiracchānagatā, na me rajjenattho, sace te mayi sineho atthi, mayā dinnāni sīlāni rakkhanto raṭṭhavāsinopi sīlaṃ rakkhāpehī”ti taṃ ovaditvā araññameva pāvisi.

The sarabha, no longer hearing the sound of the king's footsteps, turned back and, not seeing him, realized, “He must have fallen into the pit.” He went and looked, and seeing the king struggling in the deep water without a foothold, he did not hold the king's offense against him. Filled with compassion, he thought, “Let not the king perish while I am watching; I will free him from this suffering.” Standing at the edge of the pit, he said, “Do not fear, great king, I will free you from this great suffering.” As if making an effort to rescue his own beloved son, he practiced by lifting a stone to test his strength, and then he pulled the king—who had come intending to shoot him—out of the sixty-cubit pit. Having comforted him, he placed the king on his back, carried him out of the forest, set him down near the army, gave him advice, and established him in the five precepts. The king, unable to bear being apart from the Great Being, said, “Lord Sarabha, king of deer, come with me to Benares. I will give you the twelve-league kingdom of Benares; rule it.” “Great King, we are animals; I have no need for a kingdom. If you have affection for me, keep the precepts I have given you and have the people of your kingdom keep them as well.” Having advised him thus, he returned to the forest.

So assupuṇṇehi nettehi tassa guṇaṃ sarantova senaṃ pāpuṇitvā senaṅgaparivuto nagaraṃ gantvā “ito paṭṭhāya sakalanagaravāsino pañca sīlāni rakkhantū”ti dhammabheriṃ carāpesi. Mahāsattena pana attano kataguṇaṃ kassaci akathetvā sāyanhe nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā alaṅkatasayane sayitvā paccūsakāle mahāsattassa guṇaṃ saritvā uṭṭhāya sayanapiṭṭhe pallaṅkena nisīditvā pītipuṇṇena hadayena chahi gāthāhi udānesi –

With eyes full of tears, remembering the virtues of the Great Being, the king reached his army and, surrounded by his forces, entered the city. He had the drum of the Dhamma sounded throughout the land, proclaiming: “From this day forth, let all the inhabitants of the kingdom observe the five precepts.” Without telling anyone of the service the Great Being had done for him, he ate a meal of various choice delicacies in the evening and lay down on a decorated bed. At dawn, remembering the virtues of the Great Being, he rose and sat cross-legged on his bed. With a heart full of joy, he uttered these verses as an inspired exclamation:

134.

134.

“Āsīsetheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, yathā icchiṃ tathā ahu.

A person should indeed aspire; a wise person should not be disheartened. I see myself as I desired, so it has become.

135.

135.

“Āsīsetheva [V 4.0241] puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, udakā thalamubbhataṃ.

A person should indeed aspire; a wise person should not be disheartened. I see myself, drawn up from the water onto dry land.

136.

136.

“Vāyametheva [M 4.0270] puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, yathā icchiṃ tathā ahu.

A person should indeed strive; a wise person should not be disheartened. I see myself as I desired, so it has become.

137.

137.

“Vāyametheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, udakā thalamubbhataṃ.

A person should indeed strive; a wise person should not be disheartened. I see myself, drawn up from the water onto dry land.

138.

138.

“Dukkhūpanītopi naro sapañño, āsaṃ na chindeyya sukhāgamāya;

Bahū [P 4.0270] hi phassā ahitā hitā ca, avitakkitā maccumupabbajanti.

Even when beset by suffering, a wise person should not abandon hope for the coming of happiness; for many experiences, both harmful and beneficial, arise unexpectedly, even as one approaches death.

139.

139.

“Acintitampi bhavati, cintitampi vinassati;

Na hi cintāmayā bhogā, itthiyā purisassa vā”ti.

Even the unthought-of happens, the thought-of perishes; for wealth is not created by mere thought, for a woman or a man.

Tattha āsīsetheva purisoti āsacchedakakammaṃ akatvā attano kammesu āsaṃ karotheva na ukkaṇṭheyya. Yathā icchinti ahañhi saṭṭhihatthā narakā uṭṭhānaṃ icchiṃ, somhi tatheva jāto, tato uṭṭhitoyevāti dīpeti. Ahitā hitā cāti dukkhaphassā ca sukhaphassā ca, “maraṇaphassā jīvitaphassā cā”tipi attho, sattānañhi maraṇaphasso ahito jīvitaphasso hito, tesaṃ avitakkito acintitopi maraṇaphasso āgacchatīti dasseti. Acinti tampīti mayā “āvāṭe patissāmī”ti na cintitaṃ, “sarabhaṃ māressāmī”ti cintitaṃ, idāni pana me cintitaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, acintitameva jātaṃ. Bhogāti yasaparivārā. Ete cintāmayā na honti, tasmā ñāṇavatā vīriyameva kātabbaṃ. Vīriyavato hi acintitampi hotiyeva.

Here, ‘A person should indeed aspire’ means one should indeed have hope in one’s own deeds, not performing an act that cuts off hope, and not be disheartened. ‘As I desired’ means: ‘I desired to rise from the sixty-cubit pit, and so it has come to be for me; I have indeed risen from it’—this is what it illustrates. ‘Harmful and beneficial’ refers to painful contacts and pleasant contacts. The meaning is also ‘contacts of death and contacts of life,’ for among beings, the contact of death is harmful, while the contact of life is beneficial. It shows that the contact of death comes even without being thought of or considered by them. ‘Even the unthought-of’ means: ‘I did not think, “I will fall into a pit,” but I did think, “I will kill the sarabha deer.” Now, however, what I thought of is lost, and what was unthought of has come to pass.’ ‘Wealth’ refers to fame and retinue. These are not created by mere thinking; therefore, one who is wise should exert effort. For the diligent, even the unthought-of indeed comes to pass.

Tassevaṃ udānaṃ udānentasseva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahi. Purohito ca pātova sukhaseyyapucchanatthaṃ āgantvā rājadvāre ṭhito tassa udānagītasaddaṃ sutvā cintesi “rājā hiyyo migavaṃ agamāsi, tattha sarabhamigaṃ viraddho bhavissati, tato amaccehi avahasiyamāno ‘māretvā naṃ āharissāmī’ti khattiyamānena taṃ anubandhanto saṭṭhihatthe narake patito bhavissati, dayālunā sarabharājena rañño dosaṃ acintetvā rājā uddharito bhavissati, tena maññe udānaṃ udānetī”ti. Evaṃ brāhmaṇassa rañño [M 4.0271] paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ udānaṃ sutvā sumajjite ādāse mukhaṃ [V 4.0242] olokentassa chāyā viya raññā ca sarabhena ca katakāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi. So nakhaggena dvāraṃ ākoṭesi. Rājā “ko eso”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ deva purohito”ti. Athassa dvāraṃ vivaritvā “ito ehācariyā”ti āha. So pavisitvā rājānaṃ jayāpetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “ahaṃ, mahārāja, tayā araññe katakāraṇaṃ jānāmi, tvaṃ ekaṃ sarabhamigaṃ anubandhanto narake patito, atha naṃ so sarabho silāya yoggaṃ katvā [P 4.0271] narakato uddhari, so tvaṃ tassa guṇaṃ anussaritvā udānaṃ udānesī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

As he was thus uttering this inspired utterance, the dawn arose. The royal priest, coming early in the morning to inquire about the king’s well-being, stood at the palace gate. Hearing the sound of the king’s inspired song, he thought: 'Yesterday the king went hunting. There, he must have missed the sarabha deer. Then, being ridiculed by his ministers, he must have pursued it with a warrior's pride, saying, “I will kill it and bring it back.” Following it, he must have fallen into the sixty-cubit pit. But the compassionate sarabha king, not considering the king’s fault, must have rescued him. That is why, I suppose, he utters this inspired utterance.' Thus, when the brahmin heard the king’s inspired utterance, complete in its expression, the deed done by the king and the sarabha became as clear to him as the reflection of a face in a well-polished mirror. He tapped on the door with his fingernail. The king asked, 'Who is there?' 'It is I, sire, the royal priest.' Then the king opened the door for him and said, 'Come here, teacher.' Entering, the priest paid his respects to the king and stood to one side. 'Great king, I know the deed you did in the forest. You, pursuing a single sarabha deer, fell into a pit. Then that sarabha, having practiced with a rock, rescued you from the pit. Remembering his virtue, you utter this inspired utterance.' Having said this, he spoke two verses:

140.

140.

“Sarabhaṃ giriduggasmiṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ anusarī pure;

Alīnacittassa tuvaṃ, vikkantamanujīvasi.

The sarabha in the rugged mountain terrain, whom you formerly pursued—you live by the valor of that one whose mind is unshrinking.

141.

141.

“Yo taṃ viduggā narakā samuddhari, silāya yoggaṃ sarabho karitvā;

Dukkhūpanītaṃ maccumukhā pamocayi, alīnacittaṃ ta migaṃ vadesī”ti.

He who rescued you from that dreadful pit—the sarabha, having practiced with a rock—freed you from the jaws of death when you were overcome by suffering; you speak of that deer, whose mind is unshrinking.

Tattha anusarīti anubandhi. Vikkantanti uddharaṇatthāya kataparakkamaṃ. Anujīvasīti upajīvasi, tassānubhāvena tayā jīvitaṃ laddhanti attho. Samuddharīti uddhari. Ta migaṃ vadesīti taṃ suvaṇṇasarabhamigaṃ idha sirisayane nisinno vaṇṇesi.

There, ‘pursued’ (anusarī) means followed. ‘Valor’ (vikkantaṃ) means the effort made for the sake of rescue. ‘You live by’ (anujīvasī) means you survive; the meaning is that life was obtained by his power. ‘Rescued’ (samuddharī) means he pulled you out. ‘You speak of that deer’ means you praised that golden sarabha deer while seated here on the royal couch.

Taṃ sutvā rājā “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ na migavaṃ gato, sabbaṃ pavattiṃ jānāti, kathaṃ nu kho jānāti, pucchissāmi na”nti cintetvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king thought: 'This priest did not go hunting with me, yet he knows the whole story. How does he know? I will ask him.' Thus reflecting, he spoke the ninth verse:

142.

142.

“Kiṃ tvaṃ nu tattheva tadā ahosi, udāhu te koci naṃ etadakkhā;

Vivaṭacchaddo nusi sabbadassī, ñāṇaṃ nu te brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpa”nti.

Were you there at that time, or did someone tell you this? Are you one who has removed the veil, seeing all, or is your knowledge, O Brahmin, of a fearsome nature?

Tattha bhiṃsarūpanti kiṃ nu te ñāṇaṃ balavajātikaṃ, tenetaṃ jānāsīti.

Here, ‘of a fearsome nature’ means: Is your knowledge of a powerful nature, by which you know this?

Brāhmaṇo [M 4.0272] “nāhaṃ sabbaññubuddho, byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā tayā kathitagāthānaṃ pana mayhaṃ attho upaṭṭhātī”ti dīpento dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin, revealing that 'I am not an omniscient Buddha, but the meaning of the verses spoken by you occurs to me without distorting the expression,' spoke the tenth verse:

143.

143.

“Na cevahaṃ tattha tadā ahosiṃ, na cāpi me koci naṃ etadakkhā;

Gāthāpadānañca [P 4.0272] subhāsitānaṃ, atthaṃ tadānenti janinda dhīrā”ti.

I was not there at that time, nor did anyone tell me this; but the wise, O king, deduce the meaning of well-spoken verses.

Tattha [V 4.0243] subhāsitānanti byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā suṭṭhu bhāsitānaṃ. Atthaṃ tadānentīti yo tesaṃ attho, taṃ ānenti upadhārentīti.

There, ‘well-spoken’ means those spoken well without distorting the expression. ‘Deduce the meaning’ means they comprehend whatever is the meaning.

Rājā tassa tussitvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya dānādipuññābhirato ahosi, manussāpi puññābhiratā hutvā matamatā saggameva pūrayiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ rājā “lakkhaṃ vijjhissāmī”ti purohitamādāya uyyānaṃ gato. Tadā sakko devarājā bahū nave deve ca devakaññāyo ca disvā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjento sarabhamigena narakā uddharitvā rañño sīlesu patiṭṭhāpitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “rañño ānubhāvena mahājano puññāni karoti, tena devaloko paripūrati, idāni kho pana rājā lakkhaṃ vijjhituṃ uyyānaṃ gato, taṃ vīmaṃsitvā sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā sarabhamigassa guṇaṃ kathāpetvā attano ca sakkabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā ākāse ṭhito dhammaṃ desetvā mettāya ceva pañcannaṃ sīlānañca guṇaṃ kathetvā āgamissāmī”ti cintetvā uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Rājāpi “lakkhaṃ vijjhissāmī”ti dhanuṃ āropetvā saraṃ sannayhi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko rañño ca lakkhassa ca antare attano ānubhāvena sarabhaṃ dassesi. Rājā taṃ disvā saraṃ na muñci. Atha naṃ sakko purohitassa sarīre adhimuccitvā gāthaṃ abhāsi –

The king, pleased with him, gave him much wealth. From then on, he became devoted to meritorious deeds such as giving, and other people, also delighting in merit, upon their deaths, filled heaven itself. Then one day, the king, thinking, 'I will shoot a target,' went to the park, taking the priest with him. At that time, Sakka, the king of gods, seeing many new gods and celestial maidens, wondered, 'What is the reason?' Reflecting, he understood that the king had been rescued from the pit by the sarabha deer and established in the precepts. Knowing that by the king's power the great populace performed meritorious deeds, thus filling the world of the gods, he thought, 'Now the king has gone to the park to shoot a target. I will test him, cause him to utter a lion's roar, cause him to proclaim the virtues of the sarabha deer, reveal my own identity as Sakka, and, standing in the sky, I will teach the Dhamma, speak of the virtues of loving-kindness and the five precepts, and then return.' Having decided this, he went to the park. The king, intending to shoot the target, strung his bow and fitted an arrow. At that moment, Sakka, by his power, manifested a sarabha deer between the king and the target. Seeing it, the king did not release the arrow. Then Sakka, possessing the priest's body, spoke this verse:

144.

144.

“Ādāya pattiṃ paraviriyaghātiṃ, cāpe saraṃ kiṃ vicikicchase tuvaṃ;

Nunno saro sarabhaṃ hantu khippaṃ, annañhi etaṃ varapañña rañño”ti.

Taking the feathered arrow that destroys the vigor of others, why do you hesitate with the arrow on the bow? Let the impelled arrow quickly slay the sarabha, for this is indeed food for a king, O you of excellent wisdom.

Tattha [M 4.0273] pattinti vājapattehi samannāgataṃ. Paraviriyaghātinti paresaṃ vīriyaghātakaṃ. Cāpe saranti etaṃ pattasahitaṃ saraṃ cāpe ādāya sannayhitvā idāni tvaṃ kiṃ vicikicchasi. Hantūti tayā vissaṭṭho hutvā esa saro [P 4.0273] khippaṃ imaṃ sarabhaṃ hanatu. Annañhi etanti varapañña, mahārāja, sarabho nāma rañño āhāro bhakkhoti attho.

There, ‘pattiṃ’ means endowed with wing-feathers. ‘Paraviriyaghātiṃ’ means destructive of the vigor of others. ‘Cāpe saraṃ’ means: having taken this feathered arrow and fitted it on the bow, why do you now hesitate? ‘Hantu’ means: may this arrow, shot by you, swiftly slay this sarabha. ‘Annañhi etaṃ’ means: O you of excellent wisdom, great king, a sarabha is food for a king, meaning it is to be eaten.

Tato rājā gāthamāha –

Then the king spoke this verse:

145.

145.

“Addhā pajānāmi ahampi etaṃ, annaṃ migo brāhmaṇa khattiyassa;

Pubbe katañca apacāyamāno, tasmā migaṃ sarabhaṃ no hanāmī”ti.

Surely, I too understand this: O brahmin, a deer is food for a noble. But respecting what was done before, therefore I will not kill the sarabha deer.

Tattha [V 4.0244] pubbe katañcāti brāhmaṇa, ahametaṃ ekaṃsena jānāmi yathā migo khattiyassa annaṃ, pubbe pana iminā mayhaṃ kataguṇaṃ pūjemi, tasmā taṃ na hanāmīti.

There, ‘pubbe katañca’ means: O brahmin, I know this with certainty, that a deer is food for a warrior. But I honor the good deed done for me by this one in the past; therefore, I will not kill it.

Tato sakko gāthādvayamāha –

Then Sakka spoke these two verses:

146.

146.

“Neso migo mahārāja, asureso disampati;

Etaṃ hantvā manussinda, bhavassu amarādhipo.

This is no deer, O great king; it is the lord of Asuras, the ruler of the quarters. Slay him, O lord of men, and become the ruler of the immortals.

147.

147.

“Sace ca rājā vicikicchase tuvaṃ, hantuṃ migaṃ sarabhaṃ sahāyakaṃ;

Saputtadāro naravīraseṭṭha, gantā tuvaṃ vetaraṇiṃ yamassā”ti.

And if you, O king, hesitate to slay your companion, the sarabha deer, then you, foremost of heroic men, along with your sons and wife, will go to Yama's Vetaraṇī.

Tattha asuresoti asuro eso, asurajeṭṭhako sakko esoti adhippāyena vadati. Amarādhipoti tvaṃ etaṃ sakkaṃ māretvā sayaṃ sakko devarājā hohīti vadati. Vetaraṇiṃ yamassāti “sace etaṃ ‘sahāyo me’ti cintetvā na māressasi, saputtadāro yamassa vetaraṇinirayaṃ gato bhavissasī”ti naṃ tāsesi.

Here, ‘asureso’ means ‘this is an Asura’; he speaks with the intention, ‘This is Sakka, the chief of the Asuras.’ ‘Amarādhipo’ means: he says, ‘By killing this Sakka, you yourself shall become Sakka, the king of the gods.’ ‘Vetaraṇiṃ yamassā’ means: he threatened him, saying, ‘If you think, “He is my friend,” and do not kill him, you, along with your sons and wife, will go to Yama’s Vetaraṇī hell.’

Tato [M 4.0274] rājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke these two verses:

148.

148.

“Kāmaṃ ahaṃ jānapadā ca sabbe, puttā ca dārā ca sahāyasaṅghā;

Gacchemu taṃ vetaraṇiṃ yamassa, na tveva hañño mama pāṇado yo.

Willingly let me, and all the people of the country, my sons and wife, and my company of friends, go to that Vetaraṇī of Yama, but I will not slay the one who gave me my life.

149.

149.

“Ayaṃ [P 4.0274] migo kicchagatassa mayhaṃ, ekassa kattā vivanasmi ghore;

Taṃ tādisaṃ pubbakiccaṃ saranto, jānaṃ mahābrahme kathaṃ haneyya”nti.

This deer was the benefactor for me when I had fallen into distress, alone in the dreadful wilderness. Remembering such a prior deed, knowing it well, O great Brahmin, how could I slay him?

Tattha mama pāṇado yoti brāhmaṇa, yo mama pāṇadado yena me piyaṃ jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ, narakaṃ pavisantena mayā so na tveva hañño na hanitabbo, avajjho esoti vadati. Ekassa kattā vivanasmi ghoreti dāruṇe araññe paviṭṭhassa sato ekassa asahāyakassa mama kattā kārako jīvitassa dāyako, svāhaṃ taṃ iminā kataṃ tādisaṃ pubbakiccaṃ sarantoyeva taṃ guṇaṃ jānantoyeva kathaṃ haneyyaṃ.

Here, ‘mama pāṇado yo’ means: O brahmin, he who gave me life, by whom precious life was given to me—even if I were to enter hell, he is not to be slain by me, he is not to be killed; he is not to be harmed, thus he declares. ‘Ekassa kattā vivanasmi ghore’ means: he was the benefactor, the doer, the giver of life for me, who had entered the dreadful wilderness, being alone and without companions. How could I, remembering such a prior deed done by him, knowing that virtue, slay him?

Atha [V 4.0245] sakko purohitassa sarīrato apagantvā sakkattabhāvaṃ māpetvā ākāse ṭhatvā rañño guṇaṃ pakāsento gāthādvayamāha –

Then Sakka, departing from the chaplain's body, manifested his own form as Sakka, stood in the sky, and proclaiming the king's virtues, spoke these two verses:

150.

150.

“Mittābhirādhī cirameva jīva, rajjaṃ imaṃ dhammaguṇe pasāsa;

Nārīgaṇehi paricāriyanto, modassu raṭṭhe tidiveva vāsavo.

O you who delight in your friends, may you live long! Rule this kingdom with righteous qualities. Being attended by throngs of women, may you rejoice in your realm, like Vāsava in the heaven of the thirty-three.

151.

151.

“Akkodhano niccapasannacitto, sabbātithī yācayogo bhavitvā;

Datvā ca bhutvā ca yathānubhāvaṃ, anindito saggamupehi ṭhāna”nti.

Free from anger, ever serene of mind, having become one fit for all guests to approach, giving and enjoying according to your means, blameless, go to the heavenly state.

Tattha [M 4.0275] mittābhirādhīti mitte ārādhento tosento tesu adubbhamāno. Sabbātithīti sabbe dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇe atithī pāhunakeyeva katvā pariharanto yācitabbayuttako hutvā. Aninditoti dānādīni puññāni karaṇena pamudito devalokena abhinandito hutvā saggaṭṭhānaṃ upehīti.

Here, 'delight in friends' means pleasing and satisfying friends, not being treacherous towards them. 'All guests' means attending to all righteous ascetics and brahmins, having made them honored guests, thus becoming worthy to be requested. 'Blameless' means, having rejoiced in performing meritorious deeds such as giving and having been praised by the heavenly world, you go to the heavenly abode.

Evaṃ [P 4.0275] vatvā sakko “ahaṃ mahārājaṃ taṃ pariggaṇhituṃ āgato, tvaṃ attānaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ nādāsi, appamatto hohī”ti taṃ ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Having said this, Sakka said, "Great king, I came to test you, but you did not allow yourself to be caught; be heedful!" After advising him thus, he returned to his own abode.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi sāriputto saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ jānātiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, purohito sāriputto, sarabhamigo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, "Not only now, monks, but also in the past Sāriputta understood the detailed meaning of what was spoken concisely." Then he identified the birth: "At that time Ānanda was the king, Sāriputta was the chaplain, and I myself was the Sarabha deer."

Sarabhamigajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Sarabha Deer Jātaka is the tenth.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Summary of the Jātakas:

Amba phandana javana, nārada dūta kaliṅgā;

Akitti takkāriyaṃ ruru, sarabhaṃ dasa terase.

Amba, Phandana, Javana, Nārada, Dūta, Kaliṅga; Akitti, Takkāriya, Ruru, Sarabha—the ten of the Thirteenth Nipāta.

Terasakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of Thirteens is finished.

14. Pakiṇṇakanipāto

14. The Miscellaneous Nipāta

[484] 1. Sālikedārajātakavaṇṇanā

[484] 1. The Commentary on the Sālikedāra Jātaka

Sampannaṃ [V 4.0246][P 4.0276][M 4.0276] sālikedāranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu sāmajātake (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu gihī posesī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃ te hontī”ti vatvā “mātāpitaro me, bhante”ti vutte “sādhu bhikkhu, porāṇakapaṇḍitā tiracchānā hutvā suvayoniyaṃ nibbattitvāpi jiṇṇe mātāpitaro kulāvake nipajjāpetvā mukhatuṇḍakena gocaraṃ āharitvā posesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Sampannaṃ sālikedāranti." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who supported his mother. The present story will become clear in the Sāma Jātaka. The Teacher had that monk summoned and asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you support laypeople?" When he said, "It is true, venerable sir," he asked him, "How are they related to you?" When he said, "They are my parents, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Good, monk! The wise of old, though born as animals in the parrot species, still had their aged parents lie down in a nest and nourished them by bringing food in their beaks." Then he related the past.

Atīte rājagahe magadharājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā nagarato pubbuttaradisāya sāliddiyo nāma brāhmaṇagāmo ahosi. Tassa pubbuttaradisāya magadhakhettaṃ atthi, tattha kosiyagotto nāma sāliddiyavāsī brāhmaṇo sahassakarīsamattaṃ khettaṃ gahetvā sāliṃ vapāpesi. Uṭṭhite ca pana sasse vatiṃ thiraṃ kāretvā kassaci paṇṇāsakarīsamattaṃ, kassaci saṭṭhikarīsamattanti evaṃ pañcasatakarīsamattaṃ khettaṃ attano purisānaṃyeva ārakkhaṇatthāya datvā sesaṃ [P 4.0277] pañcasatakarīsamattaṃ khettaṃ bhatiṃ katvā ekassa bhatakassa adāsi. So tattha kuṭiṃ katvā rattindivaṃ vasati. Khettassa pana pubbuttaradisābhāge ekasmiṃ sānupabbate mahantaṃ simbalivanaṃ atthi, tattha anekāni suvasatāni vasanti. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ suvasaṅghe suvarañño putto hutvā nibbatti. So vayappatto abhirūpo thāmasampanno sakaṭanābhipamāṇasarīro ahosi. Athassa pitā mahallakakāle “ahaṃ idāni dūraṃ gantuṃ na sakkomi, tvaṃ imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharā”ti gaṇaṃ niyyādesi. So punadivasato paṭṭhāya mātāpitūnaṃ gocaratthāya gantuṃ nādāsi, suvagaṇaṃ pariharanto himavantaṃ gantvā sayaṃjātasālivane yāvadatthaṃ [M 4.0277] sāliṃ khāditvā āgamanakāle mātāpitūnaṃ pahonakaṃ gocaraṃ āharitvā mātāpitaro posesi.

In the past, in Rājagaha, a king of Magadha ruled. At that time, to the northeast of the city, there was a brahmin village called Sāliddiya. To the northeast of that village lay the Magadha fields, where a brahmin of the Kosiyagotta, a resident of Sāliddiya, took possession of a field of a thousand karisas and had rice sown. When the crop grew, he had a strong fence built and gave fifty karisas to some, sixty karisas to others—thus distributing five hundred karisas to his own men for the purpose of guarding it. The remaining five hundred karisas he gave to a single laborer on hire. That laborer built a hut there and lived day and night. In the northeastern part of the field, on a mountain slope, there was a large silk-cotton forest where many parrots lived. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of the parrot king in that flock of parrots. When he came of age, he was handsome, strong, and had a body the size of a cart hub. Then, in his old age, his father said, "I can no longer travel far. You must take care of this flock," and entrusted the flock to him. From the next day onward, he did not allow his parents to go in search of food. Leading the flock of parrots, he went to the Himalayas, ate his fill of rice in the self-grown rice forest, and upon returning, brought back sufficient food for his parents, sustaining them.

Athassa ekadivasaṃ suvā ārocesuṃ “pubbe imasmiṃ kāle magadhakhette sāli paccati, idāni [V 4.0247] kiṃ nu kho jāta”nti? “Tena hi jānāthā”ti dve suve pahiṇiṃsu. Te gantvā magadhakhette otarantā tassa bhatiyā rakkhaṇapurisassa khette otaritvā sāliṃ khāditvā ekaṃ sālisīsaṃ ādāya simbalivanaṃ gantvā sālisīsaṃ mahāsattassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā “tattha evarūpo sālī”ti vadiṃsu. So punadivase suvagaṇaparivuto tattha gantvā tasmiṃ bhatakassa khette otari. So pana puriso suve sāliṃ khādante disvā ito cito ca dhāvitvā vārentopi vāretuṃ na sakkoti. Sesā suvā yāvadatthaṃ sāliṃ khāditvā tucchamukhāva gacchanti. Suvarājā pana bahūni sālisīsāni ekato katvā tehi parivuto hutvā āharitvā mātāpitūnaṃ deti. Suvā punadivasato paṭṭhāya tattheva sāliṃ khādiṃsu. Atha so puriso “sace ime aññaṃ [P 4.0278] katipāhaṃ evaṃ khādissanti, kiñci na bhavissati, brāhmaṇo sāliṃ agghāpetvā mayhaṃ iṇaṃ karissati, gantvā tassa ārocessāmī”ti sālimuṭṭhinā saddhiṃ tathārūpaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā sāliddiyagāmaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇaṃ passitvā vanditvā paṇṇākāraṃ datvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “kiṃ, bho purisa, sampannaṃ sālikhetta”nti puṭṭho “āma, brāhmaṇa, sampanna”nti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

One day, the parrots reported to him: "Previously, at this time, rice ripened in the Magadha field. Now, what has happened?" "Then find out," he said, and sent two parrots. They went and, descending into the Magadha field, landed in the field of the hired guard, ate the rice, and took one head of rice. Then they went to the silk-cotton forest, placed the head of rice at the feet of the Great Being, and said, "Such rice is there." The next day, the parrot king, surrounded by his flock, went there and landed in that hired laborer's field. The man, seeing the parrots eating the rice, ran here and there trying to drive them away but could not stop them. The other parrots ate their fill of rice and flew away with empty beaks. But the parrot king, having gathered many heads of rice into one, brought them back, surrounded by the flock, to give to his parents. From that day onward, the parrots continued to eat the rice there. Then the man thought, "If they keep eating like this for a few more days, nothing will be left. The brahmin will assess the value of the rice and put me in debt. I must go and inform him." So he took a handful of rice and a suitable gift, went to the village of Sāliddiya, met the brahmin, paid his respects, offered the gift, and stood to one side. When asked, "Is the rice field flourishing, good man?" he replied, "Yes, brahmin, it is flourishing," and wishing to report how the parrots eat and take the rice, he recited two verses:

1.

1.

“Sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na ne vāretumussahe.

"The rice field is abundant, O Kosiya, but parrots are eating it. I report this to you, O Brahmin; I am unable to restrain them."

2.

2.

“Eko ca tattha sakuṇo, yo nesaṃ sabbasundaro;

Bhutvā sāliṃ yathākāmaṃ, tuṇḍenādāya gacchatī”ti.

"And there is one bird there, the most beautiful of them all; having eaten rice as it pleases, it takes more in its beak and departs."

Tattha sampannanti paripuṇṇaṃ avekallaṃ. Sālikedāranti sālikhettaṃ. Sabbasundaroti sabbehi koṭṭhāsehi sundaro rattatuṇḍo jiñjukasannibhaakkhi rattapādo tīhi rattarājīhi parikkhittagīvo mahāmayūrapamāṇo so yāvadatthaṃ sāliṃ khāditvā aññaṃ tuṇḍena gahetvā gacchatīti.

In those verses, 'abundant' means complete and without deficiency. 'Rice field' refers to the field of rice. 'Most beautiful of all' means beautiful in every aspect: with a red beak, eyes like the jiñjuka seed, red feet, a neck encircled by three red stripes, and the size of a great peacock. Having eaten his fill of rice, he takes more with his beak and departs.

Brāhmaṇo [M 4.0278] tassa kathaṃ sutvā suvarāje sinehaṃ uppādetvā khettapālaṃ pucchi “ambho purisa, pāsaṃ oḍḍetuṃ jānāsī”ti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. Atha naṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

The brahmin, having heard the man's words and developing affection for the parrot king, asked the field-keeper, "My good man, do you know how to set a snare?" "Yes, I know," he replied. Then the brahmin addressed him in verse:

3.

3.

“Oḍḍentu vālapāsāni, yathā bajjhetha so dijo;

Jīvañca naṃ gahetvāna, ānayehi mamantike”ti.

"Set the snares of hair, so that that bird might be caught; seize it alive and bring it into my presence."

Tattha [V 4.0248] oḍḍentūti oḍḍayantu. Vālapāsānīti assavālādirajjumayapāsāni. Jīvañca nanti jīvantaṃ eva naṃ. Ānayehīti ānehi.

In that verse, 'oḍḍentū' means let them set. 'Vālapāsāni' means snares made of ropes of horsehair and such. 'Jīvañca naṃ' means him alive indeed. 'Ānayehi' means bring.

Taṃ sutvā khettapālo sāliṃ agghāpetvā iṇassa akatabhāvena tuṭṭho gantvā assavāle vaṭṭetvā “ajja imasmiṃ ṭhāne otarissatī”ti suvarañño otaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā punadivase pātova cāṭipamāṇaṃ pañjaraṃ katvā pāsañca oḍḍetvā suvānaṃ āgamanaṃ olokento kuṭiyaṃ nisīdi. Suvarājāpi suvagaṇaparivuto āgantvā aloluppacāratāya hiyyo khāditaṭṭhāne [P 4.0279] oḍḍitapāse pādaṃ pavesantova otari. So attano baddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā cintesi “sacāhaṃ idāneva baddharavaṃ ravissāmi, ñātakāme bhayatajjitā gocaraṃ aggahetvāva palāyissanti, yāva etesaṃ gocaraggahaṇaṃ, tāva adhivāsessāmī”ti. So tesaṃ suhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā maraṇabhayatajjito hutvā tikkhattuṃ baddharavaṃ ravi. Atha sabbe te suvā palāyiṃsu. Suvarājā “ettakesu me ñātakesu nivattitvā olokento ekopi natthi, kiṃ nu kho mayā pāpaṃ kata”nti vilapanto gāthamāha –
