Hearing that, the field guard, being pleased because the debt would not be charged against him by valuing the rice, went and twisted horsehair into snares. Marking the spot where the parrot king would land, thinking, "Today he will descend here," early the next day he made a hollow the size of a large jar, set the snare, and sat in the hut watching for the parrots' arrival. The parrot king, surrounded by his flock, arrived and, because he was not greedy in his conduct, descended at the very spot where he had eaten the day before, placing his foot right into the set snare. Realizing he was trapped, he thought, "If I let out the cry of the captured now, my relatives, terrified by the fear of death, will flee without gathering their food. I will endure until they have gathered their fill." Knowing they were satisfied, and though stricken by the fear of death, he let out the cry of the captured three times. Then all those parrots fled. The parrot king lamented, "Among all these relatives of mine, not one has turned back to look. What evil have I done?" and spoke this verse:

4.

4.

“Ete bhutvā pivitvā ca, pakkamanti vihaṅgamā;

Eko baddhosmi pāsena, kiṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā”ti.

"Having eaten and drunk, these birds fly away; I alone am bound by the snare—what evil have I done?"

Khettapālo suvarājassa baddharavaṃ suvānañca ākāse pakkhandanasaddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ nu kho”ti kuṭiyā oruyha pāsāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā suvarājānaṃ disvā “yasseva me pāso oḍḍito, sveva baddho”ti tuṭṭhamānaso suvarājānaṃ pāsato mocetvā dve pāde ekato bandhitvā daḷhaṃ ādāya sāliddiyagāmaṃ [M 4.0279] gantvā suvarājaṃ brāhmaṇassa adāsi. Brāhmaṇo balavasinehena mahāsattaṃ ubhohi hatthehi daḷhaṃ gahetvā aṅke nisīdāpetvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The field-guard, hearing the cry of distress of the parrot king and the sound of the other parrots taking flight into the sky, thought, "What is this?" Descending from his hut, he went to the location of the snare. Seeing the parrot king, he joyfully thought, "The very one for whom my snare was set is now caught!" Freeing the parrot king from the snare, he tightly bound his two feet together and, taking him firmly, went to the village of Sāliddiya. There, he gave the parrot king to the brahmin. The brahmin, with strong affection, firmly grasped the Great Being with both hands, seated him on his lap, and while conversing with him, spoke these two verses:

5.

5.

“Udaraṃ nūna aññesaṃ, suva accodaraṃ tava;

Bhutvā sāliṃ yathākāmaṃ, tuṇḍenādāya gacchasi.

"Surely the bellies of others are ordinary, but yours, O parrot, is an excessive belly. Having eaten rice as you please, you take some with your beak and go."

6.

6.

“Koṭṭhaṃ nu tattha pūresi, suva veraṃ nu te mayā;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kuhiṃ sāliṃ nidāhasī”ti.

"Do you fill a granary there, O parrot, or is there enmity between you and me? Asked by me, dear friend, explain, where do you deposit the rice?"

Tattha [V 4.0249] udaraṃ nūnāti aññesaṃ udaraṃ udarameva maññe, tava udaraṃ pana atiudaraṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ simbalivane. Pūresīti vassārattatthāya pūresi. Nidāhasīti nidhānaṃ katvā ṭhapesi, “nidhīyasī”tipi pāṭho.

Here, 'udaraṃ nūnāti' means, 'I suppose others' bellies are just bellies, but your belly is an excessive belly.' 'Tatthāti' means 'in that silk-cotton tree forest.' 'Pūresīti' means 'you filled it for the purpose of the rainy season.' 'Nidāhasīti' means 'you placed it after making a deposit'; there is also a variant reading 'nidhīyasīti'.

Taṃ sutvā suvarājā madhurāya manussabhāsāya sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the parrot king spoke the seventh verse in a sweet human voice:

7.

7.

“Na [P 4.0280] me veraṃ tayā saddhiṃ, koṭṭho mayhaṃ na vijjati;

Iṇaṃ muñcāmiṇaṃ dammi, sampatto koṭasimbaliṃ;

Nidhimpi tattha nidahāmi, evaṃ jānāhi kosiyā”ti.

"There is no enmity between me and you; I have no granary. I release a debt, I give a loan, having reached the Koṭasimbali tree. There I also deposit a treasure; know this, O Kosiya."

Tattha iṇaṃ muñcāmiṇaṃ dammīti tava sāliṃ haritvā iṇaṃ muñcāmi ceva dammi cāti vadati. Nidhimpīti ekaṃ tattha simbalivane anugāmikanidhimpi nidahāmi.

Here, regarding 'I release a debt, I give a loan,' he says, 'Taking your rice, I both release a debt and give a loan.' Regarding 'I also deposit a treasure,' it means, 'There, in the silk-cotton grove, I also deposit a treasure that follows one.'

Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo pucchi –

Then the brahmin asked him:

8.

8.

“Kīdisaṃ te iṇadānaṃ, iṇamokkho ca kīdiso;

Nidhinidhānamakkhāhi, atha pāsā pamokkhasī”ti.

"What kind of giving of loans is yours, and what kind of release from debt? Explain the depositing of treasure; then you will be released from the snare."

Tattha iṇadānanti iṇassa dānaṃ. Nidhinidhānanti nidhino nidhānaṃ.

Here, 'iṇadānanti' means the giving of a loan. 'Nidhinidhānamakkhāhi' means the depositing of treasure.

Evaṃ brāhmaṇena puṭṭho suvarājā tassa byākaronto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus questioned by the brahmin, the parrot king, answering him, spoke four verses:

9.

9.

“Ajātapakkhā taruṇā, puttakā mayha kosiya;

Te maṃ bhatā bharissanti, tasmā tesaṃ iṇaṃ dade.

"Unfledged and young are my sons, O Kosiya; they, having been supported, will support me, therefore I give them a loan."

10.

10.

“Mātā pitā ca me vuddhā, jiṇṇakā gatayobbanā;

Tesaṃ tuṇḍena hātūna, muñce pubbakataṃ iṇaṃ.

"My mother and father are old, aged, and past their youth; having carried food for them with my beak, I release the debt formerly made."

11.

11.

“Aññepi [V 4.0250][M 4.0280] tattha sakuṇā, khīṇapakkhā sudubbalā;

Tesaṃ puññatthiko dammi, taṃ nidhiṃ āhu paṇḍitā.

"Other birds are also there, with worn-out wings, very weak; to them, seeking merit, I give; the wise call that a treasure."

12.

12.

“Īdisaṃ me iṇadānaṃ, iṇamokkho ca īdiso;

Nidhinidhānamakkhāmi, evaṃ jānāhi kosiyā”ti.

"Such is my giving of loans, and such is my release from debt; I explain the depositing of treasure; understand this, O Kosiya."

Tattha hātūnāti haritvā. Taṃ nidhinti taṃ puññakammaṃ paṇḍitā anugāmikanidhiṃ nāma kathenti. Nidhinidhānanti nidhino nidhānaṃ, “nidhānanidhi”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho.

Here, 'hātūnāti' means 'having carried.' Regarding 'taṃ nidhiṃ,' the wise call that meritorious deed a treasure that follows one. 'Nidhinidhānanti' means 'the depositing of treasure'; there is also the reading 'nidhānanidhi'—the meaning is the same.

Brāhmaṇo mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasannacitto dve gāthā abhāsi.

The brahmin, having heard the Great Being's discourse on the Dhamma, with a pleased mind, spoke two verses:

13.

13.

“Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Ekaccesu manussesu, ayaṃ dhammo na vijjati.

"Excellent indeed is this bird, a twice-born one of the highest righteousness! This quality is not found among some humans."

14.

14.

“Bhuñja [P 4.0281] sāliṃ yathākāmaṃ, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Punāpi suva passemu, piyaṃ me tava dassana”nti.

"Eat rice as you please, together with all your relatives; may we see you again, O parrot; your sight is dear to me."

Tattha bhuñja sālinti ito paṭṭhāya nibbhayo hutvā bhuñjāti karīsasahassampi tasseva niyyādento evamāha. Passemūti attano ruciyā āgataṃ aññesupi divasesu taṃ passeyyāmāti.

Here, regarding 'eat the rice,' it means, 'From now on, being fearless, eat,' thus he spoke while assigning even a thousand karīsa of land to him. Regarding 'may we see,' it means, 'may we see him again on other days, when he comes according to his liking.'

Evaṃ brāhmaṇo mahāsattaṃ yācitvā piyaputtaṃ viya muducittena olokento pādato bandhanaṃ mocetvā satapākatelena pāde makkhetvā bhaddapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā kañcanataṭṭake madhulāje khādāpetvā sakkharodakaṃ pāyesi. Athassa suvarājā “appamatto hohi, brāhmaṇā”ti vatvā ovādaṃ dento āha –

Thus, having requested the Great Being, the brahmin, gazing at him with a tender heart as if toward a beloved son, released the bonds from his feet, anointed his feet with hundredfold-refined oil, seated him on a fine seat, fed him honeyed roasted grain from a golden platter, and gave him sugar-water to drink. Then the parrot king, saying, 'Be heedful, O brahmin,' and giving advice, spoke:

15.

15.

“Bhuttañca pītañca tavassamamhi, ratī ca no kosiya te sakāse;

Nikkhittadaṇḍesu dadāhi dānaṃ, jiṇṇe ca mātāpitaro bharassū”ti.

"I have eaten and drunk in your hermitage, and delight was ours in your presence, O Kosiya. Give alms to those who have laid down the rod, and support your aged mother and father."

Tattha tavassamamhīti tava nivesane. Ratīti abhirati.

Here, 'in your hermitage' means in your dwelling. 'Delight' means joy.

Taṃ [V 4.0251][M 4.0281] sutvā brāhmaṇo tuṭṭhamānaso udānaṃ udānento gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the brahmin, with a joyful mind, uttered an inspired utterance in verse:

16.

16.

“Lakkhī vata me udapādi ajja, yo addasāsiṃ pavaraṃ dijānaṃ;

Suvassa sutvāna subhāsitāni, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

"Today, truly good fortune has arisen for me, for I have seen the noblest of the twice-born. Having heard the well-spoken words of the parrot, I will perform abundant meritorious deeds."

Tattha lakkhīti sirīpi puññampi paññāpi.

Here, 'lakkhīti' means glory, merit, and wisdom.

Mahāsatto brāhmaṇena attano dinnaṃ karīsasahassamattaṃ paṭikkhipitvā aṭṭhakarīsameva gaṇhi. Brāhmaṇo thambhe nikhanitvā tassa khettaṃ niyyādetvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā khamāpetvā “gaccha sāmi, assumukhe rodamāne mātāpitaro assāsehī”ti vatvā taṃ uyyojesi. So tuṭṭhamānaso sālisīsaṃ ādāya gantvā mātāpitūnaṃ purato nikkhipitvā “ammatātā, uṭṭhethā”ti āha. Te assumukhā rodamānā uṭṭhahiṃsu, tāvadeva suvagaṇā [P 4.0282] sannipatitvā “kathaṃ muttosi, devā”ti pucchiṃsu. So tesaṃ sabbaṃ vitthārato kathesi. Kosiyopi suvarañño ovādaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ mahādānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā osānagāthamāha –

The Great Being, refusing the thousand karisas of land offered by the brahmin, accepted only eight karisas. The brahmin, having buried the boundary posts and assigned the field to him, honored him with perfumes and garlands, and begged forgiveness, saying, "Go, lord, console your weeping parents." Thus he sent him off. The Great Being, with a joyful heart, took a head of rice and went, placing it before his parents, and said, "Mother, father, arise!" They rose, their faces wet with tears, and immediately the flock of parrots gathered and asked, "How were you freed, lord?" He explained everything in detail to them. Kosiya, hearing the advice of the parrot king, thereafter established great alms for righteous ascetics and brahmins. To illustrate this matter, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:

17.

17.

“So kosiyo attamano udaggo, annañca pānañcabhisaṅkharitvā;

Annena pānena pasannacitto, santappayi samaṇabrāhmaṇe cā”ti.

"Thus Kosiya, pleased and uplifted, having prepared food and drink, with a gladdened heart satisfied ascetics and brahmins with food and drink."

Tattha santappayīti gahitagahitāni bhājanāni pūrento santappesīti.

Here, 'santappayīti' means he satisfied them by filling the vessels as they were taken up.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhu mātāpitūnaṃ posanaṃ nāma paṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā suvagaṇā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, khettapālo channo, brāhmaṇo ānando, suvarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, supporting one's parents is the tradition of the wise." He revealed the Truths and then connected the Jātaka. At the end of the exposition of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the flock of parrots was the Buddha's assembly, the parents were the great royal family, the field-guardian was Channa, the brahmin was Ānanda, but the parrot king was indeed myself.

Sālikedārajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The commentary on the Sālikedāra Jātaka, the first.

[485] 2. Candakinnarījātakavaṇṇanā

[485] 2. The Commentary on the Candakinnarī Jātaka

Upanīyatidaṃ [V 4.0252][M 4.0282] maññeti idaṃ satthā kapilavatthupuraṃ upanissāya nigrodhārāme viharanto rājanivesane rāhulamātaraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Idaṃ pana jātakaṃ dūrenidānato paṭṭhāya kathetabbaṃ. Sā panesā nidānakathā yāva laṭṭhivane uruvelakassapasīhanādā apaṇṇakajātake kathitā, tato paraṃ yāva kapilavatthugamanā vessantarajātake āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana pitu nivesane nisīditvā antarabhattasamaye mahādhammapālajātakaṃ (jā. 1.10.92 ādayo) kathetvā katabhattakicco “rāhulamātu nivesane nisīditvā tassā guṇaṃ vaṇṇento candakinnarījātakaṃ (jā. 1.14.18 ādayo) kathessāmī”ti rājānaṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā dvīhi aggasāvakehi saddhiṃ rāhulamātu nivesanaṭṭhānaṃ pāyāsi. Tadā tassā sammukhā cattālīsasahassanāṭakitthiyo vasanti tāsu khattiyakaññānaṃyeva navutiadhikasahassaṃ. Sā tathāgatassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā “sabbā kāsāvāneva nivāsentū”ti tāsaṃ ārocāpesi. Tā tathā kariṃsu. Satthā āgantvā paññattāsane [P 4.0283] nisīdi. Atha tā sabbāpi ekappahāreneva viraviṃsu, mahāparidevasaddo ahosi. Rāhulamātāpi paridevitvā sokaṃ vinodetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā rājagatena bahumānena sagāravena nisīdi. Rājā tassā guṇakathaṃ ārabhi, “bhante, mama suṇhā ‘tumhehi kāsāvāni nivatthānī’ti sutvā kāsāvāneva nivāsesi, ‘mālādīni pariccattānī’ti sutvā mālādīni pariccaji, ‘bhūmiyaṃ sayatī’ti sutvā bhūmisayanāva jātā, tumhākaṃ pabbajitakāle vidhavā hutvā aññehi rājūhi pesitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ na gaṇhi, evaṃ tumhesu asaṃhīracittā esā”ti nānappakārehi tassā guṇakathaṃ kathesi. Satthā “anacchariyaṃ, mahārāja, yaṃ esā idāni mama pacchime attabhāve mayi sasinehā asaṃhīracittā anaññaneyyā bhaveyya. Esā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattāpi mayi asaṃhīracittā anaññaneyyā ahosī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling near the city of Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Grove, told this story concerning Rāhula’s mother in the royal palace, beginning with the words, 'This is drawing near, I think.' This Jātaka should be told starting from the distant introduction. That introductory story, up to the lion's roar of Uruvela Kassapa in the Laṭṭhivana forest, has been told in the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka. From there onward, up to the journey to Kapilavatthu, it will become manifest in the Vessantara Jātaka. The Teacher, having seated himself in his father’s palace and, during the interval of the meal, recounted the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka; after finishing his meal, he thought, 'I will sit in Rāhula’s mother’s dwelling and, while praising her virtues, tell the Candakinnarī Jātaka.' Having had the king take his bowl, he set out for Rāhula’s mother’s residence with his two chief disciples. At that time, forty thousand court ladies lived in her presence, among whom there were one thousand and ninety princesses. Knowing of the Tathāgata’s arrival, she had it announced to them, 'Let all of you wear only ochre robes.' They did so. The Teacher arrived and sat on the prepared seat. Then, all of them cried out at once, and a great sound of lamentation arose. Rāhula’s mother also lamented, but then dispelled her sorrow, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down with great reverence and respect in a manner befitting royalty. The king began to speak of her virtues: 'Venerable sir, my daughter-in-law, upon hearing that you wear ochre robes, wore only ochre robes; upon hearing that you have given up garlands and the like, she gave them up; upon hearing that you sleep on the ground, she has taken to sleeping on the ground. When you went forth, she became a widow, yet she did not accept the gifts sent by other kings. Thus, her mind was unwavering toward you.' In many ways, he praised her virtues. The Teacher replied, 'It is no surprise, great king, that now, in my final existence, she should be devoted to me, with an unwavering mind and not to be led by another. Even when reborn in the animal realm, she had an unwavering mind toward me and was not to be led by another.' Being thus entreated by the king, he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte [M 4.0283] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente mahāsatto himavantapadese kinnarayoniyaṃ nibbatti, candā nāmassa bhariyā. Te ubhopi candanāmake rajatapabbate vasiṃsu. Tadā bārāṇasirājā amaccānaṃ rajjaṃ niyyādetvā dve kāsāyāni nivāsetvā sannaddhapañcāvudho ekakova himavantaṃ pāvisi. So migamaṃsaṃ khādanto ekaṃ khuddakanadiṃ anusañcaranto uddhaṃ abhiruhi. Candapabbatavāsino kinnarā vassārattasamaye anotaritvā pabbateyeva vasanti, nidāghasamaye otaranti. Tadā ca so candakinnaro attano bhariyāya saddhiṃ otaritvā tesu tesu ṭhānesu gandhe vilimpanto pupphareṇuṃ khādanto pupphapaṭe nivāsento pārupanto latādolāhi kīḷanto [V 4.0253] madhurassarena gāyanto taṃ khuddakanadiṃ patvā ekasmiṃ nivattanaṭṭhāne otaritvā udake pupphāni vikiritvā udakakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā pupphapaṭe nivāsetvā pārupitvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇāya vālukāya pupphāsanaṃ paññapetvā ekaṃ veḷu daṇḍakaṃ gahetvā sayane nisīdi[P 4.0284]. Tato candakinnaro veḷuṃ vādento madhurasaddena gāyi. Candakinnarī muduhatthe nāmetvā tassa avidūre ṭhitā nacci ceva gāyi ca. So rājā tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā padasaddaṃ asāvento saṇikaṃ gantvā paṭicchanne ṭhatvā te kinnare disvā kinnariyā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā “taṃ kinnaraṃ vijjhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā imāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappessāmī”ti ṭhatvā candakinnaraṃ vijjhi. So vedanāppatto paridevamāno catasso gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the kinnara realm in the Himalayan region; his wife was named Candā. Both of them lived on the Silver Mountain named Canda. At that time, the king of Benares, having handed over the kingdom to his ministers, donned two saffron robes, armed himself with the five weapons, and entered the Himalayas alone. Eating the flesh of wild game and wandering along a small river, he went upstream. The kinnaras dwelling on Mount Canda do not descend during the rainy season but remain on the mountain; they descend during the hot season. At that time, that Candakinnara descended with his wife Candā. Anointing themselves with perfumes in various places, eating flower pollen, wearing and cloaking themselves in garments of flowers, playing on swings of vines and such, and singing with sweet voices, they reached that small river. Descending at a bend in the river, they scattered flowers in the water and played water games. Then, having dressed and cloaked themselves in garments of flowers, they prepared a flower-seat on the sand which had the color of a silver plate, took a bamboo flute, and sat upon that seat. Then the Candakinnara played the flute and sang with a sweet voice. The kinnarī Candā, gesturing with her gentle hands, stood nearby and both danced and sang. Hearing their sounds, the king, making no sound with his feet, went slowly and stood in a hidden place. Seeing the kinnaras, he became infatuated with the kinnarī and thought, 'I will shoot that male kinnara, bring his life to an end, and live with this female kinnarī.' Standing firm, he shot the Candakinnara. Stricken with pain, he lamented and uttered four verses:

18.

18.

“Upanīyatidaṃ maññe, cande lohitamaddane;

Ajja jahāmi jīvitaṃ, pāṇā me cande nirujjhanti.

"'This is drawing near, I think, O Candā, smeared with blood; today I forsake my life. My life-breaths are ceasing, O Candā.'"

19.

19.

“Osīdi me dukkhaṃ hadayaṃ, me ḍayhate nitammāmi;

Tava candiyā socantiyā, na naṃ aññehi sokehi.

"'My heart sinks with sorrow, it burns within me, I am greatly exhausted; because of your grieving, O Candiyā, and not through other griefs.'"

20.

20.

“Tiṇamiva vanamiva milāyāmi, nadī aparipuṇṇāva sussāmi;

Tava candiyā socantiyā, na naṃ aññehi sokehi.

"'Like grass, like a forest, I wither; like a river not yet full, I dry up; because of your grieving, O Candiyā, and not by other sorrows.'"

21.

21.

“Vassamiva sare pāde, imāni assūni vattare mayhaṃ;

Tava candiyā socantiyā, na naṃ aññehi sokehī”ti.

"'Like rain at the foot of a mountain, these tears of mine flow; because of your grieving, O Candiyā, and not by other sorrows.'"

Tattha [M 4.0284] upanīyatīti santativicchedaṃ upanīyati. Idanti jīvitaṃ. Pāṇā meti bhadde, cande mama jīvitapāṇā nirujjhanti. Osīdi meti jīvitaṃ me osīdati. Nitammāmīti atikilamāmi. Tava candiyāti idaṃ mama dukkhaṃ, na naṃ aññehi sokehi, atha kho tava candiyā socantiyā sokahetu yasmā tvaṃ mama viyogena socissasi, tasmāti attho. Tiṇamiva vanamiva milāyāmīti tattapāsāṇe khittatiṇamiva mūlachinnavanamiva milāyāmīti vadati. Sare pādeti yathā nāma pabbatapāde patitavassaṃ saritvā acchinnadhāraṃ vattati.

In those verses, 'upanīyatī' means it brings near the breaking of the continuity of life. 'Idaṃ' means life. 'Pāṇā me ti' means 'O dear Candā, my life-breaths are ceasing.' 'Osīdi me ti' means 'My life is sinking.' 'Nitammāmīti' means 'I am greatly exhausted.' 'Tava candiyā ti' means 'This suffering of mine is not from other sorrows, but rather the cause of sorrow is your grieving, Candā; because you will grieve due to separation from me.' 'Tiṇamiva vanamiva milāyāmīti': 'Like grass thrown on a heated stone, or like a forest cut at the root, I wither away,' so he speaks. 'Sare pādeti' means just as rain fallen at the foot of a mountain flows on in an unbroken stream.

Mahāsatto imāhi catūhi gāthāhi paridevitvā pupphasayane nipannova satiṃ vissajjetvā parivatti. Rājā patiṭṭhitova. Itarā mahāsatte paridevante attano ratiyā mattā hutvā tassa [P 4.0285] viddhabhāvaṃ [V 4.0254] na jānāti, visaññaṃ pana naṃ parivattitvā nipannaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho me piyasāmikassa dukkha”nti upadhārentī pahāramukhato paggharantaṃ lohitaṃ disvā piyasāmike uppannaṃ balavasokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontī mahāsaddena paridevi. Rājā “kinnaro mato bhavissatī”ti nikkhamitvā attānaṃ dassesi. Candā taṃ disvā “iminā me corena piyasāmiko viddho bhavissatī”ti kampamānā palāyitvā pabbatamatthake ṭhatvā rājānaṃ paribhāsantī pañca gāthā abhāsi –

The Great Being, having lamented with these four verses, lay down on the flower bed and, losing consciousness, rolled about. The king stood right there. The other kinnarī, while the Great Being was lamenting, being intoxicated with her own delight, did not know of his being wounded. But seeing him turned over and lying there unconscious, she wondered, 'What could be the suffering of my dear husband?' Seeing blood flowing from the wound, unable to bear the intense sorrow that arose for her dear husband, she wailed loudly. The king, thinking, 'The kinnara must be dead,' came out and revealed himself. Seeing him, Candā, trembling, thought, 'By this thief my dear husband must have been wounded!' Fleeing, she stood on the mountain peak and, rebuking the king, spoke five verses:

22.

22.

“Pāpo khosi rājaputta, yo me icchitaṃ patiṃ varākiyā;

Vijjhasi vanamūlasmiṃ, soyaṃ viddho chamā seti.

"Evil indeed are you, O prince, who at the foot of the forest shoots my desired husband, making me a wretched widow; he, pierced, now lies on the ground.

23.

23.

“Imaṃ mayhaṃ hadayasokaṃ, paṭimuñcatu rājaputta tava mātā;

Yo mayhaṃ hadayasoko, kimpurisaṃ avekkhamānāya.

"May your mother, O prince, experience this sorrow of my heart; this sorrow in my heart, as I gaze upon the kimpurisa.

24.

24.

“Imaṃ mayhaṃ hadayasokaṃ, paṭimuñcatu rājaputta tava jāyā;

Yo mayhaṃ hadayasoko, kimpurisaṃ avekkhamānāya.

"May your wife, O prince, experience this sorrow of my heart; this sorrow in my heart as I gaze upon the kimpurisa.

25.

25.

“Mā ca puttaṃ mā ca patiṃ, addakkhi rājaputta tava mātā;

Yo kimpurisaṃ avadhi, adūsakaṃ mayha kāmā hi.

"May your mother, O prince, not see her son nor her husband, you who killed the innocent kimpurisa because of your desire for me.

26.

26.

“Mā ca puttaṃ mā ca patiṃ, addakkhi rājaputta tava jāyā;

Yo kimpurisaṃ avadhi, adūsakaṃ mayha kāmā hī”ti.

"May your wife, O prince, not see her son nor her husband, you who killed the innocent kimpurisa because of your desire for me."

Tattha [M 4.0285] varākiyāti kapaṇāya. Paṭimuñcatūti paṭilabhatu phusatu pāpuṇātu. Mayha kāmā hīti mayhaṃ kāmena.

Herein, 'varākiyā' means 'of a wretched one' or 'to make me a widow.' 'Paṭimuñcatu' means may she obtain, experience, or attain. 'Mayha kāmā hi' means 'because of desire for me.'

Rājā naṃ pañcahi gāthāhi paribhāsitvā pabbatamatthake ṭhitaṃyeva assāsento gāthamāha –

The king, having been rebuked by her with five verses, comforted her as she stood on the mountain peak, speaking this verse:

27.

27.

“Mā tvaṃ cande rodi mā sopi, vanatimiramattakkhi;

Mama tvaṃ hehisi bhariyā, rājakule pūjitā nārībhī”ti.

"Do not weep, O Candā, do not grieve, O you with eyes as dark as the forest blossom; you shall be my wife, honored among women in the royal household."

Tattha [V 4.0255][P 4.0286] candeti mahāsattassa paridevanakāle nāmassa sutattā evamāha. Vanatimiramattakkhīti vanatimirapupphasamānaakkhi. Pūjitā nārībhīti soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhikā aggamahesī hessasi.

Herein, 'Candā' is used because her name was heard during the Great Being's lamentation; thus he spoke. 'Vanatimiramattakkhī' means 'having eyes like the dark forest flower.' 'Pūjitā nārībhī' means 'you will be the chief queen among sixteen thousand women.'

Candā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “tvaṃ kiṃ maṃ vadesī”ti sīhanādaṃ nadantī anantaragāthamāha –

Hearing his words, Candā, roaring a lion's roar, said, "What are you saying to me?" and immediately uttered the following verse:

28.

28.

“Api nūnahaṃ marissaṃ, nāhaṃ rājaputta tava hessaṃ;

Yo kimpurisaṃ avadhi, adūsakaṃ mayha kāmā hī”ti.

"Surely I would rather die; I shall not be yours, O prince, you who killed the innocent kimpurisa because of your desire for me."

Tattha api nūnahanti api ekaṃseneva ahaṃ marissaṃ.

Herein, 'api nūnahaṃ' means 'surely I will die.'

So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā nicchandarāgo hutvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard her words, he became free from desire and passion, and then spoke this other verse:

29.

29.

“Api bhīruke api jīvitukāmike, kimpurisi gaccha himavantaṃ;

Tālīsatagarabhojanā, aññe taṃ migā ramissantī”ti.

"O timid one, O you who wish to live, O Kimpurisī, go to the Himālaya! You who feed on tālīsa and tagara leaves, other beasts will delight in you."

Tattha api bhīruketi bhīrujātike. Tālīsatagarabhojanāti tvaṃ tālīsapattatagarapattabhojanā migī, tasmā aññe taṃ migā ramissanti, na tvaṃ rājakulārahā, gacchāti naṃ avaca, vatvā ca pana nirapekkho hutvā pakkāmi.

Herein, 'O timid one' means 'O you of a timid nature.' 'You who feed on tālīsa and tagara' means, 'You are a female beast who feeds on the leaves of the tālīsa and tagara. Therefore, other beasts will delight in you; you are not worthy of the royal household. Go!' Thus he spoke to her, and having spoken, he departed without concern.

Sā tassa gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā oruyha mahāsattaṃ āliṅgitvā pabbatamatthakaṃ āropetvā pabbatatale nipajjāpetvā sīsamassa attano ūrūsu katvā balavaparidevaṃ paridevamānā dvādasa gāthā abhāsi –

Knowing he had departed, she descended, embraced the Great Being, carried him up to the mountain peak, laid him down on the mountain plateau, placed his head on her thighs, and weeping with great lamentation, she spoke these twelve verses:

30.

30.

“Te [M 4.0286] pabbatā tā ca kandarā, tā ca giriguhāyo tatheva tiṭṭhanti;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"Those mountains and those ravines, those mountain caves remain just as they were; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

31.

31.

“Te paṇṇasanthatā ramaṇīyā, vāḷamigehi anuciṇṇā;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"Those delightful leaf-beds, frequented by wild beasts; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

32.

32.

“Te [V 4.0256] pupphasanthatā ramaṇīyā, vāḷamigehi anuciṇṇā;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"Those delightful flower-beds, frequented by wild beasts; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

33.

33.

“Acchā [P 4.0287] savanti girivananadiyo, kusumābhikiṇṇasotāyo;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"Clear flow the mountain forest rivers, their streams strewn with flowers; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

34.

34.

“Nīlāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, sapphire-blue and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

35.

35.

“Pītāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, golden-yellow and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

36.

36.

“Tambāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, copper-red and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

37.

37.

“Tuṅgāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, lofty and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

38.

38.

“Setāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, silver-white and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

39.

39.

“Citrāni himavato pabbatassa, kūṭāni dassanīyāni;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"The peaks of the Himālaya mountain, variegated with jewels and delightful to behold; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

40.

40.

“Yakkhagaṇasevite gandhamādane, osadhebhi sañchanne;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassaṃ.

"In Gandhamādana, frequented by hosts of spirits, overgrown with medicinal herbs; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?

41.

41.

“Kimpurisasevite [M 4.0287] gandhamādane, osadhebhi sañchanne;

Tattheva taṃ apassantī, kimpurisa kathaṃ ahaṃ kassa”nti.

"In Gandhamādana, frequented by kimpurisas, overgrown with medicinal herbs; not seeing you there, O Kimpurisa, what shall I do?"

Tattha [V 4.0257] te pabbatāti yesu mayaṃ ekatova abhiramimha, ime te pabbatā tā ca kandarā tā ca giriguhāyo tatheva ṭhitā. Tesu ahaṃ idāni taṃ apassantī kathaṃ kassaṃ, kiṃ karissāmi, tesu pupphaphalapallavādisobhaṃ taṃ apassantī kathaṃ adhivāsetuṃ sakkhissāmīti paridevati. Paṇṇasanthatāti tālīsapattādigandhapaṇṇasantharā. Acchāti vippasannodakā. Nīlānīti nīlamaṇimayāni. Pītānīti sovaṇṇamayāni. Tambānīti manosilamayāni. Tuṅgānīti uccāni tikhiṇaggāni. Setānīti rajatamayāni. Citrānīti sattaratanamissakāni. Yakkhagaṇaseviteti bhummadevatāhi sevite.

Here, ‘those mountains’ means: ‘These are those mountains, those ravines, and those mountain caves where we once delighted together, and they remain just as they were. Not seeing you there now, how shall I fare? What shall I do? How can I bear to dwell in them, with their splendor of flowers, fruits, and foliage, while not seeing you?’ Thus she lamented. ‘Leaf-beds’ means beds of fragrant leaves such as those of the tālī palm. ‘Clear’ means with very clear water. ‘Blue’ means made of sapphires. ‘Yellow’ means made of gold. ‘Red’ means made of realgar. ‘Lofty’ means high and sharp-peaked. ‘White’ means made of silver. ‘Variegated’ means mixed with the seven precious gems. ‘Frequented by hosts of yakkhas’ means frequented by earth deities.

Iti sā dvādasahi gāthāhi paridevitvā mahāsattassa ure hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā santāpabhāvaṃ ñatvā “cando jīvatiyeva, devujjhānakammaṃ katvā jīvitamassa dassāmī”ti cintetvā “kiṃ nu kho lokapālā nāma natthi, udāhu vippavutthā, adu matā[P 4.0288], te me piyasāmikaṃ na rakkhantī”ti devujjhānakammaṃ akāsi. Tassā sokavegena sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā brāhmaṇavaṇṇena vegeneva āgantvā kuṇḍikato udakaṃ gahetvā mahāsattaṃ āsiñci. Tāvadeva visaṃ antaradhāyi, vaṇo ruhi, imasmiṃ ṭhāne viddhotipi na paññāyi. Mahāsatto sukhito uṭṭhāsi. Candā piyasāmikaṃ arogaṃ disvā somanassappattā sakkassa pāde vandantī anantaragāthamāha –

Thus, after lamenting with twelve verses, she placed her hand on the Great Being’s chest and, sensing the heat, thought, “Canda still lives! By making a complaint to the deities, I shall restore his life.” Then she thought, “Are there no world protectors, or are they absent, or are they dead, that they do not protect my beloved husband?” She then made a complaint to the deities. Due to the power of her grief, Sakka’s throne grew hot. Sakka, reflecting, understood the reason and swiftly came in the guise of a brahmin. Taking water from his pitcher, he sprinkled it on the Great Being. Instantly, the poison vanished, the wound healed, and not even a trace of having been pierced was visible in that place. The Great Being rose up, well and happy. Seeing her beloved husband healthy, Candā, filled with joy, bowed at Sakka’s feet and spoke the following verse:

42.

42.

“Vande te ayirabrahme, yo me icchitaṃ patiṃ varākiyā;

Amatena abhisiñci, samāgatāsmi piyatamenā”ti.

“I revere you, noble brahmin, who sprinkled my desired husband with the nectar of immortality; I, a wretched woman, am reunited with my dearest one.”

Tattha amatenāti udakaṃ “amata”nti maññamānā evamāha. Piyatamenāti piyatarena, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Here, “with the deathless” means she spoke thus, thinking the water was “the deathless.” “With the dearest” means with the more beloved; or this may be the reading.

Sakko tesaṃ ovādamadāsi “ito paṭṭhāya candapabbatato oruyha manussapathaṃ mā gamittha, idheva vasathā”ti. Evañca pana vatvā te ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva [M 4.0288] gato. Candāpi “kiṃ no sāmi iminā paripanthaṭṭhānena, ehi candapabbatameva gacchāmā”ti vatvā osānagāthamāha –

Sakka gave them this advice: “From now on, do not descend from Mount Canda to the path of humans; dwell right here.” Having thus spoken and advised them, he returned to his own place. Then Candā said, “My lord, what use have we for this dangerous place? Come, let us go back to Mount Canda,” and she spoke the concluding verse:

43.

43.

“Vicarāma dāni girivananadiyo, kusumābhikiṇṇasotāyo;

Nānādumavasanāyo, piyaṃvadā aññamaññassā”ti.

“Now let us wander among the mountains, forests, and rivers, their streams strewn with flowers, and covered with various trees, speaking lovingly to one another.”

Satthā [V 4.0258] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na idāneva, pubbepesā mayi asaṃhīracittā anaññaneyyā evā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā devadatto ahosi, sakko anuruddho, candā rāhulamātā, candakinnaro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, “Not only now, O King, but also in the past, she was unwavering in her heart toward me, and was not to be led away by others.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time, the king was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, Candā was Rāhula’s mother, and the Candakinnara was I myself.”

Candakinnarījātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Candakinnarī Jātaka, the second.

[486] 3. Mahāukkusajātakavaṇṇanā

[486] 3. The Commentary on the Mahāukkusa Jātaka

Ukkā cilācā bandhantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mittabandhakaupāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ parijiṇṇassa kulassa [P 4.0289] putto sahāyaṃ pesetvā aññataraṃ kuladhītaraṃ vārāpetvā “atthi panassa uppannakiccaṃ nittharaṇasamattho mitto vā sahāyo vā”ti vutte “natthī”ti vatvā “tena hi mitte tāva bandhatū”ti vutte tasmiṃ ovāde ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ tāva catūhi dovārikehi saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi, athānupubbena nagaraguttikagaṇakamahāmattādīhi saddhiṃ mettiṃ katvā senāpatināpi uparājenāpi saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi. Tehi pana saddhiṃ ekato hutvā raññā saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi. Tato asītiyā mahātherehi saddhiṃ ānandattherenapi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā tathāgatena saddhiṃ mettiṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ satthā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpesi, rājāpissa issariyamadāsi. So mittabandhakoyevāti pākaṭo jāto. Athassa rājā mahantaṃ gehaṃ datvā āvāhamaṅgalaṃ kāresi. Rājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā mahājano paṇṇākāre pahiṇi. Athassa bhariyā raññā pahitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ uparājassa, uparājena pahitaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ senāpatissāti etena upāyena sakalanagaravāsino ābandhitvā gaṇhi. Sattame divase [M 4.0289] mahāsakkāraṃ katvā dasabalaṃ nimantetvā pañcasatassa buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā bhattakiccāvasāne satthārā kathitaṃ anumodanaṃ sutvā ubhopi jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

“Torches of pine-wood they bind”—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the lay follower Mittabandhaka. It is said that in Sāvatthī, he was the son of a family that had fallen into decay. After sending a friend to ask for the hand of a certain maiden of good family, he was asked, “Does he have any friend or companion capable of helping him if a need arises?” When told “No,” he was advised, “Then let him first make friends.” Abiding by that advice, he first made friends with the four gatekeepers, then gradually with the city guards, accountants, ministers, and so on, and also with the commander-in-chief and the viceroy. Having joined with them, he made friends with the king. Then, after joining with the eighty great elders and also with the Elder Ānanda, he made friends with the Tathāgata. Then the Teacher established him in the refuges and the precepts, and the king gave him authority. He became famous as Mittabandhaka. Then the king gave him a large house and had a wedding ceremony performed. The public, beginning with the king, sent gifts. His wife, by giving the gift sent by the king to the viceroy, and the gift sent by the viceroy to the commander-in-chief, won over all the city residents by this means. On the seventh day, after making a great honor, he invited the One of Ten Powers and gave a great gift to the Sangha of five hundred monks with the Buddha at its head. At the conclusion of the meal, having heard the Teacher’s words of appreciation, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, mittabandhakaupāsako attano bhariyaṃ nissāya tassā vacanaṃ katvā sabbehi mettiṃ katvā rañño santikā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhi, tathāgatena pana saddhiṃ mettiṃ katvā ubhopi jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva so etaṃ mātugāmaṃ nissāya mahantaṃ yasaṃ sampatto, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi panesa etissā vacanena bahūhi saddhiṃ mettiṃ katvā puttasokato muttoyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, the lay follower Mittabandhaka, relying on his wife and following her advice, made friends with everyone and received great honor from the king; and by making friends with the Tathāgata, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.” The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here now?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, it is not only now that he has attained great fame by relying on this woman. Even in the past, when born in the animal realm, by her word he made friends with many and was freed from sorrow for his son.” Having been requested by them, he recounted the past.

Atīte [V 4.0259] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente ekacce paccantavāsino yattha yattha bahuṃ maṃsaṃ labhanti, tattha tattha gāmaṃ nivāsetvā araññe caritvā migādayo māretvā maṃsaṃ āharitvā puttadāre [P 4.0290] posenti. Tesaṃ gāmato avidūre mahājātassaro atthi. Tassa dakkhiṇapasse eko senasakuṇo, pacchimapasse ekā senasakuṇī, uttarapasse sīho migarājā, pācīnapasse ukkusasakuṇarājā vasati. Jātassaramajjhe pana unnataṭṭhāne kacchapo vasati. Tadā seno seniṃ “bhariyā me hohī”ti vadati. Atha naṃ sā āha – “atthi pana te koci mitto”ti? “Natthi bhadde”ti. Amhākaṃ uppannaṃ bhayaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā haraṇasamatthaṃ mittaṃ vā sahāyaṃ vā laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, mitte tāva gaṇhāhīti. “Kehi saddhiṃ mettiṃ karomi bhadde”ti? Pācīnapasse vasantena ukkusarājena, uttarapasse sīhena, jātassaramajjhe kacchapena saddhiṃ mettiṃ karohīti. So tassā vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tathā akāsi. Tadā te ubhopi saṃvāsaṃ kappetvā tasmiṃyeva sare ekasmiṃ dīpake kadambarukkho atthi samantā udakena parikkhitto, tasmiṃ kulāvakaṃ katvā paṭivasiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, some border dwellers would settle in villages wherever they could obtain abundant meat. They would roam the forest, kill deer and other animals, bring back the meat, and support their wives and children. Not far from their village was a great natural lake. On its southern side lived a male hawk, on its western side a female hawk, on its northern side a lion, the king of beasts, and on its eastern side lived the osprey king. In the middle of the lake, on a high spot, lived a turtle. Then the male hawk said to the female hawk, “Be my wife.” She replied, “But do you have any friends?” “No, my dear.” “It is proper for us to have a friend or companion who is capable of removing any danger or suffering that may arise. First, make some friends.” “With whom should I make friends, my dear?” “Make friends with the osprey king living on the eastern side, the lion on the northern side, and the turtle in the middle of the lake.” Accepting her words, he did so. Then the two of them began to live together, and they made a nest on a kadamba tree on an islet in that very lake, which was surrounded by water on all sides, and dwelt there.

Tesaṃ [M 4.0290] aparabhāge dve sakuṇapotakā jāyiṃsu. Tesaṃ pakkhesu asañjātesuyeva ekadivasaṃ te jānapadā divasaṃ araññe caritvā kiñci alabhitvā “na sakkā tucchahatthena gharaṃ gantuṃ, macche vā kacchape vā gaṇhissāmā”ti saraṃ otaritvā taṃ dīpakaṃ gantvā tassa kadambassa mūle nipajjitvā makasādīhi khajjamānā tesaṃ palāpanatthāya araṇiṃ manthetvā aggiṃ nibbattetvā dhūmaṃ kariṃsu. Dhumo uggantvā sakuṇe pahari, sakuṇapotakā viraviṃsu. Jānapadā taṃ sutvā “ambho, sakuṇapotakānaṃ sūyati saddo, uṭṭhetha ukkā bandhatha, chātā sayituṃ na sakkoma, sakuṇamaṃsaṃ khāditvāva sayissāmā”ti vatvā aggiṃ jāletvā ukkā bandhiṃsu. Sakuṇikā tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā “ime amhākaṃ potake khāditukāmā, mayaṃ evarūpassa bhayassa haraṇatthāya mitte gaṇhimha, sāmikaṃ ukkusarājassa santikaṃ pesessāmī”ti cintetvā “gaccha, sāmi[P 4.0291], puttānaṃ no uppannabhayaṃ ukkusarājassa ārocehī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In due course, two young birds were born to them. Before their wings had even grown, one day those country-folk, having wandered in the forest all day without finding anything, thought, 'It is not possible to go home empty-handed; we will catch some fish or turtles.' They descended into the lake, went to that islet, and lay down at the foot of the kadamba tree. Being bitten by mosquitoes and other insects, to drive them away, they twirled a fire-stick, produced a fire, and made smoke. The smoke rose and afflicted the birds, and the young birds cried out. Hearing that, the country-folk said, 'Hey, the sound of young birds can be heard! Get up, prepare torches! We cannot sleep hungry; we will eat the birds' flesh and only then will we sleep.' So saying, they lit a fire and prepared torches. Hearing their noise, the female bird thought, 'These men want to eat our young. We have made friends to dispel such a danger; I will send my husband to the osprey king.' Thinking thus, she said, 'Go, my lord, and inform the osprey king of the danger that has arisen for our children.' Then she spoke the first verse:

44.

44.

“Ukkā cilācā bandhanti dīpe, pajā mamaṃ khādituṃ patthayanti;

Mittaṃ sahāyañca vadehi senaka, ācikkha ñātibyasanaṃ dijāna”nti.

“The country-folk are preparing torches on the islet; they desire to eat my young. O Senaka, speak to our friend and companion; announce the calamity of the birds, our kinsmen.”

Tattha cilācāti jānapadā. Dīpeti dīpakamhi. Pajā mamanti mama puttake. Senakāti senakasakuṇaṃ [V 4.0260] nāmenālapati. Ñātibyasananti puttānaṃ byasanaṃ. Dijānanti amhākaṃ ñātīnaṃ dijānaṃ idaṃ byasanaṃ ukkusarājassa santikaṃ gantvā ācikkhāhīti vadati.

Herein, 'cilācā' means country-folk. 'Dīpe' means on the islet. 'Pajā mamaṃ' means my young. 'Senaka' is how she addresses the hawk by name. 'Ñātibyasanaṃ' means the calamity of the young. 'Dijānaṃ' means she says, 'Go to the osprey king and announce this calamity of our kinsmen, the birds.'

So vegena tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vassitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā katokāso upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “kiṃkāraṇā āgatosī”ti puṭṭho āgatakāraṇaṃ dassento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

He, going quickly to his dwelling place and uttering a call to make his arrival known, having been given an opportunity, approached, paid homage, and when asked, 'For what reason have you come?' he, explaining the reason for his coming, spoke the second verse:

45.

45.

“Dijo dijānaṃ pavarosi pakkhima, ukkusarāja saraṇaṃ taṃ upema;

Pajā mamaṃ khādituṃ patthayanti, luddā cilācā bhava me sukhāyā”ti.

“O bird, you are the best of birds, O winged one, O osprey king, we come to you for refuge. Cruel country-folk desire to eat my young. Be a source of our well-being!”

Tattha dijoti tvaṃ dijo ceva dijānaṃ pavaro ca.

Herein, 'dijo' means you are both a bird and the best among birds.

Ukkusarājā [M 4.0291] “senaka mā bhāyī”ti taṃ assāsetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The osprey king, having reassured him by saying, 'Senaka, do not be afraid,' spoke the third verse:

46.

46.

“Mittaṃ sahāyañca karonti paṇḍitā, kāle akāle sukhamesamānā;

Karomi te senaka etamatthaṃ, ariyo hi ariyassa karoti kicca”nti.

“The wise make friends and companions, seeking happiness in season and out of season. I shall do this for you, Senaka, for a noble one indeed performs the duty for a noble one.”

Tattha kāle akāleti divā ca rattiñca. Ariyoti idha ācāraariyo adhippeto. Ācārasampanno hi ācārasampannassa kiccaṃ karoteva, kimettha karaṇīyanti vadati.

Herein, 'in season and out of season' means by day and by night. By 'noble,' one noble in conduct is intended here. For one accomplished in conduct indeed performs the duty for one accomplished in conduct; what need is there to say what is to be done in this matter?

Atha [P 4.0292] naṃ pucchi “kiṃ, samma, rukkhaṃ abhiruḷhā cilācā”ti? Na tāva abhiruḷhā, ukkāyeva bandhantīti. Tena hi tvaṃ sīghaṃ gantvā mama sahāyikaṃ assāsetvā mamāgamanabhāvaṃ ācikkhāhīti. So tathā akāsi. Ukkusarājāpi gantvā kadambassa avidūre cilācānaṃ abhiruhanaṃ olokento ekasmiṃ rukkhagge nisīditvā ekassa cilācassa abhiruhanakāle tasmiṃ kulāvakassa avidūraṃ abhiruḷhe sare nimujjitvā pakkhehi ca mukhena ca udakaṃ āharitvā ukkāya upari āsiñci, sā nibbāyi. Cilācā “imañca senakasakuṇapotake cassa khādissāmī”ti otaritvā puna ukkaṃ jālāpetvā abhiruhiṃsu. Puna so ukkaṃ vijjhāpesi. Etenupāyena baddhaṃ baddhaṃ vijjhāpentassevassa aḍḍharatto jāto. So ativiya kilami, heṭṭhāudare kilomakaṃ tanutaṃ gataṃ, akkhīni rattāni jātāni. Taṃ disvā sakuṇī sāmikaṃ āha – “sāmi, ativiya kilanto [V 4.0261] ukkusarājā, etassa thokaṃ vissamanatthāya gantvā kacchaparājassa kathehī”ti. So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā ukkusaṃ upasaṅkamitvā gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

Then he asked, 'Friend, have the country-folk climbed the tree?' 'They have not yet climbed; they are only preparing the torches.' 'Then go quickly, reassure my companion, and tell her of my coming.' He did so. The osprey king also went and, observing the climbing of the country-folk from a treetop not far from the kadamba tree, he perched there. When one of the country-folk was climbing and had gotten near the nest, the osprey king dived into the lake, brought water with his wings and beak, and sprinkled it over the torch, and it was extinguished. The country-folk, thinking, 'We will eat these chicks of the hawk,' descended, lit the torch again, and climbed. Again, he caused it to be extinguished. By this method, as he kept extinguishing the torch each time it was prepared, half the night passed. He became extremely weary; the feathers on his lower belly became sparse, and his eyes became red. Seeing this, the female hawk said to her mate, 'My lord, the osprey king is extremely weary. Go and speak to the turtle king so that the osprey may rest for a little while.' Hearing her words, he approached the osprey and addressed him with a verse:

47.

47.

“Yaṃ hoti kiccaṃ anukampakena, ariyassa ariyena kataṃ tayīdaṃ;

Attānurakkhī bhava mā aḍayhi, lacchāma putte tayi jīvamāne”ti.

“Whatever duty is to be done by a compassionate one, that has been done by you, a noble one for a noble one. Protect yourself, do not be consumed; we shall have our young while you are living.”

Tattha tayīdanti tayā idaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Herein, 'tayīdaṃ' means 'by you this,' or that is the reading itself.

So [M 4.0292] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sīhanādaṃ nadanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words and letting out a lion's roar, he spoke the fifth verse:

48.

48.

“Taveva rakkhāvaraṇaṃ karonto, sarīrabhedāpi na santasāmi;

Karonti heke sakhinaṃ sakhāro, pāṇaṃ cajantā satamesa dhammo”ti.

“While providing you protection and shelter, I do not fear even the breaking up of the body. Some friends act for their friend even giving up their own life; this is the nature of the virtuous.”

Chaṭṭhaṃ [P 4.0293] pana satthā abhisambuddho hutvā tassa guṇaṃ vaṇṇento āha –

But the sixth verse the Teacher spoke, having become fully enlightened, in praise of his virtue:

49.

49.

“Sudukkaraṃ kammamakāsi, aṇḍajāyaṃ vihaṅgamo;

Atthāya kuraro putte, aḍḍharatte anāgate”ti.

“A very difficult deed did the osprey, the bird born from an egg, perform for the sake of the young before midnight arrived.”

Tattha kuraroti ukkusarājā. Putteti senakassa putte rakkhanto tesaṃ atthāya aḍḍharatte anāgate yāva diyaḍḍhayāmā vāyāmaṃ karonto dukkaraṃ akāsi.

Herein, 'kuraro' means the osprey king. 'Putte' means: protecting the young of Senaka, for their sake he performed a difficult deed, striving before midnight arrived, for as long as one and a half watches.

Senopi ukkusaṃ “thokaṃ vissamāhi, sammā”ti vatvā kacchapassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ uṭṭhāpetvā “kiṃ, samma, āgatosī”ti vutto “evarūpaṃ nāma bhayaṃ uppannaṃ, ukkusarājā paṭhamayāmato paṭṭhāya vāyamanto kilami, tenamhi tava santikaṃ āgato”ti vatvā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Senaka, having said to the osprey, 'Rest a little, friend,' went to the turtle and roused him. When asked by the turtle, 'Why, friend, have you come?' Senaka replied, 'A danger of this sort has arisen. The osprey king has been striving since the first watch and is exhausted. That is why I have come to you,' and then he spoke the seventh verse:

50.

50.

“Cutāpi heke khalitā sakammunā, mittānukampāya patiṭṭhahanti;

Puttā mamaṭṭā gatimāgatosmi, atthaṃ caretho mama vāricarā”ti.

“Some, though fallen and stumbled by their own doing, are re-established through the compassion of friends. My young are afflicted; I have come to you as a refuge. O water-dweller, act for my benefit!”

Tassattho – sāmi, ekacce hi yasato vā dhanato vā cutāpi sakammunā khalitāpi mittānaṃ [V 4.0262] anukampāya patiṭṭhahanti, mama ca puttā aṭṭā āturā, tenāhaṃ taṃ gatiṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ katvā āgatosmi, puttānaṃ jīvitadānaṃ dadanto atthaṃ me carāhi vāricarāti.

Its meaning is: Lord, some, though fallen from fame or wealth and stumbled by their own doing, are re-established through the compassion of friends. And my young are afflicted and sick; therefore I have come, having made you my refuge and resort. Giving the gift of life to my young, act for my benefit, O water-dweller.

Taṃ sutvā kacchapo itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the turtle spoke another verse:

51.

51.

“Dhanena dhaññena ca attanā ca, mittaṃ sahāyañca karonti paṇḍitā;

Karomi te senaka etamatthaṃ, ariyo hi ariyassa karoti kicca”nti.

“With wealth, with grain, and with themselves, the wise make friends and companions. I shall do this for you, Senaka, for a noble one indeed performs the duty for a noble one.”

Athassa [M 4.0293] putto avidūre nipanno pitu vacanaṃ sutvā “mā me pitā kilamatu, ahaṃ pitu kiccaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then his son, who was lying not far away, heard his father’s words and thought, 'May my father not become weary; I shall perform my father’s duty.' And he spoke the ninth verse:

52.

52.

“Appossukko tāta tuvaṃ nisīda, putto pitu carati atthacariyaṃ;

Ahaṃ [P 4.0294] carissāmi tavetamatthaṃ, senassa putte paritāyamāno”ti.

“Be without care, father, and sit down; a son acts for his father's welfare. I shall carry out this task for you, protecting the young of Senaka.”

Atha naṃ pitā gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

Then his father addressed him with a verse:

53.

53.

“Addhā hi tāta satamesa dhammo, putto pitu yaṃ care atthacariyaṃ;

Appeva maṃ disvāna pavaḍḍhakāyaṃ, senassa puttā na viheṭhayeyyu”nti.

“Truly, dear son, this is the nature of the virtuous: that a son should act for his father's welfare. Perhaps, upon seeing my large body, the country-folk will not harm the young of Senaka.”

Tattha satamesa dhammoti paṇḍitānaṃ esa dhammo. Puttāti senassa putte cilācā na heṭhayeyyunti.

Herein, 'this is the nature of the virtuous' means this is the way of the wise. 'Puttā' refers to the fact that the country-folk would not harm the hawk's young.

Evaṃ vatvā mahākacchapo “samma, mā bhāyi, tvaṃ purato gaccha, idānāhaṃ āgamissāmī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā udake patitvā kalalañca sevālañca saṃkaḍḍhitvā ādāya dīpakaṃ gantvā aggiṃ vijjhāpetvā nipajji. Cilācā “kiṃ no senapotakehi, imaṃ kāḷakacchapaṃ parivattetvā māressāma, ayaṃ no sabbesaṃ pahossatī”ti valliyo uddharitvā jiyā gahetvā nivatthapilotikāpi mocetvā tesu tesu ṭhānesu bandhitvā kacchapaṃ parivattetuṃ na sakkonti. Kacchapo te ākaḍḍhanto gantvā gambhīraṭṭhāne udake pati. Tepi kacchapalobhena saddhiṃyeva patitvā udakapuṇṇāya kucchiyā kilantā nikkhamitvā “bho ekena no ukkusena yāva aḍḍharattā ukkā vijjhāpitā, idāni iminā kacchapena udake pātetvā udakaṃ pāyetvā mahodarā [V 4.0263] katamha, puna aggiṃ karitvā aruṇe uggatepi ime senakapotake khādissāmā”ti aggiṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Sakuṇī tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “sāmi, ime yāya kāyaci velāya amhākaṃ puttake khāditvā gamissanti, sahāyassa no sīhassa santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti āha. So taṅkhaṇaññeva sīhassa [P 4.0295] santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ avelāya āgatosī”ti [M 4.0294] vutte ādito paṭṭhāya taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā ekādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, the great turtle said, “Friend, do not fear, you go ahead. I will come now.” Having dismissed him, he plunged into the water, gathered mud and algae, took them to the shore, extinguished the fire, and lay down. The country-folk thought, “What use are these young hawks to us? Let us turn over this black turtle and kill him—he will suffice for all of us.” They pulled out vines, took them as bowstrings, removed even their loincloths, and tied them in various places, but they could not turn the turtle over. The turtle dragged them along and plunged into deep water. Overcome by their greed for the turtle, they too fell in, and exhausted, with their bellies full of water, they struggled to emerge. “Friend, a single osprey extinguished our firebrand, leaving us without fire until midnight. Now, this turtle has made us fall into the water and drink until we have big bellies. Let us make a fire again, and at dawn we will eat these young hawks,” they said, and began to make a fire. Hearing their conversation, the female bird said, “Master, these country-folk will devour our young at any moment. Go to our friend, the lion.” At that very moment, he went to the lion. When asked, “Why have you come at this untimely hour?” he recounted the entire incident from the beginning and spoke the eleventh verse:

54.

54.

“Pasū manussā migavīraseṭṭha, bhayaṭṭitā seṭṭhamupabbajanti;

Puttā mamaṭṭā gatimāgatosmi, tvaṃ nosi rājā bhava me sukhāyā”ti.

“Beasts and men, O best of heroes among wild creatures, seek refuge in the best when afflicted by fear. My children are distressed; I have come to you for refuge. You are our king; be for my happiness.”

Tattha pasūti sabbatiracchāne āha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sāmi, migesu vīriyena seṭṭha, sabbalokasmiñhi sabbe tiracchānāpi manussāpi bhayaṭṭitā hutvā seṭṭhaṃ upagacchanti, mama ca puttā aṭṭā āturā. Tasmāhaṃ taṃ gatiṃ katvā āgatomhi, tvaṃ amhākaṃ rājā sukhāya me bhavāhī”ti.

Herein, “beasts” refers to all animals. The meaning is this: “O lord, best in strength among wild creatures, for in the whole world all animals and men, being afflicted by fear, approach the best for refuge. And my children are distressed and afflicted. Therefore, having made you my refuge, I have come. You are our king; be for my happiness.”

Taṃ sutvā sīho gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the lion spoke a verse:

55.

55.

“Karomi te senaka etamatthaṃ, āyāmi te taṃ disataṃ vadhāya;

Kathañhi viññū pahu sampajāno, na vāyame attajanassa guttiyā”ti.

“I shall do this for you, Senaka; I come for the destruction of those enemies of yours. For how indeed could an intelligent, capable, and mindful person not strive for the protection of his own people?”

Tattha taṃ disatanti taṃ disasamūhaṃ, taṃ tava paccatthikagaṇanti attho. Pahūti amitte hantuṃ samattho. Sampajānoti mittassa bhayuppattiṃ jānanto. Attajanassāti attasamassa aṅgasamānassa janassa, mittassāti attho.

Herein, “those enemies” means that group of foes, your host of adversaries. “Capable” means able to destroy enemies. “Mindful” means knowing of the danger that has arisen for a friend. “Of his own people” means of a person like oneself, a person like one’s own limbs—that is to say, a friend.

Evañca pana vatvā “gaccha tvaṃ putte samassāsehī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā maṇivaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ maddamāno pāyāsi. Cilācā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “kurarena tāva amhākaṃ ukkā vijjhāpitā, tathā kacchapena amhe nivatthapilotikānampi assāmikā katā, idāni pana naṭṭhamhā, sīho no jīvitakkhayameva pāpessatī”ti maraṇabhayatajjitā yena vā tena vā palāyiṃsu. Sīho āgantvā rukkhamūle na kiñci addasa. Atha naṃ kuraro [P 4.0296] ca kacchapo ca seno ca upasaṅkamitvā vandiṃsu. So tesaṃ mittānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā “ito paṭṭhāya mittadhammaṃ abhinditvā appamattā hothā”ti ovaditvā pakkāmi, tepi sakaṭhānāni gatā. Senasakuṇī [V 4.0264][M 4.0295] attano putte oloketvā “mitte nissāya amhehi dārakā laddhā”ti sukhanisinnasamaye senena saddhiṃ sallapantī mittadhammaṃ pakāsamānā cha gāthā abhāsi –

And having spoken thus, he dismissed the hawk, saying, “Go and comfort your young.” Then, treading upon the jewel-colored water, the lion set out. The villagers, seeing the lion approaching, thought, “First, the osprey extinguished our torches; then the tortoise made us lose even the worn-out clothes we were wearing; and now we are lost. The lion will surely bring our lives to an end.” Terrified by the fear of death, they fled in all directions. The lion arrived at the foot of the tree and saw nothing. Then the osprey, the tortoise, and the hawk approached and paid homage to him. He spoke to them of the benefits of friendship and advised them, “From this day forth, do not break the principle of friendship and be diligent,” and then he departed. They too went to their own places. The female hawk, looking at her young and thinking, “By relying on friends, we have regained our children,” while sitting comfortably and conversing with her mate, the hawk, spoke these six verses illustrating the principle of friendship:

56.

56.

“Mittañca kayirātha suhadayañca, ayirañca kayirātha sukhāgamāya;

Nivatthakocova sarebhihantvā, modāma puttehi samaṅgibhūtā.

“One should make a friend and a good-hearted companion; one should make a protector for the sake of attaining happiness. Like one wearing armor repelling arrows, we rejoice, being united with our children.”

57.

57.

“Sakamittassa kammena, sahāyassāpalāyino;

Kūjantamupakūjanti, lomasā hadayaṅgamaṃ.

“Through the deed of one’s own friend, a companion who does not flee, the feathered young ones chirp in response to your chirping, making sounds that are heart-pleasing.”

58.

58.

“Mittaṃ sahāyaṃ adhigamma paṇḍito, so bhuñjatī putta pasuṃ dhanaṃ vā;

Ahañca puttā ca patī ca mayhaṃ, mittānukampāya samaṅgibhūtā.

“Having obtained a friend and companion, a wise person enjoys children, cattle, or wealth. And I, my children, and my husband are united through the compassion of our friends.”

59.

59.

“Rājavatā sūravatā ca attho, sampannasakhissa bhavanti hete;

So mittavā yasavā uggatatto, asmiṃdhaloke modati kāmakāmī.

“One who has a king as a friend and one who has heroes as friends can achieve their purpose; these things are for one who is accomplished in friendship. Such a one, possessed of friends, fame, and an exalted nature, rejoices in this world, O lover of desires.”

60.

60.

“Karaṇīyāni mittāni, daliddenāpi senaka;

Passa mittānukampāya, samaggamhā sañātake.

“Friends should be made even by a poor person, O Senaka. See how, through the compassion of friends, we are reunited with our kin.”

61.

61.

“Sūrena balavantena, yo mitte kurute dijo;

Evaṃ so sukhito hoti, yathāhaṃ tvañca senakā”ti.

“The bird who makes friends with a hero, with one who is powerful, becomes happy in this way, just as I and you are, O Senaka.”

Tattha mittañcāti yaṃkiñci attano mittañca suhadayañca suhadayasahāyañca sāmikasaṅkhātaṃ ayirañca karotheva. Nivatthakocova sarebhihantvāti ettha kocoti kavaco. Yathā nāma paṭimukkakavaco sare abhihanati nivāreti, evaṃ mayampi mittabalena paccatthike abhihantvā [M 4.0296] puttehi saddhiṃ [P 4.0297] modāmāti vadati. Sakamittassa kammenāti sakassa mittassa parakkamena. Sahāyassāpalāyinoti sahāyassa apalāyino migarājassa. Lomasāti pakkhino amhākaṃ puttakā mañca tañca kūjantaṃ hadayaṅgamaṃ madhurassaraṃ nicchāretvā upakūjanti. Samaṅgibhūtāti ekaṭṭhāne ṭhitā.

Herein, “and a friend” means one should indeed make as a friend whomever is one's own friend, a good-hearted companion, or a protector called a master. In “Like one wearing armor repelling arrows,” “koco” here means armor. Just as one who has put on armor repels and wards off arrows, so too do we, by the strength of our friends, repel our enemies and rejoice together with our children. “By the deed of one's own friend” means by the prowess of one's own friend. “Of the companion who does not flee” means of the companion who does not flee, the king of beasts. “The feathered ones” means the birds, our young ones, who, while you and I are chirping, emit a sweet and heart-pleasing sound and chirp in response. “Being united” means standing together in one place.

Rājavatā sūravatā ca atthoti yassa sīhasadiso rājā ukkusakacchapasadisā ca sūrā mittā [V 4.0265] honti, tena rājavatā sūravatā ca attho sakkā pāpuṇituṃ. Bhavanti heteti yo ca sampannasakho paripuṇṇamittadhammo, tassa ete sahāyā bhavanti. Uggatattoti sirisobhaggena uggatasabhāvo. Asmiṃdhaloketi idhalokasaṅkhāte asmiṃ loke modati. Kāmakāmīti sāmikaṃ ālapati. So hi kāme kāmanato kāmakāmī nāma. Samaggamhāti samaggā jātamhā. Sañātaketi ñātakehi puttehi saddhiṃ.

“The purpose is served by one with a king and one with heroes” means: for one who has a king like a lion and heroic friends like the osprey and the tortoise, the purpose can be attained through having a king and through having heroes. “These are for him” means for one who is an accomplished friend, having fulfilled the duties of friendship, these become his companions. “Exalted nature” means one whose nature is elevated by glory and splendor. “In this world” means he rejoices in this world, known as the world of the present. “O lover of desires”—she is addressing her husband; for he is called “lover of desires” because he desires desires. “We have become united” means we have become harmonious. “With our kin” means together with our children, who are our kin.

Evaṃ sā chahi gāthāhi mittadhammassa guṇakathaṃ kathesi. Te sabbepi sahāyakā mittadhammaṃ abhinditvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Thus, in six verses, she spoke on the virtues of the principle of friendship. All those companions, without breaking the principle of friendship, remained so for as long as they lived and then passed on according to their kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva so bhariyaṃ nissāya sukhappatto, pubbepi sukhappattoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā seno ca senī ca jayampatikā ahesuṃ, puttakacchapo rāhulo, pitā mahāmoggallāno, ukkuso sāriputto, sīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, “Bhikkhus, not only now has this householder reached happiness by relying on his wife; in the past too, he reached it.” Then he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the hawk and the female hawk were this husband and wife, the young tortoise was Rāhula, the father turtle was Mahāmoggallāna, the osprey was Sāriputta, and the lion was I myself.”

Mahāukkusajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Third, the Great Osprey Jātaka.

[487] 4. Uddālakajātakavaṇṇanā

[487] 4. 4. The Uddālaka Jātaka

Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvāpi catupaccayatthāya tividhaṃ kuhakavatthuṃ pūresi. Athassa aguṇaṃ pakāsentā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā kuhanaṃ nissāya [M 4.0297] jīvikaṃ kappetī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantā.” The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Uddālaka Jātaka concerning a deceitful monk. For he, though having gone forth in this dispensation that leads out of suffering, practiced various forms of deceit for the sake of the four requisites. Then the monks, exposing his lack of virtue, started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the monk of such-and-such a name, having gone forth in such a dispensation of the Buddha that leads out of suffering, makes his living by means of deceit.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what discussion, monks, are you now sitting together?” and when they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, this monk was a deceiver,” and he related the story of the past.

Atīte [P 4.0298] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohito ahosi paṇḍito byatto. So ekadivasaṃ uyyānakīḷaṃ gato ekaṃ abhirūpaṃ gaṇikaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā taṃ paṭicca gabbhaṃ paṭilabhi. Gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ āha – “sāmi, gabbho me patiṭṭhito, jātakāle nāmaṃ karontī assa kiṃ nāmaṃ karomī”ti? So “vaṇṇadāsiyā kucchimhi nibbattattā na sakkā kulanāmaṃ kātu”nti [V 4.0266] cintetvā “bhadde, ayaṃ vātaghātarukkho uddālo nāma, idha paṭiladdhattā ‘uddālako’tissa nāmaṃ kareyyāsī”ti vatvā aṅgulimuddikaṃ adāsi. “Sace dhītā hoti, imāya naṃ poseyyāsi, sace putto, atha naṃ vayappattaṃ mayhaṃ dasseyyāsī”ti āha. Sā aparabhāge puttaṃ vijāyitvā “uddālako”tissa nāmaṃ akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain, wise and skilled. One day, having gone for sport in the park, he saw a beautiful courtesan and, his heart becoming bound to her, he cohabited with her. Through him, she conceived. Knowing that the pregnancy was established, she said to him, "Master, my pregnancy is established. At the time of birth, when giving a name, what name shall I give him?" He, thinking, "Since the child is born from the womb of a courtesan, it is not possible to give a family name," said, "Good lady, this wind-striking tree is called Uddāla. Since the child was obtained here, you should give him the name 'Uddālaka,'" and he gave her his signet ring. "If it is a daughter, you should support her with this. If it is a son, then when he has come of age, you should show him to me," he said. In due course, she gave birth to a son and gave him the name "Uddālaka."

So vayappatto mātaraṃ pucchi – “amma, ko me pitā”ti? “Purohito tātā”ti. “Yadi evaṃ vede uggaṇhissāmī”ti mātu hatthato muddikañca ācariyabhāgañca gahetvā takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanto ekaṃ tāpasagaṇaṃ disvā “imesaṃ santike varasippaṃ bhavissati, taṃ uggaṇhissāmī”ti sippalobhena pabbajitvā tesaṃ vattapaṭivattaṃ katvā “ācariyā maṃ tumhākaṃ jānanasippaṃ sikkhāpethā”ti āha. Te attano attano jānananiyāmeneva taṃ sikkhāpesuṃ. Pañcannaṃ tāpasasatānaṃ ekopi tena atirekapañño nāhosi, sveva tesaṃ paññāya aggo. Athassa te sannipatitvā ācariyaṭṭhānaṃ adaṃsu. Atha ne so āha – “mārisā, tumhe niccaṃ vanamūlaphalāhārā araññeva vasatha, manussapathaṃ kasmā na gacchathā”ti? “Mārisa, manussā nāma mahādānaṃ datvā anumodanaṃ kārāpenti, dhammiṃ kathaṃ bhaṇāpenti, pañhaṃ pucchanti, mayaṃ tena bhayena tattha na gacchāmā”ti. “Mārisā, sacepi cakkavattirājā bhavissati, manaṃ gahetvā kathanaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro, tumhe mā bhāyathā”ti vatvā tehi saddhiṃ cārikaṃ caramāno [M 4.0298] anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā [P 4.0299] rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase sabbehi saddhiṃ dvāragāme bhikkhāya cari, manussā mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Tāpasā punadivase nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu manussā mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Uddālakatāpaso dānānumodanaṃ karoti, maṅgalaṃ vadati, pañhaṃ vissajjeti, manussā pasīditvā bahupaccaye adaṃsu. Sakalanagaraṃ “paṇḍito gaṇasatthā dhammikatāpaso āgato”ti saṅkhubhi, taṃ raññopi kathayiṃsu.

When he came of age, he asked his mother, "Mother, who is my father?" "The chaplain, my dear." "If so, I shall learn the Vedas," he said. Taking the signet ring and the teacher's fee from his mother's hand, he went to Takkasilā. While learning the arts in the presence of the world-renowned teacher, he saw a group of ascetics and thought, "There must be a superior art in their presence; I shall learn it." With a desire for this art, he went forth, performed the major and minor duties for them, and said, "Teachers, teach me the art that you know." They taught him, each according to their own system. Among the five hundred ascetics, not one surpassed him in wisdom; he alone was foremost among them in wisdom. Then they assembled and gave him the position of teacher. Then he said to them, "Sirs, you always dwell in the forest, living on forest roots and fruits. Why do you not go to the haunts of men?" "Sir, men give great alms and have blessings recited, they have Dhamma talks given, and they ask questions. For fear of this, we do not go there." "Sirs, even if it were a wheel-turning monarch, winning their minds and speaking is my responsibility. You should not be afraid." Traveling with them on tour, he gradually reached Benares, stayed in the royal park, and on the next day, went for alms with all of them in a village at the gate. The people gave great alms. The next day, the ascetics entered the city, and the people gave great alms. The ascetic Uddālaka gave the blessing after the alms, spoke auspicious words, and answered questions. The people were pleased and gave many requisites. The entire city was stirred with the news: "A wise leader of a group, a righteous ascetic, has arrived." They also reported this to the king.

Rājā “kuhiṃ vasatī”ti pucchitvā “uyyāne”ti sutvā “sādhu ajja tesaṃ dassanāya gamissāmī”ti āha. Eko puriso gantvā “rājā kira vo passituṃ āgacchissatī”ti uddālakassa kathesi. Sopi isigaṇaṃ āmantetvā “mārisā, rājā kira āgamissati, issare nāma ekadivasaṃ ārādhetvā yāvajīvaṃ alaṃ hotī”ti. “Kiṃ pana kātabbaṃ ācariyā”ti? So evamāha – “tumhesu ekacce vaggulivataṃ carantu, ekacce ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuñjantu, ekacce kaṇṭakāpassayikā bhavantu, ekacce pañcātapaṃ tapantu, ekacce udakorohanakammaṃ karontu, ekacce tattha tattha mante sajjhāyantū”ti. Te tathā kariṃsu. Sayaṃ pana aṭṭha vā dasa vā paṇḍitavādino gahetvā manorame ādhārake ramaṇīyaṃ potthakaṃ [V 4.0267] ṭhapetvā antevāsikaparivuto supaññatte sāpassaye āsane nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā purohitaṃ ādāya mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā te micchātapaṃ carante disvā “apāyabhayamhā muttā”ti pasīditvā uddālakassa santikaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisinno tuṭṭhamānaso purohitena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king asked, "Where does he reside?" and hearing, "In the park," he said, "Good, today I shall go to see them." A certain man went and told Uddālaka, "The king, it is said, will come to see you." He, too, addressed the group of seers, "Sirs, the king, it is said, will come. If one pleases the powerful for a single day, it is sufficient for a lifetime." "But what is to be done, teacher?" He spoke thus: "Let some among you practice the bat-vow, let some engage in the squatting-exertion, let some become thorn-bed recliners, let some practice the five-fire austerity, let some perform the act of descending into water, and let some recite mantras here and there." They did so. He himself, taking eight or ten who claimed to be wise, placed a charming book on a beautiful stand and, surrounded by his pupils, sat on a well-prepared seat with a backrest. At that moment, the king, taking his chaplain, went to the park with a great retinue. Seeing them practicing false austerities, he was pleased, thinking, "They are freed from the fear of the states of woe." He approached Uddālaka, and after exchanging friendly greetings, he sat to one side. With a delighted mind, he conversed with the chaplain and spoke the first verse:

62.

62.

“Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantā, dummakkharūpā ye mantaṃ jappanti;

Kaccinnu te mānusake payoge, idaṃ vidū parimuttā apāyā”ti.

"Wearing rough hides, with matted hair and teeth stained with mire, repulsive in appearance, they mutter a sacred text; I wonder, do they who know this, through such human endeavor, become freed from the states of woe?"

Tattha [P 4.0300] kharājināti sakhurehi ajinacammehi samannāgatā. Paṅkadantāti dantakaṭṭhassa akhādanena malaggahitadantā. Dummakkharūpāti anañjitakkhā amaṇḍitarūpā [M 4.0299] lūkhasaṅghāṭidharā. Mānusake payogeti manussehi kattabbavīriye. Idaṃ vidūti idaṃ tapacaraṇañca mantasajjhāyanañca jānantā. Apāyāti kacci ācariya, ime catūhi apāyehi muttāti pucchati.

Therein, 'wearing rough hides' means endowed with animal skins complete with hooves. 'Teeth stained with mire' means teeth covered in dirt from not chewing a tooth-stick. 'Repulsive in appearance' means with unanointed eyes, unadorned form, wearing coarse outer robes. 'In human endeavor' means in the effort to be made by humans. 'Who know this' means knowing this practice of austerity and recitation of sacred texts. 'From the states of woe'—he asks, "Teacher, I wonder, are these freed from the four states of woe?"

Taṃ sutvā purohito “ayaṃ rājā aṭṭhāne pasanno, tuṇhī bhavituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the chaplain, thinking, "This king is pleased on the wrong occasion; it is not proper to remain silent," spoke the second verse:

63.

63.

“Pāpāni kammāni karetha rāja, bahussuto ce na careyya dhammaṃ;

Sahassavedopi na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamucce caraṇaṃ apatvā”ti.

"A learned person may still do evil deeds, O king, if they do not practice the Dhamma. Though versed in a thousand Vedas, one is not freed from suffering on account of it, without having attained right conduct."

Tattha bahussuto ceti sace mahārāja, “ahaṃ bahussutomhī”ti paguṇavedopi dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ na careyya, tīhi dvārehi pāpāneva kareyya, tiṭṭhantu tayo vedā, sahassavedopi samāno taṃ bāhusaccaṃ paṭicca aṭṭhasamāpattisaṅkhātaṃ caraṇaṃ appatvā apāyadukkhato na mucceyyāti.

Therein, 'if a learned person' means: If, great king, one who is skilled in the Vedas says, 'I am very learned,' but does not practice the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action, and instead commits evil deeds through the three doors—let the three Vedas be, even one versed in a thousand Vedas, on account of that great learning, without having attained the conduct designated as the eight attainments, would not be freed from the suffering of the states of woe.

Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā uddālako cintesi “rājā yathā vā tathā vā isigaṇassa pasīdi, ayaṃ pana brāhmaṇo carantaṃ goṇaṃ daṇḍena paharanto viya vaḍḍhitabhatte kacavaraṃ khipanto viya kathesi, tena saddhiṃ kathessāmī”ti. So tena saddhiṃ kathento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, Uddālaka thought, 'The king is pleased with the group of seers one way or another, but this brahmin spoke as if striking a grazing ox with a stick or as if throwing rubbish into a served meal. I will speak with him.' So, speaking with him, he uttered the third verse:

64.

64.

“Sahassavedopi na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamucce caraṇaṃ apatvā;

Maññāmi vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇaññeva sacca”nti.

Though versed in a thousand Vedas, one is not freed from suffering on account of it, without having attained right conduct. I think the Vedas are fruitless; only conduct together with self-restraint is truth.

Tattha [V 4.0268] aphalāti tava vāde vedā ca sesasippāni ca aphalāni āpajjanti, tāni kasmā uggaṇhanti, sīlasaṃyamena saddhiṃ caraṇaññeva ekaṃ saccaṃ āpajjatīti.

Here, 'fruitless' means that in your doctrine both the Vedas and the other arts become fruitless. Why do they study them? Only conduct together with moral restraint becomes the sole truth.

Tato [P 4.0301][M 4.0300] purohito catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the chaplain spoke the fourth verse.

65.

65.

“Na heva vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇaññeva saccaṃ;

Kittiñhi pappoti adhicca vede, santiṃ puṇāti caraṇena danto”ti.

Indeed, the Vedas are not fruitless; conduct with self-restraint is indeed the truth. For one attains fame by studying the Vedas, and the self-controlled one gains peace through conduct.

Tattha na hevāti nāhaṃ “vedā aphalā”ti vadāmi, apica kho pana sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇaṃ saccameva sabhāvabhūtaṃ uttamaṃ. Tena hi sakkā dukkhā muccituṃ. Santiṃ puṇātīti samāpattisaṅkhātena caraṇena danto bhayasantikaraṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Here, 'indeed not' means: I do not say that the Vedas are fruitless. Moreover, conduct with self-restraint is truly the supreme reality. By this, one can be freed from suffering. 'Gains peace' means the disciplined one attains Nibbāna, which stills fear, through conduct consisting of meditative attainments.

Taṃ sutvā uddālako “na sakkā iminā saddhiṃ paṭipakkhavasena ṭhātuṃ, ‘putto tavāha’nti vutte sinehaṃ akaronto nāma natthi, puttabhāvamassa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Uddālaka thought, 'It is not possible to stand against him in opposition. When told, "I am your son," there is no one who would not show affection. I will tell him of his sonship.' Reflecting thus, he spoke the fifth verse:

66.

66.

“Bhaccā mātā pitā bandhū, yena jāto sayeva so;

Uddālako ahaṃ bhoto, sottiyākulavaṃsako”ti.

Dependents, mother, father, relatives—by whom one is born, that very one he is. I am Uddālaka, good sir, of the Sottiya family lineage.

Tattha bhaccāti mātā ca pitā ca sesabandhū ca bharitabbā nāma. Yena pana jāto, soyeva so hoti. Attāyeva hi attano jāyati, ahañca tayāva uddālakarukkhamūle janito, tayā vuttameva nāmaṃ kataṃ, uddālako ahaṃ bhoti.

Here, 'dependents' means mother, father, and other relatives are to be supported. But by whom one is born, that very one he is. Indeed, one is born of oneself. And I was born by you at the foot of the uddālaka tree, and was given the very name you spoke. I am Uddālaka, good sir.

So “ekaṃsena tvaṃ uddālakosī”ti vutte “āmā”ti vatvā “mayā te mātu saññāṇaṃ dinnaṃ, taṃ kuhi”nti vutte “idaṃ brāhmaṇā”ti muddikaṃ tassa hatthe ṭhapesi. Brāhmaṇo muddikaṃ sañjānitvā nicchayena “tvaṃ brāhmaṇadhammaṃ pajānāsī”ti vatvā brāhmaṇadhammaṃ pucchanto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

When told, 'You are undoubtedly Uddālaka,' he replied, 'Yes.' Asked, 'Where is the token I gave to your mother?' he placed the ring in the brahmin's hand, saying, 'Here, Brahmin.' Recognizing the ring, the brahmin said with certainty, 'You know the brahmin's duty.' Then, questioning him about the brahmin's duty, he spoke the sixth verse:

67.

67.

“Kathaṃ [P 4.0302] bho brāhmaṇo hoti, kathaṃ bhavati kevalī;

Kathañca parinibbānaṃ, dhammaṭṭho kinti vuccatī”ti.

How, good sir, does one become a brahmin? How does one become perfected? And how is there final Nibbāna? How is one called 'righteous'?

Uddālakopi [V 4.0269][M 4.0301] tassa ācikkhanto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Uddālaka, explaining to him, spoke the seventh verse:

68.

68.
