“Niraṃkatvā aggimādāya brāhmaṇo, āpo siñcaṃ yajaṃ usseti yūpaṃ;

Evaṃkaro brāhmaṇo hoti khemī, dhamme ṭhitaṃ tena amāpayiṃsū”ti.

Having made it continuous and taken up the fire, the brahmin, sprinkling water and sacrificing, raises the sacrificial post. Acting thus, the brahmin becomes secure; by that, they esteemed him to be established in the Dhamma.

Tattha niraṃkatvā aggimādāyāti nirantaraṃ katvā aggiṃ gahetvā paricarati. Āpo siñcaṃ yajaṃ usseti yūpanti abhisecanakakammaṃ karonto sammāpāsaṃ vā vājapeyyaṃ vā niraggaḷaṃ vā yajanto suvaṇṇayūpaṃ ussāpeti. Khemīti khemappatto. Amāpayiṃsūti teneva ca kāraṇena dhamme ṭhitaṃ kathayiṃsu.

Here, 'having made it continuous and taken up the fire' means having made the fire continuous, he takes it and tends to it. 'Sprinkling water and sacrificing, raises the sacrificial post' means that while performing the consecration rite, sacrificing the Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeya, or the Niraggaḷa, he sets up the golden sacrificial post. 'Secure' means one who has attained security. 'They esteemed him' means for that very reason they declared him to be established in the Dhamma.

Taṃ sutvā purohito tena kathitaṃ brāhmaṇadhammaṃ garahanto aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the chaplain, censuring the brahmin's duty spoken by him, recited the eighth verse:

69.

69.

“Na suddhi secanenatthi, nāpi kevalī brāhmaṇo;

Na khantī nāpi soraccaṃ, nāpi so parinibbuto”ti.

There is no purity by sprinkling, nor is a brahmin perfected; there is no patience nor gentleness, nor is he thus fully extinguished.

Tattha secanenāti tena vuttesu brāhmaṇadhammesu ekaṃ dassetvā sabbaṃ paṭikkhipati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “aggiparicaraṇena vā udakasecanena vā pasughātayaññena vā suddhi nāma natthi, nāpi ettakena brāhmaṇo kevalaparipuṇṇo hoti, na adhivāsanakhanti, na sīlasoraccaṃ, nāpi kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto nāma hotī”ti.

Here, 'by sprinkling' means that by pointing to one of the brahmin's duties spoken by him, he rejects them all. This is what is said: 'There is no purity through tending the fire, through sprinkling with water, or through animal sacrifice. Nor by that much does a brahmin become perfected and complete; there is no patient endurance, no virtuous gentleness, nor is one called "fully extinguished" by the extinguishing of the defilements.'

Tato naṃ uddālako “yadi evaṃ brāhmaṇo na hoti, atha kathaṃ hotī”ti pucchanto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Uddālaka, questioning him, 'If a brahmin is not thus, then how is one so?' spoke the ninth verse:

70.

70.

“Kathaṃ so brāhmaṇo hoti, kathaṃ bhavati kevalī;

Kathañca parinibbānaṃ, dhammaṭṭho kinti vuccatī”ti.

How is one a brahmin? How does one become perfected? And how is there final Nibbāna? How is one called 'righteous'?

Purohitopissa [P 4.0303][M 4.0302] kathento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

The chaplain, explaining to him, recited the other verse:

71.

71.

“Akhettabandhū amamo nirāso, nillobhapāpo bhavalobhakhīṇo;

Evaṃkaro brāhmaṇo hoti khemī, dhamme ṭhitaṃ tena amāpayiṃsū”ti.

Without fields or relatives, without possessiveness, without longing, without evil greed, with lust for existence destroyed; acting thus, the brahmin becomes secure; by that, they esteemed him to be established in the Dhamma.

Tattha [V 4.0270] akhettabandhūti akkhetto abandhu, khettavatthugāmanigamapariggahena ceva ñātibandhavagottabandhavamittabandhavasahāyabandhavasippabandhavapariggahena ca rahito. Amamoti sattasaṅkhāresu taṇhādiṭṭhimamāyanarahito. Nirāsoti lābhadhanaputtajīvitāsāya rahito. Nillobhapāpoti pāpalobhavisamalobhena rahito. Bhavalobhakhīṇoti khīṇabhavarāgo.

Here, 'without fields or relatives' means without a field and without a relative, devoid of the possession of fields, property, villages, and towns, and of the possession of relatives, clan, friends, companions, and craft associates. 'Without possessiveness' means free from craving, views, and 'mine'-making regarding beings and formations. 'Without longing' means free from longing for gain, wealth, children, or life. 'Without evil greed' means free from evil greed and unrighteous greed. 'With lust for existence destroyed' means one whose lust for existence is destroyed.

Tato uddālako gāthamāha –

Then Uddālaka spoke a verse:

72.

72.

“Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Sabbeva soratā dantā, sabbeva parinibbutā;

Sabbesaṃ sītibhūtānaṃ, atthi seyyotha pāpiyo”ti.

Nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcasts, and scavengers—all gentle and self-controlled, all fully extinguished. For all who have become cool, is there a superior or an inferior?

Tattha atthi seyyotha pāpiyoti ete khattiyādayo sabbepi soraccādīhi samannāgatā honti, evaṃ bhūtānaṃ pana tesaṃ ayaṃ seyyo, ayaṃ pāpiyoti evaṃ hīnukkaṭṭhatā atthi, natthīti pucchati.

Here, 'is there a superior or an inferior?' means: all these, from the nobles onwards, are endowed with gentleness and so on. But among those who are thus, he asks whether a distinction of high and low, such as 'this one is superior, this one is inferior,' exists or not.

Athassa “arahattuppattito paṭṭhāya hīnukkaṭṭhatā nāma natthī”ti dassetuṃ brāhmaṇo gāthamāha –

Then, to demonstrate to him that "from the attainment of arahantship onwards, there is no such thing as high or low," the chaplain spoke a verse:

73.

73.

“Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Sabbeva soratā dantā, sabbeva parinibbutā;

Sabbesaṃ sītibhūtānaṃ, natthi seyyotha pāpiyo”ti.

"Nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcasts, and scavengers—all gentle and self-controlled, all fully extinguished. For all who have become cool, there is no superior or inferior."

Atha naṃ garahanto uddālako gāthādvayamāha –

Then, censuring him, Uddālaka spoke two verses:

74.

74.

“Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Sabbeva soratā dantā, sabbeva parinibbutā.

"Nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcasts, and scavengers—all gentle and self-controlled, all fully extinguished."

75.

75.

“Sabbesaṃ [M 4.0303] sītibhūtānaṃ, natthi seyyotha pāpiyo;

Panaṭṭhaṃ carasi brahmaññaṃ, sottiyākulavaṃsata”nti.

"For all who have become cool, there is no superior or inferior. Why then do you practice a ruined brahminhood, destroying the lineage of the Sottiya clan?"

Tassattho [V 4.0271][P 4.0304] – yadi etehi guṇehi samannāgatānaṃ viseso natthi, eko vaṇṇova hoti, evaṃ sante tvaṃ ubhato sujātabhāvaṃ nāsento panaṭṭhaṃ carasi brahmaññaṃ, caṇḍālasamo hosi, sottiyakulavaṃsataṃ nāsesīti.

The meaning is: If there is no distinction among those endowed with these qualities, if there is only one caste, then you, destroying your well-born status on both sides, practice a ruined brahminhood, you are equal to an outcast, you destroy the lineage of the Sottiya clan.

Atha naṃ purohito upamāya saññāpento gāthādvayamāha –

Then the chaplain, instructing him by means of a simile, spoke two verses:

76.

76.

“Nānārattehi vatthehi, vimānaṃ bhavati chāditaṃ;

Na tesaṃ chāyā vatthānaṃ, so rāgo anupajjatha.

"A pavilion is covered with cloths of various colors; the shadow of those cloths does not take on those colors."

77.

77.

“Evameva manussesu, yadā sujjhanti māṇavā;

Te sajātiṃ pamuñcanti, dhammamaññāya subbatā”ti.

"Just so among humans, when they are purified, they abandon their birth, having understood the Dhamma and being of good vows."

Tattha vimānanti gehaṃ vā maṇḍapaṃ vā. Chāyāti tesaṃ vatthānaṃ chāyā so nānāvidho rāgo na upeti, sabbā chāyā ekavaṇṇāva honti. Evamevāti manussesupi evameva ekacce aññāṇabrāhmaṇā akāraṇeneva cātuvaṇṇe suddhiṃ paññāpenti, esā atthīti mā gaṇhi. Yadā ariyamaggena māṇavā sujjhanti, tadā tehi paṭividdhaṃ nibbānadhammaṃ jānitvā subbatā sīlavantā paṇḍitapurisā te sajātiṃ muñcanti. Nibbānappattito paṭṭhāya hi jāti nāma niratthakāti.

Herein, 'pavilion' means a house or a hall. 'Shadow' means that the diverse color of those cloths does not appear in the shadow, for all shadows are of one color. Similarly, among humans, some ignorant brahmins declare purity among the four castes without reason—do not take this as true. When young men are purified by the noble path, having known the Nibbāna-Dhamma realized by them, the well-behaved, virtuous, wise people abandon their birth. For from the attainment of Nibbāna onwards, birth is meaningless.

Uddālako pana paccāharituṃ asakkonto appaṭibhānova nisīdi. Atha brāhmaṇo rājānaṃ āha – “sabbe ete, mahārāja, kuhakā sakalajambudīpe kohaññeneva nāsenti, uddālakaṃ uppabbājetvā upapurohitaṃ karotha, sese uppabbājetvā phalakāvudhāni datvā sevake karothā”ti. “Sādhu, ācariyā”ti rājā tathā kāresi. Te rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahantāva yathākammaṃ gatā.

Unable to reply, Uddālaka sat silent, at a loss for words. Then the chaplain said to the king, 'Great king, all these are deceivers who ruin the whole of Jambudīpa by their deceit. Disrobe Uddālaka and appoint him as your assistant chaplain. Disrobe the rest, give them weapons, and make them servants.' 'Very well, teacher,' said the king, and he did so. While attending upon the king, they went according to their deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā uddālako [M 4.0304] kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, rājā ānando, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too he was a hypocrite." Then he made the connection to the birth story: "At that time, Uddālaka was the hypocritical monk, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was none other than myself."

Uddālakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Uddālaka Jātaka, the fourth.

[488] 5. Bhisajātakavaṇṇanā

[488] 5. Commentary on the Bhisa Jātaka

Assaṃ [V 4.0272] gavaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana kusajātake (jā. 2.20.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā [P 4.0305] pana satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃ paṭiccā”ti vatvā “kilesaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā kasmā kilesaṃ paṭicca ukkaṇṭhitosi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppanne buddhe bāhirakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vatthukāmakilesakāme ārabbha uppajjanakasaññaṃ sapathaṃ katvā vihariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Horses, cattle, silver, and gold'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a discontented monk. The story, however, will appear in the Kusa Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true, venerable sir,' the Teacher asked, 'On account of what?' When he replied, 'On account of defilements, venerable sir,' the Teacher then said, 'Monk, having gone forth in such a liberating teaching, why are you discontented on account of defilements? Wise men of old, when a Buddha had not arisen, having gone forth into an external renunciation, lived having made an oath regarding the arising of perceptions of sensual desire.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇamahāsālakulassa putto hutvā nibbatti, “mahākañcanakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Athassa padasā vicaraṇakāle aparopi putto jāyi, “upakañcanakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā satta puttā ahesuṃ. Sabbakaniṭṭhā panekā dhītā, tassā “kañcanadevī”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Mahākañcanakumāro vayappatto takkasilato sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā āgacchi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro gharāvāsena bandhitukāmā “attanā samānajātiyakulato te dārikaṃ ānessāma, gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapehī”ti vadiṃsu. “Ammatātā, na mayhaṃ gharāvāsenattho, mayhañhi tayo bhavā ādittā viya sappaṭibhayā, bandhanāgāraṃ viya palibuddhā, ukkārabhūmi viya jegucchā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, mayā supinenapi methunadhammo na diṭṭhapubbo, aññe vo puttā atthi, te gharāvāsena nimantethā”ti vatvā punappunaṃ yācitopi sahāye pesetvā tehi yācitopi na icchi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of a great brahmin family possessing eighty crores of wealth. They named him "Mahākañcanakumāra." Later, when he was able to walk, another son was born to them, whom they named "Upakañcanakumāra." In this manner, seven sons were born in succession. The very youngest, however, was a daughter, and they named her "Kañcanadevī." When Mahākañcanakumāra came of age, he went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and returned. Then his parents, wishing to bind him to household life, said, "We will bring you a maiden from a family of equal birth. Establish yourself in household life." He replied, "Mother and father, I have no need for household life. For me, the three realms of existence appear as if burning, fraught with danger; like a prison, entangled; like a refuse heap, disgusting. Not even in a dream have I ever seen the act of sexual intercourse. You have other sons—invite them to household life." Though they repeatedly entreated him and even sent friends to persuade him, he remained unwilling.

Atha [M 4.0305] naṃ sahāyā “samma, kiṃ pana tvaṃ patthento kāme paribhuñjituṃ na icchasī”ti pucchiṃsu. So tesaṃ nekkhammajjhāsayataṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā mātāpitaro sesaputte nimantesuṃ, tepi na icchiṃsu. Kañcanadevīpi na icchiyeva. Aparabhāge mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Mahākañcanapaṇḍito mātāpitūnaṃ kattabbakiccaṃ katvā asītikoṭidhanena kapaṇaddhikānaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā cha bhātaro bhaginiṃ ekaṃ dāsaṃ ekaṃ dāsiṃ ekaṃ sahāyakañca ādāya mahābhinikkhamanaṃ [P 4.0306] nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pāvisi. Te tattha ekaṃ padumasaraṃ nissāya ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge assamaṃ katvā pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhārehi yāpayiṃsu. Te araññaṃ gacchantā ekatova gantvā yattha eko phalaṃ vā pattaṃ vā passati, tattha itarepi pakkositvā diṭṭhasutādīni [V 4.0273] kathentā uccinanti, gāmassa kammantaṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti. Atha ācariyo mahākañcanatāpaso cintesi “amhākaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajitānaṃ evaṃ loluppacāravasena phalāphalatthāya vicaraṇaṃ nāma appatirūpaṃ, ito paṭṭhāya ahameva phalāphalaṃ āharissāmī”ti. So assamaṃ patvā sabbepi te sāyanhasamaye sannipātetvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “tumhe idheva samaṇadhammaṃ karontā acchatha, ahaṃ phalāphalaṃ āharissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ upakañcanādayo “mayaṃ ācariya, tumhe nissāya pabbajitā, tumhe idheva samaṇadhammaṃ karotha, bhaginīpi no idheva hotu, dāsīpi tassā santike acchatu, mayaṃ aṭṭha janā vārena phalāphalaṃ āharissāma, tumhe pana tayo vāramuttāva hothā”ti vatvā paṭiññaṃ gaṇhiṃsu.

Then his friends asked him, "Friend, what then are you longing for, that you do not wish to enjoy sensual pleasures?" He informed them of his intent for renunciation. Hearing this, his parents invited their other sons, but they too did not wish for it. Kañcanadevī also did not wish it. Later, his parents passed away. The wise Mahākañcana performed the necessary duties for his parents and gave a great donation of eighty crores to the destitute and wayfarers. Taking his six brothers, one sister, one male servant, one female servant, and one companion, he made the Great Renunciation and entered the Himalayas. There, near a lotus lake in a delightful region, they built a hermitage, went forth, and sustained themselves on forest roots and fruits. When they went into the forest, they would go together; wherever one saw a fruit or a leaf, they would call the others and, speaking of what they had seen or heard, they would gather them; it was like a village place of work. Then the teacher, the ascetic Mahākañcana, thought, 'For us who have abandoned eighty crores of wealth to go forth, this kind of wandering for various fruits by way of restless conduct is unbecoming. From now on, I alone will gather the fruits.' Returning to the hermitage, he gathered them all in the evening, informed them of the matter, and said, 'You stay here practicing the ascetic's duties; I will gather the fruits.' Then Upakañcana and the others said, 'Teacher, we have gone forth depending on you. You stay here practicing the ascetic's duties; let our sister remain here too, and let the maidservant stay with her. The eight of us will take turns gathering the fruits, while you three shall be exempt from the turn.' Having said this, they received his consent.

Tato paṭṭhāya aṭṭhasupi janesu ekeko vāreneva phalāphalaṃ āharati. Sesā attano attano paṇṇasālāyameva honti, akāraṇena ekato bhavituṃ na labhanti. Vārappatto phalāphalaṃ āharitvā eko māḷako atthi, tattha pāsāṇaphalake ekādasa koṭṭhāse katvā ghaṇḍisaññaṃ katvā attano koṭṭhāsaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisati. Sesā ghaṇḍisaññāya nikkhamitvā loluppaṃ akatvā [M 4.0306] gāravaparihārena gantvā attano pāpuṇanakoṭṭhāsaṃ ādāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonti. Te aparabhāge bhisāni āharitvā khādantā tattatapā ghoratapā paramājitindriyā kasiṇaparikammaṃ karontā vihariṃsu. Atha tesaṃ sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakkopi āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “kāmādhimuttā nu kho ime isayo[P 4.0307], no”ti āsaṅkaṃ karotiyeva. So “ime tāva isayo pariggaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā attano ānubhāvena mahāsattassa koṭṭhāsaṃ tayo divase antaradhāpesi. So paṭhamadivase koṭṭhāsaṃ adisvā “mama koṭṭhāsaṃ pamuṭṭho bhavissatī”ti cintesi, dutiyadivase “mama dosena bhavitabbaṃ, paṇāmanavasena mama koṭṭhāsaṃ na ṭhapesi maññe”ti cintesi, tatiyadivase “kena nu kho kāraṇena mayhaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ na ṭhapenti, sace me doso atthi, khamāpessāmī”ti sāyanhasamaye ghaṇḍisaññaṃ adāsi.

From then on, among the eight people, each one brought various fruits in turn. The rest remained each in his own leaf-hut; they were not allowed to gather together without a reason. The one whose turn it was, having brought the fruits, there was a certain pavilion; there, having made eleven portions on a stone slab and giving a gong signal, he would take his own portion and enter his dwelling place. The rest, upon the gong signal, would come out without greed and, proceeding with respectful conduct, take their allotted portions, go to their dwelling places, and after consuming them, perform the ascetic's duties. Later, they lived bringing and eating lotus stalks, practicing intense and severe austerities, with supreme mastery over their senses, and performing the preliminary kasiṇa meditations. Then, by the power of their virtue, Sakka’s abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting and knowing the reason, became apprehensive, wondering, 'Are these hermits still intent on sensual pleasures or not?' Thinking, 'I will test these hermits first,' he used his power to make the Great Being's portion disappear for three days. On the first day, not seeing his portion, the Great Being thought, 'The one making the portions must have forgotten mine.' On the second day, he thought, 'It must be due to some fault of mine; I suppose he did not set aside my portion by way of my exclusion.' On the third day, he thought, 'For what reason is my portion not being set aside? If I have a fault, I shall ask for forgiveness.' In the evening, he gave the gong signal.

Sabbe sannipatitvā “kena ghaṇḍisaññā dinnā”ti āhaṃsu. “Mayā tātā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā ācariyā”ti? “Tātā tatiyadivase kena phalāphalaṃ ābhata”nti? Tesu eko uṭṭhāya “mayā ācariyā”ti vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Koṭṭhāse karontena te mayhaṃ koṭṭhāso katoti. “Āma, ācariya, jeṭṭhakakoṭṭhāso me kato”ti. “Hiyyo kenābhata”nti? “Mayā”ti aparo uṭṭhāya vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Koṭṭhāsaṃ karonto maṃ anussarīti. “Tumhākaṃ me jeṭṭhakakoṭṭhāso ṭhapito”ti. “Ajja kenābhata”nti. “Mayā”ti aparo uṭṭhāya vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Koṭṭhāsaṃ karonto maṃ anussarīti. “Tumhākaṃ me [V 4.0274] jeṭṭhakakoṭṭhāso kato”ti. “Tātā, ajja mayhaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ alabhantassa tatiyo divaso, paṭhamadivase koṭṭhāsaṃ adisvā ‘koṭṭhāsaṃ karonto maṃ pamuṭṭho bhavissatī’ti cintesiṃ, dutiyadivase “mama koci doso bhavissatī”ti cintesiṃ, ajja pana “sace me doso atthi, khamāpessāmī”ti cintetvā ghaṇḍisaññāya tumhe sannipātesiṃ. Ete bhisakoṭṭhāse tumhe “karimhā”ti vadatha, ahaṃ na labhāmi, etesaṃ thenetvā khādakaṃ ñātuṃ vaṭṭati, kāme pahāya pabbajitānaṃ bhisamattaṃ [M 4.0307] thenanaṃ nāma appatirūpanti. Te tassa kathaṃ sutvā “aho sāhasikakamma”nti [P 4.0308] sabbeva ubbegappattā ahesuṃ.

All gathered together and asked, 'By whom was the gong signal given?' 'By me, my dears.' 'For what reason, teacher?' 'My dears, who brought the fruits on the third day ago?' Among them, one stood up, bowed, and said, 'I did, teacher.' 'While making the portions, did you make my portion?' 'Yes, teacher, I made the portion for the eldest.' 'Who brought them yesterday?' 'I did,' another stood up and bowed. 'While making the portion, did you remember me?' 'The eldest's portion was set aside for you.' 'Who brought them today?' 'I did,' another stood up and bowed. 'While making the portion, did you remember me?' 'The eldest's portion was made for you.' 'My dears, today is the third day that I have not received my portion. On the first day, not seeing the portion, I thought, "The one making the portion has forgotten me." On the second day, I thought, "I must have some fault." Today, however, thinking, "If I have a fault, I will ask for forgiveness," I have gathered you with the gong signal. You say, "We have made these portions of lotus stalks," but I do not receive them. It is proper to know who is stealing and eating them. For those who have renounced sensual pleasures and gone forth, stealing even a mere lotus stalk is unbecoming.' Hearing his words, they were all struck with agitation, thinking, 'Oh, what a rash deed!'

Tasmiṃ assamapade vanajeṭṭhakarukkhe nibbattadevatāpi otaritvā āgantvā tesaṃyeva santike nisīdi. Āneñjakaraṇaṃ kāriyamāno dukkhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto āḷānaṃ bhinditvā palāyitvā araññaṃ paviṭṭho eko vāraṇo kālena kālaṃ isigaṇaṃ vandati, sopi āgantvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Sappakīḷāpanako eko vānaro ahituṇḍikassa hatthato muccitvā palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattheva assame vasati. Sopi taṃ divasaṃ isigaṇaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Sakko “isigaṇaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti tesaṃ santike adissamānakāyo aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇeva bodhisattassa kaniṭṭho upakañcanatāpaso uṭṭhāyāsanā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā sesānaṃ apacitiṃ dassetvā “ācariya, ahaṃ aññe apaṭṭhapetvā attānaññeva sodhetuṃ labhāmī”ti pucchi. “Āma, labhasī”ti. So isigaṇamajjhe ṭhatvā “sace te mayā bhisāni khāditāni, evarūpo nāma hotū”ti sapathaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, in the hermitage grounds, a deity born in the chief tree of the forest descended and came to sit near them. An elephant, unable to endure the pain of being trained to be motionless, broke its tethering post, fled, and entered the forest. From time to time, it would come to pay respects to the group of sages. That day, it too came and stood in a suitable place. A monkey used by a snake-charmer, having escaped from his hand, fled into the forest and lived there in the hermitage. That day, it also came to pay respects to the sages and sat in a suitable place. Sakka, thinking, 'I shall test the group of sages,' stood invisibly near them. At that moment, the youngest ascetic, Upakañcana, the Bodhisatta's younger brother, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, showed respect to the others, and asked, 'Teacher, without implicating others, may I purify myself?' 'Yes, you may.' Standing in the midst of the group of sages, he made an oath, saying, 'If I have eaten your lotus roots, may such a thing happen to me,' and then recited the first verse:

78.

78.

“Assaṃ gavaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ, bhariyañca so idha labhataṃ manāpaṃ;

Puttehi dārehi samaṅgi hotu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī”ti.

“May he obtain horses, cattle, silver, gold, and a pleasing wife in this world; may he be endowed with sons and wives, O Brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

Tattha “assaṃ gava”nti idaṃ “so ‘yattakāni piyavatthūni honti, tehi vippayoge tattakāni sokadukkhāni uppajjantī’ti vatthukāme garahanto abhāsī”ti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, 'horses and cattle' should be understood as spoken by one censuring sensual pleasures based on material things, saying, 'However many beloved things one has, from separation from them arises a corresponding amount of sorrow and suffering.'

Taṃ sutvā isigaṇo “mārisa, mā evaṃ kathetha, atibhāriyo te sapatho”ti kaṇṇe pidahi. Bodhisattopi naṃ “tāta, atibhāriyo te sapatho, na tvaṃ khādasi, tava pattāsane nisīdā”ti [V 4.0275] āha. Tasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ sapathaṃ katvā nisinne dutiyopi bhātā sahasā uṭṭhāya mahāsattaṃ vanditvā sapathena attānaṃ sodhento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the group of sages covered their ears, saying, 'Venerable sir, do not speak thus; your oath is too grave.' The Bodhisatta also said to him, 'Dear Upakañcana, your oath is too grave; you did not eat them; sit on your seat.' After that first one had taken the oath and sat down, the second brother suddenly rose, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and purifying himself with an oath, spoke the second verse:

79.

79.

“Mālañca [P 4.0309][M 4.0308] so kāsikacandanañca, dhāretu puttassa bahū bhavantu;

Kāmesu tibbaṃ kurutaṃ apekkhaṃ, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī”ti.

“May he wear garlands and Kasi sandalwood; may he have many sons; may he have intense longing for sensual pleasures, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

Tattha tibbanti vatthukāmakilesakāmesu bahalaṃ apekkhaṃ karotūti. Idaṃ so “yassetesu tibbā apekkhā honti, so tehi vippayoge mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti dukkhapaṭikkhepavaseneva āha.

Herein, 'intense' means 'may he have a strong longing for sensual pleasures, both of objects and of defilements.' He said this by way of rejecting suffering, meaning: 'Whoever has such intense longing for these, upon separation from them, experiences great suffering.'

Tasmiṃ nisinne sesāpi attano attano ajjhāsayānurūpena taṃ taṃ gāthaṃ abhāsiṃsu –

When he had sat down, the others also spoke their respective verses according to their own inclinations:

80.

80.

“Pahūtadhañño kasimā yasassī, putte gihī dhanimā sabbakāme;

Vayaṃ apassaṃ gharamāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be a glorious householder, a farmer with abundant grain, with sons, wealthy, and with all sensual pleasures. May he live at home without regarding old age, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

81.

81.

“So khattiyo hotu pasayhakārī, rājābhirājā balavā yasassī;

Sa cāturantaṃ mahimāvasātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be a warrior, one who acts by force; a mighty and glorious king of kings. May he rule the earth bounded by the four oceans, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

82.

82.

“So brāhmaṇo hotu avītarāgo, muhuttanakkhattapathesu yutto;

Pūjetu naṃ raṭṭhapatī yasassī, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be a brahmin, not free from passion, devoted to the science of auspicious moments and constellations. May the glorious ruler of the country honor him, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

83.

83.

“Ajjhāyakaṃ sabbasamantavedaṃ, tapassinaṃ maññatu sabbaloko;

Pūjentu naṃ jānapadā samecca, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May the whole world regard him as a scholar, versed in all the Vedas, and as a practitioner of austerities. May the country folk assemble to honor him, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

84.

84.

“Catussadaṃ gāmavaraṃ samiddhaṃ, dinnañhi so bhuñjatu vāsavena;

Avītarāgo maraṇaṃ upetu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he enjoy a prosperous, excellent village, complete with the four attributes, as if given by Vāsava. May he, not free from passion for the village, meet his death, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

85.

85.

“So [P 4.0310][M 4.0309] gāmaṇī hotu sahāyamajjhe, naccehi gītehi pamodamāno;

So rājato byasana mālattha kiñci, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be a village headman among companions, rejoicing in dances and songs. May he never suffer any misfortune from the king, O brahmin, he who stole your lotus roots.”

86.

86.

“Yaṃ [V 4.0276] ekarājā pathaviṃ vijetvā, itthīsahassāna ṭhapetu aggaṃ;

Sīmantinīnaṃ pavarā bhavātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yā ahāsi.

“Having conquered the earth, may a sole monarch place her as the foremost of thousands of women. May she be the best among women, O brahmin, she who stole your lotus roots.”

87.

87.

“Isīnañhi sā sabbasamāgatānaṃ, bhuñjeyya sāduṃ avikampamānā;

Carātu lābhena vikatthamānā, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yā ahāsi.

“Indeed, among all the assembled seers, may she enjoy sweet food without trembling. May she wander boasting of her gain, O brahmin, she who took away your lotus roots.”

88.

88.

“Āvāsiko hotu mahāvihāre, navakammiko hotu gajaṅgalāyaṃ;

Ālokasandhiṃ divasaṃ karotu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be a resident in a great monastery; may he be in charge of new construction in Gajaṅgala. May he work on a window all day long, O brahmin, he who took away your lotus roots.”

89.

89.

“So bajjhatū pāsasatehi chabbhi, rammā vanā niyyatu rājadhāniṃ;

Tuttehi so haññatu pācanehi, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsi.

“May he be bound with hundreds of snares in six places; may he be led from the lovely forest to the royal capital. May he be struck with prods and goads, O brahmin, he who took away your lotus roots.”

90.

90.

“Alakkamālī tipukaṇṇaviddho, laṭṭhīhato sappamukhaṃ upetu;

Sakacchabandho visikhaṃ carātu, bhisāni te brāhmaṇa yo ahāsī”ti.

“Wearing a garland of milkweed, his ears pierced with tin ornaments; beaten with a staff, may he approach a snake’s mouth. May he walk the streets with his loincloth tucked up, O brahmin, he who took away your lotus roots.”

Tattha tatiyena vuttagāthāya kasimāti sampannakasikammo. Putte gihī dhanimā sabbakāmeti putte labhatu, gihī hotu, sattavidhena ratanadhanena dhanimā hotu, rūpādibhede sabbakāme labhatu. Vayaṃ apassanti mahallakakāle pabbajjānurūpampi attano vayaṃ apassanto pañcakāmaguṇasamiddhaṃ [M 4.0310] gharameva āvasatūti. Idaṃ so “pañcakāmaguṇagiddho kāmaguṇavippayogena mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti dassetuṃ kathesi.

Here, in the verse spoken by the third, 'kasimā' means 'one accomplished in farming.' 'A householder with sons, wealthy, enjoying all pleasures' means 'may he obtain sons, may he be a householder, may he be wealthy with the seven kinds of treasure, may he obtain all desires in the categories of form, etc.' 'Not seeing old age' means 'not seeing his own age, even that suitable for renunciation in old age, may he dwell at home, rich in the five strands of sensual pleasure.' He said this to show that 'one greedy for the five strands of sensual pleasure meets with great ruin through separation from sensual pleasures.'

Catutthena vuttagāthāya [P 4.0311] rājābhirājāti rājūnaṃ antare abhirājāti. Idaṃ so “issarānaṃ nāma issariye parigalite mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjatī”ti rajje dosaṃ dassento kathesi. Pañcamena vuttagāthāya avītarāgoti purohitaṭṭhānataṇhāya sataṇhoti. Idaṃ so “purohitassa purohitaṭṭhāne parigalite mahantaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatī”ti dassetuṃ kathesi. Chaṭṭhena vuttagāthāya tapassinanti tapasīlasampannoti taṃ maññatu. Idaṃ so “lābhasakkārāpagamena mahantaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatī”ti lābhasakkāragarahavasena kathesi.

In the verse spoken by the fourth, 'king of kings' means 'supreme king among kings.' He said this showing the fault in kingship, that 'for rulers, when their rule is lost, great suffering arises.' In the verse spoken by the fifth, 'not free from craving' means 'craving for the position of chaplain.' He said this to show that 'for a chaplain, when his position is lost, great sorrow arises.' In the verse spoken by the sixth, 'ascetic' means 'may one regard him as accomplished in ascetic practice and virtue.' He said this by way of criticizing gain and honor, showing that 'when gain and honor are lost, great sorrow arises.'

Sahāyatāpasena vuttagāthāya catussadanti ākiṇṇamanussatāya manussehi, pahūtadhaññatāya dhaññena, sulabhadārutāya dārūhi, sampannodakatāya udakenāti catūhi ussannaṃ, catussadasamannāgatanti [V 4.0277] attho. Vāsavenāti vāsavena dinnaṃ viya acalaṃ, vāsavato laddhavarānubhāvena ekaṃ rājānaṃ ārādhetvā tena dinnantipi attho. Avītarāgoti kaddame sūkaro viya kāmapaṅke nimuggova hutvā. Iti sopi kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ kathento evamāha.

In the verse spoken by the companion ascetic, 'catussada' means 'abundant in four ways: with people due to being crowded with people, with grain due to abundant grain, with wood due to easily obtainable wood, and with water due to abundant water—this is the meaning of 'endowed with four abundances'.' 'By Vāsava' means 'unshakable like that given by Vāsava,' or it means 'given by a king after having pleased him by the power of a boon obtained from Vāsava.' 'Not free from craving' means 'having become as if submerged in the mire of sensual pleasures, like a pig in mud.' Thus, he too, explaining the dangers of sensual pleasures, said this.

Dāsena vuttagāthāya gāmaṇīti gāmajeṭṭhako. Ayampi kāme garahantoyeva evamāha. Kañcanadeviyā vuttagāthāya yanti yaṃ itthinti attho. Ekarājāti aggarājā. Itthisahassānanti vacanamaṭṭhatāya vuttaṃ, soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapetūti attho. Sīmantinīnanti sīmantadharānaṃ itthīnanti attho. Iti sā itthibhāve ṭhatvāpi duggandhagūtharāsiṃ viya kāme garahantīyeva evamāha. Dāsiyā vuttagāthāya sabbasamāgatānanti sabbesaṃ sannipatitānaṃ majjhe nisīditvā avikampamānā anosakkamānā sādurasaṃ bhuñjatūti attho. Dāsīnaṃ kira sāmikassa santike nisīditvā bhuñjanaṃ nāma appiyaṃ. Iti sā attano appiyatāya evamāha. Carātūti caratu. Lābhena vikatthamānāti lābhahetu kuhanakammaṃ karontī lābhasakkāraṃ uppādentī caratūti attho. Iminā sā dāsibhāve ṭhitāpi kilesakāmavatthukāme garahati.

In the verse spoken by the slave, 'village headman' means 'village elder.' He too, condemning sensual pleasures, spoke thus. In the verse spoken by Kañcanadevī, 'yaṃ' means 'which woman.' 'The sole king' means 'the supreme king.' 'A thousand women' is said for emphasis; it means 'may he place her in the highest position of sixteen thousand women.' 'Among women' means 'among women who wear a parting in their hair.' Thus, even while remaining in womanhood, she condemns sensual pleasures like a heap of foul-smelling excrement and speaks thus. In the verse spoken by the female slave, 'all assembled' means 'sitting unshaken and without shrinking back in the midst of all who have gathered, may she enjoy delicious food.' Indeed, for female slaves, eating while sitting near their master is unpleasant. Thus, she speaks of her own displeasure. 'Let her roam' means 'let her wander.' 'Boasting of gain' means 'wandering about practicing deceit for the sake of gain, generating gain and honor.' Through this, even while remaining in the state of slavery, she condemns sensual pleasures and the objects of sensual pleasure rooted in defilements.

Devatāya [M 4.0311] vuttagāthāya āvāsikoti āvāsajagganako. Gajaṅgalāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tattha kira dabbasambhārā sulabhā. Ālokasandhiṃ divasanti ekadivaseneva vātapānaṃ karotu. So kira devaputto kassapabuddhakāle gajaṅgalanagaraṃ nissāya yojanike jiṇṇamahāvihāre āvāsikasaṅghatthero hutvā jiṇṇavihāre navakammaṃ karontoyeva mahādukkhaṃ anubhavi. Tasmā tadeva dukkhaṃ ārabbha evamāha. Hatthinā vuttagāthāya pāsasatehīti bahūhi pāsehi. Chabbhīti catūsu pādesu gīvāya kaṭibhāge cāti chasu ṭhānesu. Tuttehīti dvikaṇḍakāhi dīghalaṭṭhīhi. Pācanehīti dasapācanehi aṅkusehi vā. So kira attano anubhūtadukkhaññeva ārabbha evamāha.

In the verse spoken by the deity, 'resident' means 'one who maintains the monastery.' 'In Gajaṅgala' means 'in a city of that name.' It is said that building materials were easily available there. 'A window in a day' means 'may he make a window in a single day.' It is said that this deity, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, having lived near Gajaṅgala city, was a resident elder monk in a dilapidated great monastery extending a league. While undertaking renovations to the old monastery, he experienced great suffering. Therefore, concerning that very suffering, he spoke thus. In the verse spoken by the elephant, 'pāsasatehi' means 'with many fetters.' 'Chabbhi' means 'on the four feet, the neck, and the waist—in six places.' 'Tuttehi' means 'with two-pronged long sticks.' 'Pācanehi' means 'with ten goads or hooks.' It is said that he spoke thus, concerning the suffering he himself had experienced.

Vānarena vuttagāthāya alakkamālīti ahituṇḍikena kaṇṭhe parikkhipitvā ṭhapitāya alakkamālāya samannāgato. Tipukaṇṇaviddhoti tipupiḷandhanena piḷandhakaṇṇo. Laṭṭhīhatoti sappakīḷaṃ sikkhāpayamāno laṭṭhiyā hato hutvā. Esopi ahituṇḍikassa hatthe attano anubhūtadukkhameva sandhāya evamāha.

In the verse spoken by the monkey, 'Alakkamālī' means 'adorned with an alakka garland placed around the neck by a snake-charmer.' 'Tipukaṇṇaviddho' means 'having ears adorned with tin ornaments.' 'Laṭṭhīhato' means 'being struck with a staff while being taught the snake-charmers' play.' He too, referring to his own experienced suffering in the hands of the snake-charmer, spoke thus.

Evaṃ [P 4.0312] tehi terasahi janehi sapathe kate mahāsatto cintesi “kadāci ime ‘ayaṃ anaṭṭhameva [V 4.0278] naṭṭhanti kathetī’ti mayi āsaṅkaṃ kareyyuṃ, ahampi sapathaṃ karomī”ti. Atha naṃ karonto cuddasamaṃ gāthamāha –

When those thirteen people had made their oaths, the Bodhisatta thought, 'Perhaps these might suspect me, thinking, "This teacher of ours says it is lost even though it is not lost." I too shall make an oath.' Then, intending to make it, he spoke the fourteenth verse:

91.

91.

“Yo ve anaṭṭhaṃva naṭṭhanti cāha, kāmeva so labhataṃ bhuñjatañca;

Agāramajjhe maraṇaṃ upetu, yo vā bhonto saṅkati kañcidevā”ti.

“Whoever indeed declares as lost what is not lost, may he obtain and enjoy sensual pleasures. May he meet death in the midst of a household, or whoever among you, sirs, suspects anyone.”

Tattha bhontoti ālapanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhavanto yo anaṭṭhe koṭṭhāse “naṭṭhaṃ me”ti vadati, yo vā tumhesu kañci āsaṅkati, so pañca kāmaguṇe labhatu ceva bhuñjatu ca, ramaṇīyameva pabbajjaṃ alabhitvā agāramajjheyeva maratūti.

There, 'bhonto' is a form of address. This is what is meant: "Honorable ones, whoever says, 'It is lost,' regarding a portion that is not lost, or whoever suspects any one of you, may that person obtain and enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure; without attaining the lovely life of a renunciant, may that person die right in the midst of household life."

Evaṃ [M 4.0312] isīhi sapathe kate sakko bhāyitvā “ahaṃ ime vīmaṃsanto bhisāni antaradhāpesiṃ. Ime ca chaḍḍitakheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya kāme garahantā sapathaṃ karonti, kāme garahakāraṇaṃ te pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā dissamānarūpo bodhisattaṃ vanditvā pucchanto anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, when the sages had made their oaths, Sakka, becoming afraid, thought, "While I was testing these sages, I made the lotus roots disappear. Now, as if they were reviling a lump of spit, they revile sense pleasures and make their oaths. I will ask them the reason for their reviling sense pleasures." Having thought this, appearing in visible form, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta and, questioning him, immediately spoke this verse:

92.

92.

“Yadesamānā vicaranti loke, iṭṭhañca kantañca bahūnametaṃ;

Piyaṃ manuññaṃ cidha jīvaloke, kasmā isayo nappasaṃsanti kāme”ti.

“That which beings wander in the world seeking, which is desirable and pleasing to many, and dear and delightful here in the world of the living—why then do the sages not praise sense pleasures?”

Tattha yadesamānāti yaṃ vatthukāmaṃ kilesakāmañca kasigorakkhādīhi samavisamakammehi pariyesamānā sattā loke vicaranti, etaṃ bahūnaṃ devamanussānaṃ iṭṭhañca kantañca piyañca manuññañca, kasmā isayo nappasaṃsanti kāmeti attho. “Kāme”ti iminā taṃ vatthuṃ sarūpato dasseti.

In this context, 'yadesamānā' refers to beings who wander the world seeking sensual objects and sensual defilements through actions both proper and improper, such as farming, cattle-rearing, and so on. This is what is desired, liked, dear, and pleasing to many gods and humans. 'Why do the sages not praise sense pleasures?'—this is the meaning. By the word 'kāme', it indicates those very objects in their own form.

Athassa pañhaṃ vissajjento mahāsatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, answering his question, spoke these two verses:

93.

93.

“Kāmesu ve haññare bajjhare ca, kāmesu dukkhañca bhayañca jātaṃ;

Kāmesu bhūtādhipatī pamattā, pāpāni kammāni karonti mohā.

Indeed, for the sake of sense pleasures they are killed and bound; in sense pleasures, suffering and fear are born. In sense pleasures, lords of beings become heedless; they commit evil deeds out of delusion.

94.

94.

“Te pāpadhammā pasavetva pāpaṃ, kāyassa bhedā nirayaṃ vajanti;

Ādīnavaṃ [P 4.0313] kāmaguṇesu disvā, tasmā isayo nappasaṃsanti kāme”ti.

Those of evil nature, having produced evil, at the dissolution of the body, go to hell. Seeing the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, therefore the sages do not praise sense pleasures.

Tattha [V 4.0279] kāmesūti kāmahetu, kāme nissāya kāyaduccaritādīni karontīti attho. Haññareti daṇḍādīhi haññanti. Bajjhareti rajjubandhanādīhi bajjhanti. Dukkhanti kāyikacetasikaṃ asātaṃ dukkhaṃ. Bhayanti attānuvādādikaṃ sabbampi bhayaṃ. Bhūtādhipatīti sakkaṃ ālapati. Ādīnavanti evarūpaṃ dosaṃ. So panesa ādīnavo dukkhakkhandhādīhi suttehi (ma. ni. 1.163-180) dīpetabbo.

In this context, 'in sense pleasures' means on account of sense pleasures; the meaning is that relying on sense pleasures, they commit bodily misconduct and so forth. 'They are killed' means they are killed with sticks and so on. 'They are bound' means they are tied with ropes and the like. 'Suffering' means bodily and mental unpleasantness. 'Fear' means every kind of fear, such as self-reproach. 'Lord of beings' is an address to Sakka. 'Danger' means faults of this nature. This danger should be explained by means of the discourses on the mass of suffering (Majjhima Nikāya 1.163-180).

Sakko [M 4.0313] mahāsattassa kathaṃ sutvā saṃviggamānaso anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard the words of the Great Being, Sakka, with a stirred mind, spoke the following verse:

95.

95.

“Vīmaṃsamāno isino bhisāni, tīre gahetvāna thale nidhesiṃ;

Suddhā apāpā isayo vasanti, etāni te brahmacārī bhisānī”ti.

"Testing the sage, I took the lotus stalks from the bank and placed them on dry land. The sages dwell pure and without evil; these are your lotus stalks, O practitioner of the holy life."

Tattha vimaṃsamānoti bhante, ahaṃ “ime isayo kāmādhimuttā vā, no vā”ti vīmaṃsanto. Isinoti tava mahesino santakāni bhisāni. Tīre gahetvānāti tīre nikkhittāni gahetvā thale ekamante nidhesiṃ. Suddhāti idāni mayā tumhākaṃ sapathakiriyāya ñātaṃ “ime isayo suddhā apāpā hutvā vasantī”ti.

In this context, 'testing' means: 'Venerable sir, I was testing whether these sages were devoted to sense pleasures or not.' 'Of the sage' refers to the lotus stalks belonging to you, the great sage. 'Taking them from the bank' means taking those laid on the bank and placing them in a suitable place on dry land. 'Pure' means that now, through your taking of oaths, I know that 'these sages dwell pure and without evil'.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta uttered a verse:

96.

96.

“Na te naṭā no pana kīḷaneyyā, na bandhavā no pana te sahāyā;

Kismiṃ vupatthambha sahassanetta, isīhi tvaṃ kīḷasi devarājā”ti.

"We are not your actors, nor are we your playthings; we are not your relatives, nor are we your friends. Relying on what, O Thousand-eyed One, do you play with the sages, O King of Gods?"

Tattha na te naṭā noti devarāja, mayaṃ tava naṭā vā kīḷitabbayuttakā vā keci na homa, nāpi tava ñātakā, na sahāyā, atha tvaṃ kiṃ vā upatthambhaṃ katvā kiṃ nissāya isīhi saddhiṃ kīḷasīti attho.

Here, 'not your actors' means, "O King of Devas, we are neither your actors nor suitable to be played with in any way. Nor are we your relatives, nor your friends. So, relying on what support and depending on what, do you play with the sages?" This is the meaning.

Atha naṃ sakko khamāpento vīsatimaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka, asking for forgiveness, spoke this verse:

97.

97.

“Ācariyo mesi pitā ca mayhaṃ, esā patiṭṭhā khalitassa brahme;

Ekāparādhaṃ khama bhūripañña, na paṇḍitā kodhabalā bhavantī”ti.

"You are my teacher and also my father; you are the refuge for one who has slipped, O holy man. Forgive this one offense, O one of vast wisdom, for the wise are not those whose strength is anger."

Tattha [V 4.0280] esā patiṭṭhāti esā tava pādacchāyā ajja mama khalitassa aparaddhassa patiṭṭhā hotu. Kodhabalāti paṇḍitā nāma khantibalā bhavanti, na kodhabalāti.

In this context, 'this is the refuge' means: 'May the shadow of your feet be the refuge today for me who has slipped in error.' 'Whose strength is anger' means that the wise are those whose strength is patience, not those whose strength is anger.

Atha [P 4.0314][M 4.0314] mahāsatto sakkassa devarañño khamitvā sayaṃ isigaṇaṃ khamāpento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, having forgiven Sakka, the king of the gods, and wishing to have the group of sages forgive him as well, spoke this verse:

98.

98.

“Suvāsitaṃ isinaṃ ekarattaṃ, yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiddasāma;

Sabbeva bhonto sumanā bhavantu, yaṃ brāhmaṇo paccupādī bhisānī”ti.

"It was a well-spent single night for the sages, in that we saw Vāsava, the lord of beings. May all you venerable ones be glad, for the brahmin has received the lotus stalks."

Tattha suvāsitaṃ isinaṃ ekarattanti āyasmantānaṃ isīnaṃ ekarattampi imasmiṃ araññe vasitaṃ suvasitameva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiṃ addasāma, sace hi mayaṃ nagare avasimha, imaṃ na addasāma. Bhontoti bhavanto sabbepi sumanā bhavantu, tussantu, sakkassa devarañño khamantu. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yaṃ brāhmaṇo paccupādī bhisāni, yasmā tumhākaṃ ācariyo bhisāni paṭilabhīti.

In this context, 'well-spent is the sages' single night' means that even a single night's dwelling of the venerable sages in this forest is indeed well-spent. For what reason? Because we saw Vāsava, the lord of beings; for had we lived in a city, we would not have seen him. 'Venerable ones' means may all of you be glad and satisfied, and forgive Sakka, the king of gods. For what reason? Because the brahmin has received back the lotus stalks, that is, since your teacher has regained the lotus stalks.

Sakko isigaṇaṃ vanditvā devalokameva gato. Isigaṇopi jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Sakka, having paid homage to the group of sages, went back to the celestial world. The group of sages, too, having attained meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitā sapathaṃ katvā kilese pajahiṃsū”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Jātakaṃ samodhānento puna satthā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, 'Thus, monks, the wise of old, having taken oaths, abandoned their defilements.' Having said this, he revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Concluding the Jātaka, the Teacher then recited these three verses:

99.

99.

“Ahañca sāriputto ca, moggallāno ca kassapo;

Anuruddho puṇṇo ānando, tadāsuṃ satta bhātaro.

"I and Sāriputta, Moggallāna and Kassapa, Anuruddha, Puṇṇa, and Ānanda—we were the seven brothers then."

100.

100.

“Bhaginī uppalavaṇṇā ca, dāsī khujjuttarā tadā;

Citto gahapati dāso, yakkho sātāgiro tadā.

"The sister was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the maidservant was Khujjuttarā then; Citta the householder was the servant, and the yakkha was Sātāgira then."

101.

101.

“Pālileyyo tadā nāgo, madhudo seṭṭhavānaro;

Kāḷudāyī tadā sakko, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti.

"Pālileyya was the elephant then, and Madhudo was the chief monkey; Kāḷudāyī was Sakka then—thus remember the Jātaka."

Bhisajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Bhisa Jātaka is the fifth.

[489] 6. Surucijātakavaṇṇanā

[489] 6. 6. Suruci Jātaka

Mahesī [V 4.0281][M 4.0315] surucino bhariyāti idaṃ satthā sāvatthiṃ upanissāya migāramātupāsāde viharanto visākhāya mahāupāsikāya laddhe aṭṭha vare ārabbha kathesi. Sā hi ekadivasaṃ jetavane dhammakathaṃ sutvā bhagavantaṃ saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena svātanāya nimantetvā pakkāmi. Tassā pana rattiyā accayena cātuddīpiko mahāmegho pāvassi[P 4.0315]. Bhagavā bhikkhū āmantetvā “yathā, bhikkhave, jetavane vassati, evaṃ catūsu dīpesu vassati, ovassāpetha, bhikkhave, kāyaṃ, ayaṃ pacchimako cātuddīpiko mahāmegho”ti vatvā ovassāpitakāyehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ iddhibalena jetavane antarahito visākhāya koṭṭhake pāturahosi. Upāsikā “acchariyaṃ vata bho, abbhutaṃ vata bho, tathāgatassa mahiddhikatā mahānubhāvatā, yatra hi nāma jāṇukamattesupi oghesu vattamānesu kaṭimattesupi oghesu vattamānesu na hi nāma ekabhikkhussapi pādā vā cīvarāni vā allāni bhavissantī”ti haṭṭhā udaggā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisitvā katabhattakiccaṃ bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “aṭṭhāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ varāni yācāmī”ti. “Atikkantavarā kho, visākhe, tathāgatā”ti. “Yāni ca, bhante, kappiyāni yāni ca anavajjānī”ti. “Vadehi visākhe”ti. “Icchāmahaṃ, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghassa yāvajīvaṃ vassikasāṭikaṃ dātuṃ, āgantukabhattaṃ dātuṃ, gamikabhattaṃ dātuṃ, gilānabhattaṃ dātuṃ, gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ dātuṃ, gilānabhesajjaṃ dātuṃ, dhuvayāguṃ dātuṃ, bhikkhunisaṅghassa yāvajīvaṃ udakasāṭikaṃ dātu”nti.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Migāramātupāsāda near Sāvatthī, told this Suruci Jātaka, which begins with the verse 'Suruci’s wife is the queen,' on account of the eight boons obtained by the great lay follower Visākhā. For one day, after hearing the Dhamma discourse at Jetavana, she invited the Blessed One along with the Sangha of monks for the next day’s meal and departed. When that night had passed, a great rainstorm covering the four continents poured down. The Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, just as it rains in Jetavana, so it rains on the four continents. Monks, let the rain soak your bodies; this is the last great rainstorm covering the four continents.' Having spoken thus, he vanished from Jetavana by psychic power along with the monks whose bodies had been soaked by the rain and appeared at Visākhā’s gatehouse. The lay follower, joyful and elated, thought: 'How wonderful, how marvelous is the Tathāgata’s great power and majesty! For though the floods are flowing knee-deep and waist-deep, not even a single monk’s feet or robes are wet!' She joyfully served the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha, and after the meal service was finished, she said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, I ask the Blessed One for eight boons.' 'Visākhā, the Tathāgatas have gone beyond boons.' 'Venerable sir, they are boons that are allowable and blameless.' 'Speak, Visākhā.' 'Venerable sir, I wish to give rain-cloths to the Sangha of monks for as long as I live, to give meals for incoming monks, to give meals for traveling monks, to give meals for sick monks, to give meals for those who attend the sick, to give medicine for the sick, to give a constant supply of rice-gruel, and to give bathing cloths to the Sangha of nuns for as long as I live.'

Satthā “kaṃ pana tvaṃ, visākhe, atthavasaṃ sampassamānā tathāgataṃ aṭṭha varāni yācasī”ti pucchitvā tāya varānisaṃse kathite “sādhu sādhu, visākhe, sādhu kho tvaṃ, visākhe, imaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ sampassamānā tathāgataṃ aṭṭha varāni yācasī”ti vatvā “anujānāmi te, visākhe, aṭṭha varānī”ti aṭṭha vare datvā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Athekadivasaṃ satthari pubbārāme viharante bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, visākhā mahāupāsikā mātugāmattabhāve ṭhatvāpi dasabalassa santike aṭṭha vare labhi, aho mahāguṇā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya [M 4.0316] nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, visākhā idāneva mama santikā vare labhati, pubbepesā labhiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher asked, 'But Visākhā, seeing what advantage do you ask the Tathāgata for these eight boons?' After she had explained the benefits of the boons, he said, 'Good, good, Visākhā! It is good indeed, Visākhā, that you, seeing this advantage, ask the Tathāgata for these eight boons.' Then, saying, 'Visākhā, I grant you the eight boons,' the Blessed One granted the eight boons, expressed his approval, and departed. Then one day, while the Teacher was dwelling in the Pubbārāma, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, the great lay follower Visākhā, though staying in the state of a woman, obtained eight boons from the One of Ten Powers. How great are her virtues!' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you assembled here now?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Visākhā obtains boons from me; she obtained them in the past as well.' Then he related the story of the past.

Atīte mithilāyaṃ suruci nāma rājā rajjaṃ kārento puttaṃ paṭilabhitvā tassa “surucikumāro”tveva [V 4.0282] nāmaṃ akāsi. So vayappatto “takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhissāmī”ti gantvā nagaradvāre sālāyaṃ nisīdi. Bārāṇasiraññopi putto brahmadattakumāro [P 4.0316] nāma tatheva gantvā surucikumārassa nisinnaphalakeyeva nisīdi. Te aññamaññaṃ pucchitvā vissāsikā hutvā ekatova ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā ācariyabhāgaṃ datvā sippaṃ paṭṭhapetvā na cirasseva niṭṭhitasippā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā thokaṃ maggaṃ ekatova gantvā dvedhāpathe ṭhitā aññamaññaṃ āliṅgitvā mittadhammānurakkhaṇatthaṃ katikaṃ kariṃsu “sace mama putto jāyati, tava dhītā, tava putto, mama dhītā, tesaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karissāmā”ti. Tesu rajjaṃ kārentesu surucimahārājassa putto jāyi, “surucikumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Brahmadattassa dhītā jāyi, “sumedhā”tissā nāmaṃ kariṃsu.

In the past, when a king named Suruci was ruling in Mithilā, he obtained a son and named him Prince Suruci. When the prince came of age, he went to Takkasilā to learn a craft and sat in a hall at the city gate. Prince Brahmadatta, the son of the king of Bārāṇasī, also went there and sat on the very same wooden bench where Prince Suruci was sitting. They questioned each other, became intimate friends, and together went to the teacher. Having paid the teacher’s fee, they began their studies. Not long after, having mastered the craft, they took leave of the teacher and traveled a short distance together. Standing at a crossroads, they embraced each other and made a pact to maintain their friendship: 'If a son is born to me and a daughter to you, or a son to you and a daughter to me, we will perform a marriage ceremony for them.' When they were ruling as kings, a son was born to King Suruci, and they named him Prince Suruci. A daughter was born to Brahmadatta, and they named her Sumedhā.

Surucikumāro vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā āgacchi. Atha naṃ pitā rajje abhisiñcitukāmo hutvā “sahāyassa kira me bārāṇasirañño dhītā atthi, tamevassa aggamahesiṃ karissāmī”ti tassā atthāya bahuṃ paṇṇākāraṃ datvā amacce pesesi. Tesaṃ anāgatakāleyeva bārāṇasirājā deviṃ pucchi “bhadde, mātugāmassa nāma kiṃ atirekadukkha”nti? “Sapattirosadukkhaṃ devā”ti. “Tena hi, bhadde, amhākaṃ ekaṃ dhītaraṃ sumedhādeviṃ tamhā dukkhā mocetvā yo etaṃ ekikameva gaṇhissati, tassa dassāmā”ti āha. So tehi amaccehi āgantvā tassā nāme gahite “tātā, kāmaṃ mayā pubbe mayhaṃ sahāyassa paṭiññā katā, imaṃ pana mayaṃ itthighaṭāya antare na khipitukāmā, yo etaṃ ekikameva gaṇhāti, tassa dātukāmamhā”ti āha. Te rañño santikaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Rājā pana “amhākaṃ rajjaṃ mahantaṃ, sattayojanikaṃ mithilanagaraṃ, tīṇi yojanasatāni raṭṭhaparicchedo, heṭṭhimantena soḷasa itthisahassāni laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā na rocesi.

When Prince Suruci came of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned the craft, and returned. Then his father, wishing to anoint him in the kingdom, thought, 'I have heard that my friend, the king of Bārāṇasī, has a daughter. I will make her his chief queen.' So he sent ministers with many gifts for her sake. Before they arrived, the king of Bārāṇasī asked his queen, 'Dear, what indeed is the greatest suffering for women?' 'The suffering of co-wife rivalry, my lord,' she replied. 'In that case, dear, we have an only daughter, Princess Sumedhā. Let us rescue her from that suffering and give her to whoever will take her as his only wife.' When those ministers arrived and her name was mentioned, the king said: 'Sirs, it is true that I previously made a promise to my friend, but we do not wish to cast her into the midst of a crowd of women. We wish to give her to whoever will take her alone.' The ministers sent word to their king. But the king said, 'Our kingdom is large—the city of Mithilā is seven leagues, the realm's extent is three hundred leagues; at the very least, one is entitled to have sixteen thousand women.' Thus, he was not pleased.

Surucikumāro [M 4.0317] pana sumedhāya rūpasampadaṃ sutvā savanasaṃsaggena [P 4.0317] bajjhitvā “ahaṃ taṃ ekikameva gaṇhissāmi, na mayhaṃ itthighaṭāya attho, tameva ānentū”ti mātāpitūnaṃ pesesi. Te tassa manaṃ abhinditvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ pesetvā mahantena parivārena taṃ ānetvā kumārassa aggamahesiṃ katvā ekatova abhisiñciṃsu. So surucimahārājā nāma hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento tāya saddhiṃ piyasaṃvāsaṃ vasi. Sā pana dasa vassasahassāni tassa gehe vasantī neva puttaṃ, na dhītaraṃ labhi. Atha nāgarā sannipatitvā rājaṅgaṇe upakkositvā “kimeta”nti vutte “rañño doso natthi, vaṃsānupālako pana vo putto na vijjati, tumhākaṃ ekāva devī, rājakule ca nāma heṭṭhimantena soḷasahi itthisahassehi bhavitabbaṃ, itthighaṭaṃ gaṇha, deva, addhā tāsu [V 4.0283] puññavatī puttaṃ labhissatī”ti vatvā “tātā, kiṃ kathetha, ‘ahaṃ aññaṃ na gaṇhissāmī’ti paṭiññaṃ datvā mayā esā ānītā, na sakkā musāvādaṃ kātuṃ, na mayhaṃ itthighaṭāya attho”ti raññā paṭikkhittā pakkamiṃsu.

Prince Suruci, however, hearing of Sumedhā’s perfection of beauty, became captivated through the report of her and sent word to his parents: "I will take her alone; I have no need for a multitude of women. Bring her to me." Not opposing his will, they sent much wealth and brought her with a great retinue, and having made her the prince’s chief queen, they anointed them together. He became known as King Suruci and, ruling righteously, lived in pleasant association with her. However, while she lived in his house for ten thousand years, she obtained neither son nor daughter. Then the citizens gathered in the royal courtyard and cried out. When asked, "What is this?", they said, "There is no fault in the king, but there is no son to maintain your lineage. You have only one queen, but in a royal house there should be at least sixteen thousand women. O King, take a multitude of women; surely among them a meritorious one will obtain a son." But when the king refused, saying, "Friends, what are you saying? I brought her after giving my word, 'I will take no other.' I cannot speak a lie; I have no need for a multitude of women," they departed.

Sumedhā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā “rājā tāva saccavāditāya aññā itthiyo na ānesi, ahameva panassa ānessāmī”ti rañño mātusamabhariyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano ruciyāva khattiyakaññānaṃ sahassaṃ, amaccakaññānaṃ sahassaṃ, gahapatikaññānaṃ sahassaṃ, sabbasamayanāṭakitthīnaṃ sahassanti cattāri itthisahassāni ānesi. Tāpi dasa vassasahassāni rājakule vasitvā neva puttaṃ, na dhītaraṃ labhiṃsu. Etenevupāyena aparānipi tikkhattuṃ cattāri cattāri sahassāni ānesi. Tāpi neva puttaṃ, na dhītaraṃ labhiṃsu. Ettāvatā soḷasa itthisahassāni ahesuṃ. Cattālīsa vassasahassāni atikkamiṃsu, tāni tāya ekikāya vutthehi dasahi sahassehi saddhiṃ paññāsa vassasahassāni honti. Atha nāgarā sannipatitvā puna upakkositvā “kimeta”nti vutte “deva, tumhākaṃ itthiyo [P 4.0318] puttaṃ patthetuṃ āṇāpethā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “tumhe puttaṃ patthethā”ti āha. Tā tato paṭṭhāya puttaṃ patthayamānā nānādevatā namassanti, nānāvatāni caranti, putto nuppajjateva. Atha rājā sumedhaṃ āha “bhadde, tvampi puttaṃ patthehī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti pannarasauposathadivase aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ samādāya sirigabbhe sīlāni āvajjamānā kappiyamañcake nisīdi[M 4.0318]. Sesā ajavatagovatā hutvā puttaṃ alabhitvā uyyānaṃ agamaṃsu.

Hearing this, the chief queen Sumedhā thought, "The king does not bring other women because of his truthfulness; however, I myself will bring them for him." Standing in the position of a wife who is like a mother to the king, by her own choice she brought four thousand women: a thousand noble maidens, a thousand daughters of ministers, a thousand daughters of householders, and a thousand female dancers skilled in all the arts. They too lived in the royal household for ten thousand years but obtained neither son nor daughter. In this same way, she brought another four thousand women on three separate occasions. Thus there were sixteen thousand women. Forty thousand years passed, which together with the ten thousand years she had lived alone, made fifty thousand years in total. Then the citizens gathered and cried out again. When asked, "What is this?", they said, "Your Majesty, command your women to pray for a son." The king agreed, saying, "Very well," and said, "Pray for a son." From then on, longing for a son, they worshipped various deities and performed various vows, but no son was born. Then the king said to Sumedhā, "My dear, you too pray for a son." She agreed, and on the fifteenth-day Uposatha, she undertook the Uposatha of eight factors. Residing in the auspicious chamber, she reflected on her virtues while seated on a suitable couch. The rest of the women, practicing the goat-vow and cow-vow, yet failing to obtain a son, went to the garden.

Sumedhāya sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Tadā sakko āvajjento “sumedhā puttaṃ pattheti, puttamassā dassāmi, na kho pana sakkā yaṃ vā taṃ vā dātuṃ, anucchavikamassā puttaṃ upadhāressāmī”ti upadhārento naḷakāradevaputtaṃ passi. So hi puññasampanno satto purimattabhāve bārāṇasiyaṃ vasanto vappakāle khettaṃ gacchanto ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā dāsakammakare “vapathā”ti pahiṇi. Sayaṃ nivattitvā paccekabuddhaṃ gehaṃ netvā bhojetvā puna gaṅgātīraṃ ānetvā puttena saddhiṃ ekato hutvā udumbarabhittipādaṃ naḷabhittikaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ katvā dvāraṃ yojetvā caṅkamaṃ katvā paccekabuddhaṃ tattheva temāsaṃ vasāpetvā vutthavassaṃ dve pitāputtā ticīvarena acchādetvā uyyojesuṃ. Eteneva niyāmena sattaṭṭha paccekabuddhe tāya paṇṇasālāya vasāpetvā ticīvarāni adaṃsu. “Dve pitāputtā naḷakārā hutvā gaṅgātīre veḷuṃ upadhārentā paccekabuddhaṃ disvā evamakaṃsū”tipi vadantiyeva.

Through the power of Sumedhā's virtue, Sakka’s abode trembled. Then Sakka, reflecting, thought: "Sumedhā prays for a son; I will give her one. However, it is not possible to give just anyone; I will look for a son suitable for her." While searching, he saw the deity Naḷakāra. He was a being rich in merit. In a previous life, while living in Bārāṇasī, as he was going to the field during the sowing season, he saw a Paccekabuddha and sent his workers, saying, "Do the sowing." He himself turned back, led the Paccekabuddha home, and after feeding him, led him to the bank of the Ganges. Together with his son, he built a leaf-hut with a foundation of fig-wood walls and reed walls, fitted a door, and made a walking path. He had the Paccekabuddha stay there for the three months of the rainy season. When the rains ended, the father and son provided him with the three robes and sent him on his way. In this manner, they had seven or eight Paccekabuddhas stay in that leaf-hut and gave them the three robes. Some also say: "The father and son were reed-workers, and while searching for bamboo on the bank of the Ganges, they saw a Paccekabuddha and acted in this way."

Te [V 4.0284] kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattitvā chasu kāmāvacarasaggesu anulomapaṭilomena mahantaṃ devissariyaṃ anubhavantā vicaranti. Te tato cavitvā uparidevaloke nibbattitukāmā honti. Sakko tathā gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā tesu ekassa [P 4.0319] vimānadvāraṃ gantvā taṃ āgantvā vanditvā ṭhitaṃ āha – “mārisa, tayā manussalokaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Mahārāja, manussaloko nāma jeguccho paṭikūlo, tattha ṭhitā dānādīni puññāni katvā devalokaṃ patthenti, tattha gantvā kiṃ karissāmī”ti. “Mārisa, devaloke paribhuñjitabbasampattiṃ manussaloke paribhuñjissasi, pañcavīsatiyojanubbedhe navayojanaāyāme aṭṭhayojanavitthāre ratanapāsāde vasissasi, adhivāsehī”ti. So adhivāsesi. Sakko tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā isivesena rājuyyānaṃ gantvā tāsaṃ itthīnaṃ upari ākāse caṅkamanto attānaṃ dassetvā “kassāhaṃ puttavaraṃ dammi, kā puttavaraṃ gaṇhissatī”ti āha. “Bhante, mayhaṃ dehi, mayhaṃ dehī”ti soḷasa itthisahassāni hatthe ukkhipiṃsu. Tato sakko [M 4.0319] āha – “ahaṃ sīlavatīnaṃ puttaṃ dammi, tumhākaṃ kiṃ sīlaṃ, ko ācāro”ti. Tā ukkhittahatthe samañchitvā “sace sīlavatiyā dātukāmo, sumedhāya santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti vadiṃsu. So ākāseneva gantvā tassā vāsāgāre sīhapañjare aṭṭhāsi.

Having passed away, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and, enjoying great divine sovereignty throughout the six sensual heavens in forward and reverse order, they wandered. Then, wishing to be reborn in higher heavenly realms after passing away from there, Sakka, knowing their intention, went to the door of one of their mansions and, having approached and paid respects to him as he stood there, said: “Dear sir, it is fitting for you to go to the human world.” “Great king, the human world is indeed disgusting and repulsive. Those who dwell there perform meritorious deeds like giving and aspire to the heavenly realms. What shall I do by going there?” “Dear sir, you will enjoy in the human world the prosperity that is to be enjoyed in the heavenly realms. You will dwell in a jeweled palace twenty-five yojanas in height, nine yojanas in length, and eight yojanas in width. Please consent.” He consented. Sakka, having obtained his promise, went to the royal park in the guise of an ascetic and, walking in the sky above those women, showed himself and said, “To whom shall I give a noble son? Who will accept a noble son?” “Lord, give to me, give to me!” Sixteen thousand women raised their hands. Then Sakka said, “I give a son to the virtuous. What is your virtue? What is your conduct?” They lowered their raised hands and said, “If you wish to give to a virtuous woman, go to Sumedhā.” He went through the sky and stood in the lion-window of her dwelling.

Athassā tā itthiyo ārocesuṃ “etha, devi, sakko devarājā ‘tumhākaṃ puttavaraṃ dassāmī’ti ākāsenāgantvā sīhapañjare ṭhito”ti. Sā garuparihārenāgantvā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā “saccaṃ kira, bhante, tumhe sīlavatiyā puttavaraṃ dethā”ti āha. “Āma devī”ti. “Tena hi mayhaṃ dethā”ti. “Kiṃ pana te sīlaṃ, kathehi, sace me ruccati, dassāmi te puttavara”nti. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “tena hi suṇāhī”ti vatvā attano sīlaguṇaṃ kathentī pannarasa gāthā abhāsi –

Then those women informed her, “Come, queen, Sakka, the king of gods, has come through the sky and stands in the lion-window, saying, ‘I will give you a noble son.’” She came with great ceremony, opened the lion-window, and said, “Is it true, lord, that you give a noble son to a virtuous woman?” “Yes, queen.” “Then give one to me.” “But what is your virtue? Tell me. If it pleases me, I will give you a noble son.” Hearing his words, she said, “Then listen,” and describing her virtuous qualities, she spoke fifteen verses:

102.

102.

“Mahesī surucino bhariyā, ānītā paṭhamaṃ ahaṃ;

Dasa vassasahassāni, yaṃ maṃ surucimānayi.

“I am the chief queen, wife of Suruci, brought here first; for ten thousand years it has been so, since Suruci brought me.

103.

103.

“Sāhaṃ brāhmaṇa rājānaṃ, vedehaṃ mithilaggahaṃ;

Nābhijānāmi kāyena, vācāya uda cetasā;

Suruciṃ atimaññittha, āvi vā yadi vā raho.

“O brahmin, I do not recall ever having disrespected King Suruci, the Videhan, lord of Mithila, with body, speech, or mind, whether openly or in secret.

104.

104.

“Etena [V 4.0285][P 4.0320] saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.

105.

105.

“Bhattu mama sassu mātā, pitā cāpi ca sassuro;

Te maṃ brahme vinetāro, yāva aṭṭhaṃsu jīvitaṃ.

“My husband's mother, my mother-in-law, and his father, my father-in-law—they, O brahmin, were my instructors for as long as they lived.

106.

106.

“Sāhaṃ ahiṃsāratinī, kāmasā dhammacārinī;

Sakkaccaṃ te upaṭṭhāsiṃ, rattindivamatanditā.

“I, delighting in non-violence and steadfastly practicing the Dhamma, respectfully served them, untiring day and night.

107.

107.

“Etena saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”

108.

108.

“Soḷasitthisahassāni[M 4.0320], sahabhariyāni brāhmaṇa;

Tāsu issā vā kodho vā, nāhu mayhaṃ kudācanaṃ.

“O brahmin, towards the sixteen thousand women who were my co-wives, never at any time did jealousy or anger arise in me.

109.

109.

“Hitena tāsaṃ nandāmi, na ca me kāci appiyā;

Attānaṃvānukampāmi, sadā sabbā sapattiyo.

“I rejoice in their welfare, and not one of them is displeasing to me; I always have compassion for all my co-wives, as I do for myself.

110.

110.

“Etena saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”

111.

111.

“Dāse kammakare pesse, ye caññe anujīvino;

Pesemi sahadhammena, sadā pamuditindriyā.

“Slaves, workers, messengers, and other dependents—I direct them in accordance with the Dhamma, always with joyful faculties.

112.

112.

“Etena saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”

113.

113.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe cāpi, aññe cāpi vanibbake;

Tappemi annapānena, sadā payatapāṇinī.

“Ascetics, brahmins, and other mendicants, I satisfy with food and drink, always with purified hands.

114.

114.

“Etena [V 4.0286] saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”

115.

115.

“Cātuddasiṃ pañcaddasiṃ, yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī;

Pāṭihāriyapakkhañca, aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ;

Uposathaṃ upavasāmi, sadā sīlesu saṃvutā.

“On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, and also during the special observance period, I observe the Uposatha, perfectly endowed with its eight factors, ever restrained in my virtues.

116.

116.

“Etena saccavajjena, putto uppajjataṃ ise;

Musā me bhaṇamānāya, muddhā phalatu sattadhā”ti.

“By this utterance of truth, O sage, may a son be born to me; if I am speaking falsely, may my head split into seven pieces.”

Tattha mahesīti aggamahesī. Surucinoti surucirañño. Paṭhamanti soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ. Yaṃ manti yasmiṃ kāle maṃ suruci ānayi, tato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ dasa vassasahassāni ekikāva imasmiṃ gehe vasiṃ. Atimaññitthāti muhuttampi sammukhā vā parammukhā vā atimaññinti idaṃ atikkamitvā maññanaṃ na jānāmi na sarāmi. Iseti taṃ ālapati.

Here, ‘mahesī’ means chief queen. ‘Surucino’ means of King Suruci. ‘Paṭhamaṃ’ means the very first among the sixteen thousand women. ‘Yaṃ maṃ’ means: from the time Suruci brought me, from then on I lived alone in this house for ten thousand years. ‘Atimaññittha’ means: I do not know or recall ever having for a moment, whether in his presence or absence, the thought of disrespecting him. ‘Ise’ is how she addresses him.

Te [M 4.0321] manti sasuro ca sassu cāti te ubhopi maṃ vinetāro, tehi vinītā amhi, te [P 4.0321] me yāva jīviṃsu, tāva ovādamadaṃsu. Ahiṃsāratinīti ahiṃsāsaṅkhātāya ratiyā samannāgatā. Mayā hi kunthakipillikopi na hiṃsitapubbo. Kāmasāti ekanteneva. Dhammacārinīti dasakusalakammapathesu pūremi. Upaṭṭhāsinti pādaparikammādīni kiccāni karontī upaṭṭhahiṃ.

‘Te maṃ’ means: both her father-in-law and mother-in-law were her instructors; she was trained by them, and they gave her advice as long as they lived. ‘Ahiṃsāratinī’ means: endowed with the delight known as non-violence; for by her not even an insect or an ant has ever been harmed. ‘Kāmasā’ means: absolutely. ‘Dhammacārinī’ means: she fulfills the ten wholesome courses of action. ‘Upaṭṭhāsiṃ’ means: she served them by performing duties such as caring for their feet.

Sahabhariyānīti mayā saha ekasāmikassa bhariyabhūtāni. Nāhūti kilesaṃ nissāya issādhammo vā kodhadhammo vā mayhaṃ na bhūtapubbo. Hitenāti yaṃ tāsaṃ hitaṃ, teneva nandāmi, ure vutthadhītaro viya tā disvā tussāmi. Kācīti tāsu ekāpi mayhaṃ appiyā nāma natthi, sabbāpi piyakāyeva. Anukampāmīti muducittena sabbā soḷasasahassāpi tā attānaṃ viya anukampāmi.

‘Sahabhariyāni’ means: those who became fellow wives of one husband together with me. ‘Nāhu’ means: a state of jealousy or a state of anger, arising from defilement, has never ever existed for me. ‘Hitena’ means: I rejoice in their welfare; seeing them, I am as pleased as if I were seeing daughters who have grown up at my own breast. ‘Kāci’ means: not even one among them is a person I dislike; all are indeed dear. ‘Anukampāmi’ means: with a tender heart, I have compassion for all sixteen thousand of them as I do for myself.

Sahadhammenāti nayena kāraṇena yo yaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, taṃ tasmiṃ kamme payojemīti attho. Pamuditindriyāti pesentī ca niccaṃ pamuditindriyāva hutvā pesemi, “are duṭṭha dāsa idaṃ [V 4.0287] nāma karohī’ti evaṃ kujjhitvā na me koci katthaci pesitapubbo. Payatapāṇinīti dhotahatthā pasāritahatthāva hutvā. Pāṭihāriyapakkhañcāti aṭṭhamīcātuddasīpannarasīnaṃ paccuggamanānuggamanavasena cattāro divasā. Sadāti niccakālaṃ pañcasu sīlesu saṃvutā, tehi pihitagopitattabhāvāva homīti.

‘Sahadhammena’ means: I employ each one in a task they are capable of, in accordance with the rules and with reason. ‘Pamuditindriyā’ means: when sending them on tasks, I always do so with joyful faculties. No one has ever been sent anywhere by me with anger, saying, ‘Hey, you wicked slave, do this!’ ‘Payatapāṇinī’ means: having washed and outstretched hands. ‘Pāṭihāriyapakkhañca’ means: the four days consisting of the preceding and following days of the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days. ‘Sadā’ means: always restrained in the five precepts, I am one whose self is well-guarded and protected by them.

Evaṃ tassā gāthāya satenapi sahassenapi vaṇṇiyamānānaṃ guṇānaṃ pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi, tāya pannarasahi gāthāhi attano guṇānaṃ vaṇṇitakāleyeva sakko attano bahukaraṇīyatāya tassā kathaṃ avicchinditvā “pahūtā abbhutāyeva te guṇā”ti taṃ pasaṃsanto gāthādvayamāha –

Thus, there is no limit to her virtues, which could be praised in a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand verses. Because there is no limit, while her virtues were being extolled in those fifteen verses, Sakka—on account of his many duties—interrupted her speech, saying, ‘Abundant and marvelous indeed are your virtues,’ and wanting to praise Queen Sumedhā, he spoke these two verses:

117.

117.

“Sabbeva te dhammaguṇā, rājaputti yasassini;

Saṃvijjanti tayi bhadde, ye tvaṃ kittesi attani.

“All these virtuous qualities, O glorious princess, exist in you, O noble lady, which you have proclaimed of yourself.

118.

118.

“Khattiyo [M 4.0322] jātisampanno, abhijāto yasassimā;

Dhammarājā videhānaṃ, putto uppajjate tavā”ti.

“A noble warrior of excellent birth, high-born and glorious, a righteous king of the Videhans—such a son shall be born to you.”

Tattha dhammaguṇāti sabhāvaguṇā bhūtaguṇā. Saṃvijjantīti ye tayā vuttā, te sabbeva tayi upalabbhanti. Abhijātoti atijāto suddhajāto. Yasassimāti yasasampannena parivārasampannena samannāgato. Uppajjateti evarūpo putto tava uppajjissati, mā cintayīti.

In those verses, ‘dhammaguṇā’ means qualities of nature, or true qualities. ‘Saṃvijjanti’ means all those mentioned by you are found in you. ‘Abhijāto’ means highly born or of pure birth. ‘Yasassimā’ means endowed with glory and possessed of a large retinue. ‘Uppajjate’ means such a son will be born for you; do not worry.

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā somanassajātā taṃ pucchantī dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing Sakka’s words, Queen Sumedhā was filled with joy, and wishing to question him, she spoke these two verses:

119.

119.

“Dummī [P 4.0322] rajojalladharo, aghe vehāyasaṃ ṭhito;

Manuññaṃ bhāsase vācaṃ, yaṃ mayhaṃ hadayaṅgamaṃ.

“O ascetic, you with an unadorned face, covered in dust and dirt, wearing bark garments, and standing in the unobstructed sky; you speak delightful words that are agreeable to my heart.

120.

120.

“Devatānusi saggamhā, isi vāsi mahiddhiko;

Ko vāsi tvaṃ anuppatto, attānaṃ me pavedayā”ti.

“Are you a deity from the heavenly realm, or are you a sage of great power? Who are you who have arrived here? Declare yourself to me.”

Tattha dummīti anañjitāmaṇḍito sakko āgacchanto ramaṇīyena tāpasavesena āgato, pabbajitavesena āgatattā pana sā evamāha. Agheti appaṭighe ṭhāne. Yaṃ mayhanti yaṃ etaṃ manuññaṃ [V 4.0288] vācaṃ mayhaṃ bhāsasi, taṃ bhāsamāno tvaṃ devatānusi saggamhā idhāgato. Isi vāsi mahiddhikoti yakkhādīsu ko vā tvaṃ asi idhānuppatto, attānaṃ me pavedaya, yathābhūtaṃ kathehīti vadati.

In those verses, ‘dummī’ means Sakka arrived in a pleasing ascetic guise, unanointed and unadorned; because he arrived in the guise of a renunciant, she spoke thus. ‘Aghe’ means in a place without obstruction. ‘Yaṃ mayhaṃ’ refers to: ‘This delightful speech you are saying to me; as you speak thus, are you a deity who has come here from heaven?’ ‘Isi vāsi mahiddhiko’ means: ‘Who among the yakkhas and others are you that have arrived here? Reveal yourself to me; tell it as it truly is,’ she says.

Sakko tassā kathento cha gāthā abhāsi –

Sakka, informing Queen Sumedhā, spoke these six verses:

121.

121.

“Yaṃ devasaṅghā vandanti, sudhammāyaṃ samāgatā;

Sohaṃ sakko sahassakkho, āgatosmi tavantike.

“Whom the assembly of devas worship when they are gathered in the Sudhammā Hall—I am that Sakka, the thousand-eyed; I have come to your presence.

122.

122.

“Itthiyo jīvalokasmiṃ, yā hoti samacārinī;

Medhāvinī sīlavatī, sassudevā patibbatā.

“Among women in the world of the living, she who is even-tempered in conduct through the three doors, wise, virtuous, reveres her mother-in-law like a deity, and is devoted to her husband—

123.

123.

“Tādisāya [M 4.0323] sumedhāya, sucikammāya nāriyā;

Devā dassanamāyanti, mānusiyā amānusā.

“To such a woman as Sumedhā, of excellent wisdom and pure deeds, the non-human devas come to see her, even though she is human.

124.

124.

“Tvañca bhadde suciṇṇena, pubbe sucaritena ca;

Idha rājakule jātā, sabbakāmasamiddhinī.

“And you, noble lady, through your well-practiced and good conduct in the past, were born here in this royal family, with the fulfillment of all desires.

125.

125.

“Ayañca te rājaputti, ubhayattha kaṭaggaho;

Devalokūpapattī ca, kittī ca idha jīvite.

“And this, O princess, is a winning throw for you in both respects: rebirth in the heavenly realm and fame in this life.

126.

126.

“Ciraṃ sumedhe sukhinī, dhammamattani pālaya;

Esāhaṃ tidivaṃ yāmi, piyaṃ me tava dassana”nti.

“For a long time, O Sumedhā, being happy, protect the Dhamma within yourself. I am now going to the heaven of the Thirty-Three; seeing you is a pleasure for me.”

Tattha sahassakkhoti atthasahassassa taṃmuhuttaṃ dassanavasena sahassakkho. Itthiyoti itthī. Samacārinīti tīhi dvārehi samacariyāya samannāgatā. Tādisāyāti tathārūpāya. Sumedhāyāti supaññāya. Ubhayattha kaṭaggahoti ayaṃ tava imasmiñca attabhāve anāgate ca jayaggāho. Tesu anāgate devalokuppatti ca idha jīvite pavattamāne kitti cāti ayaṃ ubhayattha kaṭaggaho nāma. Dhammanti evaṃ sabhāvaguṇaṃ ciraṃ attani pālaya. Esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Piyaṃ meti mayhaṃ tava dassanaṃ piyaṃ.

In those verses, ‘sahassakkho’ means he is called thousand-eyed because of his ability to see a thousand matters in a single moment. ‘Itthiyo’ means woman. ‘Samacārinī’ means endowed with right conduct through the three doors. ‘Tādisāya’ means to one of such nature. ‘Sumedhāyā’ means to one of excellent wisdom. ‘Ubhayattha kaṭaggaho’ means this is your victory in both this present existence and the future.
