Among these, rebirth in the heavenly realm in the future and fame while living in this life is what is called a ‘winning throw in both respects.’ ‘Dhammaṃ’ means protect such natural virtues within yourself for a long time. ‘Esāhaṃ’ means ‘this is I.’ ‘Piyaṃ me’ means ‘your sight is dear to me.’

Devaloke [V 4.0289][P 4.0323] pana me kiccakaraṇīyaṃ atthi, tasmā gacchāmi, tvaṃ appamattā hohīti tassā ovādaṃ datvā pakkāmi. Naḷakāradevaputto pana paccūsakāle cavitvā tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā rañño ārocesi, rājā gabbhassa parihāraṃ adāsi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi, “mahāpanādo”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Ubhayaraṭṭhavāsino “sāmiputtassa no khīramūla”nti ekekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ rājaṅgaṇe khipiṃsu, mahādhanarāsi ahosi. Raññā paṭikkhittāpi “sāmiputtassa no vaḍḍhitakāle paribbayo bhavissatī”ti aggahetvāva pakkamiṃsu. Kumāro pana mahāparivārena vaḍḍhitvā vayappatto soḷasavassakāleyeva sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā puttassa vayaṃ oloketvā [M 4.0324] deviṃ āha – “bhadde, puttassa me rajjābhisekakālo, ramaṇīyamassa pāsādaṃ kāretvā abhisekaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā “sādhu devā”ti sampaṭicchi. Rājā vatthuvijjācariye pakkosāpetvā “tātā, vaḍḍhakiṃ gahetvā amhākaṃ nivesanato avidūre puttassa me pāsādaṃ māpetha, rajjena naṃ abhisiñcissāmā”ti āha. Te “sādhu, devā”ti bhūmippadesaṃ vīmaṃsanti.

Now, I have some duties to attend to in the heavenly realm, so I will go. You must remain vigilant." Having given her this advice, he departed. The god Naḷakāra, at dawn, passed away and was conceived in her womb. Realizing the pregnancy had taken hold, she informed the king, who arranged for her care. After ten months, she gave birth to a son, and they named him "Mahāpanāda." The inhabitants of both kingdoms said, "This is for our lord's son's milk money," and each threw a coin into the royal courtyard, resulting in a great heap of wealth. Though the king tried to refuse, they insisted, saying, "When the lord's son grows up, this will be for his expenses," and left without taking it back. The prince, raised with a great retinue, reached the age of sixteen and mastered all arts. Observing his son's maturity, the king said to the queen, "My dear, the time has come for my son's coronation. Let us build a splendid palace for him and perform the ceremony." She agreed, saying, "Very well, my lord." The king summoned masters of the science of sites and said, "Fathers, take the builders and construct a palace for my son not far from our residence. I will anoint him as king." They replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and began surveying the site.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vissakammaṃ āmantetvā “gaccha, tāta, mahāpanādakumārassa āyāmena navayojanikaṃ, vitthārato aṭṭhayojanikaṃ, ubbedhena pañcavīsatiyojanikaṃ, ratanapāsādaṃ māpehī”ti pesesi. So vaḍḍhakīvesena vaḍḍhakīnaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “tumhe pātarāsaṃ bhuñjitvā ethā”ti te pesetvā daṇḍakena bhūmiṃ pahari, tāvadeva vuttappakāro sattabhūmiko pāsādo uṭṭhahi. Mahāpanādassa pāsādamaṅgalaṃ, chattamaṅgalaṃ, āvāhamaṅgalanti tīṇi maṅgalāni ekatova ahesuṃ. Maṅgalaṭṭhāne ubhayaraṭṭhavāsino sannipatitvā maṅgalacchaṇena satta vassāni vītināmesuṃ. Neva ne rājā uyyojesi, tesaṃ vatthālaṅkārakhādanīyabhojanīyādi [P 4.0324] sabbaṃ rājakulasantakameva ahosi. Te sattasaṃvaccharaccayena upakkositvā surucimahārājena “kimeta”nti puṭṭhā “mahārāja, amhākaṃ maṅgalaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ satta vassāni gatāni, kadā maṅgalassa osānaṃ bhavissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Tato rājā “tātā, puttena me ettakaṃ kālaṃ na hasitapubbaṃ, yadā so hasissati, tadā gamissathā”ti āha. Atha mahājano bheriṃ carāpetvā naṭe sannipātesi. Cha naṭasahassāni sannipatitvā satta koṭṭhāsā hutvā naccantā rājānaṃ hasāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tassa kira dīgharattaṃ dibbanāṭakānaṃ diṭṭhattā tesaṃ naccaṃ amanuññaṃ ahosi.

At that moment, Sakka's residence showed a sign of heat. Knowing the reason, he summoned Vissakamma and said, "Go, dear one, and construct a palace of gems for Prince Mahāpanāda, nine yojanas in length, eight yojanas in width, and twenty-five yojanas in height." Assuming the guise of a carpenter, he went to the carpenters and said, "Come here after you have eaten your breakfast." Having sent them away, he struck the ground with his staff, and instantly a seven-storied palace of the described type arose. For Mahāpanāda, three auspicious ceremonies—the palace dedication, the parasol dedication, and the wedding dedication—were all held together. People from both kingdoms gathered at the auspicious site and spent seven years celebrating with auspicious festivities. The king did not dismiss them; all their clothing, ornaments, food, and drink were entirely provided by the royal family. After seven years had passed, they clamored, and when asked by King Suruci, "What is this?", they replied, "Great king, seven years have passed while we have been enjoying the festivities. When will the conclusion of the ceremony be?" Then the king said, "Dear ones, my son has never laughed in all this time. When he laughs, then you may go." Thereupon, the people had drums beaten and gathered actors. Six thousand actors assembled and divided into seven groups, but they could not make the king laugh. It is said that because he had long seen divine dramas, their dancing was not pleasing to him.

Tadā bhaṇḍukaṇḍo ca paṇḍukaṇḍo cāti dve nāṭakajeṭṭhakā “mayaṃ rājānaṃ hasāpessāmā”ti rājaṅgaṇaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tesu bhaṇḍukaṇḍo tāva rājadvāre mahantaṃ atulaṃ nāma ambaṃ [V 4.0290] māpetvā suttaguḷaṃ khipitvā tassa sākhāya laggāpetvā suttena atulambaṃ abhiruhi. Atulamboti kira [M 4.0325] vessavaṇassa ambo. Atha tampi vessavaṇassa dāsā gahetvā aṅgapaccaṅgāni chinditvā pātesuṃ, sesanāṭakā tāni samodhānetvā udakena abhisiñciṃsu. So pupphapaṭaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca naccantova uṭṭhahi. Mahāpanādo tampi disvā neva hasi. Paṇḍukaṇḍo naṭo rājaṅgaṇe dārucitakaṃ kāretvā attano parisāya saddhiṃ aggiṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ nibbute citakaṃ udakena abhisiñciṃsu. So sapariso pupphapaṭaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca naccantova uṭṭhahi. Tampi disvā rājā neva hasi. Iti taṃ hasāpetuṃ asakkontā manussā upaddutā ahesuṃ.

Then two chief actors, Bhaṇḍukaṇḍa and Paṇḍukaṇḍa, thinking, "We will make the king laugh," entered the royal courtyard. First, Bhaṇḍukaṇḍa created a huge mango tree named Atula at the king's gate, threw a ball of thread, fastened it to a branch, and climbed up the Atula mango by the thread. It is said that the Atula mango belonged to Vessavaṇa. Then Vessavaṇa's servants seized him, cut off his limbs, and threw them down. The remaining actors gathered the pieces, sprinkled them with water, and he rose up dancing, dressed and covered in floral garments. Seeing this, Mahāpanāda did not laugh. Next, the actor Paṇḍukaṇḍa had a wooden pyre built in the royal courtyard and entered the fire with his company. When the pyre had been extinguished, they sprinkled it with water. He and his company rose up dancing, dressed and covered in floral garments. Seeing this too, the king did not laugh. Thus, unable to make him laugh, the people were distressed.

Sakko taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “gaccha, tāta, mahāpanādaṃ hasāpetvā ehī”ti devanaṭaṃ pesesi. So āgantvā rājaṅgaṇe ākāse ṭhatvā upaḍḍhaaṅgaṃ nāma [P 4.0325] dassesi, ekova hattho, ekova pādo, ekaṃ akkhi, ekā dāṭhā naccati calati phandati, sesaṃ niccalamahosi. Taṃ disvā mahāpanādo thokaṃ hasitaṃ akāsi. Mahājano pana hasanto hasanto hāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto aṅgāni vissajjetvā rājaṅgaṇeyeva pati, tasmiṃ kāle maṅgalaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ. Sesamettha “panādo nāma so rājā, yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayo”ti mahāpanādajātakena vaṇṇetabbaṃ. Rājā mahāpanādo dānādīni puññāni katvā āyupariyosāne devalokameva gato.

Knowing the reason, Sakka sent a divine dancer, saying, "Go, dear one, make Mahāpanāda laugh and then come back." The dancer arrived and, standing in the air above the royal courtyard, performed the "Half-Body" dance—only one hand, one foot, one eye, and one tooth danced, moved, and trembled, while the rest remained perfectly still. Seeing this, Mahāpanāda gave a slight laugh. But the great crowd, laughing and laughing, unable to contain their laughter or establish mindfulness, let go of their limbs and collapsed right there in the royal courtyard. At that moment, the auspicious ceremony was completed. The rest of this story is to be described in the Mahāpanāda Jātaka: "Panāda was the king whose sacrificial post was golden." King Mahāpanāda, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, at the end of his life went to the heavenly realm.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, visākhā pubbepi mama santikā varaṃ labhiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahāpanādo bhaddaji ahosi, sumedhādevī visākhā, vissakammo ānando, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, Visākhā obtained a boon from me even in the past." Then he identified the birth: "At that time, Mahāpanāda was Bhaddaji, Sumedhādevī was Visākhā, Vissakamma was Ānanda, and Sakka was none other than myself."

Surucijātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Suruci Jātaka, the Sixth.

[490] 7. Pañcuposathajātakavaṇṇanā

[490] 7. The Commentary on the Pañcuposatha Jātaka

Appossukko dāni tuvaṃ kapotāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathike pañcasate upāsake ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā dhammasabhāyaṃ catuparisamajjhe alaṅkatabuddhāsane nisīditvā muducittena parisaṃ oloketvā “ajja upāsakānaṃ kathaṃ paṭicca desanā [M 4.0326] samuṭṭhahissatī”ti ñatvā upāsake āmantetvā “uposathikattha upāsakā”ti pucchitvā “āma[V 4.0291], bhante”ti vutte “sādhu vo kataṃ, uposatho nāmesa porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi rāgādikilesaniggahatthaṃ uposathavāsaṃ vasiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this story, beginning with 'Are you now free from care, pigeon?' concerning five hundred lay devotees observing the Uposatha. At that time, the Teacher, seated on a beautifully adorned Buddha-throne in the Dhamma hall amidst a fourfold assembly, surveyed the gathering with a gentle mind. Knowing that a discourse concerning the lay devotees would arise today, he addressed the lay devotees, asking, 'Lay devotees, are you observing the Uposatha?' When they replied, 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' he said, 'Well done! The Uposatha is indeed the lineage of the ancient wise, for the ancient wise observed the Uposatha to subdue defilements such as lust.' Requested by them, he then recounted the past.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ raṭṭhānaṃ antare aṭavī ahosi. Bodhisatto magadharaṭṭhe brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya nikkhamitvā taṃ aṭaviṃ pavisitvā assamaṃ katvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa pana assamassa avidūre ekasmiṃ veḷugahane attano bhariyāya saddhiṃ kapotasakuṇo [P 4.0326] vasati, ekasmiṃ vammike ahi, ekasmiṃ vanagumbe siṅgālo, ekasmiṃ vanagumbe accho. Te cattāropi kālena kālaṃ isiṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇanti.

In the past, there was a forest between three kingdoms, including Magadha. The Bodhisatta, born into a wealthy brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha, came of age, renounced sensual pleasures, and went forth. He entered that forest, built a hermitage, and embraced the ascetic life, dwelling there. Not far from his hermitage, in a bamboo grove, lived a pigeon with his mate; in an anthill, a snake; in a jungle thicket, a jackal; and in another thicket, a bear. These four would visit the sage from time to time to listen to the Dhamma.

Athekadivasaṃ kapoto bhariyāya saddhiṃ kulāvakā nikkhamitvā gocarāya pakkāmi. Tassa pacchato gacchantiṃ kapotiṃ eko seno gahetvā palāyi. Tassā viravasaddaṃ sutvā kapoto nivattitvā olokento taṃ tena hariyamānaṃ passi. Senopi naṃ viravantiṃyeva māretvā khādi. Kapoto tāya viyogena rāgapariḷāhena pariḍayhamāno cintesi “ayaṃ rāgo maṃ ativiya kilameti, na idāni imaṃ aniggahetvā gocarāya pakkamissāmī”ti. So gocarapathaṃ pacchinditvā tāpasassa santikaṃ gantvā rāganiggahāya uposathaṃ samādiyitvā ekamantaṃ nipajji.

Then one day, a pigeon, having left its nest with his mate, went out for foraging. A hawk, following behind her, seized the female pigeon and flew away. Hearing her cry of distress, the pigeon turned back and, looking, saw her being carried away by it. The hawk killed and ate her while she was still crying. The pigeon, consumed by the burning pain of separation and the fever of lust, thought, 'This lust greatly torments me. I will not go foraging until I have restrained it.' So, cutting off the path for food, he went to the ascetic, undertook the Uposatha observance to subdue lust, and lay down to one side.

Sappopi “gocaraṃ pariyesissāmī”ti vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhamitvā paccantagāme gāvīnaṃ vicaraṇaṭṭhāne gocaraṃ pariyesati. Tadā gāmabhojakassa sabbaseto maṅgalausabho gocaraṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ vammikapāde jaṇṇunā patiṭṭhāya siṅgehi mattikaṃ gaṇhanto kīḷati, sappo gāvīnaṃ padasaddena bhīto taṃ vammikaṃ pavisituṃ pakkanto. Atha naṃ usabho pādena akkami. So taṃ kujjhitvā ḍaṃsi, usabho tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto. Gāmavāsino “usabho kira mato”ti sutvā sabbe ekato āgantvā roditvā kanditvā taṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā āvāṭe nikhaṇitvā pakkamiṃsu. Sappo tesaṃ gatakāle nikkhamitvā “ahaṃ kodhaṃ nissāya imaṃ jīvitā voropetvā mahājanassa hadaye sokaṃ pavesesiṃ, na [M 4.0327] dāni imaṃ kodhaṃ aniggahetvā gocarāya pakkamissāmī”ti cintetvā nivattitvā taṃ assamaṃ gantvā kodhaniggahāya uposathaṃ samādiyitvā ekamantaṃ nipajji.

The snake also, thinking, "I will search for food," left its dwelling and searched for food in the cattle-grazing area of a border village. At that time, the village headman’s all-white auspicious bull, having finished grazing, was kneeling at the base of an anthill, playfully scooping up earth with its horns. Frightened by the sound of the cattle’s footsteps, the snake set out to enter that anthill. Then the bull stepped on it with its foot. Enraged, the snake bit it, and the bull died right there. Hearing that the bull had died, the villagers all gathered together, weeping and wailing. They honored it with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, buried it in a pit, and departed. After they had gone, the snake emerged and thought, "Because of my anger, I have deprived this bull of life and caused sorrow to enter the hearts of many people. Now, I will not go out for food without subduing this anger." Having so thought, it turned back, went to that hermitage, undertook the Uposatha observance to subdue its anger, and lay down to one side.

Siṅgālopi [V 4.0292] gocaraṃ pariyesanto ekaṃ matahatthiṃ disvā “mahā me gocaro laddho”ti tuṭṭho gantvā soṇḍāyaṃ ḍaṃsi, thambhe daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Tattha assādaṃ alabhitvā dante ḍaṃsi, pāsāṇe daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Kucchiyaṃ ḍaṃsi, kusule daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Naṅguṭṭhe ḍaṃsi, ayasalāke [P 4.0327] daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Vaccamagge ḍaṃsi, ghatapūve daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. So lobhavasena khādanto antokucchiyaṃ pāvisi, tattha chātakāle maṃsaṃ khādati, pipāsitakāle lohitaṃ pivati, nipajjanakāle antāni ca papphāsañca avattharitvā nipajji. So “idheva me annapānañca sayanañca nipphannaṃ, aññattha kiṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā tattheva abhirato bahi anikkhamitvā antokucchiyaṃyeva vasi. Aparabhāge vātātapena hatthikuṇape sukkhante karīsamaggo pihito, siṅgālo antokucchiyaṃ nipajjamāno appamaṃsalohito paṇḍusarīro hutvā nikkhamanamaggaṃ na passi. Athekadivasaṃ akālamegho vassi, karīsamaggo temiyamāno mudu hutvā vivaraṃ dassesi. Siṅgālo chiddaṃ disvā “aticiramhi kilanto, iminā chiddena palāyissāmī”ti karīsamaggaṃ sīsena pahari. Tassa sambādhaṭṭhānena vegena nikkhantassa sinnasarīrassa sabbāni lomāni karīsamagge laggāni, tālakando viya nillomasarīro hutvā nikkhami. So “lobhaṃ nissāya mayā idaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhūtaṃ, na dāni imaṃ aniggahetvā gocaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā taṃ assamaṃ gantvā lobhaniggahatthāya uposathaṃ samādiyitvā ekamantaṃ nipajji.

The jackal, while searching for food, saw a dead elephant and, thinking, 'A great store of food has been found by me!' went joyfully and bit its trunk; it was as if he were biting a pillar. Not finding any pleasure there, he bit the tusks; it was as if he were biting stones. He bit the belly; it was as if he were biting a granary. He bit the tail; it was as if he were biting an iron rod. He bit the rectum; it was as if he were biting a ghee-cake. Driven by greed, he ate his way into the belly. There, when hungry, he ate the flesh; when thirsty, he drank the blood; and when it was time to lie down, he spread out the intestines and lungs and lay down. Thinking, 'Right here my food, drink, and bed are provided; what shall I do elsewhere?' he delighted in staying right there and lived inside the belly without going out. Later on, as the elephant carcass dried up from the wind and sun, the rectum—the path of excrement—closed. The jackal, as he lay inside the belly, became thin with little flesh or blood and a pale body, and he could not see a way out. Then one day, an untimely rain-cloud poured down rain. The rectum, being moistened, became soft and revealed an opening. Seeing the hole, the jackal thought, 'I have been suffering for a very long time; I will escape through this hole!' and struck the rectum with his head. As he burst out swiftly from the narrow place, his body being sodden, all his fur stuck to the rectum, and he emerged hairless like a palm sprout. Thinking, 'It is because of greed that I have experienced this suffering; I will not take food now without having restrained this greed,' he went to that hermitage, undertook the Uposatha observance to curb his greed, and lay down to one side.

Acchopi araññā nikkhamitvā atricchābhibhūto mallaraṭṭhe paccantagāmaṃ gato. Gāmavāsino “accho kira āgato”ti dhanudaṇḍādihatthā nikkhamitvā tena paviṭṭhaṃ gumbaṃ parivāresuṃ. So mahājanena parivāritabhāvaṃ ñatvā nikkhamitvā palāyi, palāyantameva taṃ dhanūhi ceva daṇḍādīhi ca pothesuṃ. So bhinnena sīsena lohitena galantena attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [M 4.0328] gantvā “idaṃ dukkhaṃ mama atricchālobhavasena uppannaṃ, na dāni imaṃ aniggahetvā gocaraṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā taṃ assamaṃ gantvā atricchāniggahāya uposathaṃ samādiyitvā [P 4.0328] ekamantaṃ nipajji.

The bear also, having left the forest and being overcome by excessive greed, went to a border village in the Malla country. The villagers, hearing that a bear had come, went out with bows, sticks, and other weapons in hand and surrounded the thicket into which it had entered. Realizing it was surrounded by the crowd, the bear came out and fled; as it fled, they struck it with bows, sticks, and the like. With its head broken and blood streaming down, it returned to its own dwelling place. Reflecting, "This suffering has arisen because of my excessive greed. Now, without restraining this greed, I will not take food," it went to that hermitage, undertook the Uposatha observance to restrain its excessive greed, and lay down in a suitable place.

Tāpasopi attano jātiṃ nissāya mānavasiko hutvā jhānaṃ uppādetuṃ na sakkoti. Atheko paccekabuddho tassa mānanissitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ na lāmakasatto, buddhaṅkuro esa, imasmiṃyeva bhaddakappe sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇissati, imassa mānaniggahaṃ katvā samāpattinibbattanākāraṃ karissāmī”ti tasmiṃ paṇṇasālāya nisinneyeva uttarahimavantato āgantvā tassa pāsāṇaphalake nisīdi. So nikkhamitvā taṃ attano āsane nisinnaṃ disvā [V 4.0293] mānanissitabhāvena anattamano hutvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā accharaṃ paharitvā “nassa, vasala, kāḷakaṇṇi, muṇḍaka, samaṇaka, kimatthaṃ mama nisinnaphalake nisinnosī”ti āha. Atha naṃ so “sappurisa, kasmā mānanissitosi, ahaṃ paṭividdhapaccekabodhiñāṇo, tvaṃ imasmiṃyeva bhaddakappe sabbaññubuddho bhavissasi, buddhaṅkurosi, pāramiyo pūretvā āgato aññaṃ ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ atikkamitvā buddho bhavissasi, buddhattabhāve ṭhito siddhattho nāma bhavissasī”ti nāmañca gottañca kulañca aggasāvakādayo ca sabbe ācikkhitvā “kimatthaṃ tvaṃ mānanissito hutvā pharuso hosi, nayidaṃ tava anucchavika”nti ovādamadāsi. So tena evaṃ vuttopi neva naṃ vandi, na ca “kadāhaṃ buddho bhavissāmī”tiādīni pucchi. Atha naṃ paccekabuddho “tava jātiyā mama guṇānaṃ mahantabhāvaṃ jāna, sace sakkosi, ahaṃ viya ākāse vicarāhī”ti vatvā ākāse uppatitvā attano pādapaṃsuṃ tassa jaṭāmaṇḍale vikiranto uttarahimavantameva gato.

The ascetic, relying on his own birth, was under the power of pride and could not produce jhāna. Then a Paccekabuddha, knowing his prideful state, thought: "This is no inferior being; he is a Buddha-to-be. In this very auspicious aeon, he will attain omniscience. I will subdue his pride and create the conditions for him to attain meditative fulfillments." While the ascetic was in his leaf hut, the Paccekabuddha came from the northern Himalayas and sat on his stone slab. When the ascetic came out and saw him sitting on his seat, he became displeased due to his pride. Approaching him, he snapped his fingers and said: "Be gone, you wretch, you ill-omened one, you shaveling, you little ascetic! Why are you sitting on my stone slab?" Then the Paccekabuddha said to him: "Good man, why are you so prideful? I am one who has penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabodhi. In this very auspicious aeon, you will become a fully omniscient Buddha. You are a Buddha-to-be, one who has fulfilled the perfections. After such a long time has passed, you will become a Buddha named Siddhattha." He then revealed everything—his name, clan, family, chief disciples, and so on—and advised him: "Why are you so prideful and harsh? This pride is not suitable for you." Even after being spoken to in this way, the ascetic neither paid him homage nor asked questions such as, "When will I become a Buddha?" Then the Paccekabuddha said: "Know the greatness of my qualities despite your pride of birth. If you are able, wander in the sky like me." Having said this, he rose into the air, and scattering dust from his feet onto the ascetic's matted hair, he returned to the northern Himalayas.

Tāpaso tassa gatakāle saṃvegappatto hutvā “ayaṃ samaṇo evaṃ garusarīro vātamukhe khittatūlapicu viya ākāse pakkhando, ahaṃ jātimānena evarūpassa paccekabuddhassa neva pāde vandiṃ, na ca “kadāhaṃ buddho bhavissāmī’ti pucchiṃ, jāti nāmesā kiṃ karissati, imasmiṃ loke sīlacaraṇameva mahantaṃ, ayaṃ kho pana [P 4.0329] me māno vaḍḍhanto nirayaṃ upanessati, na idāni imaṃ mānaṃ aniggahetvā phalāphalatthāya gamissāmī”ti paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā mānaniggahāya uposathaṃ samādāya kaṭṭhattharikāya [M 4.0329] nisinno mahāñāṇo kulaputto mānaṃ niggahetvā kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍhetvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā nikkhamitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pāsāṇaphalake nisīdi. Atha naṃ kapotādayo upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Mahāsatto kapotaṃ pucchi “tvaṃ aññesu divasesu na imāya velāya āgacchasi, gocaraṃ pariyesasi, kiṃ nu kho ajja uposathiko jātosī”ti? “Āma bhante”ti. Atha naṃ “kena kāraṇenā”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

After the Paccekabuddha had gone, the ascetic was overcome with spiritual urgency and thought: "This ascetic, with such a heavy body, leaps into the sky like a tuft of cotton thrown into the mouth of the wind. Due to my pride of birth, I did not even pay homage at the feet of such a Paccekabuddha, nor did I ask, 'When shall I become a Buddha?' What will this thing called birth do for me? In this world, virtuous conduct alone is great. If this pride of mine grows, it will lead me to hell. I will not go out to seek fruits now without first subduing this pride." Entering his leaf-hut, he undertook the Uposatha observance to subdue his pride. Seated on a spread of sticks, the noble youth of great wisdom subdued his pride, developed the kasiṇa, and produced the five higher knowledges and eight meditative attainments. Emerging, he sat on a stone slab at the end of his walking path. Then, the dove and the three others approached him, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Great Being asked the dove, "On other days you do not come at this time; you are searching for food. Why is it? Have you undertaken the Uposatha today?" "Yes, venerable sir," it replied. Then, wishing to ask for what reason, he spoke the first verse:

127.

127.

“Appossukko dāni tuvaṃ kapota, vihaṅgama na tava bhojanattho;

Khudaṃ pipāsaṃ adhivāsayanto, kasmā bhavaṃposathiko kapotā”ti.

"Now you are free from care, O dove; O bird, you have no need for food. Enduring hunger and thirst, why, good sir, are you observing the Uposatha, O dove?"

Tattha appossukkoti nirālayo. Na tava bhojanatthoti kiṃ ajja tava bhojanena attho natthi.

In the verse, 'appossukko' means without attachment. 'Na tava bhojanattho' means 'is it that today you have no need for food?'

Taṃ [V 4.0294] sutvā kapoto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the dove spoke two verses to explain the reason for its Uposatha observance:

128.

128.

“Ahaṃ pure giddhigato kapotiyā, asmiṃ padesasmimubho ramāma;

Athaggahī sākuṇiko kapotiṃ, akāmako tāya vinā ahosiṃ.

"Formerly, I was infatuated with a female dove; in this very place, we both delighted in sensual pleasure. Then a hawk seized that female dove; against my will, I was separated from her."

129.

129.

“Nānābhavā vippayogena tassā, manomayaṃ vedana vedayāmi;

Tasmā ahaṃposathaṃ pālayāmi, rāgo mamaṃ mā punarāgamāsī”ti.

"Because of the separation caused by her death, I experience mental anguish. Therefore, I observe the Uposatha, so that lust may never come to me again."

Tattha ramāmāti imasmiṃ bhūmibhāge kāmaratiyā ramāma. Sākuṇikoti senasakuṇo.

In the verse, 'ramāma' means we delight in sensual pleasure on this ground. 'Sākuṇiko' means a hawk bird.

Kapotena [P 4.0330] attano uposathakamme vaṇṇite mahāsatto sappādīsu ekekaṃ pucchi. Tepi yathābhūtaṃ byākariṃsu –

When the dove had described the reason for its observance, the Great Being asked the others one by one, starting with the snake. They too wished to explain the truth:

130.

130.

“Anujjugāmī [M 4.0330] uragā dujivha, dāṭhāvudho ghoravisosi sappa;

Khudaṃ pipāsaṃ adhivāsayanto, kasmā bhavaṃposathiko nu dīgha.

"O crooked-going serpent with a forked tongue, armed with fangs, you are a snake of fearsome venom. Enduring hunger and thirst, why, O long one, are you observing the Uposatha?"

131.

131.

“Usabho ahū balavā gāmikassa, calakkakū vaṇṇabalūpapanno;

So maṃ akkami taṃ kupito aḍaṃsiṃ, dukkhābhituṇṇo maraṇaṃ upāgā.

"There was a strong bull belonging to the village headman, with a swaying hump, endowed with beauty and strength. It stepped on me, and in my anger, I bit it; overcome by suffering, it met its death."

132.

132.

“Tato janā nikkhamitvāna gāmā, kanditvā roditvā apakkamiṃsu;

Tasmā ahaṃposathaṃ pālayāmi, kodho mamaṃ mā punarāgamāsi.

"Then the people came out from the village, and after weeping and wailing, they departed. Therefore, I observe the Uposatha, so that anger may not come to me again."

133.

133.

“Matāna maṃsāni bahū susāne, manuññarūpaṃ tava bhojane taṃ;

Khudaṃ pipāsaṃ adhivāsayanto, kasmā bhavaṃposathiko siṅgāla.

"The flesh of the dead is plentiful in the charnel ground, a pleasing sight for your meal. Enduring hunger and thirst, why, good jackal, are you observing the Uposatha?"

134.

134.

“Pavisi kucchiṃ mahato gajassa, kuṇape rato hatthimaṃsesu giddho;

Uṇho ca vāto tikhiṇā ca rasmiyo, te sosayuṃ tassa karīsamaggaṃ.

I entered the belly of a great elephant, delighting in the carcass, greedy for elephant flesh. Hot winds and sharp rays dried up its rectum.

135.

135.

“Kiso ca paṇḍū ca ahaṃ bhadante, na me ahū nikkhamanāya maggo;

Mahā ca megho sahasā pavassi, so temayī tassa karīsamaggaṃ.

I became gaunt and pale, O venerable one; there was no way for me to escape. Then a great cloud suddenly poured down rain, and it moistened its rectum.

136.

136.

“Tato [V 4.0295] ahaṃ nikkhamisaṃ bhadante, cando yathā rāhumukhā pamutto;

Tasmā [P 4.0331] ahaṃposathaṃ pālayāmi, lobho mamaṃ mā punarāgamāsi.

Then I emerged, venerable sir, like the moon freed from the mouth of Rāhu. Therefore, I observe the Uposatha, so that greed may never come to me again.

137.

137.

“Vammīkathūpasmiṃ [M 4.0331] kipillikāni, nippothayanto tuvaṃ pure carāsi;

Khudaṃ pipāsaṃ adhivāsayanto, kasmā bhavaṃposathiko nu accha.

Formerly, you would roam about, crushing the ants on the anthill. Enduring hunger and thirst, why, good bear, are you observing the Uposatha?

138.

138.

“Sakaṃ niketaṃ atihīḷayāno, atricchatā mallagāmaṃ agacchiṃ;

Tato janā nikkhamitvāna gāmā, kodaṇḍakena paripothayiṃsu maṃ.

Disregarding my own dwelling due to excessive greed, I went to a village of the Mallas. Then the people came out from the village and battered me with a bow-staff.

139.

139.

“So bhinnasīso ruhiramakkhitaṅgo, paccāgamāsiṃ sakaṃ niketaṃ;

Tasmā ahaṃposathaṃ pālayāmi, atricchatā mā punarāgamāsī”ti.

With a split head and a body smeared with blood, I returned to my own dwelling. Therefore, I observe the Uposatha, so that excessive greed may never come to me again.

Tattha anujjugāmītiādīhi taṃ ālapati. Calakkakūti calamānakakudho. Dukkhābhituṇṇoti so usabho dukkhena abhituṇṇo āturo hutvā. Bahūti bahūni. Pavisīti pāvisiṃ. Rasmiyoti sūriyarasmiyo. Nikkhamisanti nikkhamiṃ. Kipillikānīti upacikāyo. Nippothayantoti khādamāno. Atihīḷayānoti atimaññanto nindanto garahanto. Kodaṇḍakenāti dhanudaṇḍakehi ceva muggarehi ca.

Herein, with Anujjugāmī ('O crooked-going one') and so on, he addresses him. Calakkakū means one with a swaying hump. Dukkhābhituṇṇo means that bull, being overwhelmed and afflicted by suffering. Bahū means many. Pavisi means 'I entered.' Rasmiyo means the rays of the sun. Nikkhamisaṃ means 'I emerged.' Kipillikāni means ants. Nippothayanto means devouring. Atihīḷayāno means disdaining, blaming, censuring. Kodaṇḍakena means with bow-staves and clubs.

Evaṃ te cattāropi attano uposathakammaṃ vaṇṇetvā uṭṭhāya mahāsattaṃ vanditvā “bhante, tumhe aññesu divasesu imāya velāya phalāphalatthāya gacchatha, ajja agantvā kasmā uposathikatthā”ti pucchantā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Thus, the four of them, having each described their own observance of the Uposatha, rose and paid homage to the Great Being, and asking, “Venerable sir, on other days at this time you go out for the sake of various fruits; why is it that today you have not gone but are observing the Uposatha?” they spoke this verse:

140.

140.

“Yaṃ no apucchittha tuvaṃ bhadante, sabbeva byākarimha yathāpajānaṃ;

Mayampi pucchāma tuvaṃ bhadante, kasmā bhavaṃposathiko nu brahme”ti.

“What you asked us, venerable sir, we have all explained according to our understanding; we also ask you, venerable sir, why do you, O holy man, observe the Uposatha?”

Sopi [P 4.0332][M 4.0332] nesaṃ byākāsi –

He also explained it to them:

141.

141.

“Anūpalitto mama assamamhi, paccekabuddho muhuttaṃ nisīdi;

So maṃ avedī gatimāgatiñca, nāmañca gottaṃ caraṇañca sabbaṃ.

“An unsullied Paccekabuddha sat for a moment in my hermitage; he revealed to me my future and past, my name and clan, and all my conduct.”

142.

142.

“Evampahaṃ [V 4.0296] na vandi tassa pāde, na cāpi naṃ mānagatena pucchiṃ;

Tasmā ahaṃposathaṃ pālayāmi, māno mamaṃ mā punarāgamāsī”ti.

“Even so, I did not pay homage at his feet, nor did I question him because of my conceit; therefore, I observe the Uposatha, so that conceit may never come to me again.”

Tattha yaṃ noti yaṃ atthaṃ tvaṃ amhe apucchi. Yathāpajānanti attano pajānananiyāmena taṃ mayaṃ byākarimha. Anūpalittoti sabbakilesehi alitto. So maṃ avedīti so mama idāni gantabbaṭṭhānañca gataṭṭhānañca “anāgate tvaṃ evaṃnāmo buddho bhavissasi evaṃgotto, evarūpaṃ te sīlacaraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ nāmañca gottañca caraṇañca sabbaṃ maṃ avedi jānāpesi, kathesīti attho. Evampahaṃ na vandīti evaṃ kathentassapi tassa ahaṃ attano mānaṃ nissāya pāde na vandinti.

Therein, ‘yaṃ no’ means ‘that matter which you asked us.’ ‘Yathāpajānaṃ’ means ‘we have explained it according to our own understanding.’ ‘Anūpalitto’ means ‘unstained by all defilements.’ ‘So maṃ avedī’ means he informed me of my future destination and my past, saying, “In the future, you will become a Buddha of such a name, of such a clan, and your virtuous conduct will be such.” Thus he revealed to me my name, clan, and all my conduct—that is, he made it known to me, he told me. ‘Evampahaṃ na vandi’ means: ‘Even though he spoke thus, because of my own pride, I did not pay homage at his feet.’”

Evaṃ mahāsatto attano uposathakāraṇaṃ kathetvā te ovaditvā uyyojetvā paṇṇasālaṃ pāvisi, itarepi yathāṭṭhānāni agamaṃsu. Mahāsatto aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi, itare ca tassovāde ṭhatvā saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Thus, the Great Being, having explained the reason for his own observance of the Uposatha, exhorted and dismissed them, and then entered the leaf-hut. The others also returned to their respective places. The Great Being, with his meditation unimpaired, was destined for the Brahma world, while the others, abiding by his exhortation, were destined for the heaven world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ upāsakā, uposatho nāmesa porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, upavasitabbo uposathavāso”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kapoto anuruddho ahosi, accho kassapo, siṅgālo moggallāno, sappo sāriputto, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, “Thus, lay followers, this observance of the Uposatha is the lineage of the ancient wise ones; the Uposatha should indeed be observed.” Then he connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the pigeon was Anuruddha, the bear was Kassapa, the jackal was Moggallāna, the snake was Sāriputta, and the ascetic was I myself.”

Pañcuposathajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh, the Pañcuposatha Jātaka, is finished.

[491] 8. Mahāmorajātakavaṇṇanā

[491] 8. 8. Mahāmora Jātaka

Sace [M 4.0333] hi tyāhaṃ dhanahetu gāhitoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ [P 4.0333] ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu ayaṃ nandīrāgo tādisaṃ kiṃ nāma nālolessati, na hi sineruubbāhanakavāto sāmante purāṇapaṇṇassa lajjati, pubbe satta vassasatāni antokilesasamudācāraṃ vāretvā viharante visuddhasattepesa ālolesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“If indeed I had seized you for the sake of wealth…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain discontented monk. The Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Monk, why would this delight in lust not agitate one such as you? Indeed, a wind capable of uprooting Mount Sineru is not held back by a nearby withered leaf. In the past, even purified beings who lived for seven hundred years restraining the arising of inner defilements were agitated by it.” Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte [V 4.0297] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto paccantapadese morasakuṇiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Gabbhe paripākagate mātā gocarabhūmiyaṃ aṇḍaṃ pātetvā pakkāmi. Aṇḍañca nāma mātu arogabhāve sati aññasmiṃ dīghajātikādiparipanthe ca avijjamāne na nassati. Tasmā taṃ aṇḍaṃ kaṇikāramakulaṃ viya suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ hutvā pariṇatakāle attano dhammatāya bhijji, suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moracchāpo nikkhami. Tassa dve akkhīni jiñjukāphalasadisāni, tuṇḍaṃ pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ, tisso rattarājiyo gīvaṃ parikkhipitvā piṭṭhimajjhena agamaṃsu. So vayappatto bhaṇḍasakaṭamattasarīro abhirūpo ahosi. Taṃ sabbe nīlamorā sannipatitvā rājānaṃ katvā parivārayiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of a peahen in a border region. When the pregnancy reached full term, the mother laid the egg in the feeding ground and departed. An egg does not perish if the mother is healthy and if no dangers such as long-bodied creatures are present. Therefore, that egg, becoming golden like a kaṇikāra bud, hatched in due time by its own nature, and a golden peacock chick emerged. His two eyes were like jiñjuka seeds, his beak was the color of coral, and three red stripes encircled his neck and ran down the middle of his back. When he reached maturity, his body was the size of a goods-cart and was exceedingly beautiful. All the blue peacocks gathered, made him their king, and attended upon him.

So ekadivasaṃ udakasoṇḍiyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivanto attano rūpasampattiṃ disvā cintesi “ahaṃ sabbamorehi atirekarūpasobho, sacāhaṃ imehi saddhiṃ manussapathe vasissāmi, paripantho me uppajjissati, himavantaṃ gantvā ekakova phāsukaṭṭhāne vasissāmī”ti. So rattibhāge moresu paṭisallīnesu kañci ajānāpetvā uppatitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā tisso pabbatarājiyo atikkamma catutthāya pabbatarājiyā ekasmiṃ araññe padumasañchanno jātassaro atthi, tassa avidūre ekaṃ pabbataṃ nissāya ṭhito mahānigrodharukkho atthi, tassa sākhāya nilīyi. Tassa pana pabbatassa vemajjhe manāpā guhā atthi. So tattha vasitukāmo hutvā tassā pamukhe pabbatatale nilīyi. Taṃ pana ṭhānaṃ neva heṭṭhābhāgena [M 4.0334] abhiruhituṃ, na uparibhāgena otarituṃ sakkā, biḷāladīghajātikamanussabhayehi [P 4.0334] vimuttaṃ. So “idaṃ me phāsukaṭṭhāna”nti taṃ divasaṃ tattheva vasitvā punadivase pabbataguhāto uṭṭhāya pabbatamatthake puratthābhimukho nisinno udentaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ disvā attano divārakkhāvaraṇatthāya “udetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā”ti parittaṃ katvā gocarabhūmiyaṃ otaritvā gocaraṃ gahetvā sāyaṃ āgantvā pabbatamatthake pacchābhimukho nisinno atthaṅgataṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ disvā attano rattirakkhāvaraṇatthāya “apetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā”ti parittaṃ katvā etenupāyena vasati.

One day, while drinking water at a natural pool, seeing his own perfect beauty, the Bodhisatta thought, "I surpass all other peacocks in beauty. If I live with them in the human realm, danger will arise for me. I will go to the Himalayas and dwell all alone in a comfortable place." So, at night, when the other peacocks were asleep, without letting anyone know, he flew up, entered the Himalayas, and having crossed three mountain ranges, he found a forest in the fourth mountain range where there was a natural lake covered with lotuses. Not far from that lake, there was a great banyan tree standing against a mountain, and he perched on its branch. In the middle of that mountain, there was a pleasant cave. Wishing to live there, he settled on the mountain plateau at its entrance. That place could be neither ascended from below nor descended upon from above; it was free from the dangers of cats, snakes, and humans. Thinking, "This is a comfortable place for me," he stayed there that day. The next day, rising from the mountain cave, he sat on the mountaintop facing east. Seeing the rising orb of the sun, he performed a protection for his safety during the day, reciting: "There rises the seeing one, the sole king," and so on. Then he descended to the feeding ground, took his food, and returned in the evening. Sitting on the mountaintop facing west, he saw the setting orb of the sun and performed a protection for his safety during the night, reciting: "There departs the seeing one, the sole king," and in this way he lived.

Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ eko luddaputto araññe vicaranto pabbatamatthake nisinnaṃ moraṃ disvā attano nivesanaṃ āgantvā maraṇāsannakāle puttaṃ āha – “tāta, catutthāya pabbatarājiyā araññe suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro atthi, sace rājā pucchati, ācikkheyyāsī”ti. Athekasmiṃ divase bārāṇasirañño khemā nāma aggamahesī paccūsakāle supinaṃ passi. Evarūpo supino ahosi – “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro dhammaṃ deseti, sā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇāti, moro dhammaṃ desetvā uṭṭhāya pakkāmi”. Sā “morarājā gacchati, gaṇhatha [V 4.0298] na”nti vadantīyeva pabujjhi, pabujjhitvā ca pana supinabhāvaṃ ñatvā “supinoti vutte rājā na ādaraṃ karissati, ‘dohaḷo me’ti vutte karissatī”ti cintetvā dohaḷinī viya hutvā nipajji. Atha naṃ rājā upasaṅkamitvā pucchi “bhadde, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti. “Dohaḷo me uppanno”ti. “Kiṃ icchasi bhadde”ti? “Suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa morassa dhammaṃ sotuṃ devā”ti. “Bhadde, kuto evarūpaṃ moraṃ lacchāmī”ti? “Deva, sace na labhāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthī”ti. “Bhadde, mā cintayi, sace katthaci atthi, labhissasī”ti rājā naṃ assāsetvā gantvā rājāsane nisinno amacce pucchi “ambho, devī suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa morassa dhammaṃ sotukāmā, morā [P 4.0335] nāma suvaṇṇavaṇṇā hontī”ti? “Brāhmaṇā jānissanti devā”ti.

Then one day, a hunter's son, wandering in the forest, saw the peacock seated on the mountaintop. Returning to his home, when he was near death, he said to his son: "My dear, in the forest of the fourth mountain range, there is a golden-colored peacock. If the king asks, you must tell him." One day, Khemā, the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī, saw a dream at dawn. The dream was like this: A golden-colored peacock was teaching the Dhamma. She, crying out "Sādhu!", listened to the Dhamma. The peacock, having taught the Dhamma, rose and departed. While she was crying, "The peacock king is leaving, seize him! Seize him!", she woke up. Upon waking, knowing it was a dream, she thought, "If I say it was a dream, the king will not pay attention. But if I say I have a craving, he will." So she pretended to have a craving and lay down. Then the king approached her and asked, "Queen, what is your discomfort?" "Great King, a craving has arisen in me." "What do you desire, Queen?" "Great King, I wish to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock." "Queen, where can we find such a peacock?" "Great King, if I do not get it, I will die." "Queen, do not worry. If it exists anywhere, we shall get it." The king consoled her and, seated on the royal throne, asked his ministers, "Ministers, the queen wishes to hear the Dhamma from a golden-colored peacock. Are there indeed golden-colored peacocks?" "The brahmins will know, your majesty," they replied.

Rājā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpetvā pucchi. Brāhmaṇā evamāhaṃsu “mahārāja jalajesu macchakacchapakakkaṭakā, thalajesu migā haṃsā morā tittirā ete tiracchānagatā ca manussā ca suvaṇṇavaṇṇā hontīti amhākaṃ lakkhaṇamantesu āgata”nti. Rājā attano vijite luddaputte sannipātetvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro vo diṭṭhapubbo”ti pucchi. Sesā “na [M 4.0335] diṭṭhapubbo”ti āhaṃsu. Yassa pana pitarā ācikkhitaṃ, so āha – “mayāpi na diṭṭhapubbo, pitā pana me ‘asukaṭṭhāne nāma suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro atthī’ti kathesī”ti. Atha naṃ rājā “samma, mayhañca deviyā ca jīvitaṃ dinnaṃ bhavissati, gantvā taṃ bandhitvā ānehī”ti bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā uyyojesi. So puttadārassa dhanaṃ datvā tattha gantvā mahāsattaṃ disvā pāse oḍḍetvā “ajja bajjhissati, ajja bajjhissatī”ti abajjhitvāva mato, devīpi patthanaṃ alabhantī matā. Rājā “taṃ moraṃ nissāya piyabhariyā me matā”ti kujjhitvā kodhavasiko hutvā “himavante catutthāya pabbatarājiyā suvaṇṇavaṇṇo moro carati, tassa maṃsaṃ khāditvā ajarā amarā hontī”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā taṃ paṭṭaṃ sāramañjūsāyaṃ ṭhapetvā kālamakāsi.

The king summoned the brahmins and asked them. The brahmins replied, "Great king, it is stated in our treatises on omens that among water-born creatures like fish, turtles, and crabs; among land-born creatures like deer, swans, peacocks, and partridges; and among humans, there are those who are golden-colored." The king then gathered the hunters in his kingdom and asked, "Have you ever seen a golden-colored peacock?" The others said, "We have not seen one." But the hunter whose father had told him said, "I have not seen it, but my father told me, 'In such and such a place, there is a golden-colored peacock.'" Then the king said to him, "Friend, you will be giving life to both the queen and me. Go, capture that peacock and bring him back." He gave him much wealth and sent him off. The hunter gave the wealth to his wife and children, went to that place, and saw the Great Being. He set a snare, thinking, "Today he will be caught, today he will be caught," but he died without capturing him. The queen, too, unable to obtain her wish, died. The king, enraged, thinking, "My beloved wife died because of that peacock," and overcome by anger, had an inscription written on a golden plaque: "In the fourth mountain range of the Himalayas, a golden-colored peacock roams. Whoever eats its flesh will become ageless and immortal." He placed the plaque in a treasure chest and then passed away.

Atha añño rājā ahosi. So suvaṇṇapaṭṭe akkharāni disvā “ajaro amaro bhavissāmī”ti tassa gahaṇatthāya ekaṃ luddaputtaṃ pesesi. Sopi tattheva mato. Evaṃ cha rājaparivaṭṭā gatā, cha luddaputtā himavanteyeva matā. Sattamena pana raññā pesito sattamo luddo “ajja ajjevā”ti satta saṃvaccharāni bajjhituṃ asakkonto cintesi “kiṃ nu kho imassa morarājassa pāde pāsassa asañcaraṇakāraṇa”nti? Atha naṃ pariggaṇhanto sāyaṃpātaṃ parittaṃ karontaṃ disvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne añño moro natthi, iminā brahmacārinā bhavitabbaṃ, brahmacariyānubhāvena [P 4.0336] ceva parittānubhāvena cassa pādo pāse na bajjhatī”ti nayato pariggahetvā [V 4.0299] paccantajanapadaṃ gantvā ekaṃ moriṃ bandhitvā yathā sā accharāya pahaṭāya vassati, pāṇimhi pahaṭe naccati, evaṃ sikkhāpetvā ādāya gantvā bodhisattassa parittakaraṇato puretarameva pāsaṃ oḍḍetvā accharaṃ paharitvā moriṃ vassāpesi. Moro tassā saddaṃ suṇi, tāvadevassa satta vassasatāni sannisinnakileso phaṇaṃ karitvā daṇḍena pahaṭāsīviso viya uṭṭhahi. So kilesāturo hutvā parittaṃ kātuṃ asakkuṇitvāva vegena tassā santikaṃ gantvā pāse pādaṃ pavesentoyeva ākāsā otari. Satta vassasatāni asañcaraṇakapāso taṅkhaṇaññeva sañcaritvā pādaṃ bandhi.

Then another king arose. He saw the inscription on the golden plate and, thinking, “I shall become ageless and deathless,” sent a hunter to capture him. That hunter also died right there. In this manner, six royal successions passed, and six hunters who went to the Himalayas died there as well. But the seventh hunter, sent by the seventh king, was unable to capture him for seven years, though thinking, “Today I will catch him, today I will catch him!” He wondered, “What could be the reason that the snare does not tighten around this peacock king's foot?” Then, while observing him, he saw him reciting his evening and morning protection and realized, “There is no other peahen in this place; this peacock must be a practitioner of the holy life. It is due to the power of his holy life and the power of his protection that the snare cannot tighten around his foot.” Having understood this by inference, he went to a border region, captured a peahen, and trained her so that when he snapped his fingers, she would cry out, and when he clapped his hands, she would dance. Taking her along, he went and, before the Bodhisatta could recite his protection, he set the snare and snapped his fingers, making the peahen cry out. The peacock heard her cry, and instantly, the defilements that had lain dormant for seven hundred years arose, like a poisonous snake struck by a stick raising its hood. Overcome by defilement and unable to recite his protection, he swiftly approached her. As he placed his foot into the snare, he descended from the sky. The snare, which had not tightened for seven hundred years, tightened in that very moment and bound his foot.

Atha naṃ luddaputto yaṭṭhiagge olambantaṃ disvā cintesi “imaṃ morarājaṃ cha luddaputtā bandhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, ahampi satta vassāni nāsakkhiṃ, ajja [M 4.0336] panesa imaṃ moriṃ nissāya kilesāturo hutvā parittaṃ kātuṃ asakkuṇitvā āgamma pāse baddho heṭṭhāsīsako olambati, evarūpo me sīlavā kilamito, evarūpaṃ rañño paṇṇākāratthāya netuṃ ayuttaṃ, kiṃ me raññā dinnena sakkārena, vissajjessāmi na”nti. Puna cintesi “ayaṃ nāgabalo thāmasampanno mayi upasaṅkamante ‘esa maṃ māretuṃ āgacchatī’ti maraṇabhayatajjito phandamāno pādaṃ vā pakkhaṃ vā bhindeyya, anupagantvā pana paṭicchanne ṭhatvā khurappenassa pāsaṃ chindissāmi, tato sayameva yathāruciyā gamissatī”ti. So paṭicchanne ṭhatvā dhanuṃ āropetvā khurappaṃ sannayhitvā ākaḍḍhi. Moropi “ayaṃ luddako maṃ kilesāturaṃ katvā baddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā nirāsaṅko āgacchissati, kahaṃ nu kho so”ti cintetvā ito cito ca viloketvā dhanuṃ āropetvā ṭhitaṃ disvā “māretvā [P 4.0337] maṃ ādāya gantukāmo bhavissatī”ti maññamāno maraṇabhayatajjito hutvā jīvitaṃ yācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the hunter, seeing the peacock king hanging from the end of the pole, thought: “Six other hunters could not capture this peacock king, nor could I for seven years. But today, this peacock king, seeing this peahen and being overcome by defilement, was unable to recite his protection; thus he came, was caught in the snare, and now hangs head down. I have afflicted such a virtuous peacock king. It is not right to take such a virtuous one as a gift for the king. What will I do with the honor given by the king? I will release him.” Then he thought again: “This peacock king has strength equal to that of an elephant and is full of power. If I approach, he might think, ‘This hunter comes to kill me,’ and, terrified by the fear of death, he might thrash about and break his foot or wings. Without approaching, I will stand in a hidden place and cut the snare with an arrow. When it is cut, he will go according to his own will.” Having so thought, the hunter stood in a hidden place, strung his bow, fitted the arrow, and drew it. The peacock king, thinking, “This hunter, knowing that he caught me by making me overcome with defilement, will come without hesitation; where is he?” looked here and there and saw him standing with his bow drawn. Thinking, “He must want to take me after killing me,” and being terrified by the fear of death, he desired to beg for his life and spoke the first verse:

143.

143.

“Sace hi tyāhaṃ dhanahetu gāhito, mā maṃ vadhī jīvagāhaṃ gahetvā;

Rañño ca maṃ samma upantikaṃ nehi, maññe dhanaṃ lacchasinapparūpa”nti.

“If indeed I was seized by you for the sake of wealth, do not kill me; take me alive. And bring me to the king's presence, friend; I think you will receive no small amount of wealth.”

Tattha sace hi tyāhanti sace hi te ahaṃ. Upantikaṃ nehīti upasantikaṃ nehi. Lacchasinapparūpanti lacchasi anappakarūpaṃ.

In the verse, ‘sace hi tyāhaṃ’ means ‘sace hi te ahaṃ’ (if indeed I by you). ‘Upantikaṃ nehi’ means ‘bring into the presence of’. ‘Lacchasinapparūpaṃ’ means ‘lacchasi anappakarūpaṃ’ (you will receive a form that is not small, i.e., much).

Taṃ sutvā luddaputto cintesi – “morarājā, ‘ayaṃ maṃ vijjhitukāmatāya khurappaṃ sannayhī’ti maññati, assāsessāmi na”nti. So assāsento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the peacock king's words, the hunter thought: “The peacock king thinks, ‘He has fitted the arrow because he wants to kill me.’ I will reassure him.” So, to reassure the Bodhisatta, he spoke the second verse:

144.

144.

“Na [V 4.0300] me ayaṃ tuyha vadhāya ajja, samāhito cāpadhure khurappo;

Pāsañca tyāhaṃ adhipātayissaṃ, yathāsukhaṃ gacchatu morarājā”ti.

“This arrow of mine, fitted to the bow, is not for your death today. I will cut the snare for you; may the peacock king go as he pleases.”

Tattha adhipātayissanti chindayissaṃ.

In the verse, ‘adhipātayissaṃ’ means ‘I will cut’.

Tato [M 4.0337] morarājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the peacock king, wishing to ask the hunter the reason for his release, spoke these two verses:

145.

145.

“Yaṃ satta vassāni mamānubandhi, rattindivaṃ khuppipāsaṃ sahanto;

Atha kissa maṃ pāsavasūpanītaṃ, pamuttave icchasi bandhanasmā.

“Since for seven years you followed me, enduring hunger and thirst day and night, why then do you wish to release me from this bond, I who have been brought under the power of the snare?

146.

146.

“Pāṇātipātā virato nusajja, abhayaṃ nu te sabbabhūtesu dinnaṃ;

Yaṃ maṃ tuvaṃ pāsavasūpanītaṃ, pamuttave icchasi bandhanasmā”ti.

“Have you today refrained from killing living beings? Has fearlessness indeed been given by you to all creatures? Why then do you wish to release me from this bond, I who have been brought under the power of the snare?”

Tattha yanti yasmā maṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ tvaṃ anubandhi, tasmā taṃ pucchāmi, atha kissa maṃ pāsavasaṃ upanītaṃ bandhanasmā pamocetuṃ icchasīti attho. Virato nusajjāti virato nusi ajja. Sabbabhūtesūti sabbasattānaṃ.

In those verses, ‘yaṃ’ means ‘because’. The meaning is: ‘Because you followed me for so much time, I ask you: why do you wish to release me from this bond, I who have been brought under the power of the snare?’ ‘Virato nusajja’ means ‘virato nu si ajja’ (have you indeed refrained today?). ‘Sabbabhūtesu’ means ‘to all beings’.

Ito [P 4.0338] paraṃ –

Henceforth, the hunter, wishing to urge the Bodhisatta to explain the benefit of refraining from killing and giving fearlessness to all beings, spoke this verse:

147.

147.

“Pāṇātipātā viratassa brūhi, abhayañca yo sabbabhūtesu deti;

Pucchāmi taṃ morarājetamatthaṃ, ito cuto kiṃ labhate sukhaṃ so.

“Tell me of the benefit for one who refrains from killing and who gives fearlessness to all creatures. I ask you this matter, O king of peacocks: having passed away from here, what happiness does such a one obtain?”

148.

148.

“Pāṇātipātā viratassa brūmi, abhayañca yo sabbabhūtesu deti;

Diṭṭheva dhamme labhate pasaṃsaṃ, saggañca so yāti sarīrabhedā.

The Bodhisatta, wishing to explain to the hunter the benefit of refraining from killing and giving fearlessness to all creatures, spoke this verse: “I tell you of the benefit for one who refrains from killing and who gives fearlessness to all creatures: in this very life, he obtains praise, and after the breaking up of the body, he goes to heaven.”

149.

149.

“Na santi devā iti āhu eke, idheva jīvo vibhavaṃ upeti;

Tathā phalaṃ sukatadukkaṭānaṃ, dattupaññattañca vadanti dānaṃ;

Tesaṃ vaco arahataṃ saddahāno, tasmā ahaṃ sakuṇe bādhayāmī”ti. –

Hearing those words, the hunter, wishing to inform the peacock king of his own views, spoke this verse: “Some say, ‘There are no gods’; that right here a being comes to annihilation. Likewise, they say there is no fruit of good and bad deeds, and that giving is a practice prescribed by fools. Believing the words of those teachers whom I consider worthy ones, therefore I harm birds.”

Imā uttānasambandhagāthā pāḷinayena veditabbā.

These verses, whose connections are straightforward, are to be understood according to the Pali method.

Tattha [V 4.0301][M 4.0338] iti āhu eketi ekacce samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃ kathenti. Tesaṃ vaco arahataṃ saddahānoti tassa kira kulūpakā ucchedavādino naggasamaṇakā. Te taṃ paccekabodhiñāṇassa upanissayasampannampi sattaṃ ucchedavādaṃ gaṇhāpesuṃ. So tehi saṃsaggena “kusalākusalaṃ natthī”ti gahetvā sakuṇe māreti. Evaṃ mahāsāvajjā esā asappurisasevanā nāma. Teyeva ayaṃ “arahanto”ti maññamāno evamāha.

Herein, 'iti āhu eke' means 'some ascetics and brahmins speak thus'. Regarding 'Believing the words of those... arahants': it is said that his family's associates were annihilationist naked ascetics. They caused even that being, who was endowed with the supporting conditions for the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, to adopt the doctrine of annihilation. Through association with them, having adopted the view that 'there is no wholesome or unwholesome,' he killed birds. Thus, this association with ignoble persons is indeed greatly blameworthy. It was of them that he, thinking, 'These are arahants,' spoke thus.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “tasseva paralokassa atthibhāvaṃ kathessāmī”ti pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ adhosiro olambamānova imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Great Being, thinking, “I will explain to this hunter the existence of the other world,” while hanging head-down from the end of the snare-stick, spoke this verse:

150.

150.

“Cando ca suriyo ca ubho sudassanā, gacchanti obhāsayamantalikkhe;

Imassa lokassa parassa vā te, kathaṃ nu te āhu manussaloke”ti.

“The moon and the sun, both fair to see, travel illuminating the sky. Are they of this world or of the next? How indeed do people in the human world speak of them?”

Tattha [P 4.0339] imassāti kiṃ nu te imassa lokassa santi, udāhu paralokassāti. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Kathaṃ nu teti etesu vimānesu candimasūriyadevaputte kathaṃ nu kathenti, kiṃ atthīti kathenti, udāhu natthīti, kiṃ vā devā, udāhu manussāti?

Herein, 'imassa' means: 'Do they indeed belong to this world, or to the other world?' Or this genitive is used in the sense of the locative. 'Kathaṃ nu te' means: 'How indeed do they speak of the divine sons, the moon and sun, in their celestial mansions? Do they say they exist, or do they not exist? Or are they gods, or are they humans?'

Luddaputto gāthamāha –

The hunter's son, wishing to answer the Bodhisatta, spoke this verse:

151.

151.

“Cando ca suriyo ca ubho sudassanā, gacchanti obhāsayamantalikkhe;

Parassa lokassa na te imassa, devāti te āhu manussaloke”ti.

"The moon and the sun, both fair to see, travel illuminating the sky. They belong to the other world, not to this one; in the human world, people call them gods."

Atha naṃ mahāsatto āha –

Then the Great Being, wishing to refute the hunter's view, said to him:

152.

152.

“Ettheva te nīhatā hīnavādā, ahetukā ye na vadanti kammaṃ;

Tathā phalaṃ sukatadukkaṭānaṃ, dattupaññattaṃ ye ca vadanti dāna”nti.

"Right here your holders of base views are refuted—those who deny a cause and do not speak of kamma; likewise those who deny the fruit of good and bad deeds, and those who say that giving is merely prescribed by fools."

Tattha [M 4.0339] ettheva te nihatā hīnavādāti sace candimasūriyā devaloke ṭhitā, na manussaloke, sace ca te devā, na manussā, ettheva ettake byākaraṇe te tava kulūpakā hīnavādā nīhatā honti. Ahetukā “visuddhiyā vā saṃkilesassa vā hetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ natthī”ti evaṃvādā. Dattupaññattanti ye ca dānaṃ “bālakehi paññatta”nti vadanti.

Herein, 'ettheva te nihatā hīnavādā' means: If the moon and sun are established in the divine world, not the human world, and if they are gods, not humans, then right here, by this much of an explanation, those teachers of yours who hold base views are refuted. 'Ahetukā' are those who hold the view: 'There is no kamma that serves as a cause for purity or for defilement.' 'Dattupaññattaṃ' refers to those who say that giving is 'prescribed by fools'.

So [V 4.0302] mahāsatte kathente sallakkhetvā gāthādvayamāha –

The hunter, having carefully considered while the Great Being was speaking and being reminded of the truth, uttered a pair of verses to ask and urge him to preach the matter:

153.

153.

“Addhā hi saccaṃ vacanaṃ tavedaṃ, kathañhi dānaṃ aphalaṃ bhaveyya;

Tathā phalaṃ sukatadukkaṭānaṃ, dattupaññattañca kathaṃ bhaveyya.

"Indeed, this word of yours is true. For how could giving be fruitless? Likewise, how could there be no fruit of good and bad deeds, and how could giving be merely prescribed by fools?"

154.

154.

“Kathaṃkaro kintikaro kimācaraṃ, kiṃ sevamāno kena tapoguṇena;

Akkhāhi me morarājetamatthaṃ, yathā ahaṃ no nirayaṃ pateyya”nti.

"By doing what, by what reason, with what conduct, by practicing what, and by what ascetic virtue—explain this matter to me, O king of peacocks, so that I may not fall into hell."

Tattha [P 4.0340] dattupaññattañcāti dānañca dattupaññattaṃ nāma kathaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Kathaṃkaroti katarakammaṃ karonto. Kintikaroti kena kāraṇena karonto ahaṃ nirayaṃ na gaccheyyaṃ. Itarāni tasseva vevacanāni.

Herein, 'dattupaññattañca' means: 'And how could giving be something called prescribed by fools?' This is the meaning. 'Kathaṃkaro' means: 'Doing what action?' 'Kintikaro' means: 'For what reason, so that I might not go to hell?' The other terms are synonyms for this.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ na kathessāmi, manussaloko tuccho viya kato bhavissati, tathevassa dhammikānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ kathessāmī”ti cintetvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Great Being thought: 'If I do not answer this question, it will be as if I have made the human world empty. Therefore, I will declare to this hunter the existence of righteous ascetics and brahmins.' Thinking thus, he spoke two verses:

155.

155.

“Ye keci atthi samaṇā pathabyā, kāsāyavatthā anagāriyā te;

Pātova piṇḍāya caranti kāle, vikālacariyā viratā hi santo.

"Whatever ascetics there are on earth, they are clad in ochre robes and are homeless. At the proper time in the morning, they wander for alms, for these good people are restrained from untimely conduct."

156.

156.

“Te [M 4.0340] tattha kālenupasaṅkamitvā, pucchāhi yaṃ te manaso piyaṃ siyā;

Te te pavakkhanti yathāpajānaṃ, imassa lokassa parassa cattha”nti.

"Having approached them at the proper time, ask whichever one is dear to your mind. They will explain to you according to their knowledge the truth of this world and of the next."

Tattha santoti santapāpā paṇḍitā paccekabuddhā. Yathāpajānanti te tuyhaṃ attano pajānananiyāmena vakkhanti, kaṅkhaṃ te chinditvā kathessanti. Imassa lokassa parassa catthanti iminā nāma kammena manussaloke nibbattanti, iminā devaloke, iminā nirayādīsūti evaṃ imassa ca parassa ca lokassa atthaṃ ācikkhissanti, te pucchāti.

Herein, 'santo' means the wise, the Paccekabuddhas, who have pacified evil. 'Yathāpajānaṃ' means: they will speak to you according to their own way of knowing; having cut off your doubt, they will explain. 'Imassa lokassa parassa cattha' means: 'By this kamma one is reborn in the human world, by this in the divine world, by this in hell and so on'—thus they will declare the meaning of this world and the next; 'pucchāhi' means 'ask them'.

Evañca pana vatvā nirayabhayena tajjesi. So pana pūritapāramī paccekabodhisatto sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ oloketvā ṭhitaṃ pariṇatapadumaṃ viya paripākagatañāṇo vicarati. So tassa dhammakathaṃ suṇanto ṭhitapadeneva ṭhito saṅkhāre pariggaṇhitvā tilakkhaṇaṃ sammasanto paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ [V 4.0303] paṭivijjhi. Tassa paṭivedho ca mahāsattassa pāsato mokkho ca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Paccekabuddho sabbakilese padāletvā bhavapariyante ṭhitova udānaṃ udānanto gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, he threatened him with the fear of hell. But that hunter, being a Paccekabodhisatta who had fulfilled the perfections, possessed ripened wisdom like a mature lotus standing open to the touch of the sun's rays. Listening to the Great Being's Dhamma talk, while standing in that very posture, he comprehended the conditioned formations, contemplated the three characteristics, and penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. His penetration and the Great Being’s release from the snare occurred in the very same moment. The Paccekabuddha, having shattered all defilements and standing at the very end of existence, wishing to utter an inspired utterance, spoke this verse:

157.

157.

“Tacaṃva [P 4.0341] jiṇṇaṃ urago purāṇaṃ, paṇḍūpalāsaṃ harito dumova;

Esappahīno mama luddabhāvo, jahāmahaṃ luddakabhāvamajjā”ti.

"As a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin, as a green tree its yellowed leaf, so have I abandoned this cruel nature of mine. Today I abandon the hunter's state."

Tassattho – yathā jiṇṇaṃ purāṇaṃ tacaṃ urago jahati, yathā ca harito sampajjamānanīlapatto dumo katthaci ṭhitaṃ paṇḍupalāsaṃ jahati, evaṃ ahampi ajja luddabhāvaṃ dāruṇabhāvaṃ jahitvā ṭhito, so dāni esa pahīno mama luddabhāvo, sādhu vata jahāmahaṃ luddakabhāvamajjāti. Jahāmahanti pajahiṃ ahanti attho.

Its meaning is: Just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin, and just as a green tree with fresh green leaves sheds a yellowed leaf remaining on it, so too have I, having today abandoned my cruel and fierce nature, now stand free. Now this cruel nature of mine is abandoned. It is indeed good that I have abandoned the hunter's state today! 'Jahāmahaṃ' means 'I have abandoned'.

So imaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā “ahaṃ tāva sabbakilesabandhanehi mutto, nivesane pana me bandhitvā ṭhapitā bahū sakuṇā atthi, te kathaṃ mocessāmī”ti cintetvā mahāsattaṃ pucchi – “morarāja, nivesane me bahū sakuṇā [M 4.0341] baddhā atthi, te kathaṃ mocessāmī”ti? Paccekabuddhatopi sabbaññubodhisattānaññeva upāyapariggahañāṇaṃ mahantataraṃ hoti, tena naṃ āha “yaṃ vo maggena kilese khaṇḍetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, taṃ ārabbha saccakiriyaṃ karotha, sakalajambudīpe bandhanagato satto nāma na bhavissatī”ti. So bodhisattena dinnanayadvāre ṭhatvā saccakiriyaṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Having uttered this inspired utterance, he thought, "I am now freed from all the bonds of the defilements, but in my house many birds are kept in bondage—how shall I release them?" Reflecting thus, he asked the Great Being: "O king of peacocks, many birds are bound in my house—how shall I release them?" This is true: the knowledge of encompassing skillful means possessed by all-knowing Bodhisattas is far greater even than that of Paccekabuddhas. Because of that great knowledge, the Bodhisatta peacock king said to him: "Venerable sir, make an act of truth concerning that path of Arahantship by which you have shattered the defilements and penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. Then there will not be a single being in all of Jambudīpa who remains in bondage." Standing at the gateway of the method given by the Bodhisatta, the Paccekabuddha, wishing to make an act of truth, spoke this verse:

158.

158.

“Ye cāpi me sakuṇā atthi baddhā, satāninekāni nivesanasmiṃ;

Tesampahaṃ jīvitamajja dammi, mokkhañca te pattā sakaṃ niketa”nti.

"Whatever birds of mine are bound, many hundreds in my dwelling; to them I give their lives today, and may they attain freedom and return to their own homes."

Tattha mokkhañca te pattāti svāhaṃ mokkhaṃ patto paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito, te satte jīvitadānena anukampāmi, etena saccena. Sakaṃ niketanti sabbepi te sattā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantūti vadati.

Therein, 'and may they attain freedom' means: 'I myself have attained freedom, having penetrated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and so I stand. Out of compassion, I grant life to these beings. By this truth, let them reach freedom.' 'And their own homes' means: 'May all those beings go to their own respective dwelling places.' Thus he speaks.

Athassa [P 4.0342] saccakiriyāsamakālameva sabbe bandhanā muccitvā tuṭṭhiravaṃ ravantā sakaṭṭhānameva agamiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tesaṃ tesaṃ gehesu biḷāle ādiṃ katvā sakalajambudīpe bandhanagato satto nāma nāhosi. Paccekabuddho hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā sīsaṃ parāmasi. Tāvadeva gihiliṅgaṃ [V 4.0304] antaradhāyi, pabbajitaliṅgaṃ pāturahosi. So saṭṭhivassikatthero viya ākappasampanno aṭṭhaparikkhāradharo hutvā “tvameva mama patiṭṭhā ahosī”ti morarājassa añjaliṃ paggayha padakkhiṇaṃ katvā ākāse uppatitvā nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Morarājāpi yaṭṭhiaggato uppatitvā gocaraṃ gahetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gato. Idāni luddassa satta vassāni pāsahatthassa caritvāpi morarājānaṃ nissāya dukkhā muttabhāvaṃ pakāsento satthā osānagāthamāha –

Then, at the very moment of his act of truth, all [the birds] were freed from their bonds and, uttering joyful cries, went to their own places. At that instant, starting with cats in their respective houses, throughout all of Jambudīpa, there was not a single being in bondage. The Paccekabuddha raised his hand and touched his head. Instantly, his lay appearance vanished, and the appearance of a monk manifested. Endowed with the deportment of an elder of sixty years and bearing the eight requisites, he raised his hands in reverence to the peacock king, performed a right-sided circumambulation, and said, 'You alone have been my support.' Then he rose into the air and went to the Nandamūla cave. The peacock king, too, flew up from the tip of the snare-pole, gathered his food, and went to his own dwelling place. Now, the Teacher, in order to make clear how the hunter, after wandering for seven years with a snare in hand, was freed from the suffering of the round of rebirths by relying on the peacock king, spoke this concluding verse:

159.

159.

“Luddo [M 4.0342] carī pāsahattho araññe, bādhetu morādhipatiṃ yasassiṃ;

Bandhitvā morādhipatiṃ yasassiṃ, dukkhā sa pamucci yathāhaṃ pamutto”ti.

"A hunter with a snare in hand wandered the forest to harm the glorious lord of peacocks; having bound the glorious lord of peacocks, he was released from suffering, just as I am released."

Tattha bādhetūti māretuṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Bandhitvāti bandhitvā ṭhitassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaṃvego hutvāti attho. Yathāhanti yathā ahaṃ sayambhuñāṇena mutto, evameva sopi muttoti.

Therein, 'to harm' (bādhetuṃ) means to kill; or this is the reading itself. 'Having bound' (bandhitvā) means: having heard the Dhamma talk of the one who stood bound, he became filled with spiritual urgency—this is the meaning. 'Just as I' (yathāhaṃ) means: just as I was freed by the knowledge of self-enlightenment (sayambhuñāṇa), so too was he freed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā morarājā ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had been longing for the lay life attained Arahantship. At that time, I myself was the peacock king.

Mahāmorajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Mahā-Mora Jātaka, the eighth.

[492] 9. Tacchasūkarajātakavaṇṇanā

[492] 9. The Commentary on the Tacchasūkara Jātaka

Yadesamānā vicarimhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve mahallakatthere ārabbha kathesi. Mahākosalo kira rañño bimbisārassa dhītaraṃ dento dhītu nhānīyamūlatthāya kāsigāmaṃ adāsi. Pasenadi rājā ajātasattunā [P 4.0343] pitari mārite taṃ gāmaṃ acchindi. Tesu tassatthāya yujjhantesu paṭhamaṃ ajātasattussa jayo ahosi. Kosalarājā parājayappatto amacce pucchi “kena nu kho upāyena ajātasattuṃ gaṇheyyāmā”ti. Mahārāja, bhikkhū nāma mantakusalā honti, carapurise pesetvā vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Rājā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā “etha, tumhe vihāraṃ gantvā paṭicchannā hutvā bhadantānaṃ kathaṃ pariggaṇhathā”ti carapurise payojesi. Jetavanepi bahū rājapurisā pabbajitā honti. Tesu dve mahallakattherā vihārapaccante [V 4.0305] paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasanti, eko dhanuggahatissatthero nāma, eko mantidattatthero nāma. Te sabbarattiṃ supitvā paccūsakāle pabujjhiṃsu.

"While we wandered searching," this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning two elderly elders. It is said that King Mahākosala, when giving his daughter to King Bimbisāra, gave a village in Kāsī for the cost of her bathing powder. When Ajātasattu killed his father, King Pasenadi seized that village. When they fought for its sake, Ajātasattu was at first victorious. The defeated King of Kosala asked his ministers, "By what means can we capture Ajātasattu?" "Great King, monks are indeed skilled in counsel. It is proper to send spies to overhear the monks' conversation in the monastery." The King agreed, saying, "Good," and dispatched spies, saying, "Go to the monastery, remain concealed, and overhear the venerable sirs' conversation." In Jetavana, many of the king's men had gone forth. Among them, two elderly elders lived in a leaf-hut on the outskirts of the monastery; one was named Elder Dhanuggahatissa, the other Elder Mantidatta. Having slept the whole night, they awoke at dawn.

Tesu [M 4.0343] dhanuggahatissatthero aggiṃ jāletvā āha “bhante, mantidattattherā”ti. “Kiṃ bhante”ti. “Niddāyatha tumhe”ti. “Na niddāyāmi, kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Bhante, lālako vatāyaṃ kosalarājā cāṭimattabhojanameva bhuñjituṃ jānātī”ti. “Atha kiṃ bhante”ti. “Attano kucchimhi pāṇakamattena ajātasattunā parājito rājā”ti. “Kinti pana bhante kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Bhante, mantidattatthera yuddhaṃ nāma sakaṭabyūhacakkabyūhapadumabyūhavasena tividhaṃ. Tesu bhāgineyyaṃ ajātasattuṃ gaṇhantena sakaṭabyūhaṃ katvā gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, asukasmiṃ nāma pabbatakaṇṇe dvīsu passesu sūrapurise ṭhapetvā purato balaṃ dassetvā anto paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā naditvā vaggitvā kumine paviṭṭhamacchaṃ viya antomuṭṭhiyaṃ katvāva naṃ gahetuṃ sakkā”ti.

Among them, Elder Dhanuggahatissa lit a fire and said, "Venerable Elder Mantidatta!" "What is it, venerable sir?" "Are you sleeping?" "I am not sleeping. What is to be done?" "Venerable sir, this King of Kosala is surely a simpleton; he knows only how to eat a pot-sized meal." "What of it, venerable sir?" "The King has been defeated by Ajātasattu, who is like a mere small creature in his own belly." "But what, venerable sir, should be done?" "Venerable Mantidatta, battle formations are of three kinds: the wagon formation, the wheel formation, and the lotus formation. Among these, to capture his nephew Ajātasattu, one should use the wagon formation. At a certain mountain bend, having stationed brave men on both sides and showing a force in front, and then knowing he has entered within—by shouting and charging, one can capture him, making him like a fish that has entered a trap, as if held within one's fist."

Payojitapurisā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā mahatiyā senāya gantvā tathā katvā ajātasattuṃ gahetvā saṅkhalikabandhanena bandhitvā katipāhaṃ nimmadaṃ katvā “puna evarūpaṃ mā karī”ti assāsetvā mocetvā dhītaraṃ vajirakumāriṃ nāma tassa datvā mahantena parivārena vissajjesi. “Kosalaraññā dhanuggahatissattherassa saṃvidhānena ajātasattu gahito”ti bhikkhūnaṃ antare kathā samuṭṭhahi, dhammasabhāyampi tameva kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi dhanuggahatisso yuddhasaṃvidhāne chekoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The spies heard this conversation and reported it to the king. The King of Kosala set out with a great army and, following the instructions of the old monk, captured Ajātasattu. He bound him with shackles and subdued him for two or three days. Then, after warning him, 'Do not do such a thing again,' he released him, gave him his daughter named Vajirakumārī, and sent him away with a large retinue. A discussion arose among the monks: 'The King of Kosala captured Ajātasattu through the strategy of Elder Dhanuggahatissa.' They also raised this same topic in the hall of Dhamma. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Dhanuggahatissa was skilled in battle strategy.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 4.0344] bārāṇasinagarassa dvāragāmavāsī eko vaḍḍhakī dāruatthāya araññaṃ gantvā āvāṭe patitaṃ ekaṃ sūkarapotakaṃ disvā ānetvā “tacchasūkaro”tissa nāmaṃ katvā posesi. So tassa upakārako ahosi. Tuṇḍena rukkhe parivattetvā deti, dāṭhāya veṭhetvā kāḷasuttaṃ kaḍḍhati, mukhena ḍaṃsitvā vāsinikhādanamuggare āharati. So vuḍḍhippatto mahābalo mahāsarīro ahosi. Atha vaḍḍhakī tasmiṃ puttapemaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā “imaṃ idha vasantaṃ kocideva hiṃseyyā”ti araññe vissajjesi. So cintesi “ahaṃ imasmiṃ araññe ekakova vasituṃ na sakkhissāmi, ñātake pariyesitvā tehi [M 4.0344] parivuto vasissāmī”ti. So vanaghaṭāya sūkare pariyesanto bahū sūkare disvā tussitvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, a carpenter living in a gate-village of the city of Bārāṇasī went into the forest for wood. He saw a young boar that had fallen into a pit, brought it home, named it 'Tacchasūkara,' and raised it. It was helpful to him. With its snout, it would turn logs; with its tusks, it would wind and pull the marking string; and with its mouth, it would seize and bring the adze, chisel, and mallet. It grew, becoming very strong and large-bodied. Then the carpenter, developing fatherly love for it, thought, 'Someone living here might harm it,' and released it into the forest. The boar thought, 'I cannot live alone in this forest. I must seek out my kinsmen and live surrounded by them.' Searching for boars in the forest thicket, it saw many boars and, delighted, uttered three verses:

160.

160.

“Yadesamānā [V 4.0306] vicarimha, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Anvesaṃ vicariṃ ñātī, teme adhigatā mayā.

"Seeking whom we wandered through mountains and forests; I wandered searching for kinsmen, and they have been found by me.

161.

161.

“Bahuñcidaṃ mūlaphalaṃ, bhakkho cāyaṃ anappako;

Rammā cimā girīnajjo, phāsuvāso bhavissati.

"Here are many roots and fruits, and this food is plentiful; delightful are these mountain rivers, it will be a pleasant dwelling.

162.

162.

“Idhevāhaṃ vasissāmi, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Appossukko nirāsaṅkī, asoko akutobhayo”ti.

"Here indeed I shall dwell, with all my kinsmen; unconcerned, without suspicion, sorrowless, and with no fear from any quarter."

Tattha yadesamānāti yaṃ ñātigaṇaṃ pariyesantā mayaṃ vicarimha. Anvesanti ciraṃ vata anvesanto vicariṃ. Temeti te ime. Bhakkhoti sveva vanamūlaphalasaṅkhāto bhakkho. Appossukkoti anussukko hutvā.

Therein, 'yadesamānā' means: 'the kinsmen whom we wandered searching for.' 'Anvesaṃ' means: 'for a long time indeed, searching, I wandered.' 'Teme' means: 'those are these.' 'Bhakkhoti' means: 'that very food reckoned as forest roots and fruits.' 'Appossukko' means: 'being free from care.'

Sūkarā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā catutthaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Having heard his words, the boars spoke the fourth verse:

163.

163.

“Aññampi leṇaṃ pariyesa, sattu no idha vijjati;

So taccha sūkare hanti, idhāgantvā varaṃ vara”nti.

"Seek another shelter, for our enemy is found here. That one, O Tacchaka, slays the choicest of boars, having come here."

Tattha tacchāti taṃ nāmenālapanti. Varaṃ varanti sūkare hananto thūlamaṃsaṃ varaṃ varaññeva hanati.

Therein, 'tacchā' is how they address him by name. 'Varaṃ varaṃ' means: while killing boars, he kills the fat-fleshed ones, the very best.

Ito paraṃ uttānasambandhagāthā pāḷinayena veditabbā –

From this point onwards, the verses with a clear connection should be understood according to the method of the Pāli text.

164.

164.

“Ko numhākaṃ idha sattu, ko ñātī susamāgate;

Duppadhaṃse padhaṃseti, taṃ me akkhātha pucchitā.

"Who indeed is our enemy here, who assails our well-assembled, unassailable kinsmen? Tell me this, when you are asked."

165.

165.

“Uddhaggarājī [P 4.0345] migarājā, balī dāṭhāvudho migo;

So taccha sūkare hanti, idhāgantvā varaṃ varaṃ.

"The king of beasts with upward-pointing stripes, mighty, a beast armed with fangs; he, O Tacchaka, slays the choicest boars, having come here."

166.

166.

“Na [V 4.0307] no dāṭhā na vijjanti, balaṃ kāye samohitaṃ;

Sabbe samaggā hutvāna, vasaṃ kāhāma ekakaṃ.

"It is not that we lack fangs, and strength is well-established in our bodies; all of us, having united, will bring the solitary one under our power."

167.

167.

“Hadayaṅgamaṃ [M 4.0345] kaṇṇasukhaṃ, vācaṃ bhāsasi tacchaka;

Yopi yuddhe palāyeyya, tampi pacchā hanāmase”ti.

"O Tacchaka, you speak words pleasing to the heart and delightful to the ear; whoever might flee in battle, we would strike even them down afterwards."

Tattha ko numhākanti ahaṃ tumhe disvāva “ime sūkarā appamaṃsalohitā, bhayena nesaṃ bhavitabba”nti cintesiṃ, tasmā me ācikkhatha, ko nu amhākaṃ idha sattu. Uddhaggarājīti uddhaggāhi sarīrarājīhi samannāgato. Byagghaṃ sandhāyevamāhaṃsu. Yopīti yo amhākaṃ antare ekopi palāyissati, tampi mayaṃ pacchā hanissāmāti.

Therein, 'Ko nu amhākaṃ' means: 'Seeing you, I thought, "These boars have little flesh and blood; they must be fearful." Therefore, tell me, who indeed is our enemy here?' 'Uddhaggarājī' means 'endowed with raised body-stripes.' They spoke thus referring to the tiger. 'Yopi' means: 'Whoever among us, even one, flees, we will kill even him afterwards.'

Tacchasūkaro sabbe sūkare ekacitte katvā pucchi “kāya velāya byaggho āgamissatī”ti. Ajja pātova ekaṃ gahetvā gato, sve pātova āgamissatīti. So yuddhakusalo “imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitena sakkā jetu”nti bhūmisīsaṃ pajānāti, tasmā ekaṃ padesaṃ sallakkhetvā rattimeva sūkare gocaraṃ gāhāpetvā balavapaccūsato paṭṭhāya “yuddhaṃ nāma sakaṭabyūhādivasena tividhaṃ hotī”ti vatvā padumabyūhaṃ saṃvidahati. Majjhe ṭhāne khīrapivake sūkarapotake ṭhapesi. Te parivāretvā tesaṃ mātaro, tā parivāretvā vañjhā sūkariyo, tāsaṃ anantarā sūkarapotake, tesaṃ anantarā makuladāṭhe taruṇasūkare, tesaṃ anantarā mahādāṭhe, tesaṃ anantarā jiṇṇasūkare, tato tattha tattha dasavaggaṃ vīsativaggaṃ tiṃsavaggañca katvā balagumbaṃ ṭhapesi. Attano atthāya ekaṃ āvāṭaṃ, byagghassa patanatthāya ekaṃ suppasaṇṭhānaṃ pabbhāraṃ katvā khaṇāpesi. Dvinnaṃ āvāṭānaṃ antare attano vasanatthāya pīṭhakaṃ kāresi. So thāmasampanne yodhasūkare gahetvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne sūkare assāsento vicari. Tassevaṃ [P 4.0346] karontasseva sūriyo uggacchati.

The Tacchasūkara united all the boars in purpose and asked, "At what time will the tiger come?" "Today at dawn, he took one and left; tomorrow at dawn he will come."
