Being skilled in battle, he thought, "By standing in this position, it is possible to win," as he understood the auspiciousness of the site. Therefore, after marking out one area, he had the boars graze at night. Starting from early dawn, he said, "Battle formations are of three kinds, such as the wagon formation and others," and arranged a lotus formation. In the central position, he placed the suckling piglets. Surrounding them were their mothers; around them were the barren sows; next to them were the young boars; beyond them were the young boars with budding tusks; further out were the large-tusked boars; and beyond them were the old boars. Then, here and there, he formed groups of ten, twenty, and thirty, creating defensive units. For his own purpose, he had one pit dug, and for the tiger's downfall, he had a well-concealed pit like a mantra-hole excavated. Between the two pits, he had a platform made for himself to sit on. Taking the strongest warrior boars, he moved about, encouraging the boars in their respective positions. While he was thus arranging things, the sun rose.

Atha byaggharājā kūṭajaṭilassa assamapadā nikkhamitvā pabbatatale aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā sūkarā “āgato no bhante verī”ti vadiṃsu. Mā bhāyatha, yaṃ yaṃ esa karoti, taṃ sabbaṃ sarikkhā hutvā karothāti. Byaggho sarīraṃ vidhunitvā osakkanto viya passāvamakāsi, sūkarāpi tatheva kariṃsu. Byaggho sūkare oloketvā mahānadaṃ nadi, tepi tatheva kariṃsu. So tesaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā cintesi “na ime pubbasadisā, ajja [M 4.0346] mayhaṃ paṭisattuno hutvā vaggavaggā ṭhitā, saṃvidahako nesaṃ senānāyakopi atthi, ajja mayā etesaṃ [V 4.0308] santikaṃ gantuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti maraṇabhayatajjito nivattitvā kūṭajaṭilassa santikaṃ gato. Atha naṃ so tucchahatthaṃ disvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the tiger king, having emerged from the hermitage of the deceitful ascetic, stood on the mountain slope. Seeing him, the boars cried out, "Our enemy has come, sir!" "Do not fear. Whatever he does, do exactly the same in imitation," he said. The tiger shook his body and, as if retreating, urinated; the boars also did the same. The tiger looked at the boars and roared loudly; they too did the same. Observing their behavior, he thought, "These are not as they were before. Today they have become my adversaries, standing in groups. They even have a coordinator, an army commander. It is not right for me to go near them today." Terrified by the fear of death, he turned back and went to the deceitful ascetic. Then the ascetic, seeing him empty-handed, spoke the ninth verse:

168.

168.

“Pāṇātipātā virato nu ajja, abhayaṃ nu te sabbabhūtesu dinnaṃ;

Dāṭhā nu te migavadhāya na santi, yo saṅghapatto kapaṇova jhāyasī”ti.

"Have you abstained from killing today? Have you given safety to all beings? Do you have no fangs for slaying beasts, that you, having reached the herd, brood like a miserable wretch?"

Tattha saṅghapattoti yo tvaṃ sūkarasaṅghapatto hutvā kiñci gocaraṃ alabhitvā kapaṇo viya jhāyasīti.

Therein, 'saṅghapatto' means: 'You, having gone to the boar-herd and obtaining no prey, brood like a wretch.'

Atha byaggho tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the tiger spoke three verses:

169.

169.

“Na me dāṭhā na vijjanti, balaṃ kāye samohitaṃ;

Ñātī ca disvāna sāmaggī ekato, tasmā ca jhāyāmi vanamhi ekako.

"It is not that I lack fangs, and strength is well-established in my body; but having seen the kinsmen united as one, therefore I brood alone in the forest."

170.

170.

“Imassudaṃ yanti disodisaṃ pure, bhayaṭṭitā leṇagavesino puthu;

Te dāni saṅgamma vasanti ekato, yatthaṭṭhitā duppasahajja te mayā.

"Formerly, these used to go in all directions, stricken with fear, seeking shelters separately. Now they gather and dwell together; where they stand, they are hard for me to overcome today."

171.

171.

“Pariṇāyakasampannā[P 4.0347], sahitā ekavādino;

Te maṃ samaggā hiṃseyyuṃ, tasmā nesaṃ na patthaye”ti.

"Endowed with a leader, united, speaking with one voice, they might harm me in concord; therefore, I do not desire them."

Tattha sāmaggī ekatoti sahitā hutvā ekato ṭhite. Imassudanti ime sudaṃ mayā akkhīni ummīletvā olokitamattāva pubbe disodisaṃ gacchanti. Puthūti visuṃ visuṃ. Yatthaṭṭhitāti yasmiṃ bhūmibhāge ṭhitā. Pariṇāyakasampannāti senānāyakena sampannā. Tasmā nesaṃ na patthayeti tena kāraṇena etesaṃ na patthemi.

Therein, 'sāmaggī ekato' means 'having become united, standing together as one.' 'Imassudaṃ' means: 'Formerly, these indeed used to flee in all directions merely upon my opening my eyes and looking at them, being oppressed by fear.' 'Puthū' means 'separately, individually.' 'Yatthaṭṭhitā' means 'standing on whichever part of the ground.' 'Pariṇāyakasampannā' means 'endowed with a leader.' 'Tasmā nesaṃ na patthaye' means: 'For that reason, I do not desire them.'

Taṃ [M 4.0347] sutvā kūṭajaṭilo tassa ussāhaṃ janayanto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the deceitful matted-hair ascetic, wishing to rouse the tiger’s effort, spoke a verse:

172.

172.

“Ekova indo asure jināti, ekova seno hanti dije pasayha;

Ekova byaggho migasaṅghapatto, varaṃ varaṃ hanti balañhi tādisa”nti.

Alone, Indra conquers the Asuras; alone, the hawk slays the birds by force. Alone, the tiger, having reached a herd of beasts, slays the very best—for such is his strength.

Tattha [V 4.0309] migasaṅghapattoti migagaṇapatto hutvā varaṃ varaṃ migaṃ hanti. Balañhi tādisanti tādisañhi tassa balaṃ.

Therein, 'migasaṅghapatto' means: 'having reached a herd of beasts, he kills the very best beast.' 'Balañhi tādisaṃ' means: 'For such indeed is his strength.'

Atha byaggho gāthamāha –

Then the tiger, wishing to reject the words of that deceitful ascetic, spoke a verse:

173.

173.

“Na heva indo na seno, napi byaggho migādhipo;

Samagge sahite ñātī, na byagghe kurute vase”ti.

Neither Indra, nor a hawk, nor even a tiger, the king of beasts, can conquer them; when kinsmen are united and harmonious, a tiger cannot bring them under his control.

Tattha byaggheti byagghasadise hutvā sarīravidhūnanādīni katvā ṭhite vase na kurute, attano vase vattāpetuṃ na sakkotīti attho.

Therein, 'byagghe' means: even acting like a tiger, by shaking the body and so forth, he does not bring them under his control; the meaning is that he is unable to make them act according to his will.

Puna jaṭilo taṃ ussāhento dve gāthā abhāsi –

The deceitful ascetic, once again wishing to rouse the tiger, spoke these two verses:

174.

174.

“Kumbhīlakā sakuṇakā, saṅghino gaṇacārino;

Sammodamānā ekajjhaṃ, uppatanti ḍayanti ca.

Kumbhīlaka birds, birds that flock together, moving in groups, rejoicing together, rise up and fly about.

175.

175.

“Tesañca ḍayamānānaṃ, ekettha apasakkati;

Tañca seno nitāḷeti, veyyagghiyeva sā gatī”ti.

And among those who are flying, if one here retreats, the hawk strikes that one down—such is indeed the way of a tiger.

Tattha [P 4.0348] kumbhīlakāti evaṃnāmakā khuddakasakuṇā. Uppatantīti gocaraṃ carantā uppatanti. Ḍayanti cāti gocaraṃ gahetvā ākāsena gacchanti. Ekettha apasakkatīti eko etesu osakkitvā vā ekapassena vā visuṃ gacchati. Nitāḷetīti paharitvā gaṇhāti. Veyyagghiyeva sā gatīti byagghānaṃ esāti veyyagghi, samaggānaṃ gacchantānampi esā evarūpā gati byagghānaṃ gatiyeva nāma hoti. Na hi sakkā sabbehi ekatova gantuṃ, tasmā yo evaṃ tattha eko gacchati, taṃ gaṇhāti.

There, `kumbhīlakā` are small birds of that name. `Uppatanti` means they fly up while foraging for food. `Ḍayanti` means having taken their food, they fly through the sky. `Ekettha apasakkati` means one among them retreats or goes separately to one side. `Nitāḷeti` means [a hawk] strikes and seizes it. `Veyyagghiyeva sā gati`—`veyyagghi` means 'belonging to tigers'; this is their way. Even for those moving together in harmony, such a fate is indeed known as the 'way of tigers'. For it is not possible for all to go as one; therefore, it seizes whichever one goes separately there in that way.

Evañca pana vatvā “byaggharāja tvaṃ attano balaṃ na jānāsi, mā bhāyi, kevalaṃ tvaṃ naditvā pakkhanda, dve ekato gacchantā nāma na bhavissantī”ti ussāhesi[M 4.0348]. So tathā akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, he encouraged him, saying, 'Tiger king, you do not know your own strength. Do not fear. Simply roar and charge; even two boars will not be able to go together.' He did so. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

176.

176.

“Ussāhito [V 4.0310] jaṭilena, luddenāmisacakkhunā;

Dāṭhī dāṭhīsu pakkhanti, maññamāno yathā pure”ti.

“Urged on by the ascetic, the cruel one with eyes for prey, the tusked one charged at the tusked ones, thinking as he did before.”

Tattha dāṭhīti sayaṃ dāṭhāvudho itaresu dāṭhāvudhesu pakkhandi. Yathā pureti yathā pubbe maññati, tatheva maññamāno.

There, `dāṭhī` means he himself, armed with tusks, charged among the others who were armed with tusks. `Yathā pure` means thinking just as he had thought previously.

So kira gantvā pabbatatale tāva aṭṭhāsi. Sūkarā “punāgato sāmi, coro”ti tacchassa ārocesuṃ. So “mā bhāyathā”ti te assāsetvā uṭṭhāya dvinnaṃ āvāṭānaṃ antare pīṭhakāya aṭṭhāsi. Byaggho vegaṃ janetvā tacchasūkaraṃ sandhāya pakkhandi. Tacchasūkaro parivattitvā pacchāmukho purimaāvāṭe pati. Byaggho ca vegaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto gantvā suppapabbhāre āvāṭe patitvā puñjakitova aṭṭhāsi. Tacchasūkaro vegena uṭṭhāya tassa antarasatthimhi dāṭhaṃ otāretvā yāva hadayā phāletvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā mukhena ḍaṃsitvā bahiāvāṭe pātetvā “gaṇhathimaṃ dāsa”nti āha. Paṭhamāgatā [P 4.0349] ekavārameva tuṇḍotāraṇamattaṃ labhiṃsu, pacchā āgatā alabhitvā “byagghamaṃsaṃ nāma kīdisa”nti vadiṃsu. Tacchasūkaro āvāṭā uttaritvā sūkare oloketvā “kiṃ nu kho na tussathā”ti āha. “Sāmi, eko tāva byaggho gahito, añño paneko dasabyagghagghanako atthī”ti? “Ko nāmeso”ti? “Byagghena ābhatābhatamaṃsaṃ khādako kūṭajaṭilo”ti. “Tena hi etha, gaṇhissāma na”nti tehi saddhiṃ vegena pakkhandi.

He went and stood at the base of the mountain. The boars reported to the Takkha boar, 'Master, the thief has come again!' Reassuring them, he said, 'Do not fear,' and standing up, he took his position on a mound between the two pits. The tiger, gathering speed, leaped toward the Takkha boar. The Takkha boar turned around and, facing backward, dropped into the first pit. The tiger, unable to check its momentum, went on and fell into the cavernous pit, landing in a heap. The Takkha boar quickly got up, drove its tusk into the tiger’s inner thigh, split it open to the heart, ate some flesh, bit it with its mouth, threw it out of the pit, and said, 'Seize this slave!' Those who arrived first got only enough for a mere taste, while those who came later got nothing and asked, 'What does tiger meat taste like?' The Takkha boar climbed out of the pit, looked at the boars, and asked, 'Are you not satisfied?' They replied, 'Master, one tiger has been caught, but there is another, the tiger's servant.' 'Who is he?' 'The deceitful ascetic who eats the meat the tiger brings.' 'In that case, come, let us catch him,' and he charged away swiftly with them.

Jaṭilo “byaggho cirāyatī”ti tassa āgamanamaggaṃ olokento bahū sūkare āgacchante disvā “ime byagghaṃ māretvā mama māraṇatthāya āgacchanti maññe”ti palāyitvā ekaṃ udumbararukkhaṃ abhiruhi. Sūkarā “esa rukkhaṃ āruḷho”ti vadiṃsu. “Kiṃ rukkha”nti. “Udumbararukkha”nti. “Tena hi mā cintayittha, idāni naṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti taruṇasūkare pakkositvā rukkhamūlatā [M 4.0349] paṃsuṃ apabyūhāpesi, sūkarīhi mukhapūraṃ udakaṃ āharāpesi, mahādāṭhasūkarehi samantā mūlāni chindāpesi. Ekaṃ ujukaṃ otiṇṇamūlameva aṭṭhāsi. Tato sesasūkare “tumhe apethā”ti ussāretvā jaṇṇukehi patiṭṭhahitvā dāṭhāya mūlaṃ pahari, pharasunā pahaṭaṃ viya chijjitvā gataṃ. Rukkho parivattitvā pati. Taṃ kūṭajaṭilaṃ patantameva sampaṭicchitvā maṃsaṃ bhakkhesuṃ. Taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā rukkhadevatā gāthamāha –

The deceitful ascetic, thinking, 'The tiger is taking too long,' looked along the path of his return and saw many boars coming. 'These boars must have killed the tiger and are coming to kill me,' he thought, and fled, climbing an udumbara tree. The boars said, 'He has climbed a tree.' 'What tree?' 'An udumbara tree.' 'If that is so, do not worry; we will catch him now.' The leader of the boars summoned the young boars and had them clear away the soil from the base of the tree; he had the sows bring mouthfuls of water; and he had the boars with large tusks cut the roots all around. Only one straight, downward-growing root remained. Then, having made the other boars step aside, he braced himself on his knees and struck the root with his tusk. It was cut as if struck by an axe, and the tree overturned and fell. Catching that deceitful ascetic even as he fell, they devoured his flesh. Seeing that wonder, the tree deity spoke a verse:

177.

177.

“Sādhu [V 4.0311] sambahulā ñātī, api rukkhā araññajā;

Sūkarehi samaggehi, byaggho ekāyane hato”ti.

“Good are many kinsmen, even trees born in the forest; by united boars, the tiger was killed in a single go.”

Tattha ekāyane hatoti ekagamanasmiṃyeva hato.

Here, 'ekāyane hato' means killed in a single movement.

Ubhinnaṃ pana nesaṃ hatabhāvaṃ pakāsento satthā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

To reveal that both of them were killed, the Teacher spoke another verse:

178.

178.

“Brāhmaṇañceva byagghañca, ubho hantvāna sūkarā;

Ānandino pamuditā, mahānādaṃ panādisu”nti.

“Having slain both the brahmin and the tiger, the boars, joyful and elated, raised a great shout.”

Puna [P 4.0350] tacchasūkaro te pucchi “aññepi vo amittā atthī”ti? Sūkarā “natthi, sāmī”ti vatvā “taṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ karissāmā”ti udakaṃ pariyesantā jaṭilassa pānīyasaṅkhaṃ disvā taṃ dakkhiṇāvaṭṭaṃ saṅkharatanaṃ pūretvā udakaṃ abhiharitvā tacchasūkaraṃ udumbararukkhamūleyeva abhisiñciṃsu. Abhisekaudakaṃ āsittaṃ, sūkarimevassa aggamahesiṃ kariṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya udumbarabhaddapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇāvaṭṭasaṅkhena abhisekakaraṇaṃ pavattaṃ. Tampi atthaṃ pakāsento satthā osānagāthamāha –

Again, the carpenter boar asked them, “Do you have any other enemies?” The boars replied, “No, master,” and said, “We will consecrate you as king.” Searching for water, they saw the ascetic's water conch. Filling that right-spiraling conch-shell treasure with water, they brought it and consecrated the carpenter boar right at the foot of the udumbara tree. The sow upon whom the consecration water was poured was made his chief queen. From then on, after seating him on an auspicious udumbara seat, the custom of performing the consecration ceremony with a right-spiraling conch shell began. To explain this meaning, the Teacher spoke the concluding verse:

179.

179.

“Te su udumbaramūlasmiṃ, sūkarā susamāgatā;

Tacchakaṃ abhisiñciṃsu, tvaṃ no rājāsi issaro”ti.

“Those boars, well assembled at the foot of the udumbara tree, consecrated the carpenter boar: ‘You are our king and lord.’”

Tattha te sūti te sūkarā, su-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Udumbaramūlasminti udumbarassa mūle.

In that verse, 'te su' means those boars; 'su' is merely a particle. 'Udumbaramūlasmiṃ' means at the foot of the udumbara tree.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi dhanuggahatissatthero yuddhasaṃvidahane chekoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi [M 4.0350] – “tadā kūṭajaṭilo devadatto ahosi, tacchasūkaro dhanuggahatisso, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past also, the Elder Dhanuggahatissa was skilled in the arrangement of battle.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time, the deceitful ascetic was Devadatta, the carpenter boar was Dhanuggahatissa, and I myself was the tree deity.”

Tacchasūkarajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the Commentary on the Tacchasūkara Jātaka, is finished.

[493] 10. Mahāvāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā

[493] 10. 10. Commentary on the Mahāvāṇija Jātaka

Vāṇijā [V 4.0312] samitiṃ katvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāvatthivāsino vāṇije ārabbha kathesi. Te kira vohāratthāya gacchantā satthu mahādānaṃ datvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāya “bhante, sace arogā āgamissāma, puna tumhākaṃ pāde vandissāmā”ti vatvā pañcamattehi sakaṭasatehi nikkhamitvā kantāraṃ patvā maggaṃ asallakkhetvā maggamūḷhā nirudake nirāhāre araññe vicarantā ekaṃ nāgapariggahitaṃ nigrodharukkhaṃ disvā sakaṭāni mocetvā rukkhamūle nisīdiṃsu. Te tassa udakatintāni viya nīlāni siniddhāni pattāni udakapuṇṇā viya ca sākhā disvā cintayiṃsu “imasmiṃ rukkhe udakaṃ sañcarantaṃ viya paññāyati, imassa purimasākhaṃ chindāma, pānīyaṃ no dassatī”ti. Atheko [P 4.0351] rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā sākhaṃ chindi, tato tālakkhandhappamāṇā udakadhārā pavatti. Te tattha nhatvā pivitvā ca dakkhiṇasākhaṃ chindiṃsu, tato nānaggarasabhojanaṃ nikkhami. Taṃ bhuñjitvā pacchimasākhaṃ chindiṃsu, tato alaṅkataitthiyo nikkhamiṃsu. Tāhi saddhiṃ abhiramitvā uttarasākhaṃ chindiṃsu, tato satta ratanāni nikkhamiṃsu. Tāni gahetvā pañca sakaṭasatāni pūretvā sāvatthiṃ paccāgantvā dhanaṃ gopetvā gandhamālādihatthā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pūjetvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā dhammakathaṃ sutvā nimantetvā punadivase mahādānaṃ datvā “bhante, imasmiṃ dāne amhākaṃ dhanadāyikāya rukkhadevatāya pattiṃ demā”ti pattiṃ adaṃsu. Satthā niṭṭhitabhattakicco “katararukkhadevatāya pattiṃ dethā”ti pucchi. Vāṇijā nigrodharukkhe dhanassa laddhākāraṃ tathāgatassārocesuṃ. Satthā “tumhe tāva mattaññutāya taṇhāvasikā ahutvā dhanaṃ labhittha, pubbe pana amattaññutāya taṇhāvasikā dhanañca jīvitañca vijahiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“The merchants held a meeting”—this the Teacher related while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the merchants of Sāvatthī. It is said that when they were setting out for trade, they gave a great offering to the Teacher, became established in the refuges and the precepts, and said, “Venerable sir, if we return in good health, we will pay homage at your feet again.” Then, they departed with five hundred carts. Having reached a wilderness and losing their way, they wandered in a waterless and foodless forest. There, they saw a banyan tree protected by a nāga. Unyoking their carts, they sat at the foot of the tree. Seeing its leaves as dark and glossy as if soaked in water, and its branches as if full of water, they thought, “It appears as if water flows within this tree. Let us cut its eastern branch; it will give us water.” Then one of them climbed the tree and cut a branch; from it gushed a stream of water as thick as a palm trunk. They bathed and drank. Next, they cut the southern branch, and from it emerged foods of various excellent flavors. Having eaten, they cut the western branch, and from it emerged beautifully adorned women. After delighting in their company, they cut the northern branch, and from it emerged the seven kinds of jewels. Taking these jewels, they filled five hundred carts and returned to Sāvatthī. After securing their wealth, they went to Jetavana with perfumes and garlands in hand, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. After listening to the Dhamma talk, they invited him for the next day and gave a great offering, saying, “Venerable sir, in this offering, we share the merit with the tree deity who gave us wealth.” Having finished his meal, the Teacher asked, “To which tree deity do you share the merit?” The merchants then recounted to the Tathāgata how they had obtained the wealth from the banyan tree. The Teacher said, “By being moderate and not enslaved by craving, you have obtained wealth. But in the past, by being immoderate and enslaved by craving, others lost both wealth and life.” Being entreated by them, he related a past event.

Atīte [M 4.0351] bārāṇasinagare tadeva pana kantāraṃ sveva nigrodho. Vāṇijā maggamūḷhā hutvā tameva nigrodhaṃ passiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ satthā abhisambuddho hutvā kathento imā gāthā āha –

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was that same wilderness and that same banyan tree. The merchants, having lost their way, saw that very banyan tree. To explain this matter, the Teacher, having become fully enlightened, spoke these verses:

180.

180.

“Vāṇijā samitiṃ katvā, nānāraṭṭhato āgatā;

Dhanāharā pakkamiṃsu, ekaṃ katvāna gāmaṇiṃ.

“Merchants, having formed an assembly, came from various countries; seeking to bring back wealth, they departed, having appointed one as their leader.

181.

181.

“Te taṃ kantāramāgamma, appabhakkhaṃ anodakaṃ;

Mahānigrodhamaddakkhuṃ, sītacchāyaṃ manoramaṃ.

“Reaching that wilderness, with little food and no water, they saw a great banyan tree, cool-shaded and delightful.

182.

182.

“Te [V 4.0313] ca tattha nisīditvā, tassa rukkhassa chāyayā;

Vāṇijā samacintesuṃ, bālā mohena pārutā.

“And having sat there in the shade of that tree, the merchants, being foolish and shrouded in delusion, deliberated together.

183.

183.

“Allāyate ayaṃ rukkho, api vārīva sandati;

Iṅghassa purimaṃ sākhaṃ, mayaṃ chindāma vāṇijā.

“‘This tree is moist, indeed it seems as if water flows from it. Come, merchants, let us cut its eastern branch.’

184.

184.

“Sā ca chinnāva pagghari, acchaṃ vāriṃ anāvilaṃ;

Te tattha nhatvā pivitvā, yāvaticchiṃsu vāṇijā.

“And as soon as it was cut, it gushed forth clear, untroubled water. There the merchants bathed and drank as much as they wished.

185.

185.

“Dutiyaṃ samacintesuṃ, bālā mohena pārutā;

Iṅghassa dakkhiṇaṃ sākhaṃ, mayaṃ chindāma vāṇijā.

“A second time they deliberated together, foolish and shrouded in delusion: ‘Come, merchants, let us cut the southern branch.’

186.

186.

“Sā [P 4.0352] ca chinnāva pagghari, sālimaṃsodanaṃ bahuṃ;

Appodavaṇṇe kummāse, siṅgiṃ vidalasūpiyo.

“And as soon as it was cut, it poured forth abundant rice mixed with meat, thick barley gruel, ginger and spices, and soups of split pulses.

187.

187.

“Te tattha bhutvā khāditvā, yāvaticchiṃsu vāṇijā;

Tatiyaṃ samacintesuṃ, bālā mohena pārutā;

Iṅghassa pacchimaṃ sākhaṃ, mayaṃ chindāma vāṇijā.

“There the merchants ate and consumed as much as they wished. A third time they deliberated together, foolish and shrouded in delusion: ‘Come, merchants, let us cut the western branch.’

188.

188.

“Sā ca chinnāva pagghari, nāriyo samalaṅkatā;

Vicitravatthābharaṇā, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā.

“And as soon as it was cut, it streamed forth well-adorned women, wearing various garments and ornaments, and jeweled earrings.

189.

189.

“Api su vāṇijā ekā, nāriyo paṇṇavīsati;

Samantā parivāriṃsu, tassa rukkhassa chāyayā;

Te tāhi paricāretvā, yāvaticchiṃsu vāṇijā.

“For each merchant there was one woman, and for the leader, twenty-five; they surrounded them on all sides in the shade of that tree. Having enjoyed themselves with them, the merchants took as many as they wished.

190.

190.

“Catutthaṃ [M 4.0352] samacintesuṃ, bālā mohena pārutā;

Iṅghassa uttaraṃ sākhaṃ, mayaṃ chindāma vāṇijā.

“A fourth time they deliberated together, foolish and shrouded in delusion: ‘Come, merchants, let us cut the northern branch.’

191.

191.

“Sā [V 4.0314] ca chinnāva pagghari, muttā veḷuriyā bahū;

Rajataṃ jātarūpañca, kuttiyo paṭiyāni ca.

“And as soon as it was cut, it showered forth many pearls and beryl gems, silver and gold, and woolen rugs and coverlets.”

192.

192.

“Kāsikāni ca vatthāni, uddiyāni ca kambalā;

Te tattha bhāre bandhitvā, yāvaticchiṃsu vāṇijā.

And fabrics from Kāsī, and blankets from Uddiya; there, the merchants bound them into loads, as much as they desired.

193.

193.

“Pañcamaṃ samacintesuṃ, bālā mohena pārutā;

Iṅghassa mūlaṃ chindāma, api bhiyyo labhāmase.

A fifth time they deliberated, fools shrouded in delusion: 'Come, let us cut the root of this tree; perhaps we may obtain even more.'

194.

194.

“Athuṭṭhahi satthavāho, yācamāno katañjalī;

Nigrodho kiṃ parajjhati, vāṇijā bhaddamatthu te.

Then the caravan leader arose, entreating with hands joined in reverence: 'How does the banyan tree offend? Merchants, may it be well with you!'

195.

195.

“Vāridā purimā sākhā, annapānañca dakkhiṇā;

Nāridā pacchimā sākhā, sabbakāme ca uttarā;

Nigrodho kiṃ parajjhati, vāṇijā bhaddamatthu te.

The eastern branch gave water, the southern, food and drink; the western branch gave women, and the northern, all desires. How does the banyan tree offend? Merchants, may it be well with you!

196.

196.

“Yassa rukkhassa chāyāya, nisīdeyya sayeyya vā;

Na tassa sākhaṃ bhañjeyya, mittadubbho hi pāpako.

In the shade of whatever tree one might sit or lie, one should not break a branch of it, for to betray a friend is an evil thing.

197.

197.

“Te ca tassānādiyitvā, ekassa vacanaṃ bahū;

Nisitāhi kuṭhārīhi, mūlato naṃ upakkamu”nti.

But they, the many, not heeding the word of that one, set upon it at the root with sharpened axes.

Tattha samitiṃ katvāti bārāṇasiyaṃ samāgamaṃ katvā, bahū ekato hutvāti attho. Pakkamiṃsūti pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bārāṇaseyyakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya pakkamiṃsu. Gāmaṇinti ekaṃ paññavantataraṃ satthavāhaṃ katvā[P 4.0353]. Chāyayāti chāyāya. Allāyateti udakabharito viya allo hutvā paññāyati. Chinnāva paggharīti eko rukkhārohanakusalo abhiruhitvā taṃ chindi, sā chinnamattāva paggharīti dasseti. Paratopi eseva nayo.

Herein, having formed an assembly means having gathered in Bārāṇasī; the meaning is that many came together. They departed means they departed with five hundred carts, taking merchandise from Bārāṇasī. Having appointed a leader means having made one who was more intelligent the caravan leader. Chāyayā is used in the sense of 'in the shade.' Is moist means it appears moist, as if filled with water. As soon as it was cut, it gushed forth shows that one skilled in climbing trees climbed and cut it, and it gushed forth the very moment it was cut. This same principle applies hereafter.

Appodavaṇṇe [M 4.0353] kummāseti appodakapāyāsasadise kummāse. Siṅginti siṅgiverādikaṃ uttaribhaṅgaṃ. Vidalasūpiyoti muggasūpādayo. Vāṇijā ekāti ekekassa vāṇijassa yattakā vāṇijā[V 4.0315], tesu ekekassa ekekāva, satthavāhassa pana santike pañcavīsatīti attho. Parivāriṃsūti parivāresuṃ. Tāhi pana saddhiṃyeva nāgānubhāvena sāṇivitānasayanādīni pagghariṃsu.

Gruel with little water means gruel resembling rice porridge with little water. Ginger means ginger and other condiments. Soups of split pulses means soups of mung beans and so forth. For each merchant, one means that for each and every merchant, there was one woman, but in the presence of the caravan leader, there were twenty-five. They surrounded is simply parivāresuṃ. And along with them, by the power of the nāga, hempen canopies, beds, and so forth also gushed forth.

Kuttiyoti hatthattharādayo. Paṭiyānicāti uṇṇāmayapaccattharaṇāni. “Setakambalānī”tipi vadantiyeva. Uddiyāni ca kambalāti uddiyāni nāma kambalā atthi. Te tattha bhāre bandhitvāti yāvatakaṃ icchiṃsu, tāvatakaṃ gahetvā pañca sakaṭasatāni pūretvāti attho. Vāṇijā bhaddamatthu teti ekekaṃ vāṇijaṃ ālapanto “bhaddaṃ te atthū”ti āha. Annapānañcāti annañca pānañca adāsi. Sabbakāme cāti sabbakāme ca adāsi. Mittadubbho hīti mittānaṃ dubbhanapuriso hi pāpako lāmako nāma. Anādiyitvāti tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā. Upakkamunti mohāva chindituṃ ārabhiṃsu.

Carpets means carpets for elephants and so forth. Coverlets means woolen spreads. Some just say 'white blankets.' And blankets from Uḍḍiyāna means there are blankets by the name of Uḍḍiyāna. There they bound them into bundles means having taken as much as they wished, they filled the five hundred carts. Merchants, may it be well with you means, addressing each merchant, he said, 'May it be well with you.' And food and drink means it gave food and drink. And all desires means it gave all desirable things. For to injure a friend means a person who harms friends is indeed called wicked and base. Not heeding means not taking his word. They set upon it means out of delusion they began to cut.

Atha ne chindanatthāya rukkhaṃ upagate disvā nāgarājā cintesi “ahaṃ etesaṃ pipāsitānaṃ pānīyaṃ dāpesiṃ, tato dibbabhojanaṃ, tato sayanādīni ceva paricārikā ca nāriyo, tato pañcasatasakaṭapūraṃ ratanaṃ, idāni panime “rukkhaṃ mūlato chindissāmā’ti vadanti, ativiya luddhā ime, ṭhapetvā satthavāhaṃ avasese māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So “ettakā sannaddhayodhā nikkhamantu, ettakā dhanuggahā, ettakā vammino”ti senaṃ vicāresi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā gāthamāha –

Then, seeing them approach the tree to cut it down, the nāga king thought, 'I gave water to these thirsty ones, then divine food, then beds and the like and serving women, then treasures to fill five hundred carts. But now they say, "We will cut the tree from the root." They are exceedingly greedy. It is fitting to kill all except the caravan leader.' He arrayed his army, saying, 'Let this many armed warriors come forth, this many archers, this many armored men.' The Teacher, revealing this meaning, spoke a verse:

198.

198.

“Tato nāgā nikkhamiṃsu, sannaddhā paṇṇavīsati;

Dhanuggahānaṃ tisatā, chasahassā ca vammino”ti.

Then the nāgas came forth, twenty-five arrayed in armor; three hundred archers, and six thousand armored men.

Tattha sannaddhāti suvaṇṇarajatādivammakavacikā. Dhanuggahānaṃ tisatāti meṇḍavisāṇadhanuggahānaṃ tīṇi satāni. vamminoti kheṭakaphalakahatthā chasahassā.

There, 'sannaddhā' means clad in armor of gold, silver, and the like. 'Three hundred archers' means three hundred archers with ram's horn bows. 'Vammino' means six thousand with shields and bucklers in hand.

199.

199.

“Ete [P 4.0354][M 4.0354] hanatha bandhatha, mā vo muñcittha jīvitaṃ;

Ṭhapetvā satthavāhaṃva, sabbe bhasmaṃ karotha ne”ti. – ayaṃ nāgarājena vuttagāthā;

Kill them, bind them, do not let them live; except for the caravan leader, reduce them all to ashes.' —This verse was spoken by the nāga king.

Tattha mā vo muñcittha jīvitanti kassaci ekassapi jīvitaṃ mā muñcittha.

There, 'mā vo muñcittha jīvitaṃ' means: do not spare the life of even a single one.

Nāgā [V 4.0316] tathā katvā attharaṇādīni pañcasu sakaṭasatesu āropetvā satthavāhaṃ gahetvā sayaṃ tāni sakaṭāni pājentā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā sabbaṃ dhanaṃ tassa gehe paṭisāmetvā taṃ āpucchitvā attano nāgabhavanameva gatā. Tamatthaṃ viditvā satthā ovādavasena gāthādvayamāha –

The nāgas, having done so, loaded the rugs and other items onto five hundred carts, took the caravan leader, and themselves drove those carts to Bārāṇasī. They deposited all the wealth in his house, took their leave of him, and returned to their own nāga abode. Understanding this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses by way of admonition:

200.

200.

“Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano;

Lobhassa na vasaṃ gacche, haneyyārisakaṃ manaṃ.

Therefore, a wise person, seeing their own benefit, should not go under the sway of greed; they should slay the mind that belongs to the enemy (greed).

201.

201.

“Evamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, taṇhā dukkhassa sambhavaṃ;

Vītataṇho anādāno, sato bhikkhu paribbaje”ti.

Having known such a danger, and that craving is the origin of suffering, a bhikkhu, rid of craving, not grasping, should wander mindfully.

Tattha tasmāti yasmā lobhavasikā mahāvināsaṃ pattā, satthavāho uttamasampattiṃ, tasmā. Haneyyārisakaṃ mananti anto uppajjamānānaṃ nānāvidhānaṃ lobhasattūnaṃ santakaṃ manaṃ, lobhasampayuttacittaṃ haneyyāti attho. Evamādīnavanti evaṃ lobhe ādīnavaṃ jānitvā. Taṇhā dukkhassa sambhavanti jātiādidukkhassa taṇhā sambhavo, tato etaṃ dukkhaṃ nibbattati, evaṃ taṇhāva dukkhassa sambhavaṃ ñatvā vītataṇho taṇhāādānena anādāno maggena āgatāya satiyā sato hutvā bhikkhu paribbaje iriyetha vattethāti arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhi.

Here, 'tasmā' means: because those under the sway of greed met with great destruction, and the caravan leader attained the highest success, therefore. 'Haneyyārisakaṃ manaṃ' means one should destroy the mind that belongs to the various enemies in the form of greed arising within; that is, the mind associated with greed. 'Evamādīnavaṃ' means knowing the danger in greed in this way. 'Taṇhā dukkhassa sambhavaṃ' means craving is the origin of suffering such as birth and so on, from which this suffering originates; thus, knowing craving itself as the origin of suffering, a bhikkhu, rid of craving, not grasping through the attachment of craving, being mindful with mindfulness that has come by way of the path, should wander or conduct himself—he brought the teaching to its culmination with Arahantship.

Imañca pana dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ upāsakā pubbe lobhavasikā vāṇijā mahāvināsaṃ pattā, tasmā lobhavasikena na bhavitabba”nti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne te vāṇijā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. Tadā nāgarājā sāriputto ahosi, satthavāho pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, he said, "Thus, lay followers, merchants in the past, being under the sway of greed, met with great ruin. Therefore, one should not be under the sway of greed." Having declared the truths, he connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the truths, those merchants were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the nāga king was Sāriputta, and the caravan leader was I myself.

Mahāvāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Great Merchant Jātaka, the Tenth.

[494] 11. Sādhinajātakavaṇṇanā

[494] 11. The Explanation of the Sādhina Jātaka

Abbhuto [P 4.0355][M 4.0355] vata lokasminti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathike upāsake ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “upāsakā porāṇakapaṇḍitā attano uposathakammaṃ nissāya manussasarīreneva devalokaṃ gantvā ciraṃ vasiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'Wonderful indeed in the world!'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the lay devotees observing the Uposatha. At that time, the Teacher, having said, 'Lay devotees, the wise of ancient times, relying on their Uposatha observance, went to the world of the devas in their human bodies and lived there for a long time,' and being requested by them, related a past event.

Atīte [V 4.0317] mithilāyaṃ sādhino nāma rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. So catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāre cāti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi, devasikaṃ cha satasahassāni vayakaraṇaṃ gacchanti, pañca sīlāni rakkhati, uposathaṃ upavasati. Raṭṭhavāsinopi tassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā matamatā devanagareyeva nibbattiṃsu. Sudhammadevasabhaṃ pūretvā nisinnā devā rañño sīlādiguṇameva vaṇṇayanti. Taṃ sutvā sesadevāpi rājānaṃ daṭṭhukāmā ahesuṃ. Sakko devarājā tesaṃ manaṃ viditvā āha – “sādhinarājānaṃ daṭṭhukāmatthā”ti. “Āma devā”ti. So mātaliṃ āṇāpesi “gaccha tvaṃ vejayantarathaṃ yojetvā sādhinarājānaṃ ānehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rathaṃ yojetvā videharaṭṭhaṃ agamāsi, tadā puṇṇamadivaso hoti. Mātali manussānaṃ sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā gharadvāresu sukhakathāya nisinnakāle candamaṇḍalena saddhiṃ rathaṃ pesesi. Manussā “dve candā uṭṭhitā”ti vadantā puna candamaṇḍalaṃ ohāya rathaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “nāyaṃ cando, ratho eso, devaputto paññāyati, kassesa etaṃ manomayasindhavayuttaṃ dibbarathaṃ āneti, na aññassa, amhākaṃ rañño bhavissati, rājā hi no dhammiko dhammarājā”ti somanassajātā hutvā añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhitā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

In the past, in Mithilā, a king named Sādhina ruled the kingdom righteously. He had six alms halls established: at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at his own palace gate. Having suspended the ploughing throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he instituted a great giving. Daily, six hundred thousand were spent; he observed the five precepts and undertook the Uposatha. The inhabitants of the kingdom, abiding by his instruction, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, whenever they died, were reborn in the city of the devas. The devas, seated filling the Sudhammā assembly hall, praised the king’s virtues of morality and the like. Hearing this, the other devas also became desirous of seeing the king. Sakka, the king of devas, knowing their thought, said, 'Do you wish to see King Sādhina?' 'Yes, lord.' He then commanded Mātali, 'Go, yoke the Vejayanta chariot and bring King Sādhina.' Saying, 'Very well,' he consented, yoked the chariot, and went to the Videha kingdom. It was then a full moon day. Mātali sent the chariot along with the moon's orb at the time when humans, having eaten their evening meal, were sitting at their doorsteps engaged in pleasant conversation. The people, saying, 'Two moons have risen!' then saw the chariot coming, leaving the moon's orb behind, and said, 'This is no moon, it is a chariot! A son of the devas is visible! For whom does he bring this mind-made, divine chariot yoked with Sindh horses? Surely for none other than our king, for our king is righteous, a king of righteousness.' Filled with joy, they stood with hands reverently joined and recited the first verse:

202.

202.

“Abbhuto vata lokasmiṃ, uppajji lomahaṃsano;

Dibbo ratho pāturahu, vedehassa yasassino”ti.

"A wonder, indeed, has arisen in the world, a hair-raising event; a divine chariot has appeared for the glorious Videhan."

Tassattho [P 4.0356] – abbhuto vatesa amhākaṃ rājā, lokasmiṃ lomahaṃsano uppajji, yassa dibbo ratho pāturahosi vedehassa yasassinoti.

Its meaning is: A wonder, indeed, for our king, a hair-raising event has arisen in the world, in that a divine chariot has appeared for the glorious Videhan.

Mātalipi [M 4.0356] taṃ rathaṃ ānetvā manussesu gandhamālādīhi pūjentesu tikkhattuṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rañño nivesanadvāraṃ gantvā rathaṃ nivattetvā pacchābhāgena sīhapañjaraummāre ṭhapetvā ārohaṇasajjaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ divasaṃ rājāpi dānasālāyo oloketvā “iminā niyāmena dānaṃ dethā”ti āṇāpetvā uposathaṃ samādiyitvā divasaṃ vītināmetvā amaccagaṇaparivuto alaṅkatamahātale pācīnasīhapañjarābhimukho dhammayuttaṃ kathento nisinno hoti. Atha naṃ mātali rathābhiruhanatthaṃ nimantetvā ādāya agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Mātali, having brought that chariot, while the people honored it with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, circumambulated the city three times and went to the gate of the king’s residence. He turned the chariot around, placed it with its rear part at the ledge of the lion-window, made it ready for mounting, and stood by. That day, the king, after inspecting the alms halls and ordering, 'Give alms in this manner,' undertook the Uposatha observance and spent the day. Surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he was seated on the great decorated terrace, facing the eastern lion-window, and was engaged in a conversation connected with the Dhamma. Then Mātali invited him to mount the chariot and took him away. To explain this matter, the Teacher spoke these verses:

203.

203.

“Devaputto [V 4.0318] mahiddhiko, mātali devasārathi;

Nimantayittha rājānaṃ, vedehaṃ mithilaggahaṃ.

"The son of the devas of great power, Mātali, the charioteer of the devas, invited King Videha, the lord of Mithilā."

204.

204.

“Ehimaṃ rathamāruyha, rājaseṭṭha disampati;

Devā dassanakāmā te, tāvatiṃsā saindakā;

Saramānā hi te devā, sudhammāyaṃ samacchare.

"Come, mount this chariot, O best of kings, lord of the land. The Tāvatiṃsa devas, together with Indra, desire to see you. For those devas, longing for you, are assembled in the Sudhammā Hall."

205.

205.

“Tato ca rājā sādhino, vedeho mithilaggaho;

Sahassayuttamāruyha, agā devāna santike;

Taṃ devā paṭinandiṃsu, disvā rājānamāgataṃ.

"Then King Sādhina, the Videhan, the lord of Mithilā, having mounted the chariot yoked with a thousand horses, went into the presence of the devas. Seeing the king had arrived, the devas welcomed him."

206.

206.

“Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Nisīda dāni rājīsi, devarājassa santike.

"Welcome to you, great king; and your coming is not ill-come. Be seated now, O royal sage, in the presence of the king of the devas."

207.

207.

“Sakkopi paṭinandittha, vedehaṃ mithilaggahaṃ;

Nimantayittha kāmehi, āsanena ca vāsavo.

"Sakka also welcomed the Videhan, the lord of Mithilā; Vāsava invited him with sensual pleasures and with a seat."

208.

208.

“Sādhu khosi anuppatto, āvāsaṃ vasavattinaṃ;

Vasa devesu rājīsi, sabbakāmasamiddhisu;

Tāvatiṃsesu devesu, bhuñja kāme amānuse”ti.

"Well indeed have you reached the abode of those who exercise mastery. Dwell among the gods, O royal sage, who are fulfilled in all desires. Among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, enjoy superhuman pleasures."

Tattha samacchareti acchanti. Agā devāna santiketi devānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiñhi rathaṃ abhiruhitvā ṭhite ratho ākāsaṃ pakkhandi, so mahājanassa olokentasseva antaradhāyi. Mātali rājānaṃ devalokaṃ nesi[P 4.0357]. Taṃ disvā devatā ca sakko ca haṭṭhatuṭṭhā paccuggamanaṃ katvā [M 4.0357] paṭisanthāraṃ kariṃsu. Tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “taṃ devā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭinandiṃsūti punappunaṃ nandiṃsu. Āsanena cāti rājānaṃ āliṅgitvā “idha nisīdā”ti attano paṇḍukambalasilāsanena ca kāmehi ca nimantesi, upaḍḍharajjaṃ datvā ekāsane nisīdāpesīti attho.

There, 'samacchare' means they stay or sit. 'Agā devāna santike' means he went to the presence of the devas. For when he stood there having mounted the chariot, the chariot sprang into the sky; it vanished even as the great crowd watched. Mātali led the king to the deva world. Seeing him, the devas and Sakka, delighted and joyful, went out to meet him and performed the duties of hospitality. To show that matter, 'taṃ devā' and so forth was said. There, 'paṭinandiṃsu' means they rejoiced again and again. 'Āsanena ca' means embracing the king and saying, 'Sit here,' he invited him with his own Paṇḍukambala stone seat and with sensual pleasures; he seated him on the same seat, having given him half of the kingdom—this is the meaning.

Tattha sakkena devaraññā dasayojanasahassaṃ devanagaraṃ aḍḍhatiyā ca accharākoṭiyo vejayantapāsādañca [V 4.0319] majjhe bhinditvā dinnaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavantassa manussagaṇanāya satta vassasatāni atikkantāni. Tenattabhāvena devaloke vasanakaṃ puññaṃ khīṇaṃ, anabhirati uppannā, tasmā sakkena saddhiṃ sallapanto gāthamāha –

There, while King Sādhina was enjoying the divine prosperity given by Sakka, the king of the devas—who had divided in half the divine city of ten thousand yojanas, the twenty-five million celestial nymphs, and the Vejayanta palace—seven hundred human years passed. Due to that existence, the merit for dwelling in the deva world was exhausted and discontent arose. Therefore, while conversing with Sakka, he spoke this verse:

209.

209.

“Ahaṃ pure saggagato ramāmi, naccehi gītehi ca vāditehi;

So dāni ajja na ramāmi sagge, āyuṃ nu khīṇo maraṇaṃ nu santike;

Udāhu mūḷhosmi janindaseṭṭhā”ti.

"Formerly, having reached heaven, I delighted in dances, songs, and instrumental music. But today I no longer delight in heaven. Is my lifespan exhausted, or is death near? Or am I deluded, O best of the lords of people?"

Tattha āyuṃ nu khīṇoti kiṃ nu mama sarasena jīvitindriyaṃ khīṇaṃ, udāhu upacchedakakammavasena maraṇaṃ santike jātanti pucchati. Janindaseṭṭhāti janindānaṃ devānaṃ seṭṭha.

Here, 'āyuṃ nu khīṇo' means he asks, 'Is the life-faculty of my own natural course exhausted, or has death come near by way of destructive kamma?' 'Janindaseṭṭha' means the best among the lords of people, the devas.

Atha naṃ sakko āha –

Then Sakka said to him:

210.

210.

“Na tāyu khīṇaṃ maraṇañca dūre, na cāpi mūḷho naravīraseṭṭha;

Tuyhañca puññāni parittakāni, yesaṃ vipākaṃ idha vedayittho.

"Your life is not exhausted and death is far off, nor are you deluded, O best of heroic men. But your merits are limited, the result of which you have experienced here."

211.

211.

“Vasa devānubhāvena, rājaseṭṭha disampati;

Tāvatiṃsesu devesu, bhuñja kāme amānuse”ti.

"Dwell by the power of the devas, O best of kings, lord of the land. Among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, enjoy superhuman pleasures."

Tattha “parittakānī”ti idaṃ tena attabhāvena devaloke vipākadāyakāni puññāni sandhāya vuttaṃ, itarāni panassa puññāni pathaviyaṃ paṃsu viya appamāṇāni. Vasa devānubhāvenāti ahaṃ te attano puññāni [M 4.0358] majjhe bhinditvā dassāmi, mamānubhāvena vasāti taṃ samassāsento āha.

There, 'parittakāni' was said with reference to the merits that were yielding their result in the deva world in that existence; but his other merits were immeasurable like the dust on the earth. 'Vasa devānubhāvena' means, 'I will divide my own merits in half and give them to you; dwell by my power.' Reassuring him, Sakka said this.

Atha [P 4.0358] naṃ paṭikkhipanto mahāsatto āha –

Then the Great Being, rejecting him, said:

212.

212.

“Yathā yācitakaṃ yānaṃ, yathā yācitakaṃ dhanaṃ;

Evaṃsampadamevetaṃ, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā.

"Just like a borrowed vehicle or borrowed wealth, so indeed is this attainment which is due to a gift from another."

213.

213.

“Na [V 4.0320] cāhametamicchāmi, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā;

Sayaṃkatāni puññāni, taṃ me āveṇikaṃ dhanaṃ.

"I do not desire this which is due to a gift from another; merits done by myself, that is my own exclusive treasure."

214.

214.

“Sohaṃ gantvā manussesu, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahuṃ;

Dānena samacariyāya, saṃyamena damena ca;

Yaṃ katvā sukhito hoti, na ca pacchānutappatī”ti.

"Having gone among humans, I will do much merit through generosity, righteous conduct, restraint, and self-control; having done which, one is happy and does not regret it later."

Tattha yaṃ parato dānapaccayāti yaṃ parena dinnattā labbhati, taṃ yācitakasadisameva hoti. Yācitakañhi tuṭṭhakāle denti, atuṭṭhakāle acchinditvā gaṇhantīti vadati. Samacariyāyāti kāyādīhi pāpassa akaraṇena. Saṃyamenāti sīlasaṃyamena. Damenāti indriyadamanena. Yaṃ katvāti yaṃ karitvā sukhito ceva hoti na ca pacchānutappati, tathārūpameva kammaṃ karissāmīti.

There, 'yaṃ parato dānapaccayā' means what is obtained because it is given by another is just like a borrowed thing. For he says that people give a borrowed thing when they are pleased and take it back when they are not pleased. 'Samacariyāya' means by not doing evil through the body and so forth. 'Saṃyamena' means by the restraint of virtue. 'Damena' means by the control of the senses. 'Yaṃ katvā' means, 'I will do just such an action by which, having done it, one is happy and does not regret it later.'

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā sakko mātaliṃ āṇāpesi “gaccha, tāta, sādhinarājānaṃ mithilaṃ netvā uyyāne otārehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Rājā uyyāne caṅkamati. Atha naṃ uyyānapālo disvā pucchitvā gantvā nāradarañño ārocesi. So rañño āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā “tvaṃ purato gantvā uyyānaṃ sajjetvā tassa ca mayhañca dve āsanāni paññāpehī”ti uyyānapālaṃ uyyojesi. So tathā akāsi. Atha naṃ rājā pucchi “kassa dve āsanāni paññāpesī”ti? “Ekaṃ tumhākaṃ, ekaṃ amhākaṃ rañño”ti. Atha naṃ rājā “ko añño satto mama santike āsane nisīdissatī”ti vatvā ekasmiṃ nisīditvā ekasmiṃ pāde ṭhapesi. Nāradarājā āgantvā tassa pāde vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. So kirassa sattamo panattā. Tadā kira vassasatāyukakālova hoti. Mahāsatto pana attano puññabalena ettakaṃ kālaṃ vītināmesi. So nāradaṃ hatthe gahetvā uyyāne vicaranto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard his words, Sakka commanded Mātali: “Go, dear boy, take King Sādhina to Mithilā and set him down in the park.” He did so. The king walked in the park. Then the park-keeper saw him, asked who he was, and went to inform King Nārada. Hearing of the king's arrival, he sent the park-keeper, saying: “You go ahead, prepare the park, and set up two seats, one for him and one for me.” He did so. Then the king asked him: “For whom have you prepared these two seats?” “One for you, and one for our king.” Then the king said: “What other being would sit on a seat beside me?” and sat on one seat while placing his feet on the other. King Nārada arrived, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. It is said that he was the king's seventh descendant. At that time, it is said, the human lifespan was one hundred years. But the Great Being, through the power of his merit, had passed such a long time. Taking Nārada by the hand and wandering through the park, he spoke three verses:

215.

215.

“Imāni [M 4.0359] tāni khettāni, imaṃ nikkhaṃ sukuṇḍalaṃ;

Imā tā haritānūpā, imā najjo savantiyo.

“These are those fields, this is the beautifully ringed water-conduit; these are those green lands by the water, these are those flowing rivers.

216.

216.

“Imā [P 4.0359] tā pokkharaṇī rammā, cakkavākapakūjitā;

Mandālakehi sañchannā, padumuppalakehi ca;

Yassimāni mamāyiṃsu, kiṃ nu te disataṃ gatā.

“These are those lovely lotus ponds, resounding with the calls of ruddy sheldrakes, covered with Mandālaka flowers, and with lotuses and water lilies. Those who cherished these things as mine—to what region have they gone?”

217.

217.

“Tānīdha [V 4.0321] khettāni so bhūmibhāgo, teyeva ārāmavanūpacārā;

Tameva mayhaṃ janataṃ apassato, suññaṃva me nārada khāyate disā”ti.

“These are the fields here, that very portion of land, those very park and woodland precincts. But not seeing those same people of mine, the quarters appear empty to me, Nārada.”

Tattha khettānīti bhūmibhāge sandhāyāha. Imaṃ nikkhanti imaṃ tādisameva udakaniddhamanaṃ. Sukuṇḍalanti sobhanena musalapavesanakuṇḍalena samannāgataṃ. Haritānūpāti udakaniddhamanassa ubhosu passesu haritatiṇasañchannā anūpabhūmiyo. Yassimāni mamāyiṃsūti tāta nārada, ye mama upaṭṭhākā ca orodhā ca imasmiṃ uyyāne mahantena yasena mayā saddhiṃ vicarantā imāni ṭhānāni mamāyiṃsu piyāyiṃsu, kataraṃ nu te disataṃ gatā, kattha te pesitā. Tānīdha khettānīti imasmiṃ uyyāne tāneva etāni uparopanakaviruhanaṭṭhānāni. Teyeva ārāmavanūpacārāti ime teyeva ārāmavanūpacārā, vihārabhūmiyoti attho.

In this passage, 'khettāni' is said with reference to portions of ground. 'Imaṃ nikkhaṃ' means this same water-conduit. 'Sukuṇḍalaṃ' means provided with a beautiful ringed socket for inserting a bolt. 'Haritānūpā' refers to the lands near the water covered with green grass on both sides of the water-conduit. 'Yassimāni mamāyiṃsu' means: 'Dear Nārada, those attendants and women of the harem of mine who, wandering in this park with me in great glory, cherished these places, holding them dear—to what region have they gone? Where have they been sent?' 'Tānīdha khettāni' means these very places for planting and growing in this park. 'Teyeva ārāmavanūpacārā' means these are those same park and woodland precincts, meaning the grounds for dwelling.

Atha naṃ nārado āha – “deva, tumhākaṃ devalokagatānaṃ idāni satta vassasatāni, ahaṃ vo sattamo panattā, tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhākā ca orodhā ca maraṇamukhaṃ pattā, idaṃ vo attano santakaṃ rajjaṃ, anubhavatha na”nti. Rājā “tāta nārada, nāhaṃ idhāgacchanto rajjatthāya āgato, puññakaraṇatthāyamhi āgato, ahaṃ puññameva karissāmī”ti vatvā gāthā āha –

Then Nārada said to him: “Great King, it is now seven hundred years since you went to the world of the gods. I am your seventh descendant. Your attendants and the women of your harem have gone into the mouth of death. This kingdom is your own property; rule over it!” The king said: “Dear Nārada, when I came here, I did not come for the sake of the kingdom; I came for the sake of performing merit. I will perform merit only.” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

218.

218.

“Diṭṭhā mayā vimānāni, obhāsentā catuddisā;

Sammukhā devarājassa, tidasānañca sammukhā.

“I have seen celestial mansions, illuminating the four directions, in the presence of the King of the Gods, and in the presence of the Thirty-three gods.

219.

219.

“Vutthaṃ [M 4.0360] me bhavanaṃ dibyaṃ, bhuttā kāmā amānusā;

Tāvatiṃsesu devesu, sabbakāmasamiddhisu.

“I have dwelt in a divine abode, superhuman pleasures have been enjoyed among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, who abound in all desires.

220.

220.

“Sohaṃ etādisaṃ hitvā, puññāyamhi idhāgato;

Dhammameva carissāmi, nāhaṃ rajjena atthiko.

“Having abandoned such as this, I have come here for the sake of merit; I will practice only the Dhamma, I have no need for a kingdom.

221.

221.

“Adaṇḍāvacaraṃ [V 4.0322][P 4.0360] maggaṃ, sammāsambuddhadesitaṃ;

Taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjissaṃ, yena gacchanti subbatā”ti.

“I shall follow that path taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the path frequented by the non-violent, by which the well-conducted go.”

Tattha vutthaṃ me bhavanaṃ dibyanti vejayantaṃ sandhāya āha. Sohaṃ etādisanti tāta nārada, sohaṃ buddhañāṇena aparicchindanīyaṃ evarūpaṃ kāmaguṇasampattiṃ pahāya puññakaraṇatthāya idhāgato. Adaṇḍāvacaranti adaṇḍehi nikkhittadaṇḍahatthehi avacaritabbaṃ sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāraṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ. Subbatāti yena maggena subbatā sabbaññubuddhā gacchanti, ahampi agatapubbaṃ disaṃ gantuṃ bodhitale nisīditvā tameva maggaṃ paṭipajjissāmīti.

In this passage, 'vutthaṃ me bhavanaṃ dibyaṃ' was said with reference to the Vejayanta palace. 'Sohaṃ etādisaṃ' means: 'Dear Nārada, I, having abandoned such a wealth of sensual pleasures, which is immeasurable even by a Buddha's knowledge, have come here for the sake of performing merit.' 'Adaṇḍāvacaraṃ' means the Eightfold Path preceded by right view, which is to be frequented by those without sticks, those who have laid down the stick in their hands. 'Subbatā' means that path by which the well-conducted, the All-Knowing Buddhas, go; I too, in order to go to the region never reached before, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will follow that very path.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imā gāthāyo sabbaññutaññāṇena saṅkhipitvā kathesi. Nārado punapi āha – “rajjaṃ, deva, anusāsā”ti. “Tāta, na me rajjenattho, satta vassasatāni vigataṃ dānaṃ sattāheneva dātukāmamhī”ti. Nārado “sādhū”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā mahādānaṃ paṭiyādesi. Rājā sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā sattame divase kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavaneyeva nibbatti.

Thus, the Bodhisatta summarized these verses with the knowledge of omniscience and spoke them. Nārada spoke again: “Great king, rule the kingdom!” “Dear boy, I have no need for a kingdom; for seven hundred years giving was absent, and I wish to give it in just seven days.” Nārada, saying “Very well,” accepted his word and prepared a great almsgiving. The king, having given alms for seven days, died on the seventh day and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ vasitabbayuttakaṃ uposathakammaṃ nāmā”ti dassetvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne uposathikesu upāsakesu keci sotāpattiphale, keci sakadāgāmiphale, keci anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tadā nāradarājā sāriputto ahosi, mātali ānando, sakko anuruddho, sādhinarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, showing, “This is what is called the observance of the Uposatha that should be performed in this way,” revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some of the lay devotees who were observers of the Uposatha were established in the fruit of stream-entry, some in the fruit of once-returning, and some in the fruit of non-returning. At that time, King Nārada was Sāriputta, Mātali was Ānanda, Sakka was Anuruddha, but King Sādhina was indeed myself.

Sādhinajātakavaṇṇanā ekādasamā.

The commentary on the Sādhina Jātaka, the eleventh.

[495] 12. Dasabrāhmaṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[495] 12. The commentary on the Dasabrāhmaṇa Jātaka

Rājā [M 4.0361] avoca vidhuranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto asadisadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ aṭṭhakanipāte ādittajātake (jā. 1.8.69 ādayo) vitthāritameva. Rājā kira taṃ dānaṃ dadanto satthāraṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pañca bhikkhusatāni vicinitvā gaṇhitvā mahākhīṇāsavānaṃyeva adāsi. Athassa guṇakathaṃ kathentā “āvuso, rājā asadisadānaṃ dadanto vicinitvā mahapphalaṭṭhāne adāsī”ti dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya [V 4.0323] nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ kosalarājā [P 4.0361] mādisassa buddhassa upaṭṭhāko hutvā viceyyadānaṃ deti, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppanne buddhepi viceyyadānaṃ adaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher gave this discourse, "The king addressed Vidhura," while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the unequaled gift. It is detailed in the Aṭṭhakanipāta in the Ādittajātaka (Jā. 1.8.69, etc.). The king, while giving that gift, is said to have made the Teacher his leader and selected five hundred monks, taking only great arahants. Then, while speaking of his virtues, they raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, ‘Friends, the king, in giving the unequaled gift, selected and gave to those in a place of great fruit.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Monks, with what discussion are you assembled here now?’ When they replied, ‘With this one,’ he said, ‘It is no wonder, monks, that the king of Kosala, being a supporter of a Buddha like me, gives a selective gift. Even the wise of old gave selective gifts when a Buddha had not yet arisen.’ Then he brought up a past story.

Atīte kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare yudhiṭṭhilagotto korabyo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa vidhuro nāma amacco atthañca dhammañca anusāsati. Rājā sakalajambudīpaṃ khobhetvā mahādānaṃ deti. Taṃ gahetvā bhuñjantesu ekopi pañcasīlamattaṃ rakkhanto nāma natthi, sabbe dussīlāva, dānaṃ rājānaṃ na toseti. Rājā “viceyyadānaṃ mahapphala”nti sīlavantānaṃ dātukāmo hutvā cintesi “vidhurapaṇḍitena saddhiṃ mantayissāmī”ti. So taṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ āsane nisīdāpetvā pañhaṃ pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

In the past, in the Kuru country, in the city of Indapatta, King Korabya of the Yudhiᅩᅩhila lineage ruled. His minister, named Vidhura, advised him on both material and spiritual matters. The king, having stirred up all of Jambudĩpa, gave a great donation. But among those who received and enjoyed it, not even one observed merely the five precepts—all were immoral, and the donation did not satisfy the king. The king thought, ‘A selective donation is of great fruit,’ and desiring to give to the virtuous, he considered, ‘I will consult with the wise Vidhura.’ When he came to attend him, the king seated him on a seat and asked a question. To explain that matter, the Teacher spoke half a verse:

222.

222.

“Rājā avoca vidhuraṃ, dhammakāmo yudhiṭṭhilo”ti;

‘The king Yudhiᅩᅩhila, a lover of Dhamma, addressed Vidhura.’

Parato rañño ca vidhurassa ca vacanapaṭivacanaṃ hoti –

Then there was a conversation between the king and Vidhura:

“Brāhmaṇe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘Vidhura, seek out brahmins who are virtuous and very learned.’

223.

223.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

“Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them we shall rightly give offerings, where a gift bears great fruit.

224.

224.

“Dullabhā brāhmaṇā deva, sīlavanto bahussutā;

Viratā methunā dhammā, ye te bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ.

‘Hard to find, O king, are brahmins who are virtuous and very learned, abstaining from sexual conduct, who may partake of your food.’

225.

225.

“Dasa [M 4.0362] khalu mahārāja, yā tā brāhmaṇajātiyo;

Tesaṃ vibhaṅgaṃ vicayaṃ, vitthārena suṇohi me.

‘Great king, there are indeed ten types of brahmins; listen to my detailed analysis and investigation of them from me.’

226.

226.

“Pasibbake gahetvāna, puṇṇe mūlassa saṃvute;

Osadhikāyo ganthenti, nhāpayanti japanti ca.

‘Taking bags filled with roots and tied shut, they prepare medicinal remedies, perform ritual bathing, and chant.’

227.

227.

“Tikicchakasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

‘Like physicians, O king, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king; shall we pay homage to such as these?’

228.

228.

“Apetā [V 4.0324][P 4.0362] te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

229.

229.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

‘Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them, friend, we shall give the offering, where a gift bears great fruit.’

230.

230.

“Kiṅkiṇikāyo gahetvā, ghosenti puratopi te;

Pesanānipi gacchanti, rathacariyāsu sikkhare.

‘Taking up small bells, they make a noise before them; they also go on errands and are trained in the driving of chariots.’

231.

231.

“Paricārakasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

‘Like attendants, O king, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king; shall we pay homage to such as these?’

232.

232.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

233.

233.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

‘Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them, friend, we shall give the offering, where a gift bears great fruit.’

234.

234.

“Kamaṇḍaluṃ gahetvāna, vaṅkadaṇḍañca brāhmaṇā;

Paccupessanti rājāno, gāmesu nigamesu ca;

Nādinne vuṭṭhahissāma, gāmamhi vā vanamhi vā.

‘Taking up a water pot and a crooked staff, the brahmins will approach kings in villages and towns, saying: ’We shall not rise until something is given, whether in village or in forest.’’

235.

235.

“Niggāhakasamā [M 4.0363] rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

“Like tax-collectors, O king, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king, and we do not bow down to such as these.

236.

236.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

237.

237.

“Virate [V 4.0325] methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

‘Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them, friend, we shall give the offering, where a gift bears great fruit.’

238.

238.

“Parūḷhakacchanakhalomā, paṅkadantā rajassirā;

Okiṇṇā rajareṇūhi, yācakā vicaranti te.

‘With overgrown armpit hair, nails, and body hair, with mud-stained teeth and dusty heads, covered with dust and dirt, those beggars wander about.’

239.

239.

“Khāṇughātasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

‘Like those who dig up stumps, O king, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king; shall we pay homage to such as these?’

240.

240.

“Apetā [P 4.0363] te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

241.

241.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

‘Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them, friend, we shall give the offering, where a gift bears great fruit.’

242.

242.

“Harītakaṃ āmalakaṃ, ambaṃ jambuṃ vibhītakaṃ;

Labujaṃ dantapoṇāni, beluvā badarāni ca.

‘Haritaki and amalaka, mango, jambu, and vibhitaka; labuja, tooth-cleaners, beluva, and jujube fruits.’

243.

243.

“Rājāyatanaṃ ucchupuṭaṃ, dhūmanettaṃ madhuañjanaṃ;

Uccāvacāni paṇiyāni, vipaṇenti janādhipa.

‘Rajayatana fruits, sugarcane packets, smoking pipes, honey, and ointments; various wares they sell, O lord of men.’

244.

244.

“Vāṇijakasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

‘Like merchants, O king, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king; shall we pay homage to such as these?’

245.

245.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

246.

246.

“Virate [V 4.0326][M 4.0364] methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

‘Those who abstain from sexual conduct, who would partake of my food; to them, friend, we shall give the offering, where a gift bears great fruit.’

247.

247.

“Kasivāṇijjaṃ kārenti, posayanti ajeḷake;

Kumāriyo pavecchanti, vivāhantāvahanti ca.

‘They engage in agriculture and trade, they raise goats and sheep; they give maidens in marriage and take wives for their sons.’

248.

248.

“Samā ambaṭṭhavessehi, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

‘Equal to Ambaᅩᅩhas and Vessas, they too are called brahmins; they have been pointed out, great king; shall we pay homage to such as these?’

249.

249.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

‘They are devoid of brahminhood, (so said King Korabya) they are not called brahmins; seek others, Vidhura, who are virtuous and very learned.’

250.

250.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

Those who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat my food; friend Vidhura, we shall give an offering to them, where what is given bears great fruit.

251.

251.

“Nikkhittabhikkhaṃ [P 4.0364] bhuñjanti, gāmesveke purohitā;

Bahū te paripucchanti, aṇḍacchedā nilañchakā.

Some priests in villages eat food regularly set aside; many people consult them; they are castrators and branders of cattle.

252.

252.

“Pasūpi tattha haññanti, mahiṃsā sūkarā ajā;

Goghātakasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

Animals are also slain there—buffaloes, pigs, and goats. Like cattle-slaughterers, O king, they too are called brahmins. They have been described, O great king; shall we attend upon such as these?

253.

253.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

They have departed from brahminhood, (thus spoke King Korabya,) they are not called brahmins. Seek others, O Vidhura, who are virtuous and deeply learned.

254.

254.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

Those who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat my food; friend Vidhura, we shall give an offering to them, where what is given bears great fruit.

255.

255.

“Asicammaṃ [V 4.0327] gahetvāna, khaggaṃ paggayha brāhmaṇā;

Vessapathesu tiṭṭhanti, satthaṃ abbāhayantipi.

Taking up sword and shield and brandishing a blade, these brahmins stand on the trade routes and even escort caravans for a fee.

256.

256.

“Samā gopanisādehi, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

They are equal to cowherds and hunters, yet they too are called brahmins. They have been described, O great king; shall we attend upon such as these?

257.

257.

“Apetā [M 4.0365] te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

They have departed from brahminhood, (thus spoke King Korabya,) they are not called brahmins. Seek others, O Vidhura, who are virtuous and deeply learned.

258.

258.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

Those who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat my food; friend Vidhura, we shall give an offering to them, where what is given bears great fruit.

259.

259.

“Araññe kuṭikaṃ katvā, kuṭāni kārayanti te;

Sasabiḷāre bādhenti, āgodhā macchakacchapaṃ.

Having built a hut in the forest, they set traps; they slay hares, cats, iguanas, fish, and turtles.

260.

260.

“Te luddakasamā rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

They are like hunters, O king, yet they too are called brahmins. They have been described, O great king; shall we attend upon such as these?

261.

261.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

They have departed from brahminhood, (thus spoke King Korabya,) they are not called brahmins. Seek others, O Vidhura, who are virtuous and deeply learned.

262.

262.

“Virate [P 4.0365] methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

Those who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat my food; friend Vidhura, we shall give an offering to them, where what is given bears great fruit.

263.

263.

“Aññe dhanassa kāmā hi, heṭṭhāmañce pasakkitā;

Rājāno upari nhāyanti, somayāge upaṭṭhite.

Others, indeed, desiring wealth, lie beneath the couch while kings bathe above when the Soma sacrifice is prepared.

264.

264.

“Malamajjakasamā [V 4.0328] rāja, tepi vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase.

Like bath-attendants, O king, they too are called brahmins. They have been described, O great king; shall we attend upon such as these?

265.

265.

“Apetā te ca brahmaññā, (iti rājā korabyo)

Na te vuccanti brāhmaṇā;

Aññe vidhura pariyesa, sīlavante bahussute.

They have departed from brahminhood, (thus spoke King Korabya,) they are not called brahmins. Seek others, O Vidhura, who are virtuous and deeply learned.

266.

266.

“Virate methunā dhammā, ye me bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ;

Dakkhiṇaṃ samma dassāma, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti.

Those who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat my food; friend Vidhura, we shall give an offering to them, where what is given bears great fruit. Thus spoke King Korabya.

Tattha sīlavanteti maggenāgatasīle. Bahussuteti paṭivedhabahussute. Dakkhiṇanti dānaṃ. Ye teti ye dhammikā samaṇabrāhmaṇā tava dānaṃ [M 4.0366] bhuñjeyyuṃ, te dullabhā. Brāhmaṇajātiyoti brāhmaṇakulāni. Tesaṃ vibhaṅgaṃ vicayanti tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vibhaṅgaṃ mama paññāya vicitabhāvaṃ vitthārena suṇohi. Saṃvuteti baddhamukhe. Osadhikāyo ganthentīti “idaṃ imassa rogassa bhesajjaṃ, idaṃ imassa rogassa bhesajja”nti evaṃ siloke bandhitvā manussānaṃ denti. Nhāpayantīti nahāpanaṃ nāma karonti. Japanti cāti bhūtavijjaṃ parivattenti. Tikicchakasamāti vejjasadisā. Tepi vuccantīti tepi “brāhmaṇā vā mayaṃ, abrāhmaṇā vā”ti ajānitvā vejjakammena jīvikaṃ kappentā vohārena “brāhmaṇā”ti vuccanti. Akkhātā teti ime te mayā vejjabrāhmaṇā nāma akkhātā. Nipatāmaseti vadehi dāni, kiṃ tādise brāhmaṇe nipatāma, nimantanatthāya upasaṅkamāma, atthi te etehi atthoti pucchati. Brahmaññāti brāhmaṇadhammato. Na te vuccantīti te bāhitapāpatāya brāhmaṇā nāma na vuccanti.

Herein, 'virtuous' means possessing virtue attained through the path. 'Deeply learned' means deeply learned in penetration. 'An offering' means a gift. 'Those who' means those righteous ascetics and brahmins who would partake of your gift; they are rare. 'Of brahmin birth' means brahmin families. 'Their classification, examine' means: listen in detail to the classification of those brahmins, a distinction made by my wisdom. 'Restrained' means with a bound mouth. 'They bind medicinal herbs' means they compose verses, saying, 'This is the medicine for this illness, this is the medicine for that illness,' and give them to people. 'They bathe' means they perform a bathing ritual. 'And they chant' means they recite spirit-lore. 'Like physicians' means similar to doctors. 'They too are called' means: not knowing whether they are brahmins or not, they make a living through the practice of medicine and are called 'brahmins' by convention. 'They have been described' means: these physician-brahmins have been described by me. 'Shall we pay homage?' means: he asks, 'Speak now, shall we pay homage to such brahmins? Shall we approach them for the purpose of an invitation? Do you have any business with them?' 'From brahminhood' means from the nature of a brahmin. 'They are not called' means: they are not called brahmins, for a brahmin is so called because he has banished evil.

Kiṅkiṇikāyoti mahārāja, aparepi brāhmaṇā attano brāhmaṇadhammaṃ chaḍḍetvā jīvikatthāya rājarājamahāmattānaṃ purato kaṃsatāḷe gahetvā vādentā gāyantā gacchanti. Pesanānipīti dāsakammakarā viya pesanānipi gacchanti. Rathacariyāsūti rathasippaṃ sikkhanti. Paricārakasamāti dāsakammakarasadisā. Vaṅkadaṇḍanti [P 4.0366] vaṅkadaṇḍakaṭṭhaṃ. Paccupessanti rājānoti rājarājamahāmatte paṭicca āgamma sandhāya upasevanti. Gāmesu nigamesu cāti tesaṃ nivesanadvāre nisīdanti. Niggāhakasamāti niggahakārakehi balisādhakarājapurisehi samā. Yathā te purisā “aggahetvā na gamissāmā”ti niggahaṃ katvā gaṇhantiyeva, tathā “gāme vā [V 4.0329] vane vā aladdhā marantāpi na vuṭṭhahissāmā”ti upavasanti. Tepīti tepi balisādhakasadisā pāpadhammā.

'With a small bell' means: O great king, other brahmins, abandoning their brahmin duty for the sake of a livelihood, take up bronze cymbals and go before kings and royal ministers, playing and singing. 'And on errands' means they go on errands like slaves and workers. 'In charioteering' means they learn the craft of the chariot. 'Like attendants' means similar to slaves and workers. 'A crooked staff' means a crooked piece of wood. 'They attend upon kings' means they serve kings and royal ministers, relying on them, coming to them, and depending on them. 'And in villages and towns' means they sit at the doors of their dwellings. 'Like constrainers' means like royal officers who are enforcers and tax-collectors. Just as those men, having made a constraint, seize, thinking, 'We will not go without taking,' so too they fast, thinking, 'Even if we die without getting anything in the village or the forest, we will not get up.' 'They too' means those brahmins of evil nature are also like tax-collectors.

Rajareṇūhīti rajehi ca paṃsūhi ca okiṇṇā. Yācakāti dhanayācakā. Khāṇughātasamāti malīnasarīratāya jhāmakhette khāṇughātakehi bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā jhāmakhāṇukauddharaṇakamanussehi samānā, “aggahetvā na gamissāmā”ti niccalabhāvena ṭhitattā nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitavatikhāṇukā viyātipi attho. Tepīti tepi tathā laddhaṃ dhanaṃ vaḍḍhiyā payojetvā puna tatheva ṭhitattā dussīlā brāhmaṇā.

'With dust and dirt' means strewn with dust and dirt. 'Beggars' means beggars of wealth. 'Like stump-strikers' means: because of their soiled bodies, they are like men who pull out burnt stumps, having dug the ground in a burnt field with stump-strikers; and also, because they stand immovably thinking, 'We will not go without taking,' the meaning is that they are like boundary-posts dug in and set up. 'They too' means those immoral brahmins who, having thus obtained wealth and invested it at interest, stand there again in the same way.

Ucchupuṭanti [M 4.0367] ucchuñceva phāṇitapuṭañca. Madhuañjananti madhuñceva añjanañca. Uccāvacānīti mahagghaappagghāni. Paṇiyānīti bhaṇḍāni. Vipaṇentīti vikkiṇanti. Tepīti tepi imāni ettakāni vikkiṇitvā jīvikakappakā vāṇijakabrāhmaṇā. Posayantīti gorasavikkayena jīvikakappanatthaṃ posenti. Pavecchantīti attano dhītaro hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā paresaṃ denti. Te evaṃ paresaṃ dadamānā vivāhanti nāma, attano puttānaṃ atthāya gaṇhamānā āvāhanti nāma. Ambaṭṭhavessehīti kuṭumbikehi ceva gahapatīhi ca samā, tepi vohāravasena “brāhmaṇā”ti vuccanti.

'Sugarcane packets' means both sugarcane and packets of molasses. 'Honey and ointment' means both honey and collyrium. 'Various' means of great and small value. 'Wares' means goods. 'They sell' means they sell. 'They too' means these merchant brahmins who make a living by selling so many things. 'They rear' means they rear animals for the purpose of making a living by selling dairy products. 'They give away' means they give their own daughters to others after taking gold and silver. Those giving to others in this way are performing a vivāha (giving in marriage); those taking for the sake of their own sons are performing an āvāha (taking a bride). 'With Ambaṭṭhas and Vessas' means equal to householders and heads of households; they too are called 'brahmins' by convention.

Nikkhittabhikkhanti gāmapurohitā hutvā attano atthāya nibaddhabhikkhaṃ. Bahū teti bahū janā ete gāmapurohite nakkhattamuhuttamaṅgalāni pucchanti. Aṇḍacchedā nilañchakāti bhatiṃ gahetvā balibaddānaṃ aṇḍacchedakā ceva tisūlādiaṅkakaraṇena lañchakā ca, lakkhaṇakārakāti attho. Tatthāti tesaṃ gāmapurohitānaṃ gehesu maṃsavikkiṇanatthaṃ ete pasuādayopi haññanti. Tepīti tepi goghātakasamā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti.

Fixed alms—those who, having become village priests, receive fixed alms for their own benefit. Many—many people ask these village priests about constellations, auspicious times, and auspicious rites. Castrators and markers—those who, taking payment, castrate bulls and mark them with tridents and other signs; that is, those who make marks. There—in the houses of these village priests, even these animals and so on are killed for the purpose of selling meat. Even these—even these are called brahmins similar to cow-slaughterers.

Asicammanti asilaṭṭhiñceva kaṇḍavāraṇañca. Vessapathesūti vāṇijānaṃ gamanamaggesu. Satthaṃ abbāhayantīti satthavāhānaṃ hatthato satampi sahassampi gahetvā satthe corāṭaviṃ atibāhenti. Gopanisādehīti gopālakehi ceva nisādehi ca gāmaghātakacorehi samāti vuttaṃ. Tepīti tepi evarūpā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti. Kuṭāni kārayanti teti kūṭapāsādīni ropenti. Sasabiḷāreti sase ceva biḷāre ca. Etena thalacare mige dasseti. Āgodhā macchakacchapanti thalajesu tāva āgodhato mahante ca khuddake ca pāṇayo bādhenti mārenti, jalajesu macchakacchape. Tepīti tepi luddakasamā [P 4.0367] brāhmaṇāti vuccanti.

Swords and shields—both sword-sticks and leather armor. On trade routes—on the roads where traders travel. They escort caravans—taking hundreds or thousands from the caravan leaders, they lead the caravans through robber-infested wilderness. With herdsmen and hunters—meaning they are like herdsmen, hunters, and village-destroying robbers. Even these—even these of such a kind are called brahmins. They build huts—they erect false pavilions. Hares and cats—by this, land-dwelling animals are shown. Iguanas, fish, and turtles—on land, they harm and kill creatures large and small, beginning with iguanas; in water, fish and turtles. Even these—even these are called brahmins similar to hunters.

Aññe [V 4.0330] dhanassa kāmā hīti apare brāhmaṇā dhanaṃ patthentā. Heṭṭhāmañce pasakkitāti “kalipavāhakammaṃ kāressāmā”ti ratanamayaṃ mañcaṃ kāretvā tassa heṭṭhā nipannā acchanti. Atha nesaṃ somayāge upaṭṭhite rājāno upari nahāyanti, te kira somayāge niṭṭhite āgantvā [M 4.0368] tasmiṃ mañce nisīdanti. Atha ne aññe brāhmaṇā “kaliṃ pavāhessāmā”ti nahāpenti. Ratanamañco ceva rañño rājālaṅkāro ca sabbo heṭṭhāmañce nipannasseva hoti. Tepīti tepi malamajjakehi nahāpitehi sadisā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti.

Others, indeed, desiring wealth—meaning other brahmins seeking wealth. They lie beneath a couch—thinking, "We will perform the Kali-pavāha (evil-washing) ritual." They have a jeweled couch made and stay lying beneath it. Then, when the Soma sacrifice is ready, kings bathe above them; it is said that when the Soma sacrifice is finished, they come and sit on that couch. Then, other brahmins bathe them, intending to "wash away the Kali (bad luck)." The jeweled couch and all the royal ornaments belong only to the one lying beneath the couch. Even they—these are called brahmins similar to bath-attendants who clean away dirt.

Evañcime vohāramattabrāhmaṇe dassetvā idāni paramatthabrāhmaṇe dassento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having thus shown these brahmins by mere convention, now, showing the brahmins in the ultimate sense, he spoke two verses:

267.

267.

“Atthi kho brāhmaṇā deva, sīlavanto bahussutā;

Viratā methunā dhammā, ye te bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ.

Indeed, O king, there are virtuous and deeply learned brahmins who abstain from sexual conduct and would eat your food.

268.

268.

“Ekañca bhattaṃ bhuñjanti, na ca majjaṃ pivanti te;

Akkhātā te mahārāja, tādise nipatāmase”ti.

They eat only one meal and they do not drink intoxicants. They have been described, O great king; let us attend upon such ones.

Tattha sīlavantoti ariyasīlena samannāgatā. Bahussutāti paṭivedhabāhusaccena samannāgatā. Tādiseti evarūpe bāhitapāpe paccekabuddhabrāhmaṇe nimantanatthāya upasaṅkamāmāti.
