There, 'virtuous' means endowed with noble virtue. 'Deeply learned' means endowed with the great learning of penetration. 'Such ones' means: let us approach for the purpose of inviting those Paccekabuddha Brahmins of such a kind, who have eliminated evil.

Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā pucchi “samma vidhura, evarūpā aggadakkhiṇeyyā brāhmaṇā kahaṃ vasantī”ti? Uttarahimavante nandamūlakapabbhāre, mahārājāti. “Tena hi, paṇḍita, tava balena mayhaṃ te brāhmaṇe pariyesā”ti tuṭṭhamānaso gāthamāha –

The king, having heard his words, asked, "Good Vidhura, where do such brahmins, worthy of the highest offerings, dwell?" "In the northern Himalayas, on the slopes of Mount Nandamūla, great king." "Then, wise one, by your power, seek out those brahmins for me," he said with a delighted mind, and spoke this verse:

269.

269.

“Ete kho brāhmaṇā vidhura, sīsavanto bahussutā;

Ete vidhura pariyesa, khippañca ne nimantayā”ti.

These, Vidhura, are the brahmins who are virtuous and deeply learned. Seek them out, Vidhura, and quickly invite them.

Mahāsatto “sādhū”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā “tena hi, mahārāja, nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā sabbe nagaravāsino dānaṃ datvā uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya samādinnasīlā hontū”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā “tumhepi saddhiṃ parijanena uposathaṃ samādiyathā”ti vatvā sayaṃ pātova bhuñjitvā uposathaṃ samādāya sāyanhasamaye jātipupphapuṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇasamuggaṃ āharāpetvā raññā [V 4.0331] saddhiṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā [P 4.0368] paccekabuddhānaṃ guṇe anussaritvā vanditvā “uttarahimavante nandamūlakapabbhāravāsino pañcasatā paccekabuddhā sve amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhantū”ti nimantetvā ākāse aṭṭha pupphamuṭṭhiyo vissajjesi. Tadā tattha pañcasatā paccekabuddhā vasanti, pupphāni gantvā tesaṃ upari patiṃsu. Te āvajjentā taṃ kāraṇaṃ [M 4.0369] ñatvā “mārisā, vidhurapaṇḍitena nimantitamha, na kho panesa ittarasatto, buddhaṅkuro esa, imasmiṃyeva kappe buddho bhavissati, karissāmassa saṅgaha”nti nimantanaṃ adhivāsayiṃsu. Mahāsatto pupphānaṃ anāgamanasaññāya adhivāsitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “mahārāja, sve paccekabuddhā āgamissanti, sakkārasammānaṃ karohī”ti āha. Rājā punadivase mahāsakkāraṃ katvā mahātale mahārahāni āsanāni paññapesi. Paccekabuddhā anotattadahe katasarīrapaṭijagganā velaṃ sallakkhetvā ākāsenāgantvā rājaṅgaṇe otariṃsu. Rājā ca bodhisatto ca pasannamānasā tesaṃ hatthato pattāni gahetvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisiṃsu. Bhattakiccapariyosāne ca punadivasatthāyāti evaṃ satta divase nimantetvā mahādānaṃ datvā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāre adaṃsu. Te anumodanaṃ katvā ākāsena tattheva gatā, parikkhārāpi tehi saddhiṃyeva gatā.

The Great Being Vidhura the Wise, accepting his words by saying "Very well," told the king, "Then, O great king, have the city adorned, and let all the city-dwellers give alms, observe the Uposatha, and undertake the precepts." Having had this proclaimed by drum, he said, "You too, along with your retinue and ministers, should observe the Uposatha." Then, having eaten early in the morning himself and undertaking the Uposatha, he had a golden casket filled with jasmine flowers brought in the evening. Together with the king, he performed the prostration with the five points of contact, recollected the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas, paid homage, and invited them, saying, "May the five hundred Paccekabuddhas dwelling in the Nandamūla cave in the northern Himalayas receive our alms tomorrow." Then he scattered eight handfuls of flowers into the sky. At that time, five hundred Paccekabuddhas were dwelling in the Nandamūla cave. The flowers traveled and fell upon those five hundred Paccekabuddhas. Reflecting, they understood the reason and said, "Sirs, we have been invited by Vidhura the Wise. Truly, he is no ordinary being; he is a Buddha-sprout who will become a Buddha in this very aeon. Let us favor Vidhura the Wise." Thus they accepted the invitation. The Great Being, knowing they had accepted by the sign of the flowers not returning, said, "O great king, tomorrow the Paccekabuddhas will come. Prepare honors and respect." On the following day, the king Korabya prepared great honors and had seats fit for noble ones set out on the palace terrace. The Paccekabuddhas, having washed in Lake Anotatta and noting the time, came through the sky and descended into the royal courtyard. Both King Korabya and the Bodhisatta Vidhura, with hearts full of faith, took the bowls from their hands, led them up to the palace, offered the water of dedication, and served them with delicious hard and soft food. At the end of the meal, they invited them for the next day, and so for seven days they gave a great gift. On the seventh day, they offered all the requisites. After giving their blessing, the Paccekabuddhas departed through the sky to the Nandamūla cave, and the requisites also went with them. King Korabya and the minister Vidhura, along with their retinues, having given great alms, filled the heavenly realm at the end of their lives.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, kosalarañño mama upaṭṭhākassa sato viceyyadānaṃ dātuṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppannepi buddhe dānaṃ adaṃsuyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, vidhurapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: "Bhikkhus, it is no wonder that the King of Kosala, being my attendant, gives a discriminating gift. Even in ancient times, wise men gave discriminating gifts even before the Buddha had arisen." Then he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Korabya was Ānanda, and the minister named Vidhura was I myself."

Dasabrāhmaṇajātakavaṇṇanā dvādasamā.

The Commentary on the Dasabrāhmaṇa Jātaka is the twelfth. The blessing of giving to those who possess virtue is complete.

[496] 13. Bhikkhāparamparajātakavaṇṇanā

[496] 13. 13. The Bhikkhāparampara Jātaka: How almsfood reaches the appropriate place through the honoring of the Dhamma-jewel.

Sukhumālarūpaṃ [P 4.0369] disvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira saddho ahosi pasanno, tathāgatassa ceva saṅghassa ca nibaddhaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karoti. Athekadivasaṃ cintesi “ahaṃ buddharatanassa ceva saṅgharatanassa ca paṇītāni khādanīyabhojanīyāni ceva sukhumavatthāni ca dento niccaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karomi, idāni dhammaratanassapi karissāmi, kathaṃ nu kho tassa sakkāraṃ karontena [M 4.0370] kattabba”nti. So bahūni gandhamālādīni [V 4.0332] ādāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pucchi “ahaṃ, bhante, dhammaratanassa sakkāraṃ kattukāmomhi, kathaṃ nu kho tassa sakkāraṃ karontena kattabba”nti. Atha naṃ satthā āha – “sace dhammaratanassa sakkāraṃ kattukāmo, dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa ānandassa sakkāraṃ karohī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā theraṃ nimantetvā punadivase mahantena sakkārena attano gehaṃ netvā mahārahe āsane nisīdāpetvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ datvā mahagghe ticīvarappahonake sāṭake adāsi. Theropi “ayaṃ sakkāro dhammaratanassa kato, na mayhaṃ anucchaviko, aggasāvakassa dhammasenāpatissa anucchaviko”ti cintetvā piṇḍapātañca vatthāni ca vihāraṃ haritvā sāriputtattherassa adāsi. Sopi “ayaṃ sakkāro dhammaratanassa kato, ekantena dhammassāmino sammāsambuddhasseva anucchaviko”ti cintetvā dasabalassa adāsi. Satthā attano uttaritaraṃ adisvā piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji, cīvarasāṭake aggahesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Bhikkhāparampara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Seeing the delicate form,' regarding a certain householder. That householder was faithful and devoted, constantly showing great honor to the Buddha and the Sangha. One day, he thought: "I have always shown great honor to the Buddha-jewel and the Sangha-jewel by offering delicious hard and soft food and delicate cloths. Now, I shall also show great honor to the Dhamma-jewel. How should I act to honor the Dhamma-jewel?" Taking many perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he went to Jetavana, paid respects to the Teacher, and asked, "Venerable sir, I wish to honor the Dhamma-jewel. How should I perform this honoring of the Dhamma-jewel?" Then the Teacher said to him, "Householder, if you wish to honor the Dhamma-jewel, honor Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma." He replied, "Very well," and invited the Venerable Ānanda. The next day, he led him to his home with great honor, seated him on a costly seat, honored him with perfumes and flowers, served various superior foods, and offered cloths sufficient for the three robes. The Venerable Ānanda thought, "This honor was intended for the Dhamma-jewel; it is not fitting for me. It is fitting for the chief disciple, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta." So he took the almsfood and the cloths to the monastery and gave them to Venerable Sāriputta. The General of the Dhamma also thought, "This honor was intended for the Dhamma-jewel. Truly, it is fitting only for the Blessed Buddha, the Master of the Dhamma." So he gave them to the Buddha. The Teacher, seeing no one superior to himself, partook of the almsfood and accepted the robe-cloths.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma kuṭumbiko ‘dhammaratanassa sakkāraṃ karomī’ti dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa ānandattherassa adāsi. Thero ‘nāyaṃ mayhaṃ anucchaviko’ti dhammasenāpatino adāsi, sopi ‘nāyaṃ mayhaṃ anucchaviko’ti tathāgatassa adāsi. Tathāgato aññaṃ uttaritaraṃ apassanto attano dhammassāmitāya ‘mayhameveso anucchaviko’ti taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji, cīvarasāṭakepi gaṇhi, evaṃ so piṇḍapāto yathānucchavikatāya dhammassāminova pādamūlaṃ gato”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva piṇḍapāto paramparā yathānucchavikaṃ gacchati, pubbepi anuppanne buddhe agamāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, a certain householder, intending to honor the Dhamma-jewel, gave to the treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda. The Elder, thinking, 'This is not fitting for me,' gave it to the General of the Dhamma. He too, thinking, 'This is not fitting for me,' gave it to the Buddha. The Buddha, seeing no one superior to himself and being the Master of the Dhamma, thought, 'The gift intended for the Dhamma-jewel is fitting only for the Buddha,' and thus partook of the almsfood and accepted the robe-cloths. In this manner, because of its suitability, the almsfood reached the feet of the Master of the Dhamma through a succession of givers." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they told him, he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that almsfood reaches the appropriate place in succession; it also reached it in the past before a Buddha had arisen." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 4.0370] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto agatigamanaṃ pahāya dasa rājadhamme akopento dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Evaṃ santepissa vinicchayo suñño viya ahosi. Rājā attano aguṇagavesako hutvā antonivesanādīni [M 4.0371] pariggaṇhanto antepure ca antonagare ca dvāragāmesu ca attano aguṇaṃ kathentaṃ adisvā “janapade gavesissāmī”ti amaccānaṃ rajjaṃ niyyādetvā purohitena saddhiṃ aññātakaveseneva kāsiraṭṭhe caranto kañci aguṇaṃ kathentaṃ adisvā paccante ekaṃ nigamaṃ patvā bahidvārasālāyaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe nigamavāsī asītikoṭivibhavo kuṭumbiko mahantena parivārena nhānatitthaṃ gacchanto sālāyaṃ nisinnaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sukhumālasarīraṃ rājānaṃ disvā uppannasineho sālaṃ pavisitvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “idheva [V 4.0333] hothā”ti vatvā gehaṃ gantvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ sampādetvā mahantena parivārena bhattabhājanāni gāhāpetvā agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe himavantavāsī pañcābhiñño tāpaso āgantvā tattheva nisīdi. Nandamūlakapabbhārato paccekabuddhopi āgantvā tattheva nisīdi.

In the past, in Benares, King Brahmadatta, having abandoned the wrong courses of action and not violating the ten royal virtues, ruled righteously. Even so, his court of justice was as if empty. The king, seeking his own faults, investigated his inner palace and other places—within the royal compound, the inner city, and the gate-villages—but finding no one speaking of his faults, thinking, 'I will search in the countryside,' he entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and, in the guise of an unknown person, traveled through the Kasi country with his chaplain. Not finding anyone speaking of his faults, he reached a market town on the border and sat in a hall outside the gate. At that moment, a householder from the town, possessing eighty crores of wealth, was going to the bathing place with a large retinue. Seeing the king—golden-hued and with a delicate body—seated in the hall, affection arose in him. Entering the hall, he made a friendly greeting and said, 'Please stay right here.' Then he went home, prepared a meal with various excellent flavors, and returned with a large retinue having food vessels brought. At that same time, an ascetic dwelling in the Himalayas, possessing the five supernormal knowledges, arrived and sat there. A Paccekabuddha from the Nandamũlaka cave also arrived and sat there.

Kuṭumbiko rañño hatthadhovanaudakaṃ datvā nānaggarasehi sūpabyañjanehi bhattapātiṃ sajjetvā rañño upanesi. Rājā naṃ gahetvā purohitassa brāhmaṇassa adāsi. Brāhmaṇo gahetvā tāpasassa adāsi. Tāpaso paccekabuddhassa santikaṃ gantvā vāmahatthena bhattapātiṃ, dakkhiṇahatthena kamaṇḍaluṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā patte bhattaṃ pakkhipi. So kañci animantetvā anāpucchitvā paribhuñji. Tassa bhattakiccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko cintesi “mayā rañño bhattaṃ dinnaṃ, raññā brāhmaṇassa, brāhmaṇena tāpasassa, tāpasena paccekabuddhassa, paccekabuddho kañci anāpucchitvā paribhuñji, kiṃ nu kho imesaṃ ettakaṃ dānakāraṇaṃ, kiṃ imassa kañci anāpucchitvāva [P 4.0371] bhuñjanakāraṇaṃ, anupubbena te pucchissāmī”ti. So ekekaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā pucchi. Tepissa kathesuṃ –

The householder, having given the king water for washing his hands, prepared a food bowl with soups and curries of various excellent flavors and presented it to the king. The king took it and gave it to the brahmin chaplain. The brahmin took it and gave it to the ascetic. The ascetic went to the Paccekabuddha, took the food bowl with his left hand and the water pot with his right, poured the water of dedication, and placed the food in the bowl. He partook of it without inviting or asking permission from anyone. When the meal was finished, the householder thought, 'I gave food to the king, the king to the brahmin, the brahmin to the ascetic, and the ascetic to the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha partook of it without asking anyone. What, I wonder, is the reason for this chain of giving? And what is the reason for his eating without asking anyone? I will ask them in sequence.' He approached each one, paid respects, and asked. And they told him:

270.

270.

“Sukhumālarūpaṃ disvā, raṭṭhā vivanamāgataṃ;

Kuṭāgāravarūpetaṃ, mahāsayanamupāsitaṃ.

Seeing your delicate form, come from a kingdom to the wilderness, you who are accustomed to a fine gabled palace and a grand couch,

271.

271.

“Tassa te pemakenāhaṃ, adāsiṃ vaḍḍhamodanaṃ;

Sālīnaṃ vicitaṃ bhattaṃ, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ.

Out of affection for you, I gave you an excellent meal: choice rice, pure food with meat sauces.

272.

272.

“Taṃ tvaṃ bhattaṃ paṭiggayha, brāhmaṇassa adāsayi;

Attānaṃ anasitvāna, koyaṃ dhammo namatthu te.

You received that meal and gave it to the brahmin, without eating it yourself. What is this custom? Homage to you!

273.

273.

“Ācariyo [M 4.0372] brāhmaṇo mayhaṃ, kiccākiccesu byāvaṭo;

Garu ca āmantanīyo ca, dātumarahāmi bhojanaṃ.

The brahmin is my teacher, occupied with my affairs; he is venerable and worthy of being invited. I am fit to give him food.

274.

274.

“Brāhmaṇaṃ dāni pucchāmi, gotamaṃ rājapūjitaṃ;

Rājā te bhattaṃ pādāsi, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ.

Now I ask the brahmin Gotama, honored by the king: The king gave you food, pure and with meat sauces.

275.

275.

“Taṃ [V 4.0334] tvaṃ bhattaṃ paṭiggayha, isissa bhojanaṃ adā;

Akhettaññūsi dānassa, koyaṃ dhammo namatthu te.

You received that meal and gave food to the ascetic. Are you ignorant of the field of giving? What is this custom? Homage to you!

276.

276.

“Bharāmi puttadāre ca, gharesu gadhito ahaṃ;

Bhuñje mānusake kāme, anusāsāmi rājino.

I support a wife and children; I am attached to the household. I enjoy human sensual pleasures and I advise the king.

277.

277.

“Āraññikassa isino, cirarattaṃ tapassino;

Vuḍḍhassa bhāvitattassa, dātumarahāmi bhojanaṃ.

To the forest-dwelling ascetic, who has practiced austerities for a long time, who is mature and of developed mind, I am fit to give food.

278.

278.

“Isiñca dāni pucchāmi, kisaṃ dhamanisanthataṃ;

Parūḷhakacchanakhalomaṃ, paṅkadantaṃ rajassiraṃ.

Now I ask the ascetic, lean and covered with veins, with overgrown armpit hair, nails, and body hair, with stained teeth and a dusty head,

279.

279.

“Eko araññe viharasi, nāvakaṅkhasi jīvitaṃ;

Bhikkhu kena tayā seyyo, yassa tvaṃ bhojanaṃ adā.

You dwell alone in the forest, not longing for life. In what way is this monk superior to you, that you gave him food?

280.

280.

“Khaṇantālukalambāni, bilālitakkalāni ca;

Dhunaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ, saṅghāriyaṃ pasāriyaṃ.

Digging up various tubers and roots, and threshing wild rice and grains, then gathering and spreading them out to dry,

281.

281.

“Sākaṃ bhisaṃ madhuṃ maṃsaṃ, badarāmalakāni ca;

Tāni āharitvā bhuñjāmi, atthi me so pariggaho.

Greens, lotus roots, honey, meat, jujubes, and myrobalans—collecting these, I eat them; such is my possession.

282.

282.

“Pacanto [P 4.0372] apacantassa, amamassa sakiñcano;

Anādānassa sādāno, dātumarahāmi bhojanaṃ.

I, who cook, am fit to give food to one who does not cook; I, who have impediments, to one who is without attachment; I, who grasp, to one who does not grasp.

283.

283.

“Bhikkhuñca dāni pucchāmi, tuṇhīmāsīna subbataṃ;

Isi te bhattaṃ pādāsi, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ.

Now I ask the monk, sitting in silence and of good vows: The ascetic gave you food, pure and with meat sauces.

284.

284.

“Taṃ tvaṃ bhattaṃ paṭiggayha, tuṇhī bhuñjasi ekako;

Nāññaṃ kañci nimantesi, koyaṃ dhammo namatthu te.

Having received that food, you eat alone in silence; you do not invite anyone else. What is this custom? Homage to you!

285.

285.

“Na [V 4.0335] pacāmi na pācemi, na chindāmi na chedaye;

Taṃ maṃ akiñcanaṃ ñatvā, sabbapāpehi ārataṃ.

I do not cook nor cause to cook; I do not cut nor cause to cut. Knowing me to be without impediments and abstaining from all evil,

286.

286.

“Vāmena [M 4.0373] bhikkhamādāya, dakkhiṇena kamaṇḍaluṃ;

Isi me bhattaṃ pādāsi, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ.

Taking the alms-food with the left hand and the water-pot with the right, the ascetic gave me food, pure and with meat sauces.

287.

287.

“Ete hi dātumarahanti, samamā sapariggahā;

Paccanīkamahaṃ maññe, yo dātāraṃ nimantaye”ti.

Indeed, those with possessiveness and with possessions are fit to give. I consider it contrary to practice for one to invite the giver.

Tattha vivananti nirudakāraññasadisaṃ imaṃ paccantaṃ āgataṃ. Kūṭāgāravarūpetanti kūṭāgāravarena upagataṃ, ekaṃ varakūṭāgāravāsinanti attho. Mahāsayanamupāsitanti tattheva supaññattaṃ sirisayanaṃ upāsitaṃ. Tassa teti evarūpaṃ taṃ disvā ahaṃ pemamakāsiṃ, tassa te pemakena. Vaḍḍhamodananti uttamodanaṃ. Vicitanti apagatakhaṇḍakāḷakehi vicitataṇḍulehi kataṃ. Adāsayīti adāsi. Attānanti attanā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Anasitvānāti abhuñjitvā. Koyaṃ dhammoti mahārāja, ko esa tumhākaṃ sabhāvo. Namatthu teti namo tava atthu, yo tvaṃ attanā abhuñjitvā parassa adāsi.

There, `vivananti` means 'having arrived at this remote region, which is like a waterless wilderness.' `Kūṭāgāravarūpetaṃ` means 'endowed with an excellent gabled chamber,' meaning 'one who dwells in an excellent gabled chamber.' `Mahāsayanamupāsitaṃ` means 'the splendid bed, well-prepared right there, was used.' `Tassa te` means 'seeing such a one, I felt affection for him; because of that affection for you.' `Vaḍḍhamodanaṃ` means 'excellent cooked rice.' `Vicitaṃ` means 'made with choice grains of rice, free from broken or black grains.' `Adāsayi` means 'gave.' `Attānaṃ` means 'by oneself,' or this may also be the reading. `Anasitvāna` means 'without having eaten.' `Koyaṃ dhammo` means, 'O great king, what is this nature of yours?' `Namatthu te` means 'homage be to you,' who, without eating yourself, gave to another.

Ācariyoti kuṭumbika esa mayhaṃ ācārasikkhāpako ācariyo. Byāvaṭoti ussuko. Āmantanīyoti āmantetabbayuttako mayā dinnaṃ bhattaṃ gahetuṃ anurūpo. Dātumarahāmīti “ahaṃ evarūpassa ācariyassa bhojanaṃ dātuṃ arahāmī”ti rājā brāhmaṇassa guṇaṃ vaṇṇesi. Akhettaññūsīti nāhaṃ dānassa khettaṃ, mayi dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ na hotīti evaṃ attānaṃ dānassa akhettaṃ jānāsi maññeti. Anusāsāmīti attano atthaṃ pahāya rañño atthañca dhammañca anusāsāmi.

`Ācariyo` means, 'O householder, this is my teacher, my instructor in conduct.' `Byāvaṭo` means 'diligent.' `Āmantanīyo` means 'suitable to be invited,' 'fit to receive the food given by me.' `Dātumarahāmi` means 'I am fit to give food to such a teacher'—thus the king described the brahmin's virtues. `Akhettaññūsi` means 'you know yourself to be an unfit field for gifts, thinking: "I am not a field for gifts; what is given to me does not bear great fruit."' `Anusāsāmi` means 'I set aside my own benefit and instruct the king in both his benefit and the Dhamma.'

Evaṃ attano aguṇaṃ kathetvā āraññikassāti isino guṇaṃ kathesi. Isinoti sīlādiguṇapariyesakassa. Tapassinoti tapanissitassa. Vuḍḍhassāti [P 4.0373] paṇḍitassa guṇavuḍḍhassa. Nāvakaṅkhasīti sayaṃ dullabhabhojano hutvā evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ aññassa desi, kiṃ attano jīvitaṃ na kaṅkhasi. Bhikkhu kenāti ayaṃ bhikkhu katarena guṇena tayā seṭṭhataro.

Having thus spoken of his own lack of virtue, he then praised the virtue of the forest-dwelling ascetic. `Isino` means 'of one who seeks virtues such as morality.' `Tapassino` means 'of one devoted to austerity.' `Vuḍḍhassa` means 'of the wise one, grown in virtue.' `Nāvakaṅkhasi` means 'though you yourself have scarce food, you gave such food to another; do you not long for your own life?' `Bhikkhu kena` means 'by what quality is this monk superior to you?'

Khaṇantālukalambānīti [V 4.0336][M 4.0374] khaṇanto ālūni ceva tālakandāni ca. Bilālitakkalāni cāti bilālikandatakkalakandāni ca. Dhunaṃ sāmākanīvāranti sāmākañca nīvārañca dhunitvā. Saṅghāriyaṃ pasāriyanti ete sāmākanīvāre dhunanto saṅghāretvā puna sukkhāpite pasāretvā suppena papphoṭetvā koṭṭetvā taṇḍule ādāya pacitvā bhuñjāmīti vadati. Sākanti yaṃ kiñci sūpeyyapaṇṇaṃ. Maṃsanti sīhabyagghavighāsādimaṃsaṃ. Tāni āharitvāti tāni sākādīni āharitvā. Amamassāti taṇhādiṭṭhimamattarahitassa. Sakiñcanoti sapalibodho. Anādānassāti niggahaṇassa. Dātumarahāmīti evarūpassa paccekabuddhassa attanā laddhabhojanaṃ dātuṃ arahāmi.

`Khaṇantālukalambāni` means 'digging up yams and palm roots.' `Bilālitakkalāni ca` means 'bilāli roots and takkala roots.' `Dhunaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ` means 'threshing wild millet and wild rice.' `Saṅghāriyaṃ pasāriyaṃ` means 'gathering and spreading.' He says: 'Having threshed this wild millet and wild rice, gathering it, spreading it out again when dried, winnowing it with a basket, pounding it, taking the grains, I cook and eat.' `Sākaṃ` means 'whatever greens are suitable for soup.' `Maṃsaṃ` means 'meat such as the leavings of lions, tigers, and so on.' `Tāni āharitvā` means 'having brought those greens and so on.' `Amamassa` means 'of one without the possessiveness of craving and wrong views.' `Sakiñcano` means 'with encumbrances.' `Anādānassa` means 'of one who does not grasp.' `Dātumarahāmi` means 'I am worthy to give food obtained by myself to such a Paccekabuddha.'

Tuṇhīmāsīnanti kiñci avatvā nisinnaṃ. Akiñcananti rāgakiñcanādīhi rahitaṃ. Āratanti virataṃ sabbapāpāni pahāya ṭhitaṃ. Kamaṇḍalunti kuṇḍikaṃ. Ete hīti ete rājādayo tayo janāti hatthaṃ pasāretvā te niddisanto evamāha. Dātumarahantīti mādisassa dātuṃ arahanti. Paccanīkanti paccanīkapaṭipadaṃ. Dāyakassa hi nimantanaṃ ekavīsatiyā anesanāsu aññatarāya piṇḍapātapariyesanāya jīvikakappanasaṅkhātā micchājīvapaṭipatti nāma hoti.

`Tuṇhīmāsīnaṃ` means 'sitting without saying anything.' `Akiñcanaṃ` means 'devoid of impediments such as the impediment of greed.' `Ārataṃ` means 'abstained, steadfast, having abandoned all evil deeds.' `Kamaṇḍaluṃ` means 'a water pot.' `Ete hi` means 'these three people, the king and others'—extending his hand and pointing them out, he said thus. `Dātumarahanti` means 'they are worthy to give to one such as me.' `Paccanīkaṃ` means 'an opposing practice.' Indeed, an invitation from a donor is one of the twenty-one improper ways of seeking alms-food, a practice called wrong livelihood, which consists of making a living in this way.

Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā kuṭumbiko attamano dve osānagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, the householder was pleased and recited these two concluding verses:

288.

288.

“Atthāya vata me ajja, idhāgacchi rathesabho;

Sohaṃ ajja pajānāmi, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

Indeed, for my benefit today, the noble king has come here; today I understand where a gift bears great fruit.

289.

289.

“Raṭṭhesu giddhā rājāno, kiccākiccesu brāhmaṇā;

Isī mūlaphale giddhā, vippamuttā ca bhikkhavo”ti.

Kings are greedy for kingdoms, brahmins for their various duties; ascetics are greedy for roots and fruits, but monks are truly liberated.

Tattha rathesabhoti rājānaṃ sandhāyāha. Kiccākiccesūti rañño kiccakaraṇīyesu. Bhikkhavoti paccekabuddhā bhikkhavo pana sabbabhavehi vippamuttā.

Herein, 'noble king' (rathesabho) refers to the king. 'Various duties' (kiccākiccesu) means the king's duties to be performed. 'Monks' (bhikkhavo) refers to the Paccekabuddhas; monks, however, are freed from all existences.

Paccekabuddho [M 4.0375] tassa dhammaṃ desetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato, tathā tāpaso. Rājā pana katipāhaṃ tassa santike vasitvā bārāṇasimeva gato.

The Paccekabuddha, having taught him the Dhamma, went to his own place, and so did the ascetic. The king, after staying with him for a few days, went back to Benares.

Satthā [P 4.0374] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva piṇḍapāto yathānucchavikaṃ gacchati[V 4.0337], pubbepi gatoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kuṭumbiko dhammaratanassa sakkārakārako kuṭumbiko ahosi, rājā ānando, purohito sāriputto, himavantatāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that the alms-food reaches the one who is worthy of it; it also did so in the past.' Then he connected the birth story: 'At that time, the householder who paid respect to the jewel of the Dhamma was the householder of today; Ānanda was the king; Sāriputta was the chaplain; and the ascetic of the Himalayas was I myself.'

Bhikkhāparamparajātakavaṇṇanā terasamā.

The Conclusion of the Commentary on the Bhikkhāparampara Jātaka.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kedāraṃ candakinnarī, ukkusuddālabhisakaṃ;

Suruci pañcuposathaṃ, mahāmorañca tacchakaṃ.

Kedāra, Candakinnarī, Ukkusa, Uddāla, Bhisa; Suruci, Pañcuposatha, Mahāmora, and Tacchaka.

Mahāvāṇija sādhinaṃ, dasabrāhmaṇajātakaṃ;

Bhikkhāparamparāpi ca, terasāni pakiṇṇake.

Mahāvāṇija, Sādhina, the Dasabrāhmaṇa Jātaka, and also Bhikkhāparamparā—these thirteen are in the Miscellaneous Section.

Pakiṇṇakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Miscellaneous Section is concluded.

15. Vīsatinipāto

The Section of Twenty

[497] 1. Mātaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā

[497] 1. 1. The Mātaṅga Jātaka

(On the harassment of monks)

Kuto [V 4.0338][P 4.0375][M 4.0376] nu āgacchasi dummavāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto udenaṃ nāma vaṃsarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo jetavanato ākāsena gantvā yebhuyyena kosambiyaṃ udenassa rañño uyyānaṃ divāvihārāya gacchati. Thero kira purimabhave rajjaṃ kārento dīghamaddhānaṃ tasmiṃ uyyāne mahāparivāro sampattiṃ anubhavi. So tena pubbāciṇṇena yebhuyyena tattheva divāvihāraṃ nisīditvā phalasamāpattisukhena vītināmeti. Tasmiṃ ekadivasaṃ tattha gantvā supupphitasālamūle nisinne udeno sattāhaṃ mahāpānaṃ pivitvā “uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe aññatarāya itthiyā aṅke nipanno surāmadamattatāya niddaṃ okkami. Gāyantā nisinnitthiyo tūriyāni chaḍḍetvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā pupphaphalādīni vicinantiyo theraṃ disvā gantvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Thero tāsaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathento nisīdi. Itarāpi itthī aṅkaṃ cāletvā rājānaṃ pabodhetvā “kuhiṃ tā vasaliyo gatā”ti vutte “ekaṃ samaṇaṃ parivāretvā nisinnā”ti āha. So kuddho gantvā theraṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā “handāhaṃ, taṃ samaṇaṃ tambakipillakehi khādāpessāmī”ti kodhavasena therassa sarīre tambakipillakapuṭaṃ bhindāpesi. Thero ākāse ṭhatvā tassovādaṃ datvā jetavane gandhakuṭidvāreyeva otaritvā tathāgatena “kuto āgatosī”ti puṭṭho thero tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, bhāradvāja, udeno idāneva pabbajite viheṭheti, pubbepi viheṭhesiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"Where do you come from, ill-clad one?"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning King Udena of the Vaṃsas. At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, having traveled through the sky from Jetavana, would usually go to King Udena’s park in Kosambi for his midday rest. It is said that in a past life, the elder, while ruling as king, had long enjoyed great prosperity in that very park with a large retinue. Due to that past habit, he often sat there for his midday rest, passing the time in the bliss of fruition attainment. One day, while he was sitting at the foot of a well-flowered sāla tree, King Udena, having drunk heavily for seven days, went to the park with a large retinue, saying, "I will enjoy the pleasures of the park." Intoxicated with liquor, he lay down on the lap of a certain woman on the auspicious stone slab and fell asleep. The women who were sitting and singing, having set aside their instruments, entered the park to gather flowers and fruits. Seeing the elder, they approached, paid homage, and sat down. The elder sat there, teaching them the Dhamma. The other woman, shaking the king’s lap, woke him, and when he asked, "Where have those wretches gone?" she said, "They are sitting around an ascetic." The king, enraged, went and abused the elder, insulting him. In his fury, he said, "Come now, I will have this ascetic devoured by red ants!" and he had a nest of red ants broken over the elder’s body. The elder, standing in the air, gave him an admonition and then descended right at the door of the Perfumed Chamber in Jetavana. When asked by the Tathāgata, "Where have you come from?" the elder related the matter. The Teacher said, "Bhāradvāja, Udena does not harass monks only now; he harassed them in the past as well." And being requested, he related a past incident.

Atīte [P 4.0376] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tadā mahāsatto bahinagare caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbatti, “mātaṅgo”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Aparabhāge [M 4.0377] viññutaṃ patto “mātaṅgapaṇḍito”ti pākaṭo ahosi. Tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dhītā diṭṭhamaṅgalikā nāma ekamāsadvemāsavārena mahāparivārā uyyānaṃ kīḷituṃ gacchati. Athekadivasaṃ mahāsatto kenaci kammena nagaraṃ pavisanto antaradvāre diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ disvā ekamantaṃ apagantvā allīyitvā aṭṭhāsi. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā [V 4.0339] sāṇiyā antarena olokentī taṃ disvā “ko eso”ti pucchitvā “caṇḍālo ayye”ti vutte “adiṭṭhapubbayuttakaṃ vata passāmī”ti gandhodakena akkhīni dhovitvā tato nivatti. Tāya saddhiṃ nikkhantajano “are, duṭṭha caṇḍāla, ajja taṃ nissāya amhākaṃ amūlakaṃ surābhattaṃ naṭṭha”nti kodhābhibhūto mātaṅgapaṇḍitaṃ hatthehi ca pādehi ca pothetvā visaññiṃ katvā pakkāmi. So muhuttaṃ vītināmetvā paṭiladdhasañño cintesi “diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya parijano maṃ niddosaṃ akāraṇena pothesi, diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ labhitvāva uṭṭhahissāmi, no alabhitvā”ti adhiṭṭhāya gantvā tassā pitu nivesanadvāre nipajji. So “kena kāraṇena nipannosī”ti vutte “aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthi, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya me attho”ti āha. Eko divaso atīto, tathā dutiyo, tatiyo, catuttho, pañcamo, chaṭṭho ca. Bodhisattānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ nāma samijjhati, tasmā sattame divase diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ nīharitvā tassa adaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Varanasi, the Great Being was born in a family of outcastes outside the city, and they named him "Mātaṅga." Later, when he attained maturity, he became known as "Mātaṅga the Wise." At that time, the daughter of the chief merchant of Varanasi, named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, used to go to the park with a large retinue to play once every month or two. One day, the Great Being, entering the city for some business, saw Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā at the inner gate, stepped aside, and stood close to a wall to hide. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, peering through the gap in a curtain, saw him and asked, "Who is that?" When told, "He is an outcaste, lady," she said, "Truly, I have seen a sight that should not be seen," and after washing her eyes with scented water, she turned back. The people who had gone out with her, overcome with anger, cried, "Ah, you wicked outcaste! Because of you today, our free feast of liquor and rice is ruined!" and they beat Mātaṅga the Wise with their hands and feet until he lost consciousness, and then they left. After a while, regaining consciousness, he thought, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's retinue beat me without fault or reason. I will get up only after obtaining Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, not otherwise." Resolving thus, he went and lay down at the gate of her father's house. When asked, "For what reason are you lying here?" he replied, "There is no other reason—I desire Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā." One day passed, then a second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth. The resolve of Bodhisattas is always successful, so on the seventh day, they brought out Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā and gave her to him.

Atha naṃ sā “uṭṭhehi, sāmi, tumhākaṃ gehaṃ gacchāmā”ti āha. Bhadde, tava parijanenamhi supothito dubbalo, maṃ ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā ādāya gacchāhīti. Sā tathā katvā nagaravāsīnaṃ passantānaññeva nagarā nikkhamitvā caṇḍālagāmakaṃ gatā. Atha naṃ mahāsatto jātisambhedavītikkamaṃ akatvāva katipāhaṃ gehe vasāpetvā cintesi “ahametaṃ lābhaggayasaggappattaṃ karonto pabbajitvāva kātuṃ sakkhissāmi, na itarathā”ti[P 4.0377]. Atha naṃ āmantetvā ‘bhadde, mayi araññato kiñci anāharante amhākaṃ jīvikā nappavattati, yāva mamāgamanā mā ukkaṇṭhi, ahaṃ araññaṃ gamissāmī”ti vatvā gehavāsinopi “imaṃ mā pamajjitthā”ti ovaditvā araññaṃ gantvā samaṇapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā appamatto sattame divase aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca pañca abhiññāyo ca uppādetvā “idāni diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya [M 4.0378] avassayo bhavituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti iddhiyā gantvā caṇḍālagāmadvāre otaritvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Sā tassāgamanaṃ sutvā gehato nikkhamitvā “sāmi, kasmā maṃ anāthaṃ katvā pabbajitosī”ti paridevi. Atha naṃ “bhadde, mā cintayi, tava porāṇakayasato idāni mahantataraṃ yasaṃ karissāmi, apica kho pana ‘na mayhaṃ mātaṅgapaṇḍito sāmiko, mahābrahmā me sāmiko’ti ettakaṃ parisamajjhe vattuṃ sakkhissasī’ti āha. “Āma, sāmi, sakkhissāmī”ti. “Tena hi “idāni te sāmiko kuhinti puṭṭhā ‘brahmalokaṃ gato’ti vatvā ‘kadā āgamissatī’ti vutte ‘ito sattame divase puṇṇamāyaṃ candaṃ bhinditvā āgamissatī’ti vadeyyāsī”ti naṃ vatvā mahāsatto himavantameva gato.

Then she said to him, "Rise, my lord, let us go to your home." "Dear one, I am weak, having been severely beaten by your retinue. Pick me up, place me on your back, and take me away." She did so and, while the city-dwellers watched, they left the city and went to the outcaste village. Then the Great Being, after having her stay in his house for a few days without violating the integrity of her caste, thought, "I will be able to bring her to the highest state of gain and glory only by going forth as an ascetic, not otherwise." Then he addressed her, "Dear one, if I do not bring anything from the forest, our livelihood will not continue. Do not be anxious until I return. I will go to the forest." He also advised the inhabitants of the house, "Do not be heedless of her," and then went to the forest. After going forth as an ascetic, being diligent, on the seventh day he produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges. Thinking, "Now I can be a support for Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā," he traveled by psychic power and descended at the gate of the outcaste village. He then went to the door of Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā’s house. Hearing of his arrival, she came out of the house and lamented, "My lord, why have you gone forth, leaving me without a protector?" He replied, "Dear one, do not worry. I will now bring you a glory greater than your former glory. Moreover, will you be able to declare this much in the midst of an assembly: 'Mātaᅅga the wise is not my husband—the Great Brahmā is my husband'?" "Yes, my lord, I will be able to," she said. "Then, when asked where your husband is now, say, 'He has gone to the Brahmā world.' And when asked when he will return, say, 'On the seventh day from now, on the full moon day, he will return after splitting the moon.'" Having said this to her, the Great Being went to the Himalayas.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāpi [V 4.0340] bārāṇasiyaṃ mahājanassa majjhe tesu tesu ṭhānesu tathā kathesi. Mahājano “aho mahābrahmā samāno diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ na gacchati, evametaṃ bhavissatī”ti saddahi. Bodhisattopi puṇṇamadivase candassa gaganamajjhe ṭhitakāle brahmattabhāvaṃ māpetvā sakalaṃ kāsiraṭṭhaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasinagarañca ekobhāsaṃ katvā candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā otaritvā bārāṇasiyā uparūpari tikkhattuṃ paribbhamitvā mahājanena gandhamālādīhi pūjiyamāno caṇḍālagāmakābhimukho ahosi. Brahmabhattā sannipatitvā caṇḍālagāmakaṃ gantvā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya gehaṃ suddhavatthehi chādetvā bhūmiṃ catujjātiyagandhehi opuñchitvā pupphāni vikiritvā dhūmaṃ [P 4.0378] datvā celavitānaṃ pasāretvā mahāsayanaṃ paññapetvā gandhatelehi dīpaṃ jāletvā dvāre rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇavālukaṃ okiritvā pupphāni vikiritvā dhaje bandhiṃsu. Evaṃ alaṅkate gehe mahāsatto otaritvā anto pavisitvā thokaṃ sayanapiṭṭhe nisīdi.

Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā also spoke thus in various places amidst the great populace in Bārāᅃasĩ. The great populace believed, saying, "Ah, being the Great Brahmā, he does not forsake Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā; so it must be true." On the full moon day, when the moon was in the midst of the sky, the Bodhisatta, having manifested the form of a Brahmā, making the entire Kāsi kingdom, twelve yojanas in extent, and the city of Bārāᅃasĩ a single blaze of light, broke through the orb of the moon, descended, and circled three times above Bārāᅃasĩ. Worshipped by the great populace with perfumes, garlands, and so on, he headed towards the outcaste village. The devotees of Brahmā gathered, went to the outcaste village, covered Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā’s house with clean cloths, sprinkled the ground with perfumes of the four kinds, scattered flowers, offered incense, spread a cloth canopy, prepared a grand bed, lit lamps with fragrant oils, poured silver-colored sand at the door, scattered flowers, and tied up flags. In this adorned house, the Great Being descended, entered, and sat for a while on the bed.

Tadā diṭṭhamaṅgalikā utunī hoti. Athassā aṅguṭṭhakena nābhiṃ parāmasi, kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto āmantetvā “bhadde, gabbho te patiṭṭhito, tvaṃ puttaṃ vijāyissasi, tvampi puttopi te lābhaggayasaggappattā bhavissatha, tava pādadhovanaudakaṃ sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ abhisekodakaṃ bhavissati, nahānodakaṃ pana te amatosadhaṃ bhavissati, ye taṃ sīse āsiñcissanti, te sabbarogehi muccissanti, kāḷakaṇṇiṃ [M 4.0379] parivajjessanti, tava pādapiṭṭhe sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā vandantā sahassaṃ dassanti, sotapathe ṭhatvā vandantā sataṃ dassanti, cakkhupathe ṭhatvā vandantā ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ datvā vandissanti, appamattā hohī”ti naṃ ovaditvā gehā nikkhamitvā mahājanassa passantasseva uppatitvā candamaṇḍalaṃ pāvisi. Brahmabhattā sannipatitvā ṭhitakāva rattiṃ vītināmetvā pātova diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ suvaṇṇasivikaṃ āropetvā sīsena ukkhipitvā nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. “Mahābrahmabhariyā”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā mahājano gandhamālādīhi pūjesi. Pādapiṭṭhe sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā vandituṃ labhantā sahassatthavikaṃ denti, sotapathe ṭhatvā vandituṃ labhantā sataṃ denti, cakkhupathe ṭhatvā vandituṃ labhantā ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ denti. Evaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasiṃ taṃ gahetvā vicarantā aṭṭhārasakoṭidhanaṃ labhiṃsu.

At that time, Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā was in her fertile period. Then, touching her navel with his thumb, an embryo was established in her womb. Then the Great Being addressed her: "Dear one, an embryo has been established in your womb. You will give birth to a son, and both you and your son will attain the highest gain and honor. The water used for washing your feet will become the consecration water for kings throughout all of Jambudĩpa. Your bathing water will become a deathless medicine. Those who pour it on their heads will be freed from all diseases and will avoid misfortune. Those who bow, placing their heads on the insteps of your feet, will give a thousand. Those who bow, standing within earshot, will give a hundred. Those who bow, standing within sight, will give one kahāpaᅃa and then bow. Be heedful." Having advised her thus, he left the house and, as the great crowd looked on, rose up and entered the disc of the moon. The devotees of Brahmā gathered and, remaining standing all night, at dawn placed Diᅦᅥhamaᅅgalikā on a golden palanquin, lifted it onto their heads, and entered the city. Approaching her as "the wife of the Great Brahmā," the great crowd honored her with perfumes, garlands, and so on. Those who were able to bow, placing their heads on the insteps of her feet, gave a purse of a thousand. Those who were able to bow, standing within earshot, gave a hundred. Those who were able to bow, standing within sight, gave one kahāpaᅃa. Thus, carrying her through the twelve-yojana city of Bārāᅃasĩ, they obtained eighteen crores of wealth.

Atha naṃ nagaraṃ pariharitvā ānetvā nagaramajjhe mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā mahāsayanaṃ paññapetvā mahantena sirisobhaggena tattha vasāpesuṃ. Maṇḍapasantikeyeva sattadvārakoṭṭhaṃ sattabhūmikaṃ pāsādaṃ kātuṃ ārabhiṃsu, mahantaṃ navakammaṃ ahosi. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā maṇḍapeyeva puttaṃ vijāyi. Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase brāhmaṇā sannipatitvā [V 4.0341][P 4.0379] maṇḍape jātattā “maṇḍabyakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Pāsādo pana dasahi māsehi niṭṭhito. Tato paṭṭhāya sā mahantena yasena tasmiṃ vasati, maṇḍabyakumāropi mahantena parivārena vaḍḍhati. Tassa sattaṭṭhavassakāleyeva jambudīpatale uttamācariyā sannipatiṃsu. Te taṃ tayo vede uggaṇhāpesuṃ. So soḷasavassakālato paṭṭhāya brāhmaṇānaṃ bhattaṃ paṭṭhapesi, nibaddhaṃ soḷasa brāhmaṇasahassāni bhuñjanti. Catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake brāhmaṇānaṃ dānaṃ deti.

Then, after leading her in procession around the city and bringing her back, they had a great pavilion built in the city center. They enclosed it with a curtain, prepared a grand couch, and with great splendor and magnificence, they had her reside there. Near the pavilion itself, they began to construct a seven-storied palace with seven gatehouses—it was a great new construction project. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā gave birth to a son right there in the pavilion. On the day of his naming ceremony, the brahmins gathered and, because he was born in the pavilion (maṇḍapa), they gave him the name 'Prince Maṇḍabya.' The palace, however, was completed in ten months. From that time on, she lived there with great honor, and Prince Maṇḍabya also grew up with a large retinue. When he was seven or eight years old, the most excellent teachers in all of Jambudīpa gathered. They had the young Maṇḍabya taught the three Vedas. Starting from the age of sixteen, he established a regular meal service for the brahmins; sixteen thousand brahmins would eat there regularly. He gave alms to the brahmins at the fourth gatehouse.

Athekasmiṃ mahāmahadivase gehe bahuṃ pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādesuṃ. Soḷasa brāhmaṇasahassāni catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake nisīditvā suvaṇṇarasavaṇṇena navasappinā pakkamadhukhaṇḍasakkharāhi ca abhisaṅkhataṃ pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjanti. Kumāropi sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito suvaṇṇapādukā āruyha hatthena kañcanadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā “idha sappiṃ detha, idha madhu”nti vicārento carati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mātaṅgapaṇḍito himavante assamapade [M 4.0380] nisinno “kā nu kho diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya puttassa pavattī”ti olokento tassa atitthe pakkhandabhāvaṃ disvā “ajjeva gantvā māṇavaṃ dametvā yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, tattha dānaṃ dāpetvā āgamissāmī”ti cintetvā ākāsena anotattadahaṃ gantvā mukhadhovanādīni katvā manosilātale ṭhito rattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā paṃsukūlasaṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā mattikāpattaṃ ādāya ākāsenāgantvā catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake dānaggeyeva otaritvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Maṇḍabyo kumāro ito cito ca olokento taṃ disvā “evaṃvirūpo saṅkārayakkhasadiso ayaṃ pabbajito imaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchanto kuto nu kho āgacchatī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, on a certain day when many brahmins gathered, much milk-porridge was prepared in the house. Sixteen thousand brahmins, seated in the fourth gatehouse, partook of the milk-porridge prepared with fresh ghee the color of liquid gold, honeycomb, and the like. The prince, adorned with all his ornaments, having put on golden sandals and holding a golden staff in his hand, walked about supervising, saying, 'Give ghee in this bowl, give honey in this bowl.' At that moment, the wise Mātaṅga, living in his hermitage in the Himalayas, considering, 'What is the condition of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's son?' and seeing his state of having embarked on an improper course, thought, 'Today I shall go and tame the young man, and having caused him to give a gift where it is of great fruit, I will return.' Traveling through the air to Lake Anotatta, he performed his morning ablutions and other duties. Standing on the Manosilā plateau, he adjusted his red double-layered robe, fastened his waistband, draped himself in a robe of discarded cloth, took his clay bowl, and came through the air. Descending right at the alms-hall at the fourth gatehouse, he stood in a suitable place. Prince Maṇḍabya, looking this way and that, saw the Bodhisatta and thought, 'From where has this ascetic come to this place, looking like a spirit of the rubbish heap?' Wishing to converse with him, Prince Maṇḍabya spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Kuto [P 4.0380] nu āgacchasi dummavāsī, otallako paṃsupisācakova;

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe, ko re tuvaṃ hosi adakkhiṇeyyo”ti.

1. "From where have you come, you ill-clad one, looking like a lowly wretch, a goblin from the dust? Wearing a rag from the rubbish heap around your neck, who are you, you wretch, who are unworthy of offerings?"

Tattha dummavāsīti anañjitaamaṇḍitaghaṭitasaṅghāṭikapilotikavasano. Otallakoti lāmako olambavilambanantakadharo vā. Paṃsupisācakovāti saṅkāraṭṭhāne pisācako viya. Saṅkāracoḷanti saṅkāraṭṭhāne laddhapilotikaṃ. Paṭimuñcāti paṭimuñcitvā. Adakkhiṇeyyoti tvaṃ adakkhiṇeyyo imesaṃ paramadakkhiṇeyyānaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ eko hutvā kuto āgato.

1. Herein, 'dummavāsī' means one wearing a dull, tattered robe. 'Otallako' means inferior, or one who wears a garment with hanging threads. 'Paṃsupisācakova' means like a goblin in a rubbish heap. 'Saṅkāracoḷaṃ' means a tattered cloth obtained from a place where rubbish is discarded. 'Paṭimuñca' means having put it around the neck. 'Adakkhiṇeyyo' means: you are not a worthy recipient of offerings, but a base one. Who are you, wretch?

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto muducitteneva tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the words of Prince Maṇḍabya, the Bodhisatta, with a gentle mind and wishing to converse with him, spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Annaṃ [V 4.0342] tavedaṃ pakataṃ yasassi, taṃ khajjare bhuñjare piyyare ca;

Jānāsi maṃ tvaṃ paradattūpajīviṃ, uttiṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ labhataṃ sapāko”ti.

2. "This food of yours is prepared, O glorious one; it is eaten, enjoyed, and drunk. You know me as one who lives on what is given by others; let the outcaste also receive the alms given to one who stands and waits."

Tattha pakatanti paṭiyattaṃ. Yasassīti parivārasampanna. Taṃ khajjareti taṃ khajjanti ca bhuñjanti ca pivanti ca. Kiṃkāraṇā mayhaṃ kujjhasi? Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍanti upatiṭṭhitvā [M 4.0381] labhitabbapiṇḍaṃ, uṭṭhāya ṭhitehi vā dīyamānaṃ heṭṭhā ṭhatvā labhitabbapiṇḍaṃ. Labhataṃ sapākoti sapāko caṇḍālopi labhatu. Jātisampannā hi yattha katthaci labhanti, sapākacaṇḍālassa pana ko deti, dullabhapiṇḍo ahaṃ, tasmā me jīvitapavattanatthaṃ bhojanaṃ dāpehi, kumārāti.

2. 'Yasassī' means Maṇḍabya, who has a great retinue. 'Pakatam' means prepared. 'Taṃ khajjare...' means the brahmins eat the hard food, the soft food, and the drink. You know me as one who lives on the gifts of others. 'Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ' means alms received by standing nearby, or alms given by one standing above to be received by one standing below. 'Labhataṃ sapāko' means let even a caṇḍāla, an outcaste, receive it. Why are you angry with me? High-born people receive alms anywhere, but who gives to an outcaste caṇḍāla? I am one for whom alms are difficult to obtain; therefore, Prince, have food given to me to sustain my life.

Tato [V 4.0343] maṇḍabyo gāthamāha –

Thereafter, Prince Maṇḍabya, wishing to revile the Bodhisatta, spoke the third verse:

3.

3.

“Annaṃ mamedaṃ pakataṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ, attatthāya saddahato mamedaṃ;

Apehi etto kimidhaṭṭhitosi, na mādisā tumhaṃ dadanti jammā”ti.

3. "This food of mine is prepared for brahmins; it is for my own benefit, as I believe in the fruit of merit. Go away from here! Why do you stand here? Those like me do not give to you, you wretch!"

Tattha [P 4.0381] attatthāyāti attano vaḍḍhiatthāya. Apehi ettoti imamhā ṭhānā apagaccha. Na mādisāti mādisā jātisampannānaṃ udiccabrāhmaṇānaṃ dānaṃ denti, na tuyhaṃ caṇḍālassa, gaccha, jammāti.

3. 'Attatthāya' means for the sake of my own growth and benefit. 'Saddahato' means one who believes in the fruit. 'Apehi etto' means depart from this place. Why do you stand here? 'Jamma' means low-born outcaste. Those like me, of high birth, give gifts to high-class brahmins, not to you, an outcaste.

Tato mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Thereafter, the Bodhisatta, wishing to persuade Prince Maṇḍabya, spoke the fourth verse:

4.

4.

“Thale ca ninne ca vapanti bījaṃ, anūpakhette phalamāsamānā;

Etāya saddhāya dadāhi dānaṃ, appeva ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyye”ti.

4. "On high ground, on low ground, and in well-watered fields, they sow the seed, hoping for fruit. With such faith, give your gift; perhaps you might satisfy those who are worthy of offerings."

Tassattho – kumāra, sassaphalaṃ āsīsamānā tīsupi khettesu bījaṃ vapanti. Tattha ativuṭṭhikāle thale sassaṃ sampajjati, ninne pūtikaṃ hoti, anūpakhette nadiñca taḷākañca nissāya kataṃ oghena vuyhati. Mandavuṭṭhikāle thale khette vipajjati, ninne thokaṃ sampajjati, anūpakhette sampajjateva. Samavuṭṭhikāle thale khette thokaṃ sampajjati, itaresu sampajjateva. Tasmā yathā phalamāsīsamānā tīsupi khettesu vapanti, tathā tvampi etāya phalasaddhāya āgatāgatānaṃ sabbesaṃyeva dānaṃ dehi, appeva nāma evaṃ dadanto dakkhiṇeyye ārādheyyāsi labheyyāsīti.

4. Its meaning is: Prince, those hoping for a harvest sow seeds in all three types of fields. In a time of excessive rain, the crop thrives on high ground, rots in the lowlands, and in well-watered fields near rivers or ponds, it is swept away by the flood. In a time of scanty rain, the crop fails on high ground, succeeds slightly in the lowlands, and succeeds fully in well-watered fields. In a time of moderate rain, it succeeds slightly on high ground and fully in the others. Therefore, just as they sow in all three fields hoping for fruit, so you too, with this faith in the fruit of merit, give gifts to all who come—lowly, middling, or excellent. By giving thus, you might please and find those who are truly worthy of offerings.

Tato [M 4.0382] maṇḍabyo gāthamāha –

Then the youth Maᅆᄁabya, wishing to speak of the nobility of the recipients, uttered this verse:

5.

5.

“Khettāni mayhaṃ viditāni loke, yesāhaṃ bījāni patiṭṭhapemi;

Ye brāhmaṇā jātimantūpapannā, tānīdha khettāni supesalānī”ti.

"The fields in the world are known to me, in which I plant the seeds; those brahmins who are endowed with birth and mantras, they are the excellent fields here."

Tattha yesāhanti yesu ahaṃ. Jātimantūpapannāti jātiyā ca mantehi ca upapannā.

There, 'yesāhaᅃ' means 'in whom I.' 'Jātimantũpapannā' means 'endowed with birth and mantras.'

Tato mahāsatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Great Being, wishing to show the inferiority and superiority of the recipients, uttered these two verses:

6.

6.

“Jātimado ca atimānitā ca, lobho ca doso ca mado ca moho;

Ete aguṇā yesu ca santi sabbe, tānīdha khettāni apesalāni.

"Pride of birth and excessive conceit, greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion; those in whom all these demerits exist, they are the unvirtuous fields here."

7.

7.

“Jātimado ca atimānitā ca, lobho ca doso ca mado ca moho;

Ete [P 4.0382] aguṇā yesu na santi sabbe, tānīdha khettāni supesalānī”ti.

"Pride of birth and excessive conceit, greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion; those in whom all these demerits are not found, they are the excellent fields here."

Tattha jātimadoti “ahamasmi jātisampanno”ti evaṃ uppannamāno. Atimānitā cāti “añño mayā saddhiṃ jātiādīhi sadiso natthī”ti atikkamma pavattamāno. Lobhādayo lubbhanadussanamajjanamuyhanamattāva. Apesalānīti evarūpā puggalā āsīvisabharitā viya vammikā appiyasīlā honti. Evarūpānaṃ dinnaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti, tasmā mā etesaṃ supesalakhettabhāvaṃ maññittha. Na hi jātimantā saggadāyakā. Ye pana jātimānādirahitā ariyā, tāni khettāni supesalāni, tesu dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, te saggadāyakā hontīti.

There, 'pride of birth' means the conceit that arises thus: 'I am endowed with birth.' 'Excessive conceit' is the conceit that arises surpassing others thus: 'No one else is equal to me in birth and other such qualities.' Greed and the like are simply the states of greed, hatred, intoxication, and delusion. 'Unvirtuous' means individuals of this kind are like anthills filled with poisonous snakes, having disagreeable conduct. What is given to them is not of great fruit; therefore, do not consider them to be excellent fields. Indeed, those merely endowed with birth are not givers of heaven. But those Noble Ones who are free from pride of birth and the rest—they are the excellent fields; what is given to them is of great fruit, and they are givers of heaven.

Iti so mahāsatte punappunaṃ kathente kujjhitvā “ayaṃ ativiya bahuṃ vippalapati, kuhiṃ gatā ime dovārikā, nayimaṃ caṇḍālaṃ nīharantī”ti gāthamāha –

As the Great Being spoke thus again and again, Maᅆᄁabya became angry and said, 'This one babbles excessively. Where have these gatekeepers gone? Why do they not drive this outcaste away?' and he uttered this verse:

8.

8.

“Kvettha [M 4.0383] gatā upajotiyo ca, upajjhāyo atha vā gaṇḍakucchi;

Imassa daṇḍañca vadhañca datvā, gale gahetvā khalayātha jamma”nti.

"Where have Upajoti, Upajjhāya, or Gaᅆᄁakucchi gone? Having given him a stick and a beating, seize him by the neck and cast out this wretch!"

Tattha kvettha gatāti imesu tīsu dvāresu ṭhapitā upajotiyo ca upajjhāyo ca gaṇḍakucchi cāti tayo dovārikā kuhiṃ gatāti attho.

There, 'kvettha gatā' means: where have the three gatekeepers—Upajoti, Upajjhāya, and Gaᅆᄁakucchi—who were stationed at these three gates, gone?

Tepi [V 4.0344] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā vegenāgantvā vanditvā “kiṃ karoma devā”ti āhaṃsu. “Ayaṃ vo jammo caṇḍālo diṭṭho”ti? “Na passāma deva, kutoci āgatabhāvaṃ na jānāmā”ti. “Ko cesa māyākāro vā vijjādharo vā bhavissati, idāni kiṃ tiṭṭhathā”ti. “Kiṃ karoma devā”ti? “Imassa mukhameva pothetvā bhindantā daṇḍaveḷupesikāhi piṭṭhicammaṃ uppāṭentā vadhañca datvā gale gahetvā etaṃ jammaṃ khalayātha, ito nīharathā”ti.

They too, hearing his words, quickly came, paid homage, and said, 'What shall we do, lord?' 'Have you seen this wretched outcaste?' 'We do not see him, lord; we do not know from where he has come.' 'Who might this be, a magician or a sorcerer? Why do you stand there now?' 'What shall we do, lord?' 'Striking and smashing his face, tearing the skin from his back with sticks and bamboo splinters, and giving him a beating, seize him by the neck, cast this wretch out, and remove him from this place!'

Mahāsatto tesu attano santikaṃ anāgatesveva uppatitvā ākāse ṭhito gāthamāha –

The Great Being, even before they came near him, rose up into the sky and, standing in the air, uttered a verse, wishing to show the fault of reviling:

9.

9.

“Giriṃ [P 4.0383] nakhena khaṇasi, ayo dantehi khādasi;

Jātavedaṃ padahasi, yo isiṃ paribhāsasī”ti.

"You dig into a mountain with your fingernail; you chew iron with your teeth; you strive to swallow fire, you who revile a sage!"

Tattha jātavedaṃ padahasīti aggiṃ gilituṃ vāyamasi.

There, 'you strive to swallow fire' (jātavedaᅃ padahasi) means you strive to swallow fire.

Imañca pana gāthaṃ vatvā mahāsatto passantasseva māṇavassa ca brāhmaṇānañca ākāse pakkhandi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken this verse, the Great Being flew into the sky while the youth and the brahmins were looking on. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

10.

10.

“Idaṃ vatvāna mātaṅgo, isi saccaparakkamo;

Antalikkhasmiṃ pakkāmi, brāhmaṇānaṃ udikkhata”nti.

"Having said this, Mātaᅄga, the sage of true endeavor, departed into the sky as the brahmins looked on."

Tattha saccaparakkamoti sabhāvaparakkamo.

There, 'saccaparakkamo' means 'genuine effort.'

So pācīnadisābhimukho gantvā ekāya vīthiyā otaritvā “padavaḷañjaṃ paññāyatū”ti adhiṭṭhāya pācīnadvārasamīpe piṇḍāya caranto missakabhattaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā ekissaṃ sālāyaṃ nisīditvā missakabhattaṃ paribhuñji[M 4.0384]. Nagaradevatā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ ayyaṃ viheṭhetvā kathetī”ti asahamānā āgamiṃsu. Athassa jeṭṭhakayakkho maṇḍabyassa gīvaṃ gahetvā parivattesi, sesadevatā sesabrāhmaṇānaṃ gīvaṃ gaṇhitvā parivattesuṃ. Bodhisatte muducittatāya pana “tassa putto”ti naṃ na mārenti, kevalaṃ kilamentiyeva. Maṇḍabyassa sīsaṃ parivattitvā piṭṭhipassābhimukhaṃ jātaṃ, hatthapādā ujukā thaddhāva aṭṭhaṃsu, akkhīni kālakatasseva parivattiṃsu. So thaddhasarīrova nipajji, sesabrāhmaṇā mukhena kheḷaṃ vamantā aparāparaṃ parivattanti[V 4.0345]. Māṇavā “ayye, puttassa te kiṃ jāta”nti diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya ārocayiṃsu. Sā vegena gantvā puttaṃ disvā “kimeta”nti vatvā gāthamāha –

He went towards the eastern quarter, descended on a certain street, and made a determination: 'Let my footprints be visible.' Wandering for alms near the eastern gate, he collected mixed food, sat in a certain hall, and consumed it. The city deities, unable to endure it, thinking, 'This person speaks after harassing our master,' arrived. Then the chief yakkha seized Maᅆᄁabya by the neck and twisted it; the other deities seized the necks of the other brahmins and twisted them. However, due to the Bodhisatta's gentle nature, they did not kill him, thinking 'he is her son'; they merely tormented him. Maᅆᄁabya's head was twisted around to face his back, his hands and feet became straight and rigid, and his eyes rolled like those of a dead man. He lay there with a stiff body, while the other brahmins, vomiting saliva from their mouths, writhed back and forth. The youths reported to Diᄁᄁhamaᅄgalikā, 'Madam, what has happened to your son?' She hurried there, saw her son, asked 'What is this?' and uttered this verse:

11.

11.

“Āvellitaṃ piṭṭhito uttamaṅgaṃ, bāhuṃ pasāreti akammaneyyaṃ;

Setāni akkhīni yathā matassa, ko me imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti.

"His head is twisted to the back; his arms are outstretched and unworkable. His eyes are white like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?"

Tattha [P 4.0384] āvellitanti parivattitaṃ.

There, 'ivellitaᅃ' means 'twisted around.'

Athassā tasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitajano ārocetuṃ gāthamāha –

Then the people standing in that place, wishing to inform Diᄁᄁhamaᅄgalikā, uttered this verse:

12.

12.

“Idhāgamā samaṇo dummavāsī, otallako paṃsupisācakova;

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe, so te imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti.

"An ascetic wearing wretched clothes arrived here, a base person like a dust-demon. Wearing a rag from a rubbish heap on his neck, he is the one who made your son like this."

Sā taṃ sutvāva cintesi “aññassetaṃ balaṃ natthi, nissaṃsayaṃ mātaṅgapaṇḍito bhavissati, sampannamettābhāvano kho pana dhīro na ettakaṃ janaṃ kilametvā gamissati, kataraṃ nu kho disaṃ gato bhavissatī”ti. Tato pucchantī gāthamāha –

Hearing this, she thought: 'No one else has such power; undoubtedly, it must be the wise Mātaᅄga. But surely a wise person, accomplished in the development of loving-kindness, would not depart after causing so many people to suffer. In which direction could he have gone?' Then, inquiring, she uttered this verse:

13.

13.

“Katamaṃ disaṃ agamā bhūripañño, akkhātha me māṇavā etamatthaṃ;

Gantvāna taṃ paṭikaremu accayaṃ, appeva naṃ putta labhemu jīvita”nti.

"To which direction did the one of vast wisdom go? Tell me this matter, O young men! Having gone to him, we will make amends for the transgression; perhaps we might regain our son's life."

Tattha [M 4.0385] gantvānāti tassa santikaṃ gantvā. Taṃ paṭikaremu accayanti taṃ accayaṃ paṭikarissāma desessāma, khamāpessāma nanti. Putta labhemu jīvitanti appeva nāma puttassa jīvitaṃ labheyyāma.

There, 'having gone' (gantvāna) means having gone to his presence. 'We will make amends for that transgression' (taᅃ paᄁikaremu accayaᅃ) means we will make amends for that transgression, we will confess it, and we will ask for forgiveness. 'Perhaps we might regain our son's life' means maybe we might obtain the son's life.

Athassā tattha ṭhitā māṇavā kathentā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then the young men standing there, wishing to speak to her, uttered this verse:

14.

14.

“Vehāyasaṃ agamā bhūripañño, pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando;

Api cāpi so purimadisaṃ agacchi, saccappaṭiñño isi sādhurūpo”ti.

"The one of vast wisdom went through the air, like the moon on the fifteenth day in the middle of its path; moreover, he went toward the eastern direction, the sage true to his promise and of noble nature."

Tattha [V 4.0346] pathaddhunoti ākāsapathasaṅkhātassa addhuno majjhe ṭhito pannarase cando viya. Api cāpi soti apica kho pana so puratthimaṃ disaṃ gato.

In that verse, 'pathaddhuno' means like the moon on the fifteenth day, standing in the middle of the distance known as the path through the sky. 'Api cāpi so' means that, moreover, he went toward the eastern direction.

Sā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “mama sāmikaṃ upadhāressāmī”ti suvaṇṇakalasasuvaṇṇasarakāni gāhāpetvā dāsigaṇaparivutā tena padavaḷañjassa adhiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ patvā tenānusārena gacchantī tasmiṃ pīṭhikāya nisīditvā bhuñjamāne tassa santikaṃ gantvā [P 4.0385] vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. So taṃ disvā thokaṃ odanaṃ patte ṭhapesi. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā suvaṇṇakalasena tassa udakaṃ adāsi. So tattheva hatthaṃ dhovitvā mukhaṃ vikkhālesi. Atha naṃ sā “kena me puttassa so vippakāro kato”ti pucchantī gāthamāha –

Hearing their words, she thought, 'I will investigate my husband,' and had large and small golden vessels brought. Surrounded by a retinue of female servants, she reached the place where the footprints had been determined and, following that track, she approached him as he was sitting on a seat and eating, paid homage, and stood there. Seeing her, he left a little rice in his bowl. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā gave him water with a golden vessel. There, he washed his hands and rinsed his mouth. Then, wishing to ask, 'Who has caused this distortion in my son?', she spoke this verse:

15.

15.

“Āvellitaṃ piṭṭhito uttamaṅgaṃ, bāhuṃ pasāreti akammaneyyaṃ;

Setāni akkhīni yathā matassa, ko me imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti.

"His head is twisted back; his arms are outstretched and unmanageable. His eyes are white like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?"

Tato parā tesaṃ vacanapaṭivacanagāthā honti –

Thereafter followed their verses of dialogue and reply:

16.

16.

“Yakkhā have santi mahānubhāvā, anvāgatā isayo sādhurūpā;

Te duṭṭhacittaṃ kupitaṃ viditvā, yakkhā hi te puttamakaṃsu evaṃ.

"Indeed, there are powerful spirits who follow sages of noble form. Knowing his wicked and angry mind, those spirits have done this to your son."

17.

17.

“Yakkhā [M 4.0386] ca me puttamakaṃsu evaṃ, tvaññeva me mā kuddho brahmacāri;

Tumheva pāde saraṇaṃ gatāsmi, anvāgatā puttasokena bhikkhu.

"The spirits have indeed done this to my son; but you, O holy man, be not angry with him. I have gone to your feet alone for refuge; I have come here, O monk, out of grief for my son."

18.

18.

“Tadeva hi etarahi ca mayhaṃ, manopadoso na mamatthi koci;

Putto ca te vedamadena matto, atthaṃ na jānāti adhicca vede.

"Indeed, both then and now, I have no ill will whatsoever. But your son, intoxicated with pride in the Vedas, does not understand what is beneficial, even though he has studied the Vedas."

19.

19.

“Addhā have bhikkhu muhuttakena, sammuyhateva purisassa saññā;

Ekāparādhaṃ khama bhūripañña, na paṇḍitā kodhabalā bhavantī”ti.

"Indeed, O monk, in just a moment a person's perception can become confused. Forgive this one offense, O one of vast wisdom; the wise do not make anger their strength."

Tattha yakkhāti nagarapariggāhakayakkhā. Anvāgatāti anu āgatā, isayo sādhurūpā guṇasampannāti evaṃ jānamānāti attho. Teti te isīnaṃ guṇaṃ ñatvā tava puttaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ kupitacittaṃ viditvā. Tvaññeva meti sace [P 4.0386] yakkhā kupitā evamakaṃsu, karontu, devatā nāma [V 4.0347] pānīyauḷuṅkamattena santappetuṃ sakkā, tasmāhaṃ tesaṃ na bhāyāmi, kevalaṃ tvaññeva me puttassa mā kujjhi. Anvāgatāti āgatāsmi. Bhikkhūti mahāsattaṃ ālapantī puttassa jīvitadānaṃ yācati. Tadeva hīti diṭṭhamaṅgalike tadā tava puttassa maṃ akkosanakāle ca mayhaṃ manopadoso natthi, etarahi ca tayi yācamānāyapi mama tasmiṃ manopadoso natthiyeva. Vedamadenāti “tayo vedā me uggahitā”ti madena. Adhiccāti vede uggahetvāpi atthānatthaṃ na jānāti. Muhuttakenāti yaṃ kiñci uggahetvā muhuttakeneva.

In those verses, 'yakkhā' refers to the spirits who guard the city. 'Anvāgatā' means 'those who followed'; the meaning is that they knew the sages were of noble form and endowed with virtue. 'Te' means they, knowing the virtue of the sages and recognizing your son’s malicious and angry mind, acted. 'Tvaññeva me' means: 'If the spirits were angry and did so, let them be; deities can be satisfied with just a ladleful of water, so I do not fear them. Only you, do not be angry with my son.' 'Anvāgatā' means 'I have come.' 'Bhikkhu' is her addressing the Great Being as she begs for the gift of her son’s life. 'Tadeva hi' means: 'O Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, both then, when your son was abusing me, and now, as you plead with me, I have no ill will toward him.' 'Vedamadena' means with the pride of thinking, 'I have mastered the three Vedas.' 'Adhicca' means that even though he has studied the Vedas, he does not know what is beneficial and what is not. 'Muhuttakena' means that whatever little one has learned, in just a moment perception is confused.

Evaṃ tāya khamāpiyamāno mahāsatto “tena hi etesaṃ yakkhānaṃ palāyanatthāya amatosadhaṃ dassāmī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Thus, as she was asking for his forgiveness, the Great Being said, 'In that case, I will give the ambrosial medicine to make those spirits flee,' and spoke this verse:

20.

20.

“Idañca [M 4.0387] mayhaṃ uttiṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ, tava maṇḍabyo bhuñjatu appapañño;

Yakkhā ca te naṃ na viheṭhayeyyuṃ, putto ca te hessati so arogo”ti.

"Let your son Maṇḍabya, who has little wisdom, eat this leftover almsfood of mine; then the spirits will not harm him, and your son will become free from disease."

Tattha uttiṭṭhapiṇḍanti ucchiṭṭhakapiṇḍaṃ, “ucchiṭṭhapiṇḍa”ntipi pāṭho.

Here, 'uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa' means leftover almsfood; 'ucchiṭṭhapiṇḍa' is another reading.

Sā mahāsattassa vacanaṃ sutvā “detha, sāmi, amatosadha”nti suvaṇṇasarakaṃ upanāmesi. Mahāsatto ucchiṭṭhakakañjikaṃ tattha āsiñcitvā “paṭhamaññeva ito upaḍḍhaṃ tava puttassa mukhe osiñcitvā sesaṃ cāṭiyaṃ udakena missetvā sesabrāhmaṇānaṃ mukhe osiñcehi, sabbepi nirogā bhavissantī”ti vatvā uppatitvā himavantameva gato. Sāpi taṃ sarakaṃ sīsenādāya “amatosadhaṃ me laddha”nti vadantī nivesanaṃ gantvā paṭhamaṃ puttassa mukhe kañjikaṃ osiñci, yakkho palāyi. Itaro paṃsuṃ puñchanto uṭṭhāya “amma kimeta”nti āha. Tayā kataṃ tvameva jānissasi. Ehi, tāta, tava dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ tesaṃ vippakāraṃ passāti. So te disvā vippaṭisārī ahosi. Atha [P 4.0387] naṃ mātā “tāta maṇḍabya, tvaṃ bālo dānassa mahapphalaṭṭhānaṃ na jānāsi, dakkhiṇeyyā nāma evarūpā na honti, mātaṅgapaṇḍitasadisāva honti, ito paṭṭhāya mā etesaṃ dussīlānaṃ dānamadāsi, sīlavantānaṃ dehī”ti vatvā āha –

Hearing the Great Being’s words, she said, 'Give it, lord, the ambrosial medicine,' and offered a golden bowl. The Great Being poured the leftover food into it and said, 'First, pour half of this into your son’s mouth, then mix the rest with water in a large pot and pour it into the mouths of the remaining brahmins; all of them will become free from illness.' Having said this, he flew into the air and departed to the Himalayas. She took the bowl upon her head, exclaiming, 'I have obtained the ambrosial medicine!' and returned home. First, she poured the leftover food into her son’s mouth, and the spirit fled. The other, wiping off the dust, stood up and asked, 'Mother, what is this?' 'You will know for yourself the deed you have done. Come, dear, see the distorted state of those worthy of your offerings.' Seeing them, he was troubled at heart. Then his mother said, 'Dear Maṇḍabya, you are a fool and do not know the place of great fruit for giving. Those worthy of offerings are not like these; they are like the wise Mātanga. From this day forward, do not give alms to these immoral ones; give only to the virtuous,' and she spoke these verses:

21.

21.

“Maṇḍabya bālosi parittapañño, yo puññakkhettānamakovidosi;

Mahakkasāvesu dadāsi dānaṃ, kiliṭṭhakammesu asaññatesu.

"Maṇḍabya, you are a fool of little wisdom, unskilled in knowing the fields of merit. You give gifts to those of great defilements, who are of tainted actions and unrestrained."

22.

22.

“Jaṭā [V 4.0348] ca kesā ajinā nivatthā, jarūdapānaṃva mukhaṃ parūḷhaṃ;

Pajaṃ imaṃ passatha dummarūpaṃ, na jaṭājinaṃ tāyati appapaññaṃ.

"With matted hair and clad in hides, their faces are overgrown with hair like an old well. Behold these people of ugly appearance; matted hair and hides do not protect one of little wisdom."

23.

23.

“Yesaṃ [M 4.0388] rāgo ca doso ca, avijjā ca virājitā;

Khīṇāsavā arahanto, tesu dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti.

"Those for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance are dispelled—the Arahants, whose taints are destroyed—what is given to them brings great fruit."

Tattha mahakkasāvesūti mahākasāvesu mahantehi rāgakasāvādīhi samannāgatesu. Jaṭā ca kesāti tāta maṇḍabya, tava dakkhiṇeyyesu ekaccānaṃ kesā jaṭā katvā baddhā. Ajinā nivatthāti sakhurāni ajinacammāni nivatthā. Jarūdapānaṃ vāti tiṇagahanena jiṇṇakūpo viya mukhaṃ dīghamassutāya parūḷhaṃ. Pajaṃ imanti imaṃ evarūpaṃ anañjitāmaṇḍitalūkhavesaṃ pajaṃ passatha. Na jaṭājinanti etaṃ jaṭājinaṃ imaṃ appapaññaṃ pajaṃ tāyituṃ na sakkoti, sīlapaññāṇatapokammāneva imesaṃ sattānaṃ patiṭṭhā honti. Yesanti yasmā yesaṃ ete rajjanadussanamuyhanasabhāvā rāgādayo aṭṭhavatthukā ca avijjā virājitā vigatā, vigatattāyeva ca etesaṃ kilesānaṃ ye khīṇāsavā arahanto, tesu dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, tasmā tvaṃ, tāta, ito paṭṭhāya evarūpānaṃ dussīlānaṃ adatvā ye loke aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino pañcābhiññā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā ca paccekabuddhā ca santi, tesaṃ dānaṃ dehi. Ehi, tāta, tava kulūpake amatosadhaṃ pāyetvā aroge [P 4.0388] karissāmāti vatvā ucchiṭṭhakañjikaṃ gāhāpetvā udakacāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā soḷasannaṃ brāhmaṇasahassānaṃ mukhesu āsiñcāpesi.

Here, 'mahakkasāvesu' means 'mahākasāvesu', those who are endowed with great stains such as the stain of passion. 'Jaṭā ca kesā' means: 'Dear Maṇḍabya, among those you deem worthy of offerings, some have their hair matted and tied up.' 'Ajinā nivatthā' means wearing antelope skins with the hooves. 'Jarūdapānaṃ va' means the mouth, overgrown with a long beard, is like an old well covered by a thicket of grass. 'Pajaṃ imaṃ' means: 'behold this folk with such an unanointed, unadorned, and rough appearance.' 'Na jaṭājinaṃ' means: this matted hair and hide cannot protect this foolish folk; only virtue, wisdom, and ascetic practices are the foundation for these beings. 'Yesaṃ' means: because for those in whom these defilements—lust, hatred, and delusion, which are by nature staining, corrupting, and deluding—and ignorance with its eight grounds, are dispelled and gone, and precisely because of the absence of these defilements, they are Arahants whose taints are destroyed—to them, what is given bears great fruit. Therefore, dear, from now on, instead of giving to such immoral ones, give to those in the world who possess the eight attainments, the five higher knowledges, righteous ascetics and brahmins, and Solitary Buddhas. 'Come, dear, let us give your teachers the deathless medicine to drink and make them free from disease.' Having said this, he had the leftover rice gruel taken, placed in a water pot, and had it poured into the mouths of the sixteen thousand brahmins.

Ekeko paṃsuṃ puñchantova uṭṭhahi. Atha ne brāhmaṇā “imehi caṇḍālucchiṭṭhakaṃ pīta”nti abrāhmaṇe kariṃsu. Te lajjitā bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā majjharaṭṭhaṃ gantvā majjharañño santike vasiṃsu, maṇḍabyo pana tattheva vasi. Tadā vettavatīnagaraṃ upanissāya vettavatīnadītīre jātimanto nāmeko brāhmaṇo pabbajito jātiṃ nissāya mahantaṃ mānamakāsi. Mahāsatto “etassa mānaṃ bhindissāmī”ti taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā tassa santike uparisote vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā “imaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ jātimantassa jaṭāsu laggatū”ti adhiṭṭhāya nadiyaṃ pātesi. Taṃ tassa udakaṃ ācamantassa jaṭāsu laggi. So taṃ disvāva “nassa vasalā”ti vatvā “kuto ayaṃ kāḷakaṇṇī āgato, upadhāressāmi na”nti uddhaṃsotaṃ gacchanto mahāsattaṃ disvā “kiṃjātikosī”ti pucchi. “Caṇḍālosmī”ti. “Tayā nadiyā dantakaṭṭhaṃ pātita”nti[M 4.0389]? “Āma, mayā”ti. “Nassa, vasala, caṇḍāla kāḷakaṇṇi mā idha vasi, heṭṭhāsote vasāhī”ti vatvā heṭṭhāsote vasantenapi tena pātite dantakaṭṭhe [V 4.0349] paṭisotaṃ āgantvā jaṭāsu laggante so “nassa vasala, sace idha vasissasi, sattame divase sattadhā muddhā phalissatī”ti āha.

Each one stood up, wiping off the dust. Then the brahmins declared, 'These men have drunk the leavings of an outcaste!' and made them non-brahmins. Ashamed, they left Varanasi and went to the Middle Country, where they settled near the king of the Middle Country. But Maṇḍabya remained right there. At that time, near the city of Vettavatī, on the banks of the Vettavatī River, lived a brahmin named Jātimanta who had gone forth as an ascetic. Proud of his birth, he displayed great arrogance. The Great Being, thinking, 'I will shatter his pride,' went to that place and took up residence upstream from him. One day, after chewing a toothstick, he made a resolution: 'May this toothstick cling to Jātimanta’s matted hair,' and then threw it into the river. As Jātimanta was rinsing his mouth, the toothstick stuck in his matted locks. Seeing it, he exclaimed, 'Perish, you wretch!' and said, 'Whence has this unlucky one come? I will investigate him.' Going upstream, he saw the Great Being and asked, 'Of what caste are you?' 'I am an outcaste,' he replied. 'Did you throw the toothstick into the river?' 'Yes, I did.' 'Perish, you wretch, you outcaste, you unlucky one! Do not stay here—go live downstream!' But even when he lived downstream, the toothstick he had thrown floated back upstream and stuck in Jātimanta’s hair. Then he declared, 'Perish, you wretch! If you stay here, on the seventh day your head will split into seven pieces!'

Mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ etassa kujjhissāmi, sīlaṃ me arakkhitaṃ bhavissati, upāyenevassa mānaṃ bhindissāmī”ti sattame divase sūriyuggamanaṃ nivāresi. Manussā ubbāḷhā jātimantaṃ tāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, tumhe sūriyuggamanaṃ na dethā”ti pucchiṃsu. So āha – “na me taṃ kammaṃ, nadītīre paneko caṇḍālo vasati, tassetaṃ kammaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Manussā mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tumhe, bhante, sūriyuggamanaṃ [P 4.0389] na dethā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Āmāvuso”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti. “Tumhākaṃ kulūpako tāpaso maṃ niraparādhaṃ abhisapi, tasmiṃ āgantvā khamāpanatthāya mama pādesu patite sūriyaṃ vissajjessāmī”ti. Te gantvā taṃ kaḍḍhantā ānetvā mahāsattassa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā khamāpetvā āhaṃsu “sūriyaṃ vissajjetha bhante”ti. “Na sakkā vissajjetuṃ, sacāhaṃ vissajjessāmi, imassa sattadhā muddhā phalissatī”ti. “Atha, bhante, kiṃ karomā”ti? So “mattikāpiṇḍaṃ āharathā”ti āharāpetvā “imaṃ tāpasassa sīse ṭhapetvā tāpasaṃ otāretvā udake ṭhapethā”ti ṭhapāpetvā sūriyaṃ vissajjesi. Sūriyarasmīhi pahaṭamatte mattikāpiṇḍo sattadhā bhijji, tāpaso udake nimujji.

The Great Being thought, 'If I become angry with him, my virtue will be unprotected. I must break his pride by some stratagem,' and on the seventh day, he prevented the sun from rising. The people, distressed, approached the ascetic Jātimanta and asked, 'Venerable sir, do you not allow the sun to rise?' He replied, 'That is not my doing. There is a certain outcaste living by the river—this must be his deed.' The people then approached the Great Being and asked, 'Venerable sir, do you not allow the sun to rise?' He answered, 'Yes, friends.' 'For what reason?' 'Your family ascetic cursed me without any offense. When he comes and falls at my feet to ask for forgiveness, I will release the sun.' They went, and dragging him along, brought him and made him prostrate at the Great Being’s feet. Having made him ask for forgiveness, they said, 'Venerable sir, release the sun.' 'It cannot be released. If I release it, his head will split into seven pieces.' 'Then, venerable sir, what should we do?' He said, 'Bring a lump of clay.' They brought it, and he instructed, 'Place this on the ascetic’s head, then lower the ascetic into the water and have him stand there.' They did so, and the Great Being released the sun. As soon as the sun’s rays struck it, the lump of clay split into seven pieces, and the ascetic sank into the water.

Mahāsatto taṃ dametvā “kahaṃ nu kho dāni soḷasa brāhmaṇasahassāni vasantī”ti upadhārento “majjharañño santike”ti ñatvā “te damessāmī”ti iddhiyā gantvā nagarasāmante otaritvā pattaṃ ādāya nagare piṇḍāya cari. Brāhmaṇā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ idha ekaṃ dve divase vasantopi amhe appatiṭṭhe karissatī”ti vegena gantvā “mahārāja, māyākāro eko vijjādharo coro āgato, gaṇhāpetha na”nti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Mahāsattopi missakabhattaṃ ādāya aññataraṃ kuṭṭaṃ nissāya pīṭhikāya nisinno bhuñjati. Atha naṃ aññavihitakaṃ āhāraṃ paribhuñjamānameva raññā pahitapurisā asinā [M 4.0390] gīvaṃ paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesuṃ. So kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatti. Imasmiṃ kira jātake bodhisatto koṇḍadamako ahosi. So teneva paratantiyuttabhāvena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Devatā kujjhitvā sakalameva majjharaṭṭhaṃ uṇhaṃ kukkuḷavassaṃ vassāpetvā raṭṭhaṃ araṭṭhamakaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Great Being, having tamed him, considered, "Where do those sixteen thousand brahmins now dwell?" Learning that they were near the king of the Middle Country, he resolved, "I will tame them." Using his supernatural power, he went and alighted near the city, took his bowl, and wandered for alms in the city. The brahmins saw him and thought, "This one, staying here even for a day or two, will cause us to lose our standing." They quickly went and reported to the king, "Great king, a magician, a sorcerer, and a thief has come. Have him seized!" The king agreed, saying, "Very well." The Great Being, having received mixed alms-food, sat on a bench leaning against a wall and ate. Then, while he was eating his food, his mind occupied with other thoughts, the men sent by the king struck his neck with a sword, bringing his life to an end. Having passed away, he was reborn in the Brahma world. In this birth, it is said, the Bodhisatta was Koṇḍadamaka. It was due to that very state of being subject to others that he met his end. The deities, enraged, caused a rain of hot embers to fall over the entire Middle Country, reducing the kingdom to a wasteland. Therefore, it is said—

“Upahacca [V 4.0350] manaṃ majjho, mātaṅgasmiṃ yasassine;
