Sapārisajjo ucchinno, majjhāraññaṃ tadā ahū”ti. (jā. 2.19.96);

Having wronged in his mind the glorious Mātaṅga, Majjha, with his retinue, was utterly destroyed; the Middle Kingdom then became a wilderness.

Satthā [P 4.0390] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na idāneva, pubbepi udeno pabbajite viheṭhesiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā maṇḍabyo udeno ahosi, mātaṅgapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, "Not only now, but in the past too, Udena harassed those who had gone forth." Then he made the connection for the Jātaka: "At that time, Maṇḍabya was Udena, and the wise Mātaṅga was none other than myself."

Mātaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Mātaṅga Jātaka, the First.

[498] 2. Cittasambhūtajātakavaṇṇanā

[498] 2. The Commentary on the Cittasambhūta Jātaka

Sabbaṃ narānaṃ saphalaṃ suciṇṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmato mahākassapassa piyasaṃvāse dve saddhivihārike bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Te kira aññamaññaṃ appaṭivibhattabhogā paramavissāsikā ahesuṃ, piṇḍāya carantāpi ekatova gacchanti, ekatova āgacchanti, vinā bhavituṃ na sakkonti. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū tesaṃyeva vissāsaṃ vaṇṇayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, imesaṃ ekasmiṃ attabhāve vissāsikattaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā tīṇi cattāri bhavantarāni gacchantāpi mittabhāvaṃ na vijahiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'All that men have well done is fruitful'—this the Teacher said while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning two monk disciples of the Venerable Mahākassapa who were dear companions. It seems they shared their possessions without division and trusted each other completely. When going for alms, they went together and returned together, unable to be apart. In the Hall of the Dhamma, monks sat praising their mutual trust. The Teacher arrived and asked, "For what talk, monks, are you now gathered together?" When they told him, he said, "It is no surprise, monks, that they trust each other so deeply in this one existence. Wise men of old, even passing through three or four existences, never abandoned their friendship." Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte avantiraṭṭhe ujjeniyaṃ avantimahārājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā ujjeniyā bahi caṇḍālagāmako ahosi. Mahāsatto tattha nibbatti, aparopi satto tasseva mātucchāputto hutvā nibbatti. Tesu eko citto nāma ahosi, eko sambhūto nāma. Te ubhopi [M 4.0391] vayappattā caṇḍālavaṃsadhovanaṃ nāma sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā ekadivasaṃ “ujjenīnagaradvāre sippaṃ dassessāmā”ti eko uttaradvāre sippaṃ dassesi, eko pācīnadvāre. Tasmiñca nagare dve diṭṭhamaṅgalikāyo ahesuṃ, ekā seṭṭhidhītā, ekā purohitadhītā. Tā bahukhādanīyabhojanīyamālāgandhādīni gāhāpetvā “uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti ekā uttaradvārena nikkhami, ekā pācīnadvārena. Tā te caṇḍālaputte sippaṃ dassente disvā “ke ete”ti pucchitvā “caṇḍālaputtā”ti sutvā “apassitabbayuttakaṃ vata passimhā”ti gandhodakena [P 4.0391] akkhīni dhovitvā nivattiṃsu. Mahājano “are duṭṭhacaṇḍāla, tumhe nissāya mayaṃ amūlakāni surābhattādīni na labhimhā”ti te ubhopi bhātike pothetvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpesi.

In the past, in the city of Ujjeni in the country of Avanti, a king named Avantimahārājā ruled. At that time, outside Ujjeni, there was a village of outcastes. The Great Being was reborn there, and another being was reborn as his maternal cousin. One was named Citta and the other Sambhūta. Both, having come of age, learned the craft called 'the washing of the outcaste lineage,' and one day decided, "We will display our craft at the gates of Ujjeni city." One displayed his craft at the northern gate, the other at the eastern gate. In that city, there were two women whose sight was considered auspicious—one the merchant’s daughter, the other the high priest’s daughter. Taking various foods, drinks, garlands, perfumes, and other items, they set out, thinking, "We will go to the pleasure garden to play." One left through the northern gate, the other through the eastern gate. Seeing those outcaste boys displaying their craft, they asked, "Who are these?" Hearing they were outcaste boys, they said, "Alas, we have seen what ought not to be seen," and washed their eyes with scented water before turning back. The great crowd of people cried, "Ah, you wicked outcastes! Because of you, we did not receive the free liquor and food!" They beat both brothers and brought them to ruin.

Te [V 4.0351] paṭiladdhasaññā uṭṭhāya aññamaññassa santikaṃ gacchantā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne samāgantvā aññamaññassa taṃ dukkhuppattiṃ ārocetvā roditvā paridevitvā “kinti karissāmā”ti mantetvā “imaṃ amhākaṃ jātiṃ nissāya dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ, caṇḍālakammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissāma, jātiṃ paṭicchādetvā brāhmaṇamāṇavavaṇṇena takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhissāmā”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā tattha gantvā dhammantevāsikā hutvā disāpāmokkhācariyassa santike sippaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. Jambudīpatale “dve kira caṇḍālā jātiṃ paṭicchādetvā sippaṃ uggaṇhantī”ti sūyittha. Tesu cittapaṇḍitassa sippaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ, sambhūtassa na tāva niṭṭhāti.

Those who had regained consciousness rose and went to each other's presence. Gathering in one place, they told each other of that suffering, and weeping and lamenting, they deliberated, saying, "What shall we do?" Having resolved, "Suffering has arisen because of this birth of ours. We will not be able to perform the work of outcastes. Concealing our birth, we shall go to Takkasilā in the guise of Brahmin youths and learn a craft," they made a determination and went there. Becoming resident pupils, they began learning a craft in the presence of the world-renowned teacher. Throughout the land of Jambudīpa, it was rumored, "Two outcastes, it seems, are learning a craft while concealing their birth." Among them, Cittapaṇḍita completed the craft, but Sambhūta had not yet done so.

Athekadivasaṃ eko gāmavāsī “brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ karissāmī”ti ācariyaṃ nimantesi. Tameva rattiṃ devo vassitvā magge kandarādīni pūresi. Ācariyo pātova cittapaṇḍitaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, ahaṃ gantuṃ na sakkhissāmi, tvaṃ māṇavehi saddhiṃ gantā maṅgalaṃ vatvā tumhehi laddhaṃ bhuñjitvā amhehi laddhaṃ āharā”ti pesesi. So “sādhū”ti māṇavake gahetvā gato. Yāva māṇavā nhāyanti ceva mukhāni ca dhovanti, tāva manussā pāyāsaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nibbātūti ṭhapesuṃ. Māṇavā tasmiṃ anibbuteyeva āgantvā nisīdiṃsu. Manussā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā tesaṃ purato pātiyo ṭhapesuṃ. Sambhūto luddhadhātuko viya hutvā “sītalo”ti saññāya pāyāsapiṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhe ṭhapesi, so tassa [M 4.0392] ādittaayoguḷo viya mukhaṃ dahi. So kampamāno satiṃ anupaṭṭhāpetvā cittapaṇḍitaṃ oloketvā caṇḍālabhāsāya eva “khaḷu khaḷū”ti āha[P 4.0392]. Sopi tatheva satiṃ anupaṭṭhāpetvā caṇḍālabhāsāya eva “niggala niggalā”ti āha. Māṇavā aññamaññaṃ oloketvā “kiṃ bhāsā nāmesā”ti vadiṃsu. Cittapaṇḍito maṅgalaṃ abhāsi. Māṇavā bahi nikkhamitvā vaggavaggā hutvā tattha tattha nisīditvā bhāsaṃ sodhentā “caṇḍālabhāsā”ti ñatvā “are duṭṭhacaṇḍālā, ettakaṃ kālaṃ ‘brāhmaṇāmhā’ti vatvā vañcayitthā”ti ubhopi te pothayiṃsu. Atheko sappuriso “apethā”ti vāretvā “ayaṃ tumhākaṃ jātiyā doso, gacchatha katthaci deseva pabbajitvā jīvathā”ti te ubho uyyojesi. Māṇavā tesaṃ caṇḍālabhāvaṃ ācariyassa ārocesuṃ.

Then one day, a villager, thinking, "I will perform a gift involving the recitation of the Vedas by brahmins," invited the teacher. That very night, it rained heavily, filling the ravines and gullies along the road. Early in the morning, the teacher summoned Cittapaṇḍita and said, "Dear one, I cannot go. You go with the young men, recite the blessings, eat what is given to you, and bring back the portion given to us." Saying, "Very well," he took the young men and left. While the young men were bathing and washing their faces, the people served the rice-porridge and set it out to cool. The young men arrived before it had cooled and sat down. The people performed the water-dedication and placed bowls of rice-porridge in front of them. Sambhūta, being of a greedy nature, thinking it was cool, picked up a lump of rice-porridge and put it in his mouth—it burned his mouth like a red-hot iron ball. Trembling and unable to maintain his composure, he looked at Cittapaṇḍita and cried out in the caṇḍāla language, "Khaḷu, khaḷu!" Meaning, "It's burning! It's burning!" He too, losing his composure, replied in the caṇḍāla language, "Niggala, niggala!" Meaning, "Spit it out! Spit it out!" The young men looked at each other and asked, "What language is this?" Cittapaṇḍita recited the blessings. The young men went outside, formed into groups, and as they examined the language, they realized it was the caṇḍāla language. "Ah, you wicked caṇḍālas! All this time you have deceived us, claiming to be brahmins!" They beat both brothers. Then a good man intervened, saying, "Stop, step back!" and told them, "This is the fault of your birth. Go, ordain somewhere and make your living." He sent them both away. The young men then reported the caṇḍāla status of the brothers to the teacher.

Tepi araññaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā na cirasseva tato cavitvā nerañjarāya tīre migiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattiṃsu. Te mātukucchito nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya ekatova vicaranti, vinā bhavituṃ na sakkonti. Te ekadivasaṃ gocaraṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle sīsena sīsaṃ, siṅgena siṅgaṃ, tuṇḍena tuṇḍaṃ allīyāpetvā romanthayamāne ṭhite disvā eko luddako sattiṃ khipitvā ekappahāreneva jīvitā voropesi. Tato cavitvā nammadānadītīre [V 4.0352] ukkusayoniyaṃ nibbattiṃsu. Tatrāpi vuddhippatte gocaraṃ gahetvā sīsena sīsaṃ, tuṇḍena tuṇḍaṃ allīyāpetvā ṭhite disvā eko yaṭṭhiluddako ekappahāreneva bandhitvā vadhi. Tato pana cavitvā cittapaṇḍito kosambiyaṃ purohitassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Sambhūtapaṇḍito uttarapañcālarañño putto hutvā nibbatti. Te nāmaggahaṇadivasato paṭṭhāya attano jātiṃ anussariṃsu. Tesu sambhūtapaṇḍito nirantaraṃ sarituṃ asakkonto catutthaṃ caṇḍālajātimeva anussarati, cittapaṇḍito paṭipāṭiyā catassopi jātiyo. So soḷasavassakāle nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā [P 4.0393] jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā jhānasukhena vītināmento vasi. Sambhūtapaṇḍitopi pitu accayena chattaṃ ussāpetvā chattamaṅgaladivaseyeva mahājanamajjhe maṅgalagītaṃ katvā udānavasena dve gāthā [M 4.0393] abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā “amhākaṃ rañño maṅgalagīta”nti orodhāpi gandhabbāpi tameva gītaṃ gāyanti. Anukkameneva “rañño piyagīta”nti sabbepi nagaravāsino manussā tameva gāyanti.

The two brothers entered the forest and ordained as ascetics. Not long after, they passed away and were reborn in the womb of a doe on the banks of the Nerañjarā River. From the moment they were born, they wandered together, unable to be apart. One day, after feeding, they stood at the foot of a tree with their heads together, horns intertwined, and snouts touching, chewing their cud. A hunter saw them and, throwing a spear, killed them both at once. After passing away from that birth, they were reborn as ospreys on the banks of the Nammadā River. In that life as ospreys, when they had grown to maturity, a hunter saw them standing with their heads and beaks together and necks intertwined after feeding; he captured and killed them both at once with a trap. After passing away from the life of ospreys, Cittapaṇḍita was reborn as the son of the king's chaplain in Kosambī, while Sambhūtapaṇḍita was reborn as the son of the king of Uttarapañcāla. From the day of their naming, they both remembered their past lives. Among them, Sambhūtapaṇḍita was unable to remember them continuously, remembering only his fourth life as a caṇḍāla, while Cittapaṇḍita remembered all four births in succession. At sixteen, Cittapaṇḍita left home, entered the Himalayas, ordained as an ascetic, and having attained the meditative absorptions and higher knowledge, lived enjoying the bliss of absorption. Sambhūtapaṇḍita, after the death of his father, had the umbrella raised in coronation. On the very day of the umbrella festival, amidst a great crowd, he composed an auspicious song and uttered two verses as an inspired utterance. Hearing this, the women of the court and the musicians sang the same song, saying, "It is our king's auspicious song." Gradually, all the townspeople sang it, saying, "It is the king's beloved song."

Cittapaṇḍitopi himavantapadese vasantoyeva “kiṃ nu kho mama bhātikena sambhūtena chattaṃ laddhaṃ, udāhu na vā”ti upadhārento laddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “navarajjaṃ tāva idāni gantvāpi bodhetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, mahallakakāle naṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ kathetvā pabbājessāmī”ti cintetvā paṇṇāsa vassāni agantvā rañño puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhitakāle iddhiyā gantvā uyyāne otaritvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko dārako taṃ gītaṃ gāyanto dārūni uddharati. Cittapaṇḍito taṃ pakkosi. So āgantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ āha – “tvaṃ pātova paṭṭhāya imameva gītaṃ gāyasi, kiṃ aññaṃ na jānāsī”ti. “Bhante, aññānipi bahūni jānāmi, imāni pana dve rañño piyagītāni, tasmā imāneva gāyāmī”ti. “Atthi pana rañño gītassa paṭigītaṃ gāyanto”ti? “Natthi bhante”ti. “Sakkhissasi pana tvaṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyitu”nti? “Jānanto sakkhissāmī”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ raññā dvīsu gītesu gāyitesu idaṃ tatiyaṃ katvā gāyassū”ti gītaṃdatvā “gantvā rañño santike gāyissasi, rājā te pasīditvā mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dassatī”ti uyyojesi.

Cittapaṇḍita, while dwelling in the Himalayan region, pondered, "Has my brother Sambhūta obtained the royal umbrella or not?" Knowing that he had, he thought, "If I go now, I will not be able to make him understand since he is a new king. When he is older, I will approach him, teach the Dhamma, and have him ordain." After fifty years had passed and the king had been blessed with sons and daughters, he went by psychic power and descended in the royal garden, sitting on the auspicious stone slab like a golden statue. At that moment, a boy was gathering firewood while singing that song. Cittapaṇḍita called him. The boy came, paid his respects, and stood there. Then Cittapaṇḍita said to him, "From early morning, you have been singing only this song. Do you not know any other?" "Venerable sir, I know many others, but these two verses are the king's favorite songs, so I sing only these." "Is there anyone who can sing a response to the king's song?" "No, venerable sir," he replied. "Would you be able to sing a response?" "If I know it, I will be able to," he said. "In that case, when the king has sung his two verses, you should sing this third verse as a response." Having taught him the song, he sent him off, saying, "Go and sing it in the king's presence. The king, being pleased with you, will grant you great wealth and status."

So sīghaṃ mātu santikaṃ gantvā attānaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā rājadvāraṃ gantvā “eko kira dārako tumhehi saddhiṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyissatī”ti rañño ārocāpetvā “āgacchatū”ti vutte gantvā vanditvā “tvaṃ kira, tāta, paṭigītaṃ gāyissasī”ti [P 4.0394] puṭṭho “āma, deva, sabbaṃ rājaparisaṃ sannipātethā”ti sannipatitāya parisāya rājānaṃ āha “tumhe tāva, deva, tumhākaṃ gītaṃ gāyatha, athāhaṃ paṭigītaṃ gāyissāmī”ti. Rājā gāthādvayamāha –

He quickly went to his mother’s side, had himself adorned, and went to the palace gate. Having had it announced to the king, 'A certain boy, they say, will sing a responsive song with you,' and being told, 'Let him come,' he went, paid homage, and when asked, 'Is it true, dear boy, that you will sing in response?' he replied, 'Yes, Lord. Gather the entire royal assembly.' When the assembly had gathered, he said to the king, 'First, Lord, sing your song; then I will sing the response.' The king then recited two verses.

24.

24.

“Sabbaṃ [V 4.0353] narānaṃ saphalaṃ suciṇṇaṃ, na kammunā kiñcana moghamatthi;

Passāmi sambhūtaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ, sakammunā puññaphalūpapannaṃ.

Everything well-done by men is fruitful; no deed is ever in vain. I see Sambhūta, of great power, endowed with the fruit of merit through his own deeds.

25.

25.

“Sabbaṃ [M 4.0394] narānaṃ saphalaṃ suciṇṇaṃ, na kammunā kiñcana moghamatthi;

Kaccinnu cittassapi evamevaṃ, iddho mano tassa yathāpi mayha”nti.

Everything well-done by men is fruitful; no deed is ever in vain. I wonder, is it the same for Citta too? Is his mind as prosperous as mine?

Tattha na kammunā kiñcana moghamatthīti sukatadukkaṭesu kammesu kiñcana ekakammampi moghaṃ nāma natthi, nipphalaṃ na hoti, vipākaṃ datvāva nassatīti aparāpariyavedanīyakammaṃ sandhāyāha. Sambhūtanti attānaṃ vadati, passāmahaṃ āyasmantaṃ sambhūtaṃ sakena kammena puññaphalūpapannaṃ, sakammaṃ nissāya puññaphalena upapannaṃ taṃ passāmīti attho. Kaccinnu cittassapīti mayañhi dvepi janā ekato hutvā na ciraṃ sīlaṃ rakkhimha, ahaṃ tāva tassa phalena mahantaṃ yasaṃ patto, kacci nu kho me bhātikassa cittassapi evameva mano iddho samiddhoti.

Here, 'not even a single deed is fruitless' means that among good and bad deeds, not even a single deed is in vain or without result; it gives its result and then ceases—this refers to deeds ripening in subsequent existences. 'Sambhūta' refers to himself, meaning, 'I see the venerable Sambhūta endowed with the fruit of merit through his own deeds; I see him reborn supported by his own meritorious deeds.' 'Is Citta's mind also thus?' means, 'Indeed, we two people, having come together, did not keep the precepts for long. Yet, I have already attained great fame as a result of that. Could it be that my brother Citta's mind is also thus successful and prosperous?'

Tassa gītāvasāne dārako gāyanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

At the end of the king's song, the boy, singing, spoke the third verse:

26.

26.

“Sabbaṃ narānaṃ saphalaṃ suciṇṇaṃ, na kammunā kiñcana moghamatthi;

Cittampi jānāhi tatheva deva, iddho mano tassa yathāpi tuyha”nti.

Everything well-done by men is fruitful; no deed is ever in vain. Know that for Citta too, O King, it is just the same; his mind is as prosperous as yours.

Taṃ sutvā rājā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the fourth verse:

27.

27.

“Bhavaṃ nu citto sutamaññato te, udāhu te koci naṃ etadakkhā;

Gāthā sugītā na mamatthi kaṅkhā, dadāmi te gāmavaraṃ satañcā”ti.

Are you Citta, or did you hear this from another? Or did someone tell this to you? The verse is well-sung; I have no doubt. I give you a hundred choice villages.

Tattha [P 4.0395] sutamaññato teti ahaṃ sambhūtassa bhātā citto nāmāti vadantassa cittasseva nu te santikā sutanti attho. Koci nanti udāhu mayā sambhūtassa rañño bhātā citto diṭṭhoti koci te etamatthaṃ ācikkhi. Sugītāti sabbathāpi ayaṃ gāthā sugītā, natthettha mama kaṅkhā. Gāmavaraṃ satañcāti gāmavarānaṃ te sataṃ dadāmīti vadati.

Here, 'sutamaññato te' means: 'Did you hear it from another, that is, from the presence of Citta himself, who says, "I am Citta, the brother of Sambhūta"?' 'Koci naṃ' means: 'Or did someone tell you this matter, saying, "I have seen Citta, the brother of King Sambhūta"?' 'Sugītā' means: 'In every way, this verse is well-sung; I have no doubt about it.' 'Gāmavaraṃ satañca' means: 'I give you a hundred choice villages.'

Tato [M 4.0395] dārako pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the boy spoke the fifth verse:

28.

28.

“Na [V 4.0354] cāhaṃ citto sutamaññato me, isī ca me etamatthaṃ asaṃsi;

Gantvāna rañño paṭigāhi gāthaṃ, api te varaṃ attamano dadeyyā”ti.

I am not Citta, nor was it heard from another by me; a sage told me this matter: 'Go and sing the response to the king's verse; perhaps he, being pleased, will grant you a boon.'

Tattha etamatthanti tumhākaṃ uyyāne nisinno eko isi mayhaṃ etamatthaṃ ācikkhi.

Here, 'this matter' means: 'A certain sage sitting in your park told me this matter.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā “so mama bhātā citto bhavissati, idāneva naṃ gantvā passissāmī”ti purise āṇāpento gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, the king, thinking, 'He must be my brother Citta; I will go and see him now,' commanded his men and spoke two verses:

29.

29.

“Yojentu ve rājarathe, sukate cittasibbane;

Kacchaṃ nāgānaṃ bandhatha, gīveyyaṃ paṭimuñcatha.

Yoke the royal chariots, well-made and with variegated coverings; bind the girths of the elephants and fasten the neck-ornaments.

30.

30.

“Āhaññantu bherimudiṅgasaṅkhe, sīghāni yānāni ca yojayantu;

Ajjevahaṃ assamaṃ taṃ gamissaṃ, yattheva dakkhissamisiṃ nisinna”nti.

Let the drums, kettledrums, and conchs be sounded; let them yoke the swift vehicles. This very day I will go to that hermitage where I shall see the seated sage.

Tattha āhaññantūti āhanantu. Assamaṃ tanti taṃ assamaṃ.

Here, 'āhaññantu' means 'let them strike'. 'Assamaṃ taṃ' means 'that hermitage'.

So evaṃ vatvā rathaṃ abhiruyha sīghaṃ gantvā uyyānadvāre rathaṃ ṭhapetvā cittapaṇḍitaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno tuṭṭhamānaso aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he mounted his chariot, went swiftly, and stopped the chariot at the park gate. He approached the wise Citta, paid homage, and sat down to one side with a joyful mind. Then he spoke the eighth verse:

31.

31.

“Suladdhalābho vata me ahosi, gāthā sugītā parisāya majjhe;

Svāhaṃ isiṃ sīlavatūpapannaṃ, disvā patīto sumanohamasmī”ti.

Truly, a well-gained acquisition was mine, that a verse was well-sung in the midst of the assembly. Having seen the sage endowed with virtue, I am pleased and joyful in mind.

Tassattho [P 4.0396] – suladdhalābho vata mayhaṃ chattamaṅgaladivase parisāya majjhe gītagāthā sugītāva ahosi, svāhaṃ ajja sīlavatasampannaṃ isiṃ disvā pītisomanassappatto jātoti.

Its meaning is: 'Truly, a great gain was mine! On the day of the umbrella-festival, in the midst of the assembly, the song-verse was well-sung. Today, having seen the sage endowed with virtue, I have attained joy and gladness.'

So [M 4.0396] cittapaṇḍitassa diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya somanassappatto “bhātikassa me pallaṅkaṃ attharathā”tiādīni āṇāpento navamaṃ gāthamāha –

From the moment he saw the wise Citta, filled with gladness, he gave orders such as, 'Prepare my brother's seat,' and spoke the ninth verse:

32.

32.

“Āsanaṃ udakaṃ pajjaṃ, paṭiggaṇhātu no bhavaṃ;

Agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma, agghaṃ kurutu no bhava”nti.

May the venerable one accept a seat, water, and water for the feet from us. We invite the venerable one for a hospitality-offering; may the venerable one accept our offering.

Tattha [V 4.0355] aggheti atithino dātabbayuttakasmiṃ agghe bhavantaṃ āpucchāma. Kurutu noti imaṃ no agghaṃ bhavaṃ paṭiggaṇhātu.

Here, 'agghe' means: 'In the matter of the hospitality-gift that ought to be given to a guest, we invite the venerable one.' 'Kurutu no' means: 'May the venerable one accept this offering from us.'

Evaṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā rajjaṃ majjhe bhinditvā dento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus made a sweet and kind welcome, offering to divide the kingdom in half, he spoke another verse:

33.

33.

“Rammañca te āvasathaṃ karontu, nārīgaṇehi paricārayassu;

Karohi okāsamanuggahāya, ubhopimaṃ issariyaṃ karomā”ti.

Let them make a delightful dwelling for you; be attended by troops of women. Grant us the opportunity to favor you; let us both exercise this sovereignty.

Tattha imaṃ issariyanti kapilaraṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagare rajjaṃ majjhe bhinditvā dvepi janā karoma anubhavāma.

Here, 'this sovereignty' means: 'Let us both exercise and enjoy the sovereignty, having divided the kingdom in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the country of Kapila in half.'

Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cittapaṇḍito dhammaṃ desento cha gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, the wise Citta, teaching the Dhamma, spoke six verses:

34.

34.

“Disvā phalaṃ duccaritassa rāja, attho suciṇṇassa mahāvipākaṃ;

Attānameva paṭisaṃyamissaṃ, na patthaye putta pasuṃ dhanaṃ vā.

Seeing the fruit of misconduct, O King, and also the great result of what is well-practiced, I shall restrain myself alone; I do not desire sons, cattle, or wealth.

35.

35.

“Dasevimā vassadasā, maccānaṃ idha jīvitaṃ;

Apattaññeva taṃ odhiṃ, naḷo chinnova sussati.

Ten are these decades of years—the life of mortals here. Even without reaching that limit, one dries up like a severed reed.

36.

36.

“Tattha kā nandi kā khiḍḍā, kā ratī kā dhanesanā;

Kiṃ me puttehi dārehi, rāja muttosmi bandhanā.

In that, what delight, what sport, what pleasure, what search for wealth? What use are sons and wives to me? O King, I am freed from bondage.

37.

37.

“Sohaṃ evaṃ pajānāmi, maccu me nappamajjati;

Antakenādhipannassa, kā ratī kā dhanesanā.

I understand it thus: Death does not neglect me. For one seized by the End-maker, what pleasure, what search for wealth?

38.

38.

“Jāti [P 4.0397][M 4.0397] narānaṃ adhamā janinda, caṇḍālayoni dvipadākaniṭṭhā;

Sakehi kammehi supāpakehi, caṇḍālagabbhe avasimha pubbe.

Birth among humans is low, O lord of men; the caṇḍāla womb is the lowest of bipeds. Because of our own very evil deeds, we formerly dwelt in a caṇḍāla womb.

39.

39.

“Caṇḍālāhumha avantīsu, migā nerañjaraṃ pati;

Ukkusā nammadātīre, tyajja brāhmaṇakhattiyā”ti.

“We were outcasts in Avanti, deer by the Nerañjarā, ospreys on the Nammadā's bank; today we are a brahmin and a khattiya.”

Tattha [V 4.0356] duccaritassāti mahārāja, tvaṃ sucaritasseva phalaṃ jānāsi, ahaṃ pana duccaritassapi phalaṃ passāmiyeva. Mayañhi ubho duccaritassa phalena ito catutthe attabhāve caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbattā. Tattha na ciraṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā tassa phalena tvaṃ khattiyakule nibbatto, ahaṃ brāhmaṇakule, evāhaṃ duccaritassa ca phalaṃ suciṇṇassa ca mahāvipākaṃ disvā attānameva sīlasaṃyamena paṭisaṃyamissaṃ, puttaṃ vā pasuṃ vā dhanaṃ vā na patthemi.

Therein, 'of misconduct' means: O great king, you know only the fruit of good conduct, but I see the fruit of misconduct as well. For we were both reborn in an outcast's womb in the fourth existence from this one due to the fruit of misconduct. There, having maintained virtue for a short time, by the fruit of that you were reborn in a khattiya family, and I in a brahmin family. Thus, having seen the fruit of misconduct and the great result of good conduct, I shall restrain myself through the restraint of virtue; I do not desire a son, livestock, or wealth.

Dasevimā vassadasāti mahārāja, mandadasakaṃ khiḍḍādasakaṃ vaṇṇadasakaṃ baladasakaṃ paññādasakaṃ hānidasakaṃ pabbhāradasakaṃ vaṅkadasakaṃ momūhadasakaṃ sayanadasakanti imesañhi dasannaṃ dasakānaṃ vasena daseva vassadasā imesaṃ maccānaṃ idha manussaloke jīvitaṃ. Tayidaṃ na niyamena sabbā eva etā dasā pāpuṇāti, atha kho appattaññeva taṃ odhiṃ naḷo chinnova sussati. Yepi sakalaṃ vassasataṃ jīvanti, tesampi mandadasake pavattā rūpārūpadhammā vicchinditvā ātape khittanaḷo viya tattheva sussanti antaradhāyanti, taṃ odhiṃ atikkamitvā khiḍḍādasakaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tathā khiṭṭādasakādīsu pavattā vaṇṇadasakādīni.

O great king, ‘these ten decades’ means: the decade of infancy, the decade of play, the decade of beauty, the decade of strength, the decade of wisdom, the decade of decline, the decade of stooping, the decade of crookedness, the decade of delusion, and the decade of lying down. By means of these ten decades, the life of mortals here in the human world consists of only ten decades. It is not certain that one reaches all these decades; rather, without even reaching that limit, one withers like a cut reed. Even for those who live a full hundred years, the material and immaterial phenomena that occur in the decade of infancy cease and, like a reed thrown in the sun, dry up and vanish right there, not reaching the decade of play. Similarly, what occurs in the decade of play and so on does not reach the decade of beauty and so on.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ evaṃ sussamāne jīvite kā pañca kāmaguṇe nissāya abhinandī, kā kāyakīḷādivasena khiḍḍā, kā somanassavasena rati, kā dhanesanā, kiṃ me puttehi, kiṃ dārehi, muttosmi tamhā puttadārabandhanāti attho. Antakenādhipannassāti jīvitantakarena maccunā abhibhūtassa. Dvipadākaniṭṭhāti dvipadānaṃ antare lāmakā. Avasimhāti dvepi mayaṃ vasimha.

Therein, in this life that is thus withering away, what is the use of delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure? What is the use of sport such as bodily play? What is the use of pleasure through mental joy? What is the use of the search for wealth? What use are sons to me? What use are wives? The meaning is: I am freed from that bondage of sons and wives. 'Oppressed by the end-maker' means overwhelmed by death, the one who makes an end of life. 'The lowest of bipeds' means the most inferior among bipeds. 'We have lived' means we both have lived.

Caṇḍālāhumhāti [M 4.0398] mahārāja, ito pubbe catutthaṃ jātiṃ avantiraṭṭhe ujjeninagare caṇḍālā ahumha, tato cavitvā nerañjarāya nadiyā tīre ubhopi migā ahumha. Tattha dvepi amhe ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle aññamaññaṃ nissāya ṭhite eko luddako ekeneva sattipahārena jīvitā voropesi, tato cavitvā nammadānadītīre kurarā ahumha. Tatrāpi no nissāya ṭhite eko nesādo ekappahāreneva bandhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi, tato cavitvā te [P 4.0398] mayaṃ ajja brāhmaṇakhattiyā jātā. Ahaṃ kosambiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatto, tvaṃ idha rājā jātoti.

O great king, 'We were outcasts' means that in the fourth birth before this one, we were outcasts in the city of Ujjenī in the Avanti country. After passing away from there, we were both deer on the bank of the Nerañjarā River. There, while we both stood relying on each other at the foot of a single tree, a hunter deprived us of life with a single spear thrust. After passing away from there, we became ospreys on the bank of the Nammadā River. There too, while we stood relying on each other, a hunter captured us with a single strike and brought us to the end of our lives. After passing away from there, we are today born as a brahmin and a khattiya. I was born in a brahmin family in Kosambī, and you were born here as a king.

Evamassa atīte lāmakajātiyo pakāsetvā idāni imissāpi jātiyā āyusaṅkhāraparittataṃ dassetvā puññesu ussāhaṃ janento catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Having thus revealed his past inferior births, and now showing the brevity of the lifespan in this very birth and inspiring effort in meritorious deeds, he spoke these four verses:

40.

40.

“Upanīyati [V 4.0357] jīvitamappamāyu, jarūpanītassa na santi tāṇā;

Karohi pañcāla mameta vākyaṃ, mākāsi kammāni dukkhudrayāni.

“Life is being led away, the lifespan is short; for one led away by old age, there are no protections. Heed these words of mine, O Pañcāla, do not perform deeds that have painful consequences.”

41.

41.

“Upanīyati jīvitamappamāyu, jarūpanītassa na santi tāṇā;

Karohi pañcāla mameta vākyaṃ, mākāsi kammāni dukkhapphalāni.

“Life is being led away, the lifespan is short; for one led away by old age, there are no protections. Heed these words of mine, O Pañcāla, do not perform deeds that bear painful fruits.”

42.

42.

“Upanīyati jīvitamappamāyu, jarūpanītassa na santi tāṇā;

Karohi pañcāla mameta vākyaṃ, mākāsi kammāni rajassirāni.

“Life is being led away, the lifespan is short; for one led away by old age, there are no protections. Heed these words of mine, O Pañcāla, do not perform deeds that result in heads covered with the dust of defilement.”

43.

43.

“Upanīyati jīvitamappamāyu, vaṇṇaṃ jarā hanti narassa jiyyato;

Karohi pañcāla mameta vākyaṃ, mākāsi kammaṃ nirayūpapattiyā”ti.

“Life is being led away, the lifespan is short; old age destroys the beauty of a person who is aging. Heed these words of mine, O Pañcāla, do not perform a deed that leads to rebirth in hell.”

Tattha [M 4.0399] upanīyatīti mahārāja, idaṃ jīvitaṃ maraṇaṃ upagacchati. Idañhi imesaṃ sattānaṃ appamāyu sarasaparittatāyapi ṭhitiparittatāyapi parittakaṃ, sūriyuggamane tiṇagge ussāvabindusadisaṃ. Na santi tāṇāti na hi jarāya maraṇaṃ upanītassa puttādayo tāṇā nāma honti. Mameta vākyanti mama etaṃ vacanaṃ. Mākāsīti mā rūpādikāmaguṇahetu pamādaṃ āpajjitvā nirayādīsu dukkhavaḍḍhanāni kammāni kari. Dukkhapphalānīti dukkhavipākāni. Rajassirānīti kilesarajena okiṇṇasīsāni. Vaṇṇanti jīramānassa narassa sarīravaṇṇaṃ jarā hanti. Nirayūpapattiyāti nirassāde niraye uppajjanatthāya.

Therein, 'is being led away' means, O great king, this life approaches death. For the lifespan of these beings is short; it is small both due to the brevity of its essence and the brevity of its duration—like a dewdrop on a blade of grass at sunrise. 'There are no protections' means that for one led to death by old age, children and others are not true protections. 'This word of mine' means this speech of mine. 'Do not perform' means: do not, by falling into negligence for the sake of sensual pleasures such as forms and so on, perform deeds that increase suffering in hell and other such places. 'Having painful fruits' means having painful results. 'With heads covered in dust' means heads covered with the dust of defilements. 'Beauty' means old age destroys the bodily complexion of an aging person. 'For rebirth in hell' means for the purpose of arising in the joyless hell.

Evaṃ [P 4.0399] mahāsatte kathente rājā tussitvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

While the Great Being was speaking thus, the king, pleased, spoke these three verses:

44.

44.

“Addhā hi saccaṃ vacanaṃ tavetaṃ, yathā isī bhāsasi evametaṃ;

Kāmā ca me santi anapparūpā, te duccajā mādisakena bhikkhu.

“Indeed, this word of yours is true; it is just as you speak, O sage. But I have numerous sensual pleasures, and they are hard for one like me to abandon, O monk.”

45.

45.

“Nāgo yathā paṅkamajjhe byasanno, passaṃ thalaṃ nābhisambhoti gantuṃ;

Evampahaṃ kāmapaṅke byasanno, na bhikkhuno maggamanubbajāmi.

“Just as an elephant sunk in the mud, though seeing dry land, is unable to go there; even so, I am sunk in the mire of sensual pleasures and do not follow the monk's path.”

46.

46.

“Yathāpi mātā ca pitā ca puttaṃ, anusāsare kinti sukhī bhaveyya;

Evampi maṃ tvaṃ anusāsa bhante, yathā ciraṃ pecca sukhī bhaveyya”nti.

“Just as a mother and father would advise their son, 'How might he be happy?'; even so, O venerable sir, advise me, so that I may be happy for a long time after passing away.”

Tattha [V 4.0358] anapparūpāti aparittajātikā bahū aparimitā. Te duccajā mādisakenāti bhātika, tvaṃ kilese pahāya ṭhito, ahaṃ pana kāmapaṅke nimuggo, tasmā mādisakena te kāmā duccajā. “Nāgo yathā”ti iminā attano kāmapaṅke nimuggabhāvassa upamaṃ dasseti. Tattha byasannoti visanno anupaviṭṭho ayameva vā pāṭho. Magganti tumhākaṃ [M 4.0400] ovādānusāsanīmaggaṃ nānubbajāmi pabbajituṃ na sakkomi, idheva pana me ṭhitassa ovādaṃ dethāti. Anusāsareti anusāsanti.

Therein, 'anapparūpā' means of no small kind, many, immeasurable. 'Te duccajā mādisakena' means: 'O brother, you stand having abandoned the defilements, while I am sunk in the mire of sensual pleasures; therefore, for one like me, those sensual pleasures are hard to abandon.' By 'Nāgo yathā', he gives a simile for his own state of being sunk in the mire of sensual pleasures. Therein, 'byasanno' means sunk down or entered into; this is also an alternative reading. 'Maggaṃ' means: 'I do not follow the path of your advice and instruction; I am unable to go forth. But give me advice while I remain here.' 'Anusāsare' means 'they advise'.

Atha naṃ mahāsatto āha –

Then the Great Being said to him:

47.

47.

“No ce tuvaṃ ussahase janinda, kāme ime mānusake pahātuṃ;

Dhammiṃ baliṃ paṭṭhapayassu rāja, adhammakāro tava māhu raṭṭhe.

If you are not able, O lord of men, to abandon these human sensual pleasures, then establish a righteous tax, O king; let there be no unrighteous practice in your kingdom.

48.

48.

“Dūtā vidhāvantu disā catasso, nimantakā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ;

Te annapānena upaṭṭhahassu, vatthena senāsanapaccayena ca.

Let messengers hasten to the four directions to invite ascetics and brahmins. Serve them with food and drink, and with clothing, lodgings, and requisites.

49.

49.

“Annena [P 4.0400] pānena pasannacitto, santappaya samaṇabrāhmaṇe ca;

Datvā ca bhutvā ca yathānubhāvaṃ, anindito saggamupehi ṭhānaṃ.

With a gladdened heart, satisfy the ascetics and brahmins with food and drink. Having given and enjoyed according to your ability, blameless, reach the heavenly realm.

50.

50.

“Sace ca taṃ rāja mado saheyya, nārīgaṇehi paricārayantaṃ;

Imameva gāthaṃ manasī karohi, bhāsesi cenaṃ parisāya majjhe.

And if, O king, intoxication should overcome you while being entertained by groups of women, keep this very verse in mind and recite it in the midst of the assembly.

51.

51.

“Abbhokāsasayo jantu, vajantyā khīrapāyito;

Parikiṇṇo suvānehi, svājja rājāti vuccatī”ti.

A being who sleeps in the open air, fed milk while [his mother] was away, surrounded by dogs—he today is called a king!

Tattha ussahaseti ussahasi. Dhammiṃ balinti dhammena samena anatirittaṃ baliṃ gaṇhāti attho. Adhammakāroti porāṇakarājūhi ṭhapitaṃ vinicchayadhammaṃ bhinditvā pavattā adhammakiriyā. Nimantakāti dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇe nimantetvā pakkosakā. Yathānubhāvanti yathābalaṃ yathāsattiṃ. Imameva gāthanti idāni vattabbaṃ sandhāyāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – “mahārāja, sace taṃ mado abhibhaveyya, sace te nārīgaṇaparivutassa [M 4.0401] rūpādayo vā kāmaguṇe rajjasukhaṃ vā ārabbha māno uppajjeyya, athevaṃ cinteyyāsi ‘ahaṃ pure caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbatto channassa tiṇakuṭimattassapi [V 4.0359] abhāvā abbhokāsasayo ahosiṃ, tadā hi me mātā caṇḍālī araññaṃ dārupaṇṇādīnaṃ atthāya gacchantī maṃ kukkuragaṇassa majjhe abbhokāse nipajjāpetvā attano khīraṃ pāyetvā gacchati, sohaṃ kukkurehi parivārito tehiyeva saddhiṃ sunakhiyā khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhito, evaṃ nīcajacco hutvā ajja rājā nāma jāto’ti. ‘Iti kho, tvaṃ mahārāja, iminā atthena attānaṃ ovadanto yo so pubbe abbhokāsasayo jantu araññe vajantiyā caṇḍāliyā ito cito ca anusañcarantiyā sunakhiyā ca khīraṃ pāyito sunakhehi parikiṇṇo vaḍḍhito, so ajja rājāti vuccatī’ti imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāseyyāsī”ti.

There, 'ussahaseti' means you are able. 'Dhammiṃ baliṃ' means taking a tax that is just and equitable, not excessive. 'Adhammakāro' refers to unrighteous deeds carried out by breaking the law of judgment established by ancient kings. 'Nimantakā' means those who invite and summon righteous ascetics and brahmins. 'Yathānubhāvaṃ' means according to one's power and capacity. 'Imameva gāthaṃ' refers to the verse now to be spoken. Here is the intended meaning: 'Great king, if intoxication were to overcome you, if conceit were to arise in you regarding the sensual pleasures of form and so on, or regarding the joy of sovereignty while surrounded by a retinue of women, then you should reflect thus: "In the past, I was born into an outcast womb, and because of the absence of even a simple thatched hut, I slept in the open. At that time, my outcast mother, going into the forest for wood, leaves, and so on, would lay me down in the open among a pack of dogs, give me her own milk to drink, and then depart. I, surrounded by those dogs, grew up drinking the milk of a female dog along with them. Having been of such low birth, today I am called a king." Thus, great king, admonishing yourself with this meaning, you should recite this verse: "That being who formerly lay in the open, fed milk while the outcast woman was away wandering here and there in the forest, and who grew up surrounded by dogs—he is today called a king!"'

Evaṃ mahāsatto tassa ovādaṃ datvā “dinno te mayā ovādo, idāni tvaṃ pabbaja vā mā vā, attanāva attano kammassa vipākaṃ paṭisevissatī”ti vatvā ākāse uppatitvā tassa matthake pādarajaṃ pātento himavantameva gato. Rājāpi taṃ disvā [P 4.0401] uppannasaṃvego jeṭṭhaputtassa rajjaṃ datvā balakāyaṃ nivattetvā himavantābhimukho pāyāsi. Mahāsatto tassāgamanaṃ ñatvā isigaṇaparivuto āgantvā taṃ ādāya gantvā pabbājetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ ācikkhi. So jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattesi. Iti te ubhopi brahmalokūpagā ahesuṃ.

Thus, the Great Being gave him this advice and said, 'I have given you advice; now, whether you go forth or not, you yourself will experience the result of your own actions.' Having spoken thus, he rose into the sky, and shedding the dust from his feet upon the king's head, he departed to the Himalayas. The king, seeing this, was filled with a sense of spiritual urgency. He handed over the kingdom to his eldest son, dismissed his army, and set out toward the Himalayas. The Great Being, knowing of his arrival, came surrounded by a company of seers, took him along, gave him the going forth, and taught him the preparatory meditation on the kasiṇas. He developed the jhānas and the higher knowledges. Thus, both of them were reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā tīṇi cattāri bhavantarāni gacchantāpi daḷhavissāsāva ahesu”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sambhūtapaṇḍito ānando ahosi, cittapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, 'Thus, monks, even after passing through three or four intervening existences, the wise of old remained steadfastly affectionate and intimate.' Then he connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, Sambhūta the Wise was Ānanda, and Citta the Wise was myself.'

Cittasambhūtajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā

The Explanation of the Cittasambhūta Jātaka, the Second.

[499] 3. Sivijātakavaṇṇanā

[499] 3. The Explanation of the Sivi Jātaka

Dūre [M 4.0402] apassaṃ therovāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto asadisadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ aṭṭhakanipāte sivijātake vitthāritameva. Tadā pana rājā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāre datvā anumodanaṃ yāci, satthā akatvāva pakkāmi. Rājā bhuttapātarāso vihāraṃ gantvā “kasmā, bhante, anumodanaṃ na karitthā”ti āha. Satthā “aparisuddhā, mahārāja, parisā”ti vatvā “na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajantī”ti (dha. pa. 177) gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi. Rājā pasīditvā satasahassagghanakena sīveyyakena uttarāsaṅgena tathāgataṃ pūjetvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Punadivase dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, kosalarājā asadisadānaṃ datvā tādisenapi [V 4.0360] dānena atitto dasabalena dhamme desite puna satasahassagghanakaṃ sīveyyakavatthaṃ adāsi, yāva atitto vata āvuso dānena rājā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā ‘imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, bāhirabhaṇḍaṃ nāma sudinnaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassapariccāgena dānaṃ dadamānāpi bāhiradānena atittā ‘piyassa dātā piyaṃ labhatī’ti sampattayācakānaṃ akkhīni uppāṭetvā adaṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Seeing the elder from afar”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the incomparable gift. That has been detailed in the Sivi Jātaka in the Book of Eights. At that time, the king, on the seventh day, having given all the requisites, requested the words of appreciation. But the Teacher departed without giving them. The king, having eaten his morning meal, went to the monastery and asked, “Venerable sir, why did you not give the words of appreciation?” The Teacher replied, “Great king, the assembly was not pure,” and then taught the Dhamma with the verse: “Misers do not go to the world of the gods” (Dhammapada 177). The king, pleased, honored the Tathāgata with an upper robe of Siveyyaka cloth worth a hundred thousand and entered the city. The next day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: “Friends, the king of Kosala, having given an incomparable gift, was still not satisfied even with such a gift. When the Dhamma was taught by the One of Ten Powers, he again gave a Siveyyaka cloth worth a hundred thousand. How insatiable, friends, is the king in giving!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When told, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, external goods are indeed a good gift; however, the wise of old, having made the whole of Jambudīpa like a single level field and giving daily gifts with an expenditure of six hundred thousand, were still not satisfied with external giving. Thinking, ‘The giver of what is dear receives what is dear,’ they even tore out their own eyes and gave them to the supplicants who had come.” Thus, he related the past.

Atīte siviraṭṭhe ariṭṭhapuranagare sivimahārāje rajjaṃ kārente mahāsatto tassa putto hutvā nibbatti, “sivikumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā uggahitasippo [P 4.0402] āgantvā pitu sippaṃ dassetvā uparajjaṃ labhitvā aparabhāge pitu accayena rājā hutvā agatigamanaṃ pahāya dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā catūsu dvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāre cāti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā devasikaṃ chasatasahassapariccāgena mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Aṭṭhamiyaṃ cātuddasiyaṃ pannarasiyañca niccaṃ dānasālaṃ gantvā dānaṃ olokesi. So ekadā puṇṇamadivase pātova samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno attanā dinnadānaṃ āvajjento bāhiravatthuṃ [M 4.0403] attanā adinnaṃ nāma adisvā “mayā bāhiravatthu adinnaṃ nāma natthi, na maṃ bāhiradānaṃ toseti, ahaṃ ajjhattikadānaṃ dātukāmo, aho vata ajja mama dānasālaṃ gatakāle kocideva yācako bāhiravatthuṃ ayācitvā ajjhattikassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, sace hi me koci hadayamaṃsassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, kaṇayena uraṃ paharitvā pasannaudakato sanāḷaṃ padumaṃ uddharanto viya lohitabindūni paggharantaṃ hadayaṃ nīharitvā dassāmi. Sace sarīramaṃsassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, avalekhanasatthakena telasiṅgaṃ likhanto viya sarīramaṃsaṃ otāretvā dassāmi. Sace lohitassa nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, yantamukhe pakkhanditvā upanītaṃ bhājanaṃ pūretvā lohitaṃ dassāmi. Sace vā pana koci ‘gehe me kammaṃ nappavattati, gehe me dāsakammaṃ karohī’ti vadeyya, rājavesaṃ apanetvā bahi ṭhatvā attānaṃ sāvetvā dāsakammaṃ karissāmi. Sace me koci akkhino nāmaṃ gaṇheyya, tālamiñjaṃ nīharanto viya akkhīni uppāṭetvā dassāmī”ti cintesi.

In the past, in the Sivi kingdom, in the city of Ariṭṭhapura, while King Sivi the Great was ruling, the Great Being was born as his son. They named him “Prince Sivi.” When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, mastered the arts, returned, demonstrated his skill to his father, and received the position of sub-king. Later, after his father’s passing, he became king. Abandoning the four wrong courses of action and not violating the ten royal duties, he ruled righteously. He had six alms halls built—at the four city gates, in the city center, and at the palace gate—and daily dispensed great alms with an expenditure of six hundred thousand. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, he would always go to the alms hall to oversee the giving. One day, on the full moon day, early in the morning, seated on the royal throne under a raised white parasol, he reflected on the gifts he had given. Seeing no external object that had not been given by him, he thought, “There is no external object that remains ungiven by me, but external giving does not satisfy me. I wish to give an internal gift. Oh, if only today, when I go to the alms hall, some supplicant would not ask for an external object but would name something internal! If someone were to ask for the flesh of my heart, I would strike my chest with a spear, and like pulling a lotus with its stalk from clear water, I would draw out my heart, with drops of blood trickling, and give it. If someone were to ask for the flesh of my body, I would carve it off with a scraping knife, like scraping a horn for oil, and give it. If someone were to ask for my blood, I would leap into the mouth of a press, fill the vessel brought to me, and give my blood. Or if someone were to say, ‘The work in my house does not get done; do the work of a slave in my house,’ I would remove my royal attire, stand outside, announce myself, and perform the work of a slave. If someone were to ask for my eyes, I would pluck them out like extracting the kernel of a palm fruit and give them.”

Iti so –

Thus he thought:

“Yaṃkiñci mānusaṃ dānaṃ, adinnaṃ me na vijjati;

Yopi yāceyya maṃ cakkhuṃ, dadeyyaṃ avikampito”ti. (cariyā. 1.52) –

“Whatever human gift there is, none remains ungiven by me; should someone ask me even for my eye, I would give it, unwavering.”

Cintetvā [V 4.0361] soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato [P 4.0403] dānaggaṃ agamāsi. Sakko tassa ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā “sivirājā ‘ajja sampattayācakānaṃ cakkhūni uppāṭetvā dassāmī’ti cintesi, sakkhissati nu kho dātuṃ, udāhu no”ti tassa vimaṃsanatthāya jarāpatto andhabrāhmaṇo viya hutvā rañño dānaggagamanakāle ekasmiṃ unnatappadese hatthaṃ pasāretvā rājānaṃ jayāpetvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā tadabhimukhaṃ vāraṇaṃ pesetvā “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ vadesī”ti pucchi. Atha naṃ sakko “mahārāja, tava dānajjhāsayaṃ nissāya samuggatena kittighosena sakalalokasannivāso nirantaraṃ phuṭo, ahaṃ andho, tvaṃ dvicakkhuko”ti vatvā cakkhuṃ yācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having considered this, he bathed with sixteen pots of scented water, adorned himself with all ornaments, ate various foods of excellent flavor, mounted a decorated noble elephant, and went to the alms hall. Sakka, knowing his intention, thought, “King Sivi thought, ‘Today I will pluck out my eyes and give them to the supplicants who have arrived.’ Will he be able to give them, or not?” To test him, Sakka took the form of an old blind brahmin and, as the king was going to the alms hall, stood on an elevated spot, stretching out his hand and shouting a cry of victory for the king. The king turned the elephant toward him and asked, “Brahmin, what do you say?” Then Sakka said to him, “Great king, because of your intention to give, the sound of your fame has arisen and continuously pervaded the entire world. I am blind; you have two eyes,” and asking for an eye, he spoke the first verse:

52.

52.

“Dūre [M 4.0404] apassaṃ therova, cakkhuṃ yācitumāgato;

Ekanettā bhavissāma, cakkhuṃ me dehi yācito”ti.

“From afar, not seeing, like an old elder, I have come to ask for an eye. We shall both be one-eyed; give me an eye, as you are asked.”

Tattha dūreti ito dūre vasanto. Theroti jarājiṇṇathero. Ekanettāti ekaṃ nettaṃ mayhaṃ dehi, evaṃ dvepi ekekanettā bhavissāmāti.

There, ‘dūre’ means living far from here. ‘Thero’ means an elder, worn out by old age. ‘Ekanettā’ means, “Give me one eye, and thus we shall both be one-eyed.”

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “idānevāhaṃ pāsāde nisinno cintetvā āgato, aho me lābho, ajjeva me manoratho matthakaṃ pāpuṇissati, adinnapubbaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī”ti tuṭṭhamānaso dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being thought: “Just now, while sitting in the palace, I considered this and came here. Oh, what a gain for me! Today my wish will reach its culmination. I shall give a gift never given before.” With a delighted mind, he spoke the second verse:

53.

53.

“Kenānusiṭṭho idha māgatosi, vanibbaka cakkhupathāni yācituṃ;

Suduccajaṃ yācasi uttamaṅgaṃ, yamāhu nettaṃ purisena ‘duccaja’nti.

"By whom were you instructed to come here, mendicant, to beg for eyes? You ask for the supreme limb, which is very hard to give; that which is called the eye is said by people to be hard to relinquish."

Tattha vanibbakāti taṃ ālapati. Cakkhupathānīti cakkhūnametaṃ nāmaṃ. Yamāhūti yaṃ paṇḍitā “duccaja”nti kathenti.

Here, 'vanibbaka' is an address to him. 'Cakkhupathāni' is a name for the eyes. 'Yamāhu' means what the wise call 'hard to relinquish'.

Ito paraṃ uttānasambandhagāthā pāḷinayeneva veditabbā –

Henceforth, the connection of the verses is to be understood according to the Pāli text itself.

54.

54.

“Yamāhu devesu sujampatīti, maghavāti naṃ āhu manussaloke;

Tenānusiṭṭho [P 4.0404] idha māgatosmi, vanibbako cakkhupathāni yācituṃ.

"He who is called Sujampati among the gods, and Maghavā in the human world; instructed by him, I have come here, a mendicant, to beg for eyes."

55.

55.

“Vanibbato [V 4.0362] mayha vaniṃ anuttaraṃ, dadāhi te cakkhupathāni yācito;

Dadāhi me cakkhupathaṃ anuttaraṃ, yamāhu nettaṃ purisena duccajaṃ.

"To me, the mendicant, grant my supreme request: give your eyes, as you are asked. Give me the supreme eye, which they say is hard for a man to relinquish."

56.

56.

“Yena atthena āgacchi, yamatthamabhipatthayaṃ;

Te te ijjhantu saṅkappā, labha cakkhūni brāhmaṇa.

"For the purpose for which you came, for the goal which you desired, may those resolves of yours succeed. Receive the eyes, O brahmin."

57.

57.

“Ekaṃ [M 4.0405] te yācamānassa, ubhayāni dadāmahaṃ;

Sa cakkhumā gaccha janassa pekkhato, yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatū”ti.

"Though you ask for one, I shall give you both. Go forth endowed with eyes while the people look on. Whatever you desire, may that be fulfilled for you."

Tattha vanibbatoti yācantassa. Vaninti yācanaṃ. Te teti te tava tassa atthassa saṅkappā. Sa cakkhumāti so tvaṃ mama cakkhūhi cakkhumā hutvā. Yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatūti yaṃ tvaṃ mama santikā icchasi, taṃ te samijjhatūti.

Here, 'vanibbatoti' means 'of the requester'. 'Vaninti' means 'begging' or 'request'. 'Te te' means 'those resolves of yours for that purpose'. 'Sa cakkhumā' means 'you, having become endowed with eyes through my eyes'. 'Yadicchase tvaṃ tadate samijjhatu' means 'whatever you desire from me, may that be fulfilled for you'.

Rājā ettakaṃ kathetvā “idheva mayā akkhīni uppāṭetvā dātuṃ asāruppa”nti cintetvā brāhmaṇaṃ ādāya antepuraṃ gantvā rājāsane nisīditvā sīvikaṃ nāma vejjaṃ pakkosāpetvā “akkhiṃ me sodhehī”ti āha. “Amhākaṃ kira rājā akkhīni uppāṭetvā brāhmaṇassa dātukāmo”ti sakalanagare ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Atha senāpatiādayo rājavallabhā ca nāgarā ca orodhā ca sabbe sannipatitvā rājānaṃ vārentā tisso gāthā avocuṃ –

Having spoken thus, the king thought: "It is not proper for me to pluck out my eyes here and give them." So, taking the brahmin, he went to the inner palace, sat on the royal throne, and summoned a physician named Sīvaka, saying, "Prepare my eye." Then, throughout the entire city, a great commotion arose: "Our king, they say, intends to pluck out his eyes and give them to the brahmin!" Then the commander-in-chief and others, the royal favorites, the citizens, and the women of the inner court all gathered together and, trying to prevent the king, spoke these three verses:

58.

58.

“Mā no deva adā cakkhuṃ, mā no sabbe parākari;

Dhanaṃ dehi mahārāja, muttā veḷuriyā bahū.

"O king, do not give your eye; do not abandon us all. Give wealth, great king; there are many pearls and lapis lazuli."

59.

59.

“Yutte deva rathe dehi, ājānīye calaṅkate;

Nāge dehi mahārāja, hemakappanavāsase.

"O king, give chariots yoked with well-bred, adorned horses. Great king, give elephants clothed in golden trappings."

60.

60.

“Yathā [P 4.0405] taṃ sivayo sabbe, sayoggā sarathā sadā;

Samantā parikireyyuṃ, evaṃ dehi rathesabhā”ti.

"So that all the Sivis, with their teams and chariots, might always surround you on all sides, give in such a way, O lord of chariots."

Tattha parākarīti pariccaji. Akkhīsu hi dinnesu rajjaṃ tvaṃ na kāressasi, añño rājā [V 4.0363] bhavissati, evaṃ tayā mayaṃ pariccattā nāma bhavissāmāti adhippāyenevamāhaṃsu. Parikireyyunti parivāreyyuṃ. Evaṃ dehīti yathā taṃ avikalacakkhuṃ sivayo parivāreyyuṃ, evaṃ bāhiradhanamevassa dehi, mā akkhīni. Akkhīsu hi dinnesu na taṃ sivayo parivāressantīti.

Here, 'parākari' means 'abandoned'. Their intention was: 'If your eyes are given away, you will not be able to rule the kingdom; another will become king. Thus, we will be abandoned by you.' 'Parikireyyuṃ' means 'they would surround'. 'Evaṃ dehi' means: 'Give only external wealth, not your eyes, so that the Sivis may surround you as one with unimpaired eyes. For if your eyes are given, the Sivis will not surround you.'

Atha [M 4.0406] rājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke three verses:

61.

61.

“Yo ve dassanti vatvāna, adāne kurute mano;

Bhūmyaṃ so patitaṃ pāsaṃ, gīvāyaṃ paṭimuñcati.

"He who, having said 'I will give,' then sets his mind on not giving, fastens to his neck a snare that has fallen on the ground."

62.

62.

“Yo ve dassanti vatvānaṃ, adāne kurute mano;

Pāpā pāpataro hoti, sampatto yamasādhanaṃ.

"He who, having said 'I will give,' then sets his mind on not giving, becomes worse than the wicked, having reached Yama's domain."

63.

63.

“Yañhi yāce tañhi dade, yaṃ na yāce na taṃ dade;

Svāhaṃ tameva dassāmi, yaṃ maṃ yācati brāhmaṇo”ti.

"Whatever one is asked for, that one should give; what one is not asked for, that one should not give. Therefore, I shall give only that which the brahmin asks of me."

Tattha paṭimuñcatīti paveseti. Pāpā pāpataroti lāmakāpi lāmakataro nāma hoti. Sampatto yamasādhananti yamassa āṇāpavattiṭṭhānaṃ ussadanirayaṃ esa pattoyeva nāma hoti. Yañhi yāceti yaṃ yācako yāceyya, dāyakopi tameva dadeyya, na ayācitaṃ, ayañca brāhmaṇo maṃ cakkhuṃ yācati, na muttādikaṃ dhanaṃ, tadevassāhaṃ dassāmīti vadati.

Here, 'paṭimuñcati' means 'he fastens' or 'he puts on'. 'Pāpā pāpataro' means he becomes even more wretched than the wretched. 'Sampatto yamasādhanaṃ' means he has reached the Ussada hell, the place where Yama's authority is exercised. 'Yañhi yāce' means: whatever a beggar asks for, the giver should give just that, and not something unasked. Since this brahmin asks for my eye and not for wealth such as pearls, I shall give him just that.

Atha naṃ amaccā “kiṃ patthetvā cakkhūni desī”ti pucchantā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then the ministers, asking, "Aspiring to what do you give your eyes?" spoke a verse:

64.

64.

“Āyuṃ nu vaṇṇaṃ nu sukhaṃ balaṃ nu, kiṃ patthayāno nu janinda desi;

Kathañhi rājā sivinaṃ anuttaro, cakkhūni dajjā paralokahetū”ti.

"Is it for long life, or beauty, or happiness, or strength? Aspiring to what, O lord of men, do you give? How indeed could the unsurpassed king of the Sivis give his eyes for the sake of the next world?"

Tattha paralokahetūti mahārāja, kathaṃ nāma tumhādiso paṇḍitapuriso sandiṭṭhikaṃ issariyaṃ pahāya paralokahetu cakkhūni dadeyyāti.

Here, 'paralokahetū' means: 'Great king, how could a wise man like you, abandoning sovereignty visible in this life, give away his eyes for the sake of the next world?'

Atha [P 4.0406] nesaṃ kathento rājā gāthamāha –

Then, speaking to them, the king spoke a verse:

65.

65.

“Na [V 4.0364] vāhametaṃ yasasā dadāmi, na puttamicche na dhanaṃ na raṭṭhaṃ;

Satañca dhammo carito purāṇo, icceva dāne ramate mano mamā”ti.

"I do not give this for fame, nor do I desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom. But this is the ancient Dhamma of the virtuous, practiced of old; for this reason my mind delights in giving."

Tattha [M 4.0407] na vāhanti na ve ahaṃ. Yasasāti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā yasassa kāraṇā. Na puttamiccheti imassa cakkhudānassa phalena nevāhaṃ puttaṃ icchāmi, na dhanaṃ na raṭṭhaṃ, apica sataṃ paṇḍitānaṃ sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ esa āciṇṇo samāciṇṇo porāṇakamaggo, yadidaṃ pāramīpūraṇaṃ nāma. Na hi pāramiyo apūretvā bodhipallaṅke sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho nāma atthi, ahañca pāramiyo pūretvā buddho bhavitukāmo. Icceva dāne ramate mano mamāti iminā kāraṇena mama mano dāneyeva niratoti vadati.

Here, 'na vāhaṃ' means 'not indeed I'. 'Yasasā' means for the sake of divine or human fame. 'Na puttamicche' means: I do not desire a son, nor wealth, nor a kingdom as a result of this gift of eyes. Rather, this is the ancient path practiced and followed by the wise Bodhisattas who seek omniscience—namely, the fulfillment of the perfections. For without fulfilling the perfections, no one is able to attain omniscience on the seat of enlightenment. I, too, wish to fulfill the perfections and become a Buddha. 'Icceva dāne ramate mano mamā' means: for this reason, my mind delights only in giving.

Sammāsambuddhopi dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa cariyāpiṭakaṃ desento “mayhaṃ dvīhi cakkhūhipi sabbaññutaññāṇameva piyatara”nti dīpetuṃ āha –

The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, while expounding the Cariyāpiṭaka to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, said this to illustrate the point: 'Omniscient knowledge is dearer to me even than both my eyes':

“Na me dessā ubho cakkhū, attānaṃ me na dessiyaṃ;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā cakkhuṃ adāsaha”nti. (cariyā. 1.66);

"My two eyes are not hateful to me, nor is my self hateful to me; omniscience is dear to me, therefore I gave my eye." (Cariyā. 1.66)

Mahāsattassa pana kathaṃ sutvā amaccesu appaṭibhāṇesu ṭhitesu mahāsatto sīvikaṃ vejjaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

When he heard the words of the Great Being, and the ministers stood speechless, the Great Being addressed the physician Sīvaka in verse:

66.

66.

“Sakhā ca mitto ca mamāsi sīvika, susikkhito sādhu karohi me vaco;

Uddharitvā cakkhūni mamaṃ jigīsato, hatthesu ṭhapehi vanibbakassā”ti.

“Sīvaka, you are my friend and companion; you are well-trained, so follow my words well. Having plucked out my eyes as I desire to give them, place them in the hands of the mendicant.”

Tassattho – samma sīvika, tvaṃ mayhaṃ sahāyo ca mitto ca vejjasippe cāsi susikkhito, sādhu me vacanaṃ karohi. Mama jigīsato upadhārentassa olokentasseva tālamiñjaṃ viya me akkhīni uddharitvā imassa yācakassa hatthesu ṭhapehīti.

The meaning is this: My dear Sīvaka, you are my companion and friend, and you are well-trained in the medical art. Follow my words well. As I desire to give, as I am reflecting and looking on, pluck out my eyes as if they were palm kernels and place them in the hands of this mendicant.

Atha naṃ sīviko āha “cakkhudānaṃ nāma bhāriyaṃ, upadhārehi, devā”ti. Sīvika, upadhāritaṃ mayā, tvaṃ mā papañcaṃ [P 4.0407] karohi, mā mayā saddhiṃ bahuṃ kathehīti. So cintesi “ayuttaṃ mādisassa susikkhitassa vejjassa rañño akkhīsu satthapātana”nti. So nānābhesajjāni ghaṃsitvā bhesajjacuṇṇena nīluppalaṃ [M 4.0408] paribhāvetvā dakkhiṇakkhiṃ upasiṅghāpesi, akkhi [V 4.0365] parivatti, dukkhavedanā uppajji. “Sallakkhehi, mahārāja, paṭipākatikakaraṇaṃ mayhaṃ bhāro”ti. “Alañhi tāta mā papañcaṃ karī”ti. So paribhāvetvā puna upasiṅghāpesi, akkhi akkhikūpato mucci, balavatarā vedanā udapādi. “Sallakkhehi mahārāja, sakkomahaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ kātu”nti. “Mā papañcaṃ karī”ti. So tatiyavāre kharataraṃ paribhāvetvā upanāmesi. Akkhi osadhabalena paribbhamitvā akkhikūpato nikkhamitvā nhārusuttakena olambamānaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Sallakkhehi narinda, puna pākatikakaraṇaṃ mayhaṃ balanti. Mā papañcaṃ karīti. Adhimattā vedanā udapādi, lohitaṃ pagghari, nivatthasāṭakā lohitena temiṃsu. Orodhā ca amaccā ca rañño pādamūle patitvā “deva akkhīni mā dehī”ti mahāparidevaṃ parideviṃsu.

Then Sīvaka said to him, “Your Majesty, the gift of eyes is a difficult task; please consider it further.” “Sīvaka, I have already considered it; do not delay, and do not speak much with me.” He thought, “It is not fitting for a well-trained physician like me to apply a knife to the King's eyes.” So that physician ground various medicines, imbued a blue lotus with the medicinal powder, and had him inhale it into his right eye. The eye spun around and painful sensations arose. “Great King, consider it further; restoring it to its original state is my responsibility.” “My dear man, just pluck it out; do not delay.” When he had said this, the physician prepared the medicine and applied it again. The eye was loosened from its socket, and intense pain arose. “Great King, consider it further; I am still able to restore it to its original state.” “Do not delay,” the King replied. For the third time, the physician prepared a very sharp medicine and applied it. By the power of the medicine, the eye spun around and came out of its socket, hanging by a sinew thread. “O Lord of Men, consider it further; it is within my power to restore it to its original state.” “Physician, do not delay,” the King said, while suffering intense pain. Blood gushed forth and his garments were soaked with blood. The ladies of the court and the ministers fell at the King’s feet and wept loudly, saying, “Your Majesty, do not give away your eyes!”

Rājā vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā “tāta, mā papañcaṃ karī”ti āha. So “sādhu, devā”ti vāmahatthena akkhiṃ dhāretvā dakkhiṇahatthena satthakaṃ ādāya akkhisuttakaṃ chinditvā akkhiṃ gahetvā mahāsattassa hatthe ṭhapesi. So vāmakkhinā dakkhiṇakkhiṃ oloketvā vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā “ehi brāhmaṇā”ti brāhmaṇaṃ pakkositvā “mama ito akkhito sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇakkhimeva piyataraṃ, tassa me idaṃ paccayo hotū”ti vatvā brāhmaṇassa akkhiṃ adāsi. So taṃ ukkhipitvā attano akkhimhi ṭhapesi. Taṃ tassānubhāvena vikasitanīluppalaṃ viya hutvā patiṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto vāmakkhinā tassa taṃ akkhiṃ disvā “aho, sudinnaṃ mayā akkhidāna”nti anto samuggatāya [P 4.0408] pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭo hutvā itarampi akkhiṃ adāsi. Sakko tampi attano akkhimhi ṭhapetvā rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā mahājanassa olokentasseva nagarā nikkhamitvā devalokameva gato. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā diyaḍḍhagāthamāha –

The King endured the pain and said, “My dear physician, do not delay.” He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and holding the eye with his left hand, he took a small knife with his right hand, cut the tendon, and taking the eye, placed it in the hand of the Great Being. The Great Being looked at the right eye with his left eye, and enduring the pain, called out, “Brahmin, come here.” He then said, “The eye of omniscience is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold dearer to me than this eye of mine. May this gift of eyes be a supporting condition for attaining that omniscience.” Having spoken thus, he gave the eye to the Brahmin. The Brahmin took it and placed it in his own eye socket. By the power of Sakka, it appeared there like a blooming blue lotus. The Great Being, seeing that Brahmin's eye with his left eye, was pervaded by internal joy, thinking, ‘Ah, I have indeed given the gift of an eye!’ and he plucked out and gave the other eye as well. Sakka placed that eye also in his own socket and, while the people were watching, left the King's palace, departed from the city, and went straight to the heavenly realm. Desiring to clarify this matter, the Teacher, having attained Buddhahood, spoke these verses:

67.

67.

“Codito sivirājena, sīviko vacanaṃkaro;

Rañño cakkhūnuddharitvā, brāhmaṇassūpanāmayi;

Sacakkhu brāhmaṇo āsi, andho rājā upāvisī”ti.

“Urged by the Sivi King, Sīvaka, who followed his word, having plucked out the King's eyes, presented them to the Brahmin. The Brahmin became possessed of sight, while the King sat blind.”

Rañño [M 4.0409] na cirasseva akkhīni ruhiṃsu, ruhamānāni ca āvāṭabhāvaṃ appatvā kambalageṇḍukena viya uggatena maṃsapiṇḍena pūretvā cittakammarūpassa viya akkhīni ahesuṃ, vedanā pacchijji. Atha mahāsatto katipāhaṃ pāsāde vasitvā “kiṃ andhassa rajjena, amaccānaṃ rajjaṃ niyyādetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā amacce [V 4.0366] pakkosāpetvā tesaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “eko mukhadhovanādidāyako kappiyakārakova mayhaṃ santike bhavissati, sarīrakiccaṭṭhānesupi me rajjukaṃ bandhathā”ti vatvā sārathiṃ āmantetvā “rathaṃ yojehī”ti āha. Amaccā panassa rathena gantuṃ adatvā suvaṇṇasivikāya naṃ netvā pokkharaṇītīre nisīdāpetvā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidhāya paṭikkamiṃsu. Rājā pallaṅkena nisinno attano dānaṃ āvajjesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. So āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “mahārājassa varaṃ datvā cakkhuṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā tattha gantvā mahāsattassa avidūre aparāparaṃ caṅkami. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā imā gāthā āha –

Before long, the flesh of the King's eyes began to heal. Although it healed, it did not form hollows, but was filled with a mass of flesh that rose up like a crimson woolen ball. His eyes became like those of a painted image, and the intense pain ceased. Then the Great Being, after staying in the palace for two or three days, thought, ‘What is the use of a blind man ruling? I shall hand over the kingdom to the ministers, go to the park, and after becoming an ascetic, I shall practice the Dhamma of a recluse.’ He summoned the ministers, informed them of the matter, and said, ‘Only one personal attendant, who can provide water for washing my face and perform other minor duties, shall stay with me. Also, tie a small rope for me in the places where I attend to bodily functions.’ Then he called the charioteer and said, ‘Harness the chariot.’ However, the King's ministers did not allow him to go by chariot, but carried him in a golden palanquin and seated him by the side of a lotus pond, and after providing guards, they departed. The King sat cross-legged and reflected on his own gift. At that moment, Sakka's seat grew hot. Upon reflecting, Sakka saw the reason and thought, ‘I shall grant the Great King a boon and restore his eyes to their natural state.’ He went to the park and paced back and forth not far from the Great Being. To clarify this matter, the All-Knowing Buddha spoke these three verses:

68.

68.

“Tato so katipāhassa, uparūḷhesu cakkhusu;

Sūtaṃ āmantayī rājā, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano.

“Then, after a few days had passed, when his eyes had covered over with flesh, the King, the prosperer of the Sivi realm, addressed his charioteer:”

69.

69.

“Yojehi [P 4.0409] sārathi yānaṃ, yuttañca paṭivedaya;

Uyyānabhūmiṃ gacchāma, pokkharañño vanāni ca.

“‘Harness the chariot, driver, and let me know when it is yoked. We shall go to the park grounds, to the lotus ponds, and to the groves.’”

70.

70.

“So ca pokkharaṇītīre, pallaṅkena upāvisi;

Tassa sakko pāturahu, devarājā sujampatī”ti.

“And he sat by the edge of the lotus pond in a cross-legged posture. Then Sakka, the King of Gods and husband of Sujā, appeared before him.”

Sakkopi mahāsattena padasaddaṃ sutvā “ko eso”ti puṭṭho gāthamāha –

The Great Being, hearing Sakka's footsteps, asked, “Who is that?” Sakka then spoke this verse:

71.

71.

“Sakkohamasmi devindo, āgatosmi tavantike;

Varaṃ varassu rājīsi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti. –

“I am Sakka, the Lord of Gods, and I have come into your presence. Choose a boon, O royal sage, whatever your heart desires.”

Evaṃ vutte rājā gāthamāha –

When Sakka had spoken thus, the King said:

72.

72.

“Pahūtaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka, balaṃ koso canappako;

Andhassa me sato dāni, maraṇaññeva ruccatī”ti.

“Much wealth have I, O Sakka; my army and treasury are not small. But now that I am blind, only death appeals to me.”

Tattha [V 4.0367][M 4.0410] maraṇaññeva ruccatīti devarāja, idāni mayhaṃ andhabhāvena maraṇameva ruccati, taṃ me dehīti.

Here, “only death appeals to me” means: “O king of gods, now, because of my blindness, death alone pleases me—grant me that.”

Atha naṃ sakko āha “sivirāja, kiṃ pana tvaṃ maritukāmo hutvā maraṇaṃ rocesi, udāhu andhabhāvenā”ti? “Andhabhāvena devā”ti. “Mahārāja, dānaṃ nāma na kevalaṃ samparāyatthameva dīyati, diṭṭhadhammatthāyapi paccayo hoti, tvañca ekaṃ cakkhuṃ yācito dve adāsi, tena saccakiriyaṃ karohī”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā āha –

Then Sakka said to him, “King of Sivi, do you approve of death because you wish to die, or is it because of your blindness?” “Because of my blindness, lord.” “Great king, a gift is not given only for the sake of the next world; it is also a condition for benefit in this very life. You were asked for one eye, but you gave two. Therefore, make a declaration of truth.” Having set up the conversation thus, he said:

73.

73.

“Yāni saccāni dvipadinda, tāni bhāsassu khattiya;

Saccaṃ te bhaṇamānassa, puna cakkhu bhavissatī”ti.

“Whatever truths there are, O lord of men, speak them, O khattiya. As you speak the truth, your sight will be restored.”

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “sakka, sacesi mama cakkhuṃ dātukāmo, aññaṃ upāyaṃ mā kari, mama dānanissandeneva me cakkhu uppajjatū”ti vatvā sakkena “mahārāja, ahaṃ sakko devarājāpi na paresaṃ cakkhuṃ dātuṃ sakkomi, tayā dinnadānassa phaleneva te cakkhu uppajjissatī”ti vutte “tena hi mayā dānaṃ sudinna”nti vatvā saccakiriyaṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being said, “Sakka, if you wish to give me my sight, do not use any other means. Let my sight arise solely through the fruit of my gift.” When Sakka replied, “Great king, even I, Sakka, king of gods, cannot give sight to others. Your sight will arise only through the fruit of the gift you gave,” he said, “Then indeed, my gift was well given.” And making a declaration of truth, he spoke this verse:

74.

74.

“Ye [P 4.0410] maṃ yācitumāyanti, nānāgottā vanibbakā;

Yopi maṃ yācate tattha, sopi me manaso piyo;

Etena saccavajjena, cakkhu me upapajjathā”ti.

“Those who come to ask of me, beggars of various lineages; whoever asks of me there, even he is dear to my heart. By this utterance of truth, may my eye arise!”

Tattha ye manti ye maṃ yācituṃ āgacchanti, tesu yācakesu āgacchantesu yopi maṃ yācate, sopi me manaso piyo. Etenāti sace mama sabbepi yācakā piyā, saccamevetaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, etena me saccavacanena ekaṃ me cakkhu upapajjatha upapajjatūti āha.

Herein, 'ye maṃ' means 'those who come to beg from me'. Among those approaching beggars, whoever begs from me, even he is dear to my heart. 'Etenā'ti means: if all beggars are indeed dear to me, this is truly spoken by me; by this truthful declaration, he said: 'May one eye arise for me, may it arise.'

Athassa vacanānantarameva paṭhamaṃ cakkhu udapādi. Tato dutiyassa uppajjanatthāya gāthādvayamāha –

Immediately after his words, the first eye arose. Then, to bring forth the second, he recited two verses:

75.

75.

“Yaṃ maṃ so yācituṃ āgā, dehi cakkhunti brāhmaṇo;

Tassa cakkhūni pādāsiṃ, brāhmaṇassa vanibbato.

“When that brahmin came to ask of me, saying, 'Give me an eye!'; I gave my eyes to him, to that wandering beggar brahmin.”

76.

76.

“Bhiyyo [V 4.0368] maṃ āvisī pīti, somanassañcanappakaṃ;

Etena saccavajjena, dutiyaṃ me upapajjathā”ti.

“Greater joy then entered me, and no small happiness. By this utterance of truth, may my second eye arise!”

Tattha [M 4.0411] yaṃ manti yo maṃ yācati. Soti so cakkhuvikalo brāhmaṇo “dehi me cakkhu”nti yācituṃ āgato. Vanibbatoti yācantassa. Bhiyyo maṃ āvisīti brāhmaṇassa cakkhūni datvā andhakālato paṭṭhāya tasmiṃ andhakāle tathārūpaṃ vedanaṃ agaṇetvā “aho sudinnaṃ me dāna”nti paccavekkhantaṃ maṃ bhiyyo atirekatarā pīti āvisi, mama hadayaṃ paviṭṭhā, somanassañca mama anantaṃ aparimāṇaṃ uppajji. Etenāti sace mama tadā anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppannaṃ, saccamevetaṃ mayā vuttaṃ, etena me saccavacanena dutiyampi cakkhu upapajjatūti āha.

Herein, 'yaṃ maṃ' means 'he who begs from me'. 'So'ti means 'that brahmin with impaired sight came to beg, saying, “Give me an eye!”'. 'Vanibbato'ti means 'to the one begging'. 'Bhiyyo maṃ āvisī'ti means: after giving my eyes to the brahmin, from that moment of darkness onward, disregarding such physical pain and reflecting, 'Ah, my gift was well given,' an even greater joy entered me, pervaded my heart, and immeasurable happiness arose in me. 'Etenā'ti means: if at that time no small joy and happiness arose in me, this is truly spoken by me; by this truthful declaration, he said: 'May my second eye also arise.'

Taṅkhaṇaññeva dutiyampi cakkhu udapādi. Tāni panassa cakkhūni neva pākatikāni, na dibbāni. Sakkabrāhmaṇassa hi dinnaṃ cakkhuṃ puna pākatikaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, upahatavatthuno ca dibbacakkhu nāma na uppajjati, tāni panassa [P 4.0411] saccapāramitānubhāvena sambhūtāni cakkhūnīti vuttāni. Tesaṃ uppattisamakālameva sakkānubhāvena sabbā rājaparisā sannipatitāva ahesuṃ. Athassa sakko mahājanamajjheyeva thutiṃ karonto gāthādvayamāha –

At that very moment, the second eye also arose. But those eyes were neither ordinary nor divine. For the eye given to the brahmin Sakka cannot be made ordinary again, and a divine eye does not arise in one whose physical basis is impaired. Yet, it is said that those eyes arose through the power of his perfection of truth. At the very moment of their arising, the entire royal assembly had already gathered by the power of Sakka. Then, Sakka, praising him in the midst of the great crowd, spoke two verses:

77.

77.

“Dhammena bhāsitā gāthā, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Etāni tava nettāni, dibbāni paṭidissare.

“These verses are spoken righteously, O increaser of the Sivi realm; these eyes of yours appear as divine.”

78.

78.

“Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiroselaṃ, samatiggayha pabbataṃ;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, dassanaṃ anubhontu te”ti.

“Beyond walls, beyond rocks, surpassing mountains; may your eyes experience sight for a hundred leagues all around.”

Tattha dhammena bhāsitāti mahārāja, imā te gāthā dhammena sabhāveneva bhāsitā. Dibbānīti dibbānubhāvayuttāni. Paṭidissareti paṭidissanti. Tirokuṭṭanti mahārāja, imāni te cakkhūni devatānaṃ cakkhūni viya parakuṭṭaṃ paraselaṃ yaṃkiñci pabbatampi samatiggayha atikkamitvā samantā dasa disā yojanasataṃ rūpadassanaṃ anubhontu sādhentūti attho.

Herein, 'dhammena bhāsitā'ti means, 'O great king, these verses of yours were spoken by the very nature of righteousness.' 'Dibbānī'ti means 'endowed with divine power.' 'Paṭidissare'ti means 'they appear.' 'Tirokuṭṭan'ti means, 'O great king, may these eyes of yours, like the eyes of the devas, surpassing other walls, other rocks, and whatever mountains there may be, experience the seeing of forms for a hundred leagues in all ten directions'—this is the meaning.

Iti so ākāse ṭhatvā mahājanamajjhe imā gāthā bhāsitvā “appamatto hohī”ti mahāsattaṃ ovaditvā devalokameva gato. Mahāsattopi mahājanaparivuto mahantena sakkārena nagaraṃ [V 4.0369] pavisitvā sucandakaṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Tena cakkhūnaṃ paṭiladdhabhāvo sakalasiviraṭṭhe pākaṭo jāto. Athassa dassanatthaṃ sakalaraṭṭhavāsino bahuṃ paṇṇākāraṃ [M 4.0412] gahetvā āgamiṃsu. Mahāsatto “imasmiṃ mahājanasannipāte mama dānaṃ vaṇṇayissāmī”ti rājadvāre mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisinno nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā sabbaseniyo sannipātetvā “ambho, siviraṭṭhavāsino imāni me dibbacakkhūni disvā ito paṭṭhāya dānaṃ adatvā mā bhuñjathā”ti dhammaṃ desento catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, standing in the sky amidst the great crowd, he spoke these verses and, advising the Great Being with the words, "Be heedful," he departed to the world of the gods. The Great Being, surrounded by the great crowd, entered the city with great honor and ascended the splendid Sucandaka palace. The restoration of his eyes became widely known throughout the entire Sivi kingdom. Then, the inhabitants of the whole kingdom, wishing to see him, came bringing many gifts. The Great Being thought, 'I will proclaim my generosity in this great assembly,' and had a grand pavilion built at the royal gate. Seated on the royal throne under a lofty white parasol, he had drums beaten throughout the city, gathered all the troops, and teaching the Dhamma, he declared, 'O inhabitants of the Sivi kingdom, having seen these divine eyes of mine, from now on do not eat without giving alms,' and he uttered these verses:

79.

79.

“Ko nīdha vittaṃ na dadeyya yācito, api visiṭṭhaṃ supiyampi attano;

Tadiṅgha sabbe sivayo samāgatā, dibbāni nettāni mamajja passatha.

“Who here, when asked, would not give wealth, even what is most excellent and dear to oneself? Therefore, indeed, all you Sivis assembled, today behold my divine eyes.”

80.

80.

“Tirokuṭṭaṃ [P 4.0412] tiroselaṃ, samatiggayha pabbataṃ;

Samantā yojanasataṃ, dassanaṃ anubhonti me.

“Beyond walls, beyond rocks, surmounting mountains; for a hundred leagues all around, my eyes experience sight.”

81.

81.

“Na cāgamattā paramatthi kiñci, maccānaṃ idha jīvite;

Datvāna mānusaṃ cakkhuṃ, laddhaṃ me cakkhuṃ amānusaṃ.

“There is nothing whatsoever higher than the measure of giving for mortals in this life; having given the human eye, I have obtained the non-human eye.”

82.

82.

“Etampi disvā sivayo, detha dānāni bhuñjatha;

Datvā ca bhutvā ca yathānubhāvaṃ, aninditā saggamupetha ṭhāna”nti.

Seeing even this, O Sivis, give gifts and enjoy; having given and enjoyed according to your ability, being blameless, go to the heavenly place.

Tattha konīdhāti ko nu idha. Api visiṭṭhanti uttamampi samānaṃ. Cāgamattāti cāgapamāṇato aññaṃ varaṃ nāma natthi. Idha jīviteti imasmiṃ jīvaloke. “Idha jīvata”ntipi pāṭho, imasmiṃ loke jīvamānānanti attho. Amānusanti dibbacakkhu mayā laddhaṃ, iminā kāraṇena veditabbametaṃ “cāgato uttamaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Etampi disvāti etaṃ mayā laddhaṃ dibbacakkhuṃ disvāpi.

In this context, 'konīdhā' means 'ko nu idha' (who indeed here?). 'Api visiṭṭhan'ti means 'even what is excellent'. 'Cāgamattā'ti means 'beyond the measure of generosity, there is nothing else superior'. 'Idha jīvite'ti means 'in this world of living beings'. There is also a reading 'idha jīvataṃ', which means 'of those living in this world'. 'Amānusan'ti means 'the divine eye has been obtained by me'; for this reason it should be understood that 'there is nothing superior to generosity'. 'Etampi disvā'ti means 'having seen even this divine eye attained by me'.
