Iti imāhi catūhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā tato paṭṭhāya anvaddhamāsaṃ pannarasuposathesu mahājanaṃ sannipātāpetvā niccaṃ imāhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desesi. Taṃ sutvā mahājano dānādīni puññāni katvā devalokaṃ pūrentova agamāsi.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma with these four verses, from then on, every half-month on the fifteenth-day uposatha, he had the great crowd assemble and continually taught the Dhamma with these verses. Hearing that, the great crowd performed meritorious deeds such as giving and went on, filling the heavenly world.

Satthā [M 4.0413] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā bāhiradānena asantuṭṭhā [V 4.0370] sampattayācakānaṃ attano cakkhūni uppāṭetvā adaṃsū”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sīvikavejjo ānando ahosi, sakko anuruddho ahosi, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, sivirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, 'Thus, monks, the wise of old, unsatisfied with external gifts, tore out and gave their own eyes to the beggars who approached.' Having spoken thus, he revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the Sivi physician was Ānanda, Sakka was Anuruddha, the remaining assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and King Sivi was I myself.'

Sivijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Sivi Jātaka: The Third.

[500] 4. Sirīmantajātakavaṇṇanā

[500] 4. The Commentary on the Sirimanta Jātaka

83-103. Paññāyupetaṃ siriyā vihīnanti ayaṃ sirīmantapañho mahāumaṅge (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

83-103. 'Endowed with wisdom, but lacking in fortune'—this Sirimanta question will become clear in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.590 ff.).

Sirīmantajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Sirimanta Jātaka: The Fourth.

[501] 5. Rohaṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[501] 5. The Commentary on the Rohaṇa Deer Jātaka

Ete [P 4.0413] yūthā patiyantīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto āyasmato ānandassa jīvitapariccāgaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So panassa jīvitapariccāgo asītinipāte cūḷahaṃsajātake (jā. 2.21.1 ādayo) dhanapāladamane āvi bhavissati. Evaṃ tenāyasmatā satthu atthāya jīvite pariccatte dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, āyasmā ānando sekkhapaṭisambhidappatto hutvā dasabalassatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'These herds turn back'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Venerable Ānanda’s relinquishing of his life. That relinquishing of his life will become clear in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka of the Asītinipāta (Jā. 2.21.1 ff.), in the taming of Dhanapāla. Thus, when the Venerable One had relinquished his life for the sake of the Teacher, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, the Venerable Ānanda, having attained the analytical insights of a trainee, relinquished his life for the sake of the Ten-Powered One.' The Teacher, arriving, asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When told, 'For this one,' he said, 'Not only now, monks; long ago he also relinquished his life for my sake,' and he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente khemā nāmassa aggamahesī ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto himavantapadese migayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi sobhaggappatto. Kaniṭṭhopissa cittamigo nāma suvaṇṇavaṇṇova ahosi, kaniṭṭhabhaginīpissa sutanā nāma [M 4.0414] suvaṇṇavaṇṇāva ahosi. Mahāsatto pana rohaṇo nāma migarājā ahosi. So himavante dve pabbatarājiyo atikkamitvā tatiyāya antare rohaṇaṃ nāma saraṃ nissāya asītimigasahassaparivāro vāsaṃ kappesi. So andhe jiṇṇe mātāpitaro posesi. Atheko bārāṇasito avidūre nesādagāmavāsī nesādaputto himavantaṃ paviṭṭho mahāsattaṃ disvā attano gāmaṃ [V 4.0371] āgantvā aparabhāge kālaṃ karonto puttassārocesi “tāta, amhākaṃ kammabhūmiyaṃ asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne suvaṇṇavaṇṇo migo vasati, sace rājā puccheyya, katheyyāsī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, Khemā was his chief queen. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the deer realm in the Himalayan region and was golden-hued and possessed of great beauty. His younger brother was named Cittamiga and was also golden-hued, and his younger sister was named Sutanā and was likewise golden-hued. The Great Being, however, was a deer-king named Rohaṇa. Having crossed two great mountain ranges in the Himalayas, he settled near a lake called Rohaṇa within the third range, surrounded by eighty thousand deer. He supported his blind and aged parents. Meanwhile, a hunter’s son dwelling in a hunter’s village not far from Benares entered the Himalayas. Upon seeing the Great Being, he returned to his village. Later, when he was passing away, he told his son, 'Dear son, in our hunting grounds, in such-and-such a place, there lives a golden-hued deer. If the king should ask, you must tell him.'

Athekadivasaṃ khemā devī paccūsakāle supinaṃ addasa. Evarūpo supino ahosi – suvaṇṇavaṇṇo migo āgantvā kañcanapīṭhe nisīditvā suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikaṃ ākoṭento viya madhurassarena deviyā dhammaṃ deseti, sā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇāti. Migo dhammakathāya aniṭṭhitāya eva uṭṭhāya gacchati, sā “migaṃ gaṇhatha gaṇhathā”ti vadantīyeva pabujjhi. Paricārikāyo tassā saddaṃ sutvā “pihitadvāravātapānaṃ gehaṃ vātassapi okāso natthi, ayyā, imāya velāya migaṃ gaṇhāpetī”ti avahasiṃsu. Sā tasmiṃ khaṇe [P 4.0414] “supino aya”nti ñatvā cintesi “supinoti vutte rājā anādaro bhavissati, ‘dohaḷo uppanno’ti vutte pana ādarena pariyesissati, suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa migassa dhammakathaṃ suṇissāmī”ti. Sā gilānālayaṃ katvā nipajji. Rājā āgantvā “bhadde, kiṃ te aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Deva, aññaṃ natthi, dohaḷo pana me uppanno”ti. “Kiṃ icchasi devī”ti? “Suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa dhammikamigassa dhammaṃ sotukāmā devā”ti. “Bhadde, yaṃ natthi, tattha te dohaḷo uppanno, suvaṇṇavaṇṇo nāma migoyeva natthī”ti. So “sace na labhāmi, idheva me maraṇa”nti rañño piṭṭhiṃ datvā nipajji.

One day, Queen Khemā saw a dream at dawn. The dream was like this: a golden-hued deer came and sat on a golden seat, and as if striking a small golden bell, it preached the Dhamma to the queen in a sweet voice. She gave her approval and listened to the Dhamma. Before the Dhamma talk was finished, the deer rose and left. As she cried out, 'Catch the deer, catch it!' she awoke. Her attendants, hearing her cry, mocked her, saying, 'The palace is sealed with doors and windows, there is no room even for the wind; noble lady, at this hour she has someone catching a deer.' At that moment, realizing it was a dream, she thought, 'If I say it was a dream, the king will be indifferent. But if I say I have a pregnancy craving, he will search with concern, and I shall hear the Dhamma talk of the golden-hued deer.' She pretended to be ill and lay down. When the king arrived, he asked, 'My dear, what ails you?' 'My lord, it is nothing else, but a pregnancy craving has arisen in me.' 'What does the queen desire?' 'I wish to hear the Dhamma from a righteous golden-hued deer, my lord.' 'My dear, your craving is for something that does not exist; there is no such thing as a golden-hued deer.' She then turned her back on the king and lay down, saying, 'If I do not get it, I will die right here.'

Rājā “sace atthi, labhissasī”ti parisamajjhe nisīditvā morajātake (jā. 1.2.17 ādayo) vuttanayeneva amacce ca brāhmaṇe ca pucchitvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇā migā nāma hontī”ti sutvā luddake sannipātetvā “evarūpo migo kena diṭṭho, kena suto”ti pucchitvā tena nesādaputtena pitu santikā sutaniyāmena [M 4.0415] kathite “samma, tassa te migassa ānītakāle mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ karissāmi, gaccha ānehi na”nti vatvā paribbayaṃ datvā taṃ pesesi. Sopi “sacāhaṃ, deva, taṃ ānetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, cammamassa ānessāmi, taṃ ānetuṃ asakkonto lomānipissa ānessāmi, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti vatvā attano nivesanaṃ gantvā puttadārassa paribbayaṃ datvā tattha gantvā taṃ migarājānaṃ disvā “kasmiṃ nu kho ṭhāne pāsaṃ oḍḍetvā imaṃ migarājānaṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti vīmaṃsanto pānīyatitthe okāsaṃ passi. So daḷhaṃ cammayottaṃ vaṭṭetvā mahāsattassa pānīyapivanaṭṭhāne yaṭṭhipāsaṃ oḍḍesi.

The king said, ‘If it exists, you shall obtain it.’ Sitting in the midst of the assembly, he questioned his ministers and brahmins as described in the Mora Jātaka (Jā. 1.2.17, etc.). Hearing that ‘deer of golden color do exist,’ he summoned the hunters and asked, ‘By whom has such a deer been seen or heard of?’ When the hunter’s son explained, according to what he had heard from his father, the king said, ‘Good man, when you bring that deer, I will bestow great honor upon you. Go and bring it.’ Then he gave him his expenses and sent him off. The hunter replied, ‘If I, O king, am unable to bring him, I will bring his skin. If unable to bring that, I will bring his hairs. Do not worry.’ He then went to his home, provided expenses for his wife and children, went to the Himalayas, and saw the deer king. Pondering, ‘In what place can I set a snare to capture this deer king?’ he saw an opportunity at the watering place. He twisted a strong leather thong and set a stick-snare at the spot where the Great Being drank water.

Punadivase mahāsatto asītiyā migasahassehi saddhiṃ gocaraṃ caritvā “pakatitittheyeva pānīyaṃ [V 4.0372] pivissāmī”ti tattha gantvā otarantoyeva pāse bajjhi. So “sacāhaṃ idāneva baddharavaṃ ravissāmi, ñātigaṇā pānīyaṃ apivitvāva bhītā palāyissantī”ti cintetvā yaṭṭhiyaṃ [P 4.0415] allīyitvā attano vase vattetvā pānīyaṃ pivanto viya ahosi. Atha asītiyā migasahassānaṃ pānīyaṃ pivitvā uttaritvā ṭhitakāle “pāsaṃ chindissāmī”ti tikkhattuṃ ākaḍḍhi. Paṭhamavāre cammaṃ chijji, dutiyavāre maṃsaṃ chijji, tatiyavāre nhāruṃ chinditvā pāso aṭṭhiṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi. So chindituṃ asakkonto baddharavaṃ ravi, migagaṇā bhāyitvā tīhi ghaṭāhi palāyiṃsu. Cittamigo tiṇṇampi ghaṭānaṃ antare mahāsattaṃ adisvā “idaṃ bhayaṃ uppajjamānaṃ mama bhātu uppannaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā tassa santikaṃ gantvā baddhaṃ passi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto disvā “bhātika, mā idha tiṭṭha, sāsaṅkaṃ idaṃ ṭhāna”nti vatvā uyyojento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The next day, the Great Being, having grazed with eighty thousand deer, thought, ‘I will drink water at the usual ford.’ He went there and, as he was descending, was caught in the snare. He thought, ‘If I cry out in distress now, my kinsmen will be frightened and flee without having drunk water.’ So, clinging to the stick of the snare and yielding to its pull, he acted as if he were drinking water. Then, when the eighty thousand deer had drunk, emerged, and were standing by, he thought, ‘I will break the snare,’ and pulled three times. The first time, the skin tore; the second time, the flesh tore; the third time, having cut through the sinew, the snare struck the bone and held fast. Unable to break it, he cried out in distress. The herd of deer, terrified, fled in three groups. Cittamiga, not seeing the Great Being among any of the three groups, thought, ‘This danger must have befallen my brother.’ He went to his side and saw him trapped. Then the Great Being, seeing him, said, ‘Brother, do not stay here—this place is perilous,’ and urging him to leave, he spoke the first verse:

104.

104.

“Ete yūthā patiyanti, bhītā maraṇassa cittaka;

Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā sahā”ti.

“These herds are fleeing, frightened of death, O Cittaka. Go, you too, do not linger; they will live on with you.”

Tattha eteti cakkhupathaṃ atikkamitvā dūragate sandhāyāha. Patiyantīti patigacchanti, palāyantīti attho. Cittakāti taṃ ālapati. Tayā sahāti tvaṃ etesaṃ mama ṭhāne ṭhatvā rājā hohi, ete tayā saddhiṃ jīvissantīti.

Herein, ‘ete’ refers to those who have gone far away, beyond the range of sight. ‘Patiyanti’ means ‘they are returning’; the meaning is ‘they are fleeing.’ ‘Cittaka’ is a form of address to him. ‘Tayā sahā’ means: ‘You, standing in my place, shall be their leader, and they will live on with you.’

Tato [M 4.0416] ubhinnampi tisso ekantarikagāthāyo honti –

Then there are three verses spoken in alternation by the two brothers:

105.

105.

“Nāhaṃ rohaṇa gacchāmi, hadayaṃ me avakassati;

Na taṃ ahaṃ jahissāmi, idha hissāmi jīvitaṃ.

“I will not go, Rohaṇa, my heart is drawn to you; I will not abandon you, here I will relinquish my life.”

106.

106.

“Te hi nūna marissanti, andhā apariṇāyakā;

Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā saha.

“Surely they will die, blind and without a leader. Go, you too, do not linger; they will live on with you.”

107.

107.

“Nāhaṃ rohaṇa gacchāmi, hadayaṃ me avakassati;

Na taṃ baddhaṃ jahissāmi, idha hissāmi jīvita”nti.

“I will not go, Rohaṇa, my heart is drawn to you; I will not abandon you while you are bound; here I will relinquish my life.”

Tattha rohaṇāti mahāsattaṃ nāmenālapati. Avakassatīti kaḍḍhayati, sokena vā kaḍḍhīyati[V 4.0373]. Te hi nūnāti te amhākaṃ mātāpitaro ekaṃseneva dvīsupi amhesu idha matesu apariṇāyakā hutvā appaṭijaggiyamānā sussitvā marissanti, tasmā bhātika cittaka, gaccha tuvaṃ, tayā saha te jīvissantīti attho. Idha hissāmīti imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne jīvitaṃ jahissāmīti.

Herein, ‘Rohaṇa’ is a form of address to the Great Being by name. ‘Avakassati’ means ‘it pulls,’ or ‘it is pulled by grief.’ ‘Te hi nūna’ means: ‘Our parents, certainly, if both of us die here, being without a leader and uncared for, will wither away and die. Therefore, brother Cittaka, go; they will live on with you.’ ‘Idha hissāmi’ means: ‘In this very place, I will give up my life.’

Iti vatvā bodhisattassa [P 4.0416] dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya taṃ sandhāretvā assāsento aṭṭhāsi. Sutanāpi migapotikā palāyitvā migānaṃ antare ubho bhātike apassantī “idaṃ bhayaṃ mama bhātikānaṃ uppannaṃ bhavissatī”ti nivattitvā tesaṃ santikaṃ āgatā. Naṃ āgacchantiṃ disvā mahāsatto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he stood by the Bodhisatta’s right side, supporting and comforting him. The young doe Sutanā, having fled among the deer and not seeing her two brothers, thought, “This danger must have befallen my brothers,” and turned back, coming to their side. Seeing her approaching, the Great Being spoke the fifth verse:

108.

108.

“Gaccha bhīru palāyassu, kūṭe baddhosmi āyase;

Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā sahā”ti.

“Go, timid one, flee! I am bound in an iron trap. Go, you too, do not linger; they will live on with you.”

Tattha bhīrūti mātugāmo nāma appamattakenapi bhāyati, tena naṃ evaṃ ālapati. Kūṭeti paṭicchannapāse. Āyaseti so hi antoudake ayakkhandhaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha sāradāruṃ yaṭṭhiṃ bandhitvā oḍḍito, tasmā evamāha. Tayā sahāti te asītisahassā migā tayā saddhiṃ jīvissantīti.

Therein, ‘bhīru’ refers to the female kind, who is frightened even by a small thing; therefore, he addresses her thus. ‘Kūṭe’ means a hidden snare. ‘Āyase’ means that it was set up by hammering an iron stake into the water and tying a strong wooden pole to it; therefore, he spoke thus. ‘Tayā sahā’ means, ‘Those eighty thousand deer will live on with you.’

Tato [M 4.0417] paraṃ purimanayeneva tisso gāthā honti –

After that, in the same way as before, there are three verses spoken between the brother and sister:

109.

109.

“Nāhaṃ rohaṇa gacchāmi, hadayaṃ me avakassati;

Na taṃ ahaṃ jahissāmi, idha hissāmi jīvitaṃ.

“I will not go, Rohaṇa, my heart is drawn to you; I will not abandon you, here I will relinquish my life.”

110.

110.

“Te hi nūna marissanti, andhā apariṇāyakā;

Gaccha tuvampi mākaṅkhi, jīvissanti tayā saha.

“Surely they will die, blind and without a leader. Go, you too, do not linger; they will live on with you.”

111.

111.

“Nāhaṃ rohaṇa gacchāmi, hadayaṃ me avakassati;

Na taṃ baddhaṃ jahissāmi, idha hissāmi jīvita”nti.

“I will not go, Rohaṇa, my heart is drawn to you; I will not abandon you who are bound; here I will relinquish my life.”

Tattha te hi nūnāti idhāpi mātāpitaroyeva sandhāyāha.

Therein, ‘te hi nūna’ refers here too to the parents themselves.

Sāpi [V 4.0374] tatheva paṭikkhipitvā mahāsattassa vāmapassaṃ nissāya assāsayamānā aṭṭhāsi. Luddopi te mige palāyante disvā baddharavañca sutvā “baddho bhavissati migarājā”ti daḷhaṃ kacchaṃ bandhitvā migamāraṇasattiṃ ādāya vegenāgacchi. Mahāsatto taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

She too, having refused in the same way, stood near the Great Being’s left side, comforting him. The hunter, seeing those deer fleeing and hearing the cry of the trapped one, thought, “The deer king must be trapped!” Tightening his belt firmly and taking his deer-slaying spear, he came swiftly. Seeing him approach, the Great Being spoke the ninth verse to let those siblings know:

112.

112.

“Ayaṃ so luddako eti, luddarūpo sahāvudho;

Yo no vadhissati ajja, usunā sattiyā apī”ti.

“Here comes that hunter, of fierce appearance and armed; he who will kill us today, with an arrow or even with a spear.”

Tattha luddarūpoti dāruṇajātiko. Sattiyā apīti sattiyāpi no paharitvā vadhissati, tasmā yāva so nāgacchati, tāva palāyathāti.

Therein, ‘luddarūpa’ means of a fierce nature. ‘Sattiyā api’ means he will kill us by striking even with a spear; therefore, flee before he arrives.

Taṃ [P 4.0417] disvāpi cittamigo na palāyi. Sutanā pana sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī maraṇabhayabhītā thokaṃ palāyitvā – “ahaṃ dve bhātike pahāya kuhiṃ palāyissāmī”ti attano jīvitaṃ jahitvā nalāṭena maccuṃ ādāya punāgantvā bhātu vāmapasse aṭṭhāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Even upon seeing him, the deer Citta did not flee. But Sutanā, unable to remain steady due to her nature and terrified by the fear of death, fled a short distance. Then thinking, “Where shall I flee, abandoning my two brothers?”, she gave up her own life and, taking death on her forehead, returned and stood at her brother's left side. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke the tenth verse:

113.

113.

“Sā muhuttaṃ palāyitvā, bhayaṭṭā bhayatajjitā;

Sudukkaraṃ akarā bhīru, maraṇāyūpanivattathā”ti.

“She fled for a moment, oppressed by fear, terrified by fear. The timid one did what was very difficult to do; she returned to face death.”

Tattha maraṇāyūpanivattathāti maraṇatthāya upanivatti.

Therein, ‘maraṇāyūpanivattathā’ means she returned for the sake of death.

Luddopi [M 4.0418] āgantvā te tayo jane ekato ṭhite disvā mettacittaṃ uppādetvā ekakucchiyaṃ nibbattabhātaro viya te maññamāno cintesi “migarājā, tāva pāse baddho, ime pana dve janā hirottappabandhanena baddhā, kiṃ nu kho ime etassa hontī”ti? Atha naṃ pucchanto gāthamāha –

The hunter, arriving and seeing the three of them standing together, felt a thought of loving-kindness. Thinking of them as siblings born from the same womb, he wondered: “The deer king is trapped in the snare, but these two are bound by the bonds of shame and moral dread. What are they to him?” Then, questioning him, he spoke the verse:

114.

114.

“Kiṃ nu teme migā honti, muttā baddhaṃ upāsare;

Na taṃ cajitumicchanti, jīvitassapi kāraṇā”ti.

“What are these deer to you, who though free, wait upon the one who is bound? They do not wish to abandon you, even for the sake of their lives.”

Tattha kiṃ nu temeti kiṃ nu te ime. Upāsareti upāsanti.

Therein, ‘kiṃ nu teme’ means ‘what are these to you’. ‘Upāsare’ means ‘they attend upon’.

Athassa [V 4.0375] bodhisatto ācikkhi –

Then the Bodhisatta told him:

115.

115.

“Bhātaro honti me ludda, sodariyā ekamātukā;

Na maṃ cajitumicchanti, jīvitassapi kāraṇā”ti.

“They are my siblings, hunter, born of the same mother. They do not wish to abandon me, even for the sake of their lives.”

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhiyyosomattāya muducitto ahosi. Cittamigarājā tassa muducittabhāvaṃ ñatvā “samma luddaka, mā tvaṃ etaṃ migarājānaṃ ‘migamattoyevā’ti maññittha, ayañhi asītiyā migasahassānaṃ rājā sīlācārasampanno sabbasattesu muducitto mahāpañño andhe jiṇṇe mātāpitaro poseti. Sace tvaṃ evarūpaṃ dhammikaṃ migaṃ māresi, etaṃ mārento mātāpitaro ca no mañca bhaginiñca meti amhe pañcapi jane māresiyeva. Mayhaṃ pana bhātu jīvitaṃ dento pañcannampi janānaṃ jīvitadāyakosī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the hunter became even more tender-hearted. Citta the deer king, knowing his softened state, said: “Friend hunter, do not think of this deer king as just an ordinary deer. For he is the king of eighty thousand deer, endowed with virtue and good conduct, gentle-hearted towards all beings, and of great wisdom; he supports his blind and aged parents. If you kill such a righteous deer, in killing him, you would be killing our parents, us, and our sister—thus you would be killing five of us. But by giving my brother his life, you become the giver of life to five beings.” Having said this, he spoke a verse:

116.

116.

“Te [P 4.0418] hi nūna marissanti, andhā apariṇāyakā;

Pañcannaṃ jīvitaṃ dehi, bhātaraṃ muñca luddakā”ti.

“Surely they will die, blind and without a guide. Give life to the five, hunter; release my brother.”

So tassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasannacitto “mā bhāyi sāmī”ti vatvā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his Dhamma talk, the hunter, with a confident heart, said, “Do not fear, master,” and then spoke the next verse:

117.

117.

“So vo ahaṃ pamokkhāmi, mātāpettibharaṃ migaṃ;

Nandantu mātāpitaro, muttaṃ disvā mahāmiga”nti.

“I will release you, the deer who supports his parents. Let your mother and father rejoice, seeing the great deer freed.”

Tattha voti nipātamattaṃ. Muttanti bandhanā muttaṃ passitvā.

Therein, ‘vo’ is just a particle. ‘Muttaṃ’ means having seen him freed from the bond.

Evañca [M 4.0419] pana vatvā cintesi “raññā dinnayaso mayhaṃ kiṃ karissati, sacāhaṃ imaṃ migarājānaṃ vadhissāmi, ayaṃ vā me pathavī bhijjitvā vivaraṃ dassati, asani vā me matthake patissati, vissajjessāmi na”nti. So mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yaṭṭhiṃ pātetvā cammayottaṃ chinditvā migarājānaṃ āliṅgitvā udakapariyante nipajjāpetvā muducittena saṇikaṃ pāsā mocetvā nhārūhi nhāruṃ, maṃsena maṃsaṃ, cammena cammaṃ samodhānetvā udakena lohitaṃ dhovitvā mettacittena punappunaṃ parimajji. Tassa mettānubhāveneva mahāsattassa pāramitānubhāvena ca sabbāni nhārumaṃsacammāni sandhīyiṃsu, pādo sañchannachavi sañchannalomo ahosi, asukaṭṭhāne [V 4.0376] baddho ahosītipi na paññāyi. Mahāsatto sukhappatto hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā cittamigo somanassajāto luddassa anumodanaṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he reflected: “What will the status given by the king do for me? If I kill this deer king, either the earth will split open and show me a chasm, or a thunderbolt will strike my head. I will release him!” Approaching the Great Being, he threw down his staff, cut the leather strap, embraced the deer king, and made him lie down at the water’s edge. With a tender heart, he slowly freed him from the snare; joining sinew to sinew, flesh to flesh, and skin to skin, he washed away the blood with water and, with a mind of loving-kindness, massaged him again and again. By the power of his loving-kindness and the power of the Great Being’s perfections, all the sinews, flesh, and skin were joined together. The foot was covered with skin and hair, and it could not even be seen where he had been bound. The Great Being, restored to ease, stood up. Seeing this, the deer Citta, filled with joy, expressed his appreciation to the hunter and spoke a verse:

118.

118.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā mahāmiga”nti.

“In this way, hunter, may you rejoice, along with all your kinsmen, just as I rejoice today, seeing the great deer freed.”

Atha mahāsatto “kiṃ nu kho esa luddo maṃ gaṇhanto attano kāmena gaṇhi, udāhu aññassa āṇattiyā”ti cintetvā gahitakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Luddaputto āha – “sāmi, na mayhaṃ tumhehi kammaṃ atthi, rañño pana aggamahesī khemā nāma tumhākaṃ dhammakathaṃ sotukāmā, tadatthāya rañño āṇattiyā tvaṃ mayā gahito”ti. Samma, evaṃ sante maṃ vissajjento atidukkaraṃ [P 4.0419] karosi, ehi maṃ netvā rañño dassehi, deviyā dhammaṃ kathessāmīti. Sāmi, rājāno nāma kakkhaḷā, ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissati, mayhaṃ raññā dinnayasena kammaṃ natthi, gaccha tvaṃ yathāsukhanti. Puna mahāsatto “iminā maṃ vissajjentena atidukkaraṃ kataṃ, yasapaṭilābhassa upāyamassa karissāmī”ti cintetvā “samma, piṭṭhiṃ tāva me hatthena parimajjā”ti āha. “So parimajji, hattho suvaṇṇavaṇṇehi lomehi pūri”. “Sāmi, imehi lomehi kiṃ kāromī”ti. “Samma, imāni haritvā rañño ca deviyā ca dassetvā ‘imāni tassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇamigassa lomānī’ti vatvā mama ṭhāne ṭhatvā imāhi gāthāhi deviyā dhammaṃ desehi, taṃ sutvāyeva cassā dohaḷo paṭippassambhissatī”ti[M 4.0420]. “Dhammaṃ cara mahārājā”ti dasa dhammacariyagāthā uggaṇhāpetvā pañca sīlāni datvā appamādena ovaditvā uyyojesi. Luddaputto mahāsattaṃ ācariyaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā lomāni paduminipattena gahetvā pakkāmi. Tepi tayo janā thokaṃ anugantvā mukhena gocarañca pānīyañca gahetvā mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ gamiṃsu. Mātāpitaro “tāta rohaṇa, tvaṃ kira pāse baddho kathaṃ muttosī”ti pucchantā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then the Great Being thought, "Did this hunter seize me for his own purpose, or was it by another’s command?" and asked the reason for his capture. The hunter’s son replied, "Sir, I have no business with you, but the king’s chief queen, Khemā by name, desires to hear your Dhamma talk. For that purpose, by the king’s command, you were captured by me." "Friend, if that is so, even though I am captured for the king, by releasing me you are doing a very difficult thing. Come, take me and show me to the king, and I will teach the queen the Dhamma." "Sir, kings are harsh—who knows what may happen? I have no need for the wealth and honor given by the king. Go as you please, golden deer-king." Again, the Great Being thought, "By releasing me, he has done a very difficult thing. I will create a means for this hunter to obtain wealth and honor." Reflecting thus, he said, "Friend, stroke my back with your hand." He stroked it, and his hand was filled with golden-hued hairs. "Sir, what shall I do with these hairs?" "Friend, take these, show them to the king and the queen, and say, ‘These are the hairs of that golden-hued deer.’ Then, standing in my place, teach the queen the Dhamma with these verses. Upon hearing them, her pregnancy craving will be appeased." He had him learn the ten verses on righteous conduct beginning with, "Practice righteousness, great king," gave him the five precepts, exhorted him to be heedful, and sent him off. The hunter’s son, placing the Great Being in the position of a teacher, circumambulated him three times, paid homage in the four directions, took the hairs with a lotus leaf, and departed. Those three deer also followed him a short way, and having taken food and water with their mouths, went to their parents. The parents, asking, "Dear Rohaထa, though you were bound in a snare, how were you freed?" spoke this verse:

119.

119.

“Kathaṃ tvaṃ pamokkho āsi, upanītasmi jīvite;

Kathaṃ putta amocesi, kūṭapāsamha luddako”ti.

‑98. ‑ ‐How were you set free, when your life was brought near its end? How, son, did the hunter release you from the treacherous snare?‐

Tattha upanītasmīti tava jīvite maraṇasantikaṃ upanīte kathaṃ pamokkho āsi.

98. ‐Son, when your life was brought near death, how were you released? How did the hunter release you from the treacherous snare?‐

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Great Being, wishing to tell the cause to his mother and father, spoke these three verses:

120.

120.

“Bhaṇaṃ [V 4.0377] kaṇṇasukhaṃ vācaṃ, hadayaṅgaṃ hadayassitaṃ;

Subhāsitāhi vācāhi, cittako maṃ amocayi.

‑99. ‑ ‐Speaking words pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, based in the heart; with well-spoken words, Cittaka freed me.

121.

121.

“Bhaṇaṃ kaṇṇasukhaṃ vācaṃ, hadayaṅgaṃ hadayassitaṃ;

Subhāsitāhi vācāhi, sutanā maṃ amocayi.

‑100. ‑ ‐Speaking words pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, based in the heart; with well-spoken words, Sutanā freed me.

122.

122.

“Sutvā [P 4.0420] kaṇṇasukhaṃ vācaṃ, hadayaṅgaṃ hadayassitaṃ;

Subhāsitāni sutvāna, luddako maṃ amocayī”ti.

‑101. ‑ ‐Having heard speech pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, based in the heart; having heard these well-spoken words, the hunter released me.‐

Tattha bhaṇanti bhaṇanto. Hadayaṅganti hadayaṅgamaṃ. Dutiyagāthāya bhaṇanti bhaṇamānā. Sutvāti so imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ vācaṃ sutvā.

99. Cittaka, my younger brother, speaking words pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, and based in the heart; with well-spoken words, he freed me. 100. Sutanā, my sister, speaking words pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, and based in the heart; with well-spoken words, she freed me. 101. Having heard speech pleasant to the ear, reaching the heart, and based in the heart; having heard these well-spoken words, the hunter released me.

Athassa mātāpitaro anumodantā āhaṃsu –

Then his parents, wishing to express words of rejoicing to the hunter, spoke this verse:

123.

123.

“Evaṃ ānandito hotu, saha dārehi luddako;

Yathā mayajja nandāma, disvā rohaṇamāgata”nti.

‑102. ‑ ‐Thus may the hunter be delighted, together with his wife, just as we rejoice today, having seen Rohaထa returned.‐

Luddopi araññā nikkhamitvā rājakulaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā rājā gāthamāha –

The hunter, having left the forest, went to the royal palace, paid homage to the king, and stood in a suitable place. Seeing the hunter, the king, wishing to speak, said:

124.

124.

“Nanu tvaṃ avaca ludda, ‘migacammāni āhariṃ’;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, migacammāni nāharī”ti.

‑103. ‑ ‐Did you not say, hunter, ‘I will bring deer and deer hides’? Then for what reason have you not brought the deer and deer hides?‐

Tattha [M 4.0421] migacammānīti migaṃ vā cammaṃ vā. Āharinti āharissāmi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ambho ludda, nanu tvaṃ evaṃ avaca “migaṃ ānetuṃ asakkonto cammaṃ āharissāmi, taṃ asakkonto lomānī”ti, so tvaṃ kena kāraṇena neva migaṃ, na migacammaṃ āharīti?

Herein, ‘migacammāni’ means either the deer or its hide. ‘Āhariṃ’ means ‘I will bring’. This is what was said: “O hunter, did you not say, ‘If I am unable to bring the deer, I will bring its hide; and if unable to do that, its hairs’? So for what reason have you brought neither the deer nor the deer hide?”

Taṃ sutvā luddo gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the hunter, wishing to report to the king, said:

125.

125.

“Āgamā [V 4.0378] ceva hatthatthaṃ, kūṭapāsañca so migo;

Abajjhi taṃ migarājaṃ, tañca muttā upāsare.

‑104. ‑ ‐That deer came into my hands and into the treacherous snare; that deer-king was bound, and the unbound ones attended to him.

126.

126.

“Tassa me ahu saṃvego, abbhuto lomahaṃsano;

Imañcāhaṃ migaṃ haññe, ajja hissāmi jīvita”nti.

‑105. ‑ ‐Because of that, a sense of dread arose in me, amazing and hair-raising; ‘If I were to kill this deer, I would give up my life today.’‐

Tattha āgamāti mahārāja, so migo mama hatthatthaṃ hatthapāsañceva mayā oḍḍitaṃ kūṭapāsañca āgato, tasmiñca kūṭapāse abajjhi. Tañca muttā upāsareti tañca baddhaṃ apare muttā abaddhāva dve migā assāsentā taṃ nissāya aṭṭhaṃsu. Abbhutoti pubbe abhūtapubbo. Imañcāhanti atha me saṃviggassa etadahosi “sace ahaṃ imaṃ migaṃ hanissāmi, ajjeva imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne jīvitaṃ jahissāmī”ti.

104. O great king, that deer came into my hands and into the treacherous snare; that deer-king was bound. The two other deer, who were free, stood near that bound one, comforting him and staying by him. 105. If I were to kill this deer, I would give up my life today. Such dread arose in me, an amazing and hair-raising feeling that had never happened before.

Taṃ sutvā rājā āha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to ask the hunter, spoke this verse:

127.

127.

“Kīdisā te migā ludda, kīdisā dhammikā migā;

Kathaṃvaṇṇā kathaṃsīlā, bāḷhaṃ kho ne pasaṃsasī”ti.

‑106. ‑ ‐What kind of deer are they, hunter, what kind of righteous deer? What is their appearance, what is their conduct, that you praise them so highly?‐

Idaṃ so rājā vimhayavasena punappunaṃ pucchati. Taṃ sutvā luddo gāthamāha –

The king asked this repeatedly out of wonder. Hearing this, wishing to report to the king, the hunter spoke this verse:

128.

128.

“Odātasiṅgā [P 4.0421] sucivālā, jātarūpatacūpamā;

Pādā lohitakā tesaṃ, añjitakkhā manoramā”ti.

‑107. ‑ ‐They have white horns like silver, pure tails, and complexions like gold; their feet are red, their eyes are beautiful as if anointed, and they are delightful.‐

Tattha odātasiṅgāti rajatadāmasadisasiṅgā. Sucivālāti cāmarivālasadisena sucinā vālena samannāgatā. Lohitakāti rattanakhā pavāḷasadisā. Pādāti khurapariyantā. Añjitakkhāti añjitehi viya visuddhapañcapasādehi akkhīhi samannāgatā.

107. O great king, they have white horns like silver garlands. They have pure tails like a yak-tail whisk. They have complexions like gold. Their hooves are bright red like lac. They have eyes of fivefold clarity, as if anointed. They are beautiful and heart-delighting.

Iti [M 4.0422] so kathentova mahāsattassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇāni lomāni rañño hatthe ṭhapetvā tesaṃ migānaṃ sarīravaṇṇaṃ pakāsento gāthamāha –

As the hunter was speaking, he placed the golden-colored hairs of the Great Being in the king’s hand, and wishing to reveal the physical beauty and virtues of those deer, spoke this verse:

129.

129.

“Edisā [V 4.0379] te migā deva, edisā dhammikā migā;

Mātāpettibharā deva, na te so abhihāritu”nti.

‑108. ‑ ‐Such are these deer, O king, such are these righteous deer; they support their mother and father, O king, so it is not possible to bring that deer to you.‐

Tattha mātāpettibharāti jiṇṇe andhe mātāpitaro posenti, etādisā nesaṃ dhammikatā. Na te so abhihāritunti so migarājā na sakkā kenaci tava paṇṇākāratthāya abhiharitunti attho. “Abhihārayi”ntipi pāṭho, so ahaṃ taṃ te paṇṇākāratthāya nābhihārayiṃ na āharinti attho.

108. O king, these golden deer are of such a nature. These righteous deer support their mother and father. O king, it is not possible to bring that deer-king to you.

Iti so mahāsattassa ca cittamigassa ca sutanāya migapotikāya ca guṇaṃ kathetvā “mahārāja, ahaṃ tena migaraññā ‘attano lomāni dassetvā mama ṭhāne ṭhatvā dasahi rājadhammacariyagāthāhi deviyā dhammaṃ katheyyāsī’ti uggaṇhāpito āṇatto”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā rājā naṃ nhāpetvā ahatavatthāni nivāsetvā sattaratanakhacite pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā sayaṃ deviyā saddhiṃ nīcāsane ekamantaṃ nisīditvā taṃ añjaliṃ paggayha yācati. So dhammaṃ desento āha –

Having thus spoken of the virtues of the Great Being, of Citta the deer, and of Sutanā the young doe, he said: “Great king, I was taught and commanded by that deer king: ‘Having shown my hairs, and standing in my place, you should teach the Dhamma to the queen with the ten verses on the practice of royal righteousness.’” Hearing this, the king had him bathed, clothed him in new garments, and seated him on a couch adorned with the seven precious gems. The king himself, with the queen, sat on a low seat to one side, and raising his joined hands, made his request. The hunter, teaching the Dhamma, said:

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, mātāpitūsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward your mother and father, O noble one. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, puttadāresu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward your children and wife, O noble one. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, mittāmaccesu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward your friends and ministers, O noble one. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, vāhanesu balesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward your vehicles and troops. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, gāmesu nigamesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, in villages and towns; having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ [V 4.0380][M 4.0423] cara mahārāja, raṭṭhesu janapadesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, in kingdoms and provinces; having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu ca;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward ascetics and brahmins; having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, migapakkhīsu khattiya;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, toward beasts and birds, O noble one; having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, dhammo ciṇṇo sukhāvaho;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, rāja saggaṃ gamissasi.

“Practice the Dhamma, great king; the Dhamma, when practiced well, brings happiness. Having practiced the Dhamma here, O king, you will go to heaven.

“Dhammaṃ cara mahārāja, saindā devā sabrahmakā;

Suciṇṇena divaṃ pattā, mā dhammaṃ rāja pāmado”ti. (jā. 2.18.114-123);

“Practice the Dhamma, great king, for the gods with Indra and Brahmā attained heaven through good conduct. O king, do not be negligent in the Dhamma.” (Jātaka 2.18.114-123)

Iti nesādaputto mahāsattena desitaniyāmena ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya buddhalīlāya dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājano sādhukārasahassāni pavattesi. Dhammakathaṃ sutvāyeva deviyā [P 4.0422] dohaḷo paṭippassambhi. Rājā tussitvā luddaputtaṃ mahantena yasena santappento tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus the hunter’s son, following the method taught by the Great Being, preached the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges. The great crowd raised thousands of cries of approval. Upon hearing the Dhamma discourse, the queen’s craving subsided. The king, pleased, honored the hunter’s son with great glory and spoke these three verses:

130.

130.

“Dammi nikkhasataṃ ludda, thūlañca maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Catussadañca pallaṅkaṃ, umāpupphasarinnibhaṃ.

“I give you a hundred nikkhas, O hunter, and a splendid jeweled earring; a couch with four cushions, radiant like the umā flowers.

131.

131.

“Dve ca sādisiyo bhariyā, usabhañca gavaṃ sataṃ;

Dhammena rajjaṃ kāressaṃ, bahukāro mesi luddaka.

“And two wives of similar station, a bull, and a hundred cows; I shall rule the kingdom righteously. You have been of great service to me, O hunter.

132.

132.

“Kasivāṇijjā iṇadānaṃ, ucchācariyā ca luddaka;

Etena dāraṃ posehi, mā pāpaṃ akarī punā”ti.

“By farming, trade, lending, and gleaning, O hunter, support your family; do not do evil again.”

Tattha thūlanti mahagghaṃ maṇikuṇḍalapasādhanañca te dammi. Catussadanti caturussadaṃ, catuussīsakanti [V 4.0381] attho. Umāpupphasarinnibhanti nīlapaccattharaṇattā umāpupphasadisāya nibhāya obhāsena samannāgataṃ, kāḷavaṇṇadārusāramayaṃ vā. Sādisiyoti aññamaññaṃ [P 4.0423] rūpena ca bhogena ca sadisā. Usabhañca gavaṃ satanti usabhaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā gavaṃ satañca te dammi. Kāressanti [M 4.0424] dasa rājadhamme akopento dhammeneva rajjaṃ kāressāmi. Bahukāro mesīti suvaṇṇavaṇṇassa migarañño ṭhāne ṭhatvā dhammassa desitattā tvaṃ mama bahupakāro, migarājena vuttaniyāmeneva te ahaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpito. Kasivāṇijjāti samma luddaka, ahampi migarājānaṃ adisvā tassa vacanameva sutvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhito, tvampi ito paṭṭhāya sīlavā hohi, yāni tāni kasivāṇijjāni iṇadānaṃ uñchācariyāti ājīvamukhāni, eteneva sammāājīvena tava puttadāraṃ posehi, mā puna pāpaṃ karīti.

Here, ‘splendid’ (thūlaṃ) means highly valuable, and ‘I give you the ornament of a jeweled earring.’ ‘Four-cushioned’ (catussadaṃ) means having four cushions, or four head-posts—this is the meaning. ‘Radiant like the umā flower’ (umāpupphasarinnibhaṃ) means endowed with a radiance resembling umā flowers because of its blue covering, or made of dark-colored heartwood. ‘Of similar station’ (sādisiyo) means similar to each other in appearance and fortune. ‘A bull and a hundred cows’ (usabhañca gavaṃ sataṃ) means ‘I give you a hundred cows with a bull as their leader.’ ‘I shall rule’ (kāressaṃ) means ‘I will govern righteously, without violating the ten royal virtues.’ ‘You have been of great service to me’ (bahukāro mesi) means ‘you are of great help to me because you preached the Dhamma standing in the place of the golden-colored deer-king; by you I have been established in the five precepts, in the very manner spoken of by the deer-king.’ ‘Farming and trade’ (kasivāṇijjā) means, ‘Friend hunter, I too, without seeing the deer-king, having only heard his words, was established in the five precepts. From now on, you too should be virtuous. By these means of livelihood—farming, trade, lending, and gleaning—support your children and wife, and do no more evil.’

So rañño kathaṃ sutvā “na me gharāvāsenattho, pabbajjaṃ me anujānātha devā”ti anujānāpetvā raññā dinnadhanaṃ puttadārassa datvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi. Rājāpi mahāsattassa ovāde ṭhatvā saggapuraṃ pūresi, tassa ovādo vassasahassaṃ pavatti.

Having heard the king’s words, he said, “I have no need for the household life; grant me permission to go forth, Your Majesty.” Having obtained permission, he gave the wealth given by the king to his children and wife, entered the Himalayas, and went forth into the ascetic life. He produced the eight meditative attainments and was destined for the Brahma-world. The king, too, abiding by the Great Being’s advice, filled the heavenly city. His advice prevailed for a thousand years.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhave pubbepi mamatthāya ānandena jīvitaṃ pariccattamevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddo channo ahosi, rājā sāriputto, devī khemā bhikkhunī, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, sutanā uppalavaṇṇā, cittamigo ānando, asīti migasahassāni sākiyagaṇo, rohaṇo migarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “Thus, monks, even in the past, Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake,” and he connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Channa, the king was Sāriputta, the queen was the bhikkhunī Khemā, the parents were the great royal families, the sister Sutanā was Uppalavaṇṇā, the deer Citta was Ānanda, the eighty thousand deer were the Sakyan clan, and the deer king Rohaṇa was I myself.”

Rohaṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Rohaṇa Deer Jātaka is the fifth.

[502] 6. Cūḷahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[502] 6. The Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka

Ete haṃsā pakkamantīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ānandatherassa jīvitapariccāgameva ārabbha kathesi. Tadāpi hi dhammasabhāyaṃ therassa guṇakathaṃ kathentesu bhikkhūsu satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānandena mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccattamevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“These geese are departing”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Venerable Ānanda's sacrifice of his life. For at that time, when the monks were recounting the elder's virtues in the Dhamma hall, the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When they replied, “For this,” he said, “Not only now, monks, but even in the past Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 4.0382][M 4.0425] bārāṇasiyaṃ bahuputtako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Khemā nāmassa aggamahesī ahosi. Tadā mahāsatto suvaṇṇahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā navutihaṃsasahassaparivuto cittakūṭe vasi. Tadāpi devī [P 4.0424] vuttanayeneva supinaṃ disvā rañño suvaṇṇavaṇṇahaṃsassa dhammadesanāsavanadohaḷaṃ ārocesi. Rājāpi amacce pucchitvā “suvaṇṇavaṇṇahaṃsā nāma cittakūṭapabbate vasantī”ti ca sutvā khemaṃ nāma saraṃ kāretvā nānappakārāni nivāpadhaññāni ropāpetvā catūsu kaṇṇesu devasikaṃ abhayaghosanaṃ ghosāpesi, ekañca luddaputtaṃ haṃsānaṃ gahaṇatthāya payojesi. Tassa payojitākāro ca, tena tattha sakuṇānaṃ upaparikkhitabhāvo ca, suvaṇṇahaṃsānaṃ āgatakāle rañño ārocetvā pāsānaṃ oḍḍitaniyāmo ca, mahāsattassa pāse baddhaniyāmo ca, sumukhassa haṃsasenāpatino tīsu haṃsaghaṭāsu taṃ adisvā nivattanañca sabbaṃ mahāhaṃsajātake (jā. 2.21.89 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Idhāpi mahāsatto yaṭṭhipāse bajjhitvā pāsayaṭṭhiyaṃ olambantoyeva gīvaṃ pasāretvā haṃsānaṃ gatamaggaṃ olokento sumukhaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “āgatakāle naṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti cintetvā tasmiṃ āgate tisso gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, a king named Bahuputtaka reigned. His chief queen was named Khemā. At that time, the Great Being was born into the species of golden geese and lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, surrounded by ninety thousand geese. Then, in the manner already described, the queen saw a dream and informed the king of her longing to hear the Dhamma from a golden goose. The king, consulting his ministers and hearing that ‘golden geese live on Mount Cittakūṭa,’ had a lake named Khema constructed, had various kinds of fodder grain planted, and had a proclamation of safety announced daily at the four corners. He also employed a hunter's son to capture the geese. The manner of his employment, his observation of the birds there, the method of informing the king when the golden geese arrived, the way the snare was set, the Great Being's capture in the snare, and the turning back of Sumukha, the goose general, upon not seeing him in the three flocks—all this will become clear in the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka (Jā. 2.21.89 ff.). Here too, the Great Being, caught in the pole-snare and hanging from the snare-pole, stretched out his neck and watched the path of the geese. Seeing Sumukha approaching, he thought, 'When he arrives, I will test him,' and when he came, he spoke three verses:

133.

133.

“Ete haṃsā pakkamanti, vakkaṅgā bhayameritā;

Harittaca hemavaṇṇa, kāmaṃ sumukha pakkama.

“These geese are departing, with curved necks, driven by fear; O golden-skinned, golden-colored one, Sumukha, go as you please.

134.

134.

“Ohāya maṃ ñātigaṇā, ekaṃ pāsavasaṃ gataṃ;

Anapekkhamānā gacchanti, kiṃ eko avahiyyasi.

“My kinsfolk, leaving me behind—alone and caught in the power of the snare—depart without concern. Why are you alone left behind?

135.

135.

“Pateva patataṃ seṭṭha, natthi baddhe sahāyatā;

Mā anīghāya hāpesi, kāmaṃ sumukha pakkamā”ti.

“Fly away, O best of fliers! There is no companionship for one who is bound. Do not neglect the effort for the sorrowless state; go as you please, Sumukha.”

Tattha bhayameritāti bhayeritā bhayatajjitā bhayacalitā. Harittaca hemavaṇṇāti dvīhipi vacanehi tamevālapati. Kāmanti suvaṇṇattaca, suvaṇṇavaṇṇa, sundaramukha ekaṃsena pakkamāhiyeva, kiṃ te idhāgamanenāti vadati. Ohāyāti maṃ jahitvā uppatitā. Anapekkhamānāti te mama ñātakā mayi anapekkhāva gacchanti. Patevāti uppateva. Mā anīghāyāti [M 4.0426] ito gantvā pattabbāya niddukkhabhāvāya vīriyaṃ mā hāpesi.

Here, ‘driven by fear’ (bhayameritā) means terrified by fear, shaken by fear. ‘Golden-skinned, golden-colored’ (harittaca hemavaṇṇa)—with both these words, he addresses him. ‘Go as you please’ (kāmaṃ pakkama): he is saying, 'O golden-skinned, golden-colored, beautiful-faced one, you should certainly depart; what is the point of your coming here?' ‘Leaving’ (ohāya) means abandoning me and flying up. ‘Unconcerned’ (anapekkhamānā) means 'my relatives go without concern for me.' ‘Fly away’ (pateva) means 'fly up indeed.' ‘Do not neglect the effort for the sorrowless state’ (mā anīghāya hāpesi) means 'do not neglect the effort for the state of freedom from suffering that is to be attained by going from here.'

Tato [P 4.0425] sumukho paṅkapiṭṭhe nisīditvā gāthamāha –

Then Sumukha, sitting on the surface of the mud, spoke this verse:

136.

136.

“Nāhaṃ [V 4.0383] dukkhaparetoti, dhataraṭṭha tuvaṃ jahe;

Jīvitaṃ maraṇaṃ vā me, tayā saddhiṃ bhavissatī”ti.

“I will not abandon you, Dhataraṭṭha, [thinking] 'He is overcome by sorrow.' My life or my death will be with you.”

Tattha dukkhaparetoti mahārāja, “tvaṃ maraṇadukkhapareto”ti ettakeneva nāhaṃ taṃ jahāmi.

Here, ‘overcome by suffering’ (dukkhapareto) means, ‘O great king, you are overcome by the suffering of death.’ I will not abandon you for that reason.

Evaṃ sumukhena sīhanāde kathite dhataraṭṭho gāthamāha –

When Sumukha had spoken thus with a lion's roar, Dhataraṭṭha spoke this verse:

137.

137.

“Etadariyassa kalyāṇaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ sumukha bhāsasi;

Tañca vīmaṃsamānohaṃ, patatetaṃ avassaji”nti.

‘This is the excellence of the noble, Sumukha, what you say. And as I was testing you, I uttered this word.’

Tattha etadariyassāti yaṃ tvaṃ “nāhaṃ taṃ jahe”ti bhāsasi, etaṃ ācārasampannassa ariyassa kalyāṇaṃ uttamavacanaṃ. Patatetanti ahañca na taṃ vissajjetukāmova evaṃ avacaṃ, atha kho taṃ vīmaṃsamāno “patatū”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ avassajiṃ, gacchāti taṃ avocanti attho.

Here, ‘this is the excellence of the noble’ (etadariyassa) refers to the excellent words you spoke, ‘I will not abandon you,’ fitting for a noble one accomplished in conduct. ‘I uttered this word’ (patatetaṃ avassaji) means ‘I was not wishing to abandon you when I spoke thus, but rather, testing you, I uttered the word “Let him fly,” meaning I said “go” to you.’

Evaṃ tesaṃ kathentānaññeva luddaputto daṇḍamādāya vegenāgato. Sumukho dhataraṭṭhaṃ assāsetvā tassābhimukho gantvā apacitiṃ dassetvā haṃsarañño guṇe kathesi. Tāvadeva luddo muducitto ahosi. So tassa muducittakaṃ ñatvā puna gantvā haṃsarājameva assāsento aṭṭhāsi. Luddopi haṃsarājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

While they were speaking thus, the hunter's son arrived swiftly, carrying a club. Sumukha reassured Dhataraṭṭha, approached the hunter, showed a respectful manner, and spoke of the virtues of the king of geese. Instantly, the hunter became soft-hearted. Knowing his soft-heartedness, Sumukha went again and stood there, comforting the king of geese. The hunter then approached the king of geese and spoke the sixth verse:

138.

138.

“Apadena padaṃ yāti, antalikkhacaro dijo;

Ārā pāsaṃ na bujjhi tvaṃ, haṃsānaṃ pavaruttamā”ti.

‘The sky-faring bird makes its way through the pathless sky; yet you did not perceive the snare from afar, O best and highest of geese.’

Tattha apadena padanti mahārāja, tumhādiso antalikkhacaro dijo apade ākāse padaṃ katvā yāti. Na bujjhi tvanti so tvaṃ evarūpo dūratova imaṃ pāsaṃ na bujjhi na jānīti pucchati.

Here, ‘makes its way through the pathless sky’ (apadena padaṃ) means, ‘O great king, a sky-faring bird like you moves through the sky where there are no footprints, making its way.’ ‘You did not perceive’ (na bujjhi tvaṃ) means he asks, ‘you, being such, did not perceive or know this snare even from afar.’

Mahāsatto [M 4.0427] āha –

The Great Being said:

139.

139.

“Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhatī”ti.

‘When ruin befalls a person at the end of their life, then even upon encountering a net or a snare, they do not perceive it.’

Tattha [V 4.0384][P 4.0426] yadā parābhavoti samma luddaputta, yadā parābhavo avuḍḍhi vināso sampatto hoti, atha poso jīvitasaṅkhaye patte jālañca pāsañca patvāpi na jānātīti attho.

Here, ‘when ruin befalls’ (yadā parābhavo) means, ‘Friend hunter's son, when ruin, lack of prosperity, and destruction have arrived, then a person, having reached the end of their life, does not know, even upon reaching a net and a snare’—this is the meaning.

Luddo haṃsarañño kathaṃ abhinanditvā sumukhena saddhiṃ sallapanto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The hunter, greatly delighting in the king of geese's words, and wishing to converse with Sumukha, spoke three verses:

140.

140.

“Ete haṃsā pakkamanti, vakkaṅgā bhayameritā;

Harittaca hemavaṇṇa, tvaññeva avahiyyasi.

‘These geese depart, with curved necks, driven by fear; O golden-skinned and golden-hued, you alone are left behind.’

141.

141.

“Ete bhutvā ca pivitvā ca, pakkamanti vihaṅgamā;

Anapekkhamānā vakkaṅgā, tvaññeveko upāsasi.

‘Having eaten and drunk, these birds depart; unconcerned, with curved necks, while you alone attend upon him.’

142.

142.

“Kiṃ nu tyāyaṃ dijo hoti, mutto baddhaṃ upāsasi;

Ohāya sakuṇā yanti, kiṃ eko avahiyyasī”ti.

‘What, then, is this bird to you, that though you are free, you attend upon the bound? The birds depart, having abandoned him; why are you alone left behind?’

Tattha tvaññevāti tvameva ohiyyasīti pucchati. Upāsasīti payirupāsasi.

Here, ‘you alone’ (tvaññeva) means he asks, ‘are you alone left behind?’ ‘Attend’ (upāsasi) means ‘you wait upon him.’

Sumukho āha –

Sumukha said:

143.

143.

“Rājā me so dijo mitto, sakhā pāṇasamo ca me;

Neva naṃ vijahissāmi, yāva kālassa pariyāya”nti.

‘That bird is my king and friend, a companion dear as life itself; I will never abandon him, as long as my life shall last.’

Tattha yāva kālassa pariyāyanti luddaputta, yāva jīvitakālassa pariyosānaṃ ahaṃ etaṃ na vijahissāmiyeva.

Here, ‘as long as my life shall last’ (yāva kālassa pariyāya) means, ‘O hunter's son, until the very end of my lifetime, I will not abandon him.’

Taṃ sutvā luddo pasannacitto hutvā “sacāhaṃ evaṃ sīlasampannesu imesu aparajjhissāmi, pathavīpi me vivaraṃ dadeyya, kiṃ me rañño santikā laddhena dhanena, vissajjessāmi na”nti cintetvā gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the hunter, with a gladdened heart, thought: "If I should offend these who are so accomplished in virtue, the earth itself would open up and give me a chasm. What need have I for wealth obtained from the king? I will release him." Having thought thus, he spoke this verse:

144.

144.

“Yo [M 4.0428] ca tvaṃ sakhino hetu, pāṇaṃ cajitumicchasi;

So te sahāyaṃ muñcāmi, hotu rājā tavānugo”ti.

"You who for a friend's sake wish to give up your life, for that reason I release your companion; may the king follow your will."

Tattha [V 4.0385] yo ca tvanti yo nāma tvaṃ. Soti so ahaṃ. Tavānugoti esa haṃsarājā tava vasaṃ anugato hotu, tayā saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne vasatu.

Herein, 'you who' (yo ca tvaṃ) means 'you who indeed'. 'For that reason I' (so) means 'that I' (the speaker). 'Follow your will' (tavānugo) means may this king of geese follow your authority, and may he dwell in one place with you.

Evañca pana vatvā dhataraṭṭhaṃ yaṭṭhipāsato otāretvā saratīraṃ netvā pāsaṃ muñcitvā muducittena lohitaṃ dhovitvā nhāruādīni [P 4.0427] paṭipādesi. Tassa muducittatāya mahāsattassa pāramitānubhāvena ca tāvadeva pādo sacchavi ahosi, baddhaṭṭhānampi na paññāyi. Sumukho bodhisattaṃ oloketvā tuṭṭhacitto anumodanaṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he took Dhataraṭṭha down from the stake-snare, led him to the lake shore, released the noose, and with a tender heart washed away the blood and tended to the sinews and other parts. Due to his tender-heartedness and the power of the Great Being’s perfections, the foot immediately became whole, with skin intact, and no trace of the binding was apparent. Sumukha, looking upon the Bodhisatta with a gladdened heart, expressing his appreciation, spoke this verse:

145.

145.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā dijādhipa”nti.

"Thus rejoice, O hunter, with all your kinsmen, just as I rejoice today, seeing the lord of birds released."

Taṃ sutvā luddo “gacchatha, sāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “kiṃ pana tvaṃ samma, maṃ attano atthāya bandhi, udāhu aññassa āṇattiyā”ti pucchitvā tena tasmiṃ kāraṇe ārocite “kiṃ nu kho me itova cittakūṭaṃ gantuṃ seyyo, udāhu nagara”nti vimaṃsanto “mayi nagaraṃ gate luddaputto dhanaṃ labhissati, deviyā dohaḷo paṭippassambhissati, sumukhassa mittadhammo pākaṭo bhavissati, tathā mama ñāṇabalaṃ, khemañca saraṃ abhayadakkhiṇaṃ katvā labhissāmi, tasmā nagarameva gantuṃ seyyo”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā “ludda, tvaṃ amhe kājenādāya rañño santikaṃ nehi, sace no rājā vissajjetukāmo bhavissati, vissajjessatī”ti āha. Rājāno nāma sāmi, kakkhaḷā, gacchatha tumheti. Mayaṃ tādisaṃ luddampi mudukaṃ karimha, rañño ārādhane amhākaṃ bhāro, nehiyeva no, sammāti. So tathā akāsi. Rājā haṃse disvāva somanassajāto hutvā dvepi haṃse kañcanapīṭhe nisīdāpetvā madhulāje khādāpetvā madhurodakaṃ pāyetvā añjaliṃ paggayha dhammakathaṃ āyāci. Haṃsarājā tassa sotukāmataṃ viditvā paṭhamaṃ tāva paṭisanthāramakāsi[M 4.0429]. Tatrimā haṃsassa ca rañño ca vacanapaṭivacanagāthāyo honti –

Hearing that, the hunter said, "Go, my lords." Then the Great Being asked him, "But friend, did you bind me for your own sake or at another's command?" When the hunter explained the reason, the Bodhisatta pondered, "What would be better for me now—to go from here to Cittakūṭa, or to the city?" Reflecting, he thought, "If I go to the city, the hunter's son will gain wealth, the queen's craving will be pacified, Sumukha's virtue of friendship will be revealed, and likewise my power of wisdom. I will also obtain a safe refuge, having given the gift of fearlessness to the Khema lake. Therefore, it is better to go to the city." Having made this decision, he said, "Hunter, take us on a carrying pole to the king. If the king wishes to release us, he will do so." The hunter replied, "My lords, kings are harsh and cruel. You should go." The Bodhisatta said, "We have softened even such a hunter as you; pleasing the king is our responsibility. Just take us, friend." The hunter did so. Upon reaching the city, he entered the palace and presented them to the king. Upon seeing the geese, the king became joyful. He had both geese seated on golden stools, fed them honeyed parched grain, gave them sweetened water to drink, and then, with folded hands, requested a Dhamma talk. The king of geese, perceiving his eagerness to listen, first exchanged friendly greetings. Here follow the verses of conversation between the goose and the king:

146.

146.

“Kaccinnu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ;

Kacci raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsasi.

"I trust, great king, that you are well? I trust, O king, you are in good health? I trust this kingdom of Kāsī is prosperous? Do you rule the people righteously?"

147.

147.

“Kusalaṃ [P 4.0428] ceva me haṃsa, atho haṃsa anāmayaṃ;

Atho raṭṭhamidaṃ phītaṃ, dhammena manusāsahaṃ.

"I am well indeed, O goose, and also, O goose, in good health; moreover, this kingdom is prosperous, and I rule the people righteously."

148.

148.

“Kacci [V 4.0386] bhoto amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Kacci ārā amittā te, chāyā dakkhiṇatoriva.

"I trust, O king, that no fault is found among your ministers? I trust your enemies are kept at a distance and, like a shadow facing south, they do not grow?"

149.

149.

“Athopi me amaccesu, doso koci na vijjati;

Atho ārā amittā me, chāyā dakkhiṇatoriva.

"Moreover, no fault is found among my ministers; and my enemies are kept at a distance and, like a shadow facing south, they do not grow."

150.

150.

“Kacci te sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, tava chandavasānugā.

"I trust your wives are compatible with you in birth and status, obedient and sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, and retinue, and compliant with your wishes?"

151.

151.

“Atho me sādisī bhariyā, assavā piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, mama chandavasānugā.

"Moreover, my wives are compatible with me in birth and status, obedient and sweet-spoken, endowed with children, beauty, and retinue, and they are compliant with my wishes."

152.

152.

“Kacci te bahavo puttā, sujātā raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Paññājavena sampannā, sammodanti tato tato.

"I trust you have many sons, well-born, who increase the realm, O king? Are they endowed with the swiftness of wisdom and do they joyfully carry out their various duties?"

153.

153.

“Satameko ca me puttā, dhataraṭṭha mayā sutā;

Tesaṃ tvaṃ kiccamakkhāhi, nāvarujjhanti te vaco”ti.

"I have a hundred and one sons, Dhataraṭṭha, who are renowned through me; declare their duties to them, for they will not reject your word."

Tattha kusalanti ārogyaṃ, itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Phītanti kacci te idaṃ raṭṭhaṃ phītaṃ subhikkhaṃ, dhammena ca naṃ anusāsasīti pucchati. Dosoti aparādho. Chāyā dakkhiṇatorivāti yathā nāma dakkhiṇadisābhimukhā chāyā na vaḍḍhati, evaṃ te kacci amittā na vaḍḍhantīti vadati. Sādisīti jātigottakulapadesehi samānā. Evarūpā hi aticārinī na hoti. Assavāti vacanapaṭiggāhikā. Puttarūpayasūpetāti puttehi ca rūpena [M 4.0430] ca yasena ca upetā. Paññājavenāti paññāvegena paññaṃ javāpetvā tāni tāni kiccāni paricchindituṃ samatthāti pucchati. Sammodanti tato tatoti yattha yattha niyuttā honti, tato tato sammodanteva, na virujjhantīti pucchati. Mayā sutāti mayā vissutā. Mañhi loko “bahuputtarājā”ti vadati, iti te maṃ nissāya vissutā pākaṭā jātāti mayā sutā nāma hontīti vadati. Tesaṃ tvaṃ kiccamakkhāhīti tesaṃ mama puttānaṃ “idaṃ nāma karontū”ti tvaṃ kiccamakkhāhi, na te vacanaṃ avarujjhanti, ovādaṃ nesaṃ dehīti adhippāyenevamāha.

Herein, 'kusalaṃ' (well-being) means health; the other word (anāmayaṃ) is its synonym. 'Phītaṃ' (prosperous)—he asks, "I hope your kingdom is prosperous and abundant in food, and do you rule it righteously?" 'Doso' (fault) means offense. 'Chāyā dakkhiṇatoriva' (like a shadow to the south)—just as a shadow facing south does not grow, so he says, "I hope your enemies do not grow?" 'Sādisī' (suitable) means equal in birth, lineage, family, and status. Such a woman does not transgress. 'Assavā' (attentive) means one who listens to instructions. 'Puttarūpayasūpetā' means endowed with sons, beauty, and retinue. 'Paññājavenā' (with the swiftness of wisdom)—he asks whether they are capable of discerning various duties with the speed of wisdom. 'Sammodanti tato tato' (rejoicing from place to place)—he asks, "Wherever they are assigned, do they remain agreeable and not oppose?" 'Mayā sutā' (heard of through me) means renowned through me. For the world calls me 'the king with many sons,' and so, on account of me, they have become famous—thus they are 'heard of through me.' 'Tesaṃ tvaṃ kiccamakkhāhi' means he says, "You should declare the duties for my sons, saying, 'Let them do this.' They will not reject your word—give them advice."

Taṃ [V 4.0387] sutvā mahāsatto tassa ovādaṃ dento pañca gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the Great Being, wishing to give advice to those princes, spoke five verses:

154.

154.

“Upapannopi ce hoti, jātiyā vinayena vā;

Atha pacchā kurute yogaṃ, kicche āpāsu sīdati.

"Even if one is well-endowed by birth or by discipline, yet if one only later applies oneself to effort, one sinks down when hardships and misfortunes arise."

155.

155.

“Tassa [P 4.0429] saṃhīrapaññassa, vivaro jāyate mahā;

Rattimandhova rūpāni, thūlāni manupassati.

"For one whose wisdom is unstable or unlearned, a great failing arises; like one who is night-blind, one perceives only coarse forms but not the fine details."

156.

156.

“Asāre sārayogaññū, matiṃ na tveva vindati;

Sarabhova giriduggasmiṃ, antarāyeva sīdati.

"One who considers the unessential to be essential truly does not find wisdom; like a sarabha deer fallen into a mountain gorge, one sinks down in the midst of it."

157.

157.

“Hīnajaccopi ce hoti, uṭṭhātā dhitimā naro;

Ācārasīlasampanno, nise aggīva bhāsati.

"Even if a person is of low birth, if he is energetic, resolute, and endowed with good conduct and virtue, he shines like a fire in the night."

158.

158.

“Etaṃ me upamaṃ katvā, putte vijjāsu vācaya;

Saṃvirūḷhetha medhāvī, khette bījaṃva vuṭṭhiyā”ti.

"Taking this as a simile, have your sons instructed in the sciences; the wise one will thrive like a seed in a good field when it rains."

Tattha vinayenāti ācārena. Pacchā kurute yoganti yo ce sikkhitabbasikkhāsu daharakāle yogaṃ vīriyaṃ akatvā pacchā mahallakakāle karoti, evarūpo pacchā tathārūpe dukkhe vā āpadāsu vā uppannāsu sīdati, attānaṃ uddharituṃ na sakkoti. Tassa saṃhīrapaññassāti tassa asikkhitattā tato tato haritabbapaññassa niccaṃ calabuddhino. Vivaroti bhogādīnaṃ chiddaṃ, parihānīti attho. Rattimandhoti rattandho. Idaṃ [M 4.0431] vuttaṃ hoti – “yathā rattandho rattikāṇo rattiṃ candobhāsādīhi thūlarūpāneva passati, sukhumāni passituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ asikkhito saṃhīrapañño kismiñcideva bhaye uppanne sukhumāni kiccāni passituṃ na sakkoti, oḷārikeyeva passati, tasmā tava putte daharakāleyeva sikkhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

Herein, 'vinayena' (by discipline) means by conduct. 'Pacchā kurute yogaṃ' (yet later applies oneself)—this refers to one who, in the trainings to be learned, does not put forth effort in youth but does so in old age. Such a person, when suffering or misfortunes arise later, sinks and cannot save themselves. 'Tassa saṃhīrapaññassa' (for one whose wisdom is unstable)—this means, because one has not trained, one's wisdom is always unstable, one's intellect easily carried away from place to place. 'Vivaro' (breach) means a gap in wealth and so on, meaning loss. 'Rattimandho' (night-blind) means one who is night-blind. This is what is said: "Just as a night-blind person, one who cannot see at night, sees only coarse forms at night by the light of the moon and so on, but cannot see subtle things, so too an untrained person with unstable wisdom, when some danger arises, cannot see subtle duties—they see only the obvious. Therefore, it is fitting to train your sons while they are still young."

Asāreti nissāre lokāyatavedasamaye. Sārayogaññūti sārayutto esa samayoti maññamāno. Matiṃ na tveva vindatīti bahuṃ sikkhitvāpi paññaṃ na labhatiyeva. Giriduggasminti so evarūpo yathā nāma sarabho attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge visamampi [V 4.0388] samanti maññamāno giridugge vegenāgacchanto narakapapātaṃ patitvā antarāyeva sīdati, āvāsaṃ na pāpuṇāti, evametaṃ asāraṃ lokāyatavedasamayaṃ sārasaññāya uggahetvā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā tava putte atthanissitesu vaḍḍhiāvahesu kiccesu yojetvā sikkhāpehīti. Nise aggīvāti mahārāja, hīnajātikopi uṭṭhānādiguṇasampanno rattiṃ aggikkhandho viya obhāsati. Etaṃ meti etaṃ mayā vuttaṃ rattandhañca aggikkhandhañca upamaṃ katvā tava putte vijjāsu vācaya, sikkhitabbayuttāsu sikkhāsu yojehi. Evaṃ yutto hi yathā sukhette suvuṭṭhiyā bījaṃ saṃvirūhati, tatheva medhāvī saṃvirūhati, yasena ca bhogehi ca vaḍḍhatīti.

'Asāre' (in the unessential) means in worthless worldly doctrines and vedic lore. 'Sārayogaññū' (one who considers it essential) means one who thinks, 'this doctrine is endowed with essence.' 'Matiṃ na tveva vindati' (truly does not find wisdom)—this means, even after much learning, one does not gain wisdom. 'Giriduggasminti' (in a mountain gorge)—such a person is like a sarabha deer. Just as a sarabha deer, returning to its dwelling place, considering even a rough path on the way to be smooth, rushing swiftly through the mountain gorge, falls into a chasm like a hell and perishes right there without reaching its home—so too, grasping this worthless worldly doctrine and vedic lore with the perception of it being essential, one attains great ruin. Therefore, you should instruct your sons, engaging them in tasks that lead to benefit and growth. 'Nise aggīva' (like a fire at night)—O great king, even one of low birth, if endowed with qualities like diligence, shines like a mass of fire at night. 'Etaṃ me' (this of mine)—this means, having used this simile of mine, of the night-blind person and the mass of fire, instruct your sons in the sciences and engage them in the trainings that are fitting to be learned. Thus engaged, just as a seed grows well in a fertile field with good rain, so too the wise one grows, increasing in fame and wealth.

Evaṃ [P 4.0430] mahāsatto sabbarattiṃ rañño dhammaṃ desesi, deviyā dohaḷo paṭippassambhi. Mahāsatto aruṇuggamanavelāyameva rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhapetvā appamādena ovaditvā saddhiṃ sumukhena uttarasīhapañjarena nikkhamitvā cittakūṭameva gato.

Thus, the Great Being taught the Dhamma to the king throughout the entire night, and the queen’s craving subsided. At the very break of dawn, the Great Being established the king and queen in the five precepts, exhorted them to be diligent, and together with Sumukha, departed through the northern lion-window and flew straight to Mount Cittakūṭa.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi iminā mamatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccattamevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddo channo ahosi, rājā sāriputto, devī khemābhikkhunī, haṃsaparisā sākiyagaṇo, sumukho ānando, haṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “Monks, in the past as well, this Ānanda sacrificed his life for my sake,” and then he identified the birth: “At that time, the hunter was Channa, the king was Sāriputta, Queen Khemā was the bhikkhunī Khemā, the assembly of golden swans was the Sākiyan clan, Sumukha was Ānanda, and the king of the Dhatarāṭṭha swans was I myself.”

Cūḷahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka is finished.

[503] 7. Sattigumbajātakavaṇṇanā

[503] 7. 7. Sattigumba Jātaka: The story of the difference between two parrot brothers due to their environment.

Migaluddo [M 4.0432] mahārājāti idaṃ satthā maddakucchismiṃ migadāye viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadattena hi silāya paviddhāya bhagavato pāde sakalikāya khate balavavedanā uppajji. Tathāgatassa dassanatthāya bahū bhikkhū sannipatiṃsu. Atha bhagavā parisaṃ sannipatitaṃ disvā “bhikkhave, idaṃ senāsanaṃ atisambādhaṃ, sannipāto mahā bhavissati, maṃ mañcasivikāya maddakucchiṃ nethā”ti āha. Bhikkhū tathā kariṃsu. Jīvako tathāgatassa pādaṃ phāsukaṃ akāsi. Bhikkhū satthu santike nisinnāva kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto sayampi pāpo, parisāpissa pāpā, iti so pāpo pāpaparivārova viharatī”ti. Satthā “kiṃ kathetha, bhikkhave”ti pucchitvā “idaṃ nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto pāpo pāpaparivāroyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“A deer-hunter, O great king”—this the Teacher told while dwelling in the grotto at Maddakucchi concerning Devadatta. For when Devadatta hurled a stone, a splinter struck the Blessed One’s foot, and severe pain arose. Many monks gathered to see the Tathāgata. Seeing the gathered assembly, the Blessed One said: “Monks, this lodging is too narrow; the gathering will be great. Carry me on a litter to Maddakucchi.” The monks did so. Jīvaka the physician treated the Tathāgata’s foot until it was well. While sitting near the Teacher, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, Devadatta himself is evil, and his retinue is also evil. Being evil, he maintains an evil following.” The Teacher asked, “What are you discussing, monks?” When they told him, he said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past as well, Devadatta was evil and had an evil retinue,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 4.0389] uttarapañcālanagare pañcālo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Mahāsatto araññāyatane ekasmiṃ sānupabbate simbalivane ekassa suvarañño putto hutvā nibbatti, dve bhātaro ahesuṃ. Tassa pana pabbatassa uparivāte coragāmako ahosi pañcannaṃ corasatānaṃ nivāso, adhovāte assamo pañcannaṃ isisatānaṃ nivāso. Tesaṃ suvapotakānaṃ pakkhanikkhamanakāle vātamaṇḍalikā udapādi. Tāya pahaṭo eko suvapotako coragāmake [P 4.0431] corānaṃ āvudhantare patito, tassa tattha patitattā “sattigumbo”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Eko assame vālukatale pupphantare pati, tassa tattha patitattā “pupphako”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Sattigumbo corānaṃ antare vaḍḍhito, pupphako isīnaṃ.

In the past, when King Pañcāla was reigning in the city of Uttarapañcāla, the Great Being was reborn as the son of a parrot king in a silk-cotton forest on a mountain slope in a vast wilderness; there were two brothers. On the windward side of that mountain was a thieves’ village, the dwelling of five hundred thieves; on the leeward side was a hermitage, the dwelling of five hundred seers. At the time when the young parrots’ wings were fledging, a whirlwind arose. Struck by it, one young parrot fell into the thieves’ village among their weapons; because he fell there, they named him ‘Sattigumba.’ The other fell in the hermitage on a sandy spot among flowers; because he fell there, they named him ‘Pupphaka.’ Sattigumba grew up among the thieves, while Pupphaka grew up among the seers.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito rathavaraṃ abhiruhitvā mahantena parivārena migavadhāya nagarato nātidūre supupphitaphalitaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ upagumbavanaṃ gantvā “yassa passena migo palāyati, tasseva gīvā”ti vatvā rathā oruyha paṭicchādetvā dinne koṭṭhake dhanuṃ ādāya aṭṭhāsi. Purisehi migānaṃ uṭṭhāpanatthāya vanagumbesu pothiyamānesu eko eṇimigo uṭṭhāya gamanamaggaṃ olokento rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānasseva vivittataṃ [M 4.0433] disvā tadabhimukho pakkhanditvā palāyi. Amaccā “kassa passena migo palāyito”ti pucchantā “rañño passenā”ti ñatvā raññā saddhiṃ keḷiṃ kariṃsu. Rājā asmimānena tesaṃ keḷiṃ asahanto “idāni taṃ migaṃ gahessāmī”ti rathaṃ āruyha “sīghaṃ pesehī”ti sārathiṃ āṇāpetvā migena gatamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Rathaṃ vegena gacchantaṃ parisā anubandhituṃ nāsakkhi. Rājā sārathidutiyo yāva majjhanhikā gantvā taṃ migaṃ adisvā nivattanto tassa coragāmassa santike ramaṇīyaṃ kandaraṃ disvā rathā oruyha nhatvā ca pivitvā ca paccuttari. Athassa sārathi rathassa uttarattharaṇaṃ otāretvā sayanaṃ rukkhacchāyāya paññapesi, so tattha nipajji. Sārathipi tassa pāde sambāhanto nisīdi. Rājā antarantarā niddāyati ceva pabujjhati ca.

One day, the king, adorned with all his ornaments, mounted his excellent chariot and, accompanied by a large retinue, went to a delightful grove full of flowers and fruits not far from the city to hunt deer. He said, “The one by whose side the deer escapes shall pay the penalty with his neck,” then descended from the chariot and stood with his bow in a prepared blind. As the men beat the bushes to rouse the deer, an antelope sprang up and, looking for a way out, saw the king's position was quiet and dashed straight towards him to flee. The ministers asked, “By whose side did the antelope escape?” and learning it was by the king’s side, they jested with him along with the army. Due to his pride, the king could not bear their jesting and declared, “I will catch that antelope now!” He mounted his chariot, ordered the charioteer to drive swiftly, and followed the path the antelope had taken. The retinue could not keep up with the fast-moving chariot. Accompanied only by his charioteer, the king followed until midday but did not find the antelope. Turning back, he saw a charming ravine near the thieves’ village, descended from the chariot, bathed, drank, and came out. His charioteer then took the covering from the chariot and spread it under the shade of a tree, where the king lay down. The charioteer sat massaging his feet. The king was intermittently dozing and waking.

Coragāmavāsino corāpi rañño ārakkhaṇatthāya araññameva pavisiṃsu. Coragāmake sattigumbo ceva bhattarandhako patikolambo nāmeko puriso cāti dveva ohīyiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sattigumbo gāmakā nikkhamitvā rājānaṃ disvā “imaṃ niddāyamānameva māretvā ābharaṇāni gahessāmā”ti cintetvā patikolambassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocesi. Tamatthaṃ [P 4.0432] pakāsento satthā pañca gāthā abhāsi –

The thieves of the village had also entered the forest to keep a watch for the king. Only two remained in the thieves’ village: the parrot Sattigumba and a man named Patikolamba, who was the cook. At that moment, Sattigumba left the village, saw the king, and thought, “I will kill him while he sleeps and take his ornaments.” He went to Patikolamba and informed him of the matter. To illuminate this, the Teacher, having become a Buddha, recited these five verses:

159.

159.

“Migaluddo [V 4.0390] mahārājā, pañcālānaṃ rathesabho;

Nikkhanto saha senāya, ogaṇo vanamāgamā.

148. “The great king, a hunter of deer and lord of the Pañcālas’ chariot-warriors, set out with his army; separated from his retinue, he came into the forest.”

160.

160.

“Tatthaddasā araññasmiṃ, takkarānaṃ kuṭiṃ kataṃ;

Tassā kuṭiyā nikkhamma, suvo luddāni bhāsati.

149. “There in the wilderness, he saw the settlement built by thieves; coming out from that hut, a parrot speaks cruel words.”

161.

161.

“Sampannavāhano poso, yuvā sammaṭṭhakuṇḍalo;

Sobhati lohituṇhīso, divā sūriyova bhāsati.

150. “This man with an excellent vehicle, a youth with well-polished earrings, shines with a red turban; he blazes like the sun by day.”

162.

162.

“Majjhanhike sampatike, sutto rājā sasārathi;

Handassābharaṇaṃ sabbaṃ, gaṇhāma sāhasā mayaṃ.

151. “Now at the arrival of midday, the king with his charioteer is asleep. Come, let us seize all his ornaments by force!”

163.

163.

“Nisīthepi rahodāni, sutto rājā sasārathi;

Ādāya vatthaṃ maṇikuṇḍalañca, hantvāna sākhāhi avattharāmā”ti.

152. “Now it is as secluded as midnight; the king with his charioteer is asleep. Let us take his clothing and jeweled earrings, kill them, and cover them with branches.”

Tattha [M 4.0434] migaluddoti luddo viya migānaṃ gavesanato “migaluddo”ti vutto. Ogaṇoti gaṇā ohīno parihīno hutvā. Takkarānaṃ kuṭiṃ katanti so rājā tattha araññe corānaṃ vasanatthāya kataṃ gāmakaṃ addasa. Tassāti tato corakuṭito. Luddāni bhāsatīti patikolambena saddhiṃ dāruṇāni vacanāni katheti. Sampannavāhanoti sampannaassavāhano. Lohituṇhīsoti rattena uṇhīsapaṭṭena samannāgato. Sampatiketi sampati idāni, evarūpe ṭhitamajjhanhikakāleti attho. Sāhasāti sāhasena pasayhākāraṃ katvā gaṇhāmāti vadati. Nisīthepi rahodānīti nisīthepi idānipi raho. Idaṃ vadati – yathā nisīthe aḍḍharattasamaye manussā kilantā sayanti, raho nāma hoti, idāni ṭhitamajjhanhikepi kāle tathevāti. Hantvānāti rājānaṃ māretvā vatthābharaṇānissa gahetvā atha naṃ pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā ekamante sākhāhi paṭicchādemāti.

Herein, migaluddo (deer-hunter): he is called this because he seeks deer like a hunter (luddo). Ogaṇo: separated from his group. Takkarānaṃ kuṭiṃ kataṃ (a hut made for thieves): that king saw a small village made in the forest for thieves to live in. Tassā: from that thieves’ hut. Luddāni bhāsati (speaks cruelly): he speaks harsh words with Patikolamba. Sampannavāhano: having excellent horses for a vehicle. Lohituṇhīso: endowed with a red turban-cloth. Sampatike: now, at the present time; the meaning is, at this time of high noon. Sāhasā: he says, “Let us take by force, by a violent act.” Nisīthepi rahodāni: it is now as secluded as at midnight. This is what he is saying: just as at midnight, in the middle of the night, when people are tired and asleep, it is secluded, so it is now at high noon. Hantvāna: having killed the king and taken his clothes and ornaments, then, grabbing him by the feet and dragging him aside, let us cover him with branches.

Iti so vegena sakiṃ nikkhamati, sakiṃ patikolambassa santikaṃ gacchati. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā nikkhamitvā olokento rājabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhīto gāthamāha –

Thus he went out quickly once, and once he went near Patikolamba. Hearing his words, Patikolamba went out and looked, and recognizing the king’s royal state, he became frightened and recited a verse:

164.

164.

“Kinnu [V 4.0391] ummattarūpova, sattigumba pabhāsasi;

Durāsadā hi rājāno, aggi pajjalito yathā”ti.

“Why do you speak like a madman, Sattigumba? For kings are difficult to approach, like a blazing fire.”

Atha naṃ suvo gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

Then the parrot addressed him with a verse:

165.

165.

“Atha tvaṃ patikolamba, matto thullāni gajjasi;

Mātari mayha naggāya, kinnu tvaṃ vijigucchase”ti.

“But you, Patikolamba, drunk, you roar out coarse things! Why are you disgusted, while my mother is naked?”

Tattha [P 4.0433] atha tvanti nanu tvaṃ. Mattoti corānaṃ ucchiṭṭhasuraṃ labhitvā tāya matto hutvā pubbe mahāgajjitāni gajjasi. Mātarīti corajeṭṭhakassa bhariyaṃ sandhāyāha. Sā kira tadā sākhābhaṅgaṃ nivāsetvā carati. Vijigucchaseti mama mātari naggāya kinnu tvaṃ idāni corakammaṃ jigucchasi, kātuṃ na icchasīti.

Herein, atha tvaṃ: but you. Matto: having obtained the thieves’ leftover liquor and become intoxicated by it, you used to roar great roars. Mātari: he says this referring to the wife of the chief thief. She, it is said, was then going about wearing a garment of branches. Vijigucchase: why are you now disgusted by the act of thievery and unwilling to do it, although my mother is naked?
