Rājā pabujjhitvā tassa tena saddhiṃ manussabhāsāya kathentassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sappaṭibhayaṃ idaṃ ṭhāna”nti sārathiṃ uṭṭhāpento gāthamāha –

The king awoke, and hearing the words of the parrot speaking in human language with the man, he thought, “This place is dangerous,” and rousing his charioteer, he spoke a verse:

166.

166.

“Uṭṭhehi [M 4.0435] samma taramāno, rathaṃ yojehi sārathi;

Sakuṇo me na ruccati, aññaṃ gacchāma assama”nti.

“Get up quickly, friend charioteer, and yoke the chariot! This bird does not please me; let us go to another hermitage.”

Sopi sīghaṃ uṭṭhahitvā rathaṃ yojetvā gāthamāha –

He too rose quickly, yoked the chariot, and spoke this verse:

167.

167.

“Yutto ratho mahārāja, yutto ca balavāhano;

Adhitiṭṭha mahārāja, aññaṃ gacchāma assama”nti.

“The chariot is yoked, great king, and the strong steeds are yoked. Mount, great king! Let us go to another hermitage.”

Tattha balavāhanoti balavavāhano, mahāthāmaassasampannoti attho. Adhitiṭṭhāti abhiruha.

Herein, balavāhano: having strong draft animals, that is, endowed with horses of great stamina. Adhitiṭṭha: mount.

Abhiruḷhamatteyeva ca tasmiṃ sindhavā vātavegena pakkhandiṃsu. Sattigumbo rathaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā saṃvegappatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

And just as soon as the king had mounted, the Sindh horses rushed off with the speed of the wind. Sattigumba, seeing the chariot departing, was filled with agitation and recited two verses:

168.

168.

“Ko [V 4.0392] numeva gatā sabbe, ye asmiṃ paricārakā;

Esa gacchati pañcālo, mutto tesaṃ adassanā.

“Where have all the men gone who were here? This Pañcāla king is leaving, escaped because they did not see him.

169.

169.

“Kodaṇḍakāni gaṇhatha, sattiyo tomarāni ca;

Esa gacchati pañcālo, mā vo muñcittha jīvata”nti.

“Take up your bows, spears, and lances! That Pañcāla king is getting away! Do not let him escape you alive!”

Tattha ko numeti kuhiṃ nu ime. Asminti imasmiṃ assame. Paricārakāti corā. Adassanāti etesaṃ corānaṃ adassanena mutto esa gacchatīti, etesaṃ hatthato mutto hutvā esa adassanaṃ gacchatītipi attho. Kodaṇḍakānīti dhanūni. Jīvatanti tumhākaṃ jīvantānaṃ mā muñcittha, āvudhahatthā dhāvitvā gaṇhatha nanti.

Herein, “Who indeed?” means “Where are these?” “In this” means in this hermitage. “Attendants” means the thieves. “Not seeing” means: he goes free because these thieves do not see him; or it means that having been freed from their hands, he goes unseen. “Bows” means bows. “While you live” means: do not release him while you are alive; run with weapons in hand and seize him.

Evaṃ tassa viravitvā aparāparaṃ dhāvantasseva rājā isīnaṃ assamaṃ patto. Tasmiṃ khaṇe isayo phalāphalatthāya gatā[P 4.0434]. Eko pupphakasuvova assamapade ṭhito hoti. So rājānaṃ disvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā paṭisanthāramakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, as he kept crying out and running back and forth, the king reached the hermitage of the seers. At that moment, the seers had gone out to gather fruits and roots. Only a parrot named Pupphaka was standing in the hermitage grounds. Seeing the king, he went out to meet him and offered a welcome. To clarify this matter, the Teacher uttered four stanzas:

170.

170.

“Athāparo paṭinandittha, suvo lohitatuṇḍako;

Svāgataṃ te mahārāja, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yaṃ idhatthi pavedaya.

“Then another rejoiced, a red-beaked parrot: ‘Welcome to you, great king, and your coming is not unwelcome. You have arrived as master; declare what you wish of what is here.’”

171.

171.

“Tiṇḍukāni [M 4.0436] piyālāni, madhuke kāsumāriyo;

Phalāni khuddakappāni, bhuñja rāja varaṃ varaṃ.

“Tinduka fruits, piyālas, madhukas, and kāsumārīs; these honey-like fruits, O king, eat the very best.”

172.

172.

“Idampi pānīyaṃ sītaṃ, ābhataṃ girigabbharā;

Tato piva mahārāja, sace tvaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

“This water, too, is cool, brought from a mountain cavern; drink from it, great king, if you so desire.”

173.

173.

“Araññaṃ uñchāya gatā, ye asmiṃ paricārakā;

Sayaṃ uṭṭhāya gaṇhavho, hatthā me natthi dātave”ti.

“Those who are my attendants here have gone to the forest to glean. Please get up yourself and take them, for I have no hands with which to give.”

Tattha paṭinanditthāti rājānaṃ disvāva tussi. Lohitatuṇḍakoti rattatuṇḍo sobhaggappatto[V 4.0393]. Madhuketi madhukaphalāni. Kāsumāriyoti evaṃnāmakāni phalāni, kāraphalāni vā. Tato pivāti tato pānīyamāḷato gahetvā pānīyaṃ piva. Ye asmiṃ paricārakāti mahārāja, ye imasmiṃ assame vicaraṇakā isayo, te araññaṃ uñchāya gatā. Gaṇhavhoti phalāphalāni gaṇhatha. Dātaveti dātuṃ.

Herein, “rejoiced” means he was pleased on seeing the king. “Red-beaked” means with a red beak, having attained beauty. “Madhukas” means madhuka fruits. “Kāsumārīs” means fruits of that name, or kāra fruits. “Drink from it” means: take water from the water-stand and drink. “Those who are my attendants here” means: O great king, those seers who dwell in this hermitage have gone to the forest to glean. “Take them” means: take the fruits and roots. “To give” means for giving.

Rājā tassa paṭisanthāre pasīditvā gāthādvayamāha –

The king, pleased with his welcome, spoke a pair of stanzas:

174.

174.

“Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Atheso itaro pakkhī, suvo luddāni bhāsati.

“This bird is truly excellent, a twice-born one, supremely righteous. But that other bird, the parrot, speaks cruel words.”

175.

175.

“‘Etaṃ hanatha bandhatha, mā vo muñcittha jīvataṃ’;

Iccevaṃ vilapantassa, sotthiṃ pattosmi assama”nti.

“‘Strike him, bind him, do not let him go alive!’ While it was wailing thus, I reached this hermitage in safety.”

Tattha itaroti corakuṭiyaṃ suvako. Iccevanti ahaṃ pana tassa evaṃ vilapantasseva imaṃ assamaṃ sotthinā patto.

Herein, “the other” is the parrot in the thieves’ hut. “Thus” means: while it was wailing in this way, I reached this hermitage in safety.

Rañño kathaṃ sutvā pupphako dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard the king’s speech, Pupphaka uttered two stanzas:

176.

176.

“Bhātarosma mahārāja, sodariyā ekamātukā;

Ekarukkhasmiṃ saṃvaḍḍhā, nānākhettagatā ubho.

“We are brothers, great king, from the same mother’s womb. We were raised in the same tree, but we both went to different fields.”

177.

177.

“Sattigumbo ca corānaṃ, ahañca isinaṃ idha;

Asataṃ so, sataṃ ahaṃ, tena dhammena no vinā”ti.

“Sattigumba is with the thieves, while I am here with the seers. He follows the unrighteous, I follow the righteous; from those ways we are not separate.”

Tattha [P 4.0435] bhātarosmāti mahārāja, so ca ahañca ubho bhātaro homa. Corānanti so corānaṃ santike saṃvaḍḍho, ahaṃ isīnaṃ santike[M 4.0437]. Asataṃ so, sataṃ ahanti so asādhūnaṃ dussīlānaṃ santikaṃ upagato, ahaṃ sādhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ. Tena dhammena no vināti mahārāja, taṃ sattigumbaṃ corā coradhammena corakiriyāya vinesuṃ, maṃ isayo isidhammena isisīlācārena, tasmā sopi tena coradhammena no vinā hoti, ahampi isidhammena no vinā homīti.

Herein, “we are brothers” means: great king, he and I are both brothers. “With the thieves” means: he was raised in the presence of thieves, I in the presence of seers. “He with the bad, I with the good” means: he has gone to the unrighteous and immoral, I to the righteous and virtuous. “From that nature we are not separate” means: great king, the thieves trained him in the thieves’ way, in the conduct of thieves; the seers trained me in the seers’ way, in the conduct and virtue of seers. Therefore he is not separate from that thieves’ way, and I am not separate from the seers’ way.

Idāni [V 4.0394] taṃ dhammaṃ vibhajanto gāthādvayamāha –

Now, analyzing that nature, he spoke a pair of stanzas:

178.

178.

“Tattha vadho ca bandho ca, nikatī vañcanāni ca;

Ālopā sāhasākārā, tāni so tattha sikkhati.

“There, striking and binding, deceit and cheating, plundering and violent deeds—these things he learns there.”

179.

179.

“Idha saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Āsanūdakadāyīnaṃ, aṅke vaddhosmi bhāradhā”ti.

“Here, truth and righteousness, non-harming, restraint, and taming; I have grown up in the lap of those who give seats and water, O Bhāradha.”

Tattha nikatīti patirūpakena vañcanā. Vañcanānīti ujukavañcanāneva. Ālopāti divā gāmaghātā. Sāhasākārāti gehaṃ pavisitvā maraṇena tajjetvā sāhasikakammakaraṇāni. Saccanti sabhāvo. Dhammoti sucaritadhammo. Ahiṃsāti mettāpubbabhāgo. Saṃyamoti sīlasaṃyamo. Damoti indriyadamanaṃ. Āsanūdakadāyīnanti abbhāgatānaṃ āsanañca udakañca dānasīlānaṃ. Bhāradhāti rājānaṃ ālapati.

Herein, ‘deceit’ (nikati) is cheating by means of a counterfeit. ‘Cheating’ (vañcanā) refers just to straightforward cheating. ‘Plundering’ (ālopa) is attacking a village by day. ‘Violent deeds’ (sāhasākāra) means entering a house, threatening with death, and committing violent acts. ‘Truth’ (sacca) means one's true nature. ‘Righteousness’ (dhamma) is the principle of good conduct. ‘Non-harming’ (ahiṃsā) has loving-kindness as its forerunner. ‘Restraint’ (saṃyama) is moral restraint. ‘Taming’ (dama) is the taming of the faculties. ‘Of those who give seats and water’ means of those who are in the habit of giving seats and water to guests. ‘O Bhāradha’ is an address to the king.

Idāni rañño dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Now, teaching the Dhamma to the king, he uttered these stanzas:

180.

180.

“Yaṃ yañhi rāja bhajati, santaṃ vā yadi vā asaṃ;

Sīlavantaṃ visīlaṃ vā, vasaṃ tasseva gacchati.

“Whomever one associates with, O king, whether a good person or a bad one, virtuous or unvirtuous, one falls under that one's power.”

181.

181.

“Yādisaṃ kurute mittaṃ, yādisaṃ cūpasevati;

Sopi tādisako hoti, sahavāso hi tādiso.

“Whatever kind of friend one makes, whatever kind of person one associates with, one becomes just like that, for association is of such a kind.”

182.

182.

“Sevamāno sevamānaṃ, samphuṭṭho samphusaṃ paraṃ;

Saro diddho kalāpaṃva, alittamupalimpati;

Upalepabhayā dhīro, neva pāpasakhā siyā.

“Associating with one who associates, being touched by one who touches another; like a poisoned arrow smears the quiver, it stains what was unstained. Fearing contamination, the wise person should never have a wicked friend.”

183.

183.

“Pūtimacchaṃ kusaggena, yo naro upanayhati;

Kusāpi pūti vāyanti, evaṃ bālūpasevanā.

“The man who wraps a rotten fish with kusa grass makes the kusa grass smell rotten too; such is association with a fool.”

184.

184.

“Tagarañca [V 4.0395][P 4.0436][M 4.0438] palāsena, yo naro upanayhati;

Pattāpi surabhi vāyanti, evaṃ dhīrūpasevanā.

“The man who wraps tagara in a palāsa leaf makes the leaf smell fragrant too; such is association with the wise.”

185.

185.

“Tasmā pattapuṭasseva, ñatvā sampākamattano;

Asante nopaseveyya, sante seveyya paṇḍito;

Asanto nirayaṃ nenti, santo pāpenti suggati”nti.

“Therefore, like a leaf-container, knowing one’s own ripening, the wise person should not associate with the bad but should associate with the good. The bad lead to hell; the good lead to a good destination.”

Tattha santaṃ vā yadi vā asanti sappurisaṃ vā asappurisaṃ vā. Sevamāno sevamānanti seviyamāno ācariyo sevamānaṃ antevāsikaṃ. Samphuṭṭhoti antevāsinā vā phuṭṭho ācariyo. Samphusaṃ paranti paraṃ ācariyaṃ samphusanto antevāsī vā. Alittanti taṃ antevāsikaṃ pāpadhammena alittaṃ so ācariyo visadiddho saro sesaṃ sarakalāpaṃ viya limpati. Evaṃ bālūpasevanāti bālūpasevī hi pūtimacchaṃ upanayhanakusaggaṃ viya hoti, pāpakammaṃ akarontopi avaṇṇaṃ akittiṃ labhati. Dhīrūpasevanāti dhīrūpasevī puggalo tagarādigandhajātipaliveṭhanapattaṃ viya hoti, paṇḍito bhavituṃ asakkontopi kalyāṇamittasevī guṇakittiṃ labhati. Pattapuṭassevāti duggandhasugandhapaliveṭhanapaṇṇasseva. Sampākamattanoti kalyāṇamittasaṃsaggavasena attano paripākaṃ paribhāvanaṃ ñatvāti attho. Pāpenti suggatinti santo sammādiṭṭhikā attānaṃ nissite satte saggameva pāpentīti desanaṃ yathānusandhimeva pāpesi.

Herein, ‘a good person or a bad one’ means a true person or an untrue person. ‘One who associates with an associate’ refers to the teacher being associated with who affects the student who is associating. ‘Touched’ means the teacher is touched by the student. ‘Touching another’ refers to the student touching the other, the teacher. ‘Smears the unsmeared’ means that teacher smears the student, who was unsmeared by evil qualities, just as a poisoned arrow smears the rest of the quiver. ‘Such is association with a fool’: for one who associates with a fool is like the kusa grass that wraps a rotten fish; even without doing a bad deed, one acquires a bad reputation and disrepute. ‘Such is association with the wise’: a person who associates with the wise is like the leaf that wraps tagara and other scents; even if unable to become a wise person, by associating with a good friend one acquires a reputation for good qualities. ‘Like a leaf-container’ refers to a leaf that wraps something foul-smelling or fragrant. ‘The consequence for oneself’ means having known one’s own ripening and development through association with a good friend. ‘Lead to a good destination’: the good, being of right view, lead the beings who depend on them to heaven itself. He delivered the teaching in line with this connection.

Rājā tassa dhammakathāya pasīdi, isigaṇopi āgato. Rājā isayo vanditvā “bhante, maṃ anukampamānā mama vasanaṭṭhāne vasathā”ti vatvā tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā nagaraṃ gantvā suvānaṃ abhayaṃ adāsi. Isayopi tattha agamaṃsu. Rājā isigaṇaṃ uyyāne vasāpento yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā saggapuraṃ pūresi. Athassa puttopi chattaṃ ussāpento isigaṇaṃ paṭijaggiyevāti tasmiṃ kulaparivaṭṭe satta rājāno isigaṇassa dānaṃ pavattayiṃsu. Mahāsatto araññe vasantoyeva yathākammaṃ gato.

The king was pleased with his Dhamma talk, and the group of seers also arrived. The king paid homage to the seers and said, “Venerable sirs, out of compassion for me, please dwell in my residence.” Having obtained their consent, he returned to the city and granted safety to the parrots. The seers also went there. The king, having settled the group of seers in a park, attended to them for life and filled the heavenly city. Then his son too, when raising the royal parasol, looked after the group of seers. In that family line, seven kings continued the giving to the group of seers. The Great Being, while still dwelling in the forest, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [M 4.0439] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi devadatto pāpo pāpaparivāroyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sattigumbo devadatto ahosi, corā devadattaparisā[P 4.0437], rājā ānando, isigaṇā buddhaparisā, pupphakasuvo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: “Thus, bhikkhus, in the past too Devadatta was wicked and had a wicked retinue.” Then he made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the parrot Sattigumba was Devadatta, the thieves were Devadatta’s assembly, the king was Ānanda, the group of seers was the Buddha’s assembly, but the parrot Pupphaka was myself.”

Sattigumbajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh, the Commentary on the Sattigumba Jātaka.

[504] 8. Bhallātiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[504] 8. The Commentary on the Bhallātiya Jātaka

Bhallātiyo [V 4.0396] nāma ahosi rājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mallikaṃ deviṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassā kira ekadivasaṃ raññā saddhiṃ sayanaṃ nissāya kalaho ahosi. Rājā kujjhitvā naṃ na olokesi. Sā cintesi “nanu tathāgato rañño mayi kuddhabhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti. Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā punadivase bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā rañño gehadvāraṃ gato. Rājā paccuggantvā pattaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ pāsādaṃ āropetvā paṭipāṭiyā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā paṇītenāhārena parivisitvā bhattakiccāvasāne ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā “kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, mallikā na paññāyatī”ti pucchitvā “attano sukhamadamattatāyā”ti vutte “nanu, mahārāja, tvaṃ pubbe kinnarayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā ekarattiṃ kinnariyā vinā hutvā satta vassasatāni paridevamāno vicarī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

There was a king named Bhallātiya. The Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Queen Mallikā. It is said that one day she had a quarrel with the king regarding the couch. The king became angry and would not look at her. She thought: ‘Surely the Tathāgata does not know the king's anger toward me.’ The Teacher, knowing the reason, on the following day, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, entered Sāvatthi for alms and went to the king’s palace door. The king went out to meet him, took his bowl, led the Teacher up into the palace, had the community of bhikkhus seated in order, gave the water of dedication, served them with exquisite food, and when the meal was over, sat down to one side. The Teacher asked: ‘Great king, why is Mallikā not to be seen?’ When he was told, ‘Because of her intoxication with her own prosperity,’ the Teacher said: ‘Great king, did you not in the past, having been born in a kinnara womb and being separated from a kinnarī for a single night, wander about lamenting for seven hundred years?’ Then, at the king's request, he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ bhallātiyo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kārento “aṅgārapakkamigamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ niyyādetvā sannaddhapañcāvudho susikkhitakoleyyakasuṇakhagaṇaparivuto nagarā nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā anugaṅgaṃ gantvā upari abhiruhituṃ asakkonto ekaṃ gaṅgaṃ otiṇṇanadiṃ disvā tadanusārena gacchanto migasūkarādayo vadhitvā aṅgārapakkamaṃsaṃ khādanto uccaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhi. Tattha ramaṇīyā nadikā paripuṇṇakāle thanapamāṇodakā hutvā sandati, aññadā jaṇṇukapamāṇodakā hoti. Tattha nānappakārakā macchakacchapā vicaranti. Udakapariyante [M 4.0440] rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇavālukā ubhosu tīresu nānāpupphaphalabharitavinamitā rukkhā pupphaphalarasamattehi nānāvihaṅgamabhamaragaṇehi samparikiṇṇā vividhamigasaṅghanisevitā sītacchāyā. Evaṃ ramaṇīyāya hemavatanadiyā tīre dve [P 4.0438] kinnarā aññamaññaṃ āliṅgitvā paricumbitvā nānappakārehi paridevantā rodanti.

In the past, when King Bhallātiya was ruling in Bārāṇasī, he thought, “I will eat charcoal-roasted game,” and entrusting the kingdom to his ministers, he armed himself with the five kinds of weapons, and surrounded by a pack of well-trained Koleyya hounds, he departed from the city. Entering the Himalayas, he went along the Ganges, but being unable to climb higher, he saw a river that flowed down into the Ganges and went along it. Killing deer, boars, and other animals, and eating the charcoal-roasted meat, he ascended to a high place. There a delightful little river flowed, which in the full season had water up to the breast, but at other times was only knee-deep. Various kinds of fish and turtles swam about in it. At the water’s edge was sand the color of a silver sheet, and on both banks were trees bent down, laden with various flowers and fruits, swarming with various flocks of birds and swarms of bees intoxicated with the nectar of the flowers and fruits, frequented by diverse herds of game, and offering cool shade. On the bank of this delightful Himalayan river, two kinnaras were embracing and kissing each other, and weeping and lamenting in various ways.

Rājā tassā nadiyā tīrena gandhamādanaṃ abhiruhanto te kinnare disvā “kiṃ nu kho ete evaṃ paridevanti, pucchissāmi ne”ti cintetvā sunakhe oloketvā accharaṃ pahari. Susikkhitakoleyyakasunakhā tāya saññāya gumbaṃ pavisitvā urena nipajjiṃsu. So tesaṃ paṭisallīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā dhanukalāpañceva sesāvudhāni ca rukkhaṃ nissāya ṭhapetvā padasaddaṃ akaronto saṇikaṃ tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃkāraṇā tumhe rodathā”ti kinnare pucchi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The king, while ascending Mount Gandhamādana along the bank of that river, saw those kinnaras and thought: “Why are they lamenting so? I will ask them.” Then, glancing at his dogs, he snapped his fingers. The well-trained Koleyya hounds, understanding that sign, entered a thicket and lay down on their chests. Knowing that they had become still, he leaned his bow and quiver and his other weapons against a tree and, making no sound with his footsteps, slowly went up to them and asked the kinnaras: “For what reason are you weeping?” To make this matter clear, the Teacher spoke three stanzas:

186.

186.

“Bhallātiyo [V 4.0397] nāma ahosi rājā, raṭṭhaṃ pahāya migavaṃ acāri so;

Agamā girivaraṃ gandhamādanaṃ, supupphitaṃ kimpurisānuciṇṇaṃ.

“There was a king named Bhallātiya, who left his realm and went on the hunt; he came to Gandhamādana, best of mountains, well-flowered and frequented by kimpurisas.

187.

187.

“Sāḷūrasaṅghañca nisedhayitvā, dhanuṃ kalāpañca so nikkhipitvā;

Upāgami vacanaṃ vattukāmo, yatthaṭṭhitā kimpurisā ahesuṃ.

“Having quieted the pack of hounds, and having laid down his bow and quiver, he approached, wishing to speak, to where the kimpurisas were standing.

188.

188.

“Himaccaye hemavatāya tīre, kimidhaṭṭhitā mantayavho abhiṇhaṃ;

Pucchāmi vo mānusadehavaṇṇe, kathaṃ vo jānanti manussaloke”ti.

“At winter’s end, on the bank of the Hemavatā, why do you stand here constantly conferring? I ask you, who have the appearance of human beings: how are you known in the world of humans?”

Tattha sāḷūrasaṅghanti sunakhagaṇaṃ. Himaccayeti catunnaṃ hemantamāsānaṃ atikkame. Hemavatāyāti imissā hemavatāya nadiyā tīre.

Herein, ‘the pack of hounds’ means the pack of dogs. ‘At winter’s end’ means at the passing of the four winter months. ‘Of the Hemavatā’ means on the bank of this river Hemavatā.

Rañño [M 4.0441] vacanaṃ sutvā kinnaro tuṇhī ahosi, kinnarī pana raññā saddhiṃ sallapi –

Hearing the king’s words, the male kinnara remained silent, but the female kinnarī conversed with the king:

189.

189.

“Mallaṃ giriṃ paṇḍarakaṃ tikūṭaṃ, sītodakā anuvicarāma najjo;

Migā [P 4.0439] manussāva nibhāsavaṇṇā, jānanti no kimpurisāti luddā”ti.

“We wander along the rivers of cool water: the Malla Giri, the Paṇḍaraka, and the Tikūṭa. Resembling humans in appearance, we are known to humans as kimpurisas, O hunter.”

Tattha mallaṃ girinti samma luddaka, mayaṃ imaṃ mallagiriñca paṇḍarakañca tikūṭañca imā ca najjo anuvicarāma. “Mālāgiri”ntipi pāṭho. Nibhāsavaṇṇāti nibhāsamānavaṇṇā, dissamānasarīrāti attho.

Herein, ‘Malla giri’: ‘Friend hunter, we wander about these rivers—the Malla Giri, the Paṇḍaraka, and the Tikūṭa—and these other rivers.’ There is also the reading ‘Mālāgiri’. ‘Nibhāsavaṇṇā’ means having a radiant complexion; the meaning is having a visible body.

Tato rājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke three stanzas:

190.

190.

“Sukiccharūpaṃ paridevayavho, āliṅgito cāsi piyo piyāya;

Pucchāmi vo mānusadehavaṇṇe, kimidha vane rodatha appatītā.

“You lament as if in great distress, yet your beloved is embraced by his dear one. I ask you, who have the appearance of human beings, why do you weep here in the forest, discontented?

191.

191.

“Sukiccharūpaṃ paridevayavho, āliṅgito cāsi piyo piyāya;

Pucchāmi vo mānusadehavaṇṇe, kimidha vane vilapatha appatītā.

“You lament as if in great distress, yet your beloved is embraced by his dear one. I ask you, who have the appearance of human beings, why do you wail here in the forest, discontented?

192.

192.

“Sukiccharūpaṃ [V 4.0398] paridevayavho, āliṅgito cāsi piyo piyāya;

Pucchāmi vo mānusadehavaṇṇe, kimidha vane socatha appatītā”ti.

“You lament as if in great distress, yet your beloved is embraced by his dear one. I ask you, who have the appearance of human beings, why do you grieve here in the forest, discontented?”

Tattha sukiccharūpanti suṭṭhu dukkhappattā viya hutvā. Āliṅgito cāsi piyo piyāyāti tayā piyāya tava piyo āliṅgito ca āsi. “Āliṅgiyo cāsī”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Kimidha vaneti kiṃkāraṇā idha vane antarantarā āliṅgitvā paricumbitvā piyakathaṃ kathetvā puna appatītā rodathāti.

Herein, ‘as if in great distress’ means as if having attained great suffering. ‘And your beloved is embraced by his dear one’ means: your beloved was embraced by you, his dear one. There is also the reading ‘Āliṅgiyo cāsī’; the meaning is the same. ‘Why here in the forest’ means: for what reason, here in the forest, after embracing and kissing from time to time, and speaking endearing words, do you again become discontented and weep?

Tato [M 4.0442] parā ubhinnampi ālāpasallāpagāthā honti –

Then follow the stanzas of conversation and discussion between the two:

193.

193.

“Mayekarattaṃ vippavasimha ludda, akāmakā aññamaññaṃ sarantā;

Tamekarattaṃ anutappamānā, socāma ‘sā ratti punaṃ na hossati’.

“We were separated for one night, O hunter, unwillingly, while remembering each other. Grieving over that one night, we lament, thinking: ‘That night will not come again.’”

194.

194.

“Yamekarattaṃ anutappathetaṃ, dhanaṃva naṭṭhaṃ pitaraṃva petaṃ;

Pucchāmi [P 4.0440] vo mānusadehavaṇṇe, kathaṃ vinā vāsamakappayittha.

“That you lament for one night as for lost wealth or a deceased father—I ask you, who have the appearance of human beings, how did you manage to live apart?”

195.

195.

“Yamimaṃ nadiṃ passasi sīghasotaṃ, nānādumacchādanaṃ selakūlaṃ;

Taṃ me piyo uttari vassakāle, mamañca maññaṃ anubandhatīti.

“This river that you see with its swift current, shaded by various trees, with rocky banks—my beloved crossed it during the rainy season, thinking, I believe, that he was following me.

196.

196.

“Ahañca aṅkolakamocināmi, atimuttakaṃ sattaliyothikañca;

‘Piyo ca me hehiti mālabhārī, ahañca naṃ mālinī ajjhupessaṃ’.

“And I was gathering aṅkola flowers, atimuttaka, and sattali-yothika, thinking: ‘My beloved will be a wearer of garlands, and I, adorned with garlands, will attend on him.’”

197.

197.

“Ahañcidaṃ kuravakamocināmi, uddālakā pāṭalisindhuvārakā;

‘Piyo ca me hehiti mālabhārī, ahañca naṃ mālinī ajjhupessaṃ’.

“And I was gathering these kuravaka, uddālaka, pāṭali, and sindhuvāraka flowers, thinking: ‘My beloved will be a wearer of garlands, and I, adorned with garlands, will attend on him.’”

198.

198.

“Ahañca sālassa supupphitassa, oceyya pupphāni karomi mālaṃ;

‘Piyo ca me hehiti mālabhārī, ahañca naṃ mālinī ajjhupessaṃ’.

“And having plucked flowers from the well-flowered sāla tree, I made a garland, thinking: ‘My beloved will be a wearer of garlands, and I, adorned with garlands, will attend on him.’”

199.

199.

“Ahañca sālassa supupphitassa, oceyya pupphāni karomi bhāraṃ;

Idañca no hehiti santharatthaṃ, yatthajjimaṃ viharissāma rattiṃ.

“And having plucked flowers from the well-flowered sāla tree, I made a bundle, thinking: ‘And this will be for our bedding, where we will spend this night.’”

200.

200.

“Ahañca [V 4.0399][M 4.0443] kho agaḷuṃ candanañca, silāya piṃsāmi pamattarūpā;

‘Piyo ca me hehiti rositaṅgo, ahañca naṃ rositā ajjhupessaṃ’.

“And indeed, I, in a state of heedlessness, was grinding aloe-wood and sandalwood on a stone, thinking: ‘My beloved will have his limbs anointed, and I, being anointed, will attend upon him.’”

201.

201.

“Athāgamā salilaṃ sīghasotaṃ, nudaṃ sāle salaḷe kaṇṇikāre;

Āpūratha [P 4.0441] tena muhuttakena, sāyaṃ nadī āsi mayā suduttarā.

‘Then the swift-flowing water came, carrying along the sāla, salaḷa, and kaṇṇikāra flowers. It filled up in a moment, and by evening the river became very difficult for me to cross.

202.

202.

“Ubhosu tīresu mayaṃ tadā ṭhitā, sampassantā ubhayo aññamaññaṃ;

Sakimpi rodāma sakiṃ hasāma, kicchena no āgamā saṃvarī sā.

‘We stood then on opposite banks, both of us gazing at each other. Now we would weep, now we would laugh; that night passed for us with great difficulty.

203.

203.

“Pātova kho uggate sūriyamhi, catukkaṃ nadiṃ uttariyāna ludda;

Āliṅgiyā aññamaññaṃ mayaṃ ubho, sakimpi rodāma sakiṃ hasāma.

‘Early in the morning, O hunter, when the sun had risen, having crossed the river at a shallow point, we both embraced each other. Now we would weep, now we would laugh.

204.

204.

“Tīhūnakaṃ satta satāni ludda, yamidha mayaṃ vippavasimha pubbe;

Vassekimaṃ jīvitaṃ bhūmipāla, ko nīdha kantāya vinā vaseyya.

‘It has been seven hundred years less three days, O hunter, since we were separated here before. This life is but a single century, O guardian of the earth; who here would live apart from his beloved?’

205.

205.

“Āyuñca vo kīvatako nu samma, sacepi jānātha vadetha āyuṃ;

Anussavā vuḍḍhato āgamā vā, akkhātha metaṃ avikampamānā.

‘And how long is your lifespan, friends? If you know it, please tell me. Whether by tradition or by what has come down from the elders, tell me this without hesitation.’

206.

206.

“Āyuñca no vassasahassaṃ ludda, na cantarā pāpako atthi rogo;

Appañca dukkhaṃ sukhameva bhiyyo, avītarāgā vijahāma jīvita”nti.

‘Our lifespan is a thousand years, O hunter, and no evil disease occurs in between. Suffering is little and happiness is much; still being not free from passion, we relinquish life.’

Tattha [M 4.0444] mayekarattanti mayaṃ ekarattaṃ. Vippavasimhāti vippayuttā hutvā vasimha. Anutappamānāti “anicchamānānaṃ no ekaratto atīto”ti taṃ ekarattaṃ anucintayamānā. Punaṃ na hessatīti puna na bhavissati nāgamissatīti socāma. Dhanaṃva naṭṭhaṃ pitaraṃva petanti dhanaṃ vā naṭṭhaṃ pitaraṃ vā mātaraṃ vāpetaṃ kālakataṃ kiṃ nu kho tumhe cintayamānā kena kāraṇena taṃ ekarattaṃ vinā vāsaṃ akappayittha, idaṃ me ācikkhathāti pucchati. Yamimanti yaṃ imaṃ. Selakūlanti dvinnaṃ selānaṃ antare sandamānaṃ. Vassakāleti ekassa meghassa uṭṭhāya vassanakāle[P 4.0442]. Amhākañhi imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe rativasena carantānaṃ eko megho uṭṭhahi. Atha me piyasāmiko kinnaromaṃ “pacchato āgacchatī”ti maññamāno etaṃ nadiṃ uttarīti āha.

Herein, ‘mayekarattanti’ means ‘we for one night.’ ‘Vippavasimhāti’ means ‘having been separated, we lived.’ ‘Anutappamānāti’ means ‘regretting, thinking, “Unwillingly, that one night has passed for us.”’ ‘Punaṃ na hessatīti’ means ‘“It will not happen again, it will not come again,” thus we grieve.’ ‘Dhanaṃva naṭṭhaṃ pitaraṃva petanti’ means he asks: ‘Like lost wealth or a deceased father or mother—what were you thinking, for what reason did you live apart for that one night? Tell me this.’ ‘Yamimanti’ means ‘this which.’ ‘Selakūlanti’ means ‘flowing between two rocks.’ ‘Vassakāleti’ means ‘at the time of rain, when a single cloud has arisen.’ She said: ‘For while we were wandering for pleasure in this forest grove, a single cloud arose. Then my beloved kinnara husband, thinking, “She is coming behind me,” crossed this river.’

Ahañcāti [V 4.0400] ahaṃ panetassa paratīraṃ gatabhāvaṃ ajānantī supupphitāni aṅkolakādīni pupphāni ocināmi. Tattha sattaliyothikañcāti kundālapupphañca suvaṇṇayothikañca ocinantī pana “piyo ca me mālabhārī bhavissati, ahañca naṃ mālinī hutvā ajjhupessa”nti iminā kāraṇena ocināmi. Uddālakā pāṭalisindhuvārakāti tepi mayā ocitāyevāti vadati. Oceyyāti ocinitvā. Agaḷuṃ candanañcāti kāḷāgaḷuñca rattacandanañca. Rositaṅgoti vilittasarīro. Rositāti vilittā hutvā. Ajjhupessanti sayane upagamissāmi. Nudaṃ sāle salaḷe kaṇṇikāreti etāni mayā ocinitvā tīre ṭhapitāni pupphāni nudantaṃ harantaṃ. Suduttarāti tassā hi orimatīre ṭhitakāleyeva nadiyā udakaṃ āgataṃ, taṅkhaṇaññeva sūriyo atthaṅgato, vijjulatā niccharanti, kinnarā nāma udakabhīrukā honti, iti sā otarituṃ na visahi. Tenāha “sāyaṃ nadī āsi mayā suduttarā”ti.

‘Ahañcāti’ means ‘but I, not knowing that he had gone to the far shore, was gathering fully bloomed flowers from the aṅkola tree and others.’ ‘Tattha sattaliyothikañcāti’ means ‘also gathering kundāla flowers and golden yothika flowers, thinking, “My beloved will wear this garland, and I, adorned with a garland, will approach him.”’ ‘Uddālakā pāṭalisindhuvārakāti’ means ‘those too were gathered by me, she says.’ ‘Oceyyāti’ means ‘having gathered.’ ‘Agaḷuṃ candanañcāti’ means ‘black aloe-wood and red sandalwood.’ ‘Rositaṅgoti’ means ‘his body anointed.’ ‘Rositāti’ means ‘having been anointed.’ ‘Ajjhupessanti’ means ‘I will approach him on the bed.’ ‘Nudaṃ sāle salaḷe kaṇṇikāreti’ means sweeping away and carrying off these flowers—sāla, salaḷa, and kaṇṇikāra—that had been gathered by me and placed on the shore. ‘Suduttarāti’ means ‘for when she stood on the near shore, the river’s water came, the sun set at that very moment, lightning flashed, and kinnaras are by nature afraid of water, so she was not able to enter it. Thus she said, “That evening, the river was very difficult for me to cross.”’

Sampassantāti vijjulatāniccharaṇakāle passantā. Rodāmāti andhakārakāle apassantā rodāma, vijjulatāniccharaṇakāle passantā hasāma. Saṃvarīti ratti. Catukkanti tucchaṃ. Uttariyānāti uttaritvā. Tīhūnakanti tīhi ūnāni satta vassasatāni. Yamidha mayanti yaṃ kālaṃ idha mayaṃ vippavasimha, so ito tīhi ūnakāni satta vassasatāni hontīti vadati. Vassekimanti vassaṃ ekaṃ imaṃ, tumhākaṃ ekameva vassasataṃ imaṃ jīvitanti vadati. Ko nīdhāti evaṃ parittake jīvite ko [M 4.0445] nu idha kantāya vinā bhaveyya, ayuttaṃ tava piyabhariyāya vinā bhavitunti dīpeti.

‘Sampassantāti’ means ‘seeing during the flashes of lightning.’ ‘Rodāmāti’ means ‘we weep, not seeing in the darkness; we laugh, seeing when the lightning flashes.’ ‘Saṃvarīti’ means ‘night.’ ‘Catukkanti’ means ‘shallow.’ ‘Uttariyānāti’ means ‘having crossed.’ ‘Tīhūnakanti’ means ‘seven hundred years less three.’ ‘Yamidha mayanti’ means he says: ‘The time since we were separated here is seven hundred years less three from now.’ ‘Vassekimanti’ means he says: ‘This life of yours is only one hundred years.’ ‘Ko nīdhāti’ means he explains: ‘In such a short life, who here would be without his beloved? It is unfitting for you to be without your dear wife.’

Kīvatako nūti rājā kinnariyā vacanaṃ sutvā “imesaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā “tumhākaṃ kittako āyū”ti pucchati. Anussavāti sace vo kassaci vadantassa vā sutaṃ, mātāpitūnaṃ vā vuḍḍhānaṃ mahallakānaṃ santikā āgamo atthi, atha me tato anussavā vuḍḍhato āgamā vā etaṃ avikampamānā akkhātha. Na cantarāti amhākaṃ vassasahassaṃ āyu, antarā ca no pāpako jīvitantarāyakaro rogopi natthi. Avītarāgāti aññamaññaṃ avigatapemāva hutvā.

‘Kīvatako nūti’: Hearing the kinnarī’s words, the king thought, “I will ask about their lifespan,” and he asked, “How long is your lifespan?” ‘Anussavāti’: He asks: ‘If you have heard anyone speaking, or if there is a tradition from your parents, the old, and the aged, then tell me this without wavering, based on that report or tradition from the elders.’ ‘Na cantarāti’: They reply: ‘Our lifespan is a thousand years, and in the meantime there is no evil disease that interrupts life.’ ‘Avītarāgāti’ means ‘being with unfailing love for one another.’

Taṃ sutvā rājā “ime hi nāma tiracchānagatā hutvā ekarattiṃ vippayogena satta vassasatāni rodantā vicaranti, ahaṃ pana tiyojanasatike rajje mahāsampattiṃ pahāya araññe vicarāmi, aho akiccakārimhī”ti tatova nivatto bārāṇasiṃ gantvā “kiṃ te, mahārāja, himavante [V 4.0401] acchariyaṃ diṭṭha”nti amaccehi [P 4.0443] puṭṭho sabbaṃ ārocetvā tato paṭṭhāya dānāni dadanto bhoge bhuñji. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā –

Hearing this, the king thought: ‘Even these animals, due to separation for a single night, wander weeping for seven hundred years; yet I, having abandoned great prosperity in a kingdom of three hundred yojanas, wander in the forest. Alas, I have done what should not be done!’ Then he turned back and went to Bārāṇasī. When asked by his ministers, ‘Great king, what marvel did you see in the Himalayas?’, he told them everything. From then on, he gave gifts and enjoyed his possessions. The Teacher, making this clear, said:

207.

207.

“Idañca sutvāna amānusānaṃ, bhallātiyo ittaraṃ jīvitanti;

Nivattatha na migavaṃ acari, adāsi dānāni abhuñji bhoge”ti. –

‘And having heard this from the non-humans, Bhallātiya, reflecting that life is brief, turned back and no longer went hunting; he gave gifts and enjoyed his wealth.’

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā puna ovadanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken this verse, the Teacher, further exhorting him, spoke these two verses:

208.

208.

“Idañca sutvāna amānusānaṃ, sammodatha mā kalahaṃ akattha;

Mā vo tapī attakammāparādho, yathāpi te kimpurisekarattaṃ.

‘And having heard this from the non-humans, live in harmony and do not quarrel. Let not the fault of your own actions torment you, just as that one night of separation tormented those kimpurisas.

209.

209.

“Idañca sutvāna amānusānaṃ, sammodatha mā vivādaṃ akattha;

Mā vo tapī attakammāparādho, yathāpi te kimpurisekaratta”nti.

‘And having heard this from the non-humans, live in harmony and do not dispute. Let not the fault of your own actions torment you, just as that one night of separation tormented those kimpurisas.’

Tattha [M 4.0446] amānusānanti kinnarānaṃ. Attakammāparādhoti attano kammadoso. Kimpurisekarattanti yathā te kimpurise ekarattiṃ kato attano kammadoso tapi, tathā tumhepi mā tapīti attho.

In this context, ‘amānusānaṃ’ refers to the kinnaras. ‘Attakammāparādho’ means the fault of one’s own action. ‘Kimpurisekarattaṃ’ means: just as the fault of their own action, involving a single night of separation, tormented those kimpurisas, so too let it not torment you—this is the meaning.

Mallikā devī tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā añjaliṃ paggayha dasabalassa thutiṃ karontī osānagāthamāha –

Queen Mallikā, having heard the Tathāgata’s Dhamma teaching, rose from her seat, raised her joined hands in reverence, and praised the Ten-Powered One, speaking this final verse:

210.

210.

“Vividhaṃ adhimanā suṇomahaṃ, vacanapathaṃ tava atthasaṃhitaṃ;

Muñcaṃ giraṃ nudaseva me daraṃ, samaṇa sukhāvaha jīva me cira”nti.

‘With a devoted mind, I listen to your varied words, which are full of benefit. Uttering your speech, you dispel my distress. O recluse, bringer of happiness, may you live long for my sake!’

Tattha vividhaṃ adhimanā suṇomahanti bhante, tumhehi vividhehi nānākāraṇehi alaṅkaritvā desitaṃ dhammadesanaṃ ahaṃ adhimanā pasannacittā hutvā suṇomi. Vacanapathanti taṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ vividhavacanaṃ. Muñcaṃ giraṃ nudaseva me daranti kaṇṇasukhaṃ madhuraṃ giraṃ muñcanto mama hadaye sokadarathaṃ nudasiyeva harasiyeva. Samaṇa [P 4.0444] sukhāvaha jīva me ciranti bhante buddhasamaṇa, dibbamānusalokiyalokuttarasukhāvaha mama sāmi dhammarāja, ciraṃ jīvāti.

In this context, ‘vividhaṃ adhimanā suṇomahaṃ’ means: ‘Venerable sir, with a devoted and clear mind, I listen to the Dhamma discourse taught by you, adorned with various reasons.’ ‘Vacanapathaṃ’ means the diverse speech uttered by you. ‘Muñcaṃ giraṃ nudaseva me daraṃ’ means: ‘Uttering speech that is sweet and pleasant to the ear, you surely remove the distress of sorrow from my heart.’ ‘Samaṇa sukhāvaha jīva me ciraṃ’ means: ‘Venerable Buddha-recluse, bringer of divine, human, worldly, and supramundane happiness, my lord, King of Dhamma, may you live long.’

Kosalarājā [V 4.0402] tato paṭṭhāya tāya saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasi.

From that time onward, the King of Kosala lived in harmony with her.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kinnaro kosalarājā ahosi, kinnarī mallikā devī, bhallātiyarājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: ‘At that time, the kinnara was the King of Kosala, the kinnarī was Queen Mallikā, and King Bhallātiya was I myself.’

Bhallātiyajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Eighth Commentary on the Bhallātiya Jātaka.

[505] 9. Somanassajātakavaṇṇanā

[505] 9. The Commentary on the Somanassa Jātaka

Ko taṃ hiṃsati heṭhetīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mama vadhāya parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Who harms and harasses you?’—This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him. Then the Teacher said, ‘Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past also, he schemed to kill me,’ and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 4.0447] kururaṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagare reṇu nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā mahārakkhito nāma tāpaso pañcasatatāpasaparivāro himavante ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya cārikaṃ caranto uttarapañcālanagaraṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā sapariso piṇḍāya caranto rājadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā isigaṇaṃ disvā iriyāpathe pasanno alaṅkatamahātale nisīdāpetvā paṇītenāhārena parivisitvā “bhante, imaṃ vassārattaṃ mama uyyāneyeva vasathā”ti vatvā tehi saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā vasanaṭṭhānāni kāretvā pabbajitaparikkhāre datvā vanditvā nikkhami. Tato paṭṭhāya sabbepi te rājanivesane bhuñjanti. Rājā pana aputtako puttaṃ pattheti, puttā nuppajjanti. Vassārattaccayena mahārakkhito “idāni himavanto ramaṇīyo, tattheva gamissāmā”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā raññā katasakkārasammāno nikkhamitvā antarāmagge majjhanhikasamaye maggā okkamma ekassa sandacchāyassa rukkhassa heṭṭhā taruṇatiṇapiṭṭhe saparivāro nisīdi.

In the past, when King Reṇu was ruling in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the Kuru country, an ascetic named Mahārakkhita, with a following of five hundred ascetics, lived for a long time in the Himalayas. Seeking salt and sour foods, he traveled and reached Uttarapañcāla. Staying in the royal park, he went for alms at the king’s gate with his retinue. The king, seeing the group of sages and pleased with their deportment, had them seated on a grand, adorned terrace and served them choice food. Then he said, ‘Venerable sirs, please dwell in my park for this rainy season.’ After speaking thus, he went with them to the park, had dwelling places built, provided the requisites for ascetics, paid homage, and departed. From then on, they all ate in the royal palace. The king, however, being childless, longed for a son, but no children were born to him. At the end of the rainy season, Mahārakkhita thought: ‘Now the Himalayas are delightful; we shall go there.’ Taking leave of the king, who paid him due honor and respect, he departed. Along the way, at midday, he turned off the road and sat down with his retinue beneath a densely shaded tree on a patch of fresh grass.

Tāpasā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “rājagehe vaṃsānurakkhito putto natthi, sādhu vatassa sace rājā puttaṃ labheyya, paveṇi ghaṭīyethā”ti. Mahārakkhito tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “bhavissati nu kho rañño [P 4.0445] putto, udāhu no”ti upadhārento “bhavissatī”ti ñatvā evamāha “mā bhonto cintayittha, ajja paccūsakāle eko devaputto cavitvā rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhissatī”ti. Taṃ sutvā eko kuṭajaṭilo “idāni rājakulūpako bhavissāmī”ti [V 4.0403] cintetvā tāpasānaṃ gamanakāle gilānālayaṃ katvā nipajjitvā “ehi gacchāmā”ti vutto “na sakkomī”ti āha. Mahārakkhito tassa nipannakāraṇaṃ ñatvā “yadā sakkosi, tadā āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā isigaṇaṃ ādāya himavantameva gato. Kuhakopi nivattitvā vegenāgantvā rājadvāre ṭhatvā “mahārakkhitassa upaṭṭhākatāpaso āgato”ti rañño ārocāpetvā raññā vegena pakkosāpito pāsādaṃ abhiruyha paññattāsane nisīdi. Rājā kuhakaṃ tāpasaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno isīnaṃ ārogyaṃ pucchitvā “bhante, atikhippaṃ nivattittha, vegena kenatthenāgatatthā”ti āha. “Āma, mahārāja, isigaṇo sukhanisinno ‘sādhu vatassa, sace rañño paveṇipālako putto uppajjeyyā’ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ahaṃ kathaṃ [M 4.0448] sutvā “bhavissati nu kho rañño putto, udāhu no”ti dibbacakkhunā olokento “mahiddhiko devaputto cavitvā aggamahesiyā sudhammāya kucchimhi nibbattissatī”ti disvā “ajānantā gabbhaṃ nāseyyuṃ, ācikkhissāmi nesa”nti tumhākaṃ kathanatthāya āgato. Kathitaṃ te mayā, gacchāmahaṃ, mahārājāti. Rājā “bhante, na sakkā gantu”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho pasannacitto kuhakatāpasaṃ uyyānaṃ netvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahitvā adāsi. So tato paṭṭhāya rājakule bhuñjanto vasati, “dibbacakkhuko”tvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi.

The ascetics started a discussion: “There is no son in the royal house to protect the lineage. It would be good if the king could have a son, so that the line of succession might be established.” Hearing their conversation, Mahārakkhita reflected, “Will the king have a son, or not?” Knowing that he would, he said: “Venerable sirs, do not worry. At dawn today, a deva-son will pass away and take rebirth in the womb of the king’s chief queen.” Hearing this, a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic thought, “Now I shall become a favorite of the royal family.” When the ascetics were leaving, he made a pretext of being ill and lay down. When told, “Come, let us go,” he replied, “I cannot.” Mahārakkhita, knowing the reason for his lying down, said, “When you are able, you may come,” and taking the company of seers, he went back to the Himalayas. The fraudulent ascetic turned back, went quickly to the king’s gate, and had it announced to the king: “An ascetic who attends on Mahārakkhita has arrived.” The king had him summoned quickly. He ascended to the palace and sat down on the prepared seat. The king paid homage to the fraudulent ascetic and, sitting to one side, inquired about the seers’ health and then asked: “Venerable sir, you have returned very quickly. For what purpose have you come in such a hurry?” “Yes, great king. The company of seers was comfortably seated when they started a discussion, saying: ‘It would be good if a son could be born to the king to protect the line of succession.’ Hearing this, I used my divine eye to investigate whether the king would have a son or not, and I saw that a deva-son of great power would pass away and be reborn in the womb of your chief queen, Sudhammā. I came to tell you this, thinking, ‘Lest they unknowingly destroy the embryo, I will inform them.’ I have told you. I will go now, great king.” The king, joyful, glad, and with a confident mind, said, “Venerable sir, you cannot go.” He led the fraudulent ascetic to the park, had a dwelling place prepared for him, and gave it to him. From then on, he lived there, eating at the royal court, and he became known as ‘the one with the divine eye.’”

Tadā bodhisatto tāvatiṃsabhavanā cavitvā tattha paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Jātassa cassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “somanassakumāro”tveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhati. Kuhakatāpasopi uyyānassa ekasmiṃ passe nānappakāraṃ sūpeyyasākañca valliphalāni ca ropetvā paṇṇikānaṃ hatthe vikkiṇanto dhanaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Bodhisattassa sattavassikakāle rañño paccanto [P 4.0446] kuppi. “Dibbacakkhutāpasaṃ mā pamajjī”ti kumāraṃ paṭicchāpetvā “paccantaṃ vūpasamessāmī”ti gato. Athekadivasaṃ kumāro “jaṭilaṃ passissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā kūṭajaṭilaṃ ekaṃ gaṇṭhikakāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ubhohi hatthehi dve udakaghaṭe gahetvā sākavatthusmiṃ udakaṃ āsiñcantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo attano samaṇadhammaṃ akatvā paṇṇikakammaṃ karotī”ti ñatvā “kiṃ karosi paṇṇikagahapatikā”ti taṃ lajjāpetvā avanditvāva nikkhami. Kūṭajaṭilo “ayaṃ idāneva evarūpo paccāmitto, ko jānāti kiṃ karissati, idāneva naṃ nāsetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā rañño āgamanakāle pāsāṇaphalakaṃ ekamantaṃ khipitvā pānīyaghaṭaṃ bhinditvā paṇṇasālāya tiṇāni vikiritvā sarīraṃ telena makkhetvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā mahādukkhappatto viya mañce nipajji. Rājā āgantvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nivesanaṃ apavisitvāva “mama sāmikaṃ dibbacakkhukaṃ [V 4.0404] passissāmī”ti paṇṇasāladvāraṃ gantvā taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti anto pavisitvā taṃ nipannakaṃ disvā pāde parimajjanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa world and took rebirth there. On the day of his naming ceremony, they named him Prince Somanassa. He grew up with the attendance befitting a prince. Meanwhile, the fraudulent ascetic planted various kinds of vegetables for curries and fruits from creepers on one side of the park and sold them to vegetable sellers, accumulating wealth. When the Bodhisatta was seven years old, the king's frontier revolted. Entrusting the prince [to the court] and saying, “Do not be heedless concerning the ascetic with the divine eye,” the king went to pacify the frontier. One day, the prince, thinking, “I will see the matted-hair ascetic,” went to the park. There he saw the fraudulent ascetic wearing a coarse ochre robe and another draped over him, carrying two water pots in both hands, and watering the vegetable plot. Knowing, “This fraudulent ascetic, neglecting his duty as a recluse, is doing the work of a vegetable seller,” he shamed him by saying, “What are you doing, you vegetable-selling householder?” and left without paying homage. The fraudulent ascetic thought, “He is already such an enemy. Who knows what he will do? It is proper to destroy him right now.” When the king was returning, the ascetic threw a stone slab to one side, broke a water pot, scattered grass in his leaf-hut, smeared his body with oil, entered the hut, covered himself from head to foot, and lay on the bed as if in great pain. The king arrived, circumambulated the city, and without even entering his own residence, thought, “I will see my master, the one with the divine eye.” Going to the door of the leaf-hut, he saw the disarray and wondered, “What can this be?” Entering inside, he saw him lying there and, stroking his feet, spoke the first verse:

211.

211.

“Ko [M 4.0449] taṃ hiṃsati heṭheti, kiṃ dummano socasi appatīto;

Kassajja mātāpitaro rudantu, kvajja setu nihato pathabyā”ti.

“Who harms you, who harasses you? Why are you dejected, grieving, and displeased? Whose mother and father shall weep today? Who shall lie slain upon the earth today?”

Tattha hiṃsatīti paharati. Heṭhetīti akkosati. Kvajja setūti ko ajja sayatu.

Herein, 'harms' means 'strikes'; 'harasses' means 'reviles'. 'Who shall lie today?' means 'who should lie down today?'.

Taṃ sutvā kūṭajaṭilo nitthunanto uṭṭhāya dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic got up, groaning, and spoke the second verse:

212.

212.

“Tuṭṭhosmi deva tava dassanena, cirassaṃ passāmi taṃ bhūmipāla;

Ahiṃsako [P 4.0447] reṇumanuppavissa, puttena te heṭhayitosmi devā”ti.

“I am pleased by the sight of you, Your Majesty; after a long time I see you, O protector of the earth. Though I am harmless, having entered the presence of Reṇu, I have been harassed by your son, O king.”

Ito parā uttānasambandhagāthā pāḷinayeneva veditabbā –

The following verses have a clear connection and are to be understood in accordance with the Pāli text itself.

213.

213.

“Āyantu dovārikā khaggabandhā, kāsāviyā yantu antepurantaṃ;

Hantvāna taṃ somanassaṃ kumāraṃ, chetvāna sīsaṃ varamāharantu.

“Let the sword-bearing doorkeepers come! Let the executioners go into the inner palace! Having slain Prince Somanassa and cut off his excellent head, let them bring it here.”

214.

214.

“Pesitā rājino dūtā, kumāraṃ etadabravuṃ;

Issarena vitiṇṇosi, vadhaṃ pattosi khattiya.

The messengers sent by the king said this to the prince: “You have been given up by the lord; you have come to your execution, O khattiya.”

215.

215.

“Sa rājaputto paridevayanto, dasaṅguliṃ añjaliṃ paggahetvā;

Ahampi icchāmi janinda daṭṭhuṃ, jīvaṃ maṃ netvā paṭidassayetha.

That prince, lamenting, raised his ten-fingered gesture of reverence and said: “I too wish to see the lord of men. Take me there alive and present me to him.”

216.

216.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, rañño puttaṃ adassayuṃ;

Putto ca pitaraṃ disvā, dūratovajjhabhāsatha.

Having heard his words, they presented the son to the king. And the son, seeing his father from afar, addressed him:

217.

217.

“Āgacchuṃ [M 4.0450] dovārikā khaggabandhā, kāsāviyā hantu mamaṃ janinda;

Akkhāhi me pucchito etamatthaṃ, aparādho ko nidha mamajja atthī”ti.

“The sword-bearing doorkeepers have come, the executioners, to kill me, O lord of men. Being asked, please explain this matter to me: what offense of mine is there here today?”

Tattha [V 4.0405] ahiṃsakoti ahaṃ kassaci ahiṃsako sīlācārasampanno. Reṇumanuppavissāti mahārāja reṇu, ahaṃ tava puttena mahāparivārena anupavisitvā “are kūṭatāpasa, kasmā tvaṃ idha vasasī”ti vatvā pāsāṇaphalakaṃ khipitvā ghaṭaṃ bhinditvā hatthehi ca pādehi ca koṭṭentena viheṭhitosmīti evaṃ so abhūtameva bhūtaṃ viya katvā rājānaṃ saddahāpesi. Āyantūti gacchantu. “Mama sāmimhi vippaṭipannakālato paṭṭhāya mayipi so na lajjissatī”ti kujjhitvā tassa vadhaṃ āṇāpento evamāha. Kāsāviyāti coraghātakā. Tepi pharasuhatthā attano vidhānena gacchantūti vadati. Varanti varaṃ sīsaṃ uttamasīsaṃ chinditvā āharantu.

Herein, 'O King Reṇu, he entered upon me' means: 'Great king Reṇu, I was intruded upon by your son with his great retinue, and after he said, “Hey, you fraudulent ascetic, why do you live here?” he threw a stone slab, broke a pot, and harassed me by striking me with his hands and feet.' In this way, making what was untrue seem as if it were true, he convinced the king. 'Let them come' means 'let them go.' Getting angry, thinking, 'Since he has acted wrongly toward my master, he will feel no shame toward me either,' the king ordered his execution, saying thus. 'Those in ochre robes' refers to the executioners. He says, 'Let them too, with axes in hand, go according to their procedure.' 'The excellent thing' means 'let them cut off his excellent head, his superior head, and bring it.'

Rājinoti bhikkhave, rañño santikā dūtā raññā pesitā vegena gantvā mātarā alaṅkaritvā attano aṅke nisīdāpitaṃ kumāraṃ parivāretvā etadavocuṃ. Issarenāti raññā. Vitiṇṇosīti pariccattosi. Sa rājaputtoti bhikkhave, tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjito mātu aṅkato uṭṭhāya so rājaputto[P 4.0448]. Paṭidassayethāti dassetha. Tassāti bhikkhave, te dūtā kumārassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā māretuṃ avisahantā goṇaṃ viya naṃ rajjuyā parikaḍḍhantā netvā rañño dassayuṃ. Kumāre pana nīyamāne dāsigaṇaparivutā saddhiṃ orodhehi sudhammāpi devī nāgarāpi “mayaṃ niraparādhaṃ kumāraṃ māretuṃ na dassāmā”ti tena saddhiṃyeva agamaṃsu. Āgacchunti tumhākaṃ āṇāya mama santikaṃ āgamiṃsu. Hantuṃ mamanti maṃ māretuṃ. Ko nīdhāti ko nu idha mama aparādho, yena maṃ tvaṃ māresīti pucchi.

Bhikkhus, 'from the king': the messengers sent by the king went quickly, surrounded the prince who had been adorned by his mother and seated on her lap, and said this. 'By the lord' means by the king. 'You have been given up' means you have been abandoned. 'That prince,' Bhikkhus: hearing their words, terrified by the fear of death, that prince rose from his mother's lap. 'Present me to him' means 'show me to him.' 'His,' Bhikkhus: hearing the prince's words, those messengers, unable to bring themselves to kill him, dragged him with a rope like an ox and presented him to the king. But as the prince was being led away, Queen Sudhammā with her harem and a retinue of female slaves, and the townspeople too, went along with him, saying, 'We will not allow the innocent prince to be killed.' 'They have come' means: 'By your command they have come into my presence.' 'To kill me' means 'to kill me.' 'What offense here' means he asked: 'What offense of mine is there here, for which you are having me killed?'

Rājā “bhavaggaṃ atinīcaṃ, tava doso atimahanto”ti tassa dosaṃ kathento gāthamāha –

The king, explaining his fault, said, "The summit of existence is very low; your fault is very great," and he spoke this verse:

218.

218.

“Sāyañca [M 4.0451] pāto udakaṃ sajāti, aggiṃ sadā pāricaratappamatto;

Taṃ tādisaṃ saṃyataṃ brahmacāriṃ, kasmā tuvaṃ brūsi gahappatī”ti.

Evening and morning he descends into the water; he always diligently attends to the fire. Why do you call such a restrained one, a celibate, a householder?

Tattha udakaṃ sajātīti udakorohaṇakammaṃ karoti. Taṃ tādisanti taṃ tathārūpaṃ mama sāmiṃ dibbacakkhutāpasaṃ kasmā tvaṃ gahapativādena samudācarasīti vadati.

Herein, 'descends into the water' means he performs the rite of descending to the water. 'Such a one': he is saying, 'Why do you address such a one as that—my master, the ascetic with the divine eye—with the term "householder"?'

Tato kumāro “deva, mayhaṃ gahapatiññeva ‘gahapatī’ti vadantassa ko doso”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the prince, saying, "Your Majesty, what fault is there in my calling one who is in fact a householder a 'householder'?" spoke this verse:

219.

219.

“Tālā [V 4.0406] ca mūlā ca phalā ca deva, pariggahā vividhā santimassa;

Te rakkhati gopayatappamatto, tasmā ahaṃ brūmi gahappatī”ti.

Palmyra palms, roots, and fruits, Your Majesty, various possessions are his. He guards and protects them diligently; that is why I call him a householder.

Tattha mūlāti mūlakādimūlāni. Phalāti nānāvidhāni valliphalāni. Te rakkhati gopayatappamattoti te esa tava kulūpakatāpaso paṇṇikakammaṃ karonto nisīditvā rakkhati, vatiṃ katvā gopayati appamatto, tena kāraṇena so tava brāhmaṇo gahapati nāma hoti.

Here, 'roots' means roots such as radishes and the like. 'Fruits' means various kinds of vine-fruits. 'He guards them and protects them diligently': this ascetic who serves your family, while doing his work as a green-grocer, sits down and guards them; having made a fence, he protects them diligently. For that reason, that brahmin of yours is called a householder.

Iti naṃ ahampi “gahapatī”ti kathesiṃ. Sace na saddahasi, catūsu dvāresu paṇṇike pucchāpehīti. Rājā pucchāpesi. Te [P 4.0449] “āma, mayaṃ imassa hatthato paṇṇañca phalāphalāni ca kiṇāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Paṇṇavatthumpi upadhārāpetvā paccakkhamakāsi. Paṇṇasālampissa pavisitvā kumārassa purisā paṇṇavikkayaladdhaṃ kahāpaṇamāsakabhaṇḍikaṃ nīharitvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā mahāsattassa niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā gāthamāha –

Thus, I too called him a 'householder.' If you do not believe me, have the green-grocers at the four gates questioned. The king had them questioned. They said, 'Yes, we buy leaves and various fruits from his hand.' He also had the vegetable garden investigated and made it evident. Entering his leaf-hut, the prince’s men brought out the bundle of coins and small change earned from selling leaves and showed it to the king. Realizing the Great Being's innocence, the king spoke this verse:

220.

220.

“Saccaṃ kho etaṃ vadasi kumāra, pariggahā vividhā santimassa;

Te rakkhati gopayatappamatto, sa brāhmaṇo gahapati tena hotī”ti.

“Truly, prince, you speak the truth. He has various possessions. He guards and protects them diligently; because of that, that brahmin is a householder.”

Tato mahāsatto cintesi “evarūpassa bālassa rañño santike vāsato himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajituṃ varaṃ, parisamajjheyevassa dosaṃ āvikatvā [M 4.0452] āpucchitvā ajjeva nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. So parisāya namakkāraṃ katvā gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being thought: 'Rather than living near such a foolish king, it is better to enter the Himalayas and go forth. Having revealed that deceitful ascetic's fault in the midst of the assembly, taken leave, and departed this very day, I will go forth.' Having paid homage to the assembly, he spoke this verse:

221.

221.

“Suṇantu mayhaṃ parisā samāgatā, sanegamā jānapadā ca sabbe;

Bālāyaṃ bālassa vaco nisamma, ahetunā ghātayate maṃ janindo”ti.

“Listen to me, assembled council, all you townspeople and countryfolk. This king is a fool, and having listened to a fool's word, the sovereign has me put to death without reason.”

Tattha bālāyaṃ bālassāti ayaṃ rājā sayaṃ bālo imassa bālassa kūṭajaṭilassa vacanaṃ sutvā ahetunāva maṃ ghātayateti.

Here, 'This fool, of a fool' means: this king, himself a fool, having heard the words of this foolish, deceitful matted-hair ascetic, has me put to death without any reason.

Evañca pana vatvā pitaraṃ vanditvā attānaṃ pabbajjāya anujānāpento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus and paid homage to his father, seeking permission for his own going forth, he spoke the other verse:

222.

222.

“Daḷhasmi mūle visaṭe virūḷhe, dunnikkayo veḷu pasākhajāto;

Vandāmi pādāni tava janinda, anujāna maṃ pabbajissāmi devā”ti.

“As bamboo with spreading branches, firmly rooted, widely spread and grown, is hard to pull out; I bow at your feet, O king; grant me leave, O sire, I will go forth.”

Tattha [V 4.0407] visaṭeti visāle mahante jāte. Dunnikkayoti dunnikkaḍḍhiyo.

Here, 'spread out' means: having become wide and great. 'Hard to extract' means difficult to pull out.

Tato [P 4.0450] parā rañño ca puttassa ca vacanapaṭivacanagāthā honti –

Then followed the verses of the exchange between the king and his son:

223.

223.

“Bhuñjassu bhoge vipule kumāra, sabbañca te issariyaṃ dadāmi;

Ajjeva tvaṃ kurūnaṃ hohi rājā, mā pabbajī pabbajjā hi dukkhā.

“Enjoy vast pleasures, prince; I grant you all sovereignty. Become the king of the Kurus this very day. Do not go forth, for the going forth is suffering.”

224.

224.

“Kinnūdha deva tavamatthi bhogā, pubbevahaṃ devaloke ramissaṃ;

Rūpehi saddehi atho rasehi, gandhehi phassehi manoramehi.

“What pleasures are there here of yours, O sire? I formerly delighted in the deva world with delightful forms, sounds, tastes, scents, and touches.”

225.

225.

“Bhuttā [M 4.0453] ca me bhogā tidivasmiṃ deva, parivārito accharānaṃ gaṇena;

Tuvañca bālaṃ paraneyyaṃ viditvā, na tādise rājakule vaseyyaṃ.

“I have enjoyed pleasures in the heaven of the Thirty-three, O sire, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs. And knowing you to be a fool led by others, I would not dwell in such a royal family.”

226.

226.

“Sacāhaṃ bālo paraneyyo asmi, ekāparādhaṃ khama putta mayhaṃ;

Punapi ce edisakaṃ bhaveyya, yathāmatiṃ somanassa karohī”ti.

“If I am a fool led by others, forgive me this one offense, my son. If such a thing should happen again, then, Somanassa, do as you see fit.”

Tattha dukkhāti tāta, pabbajjā nāma parapaṭibaddhajīvikattā dukkhā, mā pabbaji, rājā hohīti taṃ yāci. Kinnūdha devāti deva, ye tava bhogā, tesu kiṃ nāma bhuñjitabbaṃ atthi. Parivāritoti paricārito, ayameva vā pāṭho. Tassa kira jātissarañāṇaṃ uppajji, tasmā evamāha. Paraneyyanti andhaṃ viya yaṭṭhiyā parena netabbaṃ. Tādiseti tādisassa rañño santike na paṇḍitena vasitabbaṃ, mayā attano ñāṇabalena ajja jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, nāhaṃ tava santike vasissāmīti ñāpetuṃ evamāha. Yathāmatinti sace puna mayhaṃ evarūpo doso hoti, atha tvaṃ yathāajjhāsayaṃ karohīti puttaṃ khamāpesi.

Here, 'is suffering' means: 'Dear son, the going forth is suffering because it is a life dependent on others. Do not go forth; become king.' Thus he pleaded. 'What here, O deva' means: 'O deva, what is there to be enjoyed among your pleasures?' 'Surrounded' means attended on; or this is the reading. It is said that the knowledge of his past lives arose in him; therefore he spoke thus. 'Led by another' means: to be led by another with a stick, like a blind man. 'In such' means: a wise person should not live in the presence of such a king. He spoke thus to make it known: 'By the power of my own knowledge I have saved my life today; I will not live in your presence.' 'As you think fit' means: 'If such a fault occurs in me again, then act according to your inclination.' Thus he had his son forgive him.

Mahāsatto rājānaṃ ovadanto aṭṭha gāthā abhāsi –

The Great Being, advising the king, spoke eight verses:

227.

227.

“Anisamma [P 4.0451] kataṃ kammaṃ, anavatthāya cintitaṃ;

Bhesajjasseva vebhaṅgo, vipāko hoti pāpako.

“An action done without consideration, a thought conceived without deliberation; like the failure of a medicine, its result is evil.”

228.

228.

“Nisamma [V 4.0408] ca kataṃ kammaṃ, sammāvatthāya cintitaṃ;

Bhesajjasseva sampatti, vipāko hoti bhadrako.

“An action done with consideration, a thought conceived with proper deliberation; like the success of a medicine, its result is auspicious.”

229.

229.

“Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

“A lazy householder enjoying sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained one who has gone forth is not good. A king who acts without due consideration is not good; a wise person who is angry—that is not good.”

230.

230.

“Nisamma [M 4.0454] khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja, yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhati.

“A khattiya should act with consideration, not without consideration, O lord of the land. For the king who acts with consideration, honor and fame increase.”

231.

231.

“Nisamma daṇḍaṃ paṇayeyya issaro, vegā kataṃ tappati bhūmipāla;

Sammāpaṇīdhī ca narassa atthā, anānutappā te bhavanti pacchā.

“A ruler should impose punishment with consideration; a king regrets what is done in haste. And a person's aims that are rightly resolved do not lead to remorse afterwards.”

232.

232.

“Anānutappāni hi ye karonti, vibhajja kammāyatanāni loke;

Viññuppasatthāni sukhudrayāni, bhavanti buddhānumatāni tāni.

“Those who, having analyzed the grounds for action in the world, perform deeds that do not lead to remorse—deeds praised by the wise and yielding happiness—those deeds are approved by the enlightened.”

233.

233.

“Āgacchuṃ dovārikā khaggabandhā, kāsāviyā hantu mamaṃ janinda;

Mātuñca aṅkasmimahaṃ nisinno, ākaḍḍhito sahasā tehi deva.

“The gatekeepers came, sword-bearers, executioners to kill me, O lord of men. While I was sitting on my mother’s lap, I was suddenly dragged away by them, O King.”

234.

234.

“Kaṭukañhi sambādhaṃ sukicchaṃ patto, madhurampi yaṃ jīvitaṃ laddha rāja;

Kicchenahaṃ ajja vadhā pamutto, pabbajjamevābhimanohamasmī”ti.

“Truly, I have reached a bitter, oppressive, and most difficult state, O King, though the life I obtained was sweet and dear. Today, with difficulty, I have been freed from execution; my mind is now set only on the going forth.”

Tattha [P 4.0452] anisammāti anoloketvā anupadhāretvā. Anavatthāya cintitanti anavatthapetvā atuletvā atīretvā cintitaṃ. Vipāko hoti pāpakoti tassa hi yathā nāma bhesajjassa vebhaṅgo vipatti, evamevaṃ vipāko hoti pāpako. Asaññatoti kāyādīhi asaññato dussīlo. Taṃ na sādhūti taṃ tassa kodhanaṃ na sādhu. Nānisammāti anisāmetvā kiñci kammaṃ na kareyya. Paṇayeyyāti paṭṭhapeyya pavatteyya. Vegāti vegena sahasā. Sammāpaṇīdhī cāti yoniso ṭhapitena cittena katā narassa atthā pacchā anānutappā bhavantīti attho. Vibhajjāti “imāni kātuṃ yuttāni, imāni ayuttānī”ti evaṃ paññāya vibhajitvā. Kammāyatanānīti kammāni. Buddhānumatānīti paṇḍitehi anumatāni anavajjāni honti. Kaṭukanti [V 4.0409] deva[M 4.0455], kaṭukaṃ sambādhaṃ sukicchaṃ maraṇabhayaṃ pattomhi. Laddhāti attano ñāṇabalena labhitvā. Pabbajjamevābhimanohamasmīti pabbajjābhimukhacittoyevasmi.

Here, 'anisamma' (without consideration) means without looking into, without investigating. 'Anavatthāya cintitaṃ' (conceived without deliberation) means conceived without determining, without weighing, without judging. 'Vipāko hoti pāpako' (the result is evil) means: just as there is the failure or ruin of a medicine, even so the result is evil. 'Asaññato' (unrestrained) means unrestrained in body and so on, immoral. 'Taṃ na sādhu' means that anger of his is not good. 'Nānisamma' means one should not do any action without investigating it. 'Paṇayeyya' (should impose) means should establish or set in motion. 'Vegā' (in haste) means with haste, suddenly. 'Sammāpaṇīdhī ca' (and with right resolution) means: the aims of a person, undertaken with a mind wisely established, do not lead to later regret—this is the meaning. 'Vibhajjā' (having analyzed) means having analyzed with wisdom thus: 'These are fit to be done, these are unfit.' 'Kammāyatanāni' means actions. 'Buddhānumatāni' (approved by the enlightened) means approved by the wise; they are blameless. 'Kaṭukaṃ' means: O King, I have encountered the bitter, oppressive, and most difficult fear of death. 'Laddhā' means having obtained it by the power of his own knowledge. 'Pabbajjamevābhimanohamasmi' (my mind is set only on the going forth) means I am one whose mind is turned toward the going forth alone.”

Evaṃ mahāsattena dhamme desite rājā deviṃ āmantetvā gāthamāha –

Thus, when the Great Being had taught the Dhamma, the king addressed the queen and spoke this verse:

235.

235.

“Putto tavāyaṃ taruṇo sudhamme, anukampako somanasso kumāro;

Taṃ yācamāno na labhāmi svajja, arahasi naṃ yācitave tuvampī”ti.

“Sudhammā, this young son of yours, Prince Somanassa, is tender and pitiable. Though I entreat him today, I do not succeed; you too ought to entreat him.”

Tattha yācitaveti yācituṃ.

Here, 'yācitave' means 'to entreat'.

Sā pabbajjāyameva uyojentī gāthamāha –

She, urging him toward the going forth itself, spoke this verse:

236.

236.

“Ramassu bhikkhācariyāya putta, nisamma dhammesu paribbajassu;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ, anindito brahmamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

“Delight in the life of alms-gathering, my son; having reflected on the practices, go forth. Having laid down the rod toward all beings, blameless, one reaches the Brahma-state.”

Tattha nisammāti pabbajanto ca nisāmetvā micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ pabbajjaṃ pahāya sammādiṭṭhiyuttaṃ niyyānikapabbajjaṃ pabbaja.

Here, 'having reflected' means: when going forth, reflect, and having abandoned the going forth of those with wrong view, undertake the going forth that leads to release and is endowed with right view.

Atha rājā gāthamāha –

Then the king spoke a verse:

237.

237.

“Accherarūpaṃ vata yādisañca, dukkhitaṃ maṃ dukkhāpayase sudhamme;

Yācassu [P 4.0453] puttaṃ iti vuccamānā, bhiyyova ussāhayase kumāra”nti.

“How truly strange it is, Sudhammā! You afflict me even though I am already suffering. When told, ‘Entreat our son,’ you encourage the prince even more.”

Tattha yādisañcāti yādisaṃ idaṃ tvaṃ vadesi, taṃ acchariyarūpaṃ vata. Dukkhitanti pakatiyāpi maṃ dukkhitaṃ bhiyyo dukkhāpayasi.

Here, ‘yādisañca’ means this that you say is indeed astonishing. ‘Dukkhitaṃ’ means: you cause me, who am already suffering, even more suffering.”

Puna devī gāthamāha –

Again the queen spoke a verse:

238.

238.

“Ye [M 4.0456] vippamuttā anavajjabhogino, parinibbutā lokamimaṃ caranti;

Tamariyamaggaṃ paṭipajjamānaṃ, na ussahe vārayituṃ kumāra”nti.

“Those who are liberated, who enjoy blameless things, and who wander in this world fully cooled—I do not dare to restrain the prince who is entering upon that Noble Path.”

Tattha [V 4.0410] vippamuttāti rāgādīhi vippamuttā. Parinibbutāti kilesaparinibbānena nibbutā. Tamariyamagganti taṃ tesaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ santakaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjamānaṃ mama puttaṃ vāretuṃ na ussahāmi devāti.

Here, 'liberated' means liberated from lust and so on. 'Fully extinguished' means cooled by the full extinguishing of the defilements. 'That noble path' means: 'I do not dare to restrain my son who is practicing that path belonging to those noble ones, such as the Buddhas, O King.'

Tassā vacanaṃ sutvā rājā osānagāthamāha –

Having heard her words, the king spoke the concluding verse:

239.

239.

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Yesāyaṃ sutvāna subhāsitāni, appossukkā vītasokā sudhammā”ti.

“Truly, one should associate with the wise and the learned, those who reflect on many reasons. For having heard their well-spoken words, this Sudhammā has become free from anxiety and free from sorrow.”

Tattha bahuṭhānacintinoti bahukāraṇacintino. Yesāyanti yesaṃ ayaṃ. Somanassakumārasseva hi sā subhāsitaṃ sutvā appossukkā jātā, rājāpi tadeva sandhāyāha.

Here, 'those who reflect on many matters' means those who reflect on many reasons. 'Yesāyaṃ' means 'of whom this one.' For it was from hearing the well-spoken words of Prince Somanassa that she became free from anxiety, and the king too spoke with reference to that.

Mahāsatto mātāpitaro vanditvā “sace mayhaṃ doso atthi, khamathā”ti mahājanassa añjaliṃ katvā himavantābhimukho gantvā manussesu nivattesu manussavaṇṇenāgantvā devatāhi satta pabbatarājiyo atikkamitvā himavantaṃ nīto vissakammunā nimmitāya paṇṇasālāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Taṃ tattha yāva soḷasavassakālā rājakulaparicārikavesena devatāyeva upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Kūṭajaṭilampi mahājano pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Mahāsatto jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

The Great Being paid homage to his mother and father and, making the añjali gesture to the great crowd, said: 'If there is any fault in me, forgive me.' Then, facing the Himalayas, he departed. When the people had turned back, deities who had come in human form led him across seven mountain ranges to the Himalayas. There, in a leaf-hut created by Vissakamma, he went forth into the ascetic life. For sixteen years, deities attended on him there in the guise of royal household attendants. The great crowd beat the fraudulent ascetic to death. The Great Being, having developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal knowledges, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā [P 4.0454] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepesa mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kuhako devadatto ahosi, mātā mahāmāyā, mahārakkhito sāriputto, somanassakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: 'Thus, bhikkhus, in the past too this one strove for my murder.' Then he identified the birth: 'At that time the schemer was Devadatta, the mother was Mahāmāyā, Mahārakkhita was Sāriputta, and Prince Somanassa was none other than myself.'

Somanassajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Somanassa Jātaka, the Ninth.

[506] 10. Campeyyajātakavaṇṇanā

[506] 10. The Commentary on the Campeyya Jātaka.

Kā [M 4.0457] nu vijjurivābhāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathakammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “sādhu vo kataṃ upāsakā uposathavāsaṃ vasantehi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā nāgasampattiṃ pahāya uposathavāsaṃ vasiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Who shines like lightning?”—This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the observance of the Uposatha. For at that time the Teacher said: “It is good, lay followers, that you are observing the Uposatha. The wise of old, having abandoned the fortune of the nāgas, also observed the Uposatha.” Being entreated by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 4.0411] aṅgaraṭṭhe aṅge ca magadharaṭṭhe magadhe ca rajjaṃ kārente aṅgamagadharaṭṭhānaṃ antare campā nāma nadī, tattha nāgabhavanaṃ ahosi. Campeyyo nāma nāgarājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Kadāci magadharājā aṅgaraṭṭhaṃ gaṇhāti, kadāci aṅgarājā magadharaṭṭhaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ magadharājā aṅgena saddhiṃ yujjhitvā yuddhaparājito assaṃ āruyha palāyanto aṅgarañño yodhehi anubaddho puṇṇaṃ campānadiṃ patvā “parahatthe maraṇato nadiṃ pavisitvā mataṃ seyyo”ti asseneva saddhiṃ nadiṃ otari. Tadā campeyyo nāgarājā antodake ratanamaṇḍapaṃ nimminitvā mahāparivāro mahāpānaṃ pivati. Asso raññā saddhiṃ udake nimujjitvā nāgarañño purato otari. Nāgarājā alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ rājānaṃ disvā sinehaṃ uppādetvā āsanā uṭṭhāya “mā bhāyi, mahārājā”ti rājānaṃ attano pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā udake nimuggakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Rājā yathābhūtaṃ kathesi. Atha naṃ “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ahaṃ taṃ dvinnaṃ raṭṭhānaṃ sāmikaṃ karissāmī”ti assāsetvā sattāhaṃ mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhavitvā sattame divase magadharājena saddhiṃ nāgabhavanā nikkhami. Magadharājā nāgarājassānubhāvena aṅgarājānaṃ gahetvā jīvitā voropetvā dvīsu raṭṭhesu rajjaṃ kāresi. Tato paṭṭhāya rañño ca nāgarājassa ca vissāso thiro ahosi. Rājā anusaṃvaccharaṃ campānadītīre [P 4.0455] ratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā mahantena pariccāgena nāgarañño balikammaṃ karoti. Sopi mahantena parivārena nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā balikammaṃ sampaṭicchati. Mahājano nāgarañño sampattiṃ oloketi.

In the past, when the kings of Aṅga and Magadha were reigning in their respective kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, there was a river named Campā between the two territories. There was a nāga realm there, where a nāga king named Campeyya reigned. Sometimes the king of Magadha would conquer the Aṅga country, and sometimes the king of Aṅga would conquer the Magadha country. Then one day, the king of Magadha, having been defeated in battle with the king of Aṅga, mounted his horse and fled. Pursued by the Aṅgan king's soldiers, he reached the swollen Campā River and thought, 'It is better to die by entering the river than at the hands of the enemy,' and he plunged into the river along with his horse. At that time, the nāga king Campeyya had created a jeweled pavilion underwater and was drinking various beverages with his large retinue. The horse, with the king, sank into the water and descended before the nāga king. Seeing the king adorned and attired, the nāga king felt affection for him, rose from his seat, and said, 'Do not fear, great king.' He seated the king on his own couch and asked the reason for his plunge into the water. The king told him the truth. Then the nāga king reassured him, saying, 'Do not fear, great king, I will make you the lord of both kingdoms.' After the king had enjoyed great splendor for seven days, on the seventh day he left the nāga realm with the nāga king. By the power of the nāga king, the king of Magadha captured the king of Aṅga, deprived him of life, and reigned over both kingdoms. From then on, the friendship between the king and the nāga king was firm. Every year, the king had a jeweled pavilion built on the bank of the Campā River and made a great offering to the nāga king. The nāga king too would emerge from his realm with a large retinue to accept the offering. The people would behold the prosperity of the nāga king.

Tadā bodhisatto daliddakule nibbatto rājaparisāya saddhiṃ nadītīraṃ gantvā taṃ nāgarājassa sampattiṃ disvā lobhaṃ uppādetvā taṃ patthayamāno dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā campeyyanāgarājassa kālakiriyato sattame divase cavitvā tassa vasanapāsāde sirigabbhe sirisayanapiṭṭhe nibbatti[M 4.0458]. Sarīraṃ sumanadāmavaṇṇaṃ mahantaṃ ahosi. So taṃ disvā vippaṭisārī hutvā “mayā katakusalanissandena chasu kāmasaggesu issariyaṃ koṭṭhe paṭisāmitaṃ dhaññaṃ viya ahosi. Svāhaṃ imissā tiracchānayoniyā paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhiṃ, kiṃ me jīvitenā”ti maraṇāya cittaṃ uppādesi. Atha naṃ sumanā nāma nāgamāṇavikā disvā “mahānubhāvo satto nibbatto bhavissatī”ti sesanāgamāṇavikānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi, sabbā nānātūriyahatthā āgantvā tassa upahāraṃ kariṃsu. Tassa taṃ nāgabhavanaṃ sakkabhavanaṃ viya ahosi, maraṇacittaṃ paṭippassambhi, sappasarīraṃ vijahitvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito sayanapiṭṭhe nisīdi. Athassa tato paṭṭhāya yaso mahā ahosi.

At that time the Bodhisatta, born into a poor family, went to the riverbank with the king’s retinue. Seeing the prosperity of the nāga king, he conceived a craving for it. Aspiring to that state, he gave alms and observed the moral precepts; then, passing away on the seventh day after the death of the nāga king Campeyya, he was reborn in the nāga palace, in the splendid inner chamber upon a royal couch. His body was large and the color of a jasmine garland. Seeing his form, he was filled with distress, thinking: 'By the fruit of the wholesome deeds I have done, sovereignty in the six sensual heavens should have been mine, like grain stored in a granary. Yet I have taken rebirth in this animal womb. What use is this life to me?' And he formed the intention to die. Then a nāga maiden named Sumanā saw him and thought, 'A being of great power has been born here.' She signaled to the other nāga maidens, and they all came with various musical instruments and paid homage to him. To him, that nāga realm appeared like Sakka’s heavenly abode, and his thought of death subsided. Casting off his serpent body, he sat on the couch adorned with all ornaments. From that time onward, his glory and retinue were great.

So tattha nāgarajjaṃ kārento aparabhāge vippaṭisārī hutvā “kiṃ me imāya tiracchānayoniyā[V 4.0412], uposathavāsaṃ vasitvā ito muccitvā manussapathaṃ gantvā saccāni paṭivijjhitvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā tato paṭṭhāya tasmiṃyeva pāsāde uposathakammaṃ karoti. Alaṅkatanāgamāṇavikā tassa santikaṃ gacchanti, yebhuyyenassa sīlaṃ bhijjati. So tato paṭṭhāya pāsādā nikkhamitvā uyyānaṃ gacchati. Tā tatrāpi gacchanti, uposatho bhijjateva. So cintesi “mayā ito nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā manussalokaṃ gantvā uposathavāsaṃ vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya [P 4.0456] uposathadivasesu nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā ekassa paccantagāmassa avidūre mahāmaggasamīpe vammikamatthake “mama cammādīhi atthikā gaṇhantu, maṃ kīḷāsappaṃ vā kātukāmā karontū”ti sarīraṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā bhoge ābhujitvā nipanno uposathavāsaṃ vasati. Mahāmaggena gacchantā ca āgacchantā ca taṃ disvā gandhādīhi pūjetvā pakkamanti. Paccantagāmavāsino gantvā “mahānubhāvo nāgarājā”ti tassa upari maṇḍapaṃ karitvā samantā vālukaṃ okiritvā gandhādīhi pūjayiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya manussā mahāsatte pasīditvā pūjaṃ katvā puttaṃ patthenti, dhītaraṃ patthenti.

While ruling the nāga kingdom there, he later became remorseful and thought: 'What use is this animal birth to me?
