If I observe the Uposatha and am freed from here to reach the human world, I shall penetrate the Four Noble Truths and make an end of suffering.' From then on, he began to observe the Uposatha in that very palace. However, adorned nāga maidens would approach him, and his virtue was frequently broken. So from then on, he left the palace and went to the park. The maidens went there too, and his Uposatha observance was still broken. He reflected: 'It is right for me to leave this nāga realm and go to the human world to observe the Uposatha.' From then on, on Uposatha days, he would leave the nāga realm and lie down on top of an anthill near a border village, not far from the main road. Offering his body as a gift, he thought: 'Let those who desire my skin and so on take them; let those who wish to make me a performing snake do so.' Coiling his body, he would lie down and observe the Uposatha. Those traveling along the main road would see him, honor him with perfumes and flowers, and then depart. The inhabitants of the border village came and, saying, 'This is a mighty nāga king,' they built a pavilion over him, scattered sand all around, and honored him with perfumes and other offerings. From then on, people, placing their faith in the Great Being, made offerings and prayed for sons and daughters.

Mahāsattopi uposathakammaṃ karonto cātuddasīpannarasīsu vammikamatthake nipajjitvā pāṭipade nāgabhavanaṃ gacchati. Tassevaṃ uposathaṃ karontassa addhā vītivatto. Ekadivasaṃ sumanā aggamahesī āha “deva[M 4.0459], tvaṃ manussalokaṃ gantvā uposathaṃ upavasasi, manussaloko ca sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo, sace te bhayaṃ uppajjeyya, atha mayaṃ yena nimittena jāneyyāma, taṃ no ācikkhāhī”ti. Atha naṃ mahāsatto maṅgalapokkharaṇiyā tīraṃ netvā “sace maṃ bhadde, koci paharitvā kilamessati, imissā pokkharaṇiyā udakaṃ āvilaṃ bhavissati, sace supaṇṇo gahessati, udakaṃ pakkuthissati, sace ahituṇḍiko gaṇhissati, udakaṃ lohitavaṇṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti āha. Evaṃ tassā tīṇi nimittāni ācikkhitvā cātuddasīuposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā tattha gantvā vammikamatthake nipajji sarīrasobhāya vammikaṃ sobhayamāno. Sarīrañhissa rajatadāmaṃ viya setaṃ ahosi matthako rattakambalageṇḍuko viya. Imasmiṃ pana jātake bodhisattassa sarīraṃ naṅgalasīsapamāṇaṃ ahosi, bhūridattajātake (jā. 2.22.784 ādayo) ūruppamāṇaṃ, saṅkhapālajātake (jā. 2.17.143 ādayo) ekadoṇikanāvapamāṇaṃ.

The Great Being, while observing the Uposatha, would lie on the top of an anthill on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, and on the first day of the following fortnight he would go back to the nāga realm. As he was thus observing the Uposatha, a long time passed. One day, the chief queen named Sumanā said: 'Lord, you go to the human world to observe the Uposatha. The human world is loathsome and dangerous. If any danger should befall you, please tell us the sign by which we may know it.' Then the Great Being led her to the shore of the MaŅgala Lotus Pond and said: 'My queen, if someone should strike and harm me, the water of this pond will become turbid. If a supaᅁᅁa should seize me, the water will boil up. If a snake charmer should capture me, the water will turn the color of blood.' Having thus explained the three signs to Sumanā, and having undertaken the Uposatha of the fourteenth day, he left the nāga realm and went to the human world to lie on the top of an anthill, beautifying it with the radiance of his body. His body was as white as a silver chain, and his head was like a red woolen ball. In this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta’s body was the size of a plowshare; in the Bhũridatta Jātaka, it was the size of a thigh; and in the Saᅅkhapāla Jātaka, it was the size of a single-seater boat.

Tadā eko bārāṇasivāsī māṇavo takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike alampāyanamantaṃ [P 4.0457] uggaṇhitvā tena maggena attano gehaṃ gacchanto mahāsattaṃ disvā “imaṃ sappaṃ gahetvā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu kīḷāpento dhanaṃ uppādessāmī”ti cintetvā dibbosadhāni [V 4.0413] gahetvā dibbamantaṃ parivattetvā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Dibbamantasutakālato paṭṭhāya mahāsattassa kaṇṇesu ayasalākapavesanakālo viya jāto, matthako sikharena abhimatthiyamāno viya jāto. So “ko nu kho eso”ti bhogantarato sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā olokento ahituṇḍikaṃ disvā cintesi “mama visaṃ mahantaṃ, sacāhaṃ kujjhitvā nāsavātaṃ vissajjessāmi, etassa sarīraṃ bhasmamuṭṭhi viya vippakirissati, atha me sīlaṃ khaṇḍaṃ bhavissati, na dāni taṃ olokessāmī”ti. So akkhīni nimmīletvā sīsaṃ bhogantare ṭhapesi.

At that time, a young man living in Bārāᅁasġ went to Takkasilā, and after learning the Alampāyana art from a world-renowned teacher, he was returning to his home by that road when he saw the Great Being. He thought: 'I will capture this serpent and make it perform in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and thereby acquire wealth.' Taking divine herbs and reciting a spell that was like a divine spell, he approached the Great Being. From the moment he heard that divine-like spell, it was to the Great Being's ears as if an iron stake was being driven into them; his head felt as if it were being crushed by a peak. He thought, 'Who is this?' Raising his head from within his coils and looking around, he saw the snake-charmer and reflected: 'My venom is great. If I were to become angry and release a blast of air from my nostrils, his body would be scattered like a handful of ashes. But then my virtue would be broken. I will not look at this snake-charmer.' Having so decided, the Great Being closed his eyes and placed his head within his coils.

Ahituṇḍiko [M 4.0460] brāhmaṇo osadhaṃ khāditvā mantaṃ parivattetvā kheḷaṃ mahāsattassa sarīre opi, osadhānañca mantassa cānubhāvena kheḷena phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāne phoṭānaṃ uṭṭhānakālo viya jāto. Atha naṃ so naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā dīghaso nipajjāpetvā ajapadena daṇḍena uppīḷento dubbalaṃ katvā sīsaṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā nippīḷi, mahāsattassa mukhaṃ vivari. Athassa mukhe kheḷaṃ opitvā osadhamantaṃ katvā dante bhindi, mukhaṃ lohitassa pūri. Mahāsatto attano sīlabhedabhayena evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ adhivāsento akkhīni ummīletvā olokanamattampi nākari. Sopi “nāgarājānaṃ dubbalaṃ karissāmī”ti naṅguṭṭhato paṭṭhāyassa aṭṭhīni cuṇṇayamāno viya sakalasarīraṃ madditvā paṭṭakaveṭhanaṃ nāma veṭhesi, tantamajjitaṃ nāma majji, naṅguṭṭhaṃ gahetvā dussapothimaṃ nāma pothesi. Mahāsattassa sakalasarīraṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ ahosi. So mahāvedanaṃ adhivāsesi.

The snake-charmer brahmin, having prepared the medicine and recited the spell, spat on the Great Being’s body. Through the power of the medicine and the spell, wherever the spittle touched, it was as if blisters were rising. Then, grabbing the nāga king by the tail, the snake-charmer dragged him out, stretched him full length, and pressed down on him with a staff shaped like a goat's foot, weakening him. He seized the head firmly and squeezed it, forcing the Great Being’s mouth open. He then spat into his mouth, applied the medicine and the spell, and broke his fangs, filling his mouth with blood. Fearing the breaking of his virtue, the Great Being endured such severe suffering without even opening his eyes to look. Thinking, 'I will make the nāga king weak,' the brahmin crushed the Great Being’s entire body from the tail up as if grinding his bones, and bound him in the 'board-wrap'. He kneaded him with a technique like a weaver treading on sizing, and taking him by the tail, beat him as a laundryman thrashes clothes. The Great Being’s entire body became smeared with blood. He endured that great pain.

Athassa dubbalabhāvaṃ ñatvā vallīhi peḷaṃ [P 4.0458] karitvā tattha naṃ pakkhipitvā paccantagāmaṃ netvā mahājanamajjhe kīḷāpesi. Nīlādīsu vaṇṇesu vaṭṭacaturassādīsu saṇṭhānesu aṇuṃthūlādīsu pamāṇesu yaṃ yaṃ brāhmaṇo icchati, mahāsatto taṃtadeva katvā naccati, phaṇasataṃ phaṇasahassampi karotiyeva. Mahājano pasīditvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi. Ekadivasameva kahāpaṇasahassañceva sahassagghanake ca parikkhāre labhi. Brāhmaṇo āditova sahassaṃ labhitvā “vissajjessāmī”ti cintesi, taṃ pana dhanaṃ labhitvā “paccantagāmeyeva tāva me ettakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, rājarājamahāmaccānaṃ santike bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissāmī”ti sakaṭañca sukhayānakañca gahetvā sakaṭe parikkhāre ṭhapetvā sukhayānake nisinno mahantena parivārena mahāsattaṃ gāmanigamādīsu kīḷāpento “bārāṇasiyaṃ uggasenarañño santike kīḷāpetvā vissajjessāmī”ti agamāsi. So maṇḍūke māretvā nāgarañño deti. Nāgarājā “punappunaṃ esa maṃ nissāya māressatī”ti na khādati. Athassa madhulāje adāsi. Mahāsatto “sacāhaṃ bhojanaṃ [V 4.0414] gaṇhissāmi, antopeḷāya eva maraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti tepi na khādati. Brāhmaṇo māsamattena bārāṇasiṃ patvā dvāragāmesu kīḷāpento bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhi.

Then, knowing his weakness, the brahmin wove a basket of vines, put the nāga king inside, and took him to the frontier regions, where he made him perform in the midst of the people. In whatever colors such as blue, in whatever shapes such as round or square, and in whatever sizes small or large the brahmin desired, the Great Being performed just so and danced. He would display a hundred hoods or even a thousand hoods. The people were delighted and gave much wealth. In a single day, he received a thousand coins and requisites worth a thousand. At the beginning when he captured him, the brahmin thought: 'If I get a thousand coins, I will release him.' But having received that wealth, he thought: 'I have gained this much wealth even in a frontier village; I will get much more from the king and the king’s great ministers.' He took a wagon and a comfortable carriage, placed his wealth in the wagon, and sat in the carriage. With a large retinue, he made the Great Being perform in villages and market towns, thinking: 'I will make him perform before King Uggasena in Bārāᅁasġ, and then I will release him.' He killed frogs and gave them to the nāga king. The nāga king thought, 'This man will kill frogs repeatedly on my account,' and would not eat them. Then the brahmin gave him honeyed parched corn. The Great Being thought, 'If I were to take this food, I would die right here in the basket,' and did not eat that either. The brahmin reached Bārāᅁasġ in a month and gained much wealth by making him perform in the gate-villages.

Rājāpi [M 4.0461] naṃ pakkosāpetvā “amhākaṃ kīḷāpehī”ti āha. “Sādhu, deva, sve pannarase tumhākaṃ kīḷāpessāmī”ti. Rājā “sve nāgarājā rājaṅgaṇe naccissati, mahājano sannipatitvā passatū”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā punadivase rājaṅgaṇaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpesi. So ratanapeḷāya mahāsattaṃ netvā vicittatthare peḷaṃ ṭhapetvā nisīdi. Rājāpi pāsādā oruyha mahājanaparivuto rājāsane nisīdi. Brāhmaṇo mahāsattaṃ nīharitvā naccāpesi. Mahājano sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonto celukkhepasahassaṃ pavatteti. Bodhisattassa upari sattaratanavassaṃ vassati. Tassa gahitassa māso sampūri. Ettakaṃ kālaṃ nirāhārova ahosi. Sumanā [P 4.0459] “aticirāyati me piyasāmiko, idānissa idha anāgacchantassa māso sampuṇṇo, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti gantvā pokkharaṇiṃ olokentī lohitavaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ disvā “ahituṇḍikena gahito bhavissatī”ti ñatvā nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā vammikasantikaṃ gantvā mahāsattassa gahitaṭṭhānañca kilamitaṭṭhānañca disvā roditvā kanditvā paccantagāmaṃ gantvā pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājaṅgaṇe parisamajjhe ākāse rodamānā aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto naccantova ākāsaṃ oloketvā taṃ disvā lajjito peḷaṃ pavisitvā nipajji. Rājā tassa peḷaṃ paviṭṭhakāle “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti ito cito ca olokento taṃ ākāse ṭhitaṃ disvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king had the brahmin summoned and said: “Make him perform for us.” “Very well, Your Majesty. Tomorrow, on the fifteenth-day observance, I will make him perform for you.” The king had a drum beaten around the city, proclaiming: “Tomorrow the nāga king will dance in the royal courtyard. Let the great populace assemble and watch!” The next day, he had the royal courtyard decorated and summoned the brahmin. The brahmin brought the Great Being in a jeweled basket, placed the basket on a colorful rug, and sat down. The king, too, descended from the palace and, surrounded by a great retinue, sat on the royal throne. The brahmin brought out the Great Being and made him dance. The great crowd, unable to contain themselves, waved thousands of cloths in the air. A shower of the seven kinds of gems rained down upon the Bodhisatta. A month had passed since he had been captured, and all this time he had been without food. Sumanā thought: “My dear husband is long overdue. A full month has passed since he left and has not returned here. What could be the reason?” She went and looked at the lotus pond and saw that the water was the color of blood. Realizing, “He must have been captured by a snake-charmer,” she left the nāga abode and went to the anthill. There she saw the place where the Great Being had been captured and tormented. Weeping and wailing, she went to the frontier village, and after making inquiries and hearing what had happened, she went to Bārāṇasī. She stood weeping in the sky in the middle of the assembly in the royal courtyard. As the Great Being was dancing, he looked up into the sky and saw her. Feeling ashamed, he entered his basket and lay down. When he entered the basket, the king wondered, “What can be the reason for this?” Looking this way and that, he saw her standing in the sky and spoke the first verse:

240.

240.

“Kā nu vijjurivābhāsi, osadhī viya tārakā;

Devatā nusi gandhabbī, na taṃ maññāmī mānusi”nti.

“Who are you that shines like lightning, or like the star Osadhi? Are you a goddess or a gandhabbī? I do not think you are a human woman.”

Tattha na taṃ maññāmi mānusinti ahaṃ taṃ mānusīti na maññāmi, tayā ekāya devatāya gandhabbiyā vā bhavituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadati.

Herein, 'I do not think you are a human being' means: I do not regard you as a human woman; it is fitting that you should be a goddess or a gandhabbī.

Idāni tesaṃ vacanapaṭivacanagāthā honti –

Now follow their verses of dialogue:

241.

241.

“Namhi devī na gandhabbī, na mahārāja mānusī;

Nāgakaññāsmi bhaddante, atthenamhi idhāgatā.

“I am not a goddess, nor a gandhabbī, nor, O great king, am I a human woman. I am a nāga maiden, O noble one; I have come here for a purpose.”

242.

242.

“Vibbhantacittā [V 4.0415][M 4.0462] kupitindriyāsi, nettehi te vārigaṇā savanti;

Kiṃ te naṭṭhaṃ kiṃ pana patthayānā, idhāgatā nāri tadiṅgha brūhi.

“With a bewildered mind and distressed faculties, tears flow from your eyes. What have you lost, or what do you desire, that you have come here, O lady? Come, tell me.”

243.

243.

“Yamuggatejo uragoti cāhu, nāgoti naṃ āhu janā janinda;

Tamaggahī puriso jīvikattho, taṃ bandhanā muñca patī mameso.

“The one whom people call a serpent of fierce energy, whom they call a nāga, O lord of men—a man, seeking a livelihood, has captured him. Release him from his bonds; he is my husband.”

244.

244.

“Kathaṃ nvayaṃ balaviriyūpapanno, hatthattamāgacchi vanibbakassa;

Akkhāhi me nāgakaññe tamatthaṃ, kathaṃ vijānemu gahītanāgaṃ.

“How did he, endowed with such strength and energy, fall into the hands of a beggar? Tell me that, O nāga maiden; how are we to understand the capture of the nāga?”

245.

245.

“Nagarampi [P 4.0460] nāgo bhasmaṃ kareyya, tathā hi so balaviriyūpapanno;

Dhammañca nāgo apacāyamāno, tasmā parakkamma tapo karotī”ti.

“The nāga could reduce even a city to ashes, for he is indeed endowed with such strength and energy. But the nāga, respecting the Dhamma, exerts himself and performs ascetic practice.”

Tattha atthenamhīti ahaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca idhāgatā. Kupitindriyāti kilantindriyā. Vārigaṇāti assubindughaṭā. Uragoti cāhūti uragoti cāyaṃ mahājano kathesi. Tamaggahī purisoti ayaṃ puriso taṃ nāgarājānaṃ jīvikatthāya aggahesi. Vanibbakassāti imassa vanibbakassa kathaṃ nu esa mahānubhāvo samāno hatthattaṃ āgatoti pucchati. Dhammañcāti pañcasīladhammaṃ uposathavāsadhammañca garuṃ karonto viharati, tasmā iminā purisena gahitopi “sacāhaṃ imassa upari nāsavātaṃ vissajjessāmi, bhasmamuṭṭhi viya vikirissati, evaṃ me sīlaṃ bhijjissatī”ti sīlabhedabhayā parakkamma taṃ dukkhaṃ adhivāsetvā tapo karoti, vīriyameva karotīti āha.

Herein, for a purpose means: I have come here on account of a certain reason. Your faculties are agitated means: your faculties are weary. Torrents of water means: streams of teardrops. Whom they call a serpent means: this is what the great populace called him. A man has seized him means: this man seized that nāga king for the sake of his livelihood. Of a beggar is a question: How could this one, being so powerful, have fallen into the hands of this beggar? And the Dhamma means: he dwells revering the Dhamma of the five precepts and the observance of the Uposatha. Therefore, though captured by this man, he thinks: “If I release a blast from my nostrils upon him, he will be scattered like a handful of ashes, and thus my moral virtue will be broken.” Fearing the breaking of his moral virtue, he exerts himself, endures that suffering, and undertakes ascetic practice; that is, he makes a strenuous effort.

Rājā “kahaṃ paneso iminā gahito”ti pucchi. Athassa sā ācikkhantī gāthamāha –

The king asked: “But where was he captured by this man?” Then she, explaining it to him, spoke this verse:

246.

246.

“Cātuddasiṃ [M 4.0463] pañcadasiñca rāja, catuppathe sammati nāgarājā;

Tamaggahī puriso jīvikattho, taṃ bandhanā muñca patī mameso”ti.

“On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, O king, the nāga king keeps the fast at a crossroads. A man, seeking a livelihood, captured him there. Release him from his bonds; he is my husband.”

Tattha catuppatheti catukkamaggassa āsannaṭṭhāne ekasmiṃ vammike caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā uposathavāsaṃ vasanto nipajjatīti attho. Taṃ bandhanāti taṃ evaṃ dhammikaṃ guṇavantaṃ nāgarājānaṃ etassa dhanaṃ datvā peḷabandhanā pamuñca.

Herein, at a crossroads means: near a four-way path, at a certain anthill, having undertaken a determination endowed with four factors, he lies down observing the Uposatha. Release him from his bonds means: give wealth to this man and release that righteous and virtuous nāga king from his confinement in the basket.

Evañca [V 4.0416] pana vatvā punapi taṃ yācantī dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken thus, imploring him again, she recited two more verses:

247.

247.

“Soḷasitthisahassāni, āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Vārigehasayā nārī, tāpi taṃ saraṇaṃ gatā.

“Sixteen thousand women, adorned with jeweled earrings, dwelling in the watery palace—they too have gone to him for refuge.”

248.

248.

“Dhammena mocehi asāhasena, gāmena nikkhena gavaṃ satena;

Ossaṭṭhakāyo urago carātu, puññatthiko muñcatu bandhanasmā”ti.

“Release him righteously and without violence, by giving a village, a gold coin, and a hundred cows. Let the serpent go, with his body freed; let the one who seeks merit release him from his bonds.”

Tattha [P 4.0461] soḷasitthisahassānīti mā tvaṃ esa yo vā so vā daliddanāgoti maññittha. Etassa hi ettakā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā itthiyova, sesā sampatti aparimāṇāti dasseti. Vārigehasayāti udakacchadanaṃ udakagabbhaṃ katvā tattha sayanasīlā. Ossaṭṭhakāyoti nissaṭṭhakāyo hutvā. Carātūti caratu.

Herein, “sixteen thousand women”: Do not think, “This is some poor nāga or other.” For this shows that he has just this many women, adorned with every ornament, while his remaining wealth is immeasurable. “Dwelling in a water-house”: one accustomed to lying down there after making a water-covering, a water-chamber. “With body released”: having become one with body released. “Let it go”: let it wander.

Atha naṃ rājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the king spoke to her these three stanzas:

249.

249.

“Dhammena mocemi asāhasena, gāmena nikkhena gavaṃ satena;

Ossaṭṭhakāyo urago carātu, puññatthiko muñcatu bandhanasmā.

“I release him righteously and without violence, by giving a village, a gold coin, and a hundred cows. Let the serpent go, with his body freed; let the one who seeks merit release him from his bonds.”

250.

250.

“Dammi nikkhasataṃ ludda, thūlañca maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Catussadañca pallaṅkaṃ, umāpupphasarinnibhaṃ.

“I give you a hundred gold coins, O hunter, a large jeweled earring, and a throne with four cushions, of the color of flax flowers.”

251.

251.

“Dve [M 4.0464] ca sādisiyo bhariyā, usabhañca gavaṃ sataṃ;

Ossaṭṭhakāyo urago carātu, puññatthiko muñcatu bandhanasmā”ti.

“And two wives of similar beauty, a bull, and a hundred cows. Let the serpent go, with his body freed; let the one who seeks merit release him from his bonds.”

Tattha luddāti rājā uragaṃ mocetuṃ ahituṇḍikaṃ āmantetvā tassa dātabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ dassento evamāha. Gāthā pana heṭṭhā vuttatthāyeva.

Herein, “O hunter”: the king, in order to release the serpent, addressed the snake-charmer and spoke thus, indicating the gift that was to be given to him. The stanza, however, has the same meaning as stated above.

Atha naṃ luddo āha –

Then the hunter said to him:

252.

252.

“Vināpi [V 4.0417] dānā tava vacanaṃ janinda, muñcemu naṃ uragaṃ bandhanasmā;

Ossaṭṭhakāyo urago carātu, puññatthiko muñcatu bandhanasmā”ti.

“Even without the gift, O lord of men, at your word we will release the serpent from his bonds. Let the serpent go, with his body freed; let the one who seeks merit release him from his bonds.”

Tattha tava vacananti mahārāja, vināpi dānena tava vacanameva amhākaṃ garu. Muñcemu nanti muñcissāmi etanti vadati.

Herein, “your word”: “O great king, even without a gift, your word itself is authoritative for us.” “We will release it” means: he says, “I will release it.”

Evañca pana vatvā mahāsattaṃ peḷato nīhari. Nāgarājā nikkhamitvā pupphantaraṃ pavisitvā taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā māṇavakavaṇṇena alaṅkatasarīro hutvā pathaviṃ bhindanto viya nikkhanto aṭṭhāsi. Sumanā ākāsato otaritvā tassa santike ṭhitā. Nāgarājā añjaliṃ paggayha rājānaṃ namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tamatthaṃ [P 4.0462] pakāsento satthā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having said this, he brought the Great Being out of the basket. The nāga king emerged, went into a cluster of flowers, discarded his serpent form, and stood there with a decorated body in the guise of a young man, as if emerging by splitting the earth. Sumanā descended from the sky and stood beside him. The nāga king stood paying homage to the king with his hands raised in reverential salutation. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:

253.

253.

“Mutto campeyyako nāgo, rājānaṃ etadabravi;

Namo te kāsirājatthu, namo te kāsivaḍḍhana;

Añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmi, passeyyaṃ me nivesanaṃ.

“The freed nāga Campeyyaka said this to the king: 'Homage to you, O King of Kāsi! Homage to you, O Prosperity of Kāsi! I raise my joined hands to you; please visit my dwelling.'”

254.

254.

“Addhā hi dubbissasametamāhu, yaṃ mānuso vissase amānusamhi;

Sace ca maṃ yācasi etamatthaṃ, dakkhemu te nāga nivesanānī”ti.

“‘Truly, they say it is a difficult thing to trust when a human trusts a non-human. If you invite me for this purpose, O Nāga, we shall see your dwellings.’”

Tattha [M 4.0465] passeyyaṃ me nivesananti mama nivesanaṃ campeyyanāgabhavanaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ passitabbayuttakaṃ. Taṃ te ahaṃ dassetukāmo, taṃ sabalavāhano tvaṃ āgantvā passa, narindāti vadati. Dubbissasanti duvissāsanīyaṃ. Sace cāti sace maṃ yācasi, passeyyāma te nivesanāni, api ca kho pana taṃ na saddahāmīti vadati.

Herein, 'May you see my dwelling' means: 'My dwelling, the delightful Campeyya Nāga abode, is worth seeing. I wish to show it to you; you, O lord of men, should come with your army and see it,' he says. 'Difficult to trust' means hard to place confidence in. 'And if' means: 'If you invite me, we would see your dwellings, but yet I do not trust you,' he says.

Atha naṃ saddahāpetuṃ sapathaṃ karonto mahāsatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then, to make him believe, the Great Being, making an oath, spoke two stanzas:

255.

255.

“Sacepi vāto girimāvaheyya, cando ca suriyo ca chamā pateyyuṃ;

Sabbā ca najjo paṭisotaṃ vajeyyuṃ, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyyaṃ.

“Even if the wind were to carry away a mountain, and the moon and the sun were to fall to the earth; even if all the rivers were to flow upstream, never, O king, would I speak falsely.

256.

256.

“Nabhaṃ [V 4.0418] phaleyya udadhīpi susse, saṃvaṭṭaye bhūtadharā vasundharā;

Siluccayo meru samūlamuppate, na tvevahaṃ rāja musā bhaṇeyya”nti.

“Though the sky should split and even the ocean dry up, though the earth, the bearer of beings, should roll up, though Mount Meru, the mass of rock, be uprooted with its base—never, O king, would I speak falsely.”

Tattha saṃvaṭṭaye bhūtadharā vasundharāti ayaṃ bhūtadharāti ca vasundharāti ca saṅkhaṃ gatā mahāpathavī kilañjaṃ viya saṃvaṭṭeyya. Samūlamuppateti evaṃ mahāsinerupabbato samūlo uṭṭhāya purāṇapaṇṇaṃ viya ākāse pakkhandeyya.

In those verses, ‘though the earth, the bearer of beings, should roll up’: this great earth, known as both Bhūtadharā and Vasundharā, would roll up like a mat. ‘Be uprooted with its base’: the great Mount Sineru would rise up with its roots and leap into the sky like a dry leaf.

So mahāsattena evaṃ vuttepi asaddahanto –

But even when the Great Being had spoken thus, the king, still not believing, said:

257.

257.

“Addhā hi dubbissasametamāhu, yaṃ mānuso vissase amānusamhi;

Sace [P 4.0463] ca maṃ yācasi etamatthaṃ, dakkhemu te nāga nivesanānī”ti. –

“Indeed, they say it is difficult to trust when a human trusts in a non-human. If you invite me to this, we shall see your dwellings, O Naga.”

Punapi tameva gāthaṃ vatvā “tvaṃ mayā kataguṇaṃ jānituṃ arahasi, saddahituṃ pana yuttabhāvaṃ vā ayuttabhāvaṃ vā ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti pakāsento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken that same stanza again, he declared, “You ought to recognize the service I have done, but I shall know whether it is proper or improper to believe you,” and spoke this stanza:

258.

258.

“Tumhe [M 4.0466] khottha ghoravisā uḷārā, mahātejā khippakopī ca hotha;

Maṃkāraṇā bandhanasmā pamutto, arahasi no jānituye katānī”ti.

“You are indeed of dreadful and mighty venom; you are of great power and quick to anger. Freed from bondage on my account, you ought to recognize the deeds done by us.”

Tattha uḷārāti uḷāravisā. Jānituyeti jānituṃ.

Herein, “mighty” means: of mighty venom. “To know” means: to know.

Atha naṃ saddahāpetuṃ puna sapathaṃ karonto mahāsatto gāthamāha –

Then, to make him believe, the Great Being, again making an oath, spoke this stanza:

259.

259.

“So paccataṃ niraye ghorarūpe, mā kāyikaṃ sātamalattha kiñci;

Peḷāya baddho maraṇaṃ upetu, yo tādisaṃ kammakataṃ na jāne”ti.

“May he be tormented in a hell of dreadful form; may he find no bodily pleasure at all; bound in a basket, may he meet his death—he who does not recognize such a deed done for him.”

Tattha paccatanti paccatu. Kammakatanti katakammaṃ evaṃ guṇakārakaṃ tumhādisaṃ yo na jānāti, so evarūpo hotūti vadati.

In that stanza, ‘be tormented’ means let him be tormented. ‘Deed done’ refers to the deed done; he says, ‘Whoever does not recognize a benefactor like you who has performed such a service, may he become like this.’

Athassa rājā saddahitvā thutiṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Then the king, believing him, and wishing to give praise, spoke this stanza:

260.

260.

“Saccappaṭiññā [V 4.0419] tava mesa hotu, akkodhano hohi anupanāhī;

Sabbañca te nāgakulaṃ supaṇṇā, aggiṃva gimhesu vivajjayantū”ti.

“May this pledge of yours be true! Be free from anger, without malice. And may the Garudas avoid your entire Naga clan, as one avoids fire in the summer.”

Tattha tava mesa hotūti tava esā paṭiññā saccā hotu. Aggiṃva gimhesu vivajjayantūti yathā manussā gimhakāle santāpaṃ anicchantā jalamānaṃ aggiṃ vivajjenti, evaṃ vivajjentu dūratova pariharantu.

In that stanza, ‘may this pledge of yours be true’ means may this pledge of yours be true. ‘As one avoids fire in summer’ means just as people in the summer season, not wishing to be scorched, avoid a blazing fire, so may they avoid them and keep their distance.

Mahāsattopi rañño thutiṃ karonto itaraṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, too, wishing to praise the king, spoke this stanza:

261.

261.

“Anukampasī nāgakulaṃ janinda, mātā yathā suppiyaṃ ekaputtaṃ;

Ahañca te nāgakulena saddhiṃ, kāhāmi veyyāvaṭikaṃ uḷāra”nti.

“You have compassion for the Naga clan, O lord of men, as a mother for her beloved only son. And I, together with the Naga clan, will perform great service for you.”

Taṃ [P 4.0464][M 4.0467] sutvā rājā nāgabhavanaṃ gantukāmo senaṃ gamanasajjaṃ kātuṃ āṇāpento gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, wishing to go to the Naga abode, ordered his army to prepare for the journey and spoke this stanza:

262.

262.

“Yojentu ve rājarathe sucitte, kambojake assatare sudante;

Nāge ca yojentu suvaṇṇakappane, dakkhemu nāgassa nivesanānī”ti.

“Let them yoke the well-decorated royal chariots with well-trained mules from Kamboja. Let them also yoke the elephants with golden trappings. We shall see the dwellings of the Naga.”

Tattha kambojake assatare sudanteti susikkhite kambojaraṭṭhasambhave assatare yojentu.

In that stanza, ‘the well-trained mules from Kamboja’ means let them yoke the well-trained mules born in the country of Kamboja.

Itarā abhisambuddhagāthā –

The following are stanzas spoken after the Great Enlightenment:

263.

263.

“Bherī mudiṅgā paṇavā ca saṅkhā, avajjayiṃsu uggasenassa rañño;

Pāyāsi rājā bahu sobhamāno, purakkhato nārigaṇassa majjhe”ti.

“Kettledrums, hand-drums, small drums, and conches were sounded for King Uggasena. The king set out, shining with great beauty, surrounded in the midst of a host of women.”

Tattha bahu sobhamānoti bhikkhave, bārāṇasirājā soḷasahi nārīsahassehi purakkhato parivārito tassa nārīgaṇassa majjhe bārāṇasito nāgabhavanaṃ gacchanto ativiya sobhamāno pāyāsi.

In that stanza, ‘shining with great beauty’: O Bhikkhus, the king of Varanasi, surrounded by sixteen thousand women, set out from Varanasi for the Naga abode, shining exceedingly in the midst of that host of women.

Tassa nagarā nikkhantakāleyeva mahāsatto attano ānubhāvena nāgabhavanaṃ sabbaratanamayaṃ pākārañca dvāraṭṭālake ca dissamānarūpe katvā nāgabhavanagāmiṃ maggaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ māpesi[V 4.0420]. Rājā sapariso tena maggena nāgabhavanaṃ pavisitvā ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgañca pāsāde ca addasa. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

As soon as the king departed from the city, the Great Being, by his own power, made the Naga abode, including its ramparts and gate-towers, made entirely of the seven kinds of gems, visible, and he created an adorned and prepared road leading to the Naga abode. The king with his retinue entered the Naga abode by that road and saw the delightful grounds and the palaces. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

264.

264.

“Suvaṇṇacitakaṃ bhūmiṃ, addakkhi kāsivaḍḍhano;

Sovaṇṇamayapāsāde, veḷuriyaphalakatthate.

“The prosperer of the Kasis saw the ground strewn with golden sand, and palaces made of gold, paved with slabs of beryl.

265.

265.

“Sa rājā pāvisi byamhaṃ, campeyyassa nivesanaṃ;

Ādiccavaṇṇasannibhaṃ, kaṃsavijjupabhassaraṃ.

“That king entered the mansion, the dwelling of Campeyya, which resembled the color of the sun, gleaming like golden lightning.

266.

266.

“Nānārukkhehi [M 4.0468] sañchannaṃ, nānāgandhasamīritaṃ;

So pāvekkhi kāsirājā, campeyyassa nivesanaṃ.

“Covered with various trees, wafted with diverse scents, the king of the Kasis entered the dwelling of Campeyya.

267.

267.

“Paviṭṭhasmiṃ kāsiraññe, campeyyassa nivesanaṃ;

Dibbā tūriyā pavajjiṃsu, nāgakaññā ca naccisuṃ.

“When the king of the Kasis had entered the dwelling of Campeyya, divine musical instruments played and Naga maidens danced.

268.

268.

“Taṃ [P 4.0465] nāgakaññā caritaṃ gaṇena, anvāruhī kāsirājā pasanno;

Nisīdi sovaṇṇamayamhi pīṭhe, sāpassaye candanasāralitte”ti.

“The pleased king of the Kasis ascended to that mansion frequented by a host of Naga maidens. He sat down on a golden seat with a backrest, anointed with the essence of sandalwood.”

Tattha suvaṇṇacitakanti suvaṇṇavālukāya santhataṃ. Byamhanti alaṅkatanāgabhavanaṃ. Campeyyassāti nāgabhavanaṃ pavisitvā campeyyanāgarājassa nivesanaṃ pāvisi. Kaṃsavijjupabhassaranti meghamukhe sañcaraṇasuvaṇṇavijju viya obhāsamānaṃ. Nānāgandhasamīritanti nānāvidhehi dibbagandhehi anusañcaritaṃ. Caritaṃ gaṇenāti taṃ nivesanaṃ nāgakaññāgaṇena caritaṃ anusañcaritaṃ. Candanasāralitteti dibbasāracandanena anulitte.

In those verses, ‘strewn with gold’ means strewn with golden sand. ‘Mansion’ means the adorned Naga abode. ‘Of Campeyya’ means having entered the Naga abode, he entered the dwelling of the Naga king Campeyya. ‘Gleaming like golden lightning’ means shining like a golden lightning flash moving across the front of a cloud. ‘Wafted with various scents’ means pervaded by various kinds of divine scents. ‘Frequented by a host’ means that dwelling was frequented and pervaded by a host of Naga maidens. ‘Anointed with sandalwood essence’ means anointed with divine heartwood sandalwood.

Tattha nisinnamattassevassa nānaggarasaṃ dibbabhojanaṃ upanāmesuṃ, tathā soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ sesarājaparisāya ca. So sattāhamattaṃ sapariso dibbannapānādīni paribhuñjitvā dibbehi kāmaguṇehi abhiramitvā sukhasayane nisinno mahāsattassa yasaṃ vaṇṇetvā “nāgarāja, tvaṃ evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ pahāya manussaloke vammikamatthake nipajjitvā kasmā uposathavāsaṃ vasī”ti pucchi. Sopissa kathesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

There, as soon as he had sat down, they offered him divine food of various excellent flavors, and likewise to the sixteen thousand women and the rest of the royal retinue. Having enjoyed divine food and drink with his retinue for about a week and delighted in divine sensual pleasures, he sat on a comfortable couch, praised the glory of the Great Being, and asked: "O nāga king, having abandoned such prosperity, why did you lie on an anthill in the human world and observe the Uposatha?" The nāga king explained it to him. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

269.

269.

“So [V 4.0421] tattha bhutvā ca atho ramitvā, campeyyakaṃ kāsirājā avoca;

Vimānaseṭṭhāni imāni tuyhaṃ, ādiccavaṇṇāni pabhassarāni;

Netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"Having eaten and enjoyed himself there, the king of Kāsi then said to Campeyya: 'These are your excellent mansions, radiant and of the color of the sun. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'

270.

270.

“Tā [M 4.0469] kambukāyūradharā suvatthā, vaṭṭaṅgulī tambatalūpapannā;

Paggayha pāyenti anomavaṇṇā, netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke;

Kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"'These women, wearing golden bracelets and armlets, finely clothed, with rounded fingers and copper-red palms, of flawless beauty, hold out drinks to serve you. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'

271.

271.

“Najjo [P 4.0466] ca temā puthulomamacchā, āṭāsakuntābhirudā sutitthā;

Netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"'These rivers of yours teem with broad-scaled fish, are resonant with the calls of ospreys, and have fine bathing places. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'

272.

272.

“Koñcā mayūrā diviyā ca haṃsā, vaggussarā kokilā sampatanti;

Netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"'Curlews, peacocks, and divine swans, and sweet-voiced cuckoos fly about. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'

273.

273.

“Ambā ca sālā tilakā ca jambuyo, uddālakā pāṭaliyo ca phullā;

Netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"'Mangoes, sāla trees, tilaka trees, and rose-apples, uddālaka trees and pāṭali trees are in full bloom. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'

274.

274.

“Imā ca te pokkharañño samantato, dibbā ca gandhā satataṃ pavāyanti;

Netādisaṃ atthi manussaloke, kiṃ patthayaṃ nāga tapo karosi.

"'And these lotus ponds of yours are all around, and divine fragrances constantly waft. Nothing like this exists in the human world. What do you seek, O nāga, that you practice austerity?'"

275.

275.

“Na puttahetu na dhanassa hetu, na āyuno cāpi janinda hetu;

Manussayoniṃ abhipatthayāno, tasmā parakkamma tapo karomī”ti.

"‘Not for the sake of a son, not for the sake of wealth, nor for the sake of long life, O lord of men, but aspiring for human birth, I therefore strive and practice austerity.’"

Tattha tāti soḷasasahassanāgakaññāyo sandhāyāha. Kambukāyūradharāti suvaṇṇābharaṇadharā. Vaṭṭaṅgulīti pavāḷaṅkurasadisavaṭṭaṅgulī. Tambatalūpapannāti abhirattehi hatthapādatalehi samannāgatā. Pāyentīti [M 4.0470] dibbapānaṃ ukkhipitvā taṃ pāyenti. Puthulomamacchāti puthulapattehi nānāmacchehi samannāgatā. Āṭāsakuntābhirudāti āṭāsaṅkhātehi sakuṇehi abhirudā. Sutitthāti sundaratitthā. Diviyā ca haṃsāti dibbahaṃsā ca. Sampatantīti manuññaravaṃ ravantā rukkhato rukkhaṃ sampatanti. Dibbā ca gandhāti tāsu pokkharaṇīsu satataṃ dibbagandhā vāyanti. Abhipatthayānoti [V 4.0422] patthayanto vicarāmi. Tasmāti tena kāraṇena parakkamma vīriyaṃ paggahetvā tapo karomi, uposathaṃ upavasāmīti.

Herein, “they” refers to the sixteen thousand nāga maidens. “Wearing shell bracelets and armlets” means wearing golden ornaments. “With rounded fingers” means with fingers rounded like coral shoots. “Endowed with copper-red palms” means endowed with very red palms of hands and soles of feet. “They give to drink” means, lifting up a divine drink, they offer it to him to drink. “With broad-scaled fish” means endowed with various kinds of fish with broad scales. “Resonant with the calls of ospreys” means resonant with birds called ospreys. “With fine bathing places” means with beautiful bathing places. “And divine swans” means celestial swans. “They fly about” means, making a delightful sound, they fly from tree to tree. “And divine fragrances” means divine fragrances constantly waft in those lotus ponds. “Aspiring” means: I wander about aspiring. “Therefore” means: for that reason, having striven and exerted my energy, I practice austerity, that is, I observe the Uposatha.

Evaṃ vutte rājā āha –

When this was said, the king said:

276.

276.

“Tvaṃ lohitakkho vihatantaraṃso, alaṅkato kappitakesamassu;

Surosito lohitacandanena, gandhabbarājāva disā pabhāsasi.

"‘You, with red eyes, broad-shouldered, adorned, with well-trimmed hair and beard, well-anointed with red sandalwood, you illuminate the quarters like a king of the gandhabbas.’"

277.

277.

“Deviddhipattosi mahānubhāvo, sabbehi kāmehi samaṅgibhūto;

Pucchāmi taṃ nāgarājetamatthaṃ, seyyo ito kena manussaloko”ti.

"‘You have attained divine power, you are of great majesty, and you are endowed with all sensual pleasures. I ask you this matter, O nāga king: in what way is the human world better than this?’"

Tattha [P 4.0467] surositoti suvilitto.

Herein, ‘well-anointed’ means well-smeared.

Athassa ācikkhanto nāgarājā āha –

Then, explaining, the nāga king said:

278.

278.

“Janinda nāññatra manussalokā, suddhīva saṃvijjati saṃyamo vā;

Ahañca laddhāna manussayoniṃ, kāhāmi jātimaraṇassa anta”nti.

"‘O lord of men, not elsewhere than in the human world is purity or restraint found. And I, having obtained human birth, will make an end of birth and death.’"

Tattha suddhī vāti mahārāja, aññatra manussalokā amatamahānibbānasaṅkhātā suddhi vā sīlasaṃyamo vā natthi. Antanti manussayoniṃ laddhā jātimaraṇassa antaṃ karissāmīti tapo karomīti.

Herein, ‘purity or...’ means: O great king, apart from the human world, there is no purity—that is, the deathless, great Nibbāna—nor is there moral restraint. ‘An end’ means: ‘Having obtained human birth, I will make an end of birth and death’; it is for this reason that I practice austerity.

Taṃ sutvā rājā āha –

Hearing this, the king said:

279.

279.

“Addhā [M 4.0471] have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāriyo ca disvāna tuvañca nāga, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

"‘Indeed, one should associate with the wise, with the learned who reflect on many things. Having seen these women and you, O nāga, I will perform abundant meritorious deeds.’"

Tattha nāriyo cāti imā tava nāgakaññāyo ca tuvañca disvā bahūni puññāni karissāmīti vadati.

Herein, ‘and the women’ means: he is saying, ‘Having seen these nāga maidens of yours and you as well, I will perform many meritorious deeds.’

Atha [V 4.0423] naṃ nāgarājā āha –

Then the nāga king said to him:

280.

280.

“Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Nāriyo ca disvāna mamañca rāja, karohi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

"‘Indeed, one should associate with the wise, with the learned who reflect on many things. Having seen these women and me, O king, perform abundant meritorious deeds.’"

Tattha karohīti kareyyāsi, mahārājāti.

Herein, ‘perform’ means: ‘You should perform, O great king.’

Evaṃ vutte uggaseno gantukāmo hutvā “nāgarāja, ciraṃ vasimha, gamissāmā”ti āpucchi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “tena hi mahārāja, yāvadicchakaṃ dhanaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti dhanaṃ dassento āha –

When this was said, Uggasena, wishing to depart, took his leave, saying: "O nāga king, we have stayed a long time; we shall depart." Then the Great Being said to him, "Well then, great king, take as much wealth as you wish," and showing him the wealth, he said:

281.

281.

“Idañca me jātarūpaṃ pahūtaṃ, rāsī suvaṇṇassa ca tālamattā;

Ito haritvāna suvaṇṇagharāni, karassu rūpiyapākāraṃ karontu.

"‘Here is my abundant gold, and heaps of gold as high as palm trees. Take it from here and build golden mansions; let them build a silver rampart.’"

282.

282.

“Muttā [P 4.0468] ca vāhasahassāni pañca, veḷuriyamissāni ito haritvā;

Antepure bhūmiyaṃ santharantu, nikkaddamā hehiti nīrajā ca.

"‘Take from here five thousand loads of pearls mixed with beryl. Let them be strewn on the ground in your inner palace; it will become free of mud and dust.’"

283.

283.

“Etādisaṃ āvasa rājaseṭṭha, vimānaseṭṭhaṃ bahu sobhamānaṃ;

Bārāṇasiṃ nagaraṃ iddhaṃ phītaṃ, rajjañca kārehi anomapaññā”ti.

"‘Dwell in such a place, O best of kings, an excellent mansion, shining brightly. Rule the prosperous and thriving city of Bārāṇasī, O one of flawless wisdom.’"

Tattha [M 4.0472] rāsīti tesu tesu ṭhānesu tālapamāṇā rāsiyo. Suvaṇṇagharānīti suvaṇṇagehāni. Nikkaddamāti evaṃ te antepure bhūmi nikkaddamā ca nirajā ca bhavissati. Etādisanti evarūpaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ rajatapākāraṃ muttāveḷuriyasanthatabhūmibhāgaṃ. Phītanti phītaṃ bārāṇasinagarañca āvasa. Anomapaññāti alāmakapaññā.

Herein, heaps means heaps the size of palm trees in various places. Golden mansions means golden houses. Free of mud means: thus the ground in your inner palace will be free of mud and free of dust. Such means a place of this kind: golden, with a silver rampart, and a ground strewn with pearls and beryl. Thriving means: dwell in the thriving city of Bārāṇasī. Of flawless wisdom means of non-inferior wisdom.

Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā adhivāsesi. Atha mahāsatto nāgabhavane bheriṃ carāpesi “sabbā rājaparisā yāvadicchakaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādikaṃ dhanaṃ gaṇhantū”ti. Rañño ca anekehi sakaṭasatehi dhanaṃ pesesi. Rājā mahantena yasena nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā bārāṇasimeva gato. Tato paṭṭhāya kira jambudīpatalaṃ sahiraññaṃ jātaṃ.

The king, hearing his words, consented. Then the Great Being had a drum beaten throughout the nāga abode, announcing: "Let all the royal retinue take as much wealth—gold, silver, and so on—as they desire." He also sent treasure for the king in many hundreds of carts. The king, with great glory, departed from the nāga abode and went right to Bārāṇasī. From then on, it is said, the land of Jambudīpa became abundant in gold.

Satthā [V 4.0424] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ porāṇakapaṇḍitā nāgasampattiṃ pahāya uposathavāsaṃ vasiṃsū”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ahituṇḍiko devadatto ahosi, sumanā rāhulamātā, uggaseno sāriputto, campeyyanāgarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher said, “Thus the wise men of old, having abandoned the fortune of a nāga, observed the Uposatha,” and he identified the birth: “At that time the snake-charmer was Devadatta, Sumanā was Rāhula's mother, Uggasena was Sāriputta, and the Nāga king Campeyya was I myself.”

Campeyyajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Campeyya Jātaka, the tenth.

[507] 11. Mahāpalobhanajātakavaṇṇanā

[507] 11. The Commentary on the Mahāpalobhana Jātaka

Brahmalokā cavitvānāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto visuddhasaṃkilesaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vitthāritameva. Idha pana satthā “bhikkhu mātugāmo nāmesa visuddhasattepi saṃkiliṭṭhe karotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Having fallen from the Brahmā world...” The Teacher told this while dwelling in Jetavana concerning the defilement of a pure being. The story has been set out in detail below. Here, however, the Teacher, saying, “Bhikkhus, womankind, you know, can defile even pure beings,” related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 4.0469] bārāṇasiyanti cūḷapalobhane (jā. 1.3.37 ādayo) vuttanayeneva atītavatthu vitthāritabbaṃ. Tadā pana mahāsatto brahmalokā cavitvā kāsirañño putto hutvā nibbatti, anitthigandhakumāro nāma ahosi. Itthīnaṃ hatthe na saṇṭhāti, purisavesena naṃ thaññaṃ pāyenti, jhānāgāre vasati, itthiyo na passati. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

The story of the past should be elaborated in the same way as it was told in the Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka. At that time, however, the Great Being, having passed away from the Brahmā world, was reborn as the son of the king of Kāsi and was named Prince Anitthigandhakumāra. He would not stay in the hands of women, so they gave him milk to drink while disguised as men. He lived in a meditation chamber and did not see women. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke four verses:

284.

284.

“Brahmalokā [M 4.0473] cavitvāna, devaputto mahiddhiko;

Rañño putto udapādi, sabbakāmasamiddhisu.

“A devaputta of great psychic power, having fallen from the Brahmā world, arose as the son of a king who was endowed with all sensual pleasures.”

285.

285.

“Kāmā vā kāmasaññā vā, brahmaloke na vijjati;

Svāssu tāyeva saññāya, kāmehi vijigucchatha.

“Neither sensual pleasures nor the perception of sensual pleasures exist in the Brahmā world; and he, through that very perception, felt revulsion for sensual pleasures.”

286.

286.

“Tassa cantepure āsi, jhānāgāraṃ sumāpitaṃ;

So tattha paṭisallīno, eko rahasi jhāyatha.

“In his inner palace there was a well-made meditation chamber. There, secluded, he would meditate alone in private.”

287.

287.

“Sa rājā paridevesi, puttasokena aṭṭito;

Ekaputto cayaṃ mayhaṃ, na ca kāmāni bhuñjatī”ti.

“That king lamented, afflicted by grief for his son: ‘This is my only son, and he does not enjoy sensual pleasures.’”

Tattha [V 4.0425] sabbakāmasamiddhisūti sabbakāmānaṃ samiddhīsu sampattīsu ṭhitassa rañño putto hutvā eko devaputto nibbatti. Svāssūti so kumāro. Tāyevāti tāya brahmaloke nibbattitāya jhānasaññāya eva. Sumāpitanti pitarā suṭṭhu manāpaṃ katvā māpitaṃ. Rahasi jhāyathāti mātugāmaṃ apassanto vasi. Paridevesīti vilapi.

Herein, 'amidst the fulfillment of all sensual pleasures' means: a devaputta was reborn as the son of a king who was established in the abundance and attainment of all sensual pleasures. 'He' refers to that prince. 'Through that very...' means: through that very perception of jhāna that had arisen in the Brahmā world. 'Well-made' means made very pleasingly by his father. 'He would meditate in private' means he lived without seeing womankind. 'He lamented' means he wailed.

Pañcamā rañño paridevanagāthā –

The fifth verse is the king's lamentation:

288.

288.

“Ko nu khvettha upāyo so, ko vā jānāti kiñcanaṃ;

Yo me puttaṃ palobheyya, yathā kāmāni patthaye”ti.

“What now is the means here, or who knows of any, that could entice my son so that he might desire sensual pleasures?”

Tattha ko nu khvettha upāyoti ko nu kho ettha etassa kāmānaṃ bhuñjanaupāyo. “Ko nu kho idhupāyo so”tipi pāṭho, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ko nu kho etaṃ upavasitvā upalāpanakāraṇaṃ jānātī”ti vuttaṃ. Ko vā jānāti kiñcananti ko vā etassa palibodhakāraṇaṃ jānātīti attho.

Here, 'what indeed is the means in this matter' means what indeed is the means here for him to enjoy these sensual pleasures? The reading “What indeed is the means here?” is also found. In the commentary, however, it is said: “Who indeed, having approached this one, knows the reason for coaxing?” Or, 'who knows of any kiñcanaṃ' means: who knows the reason for his impediment? The meaning is: who knows the cause of this obstruction?

Tato paraṃ diyaḍḍhagāthā abhisambuddhagāthā –

After that, there are one and a half verses spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One:

289.

289.

“Ahu kumārī tattheva, vaṇṇarūpasamāhitā;

Kusalā naccagītassa, vādite ca padakkhiṇā.

“There was a maiden right there, endowed with beauty and form, skilled in dance and song, and adept at playing instruments.”

290.

290.

“Sā [M 4.0474] tattha upasaṅkamma, rājānaṃ etadabravī”ti;

“Having approached the king there, she said this:”

Tattha [P 4.0470] ahūti bhikkhave, tattheva antepure cūḷanāṭakānaṃ antare ekā taruṇakumārikā ahosi. Padakkhiṇāti susikkhitā.

Here, bhikkhus, “there was” means: right there in the inner palace, among the young dancers, there was a young maiden. “Adept” means well-trained.

“Ahaṃ kho naṃ palobheyyaṃ, sace bhattā bhavissatī”ti. –

“I would indeed entice him, if he would become my husband.”

Upaḍḍhagāthā kumārikāya vuttā.

A half-verse was spoken by the maiden.

Tattha sace bhattāti sace esa mayhaṃ pati bhavissatīti.

Here, “if he would be my husband” means: if he would become my lord.

291.

291.

“Taṃ [V 4.0426] tathāvādiniṃ rājā, kumāriṃ etadabravi;

Tvaññeva naṃ palobhehi, tava bhattā bhavissatīti.

“To the maiden who spoke thus, the king said this: ‘You yourself entice him; he will be your husband.’”

Tattha tava bhattāti tavesa pati bhavissati, tvaññeva tassa aggamahesī bhavissasi, gaccha naṃ palobhehi, kāmarasaṃ jānāpehīti.

Here, “he will be your husband” means: he will become your lord, and you yourself will be his chief queen. Go, entice him, make him know the taste of sensual pleasure.

Evaṃ vatvā rājā “imissā kira okāsaṃ karontū”ti kumārassa upaṭṭhākānaṃ pesesi. Sā paccūsakāle vīṇaṃ ādāya gantvā kumārassa sayanagabbhassa bahi avidūre ṭhatvā agganakhehi vīṇaṃ vādentī madhurasarena gāyitvā taṃ palobhesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having spoken thus, the king sent a message to the prince’s attendants, saying, “Let them make an opportunity for her.” At dawn, she took her lute and went and stood not far outside the prince’s bedchamber. Playing the lute with the tips of her nails and singing with a sweet voice, she enticed him. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said:

292.

292.

“Sā ca antepuraṃ gantvā, bahuṃ kāmupasaṃhitaṃ;

Hadayaṅgamā pemanīyā, citrā gāthā abhāsatha.

“And she, having gone to the inner palace, sang many varied verses connected with sensual pleasure, heart-touching and endearing.”

293.

293.

“Tassā ca gāyamānāya, saddaṃ sutvāna nāriyā;

Kāmacchandassa uppajji, janaṃ so paripucchatha.

“Having heard the sound of that woman singing, sensual desire arose in him, and he questioned the people.”

294.

294.

“Kasseso saddo ko vā so, bhaṇati uccāvacaṃ bahuṃ;

Hadayaṅgamaṃ pemanīyaṃ, aho kaṇṇasukhaṃ mama.

“Whose sound is this? Or who is it that speaks so much, high and low? It is heart-touching and endearing. Oh, what a delight to my ears!”

295.

295.

“Esā kho pamadā deva, khiḍḍā esā anappikā;

Sace tvaṃ kāme bhuñjeyya, bhiyyo bhiyyo chādeyyu taṃ.

“This, O lord, is a woman, and this is no trivial amusement. If you were to enjoy sensual pleasures, they would delight you more and more.”

296.

296.

“Iṅgha āgacchatorena, avidūramhi gāyatu;

Assamassa samīpamhi, santike mayha gāyatu.

“Come now, let her come quickly; let her sing not far off. Let her sing near my dwelling, in my presence.”

297.

297.

“Tirokuṭṭamhi gāyitvā, jhānāgāramhi pāvisi;

Bandhi naṃ anupubbena, āraññamiva kuñjaraṃ.

“Having sung from behind the wall, she entered the meditation chamber; she bound him gradually, like a forest elephant.”

298.

298.

“Tassa [V 4.0427][M 4.0475] kāmarasaṃ ñatvā, issādhammo ajāyatha;

‘Ahameva kāme bhuñjeyyaṃ, mā añño puriso ahu’.

“Having known the taste of sensual pleasure, the state of jealousy arose in him: ‘I alone should enjoy sensual pleasures; let there be no other man!’”

299.

299.

“Tato asiṃ gahetvāna, purise hantuṃ upakkami;

Ahameveko bhuñjissaṃ, mā añño puriso siyā.

“Then, having taken a sword, he set about to kill men, saying, ‘I alone will enjoy [sensual pleasures]; let there be no other man!’”

300.

300.

“Tato [P 4.0471] jānapadā sabbe, vikkandiṃsu samāgatā;

Putto tyāyaṃ mahārāja, janaṃ heṭhetyadūsakaṃ.

“Then all the country-folk, having gathered together, cried out: ‘O great king, this son of yours harms the innocent people!’”

301.

301.

“Tañca rājā vivāhesi, samhā raṭṭhā ca khattiyo;

Yāvatā vijitaṃ mayhaṃ, na te vatthabba tāvade.

“Then the khattiya king banished him from his kingdom, saying: ‘As far as my dominion extends, you must not dwell there.’”

302.

302.

“Tato so bhariyamādāya, samuddaṃ upasaṅkami;

Paṇṇasālaṃ karitvāna, vanamuñchāya pāvisi.

“Then, taking his wife, he approached the sea. Having built a leaf-hut, he entered the forest to gather wild roots and fruits.”

303.

303.

“Athettha isi māgacchi, samuddaṃ uparūpari;

So tassa gehaṃ pāvekkhi, bhattakāle upaṭṭhite.

“Then a sage came there, traveling over the sea; he entered the prince's house when the mealtime was near.”

304.

304.

“Tañca bhariyā palobhesi, passa yāva sudāruṇaṃ;

Cuto so brahmacariyamhā, iddhiyā parihāyatha.

“And the wife enticed him—see how exceedingly cruel! He fell from the holy life and lost his psychic powers.”

305.

305.

“Rājaputto ca uñchāto, vanamūlaphalaṃ bahuṃ;

Sāyaṃ kājena ādāya, assamaṃ upasaṅkami.

“And the prince, returning from gathering many wild roots and fruits, approached the hermitage in the evening, carrying them with a shoulder pole.”

306.

306.

“Isī ca khattiyaṃ disvā, samuddaṃ upasaṅkami;

‘Vehāyasaṃ gamissa’nti, sīdate so mahaṇṇave.

“And the sage, seeing the prince, approached the sea. Thinking, ‘I will travel through the air,’ he sank into the great ocean.”

307.

307.

“Khattiyo ca isiṃ disvā, sīdamānaṃ mahaṇṇave;

Tasseva anukampāya, imā gāthā abhāsatha.

“And the prince, seeing the sage sinking in the great ocean, spoke these verses out of compassion for him:”

308.

308.

“Abhijjamāne [V 4.0428] vārismiṃ, sayaṃ āgamma iddhiyā;

Missībhāvitthiyā gantvā, saṃsīdasi mahaṇṇave.

“Though you previously came by your own psychic power over the solid water without even touching it, now, having entered into association with a woman, you sink into the great ocean.”

309.

309.

“Āvaṭṭanī mahāmāyā, brahmacariyavikopanā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

“Women are like a whirlpool, full of great deceit, destroyers of the holy life. Knowing that they cause one to sink [into the lower realms], a wise man should avoid them from afar.”

310.

310.

“Analā mudusambhāsā, duppūrā tā nadīsamā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

“Insatiable despite their gentle speech, they are hard to satisfy like rivers. Knowing that they cause one to sink, a wise man should avoid them from afar.”

311.

311.

“Yaṃ [M 4.0476] etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti taṃ.

“Whomever they associate with, whether out of desire or for wealth, they quickly consume him, just as fire burns its own fuel.”

312.

312.

“Khattiyassa vaco sutvā, isissa nibbidā ahu;

Laddhā porāṇakaṃ maggaṃ, gacchate so vihāyasaṃ.

“Having heard the prince's words, disenchantment arose in the sage. Having regained his former path [of jhana], he departed through the air.”

313.

313.

“Khattiyo ca isiṃ disvā, gacchamānaṃ vihāyasaṃ;

Saṃvegaṃ alabhī dhīro, pabbajjaṃ samarocayi.

“And the prince, the wise one, seeing the sage going through the air, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and took delight in the life of renunciation.”

314.

314.

“Tato so pabbajitvāna, kāmarāgaṃ virājayi;

Kāmarāgaṃ virājetvā, brāhmalokūpago ahū”ti.

“Then, having gone forth, he dispelled sensual lust; having dispelled sensual lust, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.”

Tattha [P 4.0472] antepuranti kumārassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Bahunti bahuṃ nānappakāraṃ. Kāmupasaṃhitanti kāmanissitaṃ gītaṃ pavattayamānā. Kāmacchandassāti assa anitthigandhakumārassa kāmacchando uppajji. Jananti attano santikāvacaraṃ paricārikajanaṃ. Uccāvacanti uggatañca anuggatañca. Bhuñjeyyāti sace bhuñjeyyāsi. Chādeyyu tanti ete kāmā nāma tava rucceyyuṃ. So “pamadā”ti vacanaṃ sutvā tuṇhī ahosi. Itarā punadivasepi gāyi. Evaṃ kumāro paṭibaddhacitto hutvā tassā āgamanaṃ rocento paricārike āmantetvā “iṅghā”ti gāthamāha.

Here, “inner palace” means the prince’s dwelling place. “Many” means much and of various kinds. “Connected with sensual pleasure” means initiating a song based on sensual pleasure. “Sensual desire” means: sensual desire arose in this prince who did not know the scent of a woman. “The people” means his own attendant folk who moved about in his presence. “High and low” means raised and not raised. “You would enjoy” means “if you would enjoy.” “They would cover you” means these things called sensual pleasures would be pleasing to you. Hearing the word “woman,” he became silent. The other sang again on the next day. Thus the prince, with his mind captivated and finding delight in her arrival, addressed his attendants and spoke the verse beginning: “Come now….”

Tirokuṭṭamhīti sayanagabbhakuṭṭassa bahi. Mā aññoti añño kāme paribhuñjanto puriso nāma mā siyā. Hantuṃ upakkamīti antaravīthiṃ otaritvā māretuṃ ārabhi. Vikandiṃsūti [V 4.0429] kumārena katipayesu purisesu pahatesu purisā palāyitvā gehāni pavisiṃsu. So purise alabhanto thokaṃ vissami. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā upakkosiṃsu. Janaṃ heṭhetyadūsakanti niraparādhaṃ janaṃ heṭheti, taṃ gaṇhāpethāti vadiṃsu. Rājā upāyena kumāraṃ gaṇhāpetvā “imassa kiṃ kattabba”nti pucchi. “Deva, aññaṃ natthi, imaṃ pana kumāraṃ tāya kumārikāya saddhiṃ raṭṭhā pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte tathā akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā “tañcā”tiādimāha. Tattha vivāhesīti pabbājesi. Na te vatthabba tāvadeti yattakaṃ mayhaṃ vijitaṃ, tattake tayā na vatthabbaṃ. Uñchāyāti phalāphalatthāya.

“Behind the wall” means outside the wall of the bedchamber. “Let there not be another” means: let there not be another man enjoying sensual pleasures. “He set about to kill” means: having gone down into the street, he began to kill. “They cried out” means: when some men had been struck by the prince, the men fled and entered their houses. Not finding the men, he rested for a short while. At that moment, they gathered in the royal courtyard and cried out. “He harms the innocent people” means: they said, “He harms the innocent people, have him seized!” The king, having had the prince seized by a stratagem, asked, “What should be done to this one?” When it was said, “Your majesty, there is nothing else; it is proper to banish this prince from the kingdom along with that maiden,” he did so. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said the verse beginning “Then…” Here, vivāhesi means he banished. “You may not dwell therein” means: “As far as my dominion extends, you may not dwell in that much.” “For gleaning” means for the sake of fruits.

Tasmiṃ [M 4.0477] pana vanaṃ paviṭṭhe itarā yaṃ tattha pacitabbayuttakaṃ atthi, taṃ pacitvā tassāgamanaṃ olokentī paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdati. Evaṃ kāle gacchante ekadivasaṃ antaradīpakavāsī eko iddhimantatāpaso assamapadato nikkhamitvā maṇiphalakaṃ viya udakaṃ maddamānova ākāse uppatitvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchanto paṇṇasālāya uparibhāgaṃ patvā dhūmaṃ disvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne manussā vasanti maññe”ti paṇṇasāladvāre otari. Sā taṃ disvā nisīdāpetvā paṭibaddhacittā hutvā itthikuttaṃ dassetvā tena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ acari. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā “athetthā”tiādimāha. Tattha isi māgacchīti isi āgacchi. Samuddaṃ uparūparīti samuddassa matthakamatthakena. Passa yāva sudāruṇanti passatha, bhikkhave, tāya kumārikāya yāva sudāruṇaṃ kammaṃ katanti attho.

But when he had entered the forest, the other woman would cook whatever was suitable to be cooked there and, looking out for his arrival, would sit at the door of the leaf-hut. As time was passing thus, one day a certain ascetic with psychic powers, an island-dweller, left his hermitage and, rising into the air as if treading on the water like a crystal slab, went on his alms round. Reaching the area above the leaf-hut and seeing smoke, he thought, “I suppose people are living in this place,” and descended at the door of the leaf-hut. Seeing him, she had him sit down and, with a captivated mind, she displayed feminine wiles and engaged in misconduct with him. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said the verse beginning “Then a sage…” Here, “a sage came” means a sage came. “Over the sea” means along the very surface of the sea. “See how very cruel” means: “See, bhikkhus, how very cruel was the deed done by that maiden.”

Sāyanti sāyanhasamaye. Disvāti taṃ vijahituṃ asakkonto sakaladivasaṃ tattheva hutvā sāyanhasamaye rājaputtaṃ āgataṃ disvā palāyituṃ “vehāyasaṃ gamissa”nti uppatanākāraṃ karonto patitvā mahaṇṇave sīdati. Isiṃ disvāti anubandhamāno gantvā passitvā. Anukampāyāti sacāyaṃ bhūmiyā āgato abhavissa, palāyitvā araññaṃ paviseyya, ākāsena āgato [P 4.0473] bhavissati, tasmā samudde patitopi uppatanākārameva karotīti anukampaṃ uppādetvā tasseva anukampāya abhāsatha. Tāsaṃ pana gāthānaṃ attho tikanipāte vuttoyeva. Nibbidā ahūti kāmesu nibbedo jāto. Porāṇakaṃ magganti pubbe adhigataṃ jhānavisesaṃ. Pabbajitvānāti taṃ itthiṃ manussāvāsaṃ netvā nivattitvā araññe isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kāmarāgaṃ virājayi, virājetvā brahmalokūpago ahosīti.

“In the evening” means at evening time. “Seeing” means: unable to leave her, he stayed there the whole day; in the evening, seeing the prince arriving, he tried to flee, thinking, “I will go through the air.” Making the gesture of flying up, he fell and sank in the great ocean. “Seeing the sage” means having gone in pursuit and seen him. “Out of compassion” means: having aroused compassion, thinking, “If this one had come by land, he would have fled and entered the forest. He must have come through the air; that is why, though fallen in the sea, he still makes the gesture of flying up,” he spoke out of compassion for him. But the meaning of those verses has already been stated in the Book of the Threes. “Disenchantment arose” means disenchantment with sensual pleasures arose. “The former path” means the special meditative attainment previously attained. “Having gone forth” means: having led that woman to a human habitation and returned, he went forth into the ascetic life in the forest and became dispassionate towards sensual lust; having become dispassionate, he became one bound for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmaṃ paṭicca visuddhasattāpi saṃkilissantī”ti [V 4.0430] vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu arahattaṃ patto. Tadā anitthigandhakumāro ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: “Thus, bhikkhus, on account of women, even pure beings become defiled.” After he had proclaimed the truths, he identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, the dissatisfied bhikkhu attained arahantship. “At that time, the prince Anitthigandha was myself.”

Mahāpalobhanajātakavaṇṇanā ekādasamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāpalobhana Jātaka, the eleventh.

[508] 12. Pañcapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā

[508] 12. The Commentary on the Pañcapaṇḍita Jātaka

315-336. Pañcapaṇḍitajātakaṃ [M 4.0478] mahāumaṅge āvi bhavissati.

315-336. The Pañcapaṇḍita Jātaka will become manifest in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka.

Pañcapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā dvādasamā.

The Commentary on the Pañcapaṇḍita Jātaka, the twelfth.

[509] 13. Hatthipālajātakavaṇṇanā

[509] 13. The Commentary on the Hatthipāla Jātaka

Cirassaṃ vata passāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘After a long time, indeed, we see...’ This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Great Renunciation. For then the Teacher said: ‘Not only now, bhikkhus, but in the past too the Tathāgata made the Great Renunciation,’ and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ esukārī nāma rājā ahosi. Tassa purohito daharakālato paṭṭhāya piyasahāyo. Te ubhopi aputtakā ahesuṃ. Te ekadivasaṃ sukhasayane nisinnā mantayiṃsu “amhākaṃ issariyaṃ mahantaṃ, putto vā dhītā vā natthi, kiṃ nu kho kattabba”nti. Tato rājā purohitaṃ āha – “samma, sace tava gehe putto jāyissati, mama rajjassa sāmiko bhavissati, sace mama putto jāyissati, tava gehe bhogānaṃ sāmiko bhavissatī”ti. Evaṃ ubhopi aññamaññaṃ saṅkariṃsu.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Esukārī. His chaplain had been his dear friend from boyhood. Both were childless. One day, while seated comfortably, they consulted: ‘Our wealth and power are great, yet we have no son or daughter. What should be done?’ Then the king said to the chaplain: ‘Friend, if a son is born in your house, he shall be the lord of my kingdom; if a son is born in my house, he shall be the lord of the wealth in your house.’ Thus they both made a pact with each other.

Athekadivasaṃ purohito bhogagāmaṃ gantvā āgamanakāle dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisanto bahinagare ekaṃ bahuputtikaṃ nāma [P 4.0474] duggatitthiṃ passi. Tassā satta puttā sabbeva arogā, eko pacanabhājanakapallaṃ gaṇhi, eko sayanakaṭasārakaṃ, eko purato gacchati, eko pacchato, eko aṅguliṃ gaṇhi, eko aṅke nisinno, eko khandhe. Atha naṃ purohito pucchi “bhadde, imesaṃ dārakānaṃ pitā kuhi”nti? “Sāmi, imesaṃ pitā nāma nibaddho natthī”ti. “Evarūpe satta putte kinti katvā alatthā”ti? Sā aññaṃ gahaṇaṃ apassantī nagaradvāre ṭhitaṃ [V 4.0431] nigrodharukkhaṃ dassetvā “sāmi etasmiṃ nigrodhe adhivatthāya devatāya santike patthetvā labhiṃ, etāya me puttā dinnā”ti āha. Purohito “tena hi gaccha tva”nti rathā [M 4.0479] oruyha nigrodhamūlaṃ gantvā sākhāya gahetvā cāletvā “ambho devate, tvaṃ rañño santikā kiṃ nāma na labhasi, rājā te anusaṃvaccharaṃ sahassaṃ vissajjetvā balikammaṃ karoti, tassa puttaṃ na desi, etāya duggatitthiyā tava ko upakāro kato, yenassā satta putte adāsi. Sace amhākaṃ rañño puttaṃ na desi, ito taṃ sattame divase samūlaṃ chindāpetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ kāressāmī”ti rukkhadevataṃ tajjetvā pakkāmi. So etena niyāmeneva punadivasepīti paṭipāṭiyā cha divase kathesi. Chaṭṭhe pana divase sākhāya gahetvā “rukkhadevate ajjekarattimattakameva sesaṃ, sace me rañño puttaṃ na desi, sve taṃ niṭṭhāpessāmī”ti āha.

Then one day, the chaplain went to his revenue-yielding village. On his return, as he was entering the city through the southern gate, he saw a poor woman named Bahuputtikā outside the city. She had seven sons, all of them healthy: one held a potsherd for cooking, one a sleeping mat, one walked in front, one behind, one held her finger, one sat on her hip, and one was on her shoulder. Then the chaplain asked her: ‘Good lady, where is the father of these children?’ ‘Sir, they have no regular father.’ ‘How did you obtain seven such sons?’ Seeing no other explanation, she pointed to a banyan tree standing by the city gate and said: ‘Sir, I obtained them by praying to the deity dwelling in this banyan tree; she gave these sons to me.’ The chaplain said, ‘Very well, you may go.’ Getting down from his chariot, he went to the foot of the banyan tree, took hold of a branch, and shaking it, said: ‘O deity! What is it that you do not receive from the king? The king spends a thousand every year and makes offerings to you, yet you do not give him a son. What service did this poor woman do for you that you gave her seven sons? If you do not give a son to our king, seven days from now I will have you cut down from the root and chopped into pieces!’ Having threatened the tree-deity, he departed. He spoke in this same manner for six days in succession. On the sixth day, he took hold of a branch and said: ‘O tree-deity, only this one night remains. If you do not give a son to my king, tomorrow I will make an end of you!’

Rukkhadevatā āvajjetvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ tathato ñatvā “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo puttaṃ alabhanto mama vimānaṃ nāsessati, kena nu kho upāyena tassa puttaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Te “mayaṃ tassa puttaṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Aṭṭhavīsatiyakkhasenāpatīnaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi, tepi tathevāhaṃsu. Sakkassa devarañño santikaṃ gantvā kathesi. Sopi “labhissati nu kho rājā anucchavike putte, udāhu no”ti [P 4.0475] upadhārento puññavante cattāro devaputte passi. Te kira purimabhave bārāṇasiyaṃ pesakārā hutvā tena kammena laddhakaṃ pañcakoṭṭhāsaṃ katvā cattāro koṭṭhāse paribhuñjiṃsu. pañcamaṃ gahetvā ekatova dānaṃ adaṃsu. Te tato cutā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattiṃsu, tato yāmabhavaneti evaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ chasu devalokesu sampattiṃ anubhavantā vicaranti. Tadā pana nesaṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanato cavitvā yāmabhavanaṃ gamanavāro hoti. Sakko tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā pakkositvā “mārisā, tumhehi manussalokaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati, esukārīrañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattathā”ti āha. Te tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sādhu deva, gamissāma, na panamhākaṃ rājakulenattho, purohitassa gehe nibbattitvā daharakāleyeva kāme pahāya pabbajissāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Sakko “sādhū”ti tesaṃ paṭiññaṃ gahetvā āgantvā rukkhadevatāya tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sā tuṭṭhamānasā sakkaṃ vanditvā attano vimānameva gatā.

The tree-deity reflected and, having understood the matter as it truly was, she thought: “If this brahmin does not get a son, he will destroy my celestial abode. By what means should I give him a son?” She went to the Four Great Kings and informed them of the matter. They said: “We are unable to give him a son.” She went to the twenty-eight yakkha generals, and they too said the same. She went to Sakka, king of the devas, and spoke to him. He considered, “Will the king obtain suitable sons or not?” and he saw four meritorious devaputtas. It is said that in their previous life they were weavers in Bārāṇasī. They would divide their earnings from that work into five portions: they enjoyed four portions, and the fifth they would give as alms together. Having passed away from that life, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, then in the Yāma realm, and thus they wandered through the six deva worlds in regular and reverse order, experiencing prosperity. At that time, it was their turn to pass away from the Tāvatiṃsa realm and go to the Yāma realm. Sakka went to them, summoned them, and said: “Sirs, it is proper for you to go to the human world. Be reborn in the womb of King Esukārī’s chief consort.” Hearing his words, they replied: “Very well, lord, we will go. However, we have no desire for royalty. We shall be reborn in the house of the royal chaplain and, while still young, we will abandon sensual pleasures and go forth.” Sakka said, “Very well,” and having received their promise, he went and informed the tree-deity of the matter. Delighted, she paid homage to Sakka and returned to her own celestial abode.

Purohitopi [M 4.0480] punadivase balavapurise sannipātāpetvā vāsipharasuādīni gāhāpetvā rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā rukkhasākhāya gahetvā “ambho devate, ajja mayhaṃ taṃ yācantassa sattamo divaso, idāni te niṭṭhānakālo”ti āha. Tato rukkhadevatā mahantenānubhāvena khandhavivarato nikkhamitvā madhurasarena taṃ āmantetvā ‘brāhmaṇa, tiṭṭhatu eko putto, cattāro te [V 4.0432] putte dassāmī”ti āha. “Mama puttenattho natthi, amhākaṃ rañño puttaṃ dehī”ti. “Tuyhaṃyeva demī”ti. “Tena hi mama dve, rañño dve dehī”ti. “Rañño na demi, cattāropi tuyhameva dammi, tayā ca laddhamattāva bhavissanti, agāre pana aṭṭhatvā daharakāleyeva pabbajissantī”ti. “Tvaṃ me kevalaṃ putte dehi, apabbajanakāraṇaṃ pana amhākaṃ bhāro”ti. Sā tassa puttavaraṃ datvā attano bhavanaṃ pāvisi. Tato paṭṭhāya devatāya sakkāro mahā ahosi.

On the next day, the royal chaplain had strong men assemble, providing them with adzes, axes, and the like, and went to the foot of the tree. Taking hold of a branch, he said: “O deity, today is the seventh day since I began entreating you; now is the time for your destruction!” Then the tree-deity, by her great divine power, emerged from a cleft in the trunk and addressed the brahmin in a sweet voice: “Brahmin, let alone one son, I will give you four sons.” “I have no need of a son for myself. Give a son to our king.” “I will give them only to you.” “In that case, give two to me and two to the king.” “I will not give any to the king; I will give all four to you alone. But you will only just have them, for without staying at home, they will go forth while still young.” “You just give me the sons; preventing them from going forth will be our responsibility.” She granted him the boon of sons and entered her abode. From then on, the honor paid to the deity was great.

Jeṭṭhakadevaputto cavitvā purohitassa brāhmaṇiyā [P 4.0476] kucchimhi nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “hatthipālo”ti nāmaṃ katvā apabbajanatthāya hatthigopake paṭicchāpesuṃ. So tesaṃ santike vaḍḍhati. Tassa padasā gamanakāle dutiyo cavitvā assā kucchimhi nibbatti, tassapi jātakāle “assapālo”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So assagopakānaṃ santike vaḍḍhati. Tatiyassa jātakāle “gopālo”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So gopālehi saddhiṃ vaḍḍhati. Catutthassa jātakāle “ajapālo”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So ajapālehi saddhiṃ vaḍḍhati. Te vuḍḍhimanvāya sobhaggappattā ahesuṃ.

The eldest devaputta passed away and was reborn in the womb of the royal chaplain’s brahmin wife. On his naming day, to prevent him from going forth, they named him Hatthipāla and entrusted him to elephant keepers. He grew up among them. When he was able to walk, the second one passed away and was reborn in her womb. At his birth, they named him Assapāla. He grew up among horse keepers. At the birth of the third, they named him Gopāla. He grew up with cowherds. At the birth of the fourth, they named him Ajapāla. He grew up with goatherds. As they grew up, they attained great beauty.

Atha nesaṃ pabbajitabhayena rañño vijitā pabbajite nīhariṃsu. Sakalakāsiraṭṭhe ekapabbajitopi nāhosi. Te kumārā atipharusā ahesuṃ, yāya disāya gacchanti, tāya āhariyamānaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ vilumpanti. Hatthipālassa soḷasavassakāle kāyasampattiṃ disvā rājā ca purohito ca “kumārā mahallakā jātā, chattussāpanasamayo, tesaṃ kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti mantetvā “ete abhisittakālato paṭṭhāya atissarā bhavissanti, tato tato pabbajitā āgamissanti, te disvā pabbajissanti, etesaṃ pabbajitakāle janapado ulloḷo bhavissati, vīmaṃsissāma tāva ne, pacchā abhisiñcissāmā”ti cintetvā ubhopi isivesaṃ gahetvā bhikkhaṃ carantā hatthipālassa [M 4.0481] kumārassa nivesanadvāraṃ agamaṃsu. Kumāro te disvāva tuṭṭho pasanno upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then, for fear of their going forth, the king had all ascetics driven out of his domain. In the entire kingdom of Kāsi, there was not a single ascetic. The princes were very harsh; in whatever direction they went, they would plunder the gifts being brought. When Hatthipāla was sixteen years old, the king and the chaplain, seeing his physical perfection, consulted each other: “The princes have grown up; it is time to raise the white parasol. What should be done with them?” They thought: “From the time of their consecration, they will become supreme lords. Then ascetics will come from here and there, and seeing them, the princes will go forth. If they go forth, the country will be in an uproar. Let us first test them; afterwards, we shall consecrate them.” Both took on the guise of sages and, wandering for alms, they went to the gate of Prince Hatthipāla’s residence. As soon as the prince saw them, he was delighted and inspired. He approached, paid homage, and recited these three stanzas:

337.

337.

“Cirassaṃ vata passāma, brāhmaṇaṃ devavaṇṇinaṃ;

Mahājaṭaṃ khāridharaṃ, paṅkadantaṃ rajassiraṃ.

“After a long time indeed, we see a brahmin of divine appearance, with a great mass of matted hair, bearing a carrying-pole, with mud-stained teeth and a dusty head.

338.

338.

“Cirassaṃ vata passāma, isiṃ dhammaguṇe rataṃ;

Kāsāyavatthavasanaṃ, vākacīraṃ paṭicchadaṃ.

“After a long time indeed, we see a sage who delights in the qualities of the Dhamma, wearing a saffron-colored garment, with a covering of bark-cloth.

339.

339.

“Āsanaṃ [V 4.0433] udakaṃ pajjaṃ, paṭigaṇhātu no bhavaṃ;

Agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma, agghaṃ kurutu no bhava”nti.

“May the venerable one accept from us a seat, water, and water for the feet. We inquire of the venerable one concerning the guest-offering; may the venerable one accept our guest-offering.”

Tattha [P 4.0477] brāhmaṇanti bāhitapāpabrāhmaṇaṃ. Devavaṇṇinanti seṭṭhavaṇṇinaṃ ghoratapaṃ paramatikkhindriyaṃ pabbajitabhāvaṃ upagatanti attho. Khāridharanti khāribhāradharaṃ. Isinti sīlakkhandhādayo pariyesitvā ṭhitaṃ. Dhammaguṇe ratanti sucaritakoṭṭhāse abhirataṃ. “Āsana”nti idaṃ tesaṃ nisīdanatthāya āsanaṃ paññapetvā gandhodakañca pādabbhañjanañca upanetvā āha. Aggheti ime sabbepi āsanādayo agghe bhavantaṃ pucchāma. Kurutu noti ime no agghe bhavaṃ paṭiggaṇhatūti.

Here, 'brāhmaṇa' refers to a brahmin who has banished evil. 'Of divine appearance' means one of excellent complexion, who has undertaken the state of one gone forth—characterized by severe austerities and extremely sharp faculties—this is the meaning. 'Bearer of the khāri-pole' refers to one who bears the burden of a khāri-pole. 'Seer' refers to one who abides having sought out the aggregates of virtue and so on. 'Delighting in the qualities of the Dhamma' means one who delights in the portion of good conduct. As for 'A seat,' having prepared a seat for them to sit on and having brought fragrant water and an ointment for the feet, he spoke. As for 'Agghe,' it means: we ask you, venerable sir, concerning all these honorific gifts, the seat and so on. 'Kurutu no' means: may the venerable one accept these honorific gifts from us.

Evaṃ so tesu ekekaṃ vārenāha. Atha naṃ purohito āha – “tāta hatthipāla tvaṃ amhe ‘ke ime’ti maññamāno evaṃ kathesī”ti. “Hemavantakā isayo”ti. “Na mayaṃ, tāta, isayo, esa rājā esukārī, ahaṃ te pitā parohito”ti. “Atha kasmā isivesaṃ gaṇhitthā”ti? “Tava vīmaṃsanatthāyā”ti. “Mama kiṃ vīmaṃsathā”ti? “Sace amhe disvā na pabbajissasi, atha taṃ rajje abhisiñcituṃ āgatāmhā”ti. “Tāta na me rajjenattho, pabbajissāmahanti. Atha naṃ pitā “tāta hatthipāla, nāyaṃ kālo pabbajjāyā”ti vatvā yathājjhāsayaṃ anusāsanto catutthagāthamāha –

Thus he addressed them one by one in turn. Then the chaplain said to him: “Dear Hatthipāla, did you speak thus thinking, ‘Who are these people?’” “They are seers from the Himalayas,” he replied. “We are not seers, dear boy. This is King Esukārī, and I am your father, the chaplain.” “Then why have you taken up the guise of seers?” “To test you.” “What would you test about me?” “We have come to anoint you to the kingship, if you do not go forth upon seeing us.” “Father, I have no need for the kingship. I will go forth.” Then his father said: “Dear Hatthipāla, this is not the time for going forth,” and instructing him according to his own inclination, he spoke the fourth stanza:

340.

340.

“Adhicca [M 4.0482] vede pariyesa vittaṃ, putte gehe tāta patiṭṭhapetvā;

Gandhe rase paccanubhuyya sabbaṃ, araññaṃ sādhu muni so pasattho”ti.

“Dear one, having studied the Vedas and sought wealth, having established sons in the household, and having experienced all scents and tastes, then the forest is good; that sage is praised.”

Tattha adhiccāti sajjhāyitvā. Putteti chattaṃ ussāpetvā nāṭake vārena upaṭṭhāpetvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhitvā te putte gehe patiṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Sabbanti ete ca gandharase sesañca sabbaṃ vatthukāmaṃ anubhavitvā. Araññaṃ sādhu muni so pasatthoti pacchā mahallakakāle pabbajitassa araññaṃ sādhu laddhakaṃ hoti. Yo evarūpe kāle pabbajati, so muni buddhādīhi ariyehi pasatthoti vadati.

Here, 'having studied' means having recited.
