As to 'sons,' it means raising the parasol, establishing them in turn at entertainments, having them prosper with sons and daughters, and establishing those sons in the household—this is the meaning. As to 'all,' it refers to experiencing these scents and tastes and all other sensual pleasures. As to 'The forest is good; the sage is praised,' it means that the forest is well gained for one who goes forth in old age. A sage who goes forth at such a time, it is said, is praised by the noble ones such as the Buddhas.

Tato hatthipālo gāthamāha –

Then Hatthipāla spoke this stanza:

341.

341.

“Vedā [V 4.0434] na saccā na ca vittalābho, na puttalābhena jaraṃ vihanti;

Gandhe [P 4.0478] rase muccanamāhu santo, sakammunā hoti phalūpapattī”ti.

“The Vedas are not true, nor is the gain of wealth; the gain of sons does not ward off old age. The good declare release from scents and tastes; the attainment of fruit comes through one’s own kamma.”

Tattha na saccāti yaṃ saggañca maggañca vadanti, na taṃ sādhenti, tucchā nissārā nipphalā. Na ca vittalābhoti dhanalābhopi pañcasādhāraṇattā sabbo ekasabhāvo na hoti. Jaranti tāta, jaraṃ vā byādhimaraṇaṃ vā na koci puttalābhena paṭibāhituṃ samattho nāma atthi. Dukkhamūlā hete upadhayo. Gandhe raseti gandhe ca rase ca sesesu ārammaṇesu ca muccanaṃ muttimeva buddhādayo paṇḍitā kathenti. Sakammunāti attanā katakammeneva sattānaṃ phalūpapatti phalanipphatti hoti. Kammassakā hi, tāta, sattāti.

Here, as to 'not true': what they declare as heaven and the path, that they do not accomplish; they are empty, pithless, and fruitless. As to 'nor is the gain of wealth': the gain of wealth, too, since it is common to five things, is not entirely of one's own nature. As to 'old age': dear one, no one at all is capable of warding off old age, sickness, or death through the gain of sons. For these acquisitions are a root of suffering. As to 'from scents and tastes': the wise ones, such as the Buddhas, declare that release from scents, tastes, and the other sense objects is indeed liberation. As to 'through one's own kamma': the attainment of fruit, the accomplishment of results for beings, comes about through the kamma done by themselves. For, dear one, beings are owners of their kamma.

Kumārassa vacanaṃ sutvā rājā gāthamāha –

Hearing the prince's words, the king spoke this stanza:

342.

342.

“Addhā hi saccaṃ vacanaṃ tavetaṃ, sakammunā hoti phalūpapatti;

Jiṇṇā ca mātāpitaro tavīme, passeyyuṃ taṃ vassasataṃ aroga”nti.

“Indeed, this word of yours is true; the attainment of fruit comes through one’s own kamma. And these parents of yours are old; may they see you, healthy, for a hundred years.”

Tattha [M 4.0483] vassasataṃ aroganti ete vassasataṃ arogaṃ taṃ passeyyuṃ, tvampi vassasataṃ jīvanto mātāpitaro posassūti vadati.

Here, as to 'healthy for a hundred years': it means may they see you healthy for a hundred years. He is saying: 'And you too, living for a hundred years, should support your parents.'

Taṃ sutvā kumāro “deva, tvaṃ kiṃ nāmetaṃ vadasī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the prince said, “Your Majesty, what is this you are saying?” and then spoke two stanzas:

343.

343.

“Yassassa sakkhī maraṇena rāja, jarāya mettī naravīraseṭṭha;

Yo cāpi jaññā na marissaṃ kadāci, passeyyuṃ taṃ vassasataṃ arogaṃ.

“O king, who has a pact with death? O best of heroes, who has friendship with old age? If there were one who knew, ‘I will never die,’ then they might see him healthy for a hundred years.

344.

344.

“Yathāpi nāvaṃ puriso dakamhi, ereti ce naṃ upaneti tīraṃ;

Evampi byādhī satataṃ jarā ca, upaneti maccaṃ vasamantakassā”ti.

“Just as a person on the water, if he propels a boat, brings it to the shore, so too do sickness and old age constantly bring a mortal into the power of the Ender.”

Tattha sakkhīti mittadhammo. Maraṇenāti datto mato mitto matoti sammutimaraṇena. Jarāyāti pākaṭajarāya vā saddhiṃ yassa mettī [P 4.0479] bhaveyya, yassetaṃ maraṇañca jarā ca mittabhāvena nāgaccheyyāti attho. Ereti ce nanti mahārāja, yathā nāma puriso nadītitthe udakamhi nāvaṃ ṭhapetvā paratīragāmiṃ janaṃ āropetvā sace arittena uppīḷento phiyena kaḍḍhanto [V 4.0435] cāleti ghaṭṭeti, atha naṃ paratīraṃ neti. Evaṃ byādhi jarā ca niccaṃ antakassa maccuno vasaṃ upanetiyevāti.

Here, 'pact' means the nature of friendship. 'With death' refers to conventional death, as when one says, 'Datta is dead, my friend is dead.' 'With old age' means with manifest old age. The meaning is: one for whom this death and old age would not approach in the manner of a friend. As to 'if he propels it,' O great king, just as a person at a river ford, having placed a boat in the water and having taken aboard people going to the far shore, if he drives and impels it by pushing with a pole and pulling with an oar, then he brings it to the far shore. In the same way, sickness and old age constantly bring a mortal into the power of the Ender, Death.

Evaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitasaṅkhārassa parittabhāvaṃ dassetvā “mahārāja, tumhe tiṭṭhatha, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathayantameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchanti, appamattā hothā”ti ovādaṃ datvā rājānañca pitarañca vanditvā attano paricārake gahetvā bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya “pabbajissāmī”ti nagarato nikkhami. “Pabbajjā nāmesā sobhanā bhavissatī”ti hatthipālakumārena saddhiṃ mahājano nikkhami. Yojanikā parisā ahosi. So tāya parisāya saddhiṃ gaṅgāya tīraṃ patvā gaṅgāya udakaṃ oloketvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānāni nibbattetvā cintesi [M 4.0484] “ayaṃ samāgamo mahā bhavissati, mama tayo kaniṭṭhabhātaro mātāpitaro rājā devīti sabbe saparisā pabbajissanti, bārāṇasī suññā bhavissati, yāva etesaṃ āgamanā idheva bhavissāmī”ti. So tattheva mahājanassa ovādaṃ dento nisīdi.

Having thus shown the limited nature of the life-formation of these beings, he gave this advice: “Great king, you may stay. Even as I speak with you, sickness, old age, and death are approaching me. Be diligent.” After giving this advice, he paid respects to the king and his father, took his attendants, and abandoning the kingship in Bārāṇasī, he left the city thinking, “I will go forth.” Thinking, “This going forth will be splendid,” a great crowd departed with Prince Hatthipāla. The assembly extended for a yojana. Reaching the bank of the Ganges with that assembly, he gazed at the water of the Ganges, performed the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, developed the jhānas, and reflected: “This gathering will be great. My three younger brothers, my parents, the king, and the queen—all will go forth with their retinues. Bārāṇasī will become empty. I will stay right here until they arrive.” And so, giving advice to the great crowd, he sat down right there.

Punadivase rājā ca purohito ca cintayiṃsu “hatthipālakumāro tāva ‘rajjaṃ pahāya mahājanaṃ ādāya pabbajissāmī’ti gantvā gaṅgātīre nisinno, assapālaṃ vīmaṃsitvā abhisiñcissāmā”ti. Te isiveseneva tassapi gehadvāraṃ agamaṃsu. Sopi te disvā pasannamānaso upasaṅkamitvā “cirassaṃ vata passāmā”tiādīni vadanto tatheva paṭipajji. Tepi taṃ tatheva vatvā attano āgatakāraṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. So “mama bhātike hatthipālakumāre sante kathaṃ paṭhamataraṃ mayhameva setacchattaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti pucchitvā “tāta, bhātā, te ‘na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, pabbajissāmī’ti vatvā nikkhanto”ti vutte “kahaṃ paneso idānī”ti vatvā “gaṅgātīre [P 4.0480] nisinno”ti vutte “tāta, mama bhātarā chaḍḍitakheḷena kammaṃ natthi, bālā hi parittakapaññā sattā etaṃ kilesaṃ jahituṃ na sakkonti, ahaṃ pana jahissāmī”ti rañño ca pitu ca dhammaṃ desento dve gāthā abhāsi –

The next day, the king and the chaplain thought: “Prince Hatthipāla, having said, ‘Abandoning the kingdom and taking the great crowd with me, I will go forth,’ has gone and is now sitting on the bank of the Ganges. Let us test Assapāla and then anoint him as king.” In the guise of hermits, they went to the door of his house as well. Seeing them, he too approached with a pleased mind, saying, “We see you after a long time,” and so on, and he acted in the same way. They too spoke to him in the same way and explained the reason for their arrival. He asked, “While my elder brother, Prince Hatthipāla, is present, how is it that the white parasol comes to me first?” When he was told, “Dear boy, your brother has departed, saying, ‘I have no need for the kingdom; I will go forth,’” he asked, “Where is he now?” When he was told, “He is sitting on the bank of the Ganges,” he said: “Father, I have no use for what is like spittle spat out by my brother. Fools, beings of little wisdom, are unable to abandon this defilement, but I will abandon it.” Then, teaching the Dhamma to the king and his father, he spoke two stanzas:

345.

345.

“Paṅko ca kāmā palipo ca kāmā, manoharā duttarā maccudheyyā;

Etasmiṃ paṅke palipe byasannā, hīnattarūpā na taranti pāraṃ.

“Sensual pleasures are mud, sensual pleasures are mire; captivating, hard to cross, the domain of Death. Sunk down in this mud and mire, those of inferior nature do not cross to the far shore.”

346.

346.

“Ayaṃ pure luddamakāsi kammaṃ, svāyaṃ gahīto na hi mokkhito me;

Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmi, māyaṃ puna luddamakāsi kamma”nti.

“This self formerly did a cruel deed; now that its result is caught, there is no release from it for me. I will restrain and guard it, lest this self do a cruel deed again.”

Tattha [V 4.0436] paṅkoti yo koci kaddamo. Palipoti sukhumavālukamisso saṇhakaddamo. Tattha kāmā laggāpanavasena paṅko nāma, osīdāpanavasena palipo nāmāti vuttā. Duttarāti duratikkamā. Maccudheyyāti maccuno adhiṭṭhānā. Etesu hi laggā ceva anupaviṭṭhā ca sattā uttarituṃ asakkontā dukkhakkhandhapariyāye vuttappakāraṃ dukkhañceva maraṇañca [M 4.0485] pāpuṇanti. Tenāha – “etasmiṃ paṅke palipe byasannā hīnattarūpā na taranti pāra”nti. Tattha byasannāti sannā. “Visannā”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Hīnattarūpāti hīnacittasabhāvā. Na taranti pāranti nibbānapāraṃ gantuṃ na sakkonti.

Here, ‘mud’ is any kind of mire. ‘Mire’ (palipo) is fine mud mixed with fine sand. Here, sensual pleasures are called ‘mud’ because they cause sticking, and ‘mire’ because they cause sinking. ‘Hard to cross’ means difficult to overcome. ‘The domain of Death’ means the station of Death. For beings who are stuck and have sunk down into these, being unable to emerge, they reach suffering and death as described in the section on the mass of suffering. Therefore he said: ‘Sunk down in this mud and mire, those of inferior nature do not cross to the far shore.’ Here, ‘sunk down’ (byasannā) means immersed. There is also a reading ‘visannā’, which has the same meaning. ‘Of inferior nature’ means having an inferior state of mind. ‘Do not cross to the far shore’ means they are unable to reach the far shore of Nibbāna.

Ayanti mahārāja, ayaṃ mamattabhāvo pubbe assagopakehi saddhiṃ vaḍḍhanto mahājanassa vilumpanaviheṭhanādivasena bahuṃ luddaṃ sāhasikakammaṃ akāsi. Svāyaṃ gahītoti so ayaṃ tassa kammassa vipāko mayā gahito. Na hi mokkhito meti saṃsāravaṭṭe sati na hi mokkho ito akusalaphalato mama atthi. Orundhiyā naṃ parirakkhissāmīti idāni naṃ kāyavacīmanodvārāni pidahanto orundhitvā parirakkhissāmi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Māyaṃ puna luddamakāsi kammaṃ. Ahañhi ito paṭṭhāya pāpaṃ akatvā kalyāṇameva karissāmi.

Great king, ‘this’ refers to this self of mine; while growing up formerly with the horse-keepers, it committed many cruel and violent deeds by way of plundering and harassing the great crowd. ‘Now that it is caught’ means this result of that deed has been experienced by me. ‘There is no release from it for me’ means as long as the round of rebirths continues, there is no escape for me from this unwholesome fruit. ‘I will restrain and guard it’ means now I will restrain it by closing the doors of body, speech, and mind, and I will guard it. For what reason? ‘Lest this self do a cruel deed again.’ For from now on, I will not do evil but will do only what is good.

Evaṃ assapālakumāro dvīhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā “tiṭṭhatha tumhe, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathentameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchantī”ti ovādaṃ datvā yojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā [P 4.0481] nikkhamitvā hatthipālakumārasseva santikaṃ gato. So tassa ākāse nisīditvā dhammaṃ desetvā “bhātika, ayaṃ samāgamo mahā bhavissati, idheva tāva homā”ti āha. Itaropi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Punadivase rājā ca purohito ca tenevupāyena gopālakumārassa nivesanaṃ gantvā tenapi tatheva paṭinanditvā attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Sopi assapālakumāro viya paṭikkhipitvā “ahaṃ cirato paṭṭhāya pabbajitukāmo vane naṭṭhagoṇaṃ viya pabbajjaṃ upadhārento vicarāmi, tena me naṭṭhagoṇassa padaṃ viya bhātikānaṃ gatamaggo diṭṭho, svāhaṃ teneva maggena gamissāmī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Thus Prince Assapāla, having taught the Dhamma with two stanzas and given the advice, “You stay; even while I am speaking with you, sickness, old age, and death are approaching me,” took a retinue of a yojana and departed, going to the presence of Prince Hatthipāla. The latter, sitting in the air, taught him the Dhamma and said, “Brother, this assembly will be great. Let us just stay here for now.” The other agreed, saying, “Very well.” The next day, the king and the chaplain went by the same means to the house of Prince Gopāla. Having been welcomed by him in the same way, they told him the reason for their coming. He too, like Prince Assapāla, refused them, saying, “For a long time I have wished to go forth; like one searching for a lost cow in the forest, I have been wandering about looking for the going forth. Therefore, like the track of a lost cow, the path taken by my brothers has been seen by me. I will go by that very path.” And he spoke this stanza:

347.

347.

“Gavaṃva naṭṭhaṃ puriso yathā vane, anvesatī rāja apassamāno;

Evaṃ naṭṭho esukārī mamattho, sohaṃ kathaṃ na gaveseyyaṃ rājā”ti.

“Just as a man in the forest, O king, searches for a lost cow though he does not see it; so too, O Esukārī, my purpose is lost. How then, O king, should I not search for it?”

Tattha [M 4.0486] esukārīti rājānaṃ ālapati. Mamatthoti vane goṇo viya mama pabbajjāsaṅkhāto [V 4.0437] attho naṭṭho. Sohanti so ahaṃ ajja pabbajitānaṃ maggaṃ disvā kathaṃ pabbajjaṃ na gaveseyyaṃ, mama bhātikānaṃ gatamaggameva gamissāmi narindāti.

Therein, ‘Esukārī’ is an address to the king. ‘My purpose’ means my purpose known as the going forth is lost, like a cow in the forest. ‘So I’: “Having seen the path of those who have gone forth today, how should I not search for the going forth? I will follow the very path taken by my brothers, O ruler of men.”

Atha naṃ “tāta gopāla, ekāhaṃ dvīhaṃ āgamehi, amhe samassāsetvā pacchā pabbajissasī”ti vadiṃsu. So “mahārāja, ajja kattabbakammaṃ ‘sve karissāmī’ti na vattabbaṃ, kalyāṇakammaṃ nāma ajjeva kattabba”nti vatvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then they said to him, “Dear Gopāla, wait for a day or two. After comforting us, you may go forth.” He said, “Great king, one should not say of a task to be done today, ‘I will do it tomorrow.’ A wholesome deed should be done this very day.” Having said this, he spoke the other stanza:

348.

348.

“Hiyyoti hiyyati poso, pareti parihāyati;

Anāgataṃ netamatthīti ñatvā, uppannachandaṃ ko panudeyya dhīro”ti.

“Thinking ‘It was yesterday,’ a person falls behind; thinking ‘It is for later,’ one declines. Knowing ‘The future is not a certainty,’ what wise person would suppress a desire that has arisen?”

Tattha hiyyoti sveti attho. Pareti punadivase. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yo mahārāja, ajja kattabbaṃ kammaṃ ‘sve’ti, sve kattabbaṃ kammaṃ ‘pare’ti vatvā na karoti, so tato parihāyati, na taṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ sakkotī”ti. Evaṃ gopālo bhaddekarattasuttaṃ [P 4.0482] (ma. ni. 3.272 ādayo) nāma kathesi. Svāyamattho bhaddekarattasuttena kathetabbo. Anāgataṃ netamatthīti yaṃ anāgataṃ, taṃ “netaṃ atthī”ti ñatvā uppannaṃ kusalacchandaṃ ko paṇḍito panudeyya hareyya.

Herein, 'hiyyo' means 'tomorrow' in this context. 'Pareti' means 'the day after.' This is what is meant: 'Great king, whoever does not do a task that should be done today, saying “I will do it tomorrow,” or a task that should be done tomorrow, saying “I will do it the day after,” falls away from it; he is unable to perform that task.' Thus the cowherd taught what is called the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. This meaning should be explained by means of the Bhaddekaratta Sutta. 'The future is not a certainty': knowing that the future 'is not a certainty,' what wise person would reject an arisen wholesome desire?

Evaṃ gopālakumāro dvīhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā “tiṭṭhatha tumhe, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathentameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchantī”ti yojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā nikkhamitvā dvinnaṃ bhātikānaṃ santikaṃ gato. Hatthipālo tassapi dhammaṃ desesi. Punadivase rājā ca purohito ca tenevupāyena ajapālakumārassa nivesanaṃ gantvā tenapi tatheva paṭinanditvā attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ ācikkhitvā “chattaṃ te ussāpessāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Kumāro āha – “mayhaṃ bhātikā kuhi”nti? Te “amhākaṃ rajjenattho natthī”ti setacchattaṃ pahāya tiyojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā nikkhamitvā gaṅgātīre nisinnāti. Nāhaṃ mama bhātikehi chaḍḍitakheḷaṃ sīsenādāya vicarissāmi, ahampi pabbajissāmīti. Tāta, tvaṃ tāva daharo[M 4.0487], amhākaṃ hatthabhāro, vayappattakāle pabbajissasīti. Atha ne kumāro “kiṃ tumhe kathetha, nanu ime sattā daharakālepi mahallakakālepi marantiyeva, ‘ayaṃ daharakāle marissati, ayaṃ mahallakakāle’ti kassaci hatthe vā pāde vā nimittaṃ natthi, ahaṃ mama maraṇakālaṃ na jānāmi, tasmā idāneva pabbajissāmī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus the young cowherd, having taught the Dhamma with two verses, said, 'You remain here. Even while I am speaking with you, sickness, old age, and death are approaching me.' Taking a retinue of one yojana, he departed and went to the presence of his two brothers. Hatthipāla also taught the Dhamma to him. The next day, the king and the royal chaplain went by the same means to the dwelling of the young goatherd. Having been welcomed by him in the same way, they explained the reason for their coming, saying, 'We will raise the royal parasol for you.' The prince asked, 'Where are my brothers?' They replied, 'Saying, “We have no need for the kingdom,” they abandoned the white parasol, took a retinue of three yojanas, and departed. They are now sitting on the bank of the Ganges.' The prince said: 'I will not wander about carrying on my head the spittle discarded by my brothers. I too will go forth.' They said: 'Dear child, you are still young, a support for us. When you reach maturity, you may go forth.' Then the prince said to them: 'What are you saying? Do not beings die when young as well as when old? There is no sign on anyone’s hand or foot saying, “This one will die young, this one in old age.” I do not know the time of my own death. Therefore, I will go forth right now.' Having said this, he spoke two verses:

349.

349.

“Passāmi [V 4.0438] vohaṃ daharaṃ kumāriṃ, mattūpamaṃ ketakapupphanettaṃ;

Abhuttabhoge paṭhame vayasmiṃ, ādāya maccu vajate kumāriṃ.

“I see a young maiden, moving as if intoxicated, with eyes like the petals of a ketaka flower; in her first youth, without having enjoyed her wealth, Death seizes the maiden and departs.”

350.

350.

“Yuvā sujāto sumukho sudassano, sāmo kusumbhaparikiṇṇamassu;

Hitvāna kāme paṭikacca gehaṃ, anujāna maṃ pabbajissāmi devā”ti.

“Young, well-born, with a handsome face and lovely to behold, golden-hued, with a beard like the filaments of safflower; having abandoned sensual pleasures and the household beforehand, permit me, O King, I will go forth.”

Tattha [P 4.0483] voti nipātamattaṃ, passāmiccevāti attho. Mattūpamanti hāsabhāsavilāsehi mattaṃ viya carantiṃ. Ketakapupphanettanti ketakapupphapattaṃ viya puthulāyatanettaṃ. Abhuttabhogeti evaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ kumāriṃ paṭhamavaye vattamānaṃ abhuttabhogameva mātāpitūnaṃ upari mahantaṃ sokaṃ pātetvā maccu gahetvāva gacchati. Sujātoti susaṇṭhito. Sumukhoti kañcanādāsapuṇṇacandasadisamukho. Sudassanoti uttamarūpadhāritāya sampannadassano. Sāmoti suvaṇṇasāmo. Kusumbhaparikiṇṇamassūti sannisinnaṭṭhena sukhumaṭṭhena ca taruṇakusumbhakesarasadisaparikiṇṇamassu. Iminā evarūpopi kumāro maccuvasaṃ gacchati. Tathāvidhampi hi sineruṃ uppātento viya nikkaruṇo maccu ādāya gacchatīti dasseti. Hitvāna kāme paṭikacca gehaṃ, anujāna maṃ pabbajissāmi devāti deva, puttadārabandhanasmiñhi uppanne taṃ bandhanaṃ ducchedanīyaṃ hoti, tenāhaṃ puretaraññeva kāme ca gehañca hitvā idāneva pabbajissāmi, anujāna, manti.

Herein, 'vo' is a mere particle; the meaning is 'I see indeed.' 'Moving as if intoxicated' means moving as if intoxicated by laughter, speech, and charm. 'With eyes like ketaka flowers' means with broad and long eyes like the petals of a ketaka flower. 'Before enjoying her wealth' means that death seizes and departs with such a maiden of supreme beauty, who is in her first youth and has not yet enjoyed her wealth, causing great sorrow to fall upon her parents. 'Well-born' means well-proportioned. 'With a handsome face' means a face like a golden mirror or the full moon. 'Of lovely appearance' means endowed with a sightly appearance on account of possessing supreme beauty. 'Golden-hued' means having a golden complexion. 'With a beard like the filaments of safflower' means a beard that is thick and fine, resembling the filaments of young safflower. By this, it is shown that even such a youth falls under the power of death. It shows that merciless death seizes and carries away even such a one, as if uprooting Mount Sineru. 'Having abandoned sensual pleasures and the household beforehand, permit me, O King, I will go forth' means: O King, when the bond of children and a wife arises, that bond is hard to break. For that reason, having abandoned sensual pleasures and the home even before that, I will go forth right now. Please permit me.

Evañca [M 4.0488] pana vatvā “tiṭṭhatha tumhe, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathentameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchantī”ti te ubhopi vanditvā yojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā nikkhamitvā gaṅgātīrameva agamāsi. Hatthipālo tassapi ākāse nisīditvā dhammaṃ desetvā “samāgamo mahā bhavissatī”ti tattheva nisīdi. Punadivase purohito pallaṅkavaramajjhagato nisīditvā cintesi “mama puttā pabbajitā, idānāhaṃ ekakova manussakhāṇuko jātomhi, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti. So brāhmaṇiyā saddhiṃ mantento gāthamāha –

And having said this, 'You remain here. Even while I am speaking with you, sickness, old age, and death are approaching me,' he paid homage to both of them. Taking a retinue of one yojana, he departed and went right to the bank of the Ganges. Hatthipāla, sitting in the air, also taught the Dhamma to him, and saying, 'The assembly will be great,' he remained right there. The next day, the royal chaplain, seated in the middle of a fine couch, reflected: 'My sons have gone forth. Now I have become a mere human stump, all alone. I too will go forth.' Consulting with his brahmin wife, he spoke this verse:

351.

351.

“Sākhāhi rukkho labhate samaññaṃ, pahīnasākhaṃ pana khāṇumāhu;

Pahīnaputtassa mamajja bhoti, vāseṭṭhi bhikkhācariyāya kālo”ti.

“A tree receives its designation from its branches, but one that has lost its branches they call a stump. For me today, O lady Vāseṭṭhi, whose sons are gone, it is time for the mendicant life.”

Tattha labhate samaññanti rukkhoti vohāraṃ labhati. Vāseṭṭhīti brāhmaṇiṃ ālapati. Bhikkhācariyāyāti mayhampi pabbajjāya kālo, puttānaṃ santikameva gamissāmīti.

Herein, 'gets its name' means it receives the designation 'tree.' 'Vāseṭṭhi' is the address to the brahmin wife. 'For the mendicant life' means 'It is time for my renunciation as well; I will go right to the presence of my sons.'

So [V 4.0439] evaṃ vatvā brāhmaṇe pakkosāpesi, saṭṭhi brāhmaṇasahassāni sannipatiṃsu. Atha ne āha – “tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti [P 4.0484] tumhe pana ācariyāti. “Ahaṃ mama puttassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Na tumhākameva nirayo uṇho, mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti. So asītikoṭidhanaṃ brāhmaṇiyā niyyādetvā yojanikaṃ brāhmaṇaparisaṃ ādāya nikkhamitvā puttānaṃ santikaññeva gato. Hatthipālo tāyapi parisāya ākāse ṭhatvā dhammaṃ desesi. Punadivase brāhmaṇī cintesi “mama cattāro puttā setacchattaṃ pahāya ‘pabbajissāmā’ti gatā, brāhmaṇopi purohitaṭṭhānena saddhiṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ chaḍḍetvā puttānaññeva santikaṃ gato, ahameva ekā kiṃ karissāmi, puttānaṃ gatamaggeneva gamissāmī”ti. Sā atītaṃ udāharaṇaṃ āharantī udānagāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, he had the brahmins summoned, and sixty thousand brahmins assembled. Then he said to them, 'What will you do?' They replied, 'But you are our teacher.' He said, 'I will go forth in the presence of my son.' They replied, 'Hell is not hot for you alone; we too will go forth.' He entrusted his wealth of eighty crores to his brahmin wife and, taking a retinue of brahmins a yojana long, he departed and went right to his sons. Hatthipāla, standing in the air, taught the Dhamma to that assembly as well. The next day, the brahmin wife thought: 'My four sons have departed to go forth, having given up the white parasol. The brahmin too, abandoning his position as royal chaplain along with his wealth of eighty crores, has gone to his sons. What shall I do, all alone? I will follow the very path my sons have taken.' Recalling a past example, she uttered this inspired verse:

352.

352.

“Aghasmi koñcāva yathā himaccaye, katāni jālāni padāliya haṃsā;

Gacchanti puttā ca patī ca mayhaṃ, sāhaṃ kathaṃ nānuvaje pajāna”nti.

“As cranes in the sky at winter's end, and as swans having broken the nets, my sons and my husband go. How can I, knowing this, not follow them?”

Tattha [M 4.0489] aghasmi koñcāva yathāti yatheva ākāse koñcasakuṇā asajjamānā gacchanti. Himaccayeti vassānaccaye. Katāni jālāni padāliya haṃsāti atīte kira channavutisahassā suvaṇṇahaṃsāvassārattapahonakaṃ sāliṃ kañcanaguhāyaṃ nikkhipitvā vassabhayena bahi anikkhamitvā catumāsaṃ tattha vasanti. Atha nesaṃ uṇṇanābhi nāma makkaṭako guhādvāre jālaṃ bandhati. Haṃsā dvinnaṃ taruṇahaṃsānaṃ dviguṇaṃ vaṭṭaṃ denti. Te thāmasampannatāya taṃ jālaṃ chinditvā purato gacchanti, sesā tesaṃ gatamaggena gacchanti. Sā tamatthaṃ pakāsentī evamāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yatheva ākāse koñcasakuṇā asajjamānā gacchanti, tathā himaccaye vassānātikkame dve taruṇahaṃsā katāni jālāni padāletvā gacchanti, atha nesaṃ gatamaggena itare haṃsā. Idāni pana mama puttā taruṇahaṃsā jālaṃ viya kāmajālaṃ chinditvā gatā, mayāpi tesaṃ gatamaggena gantabbanti iminādhippāyena “gacchanti puttā ca patī ca mayhaṃ, sāhaṃ kathaṃ nānuvaje pajāna”nti āha.

Herein, “as cranes in the sky” (aghasmi koñcāva yathā) means: just as cranes go in the sky unhindered. “At winter's end” means: at the end of the rainy season. “As swans having broken the nets that were made”: In the past, it is said, ninety-six thousand golden swans stored enough rice for the rainy season in a golden cave and stayed there for four months, not going out for fear of the rains. Then a spider named Uṇṇanābhi wove a web at the entrance of the cave. The swans gave a double portion of food to two young swans. Because of their strength, they broke that web and went first, and the others followed the path they had gone. She spoke thus to clarify this meaning. This is what is said: just as cranes go unhindered in the sky, so too, at the end of the rainy season, two young swans go forth having broken the nets that were made, and then the other swans follow the path they have gone. But now my sons, like young swans, have cut through the net of sensual pleasures and have gone. I too must go by the path they have gone. With this intention she said: “My sons and my husband go; how can I, knowing this, not follow?”

Iti sā “kathaṃ ahaṃ evaṃ pajānantī na pabbajissāmi, pabbajissāmi yevā”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā brāhmaṇiyo pakkosāpetvā evamāha “tumhe kiṃ [P 4.0485] karissathā”ti? “Tumhe pana ayye”ti. “Ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti. Sā taṃ vibhavaṃ chaḍḍetvā yojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā puttānaṃ santikameva gatā. Hatthipālo tāyapi parisāya ākāse nisīditvā dhammaṃ desesi. Punadivase rājā “kuhiṃ purohito”ti pucchi. “Deva, purohito [V 4.0440] ca brāhmaṇī ca sabbaṃ dhanaṃ chaḍḍetvā dviyojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā puttānaṃ santikaṃ gatā”ti. Rājā “asāmikaṃ dhanaṃ amhākaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti tassa gehato dhanaṃ āharāpesi. Athassa aggamahesī “rājā kiṃ karotī”ti pucchitvā “purohitassa gehato dhanaṃ āharāpetī”ti vutte “purohito kuhi”nti vatvā “sapajāpatiko pabbajjatthāya nikkhanto”ti sutvā “ayaṃ rājā brāhmaṇena ca brāhmaṇiyā ca catūhi puttehi ca jahitaṃ ukkāraṃ mohena mūḷho attano gharaṃ āharāpeti, upamāya naṃ bodhessāmī”ti sūnato maṃsaṃ āharāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe rāsiṃ kāretvā ujumaggaṃ vissajjetvā [M 4.0490] jālaṃ parikkhipāpesi. Gijjhā dūratova disvā tassatthāya otariṃsu. Tattha sappaññā jālaṃ pasāritaṃ ñatvā atibhārikā hutvā “ujukaṃ uppatituṃ na sakkhissāmā”ti attanā khāditamaṃsaṃ chaḍḍetvā vamitvā jālaṃ anallīyitvā ujukameva uppatitvā gamiṃsu. Andhabālā pana tehi chaḍḍitaṃ vamitaṃ khāditvā bhāriyā hutvā ujukaṃ uppatituṃ asakkontā āgantvā jāle bajjhiṃsu. Athekaṃ gijjhaṃ ānetvā deviyā dassayiṃsu. Sā taṃ ādāya rañño santikaṃ gantvā “etha tāva, mahārāja, rājaṅgaṇe ekaṃ kiriyaṃ passissāmā”ti sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā “ime gijjhe olokehi mahārājā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus she, having made the resolution, “How can I, knowing thus, not go forth? I will certainly go forth!” summoned the brahmin women and asked, “What will you do?” “And what about you, noble lady?” “I will go forth.” “We too will go forth.” She, having abandoned that wealth and taking a retinue a yojana in size, went right to her sons. Hatthipāla, seated in the air, taught the Dhamma to that retinue as well. The next day, the king asked, “Where is the chaplain?” “Your Majesty, the chaplain and the brahmin woman have abandoned all their wealth and, taking a retinue two yojanas in size, have gone to their sons.” The king, thinking, “Ownerless wealth comes to us,” had the wealth brought from the chaplain’s house. Then his chief queen asked, “What is the king doing?” When told, “He is having the wealth brought from the chaplain’s house,” she asked, “Where is the chaplain?” Hearing, “He has gone forth with his wife for the purpose of renunciation,” she thought, “This king, deluded by folly, is having brought to his own house the excrement abandoned by the brahmin, the brahmin woman, and their four sons. I will awaken him with a simile.” She had meat brought from a slaughterhouse, had a pile made in the royal courtyard, had the direct path cleared, and had a net spread around it. Vultures, seeing it from afar, descended for it. There, the wise ones, knowing the net was spread and having become too heavy, thought, “We will not be able to fly straight up.” They dropped and vomited the meat they had eaten and, without getting caught in the net, flew straight up and departed. But the blind fools ate what the others had dropped and vomited, became heavy, and being unable to fly straight up, came and were caught in the net. Then they brought one vulture and showed it to the queen. Taking it, she went to the king and said, “Come, great king, let us see an event in the royal courtyard.” Opening the lion-window, she said, “Look at these vultures, great king,” and recited two verses:

353.

353.

“Ete bhutvā vamitvā ca, pakkamanti vihaṅgamā;

Ye ca bhutvā na vamiṃsu, te me hatthattamāgatā.

“These birds, having eaten and vomited, depart; but those who ate and did not vomit have come into my power.”

354.

354.

“Avamī [P 4.0486] brāhmaṇo kāme, so tvaṃ paccāvamissasi;

Vantādo puriso rāja, na so hoti pasaṃsiyo”ti.

“The brahmin has vomited up sensual pleasures; you are about to eat them back. A person who eats vomit, O king, is not praiseworthy.”

Tattha bhutvā vamitvā cāti maṃsaṃ khāditvā vamitvā ca. Paccāvamissasīti paṭibhuñjissasi. Vantādoti parassa vamitakhādako. Na pasaṃsiyoti so taṇhāvasiko bālo buddhādīhi paṇḍitehi pasaṃsitabbo na hoti.

Herein, “having eaten and vomited” means having eaten the meat and then vomited. “You are about to eat back” means you will consume it again. “A vomit-eater” means one who eats what another has vomited. “Not praiseworthy” means that fool, under the sway of craving, is not to be praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas.

Taṃ sutvā rājā vippaṭisārī ahosi, tayo bhavā ādittā viya upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So “ajjeva rajjaṃ pahāya mama pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti uppannasaṃvego deviyā thutiṃ karonto gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king became remorseful; the three kinds of existence appeared to him as if they were ablaze. A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him, and thinking, “It is right for me to abandon the kingdom and go forth this very day,” he praised the queen and spoke this verse:

355.

355.

“Paṅke ca posaṃ palipe byasannaṃ, balī yathā dubbalamuddhareyya;

Evampi maṃ tvaṃ udatāri bhoti, pañcāli gāthāhi subhāsitāhī”ti.

“Just as a strong man might pull out a weak one sunk and mired in the mud, so too, noble lady, O Pañcālī, have you rescued me with these well-spoken verses.”

Tattha [V 4.0441] byasannanti nimuggaṃ, “visanna”ntipi pāṭho. Uddhareyyāti kesesu vā hatthesu vā gahetvā ukkhipitvā thale ṭhapeyya. Udatārīti kāmapaṅkato uttārayi. “Udatāsī”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. “Uddhaṭāsī”tipi pāṭho, uddharīti attho. Pañcālīti pañcālarājadhīte.

Herein, “sunk” means submerged; “visanna” is also a reading. “Might pull out” means: might grasp by the hair or hands, lift up, and place on dry land. “You have rescued” means: you have lifted out from the mire of sensual pleasures. “Udatāsi” is also a reading with the same meaning. “Uddhaṭāsi” is also a reading; it means “you have lifted out.” “Pañcālī” means: O daughter of the king of Pañcāla.

Evañca [M 4.0491] pana vatvā taṅkhaṇaññeva pabbajitukāmo hutvā amacce pakkosāpetvā āha – “tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti tumhe pana, devāti? “Ahaṃ hatthipālassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi pabbajissāma, devā”ti. Rājā dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā “atthikā setacchattaṃ ussāpentū”ti amaccaparivuto tiyojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā kumārasseva santikaṃ gato. Hatthipālo tassāpi parisāya ākāse nisinno dhammaṃ desesi. Satthā rañño pabbajitabhāvaṃ pakāsento gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, desiring to go forth that very moment, he had his ministers summoned and asked, “What will you do?” “And what about you, Your Majesty?” “I will go forth in the presence of Hatthipāla.” “We too will go forth, Your Majesty.” The king, abandoning the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent, said, “Let those who desire it raise the white parasol!” Surrounded by his ministers and taking a retinue three yojanas in size, he went right to the prince. Hatthipāla, seated in the sky, taught the Dhamma to that retinue too. The Teacher, making known the fact of the king's going forth, spoke this verse:

356.

356.

“Idaṃ vatvā mahārājā, esukārī disampati;

Raṭṭhaṃ hitvāna pabbaji, nāgo chetvāva bandhana”nti.

“Having said this, the great king Esukārī, lord of the land, abandoned his kingdom and went forth, like an elephant that has broken its bonds.”

Punadivase [P 4.0487] nagare ohīnajano sannipatitvā rājadvāraṃ gantvā deviyā ārocetvā nivesanaṃ pavisitvā deviṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito gāthamāha.

The next day, the remaining people in the city gathered, went to the palace gate, and announced their arrival to the queen. Having entered her residence and paid homage to her, they stood to one side and spoke a verse:

357.

357.

“Rājā ca pabbajjamarocayittha, raṭṭhaṃ pahāya naravīraseṭṭho;

Tuvampi no hohi yatheva rājā, amhehi guttā anusāsa rajja”nti.

“The king, that best of heroic men, has taken delight in the going forth, having abandoned his kingdom. You too be for us as the king was; protected by us, rule the kingdom.”

Tattha anusāsāti amhehi guttā hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārehi.

Herein, “rule” means: being protected by us, govern the kingdom righteously.

Sā mahājanassa kathaṃ sutvā sesagāthā abhāsi –

Having heard the speech of the great crowd, she spoke the remaining verses:

358.

358.

“Rājā ca pabbajjamarocayittha, raṭṭhaṃ pahāya naravīraseṭṭho;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi loke, hitvāna kāmāni manoramāni.

“The king, that best of heroic men, has taken delight in the going forth, having abandoned his kingdom. I too will wander alone in the world, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures.”

359.

359.

“Rājā ca pabbajjamarocayittha, raṭṭhaṃ pahāya naravīraseṭṭho;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi loke, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikāni.

“The king, that best of heroic men, has taken delight in the going forth, having abandoned his kingdom. I too will wander alone in the world, having abandoned sensual pleasures in their entirety.”

360.

360.

“Accenti [V 4.0442][M 4.0492] kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahanti;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi loke, hitvāna kāmāni manoramāni.

“Times pass, nights fly by; the stages of life are successively left behind. I too will wander alone in the world, having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures.”

361.

361.

“Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahanti;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi loke, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikāni.

“Times pass, nights fly by; the stages of life are successively left behind. I too will wander alone in the world, having abandoned sensual pleasures in their entirety.”

362.

362.

“Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahanti;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi loke, sītibhūtā sabbamaticca saṅga”nti.

“Times pass, nights fly by; the stages of life are successively left behind. I too will wander alone in the world, serene, having transcended every attachment.”

Tattha [P 4.0488] ekāti puttadhītukilesasambādhehi muccitvā imasmiṃ loke ekikāva carissāmi. Kāmānīti rūpādayo kāmaguṇe. Yatodhikānīti yena yena odhinā ṭhitāni, tena tena ṭhitāneva jahissāmi, na kiñci āmasissāmīti attho. Accenti kālāti pubbaṇhādayo kālā atikkamanti. Tarayantīti atucchā hutvā āyusaṅkhāraṃ khepayamānā khādayamānā gacchanti. Vayoguṇāti paṭhamavayādayo tayo, mandadasakādayo vā dasa koṭṭhāsā. Anupubbaṃ jahantīti uparūparikoṭṭhāsaṃ appatvā tattha tattheva nirujjhanti. Sītibhūtāti uṇhakārake uṇhasabhāve kilese pahāya sītalā hutvā. Sabbamaticca saṅganti rāgasaṅgādikaṃ sabbasaṅgaṃ atikkamitvā ekā carissāmi, hatthipālakumārassa santikaṃ gantvā pabbajissāmīti.

Herein, “alone” means: having been freed from the constraints of defilements concerning sons and daughters, I will wander solitary in this world. “Sensual pleasures” means the strands of sensual pleasure, such as forms and so on. “In their entirety” means: in whatever limit they are established, in that very limit I will abandon them; I will not touch anything at all—this is the meaning. “Times pass” means: the times of day, such as morning, pass by. “Fly by” means: not being empty, they go on, depleting and consuming the life-formation. “Stages of life” means: the three stages beginning with the first stage of life, or the ten divisions such as the decade of infancy. “Are successively left behind” means: without reaching the next higher division, they cease right there in each respective division. “Having become cool” means: having abandoned the defilements that are heat-producing and have a hot nature, one has become cool. “Having transcended every attachment” means: having transcended every bond such as the bond of lust, I will wander alone; that is, I will go to Prince Hatthipāla and go forth.

Iti sā imāhi gāthāhi mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā amaccabhariyāyo pakkosāpetvā āha – “tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti tumhe pana ayyeti? “Ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi pabbajissāmā”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti rājanivesane suvaṇṇakoṭṭhāgārādīni vivarāpetvā “asukaṭṭhāne ca asukaṭṭhāne ca mahānidhi nidahita”nti suvaṇṇapaṭṭe likhāpetvā “dinnaññeva, atthikā harantū”ti vatvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭaṃ mahātale thambhe bandhāpetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā mahāsampattiṃ chaḍḍetvā nagarā nikkhami. Tasmiṃ [M 4.0493] khaṇe sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. “Rājā ca kira devī ca rajjaṃ pahāya ‘pabbajissāmā’ti nikkhamanti, mayaṃ idha kiṃ karissāmā”ti tato tato manussā yathāpūritāneva gehāni chaḍḍetvā putte hatthesu gahetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Sabbāpaṇā pasāritaniyāmeneva ṭhitā, nivattitvā olokento nāma nāhosi. Sakalanagaraṃ tucchaṃ ahosi, devīpi tiyojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā tattheva gatā. Hatthipālo tassāpi parisāya ākāse nisinno dhammaṃ desetvā dvādasayojanikaṃ parisaṃ gahetvā himavantābhimukho pāyāsi. “Hatthipālakumāro kira dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasiṃ tucchaṃ katvā ‘pabbajissāmī’ti mahājanaṃ ādāya [V 4.0443] himavantaṃ gacchati, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya”nti sakalakāsiraṭṭhaṃ saṅkhubhi. Aparabhāge parisā tiṃsayojanikā ahesuṃ, so tāya parisāya saddhiṃ himavantaṃ [P 4.0489] pāvisi.

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the great crowd with these verses, she had the ministers' wives summoned and said, “What will you do?” “And what about you, lady?” they asked. “I will go forth,” she replied. “We too will go forth.” She said, “Good.” Then, having had the golden treasuries and so on in the royal residence opened, she had golden plates inscribed with, “In such and such a place, great treasures are buried,” and declared, “It is given; let those in need take it.” She had the golden plates tied to pillars on the upper terrace, had drums beaten throughout the city, abandoned her great wealth, and left the city. At that moment, the entire city was in an uproar. “The king and queen, it is said, are renouncing the kingdom and going forth—what shall we do here?” People everywhere, leaving their homes just as they were, took their children by the hand and departed. All shops stood wide open, with no one turning back to look. The whole city was empty. The queen, taking a retinue of three yojanas, went there as well. Hatthipāla, seated in the sky, taught the Dhamma to her retinue too, and then, taking a following of twelve yojanas, set out toward the Himalayas. “Prince Hatthipāla, it is said, has emptied Bārāṇasī for twelve yojanas and is taking the people to the Himalayas to go forth—what then of us?” The entire Kāsī country was in turmoil. Later, the retinue grew to thirty yojanas. With that following, he entered the Himalayas.

Sakko āvajjento taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “hatthipālakumāro mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, samāgamo mahā bhavissati, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vissakammaṃ āṇāpesi “gaccha, āyāmato chattiṃsayojanaṃ, vitthārato pannarasayojanaṃ assamaṃ māpetvā pabbajitaparikkhāre sampādehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā gaṅgātīre ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge vuttappamāṇaṃ assamapadaṃ māpetvā paṇṇasālāsu kaṭṭhattharaṇapaṇṇattharaṇaāsanādīni paññapetvā sabbe pabbajitaparikkhāre māpesi. Ekekissā paṇṇasālāya dvāre ekeko caṅkamo rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaparicchinno katasudhāparikammo ālambanaphalako, tesu tesu ṭhānesu nānāvaṇṇasurabhikusumasañchannā pupphagacchā, ekekassa caṅkamassa koṭiyaṃ ekeko udakabharito kūpo, tassa santike ekeko phalarukkho, so ekova sabbaphalāni phalati. Idaṃ sabbaṃ devatānubhāvena ahosi. Vissakammo assamapadaṃ māpetvā paṇṇasālāsu pabbajitaparikkhāre ṭhapetvā “ye keci pabbajitukāmā ime parikkhāre gaṇhantū”ti jātihiṅgulakena bhittiyā akkharāni likhitvā attano ānubhāvena bheravasadde migapakkhī duddasike amanusse ca paṭikkamāpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Sakka, reflecting and knowing of that event, thought, "Prince Hatthipāla has set out on the Great Renunciation. A great gathering will take place, and it is fitting to provide a dwelling place." He commanded Vissakamma, "Go, create a hermitage thirty-six yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width, and furnish it with all the requisites for ascetics." Vissakamma, saying, "Very well," agreed and went to a delightful area along the bank of the Ganges. There, on a beautiful piece of ground, he created a hermitage of the specified dimensions. In the leaf huts, he prepared wooden bedding, leaf bedding, seats, and so forth, and created all the requisites for ascetics. At the entrance of each leaf hut, there was a cloister for pacing, with designated areas for use during the night and day, smoothly plastered, and with a support board. In those various places were flowering bushes covered with blossoms of many colors and fragrances. At the end of each cloister, there was a well filled with water, and nearby, a single fruit tree which bore all kinds of fruits. All this was accomplished through the power of the deities. Having created the hermitage and placed the ascetic requisites in the leaf huts, Vissakamma wrote on the walls with vermilion: 'Let anyone who wishes to renounce the world take these requisites.' Then, by his power, he drove away frightening sounds, fierce beasts and birds, and non-human beings, and returned to his own abode.

Hatthipālakumāro ekapadikamaggena sakkadattiyaṃ assamaṃ pavisitvā akkharāni disvā “sakkena mama mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantabhāvo ñāto bhavissatī”ti [M 4.0494] dvāraṃ vivaritvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaliṅgaṃ gahetvā nikkhamitvā caṅkamaṃ otaritvā katipaye vāre aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā sesajanakāyaṃ pabbājetvā assamapadaṃ vicārento taruṇaputtānaṃ itthīnaṃ majjhaṭṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ adāsi. Tato anantaraṃ mahallakitthīnaṃ, tato anantaraṃ majjhimitthīnaṃ, samantā parikkhipitvā pana purisānaṃ adāsi[P 4.0490]. Atheko rājā “bārāṇasiyaṃ kira rājā natthī”ti āgantvā alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ nagaraṃ oloketvā rājanivesanaṃ āruyha tattha tattha ratanarāsiṃ disvā “evarūpaṃ nagaraṃ pahāya pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya pabbajjā nāmesā uḷārā bhavissatī”ti surāsoṇḍe maggaṃ pucchitvā hatthipālassa santikaṃ pāyāsi. Hatthipālo tassa vanantaraṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā paṭimaggaṃ gantvā ākāse nisinno parisāya dhammaṃ desetvā assamapadaṃ netvā sabbaparisaṃ pabbājesi. Etenupāyena aññepi cha rājāno pabbajiṃsu. Satta rājāno bhoge chaḍḍayiṃsu, chattiṃsayojaniko assamo nirantaro paripūri. Yo kāmavitakkādīsu aññataraṃ vitakketi, mahāpuriso tassa dhammaṃ desetvā brahmavihārabhāvanañceva kasiṇabhāvanañca [V 4.0444] ācikkhati. Te yebhuyyena jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā tīsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāsā brahmaloke nibbattiṃsu. Tatiyakoṭṭhāsaṃ tidhā katvā eko koṭṭhāso brahmaloke nibbatti, eko chasu kāmasaggesu, eko isīnaṃ pāricariyaṃ katvā manussaloke tīsu kulasampattīsu nibbatti. Evaṃ hatthipālassa sāsanaṃ apagatanirayatiracchānayonipettivisayāsurakāyaṃ ahosi.

Prince Hatthipāla, walking along a single-track path, entered the hermitage given by Sakka. Seeing the writing, he thought, "Sakka must have known of my departure in the Great Renunciation." Opening the door, he entered the leaf hut, took on the marks of an ascetic, and came out. Descending to the walking path, he paced back and forth several times. Then, having ordained the remaining people, while arranging the hermitage grounds, he assigned leaf huts to the women with young children in the central area. Next to them, he assigned huts to the elderly women, and next to them, to the middle-aged women. Finally, surrounding them all, he assigned huts to the men. Meanwhile, a certain neighboring king, hearing that 'There is no king in Benares,' arrived. Observing the well-adorned city, he ascended to the royal palace and saw heaps of jewels everywhere. Thinking, 'If he could abandon such a city and palace to renounce the world, this state of renunciation must indeed be magnificent,' he asked some drunkards for the way and set out for Hatthipāla's presence. Knowing the king had entered the forest, Hatthipāla went to meet him. Seated in the sky, he taught the Dhamma to the assembly, then led them to the hermitage and ordained the entire company. By this method, six other neighboring kings also renounced. Seven kings in total abandoned their wealth, and the thirty-six-yojana hermitage was filled without any gap. If anyone entertained thoughts of sensual desire or the like, the Great Being would teach them the Dhamma, instructing them in the meditation on the divine abodes and the kasiṇas. Most of them developed the jhānas and higher knowledges. Two out of three groups were reborn in the Brahma world. The third group was divided into three: one part was reborn in the Brahma world, one in the six sensual heavens, and one, after serving the sages, was reborn in the human world among the three classes of prosperous families. Thus, Hatthipāla’s dispensation was free from the four states of misery: hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, and the host of asuras.

Imasmiṃ tambapaṇṇidīpe pathavicālakadhammaguttatthero, kaṭakandhakāravāsī phussadevatthero, uparimaṇḍalavāsī mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero, malayamahādevatthero, abhayagirivāsī mahādevatthero, gāmantapabbhāravāsī mahāsivatthero, kāḷavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero kuddālasamāgame mūgapakkhasamāgame cūḷasutasomasamāgame ayogharapaṇḍitasamāgame hatthipālasamāgame ca sabbapacchā nikkhantapurisā ahesuṃ. Tenevāha bhagavā –

In this island of Tambapaṇṇi, the elder Pathavicālakadhammagutta, the elder Phussadeva residing at Kaṭakandhakāra, the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita residing at Uparimaṇḍala, the elder Malayamahādeva, the elder Mahādeva residing at Abhayagiri, the elder Mahāsiva residing at Gāmantapabbhāra, and the elder Mahānāga residing at Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa were the men who went forth last of all in the assemblies of the Kuddāla, Mūgapakkha, Cūḷasutasoma, Ayogharapaṇḍita, and Hatthipāla Jātakas. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Abhittharetha [M 4.0495] kalyāṇe, pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye;

Dandhañhi karoto puññaṃ, pāpasmiṃ ramate mano”ti. (dha. pa. 116);

'Hasten in doing good; restrain your mind from evil. For the mind of one who is slow in doing merit delights in evil.'

Tasmā kalyāṇaṃ turitaturiteneva kātabbanti.

Therefore, what is good should be done with great haste.

Satthā [P 4.0491] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā esukārī rājā suddhodanamahārājā ahosi, devī mahāmāyā, purohito kassapo, brāhmaṇī bhaddakāpilānī, ajapālo anuruddho, gopālo moggallāno, assapālo sāriputto, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, hatthipālo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past the Tathāgata went forth in the Great Renunciation." Then he connected the birth story: "At that time, King Esukārī was King Suddhodana, the queen was Mahāmāyā, the chaplain was Kassapa, the brahmin woman was Bhaddakāpilānī, Ajapāla was Anuruddha, Gopāla was Moggallāna, Assapāla was Sāriputta, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Hatthipāla was indeed myself."

Hatthipālajātakavaṇṇanā terasamā.

The thirteenth, the commentary on the Hatthipāla Jātaka.

[510] 14. Ayogharajātakavaṇṇanā

[510] 14. The Commentary on the Ayoghara Jātaka

Yamekarattiṃ paṭhamanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaññeva ārabbha kathesi. Tadāpi hi so “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This discourse beginning, 'The first night,' the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Great Renunciation. On that occasion too, he said, 'Not only now, monks, but also in the past the Tathāgata went forth in the Great Renunciation,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 4.0445] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente brahmadattassa rañño aggamahesī gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā laddhagabbhaparihārā pariṇatagabbhā paccūsasamanantare puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassā purimattabhāve ekā sapattikā “tava jātaṃ jātaṃ pajaṃ khādituṃ labhissāmī”ti patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Sā kira sayaṃ vañjhā hutvā puttamātukodhena taṃ patthanaṃ katvā yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Itarā rañño aggamahesī hutvā imaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Sā yakkhinī tadā okāsaṃ labhitvā deviyā passantiyāva bībhaccharūpā hutvā āgantvā taṃ dārakaṃ gahetvā palāyi. Devī “yakkhinī me puttaṃ gahetvā palāyī”ti mahāsaddena viravi. Itarāpi dārakaṃ mūlakandaṃ viya muruṃ muruṃ karontī khāditvā deviyā hatthavikārādīhi bheravaṃ pakāsetvā tajjetvā pakkāmi. Rājā taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “kiṃ sakkā yakkhiniyā kātu”nti tuṇhī ahosi. Puna deviyā vijāyanakāle daḷhaṃ ārakkhamakāsi. Devī puttaṃ puna vijāyi. Yakkhinī āgantvā tampi khāditvā gatā. Tatiyavāre [M 4.0496] tassā kucchiyaṃ mahāsatto paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Rājā mahājanaṃ sannipātetvā “deviyā jātaṃ jātaṃ pajaṃ ekā yakkhinī khādati[P 4.0492], kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti pucchi. Atheko “yakkhā nāma tālapaṇṇassa bhāyanti, deviyā hatthapādesu tālapaṇṇaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Atheko “ayogharassa bhāyanti, ayogharaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti attano vijite kammāre sannipātetvā “ayogharaṃ karothā”ti āṇāpetvā āyuttake adāsi. Antonagareyeva ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge gehaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ, thambhe ādiṃ katvā sabbagehasambhārā ayomayāva ahesuṃ, navahi māsehi ayomayaṃ mahantaṃ caturassasālaṃ niṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ niccaṃ pajjalitapadīpameva hoti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the chief queen of King Brahmadatta conceived. Having received the protection due to a pregnant woman, when her pregnancy reached full term, she gave birth to a son at the break of dawn. In a previous existence, a co-wife of hers had made a vow: 'May I get to devour every child you give birth to.' It is said that she, being barren herself, made this vow out of resentment towards the mother of a son and was reborn in the womb of a yakkha. The other woman, having become the king's chief queen, gave birth to this son. That ogress, finding her opportunity, took on a terrifying form right before the queen's eyes, came and seized the child, and fled. The queen cried out with a loud scream: 'An ogress has seized my son and fled!' The other, devouring the child with a crunching sound as if eating a root tuber, displayed a fearsome appearance with contortions of her hands, and after threatening the queen, she departed. When the king heard her words, he remained silent, thinking: 'What can be done about an ogress?' When the queen was again about to give birth, he arranged for strong protection. The queen gave birth to another son. The ogress came, devoured that one too, and left. On the third occasion, the Great Being was conceived in her womb. The king assembled a large crowd of people and asked: 'An ogress devours every child born to the queen. What, then, should be done?' Then one person said: 'Yakkhas, it is said, are afraid of palm leaves; it would be proper to tie palm leaves to the queen's hands and feet.' Another said: 'They are afraid of an iron house; it would be proper to build an iron house.' The king said, 'Good,' and having assembled the smiths in his realm, he commanded: 'Build an iron house,' and he entrusted the task to officials. They established the house on a pleasant plot of ground right within the city. From the pillars onwards, all the house's components were made of iron. In nine months, a large, square iron hall was completed. It was always lit with blazing lamps.

Rājā deviyā gabbhaparipākaṃ ñatvā ayogharaṃ alaṅkārāpetvā taṃ ādāya ayogharaṃ pāvisi. Sā tattha dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi, “ayogharakumāro”tvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Taṃ dhātīnaṃ datvā mahantaṃ ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahitvā rājā deviṃ ādāya nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā alaṅkatapāsādatalameva abhiruhi. Yakkhinīpi udakavāraṃ gantvā vessavaṇassa udakaṃ vahantī jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā. Mahāsatto ayoghareyeva vaḍḍhitvā viññutaṃ patto tattheva sabbasippāni uggaṇhi. Rājā “ko me puttassa vayappadeso”ti amacce pucchitvā “soḷasavasso, deva, sūro thāmasampanno yakkhasahassampi paṭibāhituṃ samattho”ti sutvā “rajjamassa dassāmi, sakalanagaraṃ alaṅkaritvā ayogharato taṃ nīharitvā ānethā”ti āha. Amaccā “sādhu, devā”ti dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasiṃ alaṅkaritvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitaṃ maṅgalavāraṇaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā kumāraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā hatthikkhandhe nisīdāpetvā “deva, kulasantakaṃ [V 4.0446] alaṅkatanagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pitaraṃ kāsirājānaṃ vandatha, ajjeva setacchattaṃ labhissathā”ti āhaṃsu.

The king, knowing the queen's pregnancy had come to term, had the iron house adorned and, taking her with him, entered it. There she gave birth to a son endowed with the signs of fortune and merit, and they named him 'Prince Ayoghara' (Prince of the Iron House). Handing him over to wet-nurses and arranging for great protection, the king took the queen, circumambulated the city, and ascended to the adorned palace terrace. The ogress, for her part, had gone for her turn to carry water for Vessavana and passed away. The Great Being grew up in the iron house itself, and upon reaching maturity, he learned all the arts right there. The king asked his ministers, 'What is my son's age?' When he heard, 'He is sixteen years old, your majesty. He is a hero, endowed with strength, capable of warding off even a thousand yakkhas,' he said, 'I will give him the kingdom. Adorn the entire city, bring him out of the iron house, and lead him here.' The ministers replied, 'Very well, your majesty.' They adorned the twelve-yojana city of Benares and, taking a state elephant decorated with all ornaments, they went there. They had the prince adorned, seated him on the elephant's back, and said: 'Your highness, circumambulate the adorned city, your family inheritance, and pay homage to your father, the king of Kasi. This very day you shall receive the white umbrella.'

Mahāsatto nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto ārāmarāmaṇeyyakavanapokkharaṇibhūmirāmaṇeyyakapāsādarāmaṇeyyakādīni disvā [P 4.0493] cintesi “mama pitā maṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ bandhanāgāre vasāpesi. Evarūpaṃ alaṅkatanagaraṃ daṭṭhuṃ nādāsi, ko nu kho mayhaṃ doso”ti amacce pucchi. “Deva, natthi tumhākaṃ doso, tumhākaṃ pana dvebhātike ekā yakkhinī khādi, tena vo [M 4.0497] pitā ayoghare vasāpesi, ayogharena jīvitaṃ tumhākaṃ laddha”nti. So tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi “ahaṃ dasa māse lohakumbhiniraye viya ca gūthaniraye viya ca mātukucchimhi vasitvā mātukucchito nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya soḷasa vassāni etasmiṃ bandhanāgāre vasiṃ, bahi oloketumpi na labhiṃ, ussadaniraye khitto viya ahosiṃ, yakkhiniyā hatthato muttopi panāhaṃ neva ajaro, na amaro homi, kiṃ me rajjena, rajje ṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya dunnikkhamanaṃ hoti, ajjeva mama pitaraṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. So nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rājakulaṃ pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.

As the Great Being was circumambulating the city, he saw the delightful parks, the delightful groves and ponds, the delightful grounds, the delightful palaces, and so on, and he thought: 'My father made me live in a prison for so long. He did not let me see such an adorned city. What, I wonder, is my fault?' He asked the ministers. 'Your highness, there is no fault in you. But an ogress devoured your two brothers, so your father had you live in the iron house. It is because of the iron house that your life was preserved.' Hearing their words, he reflected: 'For ten months I dwelt in my mother’s womb as if in the Iron Cauldron hell or the Filth hell. From the time I emerged from my mother’s womb, I have lived for sixteen years in this prison. I was not able even to look outside. It was as if I were cast into an Ussada hell. But though I have escaped from the hand of the ogress, I am not free from old age or death. What use is the kingdom to me? Once one is established in a kingdom, it is difficult to leave. This very day I will ask my father for permission to go forth, and I will enter the Himalayas and become an ascetic.' Having circumambulated the city, he entered the royal palace, paid homage to the king, and stood there.

Rājā tassa sarīrasobhaṃ oloketvā balavasinehena amacce olokesi. Te “kiṃ karoma, devā”ti vadiṃsu. Puttaṃ me ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā tīhi saṅkhehi abhisiñcitvā kañcanamālaṃ setacchattaṃ ussāpethāti. Mahāsatto pitaraṃ vanditvā “na mayhaṃ rajjenattho, ahaṃ pabbajissāmi, pabbajjaṃ me anujānāthā”ti āha. Tāta rajjaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kiṃkāraṇā pabbajissasīti. “Deva ahaṃ mātukucchimhi dasa māse gūthaniraye viya vasitvā mātukucchito nikkhanto yakkhinibhayena soḷasa vassāni bandhanāgāre vasanto bahi oloketumpi na alabhiṃ, ussadaniraye khitto viya ahosiṃ, yakkhiniyā hatthato muttomhītipi ajaro amaro na homi. Maccu nāmesa na sakkā kenaci jinituṃ, bhave ukkaṇṭhitomhi, yāva me byādhijarāmaraṇāni nāgacchanti, tāvadeva pabbajitvā dhammaṃ carissāmi, alaṃ me rajjena, anujānātha maṃ, devā”ti vatvā pitu dhammaṃ desento āha –

The king, beholding his bodily beauty, looked at his ministers with strong affection. They said, “What should we do, your majesty?” “Place my son upon a heap of jewels, anoint him with water from three conch shells, and raise aloft the golden garland and the white umbrella.” The Great Being paid homage to his father and said: “I have no need for the kingdom. I will go forth. Please grant me permission to go forth.” “Dear son, why do you reject the kingdom and wish to go forth?” “Your majesty, for ten months I dwelt in my mother’s womb as if in a hell of filth. After emerging from the womb, out of fear of the ogress I lived for sixteen years in a prison, unable even to look outside. I was as if cast into a minor hell. Even though I am freed from the ogress’s hand, I am not ageless and immortal. Death, you see, cannot be conquered by anyone. I am disenchanted with existence. Before sickness, old age, and death come upon me, I will go forth and live righteously. Enough of the kingdom for me! Grant me permission, your majesty.” And teaching the Dhamma to his father, he said:

363.

363.

“Yamekarattiṃ [P 4.0494] paṭhamaṃ, gabbhe vasati māṇavo;

Abbhuṭṭhitova so yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattati.

From the very first night a person dwells in the womb, he has set out on a journey; and as he goes, he never turns back.

364.

364.

“Na [V 4.0447] yujjhamānā na balenavassitā, narā na jīranti na cāpi mīyare;

Sabbaṃ hidaṃ jātijarāyupaddutaṃ, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

It is not by fighting, nor by reliance on strength, that people avoid growing old and dying. For all this is afflicted by birth and old age. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

365.

365.

“Caturaṅginiṃ [M 4.0498] senaṃ subhiṃsarūpaṃ, jayanti raṭṭhādhipatī pasayha;

Na maccuno jayitumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Rulers of realms conquer by force with their fourfold army of terrifying appearance; but they are not able to conquer Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

366.

366.

“Hatthīhi assehi rathehi pattibhi, parivāritā muccare ekacceyyā;

Na maccuno muccitumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Surrounded by elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, some may be freed from their enemies; but they are not able to be freed from Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

367.

367.

“Hatthīhi assehi rathehi pattibhi, sūrā pabhañjanti padhaṃsayanti;

Na maccuno bhañjitumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

With elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, heroes break and destroy their foes; but they are not able to break Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

368.

368.

“Mattā gajā bhinnagaḷā pabhinnā, nagarāni maddanti janaṃ hananti;

Na maccuno madditumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Maddened elephants, with ichor streaming from their temples, crush cities and kill people; but they are not able to crush Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

369.

369.

“Issāsino katahatthāpi vīrā, dūrepātī akkhaṇavedhinopi;

Na maccuno vijjhitumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Though they be archers, heroes with practiced hands, long-range shooters who can pierce a hair-tip; they are not able to pierce Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

370.

370.

“Sarāni khīyanti saselakānanā, sabbaṃ hidaṃ khīyati dīghamantaraṃ;

Sabbaṃ hidaṃ bhañjare kālapariyāyaṃ, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Lakes dry up, along with mountains and forests; all this wastes away in the long course of time. All this is broken by the passage of time. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

371.

371.

“Sabbesamevañhi narāna nārinaṃ, calācalaṃ pāṇabhunodha jīvitaṃ;

Paṭova dhuttassa, dumova kūlajo, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Indeed, for all men and women here, the life of beings is precarious and fleeting, like a gambler’s cloth, like a tree on a riverbank. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

372.

372.

“Dumapphalāneva [P 4.0495][M 4.0499] patanti māṇavā, daharā ca vuddhā ca sarīrabhedā;

Nāriyo narā majjhimaporisā ca, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Like fruits from a tree, people fall at the breakup of the body—the young and the old, women, men, and those of middle age. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

373.

373.

“Nāyaṃ vayo tārakarājasannibho, yadabbhatītaṃ gatameva dāni taṃ;

Jiṇṇassa hī natthi ratī kuto sukhaṃ, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

This age is not like the king of the stars; what has passed is now simply gone. For one who is old there is no delight; whence could there be happiness? This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

374.

374.

“Yakkhā [V 4.0448] pisācā athavāpi petā, kupitā te assasanti manusse;

Na maccuno assasitussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Yakkhas, pisācas, or even petas, when angered, might strike human beings with their breath; but they are not able to strike Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

375.

375.

“Yakkhe pisāce athavāpi pete, kupitepi te nijjhapanaṃ karonti;

Na maccuno nijjhapanaṃ karonti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

One can appease yakkhas, pisācas, or even petas when they are angered; but one cannot appease Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

376.

376.

“Aparādhake dūsake heṭhake ca, rājāno daṇḍenti viditvāna dosaṃ;

Na maccuno daṇḍayitussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Kings punish offenders, corrupters, and harmers, having known their fault; but they are not able to punish Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

377.

377.

“Aparādhakā dūsakā heṭhakā ca, labhanti te rājino nijjhapetuṃ;

Na maccuno nijjhapanaṃ karonti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Offenders, corrupters, and harmers may be able to appease the king; but they cannot appease Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

378.

378.

“Na khattiyoti na ca brāhmaṇoti, na aḍḍhakā balavā tejavāpi;

Na maccurājassa apekkhamatthi, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

The King of Death has no regard for anyone, whether a warrior or a brahmin, whether rich, strong, or mighty. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

379.

379.

“Sīhā [M 4.0500] ca byagghā ca athopi dīpiyo, pasayha khādanti vipphandamānaṃ;

Na maccuno khāditumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Lions, tigers, and also leopards forcibly devour struggling prey; but they are not able to devour Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

380.

380.

“Māyākārā raṅgamajjhe karontā, mohenti cakkhūni janassa tāvade;

Na maccuno mohayitussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Magicians performing in the arena may delude the eyes of the people for a time; but they are not able to delude Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

381.

381.

“Āsīvisā [P 4.0496] kupitā uggatejā, ḍaṃsanti mārentipi te manusse;

Na maccuno ḍaṃsitumussahanti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Venomous snakes, angered and fiercely potent, may bite and even kill people; but they are not able to bite Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

382.

382.

“Āsīvisā kupitā yaṃ ḍaṃsanti, tikicchakā tesa visaṃ hananti;

Na maccuno daṭṭhavisaṃ hananti, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

When angered venomous snakes bite, physicians may counteract their venom; but they cannot counteract the venom of Death's bite. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

383.

383.

“Dhammantarī vettaraṇī ca bhojo, visāni hantvāna bhujaṅgamānaṃ;

Suyyanti te kālakatā tatheva, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Though Dhammantarī, Vettaraṇī, and Bhoja destroy the venoms of serpents, they too pass away in due course. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

384.

384.

“Vijjādharā [V 4.0449] ghoramadhīyamānā, adassanaṃ osadhehi vajanti;

Na maccurājassa vajantadassanaṃ, taṃ me matī hoti carāmi dhammaṃ.

Wielders of spells, studying dreadful arts, may become invisible by means of herbs; yet they do not escape the sight of the King of Death. This is my resolve: I will practice the Dhamma.

385.

385.

“Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahāti;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe, na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī.

Indeed, the Dhamma protects one who practices the Dhamma; the Dhamma, well-practiced, brings happiness. This is the benefit of Dhamma well-practiced: one who practices the Dhamma does not go to a wretched destination.

386.

386.

“Na [M 4.0501] hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”nti.

For Dhamma and non-Dhamma do not both have the same result; non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma leads to a happy destination.

Tattha yamekarattinti yebhuyyena sattā mātukucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhantā rattiyaṃyeva gaṇhanti, tasmā evamāha. Ayaṃ panettha attho – yaṃ ekarattiṃ vā divā vā paṭhamameva paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā mātukucchisaṅkhāte gabbhe vasati. Māṇavoti satto kalalabhāvena patiṭṭhāti. Abbhuṭṭhitova so yātīti so māṇavo yathā nāma valāhakasaṅkhāto abbho uṭṭhito nibbatto vāyuvegāhato paṭigacchati, tatheva –

Here, "one night" refers to how beings, for the most part, take conception in the mother’s womb at night; therefore, it is stated thus. The meaning here is this: whether for one night or one day, having first taken conception, the being dwells in the womb, known as the mother’s belly. "Young man" refers to a being established in the state of an embryo. "He goes having arisen" means that just as a cloud mass, having arisen or come into existence, when struck by the force of the wind, goes away, so too—

“Paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, kalalā hoti abbudaṃ;

Abbudā jāyate pesi, pesi nibbattatī ghano;

Ghanā pasākhā jāyanti, kesā lomā nakhāpi ca.

First, there is the embryo; from the embryo comes the second stage. From the second stage arises the third; from the third develops the fourth. From the fourth sprout limbs, hair of the head, hair of the body, and also nails.

“Yañcassa bhuñjatī mātā, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti, mātukucchigato naroti. (saṃ. ni. 1.235);

Whatever food, drink, and sustenance his mother consumes, by that he is sustained there, the person dwelling in the mother's womb.

Imaṃ mātukucchiyaṃ kalalādibhāvaṃ, mātukucchito ca nikkhanto mandadasakādibhāvaṃ āpajjamāno satataṃ samitaṃ gacchati. Sa gacchaṃ na nivattatīti sacāyaṃ [P 4.0497] evaṃ gacchanto puna abbudato kalalabhāvaṃ, pesiādito vā abbudādibhāvaṃ, khiḍḍādasakato mandadasakabhāvaṃ, vaṇṇadasakādito vā khiḍḍādasakādibhāvaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na nivattati. Yathā pana so valāhako vātavegena saṃcuṇṇiyamāno “ahaṃ asukaṭṭhāne nāma uṭṭhito puna nivattitvā tattheva gantvā pakatibhāvena ṭhassāmī”ti na labhati, yaṃ disaṃ gataṃ, taṃ gatameva, yaṃ antarahitaṃ, taṃ antarahitameva hoti, tathā sopi kalalādibhāvena gacchamāno gacchateva, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse saṅkhārā purimānaṃ purimānaṃ paccayā hutvā pacchato anivattitvā tattha tattheva bhijjanti, jarākāle [V 4.0450] saṅkhārā “amhehi esa pubbe yuvā thāmasampanno kato, puna naṃ nivattitvā tattheva karissāmā”ti na labhanti, tattha tattheva antaradhāyantīti dasseti.

In this mother’s womb, the being undergoes states from the embryo onward, and after emerging from the womb, enters states such as infancy onward, constantly and continuously moving forward. As he goes, he does not turn back—meaning that as he goes, he does not revert from the second stage back to the embryo, nor from the third stage back to the second, nor from the decade of play back to the decade of infancy, nor from the decade of beauty back to the decade of play. Just as that mass of clouds, being pulverized by the force of the wind, cannot think, "I arose in such-and-such a place, I will return there and remain in my original state," but instead, where it has gone, it has gone; what has vanished, has vanished—so too, he, progressing through the states from the embryo onward, simply moves forward. In each successive phase, conditioned phenomena, having been causes for the preceding phenomena, without turning back, disintegrate right there. At the time of aging, the conditioned phenomena cannot think, "We made him young and strong before, we will turn him back to that state again," but instead, they disappear right there—this is what is shown.

Na [M 4.0502] yujjhamānāti ubhato byūḷhe saṅgāme yujjhantā. Na balenavassitāti na kāyabalena vā yodhabalena vā upagatā samannāgatā. Na jīrantīti purima-na-kāraṃ āharitvā evarūpāpi narā na jīranti na cāpi na mīyareti attho veditabbo. Sabbaṃ hidanti mahārāja, sabbameva idaṃ pāṇamaṇḍalaṃ mahāyantena pīḷiyamānā ucchughaṭikā viya jātiyā ca jarāya ca upaddutaṃ niccaṃ pīḷitaṃ. Taṃ me matī hotīti tena kāraṇena mama “pabbajitvā dhammaṃ carāmī”ti mati hoti cittaṃ uppajjati.

"Not fighting"—means those who are fighting in a battle drawn up on both sides. "Not relying on strength"—means not endowed with or possessed of physical strength or the strength of warriors. "Not aging"—by applying the preceding negative particle, the meaning should be understood as: it is not that such men do not age, nor that they do not die. "All this"—O great king, all this sphere of living beings is oppressed by birth and old age, constantly afflicted, like a stalk of sugarcane being crushed by a great machine. "That is my resolve"—means for that reason, the thought occurs to me: "Having gone forth, I will practice the Dhamma."

Caturaṅgininti hatthiādīhi caturaṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Senaṃ subhiṃsarūpanti suṭṭhu bhiṃsanakajātikaṃ senaṃ. Jayantīti kadāci ekacce rājāno attano senāya jayanti. Na maccunoti tepi rājāno mahāsenassa maccuno senaṃ jayituṃ na ussahanti, na byādhijarāmaraṇāni maddituṃ sakkonti. Muccare ekacceyyāti etehi hatthiādīhi parivāritā ekacce paccāmittānaṃ hatthato muccanti, maccuno pana santikā muccituṃ na sakkonti. Pabhañjantīti etehi hatthiādīhi paccatthikarājūnaṃ nagarāni pabhañjanti. Padhaṃsayantīti mahājanaṃ dhaṃsentā padhaṃsentā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti. Na maccunoti tepi maraṇakāle patte maccuno bhañjituṃ na sakkonti.

"A fourfold army"—composed of the four divisions beginning with elephants. "A very fearsome army"—an army of a truly fearsome nature. "Victorious"—sometimes certain kings are victorious with their armies. "But not over Death"—even those kings are not able to conquer the army of Death, who possesses a great army; nor can they crush sickness, old age, and death. "Some may escape"—surrounded by these divisions, including elephants, some may escape from the hands of their enemies, but they cannot escape from the presence of Death. "Shattering"—with these divisions, including elephants, they shatter the cities of rival kings. "Destroying"—destroying and ruining the masses, they bring them to the loss of life. "But not over Death"—even they, when the time of death arrives, cannot shatter Death.

Bhinnagaḷā pabhinnāti tīsu ṭhānesu pabhinnā hutvā madaṃ gaḷantā, paggharitamadāti attho. Na maccunoti tepi mahāmaccuṃ maddituṃ na sakkonti. Issāsinoti issāsā dhanuggahā. Katahatthāti susikkhitā. Dūrepātīti saraṃ dūre pātetuṃ samatthā. Akkhaṇavedhinoti aviraddhavedhino, vijjuālokena vijjhanasamatthā vā. Sarānīti anotattādīni mahāsarāni khīyantiyeva. Saselakānanāti sapabbatavanasaṇḍā mahāpathavīpi khīyati. Sabbaṃ hidanti sabbamidaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ dīghamantaraṃ ṭhatvā khīyateva. Kappuṭṭhānaggiṃ [P 4.0498] patvā mahāsinerupi aggimukhe madhusitthakaṃ viya vilīyateva, aṇumattopi saṅkhāro ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Kālapariyāyanti kālapariyāyaṃ nassanakālavāraṃ patvā sabbaṃ bhañjare, sabbaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ bhijjateva. Tassa pakāsanatthaṃ sattasūriyasuttaṃ (a. ni. 7.66) āharitabbaṃ.

Broken and burst—having burst in three places, oozing with rut, meaning 'with flowing rut.' But not over death—even they cannot crush the great death. Archers—bowmen. Well-trained—highly skilled. Long-range shooters—capable of casting an arrow far. Unerring marksmen—those whose piercing does not miss, or able to pierce by the light of lightning. The lakes—even the great lakes like Anotatta dry up. With mountains and forests—even the great earth with its mountains and forest groves wastes away. All this—all conditioned things, after enduring for a long time, just perish. Having reached the fire that arises at the end of an eon, even the great Sineru just melts like honeycomb in the mouth of a fire; not even the slightest conditioned thing can endure. The cycle of time—when the turn of the time for destruction arrives, everything is shattered; all conditioned things just break apart. To illustrate this, the Seven Suns Sutta (AN 7.66) should be cited.

Calācalanti cañcalaṃ sakabhāvena ṭhātuṃ asamatthaṃ nānābhāvavinābhāvasabhāvameva. Pāṇabhunodha [V 4.0451] jīvitanti idha loke imesaṃ pāṇabhūtānaṃ jīvitaṃ[M 4.0503]. Paṭova dhuttassa, dumova kūlajoti suradhutto hi suraṃ disvāva udare baddhaṃ sāṭakaṃ datvā pivateva, nadīkūle jātadumova kūle lujjamāne lujjati, yathā esa paṭo ca dumo ca cañcalo, evaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ, devāti. Dumapphalānevāti yathā pakkāni phalāni vātāhatāni dumaggato bhūmiyaṃ patanti, tathevime māṇavā jarāvātāhatā jīvitā gaḷitvā maraṇapathaviyaṃ patanti. Daharāti antamaso kalalabhāve ṭhitāpi. Majjhimaporisāti nārīnarānaṃ majjhe ṭhitā ubhatobyañjanakanapuṃsakā.

Restless and unsteady means unstable, unable to remain in its own state, having a nature of various states and their passing away. 'Life is fleeting for living beings'—this means the life of these living beings here in this world. Like a gambler's cloth, like a tree on the riverbank—for just as a drunkard, upon seeing liquor, immediately gives the cloth tied around his belly and drinks; or as a tree born on the riverbank is destroyed when the bank collapses, so too is the life of beings, O gods. 'Like tree fruits'—just as ripe fruits, struck by the wind, fall from the treetop to the ground, so too these young men, struck by the wind of old age, slip from life and fall onto the earth of death. 'Young'—even those abiding in the state of an embryo. 'Middle persons'—those standing between women and men, hermaphrodites possessing the characteristics of both.

Tārakarājasannibhoti yathā tārakarājā kāḷapakkhe khīṇo, puna juṇhapakkhe pūrati, na evaṃ sattānaṃ vayo. Sattānañhi yaṃ abbhatītaṃ, gatameva dāni taṃ, na tassa punāgamanaṃ atthi. Kuto sukhanti jarājiṇṇassa kāmaguṇesu ratipi natthi, te paṭicca uppajjanakasukhaṃ kutoyeva. Yakkhāti mahiddhikā yakkhā. Pisācāti paṃsupisācakā. Petāti pettivisayikā. Assasantīti assāsavātena upahananti, āvisantīti vā attho. Na maccunoti maccuṃ pana tepi assāsena upahanituṃ vā āvisituṃ vā na sakkonti. Nijjhapanaṃ karontīti balikammavasena khamāpenti pasādenti. Aparādhaketi rājāparādhakārake. Dūsaketi rajjadūsake. Heṭhaketi sandhicchedādīhi lokaviheṭhake. Rājānoti rājāno. Viditvāna dosanti dosaṃ jānitvā yathānurūpena daṇḍena daṇḍentīti attho. Na maccunoti tepi maccuṃ daṇḍayituṃ na sakkonti.

Like the king of stars—just as the moon wanes in the dark fortnight and waxes again in the bright fortnight, not so is the age of beings. For beings, what has passed is indeed gone; there is no return of it. Whence happiness?—for one aged and decayed, there is no delight in sensual pleasures; whence then could happiness arise in dependence on them? Yakkhas—yakkhas of great power. Pisacas—dust-demons. Petas—those belonging to the realm of petas. They breathe upon—they strike with their out-breath, or the meaning is 'they possess'. But not over death—even they cannot strike or possess death with their breath. They make appeasement—by means of offerings, they ask for forgiveness and please them. Offenders—those who commit offenses against the king. Corrupters—those who corrupt the kingdom. Harassers—those who harass people by house-breaking and the like. Kings—kings. Knowing their fault—knowing the fault, they punish with a punishment appropriate to it; this is the meaning. But not over death—even they cannot punish death.

Nijjhapetunti sakkhīhi attano niraparādhabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā pasādetuṃ. Na aḍḍhakā balavā tejavāpīti “ime aḍḍhā, ayaṃ kāyabalañāṇabalādīhi balavā, ayaṃ tejavā”ti evampi na paccurājassa apekkhaṃ atthi, ekasmimpi satte apekkhaṃ pemaṃ sineho natthi, sabbameva abhimaddatīti dasseti. Pasayhāti balakkārena abhibhavitvā. Na maccunoti tepi maccuṃ khādituṃ na sakkonti. Karontāti māyaṃ karontā. Mohentīti abhūtaṃ bhūtaṃ katvā dassentā mohenti.
