Uggatejāti uggatena visatejena samannāgatā. Tikicchakāti visavejjā. Dhammantarī vettaraṇī ca bhojoti ete evaṃnāmakā vejjā. Ghoramadhīyamānāti ghoraṃ nāma vijjaṃ adhīyantā. Osadhehīti ghoraṃ vā gandhāriṃ [P 4.0499] vā vijjaṃ sāvetvā osadhaṃ ādāya tehi osadhehi paccatthikānaṃ adassanaṃ vajanti.

To convince—to proclaim one's own innocence through witnesses and thereby win trust. Not the rich, the mighty, or the radiant—even thus, the King of Death has no regard, thinking, 'These are rich, this one is mighty with physical strength, knowledge, and so on, this one is radiant'; he has no expectation, affection, or love even toward a single being—thus it shows that he crushes everything. By force—overpowering by force. But not over death—even they are not able to devour death. Acting—acting deceptively. Deceiving—they deceive by presenting the untrue as true. Of fierce power—endowed with the fierce power of poison. Physicians—poison-doctors. Dhammantari, Vettaraṇī, and Bhoja—these are physicians known by those names. Studying the deadly arts—studying the art called Ghora. With antidotes—after reciting the Ghora or Gandhari art, taking an antidote, with those antidotes they become invisible to their enemies.

Dhammoti [M 4.0504] sucaritadhammo. Rakkhatīti yena rakkhito, taṃ paṭirakkhati. Sukhanti chasu kāmasaggesu sukhaṃ āvahati. Pāpetīti paṭisandhivasena upaneti.

The Dhamma—it is the Dhamma of good conduct. It protects—it protects in return the one by whom it is protected. It brings happiness—it brings happiness in the six sensual heavens. It leads—it leads to a destination by way of rebirth-linking.

Evaṃ [V 4.0452] mahāsatto catuvīsatiyā gāthāhi pitu dhammaṃ desetvā “mahārāja, tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumhākameva hotu, na mayhaṃ iminā attho, tumhehi pana saddhiṃ kathentameva maṃ byādhijarāmaraṇāni upagacchanti, tiṭṭhatha, tumhe”ti vatvā ayadāmaṃ chinditvā mattahatthī viya kañcanapañjaraṃ chinditvā sīhapotako viya kāme pahāya mātāpitaro vanditvā nikkhami. Athassa pitā “mamapi rajjenattho natthī”ti rajjaṃ pahāya tena saddhiññeva nikkhami, tasmiṃ nikkhante devīpi amaccāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikādayopīti sakalanagaravāsino gehāni chaḍḍetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Samāgamo mahā ahosi, parisā dvādasayojanikā jātā. Taṃ ādāya mahāsatto himavantaṃ pāvisi. Sakko tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā vissakammaṃ pesetvā dvādasayojanāyāmaṃ sattayojanavitthāraṃ assamapadaṃ kāresi. Sabbe pabbajitaparikkhāre paṭiyādāpesi. Ito paraṃ mahāsattassa pabbajjā ca ovādadānañca brahmalokaparāyaṇatā ca parisāya anapāyagamanīyatā ca sabbā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Thus, the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to his father with twenty-four verses, said: "Great king, let your kingdom be yours alone; I have no need of it. But even as I speak with you, sickness, old age, and death approach me. You, stay here." Having said this, like a rutting elephant breaking its iron chain, and like a lion cub breaking a golden cage, he abandoned sensual pleasures, paid homage to his parents, and departed. Then his father, thinking, "I too have no need of a kingdom," renounced the kingdom and departed with him. When he departed, the queen, the ministers, the brahmins, householders, and so on—all the city-dwellers—abandoned their homes and departed. There was a great gathering; the assembly grew to be twelve yojanas in size. Taking them with him, the Great Being entered the Himalayas. Sakka, knowing of his renunciation, sent Vissakamma and had him create a hermitage twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide. He had all the requisites of the renunciant life prepared. From this point on, the Great Being’s renunciation, his giving of advice, his destiny in the Brahma world, and the fact that the assembly did not go to a state of loss, should all be understood in the manner already described.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbepi tathāgato mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, ayogharapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, said: "Thus, monks, in the past too the Tathāgata went forth in the great renunciation." Then he made the connection to the Jātaka: "At that time, the parents were the noble royal families, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the wise one of the iron house was I myself."

Ayogharajātakavaṇṇanā cuddasamā.

The fourteenth commentary on the Ayoghara Jātaka is finished.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Mātaṅgo cittasambhūto, sivi sirī ca rohaṇaṃ;

Haṃso sattigumbo bhallā, somanassaṃ campeyyakaṃ.

Mātaṅga, Cittasambhūta, Sivi, Sirī, and Rohaṇa; Haṃsa, Sattigumba, Bhalla, Somanassa, and Campeyyaka.

Palobhaṃ pañcapaṇḍitaṃ, hatthipālaṃ ayogharaṃ;

Vīsatiyamhi jātakā, catuddaseva saṅgitā.

Palobha, Pañcapaṇḍita, Hatthipāla, and Ayoghara. In the Book of Twenty, fourteen Jātakas have thus been recited.

Vīsatinipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of Twenty is concluded.

(Catuttho bhāgo niṭṭhito)

(The fourth volume is concluded.)

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Collection of Minor Texts

Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā

The Jātaka Commentary

(Pañcamo bhāgo)

(Fifth Volume)

16. Tiṃsanipāto

16. The Book of the Thirties

[511] 1. Kiṃchandajātakavaṇṇanā

[511] 1. The Commentary on the Kiṃchanda Jātaka

Kiṃchando [V 5.0001][P 5.0001][M 5.0001] kimadhippāyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathakammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi satthā bahū upāsake ca upāsikāyo ca uposathike dhammassavanatthāya āgantvā dhammasabhāyaṃ nisinne “uposathikāttha upāsakā”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “sādhu vo [V 5.0002] kataṃ uposathaṃ karontehi, porāṇakā upaḍḍhūposathakammassa nissandena mahantaṃ yasaṃ paṭilabhiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"What is the inclination, what is the intention?"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Uposatha observance. For one day, the Teacher, seeing many laymen and laywomen who had come to listen to the Dhamma and were seated in the Dhamma hall, asked them, "Are you observing the Uposatha, lay followers?" When they replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," he said, "It is good that you are observing the Uposatha. The ancients, as a result of performing the half-Uposatha observance, attained great prosperity." Being requested by them, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto dhammena rajjaṃ kārento saddho ahosi dānasīlauposathakammesu appamatto. So sesepi amaccādayo dānādīsu samādapesi. Purohito panassa parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko lañjakhādako kūṭavinicchayiko ahosi. Rājā uposathadivase amaccādayo pakkosāpetvā “uposathikā hothā”ti āha. Purohito uposathaṃ na samādiyi. Atha naṃ divā lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭaḍḍaṃ katvā upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ rājā “tumhe uposathikā”ti amacce pucchanto “tvampi ācariya uposathiko”ti pucchi. So “āmā”ti musāvādaṃ [M 5.0002] katvā pāsādā otari. Atha naṃ eko amacco “nanu tumhe na uposathikā”ti codesi. So āha – “ahaṃ velāyameva bhuñjiṃ, gehaṃ pana gantvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāya sāyaṃ [P 5.0002] na bhuñjissāmi, rattiṃ sīlaṃ rakkhissāmi, evaṃ me upaḍḍhūposathakammaṃ bhavissatī”ti? “Sādhu, ācariyā”ti. So gehaṃ gantvā tathā akāsi. Punekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ vinicchaye nisinne aññatarā sīlavatī itthī aḍḍaṃ karontī gharaṃ gantuṃ alabhamānā “uposathakammaṃ nātikkamissāmī”ti upakaṭṭhe kāle mukhaṃ vikkhāletuṃ ārabhi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe brāhmaṇassa supakkānaṃ ambaphalānaṃ ambapiṇḍi āhariyittha. So tassā uposathikabhāvaṃ ñatvā “imāni khāditvā uposathikā hohī”ti adāsi. Sā tathā akāsi. Ettakaṃ brāhmaṇassa kammaṃ.

In the past, in Benares, when King Brahmadatta ruled righteously, he was faithful and diligent in generosity, virtue, and Uposatha observances. He also encouraged his ministers and others in acts of giving and the like. However, his chaplain was a backbiter, a bribe-taker, and a deceitful judge. On the Uposatha day, the king summoned his ministers and said, "Observe the Uposatha." The chaplain, however, did not undertake the observance. Later, during the day, after taking a bribe and deciding a false case, he came to attend the king. While asking his ministers, "Are you observing the Uposatha?" the king also asked him, "Teacher, are you also observing the Uposatha?" He falsely replied, "Yes," and descended from the palace. Then an official questioned him, "Surely, you are not observing the Uposatha?" He replied, "I ate only in the morning. After returning home, I will rinse my mouth, undertake the Uposatha, refrain from eating in the evening, and keep the precepts at night. Thus, I will have the half-Uposatha observance." The official said, "Very well, Teacher." The chaplain went home and did as he said. On another day, while he was seated in judgment, a certain virtuous woman engaged in a lawsuit, being unable to return home, thought, "I must not let the Uposatha observance pass by," and as the time drew near, she began to rinse her mouth. At that moment, a cluster of ripe mangoes was brought to the brahmin. Knowing she was observing the Uposatha, he said, "Eat these and then observe the Uposatha," and gave them to her. She did so. Such was the brahmin’s deed.

So aparabhāge kālaṃ katvā himavantapadese kosikigaṅgāya tīre tiyojanike ambavane ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge sobhaggappatte kanakavimāne alaṅkatasirisayane suttappabuddho viya nibbatti alaṅkatapaṭiyatto uttamarūpadharo soḷasasahassadevakaññāparivāro. So rattiññeva taṃ sirisampattiṃ anubhoti. Vemānikapetabhāvena hissa kammasarikkhako vipāko ahosi, tasmā aruṇe uggacchante ambavanaṃ pavisati, paviṭṭhakkhaṇeyevassa dibbattabhāvo antaradhāyati, asītihatthatālakkhandhappamāṇo attabhāvo nibbattati, sakalasarīraṃ jhāyati, supupphitakiṃsuko viya hoti. Dvīsu hatthesu ekekāva aṅguli, tattha mahākuddālappamāṇā nakhā honti. Tehi nakhehi attano piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ phāletvā uppāṭetvā khādanto vedanāppatto mahāravaṃ ravanto dukkhaṃ anubhoti. Sūriye atthaṅgate taṃ sarīraṃ antaradhāyati, dibbasarīraṃ nibbattati, alaṅkatapaṭiyattā dibbanāṭakitthiyo nānātūriyāni gahetvā parivārenti. So mahāsampattiṃ anubhavanto ramaṇīye ambavane dibbapāsādaṃ abhiruhati. Iti so uposathikāya itthiyā ambaphaladānassa nissandena tiyojanikaṃ ambavanaṃ paṭilabhati[V 5.0003], lañjaṃ gahetvā kūṭaḍḍakaraṇanissandena pana piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ uppāṭetvā [P 5.0003] khādati, upaḍḍhūposathassa nissandena rattiṃ sampattiṃ anubhoti, soḷasasahassanāṭakitthīhi parivuto paricāresi.

In the course of time, after passing away, he was reborn in the Himalayan region on the bank of the Kosikī river, in a delightful three-yojana mango grove, in a beautiful spot. He appeared in a golden mansion, on a decorated and splendid couch, as if awakened from sleep—adorned and prepared, possessing supreme beauty, and surrounded by sixteen thousand celestial maidens. He enjoyed that glorious prosperity only at night. For his karmic result was commensurate with his deeds, in the state of a mansion-dwelling peta. Therefore, at dawn, he would enter the mango grove. The moment he entered, his divine form would disappear, and a body eighty cubits tall, the size of a palm tree trunk, would arise. His entire body would burn, like a kiṃsuka tree in full bloom. On each of his two hands, there was only a single finger, with nails the size of large spades. With those nails, he would rip open the flesh of his own back and eat it, and being in extreme pain, he would suffer, crying out with a great roar. When the sun set, that body would disappear, and his divine body would arise. Sixteen thousand celestial dancing girls, adorned and prepared, would surround him with various musical instruments. Enjoying great prosperity, he would ascend the divine palace in the delightful mango grove. Thus, as a result of giving mango fruits to a woman observing the Uposatha, he obtained the three-yojana mango grove. But as a result of taking bribes and giving false judgments, he ripped and ate the flesh of his own back. And as a result of the half-day Uposatha, he enjoyed prosperity at night, surrounded and attended by sixteen thousand dancing girls.

Tasmiṃ [M 5.0003] kāle bārāṇasirājā kāmesu dosaṃ disvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā adhogaṅgāya ramaṇīye bhūmipadese paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā uñchācariyāya yāpento vihāsi. Athekadivasaṃ tamhā ambavanā mahāghaṭappamāṇaṃ ambapakkaṃ gaṅgāya patitvā sotena vuyhamānaṃ tassa tāpasassa paribhogatitthābhimukhaṃ agamāsi. So mukhaṃ dhovanto taṃ majjhe nadiyā āgacchantaṃ disvā udakaṃ taranto gantvā ādāya assamapadaṃ āharitvā agyāgāre ṭhapetvā satthakena phāletvā yāpanamattaṃ khāditvā sesaṃ kadalipaṇṇehi paṭicchādetvā punappunaṃ divase divase yāva parikkhayā khādi. Tasmiṃ pana khīṇe aññaṃ phalāphalaṃ khādituṃ nāsakkhi, rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā “tameva ambapakkaṃ khādissāmī”ti nadītīraṃ gantvā nadiṃ olokento “ambaṃ alabhitvā na uṭṭhahissāmī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā nisīdi. So tattha nirāhāro ekampi divasaṃ, dvepi, tīṇi, catu, pañca, cha divasāni vātātapena parisussanto ambaṃ olokento nisīdi. Atha sattame divase nadīdevatā āvajjamānā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ tāpaso taṇhāvasiko hutvā sattāhaṃ nirāhāro gaṅgaṃ olokento nisīdi, imassa ambapakkaṃ adātuṃ na yuttaṃ, alabhanto marissati, dassāmi tassā”ti āgantvā gaṅgāya upari ākāse ṭhatvā tena saddhiṃ sallapantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, the king of Benares, seeing the fault in sensual pleasures, went forth as an ascetic. Having built a leaf-hut in a delightful spot on the lower Ganges, he lived sustaining himself by gleaning. Then one day, a ripe mango the size of a large pot fell from that mango grove into the Ganges. Carried by the current, it floated toward the landing-place used by the ascetic. While washing his face, he saw it coming in the middle of the river. Wading into the water, he took it, brought it to his hermitage, placed it in the fire-room, and after slicing it with a small knife, he ate just enough to sustain himself. He covered the rest with banana leaves and ate it bit by bit each day until it was finished. When it was gone, he was unable to eat any other fruits. Bound by the craving for its taste, thinking, 'I will eat only that ripe mango,' he went to the riverbank and, looking at the river, made a resolution: 'I will not rise unless I get a mango,' and sat down. There, without food, he sat for one day, then two, three, four, five, and six days, withering under the wind and sun, gazing for a mango. Then on the seventh day, the river deity, reflecting and knowing the situation, thought, 'This ascetic, enslaved by craving, has sat for seven days without food, gazing at the Ganges. It is not right to withhold the ripe mango from him; if he does not get it, he will die. I will give it to him.' Approaching and standing in the air above the Ganges, she spoke the first verse, wishing to converse with him:

1.

1.

“Kiṃchando kimadhippāyo, eko sammasi ghammani;

Kiṃpatthayāno kiṃ esaṃ, kena atthena brāhmaṇā”ti.

“What is your wish, what is your intent, that you sit alone in the heat? Desiring what, seeking what, for what purpose, O Brahmin?”

Tattha chandoti ajjhāsayo. Adhippāyoti cittaṃ. Sammasīti acchasi. Ghammanīti gimhe. Esanti esanto. Brāhmaṇāti pabbajitattā tāpasaṃ ālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ kiṃ adhippāyo kiṃ cintento kiṃ patthento kiṃ gavesanto kenatthena imasmiṃ gaṅgātīre gaṅgaṃ olokento nisinnoti.

There, 'chando' means intention. 'Adhippāyo' means thought. 'Sammasi' means you sit. 'Ghammani' means in the heat of summer. 'Esaṃ' means seeking. She addresses the ascetic as 'Brahmin' because he has gone forth. This is what is meant: 'Brahmin, with what intention, thinking what, desiring what, searching for what, for what reason are you sitting on this bank of the Ganges, gazing at the river?'

Taṃ [P 5.0004] sutvā tāpaso nava gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the ascetic spoke nine verses:

2.

2.

“Yathā mahā vāridharo, kumbho supariṇāhavā;

Tathūpamaṃ ambapakkaṃ, vaṇṇagandharasuttamaṃ.

“Like a great water-bearing jar of large circumference, such is the ripe mango, supreme in color, fragrance, and taste.

3.

3.

“Taṃ [V 5.0004][M 5.0004] vuyhamānaṃ sotena, disvānāmalamajjhime;

Pāṇībhi naṃ gahetvāna, agyāyatanamāhariṃ.

“Seeing it being carried by the stream in the middle of the pure water, I took it with my hands and brought it to the fire-sanctuary.

4.

4.

“Tato kadalipattesu, nikkhipitvā sayaṃ ahaṃ;

Satthena naṃ vikappetvā, khuppipāsaṃ ahāsi me.

“Then I myself placed it on plantain leaves; with a knife I sliced it, and it relieved my hunger and thirst.

5.

5.

“Sohaṃ apetadaratho, byantībhūto dukhakkhamo;

Assādaṃ nādhigacchāmi, phalesvaññesu kesuci.

“I was free from distress, my hunger was gone, and I could endure suffering. But now I find no delight in any other fruits whatsoever.

6.

6.

“Sosetvā nūna maraṇaṃ, taṃ mamaṃ āvahissati;

Ambaṃ yassa phalaṃ sādu, madhuraggaṃ manoramaṃ;

Yamuddhariṃ vuyhamānaṃ, udadhismā mahaṇṇave.

“Surely death will bring me to wither away—pining for that mango whose fruit is sweet, of supreme sweetness, and delightful; which I rescued while it was being swept away in the great flood of water.

7.

7.

“Akkhātaṃ te mayā sabbaṃ, yasmā upavasāmahaṃ;

Rammaṃ pati nisinnosmi, puthulomāyutā puthu.

“All has been told to you by me, and the reason why I fast. I sit by the delightful river, abundant with many broad-finned fish.

8.

8.

“Tvañca kho meva akkhāhi, attānamapalāyini;

Kā vā tvamasi kalyāṇi, kissa vā tvaṃ sumajjhime.

“But now you must tell me about yourself, you who do not conceal yourself; who are you, O lovely one, and to whom do you belong, O slender-waisted one?

9.

9.

“Ruppapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīva, byagghīva girisānujā;

Yā santi nāriyo devesu, devānaṃ paricārikā.

“Like a polished plate of silver, like a tigress on a mountain slope; whatever women there are among the gods, the attendants of the gods—

10.

10.

“Yā ca manussalokasmiṃ, rūpenānvāgatitthiyo;

Rūpena te sadisī natthi, devesu gandhabbamanussaloke;

Puṭṭhāsi me cārupubbaṅgi, brūhi nāmañca bandhave”ti.

“And those women in the human world endowed with beauty—none equal you in beauty among gods, gandhabbas, or humans. Asked by me, O fair-formed one, tell me your name and kindred.”

Tattha vāridharo kumbhoti udakaghaṭo. Supariṇāhavāti susaṇṭhāno. Vaṇṇagandharasuttamanti vaṇṇagandharasehi uttamaṃ. Disvānāti disvā. Amalamajjhimeti nimmalamajjhe. Devataṃ ālapanto evamāha. Pāṇībhīti hatthehi. Agyāyatanamāharinti attano aggihutasālaṃ āhariṃ. Vikappetvāti vicchinditvā. “Vikantetvā”tipi pāṭho. “Khādi”nti pāṭhaseso. Ahāsi meti [V 5.0005] taṃ jivhagge ṭhapitamattameva satta rasaharaṇisahassāni pharitvā mama [P 5.0005] khudañca pipāsañca hari. Apetadarathoti vigatakāyacittadaratho[M 5.0005]. Sudhābhojanaṃ bhuttassa viya hi tassa sabbadarathaṃ apahari. Byantībhūtoti tassa ambapakkassa vigatanto jāto, parikkhīṇaambapakko hutvāti attho. Dukhakkhamoti dukkhena asātena kāyakkhamena ceva cittakkhamena ca samannāgato. Aññesu pana kadalipanasādīsu phalesu parittakampi assādaṃ nādhigacchāmi, sabbāni me jivhāya ṭhapitamattāni tittakāneva sampajjantīti dīpeti.

Here, ‘vāridharo kumbho’ means a water pot. ‘Supariṇāhavā’ means well-formed. ‘Vaṇṇagandharasuttama’ means supreme in color, fragrance, and taste. ‘Disvānā’ means having seen. ‘Amalamajjhime’ means ‘O one with a flawless waist.’ Addressing the deity, he spoke thus. ‘Pāṇībhī’ means ‘with hands.’ ‘Agyāyatanamāhariṃ’ means ‘I brought it to my own fire-offering hall.’ ‘Vikappetvā’ means ‘having sliced.’ ‘Vikantetvā’ is another reading. ‘Khādi’ is the remainder of the reading. ‘Ahāsi me’ means that, placed merely on the tip of the tongue, it pervaded seven thousand taste-nerves and took away my hunger and thirst. ‘Apetadaratho’ means free from bodily and mental distress. For, like one who has eaten the food of the gods, it removed all his distress. ‘Byantībhūto’ means the ripe mango was finished, that is, the ripe mango was entirely consumed. ‘Dukhakkhamo’ means endowed with bodily and mental unendurability due to the lack of pleasant taste. He explains: ‘As for other fruits like plantains and jackfruit, I find not even a little enjoyment; all of them, merely placed on my tongue, become bitter.’

Sosetvāti nirāhāratāya sosetvā sukkhāpetvā. Taṃ mamanti taṃ mama. Yassāti yaṃ assa, ahosīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ phalaṃ mama sādu ahosi, yamahaṃ gambhīre puthulaudakakkhandhasaṅkhāte mahaṇṇave vuyhamānaṃ tato udadhismā uddhariṃ, taṃ ambaṃ mama maraṇaṃ āvahissatīti maññāmi, mayhaṃ taṃ alabhantassa jīvitaṃ nappavattissatīti. Upavasāmīti khuppipāsāhi upagato vasāmi. Rammaṃ pati nisinnosmīti ramaṇīyaṃ nadiṃ pati ahaṃ nisinno. Puthulomāyutā puthūti ayaṃ nadī puthulomehi macchehi āyutā puthu vipulā, api nāma me ito sotthi bhaveyyāti adhippāyo. Apalāyinīti apalāyitvā mama sammukhe ṭhiteti taṃ devataṃ ālapati. “Apalāsinī”tipi pāṭho, palāsarahite anavajjasarīreti attho. Kissa vāti kissa vā kāraṇā idhāgatāsīti pucchati.

‘Sosetvā’ means having caused to wither, having caused to dry up, due to lack of food. ‘Taṃ mamaṃ’ means ‘that for me.’ ‘Yassā’ means ‘which was’ (sweet), this is the meaning. This is what is said: ‘That fruit which was sweet to me, which I retrieved from the river—that great ocean-like mass of deep and vast water—that mango, I think, will bring about my death; for without obtaining it, my life will not continue.’ ‘Upavasāmi’ means ‘I dwell, afflicted by hunger and thirst.’ ‘Rammaṃ pati nisinnosmi’ means ‘I sit by the delightful river.’ ‘Puthulomāyutā puthū’ means ‘this river is endowed with broad-scaled fish and is broad and wide; perhaps there will be safety for me from this’—this is the intention. ‘Apalāyinī’ means ‘not fleeing, standing before me’—thus he addresses the deity. There is also a reading ‘Apalāsinī,’ meaning ‘without foliage,’ that is, with a faultless body. ‘Kissa vā’ means he asks, ‘For what reason have you come here?’

Rūpapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīvāti suṭṭhu parimajjitakañcanapaṭṭasadisī. Byagghīvāti līlāvilāsena taruṇabyagghapotikā viya. Devānanti channaṃ kāmāvacaradevānaṃ. Yā ca manussalokasminti yā ca manussaloke. Rūpenānvāgatitthiyoti rūpena anvāgatā itthiyo natthīti attano sambhāvanāya evamāha. Tava rūpasadisāya nāma na bhavitabbanti hissa adhippāyo. Gandhabbamanussaloketi mūlagandhādinissitesu gandhabbesu ca manussaloke ca. Cārupubbaṅgīti cārunā pubbaṅgena ūrulakkhaṇena samannāgate. Nāmañca bandhaveti attano nāmagottañca bandhave ca mayhaṃ akkhāhīti vadati.

‘Rūpapaṭṭapalimaṭṭhīva’ means ‘like a well-polished golden plate.’ ‘Byagghīva’ means ‘like a young female tiger cub with playful grace.’ ‘Devānaṃ’ means ‘of the six sense-sphere gods.’ ‘Yā ca manussalokasmiṃ’ means ‘and in the human world.’ ‘Rūpenānvāgatitthiyo’ means ‘There are no women endowed with such beauty’—thus he speaks out of his high esteem for her. His intention is: ‘There could not possibly be one with beauty like yours.’ ‘Gandhabbamanussaloke’ means ‘among the gandhabbas who subsist on roots, fragrances, and so on, and in the human world.’ ‘Cārupubbaṅgī’ means ‘endowed with a charming fore-body, characterized by the signs of the thighs.’ ‘Nāmañca bandhave’ means he says, ‘Tell me your name and clan, and your relatives.’

Tato devadhītā aṭṭha gāthā abhāsi –

Then the divine daughter spoke eight verses:

11.

11.

“Yaṃ tvaṃ pati nisinnosi, rammaṃ brāhmaṇa kosikiṃ;

Sāhaṃ bhusālayāvutthā, varavārivahoghasā.

“O Brahmin, by the delightful Kosiki you sit; I am she who dwells in a mansion in the fierce current, with a flood of excellent water.

12.

12.

“Nānādumagaṇākiṇṇā[V 5.0006][M 5.0006], bahukā girikandarā;

Mameva pamukhā honti, abhisandanti pāvuse.

“Many mountain gorges, teeming with various groups of trees, make me their goal; they flow toward me in the rainy season.

13.

13.

“Atho [P 5.0006] bahū vanatodā, nīlavārivahindharā;

Bahukā nāgavittodā, abhisandanti vārinā.

“And many forest waters, bearing streams of dark blue water, many with the delight of nāgas, flow toward me with their waters.

14.

14.

“Tā ambajambulabujā, nīpā tālā cudumbarā;

Bahūni phalajātāni, āvahanti abhiṇhaso.

“Those rivers constantly carry many kinds of fruits: mangoes, rose-apples, breadfruit, kadamba trees, palms, and cluster figs.

15.

15.

“Yaṃ kiñci ubhato tīre, phalaṃ patati ambuni;

Asaṃsayaṃ taṃ sotassa, phalaṃ hoti vasānugaṃ.

“Whatever fruit on either bank falls into the water, without doubt, that fruit becomes subject to the current.

16.

16.

“Etadaññāya medhāvi, puthupañña suṇohi me;

Mā rocaya mabhisaṅgaṃ, paṭisedha janādhipa.

“Knowing this, O wise one, O one of broad wisdom, listen to me. Do not delight in attachment; restrain it, O lord of men.

17.

17.

“Na vāhaṃ vaḍḍhavaṃ maññe, yaṃ tvaṃ raṭṭhābhivaḍḍhana;

Āceyyamāno rājisi, maraṇaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

“I do not consider it wisdom, O increaser of the kingdom, that you, a thriving royal sage, should long for death.

18.

18.

“Tassa jānanti pitaro, gandhabbā ca sadevakā;

Ye cāpi isayo loke, saññatattā tapassino;

Asaṃsayaṃ tepi jānanti, paṭṭhabhūtā yasassino”ti.

“The Fathers know of him, and the gandhabbas with the devas; and also those sages in the world who are self-controlled and ascetic. Without doubt, they too know, those who are foremost and illustrious.”

Tattha kosikinti yaṃ tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, rammaṃ kosikiṃ gaṅgaṃ pati nisinno. Bhusālayāvutthāti bhuse caṇḍasote ālayo yassa vimānassa, tasmiṃ adhivatthā, gaṅgaṭṭhakavimānavāsinīti attho. Varavārivahoghasāti varavārivahena oghena samannāgatā. Pamukhāti tā vuttappakārā girikandarā maṃ pamukhaṃ karonti, ahaṃ tāsaṃ pāmokkhā homīti dasseti. Abhisandantīti sandanti pavattanti, tato tato āgantvā maṃ kosikigaṅgaṃ pavisantīti attho. Vanatodāti na kevalaṃ kandarāva, atha kho bahū vanatodā tamhā tamhā vanamhā udakānipi maṃ bahūni pavisanti. Nīlavārivahindharāti maṇivaṇṇena nīlavārinā yutte udakakkhandhasaṅkhāte vahe dhārayantiyo. Nāgavittodāti nāgānaṃ vittikārena dhanasaṅkhātena vā udakena [V 5.0007] samannāgatā. Vārināti evarūpā hi bahū nadiyo maṃ vārināva abhisandanti pūrentīti dasseti.

Here, ‘kosikiṃ’ means ‘you, brahmin, who sit by the delightful Kosiki-Ganges.’ ‘Bhusālayāvutthā’ means residing in a mansion that has its abode in a fierce, turbulent current; the meaning is, dwelling in the Gaṅgāṭṭhaka mansion. ‘Varavārivahoghasā’ means endowed with a flood of excellent water. ‘Pamukhā’ shows that those mountain gorges of the type described make me their goal, that I am their chief. ‘Abhisandanti’ means they flow, they proceed; coming from here and there, they enter me, the Kosiki-Ganges—this is the meaning. ‘Vanatodā’ means not only the gorges, but also many waters from various forests enter me. ‘Nīlavārivahindharā’ means bearing streams, described as masses of water, that possess gem-colored, dark blue water. ‘Nāgavittodā’ means endowed with water that is the enjoyment of the nagas, or with water known as treasure. ‘Vārinā’ shows that many such rivers flow towards and fill me with water.

Tāti [M 5.0007] tā nadiyo. Āvahantīti etāni ambādīni ākaḍḍhanti. Sabbāni hi etāni upayogatthe paccattavacanāni. Atha vā tāti upayogabahuvacanaṃ. Āvahantīti imāni ambādīni tā nadiyo āgacchanti, upagacchantīti attho, evaṃ upagatāni pana mama sotaṃ pavisantīti adhippāyo. Sotassāti yaṃ ubhato tīre jātarukkhehi phalaṃ mama ambuni patati, sabbaṃ taṃ mama sotasseva vasānugaṃ hoti. Natthettha saṃsayoti evaṃ ambapakkassa nadīsotena āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathesi.

‘Tā’ means those rivers. ‘Āvahanti’ means they carry along these mangoes and other fruits. For all these are nominative case forms used in the sense of the accusative. Or, ‘tā’ is the accusative plural. ‘Āvahanti’ means these mangoes and other fruits come to those rivers—this is the meaning; the intention is that, having thus arrived, they enter my current. ‘Sotassa’ means whatever fruit from the trees growing on both banks falls into my water, all of it follows the will of my current. ‘Natth'ettha saṃsayo’ means thus she spoke of the reason for the ripe mango's arrival by the river’s current.

Medhāvi puthupaññāti ubhayaṃ ālapanameva. Mā rocayāti evaṃ taṇhābhisaṅgaṃ mā rocaya. Paṭisedhāti paṭisedhehi nanti rājānaṃ ovadati. Vaḍḍhavanti paññāvaḍḍhabhāvaṃ paṇḍitabhāvaṃ. Raṭṭhābhivaḍḍhanāti [P 5.0007] raṭṭhassa abhivaḍḍhana. Āceyyamānoti maṃsalohitehi āciyanto vaḍḍhanto, taruṇova hutvāti attho. Rājisīti taṃ ālapati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tvaṃ nirāhāratāya sussamāno taruṇova samāno ambalobhena maraṇaṃ abhikaṅkhasi, na ve ahaṃ tava imaṃ paṇḍitabhāvaṃ maññāmīti.

‘Medhāvi, puthupaññā’: both are forms of address. ‘Mā rocaya’ means do not delight in such attachment of craving. ‘Paṭisedha’ means she advises the king, saying, ‘Restrain it.’ ‘Vaḍḍhavaṃ’ means the state of increased wisdom, the state of being a wise man. ‘Raṭṭhābhivaḍḍhana’ means the increaser of the kingdom. ‘Āceyyamāno’ means being built up with flesh and blood, growing; the meaning is being young. ‘Rājisi’ is how she addresses him. This is what is said: ‘Since you, while wasting away from lack of food and being young, desire death out of greed for a mango, I certainly do not consider this to be wisdom on your part.’

Tassāti yo puggalo taṇhāvasiko hoti, tassa taṇhāvasikabhāvaṃ “pitaro”ti saṅkhaṃ gatā brahmāno ca saddhiṃ kāmāvacaradevehi gandhabbā ca vuttappakārā dibbacakkhukā isayo ca asaṃsayaṃ jānanti. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ te iddhimanto jāneyyuṃ, “asuko hi nāma taṇhāvasiko hotī”ti. Puna tesaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā yepi tesaṃ paṭṭhabhūtā yasassino paricārakā, tepi jānanti. Pāpakammaṃ karontassa hi raho nāma natthīti tāpasassa saṃvegaṃ uppādentī evamāha.

‘Tassa’ refers to a person who is under the sway of craving. The state of being under the sway of craving is known, without a doubt, by the Brahmās, known as “fathers,” together with the gods of the sensual realm, the gandhabbas, and the seers with divine vision as previously described. It is no wonder that those with psychic power should know, “So-and-so is indeed under the sway of craving.” Furthermore, having heard their words as they speak, even those illustrious attendants of theirs also know. For there is no such thing as secrecy for one who does evil deeds. Thus she spoke, arousing a sense of urgency in the ascetic.

Tato tāpaso catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the ascetic uttered four verses:

19.

19.

“Evaṃ viditvā vidū sabbadhammaṃ, viddhaṃsanaṃ cavanaṃ jīvitassa;

Na cīyatī tassa narassa pāpaṃ, sace na ceteti vadhāya tassa.

Having thus understood all good states and the destruction and passing away of life, evil does not accumulate for that man if he does not intend to kill him.

20.

20.

“Isipūgasamaññāte[M 5.0008], evaṃ lokyā viditā sati;

Anariyaparisambhāse, pāpakammaṃ jigīsasi.

O you who are renowned among the company of sages and thus known as a blessing to the world; O beautiful one, with your ignoble speech, you seek to bring about an evil deed.

21.

21.

“Sace [V 5.0008] ahaṃ marissāmi, tīre te puthusussoṇi;

Asaṃsayaṃ taṃ asiloko, mayi pete āgamissati.

If I die on your bank, O broad-hipped one, without a doubt, ill-repute will come to you when I am dead.

22.

22.

“Tasmā hi pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, rakkhasseva sumajjhime;

Mā taṃ sabbo jano pacchā, pakuṭṭhāyi mayi mate”ti.

Therefore, O slender-waisted one, guard against an evil deed; let not all people afterward revile you when I am dead.

Tattha evaṃ viditvāti yathā ahaṃ sīlañca aniccatañca jānāmi, evaṃ jānitvā ṭhitassa. Vidūti viduno. Sabbadhammanti sabbaṃ sucaritadhammaṃ. Tividhañhi sucaritaṃ idha sabbadhammoti adhippetaṃ. Viddhaṃsananti bhaṅgaṃ. Cavananti cutiṃ. Jīvitassāti āyuno. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – evaṃ viditvā ṭhitassa paṇḍitassa sabbaṃ sucaritadhammaṃ jīvitassa ca aniccataṃ jānantassa evarūpassa narassa pāpaṃ na cīyati na vaḍḍhati. Sace na ceteti vadhāya tassāti tassa saṅkhaṃ gatassa parapuggalassa vadhāya na ceteti na pakappeti, neva parapuggalaṃ vadhāya ceteti, nāpi parasantakaṃ vināseti, ahañca kassaci vadhāya acetetvā kevalaṃ ambapakke āsaṅgaṃ katvā gaṅgaṃ olokento nisinno, tvaṃ mayhaṃ kiṃ nāma akusalaṃ passasīti.

Here, ‘having understood thus’ means: standing having known as I know virtue and impermanence. ‘Vidū’ means the wise one. ‘Sabbadhammaṃ’ means all good conduct; for here, the threefold good conduct is intended by ‘sabbadhammaṃ’. ‘Viddhaṃsanaṃ’ means breaking up. ‘Cavanaṃ’ means passing away. ‘Jīvitassa’ means of the life-span. This is what is said: For such a person, a wise one who stands having understood thus, knowing all good conduct and the impermanence of life, evil does not accumulate or increase. ‘If he does not intend to kill him’ means: he does not intend or plan for the killing of another person; he neither intends to kill another person, nor does he destroy another’s property. And I, without intending to kill anyone, having merely developed an attachment to a ripe mango, sat looking at the Ganges; what unwholesome deed do you see in me?

Isipūgasamaññāteti [P 5.0008] isigaṇena suṭṭhu aññāte isīnaṃ sammate. Evaṃ lokyāti tvaṃ nāma pāpapavāhanena lokassa hitāti evaṃ viditā. Satīti sati sobhane uttameti ālapanametaṃ. Anariyaparisambhāseti “tassa jānanti pitaro”tiādikāya asundarāya paribhāsāya samannāgate. Jigīsasīti mayi pāpe asaṃvijjantepi maṃ evaṃ paribhāsantī ca paramaraṇaṃ ajjhupekkhantī ca attano pāpakammaṃ gavesasi uppādesi. Tīre teti tava gaṅgātīre. Puthusussoṇīti puthulāya sundarāya soṇiyā samannāgate. Peteti ambapakkaṃ alabhitvā paralokaṃ gate, mateti attho. Pakuṭṭhāyīti akkosi garahi nindi. “Pakvatthāsī”tipi pāṭho.

‘Isipūgasamaññāte’ means well-known by the company of sages, esteemed by the sages. ‘Evaṃ lokyā’ means you are thus known as beneficial to the world because of the removal of evil. ‘Sati’ is an address meaning ‘O beautiful, O excellent one.’ ‘Anariyaparisambhāse’ means endowed with unseemly abuse such as, ‘his fathers know him,’ and so forth. ‘Jigīsasi’ means even though no evil exists in me, by reviling me thus and being indifferent to another’s death, you seek and produce your own evil deed. ‘Tīre te’ means on your bank of the Ganges. ‘Puthusussoṇī’ means endowed with broad and beautiful hips. ‘Pete’ means having gone to the other world without obtaining the ripe mango; the meaning is ‘dead’. ‘Pakuṭṭhāyi’ means he abused, reproached, or reviled. There is also a reading ‘Pakvatthāsī’.

Taṃ [M 5.0009] sutvā devadhītā pañca gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the divine maiden spoke five verses:

23.

23.

“Aññātametaṃ avisayhasāhi, attānamambañca dadāmi te taṃ;

Yo dubbaje kāmaguṇe pahāya, santiñca dhammañca adhiṭṭhitosi.

This is known, O unconquerable one. I give myself and that mango to you, who, having abandoned the sense-pleasures that are difficult to give up, are established in peace and the Dhamma.

24.

24.

“Yo [V 5.0009] hitvā pubbasaññogaṃ, pacchāsaṃyojane ṭhito;

Adhammañceva carati, pāpañcassa pavaḍḍhati.

Whoever, having abandoned former ties, stands attached to later ties, practices unrighteousness, and for him evil increases.

25.

25.

“Ehi taṃ pāpayissāmi, kāmaṃ appossuko bhava;

Upanayāmi sītasmiṃ, viharāhi anussuko.

Come, I will lead you there. Do as you wish, be without anxiety. I will bring you to a cool place; dwell without worry.

26.

26.

“Taṃ puppharasamattebhi, vakkaṅgehi arindama;

Koñcā mayūrā diviyā, kolaṭṭhimadhusāḷikā;

Kūjitā haṃsapūgehi, kokilettha pabodhare.

O foe-tamer, that place resounds with those with curved necks, intoxicated with the nectar of flowers: herons, peacocks, celestial birds, kolaṭṭhi and madhusāḷikā birds. It is filled with the calls of flocks of swans, and here the cuckoos awaken.

27.

27.

“Ambettha vippasākhaggā, palālakhalasannibhā;

Kosambasalaḷā nīpā, pakkatālavilambino”ti.

Here the mango trees have branches with clear ends, resembling heaps of straw from their mass of flowers; Kosamba, Salaḷa, and Nīpa trees are here, with ripe palm fruits hanging down.

Tattha aññātametanti “garahā te bhavissatīti vadanto ambapakkatthāya vadasī”ti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ mayā aññātaṃ. Avisayhasāhīti rājāno nāma dussahaṃ sahanti, tena naṃ ālapantī evamāha. Attānanti taṃ āliṅgitvā ambavanaṃ nayantī attānañca te dadāmi tañca ambaṃ. Kāmaguṇeti kañcanamālāsetacchattapaṭimaṇḍite vatthukāme. Santiñca dhammañcāti dussīlyavūpasamena santisaṅkhātaṃ sīlañceva sucaritadhammañca. Adhiṭṭhitosīti yo tvaṃ ime guṇe upagato, etesu vā patiṭṭhitoti attho.

Here, 'Aññātametaṃ' means: 'Speaking as if saying "Reproach will come to you," you are speaking for the sake of the ripe mango'—this reason is known by me. 'Avisayhasāhi' means: kings indeed endure the unendurable; thus addressing him, she spoke. 'Attānaṃ' means: embracing him and leading him to the mango grove, she says, 'I give both myself and that mango to you.' 'Kāmaguṇe' means: the objects of sensual pleasure, such as golden garlands and white parasols. 'Santiñca dhammañca' means: virtue, known as peace through the cessation of misconduct, and the Dhamma of good conduct. 'Adhiṭṭhitosi' means: you who have attained these qualities, or are established in them.

Pubbasaññoganti purimabandhanaṃ. Pacchāsaṃyojaneti pacchimabandhane. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ambho tāpasa yo mahantaṃ rajjasirivibhavaṃ pahāya ambapakkamatte [P 5.0009] rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā vātātapaṃ agaṇetvā nadītīre sussamāno nisīdati, so mahāsamuddaṃ taritvā velante saṃsīdanapuggalasadiso. Yo puggalo rasataṇhāvasiko adhammañceva carati, rasataṇhāvasena kariyamānaṃ pāpañcassa pavaḍḍhatīti. Iti sā tāpasaṃ garahantī evamāha.

'Pubbasaññogaṃ' means: the former bond. 'Pacchāsaṃyojane' means: in the latter bond. This is what is said: 'O ascetic, one who abandons great royal splendor and glory, yet is bound by craving for the taste of a mere ripe mango, and, disregarding wind and sun, sits withering on the riverbank—such a one is like a person sinking at the shore after crossing the great ocean. For a person enslaved by craving for tastes who practices unrighteousness, the evil done through the power of that craving for tastes increases.' Thus, rebuking the ascetic, she spoke.

Kāmaṃ appossuko bhavāti ekaṃseneva ambapakke nirālayo hohi. Sītasminti sītale ambavane. Tanti evaṃ vadamānāva devatā tāpasaṃ [M 5.0010] āliṅgitvā ure nipajjāpetvā ākāse pakkhantā tiyojanikaṃ dibbaambavanaṃ disvā sakuṇasaddañca sutvā tāpasassa ācikkhantī “ta”nti evamāha. Puppharasamattebhīti puppharasena mattehi. Vakkaṅgehīti vaṅkagīvehi sakuṇehi abhināditanti [V 5.0010] attho. Idāni te sakuṇe ācikkhantī “koñcā”tiādimāha. Tattha diviyāti dibyā. Kolaṭṭhimadhusāḷikāti kolaṭṭhisakuṇā ca nāma suvaṇṇasāḷikā sakuṇā ca. Ete dibbasakuṇā ettha vasantīti dasseti. Kūjitā haṃsapūgehīti haṃsagaṇehi upakūjitā viravasaṅghaṭṭitā. Kokilettha pabodhareti ettha ambavane kokilā vassantiyo attānaṃ pabodhenti ñāpenti. Ambetthāti ambā ettha. Vippasākhaggāti phalabhārena onamitasākhaggā. Palālakhalasannibhāti pupphasannicayena sālipalālakhalasadisā. Pakkatālavilambinoti pakkatālaphalavilambino. Evarūpā rukkhā ca ettha atthīti ambavanaṃ vaṇṇeti.

'Kāmaṃ appossuko bhava' means: be completely without attachment to the ripe mango. 'Sītasmiṃ' means: in the cool mango grove. 'Taṃ' means: while speaking thus, the deity embraced the ascetic, laid him on her breast, and rising into the sky, saw the divine mango grove three leagues away and heard the sound of birds; while explaining it to the ascetic, she said 'that'. 'Puppharasamattebhi' means: by those intoxicated with the nectar of flowers. 'Vakkaṅgehi' means: by birds with bent necks; the meaning is 'resounding with'. Now, pointing out those birds to him, she says, 'Koñcā,' and so on. There, 'diviyā' means: divine. 'Kolaṭṭhimadhusāḷikā' means: birds called Kolaṭṭhi and golden sālikā birds. This shows that these divine birds dwell here. 'Kūjitā haṃsapūgehi' means: resounded by flocks of swans, filled with their calls. 'Kokilettha pabodhare' means: here in this mango grove, the cuckoos, making their calls, make their presence known. 'Ambettha' means: mango trees here. 'Vippasākhaggā' means: with branches bent down by the weight of fruit. 'Palālakhalasannibhā' means: like a threshing floor of rice stalks due to their masses of flowers. 'Pakkatālavilambino' means: with fruit hanging like ripe palm fruits. 'Such trees are also here'—thus she describes the mango grove.

Vaṇṇayitvā ca pana tāpasaṃ tattha otāretvā “imasmiṃ ambavane ambāni khādanto attano taṇhaṃ pūrehī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tāpaso ambāni khāditvā taṇhaṃ pūretvā vissamitvā ambavane vicaranto taṃ petaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantaṃ disvā kiñci vattuṃ nāsakkhi. Sūriye pana atthaṅgate taṃ nāṭakitthiparivāritaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamānaṃ disvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

After praising the mango grove and bringing the ascetic down there, she said, 'Eating mangoes in this mango grove, satisfy your craving,' and then departed. The ascetic, after eating the mangoes, satisfying his craving, and resting, was wandering in the mango grove when he saw that peta enduring suffering, but he was unable to say anything. However, when the sun had set, seeing that peta enjoying divine prosperity, surrounded by a troupe of dancing women, he spoke these three verses to inquire about the cause:

28.

28.

“Mālī kiriṭī kāyūrī, aṅgadī candanussado;

Rattiṃ tvaṃ paricāresi, divā vedesi vedanaṃ.

Garlanded, wearing a headdress, wearing bracelets and armbands, anointed with sandalwood; at night you enjoy pleasures, but by day you experience suffering.

29.

29.

“Soḷasitthisahassāni, yā temā paricārikā;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvosi, abbhuto lomahaṃsano.

Sixteen thousand women are your attendants; such is your great power, amazing and hair-raising.

30.

30.

“Kiṃ kammamakarī pubbe, pāpaṃ attadukhāvahaṃ;

Yaṃ karitvā manussesu, piṭṭhimaṃsāni khādasī”ti.

What evil deed did you previously commit, bringing suffering upon yourself, that having done it among humans, you now devour the flesh from your own back?

Tattha mālīti dibbamālādharo. Kiriṭīti dibbaveṭhanadharo. Kāyūrīti dibbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍito. Aṅgadīti dibbaṅgadasamannāgato. Candanussadoti [P 5.0010] dibbacandanavilitto. Paricāresīti indriyāni dibbavisayesu cāresi. Divāti divā [M 5.0011] pana mahādukkhaṃ anubhosi. Yā temāti yā te imā. Abbhutoti manussaloke abhūtapubbo. Lomahaṃsanoti ye taṃ passanti, tesaṃ lomāni haṃsanti. Pubbeti purimabhave. Attadukhāvahanti attano dukkhāvahaṃ. Manussesūti yaṃ manussaloke katvā idāni attano piṭṭhimaṃsāni khādasīti pucchati.

Here, 'mālī' means wearing divine garlands. 'Kiriṭī' means wearing a divine headdress. 'Kāyūrī' means adorned with divine ornaments. 'Aṅgadī' means possessing divine armlets. 'Candanussado' means anointed with divine sandalwood. 'Paricāresī' means he moved his senses among divine objects. 'Divā' means during the day, he experienced great suffering. 'Yā temā' means 'these of yours'. 'Abbhuto' means unprecedented in the human world. 'Lomahaṃsano' means for those who see him, their hairs stand on end. 'Pubbe' means in a previous existence. 'Attadukhāvahaṃ' means bringing suffering upon oneself. 'Manussesu' means the ascetic asks, 'Having done what in the human world do you now devour your own back-flesh?'

Peto [V 5.0011] taṃ sañjānitvā “tumhe maṃ na sañjānātha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ purohito ahosiṃ, idaṃ me rattiṃ sukhānubhavanaṃ tumhe nissāya katassa upaḍḍhūposathassa nissandena laddhaṃ, divā dukkhānubhavanaṃ pana mayā pakatassa pāpasseva nissandena. Ahañhi tumhehi vinicchaye ṭhapito kūṭaḍḍaṃ karitvā lañjaṃ gahetvā parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko hutvā tassa divā katassa kammassa nissandena idaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāmī”ti vatvā gāthādvayamāha –

The peta, recognizing him, said: 'Do you not recognize me? I was your family priest. This pleasure I experience at night was obtained as the result of the half-Uposatha I observed because of you. But the suffering I endure by day is the result of the evil I myself did. For I was appointed by you as a judge, and having made false judgments and taken bribes, I acted like one who eats others' back-flesh; thus I experience this suffering as the consequence of the deeds I did by day.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

31.

31.

“Ajjhenāni paṭiggayha, kāmesu gadhito ahaṃ;

Acariṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, paresaṃ ahitāyahaṃ.

Having studied the Vedas, I was greedy for sensual pleasures; for a long time I acted to the detriment of others.

32.

32.

“Yo piṭṭhimaṃsiko hoti, evaṃ ukkacca khādati;

Yathāhaṃ ajja khādāmi, piṭṭhimaṃsāni attano”ti.

Whoever is a backbiter, thus tears off and eats, just as I today eat my own back-flesh.

Tattha ajjhenānīti vede. Paṭiggayhāti paṭiggahetvā adhīyitvā. Acarinti paṭipajjiṃ. Ahitāyahanti ahitāya atthanāsanāya ahaṃ. Yo piṭṭhimaṃsikoti yo puggalo paresaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsakhādako pisuṇo hoti. Ukkaccāti ukkantitvā.

Here, 'Ajjhenāni' refers to the Vedas. 'Paṭiggayha' means having received and studied. 'Acariṃ' means I practiced. 'Ahitāya ahaṃ' means for harm, for the destruction of welfare, I. 'Yo piṭṭhimaṃsiko' means that person who is a backbiter, a slanderer of others. 'Ukkacca' means having torn off.

Idañca pana vatvā tāpasaṃ pucchi – “tumhe kathaṃ idhāgatā”ti. Tāpaso sabbaṃ vitthārena kathesi. “Idāni pana, bhante, idheva vasissatha, gamissathā”ti. “Na vasissāmi, assamapadaṃyeva gamissāmī”ti. Peto “sādhu, bhante, ahaṃ vo nibaddhaṃ ambapakkena upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti vatvā attano ānubhāvena assamapadeyeva otāretvā “anukkaṇṭhā idheva vasathā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā gato. Tato paṭṭhāya nibaddhaṃ ambapakkena upaṭṭhahi. Tāpaso taṃ paribhuñjanto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānābhiññā nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having said this, the peta asked the ascetic: “How did you come here?” The ascetic explained everything in detail. “Now, venerable sir, will you stay here or will you go?” “I will not stay; I will go to my hermitage.” The peta said: “Very well, venerable sir, I will regularly attend on you with ripe mangoes.” Having spoken thus, by his own power he set him down at the hermitage and, after taking his promise to “dwell here without discontent,” he departed. From then on, he regularly attended on him with ripe mangoes. The ascetic, partaking of them and undertaking the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, developed the jhānas and higher knowledges, and became one bound for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [P 5.0011] upāsakānaṃ imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, [M 5.0012] keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino. Tadā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse to the lay followers and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the talk on the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners. At that time, the goddess was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was myself.

Kiṃchandajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Explanation of the Kiṃchanda Jātaka, the First.

[512] 2. Kumbhajātakavaṇṇanā

[512] 2. The Explanation of the Kumbha Jātaka

Ko [V 5.0012] pāturāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto visākhāya sahāyikā surāpītā pañcasatā itthiyo ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira surāchaṇe saṅghuṭṭhe tā pañcasatā itthiyo sāmikānaṃ chaṇe kīḷamānānaṃ tikkhasuraṃ paṭiyādetvā “chaṇaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti sabbāpi visākhāya santikaṃ gantvā “sahāyike chaṇaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti vatvā “ayaṃ surāchaṇo, na ahaṃ suraṃ pivissāmī”ti vutte – “tumhe sammāsambuddhassa dānaṃ detha, mayaṃ chaṇaṃ karissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tā uyyojetvā satthāraṃ nimantāpetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā bahuṃ gandhamālaṃ ādāya sāyanhasamaye dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ tāhi parivutā jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tā panitthiyo suraṃ pivamānāva tāya saddhiṃ gantvā dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā suraṃ pivitvāva tāya saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Visākhā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, itarāsu ekaccā satthu santikeyeva nacciṃsu, ekaccā gāyiṃsu, ekaccā hatthakukkuccapādakukkuccāni, ekaccā kalahaṃ akaṃsu.

“Who appeared?”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning five hundred female companions of Visākhā who had drunk liquor. It is said that in Sāvatthī, when a liquor festival was proclaimed, these five hundred women, while their husbands were enjoying the festival, prepared strong liquor and said, “We too will enjoy the festival.” All of them went to Visākhā and said, “Friend, let us enjoy the festival.” When she replied, “This is a liquor festival; I will not drink liquor,” they said, “You give alms to the Perfectly Enlightened One, and we will celebrate the festival.” She agreed and sent them off. Then she had the Teacher invited and held a great almsgiving. Taking many perfumes and garlands, she went to Jetavana in the evening, surrounded by those women, to listen to a Dhamma talk. But those women went with her while drinking liquor. They stood at the gatehouse and drank liquor, and then went with her into the Teacher’s presence. Visākhā paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. But among the other women, some danced right in the Teacher’s presence, some sang, some made improper gestures with their hands and feet, and some quarreled.

Satthā tāsaṃ saṃvegajananatthāya bhamukalomato raṃsī vissajjesi, andhakāratimisā ahosi. Tā bhītā ahesuṃ maraṇabhayatajjitā, tena tāsaṃ surā jīri. Satthā nisinnapallaṅke antarahito sinerumuddhani ṭhatvā uṇṇalomato raṃsī vissajjesi, candasūriyasahassuggamanaṃ viya ahosi. Satthā tattha ṭhitova tāsaṃ saṃvegajananatthāya –

To arouse a sense of spiritual urgency in them, the Teacher emitted rays from the hairs of his eyebrows, and there was pitch darkness. They were frightened, terrified by the fear of death, and through that their intoxication wore off. The Teacher, having vanished from the throne on which he was sitting, stood on the summit of Mount Sineru and emitted a ray from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, and it was as if a thousand suns and moons had risen. Standing there, to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency in them, he spoke:

“Ko nu hāso kimānando, niccaṃ pajjalite sati;

Andhakārena onaddhā, padīpaṃ na gavesathā”ti. (dha. pa. 146) –

“What laughter, what joy, when all is ever burning? Enveloped by darkness, will you not seek a light?”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Gāthāpariyosāne tā pañcasatāpi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā gandhakuṭichāyāya buddhāsane nisīdi. Atha [M 5.0013] naṃ visākhā vanditvā, “bhante, idaṃ hirottappabhedakaṃ surāpānaṃ nāma kadā uppanna”nti pucchi. So tassā ācikkhanto atītaṃ āhari.

He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, all five hundred women were established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher returned and sat down on the Buddha-seat in the shade of the fragrant chamber. Then Visākhā paid homage to him and asked, “Venerable sir, when did this drinking of liquor, which destroys moral shame and moral dread, first arise?” Explaining it to her, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 5.0012] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko kāsiraṭṭhavāsī suro nāma vanacarako bhaṇḍapariyesanatthāya himavantaṃ agamāsi. Tattheko rukkho uggantvā porisamatte ṭhāne tidhākappo ahosi. Tassa tiṇṇaṃ kappānaṃ antare cāṭippamāṇo āvāṭo ahosi. So deve vassante udakena pūrito, taṃ parivāretvā harītakī āmalakī maricagaccho ca ahosi[V 5.0013], tesaṃ pakkāni phalāni chijjitvā tattha patanti. Tassāvidūre sayaṃjātasāli jāto, tato suvakā sālisīsāni āharitvā tasmiṃ rukkhe nisīditvā khādanti. Tesaṃ khādamānānaṃ sālīpi taṇḍulāpi tattha patanti. Iti taṃ udakaṃ sūriyasantāpena paccamānaṃ rasaṃ lohitavaṇṇaṃ ahosi. Nidāghasamaye pipāsitā sakuṇagaṇā āgantvā taṃ pivitvā mattā parivattitvā rukkhamūle patiṃsu, tasmiṃ thokaṃ niddāyitvā vikūjamānā pakkamanti. Rukkhasunakhamakkaṭādīsupi eseva nayo. Vanacarako taṃ disvā “sace idaṃ visaṃ bhaveyya, ime mareyyuṃ, ime pana thokaṃ niddāyitvā yathāsukhaṃ gacchanti, nayidaṃ visa”nti sayaṃ pivitvā matto hutvā maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo ahosi. Tato aggiṃ katvā rukkhamūle patite tittirakukkuṭādayo māretvā maṃsaṃ aṅgāre pacitvā ekena hatthena naccanto ekena maṃsaṃ khādanto ekāhadvīhaṃ tattheva ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a woodsman from the Kāsī country named Sura went to the Himalayas to search for forest goods. There a tree had grown up and, at the height of a man, had forked into three branches. In the hollow between the three forks was a cavity the size of a large jar. When the god rained, it filled with water. Surrounding it were yellow myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, and pepper shrubs. Their ripe fruits fell into it. Not far from it, wild rice grew. Parrots would bring heads of rice, sit on that tree, and eat them. As they were eating, both paddy and rice grains fell in there. Thus the water, fermenting in the sun’s heat, became a red-colored liquor. In the hot season, flocks of thirsty birds came and drank it. Becoming intoxicated, they tumbled down and fell at the foot of the tree. After sleeping for a little while, they flew off, chirping. The same happened with dogs, monkeys, and other animals. The woodsman saw this and thought: “If this were poison, they would die. But since they sleep for a little while and then go off as they please, this is not poison.” He drank some himself and became intoxicated, and he felt a desire to eat meat. He then made a fire, killed the partridges, fowl, and other birds that had fallen at the foot of the tree, roasted the meat on the coals, and remained there for a day or two, dancing and gesticulating with one hand while eating meat with the other.

Tato pana avidūre eko varuṇo nāma tāpaso vasati. Vanacarako aññadāpi tassa santikaṃ gacchati. Athassa etadahosi – “idaṃ pānaṃ tāpasena saddhiṃ pivissāmī”ti. So ekaṃ veḷunāḷikaṃ pūretvā pakkamaṃsena saddhiṃ āharitvā paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā, “bhante, imaṃ [P 5.0013] pivathā”ti vatvā ubhopi maṃsaṃ khādantā piviṃsu. Iti surena ca varuṇena ca diṭṭhattā tassa pānassa “surā”ti ca “varuṇā”ti ca nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Te ubhopi “attheso upāyo”ti veḷunāḷiyo pūretvā kājenādāya paccantanagaraṃ gantvā “pānakārakā nāma āgatā”ti rañño ārocāpesuṃ. Rājā ne pakkosāpesi, te tassa pānaṃ upanesuṃ. Rājā dve tayo vāre pivitvā majji, tassa taṃ ekāhadvīhamattameva ahosi. Atha [M 5.0014] ne “aññampi atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, devā”ti. “Kuhi”nti? “Himavante devā”ti. “Tena hi ānethā”ti. Te gantvā ekadve vāre ānetvā “nibaddhaṃ gantuṃ na sakkhissāmā”ti sambhāre sallakkhetvā tassa rukkhassa tacaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbasambhāre pakkhipitvā nagare suraṃ kariṃsu. Nāgarā suraṃ pivitvā pamādaṃ āpannā duggatā ahesuṃ, nagaraṃ suññaṃ viya ahosi, tena pānakārakā tato palāyitvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā “pānakārakā āgatā”ti rañño ārocāpesuṃ. Rājā ne pakkosāpetvā paribbayaṃ adāsi. Te tatthāpi suraṃ akaṃsu, tampi nagaraṃ tatheva vinassi, tato palāyitvā sāketaṃ, sāketato sāvatthiṃ agamaṃsu.

Now, not far from that tree lived an ascetic named Varuṇa. The hunter would also visit him on other occasions. Then it occurred to him: “I will drink this beverage with the ascetic.” So he filled a bamboo tube, took it along with some roasted meat, and went to the leaf-hut. He said, “Venerable sir, drink this,” and both the hunter and the ascetic ate the meat and drank the beverage. Thus, because it had been discovered by the hunter Sura and the ascetic Varuṇa, the drink came to be called ‘surā’ and ‘varuṇā.’ Both of them thought, “There is a way here,” and filling bamboo tubes and taking them on a carrying pole, they went to a border city and had it announced to the king: “Drink-makers have arrived.” The king summoned them, and they offered him the drink. The king drank it two or three times and became intoxicated. For him, that supply lasted only a day or two. Then he asked them, “Is there any more?” “There is, your majesty.” “Where?” “In the Himalayas, your majesty.” “Then go and bring it.” They went and brought it back once or twice, but then they thought, “We will not be able to keep going back and forth constantly.” They noted the ingredients—starting with the bark of that tree—and, gathering all the components, they made the liquor in the city. The townspeople drank the liquor, became heedless and impoverished, and the city became as if deserted. The drink-makers fled from there and went to Benares. They had it announced to the king: “Drink-makers have arrived.” The king summoned them and gave them their expenses. They made liquor there too, and that city was ruined in the same way. Fleeing from there, they went to Sāketa, and from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.

Tadā sāvatthiyaṃ sabbamitto nāma rājā ahosi. So tesaṃ saṅgahaṃ katvā “kena vo attho”ti pucchitvā “sambhāramūlena ceva sālipiṭṭhena ca pañcahi cāṭisatehi cā”ti vutte sabbaṃ dāpesi. Te pañcasu cāṭisatesu suraṃ saṇṭhāpetvā mūsikabhayena cāṭirakkhaṇatthāya ekekāya [V 5.0014] cāṭiyā santike ekekaṃ biḷāraṃ bandhiṃsu. Te paccitvā uttaraṇakāle cāṭikucchīsu paggharantaṃ suraṃ pivitvā mattā niddāyiṃsu. Mūsikā āgantvā tesaṃ kaṇṇanāsikadāṭhikanaṅguṭṭhe khāditvā agamaṃsu. “Biḷārā suraṃ pivitvā matā”ti [P 5.0014] āyuttakapurisā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “visakārakā ete bhavissantī”ti tesaṃ dvinnampi janānaṃ sīsāni chindāpesi. Te “suraṃ deva, madhuraṃ devā”ti viravantāva mariṃsu. Rājā te mārāpetvā “cāṭiyo bhindathā”ti āṇāpesi. Biḷārāpi surāya jiṇṇāya uṭṭhahitvā kīḷantā vicariṃsu, te disvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “sace visaṃ assa, ete mareyyuṃ, madhureneva bhavitabbaṃ, pivissāmi na”nti nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā alaṅkatamaṇḍape samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisīditvā amaccagaṇaparivuto suraṃ pātuṃ ārabhi.

At that time, a king named Sabbamitta was reigning in Sāvatthī. He gave them his patronage and asked, “What do you need?” When they replied, “The source ingredients, rice flour, and five hundred jars,” he had it all given to them. They prepared the liquor in five hundred jars and, for fear of mice, they tied one cat near each jar to guard it. When the liquor had fermented and it was time to draw it off, the cats drank the liquor that was trickling from the jars, became intoxicated, and fell asleep. Mice came and gnawed their ears, noses, teeth, and tails, and then left. The king’s men reported to him: “The cats drank the liquor and have died.” The king thought, “These men must be poison-makers,” and had both of them beheaded. They died crying out, “It is liquor, your majesty! It is sweet, your majesty!” After having them killed, the king commanded: “Break the jars!” But when the effects of the liquor had worn off, the cats got up and went about playing. Seeing this, the men reported it to the king. The king thought: “If it were poison, they would have died. It must be sweet. I will drink it.” He had the city decorated, a pavilion erected in the royal courtyard, and, seated on the royal throne under a raised white parasol in the decorated pavilion, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he began to drink the liquor.

Tadā sakko devarājā “ke nu kho mātupaṭṭhānādīsu appamattā tīṇi sucaritāni pūrentī”ti lokaṃ volokento taṃ rājānaṃ suraṃ pātuṃ nisinnaṃ disvā “sacāyaṃ suraṃ pivissati, sakalajambudīpo nassissati. Yathā na pivissati, tathā naṃ karissāmī”ti ekaṃ surāpuṇṇaṃ kumbhaṃ hatthatale ṭhapetvā brāhmaṇavesenāgantvā rañño sammukhaṭṭhāne ākāse ṭhatvā [M 5.0015] “imaṃ kumbhaṃ kiṇātha, imaṃ kumbhaṃ kiṇāthā”ti āha. Sabbamittarājā taṃ tathā vadantaṃ ākāse ṭhitaṃ disvā “kuto nu kho brāhmaṇo āgacchatī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then Sakka, king of the devas, surveying the world and wondering, “Who now are those who are heedful in such duties as ministering to parents and are fulfilling the three kinds of good conduct?” saw that king seated, about to drink liquor. He thought: “If this king drinks liquor, all of Jambudīpa will perish. I will act in such a way that he does not drink it.” Placing a pot full of liquor in the palm of his hand, he approached in the guise of a brahmin. Standing in the air in front of the king, he said, “Buy this pot, buy this pot!” King Sabbamitta, seeing him standing in the air and speaking thus, wondered, “From where has this brahmin come?” Engaging in conversation with him, he spoke three stanzas:

33.

33.

“Ko pāturāsī tidivā nabhamhi, obhāsayaṃ saṃvariṃ candimāva;

Gattehi te rasmiyo niccharanti, sateratā vijjurivantalikkhe.

“Who are you that has appeared in the sky from the triple heaven, illuminating the night like the moon? Rays issue from your limbs, like the lightning called Sateratā in the atmosphere.

34.

34.

“So chinnavātaṃ kamasī aghamhi, vehāyasaṃ gacchasi tiṭṭhasī ca;

Iddhī nu te vatthukatā subhāvitā, anaddhagūnaṃ api devatānaṃ.

“You travel through the void where the wind is cut off; you go and stand in the sky. Is this psychic power of yours well-developed and established, like that of the devas who do not travel on foot?

35.

35.

“Vehāyasaṃ gammamāgamma tiṭṭhasi, kumbhaṃ kiṇāthāti yametamatthaṃ;

Ko [P 5.0015] vā tuvaṃ kissa vā tāya kumbho, akkhāhi me brāhmaṇa etamattha”nti.

“Standing there, having come through the air, you say, ‘Buy this pot!’ Who are you, and what is this pot for? Explain this matter to me, brahmin.”

Tattha ko pāturāsīti kuto pātubhūtosi, kuto āgatosīti attho. Tidivā nabhamhīti kiṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanā āgantvā idha nabhamhi ākāse pākaṭo jātosīti pucchati. Saṃvarinti rattiṃ. Sateratāti evaṃnāmikā. Soti so tvaṃ. Chinnavātanti valāhakopi tāva vātena [V 5.0015] kamati, tassa pana sopi vāto natthi, tenevamāha. Kamasīti pavattesi. Aghamhīti appaṭighe ākāse. Vatthukatāti vatthu viya patiṭṭhā viya katā. Anaddhagūnaṃ api devatānanti yā padasā addhānaṃ agamanena anaddhagūnaṃ devatānaṃ iddhi, sā api tava subhāvitāti pucchati. Vehāyasaṃ gammamāgammāti ākāse pavattaṃ padavītihāraṃ paṭicca nissāya. “Tiṭṭhasī”ti imassa “ko vā tuva”nti iminā sambandho, evaṃ tiṭṭhamāno ko vā tvanti attho. Yametamatthanti yaṃ etaṃ vadasi. Imassa “kissa vā tāya”nti iminā sambandho, yaṃ etaṃ kumbhaṃ kiṇāthāti vadasi, kissa vā te ayaṃ kumbhoti attho.

Herein, 'ko pāturāsī' means: from where have you appeared, from where have you come? 'Tidivā nabhamhi': he asks, “Having come from the Tāvatiṃsa realm, have you become manifest here in the sky?” 'Saṃvariṃ' means the night. 'Sateratā': so-named. 'So': that is, you. 'Chinnavātaṃ': even a cloud travels by the wind, but for him there is no wind; therefore he says this. 'Kamasī' means you move or proceed. 'Aghamhi': in the unobstructed sky. 'Vatthukatā' means made like a basis or foundation. 'Anaddhagūnaṃ api devatānaṃ': he asks if your psychic power is well-developed like that of the devas, who are non-travelers because they do not go a distance on foot. 'Vehāyasaṃ gammamāgamma': based on and relying on movement through the sky. The word 'tiṭṭhasī' is connected with 'ko vā tuvaṃ'; the meaning is, “standing thus, who are you?” 'Yametamatthanti': what you say. This is connected with 'kissa vā tāya'; the meaning is, “when you say, ‘Buy this pot,’ for what purpose is this pot of yours?”

Tato [M 5.0016] sakko “tena hi suṇāhī”ti vatvā surāya dose dassento āha –

Then Sakka said, “Well then, listen,” and pointing out the dangers of liquor, he spoke:

36.

36.

“Na sappikumbho napi telakumbho, na phāṇitassa na madhussa kumbho;

Kumbhassa vajjāni anappakāni, dose bahū kumbhagate suṇātha.

“This is no pot of ghee, no pot of oil, no pot of molasses, no pot of honey. The faults of this pot are many; listen to the numerous dangers contained in the pot.

37.

37.

“Gaḷeyya yaṃ pitvā pate papātaṃ, sobbhaṃ guhaṃ candaniyoḷigallaṃ;

Bahumpi bhuñjeyya abhojaneyyaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, one would stumble and fall into a precipice, a pit, a cave, mire or a drain; one would eat much that is inedible. Buy this pot full of that!

38.

38.

“Yaṃ pitvā cittasmiṃ anesamāno, āhiṇḍatī goriva bhakkhasādī;

Anāthamāno [P 5.0016] upagāyati naccati ca, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, no longer master of his mind, he wanders about like an ox eating refuse. Helplessly he sings and dances. Buy this pot full of that!

39.

39.

“Yaṃ ve pivitvā acelova naggo, careyya gāme visikhantarāni;

Sammūḷhacitto ativelasāyī, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, naked like a naked ascetic, he would wander through the village and its lanes; with mind bewildered, sleeping excessively. Buy this pot full of that!

40.

40.

“Yaṃ pitvā uṭṭhāya pavedhamāno, sīsañca bāhuñca pacālayanto;

So naccatī dārukaṭallakova, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, he gets up trembling, shaking his head and arms; he dances like a wooden puppet. Buy this pot full of that!

41.

41.

“Yaṃ ve pivitvā aggidaḍḍhā sayanti, atho sigālehipi khāditāse;

Bandhaṃ vadhaṃ bhogajāniñcupenti, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, some lie down burned by fire, and others are eaten by jackals; they incur bondage, injury, and loss of wealth. Buy this pot full of that!

42.

42.

“Yaṃ [M 5.0017] pitvā bhāseyya abhāsaneyyaṃ, sabhāyamāsīno apetavattho;

Sammakkhito vantagato byasanno, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, one would say what should not be said; sitting in an assembly without clothes, smeared with vomit and fallen into ruin, one lies down. Buy this pot full of that!

43.

43.

“Yaṃ [V 5.0016] ve pivitvā ukkaṭṭho āvilakkho, mameva sabbapathavīti maññe;

Na me samo cāturantopi rājā, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, arrogant and with bloodshot eyes, one thinks, ‘The whole earth is mine! No king of the four quarters is my equal!’ Buy this pot full of that.

44.

44.

“Mānātimānā kalahāni pesuṇī, dubbaṇṇinī naggayinī palāyinī;

Corāna dhuttāna gatī niketo, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“It is pride and contempt, quarrels and slander; it makes one ugly, naked, and a fugitive. It is the destination and home of thieves and scoundrels. Buy this pot full of it!

45.

45.

“Iddhāni phītāni kulāni assu, anekasāhassadhanāni loke;

Ucchinnadāyajjakatānimāya, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Though there are prosperous and flourishing families in the world with wealth in the many thousands, by this liquor their inheritance is cut off. Buy this pot full of that!

46.

46.

“Dhaññaṃ dhanaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ, khettaṃ gavaṃ yattha vināsayanti;

Ucchedanī vittagataṃ kulānaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“They destroy grain, wealth, silver, and gold, fields and cattle. It is the destroyer of the wealth of families. Buy this pot full of it!

47.

47.

“Yaṃ [P 5.0017] ve pitvā dittarūpova poso, akkosati mātaraṃ pitarañca;

Sassumpi gaṇheyya athopi suṇhaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, a man as if crazed reviles his mother and father; he would even assault his mother-in-law and his daughter-in-law. Buy this pot full of that!

48.

48.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā dittarūpāva nārī, akkosatī sassuraṃ sāmikañca;

Dāsampi gaṇhe paricārikampi, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, a woman as if crazed reviles her father-in-law and husband; she would even assault a male or female servant. Buy this pot full of it!

49.

49.

“Yaṃ [M 5.0018] ve pivitvāna haneyya poso, dhamme ṭhitaṃ samaṇaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vā;

Gacche apāyampi tatonidānaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, a man might strike a recluse or a brahmin who is established in the Dhamma; on that account, he would go to a state of misery. Buy this pot full of that!

50.

50.

“Yaṃ ve pivitvā duccaritaṃ caranti, kāyena vācāya ca cetasā ca;

Nirayaṃ vajanti duccaritaṃ caritvā, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, they engage in misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in misconduct, they go to hell. Buy this pot full of that!

51.

51.

“Yaṃ yācamānā na labhanti pubbe, bahuṃ hiraññampi pariccajantā;

So taṃ pivitvā alikaṃ bhaṇāti, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, he tells a lie, which formerly he would not have told even if begged and offered much gold. Buy this pot full of that!

52.

52.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā pesane pesiyanto, accāyike karaṇīyamhi jāte;

Atthampi so nappajānāti vutto, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, when sent on an errand, if an urgent task arises, even when told he does not understand the matter. Buy this pot full of that!

53.

53.

“Hirīmanāpi [V 5.0017] ahirīkabhāvaṃ, pātuṃ karonti madanāya mattā;

Dhīrāpi santā bahukaṃ bhaṇanti, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Intoxicated by this drink, even those with a sense of shame display shamelessness; even those who are wise speak a great deal. Buy this pot full of it!

54.

54.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā ekathūpā sayanti, anāsakā thaṇḍiladukkhaseyyaṃ;

Dubbaṇṇiyaṃ āyasakyañcupenti, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, they lie in a single heap, without food, on a painful bed on the bare ground; they incur ugliness and disrepute. Buy this pot full of that!

55.

55.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā pattakhandhā sayanti, gāvo kūṭahatāva na [P 5.0018] hi vāruṇiyā;

Vego narena susahoriva, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, they lie with drooping heads, like cattle struck down; indeed, there is no impulse harder for a man to bear than that of liquor. Buy this pot full of that!

56.

56.

“Yaṃ [M 5.0019] manussā vivajjanti, sappaṃ ghoravisamiva;

Taṃ loke visasamānaṃ, ko naro pātumarahati.

“That which people avoid like a fierce, venomous snake, that which is like poison in the world—what person is fit to drink it?

57.

57.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā andhakaveṇḍaputtā, samuddatīre paricārayantā;

Upakkamuṃ musalebhi aññamaññaṃ, tassā puṇṇaṃ kumbhamimaṃ kiṇātha.

“Having drunk this, the sons of Andhakaveṇhu, while roaming on the seashore, set upon one another with clubs. Buy this pot full of that!

58.

58.

“Yaṃ ve pitvā pubbadevā pamattā, tidivā cutā sassatiyā samāyā;

Taṃ tādisaṃ majjamimaṃ niratthakaṃ, jānaṃ mahārāja kathaṃ piveyya.

“Having drunk this, the ancient devas, becoming heedless, fell from the heaven of the Thirty-three for all time. Knowing this worthless intoxicant to be such, great king, how could you drink it?

59.

59.

“Nayimasmiṃ kumbhasmiṃ dadhi vā madhu vā, evaṃ abhiññāya kiṇāhi rāja;

Evañhimaṃ kumbhagatā mayā te, akkhātarūpaṃ tava sabbamittā”ti.

“In this pot there is neither curd nor honey; having understood this, O king, buy it! Thus, the nature of what is in this pot has been explained to you by me, O Sabbamitta.”

Tattha vajjānītiādīnavā. Gaḷeyyāti gacchanto pade pade parivatteyya. Yaṃ pitvā pateti yaṃ pivitvā pateyya. Sobbhanti āvāṭaṃ. Candaniyoḷigallanti candanikañca oḷigallañca. Abhojaneyyanti bhuñjituṃ ayuttaṃ. Anesamānoti anissaro. Gorivāti goṇo viya. Bhakkhasādīti purāṇakasaṭakhādako, yathā so tattha tattha bhakkhasaṃ pariyesanto āhiṇḍati, evaṃ āhiṇḍatīti attho. Anāthamānoti niravassayo anātho viya. Upagāyatīti aññaṃ gāyantaṃ disvā upagantvā gāyati. Acelovāti acelako viya. Visikhantarānīti antaravīthiyo. Ativelasāyīti aticirampi niddaṃ okkameyya. “Ativelacārī”tipi pāṭho, ativelacārī hutvā careyyāti attho.

Herein, vajjāni means dangers. Gaḷeyya means that while walking he would stumble at every step. Yaṃ pitvā pate means: having drunk which, one would fall. Sobbhaṃ means a pit. Candaniyoḷigallaṃ means a charnel ground and a cesspool. Abhojaneyyaṃ means unfit to be eaten. Anesamāno means not being one's own master. Goriva means like an ox. Bhakkhasādī means an eater of old rubbish; the meaning is that just as such a one wanders about here and there searching for scraps, so does he wander. Anāthamāno means like one who is helpless, without support. Upagāyati means that seeing another singing, he goes up and sings along. Acelova means like a naked ascetic. Visikhantarāni means the lanes in between. Ativelasāyī means he might fall asleep for a very long time. There is also the reading ativelacārī, meaning, having become one who wanders about excessively, he would wander.

Dārukaṭallako [V 5.0018] vāti dārumayayantarūpakaṃ viya. Bhogajāniñcupentīti bhogajāniñca upenti, pāṇātipātādīni katvā daṇḍapīḷitā dhanajāniñca aññañca vadhabandhanādidukkhaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho. Vantagatoti attano vantasmiṃ [P 5.0019] gato. Byasannoti byasanāpanno. “Visanno”tipi pāṭho[M 5.0020], tasmiṃ vante osannoti attho. Ukkaṭṭhoti ahaṃ mahāyodho, ko mayā sadiso atthīti evaṃ ukkaṃsagato hutvā. Āvilakkhoti rattakkho. Sabbapathavīti sabbā pathavī. “Sabbaputhuvī”tipi pāṭho. Cāturantoti catusamuddapariyantāya pathaviyā issaro. Mānātimānāti mānakārikā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Gatīti nibbatti. Niketoti nivāso. Tassā puṇṇanti yā evarūpā, tassā puṇṇaṃ. Iddhānīti samiddhāni. Phītānīti vatthālaṅkārakappabhaṇḍehi pupphitāni. Ucchinnadāyajjakatānīti ucchinnadāyādāni niddhanāni katāni. Yattha vināsayantīti yaṃ nissāya yattha patiṭṭhitā, evaṃ bahumpi dhanadhaññādisāpateyyaṃ nāsayanti, kapaṇā honti.

“Like a wooden puppet” means like a wooden automaton. “Bhogajāniñcupenti” means they incur loss of wealth; having committed acts like killing living beings, they are oppressed by punishment and attain loss of wealth and other suffering such as execution and bondage—this is the meaning. “Vantagato” means gone into his own vomit. “Byasanno” means overtaken by disaster. Another reading is “Visanno,” meaning he has sunk into that vomit. “Ukkaṭṭho” means boasting, “I am a great warrior, who is equal to me?”—thus filled with conceit. “Āvilakkho” means red-eyed. “Sabbapathavī” means the entire earth. Another reading is “Sabbaputhuvī.” “Cāturanto” means the ruler of the earth bounded by the four oceans. “Mānātimānā” means acts of conceit. The same principle applies to the remaining terms. “Gati” means rebirth. “Niketo” means a dwelling. “Tassā puṇṇanti” means the fullness of whatever is like that. “Iddhāni” means thriving. “Phītāni” means flourishing with wealth, ornaments, and various goods. “Ucchinnadāyajjakatāni” means cut off from inheritance, made destitute. “Yattha vināsayanti” means relying on which, or being established in which, they destroy much wealth, grain, and property, becoming wretched.

Dittarūpoti dappitarūpo. Gaṇheyyāti bhariyasaññāya kilesavasena hatthe gaṇheyya. Dāsampi gaṇheti attano dāsampi kilesavasena “sāmiko me”ti gaṇheyya. Pivitvānāti pivitvā. Duccaritaṃ caritvāti evaṃ tīhi dvārehi dasavidhampi akusalaṃ katvā. Yaṃ yācamānāti yaṃ purisaṃ pubbe suraṃ apivantaṃ bahuṃ hiraññaṃ pariccajantā musāvādaṃ karohīti yācamānā na labhanti. Pitvāti pivitvā ṭhito. Nappajānāti vuttoti “kenaṭṭhena āgatosī”ti vutto sāsanassa duggahitattā taṃ atthaṃ na jānāti. Hirīmanāpīti hirīyuttacittāpi. Ekathūpāti sūkarapotakā viya hīnajaccehipi saddhiṃ ekarāsī hutvā. Anāsakāti nirāhārā. Thaṇḍiladukkhaseyyanti bhūmiyaṃ dukkhaseyyaṃ sayanti. Āyasakyanti garahaṃ.

“Dittarūpo” means arrogant in form. “He would seize” means he would seize with the hand through the defilement of perceiving her as a wife. “She would seize even a slave” means she would seize even her own slave through defilement, thinking, “He is my master.” “Having drunk” means having drunk. “Having engaged in misconduct” means having thus committed the ten kinds of unwholesome action through the three doors. “Whom they ask” refers to a man who previously did not drink liquor, whom they could not persuade to speak a falsehood even when they asked him, offering much gold. “Having drunk” means having drunk and standing. “He does not understand what was said” means when asked, “For what purpose have you come?” he does not understand the meaning because the message was poorly grasped. “Even one with shame” means even one with a mind endowed with shame. “In one heap” means like piglets, becoming one heap even with those of low birth. “Without food” means without sustenance. “The painful bed on the hard ground” means they lie on the ground, a painful bed. “Āyasakyaṃ” means blame.

Pattakhandhāti patitakkhandhā. Kūṭahatāvāti gīvāya baddhena kūṭena hatā gāvo viya, yathā tā tiṇaṃ akhādantiyo pānīyaṃ apivantiyo sayanti, tathā sayantīti attho. Ghoravisamivāti ghoravisaṃ viya. Visasamānanti visasadisaṃ. Andhakaveṇḍaputtāti dasa bhātikarājāno. Upakkamunti pahariṃsu. Pubbadevāti asurā. Tidivāti tāvatiṃsadevalokā. Sassatiyāti sassatā, dīghāyukabhāvena niccasammatā devalokāti attho. Samāyāti saddhiṃ asuramāyāhi. Jānanti evaṃ “niratthakaṃ eta”nti jānanto tumhādiso paṇḍito puriso kathaṃ piveyya[M 5.0021]. Kumbhagatā mayāti kumbhagataṃ mayā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Akkhātarūpanti sabhāvato akkhātaṃ.

“With drooping shoulders” means with fallen shoulders. “Struck by a trap” means like cows struck by a trap tied around their necks; just as they lie down not eating grass or drinking water, so they lie—this is the meaning. “Like a terrible poison” means like a terrible poison. “Resembling poison” means similar to poison. “The sons of Andhakaveṇḍa” means the ten brother-kings. “They attacked” means they struck. “The ancient gods” means the asuras. “From heaven” means from the Tāvatiṃsa deva world. “For eternity” means the eternal ones; the meaning is that the deva worlds are considered permanent on account of their long lifespan. “With magic” means together with the illusions of the asuras. “Jānaṃ” means: knowing, ‘This is pointless,’ how could a wise man like you drink it? “Kumbhagatā mayā” means ‘what is in the pot by me’; or this is the reading itself. “Akkhātarūpaṃ” means its nature is declared; that is, declared from its own nature.

Taṃ [V 5.0019] sutvā rājā surāya ādīnavaṃ ñatvā tuṭṭho sakkassa thutiṃ karonto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the king, having understood the danger of liquor, was pleased, and uttering praise of Sakka, he spoke two verses:

60.

60.

“Na [P 5.0020] me pitā vā athavāpi mātā, etādisā yādisako tuvaṃsi;

Hitānukampī paramatthakāmo, sohaṃ karissaṃ vacanaṃ tavajja.

“Neither my father nor my mother has been such as you are to me; compassionate and seeking my highest good, today I will do your bidding.

61.

61.

“Dadāmi te gāmavarāni pañca, dāsīsataṃ satta gavaṃsatāni;

Ājaññayutte ca rathe dasa ime, ācariyo hosi mamatthakāmo”ti.

“I give you five choice villages, a hundred female slaves, seven hundred cows, and these ten chariots yoked with thoroughbreds; be my teacher, you who desire my welfare.”

Tattha gāmavarānīti, brāhmaṇa, ācariyassa nāma ācariyabhāgo icchitabbo, saṃvacchare saṃvacchare satasahassuṭṭhānake tuyhaṃ pañca gāme dadāmīti vadati. Dasa imeti ime dasa purato ṭhite kañcanavicitte rathe dassento evamāha.

Therein, 'choice villages' means he says: 'Brahmin, a teacher's fee is to be desired; I will give you five villages with an income of a hundred thousand each year.' 'These ten' means he spoke while pointing to these ten chariots adorned with gold standing before him.

Taṃ sutvā sakko devattabhāvaṃ dassetvā attānaṃ jānāpento ākāse ṭhatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, Sakka revealed his divine form and, making himself known, stood in the sky and spoke two verses:

62.

62.

“Taveva dāsīsatamatthu rāja, gāmā ca gāvo ca taveva hontu;

Ājaññayuttā ca rathā taveva, sakkohamasmī tidasānamindo.

“Let the hundred female slaves be yours, O king, and let the villages and cattle be yours; let the chariots yoked with thoroughbreds be yours. I am Sakka, lord of the Thirty-three.

63.

63.

“Maṃsodanaṃ sappipāyāsaṃ bhuñja, khādassu ca tvaṃ madhumāsapūve;

Evaṃ tuvaṃ dhammarato janinda, anindito saggamupehi ṭhāna”nti.

“Eat rice with meat and milk-rice with ghee, and eat cakes made with honey. Thus, O lord of men, delighting in the Dhamma, blameless, go to the heavenly realm.”

Tattha evaṃ tuvaṃ dhammaratoti evaṃ tvaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjanto surāpānā virato tīṇi duccaritāni pahāya tividhasucaritadhammarato hutvā kenaci anindito saggaṭṭhānaṃ upehīti.

Therein, ‘thus, you delight in the Dhamma’ means: thus, while you enjoy food of various excellent flavors, abstaining from drinking liquor, having abandoned the three kinds of misconduct, delighting in the Dhamma of the threefold good conduct, unblamed by anyone, go to the heavenly realm.

Iti [M 5.0022] sakko tassa ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Sopi suraṃ apivitvā surābhājanāni bhindāpetvā sīlaṃ samādāya dānaṃ datvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi. Jambudīpepi anukkamena surāpānaṃ vepullappattaṃ jātaṃ.

Thus Sakka, having given him this advice, went to his own abode. The king too, not drinking liquor, had the liquor vessels broken, undertook the moral precepts, gave alms, and was destined for heaven. In Jambudīpa, too, the drinking of liquor gradually became widespread.

Satthā [V 5.0020] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.
