The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, but Sakka was I myself.”

Kumbhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Kumbha Jātaka, the second.

[513] 3. Jayaddisajātakavaṇṇanā

[513] 3. The Commentary on the Jayaddisa Jātaka

Cirassaṃ [P 5.0021] vata meti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu sāmajātakasadisaṃ (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo). Tadā pana satthā “porāṇakapaṇḍitā kañcanamālaṃ setacchattaṃ pahāya mātāpitaro posesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story, which begins “After a long time, indeed, for me,” concerning a certain monk who supported his mother. The present story is similar to the Sāma Jātaka. Then the Teacher, saying, “The wise ones of old, having given up a golden garland and the white parasol, supported their parents,” related the past.

Atīte kapilaraṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagare pañcālo nāma rājā ahosi. Tassa aggamahesī gabbhaṃ paṭilabhitvā puttaṃ vijāyi. Tassā purimabhave ekā sapattikā kujjhitvā “tuyhaṃ jātaṃ jātaṃ pajaṃ khādituṃ samatthā bhavissāmī”ti patthanaṃ ṭhapetvā yakkhinī ahosi. Sā tadā okāsaṃ labhitvā tassā passantiyāva taṃ allamaṃsapesivaṇṇaṃ kumārakaṃ gahetvā murumurāyantī khāditvā pakkāmi. Dutiyavārepi tatheva akāsi. Tatiyavāre pana tassā pasūtigharaṃ paviṭṭhakāle gehaṃ parivāretvā gāḷhaṃ ārakkhaṃ akaṃsu. Vijātadivase yakkhinī āgantvā puna dārakaṃ aggahesi. Devī “yakkhinī”ti mahāsaddamakāsi. Āvudhahatthā purisā āgantvā deviyā dinnasaññāya yakkhiniṃ anubandhiṃsu. Sā khādituṃ okāsaṃ alabhantī tato palāyitvā udakaniddhamanaṃ pāvisi. Dārako mātusaññāya tassā thanaṃ mukhena gaṇhi. Sā puttasinehaṃ uppādetvā tato palāyitvā susānaṃ gantvā dārakaṃ pāsāṇaleṇe ṭhapetvā paṭijaggi. Athassa anukkamena vaḍḍhamānassa manussamaṃsaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Ubhopi [M 5.0023] manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā tattha vasiṃsu. Dārako attano manussabhāvaṃ na jānāti “yakkhiniputtosmī”ti saññāya. So attabhāvaṃ jahitvā antaradhāyituṃ na sakkoti. Athassa sā antaradhānatthāya ekaṃ mūlaṃ adāsi. So mūlānubhāvena antaradhāyitvā manussamaṃsaṃ khādanto vicarati. Yakkhinī vessavaṇassa mahārājassa veyyāvaccatthāya gatā tattheva kālamakāsi. Devīpi catutthavāre aññaṃ puttaṃ [P 5.0022] vijāyi. So yakkhiniyā muttattā arogo ahosi. Paccāmittaṃ yakkhiniṃ jinitvā jātattā “jayaddisakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā chattaṃ ussāpetvā rajjamanusāsi.

In the past, in the city of Uttara Pañcāla in the Kapila country, there was a king named Pañcāla. His chief queen conceived and gave birth to a son. In a previous life, a co-wife of hers, becoming angry, made a wish, “May I be able to devour your offspring as soon as they are born,” and she became a yakkhinī. Seizing the opportunity, while the queen was watching, that yakkhinī grabbed the infant, who was the color of a lump of fresh meat, and making a crunching sound, she devoured him and departed. The second time, too, she did the same. On the third occasion, however, when the queen was about to enter the delivery chamber, they surrounded the house and set up a strong guard. On the day of the birth, the yakkhinī came and again seized the child. The queen cried out loudly, “A yakkhinī!” Men with weapons in hand came and, on a signal from the queen, pursued the yakkhinī. Not finding an opportunity to devour him, she fled from there and entered a water drain. The child, perceiving her as his mother, took her breast in his mouth. Arousing motherly love for a son, she fled from there and went to a charnel ground, where she placed the child in a rock cave and looked after him. Then, as he gradually grew up, she would bring him human flesh and give it to him. Both of them lived there, eating human flesh. The boy did not know his own human state, perceiving, “I am the son of a yakkhinī.” He was not able to abandon his physical form and disappear. Then, for the purpose of making him disappear, she gave him a root. By the power of the root, he would disappear and wander about eating human flesh. The yakkhinī went to attend upon the great king Vessavaṇa and died right there. The queen, on the fourth occasion, gave birth to another son. As he was free from the yakkhinī, he was healthy. Because he was born having conquered the enemy yakkhinī, they gave him the name Prince Jayaddisa. When he came of age, he attained perfection in all the arts, raised the parasol, and ruled the kingdom.

Tadā [V 5.0021] bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, “alīnasattukumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto uggahitasabbasippo uparājā ahosi. Sopi yakkhiniputto aparabhāge pamādena taṃ mūlaṃ nāsetvā antaradhāyituṃ asakkonto dissamānarūpova susāne manussamaṃsaṃ khādi. Manussā taṃ disvā bhītā āgantvā rañño upakkosiṃsu “deva eko yakkho dissamānarūpo susāne manussamaṃsaṃ khādati, so anukkamena nagaraṃ pavisitvā manusse māretvā khādissati, taṃ gāhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā “gaṇhatha na”nti āṇāpesi. Balakāyo gantvā susānaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Yakkhiniputto naggo ubbiggarūpo maraṇabhayabhīto viravanto manussānaṃ antaraṃ pakkhandi. Manussā “yakkho”ti maraṇabhayabhītā dvidhā bhijjiṃsu. Sopi tato palāyitvā araññaṃ pāvisi, na puna manussapathaṃ āgacchi. So ekaṃ mahāvattaniaṭaviṃ nissāya maggapaṭipannesu manussesu ekekaṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā māretvā khādanto ekasmiṃ nigrodhamūle vāsaṃ kappesi.

Then the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief queen, and they named him Prince Alīnasattu. When he came of age, having mastered all the arts, he became the viceroy. That son of the yakkhinī, however, later through negligence destroyed that root and, unable to vanish, became visible and ate human flesh in the charnel ground. People saw him and, terrified, came and cried out to the king: “Your Majesty, a visible ogre is eating human flesh in the charnel ground. In due course, he will enter the city, kill people, and devour them. He should be captured.” The king consented, saying, “Very well,” and ordered, “Seize him!” A troop of soldiers went and surrounded the charnel ground. The yakkhinī’s son, naked, looking agitated and terrified of death, rushed screaming into the midst of the people. The people, terrified of death, cried out, “An ogre!” and split into two groups. He fled from there and entered the forest, never again returning to the paths of humans. Taking up residence near the Mahāvaṭṭanī forest, he would seize travelers on the road one by one, drag them into the forest, kill and eat them, and made his home at the foot of a banyan tree.

Atheko satthavāhabrāhmaṇo aṭavipālānaṃ sahassaṃ datvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi taṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Manussayakkho viravanto pakkhandi, bhītā manussā urena nipajjiṃsu. So brāhmaṇaṃ gahetvā palāyanto khāṇunā pāde viddho aṭavipālesu anubandhantesu brāhmaṇaṃ chaḍḍetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānarukkhamūle nipajji. Tassa tattha nipannassa sattame divase jayaddisarājā migavadhaṃ āṇāpetvā nagarā nikkhami. Taṃ nagarā nikkhantamattameva [P 5.0023][M 5.0024] takkasilavāsī nando nāma mātuposakabrāhmaṇo catasso satārahagāthāyo ādāya āgantvā rājānaṃ addasa. Rājā “nivattitvā suṇissāmī”ti tassa nivāsagehaṃ dāpetvā migavaṃ gantvā “yassa passena migo palāyati, tasseva gīvā”ti āha. Atheko pasadamigo uṭṭhahitvā rañño abhimukho gantvā palāyi. Amaccā parihāsaṃ kariṃsu. Rājā khaggaṃ gahetvā taṃ anubandhitvā tiyojanamatthake patvā khaggena paharitvā dve khaṇḍāni karitvā kājenādāya āgacchanto manussayakkhassa nipannaṭṭhānaṃ patvā dabbatiṇesu nisīditvā thokaṃ vissamitvā gantuṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ so uṭṭhāya “tiṭṭha kuhiṃ gacchasi, bhakkhosi me”ti hatthe gahetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then a certain brahmin caravan leader, having given a thousand to the forest guards, set out on that road with five hundred carts. A man-eating ogre rushed out, shouting; the terrified men fell on their bellies. The ogre seized the brahmin and fled, but its foot was pierced by a stump. While the forest guards pursued, it dropped the brahmin and lay down at the foot of its dwelling-tree. On the seventh day of its lying there, King Jayaddisa, having ordered a deer hunt, set out from the city. Just as he was leaving the city, a brahmin from Takkasilā named Nanda, a supporter of his mother, arrived with four verses each worth a hundred and saw the king. The king said, 'I will listen when I return,' and having provided a dwelling for him, went to the deer hunt and declared: 'In whoever's direction a deer escapes, the penalty is his neck!' Then a spotted deer rose up and fled towards the king. The ministers jeered. The king, taking his sword, pursued it, and after three leagues he caught up with it, struck it with his sword, and cut it into two pieces. Carrying it on a shoulder-pole, he was returning when he reached the place where the man-eating ogre was lying. He sat down on some kusa grass, rested for a moment, and prepared to go. Then the ogre rose up, seized him by the hand, and said, 'Stop! Where are you going? You are my food!' and spoke the first verse:

64.

64.

“Cirassaṃ vata me udapādi ajja, bhakkho mahā sattamibhattakāle;

Kutosi kovāsi tadiṅgha brūhi, ācikkha jātiṃ vidito yathāsī”ti.

“Indeed, after a long time, a great meal has appeared for me today, at my seventh-day mealtime. Where are you from? Who are you? Come, tell me! Declare your lineage, so that you may be known for who you are.”

Tattha bhakkho mahāti mahābhakkho. Sattamibhattakāleti pāṭipadato paṭṭhāya nirāhārassa sattamiyaṃ bhattakāle. Kutosīti kuto āgatosīti.

Herein, ‘a great meal’ means a large meal. ‘At mealtime on the seventh day’ means at the mealtime on the seventh day of being without food, starting from day one. ‘Where are you from?’ means ‘From where have you come?’

Rājā [V 5.0022] yakkhaṃ disvā bhīto ūrutthambhaṃ patvā palāyituṃ nāsakkhi, satiṃ pana paccupaṭṭhāpetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, seeing the ogre, was terrified. His thighs became stiff and he was unable to flee. However, establishing mindfulness, he spoke the second verse:

65.

65.

“Pañcālarājā migavaṃ paviṭṭho, jayaddiso nāma yadissuto te;

Carāmi kacchāni vanāni cāhaṃ, pasadaṃ imaṃ khāda mamajja muñcā”ti.

“I am the king of Pañcāla who entered the hunt, Jayaddisa by name, if you have heard of me. I roam the mountain slopes and the woods. Eat this spotted deer, but release me today.”

Tattha migavaṃ paviṭṭhoti migavadhāya raṭṭhā nikkhanto. Kacchānīti pabbatapassāni. Pasadanti pasadamigaṃ.

Herein, ‘entered the hunt’ means he went out from the kingdom to hunt deer. ‘Mountain slopes’ (kacchāni) means the base of the mountains. ‘This spotted deer’ refers to the spotted deer.

Taṃ [P 5.0024][M 5.0025] sutvā yakkho tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the ogre spoke the third verse:

66.

66.

“Seneva tvaṃ paṇasi sassamāno, mamesa bhakkho pasado yaṃ vadesi;

Taṃ khādiyāna pasadaṃ jighaññaṃ, khādissaṃ pacchā na vilāpakālo”ti.

“You bargain with what is mine, vexing me! This spotted deer you speak of is my food. Having eaten that spotted deer, I, being hungry to devour, will eat you afterwards. This is no time for lamentation!”

Tattha senevāti mama santakeneva. Paṇasīti voharasi attānaṃ vikkiṇāsi. Sassamānoti vihiṃsayamāno. Taṃ khādiyānāti taṃ paṭhamaṃ khāditvā. Jighaññanti ghasitukāmo. Khādissanti etaṃ pacchā khādissāmi. Na vilāpakāloti mā vilapi. Nāyaṃ vilāpakāloti vadati.

Herein, ‘with what is mine’ means with what belongs to me alone. ‘You bargain’ means you transact, trying to buy yourself off. ‘Vexing me’ means intending to harm. ‘Having eaten that’ means having eaten that first. ‘Being hungry to devour’ means desiring to eat. ‘I will eat’ means ‘I will eat you afterwards.’ ‘This is no time for lamentation’ means ‘Do not lament.’ He is saying, ‘This is not the time for lamentation.’

Taṃ sutvā rājā nandabrāhmaṇaṃ saritvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king remembered the brahmin Nanda and spoke the fourth verse:

67.

67.

“Na catthi mokkho mama nikkayena, gantvāna pacchāgamanāya paṇhe;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti.

“If there is no release for me by ransom, then let me go on the promise to return later. Having delivered on my pledge to the brahmin, as a guardian of the truth, I will come back.”

Tattha na catthīti na ce mayhaṃ nikkayena vimokkho atthi. Gantvānāti evaṃ sante ajja imaṃ migamaṃsaṃ khāditvā mama nagaraṃ gantvā. Paṇheti pageyeva, sveva pātarāsakāle paccāgamanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhāhīti adhippāyo. Taṃ saṅgaranti mayā “dhanaṃ te dassāmī”ti brāhmaṇassa saṅgaro kato, taṃ tassa datvā imaṃ mayā vuttaṃ saccaṃ anurakkhanto ahaṃ puna āgamissāmīti attho.

Herein, ‘if there is no’ means ‘if there is no release for me by ransom.’ ‘Let me go’ means: ‘This being the case, you eat this deer meat today, and let me go to my city.’ ‘On the promise’ means early; the intention is: ‘Accept my vow to return tomorrow at breakfast time.’ ‘That pledge’ refers to the promise made by me to the brahmin, ‘I will give you wealth.’ The meaning is: ‘Having given that to him, and guarding this truth spoken by me, I will come again.’

Taṃ [V 5.0023] sutvā yakkho pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the ogre spoke the fifth verse:

68.

68.

“Kiṃ kammajātaṃ anutappate tvaṃ, pattaṃ samīpaṃ maraṇassa rāja;

Ācikkha me taṃ api sakkuṇemu, anujānituṃ āgamanāya paṇhe”ti.

“For what kind of deed do you now worry, O king, having come so near to death? Tell me that; perhaps we might be able to permit you to go on the promise of your return.”

Tattha [P 5.0025][M 5.0026] kammameva kammajātaṃ. Anutappateti taṃ anutappati. Pattanti upagataṃ. Api sakkuṇemūti api nāma taṃ tava sokakāraṇaṃ sutvā pātova āgamanāya taṃ anujānituṃ sakkuṇeyyāmāti attho.

Herein, ‘kind of deed’ is simply a deed. ‘You now worry’ means you worry over that. ‘Having come’ means approached. ‘Perhaps we might be able’ means: ‘Perhaps, having heard the cause of your sorrow, we might be able to permit you to return early in the morning.’ This is the meaning.

Rājā taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathento chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, stating the reason, spoke the sixth verse:

69.

69.

“Katā mayā brāhmaṇassa dhanāsā, taṃ saṅgaraṃ paṭimukkaṃ na muttaṃ;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajissa”nti.

“I have raised in a brahmin a hope for wealth; that pledge has been bound upon me but not yet discharged. Having delivered on that pledge to the brahmin, as a guardian of the truth, I will return.”

Tattha paṭimukkaṃ na muttanti catasso satārahā gāthā sutvā “dhanaṃ te dassāmī”ti paṭiññāya mayā attani paṭimuñcitvā ṭhapitaṃ, na pana taṃ muttaṃ dhanassa adinnattā.

Herein, ‘bound upon me but not yet discharged’ means: having heard the four verses worth a hundred each, with the promise, ‘I will give you wealth,’ it was bound upon myself, but it has not been discharged because the wealth has not yet been given.

Taṃ sutvā yakkho sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the ogre spoke the seventh verse:

70.

70.

“Yā te katā brāhmaṇassa dhanāsā, taṃ saṅgaraṃ paṭimukkaṃ na muttaṃ;

Taṃ saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassappadāya, saccānurakkhī punarāvajassū”ti.

“That hope for wealth you raised in the brahmin, that pledge bound upon you but not yet discharged—having delivered on that pledge to the brahmin, as a guardian of the truth, you must return.”

Tattha punarāvajassūti puna āgacchassu.

Herein, ‘you must return’ means ‘you must come back again.’

Evañca pana vatvā rājānaṃ vissajjesi. So tena vissaṭṭho “tvaṃ mā cintayi, ahaṃ pātova āgamissāmī”ti vatvā magganimittāni sallakkhento attano balakāyaṃ upagantvā balakāyaparivuto nagaraṃ pavisitvā nandabrāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā mahārahe āsane nisīdāpetvā tā gāthā sutvā cattāri sahassāni datvā yānaṃ āropetvā “imaṃ takkasilameva nethā”ti manusse datvā brāhmaṇaṃ uyyojetvā dutiyadivase paṭigantukāmo hutvā puttaṃ āmantetvā anusāsi. Tamatthaṃ dīpento satthā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken thus, he released the king. Released by him, the king said, “Do not worry, I will return early in the morning.” Then, taking note of the landmarks on the way, he went to his retinue. Surrounded by his troops, he entered the city, had the brahmin Nanda summoned, seated him on a magnificent seat, and after listening to the verses, gave him four thousand coins. He had him mount a vehicle and, entrusting him to some men with the instruction, “Take him to Takkasilā,” he sent the brahmin off. Then, as he wished to return the next day, he summoned his son and instructed him. Clarifying this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:

71.

71.

“Muttoca [V 5.0024][M 5.0027] so porisādassa hatthā, gantvā sakaṃ mandiraṃ kāmakāmī;

Taṃ [P 5.0026] saṅgaraṃ brāhmaṇassappadāya, āmantayī puttamalīnasattuṃ.

“Freed from the hand of the man-eater, he went to his own palace, a place of sensual delights. Having fulfilled his pledge to the brahmin, he addressed his son Alīnasattu.”

72.

72.

“Ajjeva rajjaṃ abhisiñcayassu, dhammaṃ cara sesu paresu cāpi;

Adhammakāro ca te māhu raṭṭhe, gacchāmahaṃ porisādassa ñatte”ti.

“Be consecrated in the kingdom this very day. Practice righteousness toward your own people and toward others as well. Let there be no unrighteousness in your kingdom; I am going into the presence of the man-eater.”

Tattha alīnasattunti evaṃnāmakaṃ kumāraṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “arinasattu”nti likhitaṃ. Ajjeva rajjanti putta rajjaṃ te dammi, tvaṃ ajjeva muddhani abhisekaṃ abhisiñcayassu. Ñatteti abhyāse, santiketi attho.

Herein, ‘Alīnasattu’ is the prince so named. But in the Pali it is written as ‘Arinasattu’. ‘To the kingdom this very day’ means: “Son, I give the kingdom to you; you should be consecrated with the head-anointing this very day.” ‘In the presence’ means near, or in the vicinity; this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā kumāro dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince spoke the tenth verse:

73.

73.

“Kiṃ kamma krubbaṃ tava deva pāva, nārādhayī taṃ tadicchāmi sotuṃ;

Yamajja rajjamhi udassaye tuvaṃ, rajjampi niccheyyaṃ, tayā vināha”nti.

“What deed have I done at your feet, O King, that I have displeased you? I wish to hear it. Why do you establish me in the kingdom today? For without you, I would not desire the kingdom itself.”

Tattha krubbanti karonto. Yamajjāti yena anārādhakammena ajja maṃ rajjamhi tvaṃ udassaye ussāpesi patiṭṭhāpesi, taṃ me ācikkha, ahañhi tayā vinā rajjampi na icchāmīti attho.

Herein, ‘krubbaṃ’ means doing. ‘Because of which today’ means: “Tell me the displeasing deed because of which you would today raise me up, elevate me, and establish me in the kingdom; for indeed, without you I do not desire even the kingdom.” This is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā rājā anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the next verse:

74.

74.

“Na kammunā vā vacasāva tāta, aparādhitohaṃ tuviyaṃ sarāmi;

Sandhiñca katvā purisādakena, saccānurakkhī punāhaṃ gamissa”nti.

“I do not recall any offense by you toward me, dear son, whether by deed or by word. But having made a pact with the man-eater, I will go back as a guardian of the truth.”

Tattha aparādhitoti aparādhaṃ ito. Tuviyanti tava santakaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, ahaṃ ito tava kammato vā tava vacanato vā [M 5.0028] kiñci mama appiyaṃ aparādhaṃ na sarāmīti. Sandhiñca katvāti maṃ pana migavaṃ [P 5.0027] gataṃ eko yakkho “khādissāmī”ti gaṇhi. Athāhaṃ brāhmaṇassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā tassa sakkāraṃ katvā “sve tava pātarāsakāle āgamissāmī”ti tena purisādakena sandhiṃ saccaṃ katvā āgato, tasmā taṃ saccaṃ anurakkhanto puna tattha gamissāmi, tvaṃ rajjaṃ kārehīti vadati.

Herein, ‘aparādhito’ means an offense from this source. ‘Tuviyaṃ’ means belonging to you. This is what is said: “Dear son, I do not recall any displeasing offense from you, whether from your deeds or from your words. ‘Having made a pact’ means: while I was out hunting, a yakkha seized me, saying, ‘I will eat you.’ Then, after hearing the brahmin’s Dhamma talk and honoring him, I came away after making a truthful pact with that man-eater, saying, ‘I will return tomorrow at the time of your breakfast.’ Therefore, guarding that truth, I will go back there; you rule the kingdom,” he says.

Taṃ [V 5.0025] sutvā kumāro gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince spoke a verse:

75.

75.

“Ahaṃ gamissāmi idheva hohi, natthi tato jīvato vippamokkho;

Sace tuvaṃ gacchasiyeva rāja, ahampi gacchāmi ubho na homā”ti.

“I shall go; you stay right here. From him there is no escape for one who is alive. If you go, O King, I too shall go; then we both shall cease to be.”

Tattha idhevāti tvaṃ idheva hoti. Tatoti tassa santikā jīvantassa mokkho nāma natthi. Ubhoti evaṃ sante ubhopi na bhavissāma.

Herein, ‘idheva’ means: “You stay right here.” ‘Tato’ means: from him, there is no escape for one who is alive. ‘Ubho’ means: this being so, we both shall not exist.

Taṃ sutvā rājā gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke a verse:

76.

76.

“Addhā hi tāta satānesa dhammo, maraṇā ca me dukkhataraṃ tadassa;

Kammāsapādo taṃ yadā pacitvā, pasayha khāde bhidā rukkhasūle”ti.

“Truly, dear son, this is the nature of the good. But it would be more painful for me than death if Kammāsapāda, having impaled you on a tree-stake and cooked you, should forcibly devour you.”

Tassattho – addhā ekaṃsena esa, tāta, satānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ dhammo sabhāvo, yuttaṃ tvaṃ vadasi, api ca kho pana mayhaṃ maraṇatopetaṃ dukkhataraṃ assa, yadā taṃ so kammāsapādo. Bhidā rukkhasūleti tikhiṇarukkhasūle bhitvā pacitvā pasayha balakkārena khādeyyāti.

The meaning is: “Truly, certainly, dear son, this is the nature and principle of the good and the wise; you speak what is proper. Nevertheless, it would be more painful for me even than death if that Kammāsapāda... ‘Having impaled on a tree-stake’ means: having impaled you on a sharp wooden stake, cooked you, and should forcibly, by violence, devour you.”

Taṃ sutvā kumāro gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince spoke a verse:

77.

77.

“Pāṇena te pāṇamahaṃ nimissaṃ, mā tvaṃ agā porisādassa ñatte;

Evañca te pāṇamahaṃ nimissaṃ, tasmā mataṃ jīvitassa vaṇṇemī”ti.

“I will exchange my life for your life; do not go into the presence of the man-eater. Thus I will exchange my life for yours; therefore I value my death for the sake of your life.”

Tattha [M 5.0029] nimissanti ahaṃ idheva tava pāṇena mama pāṇaṃ parivattessaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā etaṃ pāṇaṃ tava pāṇenāhaṃ nimissaṃ, tasmā tava [P 5.0028] jīvitassatthāya mama maraṇaṃ vaṇṇemi maraṇameva varemi, icchāmīti attho.

Herein, ‘nimissaṃ’ means: “I will exchange my life for your life right here.” ‘Tasmā’ means: “Since I will exchange this life of mine for your life, therefore for the sake of your life I praise my death; I choose death itself, I wish for it.” This is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā rājā puttassa balaṃ jānanto “sādhu tāta, gacchāhī”ti sampaṭicchi. So mātāpitaro vanditvā nagaramhā nikkhami. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, knowing his son's strength, consented, saying, “Very well, dear son, go.” The prince paid homage to his parents and left the city. To reveal this matter, the Teacher spoke a half-verse:

78.

78.

“Tato [V 5.0026] have dhitimā rājaputto, vanditvā mātu ca pitu ca pāde”ti.

“Then, indeed, the resolute prince, having venerated his mother’s and father’s feet,”

Tattha pādeti pāde vanditvā nikkhantoti attho;

Herein, ‘pāde’ means: having venerated their feet, he departed; this is the meaning.

Athassa mātāpitaropi bhaginīpi bhariyāpi amaccaparijanehi saddhiṃyeva nikkhamiṃsu. So nagarā nikkhamitvā pitaraṃ maggaṃ pucchitvā suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā sesānaṃ ovādaṃ datvā acchambhito kesarasīho viya maggaṃ āruyha yakkhāvāsaṃ pāyāsi. Taṃ gacchantaṃ disvā mātā sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī pathaviyaṃ pati. Pitā bāhā paggayha mahantena saddena kandi. Tampi atthaṃ pakāsento satthā –

Then his mother and father, his sister, and his wife, along with the ministers and their retinue, also departed with him. Having left the city, he asked his father the way, noted it well, venerated his parents, and gave advice to the rest. Then, unafraid like a maned lion, he set out on the road toward the yakkha’s dwelling. Seeing him go, his mother, unable to maintain her composure, fell to the earth. His father, raising his arms, wept with a loud cry. To reveal this matter too, the Teacher said:

“Dukhinissa mātā nipatā pathabyā, pitāssa paggayha bhujāni kandatī”ti. –

“His grieving mother fell upon the earth; his father, raising his arms, wept aloud.”

Upaḍḍhagāthaṃ vatvā tassa pitarā payuttaṃ āsīsavādaṃ abhivādanavādaṃ mātarā bhaginībhariyāhi ca kataṃ saccakiriyaṃ pakāsento aparāpi catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken the half-verse, revealing the blessing and words of homage uttered by his father, and the act of truth performed by his mother, sister, and wife, the Teacher spoke another four verses:

79.

79.

“Taṃ gacchantaṃ tāva pitā viditvā, parammukho vandati pañjalīko;

Somo ca rājā varuṇo ca rājā, pajāpatī candimā sūriyo ca;

Etehi gutto purisādakamhā, anuññāto sotthi paccehi tāta.

“Seeing him going, his father, knowing this, faced away and venerated with cupped hands: ‘May King Soma, King Varuṇa, Pajāpati, the Moon, and the Sun—guarded by these, and released by the man-eater, may you return in safety, dear son.’”

80.

80.

“Yaṃ [P 5.0029][M 5.0030] daṇḍakirañño gatassa mātā, rāmassakāsi sotthānaṃ suguttā;

Taṃ te ahaṃ sotthānaṃ karomi, etena saccena sarantu devā;

Anuññāto sotthi paccehi putta.

“The blessing for safety that Rāma’s well-guarded mother performed for him when he had gone to the Daṇḍaka forest—that same blessing for safety I now perform for you. By this truth, may the devas protect you! Released, return in safety, my son.”

81.

81.

“Āvī raho vāpi manopadosaṃ, nāhaṃ sare jātu malīnasatte;

Etena saccena sarantu devā, anuññāto sotthi paccehi bhātika.

“Whether openly or in secret, I do not recall ever having any ill-will in my heart toward Alīnasattu. By this truth, may the devas protect you! Released, return in safety, dear brother.”

82.

82.

“Yasmā ca me anadhimanosi sāmi, na cāpi me manasā appiyosi;

Etena saccena sarantu devā, anuññāto sotthi paccehi sāmī”ti.

“And since you have never strayed from me even in thought, my lord, and since you have never been unloved by my heart, by this truth, may the devas protect you! Released, return in safety, my lord.”

Tattha parammukhoti ayaṃ me putto parammukho mātāpitaro vanditvā gacchati, iti etaṃ parammukhaṃ [V 5.0027] gacchantaṃ disvā viditvā. Pañjalīkoti tasmiṃ kāle sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā vandati devatā namassati. Purisādakamhāti purisādassa santikā tena anuññāto sotthinā paccehi.

Herein, `parammukho` means: 'This son of mine is going, having venerated his parents, with his back turned.' Thus it means: having seen and known him going with his back turned. `Pañjalīko` means: at that time, having placed his cupped hands on his head, he venerates, he pays homage to the deities. `Purisādakamhā` means: from the man-eater; 'permitted by him, return in safety.'

Rāmassakāsīti rāmassa akāsi. Eko kira bārāṇasivāsī rāmo nāma mātuposako mātāpitaro paṭijagganto vohāratthāya gato daṇḍakirañño vijite kumbhavatīnagaraṃ gantvā navavidhena vassena sakalaraṭṭhe vināsiyamāne mātāpitūnaṃ guṇaṃ sari. Atha naṃ mātupaṭṭhānakammassa phalena devatā sotthinā ānayitvā mātu adaṃsu. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutavasenāharitvā evamāha. Sotthānanti sotthibhāvaṃ. Taṃ pana kiñcāpi devatā kariṃsu, mātupaṭṭhānaṃ nissāya nibbattattā pana mātā akāsīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ te ahanti ahampi te tameva sotthānaṃ karomi, maṃ nissāya tatheva tava sotthibhāvo hotūti attho. Atha vā karomīti icchāmi. Etena saccenāti sace devatāhi tassa sotthinā ānītabhāvo sacco, etena saccena mamapi puttaṃ sarantu devā[M 5.0031], rāmaṃ viya tampi āharitvā mama dassantūti attho. Anuññātoti porisādena “gacchā”ti anuññāto devatānaṃ ānubhāvena sotthi paṭiāgaccha puttāti vadati.

`Rāmassakāsi` means: she did for Rāma. It is said that a resident of Bārāṇasī named Rāma, a supporter of his mother, went for the purpose of trade while looking after his parents. He went to the city of Kumbhavatī in the domain of King Daṇḍaki. When the entire country was being destroyed by a nine-fold rain, he recalled the virtues of his parents. Then, as a result of his karma of attending on his mother, the devas brought him back safely and gave him to his mother. Having adduced that reason based on what she had heard, she spoke thus. `Sotthānaṃ` means the state of safety. Although the devas did it, since it arose based on his attendance on his mother, it is said that his mother did it. `Taṃ te ahaṃ` means: 'I too perform that same well-wishing for safety for you'; the meaning is, 'Relying on me, may you have the same state of safety.' Or, `karomi` means 'I wish.' `Etena saccena` means: 'If it is true that he was brought back safely by the devas, by this truth may the devas be mindful of my son too; just like Rāma, may they bring him back and show him to me'—this is the meaning. `Anuññāto` means: 'Permitted by the man-eater, "Go!"; by the power of the devas, return safely, my son,' she says.

Jātu malīnasatteti jātu ekaṃsena alīnasatte mama bhātike ahaṃ sammukhā vā parammukhā vā manopadosaṃ na sarāmi, na mayā tamhi manopadoso katapubboti evamassa kaniṭṭhā saccamakāsi. Yasmā ca me anadhimanosi[P 5.0030], sāmīti mama, sāmi alīnasattu yasmā tvaṃ anadhimanosi, maṃ abhibhavitvā atikkamitvā aññaṃ manena na patthesi. Na cāpi me manasā appiyosīti mayhampi ca manasā tvaṃ appiyo na hosi, aññamaññaṃ piyasaṃvāsāva mayanti evamassa aggamahesī saccamakāsi.

`Jātu malīnasatte` means: 'I do not recall ever, in any way, having corruption of mind towards my virtuous brother, whether in his presence or in his absence; no corruption of mind towards him has been done by me before.' Thus his younger sister made an act of truth. `Yasmā ca me anadhimanosi, sāmi` means: 'My lord, virtuous one, since you are not disdainful of me, you do not desire another with your mind, overpowering and transgressing me.' `Na cāpi me manasā appiyosi` means: 'And you are not displeasing to my mind either; we live together in mutual affection.' Thus his chief queen made an act of truth.

Kumāropi pitarā akkhātanayena rakkhāvāsamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Yakkhopi “khattiyā nāma bahumāyā honti, ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissatī”ti rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā rañño āgamanaṃ olokento nisīdi. So kumāraṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “pitaraṃ nivattetvā putto āgato bhavissati, natthi me bhaya”nti otaritvā tassa piṭṭhiṃ dassento nisīdi. So āgantvā tassa purato aṭṭhāsi. Atha yakkho gāthamāha –

The prince, too, followed the path to the yakkha’s dwelling according to the instructions given by his father. The yakkha, thinking, 'Khattiyas are full of deceit; who knows what will happen?' climbed a tree and sat watching for the king’s arrival. Seeing the prince coming, he thought, 'The son must have come after sending his father back; there is no danger for me.' He descended and sat showing his back to him. The prince came and stood before him. Then the yakkha spoke a verse:

83.

83.

“Brahā ujū cārumukho kutosi, na maṃ pajānāsi vane vasantaṃ;

Luddaṃ maṃ ñatvā ‘purisādako’si, ko sotthimājānamidhāvajeyyā”ti.

“Tall, upright, and with a charming face, from where have you come? Do you not know me, who dwells in this forest? Knowing me to be a fierce man-eater, who that values his safety would come here?”

Tattha [V 5.0028] ko sotthimājānamidhāvajeyyāti kumāra ko nāma puriso attano sotthibhāvaṃ jānanto icchanto idhāgaccheyya, tvaṃ ajānanto āgato maññeti.

Herein, `ko sotthimājānamidhāvajeyyā` means: ‘Prince, what person, knowing and wishing for his own state of safety, would come here? I think you have come without knowing.’

Taṃ sutvā kumāro gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the prince, wishing to offer himself for the yakkha to eat, spoke a verse:

84.

84.

“Jānāmi ludda purisādako tvaṃ, na taṃ na jānāmi vane vasantaṃ;

Ahañca puttosmi jayaddisassa, mamajja khāda pituno pamokkhā”ti.

“I know you are a fierce man-eater; I am well aware of you who dwells in the forest. I am the son of Jayaddisa. Eat me today for the sake of my father’s release.”

Tattha [M 5.0032] pamokkhāti pamokkhahetu ahaṃ pitu jīvitaṃ datvā idhāgato, tasmā taṃ muñca, maṃ khādāhīti attho.

Herein, `pamokkhā` means: ‘For the sake of his release I have come here, having given my life for my father. Therefore, release him; eat me’—this is the meaning.

Tato yakkho gāthamāha –

Then the yakkha, wishing to praise the prince, spoke a verse:

85.

85.

“Jānāmi puttoti jayaddisassa, tathā hi vo mukhavaṇṇo ubhinnaṃ;

Sudukkaraññeva [P 5.0031] kataṃ tavedaṃ, yo mattumicche pituno pamokkhā”ti.

“I know you are the son of Jayaddisa, for the facial complexion of you both is identical. This deed of yours is very difficult to do—that you would wish to die for your father’s release.”

Tattha tathā hi voti tādiso vo tumhākaṃ. Ubhinnampi sadisova mukhavaṇṇo hotīti attho. Kataṃ tavedanti idaṃ tava kammaṃ sudukkaraṃ.

Herein, `tathā hi vo` means: ‘such is your resemblance.’ The meaning is: ‘The facial appearance of both is indeed similar.’ `Kataṃ tavedaṃ` means: ‘this deed of yours is very difficult to do.’

Tato kumāro gāthamāha –

Then the prince, responding to the yakkha's praise and explaining the reason for his coming in his father's stead, spoke a verse:

86.

86.

“Na dukkaraṃ kiñci mahettha maññe, yo mattumicche pituno pamokkhā;

Mātu ca hetu paraloka gantvā, sukhena saggena ca sampayutto”ti.

“I consider nothing here to be difficult for one who wishes to die for his father’s release; or for his mother’s sake, for having gone to the next world, he is endowed with the happiness of heaven.”

Tattha kiñci mahettha maññeti kiñci ahaṃ ettha na maññāmi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yakkha yo puggalo pitu vā pamokkhatthāya mātu vā hetu paralokaṃ gantvā sukhena sagge nibbattanakasukhena sampayutto bhavituṃ mattumicche marituṃ icchati, tasmā ahaṃ ettha mātāpitūnaṃ atthāya jīvitapariccāge kiñci dukkaraṃ na maññāmīti.

Herein, `kiñci mahettha maññe` means: I do not consider anything here difficult. This is what is said: “Yakkha, a person who wishes to die for the sake of his father’s release or for his mother’s sake, so that after going to the next world he might be united with the happiness of rebirth in heaven—therefore, I do not consider it anything difficult to sacrifice my life for the sake of my parents.”

Taṃ [V 5.0029] sutvā yakkho “kumāra, maraṇassa abhayānakasatto nāma natthi, tvaṃ kasmā na bhāyasī”ti pucchi. So tassa kathento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the yakkha asked, “Prince, there is no being who is not afraid of death. Why are you not afraid?” Explaining the reason for his fearlessness, the prince spoke two verses:

87.

87.

“Ahañca kho attano pāpakiriyaṃ, āvī raho vāpi sare na jātu;

Saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi, yatheva me idha tathā parattha.

“I certainly do not recall ever having done an evil deed, either openly or in secret. I am one who has clearly discerned birth and death; as it is for me here, so it is in the hereafter.

88.

88.

“Khādajja [M 5.0033] maṃ dāni mahānubhāva, karassu kiccāni imaṃ sarīraṃ;

Rukkhassa vā te papatāmi aggā, chādayamāno mayhaṃ tvamadesi maṃsa”nti.

“Eat me now, O mighty one; do what you will with this body. Or I will leap down for you from the top of this tree, and you may eat my flesh with relish.”

Tattha sare na jātūti ekaṃseneva na sarāmi. Saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmīti ahaṃ ñāṇena suparicchinnajātimaraṇo, jātasatto amaraṇadhammo nāma natthīti jānāmi. Yatheva me idhāti yatheva mama idha[P 5.0032], tathā paraloke, yathā ca paraloke, tathā idhāpi maraṇato mutti nāma natthīti idampi mama ñāṇena suparicchinnaṃ. Karassu kiccānīti iminā sarīrena kattabbakiccāni kara, imaṃ te mayā nissaṭṭhaṃ sarīraṃ. Chādayamāno mayhaṃ tvamadesi maṃsanti mayi rukkhaggā patitvā mate mama sarīrato tvaṃ chādayamāno rocayamāno yaṃ yaṃ icchasi, taṃ taṃ maṃsaṃ adesi, khādeyyāsīti attho.

In this context, 'sare na jātu' means: I absolutely do not recall. 'Saṅkhātajātīmaraṇohamasmi' means: I am one whose birth and death are well-defined by wisdom; I know that there is no born being that is of a deathless nature. 'Yatheva me idha' means: just as it is for me here, so it is in the next world—there is no release from death; this too is clearly discerned by my wisdom. 'Karassu kiccāni' means: do with this body the deeds that are to be done; this body has been relinquished to you by me. 'Chādayamāno mayhaṃ tvamadesi maṃsaṃ' means: when I have leaped from the treetop and died, you, choosing and relishing whatever flesh you desire from my body, may eat it. This is the meaning.

Yakkho tassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhīto hutvā “na sakkā imassa maṃsaṃ khādituṃ, upāyena naṃ palāpessāmī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The yakkha, hearing the prince's words, became very frightened and thought, “It is not possible for me to eat this prince’s flesh. I will make him flee by some stratagem.” Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

89.

89.

“Idañca te ruccati rājaputta, cajesi pāṇaṃ pituno pamokkhā;

Tasmā hi so tvaṃ taramānarūpo, sambhañja kaṭṭhāni jalehi aggi”nti.

“And if this is pleasing to you, prince, that you give up your life for your father’s release, then you, in haste, should break up firewood and kindle a fire.”

Tattha jalehīti araññaṃ pavisitvā sāradārūni āharitvā aggiṃ jāletvā niddhūme aṅgāre kara, tattha te maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādissāmīti dīpeti.

In this context, 'jalehi' indicates: “Having entered the forest and brought back hardwood, kindle a fire and make smokeless embers. There I will cook your flesh and eat it.”

So tathā katvā tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ pakāsento satthā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

The prince did as the yakkha said and then approached him. The Teacher, making that matter clear, spoke another verse:

90.

90.

“Tato have dhitimā rājaputto, dāruṃ samāharitvā mahantamaggiṃ;

Santīpayitvā paṭivedayittha, ādīpito dāni mahāyamaggī”ti.

“Then the resolute prince, having gathered wood and kindled a great fire, announced: ‘The great fire has now been lit by me!’”

Yakkho [V 5.0030][M 5.0034] aggiṃ katvā āgataṃ kumāraṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ purisasīho, maraṇāpissa bhayaṃ natthi, mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ evaṃ nibbhayo nāma na diṭṭhapubbo”ti lomahaṃsajāto kumāraṃ punappunaṃ olokento nisīdi. Kumāro tassa kiriyaṃ disvā gāthamāha –

The yakkha looked at the prince who had returned after making the fire and thought: “This man is a lion among men, courageous and without fear of death. In all this time, I have never before seen one so fearless.” Filled with awe and with his hair standing on end, he sat gazing at the prince again and again. Seeing the yakkha's behavior, the prince urged him to eat, saying:

91.

91.

“Khādajja maṃ dāni pasayhakāri, kiṃ maṃ muhuṃ pekkhasi haṭṭhalomo;

Tathā [P 5.0033] tathā tuyhamahaṃ karomi, yathā yathā maṃ chādayamāno adesī”ti.

“Eat me now, you who act by force! Why do you keep looking at me with your hair standing on end? I will do for you exactly as you wish, so that you may eat my flesh with relish.”

Tattha muhunti punappunaṃ. Tathā tathā tuyhamahanti ahaṃ tuyhaṃ tathā tathā vacanaṃ karomi, idāni kiṃ karissāmi, yathā yathā maṃ chādayamāno rocayamāno adesi khādissasi, tasmā khādajja manti.

In this context, 'muhuṃ' means repeatedly. 'Tathā tathā tuyhamahaṃ' means: I will follow your word in every way. 'What should I do now so that you, choosing and relishing me, will eat me? Therefore, eat me now.'

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā yakkho gāthamāha –

Having heard the prince's urging, the yakkha, wishing to express his inability to do so, spoke a verse:

92.

92.

“Ko tādisaṃ arahati khāditāye, dhamme ṭhitaṃ saccavādiṃ vadaññuṃ;

Muddhāpi tassa viphaleyya sattadhā, yo tādisaṃ saccavādiṃ adeyyā”ti.

“Who could bring himself to eat such a one—established in Dhamma, truthful, and benevolent? Even the head of one who would eat such a truthful person would surely split into seven pieces.”

Taṃ sutvā kumāro “sace maṃ na khāditukāmosi, atha kasmā dārūni bhañjāpetvā aggiṃ kāresī”ti vatvā “palāyissati nu kho, noti tava pariggaṇhanatthāyā”ti vutte “tvaṃ idāni maṃ kathaṃ pariggaṇhissasi, yohaṃ tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbatto sakkassa devarañño attānaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ nādāsi”nti vatvā āha –

Hearing that, the prince said: “Yakkha, if you do not wish to eat me, then why did you have me break wood and kindle a fire?” When the yakkha replied, “I had you kindle the fire to test you, to see if you would flee,” the prince said: “Why do you test me now? For even when I was born in the animal realm, I did not [merely] give myself to Sakka, king of the devas, just to be tested.” And he said:

93.

93.

“Idañhi so brāhmaṇaṃ maññamāno, saso avāsesi sake sarīre;

Teneva so candimā devaputto, sasatthuto kāmaduhajja yakkhā”ti.

“Thinking him a brahmin, the hare offered his own body. Because of that, O yakkha, the moon god, praised because of the hare, today fulfills the world's desires.”

Tassattho – idañhi so sasapaṇḍito “brāhmaṇo eso”ti brāhmaṇaṃ maññamāno “ajja imaṃ sarīraṃ khāditvā idheva vasā”ti evaṃ sake sarīre attano sarīraṃ dātuṃ avāsesi, vasāpesīti attho. Sarīrañcassa [M 5.0035] bhakkhatthāya adāsi. Sakko pabbatarasaṃ pīḷetvā ādāya candamaṇḍale sasalakkhaṇaṃ akāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya teneva sasalakkhaṇena so candimā devaputto “sasī sasī”ti evaṃ sasatthuto lokassa kāmaduho pemavaḍḍhano ajja yakkha virocati. Kappaṭṭhiyañhetaṃ pāṭihāriyanti.

Its meaning is this: That wise hare, thinking, “This is a brahmin,” and regarding him as a brahmin, resolved to give his own body, thinking, “Let him eat this body today and dwell right here.” This is the meaning of avāsesi, ‘he made him dwell.’ And he gave his body to be eaten. Sakka squeezed the essence from a mountain and with it drew the mark of the hare on the disk of the moon. From that time on, because of that very mark of the hare, the moon god, having the mark of the hare and being named Sasī, shines today, O yakkha, fulfilling the world’s desires and increasing affection. This is a marvel that will last for the aeon.

Taṃ [V 5.0031][P 5.0034] sutvā yakkho kumāraṃ vissajjento gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the man-eater yakkha, wishing to release the prince, spoke this verse:

94.

94.

“Cando yathā rāhumukhā pamutto, virocate pannaraseva bhāṇumā;

Evaṃ tuvaṃ porisādā pamutto, viroca kappile mahānubhāva;

Āmodayaṃ pitaraṃ mātarañca, sabbo ca te nandatu ñātipakkho”ti.

“Just as the moon freed from Rāhu’s mouth, or as the sun, shines on the fifteenth day, so you, freed from the man-eater, should shine in the land of the Kapilas, O mighty one. Delighting your father and your mother, may all your kinsfolk rejoice.”

Tattha bhāṇumāti sūriyo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā pannarase rāhumukhā mutto cando vā bhāṇumā vā virocati, evaṃ tvampi mama santikā mutto kapilaraṭṭhe viroca mahānubhāvāti. Nandatūti tussatu.

Herein, ‘bhāṇumā’ means the sun. This is what is said: Just as the moon freed from Rāhu’s mouth on the fifteenth day, or as the sun, shines, so you too, freed from my presence, should shine in the kingdom of Kapila, O mighty one. ‘Nandatu’ means let them be pleased.

Gaccha mahāvīrāti mahāsattaṃ uyyojesi. Sopi taṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā pañca sīlāni datvā “yakkho nu kho esa, no”ti pariggaṇhanto “yakkhānaṃ akkhīni rattāni honti animmisāni ca, chāyā na paññāyati, acchambhitā honti. Nāyaṃ yakkho, manusso eso. Mayhaṃ pitu kira tayo bhātaro yakkhiniyā gahitā. Tesu etāya dve khāditā bhavissanti, eko puttasinehena paṭijaggito bhavissati, iminā tena bhavitabbaṃ, imaṃ netvā mayhaṃ pitu ācikkhitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpessāmī”ti cintetvā “ehi ambho, na tvaṃ yakkho, pitu me jeṭṭhabhātikosi, ehi mayā saddhiṃ gantvā kulasantake rajje chattaṃ ussāpehī”ti vatvā itarena “nāhaṃ manusso”ti vutte “na tvaṃ mayhaṃ saddahasi, atthi pana so, yassa saddahasī”ti pucchitvā “atthi asukaṭṭhāne dibbacakkhukatāpaso”ti vutte taṃ ādāya tattha agamāsi. Tāpaso te disvāva “kiṃ karontā pitāputtā araññe carathā”ti vatvā tesaṃ ñātibhāvaṃ kathesi[M 5.0036]. Porisādo tassa saddahitvā “tāta, tvaṃ gaccha, ahaṃ ekasmiññeva attabhāve dvidhā jāto, na me rajjenattho, pabbajissāmaha”nti tāpasassa santike isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Atha naṃ kumāro vanditvā nagaraṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ [P 5.0035] pakāsento satthā –

Saying, “Go, great hero,” he dismissed the Great Being Alīnasatta. The prince, in turn, tamed him, established him in the five precepts, and then, while investigating whether he was a real yakkha or not, thought: “The eyes of yakkhas are red and unblinking, they cast no shadow, and they are fearless. This is not a yakkha; he is a human. It is said that my father’s three elder brothers were taken by a yakkhinī. She must have eaten two of them, and cared for one out of love as her son. This must be that man. I will take him, inform my father the king, and establish him in the kingdom.” Thinking thus, he said: “Come, friend, you are not a yakkha; you are my father’s eldest brother. Come with me and raise the royal white umbrella over our family’s kingdom.” When the other said, “I am not a human,” the prince asked, “If you do not believe my word, is there someone you would believe?” When he was told, “There is a hermit with the divine eye in such-and-such a place,” he took the man-eater and went to him. As soon as the hermit saw them, he said, “For what purpose are you two, uncle and nephew, wandering in the forest?” and he explained their family relationship. The man-eater believed the hermit's words and said: “My dear son, you may go. I have had two different natures in this single existence; I have no need for a kingdom. I will become a monk.” And he went forth as an ascetic in the presence of the hermit. Then the prince Alīnasatta paid homage to his uncle and returned to the city. The Teacher, making this matter known, said:

95.

95.

“Tato have dhitimā rājaputto, katañjalī pariyāya porisādaṃ;

Anuññāto sotthi sukhī arogo, paccāgamā kapilamalīnasattā”ti. –

“Then indeed the wise prince Alīnasatta, with hands folded in reverence, was politely released by the man-eater. Having been given permission, he returned—safe, happy, and healthy—to Kapila.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā tassa nagaraṃ gatassa negamādīhi katakiriyaṃ dassento osānagāthamāha –

Having spoken that verse, the Teacher, showing the honors paid to the prince Alīnasatta by the townspeople and others when he returned to the city, spoke the concluding verse:

96.

96.

“Taṃ [V 5.0032] negamā jānapadā ca sabbe, hatthārohā rathikā pattikā ca;

Namassamānā pañjalikā upāgamuṃ, namatthu te dukkarakārakosī”ti.

“All the townspeople and country folk, the elephant-riders, charioteers, and foot-soldiers, approached him, paying homage with folded hands, saying: ‘Homage to you, prince, you are a doer of difficult deeds!’”

Rājā “kumāro kira āgato”ti sutvā paccuggamanaṃ akāsi. Kumāro mahājanaparivāro gantvā rājānaṃ vandi. Atha naṃ so pucchi – “tāta, kathaṃ tādisā porisādā muttosī”ti. “Tāta, nāyaṃ yakkho, tumhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātiko, esa mayhaṃ petteyyo”ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “tumhehi mama petteyyaṃ daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Rājā taṅkhaṇaññeva bheriṃ carāpetvā mahantena parivārena tāpasānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Mahātāpaso tassa yakkhiniyā ānetvā akhāditvā positakāraṇañca yakkhābhāvakāraṇañca tesaṃ ñātibhāvañca sabbaṃ vitthārato kathesi. Rājā “ehi, bhātika, rajjaṃ kārehī”ti āha. “Alaṃ mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi etha uyyāne vasissatha, ahaṃ vo catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti? “Na āgacchāmi mahārājā”ti. Rājā tesaṃ assamapadato avidūre ekaṃ pabbatantaraṃ bandhitvā mahantaṃ taḷākaṃ kāretvā kedāre sampādetvā mahaḍḍhakulasahassaṃ ānetvā mahāgāmaṃ nivāsetvā tāpasānaṃ bhikkhācāraṃ paṭṭhapesi. So gāmo cūḷakammāsadammanigamo [M 5.0037] nāma jāto. Sutasomamahāsattena [P 5.0036] porisādassa damitapadeso pana mahākammāsadammanigamoti veditabbo.

The king Jayaddisa, hearing, “The prince has come,” went out to meet him. The prince, surrounded by a great crowd, approached the king and paid homage. Then the king asked him: “Dear son, how did you escape from the hands of such a cruel man-eater?” “Great father, he is not a yakkha; he is your elder brother and my paternal uncle.” Having related the entire story, he said: “It is fitting that you, great king, go to see my uncle.” The king immediately had a drum beaten and, with a large retinue, went to the hermits. The great hermit with the divine eye explained the whole matter in detail: how the man-eater was taken by the yakkhinī but not eaten and was raised by her, how he became like a yakkha, and their family relationship. King Jayaddisa said: “Elder brother, come and rule the kingdom!” “No, great king,” he refused. “Then come and dwell in my royal park; I will attend on you with the four requisites.” “I will not come, great king.” So the king had a mountain valley dammed not far from their hermitage, created a large reservoir, prepared fields, brought a thousand noble families to settle a large village, and established a regular alms-round for the hermits. That village came to be known as the Cūḷakammāsadamma Market Town. The place where the Great Being Sutasoma tamed the man-eater is to be known as the Mahākammāsadamma Market Town.

Satthā idaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakatthero sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, tāpaso sāriputto, porisādo aṅgulimālo, kaniṭṭhā uppalavaṇṇā, aggamahesī rāhulamātā, alīnasattukumāro pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the elder who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time the mother and father were the royal family, the hermit was Sāriputta, the man-eater was Aṅgulimāla, the younger sister was Uppalavaṇṇā, the chief queen was Rāhula's mother, and the prince Alīnasatta was myself.

Jayaddisajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Jayaddisa Jātaka is finished.

[514] 4. Chaddantajātakavaṇṇanā

[514] 4. 4. Chaddanta Jātaka: The story of holding a grudge due to a misunderstanding toward one's husband. The Commentary on the Chaddanta Jātaka.

Kiṃ nu socasīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ daharabhikkhuniṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira sāvatthiyaṃ kuladhītā gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā sāsane pabbajitvā ekadivasaṃ bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ dhammasavanāya gantvā alaṅkatadhammāsane nisīditvā dhammaṃ desentassa dasabalassa aparimāṇapuññapabhāvābhinibbattaṃ uttamarūpasampattiyuttaṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā “pariciṇṇapubbā [V 5.0033] nu kho me bhavasmiṃ vicarantiyā imassa mahāpurisassa pādaparicārikā”ti cintesi. Athassā taṅkhaṇaññeva jātissarañāṇaṃ uppajji – “chaddantavāraṇakāle ahaṃ imassa mahāpurisassa pādaparicārikā bhūtapubbā”ti. Athassā sarantiyā mahantaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji. Sā pītivegena mahāhasitaṃ hasitvā puna cintesi – “pādaparicārikā nāma sāmikānaṃ hitajjhāsayā appakā, ahitajjhāsayāva bahutarā, hitajjhāsayā nu kho ahaṃ imassa mahāpurisassa ahosiṃ, ahitajjhāsayā”ti. Sā anussaramānā “ahaṃ appamattakaṃ dosaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā vīsaratanasatikaṃ chaddantamahāgajissaraṃ sonuttaraṃ nāma nesādaṃ pesetvā visapītasallena vijjhāpetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi”nti addasa. Athassā soko udapādi, hadayaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi, sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontī assasitvā passasitvā mahāsaddena parodi. Taṃ disvā satthā [M 5.0038] sitaṃ pātu karitvā “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo sitassa pātukammāyā”ti bhikkhusaṅghena puṭṭho “bhikkhave, ayaṃ daharabhikkhunī pubbe mayi kataṃ aparādhaṃ saritvā rodatī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Why do you grieve?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a young bhikkhunī. She, it seems, was a daughter of a good family in Sāvatthī who, having seen the danger in the household life, had gone forth into the Dispensation. One day, having gone with the other bhikkhunīs to hear the Dhamma, she gazed upon the personal form of the Ten-Powered One—who was sitting on the decorated Dhamma-seat and teaching the Dhamma—produced by the power of immeasurable merit and endowed with supreme beauty. She thought: “I wonder if, while wandering through states of existence, I was ever a foot-attendant to this Great Being.” At that very moment, the knowledge of recalling past lives arose in her: “During the time of the Chaddanta elephant, I was a foot-attendant to this Great Being.” As she recollected this, great joy and delight arose in her. Overcome by the force of her rapture, she laughed a great laugh. Then she thought again: “Foot-attendants who are well-disposed toward their masters are few, while those who are ill-disposed are many. I wonder, was I well-disposed or ill-disposed toward this Great Being?” Reflecting further, she realized: “I harbored a slight resentment in my heart and sent a hunter named Sonuttara to have the great elephant king Chaddanta, who was one hundred and twenty cubits long, pierced with a poisoned arrow, thereby causing his death.” Then sorrow arose in her. Her heart grew hot and, unable to contain her grief, she sighed and sobbed, and wailed aloud. Seeing this, the Teacher showed a smile. When asked by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the appearance of a smile?” he replied: “Bhikkhus, this young bhikkhunī is weeping as she remembers an offense she committed against me in the past,” and he related the story of the past.

Atīte [P 5.0037] himavantapadese chaddantadahaṃ upanissāya aṭṭhasahassā hatthināgā vasiṃsu iddhimantā vehāsaṅgamā. Tadā bodhisatto jeṭṭhakavāraṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, so sabbaseto ahosi rattamukhapādo. So aparabhāge vuddhippatto aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedho ahosi vīsaratanasatāyāmo. Aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthāya rajatadāmasadisāya soṇḍāya samannāgato. Dantā panassa parikkhepato pannarasahatthā ahesuṃ dīghato tiṃsahatthā chabbaṇṇaraṃsīhi samannāgatā. So aṭṭhannaṃ nāgasahassānaṃ jeṭṭhako ahosi, pañcasate paccekabuddhe pūjesi. Tassa dve aggamahesiyo ahesuṃ – cūḷasubhaddā, mahāsubhaddā cāti. Nāgarājā aṭṭhanāgasahassaparivāro kañcanaguhāyaṃ vasati. So pana chaddantadaho āyāmato ca vitthārato ca paṇṇāsayojano hoti. Tassa majjhe dvādasayojanappamāṇe ṭhāne sevālo vā paṇakaṃ vā natthi, maṇikkhandhavaṇṇaudakameva santiṭṭhati, tadanantaraṃ yojanavitthataṃ suddhaṃ kallahāravanaṃ, taṃ udakaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ, tadanantaraṃ yojanavitthatameva suddhaṃ nīluppalavanaṃ taṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ, tato yojanayojanavitthatāneva rattuppalasetuppalarattapadumasetapadumakumudavanāni purimaṃ purimaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitāni. Imesaṃ pana sattannaṃ vanānaṃ anantaraṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ kallahārādivanānaṃ vasena omissakavanaṃ yojanavitthatameva tāni parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tadanantaraṃ nāgānaṃ kaṭippamāṇe udake yojanavitthatameva rattasālivanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ udakapariyante yojanavitthatameva nīlapītalohitaodātasurabhisukhumakusumasamākiṇṇaṃ khuddakagacchavanaṃ, iti imāni dasa vanāni yojanavitthatāneva. Tato khuddakarājamāsamahārājamāsamuggavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ tipusaelālukalābukumbhaṇḍavallivanāni, tato pūgarukkhappamāṇaṃ [V 5.0034] ucchuvanaṃ, tato hatthidantappamāṇaphalaṃ kadalivanaṃ[P 5.0038], tato sālavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ cāṭippamāṇaphalaṃ panasavanaṃ, tato madhuraphalaṃ ciñcavanaṃ, tato ambavanaṃ, tato kapiṭṭhavanaṃ, tato omissako mahāvanasaṇḍo, tato veḷuvanaṃ, ayamassa tasmiṃ [M 5.0039] kāle sampatti. Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana idāni pavattamānasampattiyeva kathitā.

In the past, in the Himalayan region, eight thousand elephant-nāgas, possessing psychic powers and able to travel through the air, dwelt near Lake Chaddanta. At that time the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of the chief elephant. He was entirely white, with a red face and feet. In due course, having reached his full growth, he was eighty-eight cubits in height and one hundred and twenty cubits in length. He was endowed with a trunk fifty-eight cubits long, like a silver rope. His tusks were fifteen cubits in circumference and thirty cubits in length, and they radiated six-colored rays. He became the chief of the eight thousand elephants and he honored five hundred Paccekabuddhas. He had two chief consorts, Cūḷasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā. The elephant king, surrounded by eight thousand elephants, dwelt in the Golden Cave. Lake Chaddanta was fifty yojanas in length and breadth. In its middle, in an area of twelve yojanas, there was neither moss nor water-plant; only water the color of a heap of jewels remained still. Next to that, a yojana in width, was a forest of pure white water lilies, which stood encircling the water. Next to that, also a yojana in width, was a forest of pure blue lotuses, which stood encircling the former. Then, each a yojana in width, were forests of red water lilies, white water lilies, red lotuses, white lotuses, and kumuda lilies, each standing encircling the one before it. Next to these seven forests was a mixed forest, also a yojana in width, which stood encircling all of them. Next to that, in water that was waist-deep for the elephants, was a forest of red rice, a yojana in width. Next to that, at the edge of the water, was a yojana-wide grove of small shrubs strewn with fragrant and delicate flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white. Thus these ten forests were each a yojana in width. Next came a forest of small cow-peas, large cow-peas, and green gram; then forests of cucumber, gourd, pumpkin, and other vines; then a sugarcane grove as tall as areca-nut trees; then a banana grove with fruit the size of elephant tusks; then a sāl forest; then a jackfruit grove with fruit the size of large jars; then a tamarind grove with sweet fruit; then a mango grove; then a wood-apple grove; then a great mixed forest thicket; and then a bamboo grove. Such was his prosperity at that time. In the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, only his present prosperity is described.

Veḷuvanaṃ pana parikkhipitvā satta pabbatā ṭhitā. Tesaṃ bāhirantato paṭṭhāya paṭhamo cūḷakāḷapabbato nāma, dutiyo mahākāḷapabbato nāma, tato udakapabbato nāma, tato candimapassapabbato nāma, tato sūriyapassapabbato nāma, tato maṇipassapabbato nāma, sattamo suvaṇṇapassapabbato nāma. So ubbedhato sattayojaniko chaddantadahaṃ parikkhipitvā pattassa mukhavaṭṭi viya ṭhito. Tassa abbhantarimaṃ passaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ, tato nikkhantena obhāsena chaddantadaho samuggatabālasūriyo viya hoti. Bāhirapabbatesu pana eko ubbedhato chayojaniko, eko pañca, eko cattāri, eko tīṇi, eko dve, eko yojaniko, evaṃ sattapabbataparikkhittassa pana tassa dahassa pubbuttarakaṇṇe udakavātappaharaṇokāse mahānigrodharukkho atthi. Tassa khandho parikkhepato pañcayojaniko, ubbedhato sattayojaniko, catūsu disāsu catasso sākhā chayojanikā, uddhaṃ uggatasākhāpi chayojanikāva, iti so mūlato paṭṭhāya ubbedhena terasayojaniko, sākhānaṃ orimantato yāva pārimantā dvādasayojaniko, aṭṭhahi pārohasahassehi paṭimaṇḍito muṇḍamaṇipabbato viya vilāsamāno tiṭṭhati. Chaddantadahassa pana pacchimadisābhāge suvaṇṇapassapabbate dvādasayojanikā kañcanaguhā tiṭṭhati. Chaddanto nāma nāgarājā vassāratte hemante aṭṭhasahassanāgaparivuto kañcanaguhāyaṃ vasati. Gimhakāle udakavātaṃ sampaṭicchamāno mahānigrodhamūle pārohantare tiṭṭhatī.

Encircling the bamboo grove stood seven mountains. Starting from the outermost, the first is named the Lesser Black Mountain, the second the Greater Black Mountain, then the Water Mountain, then the Moon-sided Mountain, then the Sun-sided Mountain, then the Jewel-sided Mountain, and the seventh is named the Golden-sided Mountain. This last one is seven yojanas in height and stands encircling Lake Chaddanta like the rim of a bowl. Its inner side is the color of gold, and with the radiance issuing from it, Lake Chaddanta looks like the rising morning sun. As for the outer mountains, one is six yojanas in height, one five, one four, one three, one two, and one is a single yojana high. In the northeastern corner of this lake, thus surrounded by seven mountains, in a place struck by water and wind, there is a great banyan tree. Its trunk is five yojanas in circumference and seven yojanas in height. In the four directions it has four great branches, each six yojanas long, and the branch that rises straight up is also six yojanas long. Thus from its root to its top it is thirteen yojanas high, and from the near side of its branches to the far side it spans twelve yojanas. Adorned with eight thousand aerial roots, it stands resplendent like a polished jewel mountain. In the western part of Lake Chaddanta, on the Golden-sided Mountain, there is a golden cave twelve yojanas in extent. The elephant king named Chaddanta, surrounded by eight thousand elephants, dwells in the Golden Cave during the rainy and winter seasons. In the summer, to receive the cool water and breeze, he stands at the foot of the great banyan tree among its aerial roots.

Athassa ekadivasaṃ “mahāsālavanaṃ pupphita”nti taruṇanāgā āgantvā ārocayiṃsu. So saparivāro “sālakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti [P 5.0039] sālavanaṃ gantvā ekaṃ supupphitaṃ sālarukkhaṃ kumbhena pahari. Tadā cūḷasubhaddā paṭivātapasse ṭhitā, tassā sarīre sukkhadaṇḍakamissakāni purāṇapaṇṇāni ceva tambakipillikāni ca patiṃsu. Mahāsubhaddā adhovātapasse ṭhitā, tassā sarīre pupphareṇukiñjakkhapattāni patiṃsu. Cūḷasubhaddā “ayaṃ nāgarājā attano piyabhariyāya upari pupphareṇukiñjakkhapattāni pātesi, mama [M 5.0040] sarīre sukkhadaṇḍakamissāni purāṇapaṇṇāni ceva tambakipillikāni ca pātesi, hotu, kātabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti mahāsatte veraṃ bandhi.

Then one day, young elephants came and announced to him, “The great sāla grove is in bloom.” He, along with his retinue, went to the sāla grove, thinking, “I will play the sāla game,” and struck a fully blooming sāla tree with his forehead. At that time, Cūḷasubhaddā was standing on the windward side, and dry twigs mixed with old leaves and red ants fell upon her body. Mahāsubhaddā was standing on the leeward side, and flower pollen, filaments, and petals fell upon her body. Cūḷasubhaddā thought: “This elephant king let flower pollen, filaments, and petals fall on his beloved wife, but on my body he let fall dry twigs mixed with old leaves and red ants. So be it! I will know what is to be done,” and she conceived a grudge against the Great Being.

Aparampi divasaṃ nāgarājā saparivāro nhānatthāya chaddantadahaṃ otari. Atha dve taruṇanāgā soṇḍāhi [V 5.0035] usirakalāpe gahetvā kelāsakūṭaṃ majjantā viya nhāpesuṃ. Tasmiṃ nhatvā uttiṇṇe dve kareṇuyo nhāpesuṃ. Tāpi uttaritvā mahāsattassa santike aṭṭhaṃsu. Tato aṭṭhasahassanāgāsaraṃ otaritvā udakakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā sarato nānāpupphāni āharitvā rajatathūpaṃ alaṅkarontā viya mahāsattaṃ alaṅkaritvā pacchā dve kareṇuyo alaṅkariṃsu. Atheko hatthī sare vicaranto sattuddayaṃ nāma mahāpadumaṃ labhitvā āharitvā mahāsattassa adāsi. So taṃ soṇḍāya gahetvā reṇuṃ kumbhe okiritvā jeṭṭhakāya mahāsubhaddāya adāsi. Taṃ disvā itarā “idampi sattuddayaṃ mahāpadumaṃ attano piyabhariyāya eva adāsi, na mayha”nti punapi tasmiṃ veraṃ bandhi.

On another day, the elephant king with his retinue descended into Lake Chaddanta to bathe. Then two young elephants, holding bundles of usira grass with their trunks, bathed him as if polishing Mount Kelāsa. After he had bathed and emerged, the two female elephants bathed. They too emerged and stood near the Great Being. Then eight thousand elephants descended into the lake, played in the water, and, bringing various flowers from the lake, they adorned the Great Being as if adorning a silver stūpa, and afterwards they adorned the two female elephants. Then one elephant, wandering in the lake, found a great lotus named Sattuddaya, brought it, and gave it to the Great Being. He took it with his trunk, sprinkled the pollen on his forehead, and gave it to the senior one, Mahāsubhaddā. Seeing this, the other thought: “He gave this Sattuddaya lotus only to his beloved wife, not to me,” and once more she conceived a grudge against him.

Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatte madhuraphalāni ceva bhisamuḷālāni ca pokkharamadhunā yojetvā pañcasate paccekabuddhe bhojente cūḷasubhaddā attanā laddhaphalāphalaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ datvā “bhante, ito cavitvā maddarājakule nibbattitvā subhaddā nāma rājakaññā hutvā vayappattā bārāṇasirañño aggamahesibhāvaṃ patvā tassa piyā manāpā taṃ attano ruciṃ kāretuṃ samatthā hutvā tassa ācikkhitvā ekaṃ luddakaṃ pesetvā imaṃ hatthiṃ visapītena sallena vijjhāpetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiṃ [P 5.0040] vissajjente yamakadante āharāpetuṃ samatthā homī”ti patthanaṃ ṭhapesi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya gocaraṃ aggahetvā sussitvā nacirasseva kālaṃ katvā maddaraṭṭhe rājaaggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, subhaddātissā nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Atha naṃ vayappattaṃ bārāṇasirañño adaṃsu. Sā tassa piyā ahosi manāpā, soḷasannaṃ itthisahassānaṃ jeṭṭhikā hutvā jātissarañāṇañca paṭilabhi. Sā cintesi – “samiddhā me patthanā, idāni tassa nāgassa yamakadante āharāpessāmī”ti. Tato sarīraṃ telena makkhetvā kiliṭṭhavatthaṃ nivāsetvā gilānākāraṃ dassetvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā mañcake nipajji. Rājā “kuhiṃ subhaddā”ti vatvā “gilānā”ti sutvā sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā mañcake nisīditvā tassā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was feeding five hundred paccekabuddhas with sweet fruits and lotus roots and stalks mixed with lotus honey, Cūḷasubhaddā, having given the fruits she had obtained to the paccekabuddhas, made an aspiration: “Venerable sirs, after passing away from here, may I be reborn in the royal family of Madda and become a princess named Subhaddā. When I come of age, may I attain the position of chief queen to the king of Benares. Being dear and beloved to him, and able to have him do my bidding, may I then inform him, send a hunter, have this elephant shot with a poisoned arrow, and bring about his death. Then may I be able to have his pair of tusks, which emit six-colored rays, brought to me.” From that time on, she did not take her food, wasted away, and before long she died. She was reborn in the womb of the chief queen in the Madda kingdom, and they named her Subhaddā. When she came of age, they gave her to the king of Benares. She became dear and beloved to him, the chief among sixteen thousand women, and she also gained the knowledge of remembering past lives. She thought: “My aspiration has been fulfilled. Now I will have the pair of tusks of that elephant brought to me.” Then, having smeared her body with oil and put on a soiled garment, she showed the appearance of being ill, entered the royal bedchamber, and lay down on the couch. The king asked, “Where is Subhaddā?” and when he heard, “She is ill,” he entered the royal bedchamber, sat down on the couch, and while stroking her back, he spoke the first stanza:

97.

97.

“Kiṃ [M 5.0041] nu socasinuccaṅgi, paṇḍūsi varavaṇṇini;

Milāyasi visālakkhi, mālāva parimadditā”ti.

“Why do you grieve so, O golden-limbed one? Why are you pale, O you of lovely complexion? You are withering, O wide-eyed one, like a garland that has been crushed.”

Tattha anuccaṅgīti kañcanasannibhasarīre. Mālāva parimadditāti hatthehi parimadditā padumamālā viya.

Herein, ‘anuccaṅgī’ means: one with a body like gold. ‘Mālāva parimadditā’ means: like a lotus garland crushed by hands.

Taṃ sutvā sā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, she spoke this stanza:

98.

98.

“Dohaḷo [V 5.0036] me mahārāja, supinantenupajjhagā;

Na so sulabharūpova, yādiso mama dohaḷo”ti.

“A longing has arisen in me, great king, that came to me in a dream. That longing of mine is not of a kind that is easy to fulfill.”

Tattha na soti yādiso mama supinantenupajjhagā supine passantiyā mayā diṭṭho dohaḷo, so sulabharūpo viya na hoti, dullabho so, mayhaṃ pana taṃ alabhantiyā jīvitaṃ natthīti avaca.

Herein, `na so` means: the longing that arose from a dream, which I saw while dreaming, is not of a kind that is easy to fulfill; it is difficult to fulfill. She said: “But for me, if I do not fulfill it, there is no life.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke a stanza:

99.

99.

“Ye keci mānusā kāmā, idha lokamhi nandane;

Sabbe te pacurā mayhaṃ, ahaṃ te dammi dohaḷa”nti.

“Whatever human sensual pleasures exist here in this world, O delightful one, all are available to me in abundance. I will give you the object of your longing.”

Tattha pacurāti bahū sulabhā.

Herein, `pacurā` means: many and easy to obtain.

Taṃ sutvā devī, “mahārāja, dullabho mama dohaḷo, na taṃ idāni kathemi, yāvattakā pana te vijite luddā, te sabbe sannipātetha[P 5.0041], tesaṃ majjhe kathessāmī”ti dīpentī anantaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the queen, making her intention clear, said: “Great king, the object of my longing is difficult to obtain. I will not speak of it now. But assemble all the hunters in your dominion; I will speak in their midst.” Then she spoke the following stanza:

100.

100.

“Luddā deva samāyantu, ye keci vijite tava;

Etesaṃ ahamakkhissaṃ, yādiso mama dohaḷo”ti.

“Let the hunters assemble, O lord, all those who are in your dominion. To them I will declare what my longing is like.”

Rājā “sādhū”ti sirigabbhā nikkhamitvā “yāvatikā tiyojanasatike kāsikaraṭṭhe luddā, tesaṃ sannipātatthāya bheriṃ carāpethā”ti amacce āṇāpesi. Te tathā akaṃsu. Nacirasseva kāsiraṭṭhavāsino luddā yathābalaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā āgantvā āgatabhāvaṃ rañño ārocāpesuṃ[M 5.0042]. Te sabbepi saṭṭhisahassamattā ahesuṃ. Rājā tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā vātapāne ṭhito hatthaṃ pasāretvā tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ deviyā kathento āha –

The king said, “Very well,” and, emerging from the royal bedchamber, he commanded his ministers: “Have a drum beaten to assemble all the hunters in the kingdom of Kāsi, which is three hundred yojanas in extent.” They did so. Before long, the hunters dwelling in the Kāsi kingdom arrived, bringing gifts according to their ability, and had their arrival announced to the king. They numbered sixty thousand in all. When the king learned of their arrival, he stood at a window, stretched out his hand, and, informing the queen of their arrival, he said:

101.

101.

“Ime te luddakā devi, katahatthā visāradā;

Vanaññū ca migaññū ca, mamatthe cattajīvitā”ti.

“Here are these hunters, O queen, skilled and expert, who know the forest and the beasts, and who would give up their lives for my sake.”

Tattha [V 5.0037] ime teti ye tvaṃ sannipātāpesi, ime te. Katahatthāti vijjhanachedanesu katahatthā kusalā susikkhitā. Visāradāti nibbhayā. Vanaññū ca migaññū cāti vanāni ca mige ca jānanti. Mamattheti sabbepi cete mamatthe cattajīvitā, yamahaṃ icchāmi, taṃ karontīti.

Herein, `ime te` means: these are the ones you had assembled. `Katahatthā` means: skilled of hand, clever, and well-trained in shooting and cutting. `Visāradā` means: fearless. `Vanaññū ca migaññū ca` means: they know the forests and the beasts. `Mamatthe` means: for my sake; they have all given up their lives for my sake, meaning they will do whatever I wish.

Taṃ sutvā devī te āmantetvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the queen addressed them and spoke another stanza:

102.

102.

“Luddaputtā nisāmetha, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Chabbisāṇaṃ gajaṃ setaṃ, addasaṃ supine ahaṃ;

Tassa dantehi me attho, alābhe natthi jīvita”nti.

“Listen, sons of hunters, as many of you as are gathered here! I saw in a dream a white elephant with six tusks. I have need of its tusks; if I do not get them, I cannot live!”

Tattha nisāmethāti suṇātha. Chabbisāṇanti chabbaṇṇavisāṇaṃ.

Herein, `nisāmetha` means: listen. `Chabbisāṇaṃ` means: having tusks with six colors.

Taṃ sutvā luddaputtā āhaṃsu –

Hearing that, the sons of the hunters said:

103.

103.

“Na no pitūnaṃ na pitāmahānaṃ, diṭṭho suto kuñjaro chabbisāṇo;

Yamaddasā [P 5.0042] supine rājaputtī, akkhāhi no yādiso hatthināgo”ti.

“A six-tusked elephant has never been seen or heard of by our fathers or our grandfathers. O princess, tell us what kind of elephant king it is that you saw in a dream.”

Tattha pitūnanti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – devi neva amhākaṃ pitūhi, na pitāmahehi evarūpo kuñjaro diṭṭhapubbo, pageva amhehi, tasmā attanā diṭṭhalakkhaṇavasena akkhāhi no, yādiso tayā diṭṭho hatthināgoti.

Herein, `pitūnaṃ` is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental. This is what was said: “O queen, such an elephant has never been seen before by our fathers or our grandfathers, much less by us. Therefore, tell us, according to the characteristics you yourself have seen, what kind of elephant king it was.”

Anantaragāthāpi [M 5.0043] teheva vuttā –

The following stanza was also spoken by them:

104.

104.

“Disā catasso vidisā catasso, uddhaṃ adho dasa disā imāyo;

Katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā, yamaddasā supine chabbisāṇa”nti.

“The four directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—these are the ten directions. In which direction does that six-tusked elephant king dwell, whom you saw in a dream?”

Tattha disāti disāsu. Katamanti etāsu disāsu katamāya disāyāti.

Herein, `disā` is used in the sense of `disāsu` (in the directions). `Katamaṃ` means: in which of these directions.

Evaṃ vutte subhaddā sabbe ludde oloketvā tesaṃ antare patthaṭapādaṃ bhattapuṭasadisajaṅghaṃ mahājāṇukaṃ mahāphāsukaṃ bahalamassutambadāṭhikaṃ nibbiddhapiṅgalaṃ dussaṇṭhānaṃ bībhacchaṃ sabbesaṃ matthakamatthakena [V 5.0038] paññāyamānaṃ mahāsattassa pubbaveriṃ sonuttaraṃ nāma nesādaṃ disvā “esa mama vacanaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī”ti rājānaṃ anujānāpetvā taṃ ādāya sattabhūmikapāsādassa uparimatalaṃ āruyha uttarasīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā uttarahimavantābhimukhaṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

When this was said, Subhaddā surveyed all the hunters and saw among them a hunter named Sonuttara, a former enemy of the Great Being. He had large feet, calves like rice-baskets, large knees, large ribs, a thick beard and reddish-brown fangs, piercing tawny eyes, a misshapen and repulsive appearance, and was so tall that he could be seen above the heads of all the others. Thinking, “This one will be able to do my bidding,” she obtained the king’s permission, took the hunter up to the top floor of the seven-storied palace, opened the northern lion-window, and stretching out her hand towards the northern Himālaya, she spoke four stanzas to point out the place where the elephant king lived:

105.

105.

“Ito ujuṃ uttariyaṃ disāyaṃ, atikkamma so satta girī brahmante;

Suvaṇṇapasso nāma girī uḷāro, supupphito kimpurisānuciṇṇo.

“Straight to the north from here, beyond seven great mountains, there is a lofty mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa (Golden Side), well-blossomed and frequented by kimpurisas.

106.

106.

“Āruyha selaṃ bhavanaṃ kinnarānaṃ, olokaya pabbatapādamūlaṃ;

Atha [P 5.0043] dakkhasī meghasamānavaṇṇaṃ, nigrodharājaṃ aṭṭhasahassapādaṃ.

“Having climbed that mountain, the abode of the kinnaras, look down at the mountain’s base. Then you will see a kingly banyan tree, the color of a dark cloud, with eight thousand offshoots.

107.

107.

“Tatthacchatī kuñjaro chabbisāṇo, sabbaseto duppasaho parebhi;

Rakkhanti naṃ aṭṭhasahassanāgā, īsādantā vātajavappahārino.

“There dwells the six-tusked elephant, all white, unassailable by others. Eight thousand elephants guard him, with tusks like chariot-poles, who attack with the speed of the wind.

108.

108.

“Tiṭṭhanti [M 5.0044] te tumūlaṃ passasantā, kuppanti vātassapi eritassa;

Manussabhūtaṃ pana tattha disvā, bhasmaṃ kareyyuṃ nāssa rajopi tassā”ti.

“They stand there, breathing heavily; they get angry even at the stirring of the wind. But on seeing a human being there, they would reduce him to ash, so that not even his dust would remain.”

Tattha itoti imamhā ṭhānā. Uttariyanti uttarāya. Uḷāroti mahā itarehi chahi pabbatehi uccataro. Olokayāti ālokeyyāsi. Tatthacchatīti tasmiṃ nigrodhamūle gimhasamaye udakavātaṃ sampaṭicchanto tiṭṭhati. Duppasahoti aññe taṃ upagantvā pasayhakāraṃ kātuṃ samatthā nāma natthīti duppasaho parebhi. Īsādantāti rathīsāya samānadantā. Vātajavappahārinoti vātajavena gantvā paccāmitte paharaṇasīlā evarūpā aṭṭhasahassanāgā nāgarājānaṃ rakkhanti. Tumūlanti bhiṃsanakaṃ mahāsaddānubandhaṃ assāsaṃ muñcantā tiṭṭhanti. Eritassāti vātapaharitassa yaṃ saddānubandhaṃ eritaṃ calanaṃ kampanaṃ, tassapi kuppanti, evaṃpharusā te nāgā. Nāssāti tassa nāsavātena viddhaṃsetvā bhasmaṃ katassa tassa rajopi na bhaveyyāti.

Herein, `ito` means from this place. `Uttariyaṃ` means to the north. `Uḷāro` means great, being higher than the other six mountains. `Olokaya` means you should look. `Tatthacchati` means he stands there at the foot of that banyan tree during the summer season, receiving the cool breeze. `Duppasaho` means he is unassailable by others, as no one else is capable of approaching and overpowering him. `Īsādantā` means having tusks as long as chariot-poles. `Vātajavappahārino` means that these eight thousand elephants, who are accustomed to moving with the speed of the wind to strike their enemies, protect the elephant king. `Tumūlaṃ` means they stand releasing breaths accompanied by a terrifying and great sound. `Eritassa` means they become angry even at the movement, shaking, or trembling caused by the wind; so fierce are those elephants. `Nāssa` means that not even the dust of the person would remain after being destroyed and reduced to ashes by the blast from the elephant's nostrils.

Taṃ sutvā sonuttaro maraṇabhayabhīto āha –

Hearing that, Sonuttara, terrified by the fear of death, said to the queen:

109.

109.

“Bahū [V 5.0039] hime rājakulamhi santi, piḷandhanā jātarūpassa devi;

Muttā [P 5.0044] maṇī veḷuriyāmayā ca, kiṃ kāhasi dantapiḷandhanena;

Māretukāmā kuñjaraṃ chabbisāṇaṃ, udāhu ghātessasi luddaputte”ti.

"Many indeed are the ornaments of gold in the royal household, O queen; pearls, gems, and those made of beryl. What will you do with an ornament of tusk? Do you wish to kill the six-tusked elephant, or will you have the hunter's sons slain?"

Tattha piḷandhanāti ābharaṇāni. Veḷuriyāmayāti veḷuriyamayāni. Ghātessasīti udāhu piḷandhanāpadesena luddaputte ghātāpetukāmāsīti pucchati.

Here, 'ornaments' means adornments. 'Made of beryl' means made of beryl stone. 'Will you have slain' means he asks, 'Or, under the pretext of an ornament, do you wish to have the hunter's sons slain?'

Tato devī gāthamāha –

Then the queen spoke this verse to the hunter:

110.

110.

“Sā issitā dukkhitā casmi ludda, uddhañca sussāmi anussarantī;

Karohi me luddaka etamatthaṃ, dassāmi te gāmavarāni pañcā”ti.

"Jealous and afflicted am I, O hunter; agitated and remembering, I wither away. Accomplish this purpose for me, hunter, and I will give you five excellent villages."

Tattha [M 5.0045] sāti sā ahaṃ. Anussarantīti tena vāraṇena pure mayi kataṃ veraṃ anussaramānā. Dassāmi teti etasmiṃ te atthe nipphādite saṃvacchare satasahassuṭṭhānake pañca gāmavare dadāmīti.

Here, 'she' means 'that I.' 'Remembering' means remembering the enmity done to me in the past by that elephant. 'I will give you' means: 'When this matter has been accomplished for you, I will give you five excellent villages that yield an annual income of a hundred thousand each.'

Evañca pana vatvā “samma luddaputta ahaṃ ‘etaṃ chaddantahatthiṃ mārāpetvā yamakadante āharāpetuṃ samatthā homī’ti pubbe paccekabuddhānaṃ dānaṃ datvā patthanaṃ paṭṭhapesiṃ, mayā supinantena diṭṭhaṃ nāma natthi, sā pana mayā patthitapatthanā samijjhissati, tvaṃ gacchanto mā bhāyī”ti taṃ samassāsetvā pesesi. So “sādhu, ayye”ti tassā vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā “tena hi me pākaṭaṃ katvā tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kathehī”ti pucchanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, she said: 'Friend hunter's son, in the past I gave a gift to Paccekabuddhas and made an aspiration: "May I be able to have this Chaddanta elephant killed and its pair of tusks brought to me." This is not something I have merely seen in a dream, but that aspiration I made will surely be fulfilled. Go, and do not be afraid.' Having thus comforted him, she sent him off. He accepted her words, saying, 'Very well, noble lady,' and then, asking, 'In that case, please make its dwelling place clear and describe it to me,' he spoke this verse:

111.

111.

“Katthacchatī kattha mupeti ṭhānaṃ, vīthissa kā nhānagatassa hoti;

Kathañhi so nhāyati nāgarājā, kathaṃ vijānemu gatiṃ gajassā”ti.

"Where does it dwell, where does it go to rest? What is its path when it goes to bathe? How does that elephant king bathe? How may we know the way of the elephant?"
