Tattha katthacchatīti kattha vasati. Kattha mupetīti kattha upeti, kattha tiṭṭhatīti attho. Vīthissa kāti tassa nhānagatassa kā vīthi hoti, kataramaggena so gacchati. Kathaṃ vijānemu gatinti tayā akathite mayaṃ kathaṃ tassa nāgarājassa gatiṃ vijānissāma, tasmā kathehi noti attho.

Here, 'where does it dwell' means: where does it live? 'Where does it go' means: where does it approach, where does it stand? That is the meaning. 'What is its path' means: what is the path of the one who has gone to bathe; by which way does it go? 'How may we know the way' means: if you do not tell us, how can we know the way of that elephant king? Therefore, tell us. That is the meaning.

Tato [V 5.0040][P 5.0045] sā jātissarañāṇena paccakkhato diṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ tassa ācikkhantī dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then she, through the power of her knowledge of past lives, describing the place as if directly seen, spoke these two verses:

112.

112.

“Tattheva sā pokkharaṇī adūre, rammā sutitthā ca mahodikā ca;

Sampupphitā bhamaragaṇānuciṇṇā, ettha hi so nhāyati nāgarājā.

"Right there, not far away, is that lotus pond, delightful, with good bathing spots and abundant water, abloom with flowers and frequented by swarms of bees. It is here that the elephant king bathes."

113.

113.

“Sīsaṃ [M 5.0046] nahātuppalamālabhārī, sabbaseto puṇḍarīkattacaṅgī;

Āmodamāno gacchati sanniketaṃ, purakkhatvā mahesiṃ sabbabhadda”nti.

"Having bathed his head, bearing a garland of blue lotuses, all white, with limbs and skin like a white lotus, rejoicing, he goes to his dwelling, having placed his chief queen, Sabbabhaddā, at the fore."

Tattha tatthevāti tassa vasanaṭṭhāneyeva. Pokkharaṇīti chaddantadahaṃ sandhāyāha. Sampupphitāti duvidhehi kumudehi tividhehi uppalehi pañcavaṇṇehi ca padumehi samantato pupphitā. Ettha hi soti so nāgarājā ettha chaddantadahe nhāyati. Uppalamālabhārīti uppalādīnaṃ jalajathalajānaṃ pupphānaṃ mālaṃ dhārento. Puṇḍarīkattacaṅgīti puṇḍarīkasadisatacena odātena aṅgena samannāgato. Āmodamānoti āmoditapamodito. Sanniketanti attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Purakkhatvāti sabbabhaddaṃ nāma mahesiṃ purato katvā aṭṭhahi nāgasahassehi parivuto attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti.

Here, 'right there' means in his very dwelling place. 'Lotus pond': this is said referring to the Chaddanta Lake. 'Abloom with flowers' means abloom all around with two kinds of white water lilies, three kinds of blue lotuses, and five-colored lotuses. 'It is here that' means: that elephant king bathes here in the Chaddanta Lake. 'Bearing a garland of blue lotuses' means bearing a garland of lotuses and other aquatic and terrestrial flowers. 'With limbs and skin like a white lotus' means endowed with a pure body with skin like a white lotus. 'Rejoicing' means delighted and joyful. 'To his dwelling' means to his own dwelling place. 'Having placed at the fore' means: having placed the chief queen named Sabbabhaddā at the fore, surrounded by eight thousand elephants, he proceeds to his own dwelling place.

Taṃ sutvā sonuttaro “sādhu ayye, ahaṃ taṃ vāraṇaṃ māretvā tassa dante āharissāmī”ti sampaṭicchi. Athassa sā tuṭṭhā sahassaṃ datvā “gehaṃ tāva gaccha, ito sattāhaccayena tattha gamissasī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā kammāre pakkosāpetvā “tātā amhākaṃ vāsipharasu-kuddāla-nikhādana-muṭṭhikaveḷugumbacchedana-sattha-tiṇalāyana-asilohadaṇḍakakacakhāṇuka- ayasiṅghāṭakehi attho, sabbaṃ sīghaṃ katvā āharathā”ti āṇāpetvā cammakāre pakkosāpetvā “tātā amhākaṃ kumbhabhāragāhitaṃ cammabhastaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, cammayottavarattahatthipādaupāhanacammachattehipi no attho, sabbaṃ sīghaṃ katvā āharathā”ti āṇāpesi. Te ubhopi sabbāni tāni sīghaṃ katvā āharitvā [P 5.0046] adaṃsu. Sā tassa pātheyyaṃ saṃvidahitvā araṇisahitaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ upakaraṇañca baddhasattumādiṃ katvā pātheyyañca cammabhastāyaṃ pakkhipi, taṃ sabbampi kumbhabhāramattaṃ ahosi.

Hearing this, Sonuttara agreed, saying: 'Very well, noble lady. I will kill that elephant and bring its tusks.' Then she, delighted, gave him a thousand coins and dismissed him, saying: 'For now, go home. You are to go there after seven days have passed.' She had blacksmiths summoned and ordered them: 'Sirs, we have need of an adze, an axe, a spade, a chisel, a hammer, a knife for cutting bamboo thickets, a grass-cutting sickle, an iron rod, a saw, stakes, and an iron tripod. Make all this quickly and bring it.' Then she had leatherworkers summoned and ordered them: 'Sirs, it is necessary to make a leather sack that can hold a pot-load. We also have need of leather straps, thongs, elephant-foot sandals, and a leather parasol. Make all this quickly and bring it.' Both groups quickly made all these things and brought them to her. She prepared his journey-provisions, and packed all the equipment, beginning with the fire-sticks, and the provisions, beginning with tied-up parched grain, into the leather sack. All of it amounted to the measure of a pot-load.

Sonuttaropi attano parivacchaṃ katvā sattame divase āgantvā deviṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ sā “niṭṭhitaṃ te samma sabbūpakaraṇaṃ, imaṃ tāva pasibbakaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha. So pana mahāthāmo pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ [M 5.0047] dhāreti, tasmā tambūlapasibbakaṃ viya ukkhipitvā upakacchantare [V 5.0041] ṭhapetvā rittahattho viya aṭṭhāsi. Subhaddā luddassa puttadārānaṃ paribbayaṃ datvā rañño ācikkhitvā sonuttaraṃ uyyojesi. Sopi rājānañca deviñca vanditvā rājanivesanā oruyha rathe ṭhatvā mahantena parivārena nagarā nikkhamitvā gāmanigamajanapadaparamparāya paccantaṃ patvā jānapade nivattetvā paccantavāsīhi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā manussapathaṃ atikkamma paccantavāsinopi nivattetvā ekakova gacchanto tiṃsayojanaṃ patvā paṭhamaṃ dabbagahanaṃ kāsagahanaṃ tiṇagahanaṃ tulasigahanaṃ saragahanaṃ tirivacchagahananti cha gahanāni, kaṇṭakaveḷugumbagahanāni vettagahanaṃ omissakagahanaṃ naḷagahanaṃ saragahanasadisaṃ uragenapi dubbinivijjhaṃ ghanavanagahanaṃ rukkhagahanaṃ veḷugahanaṃ aparampi veḷugumbagahanaṃ kalalagahanaṃ udakagahanaṃ pabbatagahananti aṭṭhārasa gahanāni paṭipāṭiyā patvā dabbagahanādīni asitena lāyitvā tulasigahanādīni veḷugumbacchedanasatthena chinditvā rukkhe pharasunā koṭṭetvā atimahante rukkhe nikhādanena vijjhitvā maggaṃ karonto veḷuvane nisseṇiṃ katvā veḷugumbaṃ āruyha veḷuṃ chinditvā aparassa veḷugumbassa upari pātetvā veḷugumbamatthakena gantvā kalalagahane sukkharukkhapadaraṃ [P 5.0047] attharitvā tena gantvā aparaṃ attharitvā itaraṃ ukkhipitvā puna purato attharanto taṃ atikkamitvā udakagahane doṇiṃ katvā tāya udakagahanaṃ taritvā pabbatapāde ṭhatvā ayasiṅghāṭakaṃ yottena bandhitvā uddhaṃ khipitvā pabbate laggāpetvā yottenāruyha vajiraggena lohadaṇḍena pabbataṃ vijjhitvā khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha ṭhatvā siṅghāṭakaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā puna upari laggāpetvā tattha ṭhito cammayottaṃ olambetvā taṃ ādāya otaritvā heṭṭhimakhāṇuke bandhitvā vāmahatthena yottaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇahatthena muggaraṃ ādāya yottaṃ paharitvā khāṇukaṃ nīharitvā puna abhiruhati. Etenupāyena pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruyha parato otaranto purimanayeneva paṭhamaṃ pabbatamatthake khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā cammapasibbake yottaṃ bandhitvā khāṇuke veṭhetvā sayaṃ antopasibbake nisīditvā makkaṭakānaṃ makkaṭasuttavissajjanākārena yottaṃ viniveṭhento otarati. Cammachattena vātaṃ gāhāpetvā sakuṇo viya otaratītipi vadantiyeva.

Sonuttara, having prepared his own provisions, arrived on the seventh day, paid homage to the queen, and stood by. Then she said to him, “Friend, all your equipment is ready. Take this bag for now.” But he, a man of great strength, possessed the might of five elephants, so he lifted it as if it were a betel-pouch, placed it under his arm, and stood as if empty-handed. Subhaddā, having given an allowance for the hunter’s wife and children, informed the king and sent Sonuttara on his way. He, too, paid homage to the king and queen, descended from the royal palace, mounted a chariot, and left the city with a great retinue. Passing through villages, towns, and districts in succession, he reached the frontier. Having sent back the country folk, he entered the forest with the frontier dwellers. Having passed the path of humans, he sent back the frontier dwellers too and, proceeding alone, he traveled for thirty yojanas. He first came to six kinds of thickets: a thicket of dabba grass, of kāsa grass, of ordinary grass, of tulasi plants, of sara grass, and of tirivaccha grass. Then he came in succession to eighteen kinds of thickets, among them: thickets of thorny bamboo, of cane, of mixed growth, of reeds, a thicket like a thicket of sara grass, a dense forest impenetrable even to a snake, a thicket of trees, a thicket of bamboo, another thicket of bamboo clumps, an impassable mire, an impassable stretch of water, and an impassable mountain. He mowed down the thickets of dabba grass and the others with a sickle; he cut through the thickets of tulasi and the others with a bamboo-clump cutter; he chopped down the trees with an axe and pierced the huge trees with a chisel, making a path. In a bamboo forest, he made a ladder, climbed a bamboo clump, cut a bamboo stalk, and let it fall on top of another bamboo clump, and thus went across on the tops of the bamboo clumps. In the impassable mire, he spread out planks of dry wood and went across on them, spreading another plank in front, picking up the one behind, and again spreading it in front. In the impassable stretch of water, he made a canoe and crossed the water in it. Standing at the foot of the mountain, he tied an iron grappling hook to a rope, threw it up and made it catch on the mountain. He climbed up by the rope, and with an iron rod tipped with adamant he pierced the mountain and drove in a stake. Standing on that, he pulled up the grappling hook and again made it catch higher up. Standing there, he let down a leather strap, took hold of it and descended, tied it to the lower stake, and holding the strap with his left hand and taking a hammer in his right, he struck the strap, pulled out the stake, and climbed up again. By this means he climbed to the top of the mountain. Descending on the other side, he followed the same method as before. First, he drove a stake into the mountain top, tied a rope to his leather bag, wound it around the stake, and sitting inside the bag, he unwound the rope and descended in the way spiders let down their spider-thread. Some say he descended like a bird by catching the wind with a leather parasol.

Evaṃ [M 5.0048] tassa subhaddāya vacanaṃ ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā sattarasa gahanāni atikkamitvā pabbatagahanaṃ patvā tatrāpi cha pabbate atikkamitvā suvaṇṇapassapabbatamatthakaṃ āruḷhabhāvaṃ āvikaronto satthā āha –

Thus, having accepted Subhaddā’s word, the hunter left the city, passed through seventeen thickets, reached the impassable mountain region, and there too crossed six mountains. To make clear that he had climbed to the summit of the mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa, the Teacher said:

114.

114.

“Tattheva so uggahetvāna vākyaṃ, ādāya tūṇiñca dhanuñca luddo;

Vituriyati satta girī brahante, suvaṇṇapassaṃ nāma giriṃ uḷāraṃ.

“Right there, having taken her word, the hunter took his quiver and his bow; he ranged among seven great mountains, seeking the splendid mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa.”

115.

115.

“Āruyha [V 5.0042] selaṃ bhavanaṃ kinnarānaṃ, olokayī pabbatapādamūlaṃ;

Tatthaddasā meghasamānavaṇṇaṃ, nigrodharājaṃ aṭṭhasahassapādaṃ.

“Having climbed the rock, the kinnaras’ abode, he looked down at the mountain’s foot; there he saw, the color of a cloud, the kingly banyan with eight thousand aerial roots.”

116.

116.

“Tatthaddasā [P 5.0048] kuñjaraṃ chabbisāṇaṃ, sabbasetaṃ duppasahaṃ parebhi;

Rakkhanti naṃ aṭṭhasahassanāgā, īsādantā vātajavappahārino.

“There he saw the six-tusked elephant, all white, unassailable by others; eight thousand elephants guard him, with tusks like chariot-poles, striking with the speed of wind.”

117.

117.

“Tatthaddasā pokkharaṇiṃ adūre, rammaṃ sutitthañca mahodikañca;

Sampupphitaṃ bhamaragaṇānuciṇṇaṃ, yattha hi so nhāyati nāgarājā.

“There nearby he saw a lotus pond, delightful, with fine fords and ample water, covered in blossoms, frequented by swarms of bees, where that elephant king was wont to bathe.”

118.

118.

“Disvāna nāgassa gatiṃ ṭhitiñca, vīthissayā nhānagatassa hoti;

Opātamāgacchi anariyarūpo, payojito cittavasānugāyā”ti.

“Having seen the elephant’s gait and stance, his path to his resting and bathing place, the ignoble man, impelled by the power of her will, went to a place of ambush.”

Tattha soti, bhikkhave, so luddo tattheva sattabhūmikapāsādatale ṭhitāya tassā subhaddāya vacanaṃ uggahetvā saratūṇiñca mahādhanuñca ādāya pabbatagahanaṃ patvā “kataro nu kho suvaṇṇapassapabbato nāmā”ti satta [M 5.0049] mahāpabbate vituriyati, tasmiṃ kāle tuleti tīreti. So evaṃ tīrento suvaṇṇapassaṃ nāma giriṃ uḷāraṃ disvā “ayaṃ so bhavissatī”ti cintesi. Olokayīti taṃ kinnarānaṃ bhavanabhūtaṃ pabbataṃ āruyha subhaddāya dinnasaññāvasena heṭṭhā olokesi. Tatthāti tasmiṃ pabbatapādamūle avidūreyeva taṃ nigrodhaṃ addasa.

Herein, Bhikkhus, by ‘he’ is meant that hunter. Right there: having taken the word of Subhaddā as she stood on the terrace of the seven-storied palace, he took his quiver of arrows and his great bow, reached the impassable mountain region, and explored the seven great mountains, thinking: “Now which one is the mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa?” At that time, ‘explored’ means he weighed and considered. While thus considering, he saw the splendid mountain named Suvaṇṇapassa and thought: “This must be it.” He looked down: having climbed that mountain which was the abode of the kinnaras, he looked down below by means of the sign given by Subhaddā. There: at the foot of that mountain, not far off, he saw that banyan tree.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ nigrodharukkhamūle ṭhitaṃ. Tatthāti tattheva antopabbate tassa nigrodhassāvidūre yattha so nhāyati, taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ addasa. Disvānāti suvaṇṇapassapabbatā oruyha hatthīnaṃ gatakāle hatthipādaupāhanaṃ āruyha tassa nāgarañño gataṭṭhānaṃ nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānaṃ upadhārento “iminā maggena gacchati, idha nhāyati, nhatvā uttiṇṇo, idha tiṭṭhatī”ti sabbaṃ disvā ahirikabhāvena anariyarūpo tāya cittavasānugāya payojito, tasmā opātaṃ āgacchi paṭipajji, āvāṭaṃ khaṇīti attho.

‘There’ means standing at the foot of that banyan tree. ‘There’ means right there within the mountain, not far from that banyan tree, he saw that lotus pond where the elephant bathed. ‘Having seen’ means having descended from the Suvaṇṇapassa mountain at the time the elephants went out, having followed the elephant tracks and observing the movements and the regular dwelling place of that elephant king—thinking, ‘He goes by this path, he bathes here, having bathed he comes out, he stands here’—having seen all this, being of ignoble nature on account of his shamelessness, and being impelled by her (Queen Subhaddā) who followed the whims of her mind, he therefore went to a place of ambush, that is, he dug a pit. This is the meaning.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – “so kira mahāsattassa vasanokāsaṃ sattamāsādhikehi sattahi saṃvaccharehi sattahi ca divasehi patvā vuttanayeneva tassa vasanokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā “idha āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā tasmiṃ ṭhito vāraṇādhipatiṃ visapītena sallena vijjhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti vavatthapetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā thambhādīnaṃ atthāya rukkhe chinditvā dabbasambhāre [V 5.0043] sajjetvā hatthīsu [P 5.0049] nhānatthāya gatesu tassa vasanokāse mahākuddālena caturassaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā uddhatapaṃsuṃ bījaṃ vapanto viya udakena vikiritvā udukkhalapāsāṇānaṃ upari thambhe patiṭṭhapetvā tulā ca kāje ca datvā padarāni attharitvā kaṇḍappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ katvā upari paṃsuñca kacavarañca pakkhipitvā ekena passena attano pavisanaṭṭhānaṃ katvā evaṃ niṭṭhite āvāṭe paccūsakāleyeva patisīsakaṃ paṭimuñcitvā kāsāyāni paridahitvā saddhiṃ visapītena sallena dhanuṃ ādāya āvāṭaṃ otaritvā aṭṭhāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Here is the story in sequence: It is said that after seven years, seven months, and seven days, he reached the dwelling place of the Great Being. Having noted the dwelling place in the manner described, he made a resolve: ‘I will dig a pit here, and standing in it, I will shoot the lord of elephants with a poisoned arrow and bring him to his end.’ Having made this decision, he entered the forest, cut down trees for posts and other things, and prepared the materials. When the elephants had gone to bathe, he dug a square pit in the elephant king's dwelling place with a large hoe. He scattered the excavated earth and sprinkled it with water as if sowing seed. He set up posts on top of mortar-stones, placed beams and poles, and spread planks over them. He made a hole the size of an arrow-shaft and on top he threw earth and rubbish. On one side he made an entrance for himself. When the pit was thus finished, at dawn he put on a head-dress, donned saffron robes, and taking his bow along with a poisoned arrow, he descended into the pit and stood there. To illuminate this matter, the Teacher said:

119.

119.

“Khaṇitvāna kāsuṃ phalakehi chādayi, attānamodhāya dhanuñca luddo;

Passāgataṃ puthusallena nāgaṃ, samappayī dukkaṭakammakārī.

“Having dug a pit and covered it with planks, the hunter concealed himself and his bow inside; when the elephant came alongside, the doer of evil deeds struck him with a broad arrow.”

120.

120.

“Viddho [M 5.0050] ca nāgo koñcamanādi ghoraṃ, sabbe ca nāgā ninnaduṃ ghorarūpaṃ;

Tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca raṇaṃ karontā, dhāviṃsu te aṭṭha disā samantato.

“Being struck, the elephant uttered a terrible heron-like cry, and all the elephants roared a dreadful roar; crushing grass and wood to pieces, they fled in all eight directions.”

121.

121.

“Vadhissametanti parāmasanto, kāsāvamaddakkhi dhajaṃ isīnaṃ;

Dukkhena phuṭṭhassudapādi saññā, arahaddhajo sabbhi avajjharūpo”ti.

“Thinking, ‘I will kill him,’ as he was reaching out, he saw the saffron robe, the banner of the sages; though stricken with pain, the perception arose: ‘The banner of the Worthy Ones is inviolable to the virtuous.’”

Tattha odhāyāti odahitvā pavesetvā. Passāgatanti attano āvāṭassa passaṃ āgataṃ. So kira dutiyadivase āgantvā nhatvā uttiṇṇo tasmiṃ mahāvisālamālake nāma padese aṭṭhāsi. Athassa sarīrato udakaṃ nābhipadesena ogalitvā tena chiddena luddassa sarīre pati. Tāya saññāya so mahāsattassa āgantvā ṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ passāgataṃ puthunā sallena samappayi vijjhi. Dukkaṭakammakārīti tassa mahāsattassa kāyikacetasikassa dukkhassa uppādanena dukkaṭassa kammassa kārako.

In this verse, ‘concealed’ means having placed himself inside, having entered. ‘Came alongside’ means he came to the side of the pit. It is said that on the following day, the elephant came, bathed, emerged, and stood in a place called the Great Open Space. Then water dripped from his body at the navel area, fell through that hole, and landed on the hunter’s body. By that sign, the hunter knew that the Great Being had arrived and was standing there, and when he came alongside, he struck him with a broad arrow, that is, he pierced him. ‘Doer of evil deeds’ means he is the doer of a wicked deed because he caused physical and mental suffering to that Great Being.

Koñcamanādīti koñcanādaṃ akari. Tassa kira taṃ sallaṃ nābhiyaṃ pavisitvā pihakādīni sañcuṇṇetvā antāni chinditvā piṭṭhibhāgaṃ [P 5.0050] pharasunā padālentaṃ viya uggantvā ākāse pakkhandi. Bhinnarajatakumbhato rajanaṃ viya pahāramukhena lohitaṃ pagghari, balavavedanā uppajji. So vedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto vedanāppatto sakalapabbataṃ ekaninnādaṃ karonto tikkhattuṃ mahantaṃ koñcanādaṃ nadi. Sabbe cāti tepi sabbe aṭṭhasahassanāgā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayabhītā ghorarūpaṃ ninnaduṃ anuravaṃ kariṃsu. Raṇaṃ karontāti tena saddena gantvā chaddantavāraṇaṃ [V 5.0044] vedanāppattaṃ disvā “paccāmittaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karontā samantā dhāviṃsu.

‘Uttered a heron’s cry’ means he made a heron-like sound. It is said that the arrow entered his navel, crushed his spleen and other organs, severed his intestines, and then, as if splitting his back with an axe, it burst out and soared into the sky. Blood gushed from the wound like red dye from a broken silver pot, and intense pain arose. Unable to endure the pain, overcome by suffering, he made the entire mountain resound with a single roar and three times uttered a great heron-like cry. And all of them, all eight thousand elephants, hearing that sound, were terrified by the fear of death and made a dreadful roar in response. ‘Making a commotion’ means that upon hearing the sound and seeing the six-tusked elephant overcome with pain, they rushed about on all sides, crushing grass and wood to powder, thinking, ‘We will seize the enemy!’

Vadhissametanti “bhikkhave, so chaddantavāraṇo disā pakkantesu nāgesu subhaddāya kareṇuyā passe ṭhatvā sandhāretvā samassāsayamānāya vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā kaṇḍassa āgataṭṭhānaṃ sallakkhento ‘sace [M 5.0051] idaṃ puratthimadisādīhi āgataṃ abhavissa, kumbhādīhi pavisitvā pacchimakāyīdīhi nikkhamissa, idaṃ pana nābhiyā pavisitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi, tasmā pathaviyaṃ ṭhitena vissaṭṭhaṃ bhavissatī’ti upadhāretvā ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ upaparikkhitukāmo “ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissati, subhaddaṃ apanetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā “bhadde, aṭṭhasahassanāgā mama paccāmittaṃ pariyesantā disā pakkhandā, tvaṃ idha kiṃ karosī”ti vatvā, “deva, ahaṃ tumhe sandhāretvā samassāsentī ṭhitā, khamatha me”ti tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā tāya ākāsaṃ pakkhandāya nāgarājā bhūmiṃ pādanakhena pahari, padaraṃ uppatitvā gataṃ. So chiddena olokento sonuttaraṃ disvā “vadhissāmi na”nti cittaṃ uppādetvā rajatadāmavaṇṇasoṇḍaṃ pavesetvā parāmasanto buddhānaṃ isīnaṃ dhajaṃ kāsāvaṃ addakkhi. Luddo kāsāvaṃ mahāsattassa hatthe ṭhapesi. So taṃ ukkhipitvā purato ṭhapesi. Athassa tena tathārūpenapi dukkhena phuṭṭhassa “arahaddhajo nāma sabbhi paṇḍitehi avajjharūpo, aññadatthu sakkātabbo garukātabboyevā”ti ayaṃ saññā udapādi.

Monks, while the other elephants had departed in various directions, that Chaddanta elephant king, enduring the pain while the female elephant Subhaddā stood by his side, supporting and comforting him, observed the place from which the arrow had come and thought: 'If this had come from the eastern direction or the like, it would have entered through the cranial bumps and the like, and exited through the rear of my body. But this one entered my navel and leapt up into the sky. Therefore, it must have been shot by someone standing within the ground.' Reflecting thus and wanting to investigate the place where the hunter stood, he thought: 'Who knows what will happen? It is proper to send Subhaddā away.' Then he said: 'Dear one, eight thousand elephants are searching for my enemy in all directions. What are you doing here?' She replied: 'Lord, I am standing here supporting and comforting you. Forgive me.' After circumambulating him three times and paying homage at four points, she leapt into the sky. After she had departed, the elephant king struck the ground with his toenail, and the plank covering the pit was displaced. Looking through the opening, he saw Sonuttara and the thought arose: 'I will kill him.' Extending his trunk, which was the color of a silver chain, he reached out and saw the ochre robe, the banner of the Buddhas and sages. The hunter placed the ochre robe in the Great Being’s trunk. He lifted it up and placed it before him. Then, even though afflicted by such suffering, this perception arose in him: 'The banner of the Arahants is a thing not to be harmed by the virtuous and wise; on the contrary, it should be honored and revered.'

So tena saddhiṃ sallapanto gāthādvayamāha –

Conversing with him, he spoke these two verses:

122.

122.

“Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ, yo vatthaṃ paridahissati;

Apeto damasaccena, na so kāsāvamarahati.

Whoever would don the ochre robe while yet impure, devoid of self-control and truth, is not worthy of the ochre robe.

123.

123.

“Yo ca vantakasāvassa, sīlesu susamāhito;

Upeto damasaccena, sa ve kāsāvamarahatī”ti.

But one who has purged his impurities, is well established in the virtues, and is endowed with self-control and truth—he is indeed worthy of the ochre robe.

Tassattho – samma luddaputta yo puriso rāgādīhi kasāvehi anikkasāvo indriyadamena ceva vacīsaccena ca apeto anupagato tehi guṇehi kasāvarasapītaṃ kāsāvavatthaṃ paridahati, so taṃ kāsāvaṃ nārahati, nānucchaviko so tassa [P 5.0051] vatthassa. Yo pana tesaṃ kasāvānaṃ vantattā [V 5.0045] vantakasāvo assa sīlesu susamāhito supatiṭṭhito paripuṇṇasīlācāro, so taṃ kāsāvaṃ arahati nāmāti.

Its meaning is: Friend, son of a hunter, any person who is not free from the stains of lust and so on, who is devoid of sense-restraint and truthfulness in speech, and yet wears the ochre robe dyed with the essence of the dye-stains—he is not worthy of that ochre robe; he is unsuitable for that garment. But one who has purged those stains, who is well-composed and firmly established in the virtues, perfected in moral conduct—he is indeed worthy of that ochre robe.

Evaṃ vatvā mahāsatto tasmiṃ cittaṃ nibbāpetvā “samma kimatthaṃ tvaṃ maṃ vijjhasi, kiṃ attano atthāya, udāhu aññena payojitosī”ti pucchi. Tamatthaṃ āvīkaronto satthā āha –

Having said this, the Great Being, extinguishing his anger toward him, asked: 'Friend, for what reason did you shoot me? Was it for your own sake, or were you employed by another?' Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:

124.

124.

“Samappito [M 5.0052] puthusallena nāgo, aduṭṭhacitto luddakamajjhabhāsi;

Kimatthayaṃ kissa vā samma hetu, mamaṃ vadhī kassa vāyaṃ payogo”ti.

Struck by the mighty arrow, the elephant, with a mind free from malice, spoke to the hunter: 'For what purpose, friend, or for what reason, did you strike me? Whose undertaking is this?'

Tattha kimatthayanti āyatiṃ kiṃ patthento. Kissa vāti kissa hetu kena kāraṇena, kiṃ nāma tava mayā saddhiṃ veranti adhippāyo. Kassa vāti kassa vā aññassa ayaṃ payogo, kena payojito maṃ avadhīti attho.

Herein, 'for what purpose' means 'desiring what in the future?' 'For what reason' means 'for what cause?'; the intention is: 'What enmity do you have with me?' 'Whose' means 'whose undertaking is this, or another's?'; the meaning is: 'Employed by whom did you strike me?'

Athassa ācikkhanto luddo gāthamāha –

Then the hunter, explaining to him, spoke this verse:

125.

125.

“Kāsissa rañño mahesī bhadante, sā pūjitā rājakule subhaddā;

Taṃ addasā sā ca mamaṃ asaṃsi, dantehi atthoti ca maṃ avocā”ti.

Venerable Sir, the chief queen of the King of Kāsī is the lady Subhaddā, who is honored in the royal family. She saw you and informed me, and she told me: 'I have need of the tusks.'

Tattha pūjitāti aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā pūjitā. Addasāti sā kira taṃ supinante addasa. Asaṃsīti sā ca mama sakkāraṃ kāretvā “himavantapadese evarūpo nāma nāgo asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne vasatī”ti mamaṃ ācikkhi. Dantehīti tassa nāgassa chabbaṇṇaraṃsisamujjalā dantā, tehi mama attho, piḷandhanaṃ kāretukāmāmhi, te me āharāti maṃ avocāti.

Herein, 'honored' means she was honored by being established in the position of chief queen. 'She saw' means, it is said, that she saw him in a dream. 'She informed me' means that after having me shown honor, she told me: 'In the Himalayan region there is an elephant of such-and-such a kind living in such-and-such a place.' 'I have need of the tusks' means she said to me: 'That elephant's tusks are resplendent with six-colored rays. I have need of them as I wish to have an ornament made. Bring them to me.'

Taṃ sutvā “idaṃ cūḷasubhaddāya kamma”nti ñatvā mahāsatto vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā “tassā mama dantehi attho natthi, maṃ māretukāmatāya pana pahiṇī”ti dīpento gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing this, the Great Being knew, 'This is the work of Cūḷasubhaddā.' Enduring the pain, he explained, 'She has no need for my tusks; rather, she sent him because she desires to kill me,' and he spoke two verses:

126.

126.

“Bahū hime dantayugā uḷārā, ye me pitūnañca pitāmahānaṃ;

Jānāti sā kodhanā rājaputtī, vadhatthikā veramakāsi bālā.

Many are these splendid pairs of tusks here, belonging to my fathers and my grandfathers. That wrathful princess knows this; the fool, desiring my death, has created this enmity.

127.

127.

“Uṭṭhehi [V 5.0046][P 5.0052] tvaṃ ludda kharaṃ gahetvā, dante ime chinda purā marāmi;

Vajjāsi taṃ kodhanaṃ rājaputtiṃ, nāgo hato handa imassa dantā”ti.

Arise, hunter, take your saw and cut off these tusks before I die. You should tell that wrathful princess: 'The elephant is slain! Here, take his tusks!'

Tattha [M 5.0053] imeti tassa kira pitu pitāmahānaṃ dantā mā vinassantūti guhāyaṃ sannicitā, te sandhāya evamāha. Jānātīti bahūnaṃ vāraṇānaṃ idha sannicihe dante jānāti. Vadhatthikāti kevalaṃ pana sā maṃ māretukāmā appamattakaṃ dosaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā attano veraṃ akāsi, evarūpena pharusakammena matthakaṃ pāpesi. Kharanti kakacaṃ. Purā marāmīti yāva na marāmi. Vajjasīti vadeyyāsi. Handa imassa dantāti hato so mayā nāgo, manoratho te matthakappatto, gaṇha, ime tassa dantāti.

Herein, 'these' refers to the tusks of his father and grandfathers which were collected in a cave so they would not be lost; it was with reference to them that he spoke thus. 'She knows' means she knows about the many elephant tusks collected here. 'Desiring my death' means simply wishing to kill me, she harbored a slight resentment in her heart and created enmity, bringing matters to a head with such a harsh deed. 'Sharp' (kharaṃ) means a saw. 'Before I die' means as long as I have not yet died. 'You should tell' means you should say. 'Here are his tusks' means 'That elephant has been slain by me; your wish is fulfilled. Take them, these are his tusks.'

So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā nisīdanaṭṭhānā vuṭṭhāya kakacaṃ ādāya “dante chindissāmī”ti tassa santikaṃ upagato. So pana ubbedhato aṭṭhāsītihattho rajatapabbato viya ṭhito, tenassa so dantaṭṭhānaṃ na pāpuṇi. Atha mahāsatto kāyaṃ upanāmento heṭṭhāsīsako nipajji. Tadā nesādo mahāsattassa rajatadāmasadisaṃ soṇḍaṃ maddanto abhiruhitvā kelāsakūṭe viya kumbhe ṭhatvā mukhakoṭimaṃsaṃ dhanukena paharitvā anto pakkhipitvā kumbhato oruyha kakacaṃ antomukhe pavesesi, ubhohi hatthehi daḷhaṃ aparāparaṃ kaḍḍhi. Mahāsattassa balavavedanā uppajji, mukhaṃ lohitena pūri. Nesādo ito cito ca sañcārento kakacena chindituṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto mukhato lohitaṃ chaḍḍetvā vedanaṃ adhivāsetvā “kiṃ samma chindituṃ na sakkosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, sāmī”ti. Mahāsatto satiṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā “tena hi samma mama soṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā kakacakoṭiṃ gaṇhāpehi, mama sayaṃ soṇḍaṃ ukkhipituṃ balaṃ natthī”ti āha. Nesādo tathā akāsi.

Hearing his words, the hunter rose from his seat, took his saw, and approached, thinking, 'I will cut off the tusks.' But the elephant stood eighty-eight cubits high like a silver mountain, so the hunter could not reach the base of his tusks. Then the Great Being, inclining his body, lay down with his head low. Then the hunter, treading on the Great Being’s trunk that was like a silver chain, climbed up and stood on his frontal globes as if on a peak of Mount Kelāsa. Striking the flesh at the corner of his mouth with his bow and pushing it inside, he climbed down from the globes and inserted the saw into the mouth. He pulled it firmly back and forth with both hands. Intense pain arose in the Great Being, and his mouth filled with blood. The hunter, moving it this way and that, was unable to cut through with the saw. Then the Great Being, spitting out the blood from his mouth and enduring the pain, asked, 'Friend, are you not able to cut them?' 'Yes, lord,' he replied. The Great Being, establishing mindfulness, said, 'In that case, friend, lift my trunk and let it take hold of the tip of the saw. I do not have the strength to lift my trunk myself.' The hunter did as he was told.

Mahāsatto soṇḍāya kakacaṃ gahetvā aparāparaṃ cāresi, dantā kaḷīrā viya chijjiṃsu. Atha naṃ te āharāpetvā gaṇhitvā “samma luddaputta ahaṃ ime dante tuyhaṃ dadamāno neva ‘mayhaṃ appiyā’ti [P 5.0053] dammi, na sakkattamārattabrahmattāni patthento, imehi pana me dantehi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇadantāva piyatarā, sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivedhāya me idaṃ puññaṃ paccayo hotū”ti dante datvā “samma idaṃ ṭhānaṃ kittakena kālena āgatosī”ti pucchitvā “sattamāsasattadivasādhikehi sattahi saṃvaccharehī”ti vutte – “gaccha imesaṃ [M 5.0054] dantānaṃ ānubhāvena sattadivasabbhantareyeva bārāṇasiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti vatvā tassa parittaṃ katvā taṃ uyyojesi[V 5.0047]. Uyyojetvā ca pana anāgatesuyeva tesu nāgesu subhaddāya ca anāgatāya kālamakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

The Great Being took the saw with his trunk and moved it back and forth; the tusks were severed like tender shoots. Then, having the hunter bring them and taking them, he said: 'Friend, son of a hunter, in giving these tusks to you, I do not give them thinking, “They are unloved by me,” nor do I give them aspiring to the state of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā. But the tusks of omniscient knowledge are a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times dearer to me than these tusks. May this merit be a condition for my penetration of omniscient knowledge.' Having given the tusks, he asked, 'Friend, in how much time did you come to this place?' When he said, 'In seven years, seven months, and seven days,' he said, 'Go. By the power of these tusks, you will reach Bārāṇasī within just seven days.' Then he performed a protection for him and sent him away. After sending him away, before those elephants and Subhaddā had returned, he passed away. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

128.

128.

“Uṭṭhāya so luddo kharaṃ gahetvā, chetvāna dantāni gajuttamassa;

Vaggū subhe appaṭime pathabyā, ādāya pakkāmi tato hi khippa”nti.

“Having risen, that hunter took his saw, and after cutting off the tusks of the most excellent elephant—lovely, beautiful, and incomparable on earth—he quickly departed from there, taking them.”

Tattha vaggūti vilāsavante. Subheti sundare. Appaṭimeti imissaṃ pathaviyaṃ aññehi dantehi asadiseti.

Herein, 'lovely' (vaggū) means graceful. 'Beautiful' (subhe) means fair. 'Incomparable' (appaṭime) means unequaled by any other tusks on this earth.

Tasmiṃ pakkante te nāgā paccāmittaṃ adisvā āgamiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

When he had departed, those elephants, not seeing the enemy, returned. Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:

129.

129.

“Bhayaṭṭitā nāgavadhena aṭṭā, ye te nāgā aṭṭha disā vidhāvuṃ;

Adisvāna posaṃ gajapaccamittaṃ, paccāgamuṃ yena so nāgarājā”ti.

“Afflicted by fear, distressed by the slaying of the elephant, those elephants fled in the eight directions. Not seeing the person, the elephant’s enemy, they returned to where that elephant king was.”

Tattha bhayaṭṭitāti maraṇabhayena upaddutā. Aṭṭāti dukkhitā. Gajapaccamittanti gajassa paccāmittaṃ. Yena soti yattha visālamālake so nāgarājā kālaṃ katvā kelāsapabbato viya patito, taṃ ṭhānaṃ paccāgamunti attho.

Herein, 'afflicted by fear' (bhayaṭṭitā) means oppressed by the fear of death. 'Distressed' (aṭṭā) means suffering. 'The elephant’s enemy' (gajapaccamittaṃ) means the enemy of the elephant. 'To where that elephant king was' (yena soti) means: to the place in the great sāl-tree grove where that elephant king, having passed away, had fallen like Mount Kelāsa; they returned to that place. This is the meaning.

Tehi [P 5.0054] pana saddhiṃ mahāsubhaddāpi āgatā. Te sabbepi aṭṭhasahassanāgā tattha roditvā kanditvā mahāsattassa kulupakānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, tumhākaṃ paccayadāyako visapītena sallena viddho kālakato, sīvathikadassanamassa āgacchathā”ti vadiṃsu. Pañcasatā paccekabuddhāpi ākāsenāgantvā visālamālake otariṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dve taruṇanāgā nāgarañño sarīraṃ dantehi ukkhipitvā paccekabuddhe vandāpetvā citakaṃ āropetvā jhāpayiṃsu. Paccekabuddhā sabbarattiṃ āḷāhane [M 5.0055] dhammasajjhāyamakaṃsu. Aṭṭhasahassanāgā āḷāhanaṃ nibbāpetvā vanditvā nhatvā mahāsubhaddaṃ purato katvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then, along with them, Mahāsubhaddā also arrived. All those eight thousand elephants, weeping and wailing there, went to the Paccekabuddhas who were patrons of the Great Being’s family and said: “Venerable sirs, your provider of requisites has been struck by a poisoned arrow and has passed away. Please come to see his remains.” Five hundred Paccekabuddhas also came through the sky and descended in the great sāl-tree grove. At that moment, two young elephants lifted the elephant king’s body with their tusks, had it pay homage to the Paccekabuddhas, placed it on the pyre, and cremated it. The Paccekabuddhas recited the Dhamma all night at the cremation ground. The eight thousand elephants extinguished the pyre, paid homage, bathed, and, placing Mahāsubhaddā at their head, went to their own dwelling place. Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:

130.

130.

“Te tattha kanditvā roditvāna nāgā, sīse sake paṃsukaṃ okiritvā;

Agamaṃsu te sabbe sakaṃ niketaṃ, purakkhatvā mahesiṃ sabbabhadda”nti.

“Having wailed and wept there, those elephants, sprinkling dust on their own heads, all went to their own abode, placing the queen Sabbabhaddā at their head.”

Tattha [V 5.0048] paṃsukanti āḷāhanapaṃsukaṃ.

Herein, 'dust' (paṃsukaṃ) means the dust from the cremation ground.

Sonuttaropi appatteyeva sattame divase dante ādāya bārāṇasiṃ sampāpuṇi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Sonuttara, before the seventh day was reached, took the tusks and arrived at Bārāṇasī. Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:

131.

131.

“Ādāya dantāni gajuttamassa, vaggū subhe appaṭime pathabyā;

Suvaṇṇarājīhi samantamodare, so luddako kāsipuraṃ upāgami;

Upanesi so rājakaññāya dante, nāgo hato handa imassa dantā”ti.

“Having taken the tusks of the most excellent elephant—lovely, beautiful, and incomparable on earth, gleaming all around their middle with golden streaks—that hunter went to the city of Kāsī. He presented the tusks to the royal princess, saying: ‘The elephant is slain! Here, these are his tusks!’”

Tattha suvaṇṇarājīhīti suvaṇṇarājiraṃsīhi. Samantamodareti samantato obhāsante sakalavanasaṇḍaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ viya karonte. Upanesīti ahaṃ chaddantavāraṇassa chabbaṇṇaraṃsivissajjane yamakadante ādāya [P 5.0055] āgacchāmi, nagaraṃ alaṅkārāpethāti deviyā sāsanaṃ pesetvā tāya rañño ārocāpetvā devanagaraṃ viya nagare alaṅkārāpite sonuttaropi nagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādaṃ āruhitvā dante upanesi, upanetvā ca pana, “ayye, yassa kira tumhe appamattakaṃ dosaṃ hadaye karittha, so nāgo mayā hato mato, ‘matabhāvaṃ me āroceyyāsī’ti āha, tassa matabhāvaṃ tumhe jānātha, gaṇhatha, ime tassa dantā”ti dante adāsi.

Herein, 'with golden streaks' means with streaks of golden rays. 'Gleaming all around' means illuminating all around, making the entire forest grove appear as if it were the color of gold. 'He presented': having sent a message to the queen, and having had her inform the king, the city was adorned like a city of the devas. Then Sonuttara entered the city, ascended the palace, and presented the tusks. Having presented them, he said: 'Noble lady, that elephant against whom you bore a slight aversion in your heart has been killed by me; he is dead. He said, "You should inform her of my death." So know that he is dead. Take these; these are his tusks,' and he gave her the tusks.

Sā mahāsattassa chabbaṇṇaraṃsivicittadante maṇitālavaṇṭena gahetvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā purimabhave attano pirasāmikassa dante olokentī “evarūpaṃ [M 5.0056] sobhaggappattaṃ vāraṇaṃ visapītena sallena jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ime dante chinditvā sonuttaro āgato”ti mahāsattaṃ anussarantī sokaṃ uppādetvā adhivāsetuṃ nāsakkhi. Athassā tattheva hadayaṃ phali, taṃ divasameva kālamakāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

She took the Great Being’s tusks, which were variegated with six-colored rays, using a jeweled fan, and placed them on her lap. As she gazed at the tusks of her beloved husband from a previous birth, she remembered the Great Being and thought: 'Sonuttara has come after bringing such a magnificent elephant, who had attained such beauty, to the end of his life with a poisoned arrow and cutting off these tusks.' Arousing sorrow, she was unable to endure it. Then and there her heart burst, and she passed away that very day. Making this matter clear, the Teacher said:

132.

132.

“Disvāna dantāni gajuttamassa, bhattuppiyassa purimāya jātiyā;

Tattheva tassā hadayaṃ aphāli, teneva sā kālamakāsi bālā”ti.

“Having seen the tusks of the most excellent elephant, her beloved husband in a former birth, right there her heart burst, and for that very reason that foolish woman passed away.”

133.

133.

“Sambodhipatto sa mahānubhāvo, sitaṃ akāsī parisāya majjhe;

Pucchiṃsu bhikkhū suvimuttacittā, nākāraṇe pātukaronti buddhā.

“He of great power who has attained perfect enlightenment smiled in the midst of the assembly. The bhikkhus, with minds well liberated, inquired: ‘Buddhas do not manifest a smile without a reason.’”

134.

134.

“Yamaddasātha [V 5.0049] dahariṃ kumāriṃ, kāsāyavatthaṃ anagāriyaṃ carantiṃ;

Sā kho tadā rājakaññā ahosi, ahaṃ tadā nāgarājā ahosiṃ.

“The young maiden whom you saw, wearing the saffron robe and wandering in the homeless life—she was then the royal princess, and I was then the elephant king.”

135.

135.

“Ādāya dantāni gajuttamassa, vaggū subhe appaṭime pathabyā;

Yo [P 5.0056] luddako kāsipuraṃ upāgami, so kho tadā devadatto ahosi.

“The hunter who went to the city of Kāsī, taking the tusks of the most excellent elephant—lovely, beautiful, and incomparable on earth—he was Devadatta then.”

136.

136.

“Anāvasūraṃ cirarattasaṃsitaṃ, uccāvacaṃ caritamidaṃ purāṇaṃ;

Vītaddaro vītasoko visallo, sayaṃ abhiññāya abhāsi buddho.

“This ancient conduct, high and low, practiced for a long, long time and never setting—the Buddha, free from anxiety, free from sorrow, and without darts, declared this, having directly known it himself.”

137.

137.

“Ahaṃ vo tena kālena, ahosiṃ tattha bhikkhavo;

Nāgarājā tadā homi, evaṃ dhāretha jātaka”nti. –

“Bhikkhus, at that time I was there; I was then the elephant king. Thus should you remember this Jātaka.”

Imā [M 5.0057] gāthā dasabalassa guṇe vaṇṇentehi dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi ṭhapitā.

These verses were included by the elders of the Dhamma council, who were praising the virtues of the One with Ten Powers.

Tattha sitaṃ akāsīti so sambodhippatto satthā mahānubhāvo alaṅkatadhammasabhāyaṃ alaṅkatadhammāsane parisamajjhe nisinno ekadivasaṃ sitaṃ akāsi. Nākāraṇeti “bhante, buddhā nāma akāraṇe sitaṃ na karonti, tumhehi ca sitaṃ kataṃ, kena nu kho kāraṇena sitaṃ kata”nti mahākhīṇāsavā bhikkhū pucchiṃsu. Yamaddasāthāti evaṃ puṭṭho, āvuso, satthā attano sitakāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto ekaṃ daharabhikkhuniṃ dassetvā evamāha – “bhikkhave, yaṃ ekaṃ daharaṃ yobbanappattaṃ kumāriṃ kāsāyavatthaṃ anagāriyaṃ upetaṃ pabbajitvā imasmiṃ sāsane carantiṃ addasātha passatha, sā tadā ‘visapītena sallena nāgarājaṃ vijjhitvā vadhehī’”ti sonuttarassa pesetā rājakaññā ahosi. Tena gantvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpito ahaṃ tadā so nāgarājā ahosinti attho. Devadattoti, bhikkhave, idāni devadatto tadā so luddako ahosi.

Herein, 'sitaṃ akāsi' means that one day the Teacher, of great power, who had attained perfect enlightenment, was seated in the midst of the assembly on the decorated Dhamma seat in the decorated Dhamma hall, and he smiled. 'Nākāraṇe' means: 'Venerable sir, Buddhas do not smile without a reason, yet you have smiled. For what reason did you smile?' Thus the great bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed asked. 'Yamaddasātha': Being asked thus, the Teacher, explaining the reason for his smile, pointed to a young bhikkhunī and said: 'Bhikkhus, this young maiden whom you see, who has reached youth, wears the saffron robe, has gone forth into the homeless life, and is faring in this Dispensation—she was then the royal princess who sent Sonuttara, saying: "Kill the elephant king by striking him with a poisoned arrow!"' The meaning is: 'I, who was brought to the end of my life by him who went there, was then that elephant king.' 'Devadatto' means: 'Bhikkhus, he who is now Devadatta was then that hunter.'

Anāvasūranti na avasūraṃ, anatthaṅgatasūriyanti attho. Cirarattasaṃsitanti ito ciraratte anekavassakoṭimatthake saṃsitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ anuciṇṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āvuso, ito anekavassakoṭimatthake saṃsaritampi pubbaṇhe kataṃ taṃ divasameva sāyanhe saranto viya attano caritavasena uccattā tāya rājadhītāya ca sonuttarassa ca caritavasena nīcattā uccānīcaṃ caritaṃ idaṃ purāṇaṃ rāgādīnaṃ darānaṃ vigatatāya vītaddaro, ñātidhanasokādīnaṃ abhāvena vītasoko, rāgasallādīnaṃ vigatattā visallo attanāva jānitvā buddho abhāsīti. Ahaṃ voti [V 5.0050] ettha voti nipātamattaṃ, bhikkhave, ahaṃ tena kālena tattha chaddantadahe ahosinti attho. Nāgarājāti honto ca pana na añño koci tadā homi, atha kho nāgarājā homīti attho. Evaṃ cārethāti tumhe taṃ jātakaṃ evaṃ dhāretha uggaṇhātha pariyāpuṇāthāti.

'Anāvasūraṃ' means not setting; the meaning is, like a sun that has not set. 'Cirarattasaṃsitaṃ' means practiced and transmigrated through for a long time, for many crores of years past. This is what is said: 'Friends, although it was transmigrated through many crores of years ago, it is remembered as if what was done in the morning is remembered in the evening. This ancient conduct was high and low—high because of his own conduct, and low because of the conduct of that princess and Sonuttara. "Vītaddaro" means free from anxiety because the anxieties of lust and so on have departed. "Vītasoko" means free from sorrow because of the absence of grief over relatives, wealth, and so on. "Visallo" means without darts because the darts of lust and so on have departed. The Buddha spoke having known this by himself.' 'Ahaṃ vo': here 'vo' is a mere particle. The meaning is: 'Bhikkhus, at that time I was there in the Chaddanta lake.' 'Nāgarājā': The meaning is: 'And being so, I was no one else then, but I was the elephant king.' 'Evaṃ dhāretha': 'You should remember that Jātaka thus, learn it, and master it.'

Imañca [P 5.0057] pana dhammadesanaṃ sutvā bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Sā pana bhikkhunī pacchā vipassitvā arahattaṃ pattāti.

And having heard this Dhamma discourse, many attained stream-entry and the other fruits. That bhikkhunī, later on, having developed insight, attained arahantship.

Chaddantajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Chaddanta Jātaka, the Fourth.

[515] 5. Sambhavajātakavaṇṇanā

[515] 5. The Commentary on the Sambhava Jātaka

Rajjañca [M 5.0058] paṭipannāsmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu mahāumaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“We have undertaken kingship...” This the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the perfection of wisdom. The story of the present will become clear in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka (Jā 546).

Atīte pana kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare dhanañcayakorabyo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa sucirato nāma brāhmaṇo purohito atthadhammānusāsako ahosi. Rājā dānādīni puññāni karonto dhammena rajjamanusāsi. So ekadivasaṃ dhammayāgaṃ nāma pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā sucirataṃ nāma brāhmaṇaṃ purohitaṃ āsane nisīdāpetvā sakkāraṃ katvā pañhaṃ pucchanto catasso gāthāyo abhāsi –

In the past, in the kingdom of the Kurus, in the city of Indapatta, a king named Dhanañjaya Koravya was ruling the kingdom. His chaplain was a brahmin named Sucirata, an instructor in temporal and spiritual matters. The king ruled righteously, performing meritorious deeds such as giving. One day, having formulated a question called the ‘Dhamma-sacrifice,’ he had the brahmin Sucirata take a seat, paid him homage, and, in order to ask the question, recited four verses:

138.

138.

“Rajjañca paṭipannāsma, ādhipaccaṃ sucīrata;

Mahattaṃ pattumicchāmi, vijetuṃ pathaviṃ imaṃ.

“We have undertaken kingship and sovereignty, Sucirata. I wish to attain greatness, to conquer this earth.”

139.

139.

“Dhammena no adhammena, adhammo me na ruccati;

Kiccova dhammo carito, rañño hoti sucīrata.

“By Dhamma, not by non-Dhamma, for non-Dhamma does not please me. O Sucirata, Dhamma when practiced is truly the king’s duty.”

140.

140.

“Idha cevāninditā yena, pecca yena aninditā;

Yasaṃ devamanussesu, yena pappomu brāhmaṇa.

“By what means are we blameless here, and blameless hereafter? By what means, O brahmin, may we attain fame among gods and humans?”

141.

141.

“Yohaṃ [V 5.0051] atthañca dhammañca, kattumicchāmi brāhmaṇa;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, brāhmaṇakkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“I am one who wishes to accomplish both the good and the Dhamma, O brahmin. Being asked by me, O brahmin, explain that good and Dhamma.”

Tattha rajjanti, ācariya, mayaṃ imasmiṃ sattayojanike indapatthanagare rajjañca, tiyojanasatike kururaṭṭhe issarabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ādhipaccañca. Paṭipannāsmāti adhigatā bhavāma. Mahattanti idāni mahantabhāvaṃ. Pattumicchāmi vijetunti imaṃ pathaviṃ dhammena abhibhavituṃ ajjhottharituṃ icchāmi. Kiccovāti avasesajanehi rañño carito dhammo kicco karaṇīyataro. Rājānuvattako hi loko, so tasmiṃ dhammike sabbopi dhammiko hoti. Tasmā esa dhammo nāma raññova kiccoti.

Herein, O teacher, by ‘kingship’ and ‘sovereignty’ is meant kingship in this seven-yojana city of Indapatta, and sovereignty, reckoned as lordship over the three-hundred-yojana land of the Kurus. ‘We have undertaken’ means we have attained it. ‘Greatness’ means the state of greatness. ‘I wish to attain and conquer’ means: ‘I wish to conquer and overwhelm this earth righteously.’ ‘A duty’ means: the Dhamma practiced by a king is a greater duty, more to be done, than that of other people. For the world follows the king; when he is righteous, everyone becomes righteous. Therefore this Dhamma is indeed the king’s duty.

Idha cevāninditāti yena mayaṃ idhaloke paraloke [P 5.0058] ca aninditā. Yena pappomūti yena mayaṃ nirayādīsu anibbattitvā devesu ca manussesu ca yasaṃ issariyaṃ sobhaggaṃ pāpuṇeyyāma, taṃ no kāraṇaṃ kathehīti[M 5.0059]. Yohanti, brāhmaṇa, yo ahaṃ phalavipākasaṅkhātaṃ atthañca tassa atthassa hetubhūtaṃ dhammañca kattuṃ samādāya vattituṃ uppādetuñca icchāmi. Taṃ tvanti tassa mayhaṃ tvaṃ sukheneva nibbānagāmimaggaṃ āruyha apaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ patthentassa taṃ atthañca dhammañca pucchito akkhāhi, pākaṭaṃ katvā kathehīti brāhmaṇaṃ dhammayāgapañhaṃ pucchi.

‘Blameless here and hereafter’ means: by what means may we be blameless in this world and in the next world? ‘By what means may we attain’ means: by what means may we, without being reborn in hell and other such states, attain fame, lordship, and good fortune among gods and humans? Tell us that reason. ‘I am one who’ means: O brahmin, I am one who wishes to accomplish both the good, reckoned as fruit and result, and the Dhamma, which is the cause of that good—to undertake it, to live by it, and to produce it. ‘That, you’ means: since I am one who seeks a state without relinking in rebirth, having easily ascended the path leading to Nibbāna, you, being asked by me about that good and Dhamma, should explain it; speak making it plain. Thus he asked the brahmin the question about the Dhamma-sacrifice.

Ayaṃ pana pañho gambhīro buddhavisayo, sabbaññubuddhameva taṃ pucchituṃ yuttaṃ, tasmiṃ asati sabbaññutaññāṇapariyesakaṃ bodhisattanti. Sucirato pana attano abodhisattatāya pañhaṃ kathetuṃ nāsakkhi, asakkonto ca paṇḍitamānaṃ akatvā attano asamatthabhāvaṃ kathento gāthamāha –

But this question is profound, the domain of a Buddha. It is fitting to ask only an omniscient Buddha about it, or in his absence, a bodhisatta who is seeking the knowledge of omniscience. However, the brahmin Sucirata, because he himself was not a bodhisatta, was unable to answer the question. Being unable, and not feigning the conceit of a wise man, he declared his own inability by speaking a verse:

142.

142.

“Nāññatra vidhurā rāja, etadakkhātumarahati;

Yaṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, kattumicchasi khattiyā”ti.

“No one other than Vidhura, O king, is able to explain this good and Dhamma that you wish to accomplish, O khattiya.”

Tassattho – avisayo esa, mahārāja, pañho mādisānaṃ. Ahañhi nevassa ādiṃ, na pariyosānaṃ passāmi, andhakāraṃ paviṭṭho viya homi. Bārāṇasirañño pana purohito vidhuro nāma brāhmaṇo atthi, so etaṃ ācikkheyya, taṃ ṭhapetvā yaṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca kattumicchasi, etaṃ akkhātuṃ na añño arahatīti.

Its meaning is: This question, great king, is beyond the scope of one like me. For I see neither its beginning nor its end; I am like one who has entered darkness. However, there is a brahmin named Vidhura, the chaplain of the king of Bārāṇasī; he could explain this. Except for him, no one else is able to explain this good and Dhamma that you wish to accomplish.

Rājā [V 5.0052] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “tena hi, brāhmaṇa, khippaṃ tassa santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti paṇṇākāraṃ datvā taṃ pesetukāmo hutvā gāthamāha –

The king, hearing his words, said, "Well then, brahmin, go quickly to him." Then, wishing to send him, he gave him a gift and spoke this verse:

143.

143.

“Ehi kho pahito gaccha, vidhurassa upantikaṃ;

Nikkhañcimaṃ suvaṇṇassa, haraṃ gaccha sucīrata;

Abhihāraṃ imaṃ dajjā, atthadhammānusiṭṭhiyā”ti.

“Come now, as an envoy, go to the presence of Vidhura. Taking this nikkha of gold, go, Sucirata! You should give this as a presentation gift for the instruction in the good and the Dhamma.”

Tattha upantikanti santikaṃ. Nikkhanti pañcasuvaṇṇo eko nikkho. Ayaṃ pana rattasuvaṇṇassa nikkhasahassaṃ datvā evamāha. Imaṃ dajjāti tena imasmiṃ dhammayāgapañhe kathite tassa atthadhammānusiṭṭhiyā abhihārapūjaṃ karonto imaṃ nikkhasahassaṃ dadeyyāsīti.

Herein, 'to the presence of' means near. 'Nikkha' means one nikkha is five suvaṇṇas. But the king, having given a thousand nikkhas of red gold, spoke thus. 'You should give this' means: when this question of the Dhamma-sacrifice has been explained, making a presentation-offering for the instruction in its good and Dhamma, you should give this thousand nikkhas.

Evañca [P 5.0059] pana vatvā pañhavissajjanassa likhanatthāya satasahassagghanakaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭañca gamanatthāya yānaṃ, parivāratthāya balakāyaṃ, tañca paṇṇākāraṃ datvā [M 5.0060] taṅkhaṇaññeva uyyojesi. So pana indapatthanagarā nikkhamitvā ujukameva bārāṇasiṃ agantvā yattha yattha paṇḍitā vasanti, sabbāni tāni ṭhānāni upasaṅkamitvā sakalajambudīpe pañhassa vissajjetāraṃ alabhitvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nivāsaṃ gahetvā katipayehi janehi saddhiṃ pātarāsabhuñjanavelāya vidhurassa nivesanaṃ gantvā āgatabhāvaṃ ārocāpetvā tena pakkosāpito taṃ sake ghare bhuñjamānaṃ addasa. Tamatthaṃ āvikaronto satthā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, for the purpose of writing down the answer to the question, the king gave a golden plate worth a hundred thousand, a vehicle for the journey, a body of troops for an escort, and that gift, and dispatched him that very moment. He, however, departed from the city of Indapatta, and without going straight to Bārāṇasī, he approached all those places wherever wise people dwelt. But not finding anyone in all of Jambudīpa who could answer the question, he gradually reached Bārāṇasī. Having taken up residence in a certain place, he went with a few people to Vidhura’s dwelling at the time of the morning meal and had his arrival announced. Being summoned by him, he saw Vidhura eating in his own home. Making this matter clear, the Teacher spoke the seventh verse:

144.

144.

“Svādhippāgā bhāradvājo, vidhurassa upantikaṃ;

Tamaddasa mahābrahmā, asamānaṃ sake ghare”ti.

That Bhāradvāja went to the presence of Vidhura. He saw the great brahmin eating in his own home.

Tattha svādhippāgāti so bhāradvājagotto sucirato adhippāgā, gatoti attho. Mahābrahmāti mahābrāhmaṇo. Asamānanti bhuñjamānaṃ.

Herein, 'svādhippāgā' means: that Sucirata of the Bhāradvāja clan went; 'gato' is the meaning. 'Mahābrahmā' means a great brahmin. 'Asamānaṃ' means eating.

So pana tassa bālasahāyako ekācariyakule uggahitasippo, tasmā tena saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjitvā bhattakiccapariyosāne sukhanisinno “samma kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti puṭṭho āgamanakāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Now, he was his childhood friend, and they had learned their craft in the same teacher's family. Therefore, after eating together with him, when the meal was finished and he was sitting comfortably, he was asked, 'Friend, for what reason have you come?' Explaining the reason for his arrival, he spoke the eighth verse:

145.

145.

“Raññohaṃ [V 5.0053] pahito dūto, korabyassa yasassino;

‘Atthaṃ dhammañca pucchesi’, iccabravi yudhiṭṭhilo;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, vidhurakkhāhi pucchito”ti.

I am a messenger sent by the king, the glorious Korabya. 'Ask about the benefit and the Dhamma,' thus said Yudhiṭṭhila. Being asked, O Vidhura, please explain that benefit and Dhamma to me.

Tattha raññohanti ahaṃ rañño korabyassa yasassino dūto. Pahitoti tena pesito idhāgamiṃ. Pucchesīti so yudhiṭṭhilagotto dhanañcayarājā maṃ dhammayāgapañhaṃ nāma pucchi, ahaṃ kathetuṃ asakkonto “tvaṃ sakkhissasī”ti ñatvā tassa ārocesiṃ, so ca paṇṇākāraṃ datvā pañhapucchanatthāya maṃ tava santikaṃ pesento “vidhurassa santikaṃ gantvā imassa pañhassa atthañca pāḷidhammañca puccheyyāsī”ti abravi. “Taṃ tvaṃ idāni mayā pucchito akkhāhī”ti.

Herein, `rañño'haṃ` means: I am a messenger of the glorious king of the Kurus. `Pahito` means: sent by him, I have come here. `Pucchesi` means: that King Dhanañjaya of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan asked me the question called the Dhamma-sacrifice. Being unable to answer, and knowing 'you will be able,' I informed him. And he, giving a gift and sending me to your presence for the purpose of asking the question, said: 'Go to the presence of Vidhura and ask the meaning and the principle in the text of this question.' The final line means: 'That, you should now explain, being asked by me.'

Tadā [P 5.0060] pana so brāhmaṇo “mahājanassa cittaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti gaṅgaṃ pidahanto viya vinicchayaṃ vicāreti. Tassa pañhavissajjane okāso natthi. So tamatthaṃ ācikkhanto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

But at that time, that brahmin, thinking, 'I will win over the minds of the people,' was investigating a case, as if damming the Ganges. He had no opportunity to answer the question. Explaining this matter, he spoke the ninth verse:

146.

146.

“Gaṅgaṃ [M 5.0061] me pidahissanti, na taṃ sakkomi brāhmaṇa;

Apidhetuṃ mahāsindhuṃ, taṃ kathaṃ so bhavissati;

Na te sakkomi akkhātuṃ, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchito”ti.

I have the Ganges to dam, O brahmin; I am unable to dam that great river. How then will there be an opportunity? Being asked, I am unable to explain to you the benefit and the Dhamma.

Tassattho – brāhmaṇa, mayhaṃ “mahājanassa nānācittagatisaṅkhātaṃ gaṅgaṃ pidahissa”nti byāpāro uppanno, tamahaṃ mahāsindhuṃ apidhetuṃ na sakkomi, tasmā kathaṃ so okāso bhavissati, yasmā te ahaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjeyyaṃ. Iti cittekaggatañceva okāsañca alabhanto na te sakkomi akkhātuṃ atthaṃ dhammañca pucchitoti.

Its meaning is: O brahmin, a concern has arisen for me, 'I will dam the Ganges,' which is known as the various mental dispositions of the great multitude. I am not able to dam that great river. Therefore, how will there be an opportunity through which I might answer your question? Thus, obtaining neither one-pointedness of mind nor an opportunity, I am unable to explain to you the benefit and the Dhamma about which you asked.

Evañca pana vatvā “putto me paṇḍito mayā ñāṇavantataro, so te byākarissati, tassa santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti vatvā dasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, he added, 'My son is a wise man, more knowledgeable than I. He will explain it to you. Go to him,' and then he spoke the tenth verse:

147.

147.

“Bhadrakāro ca me putto, oraso mama atrajo;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, gantvā pucchassu brāhmaṇā”ti.

Bhadrakāra is my son, my breast-born, own-begotten son. Go and ask him, O brahmin, about that benefit and Dhamma.

Tattha orasoti ure saṃvaḍḍho. Atrajoti attanā jātoti.

Herein, 'oraso' means nurtured at the breast. 'Atrajo' means born from oneself.

Taṃ [V 5.0054] sutvā sucirato vidhurassa gharā nikkhamitvā bhadrakārassa bhuttapātarāsassa attano parisamajjhe nisinnakāle nivesanaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā ekādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sucirata left Vidhura's house and went to Bhadrakāra's residence at the time when Bhadrakāra had finished his morning meal and was sitting in the midst of his retinue. To make this matter clear, the Teacher spoke the eleventh verse:

148.

148.

“Svādhippāgā bhāradvājo, bhadrakārassupantikaṃ;

Tamaddasa mahābrahmā, nisinnaṃ samhi vesmanī”ti.

That Bhāradvāja went to the presence of Bhadrakāra. The great brahmin saw him seated in his own house.

Tattha vesmanīti ghare.

Herein, 'vesmanī' means in the house.

So tattha gantvā bhadrakāramāṇavena katāsanābhihārasakkāro nisīditvā āgamanakāraṇaṃ puṭṭho dvādasamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having gone there and being honored with the offer of a seat by the young man Bhadrakāra, he sat down. When asked the reason for his arrival, he spoke the twelfth verse:

149.

149.

“Raññohaṃ [P 5.0061] pahito dūto, korabyassa yasassino;

‘Atthaṃ dhammañca pucchesi’, iccabravi yudhiṭṭhilo;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, bhadrakāra pabrūhi me”ti.

I am a messenger sent by the king, the glorious Korabya. 'Ask about the benefit and the Dhamma,' thus said Yudhiṭṭhila. Tell me that benefit and Dhamma, O Bhadrakāra.

Atha naṃ bhadrakāro, “tāta, ahaṃ imesu divasesu paradārikakamme abhiniviṭṭho, cittaṃ me byākulaṃ, tena tyāhaṃ vissajjetuṃ na sakkhissāmi, mayhaṃ [M 5.0062] pana kaniṭṭho sañcayakumāro nāma mayā ativiya ñāṇavantataro, taṃ puccha, so te pañhaṃ vissajjessatī”ti tassa santikaṃ pesento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then Bhadrakāra said to him: 'Dear sir, these days I am engrossed in an affair with another's wife, and my mind is confused. Therefore I will not be able to answer you. However, my younger brother, the youth Sañcaya, is much more knowledgeable than I. Ask him; he will answer your question.' Then, sending him to Sañcaya, he spoke two verses:

150.

150.

“Maṃsakājaṃ avahāya, godhaṃ anupatāmahaṃ;

Na te sakkomi akkhātuṃ, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchito.

Having abandoned my load of meat, I am chasing an iguana. Being asked, I am unable to explain to you the benefit and the Dhamma.

151.

151.

“Sañcayo nāma me bhātā, kaniṭṭho me sucīrata;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, gantvā pucchassu brāhmaṇā”ti.

My brother is named Sañcaya, my younger brother, O Sucirata. Go and ask him, O brahmin, about that benefit and Dhamma.

Tattha maṃsakājanti yathā nāma puriso thūlamigamaṃsaṃ kājenādāya gacchanto antarāmagge godhapotakaṃ disvā maṃsakājaṃ chaḍḍetvā taṃ anubandheyya, evameva attano ghare vasavattiniṃ bhariyaṃ chaḍḍetvā parassa rakkhitagopitaṃ itthiṃ anubandhanto homīti dīpento evamāhāti.

Here, 'basket of meat' means: just as a man carrying a large piece of game meat on a carrying pole might see a young iguana on the way, discard his load of meat, and pursue it, so too, abandoning his own wife at home who is under his authority, he pursues another’s guarded and protected woman. He said this to explain it.

So [V 5.0055] tasmiṃ khaṇe sañcayassa nivesanaṃ gantvā tena katasakkāro āgamanakāraṇaṃ puṭṭho ācikkhi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dve gāthā abhāsi –

At that moment, he went to Sañcaya's residence, and having been honored by him, when asked the reason for his coming, he explained. To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:

152.

152.

“Svādhippāgā bhāradvājo, sañcayassa upantikaṃ;

Tamaddasa mahābrahmā, nisinnaṃ samhi vesmani.

That Bhāradvāja went to the presence of Sañcaya. The great brahmin saw him seated in his own house.

153.

153.

“Raññohaṃ pahito dūto, korabyassa yasassino;

‘Atthaṃ dhammañca pucchesi’, iccabravi yudhiṭṭhilo;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, sañcayakkhāhi pucchito”ti.

I am a messenger sent by the king, the glorious Korabya. 'Ask about the benefit and the Dhamma,' thus said Yudhiṭṭhila. Being asked, O Sañcaya, please explain that benefit and Dhamma to me.

Sañcayakumāro pana tadā paradārameva sevati. Athassa so “ahaṃ, tāta, paradāraṃ sevāmi, sevanto ca pana gaṅgaṃ otaritvā [P 5.0062] paratīraṃ gacchāmi, taṃ maṃ sāyañca pāto ca nadiṃ tarantaṃ maccu gilati nāma, tena cittaṃ me byākulaṃ, na tyāhaṃ ācikkhituṃ sakkhissāmi, kaniṭṭho pana me sambhavakumāro nāma atthi jātiyā sattavassiko, mayā sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇenādhikañāṇataro, so te ācikkhissati, gaccha taṃ pucchāhī”ti āha. Imamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Now at that time, Prince Sañcaya was consorting with another's wife. Then he said to the brahmin: 'Good sir, I am consorting with another's wife, and in doing so, I cross the Ganges to reach the other shore. As I cross the river evening and morning, Death, it is said, swallows me. Because of this, my mind is agitated, and I will not be able to explain it to you. However, I have a younger brother named Prince Sambhava, who is seven years old from birth and possesses wisdom a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times greater than mine. He will explain it to you; go and ask him.' To clarify this matter, the Teacher spoke two verses:

154.

154.

“Sadā [M 5.0063] maṃ gilate maccu, sāyaṃ pāto sucīrata;

Na te sakkomi akkhātuṃ, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchito.

Death always swallows me, O Sucirata, evening and morning; being asked, I am unable to explain to you the benefit and the Dhamma.

155.

155.

“Sambhavo nāma me bhātā, kaniṭṭho me sucīrata;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, gantvā pucchassu brāhmaṇā”ti.

My brother is named Sambhava, my younger brother, O Sucirata. Go and ask him, O brahmin, about the benefit and the Dhamma.

Taṃ sutvā sucirato “ayaṃ pañho imasmiṃ loke abbhuto bhavissati, imaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetuṃ samattho nāma natthi maññe”ti cintetvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, Sucirata thought, 'This question will be a wonder in this world. I think there is no one capable of answering this question,' and he spoke two verses:

156.

156.

“Abbhuto vata bho dhammo, nāyaṃ asmāka ruccati;

Tayo janā pitāputtā, te su paññāya no vidū.

This matter is indeed amazing, sir, but it is not pleasing to us. There are three of them—a father and his sons—and they do not know it through their wisdom.

157.

157.

“Na [V 5.0056] taṃ sakkotha akkhātuṃ, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchitā;

Kathaṃ nu daharo jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchito”ti.

You are not able to explain it, being asked about the benefit and the Dhamma. How indeed could a youth know when asked about the benefit and the Dhamma?

Tattha nāyanti ayaṃ pañhadhammo abbhuto, imaṃ kathetuṃ samatthena nāma na bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā yaṃ tvaṃ “kumāro kathessatī”ti vadati, nāyaṃ asmākaṃ ruccati. Te sūti ettha su-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Pitāti vidhuro paṇḍito, puttā bhadrakāro sañcayo cāti tepi tayo pitāputtā paññāya imaṃ dhammaṃ no vidū, na vijānanti, añño ko jānissatīti attho. Na tanti tumhe tayo janā pucchitā etaṃ akkhātuṃ na sakkotha, daharo sattavassiko kumāro pucchito kathaṃ nu jaññā, kena kāraṇena jānituṃ sakkhissatīti attho.

Here, nāyaṃ means: this matter of the question is amazing; there must surely be no one able to explain it. Therefore, regarding what you say, ‘The prince will explain it,’ this does not please us. In te su, the su is merely a particle. Pitā refers to the sage Vidhura, and the sons are Bhadrakāra and Sañcaya. Even these three, father and sons, do not know this matter by means of wisdom; they do not understand it. The meaning is: who else will know it? Na taṃ means: you three people, being asked, are not able to explain this. The meaning is: how indeed would a young seven-year-old prince, being asked, know it? For what reason would he be able to know it?

Taṃ sutvā sañcayakumāro, “tāta, sambhavakumāraṃ ‘daharo’ti mā uññāsi, sacepi pañhavissajjanenātthiko, gaccha naṃ pucchā”ti atthadīpanāhi upamāhi kumārassa vaṇṇaṃ pakāsento dvādasa gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard this, Prince Sañcaya said: "Dear father, do not scorn Prince Sambhava for being young. If you desire an answer to the question, go and ask him." Then, proclaiming the prince's virtues with similes that illuminate the meaning, he spoke twelve verses:

158.

158.

“Mā [P 5.0063] naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇa.

“Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.

159.

159.

“Yathāpi cando vimalo, gacchaṃ ākāsadhātuyā;

Sabbe tārāgaṇe loke, ābhāya atirocati.

“Just as the stainless moon, moving through the element of space, outshines all the hosts of stars in the world with its radiance.

160.

160.

“Evampi [M 5.0064] daharūpeto, paññāyogena sambhavo;

Mā naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇa.

“So too, though young in form, Sambhava shines through the application of wisdom. Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.

161.

161.

“Yathāpi rammako māso, gimhānaṃ hoti brāhmaṇa;

Atevaññehi māsehi, dumapupphehi sobhati.

“Just as a delightful month of summer, O brahmin, shines with the blossoms of trees, far surpassing the other months.

162.

162.

“Evampi daharūpeto, paññāyogena sambhavo;

Mā naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇa.

“So too, though young in form, Sambhava shines through the application of wisdom. Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.

163.

163.

“Yathāpi [V 5.0057] himavā brahme, pabbato gandhamādano;

Nānārukkhehi sañchanno, mahābhūtagaṇālayo;

Osadhehi ca dibbehi, disā bhāti pavāti ca.

“Just as the Himālaya, O brahmin, the mountain Gandhamādana, covered with various trees, the abode of hosts of great beings, both illuminates the quarters and wafts its fragrance with divine medicinal herbs.

164.

164.

“Evampi daharūpeto, paññāyogena sambhavo;

Mā naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇa.

“So too, though young in form, Sambhava shines through the application of wisdom. Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.

165.

165.

“Yathāpi pāvako brahme, accimālī yasassimā;

Jalamāno vane gacche, analo kaṇhavattanī.

“Just as a blazing fire, O brahmin, wreathed in flames, glorious, burning in a forest grove, the insatiable one with a blackened track.

166.

166.

“Ghatāsano dhūmaketu, uttamāhevanandaho;

Nisīthe pabbataggasmiṃ, pahūtedho virocati.

“The oblation-eater, whose banner is smoke, the burner of the best forest grove, shines brightly at midnight on a mountain peak with abundant fuel.

167.

167.

“Evampi daharūpeto, paññāyogena sambhavo;

Mā naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇa.

“So too, though young in form, Sambhava shines through the application of wisdom. Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.

168.

168.

“Javena bhadraṃ jānanti, balibaddañca vāhiye;

Dohena dhenuṃ jānanti, bhāsamānañca paṇḍitaṃ.

“By its speed they know a noble steed, and a draught ox by its hauling; by its milking they know a milch-cow, and a wise person by their speech.

169.

169.

“Evampi daharūpeto, paññāyogena sambhavo;

Mā naṃ daharoti uññāsi, apucchitvāna sambhavaṃ;

Pucchitvā sambhavaṃ jaññā, atthaṃ dhammañca brāhmaṇā”ti.

“So too, though young in form, Sambhava shines through the application of wisdom. Do not scorn him for being young without having asked Sambhava. Having asked Sambhava, O brahmin, you will know the meaning and the Dhamma.”

Tattha [M 5.0065] jaññāti jānissasi. Candoti puṇṇacando. Vimaloti abbhādimalavirahito. Evampi daharūpetoti evaṃ sambhavakumāro daharabhāvena upetopi [P 5.0064] paññāyogena sakalajambudīpatale avasese paṇḍite atikkamitvā virocati. Rammakoti cittamāso. Atevaññehīti ativiya aññehi ekādasahi māsehi. Evanti evaṃ sambhavopi paññāyogena sobhati. Himavāti himapātasamaye himayuttoti himavā, gimhakāle himaṃ vamatīti himavā. Sampattaṃ [V 5.0058] janaṃ gandhena madayatīti gandhamādano. Mahābhūtagaṇālayoti devagaṇānaṃ nivāso. Disā bhātīti sabbadisā ekobhāsā viya karoti. Pavātīti gandhena sabbadisā vāyati. Evanti evaṃ sambhavopi paññāyogena sabbadisā bhāti ceva pavāti ca.

Here, jaññā means: you will know. Cando means: the full moon. Vimalo means: devoid of the stain of clouds, etc. Evampi daharūpeto means: even so, Prince Sambhava, though endowed with youth, shines through the application of wisdom, having surpassed the remaining sages on the entire surface of Jambudīpa. Rammako means: the month of Citta. Atevaññehi means: exceedingly more than the other eleven months. Evaṃ means: even so, Sambhava too shines through the application of wisdom. Himavā means: it is connected with snow at the time of snowfall, thus Himavā; or, it emits snow in the summer, thus Himavā. Gandhamādano means: it intoxicates with its fragrance the people who have arrived. Mahābhūtagaṇālayo means: the dwelling of the hosts of devas. Disā bhāti means: it makes all directions as if a single radiance. Pavāti means: its fragrance wafts in all directions. Evaṃ means: even so, Sambhava too, through the application of wisdom, both illuminates and wafts his fragrance in all directions.

Yasassimāti tejasampattiyā yasassimā. Accimālīti accīhi yutto. Jalamāno vane gaccheti gacchasaṅkhāte mahāvane jalanto carati. Analoti atitto. Gatamaggassa kaṇhabhāvena kaṇhavattanī. Yaññe āhutivasena āhutaṃ ghataṃ asnātīti ghatāsano. Dhūmo ketukiccaṃ assa sādhetīti dhūmaketu. Uttamāhevanandahoti ahevanaṃ vuccati vanasaṇḍo, uttamaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ dahatīti attho. Nisītheti rattibhāge. Pabbataggasminti pabbatasikhare. Pahūtedhoti pahūtaindhano. Virocatīti sabbadisāsu obhāsati. Evanti evaṃ mama kaniṭṭho sambhavakumāro daharopi paññāyogena virocati. Bhadranti bhadraṃ assājānīyaṃ javasampattiyā jānanti, na sarīrena. Vāhiyeti vahitabbabhāre sati bhāravahatāya “ahaṃ uttamo”ti balibaddaṃ jānanti. Dohenāti dohasampattiyā dhenuṃ “sukhīrā”ti jānanti. Bhāsamānanti ettha “nābhāsamānaṃ jānanti, missaṃ bālehi paṇḍita”nti suttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.241) āharitabbaṃ.

Yasassimā means: glorious due to the possession of splendor. Accimālī means: endowed with flames. Jalamāno vane gacche means: it wanders blazing in the great forest called a grove. Analo means: insatiable. Kaṇhavattanī means: because of the blackness of the path it has taken. Ghatāsano means: it eats the offered ghee at a sacrifice. Dhūmaketu means: smoke serves as its banner. Uttamāhevanandaho means: ahevanaṃ is said to be a forest grove; the meaning is that it burns the best forest grove. Nisīthe means: in the night-time. Pabbataggasmiṃ means: on the mountain peak. Pahūtedho means: having abundant fuel. Virocati means: it illuminates in all directions. Evaṃ means: even so, my younger brother, Prince Sambhava, though young, shines through the application of wisdom. Bhadraṃ means: they know a noble thoroughbred horse by its possession of speed, not by its body. Vāhiye means: when there is a load to be carried, they know the bull by its carrying of the load, as the best. Dohena means: by its abundance of milk they know a milch-cow as one with good milk. Bhāsamānaṃ: here the sutta should be cited: “They do not know one who is not speaking; the wise is mixed with fools” (SN 2.241).

Sucirato evaṃ tasmiṃ sambhavaṃ vaṇṇente “pañhaṃ pucchitvā jānissāmī”ti “kahaṃ pana te kumāra kaniṭṭho”ti pucchi. Athassa so sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā “yo esa pāsādadvāre antaravīthiyā kumārakehi saddhiṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kīḷati, ayaṃ mama kaniṭṭho, upasaṅkamitvā taṃ puccha, buddhalīḷāya te pañhaṃ kathessatī”ti āha. Sucirato tassa vacanaṃ sutvā [M 5.0066] pāsādā oruyha kumārassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Kāya velāyāti? Kumārassa nivatthasāṭakaṃ mocetvā [P 5.0065] khandhe khipitvā ubhohi hatthehi paṃsuṃ gahetvā ṭhitavelāya. Tamatthaṃ āvikaronto satthā gāthamāha –

While the prince was thus praising Sambhava, Sucirata thought, “I will find out by asking the question,” and he asked, “But where, prince, is your younger brother?” Then the prince, opening the lion-window and stretching out his hand, said to him: “That golden-colored one who is playing with the boys in the street at the palace gate—he is my younger brother. Approach him and ask; he will explain the question to you with the grace of a Buddha.” Having heard his words, Sucirata descended from the palace and went to the prince. At what time? At the time when the prince stood, having untied his lower garment and thrown it over his shoulder, holding dust in both hands. Making this matter clear, the Teacher spoke a verse:

170.

170.

“Svādhippāgā bhāradvājo, sambhavassa upantikaṃ;

Tamaddasa mahābrahmā, kīḷamānaṃ bahīpure”ti.

“Bhāradvāja approached the presence of Sambhava. The great brahmin saw him playing in the outer part of the city.”

Tattha bahīpureti bahinivesane.

Here, bahīpure means: in the outer residence.

Mahāsattopi brāhmaṇaṃ āgantvā purato ṭhitaṃ disvā “tāta, kenatthenāgatosī”ti pucchitvā, “tāta, kumāra ahaṃ jambudīpatale āhiṇḍanto mayā pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ kathetuṃ samatthaṃ alabhitvā [V 5.0059] tava santikaṃ āgatomhī”ti vutte “sakalajambudīpe kira avinicchito pañho mama santikaṃ āgato, ahaṃ ñāṇena mahallako”ti hirottappaṃ paṭilabhitvā hatthagataṃ paṃsuṃ chaḍḍetvā khandhato sāṭakaṃ ādāya nivāsetvā “puccha, brāhmaṇa, buddhalīḷāya te kathessāmī”ti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi. Tato brāhmaṇo –

The Great Being, seeing the brahmin who had come and was standing before him, asked, “Dear father, for what reason have you come?” When he was told, “Dear boy, while wandering throughout Jambudīpa, I could not find anyone able to answer the question I ask, so I have come to you,” he thought, “It seems an unresolved question from all of Jambudīpa has come to me; I am mature in wisdom.” Having gained a sense of moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, he shook the dust from his hands, took his cloth from his shoulder and put it on, and made the invitation of an omniscient one: “Ask, brahmin. I will explain it to you with the grace of a Buddha.” Then the brahmin said:

171.

171.

“Raññohaṃ pahito dūto, korabyassa yasassino;

‘Atthaṃ dhammañca pucchesi’, iccabravi yudhiṭṭhilo;

Taṃ tvaṃ atthañca dhammañca, sambhavakkhāhi pucchito”ti. –

“I am a messenger sent by the king, the glorious Kuru lord; ‘Ask about the meaning and the Dhamma,’ thus spoke Yudhiṭṭhila. Being asked, O Sambhava, please explain to me that meaning and Dhamma.”

Gāthāya pañhaṃ pucchi.

He asked the question in a verse.

Tassa attho sambhavapaṇḍitassa gaganamajjhe puṇṇacando viya pākaṭo ahosi.

The meaning became as clear to the wise Sambhava as the full moon in the midst of the sky.

Atha naṃ “tena hi suṇohī”ti vatvā dhammayāgapañhaṃ vissajjento gāthamāha –

Then, saying to him, “Well then, listen,” while answering the question about the Dhamma-sacrifice, he spoke this verse:

172.

172.

“Taggha te ahamakkhissaṃ, yathāpi kusalo tathā;

Rājā ca kho taṃ jānāti, yadi kāhati vā na vā”ti.

“Indeed, I will explain it to you, just as a skilled one would; And the king himself knows whether he will act or not.”

Tassa antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā madhurassarena dhammaṃ desentassa saddo dvādasayojanikaṃ sakalabārāṇasinagaraṃ avatthari. Atha rājā ca uparājādayo ca sabbe sannipatiṃsu. Mahāsatto mahājanassa majjhe dhammadesanaṃ paṭṭhapesi.

As he stood in the middle of the street and taught the Dhamma in a sweet voice, the sound spread throughout the entire twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī. Then the king, the viceroy, and all the others assembled. The Great Being began his Dhamma discourse in the midst of the great assembly.

Tattha [P 5.0066][M 5.0067] tagghāti ekaṃsavacanaṃ. Yathāpi kusaloti yathā atikusalo sabbaññubuddho ācikkhati, tathā te ekaṃseneva ahamakkhissanti attho. Rājā ca kho tanti ahaṃ taṃ pañhaṃ yathā tumhākaṃ rājā jānituṃ sakkoti, tathā kathessāmi.
