Tato uttari rājā eva taṃ jānāti, yadi karissati vā na vā karissati, karontassa vā akarontassa vā tassevetaṃ bhavissati, mayhaṃ pana doso natthīti dīpeti.

Herein, taggha (“indeed”) is a word of certainty. Yathāpi kusalo (“just as a skilled one would”) means: “Just as the supremely skilled Omniscient Buddha would declare, so too will I explain it to you with certainty.” Rājā ca kho taṃ (“And the king himself knows”) means: “I will explain the question in such a way that your king will be able to understand it. Beyond that, the king himself knows whether he will do it or not. Whether he does it or does not do it, that will be his own affair, but there is no fault on my part”—this is what he indicates.

Evaṃ imāya gāthāya pañhakathanaṃ paṭijānitvā idāni dhammayāgapañhaṃ kathento āha –

Having thus promised with this verse to explain the question, he now spoke on the question of the Dhamma-sacrifice, saying:

173.

173.

“Ajja [V 5.0060] suveti saṃseyya, raññā puṭṭho sucīrata;

Mā katvā avasī rājā, atthe jāte yudhiṭṭhilo.

“If asked by the king, O Sucīrata, one might say, ‘Today’ or ‘Tomorrow.’ When an objective arises, let not King Yudhiṭṭhila, following such a person, remain heedless.”

174.

174.

“Ajjhattaññeva saṃseyya, raññā puṭṭho sucīrata;

Kummaggaṃ na niveseyya, yathā mūḷho acetaso.

“When asked by the king, O Sucīrata, one should speak only of what is internal. He should not enter upon a wrong path, like a deluded, mindless person.”

175.

175.

“Attānaṃ nātivatteyya, adhammaṃ na samācare;

Atitthe nappatāreyya, anatthe na yuto siyā.

“He should not transgress against himself; he should not practice unrighteousness. He should not venture into a false ford; he should not be yoked to what is unbeneficial.”

176.

176.

“Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni, kattuṃ jānāti khattiyo;

Sadā so vaḍḍhate rājā, sukkapakkheva candimā.

“The khattiya who knows how to act on these points—that king always prospers, like the moon in the bright fortnight.”

177.

177.

“Ñātīnañca piyo hoti, mittesu ca virocati;

Kāyassa bhedā sappañño, saggaṃ so upapajjatī”ti.

“He is dear to his kinsmen and shines among his friends. With the breakup of the body, that wise person is reborn in heaven.”

Tattha saṃseyyāti katheyya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, sucirata sace tumhākaṃ raññā “ajja dānaṃ dema, sīlaṃ rakkhāma, uposathakammaṃ karomā”ti koci puṭṭho, “mahārāja, ajja tāva pāṇaṃ hanāma, kāme paribhuñjāma, suraṃ pivāma, kusalaṃ pana karissāma suve”ti rañño katheyya, tassa atimahantassapi amaccassa vacanaṃ katvā tumhākaṃ rājā yudhiṭṭhilagotto tathārūpe atthe jāte taṃ divasaṃ pamādena vītināmento mā avasi, tassa vacanaṃ akatvā uppannaṃ kusalacittaṃ aparihāpetvā kusalapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kammaṃ karotuyeva, idamassa katheyyāsīti. Evaṃ mahāsatto imāya gāthāya –

Herein, saṃseyya means “one might say.” This is the meaning: “Dear Sucīrata, if your king should ask someone, ‘Shall we give alms today, observe the precepts, and perform the Uposatha observance?’ and that person should say to the king, ‘Great king, for today let us kill living beings, enjoy sensual pleasures, and drink liquor; we will do what is wholesome tomorrow’—even if this is the word of a very great minister, your king of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan, having heard it, should not spend that day in heedlessness when such an opportunity has arisen. Disregarding that person’s word and not allowing the arisen wholesome thought to diminish, he should perform the action connected with the wholesome. This is what you should tell him.” Thus the Great Being, with this verse...

“Ajjeva [M 5.0068] kiccamātappaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve”ti. (ma. ni. 3.272) –

“Today itself one should make an effort; who knows if death will come tomorrow?”

Bhaddekarattasuttañceva,

...and the Bhaddekaratta Sutta,

“Appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno pada”nti. (dha. pa. 21) –

“Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless, heedlessness is the path to death.”

Appamādovādañca kathesi.

...and he gave the exhortation on heedfulness.

Ajjhattaññevāti[V 5.0061], tāta, sucirata sambhavapaṇḍito tayā dhammayāgapañhe pucchite kiṃ kathesīti raññā puṭṭho samāno tumhākaṃ rañño ajjhattaññeva saṃseyya, niyakajjhattasaṅkhātaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ hutvā abhāvato aniccanti katheyyāsi. Ettāvatā mahāsatto –

Ajjhattaññeva: “Dear Sucīrata, when you are asked by the king, ‘What did the wise Sambhava say when you asked him the question about the Dhamma-sacrifice?’ you should speak to your king only about what is internal. You should say that the five aggregates, which are designated as one’s own internal self, are impermanent because, having come to be, they cease to exist.” By this much the Great Being...

“Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti, yadā paññāya passati”. (dha. pa. 277) –

“‘All conditioned formations are impermanent’—when one sees this with wisdom…”

“Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino”ti. (dī. ni. 2.221) –

“‘Impermanent, alas, are all formations, subject to arising and passing away.’”

Evaṃ vibhāvitaṃ aniccataṃ kathesīti.

Thus he explained impermanence, making it manifest.

Kummagganti, brāhmaṇa, yathā [P 5.0067] mūḷho acetano andhabālaputhujjano dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatasaṅkhātaṃ kummaggaṃ sevati, evaṃ tava rājā taṃ kummaggaṃ na seveyya, niyyānikaṃ dasakusalakammapathamaggameva sevatu, evamassa vadeyyāsīti.

Kummaggaṃ: “Brahmin, just as a deluded, mindless, blind, foolish worldling follows the wrong path designated as the sixty-two kinds of views, so your king should not follow that wrong path. Let him follow only the path that leads out, the supreme path of the ten wholesome courses of action. Thus you should speak to him.”

Attānanti imaṃ sugatiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ attabhāvaṃ nātivatteyya, yena kammena tisso kusalasampattiyo sabbakāmasagge atikkamitvā apāye nibbattanti, taṃ kammaṃ na kareyyāti attho. Adhammanti tividhaduccaritasaṅkhātaṃ adhammaṃ na samācareyya. Atittheti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhisaṅkhāte atitthe nappatāreyya na otāreyya. “Na tāreyyā”tipi pāṭho, attano diṭṭhānugatimāpajjantaṃ janaṃ na otāreyya. Anattheti akāraṇe. Na yutoti yuttapayutto na siyā. Brāhmaṇa, yadi te rājā dhammayāgapañhe vattitukāmo, “imasmiṃ ovāde vattatū”ti tassa katheyyāsīti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Attānaṃ: This means he should not transgress against this personality established in a good destination; he should not perform that kamma by which, having disregarded the three wholesome attainments and all the sensual heavens, one is reborn in a state of deprivation. Adhammaṃ: He should not practice the unrighteousness designated as the threefold misconduct. Atitthe: He should not venture into or descend into the non-ford designated as the sixty-two views. There is also the reading na tāreyya, meaning he should not cause people who are following their own views to descend. Anatthe: In what is unbeneficial. Na yuto: He should not be yoked or engaged. “Brahmin, if your king wishes to act upon the question of the Dhamma-sacrifice, you should tell him, ‘Let him act in accordance with this advice.’” This is the intention here.

Sadāti satataṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yo khattiyo etāni kāraṇāni kātuṃ jānāti, so rājā sukkapakkhe cando viya sadā vaḍḍhatī”ti[M 5.0069]. Virocatīti mittāmaccānaṃ majjhe attano sīlācārañāṇādīhi guṇehi sobhati virocatīti.

Sadā means constantly. This is what is said: “The khattiya who knows how to act on these points—that king always prospers, like the moon in the bright fortnight.” Virocati means he shines and is radiant among his friends and ministers on account of his own virtues such as moral discipline, good conduct, knowledge, and so on.

Evaṃ mahāsatto gaganatale candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya buddhalīḷāya brāhmaṇassa pañhaṃ kathesi. Mahājano nadanto selento apphoṭento sādhukārasahassāni adāsi, celukkhepe ca aṅguliphoṭe ca pavattesi, hatthapiḷandhanādīni khipi. Evaṃ khittadhanaṃ koṭimattaṃ ahosi. Rājāpissa tuṭṭho mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. Suciratopi nikkhasahassena pūjaṃ katvā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe jātihiṅgulakena pañhavissajjanaṃ [V 5.0062] likhitvā indapatthanagaraṃ gantvā rañño dhammayāgapañhaṃ kathesi. Rājā tasmiṃ dhamme vattitvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Thus the Great Being, as if making the moon rise in the expanse of the sky, explained the brahmin’s question with the graceful ease of a Buddha. The great crowd roared, cheered, and clapped their hands, giving thousands of acclamations of “Sādhu!” They waved their cloths and snapped their fingers, and threw down their hand-ornaments and so on. The wealth thus thrown amounted to a crore. The king, being pleased, bestowed great fame upon him. Sucīrata, too, made an offering of a thousand gold coins, and having inscribed the explanation of the question on a golden plate with vermilion, he went to the city of Indapattha and related the question of the Dhamma-sacrifice to the king. The king, having conducted himself according to that Dhamma, went on to fill the city of the devas.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato mahāpaññoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā dhanañcayarājā ānando ahosi, sucirato anuruddho, vidhuro kassapo, bhadrakāro moggallāno, sañcayamāṇavo sāriputto, sambhavapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, said, “Monks, not only now but in the past too the Tathāgata was of great wisdom,” and he identified the birth: “At that time, King Dhanañjaya was Ānanda, Sucīrata was Anuruddha, Vidhura was Kassapa, Bhadrakāra was Moggallāna, the young man Sañcaya was Sāriputta, and the wise Sambhava was myself.”

Sambhavajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Sambhava Jātaka, the Fifth.

[516] 6. Mahākapijātakavaṇṇanā

[516] 6. The Commentary on the Great Monkey Jātaka

Bārāṇasyaṃ ahū rājāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa silāpavijjhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tena hi dhanuggahe payojetvā aparabhāge [P 5.0068] silāya paviddhāya bhikkhūhi devadattassa avaṇṇe kathite satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayhaṃ silaṃ pavijjhiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“There was a king in Bārāṇasī.” The Teacher told this story while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove with reference to Devadatta’s hurling of a rock. For when, after he had employed archers, on a later occasion a rock was hurled by him, the monks spoke in dispraise of Devadatta. The Teacher said, “Monks, not only now has Devadatta hurled a rock at me; he did so in the past as well,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente kāsikagāmake eko kassakabrāhmaṇo khettaṃ kasitvā goṇe vissajjetvā kuddālakammaṃ kātuṃ ārabhi. Goṇā ekasmiṃ gacche paṇṇāni khādantā anukkamena aṭaviṃ pavisitvā palāyiṃsu. So velaṃ sallakkhetvā kuddālaṃ ṭhapetvā goṇe olokento adisvā domanassappatto te pariyesanto [M 5.0070] antoaṭaviṃ pavisitvā āhiṇḍanto himavantaṃ pāvisi. So tattha disāmūḷho hutvā sattāhaṃ nirāhāro vicaranto ekaṃ tindukarukkhaṃ disvā abhiruyha phalāni khādanto tindukarukkhato parigaḷitvā saṭṭhihatthe narakapapāte pati. Tatrassa dasa divasā vītivattā. Tadā bodhisatto kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā phalāphalāni khādanto taṃ purisaṃ disvā silāya yoggaṃ katvā taṃ purisaṃ uddharitvā silāya matthake nisīdāpetvā evamāha – “bho brāhmaṇa, ahaṃ kilamāmi, muhuttaṃ niddāyissāmi, maṃ rakkhāhī”ti. So tassa niddāyantassa silāya matthakaṃ padālesi. Mahāsatto tassa taṃ kammaṃ ñatvā uppatitvā sākhāya nisīditvā “bho purisa, tvaṃ bhūmiyā gaccha, ahaṃ sākhaggena tuyhaṃ maggaṃ ācikkhanto gamissāmī”ti taṃ purisaṃ araññato nīharitvā magge ṭhapetvā pabbatapādameva pāvisi. So puriso mahāsatte aparajjhitvā kuṭṭhī hutvā diṭṭhadhammeyeva manussapeto ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a brahmin farmer in a village of Kāsi plowed his field, and having unyoked the oxen, began to work with a hoe. The oxen, eating leaves in a thicket, gradually entered the forest and ran away. He, noticing the time, set down his hoe and looked for the oxen. Not seeing them, he became dejected. Searching for them, he entered the deep forest and, wandering about, reached the Himalayas. There, having lost his bearings, he roamed for seven days without food until he saw a tinduka tree. Climbing it, he ate the fruits, but then he slipped from the tinduka tree and fell into a deep chasm sixty cubits deep. Ten days passed for him there. At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn as a monkey. While eating various fruits, he saw the man. Having practiced with stones to test his strength, he lifted the man out, had him sit on top of the rock, and said: “Friend brahmin, I am tired. I will sleep for a moment. Please guard me.” But while he was sleeping, the man shattered his head with a stone. The Great Being, knowing this deed, leaped up, perched on a branch, and said: “Friend man, you go on the ground. I will go along the treetops pointing out the path for you.” Having led the man out of the forest and set him on the path, he returned to the foot of the mountain. That man, having wronged the Great Being, became a leper and in this very life became a ghost among humans.

So [V 5.0063] satta vassāni dukkhapīḷito vicaranto bārāṇasiyaṃ migājinaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ pavisitvā pākārantare kadalipaṇṇaṃ attharitvā vedanāppatto nipajji. Tadā bārāṇasirājā uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha vicaranto taṃ disvā “kosi tvaṃ, kiṃ vā katvā imaṃ dukkhaṃ patto”ti pucchi. Sopissa sabbaṃ vitthārato ācikkhi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

For seven years, tormented by suffering, he wandered about and entered a park named Migājina in Bārāṇasī. There, between the walls, he spread out a banana leaf and lay down, afflicted by pain. At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī went to the park, and while walking about there, he saw him and asked: “Who are you? And what have you done to come to this suffering?” The man explained the entire matter to him in detail. To make this matter clear, the Teacher said:

178.

178.

“Bārāṇasyaṃ ahū rājā, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Mittāmaccaparibyūḷho, agamāsi migājinaṃ.

“In Bārāṇasī there was a king, who made the Kāsi kingdom prosper; surrounded by friends and ministers, he went to Migājina.

179.

179.

“Tattha [P 5.0069] brāhmaṇamaddakkhi, setaṃ citraṃ kilāsinaṃ;

Viddhastaṃ koviḷāraṃva, kisaṃ dhamanisanthataṃ.

“There he saw a brahmin, white, mottled, and leprous; blighted like a koviḷāra tree, emaciated, with his veins standing out.

180.

180.

“Paramakāruññataṃ pattaṃ, disvā kicchagataṃ naraṃ;

Avaca byamhito rājā, yakkhānaṃ katamo nusi.

“Seeing the man in distress, who had met with a most pitiable state, the frightened king said: ‘Which of the yakkhas might you be?’

181.

181.

“Hatthapādā ca te setā, tato setataraṃ siro;

Gattaṃ kammāsavaṇṇaṃ te, kilāsabahulo casi.

“Your hands and feet are white, and your head is whiter still; your body is of a mottled color, and you are full of skin disease.

182.

182.

“Vaṭṭanāvaḷisaṅkāsā[M 5.0071], piṭṭhi te ninnatunnatā;

Kāḷapabbāva te aṅgā, nāññaṃ passāmi edisaṃ.

“Your back, uneven with hollows and bumps, is like a string of beads; your limbs are like dark-jointed vines; I see no other like you.

183.

183.

“Ugghaṭṭapādo tasito, kiso dhamanisanthato;

Chāto ātattarūposi, kutosi kattha gacchati.

“With dust-soiled feet, trembling, emaciated, with veins standing out, hungry, and with a withered form—where do you come from? Where are you going?

184.

184.

“Duddasī appakārosi, dubbaṇṇo bhīmadassano;

Janetti yāpi te mātā, na taṃ iccheyya passituṃ.

“You are painful to see, ill-formed, ugly, and dreadful to behold; even the mother who bore you would not wish to see you.

185.

185.

“Kiṃ kammamakaraṃ pubbe, kaṃ avajjhaṃ aghātayi;

Kibbisaṃ yaṃ karitvāna, idaṃ dukkhaṃ upāgamī”ti.

“What deed did you do in the past? Whom did you slay that should not have been slain? Having committed what cruel offense have you come to this suffering?”

Tattha bārāṇasyanti bārāṇasiyaṃ. Mittāmaccaparibyūḷhoti mittehi ca daḷhabhattīhi amaccehi [V 5.0064] ca parivuto. Migājinanti evaṃnāmakaṃ uyyānaṃ. Setanti setakuṭṭhena setaṃ kabarakuṭṭhena vicitraṃ paribhinnena kaṇḍūyanakilāsakuṭṭhena kilāsinaṃ vedanāppattaṃ kadalipaṇṇe nipannaṃ addasa. Viddhastaṃ koviḷāraṃvāti vaṇamukhehi paggharantena maṃsena viddhastaṃ pupphitakoviḷārasadisaṃ. Kisanti ekaccesu padesesu aṭṭhicammamattasarīraṃ sirājālasanthataṃ. Byamhitoti bhīto vimhayamāpanno vā. Yakkhānanti yakkhānaṃ antare tvaṃ katarayakkho nāmāsi. Vaṭṭanāvaḷisaṅkāsāti piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhāne āvunitvā ṭhapitāvaṭṭanāvaḷisadisā. Aṅgāti kāḷapabbavallisadisāni te aṅgāni. Nāññanti aññaṃ purisaṃ edisaṃ na passāmi. Ugghaṭṭapādoti rajokiṇṇapādo. Ātattarūpoti sukkhasarīro. Duddasīti dukkhena passitabbo. Appakārosīti sarīrappakārarahitosi, dussaṇṭhānosīti attho. Kiṃ kammamakaranti ito pubbe kiṃ kammaṃ akaraṃ, akāsīti attho. Kibbisanti dāruṇakammaṃ.

Herein, 'Bārāṇasyaṃ' means in Bārāṇasī. 'Mittāmaccaparibyūḷho' means surrounded by friends of firm loyalty and by ministers. 'Migājinaṃ' is a park of that name. 'Setaṃ': he saw him lying on a banana leaf, white with white leprosy, mottled with variegated leprosy, leprous with scaly, itchy, broken skin leprosy, afflicted by pain. 'Viddhastaṃ koviḷāraṃva': ruined, like a flowering koviḷāra tree, because of the flesh oozing from the openings of his sores. 'Kisaṃ': in some places a body of mere skin and bones, covered with a network of veins. 'Byamhito': frightened or struck with amazement. 'Yakkhānaṃ': means among the yakkhas, what kind of yakkha are you? 'Vaṭṭanāvaḷisaṅkāsā': like a string of beads that have been threaded and set down along the spine. 'Aṅgā': your limbs are like dark-jointed vines. 'Nāññaṃ': I do not see another man like this. 'Ugghaṭṭapādo': with dust-soiled feet. 'Ātattarūpo': with a dried-up body. 'Duddasī': to be seen with difficulty. 'Appakārosi': you are devoid of proper shape; the meaning is 'ill-formed.' 'Kiṃ kammaṃ akaraṃ': what deed did I do before this; the meaning is 'what did you do?' 'Kibbisaṃ': a cruel deed.

Tato paraṃ brāhmaṇo āha –

Then the brahmin ghost said to the king of Bārāṇasī who had questioned him:

186.

186.

“Taggha te ahamakkhissaṃ, yathāpi kusalo tathā;

“Indeed, I will explain it to you, just as a skilled person would;

Saccavādiñhi lokasmiṃ, pasaṃsantīdha paṇḍitā.

for here in this world the wise praise one who speaks the truth.

187.

187.

“Eko [P 5.0070][M 5.0072] caraṃ gogaveso, mūḷho accasariṃ vane;

Araññe irīṇe vivane, nānākuñjarasevite.

“Wandering alone in search of my oxen, bewildered, I went too far into the forest, into the wilderness, a barren waste, a jungle frequented by various elephants.

188.

188.

“Vāḷamigānucarite, vippanaṭṭhosmi kānane;

Acariṃ tattha sattāhaṃ, khuppipāsasamappito.

“In the forest frequented by beasts of prey, I was utterly lost; I wandered there for seven days, afflicted by hunger and thirst.

189.

189.

“Tattha tindukamaddakkhiṃ, visamaṭṭhaṃ bubhukkhito;

Papātamabhilambantaṃ, sampannaphaladhārinaṃ.

“There, being hungry, I saw a tinduka tree growing on uneven ground, overhanging a precipice and bearing abundant fruit.

190.

190.

“Vātassitāni bhakkhesiṃ, tāni rucciṃsu me bhusaṃ;

Atitto rukkhamārūhiṃ, tattha hessāmi āsito.

“I ate the fruits that had fallen in the wind, and they pleased me greatly. Still unsatisfied, I climbed the tree, thinking: ‘There I will eat my fill.’

191.

191.

“Ekaṃ me bhakkhitaṃ āsi, dutiyaṃ abhipatthitaṃ;

Tato sā bhañjatha sākhā, chinnā pharasunā viya.

“One fruit I had eaten, a second I was longing for, when that branch on which I climbed broke, as if cut by an axe.

192.

192.

“Sohaṃ [V 5.0065] sahāva sākhāhi, uddhaṃpādo avaṃsiro;

Appatiṭṭhe anālambe, giriduggasmi pāpataṃ.

“Then I, along with the branches, with feet up and head down, with no footing and no support, fell into a mountain abyss.

193.

193.

“Yasmā ca vāri gambhīraṃ, tasmā na samapajjisaṃ;

Tattha sesiṃ nirānando, anūnā dasa rattiyo.

“And because the water was deep, for that reason I did not strike the level ground; there I lay joyless for no less than ten nights.

194.

194.

“Athettha kapi māgañchi, gonaṅgulo darīcaro;

Sākhāhi sākhaṃ vicaranto, khādamāno dumapphalaṃ.

“Then a langur monkey came there, a dweller in ravines, moving from branch to branch, eating the fruit of the trees.”

195.

195.

“So maṃ disvā kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ, kāruññamakaraṃ mayi;

Ambho ko nāma so ettha, evaṃ dukkhena aṭṭito.

“Seeing me thin and pale, he took pity on me: ‘Hey there! Who can you be here, so afflicted by suffering?’

196.

196.

“Manusso amanusso vā, attānaṃ me pavedaya;

Tassañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā, idaṃ vacanamabraviṃ.

“‘Whether you are human or non-human, reveal yourself to me.’ Having saluted him with joined palms, I spoke these words:

197.

197.

“Manussohaṃ byasampatto, sā me natthi ito gati;

Taṃ vo vadāmi bhaddaṃ vo, tvañca me saraṇaṃ bhava.

“‘I am a human who has met with disaster; I have no other way out from here. I tell you this—blessings to you!—be my refuge.’

198.

198.

“Garuṃ silaṃ gahetvāna, vicarī pabbate kapi;

Silāya yoggaṃ katvāna, nisabho etadabravi.

“Having taken a heavy stone, the monkey moved about the mountain; having practiced with the stone, that excellent one said this:

199.

199.

“Ehi [M 5.0073] me piṭṭhimāruyha, gīvaṃ gaṇhāhi bāhubhi;

Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi, giriduggata vegasā.

“‘Come, climb onto my back and grasp my neck with your arms; I will lift you out from this mountain abyss with speed.’

200.

200.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, vānarindassa sirīmato;

Piṭṭhimāruyha dhīrassa, gīvaṃ bāhāhi aggahiṃ.

“Having heard those words of the glorious monkey king, I climbed onto the back of that wise one and grasped his neck with my arms.

201.

201.

“So maṃ tato samuṭṭhāsi, tejassī balavā kapi;

Vihaññamāno kicchena, giriduggata vegasā.

“That majestic and powerful monkey lifted me from there; though suffering and with great difficulty, he brought me with speed from the mountain abyss.

202.

202.

“Uddharitvāna [V 5.0066] maṃ santo, nisabho etadabravi;

Iṅgha maṃ samma rakkhassu, pasupissaṃ muhuttakaṃ.

“Having lifted me out, that virtuous and excellent one said this: ‘Come now, friend, please guard me; I will sleep for a moment.’

203.

203.

“Sīhā byagghā [P 5.0071] ca dīpī ca, acchakokataracchayo;

Te maṃ pamattaṃ hiṃseyyuṃ, te tvaṃ disvā nivāraya.

“‘Lions, tigers, and leopards, bears, wolves, and hyenas—they might harm me if I am heedless. If you see them, ward them off.’

204.

204.

“Evaṃ me parittātūna, pasupī so muhuttakaṃ;

Tadāhaṃ pāpikaṃ diṭṭhiṃ, paṭilacchiṃ ayoniso.

“Having thus made me his protection, he slept for a moment. Then I unwisely conceived a wicked view:

205.

205.

“Bhakkho ayaṃ manussānaṃ, yathā caññe vane migā;

Yaṃ nūnimaṃ vadhitvāna, chāto khādeyya vānaraṃ.

“‘This one is food for humans, just like other beasts in the forest. What if, being hungry, I were to kill this monkey and eat him?’

206.

206.

“Asito ca gamissāmi, maṃsamādāya sambalaṃ;

Kantāraṃ nittharissāmi, pātheyyaṃ me bhavissati.

“‘Having eaten my fill, I will go, taking the meat as provisions. I will cross the wilderness; it will serve as travel-food for me.’

207.

207.

“Tato silaṃ gahetvāna, matthakaṃ sannitāḷayiṃ;

Mama gattakilantassa, pahāro dubbalo ahu.

“Then, taking a stone, I struck him on the head. But because my body was exhausted, the blow was weak.

208.

208.

“So ca vegenudappatto, kapi ruhiramakkhito;

Assupuṇṇehi nettehi, rodanto maṃ udikkhati.

“The monkey leaped up quickly, smeared with blood; with eyes full of tears, weeping, he looked at me.

209.

209.

“Māyyo maṃ kari bhaddante, tvañca nāmedisaṃ kari;

Tvañca kho nāma dīghāvu, aññe vāretumarahasi.

“‘Good sir, do not do this to me! May you be blessed. You have indeed done such a thing! You, O long-lived one, ought to restrain others from such deeds.’

210.

210.

“Aho vata re purisa, tāvadukkarakāraka;

Edisā visamā duggā, papātā uddhato mayā.

“‘Alas, O man, you who do such a difficult evil deed! From such an uneven, difficult, precipitous abyss you were lifted up by me.

211.

211.

“Ānīto paralokāva, dubbheyyaṃ maṃ amaññatha;

Taṃ tena pāpakammena, pāpaṃ pāpena cintitaṃ.

“‘Brought back as if from the other world, you thought to betray me. Because of that evil deed, that evil was conceived by an evil person.

212.

212.

“Mā [V 5.0067][M 5.0074] heva tvaṃ adhammaṭṭha, vedanaṃ kaṭukaṃ phusi;

Mā heva pāpakammaṃ taṃ, phalaṃ veḷuṃva taṃ vadhi.

“‘O unrighteous one, may you not feel such bitter pain! May that evil deed not destroy you, just as its fruit destroys the bamboo!’

213.

213.

“Tayi me natthi vissāso, pāpadhamma asaññata;

Ehi me piṭṭhito gaccha, dissamānova santike.

“‘I have no trust in you, O evil-natured and unrestrained one! Come, walk behind me, remaining in my sight nearby.

214.

214.

“Muttosi hatthā vāḷānaṃ, pattosi mānusiṃ padaṃ;

Esa maggo adhammaṭṭha, tena gaccha yathāsukhaṃ.

“‘You are freed from the grasp of wild beasts, you have reached the place of humans. This is the path, O unrighteous one; go by it as you please.’

215.

215.

“Idaṃ vatvā giricaro, rahade pakkhalya matthakaṃ;

Assūni sampamajjitvā, tato pabbatamāruhi.

“Having said this, the mountain-dweller washed his head in a lake, and having wiped away his tears, he then climbed the mountain.

216.

216.

“Sohaṃ tenābhisattosmi, pariḷāhena aṭṭito;

Ḍayhamānena gattena, vāriṃ pātuṃ upāgamiṃ.

“I was as if cursed by him and am afflicted by a burning fever. With my body burning, I approached a lake to drink water.

217.

217.

“Agginā viya santatto, rahado ruhiramakkhito;

Pubbalohitasaṅkāso, sabbo me samapajjatha.

“The entire lake appeared to me as if scorched by fire, smeared with blood and resembling pus and blood.

218.

218.

“Yāvanto [P 5.0072] udabindūni, kāyasmiṃ nipatiṃsu me;

Tāvanto gaṇḍa jāyetha, addhabeluvasādisā.

“As many drops of water as fell upon my body, so many boils arose, as large as half a wood-apple fruit.

219.

219.

“Pabhinnā pagghariṃsu me, kuṇapā pubbalohitā;

Yena yeneva gacchāmi, gāmesu nigamesu ca.

“Bursting open, they oozed with foul-smelling pus and blood; wherever I went, through villages and market towns,

220.

220.

“Daṇḍahatthā nivārenti, itthiyo purisā ca maṃ;

Okkitā pūtigandhena, māssu orena āgamā.

“Women and men with sticks in hand drove me away; surrounded by a foul stench, they cried: ‘Do not come near us!’

221.

221.

“Etādisaṃ idaṃ dukkhaṃ, satta vassāni dāni me;

Anubhomi sakaṃ kammaṃ, pubbe dukkaṭamattano.

“I have endured such suffering as this for seven years now; I am experiencing my own kamma, the evil deed I did in the past.

222.

222.

“Taṃ [V 5.0068] vo vadāmi bhaddante, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Māssu mittāna dubbhittho, mittadubbho hi pāpako.

“This I say to you—blessings to you!—to all who are gathered here: do not be treacherous to friends, for a betrayer of friends is an evil person.

223.

223.

“Kuṭṭhī kilāsī bhavati, yo mittānidha dubbhati;

Kāyassa bhedā mittaddu, nirayaṃ sopapajjatī”ti.

“Whoever betrays friends in this world becomes a leper or one with skin disease; with the breakup of the body, the betrayer of friends is reborn in hell.”

Tattha [M 5.0075] kusaloti yathā cheko kusalo katheti, tathā vo kathessāmi. Gogavesoti naṭṭhe goṇe gavesanto. Accasarinti manussapathaṃ atikkamitvā himavantaṃ pāvisiṃ. Araññeti arājake suññe. Irīṇeti sukkhakantāre. Vivaneti vivitte. Vippanaṭṭhoti maggamūḷho. Bubhukkhitoti sañjātabubhukkho chātajjhatto. Papātamabhilambantanti papātābhimukhaṃ olambantaṃ. Sampannaphaladhārinanti madhuraphaladhārinaṃ. Vātassitānīti paṭhamaṃ tāva vātapatitāni khādiṃ. Tattha hessāmīti tasmiṃ rukkhe suhito bhavissāmīti āruḷhomhi. Tato sā bhañjatha sākhāti tassa abhipatthitassa atthāya hatthe pasārite sā mayā abhiruḷhā sākhā pharasunā chinnā viya abhañjatha. Anālambeti ālambitabbaṭṭhānarahite. Giriduggasminti girivisame. Sesinti sayitomhi.

Therein, 'skillful' means as a clever, skillful person speaks, so shall I speak to you. 'Seeking cattle' means searching for lost cattle. 'I strayed' means having passed beyond human paths, I entered the Himalayas. 'Wilderness' means a kingless, empty place. 'Barren land' means a dry wasteland. 'Desolate' means secluded. 'Lost' means bewildered on the path. 'Hungry' means overcome by hunger, consumed by starvation. 'Clutching at the precipice' means hanging downwards towards the precipice. 'Bearing ripe fruit' means bearing sweet fruit. 'Wind-fallen fruits' means first, I ate those fruits fallen by the wind. 'There I shall be' means thinking, 'I shall be content in this tree,' I climbed. 'Then the branch broke' means as I stretched out my hand for that object I desired, the branch I had climbed broke as if cut by an axe. 'Without support' means in a place lacking anything to hold on to. 'In the mountain ruggedness' means in a difficult place in the mountains. 'I lay down' means I lay down to sleep.

Kapi māgañchīti kapi āgañchi. Gonaṅguloti gunnaṃ naṅguṭṭhasadisanaṅguṭṭho. “Gonaṅguṭṭho”tipi pāṭho. “Gonaṅgulī”tipi paṭhanti. Akaraṃ mayīti akarā mayi. Ambhoti, mahārāja, so kapirājā tasmiṃ narakapapāte mama udakapothanasaddaṃ sutvā maṃ “ambho”ti ālapitvā “ko nāmeso”ti pucchi. Byasampattoti byasanaṃ patto, papātassa vasaṃ pattoti vā attho. Bhaddaṃ voti tasmā tumhe vadāmi – “bhaddaṃ tumhākaṃ hotū”ti. Garuṃ silanti, mahārāja, so kapirājā mayā evaṃ vutte “mā bhāyī”ti maṃ assāsetvā paṭhamaṃ tāva garuṃ silaṃ gahetvā yoggaṃ karonto pabbate vicari[P 5.0073]. Nisabhoti purisanisabho uttamavānarindo pabbatapapāte ṭhatvā maṃ etadabravīti.

'Kapi māgañchi' means 'the monkey came.' 'Gonaṅgulo' means one whose tail is similar to the tail of a bull. There is also a reading as 'Gonaṅguṭṭho.' Some also read it as 'Gonaṅgulī.' 'Akaraṃ mayi' means 'he did to me.' 'Ambho,' O king, means that the monkey king, hearing the sound of me striking the water in that hellish abyss, addressed me as 'Ambho' and asked, 'Who is this?' 'Byasampatto' means having met with calamity, or having fallen under the power of the abyss. 'Bhaddaṃ vo' means 'therefore I say to you, “May it be well with you.”' 'Garuṃ silaṃ,' O king, means that the monkey king, when I had spoken thus, having reassured me by saying, 'Do not fear,' first took up a heavy rock and wandered over the mountain, making it suitable. 'Nisabho' means the bull of men, the excellent king of monkeys, standing at the mountain abyss, spoke this to me.

Bāhubhīti dvīhi bāhāhi mama gīvaṃ suggahitaṃ gaṇha. Vegasāti vegena. Sirīmatoti puññavantassa. Aggahinti saṭṭhihatthaṃ narakapapātaṃ vātavegena otaritvā udakapiṭṭhe ṭhitassa ahaṃ vegena piṭṭhimabhiruhitvā ubhohi bāhāhi gīvaṃ aggahesiṃ. Vihaññamānoti kilamanto. Kicchenāti dukkhena. Santoti paṇḍito, atha vā parisanto kilanto. Rakkhassūti ahaṃ taṃ uddharanto kilanto muhuttaṃ vissamanto pasupissaṃ, tasmā maṃ rakkhāhi. Yathā caññe vane migāti [V 5.0069] sīhādīhi aññepi ye imasmiṃ vane vāḷamigā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “acchakokataracchayo”ti likhanti. Parittātūnāti, mahārāja, evaṃ so kapirājā maṃ attano [M 5.0076] parittāṇaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ pasupi. Ayonisoti ayonisomanasikārena. Bhakkhoti khāditabbayuttako. Asito dhāto suhito. Sambalanti pātheyyaṃ. Matthakaṃ sannitāḷayinti tassa vānarindassa matthakaṃ pahariṃ. “Sannitāḷaya”ntipi pāṭho. Dubbalo ahūti na balavā āsi, yathādhippāyaṃ na agamāsīti.

'Bāhubhi' means 'Grasp my neck firmly with both your arms.' 'Vegasā' means swiftly. 'Sirīmato' means of the meritorious one. 'Aggahiṃ' means: when he had descended the sixty-cubit hellish abyss with the speed of the wind and was standing on the surface of the water, I swiftly climbed onto his back and grasped his neck with both arms. 'Vihaññamāno' means becoming weary. 'Kicchena' means with difficulty. 'Santo' means wise, or else exhausted and weary. 'Rakkhassu' means: 'While rescuing you, I have become weary, and while resting for a moment, I will fall asleep; therefore, protect me.' 'Yathā caññe vane migā' means other beasts of prey in this forest, such as lions and so on. In the Pāli text, however, they write 'acchakokataracchayo.' 'Parittātūnaṃ,' O king, means that the monkey king, having entrusted his protection to me, slept for a moment. 'Ayoniso' means with unwise attention. 'Bhakkho' means fit to be eaten. 'Asito dhāto suhito' means not eaten, nourished, satisfied. 'Sambalaṃ' means provisions for a journey. 'Matthakaṃ sannitāḷayiṃ' means I struck the head of that king of monkeys. There is also a reading as 'sannitāḷaya.' 'Dubbalo ahū' means he was not strong; he did not achieve his intention.

Vegenāti mayā pahaṭapāsāṇavegena. Udappattoti uṭṭhito. Māyyoti tena mittadubbhipurisena silāya paviddhāya mahācammaṃ chinditvā olambi, ruhiraṃ pagghari. Mahāsatto vedanāppatto cintesi – “imasmiṃ ṭhāne añño natthi, idaṃ bhayaṃ imaṃ purisaṃ nissāya uppanna”nti. So maraṇabhayabhīto olambantaṃ cammabandhaṃ hatthena gahetvā uppatitvā sākhaṃ abhiruyha tena pāpapurisena saddhiṃ sallapanto “māyyo ma”ntiādimāha. Tattha māyyo maṃ kari bhaddanteti mā akari ayyo maṃ bhaddanteti taṃ nivāreti. Tvañca kho nāmāti tvaṃ nāma evaṃ mayā papātā uddhaṭo edisaṃ pharusakammaṃ mayi kari, aho te ayuttaṃ katanti. Aho vatāti taṃ garahanto evamāha. Tāvadukkarakārakāti mayi aparajjhanena atidukkarakammakāraka. Paralokāvāti paralokato viya ānīto. Dubbheyyanti dubbhitabbaṃ vadhitabbaṃ. Vedanaṃ kaṭukanti evaṃ santepi tvaṃ adhammaṭṭha yādisaṃ vedanaṃ ahaṃ phusāmi, edisaṃ vedanaṃ kaṭukaṃ mā phusi, taṃ pāpakammaṃ phalaṃ veḷuṃva taṃ mā vadhi. Iti maṃ, mahārāja, so piyaputtakaṃ viya anukampi.

'Vegena' means by the force of the stone I hurled. 'Udappatto' means he jumped up. 'Māyyo' means that when a stone was thrown by that treacherous man, it cut through the great hide, which then hung down, and blood gushed forth. The great being, struck by pain, thought: 'There is no one else in this place; this danger has arisen because of this man.' Fearing death, he grabbed the hanging strip of skin with his hand, leapt up, climbed onto a branch, and while conversing with that wicked man, he said, 'Māyyo maṃ,' and so on. Therein, 'māyyo maṃ kari bhaddante' means he restrains him, saying, 'Noble one, good sir, do not do this to me.' 'Tvañca kho nāma' means: 'You, indeed, having been pulled out from the precipice by me, have done such a cruel deed to me—ah, what an improper thing you have done!' 'Aho vata' means he spoke thus, rebuking him. 'Tāvadukkarakāraka' means a doer of an extremely difficult deed by offending me. 'Paralokāva' means as if brought from the other world. 'Dubbheyya' means one who should be harmed, who should be struck. 'Vedanaṃ kaṭukaṃ' means: 'Even so, you who are unrighteous, may you not experience such a bitter pain as I experience. May that evil deed not destroy you, just as its fruit destroys the bamboo.' Thus, great king, he had compassion for me as for a dear son.

Atha naṃ ahaṃ etadavocaṃ – “ayya, mayā kataṃ dosaṃ hadaye mā kari, mā maṃ asappurisaṃ evarūpe araññe nāsaya, ahaṃ disāmūḷho maggaṃ na jānāmi, attanā kataṃ kammaṃ mā nāsetha, jīvitadānaṃ me detha, araññā nīharitvā manussapathe ṭhapethā”ti. Evaṃ vutte so mayā saddhiṃ sallapanto “tayi me natthi vissāso”ti ādimāha. Tattha tayīti ito paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ tayi vissāso [P 5.0074] natthi. Ehīti, bho purisa, ahaṃ tayā saddhiṃ maggena na gamissāmi, tvaṃ pana ehi mama piṭṭhito avidūre dissamānasarīrova gaccha, ahaṃ rukkhaggeheva gamissāmīti. Muttosīti atha so maṃ, mahārāja, araññā nīharitvā, bho purisa, vāḷamigānaṃ hatthā muttosi. Pattosi mānusiṃ padanti manussūpacāraṃ patto āgatosi, esa te maggo, etena gacchāti āha.

Then I said to him: 'Sir, do not hold in your heart the wrong I have done; do not destroy me, an evil man, in such a wilderness. I am confused about the directions and do not know the way. Do not destroy the deed you yourself have done; grant me the gift of life. Lead me out of the forest and set me on a human path.' When this was said, he, conversing with me, said, 'I have no trust in you,' and so on. Therein, 'tayi' means 'from this point forward, I have no trust in you.' 'Ehi' means: 'Good man, I will not go with you on the path. But you, come, walk behind me, keeping your body visible not far away. I will go by the treetops.' 'Muttosi' means that then, great king, having led me out of the forest, he said: 'Good man, you are freed from the grasp of beasts of prey.' 'Pattosi mānusiṃ padaṃ' means 'You have arrived, having reached a place frequented by humans. This is your path; go by it,' he said.

Giricaroti [M 5.0077] giricārī vānaro. Pakkhalyāti dhovitvā. Tenābhisattosmīti so ahaṃ, mahārāja[V 5.0070], tena vānarena abhisatto, pāpakamme pariṇate tenābhisattosmīti maññamāno evamāha. Aṭṭitoti upadduto. Upāgaminti ekaṃ rahadaṃ upagatosmi. Samapajjathāti jāto, evarūpo hutvā upaṭṭhāsi. Yāvantoti yattakāni. Gaṇḍa jāyethāti gaṇḍā jāyiṃsu. So kira pipāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto udakañjaliṃ ukkhipitvā thokaṃ pivitvā sesaṃ sarīre siñci. Athassa tāvadeva udakabindugaṇanāya aḍḍhabeluvapakkappamāṇā gaṇḍā uṭṭhahiṃsu, tasmā evamāha. Pabhinnāti te gaṇḍā taṃ divasameva bhijjitvā kuṇapā pūtigandhikā hutvā pubbalohitāni pagghariṃsu. Yena yenāti yena yena maggena. Okkitāti pūtigandhena okiṇṇā parikkhittā parivāritā. Māssu orena āgamāti duṭṭhasatta orena māssu āgamā, amhākaṃ santikaṃ mā āgamīti evaṃ vadantā maṃ nivārentīti attho. Satta vassāni dāni meti, mahārāja, tato paṭṭhāya idāni satta vassāni mama ettakaṃ kālaṃ sakaṃ kammaṃ anubhomi.

'Giricaro' means a mountain-roaming monkey. 'Pakkhalyā' means having washed. 'Tenābhisattosmi' means, O king, that he spoke thus, thinking: 'I was cursed by that monkey, and when the evil deed ripened, I was cursed by it.' 'Aṭṭito' means afflicted. 'Upāgamiṃ' means I approached a certain lake. 'Samapajjatha' means it arose; having become of such a form, it appeared. 'Yāvanto' means as many as. 'Gaṇḍā jāyetha' means boils arose. It seems that, unable to endure his thirst, he scooped up a handful of water, drank a little, and sprinkled the rest on his body. Then, at that very moment, boils the size of half a beluva fruit arose, equal in number to the drops of water; that is why he spoke thus. 'Pabhinnā' means those boils burst that very day and, becoming putrid, foul-smelling corpses, they oozed pus and blood. 'Yena yena' means by whatever path. 'Okkitā' means strewn, surrounded, and enveloped by the foul stench. 'Māssu orena āgamā' means that people, saying, 'Evil being, do not come this way, do not come near us,' restrained me; this is the meaning. 'Satta vassāni dāni me' means, 'Great king, from that time until now is seven years; for this long I experience my own kamma.'

Iti so attano mittadubbhikammaṃ vitthāretvā, “mahārāja, maññeva oloketvā evarūpaṃ kammaṃ na kenaci kattabba”nti vatvā “taṃ vo”tiādimāha. Tattha tanti tasmā. Yasmā evarūpaṃ kammaṃ evaṃ dukkhavipākaṃ, tasmāti attho.

Having thus elaborated on his own act of treachery towards a friend, he said, 'Great king, looking at me, such an act should not be committed by anyone,' and then spoke the words beginning with 'Taṃ vo.' Herein, 'taṃ' means 'therefore.' Because such an act has such a painful result, that is the meaning.

223.

223.

“Kuṭṭhī kilāsī bhavati, yo mittānidha dubbhati;

Kāyassa bhedā mittaddu, nirayaṃ sopapajjatī”ti. –

He becomes a leper, afflicted with skin disease, who here is treacherous to friends; upon the breaking up of the body, the betrayer of friends is reborn in hell.

Ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā. Bhikkhave, yo idha loke mittāni dubbhati hiṃsati, so evarūpo hotīti attho.

This is a verse of the Fully Enlightened One. Monks, whoever in this world is treacherous to friends and harms them, such a person becomes like this—this is the meaning.

Tassapi purisassa raññā saddhiṃ kathentasseva pathavī vivaraṃ adāsi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva cavitvā avīcimhi nibbatto. Rājā tasmiṃ pathaviṃ paviṭṭhe uyyānā nikkhamitvā nagaraṃ paviṭṭho.

Even as that man was speaking with the king, the earth opened up for him. At that very moment, he passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. When the man had been swallowed by the earth, the king departed from the park and entered the city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayhaṃ silaṃ paṭivijjhiyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā [M 5.0078] mittadubbhī puriso devadatto ahosi, kapirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse and said: 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta has struck me with a rock.' Then he made the connection with the Jātaka: 'At that time the man who was treacherous to his friend was Devadatta, but the monkey king was I myself.'

Mahākapijātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Great Monkey Jātaka, the Sixth.

[517] 7. Dakarakkhasajātakavaṇṇanā

[517] 7. The Commentary on the Water-Ogre Jātaka

224-257. Sace [V 5.0071][P 5.0075] vo vuyhamānānanti dakarakkhasajātakaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ mahāumaṅgajātake āvi bhavissatīti.

224-257. 'If you are being swept away'—this is the Water-Ogre Jātaka. All of this will become clear in the Mahāummagga Jātaka.

Dakarakkhasajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Water-Ogre Jātaka, the Seventh.

[518] 8. Paṇḍaranāgarājajātakavaṇṇanā

[518] 8. The Commentary on the Paṇḍara Nāga-King Jātaka

Vikiṇṇavācanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto musāvādaṃ katvā devadattassa pathavippavesanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā bhikkhūhi tassa avaṇṇe kathite “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto musāvādaṃ katvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story beginning with the words, 'Scattered speech,' concerning Devadatta's being swallowed by the earth for having told a lie. For at that time, when the monks were speaking in dispraise of him, the Teacher said: 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta was swallowed by the earth for having told a lie,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente pañcasatavāṇijā nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhanditvā sattame divase atīradassaniyā nāvāya samuddapiṭṭhe bhinnāya ṭhapetvā ekaṃ avasesā macchakacchapabhakkhā ahesuṃ, eko pana vātavegena karampiyapaṭṭanaṃ nāma pāpuṇi. So samuddato uttaritvā naggabhogo tasmiṃ paṭṭaneyeva bhikkhāya cari. Tamenaṃ manussā “ayaṃ samaṇo appiccho santuṭṭho”ti sambhāvetvā sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. So “laddho me jīvikūpāyo”ti tesu nivāsanapārupanaṃ dentesupi na icchi. Te “natthi ito uttari appiccho samaṇo”ti bhiyyo bhiyyo pasīditvā tassa assamapadaṃ katvā tattha naṃ nivāsāpesuṃ. So “karampiyaacelo”ti paññāyi. Tassa tattha vasantassa mahālābhasakkāro udapādi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, five hundred merchants embarked on a ship and set out on the ocean. On the seventh day, with the shore no longer visible, their ship broke apart on the surface of the sea. All except one became food for fish and turtles. One, however, borne by the force of the wind, reached a seaport named Karampiya. Having come ashore from the sea, he wandered about naked for alms in that very port. People, thinking, 'This ascetic is of few desires and content,' showed him respect. Thinking, 'I have found a means of livelihood,' he did not want the lower and upper garments they offered him. They, believing, 'There is no ascetic with fewer desires than this,' grew even more confident in him and built him a hermitage, where they had him dwell. He became known as 'Karampiya the Naked.' While dwelling there, great gain and honor arose for him.

Eko [M 5.0079] nāgarājāpissa supaṇṇarājā ca upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti. Tesu nāgarājā nāmena paṇḍaro nāma. Athekadivasaṃ supaṇṇarājā tassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno evamāha – “bhante, amhākaṃ ñātakā nāge gaṇhantā bahū vinassanti, etesaṃ nāgānaṃ gahaṇaniyāmaṃ mayaṃ na jānāma, guyhakāraṇaṃ kira tesaṃ atthi, sakkuṇeyyātha nu kho tumhe ete piyāyamānā viya [P 5.0076] taṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchitu”nti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā supaṇṇarāje vanditvā pakkante nāgarājassa āgatakāle vanditvā nisinnaṃ nāgarājānaṃ pucchi – “nāgarāja, supaṇṇā kira tumhe gaṇhantā bahū vinassanti, tumhe gaṇhantā kathaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkontī”ti. Bhante, idaṃ amhākaṃ guyhaṃ rahassaṃ, mayā imaṃ kathentena ñātisaṅghassa maraṇaṃ āhaṭaṃ [V 5.0072] hotīti. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, āvuso, “ayaṃ aññassa kathessatī”ti evaṃsaññī hosi, nāhaṃ aññassa kathessāmi, attanā pana jānitukāmatāya pucchāmi, tvaṃ mayhaṃ saddahitvā nibbhayo hutvā kathehīti. Nāgarājā “na kathessāmi, bhante”ti vanditvā pakkāmi. Punadivasepi pucchi, tathāpissa na kathesi.

A Nāga king and a Supaṇṇa king used to come to attend upon him. The Nāga king’s name was Paṇḍara. One day, the Supaṇṇa king approached him, paid homage, and sat to one side, saying: 'Venerable sir, many of our Supaṇṇa kinsmen perish while seizing Nāgas. We do not know the method of their capture. It is said they have a secret. Could you, by making a show of friendship, ask them for that reason?' He agreed, saying, 'Good.' After the Supaṇṇa king had paid homage and left, when the Nāga king arrived, paid homage, and sat down, the ascetic asked him: 'Nāga king, it is said that many Supaṇṇas perish while seizing you. How is it that they are unable to capture you?' The Nāga king replied: 'Venerable sir, this is our secret and mystery; if I were to reveal it, I would bring death to my kinsmen.' 'But, friend, do you think I will tell someone else? I will not tell anyone. I am asking because I myself want to know. Trust me and speak without fear.' The Nāga king paid homage and said, 'I will not tell, venerable sir,' and departed. The next day, the ascetic asked again, but still the Nāga king would not tell him.

Atha naṃ tatiyadivase āgantvā nisinnaṃ, “nāgarāja, ajja tatiyo divaso, mama pucchantassa kimatthaṃ na kathesī”ti āha. “Tumhe aññassa ācikkhissathā”ti bhayena, bhanteti. Kassaci na kathessāmi, nibbhayo kathehīti. “Tena hi, bhante, aññassa mā kathayitthā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā, “bhante, mayaṃ mahante mahante pāsāṇe gilitvā bhāriyā hutvā nipajjitvā supaṇṇānaṃ āgamanakāle mukhaṃ nibbāhetvā dante vivaritvā supaṇṇe ḍaṃsituṃ acchāma, te āgantvā amhākaṃ sīsaṃ gaṇhanti, tesaṃ amhe garubhāre hutvā nipanne uddharituṃ vāyamantānaññeva udakaṃ ottharati. Te sīdantā antoudakeyeva maranti, iminā kāraṇena bahū supaṇṇā vinassanti, tesaṃ amhe gaṇhantānaṃ kiṃ sīsena gahitena, bālā naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā amhe heṭṭhāsīsake katvā gahitaṃ gocaraṃ mukhena chaḍḍāpetvā lahuke katvā gantuṃ sakkontī”ti so attano rahassakāraṇaṃ tassa dussīlassa kathesi.

Then, on the third day, when the Nāga king came and sat down, the ascetic said to him: 'Nāga king, today is the third day. Why do you not tell me what I ask?' 'It is for fear that you will tell someone else, venerable sir.' 'I will not tell anyone; speak without fear.' Having taken his promise, the Nāga king said, 'Then, venerable sir, do not tell anyone else,' and explained: 'Venerable sir, we swallow large stones and lie down, becoming heavy. When the Supaṇṇas come, we stick out our heads, bare our fangs, and wait to bite them. They come and seize our heads. As we lie there, heavy-laden, they struggle to lift us, and the water overwhelms them. Sinking, they die right there in the water. For this reason many Supaṇṇas perish. When they seize us, what is the use of seizing us by the head? The fools! If they were to grab us by the tail, turn us upside down, and make us disgorge the food we have swallowed, they could make us light and carry us away.' Thus he revealed his secret to that immoral one.

Atha tasmiṃ pakkante supaṇṇarājā āgantvā karampiyaacelaṃ vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, pucchitaṃ te nāgarājassa guyhakāraṇa”nti āha. So “āmāvuso”ti [P 5.0077][M 5.0080] vatvā sabbaṃ tena kathitaniyāmeneva kathesi. Taṃ sutvā supaṇṇo “nāgarājena ayuttaṃ kataṃ, ñātīnaṃ nāma nassananiyāmo parassa na kathetabbo, hotu, ajjeva mayā supaṇṇavātaṃ katvā paṭhamaṃ etameva gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti supaṇṇavātaṃ katvā paṇḍaranāgarājānaṃ naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā heṭṭhāsīsaṃ katvā gahitagocaraṃ chaḍḍāpetvā uppatitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Paṇḍaro ākāse heṭṭhāsīsakaṃ olambanto “mayāva mama dukkhaṃ ābhata”nti paridevanto āha –

After the Nāga king had left, the Supaṇṇa king came, paid respects to the naked ascetic Karampiya, and asked: 'Venerable sir, did you ask the Nāga king for his secret?' 'Yes, friend,' he replied, and told him everything exactly as the Nāga had related it. Hearing this, the Supaṇṇa said: 'The Nāga king has acted improperly. One should not reveal to another the means by which one’s own kin are destroyed. So be it! Today I will create a Supaṇṇa-wind, and it is fitting that I seize this very one first.' Creating a Supaṇṇa-wind, he grabbed the Nāga king Paṇḍara by the tail, turned him upside down, made him disgorge the food he had seized, and leaping up, soared into the sky. As Paṇḍara dangled head-down in the sky, he lamented, saying:

258.

258.

“Vikiṇṇavācaṃ aniguyhamantaṃ, asaññataṃ aparicakkhitāraṃ;

Bhayaṃ tamanveti sayaṃ abodhaṃ, nāgaṃ yathā paṇḍarakaṃ supaṇṇo.

“Fear follows the foolish one of scattered speech, who does not guard a secret, who is unrestrained and undiscerning, just as the Supaṇṇa follows the Nāga Paṇḍara.”

259.

259.

“Yo guyhamantaṃ parirakkhaṇeyyaṃ, mohā naro saṃsati hāsamāno;

Taṃ bhinnamantaṃ bhayamanveti khippaṃ, nāgaṃ yathā paṇḍarakaṃ supaṇṇo.

“The person who, through delusion, reveals with a laugh a secret that should be guarded—fear quickly follows that person whose secret is betrayed, just as the Supaṇṇa follows the Nāga Paṇḍara.”

260.

260.

“Nānumitto [V 5.0073] garuṃ atthaṃ, guyhaṃ veditumarahati;

Sumitto ca asambuddhaṃ, sambuddhaṃ vā anatthavā.

“A false friend is not worthy to know a weighty, secret matter; nor is a true friend who is unwise, nor one who is wise but harmful.”

261.

261.

“Vissāsamāpajjimahaṃ acelaṃ, samaṇo ayaṃ sammato bhāvitatto;

Tassāhamakkhiṃ vivariṃ guyhamatthaṃ, atītamattho kapaṇaṃ rudāmi.

“I placed my trust in the naked ascetic, thinking, ‘This is a recluse, esteemed, and of developed self.’ To him I revealed and disclosed my secret matter. Now that my purpose is lost, I weep wretchedly.”

262.

262.

“Tassāhaṃ paramaṃ brahme guyhaṃ, vācaṃ himaṃ nāsakkhiṃ saṃyametuṃ;

Tappakkhato hi bhayamāgataṃ mamaṃ, atītamattho kapaṇaṃ rudāmi.

“O noble one, I was unable to restrain this supreme secret speech; from that, fear has come upon me. My purpose is lost, and I weep wretchedly.”

263.

263.

“Yo [P 5.0078] ve naro suhadaṃ maññamāno, guyhamatthaṃ saṃsati dukkulīne;

Dosā bhayā athavā rāgarattā, pallatthito bālo asaṃsayaṃ so.

“Whatever man, thinking someone a friend, reveals a secret to a person of low birth—whether from hatred, fear, or when inflamed by lust—that fool is without doubt ruined.”

264.

264.

“Tirokkhavāco [M 5.0081] asataṃ paviṭṭho, yo saṅgatīsu mudīreti vākyaṃ;

Āsīviso dummukhotyāhu taṃ naraṃ, ārā ārā saṃyame tādisamhā.

“One of deceitful speech who has entered the company of the wicked and utters secret words in assemblies—they call that person a foul-mouthed venomous snake. Keep far, far away from such a one.”

265.

265.

“Annaṃ pānaṃ kāsikacandanañca, manāpitthiyo mālamucchādanañca;

Ohāya gacchāmase sabbakāme, supaṇṇa pāṇūpagatāva tyamhā”ti.

“Abandoning food, drink, Kāsī sandalwood, pleasing women, garlands, and unguents, we depart from all sensual pleasures. O Supaṇṇa, we are at your mercy!”

Tattha vikiṇṇavācanti patthaṭavacanaṃ. Aniguyhamantanti appaṭicchannamantaṃ. Asaññatanti kāyadvārādīni rakkhituṃ asakkontaṃ. Aparicakkhitāranti “ayaṃ mayā kathitamantaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkhissati, na sakkhissatī”ti puggalaṃ oloketuṃ upaparikkhituṃ asakkontaṃ. Bhayaṃ tamanvetīti taṃ imehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ abodhaṃ duppaññaṃ puggalaṃ sayaṃkatameva bhayaṃ anveti, yathā maṃ paṇḍarakanāgaṃ supaṇṇo anvāgatoti. Saṃsati hāsamānoti rakkhituṃ asamatthassa pāpapurisassa hāsamāno katheti. Nānumittoti anuvattanamattena yo mitto, na hadayena, so guyhaṃ atthaṃ jānituṃ nārahatīti paridevati. Asambuddhanti asambuddhanto ajānanto, appaññoti attho. Sambuddhanti sambuddhanto jānanto, sappaññoti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yopi suhadayo mitto vā amitto vā appañño sappaññopi vā yo anatthavā anatthacaro, sopi guyhaṃ vedituṃ nārahate”ti.

Herein, 'vikiṇṇavācaṃ' means scattered speech. 'Aniguyhamantaṃ' means unconcealed counsel. 'Asaññatanti' means unable to guard the doors of the body and so on. 'Aparicakkhitāraṃ' means unable to observe or examine a person to determine: ‘Will this person be able to guard the counsel told by me, or not?’ ‘Fear follows him’ means: fear follows that unwise person of little wisdom who is endowed with these four characteristics, just as the Supaṇṇa pursued me, the Nāga Paṇḍara. ‘Reveals while laughing’ means: one tells it while laughing to a wicked person who is unable to guard it. ‘Nānumitto’ means a friend merely by association and not by heart; such a person is not worthy to know a secret matter. ‘Unwise’ means not knowing, that is, of little wisdom. ‘Wise’ means knowing, that is, possessed of wisdom. This is what is said: ‘Even a good-hearted friend or an enemy, whether unwise or wise, if they act harmfully, they too are not worthy to know a secret.’

Samaṇo ayanti ayaṃ samaṇoti ca lokasammatoti ca bhāvitattoti ca maññamāno ahaṃ [V 5.0074] etasmiṃ vissāsamāpajjiṃ. Akkhinti kathesiṃ. Atītamatthoti atītattho, atikkantattho hutvā idāni kapaṇaṃ rudāmīti paridevati. Tassāti tassa acelakassa. Brahmeti supaṇṇaṃ ālapati. Saṃyametunti imaṃ guyhavācaṃ rahassakāraṇaṃ rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃ. Tappakkhato hīti idāni idaṃ bhayaṃ mama tassa acelakassa pakkhato koṭṭhāsato santikā āgataṃ, iti atītattho [M 5.0082] kapaṇaṃ rudāmīti. Suhadanti “suhado mama aya”nti maññamāno. Dukkulīneti [P 5.0079] akulaje nīce. Dosāti etehi dosādīhi kāraṇehi yo evarūpaṃ guyhaṃ saṃsati, so bālo asaṃsayaṃ pallatthito parivattetvā pāpito, hatoyeva nāmāti attho.

‘This is an ascetic’ means: thinking ‘This is an ascetic, and he is esteemed by the world, and he is of developed self,’ I placed trust in him. ‘I spoke’ means I told it. ‘Atītamattho’ means the purpose has passed; now he laments, ‘I weep wretchedly.’ ‘His’ means of that naked ascetic. ‘Brahme’: he addresses the Supaṇṇa. ‘To restrain’ means I was unable to guard this secret speech, this confidential matter. ‘Because of that one’ means now this fear has come to me from the side of that naked ascetic, from his presence; thus, ‘the purpose is passed, I weep wretchedly.’ ‘A friend’ means thinking, ‘This is my good-hearted friend.’ ‘Of low birth’ means born of a base family. ‘From hatred’ means for these reasons such as hatred, whoever reveals such a secret is a fool; he is undoubtedly ruined, meaning he is destroyed.

Tirokkhavācoti attano yaṃ vācaṃ kathetukāmo, tassā tirokkhakatattā paṭicchannavāco. Asataṃ paviṭṭhoti asappurisānaṃ antaraṃ paviṭṭho asappurisesu pariyāpanno. Saṅgatīsu mudīretīti yo evarūpo paresaṃ rahassaṃ sutvāva parisamajjhesu “asukena asukaṃ nāma kataṃ vā vuttaṃ vā”ti vākyaṃ udīreti, taṃ naraṃ “āsīviso dummukho pūtimukho”ti āhu, tādisamhā purisā ārā ārā saṃyame, dūrato dūratova virameyya, parivajjeyya nanti attho. Mālamucchādanañcāti mālañca dibbaṃ catujjātiyagandhañca ucchādanañca. Ohāyāti ete dibbaannādayo sabbakāme ajja mayaṃ ohāya chaḍḍetvā gamissāma. Supaṇṇa, pāṇūpagatāva tyamhāti, bho supaṇṇa, pāṇehi upagatāva te amhā, saraṇaṃ no hohīti.

‘Tirokkhavāco’ means concealed speech because one makes hidden the speech one wishes to speak. ‘Entered among the wicked’ means having entered among wicked people, one is included among them. ‘Utters in assemblies’ means one who, having heard another's secret, utters the statement in the midst of an assembly: ‘Such and such was done or said by so-and-so.’ They call that person ‘a venomous snake, foul-mouthed, and rotten-mouthed.’ From such a person one should keep far, far away; one should desist from a great distance and shun them. ‘Garlands and unguents’ means both divine garlands and the four kinds of divine perfumes and unguents. ‘Abandoning’ means today we will abandon all these divine foods and all sensual pleasures, and depart. ‘O Supaṇṇa, we have come to you for our lives’ means ‘O Supaṇṇa, we have come to you with our lives; be a refuge to us.’

Evaṃ paṇḍarako ākāse heṭṭhāsīsako olambanto aṭṭhahi gāthāhi paridevi. Supaṇṇo tassa paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā, “nāgarāja attano rahassaṃ acelakassa kathetvā idāni kimatthaṃ paridevasī”ti taṃ garahitvā gāthamāha –

Thus Paṇḍaraka, hanging head down in the sky, lamented with eight verses. Hearing the sound of his lamentation, the Supaṇṇa rebuked the Nāga king, saying: ‘Nāga king, having told your secret to a naked ascetic, why do you now lament?’ and spoke this verse:

266.

266.

“Ko nīdha tiṇṇaṃ garahaṃ upeti, asmiṃdha loke pāṇabhū nāgarāja;

Samaṇo supaṇṇo athavā tvameva, kiṃkāraṇā paṇḍarakaggahīto”ti.

“Who here among the three incurs blame in this world of living beings, O Nāga king? The ascetic, the Supaṇṇa, or is it you yourself? For what reason has Paṇḍaraka been seized?”

Tattha ko nīdhāti idha amhesu tīsu janesu ko nu. Asmiṃdhāti ettha idhāti nipātamattaṃ, asmiṃ loketi attho. Pāṇabhūti pāṇabhūto. Athavā tvamevāti udāhu tvaṃyeva. Tattha samaṇaṃ tāva mā garaha, so hi upāyena taṃ rahassaṃ pucchi. Supaṇṇampi mā garaha, ahañhi tava paccatthikova. Paṇḍarakaggahītoti, samma paṇḍaraka, “ahaṃ kiṃkāraṇā supaṇṇena gahito”ti cintetvā ca pana attānameva garaha, tayā hi rahassaṃ kathentena attanāva attano anattho katoti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Herein, ‘who here’ means who indeed among us three? ‘In this’—here ‘idha’ is a mere particle; the meaning is ‘in this world.’ ‘Living being’ means one who is a living being. ‘Or is it you yourself’ means or is it you alone. In this matter, do not blame the ascetic, for he asked for the secret through a stratagem. Do not blame the Supaṇṇa either, for I am your enemy. ‘For what reason has Paṇḍaraka been seized’ means: ‘Friend Paṇḍaraka, reflect: “For what reason was I seized by the Supaṇṇa?” and blame yourself alone. For by revealing the secret, you have brought ruin upon yourself.’ This is the intention.

Taṃ [V 5.0075][M 5.0083] sutvā paṇḍarako itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Paṇḍaraka spoke another verse:

267.

267.

“Samaṇoti me sammatatto ahosi, piyo ca me manasā bhāvitatto;

Tassāhamakkhiṃ [P 5.0080] vivariṃ guyhamatthaṃ, atītamattho kapaṇaṃ rudāmī”ti.

“To me he was an ascetic, one esteemed, dear to my heart, and of developed self. To him I spoke and revealed the secret matter; now that my purpose is lost, I weep wretchedly.”

Tattha sammatattoti so samaṇo mayhaṃ “sappuriso aya”nti sammatabhāvo ahosi. Bhāvitattoti sambhāvitabhāvo ca me ahosīti.

Herein, 'highly esteemed' (sammatatto) means that ascetic was esteemed by me with the thought, 'This is a virtuous person.' 'Of developed nature' (bhāvitatto) means he was also highly regarded by me.

Tato supaṇṇo catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Supaṇṇa spoke four verses:

268.

268.

“Na catthi satto amaro pathabyā, paññāvidhā natthi na ninditabbā;

‘There is no being on earth who is immortal; there is a kind of wisdom that should not be blamed.

Saccena dhammena dhitiyā damena, alabbhamabyāharatī naro idha.

By truth, by Dhamma, by fortitude, by self-control, a person here brings about even what is unobtainable.

269.

269.

“Mātā pitā paramā bandhavānaṃ, nāssa tatiyo anukampakatthi;

Tesampi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse, mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno.

‘Mother and father are the supreme relatives; there is no third person as compassionate as they. Even to them one should not reveal a supreme secret, fearing the disclosure of counsel.

270.

270.

“Mātā pitā bhaginī bhātaro ca, sahāyā vā yassa honti sapakkhā;

Tesampi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse, mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno.

‘Mother, father, sister, and brothers, or friends who are one's allies—even to them one should not reveal a supreme secret, fearing the disclosure of counsel.

271.

271.

“Bhariyā ce purisaṃ vajjā, komārī piyabhāṇinī;

Puttarūpayasūpetā, ñātisaṅghapurakkhatā;

Tassāpi guyhaṃ paramaṃ na saṃse, mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno”ti.

‘Even if a wife is devoted to her husband—a young woman wed in her youth, sweet-spoken, endowed with sons, beauty, and fame, and honored by her kin—even to her one should not reveal a supreme secret, fearing the disclosure of counsel.’

Tattha amaroti amaraṇasabhāvo satto nāma natthi. Paññāvidhā natthīti na-kāro padasandhikaro, paññāvidhā atthīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nāgarāja[M 5.0084], loke amaropi natthi, paññāvidhāpi atthi, sā aññesaṃ paññākoṭṭhāsasaṅkhātā paññāvidhā attano jīvitahetu na ninditabbāti. Atha vā paññāvidhāti paññāsadisā na ninditabbā nāma aññā dhammajāti natthi, taṃ kasmā nindasīti. Yesaṃ pana “paññāvidhānampi na ninditabba”ntipi pāṭho, tesaṃ ujukameva. Saccenātiādīsu vacīsaccena ca sucaritadhammena ca paññāsaṅkhātāya dhitiyā ca indriyadamena ca alabbhaṃ dullabhaṃ aṭṭhasamāpattimaggaphalanibbānasaṅkhātampi visesaṃ abyāharati āvahati [V 5.0076] taṃ nipphādeti [P 5.0081] naro idha, tasmā nārahasi acelaṃ nindituṃ, attānameva garaha. Acelena hi attano paññavantatāya upāyakusalatāya ca vañcetvā tvaṃ rahassaṃ guyhaṃ mantaṃ pucchitoti attho.

Herein, 'immortal' means there is no being with an immortal nature. In 'a kind of wisdom does not exist,' the 'na' is a euphonic particle (padasandhikaro); the meaning is 'a kind of wisdom exists.' This is what is said: O Nāga king, in the world there is no immortal being, but a kind of wisdom does exist. That wisdom, reckoned as a specific kind of wisdom possessed by others, should not be blamed for the sake of one's own life. Alternatively, 'a kind of wisdom' means there is no other category of Dhamma similar to wisdom that should not be blamed; why then do you blame it? For those who have the reading 'even a specific kind of wisdom should not be blamed,' the meaning is straightforward. Regarding 'by truth,' etc.: by truth of speech, by the Dhamma of good conduct, by the fortitude known as wisdom, and by the restraint of the senses, a person here achieves even the rare and difficult distinctions consisting of the eight attainments, the Path, the Fruition, and Nibbāna. Therefore, you should not blame the naked ascetic; blame only yourself. For the naked ascetic, by his own intelligence and skill in means, deceived you and asked for your secret counsel—this is the meaning.

Paramāti ete ubho bandhavānaṃ uttamabandhavā nāma. Nāssa tatiyoti assa puggalassa mātāpitūhi añño tatiyo satto anukampako nāma natthi, mantassa bhedaṃ parisaṅkamāno paṇḍito tesaṃ mātāpitūnampi paramaṃ guyhaṃ na saṃseyya, tvaṃ pana mātāpitūnampi akathetabbaṃ acelakassa kathesīti attho. Sahāyā vāti suhadayamittā vā. Sapakkhāti petteyyamātulapitucchādayo samānapakkhā ñātayo. Tesampīti etesampi ñātimittānaṃ na katheyya, tvaṃ pana acelakassa kathesi, attanova kujjhassūti dīpeti. Bhariyā ceti komārī piyabhāṇinī puttehi ca rūpena ca yasena ca upetā evarūpā bhariyāpi ce “ācikkhāhi me tava guyha”nti vadeyya, tassāpi na saṃseyya.

'Supreme' means these two are the most excellent among relatives. 'No third for him' means for a person there is no third being as compassionate as his mother and father. A wise person, fearing the disclosure of counsel, would not tell even a supreme secret to his mother and father. Yet you told the naked ascetic what should not have been told even to your parents—this is the meaning. 'Or friends' means good-hearted companions. 'One's allies' means kinsfolk on the same side, such as paternal uncles, maternal uncles, paternal aunts, and so on. 'Even to them' means one should not tell even these relatives and friends. Yet you told the naked ascetic; this shows you should be angry only with yourself. 'And a wife' means even if a wife who was wed in her youth, who is sweet-spoken and endowed with sons, beauty, and fame, should say, 'Tell me your secret,' one should not reveal it even to her.

Tato parā –

The following verses:

272.

272.

“Na guyhamatthaṃ vivareyya, rakkheyya naṃ yathā nidhiṃ;

Na hi pātukato sādhu, guyho attho pajānatā.

‘One should not reveal a secret matter; one should guard it like a hidden treasure. For a secret matter made manifest is not praised by the wise.

273.

273.

“Thiyā guyhaṃ na saṃseyya, amittassa ca paṇḍito;

Yo cāmisena saṃhīro, hadayattheno ca yo naro.

‘A wise person should not tell a secret to a woman or to an enemy, nor to one who can be subverted by a bribe, nor to a person who is a thief of the heart.

274.

274.

“Guyhamatthaṃ asambuddhaṃ, sambodhayati yo naro;

Mantabhedabhayā tassa, dāsabhūto titikkhati.

‘If a person reveals a secret matter not yet known to another, then out of fear of that secret being disclosed, he must endure being like a slave to that person.

275.

275.

“Yāvanto [M 5.0085] purisassatthaṃ, guyhaṃ jānanti mantinaṃ;

Tāvanto tassa ubbegā, tasmā guyhaṃ na vissaje;

‘However many counselors know a person's secret matter, that many are the sources of his anxiety; therefore, one should not disclose a secret.

276.

276.

“Vivicca bhāseyya divā rahassaṃ, rattiṃ giraṃ nātivelaṃ pamuñce;

Upassutikā hi suṇanti mantaṃ, tasmā manto khippamupeti bheda”nti. –

‘One should speak a secret in seclusion by day; at night one should not speak too loudly. For eavesdroppers may hear the counsel; thus, counsel is quickly disclosed.’

Pañca [V 5.0077] gāthā umaṅgajātake pañcapaṇḍitapañhe āvi bhavissanti.

These five verses will become clear in the Question of the Five Pandits in the Umaṅga Jātaka.

Tato parāsu –

In the following verses:

277.

277.

“Yathāpi assa nagaraṃ mahantaṃ, advārakaṃ āyasaṃ bhaddasālaṃ;

Samantakhātāparikhāupetaṃ[P 5.0082], evampi me te idha guyhamantā.

‘Just as there might be a great city, gateless, made of iron, with beautiful halls, and surrounded by a dug-out moat—even so do those who keep their secret counsel appear to me here.

278.

278.

“Ye guyhamantā avikiṇṇavācā, daḷhā sadatthesu narā dujivha;

Ārā amittā byavajanti tehi, āsīvisā vā riva sattusaṅghā”ti. –

‘O two-tongued one, those men who keep their counsel secret, whose speech is not loose, and who are firm in their own welfare—from them enemies keep far away, just as a host of foes flees from a venomous snake.’

Dvīsu gāthāsu bhaddasālanti āpaṇādīhi sālāhi sampannaṃ. Samantakhātāparikhāupetanti samantakhātāhi tīhi parikhāhi upagataṃ. Evampi meti evampi mayhaṃ te purisā khāyanti. Katare? Ye idha guyhamantā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā advārakassa ayomayanagarassa manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogo antova hoti, na abbhantarimā bahi nikkhamanti, na bāhirā anto pavisanti, aparāparaṃ sañcāro chijjati, guyhamantā purisā evarūpā honti, attano guyhaṃ attano antoyeva jīrāpenti, na aññassa kathentīti. Daḷhā sadatthesūti attano atthesu thirā. Dujivhāti paṇḍarakanāgaṃ ālapati. Byavajantīti paṭikkamanti. Āsīvisā vā riva sattusaṅghāti ettha vāti nipātamattaṃ, āsīvisā sattusaṅghā rivāti attho. Yathā āsīvisato sattusaṅghā jīvitukāmā manussā [M 5.0086] ārā paṭikkamanti, evaṃ tehi guyhamantehi narehi ārā amittā paṭikkamanti, upagantuṃ okāsaṃ na labhantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the two verses, (bhaddasāla) means endowed with halls such as shops. (Samantakhātāparikhāupeta) means surrounded by three moats dug all around. (Evampi me) means ‘so too do these men appear to me.’ Which ones? Those who are of secret counsel here. This is what is said: Just as in a city without gates made of iron, the people’s enjoyment and use remain inside—those inside do not go out, and those outside do not enter, so that coming and going is cut off—so too are men of secret counsel. They let their secrets grow old within themselves, not telling them to another. (Daḷhā sadatthesu) means firm in their own purposes. (Dujivhā): he addresses the Nāga Paṇḍaraka as ‘two-tongued.’ (Byavajanti) means they retreat. (Āsīvisā vā riva sattusaṅghā): here vā is merely a particle; the meaning is ‘like a host of beings from a venomous snake.’ Just as a host of beings, people who wish to live, retreat far from a venomous snake, so too do enemies retreat far from these men of secret counsel, finding no opportunity to approach—this is what is said.

Evaṃ supaṇṇena dhamme kathite paṇḍarako āha –

When the Supaṇṇa had thus preached the Dhamma, the Nāga king Paṇḍaraka said:

279.

279.

“Hitvā gharaṃ pabbajito acelo, naggo muṇḍo carati ghāsahetu;

Tamhi nu kho vivariṃ guyhamatthaṃ, atthā ca dhammā ca apaggatāmhā.

“Having left home, he went forth as a clothless ascetic; naked and shaven-headed, he wanders for the sake of food. To him, indeed, I revealed my secret, and now I have fallen away from both my welfare and the Dhamma.”

280.

280.

“Kathaṃkaro hoti supaṇṇarāja, kiṃsīlo kena vatena vattaṃ;

Samaṇo caraṃ hitvā mamāyitāni, kathaṃkaro saggamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

“How should he act, O king of Supaṇṇas? What should be his virtue, and what vow should he observe? Faring as an ascetic, having abandoned all possessiveness, how should he act to reach the heavenly state?”

Tattha ghāsahetūti nissiriko kucchipūraṇatthāya khādanīyabhojanīye pariyesanto carati. Apaggatāmhāti [V 5.0078] apagatā parihīnāmhā. Kathaṃkaroti [P 5.0083] idaṃ nāgarājā tassa naggassa samaṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā samaṇapaṭipattiṃ pucchanto āha. Tattha kiṃsīloti katarena ācārena samannāgato. Kena vatenāti katarena vatasamādānena vattanto. Samaṇo caranti pabbajjāya caranto taṇhāmamāyitāni hitvā kathaṃ samitapāpasamaṇo nāma hoti. Sagganti kathaṃ karonto ca suṭṭhu aggaṃ devanagaraṃ so samaṇo upetīti.

Herein, 'for the sake of food' (ghāsahetu) means: being destitute, he wanders seeking edibles and meals for the sake of filling his belly. 'We have departed from' (apaggatāmhā) means: we have departed from or been deprived of. 'How does one act?' (kathaṃkaro): the Nāga king said this, asking about the practice of a recluse, since he now knew the true nature of that naked one. Herein, 'what is his virtue?' means: with what kind of conduct is he endowed? 'By what vow?' means: by undertaking what vow does he live? 'Faring as a recluse' means: living in the state of one who has gone forth, having abandoned craving and possessiveness, how is he called a recluse because he has pacified evil? 'The heavenly' means: and how, by acting thus, does that recluse reach the excellent, supreme state in the city of the gods?

Supaṇṇo āha –

The Supaṇṇa said:

281.

281.

“Hiriyā titikkhāya damenupeto, akkodhano pesuṇiyaṃ pahāya;

Samaṇo caraṃ hitvā mamāyitāni, evaṃkaro saggamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

“Endowed with moral shame, patience, and self-control, free from anger, and having abandoned slander; faring as an ascetic, having given up all possessiveness, acting thus, he reaches the heavenly state.”

Tattha hiriyāti, samma nāgarāja, ajjhattabahiddhāsamuṭṭhānehi hirottappehi titikkhāsaṅkhātāya adhivāsanakhantiyā indriyadamena ca upeto akujjhanasīlo pisuṇavācaṃ pahāya taṇhāmamāyitāni ca hitvā pabbajjāya caranto [M 5.0087] samaṇo nāma hoti, evaṃkaroyeva ca etāni hirīādīni kusalāni karonto saggamupeti ṭhānanti.

Herein, 'with conscience' means: Friend Nāga king, one is called a recluse who fares on in the homeless life endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing that arise internally and externally, with enduring patience, with restraint of the senses, and with a nature free from anger, having abandoned slanderous speech and having given up cravings and possessiveness. And it is by acting thus, by performing these wholesome deeds beginning with conscience, that one attains the heavenly state.

Idaṃ supaṇṇarājassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā paṇḍarako jīvitaṃ yācanto gāthamāha –

Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma from the king of the Supaṇṇas, Paṇḍaraka, begging for his life, spoke this verse:

282.

282.

“Mātāva puttaṃ taruṇaṃ tanujjaṃ, samphassatā sabbagattaṃ phareti;

Evampi me tvaṃ pāturahu dijinda, mātāva puttaṃ anukampamāno”ti.

“As a mother her tender, body-born son, pervades her whole body with the joy of his touch; even so you have appeared to me, O king of birds, like a mother feeling compassion for her son.”

Tassattho – yathā mātā tanujaṃ attano sarīrajātaṃ taruṇaṃ puttaṃ samphassataṃ disvā taṃ ure nipajjāpetvā thaññaṃ pāyentī puttasamphassena sabbaṃ attano gattaṃ phareti, napi mātā puttato bhāyati napi putto mātito, evampi me tvaṃ pāturahu pātubhūto dijinda dijarāja, tasmā mātāva puttaṃ mudukena hadayena anukampamāno maṃ passa, jīvitaṃ me dehīti.

Its meaning is: Just as a mother, seeing her tender son, born from her own body, touching her, lays him on her breast and gives him her milk, and with the touch of her son she pervades her entire body—the mother does not fear the son, nor does the son fear the mother—even so you have appeared to me, O king of birds. Therefore, like a mother feeling compassion for her son with a tender heart, look upon me; grant me my life.

Athassa supaṇṇo jīvitaṃ dento itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Supaṇṇa, granting him his life, spoke the other verse:

283.

283.

“Handajja tvaṃ muñca vadhā dujivha, tayo hi puttā na hi añño atthi;

Antevāsī [P 5.0084] dinnako atrajo ca, rajjassu puttaññataro me ahosī”ti.

“Come now, O two-tongued one, be released from death! For there are three sons and no other: a resident pupil, a given son, and a natural son. Rejoice! You have become one of these sons to me.”

Tattha [V 5.0079] muñcāti mucca, ayameva vā pāṭho. Dujivhāti taṃ ālapati. Aññoti añño catuttho putto nāma natthi. Antevāsīti sippaṃ vā uggaṇhamāno pañhaṃ vā suṇanto santike nivuttho. Dinnakoti “ayaṃ te putto hotū”ti parehi dinno. Rajjassūti abhiramassu. Aññataroti tīsu puttesu aññataro antevāsī putto me tvaṃ jātoti dīpeti.

Herein, 'be released' (muñca) means: be you released; or this is the reading itself. 'O two-tongued one' (dujivha): he addresses him thus. 'No other' (añño) means: there is no other, that is, a fourth kind of son. 'A resident pupil' (antevāsī) is one who lives nearby while learning a craft or listening to a teaching. 'A given son' (dinnako) is one given by others, who say, 'Let this be your son.' 'Rejoice' (rajjassu) means: delight. 'One of these sons' (aññataro): he indicates, 'Among the three sons, you have become my son, the resident pupil.'

Evañca pana vatvā ākāsā otaritvā taṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā dve gāthā abhāsi –

And having spoken thus, he descended from the sky and set him down on the ground. The Teacher, making this matter clear, spoke these two verses:

284.

284.

“Icceva [M 5.0088] vākyaṃ visajjī supaṇṇo, bhumyaṃ patiṭṭhāya dijo dujivhaṃ;

Muttajja tvaṃ sabbabhayātivatto, thalūdake hohi mayābhigutto.

“Having spoken these words, the Supaṇṇa, the twice-born bird, standing on the ground, released the two-tongued one: ‘Today you are freed, having passed beyond all fear; be protected by me on land and in water.

285.

285.

“Ātaṅkinaṃ yathā kusalo bhisakko, pipāsitānaṃ rahadova sīto;

Vesmaṃ yathā himasītaṭṭitānaṃ, evampi te saraṇamahaṃ bhavāmī”ti.

“As a skilled physician for the ailing, as a cool lake for the thirsty, as a shelter for those struck by frost and cold, even so will I be a refuge for you.”

Tattha icceva vākyanti iti evaṃ vacanaṃ vatvā taṃ nāgarājaṃ vissajji. Bhumyanti so sayampi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāya dijo taṃ dujivhaṃ samassāsento mutto ajja tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya sabbabhayāni ativatto thale ca udake ca mayā abhigutto rakkhito hohīti āha. Ātaṅkinanti gilānānaṃ. Evampi teti evaṃ ahaṃ tava saraṇaṃ bhavāmi.

Therein, 'icceva vākyaṃ' means: having spoken thus, he released that Nāga king. 'Bhumyaṃ' means: the bird himself, having stood on the ground, consoling that two-tongued one, said: ‘Today you are freed. Henceforth, having passed beyond all fears, be protected and guarded by me on land and in water.’ ‘Ātaṅkinaṃ’ means: for the sick. ‘Evampi te’ means: even so I will be your refuge.

Gaccha tvanti uyyojesi. So nāgarājā nāgabhavanaṃ pāvisi. Itaropi supaṇṇabhavanaṃ gantvā “mayā paṇḍarakanāgo sapathaṃ katvā saddahāpetvā vissajjito, kīdisaṃ nu kho mayi tassa hadayaṃ, vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā supaṇṇavātaṃ akāsi. Taṃ disvā nāgo “supaṇṇarājā maṃ gahetuṃ āgato bhavissatī”ti maññamāno byāmasahassamattaṃ attabhāvaṃ māpetvā pāsāṇe ca vālukañca gilitvā bhāriyo hutvā [P 5.0085] naṅguṭṭhaṃ heṭṭhākatvā bhogamatthake phaṇaṃ dhārayamāno nipajjitvā supaṇṇarājānaṃ ḍaṃsitukāmo viya ahosi. Taṃ disvā supaṇṇo itaraṃ gāthamāha –

He dismissed him, saying, “Go now.” That Nāga king entered the Nāga abode. The other, having gone to the Supaṇṇa abode, thought: “I made the Nāga Paṇḍaraka swear an oath, made him trust me, and then released him. What, I wonder, is in his heart toward me? I will test him.” So he went to the Nāga abode and created a Supaṇṇa-wind. Seeing this, the Nāga thought, “The Supaṇṇa king must have come to seize me.” He magically created a body a thousand fathoms in size, swallowed stones and sand to make himself heavy, placed his tail underneath, and lay down holding his hood above his coils, as if wanting to bite the Supaṇṇa king. Seeing this, the Supaṇṇa spoke the other verse:

286.

286.

“Sandhiṃ katvā amittena, aṇḍajena jalābuja;

Vivariya dāṭhaṃ sesi, kuto taṃ bhayamāgata”nti.

“O womb-born one, having made a pact with an egg-born foe, you lie with fangs bared. From where has this fear come upon you?”

Taṃ sutvā [V 5.0080] nāgarājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Nāga king spoke three verses:

287.

287.

“Saṅketheva amittasmiṃ, mittasmimpi na vissase;

Abhayā bhayamuppannaṃ, api mūlāni kantati.

“One should be wary of a foe, and even in a friend one should not place trust. Fear that has arisen from a source of safety cuts away the very roots.”

288.

288.

“Kathaṃ nu vissase tyamhi, yenāsi kalaho kato;

Niccayattena ṭhātabbaṃ, so disabbhi na rajjati.

“How indeed could I trust in you, with whom I have had a quarrel? One must always stand prepared; such a one is not ensnared by his foes.”

289.

289.

“Vissāsaye [M 5.0089] na ca taṃ vissayeyya, asaṅkito saṅkito ca bhaveyya;

Tathā tathā viññū parakkameyya, yathā yathā bhāvaṃ paro na jaññā”ti.

“One might inspire trust, but should not trust in turn; though unsuspected, one should still be wary. The wise should strive in such a way that another cannot know their disposition.”

Tattha abhayāti abhayaṭṭhānabhūtā mittamhā bhayaṃ uppannaṃ jīvitasaṅkhātāni mūlāneva kantati. Tyamhīti tasmiṃ. Yenāsīti yena saddhiṃ kalaho kato ahosi. Niccayattenāti niccapaṭiyattena. So disabbhi na rajjatīti yo niccayattena abhitiṭṭhati, so attano sattūhi saddhiṃ vissāsavasena na rajjati, tato tesaṃ yathākāmakaraṇīyo na hotīti attho. Vissāsayeti paraṃ attani vissāsaye, taṃ pana sayaṃ na vissaseyya. Parena asaṅkito attanā ca so saṅkito bhaveyya. Bhāvaṃ paroti yathā yathā paṇḍito parakkamati, tathā tathā tassa paro bhāvaṃ na jānāti, tasmā paṇḍitena vīriyaṃ kātabbamevāti dīpeti.

Therein, 'abhayā' means: fear arisen from a friend, who is a source of safety, cuts down the very roots, that is, life. 'Tyamhi' means: in that one. 'Yenāsi' means: with whom a quarrel was once made. 'Niccayattena' means: with constant readiness. 'So disabbhi na rajjati' means: one who stands firm with constant readiness is not ensnared by his enemies through trust, and thus does not become one who can be treated by them as they wish. 'Vissāsaye' means: one should make another trust in oneself, but one should not trust that person in return. One should be unsuspected by the other, but be wary oneself. 'Bhāvaṃ paro' means: in whatever way a wise person strives, in that way the other does not know his disposition. Therefore, it shows that a wise person must indeed make an effort.

Iti te aññamaññaṃ sallapitvā samaggā sammodamānā ubhopi acelakassa assamaṃ agamiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, having conversed with each other, reconciled and rejoicing together, they both went to the hermitage of the naked ascetic. The Teacher, making this matter clear, said:

290.

290.

“Te devavaṇṇā sukhumālarūpā, ubho samā sujayā puññakhandhā;

Upāgamuṃ [P 5.0086] karampiyaṃ acelaṃ, missībhūtā assavāhāva nāgā”ti.

“They of divine complexion, of delicate form, both alike, of noble birth, like heaps of merit, approached the naked ascetic Karampiya, joined together like noble elephants yoked to a chariot.”

Tattha samāti samānarūpā sadisasaṇṭhānā hutvā. Sujayāti suvayā parisuddhā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Puññakhandhāti katakusalatāya puññakkhandhā viya. Missībhūtāti hatthena hatthaṃ gahetvā kāyamissībhāvaṃ upagatā. Assavāhāva nāgāti dhure yuttakā rathavāhā dve assā viya purisanāgā tassa assamaṃ agamiṃsu.
