Herein, 'samā' means: having become similar in form and identical in appearance. 'Sujayā' means: of good age, or pure; or this is the reading itself. 'Puññakhandhā' means: like a heap of merit because of the wholesome deeds they had done. 'Missībhūtā' means: having taken each other by the hand, they attained a state of bodily mingling. 'Assavāhāva nāgā' means: the two noble men, like two chariot-drawing horses yoked to the pole, went to the hermitage of Karampiya.

Gantvā [V 5.0081] ca pana supaṇṇarājā cintesi – “ayaṃ nāgarājā acelakassa jīvitaṃ na dassati, etaṃ dussīlaṃ na vandissāmī”ti. So bahi ṭhatvā nāgarājānameva tassa santikaṃ pesesi. Taṃ sandhāya satthā itaraṃ gāthamāha.

Then the supaṇṇa king, having gone there, thought: 'This Nāga king will not give his life for the naked ascetic; I will not pay homage to this immoral one.' Standing outside, he sent only the Nāga king into the ascetic's presence. In reference to this, the Teacher spoke the other verse.

291.

291.

“Tato [M 5.0090] have paṇḍarako acelaṃ, sayamevupāgamma idaṃ avoca;

Muttajjahaṃ sabbabhayātivatto, na hi nūna tuyhaṃ manaso piyamhā”ti.

'Then indeed Paṇḍaraka, having approached the naked ascetic of his own accord, said this: "I am released today, having overcome all fear. Surely we are not dear to your heart."'

Tattha piyamhāti dussīlanaggabhoggamusāvādi nūna mayaṃ tava manaso na piyā ahumhāti paribhāsi.

Herein, by 'we are dear' he reviled him, saying: 'O immoral, naked, gluttonous, and lying one, surely we were not dear to your heart.'

Tato acelo itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the naked ascetic spoke the other verse:

292.

292.

“Piyo hi me āsi supaṇṇarājā, asaṃsayaṃ paṇḍarakena saccaṃ;

So rāgarattova akāsimetaṃ, pāpakammaṃ sampajāno na mohā”ti.

'Dear to me was the supaṇṇa king; this is undoubtedly true, O Paṇḍaraka. I, being inflamed by passion, did this evil deed, fully aware and not out of delusion.'

Tattha paṇḍarakenāti tayā paṇḍarakena so mama piyataro ahosi, saccametaṃ. Soti so ahaṃ tasmiṃ supaṇṇe rāgena ratto hutvā etaṃ pāpakammaṃ jānantova akāsiṃ, na mohena ajānantoti.

Herein, 'by Paṇḍaraka' means 'more than you, Paṇḍaraka.' He was dearer to me; this is true. 'He' refers to 'I.' I, being inflamed with passion for that supaṇṇa, knowingly committed this evil deed, not unknowingly out of delusion.

Taṃ sutvā nāgarājā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the Nāga king spoke two verses:

293.

293.

“Na me piyaṃ appiyaṃ vāpi hoti, sampassato lokamimaṃ parañca;

Susaññatānañhi viyañjanena, asaññato lokamimaṃ carāsi.

'For me, who sees this world and the next, there is nothing dear or not dear. But you, with the guise of one who is well-restrained, wander this world unrestrained.'

294.

294.

“Ariyāvakāsosi [P 5.0087] anariyovāsi, asaññato saññatasannikāso;

Kaṇhābhijātikosi anariyarūpo, pāpaṃ bahuṃ duccaritaṃ acārī”ti.

'You have the appearance of a noble one, but you are ignoble; you are unrestrained, though you resemble one who is restrained. You are of dark birth, of ignoble nature; you have practiced much evil and misconduct.'

Tattha na meti ambho dussīlanaggamusāvādi pabbajitassa hi imañca parañca lokaṃ sampassato piyaṃ vā me appiyaṃ vāpi meti na hoti, tvaṃ pana susaññatānaṃ sīlavantānaṃ byañjanena pabbajitaliṅgena asaññato hutvā imaṃ lokaṃ vañcento carasi. Ariyāvakāsosīti ariyapaṭirūpakosi[V 5.0082]. Asaññatoti [M 5.0091] kāyādīhi asaññatosi. Kaṇhābhijātikoti kāḷakasabhāvo. Anariyarūpoti ahirikasabhāvo. Acārīti akāsi.

Herein, 'for me there is not' means: O immoral, naked, lying ascetic, for a renunciant who sees this world and the next, there is no 'this is dear to me' or 'this is not dear to me.' But you, being unrestrained, wander this world deceiving it with the outward mark of a renunciant, the guise of the well-restrained and virtuous. 'You have the appearance of a noble one' means you are a counterfeit noble. 'Unrestrained' means unrestrained in body and so on. 'Of dark birth' means of an evil nature. 'Of ignoble nature' means of a shameless nature. 'You have practiced' means you have done.

Iti taṃ garahitvā idāni abhisapanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having censured him thus, he now uttered this verse, laying a curse upon him:

295.

295.

“Aduṭṭhassa tuvaṃ dubbhi, dubbhī ca pisuṇo casi;

Etena saccavajjena, muddhā te phalatu sattadhā”ti.

'You have betrayed one who was not hostile; you are a betrayer and a slanderer. By this statement of truth, may your head split into seven pieces!'

Tassattho – ambho dubbhi tvaṃ aduṭṭhassa mittassa dubbhī cāsi, pisuṇo cāsi, etena saccavajjena muddhā te sattadhā phalatūti.

Its meaning is: O betrayer, you have betrayed a blameless friend, and you are a slanderer. By this statement of truth, may your head split into seven pieces!

Iti nāgarājassa sapantasseva acelakassa sīsaṃ sattadhā phali. Nisinnaṭṭhāneyevassa bhūmi vivaraṃ adāsi. So pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīcimhi nibbatti, nāgarājasupaṇṇarājānopi attano bhavanameva agamiṃsu. Satthā tassa pathaviṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ pakāsento osānagāthamāha –

Even as the Nāga king was laying his curse, the naked ascetic's head split into seven pieces. The earth gave an opening right where he was sitting. He entered the earth and was reborn in Avīci. The Nāga king and the supaṇṇa king also returned to their own abodes. The Teacher, making known his entering the earth, spoke the concluding verse:

296.

296.

“Tasmā hi mittānaṃ na dubbhitabbaṃ, mittadubbhā pāpiyo natthi añño;

Āsittasatto nihato pathabyā, indassa vākyena hi saṃvaro hato”ti.

'Therefore one should not betray friends, for there is no one more evil than a betrayer of friends. The being drenched with the poison of his own deed was struck down to the earth; by the word of the chief, his "restraint" was destroyed.'

Tattha tasmāti yasmā mittadubbhikammassa pharuso vipāko, tasmā. Āsittasattoti āsittavisena satto. Indassāti nāgindassa vākyena. Saṃvaroti “ahaṃ saṃvare ṭhitosmī”ti paṭiññāya evaṃ paññāto ājīvako hatoti.

Herein, 'therefore' means: because the result of the act of betraying a friend is harsh, therefore... 'The being drenched with poison' means a being drenched with the poison of the deed of betraying a friend. 'Of the chief' means by the word of the Naga chief. 'Restraint' means: the Ājīvaka who was known by his claim 'I abide in restraint' was destroyed.

Satthā [P 5.0088] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto musāvādaṃ katvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā acelako devadatto ahosi, nāgarājā sāriputto, supaṇṇarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher said: 'Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta spoke falsehood and entered the earth.' Then he made the connection for the Jātaka: 'At that time, the naked ascetic was Devadatta, the Nāga king was Sāriputta, and the supaṇṇa king was myself.'

Paṇḍaranāgarājajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Paṇḍara Nāga King Jātaka, the Eighth.

[519] 9. Sambulājātakavaṇṇanā

[519] 9. The Commentary on the Sambulā Jātaka

Kā [V 5.0083][M 5.0092] vedhamānāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mallikaṃ deviṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu kummāsapiṇḍijātake (jā. 1.7.142 ādayo) vitthāritameva. Sā pana tathāgatassa tiṇṇaṃ kummāsapiṇḍikānaṃ dānānubhāvena taṃ divasaññeva rañño aggamahesibhāvaṃ patvā pubbuṭṭhāyitādīhi pañcahi kalyāṇadhammehi samannāgatā ñāṇasampannā buddhupaṭṭhāyikā patidevatā ahosi. Tassā patidevatābhāvo sakalanagare pākaṭo ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, mallikā devī kira vattasampannā ñāṇasampannā patidevatā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesā vattasampannā patidevatāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Who is trembling?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning Queen Mallikā. The story is detailed in the Kummāsapiṇḍi Jātaka. By the power of her offering of three handfuls of barley-gruel to the Tathāgata, on that very day she attained the position of chief queen to King Kosala. Endowed with the five fine qualities—rising before her husband and so on—she was possessed of wisdom, an attendant of the Buddha, and a wife devoted to her husband as if he were a god. Her devotion to her husband became well-known throughout the city of Sāvatthi. Then one day, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, Queen Mallikā, it seems, is accomplished in her duties, possessed of wisdom, and a devoted wife.” The Teacher came and asked, “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered here?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said, “Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past too, she was accomplished in her duties and a devoted wife,” and he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadattassa rañño sotthiseno nāma putto ahosi. Taṃ rājā vayappattaṃ uparajje patiṭṭhapesi, sambulā nāmassa aggamahesī ahosi uttamarūpadharā sarīrappabhāsampannā, nivāte jalamānā dīpasikhā viya khāyati. Aparabhāge sotthisenassa sarīre kuṭṭhaṃ uppajjati, vejjā tikicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. So bhijjamāne kuṭṭhe paṭikūlo hutvā vippaṭisāraṃ patvā “ko me rajjena attho, araññe anāthamaraṇaṃ marissāmī”ti rañño ārocāpetvā itthāgāraṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhami. Sambulā bahūhi upāyehi nivattiyamānāpi anivattitvāva “ahaṃ taṃ sāmikaṃ araññe paṭijaggissāmī”ti vatvā saddhiññeva nikkhami. So araññaṃ pavisitvā sulabhamūlaphalāphale chāyūdakasampanne padese paṇṇasālaṃ katvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Rājadhītā taṃ paṭijaggi. Kathaṃ? Sā hi pāto vuṭṭhāya assamapadaṃ sammajjitvā pānīyaparibhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā dantakaṭṭhañca [P 5.0089] mukhadhovanañca upanāmetvā mukhe dhote nānāosadhāni pisitvā tassa vaṇe makkhetvā madhuramadhurāni phalāphalāni khādāpetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā hatthesu dhotesu “appamatto hohi devā”ti vatvā vanditvā pacchikhaṇittiaṅkusake ādāya phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ pavisitvā phalāphalāni āharitvā ekamante ṭhapetvā ghaṭena udakaṃ āharitvā nānācuṇṇehi ca mattikāhi ca sotthisenaṃ nhāpetvā puna [M 5.0093] madhuraphalāphalāni upanāmeti. Paribhogāvasāne vāsitapānīyaṃ upanetvā sayaṃ phalāphalāni paribhuñjitvā padarasantharaṃ saṃvidahitvā tasmiṃ tattha nipanne tassa pāde dhovitvā sīsaparikammapiṭṭhiparikammapādaparikammāni katvā sayanapassaṃ upagantvā nipajjati. Etenupāyena sāmikaṃ paṭijaggi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, he had a son named Sotthisena. When the son came of age, the king established him in the viceroyalty. His chief queen was named Sambulā, who possessed supreme beauty and was endowed with bodily radiance, shining like a lamp flame in a windless place. In the course of time, leprosy arose on Sotthisena’s body, and physicians were unable to cure him. As the leprosy festered, he became repulsive and, falling into remorse, he thought, “What use is kingship to me? I will die a protectorless death in the forest.” Having informed his father, King Brahmadatta, he abandoned the delightful gold-palace and the women's quarters and departed. Although Queen Sambulā was urged by many means to turn back, she would not, saying, “I will care for my lord in the forest,” and she departed together with the prince. Having entered the forest, in a place with abundant and easily found roots and fruits, with shade and water, he built a leaf-hut and took up residence. The princess cared for him. How? Rising early in the morning, she would sweep the hermitage, set out water for drinking and use, and offer him a tooth-stick and water for washing his face. After he had rinsed his mouth, she would grind various medicinal herbs and apply them to the prince's sores, feed him sweet and delicious fruits, and after he had rinsed his mouth and washed his hands, she would say, “Be diligent, my lord,” and pay homage to him. Then, taking a basket, a digging stick, a hook, and a pole, she would enter the forest for fruits. Having brought back fruits, she would set them in a suitable place, fetch water in a pot, and bathe Prince Sotthisena with various powders and clays, then again offer him sweet fruits. At the conclusion of his meal, she would offer him scented water. Then she herself would eat some fruits, prepare a wooden bed, and when the prince lay down on it, she would wash his feet. Having performed the ministering of his head, back, and limbs, she would go to the side of his bed and lie down. In this way, she cared for her husband.

Sā [V 5.0084] ekadivasaṃ araññe phalāphalaṃ āharantī ekaṃ girikandaraṃ disvā sīsato pacchiṃ otāretvā kandaratīre ṭhapetvā “nhāyissāmī”ti otaritvā haliddāya sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭetvā nhatvā sudhotasarīrā uttaritvā vākacīraṃ nivāsetvā kandaratīre aṭṭhāsi. Athassā sarīrappabhāya vanaṃ ekobhāsaṃ ahosi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko dānavo gocaratthāya caranto taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā gāthādvayaṃ āha –

One day, while gathering fruits in the forest, she saw a mountain glen. Taking her basket down from her head, she placed it at the edge of the glen and, thinking, “I will bathe,” she went down into the water. She rubbed her body with turmeric powder, bathed, and with her body thoroughly cleansed, she came out from the water, put on a bark garment, and stood at the edge of the glen. At that moment, from the radiance of her body, the entire forest became lit up. At that moment, a dānava who was roaming in search of prey saw Princess Sambulā and, his heart captivated, desiring to ask her story, he spoke these two verses:

297.

297.

“Kā vedhamānā girikandarāyaṃ, ekā tuvaṃ tiṭṭhasi saṃhitūru;

Puṭṭhāsi me pāṇipameyyamajjhe, akkhāhi me nāmañca bandhave ca.

“Who are you, trembling, standing alone in this mountain glen, O lady with beautiful thighs? You with a waist measurable by a hand-span, I ask you: tell me your name and your relatives.”

298.

298.

“Obhāsayaṃ vanaṃ rammaṃ, sīhabyagghanisevitaṃ;

Kā vā tvamasi kalyāṇi, kassa vā tvaṃ sumajjhime;

Abhivādemi taṃ bhadde, dānavāhaṃ namatthu te”ti.

“Illuminating this lovely forest, frequented by lions and tigers, who are you, O lovely one? To whom do you belong, O slender-waisted lady? I greet you, O gracious lady. I am a dānava. Homage to you!”

Tattha kā vedhamānāti nhānamattatāya sītabhāvena kampamānā. Saṃhitūrūti sampiṇḍitūru uttamaūrulakkhaṇe. Pāṇipameyyamajjheti [P 5.0090] hatthena minitabbamajjhe. Kā vā tvanti kā nāma vā tvaṃ bhavasi. Abhivādemīti vandāmi. Dānavāhanti ahaṃ eko dānavo, ayaṃ namakkāro tava atthu, añjaliṃ te paggaṇhāmīti avaca.

Herein, ‘who, trembling’ (kā vedhamānā) means trembling due to the coldness of just having bathed. ‘With thighs held close’ (saṃhitūrū) means with excellent thighs characterized by the mark of beauty. ‘With a waist measurable by a hand-span’ (pāṇipameyyamajjhe) means with a waist that can be grasped by the hands. ‘Who are you?’ (kā vā tvaṃ) means ‘What is your name?’ ‘I greet you’ (abhivādemi) means ‘I pay homage.’ ‘I am a dānava’ (dānavāhaṃ) means ‘I am a dānava; may this homage be to you; I raise my joined palms to you.’

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing the words of the dānava, Sambulā wished to inform him of the facts and spoke these three verses:

299.

299.

“Yo putto kāsirājassa, sotthisenoti taṃ vidū;

Tassāhaṃ sambulā bhariyā, evaṃ jānāhi dānava;

Abhivādemi taṃ bhante, sambulāhaṃ namatthu te.

“He who is the son of the king of Kāsi, they know him as Sotthisena. I am his wife, Sambulā; know this, O dānava. I greet you, venerable sir; I am Sambulā, homage to you.”

300.

300.

“Vedehaputto bhaddante, vane vasati āturo;

Tamahaṃ rogasammattaṃ, ekā ekaṃ upaṭṭhahaṃ.

“The son of the Videha princess, venerable sir, dwells in the forest, afflicted. I alone attend to him alone, who is overcome by disease.”

301.

301.

“Ahañca [M 5.0094] vanamuñchāya, madhumaṃsaṃ migābilaṃ;

Yadāharāmi taṃ bhakkho, tassa nūnajja nādhatī”ti.

“And I glean from the forest honey and meat left by predators; when I bring it, that is his food. Surely today he is tormented.”

Tattha [V 5.0085] vedehaputtoti vedeharājadhītāya putto. Rogasammattanti rogapīḷitaṃ. Upaṭṭhahanti upaṭṭhahāmi paṭijaggāmi. “Upaṭṭhitā”tipi pāṭho. Vanamuñchāyāti vanaṃ uñchetvā uñchācariyaṃ caritvā. Madhumaṃsanti nimmakkhikaṃ madhuñca migābilamaṃsañca sīhabyagghamigehi khāditamaṃsato atirittakoṭṭhāsaṃ. Taṃ bhakkhoti yaṃ ahaṃ āharāmi, taṃ bhakkhova so mama sāmiko. Tassa nūnajjāti tassa maññe ajja āhāraṃ alabhamānassa sarīraṃ ātape pakkhittapadumaṃ viya nādhati upatappati milāyati.

Herein, ‘son of the Videha’ (vedehaputto) means the son of the daughter of the king of Videha. ‘Overcome by disease’ (rogasammattanti) means tormented by disease. ‘I attend’ (upaṭṭhahaṃ) means I wait upon and care for him. There is also the reading upaṭṭhitā. ‘Gleaning from the forest’ (vanamuñchāyā) means having gleaned in the forest. ‘Honey and meat’ (madhumaṃsaṃ) means honey free from flies and meat from the lairs of predators, the leftover portion from meat eaten by lions, tigers, and other beasts. ‘That is his food’ (taṃ bhakkho) means: whatever I bring, that is the food of my husband. ‘Surely today he’ (tassa nūnajjā) means: I think today, not receiving food, his body is tormented and withers like a lotus cast in the sun.

Tato paraṃ dānavassa ca tassā ca vacanapaṭivacanagāthāyo honti –

Thereafter, the dānava, wishing to entice the princess, spoke this verse:

302.

302.

“Kiṃ vane rājaputtena, āturena karissasi;

Sambule pariciṇṇena, ahaṃ bhattā bhavāmi te.

“What will you do in the forest with that afflicted prince whom you serve, O Sambulā? I will become your husband.”

303.

303.

“Sokaṭṭāya durattāya, kiṃ rūpaṃ vijjate mama;

Aññaṃ pariyesa bhaddante, abhirūpataraṃ mayā.

Wishing to reject the words of the dānava who spoke thus enticingly, Princess Sambulā said: “Afflicted by sorrow and in a wretched state, what beauty is there in me? Seek another, good sir, one more beautiful than I.”

304.

304.

“Ehimaṃ girimāruyha, bhariyā me catussatā;

Tāsaṃ tvaṃ pavarā hohi, sabbakāmasamiddhinī.

When rejected thus by Princess Sambulā, the dānava, wishing to entice her through threats, spoke these three verses: “Come, ascend this mountain. I have four hundred wives; you shall be the foremost among them, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.”

305.

305.

“Nūna tārakavaṇṇābhe, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi;

Sabbaṃ taṃ pacuraṃ mayhaṃ, ramassvajja mayā saha.

“Surely, O you who shine like a star, whatever you desire in your mind, I have all that in abundance. Enjoy yourself with me today.”

306.

306.

“No [P 5.0091] ce tuvaṃ maheseyyaṃ, sambule kārayissasi;

Alaṃ tvaṃ pātarāsāya, paṇhe bhakkhā bhavissasi.

“If you will not accept the status of my chief queen, O Sambulā, you will be enough for my breakfast; you will become my food.”

307.

307.

“Tañca sattajaṭo luddo, kaḷāro purisādako;

Vane nāthaṃ apassantiṃ, sambulaṃ aggahī bhuje.

After speaking thus enticingly, he seized the hand of Princess Sambulā, and she fell into great sorrow. To clarify this matter, the Blessed One said: “Then that cruel man-eater with seven matted locks and protruding teeth seized Sambulā by the arm, as she was in the forest without a protector.”

308.

308.

“Adhipannā pisācena, luddenāmisacakkhunā;

Sā ca sattuvasaṃ pattā, patimevānusocati.

The Blessed One spoke these two verses: “Overcome by the cruel dānava with his lustful eye, she fell under the power of her enemy, yet she grieved only for her husband.”

309.

309.

“Na [V 5.0086][M 5.0095] me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, yaṃ maṃ khādeyya rakkhaso;

Yañca me ayyaputtassa, mano hessati aññathā.

“This is not so great a sorrow for me—that the rakkhasa might devour me—as that the mind of my noble lord might become otherwise (towards me).”

310.

310.

“Na santi devā pavasanti nūna, na hi nūna santi idha lokapālā;

Sahasā karontānamasaññatānaṃ, na hi nūna santi paṭisedhitāro”ti.

“Surely there are no gods; they must be away! Surely there are no World-Protectors here! For those who act violently and without restraint, surely there are none to restrain them.”

Tattha pariciṇṇenāti tena āturena pariciṇṇena kiṃ karissasi. Sokaṭṭāyāti sokāturāya. “Sokaṭṭhāyā”tipi pāṭho, soke ṭhitāyāti attho. Durattāyāti duggatakapaṇabhāvappattāya attabhāvāya. Ehimanti mā tvaṃ durattāmhīti cintayi, etaṃ mama girimhi dibbavimānaṃ, ehi imaṃ giriṃ āruha. Catussatāti tasmiṃ me vimāne aparāpi catussatā bhariyāyo atthi. Sabbaṃ tanti yaṃ kiñci upabhogaparibhogavatthābharaṇādikaṃ icchasi, sabbaṃ taṃ nūna mayhaṃ pacuraṃ bahuṃ sulabhaṃ, tasmā mā kapaṇāmhīti cintayi, ehi mayā saha ramassūti vadati.

Herein, whom you serve means: what will you do with that afflicted one whom you serve? Afflicted by sorrow means tormented by sorrow. There is also the reading sokaṭṭhāyā, meaning abiding in sorrow. In a wretched state means having attained a miserable and wretched state of existence. Come: Do not think, ‘I am wretched.’ This is my divine mansion on the mountain; come, ascend this mountain. Four hundred: In that mansion of mine there are another four hundred wives. All that: Whatever things for use and enjoyment, garments, ornaments, and so on, you desire, I surely have all that in abundance, plentiful and easy to get. Therefore do not think, ‘I am wretched’; come, enjoy yourself with me, he says.

Maheseyyanti, “bhadde, sambule no ce me tvaṃ mahesibhāvaṃ kāressasi, pariyattā tvaṃ mama pātarāsāya, tena taṃ balakkārena vimānaṃ nessāmi, tatra maṃ asaṅgaṇhantī mama sve pātova bhakkhā bhavissasī”ti evaṃ vatvā so sattahi jaṭāhi samannāgato luddako dāruṇo nikkhantadanto taṃ tasmiṃ vane kiñci attano nāthaṃ apassantiṃ sambulaṃ bhuje aggahesi. Adhipannāti ajjhotthaṭā. Āmisacakkhunāti kilesalolena. Patimevāti attano acintetvā patimeva anusocati. Mano hessatīti maṃ cirāyantiṃ viditvā aññathā cittaṃ bhavissati. Na santi devāti idaṃ sā dānavena bhuje gahitā devatujjhāpanaṃ karontī āha. Lokapālāti evarūpānaṃ sīlavantīnaṃ patidevatānaṃ pālakā lokapālā nūna idha loke na santīti paridevati.

Chief-queenship: “Good Sambulā, if you will not accept the state of being my chief queen, you are sufficient for my breakfast. Therefore I will take you by force to my mansion; there, if you do not accept me, you will become my food tomorrow morning.” So saying, that cruel, fierce hunter with seven matted locks and protruding teeth seized Sambulā by the arm in that forest, as she saw no protector for herself. Overcome means overwhelmed. With an eye for flesh means greedy with defilement. Only for her husband: not thinking of herself, she grieves only for her husband. His mind will become otherwise: “Knowing that I am delayed, his mind will be altered.” There are no gods: this she said, seized by the arm by the dānava, reproaching the gods. World-Protectors: “Protectors of such virtuous women devoted to their husbands—such World-Protectors surely do not exist in this world,” thus she laments.

Athassā [P 5.0092] sīlatejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi, paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vajiraṃ ādāya vegena gantvā dānavassa matthake ṭhatvā itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then, by the power of her virtue, Sakka’s abode trembled, and the Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on it, understood the cause. Taking his thunderbolt, he went swiftly, and standing over the dānava’s head, he spoke the next verse:

311.

311.

“Itthīnamesā [V 5.0087][M 5.0096] pavarā yasassinī, santā samā aggirivuggatejā;

Tañce tuvaṃ rakkhasādesi kaññaṃ, muddhā ca hi sattadhā te phaleyya;

Mā tvaṃ dahī muñca patibbatāyā”ti.

“This woman is the best of women, glorious, peaceful, composed, and as radiant as a blazing fire. If you, rakkhasa, should eat this maiden, your head would surely split into seven pieces. Do not torment her! Release this woman devoted to her husband.”

Tattha santāti upasantā, atha vā paṇḍitā ñāṇasampannā. Samāti kāyavisamādivirahitā. Adesīti khādasi. Phaleyyāti iminā me indavajirena paharitvā muddhā bhijjetha. Mā tvaṃ dahīti tvaṃ imaṃ patibbataṃ mā tāpeyyāsīti.

Herein, 'peaceful' means calmed, or wise and endowed with knowledge. 'Composed' means free from bodily imbalance and the like. 'Harm' (adesi) means you eat. 'Would split' means: 'Struck by this thunderbolt of mine, your head would be split.' 'Do not torment' means: you should not cause distress to this woman devoted to her husband.

Taṃ sutvā dānavo sambulaṃ vissajjesi. Sakko “punapi esa evarūpaṃ kareyyā”ti cintetvā dānavaṃ devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā puna anāgamanāya tatiye pabbatantare vissajjesi, rājadhītaraṃ appamādena ovaditvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Rājadhītāpi atthaṅgate sūriye candālokena assamaṃ pāpuṇi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā aṭṭha gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the dānava released Sambulā. Sakka thought, “He might do such a thing again,” and so he bound the dānava with a divine chain and released him in a third mountain range, never to return. Having advised the princess about heedfulness, he returned to his own place. When the sun had set, the princess reached the hermitage by the light of the moon. The Teacher, making this matter clear, spoke eight verses:

312.

312.

“Sā ca assamamāgacchi, pamuttā purisādakā;

Nīḷaṃ paḷinaṃ sakuṇīva, gatasiṅgaṃva ālayaṃ.

And she came to the hermitage, freed from the man-eater, like a bird to its deserted nest, like a cow to the empty stall where its young calf is gone.

313.

313.

“Sā tattha paridevesi, rājaputtī yasassinī;

Sambulā utumattakkhā, vane nāthaṃ apassantī.

There the glorious princess lamented, Sambulā with eyes dimmed by distress, not seeing her protector in the forest.

314.

314.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe vande, sampannacaraṇe ise;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā.

“I pay homage to the ascetics and brahmins, the seers of accomplished conduct. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

315.

315.

“Vande sīhe ca byagghe ca, ye ca aññe vane migā;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā.

“I pay homage to the lions and tigers, and to whatever other beasts are in the forest. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

316.

316.

“Tiṇā latāni osajho, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā.

“I pay homage to the grasses, vines, and herbs, to the mountains and the forests. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

317.

317.

“Vande indīvarīsāmaṃ, rattiṃ nakkhattamāliniṃ;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā.

“I pay homage to the night, dark as a blue lotus, garlanded with constellations. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

318.

318.

“Vande [V 5.0088][P 5.0093][M 5.0097] bhāgīrathiṃ gaṅgaṃ, savantīnaṃ paṭiggahaṃ;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā.

“I pay homage to the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, the receptacle of flowing rivers. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

319.

319.

“Vande ahaṃ pabbatarājaseṭṭhaṃ, himavantaṃ siluccayaṃ;

Rājaputtaṃ apassantī, tumhaṃmhi saraṇaṃ gatā”ti.

“I pay homage to the Himavant, best of mountain kings, a mass of rock. Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge.”

Tattha nīḷaṃ paḷinaṃ sakuṇīvāti yathā sakuṇikā mukhatuṇḍakena gocaraṃ gahetvā kenaci upaddavena sakuṇapotakānaṃ paḷinattā paḷinaṃ sakuṇinīḷaṃ āgaccheyya, yathā vā gatasiṅgaṃ nikkhantavacchakaṃ ālayaṃ suññaṃ vacchakasālaṃ vacchagiddhinī dhenu āgaccheyya, evaṃ suññaṃ assamaṃ āgacchīti attho. Tadā hi sotthiseno sambulāya ciramānāya “itthiyo nāma lolā, paccāmittampi me gahetvā āgaccheyyā”ti parisaṅkanto paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā gacchantaraṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Utumattakkhāti sokavegasañjātena uṇhena utunā mandalocanā. Apassantīti tasmiṃ vane nāthaṃ attano patiṃ apassantī ito cito ca sandhāvamānā paridevesi.

Herein, 'like a bird to its deserted nest' means: just as a mother bird, having taken food with its beak, might return to find the nest deserted because the young ones have fled due to some danger; or as a cow yearning for her calf might return to the empty stall from which the calf has gone; so she came to the empty hermitage—this is the meaning. For at that time, since Sambulā was taking so long, Sotthisena became suspicious, thinking: “Women are indeed fickle; she might even bring my enemy along with her.” He left the leaf-hut, entered a thicket, and sat down. That is why this was said. 'With eyes dimmed by distress' means eyes with weakened vision due to the heat born of intense grief. 'Not seeing' means: not seeing her protector, her own husband, in that forest, she ran about here and there, lamenting.

Tattha samaṇe brāhmaṇeti samitapāpabāhitapāpe samaṇe brāhmaṇe. Sampannacaraṇeti saha sīlena aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ vasena ca sampannacaraṇe ise vandeti evaṃ vatvā rājaputtaṃ apassantī tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā amhi. Sace me sāmikassa nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ jānātha, ācikkhathāti paridevesīti attho. Sesagāthāsupi eseva nayo. Tiṇā latāni osajhoti antopheggubahisāratiṇāni ca latāni ca antosāraosadhiyo ca. Imaṃ gāthaṃ tiṇādīsu nibbattadevatā sandhāyāha. Indīvarīsāmanti indīvarīpupphasamānavaṇṇaṃ. Nakkhattamālininti nakkhattapaṭipāṭisamannāgataṃ. Tumhaṃmhīti rattiṃ sandhāya tampi amhīti āha. Bhāgīrathiṃ gaṅganti evaṃpariyāyanāmikaṃ gaṅgaṃ. Savantīnanti aññāsaṃ bahūnaṃ nadīnaṃ paṭiggāhikaṃ. Gaṅgāya nibbattadevataṃ sandhāyevamāha. Himavantepi eseva nayo.

Herein, 'ascetics and brahmins' means those who have pacified and dispelled evil. 'Of accomplished conduct' means seers endowed with virtue and the eight meditative attainments. The meaning is that she lamented, saying: “Not seeing the prince, I have gone to you for refuge. If you know the place where my master is, please tell me.” The same method applies to the remaining verses. 'Grasses, vines, and herbs' refers to grasses with soft interiors and hard exteriors, vines, and herbs with hard substances inside. She spoke this verse addressing the deities residing in the grasses and so on. 'Dark as a blue lotus' means having a color like a blue lotus flower. 'Garlanded with constellations' means endowed with a sequence of stars. 'To you' refers to the night. 'The Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā' is the Gaṅgā referred to by this synonym. 'Receptacle of flowing rivers' means the recipient of many other rivers. She spoke thus with reference to the deity residing in the Gaṅgā. The same applies to the Himavant.

Taṃ evaṃ paridevamānaṃ disvā sotthiseno cintesi – “ayaṃ ativiya paridevati, na kho panassā bhāvaṃ jānāmi, sace mayi sinehena evaṃ karoti[M 5.0098], hadayampissā phaleyya, pariggaṇhissāmi tāva na”nti gantvā paṇṇasāladvāre nisīdi. Sāpi paridevamānāva paṇṇasāladvāraṃ gantvā tassa pāde vanditvā “kuhiṃ gatosi, devā”ti āha. Atha naṃ so, “bhadde[V 5.0089], tvaṃ aññesu [P 5.0094] divasesu na imāya velāya āgacchasi, ajja atisāyaṃ āgatāsī”ti pucchanto gāthamāha –

Seeing her lamenting thus, Sotthisena thought: “She is lamenting excessively, but I do not know her true state. If she is doing this out of affection for me, her heart might break. I will first test her.” He went and sat at the door of the leaf-hut. Still lamenting, she went to the door of the leaf-hut, paid homage at his feet, and said, “Where have you been, lord?” Then, questioning her, he said: “Good lady, on other days you do not come at this time; today you have come very late,” and he spoke this verse:

320.

320.

“Atisāyaṃ vatāgañchi, rājaputti yasassini;

Kena nujja samāgacchi, ko te piyataro mayā”ti.

“Very late indeed have you come, O illustrious princess. With whom did you meet today? Who is dearer to you than I?”

Atha naṃ sā “ahaṃ, ayyaputta, phalāphalāni ādāya āgacchantī ekaṃ dānavaṃ passiṃ, so mayi paṭibaddhacitto hutvā maṃ hatthe gaṇhitvā ‘sace mama vacanaṃ na karosi, khādissāmi ta’nti āha, ahaṃ tāya velāya taññeva anusocantī evaṃ paridevi”nti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then she said to him: “My lord, while I was coming back carrying various fruits, I saw a dānava. He became infatuated with me, seized me by the hand, and said, ‘If you do not do my bidding, I will devour you.’ At that moment, grieving only for you, I lamented thus,” and she spoke this verse:

321.

321.

“Idaṃ khohaṃ tadāvocaṃ, gahitā tena sattunā;

Na me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, yaṃ maṃ khādeyya rakkhaso;

Yañca me ayyaputtassa, mano hessati aññathā”ti.

“This indeed I said then, seized by that enemy: ‘This is not such a sorrow to me, that the rākṣasa might devour me, as that the mind of my noble husband might become otherwise.’”

Athassa sesampi pavattiṃ ārocentī “tena panāhaṃ, deva, dānavena gahitā attānaṃ vissajjāpetuṃ asakkontī devatujjhāpanakammaṃ akāsiṃ, atha sakko vajirahattho āgantvā ākāse ṭhito dānavaṃ santajjetvā maṃ vissajjāpetvā taṃ devasaṅkhalikāya bandhitvā tatiye pabbatantare khipitvā pakkāmi, evāhaṃ sakkaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhi”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā sotthiseno, “bhadde, hotu, mātugāmassa antare saccaṃ nāma dullabhaṃ, himavante hi bahū vanacarakatāpasavijjādharādayo santi, ko tuyhaṃ saddahissatī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then, relating the rest of the story, she said: “Then, lord, having been seized by that dānava and being unable to get myself released, I performed an act of appealing to the devas. Then Sakka, wielder of the thunderbolt, came and, standing in the sky, threatened the dānava and had me released. He bound him with a divine chain, threw him into a third mountain gorge, and departed. Thus, by relying on Sakka, I obtained my life.” Hearing this, Sotthisena said: “Good lady, let it be. Among womankind, truth is indeed hard to find. For in the Himalayas there are many forest-wanderers, ascetics, sorcerers, and the like—who will believe your word?” And he spoke this verse:

322.

322.

“Corīnaṃ bahubuddhīnaṃ, yāsu saccaṃ sudullabhaṃ;

Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno, macchassevodake gata”nti.

“Of thievish women of many wiles, among whom truth is very hard to find, their nature is difficult to know, like the track of a fish in the water.”

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “ayyaputta, ahaṃ taṃ asaddahantaṃ mama saccabaleneva tikicchissāmī”ti udakassa kalasaṃ pūretvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā tassa sīse udakaṃ āsiñcantī gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, she said: “My lord, I will cure you, who do not believe me, by the very power of my truth.” Filling a pot with water, she performed an act of truth and, sprinkling the water on his head, spoke this verse:

323.

323.

“Tathā [V 5.0090][P 5.0095][M 5.0099] maṃ saccaṃ pāletu, pālayissati ce mamaṃ;

Yathāhaṃ nābhijānāmi, aññaṃ piyataraṃ tayā;

Etena saccavajjena, byādhi te vūpasammatū”ti.

“May the truth protect me—and it will protect me—as I know no one dearer than you. By this statement of truth, may your illness be appeased!”

Tattha tathā-saddo “ce mama”nti iminā saddhiṃ yojetabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathāhaṃ vadāmi, tathā ce mama vacanaṃ saccaṃ, atha maṃ idānipi pāletu, āyatimpi pālessati, idāni me vacanaṃ suṇātha “yathāhaṃ nābhijānāmī”ti. Potthakesu pana “tathā maṃ saccaṃ pāletī”ti likhitaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi.

Herein, the word ‘tathā’ should be connected with ‘ce mama.’ This is what is said: ‘If my word is true in the way that I speak, then may it protect me now, and it will protect me in the future. Now hear my word: “As I do not know…”’ In the manuscripts, however, it is written ‘tathā maṃ saccaṃ pāletī’ (truth protects me so), but that is not in the commentary.

Evaṃ tāya saccakiriyaṃ katvā udake āsittamatteyeva sotthisenassa kuṭṭhaṃ ambilena dhotaṃ viya tambamalaṃ tāvadeva apagacchi. Te katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā araññā nikkhamma bārāṇasiṃ patvā uyyānaṃ pavisiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā uyyānaṃ gantvā tattheva sotthisenassa chattaṃ ussāpetvā sambulaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne abhisiñcāpetvā nagaraṃ pavesetvā sayaṃ isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā uyyāne vāsaṃ kappesi, rājanivesaneyeva ca nibaddhaṃ bhuñji. Sotthisenopi sambulāya aggamahesiṭṭhānamattameva adāsi, na punassā koci sakkāro ahosi, atthibhāvampissā na aññāsi, aññāheva itthīhi saddhiṃ abhirami. Sambulā sapattidosavasena kisā ahosi upaṇḍupaṇḍukajātā dhamanīsanthatagattā. Sā ekadivasaṃ sokavinodanatthaṃ bhuñjituṃ āgatassa sasuratāpasassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ katabhattakiccaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. So taṃ milātindriyaṃ disvā gāthamāha –

When she had thus performed the act of truth, as soon as the water was sprinkled, Sotthisena's leprosy vanished at that very moment, like copper-rust washed away with acid. After living there for a few days, they left the forest, reached Bārāṇasī, and entered the park. The king, learning of their arrival, went to the park and right there raised the parasol for Sotthisena and had Sambulā consecrated in the position of chief queen. He had them enter the city, while he himself went forth into the ascetic life and took up residence in the park, though he ate regularly at the royal palace. Sotthisena, for his part, gave Sambulā only the position of chief queen; there was no further honor or respect for her, and he did not even acknowledge her presence, but delighted in the company of other women. Sambulā, on account of the neglect due to her co-wives, became thin and pale, her body covered with a network of veins. One day, to dispel her sorrow, she went to her father-in-law, the ascetic, who had come for his meal. After he had finished his meal, she paid homage to him and sat down to one side. Seeing her with her faculties withered, he spoke this verse:

324.

324.

“Ye kuñjarā sattasatā uḷārā, rakkhanti rattindivamuyyutāvudhā;

Dhanuggahānañca satāni soḷasa, kathaṃvidhe passasi bhadde sattavo”ti.

“Those seven hundred magnificent elephants, guarded by warriors with weapons drawn day and night, and those sixteen hundred archers—what kind of enemies do you see, good lady, that you look so fearful?”

Tassattho – bhadde, sambule ye amhākaṃ sattasatā kuñjarā, tesaññeva khandhagatānaṃ yodhānaṃ vasena uyyuttāvudhā, aparāni ca soḷasadhanuggahasatāni [P 5.0096] rattindivaṃ bārāṇasiṃ rakkhanti. Evaṃ surakkhite nagare kathaṃvidhe tvaṃ sattavo passasi. Bhadde, yassā tava sāsaṅkā sappaṭibhayā [M 5.0100] araññā āgatakālepi pabhāsampannaṃ sarīraṃ, idāni pana milātā paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇā ativiya kilantindriyāsi, kassa nāma tvaṃ bhāyasī”ti pucchi.

The meaning is this: “Good Sambulā, our seven hundred elephants have weapons drawn by means of the warriors mounted on their backs, and another sixteen hundred archers guard Bārāṇasī day and night. In such a well-guarded city, what kind of enemies do you see? Good lady, you whose body was endowed with radiance even when you came from the forest anxious and fearful, are now withered, the color of a pale leaf, with faculties utterly exhausted. Of whom indeed are you afraid?” he asked.

Sā [V 5.0091] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “putto te, deva, mayi na purimasadiso”ti vatvā pañca gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, she said, “Your son, O lord, is not the same towards me as he was before,” and she spoke these five verses:

325.

325.

“Alaṅkatāyo padumuttarattacā, virāgitā passati haṃsagaggarā;

Tāsaṃ suṇitvā mitagītavāditaṃ, na dāni me tāta tathā yathā pure.

“He gazes upon adorned women with skin like a lotus-petal, slender-waisted, and with voices sweet as swans. Having heard their measured song and music, now, father, he is not the same towards me as he was before.”

326.

326.

“Suvaṇṇasaṃkaccadharā suviggahā, alaṅkatā mānusiyaccharūpamā;

Senopiyā tāta aninditaṅgiyo, khattiyakaññā paṭilobhayanti naṃ.

“Wearing golden breast-bands, of fine figure, adorned like human nymphs; dear to Sena, father, these khattiya maidens of flawless limbs entice him.”

327.

327.

“Sace ahaṃ tāta tathā yathā pure, patiṃ tamuñchāya punā vane bhare;

Sammānaye maṃ na ca maṃ vimānaye, itopi me tāta tato varaṃ siyā.

“Father, if, as before, I were to support my husband in the forest again by gleaning, he would honor me and not despise me. Father, even that would be better for me than this.”

328.

328.

“Yamannapāne vipulasmi ohite, nārī vimaṭṭhābharaṇā alaṅkatā;

Sabbaṅgupetā patino ca appiyā, abajjha tassā maraṇaṃ tato varaṃ.

“Even when abundant food and drink is set out, if a woman, though adorned with polished ornaments and endowed with every good quality, is unloved by her husband, death would be better for her than that.”

329.

329.

“Api ce daliddā kapaṇā anāḷhiyā, kaṭādutīyā patino ca sā piyā;

Sabbaṅgupetāyapi appiyāya, ayameva seyyā kapaṇāpi yā piyā”ti.

“Even if she is poor, miserable, and destitute, with only a mat for a companion, if she is dear to her husband, that is better than being endowed with all qualities yet unloved. Better is the miserable one who is dear.”

Tattha padumuttarattacāti padumagabbhasadisauttarattacā. Sabbāsaṃ sarīrato suvaṇṇapabhā niccharantīti dīpeti. Virāgitāti vilaggasarīrā, tanumajjhāti [P 5.0097] attho. Haṃsagaggarāti evarūpā haṃsā viya madhurassarā nāriyo passati. Tāsanti [M 5.0101] so tava putto tāsaṃ nārīnaṃ mitagītavāditādīni suṇitvā idāni me, tāta, yathā pure, tathā na pavattatīti vadati. Suvaṇṇasaṃkaccadharāti suvaṇṇamayasaṃkaccālaṅkāradharā. Alaṅkatāti nānālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā. Mānusiyaccharūpamāti mānusiyo accharūpamā. Senopiyāti sotthisenassa piyā. Paṭilobhayanti nanti naṃ tava puttaṃ paṭilobhayanti.

Herein, ‘padumuttarattacā’ means having skin like the interior of a lotus; it indicates that a golden radiance issues from their bodies. ‘Virāgitā’ means with slender bodies; the meaning is slender-waisted. ‘Haṃsagaggarā’ means women with voices as sweet as swans. Regarding ‘Tāsaṃ…’: she is saying, ‘Having heard the measured song and music of those women, your son, father, no longer behaves towards me as he did before.’ ‘Suvaṇṇasaṃkaccadharā’ means wearing ornaments like golden breast-bands. ‘Alaṅkatā’ means adorned with various ornaments. ‘Mānusiyaccharūpamā’ means human women resembling nymphs. ‘Senopiyā’ means dear to Sotthisena. Regarding ‘paṭilobhayanti naṃ’: they entice him, your son.

Sace ahanti, tāta, yathā pure sace ahaṃ punapi taṃ patiṃ tatheva kuṭṭharogena vanaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ uñchāya tasmiṃ vane bhareyyaṃ, punapi maṃ so sammāneyya na vimāneyya, tato me itopi bārāṇasirajjato taṃ araññameva varaṃ siyā sapattidosena sussantiyāti dīpeti. Yamannapāneti yaṃ annapāne. Ohiteti ṭhapite paṭiyatte. Iminā bahunnapānagharaṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ kirassā adhippāyo [V 5.0092] – yā nārī vipulannapāne ghare ekikāva asapatti samānā vimaṭṭhābharaṇā nānālaṅkārehi alaṅkatā sabbehi guṇaṅgehi upetā patino ca appiyā hoti, abajjha gīvāya valliyā vā rajjuyā vā bandhitvā tassā tato gharāvāsato maraṇameva varataranti. Anāḷhīyāti anāḷhā. Kaṭādutīyāti nipajjanakaṭasārakadutiyā. Seyyāti kapaṇāpi samānā yā patino piyā, ayameva uttamāti.

Regarding ‘Sace ahaṃ’: she is showing that, ‘Father, if, as before, I were again to support in that forest by gleaning for that husband who had entered it with leprosy, he would again honor me and not dishonor me. Therefore, for me who am wasting away because of the fault of my co-wives, that very forest would be better than even this kingdom of Bārāṇasī.’ ‘Yamannapāne’ means ‘in food and drink.’ ‘Ohite’ means placed, prepared. By this she indicates a house full of food and drink. This, it seems, is her intention: if a woman in a house with abundant food and drink, alone and without a co-wife, with polished ornaments, adorned with various decorations, and endowed with all good qualities, is unloved by her husband, for her, death by being bound by the neck with a vine or a rope is better than that household life. ‘Anāḷhiyā’ means without refuge. ‘Kaṭādutīyā’ means having a grass sleeping mat as her second. Regarding ‘seyyā’: she who, though destitute, is dear to her husband—this one is the best.

Evaṃ tāya attano parisussanakāraṇe tāpasassa kathite tāpaso rājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, sotthisena tayi kuṭṭharogābhibhūte araññaṃ pavisante tayā saddhiṃ pavisitvā taṃ upaṭṭhahantī attano saccabalena tava rogaṃ vūpasametvā yā te rajje patiṭṭhānakāraṇamakāsi, tassā nāma tvaṃ neva ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ, na nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ jānāsi, ayuttaṃ te kataṃ, mittadubbhikammaṃ nāmetaṃ pāpaka”nti vatvā puttaṃ ovadanto gāthamāha –

When she had thus told the ascetic the reason for her own wasting away, the ascetic had King Sotthisena summoned and said: “My son, Sotthisena, when you were overwhelmed by leprosy and entering the forest, she entered with you and attended on you. By the power of her own truth she healed your disease and was the cause of your establishment in the kingdom. Yet of this very woman you do not even know her standing place or her sitting place. You have done what is improper; this is the evil deed called treachery to a friend.” Saying this, advising his son, he spoke a verse:

330.

330.

“Sudullabhitthī purisassa yā hitā, bhattitthiyā dullabho yo hito ca;

Hitā ca te sīlavatī ca bhariyā, janinda dhammaṃ cara sambulāyā”ti.

“Very rare is a woman who is beneficial to a man, and rare is a husband who is beneficial to his wife. Your wife is both beneficial and virtuous, O king of men; practice righteousness towards Sambulā.”

Tassattho [M 5.0102] – tāta, yā purisassa hitā muducittā anukampikā itthī, yo ca bhattā itthiyā hito kataguṇaṃ jānāti, ubhopete sudullabhā. Ayañca sambulā tuyhaṃ [P 5.0098] hitā ceva sīlasampannā ca, tasmā etissā dhammaṃ cara, kataguṇaṃ jānitvā muducitto hohi, cittamassā paritosehīti.

The meaning is: My son, a woman who is beneficial to a man—gentle-hearted and compassionate—and a husband who is beneficial to his wife and recognizes the good she has done: both of these are very rare. This Sambulā is both beneficial to you and endowed with virtue. Therefore, practice righteousness toward her; recognizing the good she has done, be gentle-hearted and gladden her mind.

Evaṃ so puttassa ovādaṃ datvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Rājā pitari gate sambulaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “bhadde, ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayā kataṃ dosaṃ khama, ito paṭṭhāya sabbissariyaṃ tuyhameva dammī”ti vatvā osānagāthamāha –

Having thus advised his son, he rose from his seat and departed. After his father left, the king had Sambulā summoned and said, “Good lady, forgive the offense I have committed for so long. From now on, I grant you all authority.” Then he spoke this concluding verse:

331.

331.

“Sace tuvaṃ vipule laddhabhoge, issāvatiṇṇā maraṇaṃ upesi;

Ahañca te bhadde imā rājakaññā, sabbe te vacanakarā bhavāmā”ti.

“Should you, my good lady, having obtained vast enjoyments, be overcome by jealousy and approach death, I and these royal maidens—all of us—will be obedient to your word.”

Tassattho – bhadde, sambule sace tvaṃ ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisittā aggamahesiṭṭhānavasena vipule bhoge labhitvāpi issāya otiṇṇā maraṇaṃ upesi, ahañca imā [V 5.0093] ca rājakaññā sabbe tava vacanakarā bhavāma, tvaṃ yathādhippāyaṃ imaṃ rajjaṃ vicārehīti sabbissariyaṃ tassā adāsi.

The meaning is: My good Sambulā, if you, having been set on a heap of jewels and anointed by reason of the position of chief queen, and having obtained vast enjoyments, should still be overcome by jealousy and approach death, I and these royal maidens—all of us—would be obedient to your command. Rule this kingdom as you wish. Thus he granted her full authority.

Tato paṭṭhāya ubho samaggavāsaṃ vasantā dānādīni puññāni karitvā yathākammaṃ gamiṃsu. Tāpaso jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

From then on, the two lived together in harmony, performing meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed on according to their kamma. The ascetic, having developed the meditative attainments and the higher knowledges, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi mallikā patidevatāyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā sambulā mallikā ahosi, sotthiseno kosalarājā, pitā tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: “Monks, not only now but in the past too Mallikā was devoted to her husband.” Then he identified the birth: “At that time Sambulā was Mallikā, Sotthisena was the King of Kosala, and the ascetic father was I myself.”

Sambulājātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Sambulā Jātaka, the Ninth.

[520] 10. Gandhatindukajātakavaṇṇanā

[520] 10. The Commentary on the Gandhatinduka Jātaka

Appamādoti [M 5.0103] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājovādaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Rājovādo heṭṭhā vitthāritova. Atīte pana kapilaraṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagare pañcālo nāma rājā agatigamane ṭhito adhammena pamatto rajjaṃ kāresi. Athassa amaccādayo sabbepi adhammikāva jātā. Balipīḷitā raṭṭhavāsino puttadāre ādāya araññe migā viya cariṃsu, gāmaṭṭhāne gāmo nāma nāhosi. Manussā rājapurisānaṃ [P 5.0099] bhayena divā gehe vasituṃ asakkontā gehāni kaṇṭakasākhāhi parikkhipitvā gehe rattiṃ vasitvā aruṇe uggacchanteyeva araññaṃ pavisanti. Divā rājapurisā vilumpanti, rattiṃ corā. Tadā bodhisatto bahinagare gandhatindukarukkhe devatā hutvā nibbatti, anusaṃvaccharaṃ rañño santikā sahassagghanakaṃ balikammaṃ labhati. So cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā pamatto rajjaṃ kāreti, sakalaraṭṭhaṃ vinassati, ṭhapetvā maṃ añño rājānaṃ patirūpe nivesetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, upakārako cāpi me anusaṃvaccharaṃ sahassagghanakabalinā pūjeti, ovadissāmi na”nti.

“Heedfulness…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning advice to a king. The advice to a king has been explained in detail before. In the past, in the city of Uttara Pañcāla in the Kapila country, a king named Pañcāla, established in the four wrong courses, ruled the kingdom unrighteously and heedlessly. Then all his ministers and others also became unrighteous. Oppressed by taxes, the inhabitants of the country took their children and wives and wandered in the forest like deer. In the village areas, there were no villages to speak of. Fearing the king’s men, people were unable to stay in their homes by day; having surrounded their houses with thorny branches, they would stay in their houses at night and enter the forest as soon as dawn was breaking. By day the king’s men would plunder them, by night thieves. At that time the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity in a fragrant tinduka tree outside the city. Each year he received from the king an offering worth a thousand. He thought: “This king rules heedlessly and the entire country is being ruined. Apart from me, there is no one capable of establishing the king in what is proper. And he is a benefactor to me, honoring me annually with an offering worth a thousand. I will advise him.”

So rattibhāge rañño sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā ussīsakapasse ṭhatvā obhāsaṃ vissajjetvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ bālasūriyaṃ viya jalamānaṃ disvā “kosi tvaṃ, kena vā kāraṇena idhāgatosī”ti pucchi. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “mahārāja, ahaṃ gandhatindukadevatā, ‘tuyhaṃ ovādaṃ dassāmī’ti āgatomhī”ti āha. “Kiṃ nāma ovādaṃ dassasī”ti [V 5.0094] evaṃ vutte mahāsatto, “mahārāja, tvaṃ pamatto hutvā rajjaṃ kāresi, tena te sakalaraṭṭhaṃ hataviluttaṃ viya vinaṭṭhaṃ, rājāno nāma pamādena rajjaṃ kārentā sakalaraṭṭhassa sāmino na honti, diṭṭheva dhamme vināsaṃ patvā samparāye puna mahāniraye nibbattanti. Tesu ca pamādaṃ āpannesu antojanā bahijanāpissa pamattāva honti, tasmā raññā atirekena appamattena bhavitabba”nti vatvā dhammadesanaṃ paṭṭhapento imā ekādasa gāthā āha –

At night, he entered the king’s royal chamber, stood beside his pillow, and, emitting a radiance, remained poised in the air. The king, seeing him shining like the young sun, asked, “Who are you? For what reason have you come here?” Hearing his words, the deity replied, “Great king, I am the deity of the fragrant tinduka tree. I have come to give you advice.” When asked, “What advice will you give?” the Great Being said, “Great king, you rule heedlessly, and because of this your entire kingdom is ruined as if it were plundered and destroyed. Kings who rule with heedlessness are not masters of their entire kingdom; they meet with ruin in this very life and are reborn in a great hell in the next. When they fall into heedlessness, those within and without the palace are also heedless. Therefore, a king must be exceptionally heedful.” Beginning his Dhamma discourse, he spoke these eleven verses:

332.

332.

“Appamādo amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ;

Appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā.

“Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.”

333.

333.

“Madā [M 5.0104] pamādo jāyetha, pamādā jāyate khayo;

Khayā padosā jāyanti, mā mado bharatūsabha.

“From intoxication heedlessness is born; from heedlessness, ruin is born; from ruin, faults arise. O bull among the Bharatas, do not be intoxicated.”

334.

334.

“Bahū hi khattiyā jīnā, atthaṃ raṭṭhaṃ pamādino;

Athopi gāmino gāmā, anagārā agārino.

“Indeed, many heedless nobles have been ruined in their welfare and their kingdom; so too have village headmen in their villages, and heedless renunciants and householders alike have met with ruin.”

335.

335.

“Khattiyassa [P 5.0100] pamattassa, raṭṭhasmiṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Sabbe bhogā vinassanti, rañño taṃ vuccate aghaṃ.

“O increaser of the kingdom, for a heedless noble in his realm, all possessions perish; that is called the king’s misfortune.”

336.

336.

“Nesa dhammo mahārāja, ativelaṃ pamajjasi;

Iddhaṃ phītaṃ janapadaṃ, corā viddhaṃsayanti naṃ.

“This is not the proper way, O great king, that you are so exceedingly heedless; thieves are destroying this prosperous and flourishing country.”

337.

337.

“Na te puttā bhavissanti, na hiraññaṃ na dhāniyaṃ;

Raṭṭhe viluppamānamhi, sabbabhogehi jīyasi.

“You will have no sons to continue your line, no gold, no grain; while the kingdom is being plundered, you are being deprived of all your possessions.”

338.

338.

“Sabbabhogā parijiṇṇaṃ, rājānaṃ vāpi khattiyaṃ;

Ñātimittā suhajjā ca, na taṃ maññanti māniyaṃ.

“A king or noble whose possessions are all exhausted—his kinsmen, friends, and companions no longer consider him worthy of honor.”

339.

339.

“Hatthārohā anīkaṭṭhā, rathikā pattikārakā;

Tamevamupajīvantā, na taṃ maññanti māniyaṃ.

“Elephant riders, royal guards, charioteers, and foot soldiers—even though they live in dependence on him, they do not consider him worthy of honor.”

340.

340.

“Asaṃvihitakammantaṃ[V 5.0095], bālaṃ dummantimantinaṃ;

Sirī jahati dummedhaṃ, jiṇṇaṃva urago tacaṃ.

“The fool with his affairs unmanaged, poorly advised and witless—fortune forsakes that king, as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.”

341.

341.

“Susaṃvihitakammantaṃ, kāluṭṭhāyiṃ atanditaṃ;

Sabbe bhogābhivaḍḍhanti, gāvo sausabhāmiva.

“For a king with his affairs well-managed, who rises at the proper time and is untiring—all his possessions increase, like a herd of cows with a bull.”

342.

342.

“Upassutiṃ mahārāja, raṭṭhe janapade cara;

Tattha disvā ca sutvā ca, tato taṃ paṭipajjasī”ti.

“Go incognito, great king, and wander through the kingdom and the country; having seen and heard for yourself, you should then act accordingly.”

Tattha appamādoti satiyā avippavāso. Amatapadanti amatassa nibbānassa padaṃ adhigamakāraṇaṃ. Maccuno padanti maraṇassa kāraṇaṃ. Pamattā hi vipassanaṃ avaḍḍhetvā appaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ pattuṃ asakkontā punappunaṃ saṃsāre jāyanti ceva mīyanti ca, tasmā pamādo maccuno padaṃ nāma[M 5.0105]. Na mīyantīti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā appaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ pattā puna saṃsāre anibbattattā na mīyanti nāma. Ye pamattāti, mahārāja, ye puggalā pamattā, te yathā matā, tatheva daṭṭhabbā. Kasmā? Akiccasādhanatāya. Matassapi hi “ahaṃ dānaṃ dassāmi, sīlaṃ rakkhissāmi, uposathakammaṃ karissāmi, kalyāṇakammaṃ pūressāmī”ti ābhogo vā patthanā vā pariyuṭṭhānaṃ vā natthi apagataviññāṇattā, pamattassapi appamādābhāvāti tasmā ubhopete ekasadisāva.

Therein, ‘heedfulness’ is the non-departure of mindfulness. ‘The path to the Deathless’ is the path that is the cause for attaining the Deathless, Nibbāna. ‘The path of death’ is the cause of death. For the heedless, being unable to develop insight and attain the state of non-rebirth, are repeatedly born and die in saṃsāra. Therefore, heedlessness is called the path of death. ‘They do not die’ means: those who develop insight and attain the state of non-rebirth are not born again in saṃsāra and thus are said not to die. ‘Those who are heedless’ means: O great king, those persons who are heedless should be regarded as if they were dead. Why? Because of their failure to accomplish what should be done. For a dead person has no thought, aspiration, or impulse to give alms, observe the precepts, perform the Uposatha observance, or complete wholesome deeds, since their consciousness has departed. So too for a heedless person, due to their lack of heedfulness. Therefore, both are exactly the same.

Madāti, mahārāja, ārogyayobbanajīvitamadasaṅkhātā tividhā madā pamādo nāma jāyati. So madappatto pamādāpanno pāṇātipātādīni pāpakammāni karoti. Atha naṃ rājāno chindāpenti vā hanāpenti vā, sabbaṃ vā dhanamassa haranti, evamassa pamādā ñātidhanajīvitakkhayo jāyati. Puna so dhanakkhayaṃ [P 5.0101] vā yasakkhayaṃ vā patto jīvituṃ asakkonto jīvitavuttatthāya kāyaduccaritādīni karoti, iccassa khayā padosā jāyanti, tena taṃ vadāmi mā mado bharatūsabhāti, raṭṭhabhārakajeṭṭhaka bharatūsabha mā pamādamāpajjīti attho. Atthaṃ raṭṭhanti janapadavāsīnaṃ vuddhiñceva sakalaraṭṭhañca bahū pamādino jīnā. Tesaṃ āvibhāvatthāya khantivādijātaka-mātaṅgajātaka-bharujātaka-sarabhaṅgajātaka-cetiyajātakāni kathetabbāni. Gāminoti gāmabhojakāpi te gāmāpi bahū pamādadosena jīnā parihīnā vinaṭṭhā. Anagārā agārinoti pabbajitāpi pabbajitapaṭipattito, gihīpi gharāvāsato ceva dhanadhaññādīhi ca bahū jīnā parihīnāti vadati. Taṃ vuccate aghanti, mahārāja, yasabhogaparihāni [V 5.0096] nāmetaṃ rañño dukkhaṃ vuccati. Bhogābhāvena hi niddhanassa yaso hāyati, hīnayaso mahantaṃ kāyikacetasikadukkhaṃ pāpuṇāti.

‘From intoxication’ means: O great king, from the threefold intoxication—with health, youth, and life—heedlessness is born. One overcome by intoxication and fallen into heedlessness commits evil deeds such as taking life. Then kings have him executed or killed, or they confiscate all his wealth. Thus, from his heedlessness, the loss of his relatives, wealth, and life is born. Then, having suffered the loss of wealth or fame and being unable to support himself, he engages in bodily misconduct and the like to maintain his life. Thus for him, from decline, vices are born. Therefore I say, ‘Let not intoxication overcome you, O bull among the Bharatas,’ the meaning of which is: ‘O chief bearer of the kingdom’s burden, O bull among the Bharatas, do not fall into heedlessness.’ ‘Their welfare and their kingdom’: this means the prosperity of the country-dwellers and the entire kingdom is lost by many heedless ones. To make this clear, the Khantivādi Jātaka, the Mātaṅga Jātaka, the Bharu Jātaka, the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, and the Cetiya Jātaka should be related. ‘Village headmen lost their villages’: both village headmen and their villages are lost, diminished, and destroyed through the fault of heedlessness. ‘Renunciants their homelessness, and householders their homes’: this means that many renunciants fall away from the renunciant’s practice, and many householders fall away from the household life and are ruined in regard to wealth, grain, and so on. ‘That is called the king’s misfortune’: O great king, this means that the decline of his fame and possessions is called a king’s suffering. For when one is poor through lack of possessions, one’s fame diminishes, and with diminished fame one experiences great physical and mental suffering.

Nesa dhammoti, mahārāja, esa porāṇakarājūnaṃ dhammo na hoti. Iddhaṃ phītanti annapānādinā samiddhaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādinā phītaṃ pupphitaṃ. Na te puttāti, mahārāja, paveṇipālakā te puttā na bhavissanti. Raṭṭhavāsino hi “adhammikarañño esa putto, kiṃ amhākaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ karissati, nāssa chattaṃ dassāmā”ti chattaṃ na denti. Evametesaṃ paveṇipālakā puttā na honti nāma. Parijiṇṇanti parihīnaṃ. Rājānaṃ vāpīti sacepi so rājā hoti, atha naṃ rājānaṃ samānampi. Māniyanti “ayaṃ rājā”ti garucittena [M 5.0106] sammānetabbaṃ katvā na maññanti. Upajīvantāti upanissāya jīvantāpi ete ettakā janā garucittena maññitabbaṃ na maññanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Adhammikabhāvena.

‘This is not the Dhamma,’ O great king; this is not the Dhamma of the ancient kings. ‘Prosperous and flourishing’ means prosperous with food and drink and the like, flourishing with gold and silver and so forth, blossomed. ‘They will not be your sons,’ O great king; your sons who should be guardians of the lineage will not be so. For the inhabitants of the realm say, “This is the son of an unrighteous king; what good will he do for us? We will not give him the umbrella.” Thus they do not give him the umbrella. In this way, those sons who should be guardians of the lineage are not truly sons. ‘Worn out’ means diminished. ‘Even a king’: even though he is a king, they do not esteem him. ‘They do not esteem him’ means they do not regard him with a respectful mind, thinking, “This is the king,” as one who should be honored. ‘Those who live depending on him’: even these many people who live in dependence on him do not regard him with a respectful mind. For what reason? Because of his unrighteousness.

Sirīti yasavibhavo. Tacanti yathā urago jiṇṇatacaṃ jigucchanto jahati, na puna oloketi, evaṃ tādisaṃ rājānaṃ sirī jahati. Susaṃvihitakammantanti kāyadvārādīhi pāpakammaṃ akarontaṃ. Abhivaḍḍhantīti abhimukhaṃ gacchantā vaḍḍhanti. Sausabhāmivāti sausabhā iva. Appamattassa hi sausabhajeṭṭhako gogaṇo viya bhogā vaḍḍhanti. Upassutinti janapadacārittasavanāya cārikaṃ attano sakalaraṭṭhe ca janapade ca cara. Tatthāti tasmiṃ raṭṭhe caranto daṭṭhabbaṃ disvā sotabbaṃ sutvā attano guṇāguṇaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā tato attano hitapaṭipattiṃ paṭipajjissasīti.

‘Glory’ means fame and splendor. ‘Sheds it’: just as a snake, disgusted with its old skin, sheds it and does not look back at it, so glory abandons such a king. ‘Well-ordered in action’ means not committing evil deeds through the doors of body, speech, and mind. ‘Flourishing’ means they grow as they approach. ‘Like a fine bull’ means like a herd with a fine bull. For the wealth of a diligent person grows like a herd of cattle with a fine bull as its chief. ‘Listening attentively’: you should roam on tour throughout your entire realm and country to hear about the conduct of the people in the countryside. ‘There’ means: while roaming in that realm, having seen what should be seen and heard what should be heard, and having personally ascertained your own virtues and faults, you should then undertake a practice beneficial to yourself.

Iti mahāsatto ekādasahi gāthāhi rājānaṃ ovaditvā “gaccha papañcaṃ akatvā pariggaṇha raṭṭhaṃ, mā nāsayī”ti vatvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Rājāpi tassa vacanaṃ sutvā saṃvegappatto punadivase rajjaṃ amacce paṭicchāpetvā purohitena saddhiṃ kālasseva pācīnadvārena nagarā nikkhamitvā [P 5.0102] yojanamattaṃ gato. Tattheko gāmavāsī mahallako aṭavito kaṇṭakasākhaṃ āharitvā gehadvāraṃ parikkhipitvā pidahitvā puttadāraṃ ādāya araññaṃ pavisitvā sāyaṃ rājapurisesu pakkantesu attano gharaṃ āgacchanto gehadvāre pāde kaṇṭakena viddho ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā kaṇṭakaṃ nīharanto –

Thus the Bodhisatta, having advised the king with eleven verses, said, 'Go, O king, without delay, investigate the kingdom; do not destroy it,' and returned to his own dwelling. The king, on hearing his words, was struck with a sense of urgency. The next day, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he left the city early in the morning through the eastern gate with his chaplain and traveled for about a yojana. There, an elderly villager brought thorny branches from the forest, fenced off his house door, and closed it. Taking his wife and children, he entered the forest. In the evening, when the king’s men had departed, as he was returning to his house, his foot was pierced by a thorn at the door. Sitting squatting to remove the thorn—

343.

343.

“Evaṃ vedetu pañcālo, saṅgāme saramappito;

Yathāhamajja vedemi, kaṇṭakena samappito”ti. –

“May the king of Pañcāla feel just as I feel today, struck by a thorn, when he is struck by an arrow in battle.”

Imāya [V 5.0097] gāthāya rājānaṃ akkosi. Taṃ panassa akkosanaṃ bodhisattānubhāvena ahosi. Bodhisattena adhiggahitova so akkosīti veditabbo. Tasmiṃ pana samaye rājā ca purohito ca aññātakavesena tassa santikeva aṭṭhaṃsu. Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā purohito itaraṃ gāthamāha –

With this verse, he reviled the king. But this reviling of his occurred through the Bodhisatta’s power. It should be understood that he reviled him because he was possessed by the Bodhisatta. At that time, the king and the chaplain, incognito, were standing right near him. Then, having heard his words, the chaplain spoke the other verse:

344.

344.

“Jiṇṇo dubbalacakkhūsi, na rūpaṃ sādhu passasi;

Kiṃ tattha brahmadattassa, yaṃ taṃ maggeyya kaṇṭako”ti.

“You are old and weak-eyed; you do not see things clearly. What fault is it of Brahmadatta’s that a thorn should pierce you?”

Tattha [M 5.0107] maggeyyāti vijjheyya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi tvaṃ attano abyattatāya kaṇṭakena viddho, ko ettha rañño doso. Yena rājānaṃ akkosi, kiṃ te raññā kaṇṭako oloketvāva ācikkhitabboti.

In this context, 'maggeyya' means 'should pierce.' This is what is meant: If you were pierced by a thorn due to your own inability, what fault is it of the king here? For which reason you revile the king, was the king supposed to have looked for the thorn and pointed it out to you?

Taṃ sutvā mahallako tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the old man spoke three verses:

345.

345.

“Bahvettha brahmadattassa, sohaṃ maggasmi brāhmaṇa;

Arakkhitā jānapadā, adhammabalinā hatā.

“Much here is Brahmadatta’s fault, O brahmin, as I am here on this road. The countryfolk are unprotected and oppressed by unrighteous taxes.”

346.

346.

“Rattiñhi corā khādanti, divā khādanti tuṇḍiyā;

Raṭṭhasmiṃ kūṭarājassa, bahu adhammiko jano.

“At night thieves plunder, by day the tax collectors devour; in the realm of a treacherous king, there are many unrighteous people.”

347.

347.

“Etādise bhaye jāte, bhayaṭṭā tāta māṇavā;

Nillenakāni kubbanti, vane āhatva kaṇṭaka”nti.

“When such danger has arisen, friend, people oppressed by fear bring thorns from the forest and make hiding places.”

Tattha bahvetthāti, brāhmaṇa, sohaṃ sakaṇṭake magge patito sannisinno, bahu ettha brahmadattassa doso, tvaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ rañño dosena [P 5.0103] mama sakaṇṭake magge vicaraṇabhāvaṃ na jānāsi. Tassa hi arakkhitā jānapadā…pe… kaṇṭakanti. Tattha khādantīti vilumpanti. Tuṇḍiyāti vadhabandhādīhi pīḷetvā adhammena balisādhakā. Kūṭarājassāti pāparañño. Adhammikoti paṭicchannakammanto. Tātāti purohitaṃ ālapati. Māṇavāti manussā. Nillenakānīti nilīyanaṭṭhānāni. Vane āhatva kaṇṭakanti kaṇṭakaṃ āharitvā dvārāni pidahitvā gharaṃ chaḍḍetvā puttadāraṃ ādāya vanaṃ pavisitvā tasmiṃ vane attano nilīyanaṭṭhānāni karonti[V 5.0098]. Atha vā vane yo kaṇṭako, taṃ āharitvā gharāni parikkhipanti. Iti rañño dosenevamhi kaṇṭakena viddho, mā evarūpassa rañño upatthambho hohīti.

In this context, 'bahvettha' means: Brahmin, I have fallen and am sitting on a thorny path; there is much fault of Brahmadatta in this matter. For all this time, you have not known that my wandering on a thorny path is due to the king's fault. For his subjects are unprotected... thorns. In this context, 'khādanti' means they plunder. 'Tuṇḍiyā' refers to the tax collectors who oppress by means of execution, imprisonment, and so on, collecting taxes unrighteously. 'Kūṭarājassa' means of an evil king. 'Adhammiko' means one of concealed deeds. 'Tāta' is an address to the chaplain. 'Māṇavā' means people. 'Nillenakānī' means places for hiding. 'Vane āhatva kaṇṭakaṃ' means: having brought thorns from the forest, they close the doors, abandon their houses, take their wives and children, and enter the forest, and in that forest they make hiding places for themselves. Or else, whatever thorns are in the forest, they bring those and surround their houses with them. Thus it is because of the king's fault that I am pierced by a thorn; do not be a supporter of such a king.

Taṃ sutvā rājā purohitaṃ āmantetvā, “ācariya, mahallako yuttaṃ bhaṇati, amhākameva doso, ehi nivattāma, dhammena rajjaṃ kāressāmā”ti āha. Bodhisatto purohitassa sarīre adhimuccitvā purato gantvā “pariggaṇhissāma tāva, mahārājā”ti āha. Te tamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ gacchantā antarāmagge ekissā mahallikāya saddaṃ assosuṃ. Sā kirekā dalidditthī dve dhītaro vayappattā rakkhamānā [M 5.0108] tāsaṃ araññaṃ gantuṃ na deti. Sayaṃ araññato dārūni ceva sākañca āharitvā dhītaro paṭijaggati. Sā taṃ divasaṃ ekaṃ gumbaṃ āruyha sākaṃ gaṇhantī pavaṭṭamānā bhūmiyaṃ patitvā rājānaṃ maraṇena akkosantī gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king addressed the chaplain, “Teacher, the old man speaks rightly; the fault is ours alone. Come, let us turn back. We will rule the kingdom righteously.” The Bodhisatta, having taken possession of the chaplain’s body, went before them and said, “Let us investigate further first, great king.” As they were going from that village to another, on the road between they heard the voice of an old woman. It seems she was a poor woman who was protecting two grown-up daughters and did not let them go to the forest. She herself brought firewood and vegetables from the forest and looked after her daughters. That day, while climbing a bush to gather vegetables, she slipped, fell to the ground, and reviling the king with death, she spoke this verse:

348.

348.

“Kadāssu nāmayaṃ rājā, brahmadatto marissati;

Yassa raṭṭhamhi jīyanti, appatikā kumārikā”ti.

“When, I wonder, will this King Brahmadatta die, in whose realm unmarried maidens waste away?”

Tattha appatikāti assāmikā. Sace hi tāsaṃ sāmikā assu, maṃ poseyyuṃ. Pāparañño pana rajje ahaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhomi, kadā nu kho esa marissatīti.

Here, 'unmarried' means without a husband. For if they had husbands, they would support me. But in the realm of this evil king I experience suffering. When, oh when, will he die?

Evaṃ bodhisattānubhāveneva sā akkosi. Atha naṃ purohito paṭisedhento gāthamāha –

Thus it was only through the Bodhisatta’s power that she reviled him. Then the chaplain, rebuking her, spoke this verse:

349.

349.

“Dubbhāsitañhi te jammi, anatthapadakovide;

Kuhiṃ rājā kumārīnaṃ, bhattāraṃ pariyesatī”ti.

“Your speech is ill-spoken, you wretch, unskilled in what is beneficial. Where does a king search for husbands for maidens?”

Taṃ [P 5.0104] sutvā mahallikā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the old woman spoke two verses:

350.

350.

“Na me dubbhāsitaṃ brahme, kovidatthapadā ahaṃ;

Arakkhitā jānapadā, adhammabalinā hatā.

“My speech is not ill-spoken, brahmin; I am skilled in the meaning of things. The countryfolk are unprotected, ruined by unrighteous taxes.

351.

351.

“Rattiñhi corā khādanti, divā khādanti tuṇḍiyā;

Raṭṭhasmiṃ kūṭarājassa, bahu adhammiko jano;

Dujjīve dubbhare dāre, kuto bhattā kumāriyo”ti.

“At night thieves plunder, by day the tax collectors; in the realm of a treacherous king, the people are very unrighteous. When life is hard and wives are hard to support, from where are there husbands for maidens?”

Tattha [V 5.0099] kovidatthapadāti ahaṃ atthapade kāraṇapade kovidā chekā, mā tvaṃ etaṃ pāparājānaṃ pasaṃsi. Dujjīveti dujjīve raṭṭhe dubbhare dāre jāte manussesu bhītatasitesu araññe vasantesu kuto bhattā kumāriyo, kuto kumāriyo bhattāraṃ labhissantīti attho.

Here, 'skilled in the meaning of things' means: I am skilled, clever, in the meaning and the reason; do not praise this evil king. 'When life is hard' means: when life is hard in the realm and wives are difficult to support, when people have become fearful and terrified and live in the forest, from where are there husbands for maidens? From where will maidens get a husband? This is the meaning.

Te tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “yuttaṃ sā kathetī”ti tato paraṃ gacchantā ekassa kassakassa saddaṃ assosuṃ. Tassa kira kasantassa sāliyo [M 5.0109] nāma balibaddo phālena pahaṭo sayi. So rājānaṃ akkosanto gāthamāha –

Hearing her words, they thought, “She speaks rightly,” and going on from there, they heard the voice of a certain farmer. It seems that as he was plowing, his ox named Sāliya was struck by the plowshare and lay down. He, reviling the king, spoke this verse:

352.

352.

“Evaṃ sayatu pañcālo, saṅgāme sattiyā hato;

Yathāyaṃ kapaṇo seti, hato phālena sāliyo”ti.

“May Pañcāla lie thus, struck by a spear in battle, just as this wretched Sāliya lies, struck by the plowshare.”

Tattha yathāti yathā ayaṃ vedanāppatto sāliyabalibaddo seti, evaṃ sayatūti attho.

Here, 'just as' means: ‘just as this ox Sāliya, afflicted with pain, lies down, so may he lie down’—this is the meaning.

Atha naṃ purohito paṭisedhento gāthamāha –

Then the chaplain, rebuking him, spoke this verse:

353.

353.

“Adhammena tuvaṃ jamma, brahmadattassa kujjhasi;

Yo tvaṃ sapasi rājānaṃ, aparajjhitvāna attano”ti.

“Unjustly, you wretch, you are angry with Brahmadatta, you who curse the king though he has not wronged you personally.”

Tattha adhammenāti akāraṇena asabhāvena.

Here, 'unjustly' means without cause, without justification.

Taṃ sutvā so tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, he spoke three verses:

354.

354.

“Dhammena brahmadattassa, ahaṃ kujjhāmi brāhmaṇa;

Arakkhitā jānapadā adhammabalinā hatā.

“It is justly that I am angry with Brahmadatta, brahmin. The countryfolk are unprotected, ruined by unrighteous taxes.

355.

355.

“Rattiñhi corā khādanti, divā khādanti tuṇḍiyā;

Raṭṭhasmiṃ kūṭarājassa, bahu adhammiko jano.

“At night thieves plunder, by day the tax collectors; in the realm of a treacherous king, the people are very unrighteous.

356.

356.

“Sā [P 5.0105] nūna puna re pakkā, vikāle bhattamāhari;

Bhattahāriṃ apekkhanto, hato phālena sāliyo”ti.

“Surely she, the cook, brought the food late again. While I was waiting for the food-bringer, Sāliya was struck by the plowshare.”

Tattha [V 5.0100] dhammenāti kāraṇeneva, akāraṇena akkosatīti saññaṃ mā kari. Sā nūna puna re pakkā, vikāle bhattamāharīti, brāhmaṇa, sā bhattahārikā itthī pātova mama bhattaṃ pacitvā āharantī adhammabalisādhakehi brahmadattassa dāsehi palibuddhā bhavissati, te parivisitvā puna mayhaṃ bhattaṃ pakkaṃ bhavissati, tena kāraṇena vikāle bhattaṃ āhari, “ajja vikāle bhattaṃ āharī”ti cintetvā chātajjhatto ahaṃ taṃ bhattahāriṃ olokento goṇaṃ aṭṭhāne patodena vijjhiṃ, tenesa pādaṃ ukkhipitvā phālaṃ paharanto hato phālena sāliyo. Tasmā “esa mayā hato”ti saññaṃ mā kari, pāparaññoyeva hato nāmesa, mā tassa vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇīti.

Here, 'justly' means 'with cause.' Do not think that I revile without cause. Regarding the verse, 'Surely she, the cook, brought the food late again': Brahmin, that food-bearing woman, having cooked my meal early in the morning and while bringing it, must have been obstructed by the unrighteous tax collectors, the slaves of Brahmadatta. After serving them, she must have cooked my meal again. For that reason, she brought the meal at the wrong time. Thinking, 'Today she brought the meal late,' I, being afflicted by hunger and watching for that food-bearer, pricked the ox in the wrong place with a goad. Then it lifted its foot, striking the ploughshare, and so Sāliya was struck by the ploughshare. Therefore, do not think, 'He was struck by me.' Indeed, he was struck by the evil king himself. Do not speak in his praise.

Te [M 5.0110] purato gantvā ekasmiṃ gāme vasiṃsu. Punadivase pātova ekā kūṭadhenu godohakaṃ pādena paharitvā saddhiṃ khīrena pavaṭṭesi. So brahmadattaṃ akkosanto gāthamāha –

They went on and stayed in a certain village. The next day at dawn, a deceitful cow kicked over the milkman with its foot, spilling the milk along with the pail. Reviling Brahmadatta, he spoke this verse:

357.

357.

“Evaṃ haññatu pañcālo, saṅgāme asinā hato;

Yathāhamajja pahato, khīrañca me pavaṭṭita”nti.

“Thus may the Pañcāla king be slain, killed by the sword in battle, just as I was struck today and my milk was spilled.”

Taṃ sutvā purohito paṭisedhento gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the chaplain, objecting, spoke this verse:

358.

358.

“Yaṃ pasu khīraṃ chaḍḍeti, pasupālaṃ vihiṃsati;

Kiṃ tattha brahmadattassa, yaṃ no garahate bhava”nti.

“When a beast spills milk and harms its keeper, what is that to Brahmadatta, that you, sir, should censure him?”

Brāhmaṇena gāthāya vuttāya puna so tisso gāthā abhāsi –

When the brahmin had spoken this verse, the other man spoke three more verses:

359.

359.

“Gārayho brahme pañcālo, brahmadattassa rājino;

Arakkhitā jānapadā, adhammabalinā hatā.

“Blameworthy, O brahmin, is the Pañcāla king, Brahmadatta. The countryfolk are unprotected, ruined by unrighteous taxes.

360.

360.

“Rattiñhi corā khādanti, divā khādanti tuṇḍiyā;

Raṭṭhasmiṃ kūṭarājassa, bahu adhammiko jano.

“By night thieves devour; by day tax collectors devour. In the realm of a crooked king, the people are very unrighteous.

361.

361.

“Caṇḍā aṭanakā gāvī, yaṃ pure na duhāmase;

Taṃ dāni ajja dohāma, khīrakāmehupaddutā”ti.

“A fierce and roaming cow, which we did not milk before, we now milk today, harassed by those greedy for milk.”

Tattha [V 5.0101] caṇḍāti pharusā. Aṭanakāti palāyanasīlā. Khīrakāmehīti adhammikarañño purisehi bahuṃ khīraṃ āharāpentehi upaddutā duhāma. Sace hi so dhammena rajjaṃ kāreyya, na no evarūpaṃ bhayaṃ āgaccheyyāti.

Here, 'caṇḍā' means harsh. 'Aṭanakā' means prone to fleeing. 'Harassed by those greedy for milk' means: we milk, being oppressed by the men of the unrighteous king who make us bring much milk. For if he were to rule the kingdom righteously, such fear would not come upon us.

Te [P 5.0106] “so yuttaṃ kathetī”ti tamhā gāmā nikkhamma mahāmaggaṃ āruyha nagarābhimukhā gamiṃsu. Ekasmiñca gāme balisādhakā asikosatthāya ekaṃ taruṇaṃ kabaravacchakaṃ māretvā cammaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Vacchakamātā dhenu puttasokena tiṇaṃ na khādati pānīyaṃ na pivati, paridevamānā āhiṇḍati. Taṃ disvā gāmadārakā rājānaṃ akkosantā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Thinking, 'He speaks what is proper,' they left that village, took to the highway, and went towards the city. In a certain village, tax collectors, for the sake of a sword sheath, killed a young dappled calf and took its hide. The mother cow, out of grief for her son, did not eat grass or drink water, but wandered about lamenting. Seeing this, the village boys, wishing to revile the king, spoke this verse:

362.

362.

“Evaṃ kandatu pañcālo, viputto vippasukkhatu;

Yathāyaṃ kapaṇā gāvī, viputtā paridhāvatī”ti.

“Thus may the Pañcāla king cry out, be bereft of sons, and utterly wither away, just as this wretched cow, bereft of her calf, runs about wailing.”

Tattha paridhāvatīti paridevamāno dhāvati.

Here, paridhāvati means 'runs about lamenting.'

Tato [M 5.0111] purohito itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Then the chaplain, wishing to ask the reason for the boys' reviling, spoke this verse:

363.

363.

“Yaṃ pasu pasupālassa, sambhameyya raveyya vā;

Konīdha aparādhatthi, brahmadattassa rājino”ti.

“That a beast should be agitated or cry out while its keeper is watching, what fault is there in this for King Brahmadatta?”

Tattha sambhameyya raveyya vāti bhameyya vā viraveyya vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tātā, pasu nāma pasupālassa rakkhantasseva dhāvatipi viravatipi, tiṇampi na khādati pānīyampi na pivati, idha rañño ko nu aparādhoti.

Here, sambhameyya raveyya vā means 'it might run about or cry out.' This is the meaning: 'My dears, a beast indeed runs about and cries out even while its keeper is protecting it; it does not eat grass or drink water. In this running and crying out of the cow, what fault, now, is the king's?'

Tato gāmadārakā dve gāthā abhāsiṃsu –

Then the village boys, wishing to show the king's fault to the brahmin, spoke two verses:

364.

364.

“Aparādho mahābrahme, brahmadattassa rājino;

Arakkhitā jānapadā, adhammabalinā hatā.

“The fault, great brahmin, is King Brahmadatta's. The countryfolk are unprotected, oppressed by unrighteous taxation.”

365.

365.

“Rattiñhi [V 5.0102] corā khādanti, divā khādanti tuṇḍiyā;

Raṭṭhasmiṃ kūṭarājassa, bahu adhammiko jano;

Kathaṃ no asikosatthā, khīrapā haññate pajā”ti.

“By night thieves devour; by day tax collectors devour. In the realm of a crooked king, many people are unrighteous. Why now, for a sword sheath, is a milk-drinking creature killed?”

Tattha mahābrahmeti mahābrāhmaṇa. Rājinoti rañño. Kathaṃ noti kathaṃ nu kena nāma kāraṇena. Khīrapā haññate pajāti pāparājassa sevakehi khīrapako vacchako haññati, idāni sā dhenu puttasokena paridevati, sopi rājā ayaṃ dhenu viya paridevatūti rājānaṃ akkosiṃsuyeva.
