Here, mahābrahme means 'great brahmin.' Rājino means 'of the king.' Kathaṃ no means 'how now?', 'for what reason?' 'A milk-drinking creature is killed' means: a milk-drinking calf is killed by the servants of the evil king, and now that cow laments out of grief for her son. They indeed reviled the king, saying: 'May that king also lament just like this cow!'

Te “sādhu vo kāraṇaṃ vadathā”ti vatvā pakkamiṃsu. Athantarāmagge ekissā sukkhapokkharaṇiyā kākā tuṇḍehi vijjhitvā maṇḍūke khādanti. Bodhisatto tesu taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampattesu attano ānubhāvena maṇḍūkena –

Saying, 'You speak a good reason,' they departed. Then on the way, in a dried-up lotus pond, crows were pecking frogs with their beaks and eating them. When they reached that spot, the Bodhisatta, the tree-spirit of the Gandhatinduka tree, by his own power, made a frog revile the king with this verse:

366.

366.

“Evaṃ [P 5.0107] khajjatu pañcālo, hato yuddhe saputtako;

Yathāhamajja khajjāmi, gāmikehi araññajo”ti. –

“Thus may the Pañcāla king be devoured, slain in battle with his sons, just as I, though forest-born, am devoured today by village crows.”

Rājānaṃ akkosāpesi.

Thus he caused the king to be reviled.

Tattha gāmikehīti gāmavāsīhi.

Here, gāmikehi means 'by village-dwellers.'

Taṃ [M 5.0112] sutvā purohito maṇḍūkena saddhiṃ sallapanto gāthamāha –

Hearing the frog's reviling cry, the chaplain, wishing to converse with the frog, spoke this verse:

367.

367.

“Na sabbabhūtesu vidhenti rakkhaṃ, rājāno maṇḍūka manussaloke;

Nettāvatā rājā adhammacārī, yaṃ tādisaṃ jīvamadeyyu dhaṅkā”ti.

“O frog, kings in the world of humans do not provide protection for all beings. A king is not an unrighteous ruler merely because crows might eat such a living being as you.”

Tattha jīvanti jīvantaṃ. Adeyyunti khādeyyuṃ. Dhaṅkāti kākā. Ettāvatā rājā adhammiko nāma na hoti, kiṃ sakkā araññaṃ pavisitvā raññā taṃ rakkhantena caritunti.

Here, jīvam means 'while still alive.' Adeyyuṃ means 'they would eat.' Dhaṅkā means crows. A king is not called unrighteous merely for this reason. Is it possible for a king to go about protecting you in the forest?

Taṃ sutvā maṇḍūko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing the chaplain's words, the frog, wishing to show him the reason, spoke two verses:

368.

368.

“Adhammarūpo [V 5.0103] vata brahmacārī, anuppiyaṃ bhāsasi khattiyassa;

Viluppamānāya puthuppajāya, pūjesi rājaṃ paramappamādaṃ.

“You appear unrighteous indeed, O practitioner of holy vows! You speak what is pleasing to the khattiya. While the common people are being plundered, you praise a most negligent king.”

369.

369.

“Sace idaṃ brahme surajjakaṃ siyā, phītaṃ raṭṭhaṃ muditaṃ vippasannaṃ;

Bhutvā baliṃ aggapiṇḍañca kākā, na mādisaṃ jīvamadeyyu dhaṅkā”ti.

“If, O brahmin, this realm were well-ruled—prosperous, joyful, and serene—then the crows, having eaten offerings and the choicest alms, would not eat a living being like me while I am still alive.”

Tattha brahmacārīti purohitaṃ garahanto āha. Khattiyassāti evarūpassa pāparañño. Viluppamānāyāti vilumpamānāya, ayameva vā pāṭho. Puthuppajāyāti vipulāya pajāya vināsiyamānāya. Pūjesīti pasaṃsi. Surajjakanti chandādivasena agantvā dasa rājadhamme akopentena appamattena raññā rakkhiyamānaṃ sace idaṃ surajjakaṃ bhaveyya. Phītanti devesu sammādhāraṃ anuppavecchantesu sampannasassaṃ. Na mādisanti evaṃ sante mādisaṃ jīvamānaññeva kākā na khādeyyuṃ.

Here, brahmacārī: he says this rebuking the chaplain. Khattiyassa: of such an evil king. Viluppamānāya: this means 'being plundered'. Puthuppajāya: of the vast populace that is being destroyed. Pūjesi: you praised. Surajjakaṃ: if this were well-ruled, that is, protected by a diligent king who, not following the four wrong ways (agati), does not violate the ten royal virtues. Phītaṃ: with abundant crops when the devas send down sufficient rain. Na mādisanti: this being so, the crows would not eat one like me while I am still alive.

Evaṃ chasupi ṭhānesu akkosanaṃ bodhisattasseva ānubhāvena ahosi;

Thus, in all six places, the reviling occurred through the power of the Bodhisatta alone.

Taṃ [P 5.0108] sutvā rājā ca purohito ca “araññavāsiṃ tiracchānagataṃ maṇḍūkaṃ upādāya sabbe amheyeva akkosantī”ti vatvā tato nagaraṃ [M 5.0113] gantvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā mahāsattassovāde ṭhitā dānādīni puññāni kariṃsu.

Hearing the frog's words, the king and the chaplain said, 'From the forest-dwelling animal frog onwards, everyone is reviling only us!' Then they went from there to the city, ruled the kingdom righteously, and, remaining established in the Bodhisatta's instruction, performed meritorious deeds such as giving.

Satthā kosalarañño imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā, “mahārāja, raññā nāma agatigamanaṃ pahāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāretabba”nti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā gandhatindukadevatā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse to the king of Kosala, said: 'Great King, a king should rule the kingdom righteously, having abandoned following the four wrong ways (agati).' Then he identified the birth story, saying: 'At that time, I myself was the Gandhatinduka tree-spirit.'

Gandhatindukajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Gandhatinduka Jātaka is finished.

Jātakuddānaṃ

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kiṃchanda kumbha jayaddisa chaddanta, atha paṇḍitasambhava sirakapi;

Dakarakkhasa paṇḍaranāgavaro, atha sambula tindukadevasutoti.

Kiṃchanda, Kumbha, Jayaddisa, Chaddanta; then Paṇḍitasambhava, Sīrakapi; Dakarakkhasa, Paṇḍaranāgavara; then Sambula, and Tindukadevasuta.

Tiṃsanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Thirty is finished.
